# The <term>Platonic Theology</term> of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, on the immortality of souls: newly printed with greater accuracy, and compared with the original copies of the same author.

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance. His "Platonic Theology" was a landmark attempt to prove the immortality of the soul using both Christian doctrine and the philosophy of Plato.</note>

All passages have been restored which, through the negligence of those who previously sent it to the press, were either omitted or contained errors. Recently added is a very extensive alphabetical index of everything noteworthy, along with many other features contributing to the elegance of the entire volume, as will be evident to the studious reader while reading.

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page contains the formal dedication letter for the 1525 edition of the Platonic Theology. It follows the title page, serving as an introduction by the editor, Lucas Panetius, to his patron, Girolamo Quirini. It establishes the editor's scholarly credentials and the effort put into correcting the previous, flawed editions of the text.</meta>

# Lucas Panetius, Canon of <note>modern: Ulcinj, a coastal town in Montenegro</note> Ulcinj: Professor of Arts and Laws
## To the Most Reverend Lord Girolamo Quirini, Patriarch of Venice and Primate of Dalmatia: Greetings.

I am sending as a gift to your lordship, most reverend lord, the *Platonic Theology* of Marsilio Ficino. Through the negligence of printers, it had been published full of errors, but it has now been corrected by me. This work is most suited to you, an eminent theologian, not only because of your great piety and innocence of life but also because of your learning in the liberal arts. Your wisdom will be the witness of what I have achieved and how much I have toiled in restoring it to its original brilliance, especially as you study it with your own hands. 

I have added, moreover, a very brief <term>repertorium</term> <note>a thematic index or guide</note>, in the production of which I labored for several months. I ask for your most serious judgment on how much this index contributes to the review of all the sayings, inquiries, and noteworthy points of the ancients throughout the entire volume. 

For whatever was disputed by the ancients concerning the divine essence; concerning <term>Ideas</term> <note>the Platonic concept of perfect forms</note>; concerning divine providence; the soul of the world; the <term>intelligences</term> <note>angelic or celestial beings</note>; the celestial spheres; paradise; the four elements; purgatory; limbo; hell; matter and form; genera and causes; chance and fortune; fate; motion; the infinite; place, vacuum, and time; the eternity of the world; the intellective soul; the souls of brutes and plants; <term>genii</term> <note>guardian spirits</note>; demons; the resurrection; miracles; dreams; prophets; religion; and all the problems of the ancient sages—you will be able to see it all at a single glance. You will also have plainly visible the names of all the philosophers who have existed since the beginning of the world, along with the variety of their opinions. 

Indeed, the utility of this "golden" work can be understood from this fact: that a man most learned in both Greek and Latin, as if running through the Elysian fields and flowery meadows, has selected and explained the primary secrets and hidden truths from the writings of Moses, <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note>, Zoroaster, Pythagoras, Orpheus, Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, Hesiod, Poseidonius, Xenophon, Lucretius, Ptolemy, Plotinus, Porphyry, Numenius, Origen, Iamblichus, Avicenna, <note>original: "alganteis", likely Al-Ghazali</note> Al-Ghazali, Plutarch, Averroes, Solomon, John the Evangelist, Paul the Apostle, Dionysius the Areopagite, Augustine, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, and more recent Christian theologians, and <unclear>...</unclear> has made them familiar to the learned. 

It pleased me, therefore, to dedicate everything edited by me in Marsilio’s *Platonic Theology*—however small it may be—to you, an exceptional theologian endowed with the greatest eloquence, the highest counsel, and sharp judgment. For by the law of jurisdiction, the labors of those dwelling in Venice seek to be inscribed to your lordship. I believe nature shaped you for justice, temperance, prudence, and fortitude—in short, for all virtues—and that the high God, truly the best and greatest, has very recently raised you to the summit of the patriarchal seat. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of variation." <note>A quote from the New Testament, James 1:17.</note>

Therefore, most celebrated prelate, embrace with a generous spirit this theology of Marsilio, corrected by me, than which our age has seen nothing more learned or sublime. I say it provides knowledge of wonderful things, and is indeed very profitable for human happiness, which consists in the contemplation of <term>separate substances</term> <note>beings without physical bodies, such as angels or God</note>. Meanwhile, I shall prepare many more things in both philosophy and <term>pontifical law</term> <note>canon law of the Church</note> to be sent to your highness, to whom by right of leadership all my studies (in which I have been engaged for twenty years in Venice and Padua) are deservedly directed.

->Farewell.<-

->.VXX.C.M<-

Repertory of the Platonic Theology
<note>The word "repertorium" refers to a systematic index or finding aid designed to help a reader locate specific topics across the eighteen books of Ficino's massive work.</note>

<margin>Library stamp: NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME VITTORIO EMANUELE</margin>

# Repertory of the Platonic Theology

¶ A most illustrious repertory of the *Platonic Theology* by Marsilio Ficino, the most eminent of Platonists: newly edited according to a multifaceted alphabetical sequence by Lucas Panetius, Canon of Ulcinj <note>modern Montenegro</note> and Professor of Arts and Laws.

-> A <-

**Acheron**, Styx, Phlegethon, and Cocytus <note>The four rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology</note>: what the places of the underworld are and how they are to be interpreted: Book 18, Letter E, Page 194.
**Action**: what and how many things are required for the natural perfection of any action: Book 1, Letter H, Page 1.
**Acts**: the works of acts remain incorrupt to the extent that they are preserved by the power of nature, just as a statue remains standing for a long time through the natural solidity of the stone or bronze: Book 2, Letter L, Page 14.
**Affect** <note>In this context, a deep-seated emotion or psychological state</note>: a long-standing affect, according to Hippocrates and Galen, changes the previous <term>complexion</term> <note>the balance of bodily humors</note> of the body and draws it into its own nature: Book 13, Letter A, below Page 125.
**Affects**: the four affects that follow the four humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to govern health and personality</note>: Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> described these clearly, imitating partly Plato and partly Hermes Trismegistus: Book 18, Letter L, Page 194.
**Agent**: in what way the First Agent <note>God</note> differs from the other agents that are in need: Book 2, Letter U, Page 15.
**Whiteness**: that which is on a wall, and the power of a white body: what it should properly be called according to Plato: Book 12, Letter D, Page 2.
**Alexander** the King: while he was sleeping, a dragon showed him a herb with which he might cure Ptolemy, who was severely wounded: Book 3, Letter G, Page 113.
**Alexander** of Macedon: when he heard Anaxarchus and Democritus arguing that there are innumerable worlds, he cried out, "Woe is me, for I have not yet gained possession of even one!": Book 14, Letter G, Page 133.
**Alexander** of Macedon among kings, and Empedocles among philosophers, worked like gods: Book 14, Letter H, Page 133.
**Alexander** of Aphrodisias, Themistius, Proclus, and others: what they felt concerning the immortality of the soul and the mind of Aristotle: Book 15, Letter G and following, Page 141.

---

**Friendship**: the end of friendship is the communion of life: Book 4, Letter A, Page 137.
**Angels**: even if they move the bodies of the world <note>the celestial spheres</note>, they themselves are in no way moved by the moved bodies; it is different, however, for intellective souls: Book 1, Letter G, Page 7.
**Whether** gods exist, and how Aristotle proves there are many in the eleventh book of his *Divine Matters* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>: Book 1, Letter H, Page 7.
**Angel** orders: in distinguishing the orders of angels, Dionysius the Areopagite uses the numbers three, nine, and sometimes even seven: Book 1, Letter D, Page 7.
**Angel**: is nothing other than an immobile multitude: Book 1, Letter H, Page 8.
**Angel**: whether it exists as <term>pure act</term> <note>a being that is fully realized without potential for change</note> or is composed of act and potency: Book 3, Letter A, Page 23.
**Angels**: the sublime angels, according to Plato: what rank they hold: Book 10, Letter G, Page 85.
**Angel**: beholds all and individual works of God; and in what way an angel looks back so that it sees all things; whether it directs its sight into bodies or not: Book 16, Letter F and following, Page 165.
**Angel**: whether it discerns all things through the essence of God: Book 16, Letter B, Page 165.
**Souls**: rational souls are established between eternity and time: Book 1, Letter L, Page 6.
**Soul**: its work is to provide vital motion, because it is itself a kind of life: Book 1, Letter E, Page 8.
**Soul**: we judge it to be better than the body for the reason that it is closer to the highest goodness: Book 2, Letter I, Page 11.
**Soul**: what the definition of the rational soul is: Book 3, Letter F, Page 26.
**Soul** of the earth: why it is necessary for the earth to have a rational soul: Book 4, Letter B, Page 28.
**Soul**: why its essence is said to be immobile: Book 5, Letter G, Page 40.
**Soul**: whether it is made by God in such a way that it is effected through an angel as a medium: Book 5, Letter A, Page 41.
**Soul** <note>original: "Alia," likely a typo for "Anima"</note>: when it departs, the body ceases to live; and as long as it is present in the body, it never for a moment ceases to exercise the works of life by vivifying the body: Book 5, Letter E, Page 42.
**Soul**: just as it does not perish, [it is asked] whether it might nonetheless change into a more ancient essence: Book 5, Letter A, Page 44.

<margin>/</margin> Three primary offices <note>or duties</note> of our soul are seen to exist: and what each one is: Book 6, Letter D, 46
The differences of rational souls, what they are: Book 6, Letter D, 49
<margin>/</margin> The power of the soul in the body is almost the same as the power of rennet in milk, or the force of a magnet in iron, from which it is drawn and suspended: Book 6, Letter B, 5
The soul is present in its entirety in every individual part at once: since the whole feels at once in each part: Book 6, Letter B, 56
The entire judging power of the soul, together with the entire substance of the soul itself, is present in every individual limb so that whatever happens anywhere, the whole soul immediately perceives it without a messenger; the whole soul also suffers with it, and so on, as followed there: Book 7, Letter D, 57
<margin>/</margin> The offices of the soul are two: namely, to speculate and to take counsel: Book 2, Letter B, 72
Whether the soul exhibits the meaning of a voice through the tongue: Book 1, Letter B, 89
The souls of brute animals exercise unique arts in individual species: such as insects with woolen webs <note>original: "laneam telam insecta seritia," referring to silk-producing insects</note>, spiders with linen, swallows with pottery <note>referring to the mud nests of swallows</note>, etc.: Book 11, Letter L, 101
In which parts of the brain Averroes <note>12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> places the powers of the soul: Book 15, Letter L, 143
The soul, according to Aristotle, is the <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus," the realization or fulfillment of a potential</note> of a physical, organic body having life in potential; or the soul is the principle of living, sensing, understanding, and moving according to place: Book 15, Letter L, 150
<margin>/</margin> Since the dissolution of the soul from the body is an evil according to Plotinus, it does not pertain to the soul, because she does not mix herself with the body; and many other beautiful things about this: Book 15, Letter B, 155
Why the souls of the deceased do not return, and why they are also not seen: Book 16, Letter D, with many following, 169
<margin>/</margin> The Platonists feel that rational souls imitate divine providence in four ways, and other things that follow there: Book 16, Letter D, 170
From what things the Pythagoreans and Platonists say the soul is mixed: Book 17, Letter A, 175
One must think primarily on three things regarding souls: namely, essence, life, and intelligence, and what each one is: Book 17, Letter D, 175

Book 17, Letter E, 176

Three primary species of souls: namely, the divine, those always following God, and those sometimes following: to the first, the Pythagoreans assign wisdom; to the second, right opinion; to the third, wavering opinion: Book 17, Letter L, 177
<margin>/</margin> The Soul of the World is called "necessity" for this reason: because she leads the universe by her fatal <note>or "fated"</note> power: Book 17, Letter E, 178
Iamblichus <note>Neoplatonist philosopher</note> rejected the transmigration of the soul from a human into beasts; and Porphyry rejected the infinite circuit <note>the idea of an endless cycle of reincarnation</note>: Book 15, Letter L, 177
Why Plato thought souls exist before bodies, as some Christians also thought: Book 17, Letter A, 179
Why Plato felt that the souls of men pass into beasts, and many other fictions regarding this: Book 17, Letter A, 179
What the Magi call the <term>vehicle of the soul</term> <note>the subtle, "astral" body that carries the soul between realms</note>, and what Plato and Plotinus call it, and also what Zoroaster means when he says: "Do not seat the spirit, nor increase it in the depth which is level": Book 18, Letter L, with following, 184
The souls of the elements and their courses: why they do not strive toward the celestial habitation: Book 18, Letter L, 185
Which souls, according to Plotinus, are those that care for their own, and often publicly benefit the human race with prophecies and other benefits: Book 18, Letter A, 186
Souls that have emerged from the water of Lethe <note>the mythological river of forgetfulness</note> fly out more highly: Book 18, Letter D, 187
Purified souls according to Plato, who have loved divine beauty, finally [enter] into the divine sea itself; there they not only drink of the divine liquid, but pour it out from themselves onto others: Book 18, Letter B, 187

Orpheus distributed nine regions for souls, and what each one is: Book 18, Letter D, 194
The human mind is a certain god, or a star surrounded by a cloud, or a demon <note>original: "demon," here in the sense of a guiding spirit or lesser deity</note>; it should not be called an inhabitant of the earth, but a guest: Book 10, Letter D, 84
From where souls depart from themselves: Book 1, Letter E, 88

# Platonic Theology

...beautiful: Book 18, Letter D and following, 194 <note>This is the conclusion of an entry for "Soul" from the previous page.</note>
**M**any animals exist in the earth: which have their own soul distinct from the common soul of the earth: and many other things concerning this: Book 4, Letter A, 28
No animal is more foolish than man: if that power of the mind—which is unique to man—were to deceive more than the senses—which are common to beasts: Book 6, Letter F, 47
How many species of animals are said to exist: Book 9, Letter A, 81
Every appetite <note>or desire</note> is filled by the possession of its cause: Book 10, Letter L, 90
Apollonius of Tyana, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Philolaus <note>various ancient Greek philosophers and wonder-workers</note> performed many miracles: Book 13, Letter J below, 127
Apollonius of Tyana saw from the city of Rome things that were happening in Egypt: Book 18, Letter K, 185
Certain of the Arabs should not be heard who imagine the human intellect: because it cannot attain [perfection] in individuals in this life, it should at least do so in all men collectively: Book 14, Letter B, 131 <note>This is likely a critique of the Averroist theory of a single collective intellect.</note>
Archelaus was the teacher of Socrates; Archelaus was the student of Anaxagoras; Anaxagoras of Anaximenes; Anaximenes of Anaximander; Anaximander of Thales: Book 11, Letter B, 102 <note>This trace's the intellectual "genealogy" of Socrates back to the first Greek philosopher, Thales.</note>
Archimedes of Syracuse, intent on his geometric figures, did not notice the tumultuous destruction of his dying fatherland and the innumerable enemies above his head: Book 13, Letter B, 119
Archimedes of Syracuse made a bronze heaven <note>original: "eneum celum," an orrery or mechanical planetarium</note> in which all the motions of the seven planets were seen most truly, just as they are in the sky: and the machine itself turned like the heavens: Book 13, Letter D, 124
Archytas of Tarentum made a dove out of wood by the discipline of mathematics: he balanced it and filled it with spirit <note>air or steam</note> so that it flew: Book 13, Letter D, 124
What human art is, what nature is, what a craft is, and what the work of nature is: Book 4, Letter D and following, 27
Whatever art and nature do, they lead out from a certain potentiality into act, just as a sculptor does from stone, etc.: Book 5, Letter G, 41
The triple difference of arts between men and beasts: Book 11, Letter E, 102
According to Plato, Aristotle held without controversy: that the souls of men are many and eternal: Book 15, Letter F, 142
Common art is nothing other than a memory of things experienced and accepted, joined with a certain use of the body and operation: Book 12, Letter F, 113
What astrologers bring forth when judging the birth <note><term>genesi</term>: a birth chart or horoscope</note> of anyone: Book 9, Letter A, 76
Averroes the Spaniard, Arab in tongue, devoted to the doctrine of Aristotle but ignorant of the Greek language, is said to have read the books of Aristotle in a barbarous language <note>likely referring to Latin translations from Arabic</note> perverted rather than converted from the Greek: so it is no wonder if, in certain hidden matters, the mind of that very brief writer [Aristotle] was hidden from him: Book 15, Letter E, 142
Avenzoar Albumaron, the physician, writes that he received the best remedy for his aching eye from a recently deceased physician in a dream: Book 18, Letter L, 169

## B

**B**asilisks <note>mythical serpents</note> near Cyrene kill men with the vapor of their eyes: Book 13, Letter F, 127
Blessed is he who enjoys divine flavors in God; miserable truly is he who nowhere senses any divine odor; but less blessed is he who enjoys fewer things in Him, and so likewise miserable: Book 18, Letter S, 195
How the degrees of the blessed are located, and also those of the damned: Book 18, Letter J and following, 95
Anything is in a good state then: when it is united to itself and to its principle <note>its source or beginning</note>, and remains pure, and is not mixed with exterior things: Book 2, Letter D, 9
To be well <note>well-being</note> is more excellent than simply to be: Book 8, Letter D, 70
Certain beasts named catoblepas are found among the Western Ethiopians: which kill men by their gaze alone: Book 14, Letter F, 127
According to Plato, just as beasts cannot be led happily by a beast without a man: so men cannot be led by a man without God: Book 14, Letter J, 138
All power of beasts belongs to the soul and body together: because it is drawn out from matter together with its essence: Book 15, Letter D, 147
There is nothing above Goodness: Book 2, Letter L, 9
Goodness, Unity, and Truth: according to the mind of Plato, the principle of all things is above the angels: one God, true and good: Book 2, Letter D, 9
Divine goodness is not to be called evil because it permits sins to be committed and punishes them once committed: Book 14, Letter J, 141

# Index

**Goodness** is preferred above all things: indeed, we desire the good in all things and everywhere: so freely and so joyfully that we further wish to be unable to *not* desire it: Book 1, Letter **K 9**
**Goodness** is broader than life: because it applies to more things <note>Ficino refers to the idea that even inanimate objects possess "goodness" by virtue of their existence, whereas only some things possess life</note>: Book 2, Letter **R 12**
**The Good** itself is named by Plato in his *Letters* as God the Father: but he calls the "intelligible" itself God the Son: Plotinus likewise speaks of "God from God," and "Light from Light," and the "Reason and Word of God" <note>original: "deum de deo: z de luce lumẽ z rõnẽ verbũq; dei." Ficino is famously attempting to show that Platonic philosophy mirrors the Christian Trinity</note>: Book 11, Letter **F** and following **97**
**The Good** is desired simply by all things: but they do not desire "to be" simply: but rather "to be well": and the form, if it is to be well at all, would not desire not to be, according to the opinion of Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note>: and many other things which follow there: Book 12, Letter **D 110**
**The Good** and **the One** are understood to be the same according to Plato: Book 12, Letter **K** and following **110**
The **Good of man** consists in a certain action that is unimpeded, secure, and continuous: Book 14, Letter **B 135**
**The Good** itself: as Plotinus says, creates the intellect through poured-out splendor: the intellect also, while it unfolds, expresses the rational soul: the soul itself, propagating itself, produces life and the corporal form: Book 16, Letter **C 170**
**Eternal Good** and **Evil**: whether Plato signified them just as the Christians do: Book 17, Letter **B 179**
**Brahmins** of India <note>term: <term>Brachmane</term> (the priestly caste of India, often admired by Renaissance philosophers for their perceived ancient wisdom)</note>: the Magi among the Persians: and likewise the priests among the Chaldeans: and the Greeks, according to Porphyry's opinion, devoted themselves to prayers and worshipped God: Book 14, Letter **D 138**

->L<-

**C**haos, the ancient, was what the earliest theologians called "prime matter": to which God—as the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most influential dialogues concerning the creation of the universe</note> teaches—applies power: and many other beautiful things on this: Book 10, Letter **I 89**
**Chaldeans** and **Egyptians**: these mathematicians excelled in the prediction of the future: Book 13, Letter **A 125**
**Dogs**: those who are stirred to rabies by a dog's bite: sometimes even in the very onset of the madness, they notice the insanity as it threatens: and they are terrified by horrendous dreams: they cry out against their own imagination, very often saying that they are dreaming: Book 9, Letter **F 79**
**Cause**: any cause whatever produces some effect in the order of things: Book 2, Letter **S 11**
**Cause**: just as a particular cause is present for a particular effect: so a universal cause is present for a universal effect: Book 2, Letter **D 12**
**Cause**: God is properly called "Cause": who alone produces any thing in its entirety: nor does He need to compel or require the help of another, or borrow matter from elsewhere: Book 2, Letter **N 14**
**First Cause** acts more vehemently in any effect than the remaining causes: and many other beautiful things which follow: Book 2, Letter **D 14**
**Cause**: every cause acts through "form": and the more ample a cause is, by so much more ample a form it acts: Book 5, Letter **U 15**
**Heaven's** corporeal and substantial form, in the opinion of Averroes and Aristotle, lacks matter: Book 5, Letter **H 4**
**Heaven**: by what principle it may be moved, namely by God: as if by another: Book 4, Letter **B** with many following **29, 30**
**Heaven's** motion in being moved is declared by a beautiful example: Book 4, Letter **L 32**
**Heaven** cannot stand still: because its soul cannot rest: and yet it does not wish to leave its natural place: Book 4, Letter **S 33**
**Heaven**, being sublime, encompasses the forms of the rest of the bodies either in act or by active power: Book 10, Letter **F 82**
**Heavens**: God holds the rank of the first heaven: the Minds <note>the angelic or celestial intellects</note> hold the place of the following bodies: the lowest intellect holds the place of the lowest matter: Book 10, Letter **G 82**
**Heavenly regions**: how many there are according to the Platonists and the Christians: Book 17, Letter **B 187**
**Circle** is a figure: from the center of which all lines drawn straight to the circumference are equal: Book 11, Letter **D 105**
**Complexion** <note>term: <term>Complexio</term> (in medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—that determines a person's temperament and health)</note>, the most tempered: from what things it may be indicated: Book 10, Letter **I 84**
**Composition** is nothing other than the union of many: but many things are not united except by the One: Book 7, Letter **D 59**
**Complexion**, healthy and natural: what its nature is: and many other things regarding complexions: Book 4, Letter **E 139**
**Cleombrotus**: when he had persuaded himself of the immortality of the soul, he took leave of this life out of love for the other <note>Cleombrotus of Ambracia was a youth who reportedly committed suicide after reading Plato's *Phaedo* to reach the afterlife sooner</note>: Book 14, Letter **H 140**
**Cornelius**, a most just priest: as Aulus Gellius writes, was moved in his mind by a divine power at that time when Caesar and Pompey were clashing in Thessaly: to such an extent that he saw both the time, the order, and the outcome of the battle: Book 13, Letter **D 119**
**Body**, according to Plato's opinion, consists of a certain matter and quantity: and many other things on this: Book 1, Letter **E 1**
**Bodies**, the most excellent among the Platonists are the inhabitants of heaven: and of demons <note>note: "demonũ" here refers to *daimones*, intermediary spirits in Greek philosophy, not necessarily evil spirits</note>, and of men: Book 1, Letter **B 6**

# Index

**Dimension** is nothing other than the extension of the matter itself. Book 1, Letter **F** 3
**Diogenes** the Cynic, naked, used to walk upon ice and snow in the winter, and burning sands in the summer; and meanwhile he laughed and joked. Polemon the Academic: while he felt the bites of most rabid dogs, he did not even turn pale. Anaxarchus of Abdera, the philosopher, was ordered by Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus, to be cast into a hollow stone and struck with iron hammers; but he himself, neglecting the punishment of his body, said: "Pound, pound the vessel <note>original: *vasculum*</note> of Anaxarchus, for you do not terrify Anaxarchus," and many other things on this: Book 13, Letter **D** 118
The **Divine** intelligible, according to Proclus, is to be called that very thing. The pure intellect indeed is in and of itself. The animal intellect <note>The intellect as it pertains to the soul or living beings</note> is [named] in another way; and many other things on this: Book 15, Letter **D** 146
The younger Pliny writes that there was an **infamous house** in Athens, and that Athenodorus of Tarsus, the philosopher, discovered the cause: Book 17, Letter **K** 180

## E

**Devising** <note>The act of thinking out or inventing</note> is an act of the soul: Book 16, Letter **G** 174
The **Egyptians**, as Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> relates, constructed statues of the gods in such a way that they could speak and walk: Book 13, Letter **D** 114
This is the innate condition of **effects**: that they depend on another: Book 1, Letter **F** 3
No **effect** can extend itself beyond its cause: Book 10, Letter **F** 91
**Choice** itself is in some way a work of the soul; and many other things on choice: Book 2, Letter **G** 5
Human **choice** is nothing other than a certain action following the human species, just like the discourse of reason: Book 9, Letter **L** 75
Since the **elements** consist of fluctuating matter and always mutually infect each other, they would observe no order of themselves unless they were governed by the most orderly law of celestial motion: Book 1, Letter **D** 7
The middle bodies of the **elements**, namely the four, are in time partly incorruptible and partly corruptible: Book 9, Letter **J** 81
Because of the qualities of the **elements**, jasper does not induce labor, nor does it drive away harmful apparitions; sapphire restrains sweat and contributes to grace; emerald extinguishes lust; amethyst calms drunkenness: Book 10, Letter **G** 87
Whatever the **elements** and plants do, they perform by a certain necessary affection <note>A natural disposition or state</note> of their nature, which exists as one and the same thing: Book 18, Letter **D** 181
A certain **eunuch**, according to Plutarch, being sick, was left by the physicians as if already dead; and after a short time, having been brought back to himself, he said that he had been dead and was restored again to his body; and many other things on him: Book 13, Letter **K** 112
The Pythagorean **enigma** used by Xenocrates—that the soul is a self-moving number—and how it may be solved: Book 3, Letter **G** 24
**Epimenides** of Crete slept for fifty years; Pythagoras lay hidden for ten years; Zoroaster indeed for twenty; Socrates, as Plato writes, stood immobile in the same footprints from sunrise until the next sun rose, and with eyes directed to the same place, he stood thinking and abstracted from the body: Book 13, Letter **G** 119
The **being** <note>original: *Esse*</note> of the soul is nothing other than to live: Book 5, Letter **J** 39
**Being** <note>original: *Esse*</note> is the first of all effects; the rest are indeed nothing other than certain determinations and properties of being itself: Book 2, Letter **B** 14
**Being** and **not-being** are contradictory: Book 5, Letter **F** 40
That **being** which follows after nothingness is called absolute being, since simply being follows immediately after nothing: Book 5, Letter **E** 40
**Being** does not have any contrary except not-being: Book 12, Letter **B** 117
How **being** itself is divided according to the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>: Book 16, Letter **F** 166
Since **being** differs from essence, whether it exists from essence: Book 17, Letter **D** 175
That **essence** which is the seat of the soul—which Plato also calls the "mixing bowl" <note>original: *pateram*, referring to the *Timaeus* 35a-41d</note> of souls in the *Timaeus*—has no origin from bodies, and also is not constituted from parts of quantity: Book 5, Letter **D** 35
A beautiful distinction of **essences** by Proclus.

# Platonic Theology

[Things] **devised**: <note>original: *excogitata*</note> Book 11, Letter **A** 104
The **ages** of life after the seventh or eighth seven-year cycle, and what can happen to a person: <note>Ficino refers to the ancient belief in "climacterics," where life is divided into seven-year periods that bring significant physical and spiritual changes.</note> Book 9, Letter **B** 77
Two **ages** are especially religious: namely childhood and old age: Book 14, Letter **B** 139
**Eudemus of Cyprus**, an associate of Aristotle; for what reason he prophesied many things: Book 9, Letter **E** 72

->F<-

One must not believe the **assertors of Fate** who claim that individual things [arise] from determined physical causes, and that the effect necessarily follows the cause thereafter: <note>Ficino argues here against strict determinism, protecting the concept of free will.</note> Book 9, Letter **E** 75
**Fortune-tellers** and prophets; what miracles they performed: Book 13, Letter **B** 120
The **End** <note>The final purpose or "telos" of a thing.</note> is located in the same order along with that which acts toward the end: Book 2, Letter **B** 18
The closer something is to its **natural end**, the more vehemently it approaches that end: Book 18, Letter **F** 188
There is no proportion between the **finite** and the infinite: Book 8, Letter **L** 71
**Form** is often called "act" <note>original: *actus*. In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" is the realization of a potential; form is what makes a thing what it actually is.</note> by the physicists: Book 1, Letter **A** 2
**Corporal forms** do not have sufficient generation among themselves, but require a higher cause: Book 1, Letter **I** 4
Whether **forms in God** are distinct according to a certain mode of nature—just as in fire there is light, heat, dryness, and lightness—through which He acts by a certain necessity of His nature: Book 2, Letter **E** 16
Whether God or an angel induces a **new form** into the soul, by which it may be disturbed: Book 5, Letter **B** 36
Each **form** has its own nature through its work, and a species different from others: Book 5, Letter **L** 36
A **form** implanted in bodies loses its own excellence and becomes entirely corporal when it has undergone all the conditions of the body, which are spatial extension and change according to time: Book 5, Letter **B** 38
An **intelligible form** is by no means divided into parts similar to one another: Book 8, Letter **B** 64
The **form** in the art of a work has a triple degree: Book 10, Letter **D** 86
What the order is among the **forms of the elements**: Book 10, Letter **F** 67
It was necessary for some **form** in nature to be expressed most similar to God, if indeed the divine craftsman <note>The *Demiurge*, the figure from Plato's 'Timaeus' who fashions the universe.</note> were to surpass nature, as Plato teaches: Book 10, Letter **D** 88
The **forms of things** according to Plato: just as they are transmitted through the divine mind into matter by the lowest power of the soul—that is, through the seeds of forms infused into this power—so there is no transition from the perception of corporal forms into the ideas of the divine mind, unless through the highest part of the soul—that is, through the innate formulas of the ideas: Book 12, Letter **L** 107
**Forms in bodies** according to Plato are nothing other than images of divine ideas, just like the figures that are pressed into wax from the images existing on a golden seal: Book 15, Letter **D** 144
What kind of **form** it is that the Platonists call both natural and divine, since it is the boundary between natural and divine forms: Book 15, Letter **E** 144
From where the **formulas** <note>original: *formulae*. These are the innate "blueprints" or concepts present in the human mind from birth.</note> arrive in the mind: whether from likenesses, or from the soul’s fiction, or perhaps from ideas: Book 11, Letter **F** 100
One who profits nothing **strives in vain**, and admits nothing toward that which he possesses: Book 1, Letter **B** 9

->G<-

**Galen** <note>The famous 2nd-century Greek physician.</note> when he was sick around the diaphragm, dreamed that he would be cured if he let blood from the vein that is between the thumb and index finger: Book 13, Letter **A** 122
Some **Galileans** [the Apostles] once, by God’s sudden inspiration, rose from being fishermen to become supreme theologians: Book 13, Letter **D** 119
**Generation** is the principle of nutrition and growth: Book 4, Letter **L** 26
In any **genus**, the first principle of the whole genus exists: Book 1, Letter **L** 2
In any **genus** of things, that which is the highest of that genus exists as only one: Book 2, Letter **B** 10
In any **genus**, that which is highest ought to have the pure nature of that genus, unmixed with other things, lest it be diminished by the mixture: Book 2, Letter **J** 14
In any **genus**, that which is highest has nothing of a contrary genus either mixed in or nearby...

# Index

...**most**. Book 13, Letter **B** <note>This is a fragment of an entry continued from the previous page, likely referring to the "first" or "extreme" point.</note>
The **genera** <note>original: *genera*; the basic categories or types of being.</note> of all things are distinguished by the Platonists and Proclus: and especially Unity and Mind, Soul and Nature: Book 13, Letter **L** 131
In any **genus**, that which is supreme has a certain limit beyond which the genus does not extend; many such points on this: Book 15, Letter **B** 154
**Kind spirits** <note>original: *Benii*; referring to "Agathodaemones" or good spirits.</note> or good demons, who are called "genii": these constant guides of the intellect are within the person; they lead to the right path not by force but by persuasion. Conversely, there are also evil, adversarial, and foreign ones: Book 17, Letter **B** 192
For the **terrestrial globe**, according to the Platonists, one soul is sufficient; since it is entirely one in its parts, joined in one mass; and one soul also suffices for the orb of water; and many other things on this: Book 4, Letter **Y** 28
The **degrees** of bodies, according to the Platonists, are the shadows of rational souls; moreover, the degrees of souls are the images of angels: Book 1, Letter **E** 7
Any higher **degree** works something into the lower, and receives something from the higher: Book 2, Letter **L** 11
How many **degrees** of souls there are: Book 4, Letter **F** 31
Anaxagoras introduced four **degrees** of things: namely immortal eternity, immortal time, mortal eternity, and mortal time: Book 9, Letter **B** 81.
The **degree** of souls is manifold according to the Platonists: and just as angelic lives are always separate from bodies, while brute [animal] lives are never separate, so the two middle ones are more fortunate souls which are always separate at the peak but joined at the base; and many other things concerning the matter of the soul: Book 17, Letter **D** with many following, 168
**Taste** is nothing other than a certain touch of the tongue: Book 10, Letter **K** 84

->**H**<-

A **disposition** <note>original: *habitus*; a stable quality or state of the soul.</note> stops motion; and an infinite disposition in some way terminates an unending motion: Book 10, Letter **E** 91
A **disposition** turns into nature in such a way that the inclination coming from the disposition is just like that which comes from nature: Book 18, Letter **K** 186
The Platonists think that a **disposition** remains in the imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> in some way; the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> think otherwise: Book 17, Letter **B** 195
The soul of **Hermotimus** <note>transcribed here as "Harmonis"</note> of Clazomenae was accustomed to wander after leaving the body, and reported many true things from far away, until his enemies—who were called Cantharidae—burnt his body, taking away from the returning soul its sheath, as it were; which Aristeas of Proconnesus used to do: Book 13, Letter **D** below, 119
Where the causes of **herbs** and animals born through putrefaction <note>The ancient theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from decaying matter.</note> are said to be: Book 4, Letter **S** 27
**Er** the Pamphylian <note>original: *Herus*; a character from Plato's *Republic* who died and returned to life to describe the afterlife.</note>, who rose from death, narrated many amazing things about the other state: Book 18, Letter **F** 195
The herb **Hierobotane** <note>Literally "sacred herb," often identified as Vervain.</note>, as the Magi say, is useful for the divinations of physicians; **Agate** <note>original: *Achates*</note> comforts the sight, and dulls poison; it provides strength and eloquence; **Diamond** <note>original: *adamas*</note> when present takes away what the magnet attracts; **Carnelian** <note>original: *corneola*</note> stops the flow of blood and mitigates anger; **Onyx** kindles anger and causes terror in dreams; finally, **Coral**, as Metrodorus and Zoroaster testify, removes insane terrors and repels lightning and hail: Book 4, Letter **L** 27
When **Hippocrates** went to cure **Democritus**, whom the common people thought was insane, he received [word] from God during rest that it was not Democritus who was insane, but the common people: Book 13, Letter **L** 123
No animal would be more unhappy than **man**, if [God] had assigned the same end of living to him as to the other animals: Book 1, Letter **A** 1
Why the **human** soul is not subject to the heavens, and from what things this appears: Book 9, Letter **K** 75
The nature of **man** is such that, just as the intellect relates to the principle of contemplation—which is that which is everywhere clearly true—so the will relates to the principle of action, which is the Good itself: Book 9, Letter **L** 75
Why a larger brain and a hotter heart are given to **men** than to other animals: Book 10, Letter **A** 84
Every speech of a **man**, and his entire action of life and consultation, is nothing other than a certain argumentation: Book 11, Letter **L** 105
**Man** alone among all animals laughs, and alone he cries, because the movements of the soul have the greatest command over the body: Book 13, Letter **L** 118
More ingenious **men** are often leaner in flesh; they are slender, of poor health, and their bodies vary the least during many movements; as is read concerning Aristotle, Plato, Speusippus, Carneades, Chrysippus, and Plotinus:

# Platonic Theology

Book 13, Letter **d** 118

**Men** excelling in any art, according to the opinion of Aristotle, were melancholic: whether they were born as such or became so through constant meditation: Book 13, Letter **I** 119 <note>original: "melancolici"; Ficino refers to the famous Aristotelian idea that genius and melancholy are linked.</note>

**Man**, who rules over all things both living and non-living, is a kind of god of the animals: Book 13, Letter **E** 124

**Man** possesses a nature that does not desire the impossible: and many other things regarding natural appetite: and things contrary to nature throughout the whole chapter: and Letter **I** 139 <term>natural appetite</term> <note>The inherent drive of a being toward its proper perfection or "good."</note>

**Men** alone among living creatures worship God: they alone honor God with affection, gestures, words, shrines, and sacrifices: which Plato and Pythagoras want to be the greatest proof of divinity: Book 14, Letter **B** 136

**Man** is the most foolish of all animals, and the most miserable: if he enjoys neither the present life nor the future: Book 13, Letter **S** 137

It belongs to **man** alone to contemplate divine things: nor do brutes show any sign of religion, whatever may be said about many beasts: Book 14, Letter **D** 137

**Men** are sharper [of mind] in whose birth Saturn and Mercury are most present: such as were Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Varro, Apollonius of Tyana: Book 13 with the following, 139 <note>original: "theaneus"; referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher.</note>

**Impious men** are either the most lazy, such as Epicurus is said to have been: or profligate, such as Aristippus: or insane, such as their follower Lucretius, who committed suicide: Book 13, Letter **L** 139 <note>Epicurus and Aristippus represented hedonistic philosophies that Ficino, as a Platonist, opposed.</note>

**Men** who are too curious in their studies, because of too much brain movement, when the brain dries out, usually go somewhat insane: like those who said nothing in things ever stands still: Book 13, Letter **F** 139 <note>A reference to the followers of Heraclitus who believed in universal flux.</note>

The two most excellent **acts of men** are those which are in the most excellent part of the soul and are concerned with the most excellent object: Book 13, Letter **D** 140

**Men**, as Plato testifies in the *Epinomis*, have nothing more divine than religion: Book 13, Letter **E** 40

**Men** are said in some places to be nourished by smell and odor alone, as Pliny relates: Book 16, Letter **E** 170

Aristotle saw a **man**, according to the testimony of Olympiodorus, who never slept, and lived only on air exposed to the sun's rays: Book 16, Letter **E** 170

Why **men** have a body more fragile than beasts: <note>Word fragment completed at top of next column</note>

---

Book 16, Letter **F** 171

**Man**, according to Plotinus, is the rational soul itself which, while remaining in itself, generates the animal below it: and other things that follow there: Book 16, Letter **L** 173

The **inner man**, according to the Apostle Paul, is renewed day by day: Book 17, Letter **F** 187

**Homer** and many others, blind either by nature or from infancy, wrote many things in such a way that they seem to have seen everything clearly: likewise Zoroaster and many other inventors of wisdom: Book 11, Letter **D** with the following, 101

The **human body**, if compared to other animals, possesses very little earth, and that which it has is subtle: and it possesses many more of the higher elements: Book 13, Letter **L** 118

The **melancholic humor** is cold, dry, and black: which qualities are contrary to those in which the vigor of life consists: namely heat, moisture, and clear spirit: Book 13, Letter **d** 139

The **humors** in an animal have two principles of conduct: namely natural and vital: Book 18, Letter **S** 192

->**I**<-

How the glorious God conceives diverse **Ideas**: Book 2, Letter **L** 17 <note>original: "Ideas"; in Platonic thought, these are the eternal, perfect patterns or "forms" of all things in the Divine Mind.</note>

How many **Ideas** are said to be in God according to Plato's mind: Book 2, Letter **E** with the following, 17

Every **Idea** is eternal life: because according to its nature, an idea can pursue its path in the manner of an idea, and can also achieve eternal life through the eternal manner: Book 2, Letter **A** 40

The Platonists place **less common Ideas** as born within common Ideas: and finally all types of Ideas in Being itself, the first and most common of all beings and the most perfect: which they call the supreme Intelligible: Book 11, Letter **B** 97 <term>Intelligible</term> <note>That which can only be perceived by the intellect, not the senses; the realm of ultimate reality.</note>

**Ideas** in the Good itself are only distinct from each other by certain relative reasons in the manner of a cause: but in the Intelligible itself they are distinct through proper forms and absolute forms, and are further different from each other: and many other things on this: Book 11, Letter **E** 97

How Plotinus and Proclus posit **Ideas**: and how they call them exemplary and essential forms: Book 11, Letter **B** with the following, 98

The **imagination** of a glutton infects his saliva with the taste of feasts; it makes children and pregnant women waste away; it loosens the bowels; it numbs the teeth: and causes many other effects: Book 23 <note>Ficino often discussed the physical power of the soul's imagination over the body.</note>

**Impiety** toward the gods arises not only from a disordered physical constitution but also from corrupted morals: Book 14, Letter B 140

**Lower things** were established for the sake of higher things: Book 1, Letter B 7

The name of the **Underworld** is used by the Platonics to refer only to that region of the world where the tumultuous confusion of the elements is out of harmony: Book 18, Letter B 194 <note>original: "Inferoz nōie"; Ficino is interpreting the mythological "Hades" as the physical, material realm of change.</note>

**Infinite things** in power: what those are which are said to be in nature, but not in act: Book 2, Letter Z 16 <term>in act</term> <note>A Scholastic term meaning "actually existing" or "fully realized," as opposed to having only the potential to exist.</note>

**Fire**: how it is the most effective of all the elements: Book 1, Letter L 1

**Intellectual nature**: in how many ways it exists: Book 10, Letter F 85

The **Intellectual** relates to the **Intelligible** almost as that which desires and moves, and that which can be formed, relates to the desirable mover and former: Book 11, Letter B 97

**Our intellect**, according to Plato in the seventh book of the *Republic* and the Philosopher in the second book of *Divine Matters*, relates to those things which are most manifest in nature just as the eye of an owl relates to the light of the sun: Book 6, Letter D 47 <note>The "Philosopher" refers to Aristotle, specifically his 'Metaphysics' (Divine Matters). This famous metaphor explains that human minds are blinded by the "brightness" of supreme truths.</note>

The **Human intellect**: what its quality is: Book 10, Letter B 81

The **Lowest intellect**, although it is divine, nevertheless has a certain sensory and irrational nature through which it appropriately inclines toward earthly bodies: Book 10, Letter E 83 <note>Ficino refers to the part of the soul that bridges the gap between pure reason and physical sensation.</note>

Just as the object of the **Intellect** is being itself under the aspect of truth, the object of the **Will** is being itself under the aspect of the good: Book 10, Letter D 91

The function of the **Human intellect** is nothing other than to understand divine beings: Book 12, Letter L 111 <term>numina</term> <note>Refers to divine powers, spirits, or gods.</note>

The grades of the **Intellect** according to Porphyry: how they are distinguished: Book 15, Letter F 146

The **Intellect**, according to Aristotle, is the organ of no physical act: Book 15, Letter F 156

The study of the **Intellect** is accustomed to resolving particulars into universals until it reaches the most common; and to describe being itself under an absolute definition; and to divide it most distinctly through all levels: Book 18, Letter B 189

It is proper to the **Intelligence of God** that He understands Himself: and many other things regarding the intellection of God: Book 2, Letter A with several following 15

The crowd of **Platonic interpreters** divided itself into six academies: and what each one is and thought: Book 17, Letter L 174

Some things lack **Freedom of judgment** because they have no judgment at all, like plants; others because, although they have it, they have it from nature determined toward one specific thing, like brutes: Book 9, Letter D 74

Since man does not have a **Judgment** regarding actions determined by nature toward one thing, he is necessarily free: Book 9, Letter F 74

How **John the Evangelist** on the island of Patmos saw the order of the ages; Ezekiel saw the valley filled with the bones of the dead; Isaiah saw God sitting and surrounded by seraphim: Book 13, Letter E 124

The part of **Justice** which regards human affairs must not be thought of as not pertaining to God, to whom pertains the administration of the entire world: Book 14, Letter F 141

**L**aw is necessary for man so that he may live in community; and in that law, there should be such great authority that no one believes they can or should transgress it either by violence or by trickery: Book 14, Letter B and Letter R 138

Men removed from **Law** cannot live together, according to Plato: Book 14, Letter L and following 138

There was a **Law** among the ancients that those guilty of sacrilege should be either burned or smothered, as Philo the Jew, the Platonic, writes: Book 14, Letter D 141 <note>original: "philon iudeus platonicus"; Ficino viewed Philo as a key figure linking Jewish scripture and Platonic philosophy.</note>

**Law** is God to the wise man, but lust to the foolish; and he will be blessed who humbly subjects himself to the divine law, but miserable is he who proudly despises it: Book 18, Letter F 193

**Liberty** is like an appetible good: Book 2, Letter B 18 <term>appetible</term> <note>Something capable of being desired or sought after as a good.</note>

From where **Wood and stones** experience the union of their parts according to the Platonics: Book 6, Letter D 51

All **Envy** (or spite), according to Plato, is absent from the divine chorus: Book 18, Letter A 190 <note>original: "Liuor omnis"; a reference to the 'Timaeus' where Plato states the Creator is free from jealousy.</note>

**Local motion**, which is an external motion, appears more perfect in any thing the more the internal nature of the thing is perfect: Book 2, Letter R 13

# Platonic Theology

**Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher who argued against the immortality of the soul.</note> lacked confidence in immortality for this reason: especially because, as death approaches, the powers of the mind seem to fail: Book 9, Letter E **79**

**Light**, according to Orpheus and Heraclitus, is nothing other than the visible soul, from which all things are brought back to life; the soul, however, is invisible light: Book 18, Letter F **69**

**Light** has two qualities: namely, brightness and heat. It exercises brightness in the air, yet it does not grant heat to the air; hence, when the sun sets—as Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> believes—the light is not extinguished, but the whole light withdraws at once along with the sun; however, the remains of the heat are left behind deep into the night; and many other things concerning this: Book 15, Letter E **148.**

The **Light of grace and glory** according to Christian theologians, what it may be: Book 18, Letter B **188**

---

How a **Master** <note>original: "Magister"; referring to a teacher or professor.</note> instructs a disciple, and whether he pours the knowledge he possesses into the disciple: Book 1, Letter B and following **102**

The **Enigma of the Magi**: there is a thing bright on all sides; there is a thing dark on all sides; there is a middle thing, partly bright and partly dark: Book 1, Letter A **6**

What **Zoroaster**, prince of the Magi, attained in twenty years of solitude; and also Orpheus in the deserted mountains of Thrace: Book 14, Letter H **123**

Those most powerful in **Sorceries** <note>original: "Maleficys"; referring to harmful magic or the "evil eye".</note> are those for whom, at birth, the malignant aspect of Saturn and the "earthly seed" of their parents, along with a very similar diet, have forged a physical temperament abounding in foul vapors and melancholy: Book 13, Letter D **126**

The **Power of Mars** subjects the little sparks of bile; and what effects Mars is bound to cause in men themselves: Book 13, Letter E **127**

How **Prime Matter** is one under all bodies: Book 1, Letter B **1** <term>Prime Matter</term> <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, this is the most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical objects.</note>

Why **Matter** does not decay; and many things concerning the nature of matter itself: Book 5, Letter D **34**

The first act <note>The "first act" here refers to the initial form or existence given to a thing.</note> cannot take the place of **Matter**: Book 5, Letter K **39**

**Common matter** can exist without this or that specific "act" or form; but the specific "golden matter" <note>Ficino is likely using gold as a specific example of a material with its own unique form.</note> can by no means exist without its specific form: Book 5, Letter L **39**

Whether in **Prime Matter** there remains that same indifferent potential for either [form]: Book 5, Letter D **69**

**Prime Matter** is placed by Plato between "being" and "nothing"; and many other things regarding matter and form: Book 10, Letter H and following **85**

**Prime Matter** has no power of its own to give itself form; it does, however, possess a power and preparation to be formed, which is called the "beginning of forms": Book 10, Letter H **89**

A twofold commonality belongs to **Matter**: namely, the natural and the accidental; and what each one is: Book 11, Letter E **95**

All **Melancholics**—such as were Heraclitus, Aristotle, Chrysippus, Democritus, Genocriticus, Avempace, and the Arabs—why they felt so rashly about God: Book 14, Letter A **139** <note>Ficino often explores the link between the "melancholy" temperament and either profound genius or spiritual error.</note>

If anyone should lose their **Memory** because of an injury to a part of the head: according to the Platonists and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, what effect would follow: Book 9, Letter L and following **79**

**Memory**: Mithridates, Cyrus, Julius Caesar, Scipio, Fabius Maximus, Lucullus, and Seneca excelled in it; and many other things about this: Book 13, Letter A **125**

The **Minds** that have been granted to the inhabitants of heaven, to demons, and to men, are the highest of all minds: Book 1, Letter B **6**

All **Minds** are the instruments of God: Book 2, Letter D **15**

The **Minds of men** are not moved by higher minds through the heavens as if through some instrument or medium: Book 9, Letter F **6**

Whether the **Mind** recognizes its own instrument through some other instrument, or not: Book 9, Letter F **78**

# Index

¶ When we are accustomed to speak in the manner of **Aristotle**, saying that the **Mind** recreates new species <note>original: "species"; in Renaissance psychology, these represent the mental forms or images of things perceived.</note>; we can also say, more in the **Platonic** manner, that innate species are drawn forth from the secret recesses of the mind: Book 11, Letter D **96**

¶ The **Mind**, according to **Plato**, understands through innate forms: Book 14, Letter D **132**

¶ **Aristotle** never called the **active and receptive mind** two distinct essences, nor did he posit them as such; rather, he called them parts of the soul, and said they were two different powers in the soul: Book 15, Letter F **155**

¶ The perfection of the **Mind** consists in **truth**; moreover, truth, being, and the "intelligible" are the same thing: Book 18, Letter S **188**

¶ What the nature of **Mercury and Saturn** might be: Book 13, Letter R **119**

¶ **Hermes Trismegistus**, **Joseph**, and **Daniel** interpreted all dreams truly: Book 13, Letter F **123**

¶ Intense **fear** cures hiccups and quartan fever <note>A fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, historically associated with malaria.</note>: Book 13, Letter R **118**

¶ Out of **fear**, both of his father’s death and from a desire to shout, when a certain Persian wanted to kill King **Croesus**, the son of Croesus—who had been mute until then—suddenly loosened his tongue and shouted with a loud voice: "O man, do not kill Croesus!" From then on, he was able to speak: Book 13, Letter J **118**

¶ A **Miracle** is not beyond the nature of our soul when the soul is an instrument of God; but since it is a great thing and happens rarely, it produces wonder; and many other things concerning miracles performed by men: Book 13, Letter D **125**

¶ The **miracle** that **Posidonius** <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher, politician, and astronomer.</note> writes about concerning two Arcadian friends, one of whom turned aside to stay with an innkeeper, the other with a host: Book 16, Letter N **169**

¶ Twelve **miracles** which occurred in December and January of the year 1477, when the relics of the Blessed Apostle Peter were found in the city of **Volterra**; these are signs of the resurrection: Book 18, Letter F **191**

¶ **Moses** and **Hermes Trismegistus** are the same man, according to Artabanus the historian <note>An ancient historian of Jewish history; this identification was a common theme in Renaissance attempts to harmonize pagan and Christian wisdom.</note>: Book 18, Letter A **182**

¶ What else is **morality** but a fervor—a stable appetite kindled by the clarity of the intellect? Book 8, Letter H **63**

¶ The **moral goal** is to purify and separate the soul from the divisible body; the goal of **speculation** <note>original: "speculatiue"; referring to the contemplative or theoretical life of the mind.</note>, however, is to comprehend the incorporeal and universal reasons of things situated far from individual bodies: Book 8, Letter H **63**

¶ **Character** <note>original: "Mores"</note> according to **Plato and Socrates**, is the path either to the underworld or to the heavens: Book 18, Letter D **192**

¶ **Motion** is an act running through the moments of time: Book 3, Letter A **24**

¶ Natural **straight-line motion**, according to **Aristotle**, cannot wander to infinity; otherwise, in its progress, it would not be now slower and now faster: Book 14, Letter F and following **131**

¶ All parts of the **World**, however diverse, are reconciled by a mutual order, since they constitute a single body; they borrow natures from one another and are changed: Book 2, Letter A **10**

¶ There is **one God** for one world and one set of movers, especially according to the reasoning of the **Platonists**, because He is unity: Book 2, Letter B **10**

¶ The individual parts of the **World** are referred to the "good of the order," which exists in the whole as if it were the final goal: Book 2, Letter I **16**

¶ Although the members of the **World** are contrary to one another, why do they nevertheless breathe together into one and communicate their powers to one another? Book 4, Letter D **30**

¶ Does the human soul confuse the **order of the world** by performing miracles? Book 13, Letter H **129**

¶ The **World**, according to **Plato**, is full partly of good things and partly of bad; finally, certain <term>daemons <gloss>intermediary spirits between gods and men</gloss></term> preside over men like shepherds guarding sheep; and men sin by their own will; and many other beautiful things: Book 14, Letter B **141**

¶ In the **intelligible world**, according to **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, one must proceed from the highest intelligible to the many intellects, as if from a shaper to the powers to be shaped from there: Book 15, Letter H **145**

# N
**N** Where the causes of things born through **putrefaction** <note>The early scientific theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</note> are said to be: Book 2, Letter F **27**

**Nature** moves its own matter more effectively and better than **Art** moves its own: Book 1, Letter L **3**

What belongs to someone by their own **Nature** belongs to them before that which comes to them from elsewhere: Book 2, Letter N **14**

The **Nature** of each thing is a certain form and virtue determined to one specific work in a certain way, doing whatever it does with all its might; and doing so by necessity: Book 2, Letter N **17**

**Nature and Intelligence** act through form, and produce something similar in form: Book 2, Letter L **37**

**Nature** does not fail in necessary things, nor does it abound in superfluous ones: Book 7, Letter B **55**

According to the **Platonists**, the very **Nature** of man is a kind of **rationality**: Book 8, Letter L **66**

Things produced by **Nature** are led to an end by determined means, and always come forth in the same way, since nature is determined to one thing; however, the **choices of man** tend toward an end by various paths, both in behaviors and in crafts: Book 9, Letter B **75**

According to **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian who attempted to reconcile Greek philosophy with the Bible</note>, all **Natures** that share the same principle are similar to one another: Book 9, Letter B **81**

Just as **Nature** relates to its own matter, so **God** relates almost to his own: Book 11, Letter D **107**

It is difficult to completely cast off one's **Nature**: Book 14, Letter F **138**

**Nature** in individual species does many things not for the sake of survival alone, but for the sake of **ornament**: Book 15, Letter E **157**

The **Nature of contradictories** is such that they cannot dwell together at the same time: Book 15, Letter A **164**

**Relative Necessity** has three parts: Book 11, Letter A **105**

It has been discovered that there is a certain **nerve** in the soul around the neck; those who pull it move all the animal's limbs together, so that each part is moved by its own proper motions: Book 1, Letter F **21**

**Nothing** cannot be defined under the category of being: Book 2, Letter L **11**

Natural agents cannot make something from **nothing**: Book 5, Letter B **34**

Every **number** is said to be a number according to potential: Book 1, Letter M **16**

No one can deny that the **power of numbers** is in the soul: Book 12, Letter A **114**

According to **Plato**, humans need the **protection of divine powers** (numina) because they dwell among false goods and innumerable evils; and many other beautiful things concerning the mind of the ancients are found throughout the whole chapter: Book 18, Letter D and following **185**

# O

The **opinion** of **Anebo** and **Abammon**, the Egyptian priests; also of **Plotinus** and **Iamblichus**; and of **Julian the Platonist**: that not only God, but every mind—whether angelic or animate—pours itself out whole through the infinite: Book 10, Letter F **42**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle** in the *Book of Divine Things* <note>original: "lib. diuinorum" - a common Renaissance title for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note>: that just as the order of the parts of an army among themselves and toward the whole proceeds from the order of the whole toward one leader, so the order of the parts of the world among themselves and toward the whole depends on the order of the whole toward God: Book 2, Letter B **20**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle** in the second book of *On Animals*: that the intellect is infused from without, and is the only thing that is divine, whose operation is not fulfilled through anything corporeal: Book 10, Letter I **89**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle**: that the human mind has two powers, one active <term>agent intellect: the power that abstracts universal concepts from sensory data</term> and the other receptive <term>possible intellect: the power that receives and stores those concepts</term>, and what each of them is: Book 11, Letter F **93**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle**: that there is a certain sense which truly perceives, and many other things regarding this: Book 11, Letter E **104**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle**: that the soul understands nothing without a **phantasm** <note>original: "phantasmate" - a mental image or representation derived from the senses</note>: Book 15, Letter B below **152**

The **opinion** of **Aristotle**: that the receptive intellect understands the universal reasons of natural things only when it has received their absolute and intelligible forms: Book 15, Letter D **154**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Aristotle** and **Dicaearchus** <note>A 4th-century BC Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>: that the soul does not die, but is immortal, and many other beautiful things on this matter: Book 15, Letter L **43**

The **opinion** of the **Astrologers**: that certain natures of the elements exist in heaven; hence that Gospel saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth" <note>Matthew 5:5; the astrologers interpreted "earth" here as a celestial territory</note>, and many other beautiful things on this: Book 16, Letter H **170**

The **opinion** of **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain</note> regarding the immortality of the soul, with its foundations and its refutation: Book 15, Letter I, along with several following sections **143**

The **opinion** of **Averroes**: that the intellect is joined to us only because it is formed from the **species** <note>original: "speciebus" - the mental forms or images of objects</note> received by us: Book 15, Letter D **152**

The **opinion** of **Averroes**: that the human soul possesses a "particular reason" by its own nature, and through it, it instructs the mind, etc., in the things that follow: Book 15, Letter F **153**

The **opinion** of the **Averroists** and their teacher: that the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination</note> is a motion produced by the senses: Book 15, Letter D **152**

The **opinion** of **Augustine**: that all things which we perceive through the body—even when they are not present to the senses—we nevertheless experience as images, whether in sleep or in madness, as if they were actually present; and many other things on this: Book 11, Letter D **104**

The **opinion** of **Avicebron** <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Jewish philosopher</note> and of **Christian theologians**: that all things below God consist of a receptive and formable power, and a formal act: Book 17, Letter B **175**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note> regarding the sudden creation of a man established in a perfect age <note>A reference to Avicenna's "Floating Man" thought experiment, proving the soul's self-awareness</note>: Book 6, Letter A **47**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "algatelis" - the 11th-century Persian theologian and philosopher</note>: that the soul is indeed the form of the body, but is not itself corporeal; and many other points on this: Book 15, Letter L **143**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Avicenna**: that souls, both the blessed and the wretched, in the other life—as a certain habit contracted from sensible things persists for a time—are able to imagine what they previously imagined here with a more vehement affection: Book 15, Letter L **167**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali**: that something created will exist forever, especially the soul, which religion also holds: Book 17, Letter D **183**

The **opinion** of **Avicenna**: that the soul, once separated from the contagion of the body, uses a certain celestial instrument in heaven, as if received from the body of heaven itself, through which it performs the function of imagination: Book 18, Letter L **190**

<margin>/</margin>
The **opinion** of **Avicenna**: that the soul, as if by a certain nature even without choice or meditation, both here and in the other life, is twisted away from the intelligible mode toward the sensible: Book 18, Letter D **193**

# Repertorium

Beautiful to the ear <note>original: "auditu pulchra"; likely the conclusion of a previous entry regarding aesthetics</note>: Book 10, Letter A, 83.

**The opinion of Plato:** that there are as many crowds of demons, heroes, and souls subject [to the stars] as there are stars; and under Saturn are the Saturnian ones, under Jupiter the Jovian ones, and the Martial ones under Mars <note>original: "martias nō sub marte"; the "nō" is likely a scribal abbreviation or error for "v[ero]" or similar, as the context implies the Martial spirits belong to Mars</note>, and other things that follow: Book 10, Letter B, 83.

**The opinion of Plato:** that all things are in all things, but on earth in an earthly way, in water in an aquatic way, and similarly in air and fire; also in heaven according to celestial nature, all things in the moon according to lunar nature, and in the other spheres in the same manner; so much so that any sphere, in its own way and with its own quality, exists as a whole world: Book 10, Letter B, 83.

**The opinion of Plato:** that the natural seat of intelligence is not in mortal bodies, even though they [the bodies] are mortal: Book 10, Letter F, 86.

**The opinion of Plato:** that the divine influence flowing from God, penetrating through the heavens, descending through the elements, and ending in lower matter, is itself the formative power <term>formatrix virtus</term> which he calls the reason of divine intelligence: Book 10, Letter I <note>original: "J"; in early modern printing, I and J were often the same character</note>, 89.

**The opinion of Plato** in the book *On Nature* <note>likely referring to the *Timaeus*, which deals with the creation of the universe</note>: that the rational soul <term>anima rationalis</term> is granted only by the Maker of the world, but irrational souls are granted by his ministers who assist in his work: Book 10, Letter D, 89.

**The opinion of Plato:** that neither the mind nor the senses are formed by external bodies in order to perceive anything, but [perceive] in one way or another: Book 10, Letter D, 93.

**The opinion of Plato:** that God is wonderfully delighted with his work, because pleasure is joined to the act of generation: Book 11, Letter F, 99.

**The opinion or paradox of Plato:** that bodies are not true things, because truth does not remain in them: Book 11, Letter B, 103.

**The opinion of Plato:** that there are two parts of an element, namely matter and form; that it is not called fire or water because of the matter, but because of the form: Book 11, Letter F, 103.

**The opinion of Plato** and Augustine <note>St. Augustine, the 4th-century Bishop of Hippo who integrated Platonic philosophy into Christian theology</note>: that the truths of things themselves dwell more intimately in our mind and show that their intimacy alone is perpetual: Book 11, Letter B, 106.

**The opinion of Plato:** that the act of intelligible things ought to be called truth; the act of the mind, knowledge; and the act of both [together] is the knot, which is God, and many other things: Book 11, Letter F, 108.

**The opinion of Plato:** that the most famous poets are seized by a certain divine frenzy <term>divino furore</term>, such as were Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Pindar, Ion, Linus, Chalcidius, Lucretius, and many others: Book 13, Letter B, with the following, 119.

**The opinion of Plato** in the 10th book of the *Republic*: that the virtue of the soul is not a slave; that a demon <note>original: "demonem"; referring to the 'daimon' or personal guiding spirit mentioned in the Myth of Er</note> is the guide of life, and moreover that the fortune of life is chosen by us, not we by the demon or fortune; and the blame belongs to the one choosing, not to God: Book 13, Letter E, 120.

**The opinion of Plato:** that from heaven even unto the earth, in all the spheres, different regions were distributed from the beginning to different deities; so that when in a region of the earth dedicated to certain deities, the disposition toward those same deities is specially increased—either through higher influences or through the affections of souls—miracles appropriate to such deities are often performed, either by the deities themselves or through the souls occupied by those same deities in that place: Book 13, Letter E, 128.

**The opinion of Plato** in the book *On Knowledge* <note>likely the *Theaetetus*</note>: that evils cannot be avoided altogether, because it is necessary that there always be something contrary to the good: Book 14, Letter D, 130.

**The opinion of Plato** and Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian philosopher Ibn Sina; Renaissance Platonists often harmonized his views with Plato's</note>: that man is by nature a social animal: Book 14, Letter B, 138.

**The opinion of Plato** and Avicenna: that in certain ages God sends some Mercury <note>original: "mercurium"; used here as a title for a divine messenger or prophet</note>, that is, a prophet who is the interpreter of the divine will and a lawgiver of both divine and human law: Book 14, Letter K, 138.

**The opinion of Plato:** that God makes individual things by understanding and loving them: Book 14, Letter F below, 141.

**The opinion of Plato:** that the principle of motion is in the soul, by which anyone might make themselves this or that according to their will, and many other things concerning this: Book 14, Letter B, 141.

**The opinion of Plato:** that that which has once been truly understood can never be entirely consigned to oblivion, but the appearance <note>original: "speciem"; the mental image or form</note> of the understood thing [remains] in the eternal mind
