# Platonic Theology

...to be turned into an eternal habit: Book 15, Letter D, 160.

**The opinion of Plato** that souls which knew each other here by some affection recognize each other there; and they are moved toward one another in nearly a similar way: Book 16, Letter B, 167.

**The opinion of Plato**: that sublime bodies approach sublime souls, while lower ones approach [lower] bodies; and other things that follow there: Book 16, Letter B, 171.

**The opinion of Plato** in Book 7 of the *Republic*: that the soul, falling into bodies, plunges from the highest light into the deepest darkness: Book 16, Letter A, 171.

**The opinion of Plato**: that souls descend by fate—that is, because they desire generation <note>The process of being born into a physical body</note>, and they desire it at a certain specific time; but by their own choice <term>arbitrio</term> they choose this or that kind of life; and other things that follow there: Book 17, Letter D, 177.

**The opinion of Plato and Dionysius the Areopagite**: that God is known rather by what He is not than by what He is; and by what reasoning either He relates to other things or other things relate to Him: Book 18, Letter E, 188. <note>This refers to "negative theology," the idea that the divine is so far beyond human language that we can only describe what God is not.</note>

**The opinion of Plato**: that souls possess two principles within them, since they are the cause of punishment or reward; and what each one is: Book 18, Letter G below, 192.

**The opinion of Plato**, which Origen interpreted: that there is a certain hidden cause of punishment by which the damned are affected: Book 18, Letter L, 194.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: concerning the fittingness <term>deccentia</term> of the infinite Good: Book 2, Letter E, 11.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that the divine essence is one insofar as it is God: Book 2, Letter D, 17.

**The opinion of the Platonists saying**: that God, through the specific hinge <term>cardinem</term> <note>original: "cardinem"; used here to mean a focal point or governing principle</note> of each order, turns that specific order—that is, He moves all things through one essence: Book 2, Letter D, 18.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that the rational soul, by a certain perpetual light, thinks in some way of God and the angel; from this it divines <note>original: "augurat"</note>, and desires to paint itself in their likeness; then it moves itself by gradually forming itself through speculation, morals, and action: Book 3, Letter B, 24.

---

**The opinion of the Platonists**: regarding what is called the "third essence": Book 3, Letter E, 24.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that an angel truly exists—that is, it always stands still; quality is made—that is, it is moved at some time: Book 13, Letter F, 24.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: regarding that which exists in a part of time being that which exists through all time; and many other things concerning the age <term>aevum</term> <note>A state of existence between time and eternity, often associated with angels</note> and the eternal: Book 3, Letter G, 25.

**The opinion of the Platonists** who deny many influences: Book 4, Letter D, 26.

**The opinion of the Platonists** that not only the heavens, but even the elements themselves are alive: Book 4, Letter J, 30.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that the circuit of the universe completes its interval in thirty-six thousand solar years, which they call the Great and Mundane Year; Hermes <note>original: "mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> calls this the "sentu̅" <note>original: "sentu̅"; possibly an error for "summam" (sum) or "seriem" (series)</note>, while Plato calls it the "restoration" of the world: Book 2, Letter B, 32.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that a form divided throughout a body loses its nature of simplicity and constancy in the body: Book 6, Letter G, 51.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that motion in the soul exists properly as an action, since it occurs in its own source; and it forms and agitates the body; but in the body, it is called a "passion" <term>passio</term> <note>In this context, "passion" means being the recipient of an action, the opposite of "action"</note>: Book 6, Letter F, 53.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that it is possible for the soul to be moved by itself, because in it—besides those eight motions of another nature—other motions are found: Book 6, Letter F, 54.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that reptiles have an indivisible soul, whose members live even when divided: Book 7, Letter B, 57.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that substance is by no means recognized by the imagination <term>phantasia</term>, as if it [imagination] does not recognize the rational principle of substance: Book 8, Letter G, 60.

**The opinion of the Platonists and Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>: that the particular is perceived by the intellect only through a certain secondary act: Book 8, Letter E, 61.

**The opinion of the Platonists**: that minds and souls [exist] in the world in time, and in the succession of generation...

It covers the soul's descent into the body, the nature of God's essence, the concept of the "Great Year," and the distinction between soul-action and bodily-passion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Repertorium" (Alphabetical Index or Catalogue) of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. It follows the section detailing the specific opinions of Plato himself and moves into the "Opinions of the Platonists" (Opinio Platonicorum), a broader group of philosophers following the Platonic tradition. The index links specific philosophical themes to their locations in the main text by Book, "Letter" (a subsection marker), and page number.</meta>

<header>Catalogue</header>

# Catalogue

To proceed: Book 8, Letter E, 71.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that from the substance of the rational soul, just as from the sun, the irrational life of the body is poured out like light; and that the soul is affected toward this life as if toward its own offspring; to care for which offspring the body—as the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the creation of the universe</note> teaches—is disposed through celestial minds: Book 9, Letter B, 73.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that in the soul, a motion of action occurs together with the mutability of substance: Book 9, Letter C, 81.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that they place archangels before angels, principalities before archangels, and certain intellects before principalities; these are called "gods" by a kind of participation, always full of the highest God and drunk with divine nectar: Book 10, Letter L, 83.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that perhaps a simple mind needs time <note>original: "chronon" (Greek for time)</note> after it has once produced that form in unity and retains its own: Book 10, Letter L, 88.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that nearly no less infinite power is needed for a soul to dedicate itself to the infinite God, and also to know and love the infinite under a certain logic of infinity, than is needed for something to be made from nothing: Book 10, Letter S, 91.

**The opinion of the Platonists and Peripatetics:** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</note> what is called the "first object," which presents itself at the first and direct glance; and also what constitutes an "adequate object": Book 10, Letter D, 91.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that in prime matter <term>materia prima</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance from which the universe is made</note> the beginnings of all forms to be received lie hidden; and in nature, through which matter is moved toward forms, the seeds of those forms lie concealed: Book 11, Letter D, 95.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that just as the senses—which know through external forms (called "accidental")—always reach toward accidents <note>Temporary or non-essential qualities, like color or size</note>, so conversely the mind—which defines the essences of things—understands through essential forms: Book 11, Letter D, 95.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that the images of prime matter are not true forms (which some physicists think are real), nor do they ever rest—as Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the idea that "everything flows"</note> says—because matter is in flux; instead, they become participants in eternal Ideas <note>The perfect, unchanging archetypes in the mind of God</note> according to Parmenides the Pythagorean: Book 11, Letter B, 99.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** of Avicenna <note>Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note> and Al-Ghazali <note>Persian theologian and philosopher</note> that both elemental and intellectual matter beneath the moon are subject to a certain divine mind as if to a formative power: Book 12, Letter E, 107.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that celestial bodies are in themselves dissolvable because they are both mobile and composite (either made of many creatures or of parts); yet they endure undissolved because they are joined to the immortal soul without any other intervening body: Book 11, Letter L, 112.

**The opinion of the Platonists** and Averroes: <note>Andalusian Muslim philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> that a certain unity is made from the power of the intellect and the form of the thing to be understood, because a more stable composition results from these: Book 14, Letter S, 138.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** to attribute the greatest causes of impiety to the lowest class of demons; who, through great persuasion, drive people either into false religion because of ambition, or into no religion at all because of envy: Book 14, Letter P, 140.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that the forms of irrational lives follow like shadows of the mind, proceeding through bodies: Book 15, Letter I, 145.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that the imagination <term>phantasia</term> possesses its own memory: Book 15, Letter S, 159.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that there are as many armies of souls as there are stars; and they take their nature and name from there: Book 15, Letter L, 160.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that just as higher minds contain the ideas of material things in an immaterial way and the ideas of things subject to birth in an eternal way, so they possess only universal ideas of particular things: Book 16, Letter K, 166.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that souls always have an ethereal body; but according to Christians, they will always have such a body [in the future]: <note>This refers to the glorified body in the afterlife</note> Book 16, Letter F and Letter S, 168.

<meta>This page continues the "Repertorium" (Index) of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. The previous page ended with the opinions of the Platonists and Peripatetics regarding the soul's ability to exist without a body. This page continues detailing the "Opinions of the Platonists" and transitions into the specific "Opinions of Plotinus," the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, as they relate to the soul's nature, its descent, and its ultimate return to the divine.</meta>

<header>Platonic Theology</header>

# Platonic Theology

**The opinion of the Platonists and Dionysius the Areopagite:** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century who blended Neoplatonism with Christian thought</note> that the natural duty of divine minds is: to remain in their own nature; to proceed by providing and acting; and to return to themselves and their origin by acknowledging them; and to convert the things that follow them: Book 16, Letter **B**, 170.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that the illusions and violence of demons can be purged through philosophy and sacrifices: Book 16, Letter **H**, 173.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that angelic souls proceed from God through intellectual virtue; demonic souls according to the "crafting" <note>original: "opificium," referring to the Demiurge or creator-figure</note> and providence—and therefore they build mundane things; and heroic souls according to a primarily "turning" <note>original: "conversivam," the capacity to turn back toward the divine</note> faculty; and many other beautiful things throughout the whole chapter: Book 17, Letter **E**, 176.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that there is something which has infinite lives from itself; something which has them from another; and something which has them from nothing; and many other beautiful things: Book 17, Letter **H**, 177.

**The opinion of the Platonists and Plotinus:** <note>The primary philosopher of the Neoplatonic school, whose work Ficino translated into Latin</note> that just as many images are spread from a single face through many mirrors, so from the soul of a sphere <note>The "World Soul" or the souls of celestial bodies</note> images are spread into the bodies of brute animals: Book 18, Letter **E** and Letter **F**, 183.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that the soul uses three vehicles <note>term: <term>vehicles</term> (Latin: *vehicula*). Neoplatonists believed the soul descended through the heavens, picking up subtle "envelopes" or bodies of light/ether before entering a physical body</note> and what each one is: Book 18, Letter **L**, 185.

<margin>Note Well.</margin> **The opinion of the Platonists:** Zoroaster, Plotinus, Avicenna, the Hebrews, the Christians, and the Muslims: <note>original: "mahumetenthum"</note> that when the same causes eventually return, the exact same men will return; and that divine authority asserting the resurrection is to be believed; and infinite other beautiful things: Book 18, Letter **D** with several following, 191.

**The opinion of the Platonists:** that when the soul senses something, it is said to act through the body, yet not such that the body senses at the same time; for just as the soul is the source of living according to Plato, so it is the source of sensing: Book 9, Letter **D**, 77.

**The opinion of Plotinus:** that God himself is intellection, <note>The act of pure understanding or thinking</note> not in some intellect as if a potential, nor of truth as if an external object, but existing in itself and of its own sphere: Book 1, Letter **D**, 8.

---

**The opinion of Plotinus:** that God is not as he is by chance, or as necessity compelled, but as he himself watches, acts, and wills: Book 2, Letter **A**, 19.

**The opinion of Plotinus and Proclus:** <note>A later Neoplatonist (5th century) known for his systematic philosophy</note> they think the soul is made by an angel; however, Dionysius the Areopagite, Origen, and Augustine think otherwise, believing that the soul is created by God alone: Book 5, Letter **B**, 40.

**The opinion of Plotinus and Porphyry:** <note>A student of Plotinus who edited his works</note> that the vegetative soul <note>The part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note> lacks quantity, because it is equally enclosed in the smallest things and fills the largest: Book 6, Letter **E**, 51.

**The opinion of Plotinus and Proclus:** that consultation <note>The act of deliberation or reasoning</note> should be done so that we do not subject the soul to things, but rather subject things to our soul; and many other things concerning this: Book 9, Letter **I**, 75.

**The opinion of Plotinus, Proclus, and Avicenna:** <note>The famous Persian polymath and philosopher (Ibn Sina)</note> that celestial motions are not the causes of lower things, but rather instruments obeying the divine movers as if they were craftsmen; and many other beautiful things on this matter: Book 9, Letter **G**, 76.

**The opinion of Plotinus:** what eternity <note>original: "evum." A technical term for a duration that is neither temporal time nor absolute eternity, often associated with the existence of angels or celestial souls</note> is: Book 11, Letter **B**, 100.

**The opinion of Plotinus, Theodorus of Asine, and Iamblichus:** <note>Further Neoplatonic philosophers who explored the soul's relation to the divine</note> that the human mind, which is not human but divine, lives in the intelligible world and acts continuously through the continuous intuition of the Ideas: Book 12, Letter **B**, 111.

**The opinion of Plotinus:** concerning human minds by comparison to the celestial spheres: Book 12, Letter **L**, 115.

**The opinion of Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Theodorus:** that just as an indeterminate dimension of quantity always perfects matter, so the immense power of divine magnitude—through its force in its light—continuously forms the mind toward its end with eternal Ideas: Book 12, Letter **S**, 112.

**The opinion of Plotinus and Proclus:** how the soul of Plato is distinguished from the soul of Socrates: Book 15, Letter **L** with the following, 156.

**The opinion of Plotinus or Porphyry:** that the soul, having often experienced these evils, finally clings entirely to the Parent <note>i.e., God or the One</note> and will never return to this life again: Book 16, Letter **B**, 168.

<summary>This page lists the philosophical positions of the Platonists and Neoplatonists (Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry) regarding the soul's origin, its "vehicles," its relation to the celestial spheres, and its ultimate return to God. It highlights the syncretism of Ficino’s work, linking these pagan philosophers with Christian, Jewish, and Islamic traditions on topics like the resurrection.</summary>

# Index

**The opinion of Plotinus:** <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note> that souls clearly perceive their own powers and nature through their actions; and unless all these powers are brought forth, the soul will not perfectly know itself or its own properties: Book 16, Letter **A**, 168.

**The opinion of Plotinus:** regarding why the soul’s stay here [in the body] is brief: Book 16, Letter **B**, 168.

**The opinion of Plotinus:** that just as the circle of the single world encompasses many others—the Saturnian, Jovian, Martial, Solar, and the rest in sequence—so the single inner circuit of the World Soul contains many particular souls through its various species: Book 16, Letter **E**, 170.

**The opinion of Plutarch,** Demetrius, and the philosopher Aemilianus the rhetorician regarding demons and human spirits: namely, that they are eternal; and many other things on this: Book 10, Letter **D**, 83.

**The opinion of Porphyry and Plato:** <note>Porphyry was a student of Plotinus and a key editor of his works</note> that the human mind is made pure by seeking God, and by imitating God, it becomes a god: Book 14, Letter **D**, 140.

**The opinion of Proclus:** <note>A late Neoplatonist known for his highly systematic philosophy</note> that they say there are only three kinds of bodies: Book 1, Letter **B**, 4.

**The opinion of Proclus:** that only three kinds of forms are said to exist: Book 1, Letter **C**, 4.

**The opinion of Proclus:** that since the soul is the principle of generation, it generates and gives life to itself, so that it possesses its essence from itself; and many other things on this: Book 8, Letter **E**, 70.

**The opinion of Proclus:** that the maker of the world <note>original: "mundi opifex," the Demiurge or creator-god</note> while begetting himself by contemplating himself, generates all things in himself at the same time: Book 11, Letter **K**, 98.

**The opinion of Proclus,** or a paradox: that things composed of elements possess neither eternity nor stability, but possess pure minds and life; and many other things on this: Book 11, Letter **J**, 104.

**The opinion of Proclus:** that the soul slips down from unity into a discordant multitude, and from a state of rest into a change that knows no peace: Book 16, Letter **A** below, 171.

**The opinion of Proclus:** that celestial souls also range through [discursive thought] <note>original: "discurrere," the process of moving from one thought to another rather than knowing all at once</note> while understanding; and many other things on this: Book 17, Letter **J**, 177.

---

**The opinion of Ptolemy:** <note>The famous astronomer and geographer</note> who grants that particular effects occur regarding matter—not that celestial things (which are universal and remote causes) are followed absolutely, but only insofar as intermediate causes allow and the movable disposition of matter is subjected to continuous causes; and many other things on this: Book 9, Letter **D**, 75.

**The opinion of Solomon:** <note>The biblical king, traditionally the author of Ecclesiastes</note> that "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity": Book 11, Letter **E** above, 104.

**The opinion of Serapion, Avicenna,** <note>Major figures in medieval medicine and Islamic philosophy</note> and the ancient philosophers: that demons deceive men by the provocation of black bile <note>original: "atre bilis," referring to the medical condition of melancholy</note>: Book 16, Letter **D**, 173.

**The opinion of Sixtus the Pythagorean:** <note>Likely the "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of moral maxims</note> that the human mind is made a temple of God, and the temple of the eternal God will never fall; and many other things on this: Book 14, Letter **L**, 136.

**The opinion of Socrates:** regarding the forms that lie within formed subjects: because they are imperfect, there exist forms that are self-subsistent and perfect, from which the subject-form is shaped: Book 6, Letter **J**, 47.

**The opinion of Speusippus, Xenocrates, Numenius, and Plotinus:** that the irrational form is called the "animation" and "vivification" of bodies, and that it is immortal; though Porphyry and Proclus deny this: Book 5, Letter **E** and following, 43.

**The opinion of Strato and Chrysippus:** <note>Representatives of the Peripatetic and Stoic schools</note> who confess that life is infused into the world, but that this life itself is the highest God; which the Platonists denied: Book 4, Letter **D**, 27.

**The opinion of certain theologians:** stating that God chooses for something to happen according to contingency; yet nothing deviates so much that it either disturbs the order of the universe or escapes the providence of that order: Book 2, Letter **B**, 20.

**The opinion of the theologians:** who posit that the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, fiery heaven of medieval cosmology, the dwelling place of God</note> is movable through itself in eternity; but other spheres exist in eternity and time together; and finally, composite things exist in time: Book 3, Letter **D**, 25.

**The opinion of the ancient theologians,** with whom Aristotle agreed: that the highest boundary and the ultimate form is the rational soul: Book 1, Letter **B**, 8.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical "Repertorium" (Index) of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. It moves from the general "Opinions" of Platonists into specific entries for the "Ancient," "Early," and "Christian" theologians, followed by the specific doctrines of Thomas Aquinas, Timaeus of Locri, Xenocrates, Xenophanes, and Zoroaster. These entries highlight Ficino’s project of "Ancient Theology," where he attempts to show a continuous thread of wisdom from early prophets like Zoroaster through to Christian doctrine.</meta>

<header>Platonic Theology</header>

# Platonic Theology

**The opinion of the ancient theologians**: that souls doze within bodies; and that whatever we seem to do or suffer here is nothing other than dreams; and many other things on this: Book 14, Letter **D**, 136.

**The opinion of the early theologians**: <note>Refers to the *prisci theologi*, the semi-legendary sages Ficino believed preceded Plato</note> that the glorious God tends to the trees, and leads and feeds the beasts: Book 14, Letter **E**, 137.

**The opinion of the early theologians**: that souls are many; and that these govern this or that, here or there, not by emotional attachment but by a certain providence distributed by God: Book 16, Letter **A**, 167.

**The opinion of the Christian theologians**: that God becomes the first intelligible [object], and the beginning, middle, and end of all intellectual power and action: Book 18, Letter **L**, 188.

**The opinion of the Christian theologians**: concerning the state of the soul after death: Book 18, Letter **B**, 194.

**The opinion of Thomas [Aquinas]**: <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the leading scholastic philosopher whose work Ficino often sought to reconcile with Platonism</note> that the act of the divine will, according to a certain condition or position, can be said to necessarily will this or that thing: Book 2, Letter **B**, 19.

**The opinion of Thomas [Aquinas]**: that the soul, in relation to the state and motion of another, rests and is moved at the same time in different respects; and many other things on this: Book 15, Letter **E**, 156.

**The opinion of Timaeus of Locri and Plato**: <note>Timaeus was the Pythagorean philosopher who is the main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name</note> saying that a certain essence consists of an indivisible and a divisible nature: Book 3, Letter **E**, 26.

**The opinion of Timaeus**: that above the stained and imperfect forms of matter there are other pure, complete, and separate forms: Book 11, Letter **B**, 104.

**The opinion of Timaeus and Proclus**: that the intelligible world <note>The eternal realm of Ideas or Forms</note> always indeed exists, but is never created; whereas the sensible world <note>The physical world experienced by the senses</note> is certainly always being created, but never truly *is*, or is recreated: Book 11, Letter **B**, 104.

**The opinion of Timaeus, who imitated Moses**: <note>Ficino and his contemporaries believed Plato traveled to Egypt and learned the teachings of Moses</note> that in the beginning God created the fiery heaven and the earth as the principal members of the world; and so that he might bind these two more fittingly together, he soon placed air and water between them, as if they were discovered not for their own sake, but for the sake of the others: Book 18, Letter **F**, 170.

**The opinion of Timaeus**: that the rational soul comes from God alone, but the irrational life beneath it, which is enslaved to the body, depends on the celestial gods at God's command: Book 18, Letter **L** below, 183.

**The opinion of Xenocrates, Speusippus, Iamblichus, and Plutarch**: <note>Key figures in the history of the Platonic Academy and later Neoplatonism</note> thinking that an eternal power proceeds from eternity itself, not only down to the lowest minds which are reflected back into it, but even as far as the souls of beasts. Numenius, moreover, extends it even to plants; finally, Plotinus even to the natures of things; and many other things on this: Book 10, Letter **F**, 84.

**The opinion of Xenophanes, Parmenides, Zeno, Melissus, Stilpon, Anaxagoras, and Empedocles**: <note>A list of Pre-Socratic philosophers often associated with the idea that the senses are deceptive</note> that nothing of the truth is grasped by the senses: Book 11, Letter **L**, 104.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: <note>The Persian prophet whom Ficino considered the first of the 'Ancient Theologians'</note> that the world has immobile intellectual rulers: Book 1, Letter **L**, 7.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the intelligible itself exists outside the mind: Book 1, Letter **A**, 8.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that all things are born from one fire: Book 2, Letter **F**, 13.

**The opinion of Zoroaster and the sacred [priests]**: that God in a certain way acts upon himself: Book 2, Letter **B**, 19.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that God the Father does not strike fear, but induces persuasion: Book 2, Letter **L**, 22.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that God has perfected all things and granted them to the second mind: Book 3, Letter **A**, 23.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that God snatched [all things] through himself, nor did he include his own fire within the mind that follows him; as if he had said that he has no comparison with any others: Book 3, Letter **D**, 23.

**The opinion of Zoroaster, from whom all the wisdom of the ancient theologians flowed**: saying that the heaven is carried by an eternal will, and always runs its works by necessity: Book 4, Letter **B**, 31.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the soul is in a certain way all things, since he says: it encompasses many fullnesses of the world’s limits: Book 4, Letter **J**, 32.

**The opinion of Zoroaster and Orpheus regarding Proteus changing forms**: Book 4, Letter **B** above, 32.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index (Repertorium) of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology. The previous page concluded with the views of Thomas Aquinas. This page focuses heavily on Zoroaster (the legendary Persian sage whom Ficino considered a founding father of ancient wisdom), as well as entries for Saint Paul, the Peripatetic philosophers, and various ancient sages and artists.</meta>

<header>Index</header>

# Index

[The soul] thinks it effectively returns: Book 2, Letter **B**, 32.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: <note>Zoroaster was the legendary Persian prophet whom Ficino believed founded the "Ancient Theology" (*prisca theologia*) that led to Plato and eventually Christianity.</note> that the heavens constantly revolve for us: Book 4, Letter **B**, 33.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the soul remains immortal and is the mistress of life: Book 5, Letter **A**, 42.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that man must ascend to his own light and the rays of his homeland <note>original: *patrie*; refers to the celestial origin of the soul</note>, from whence the soul itself was infused, surrounded by the great light of the mind: Book 10, Letter **B**, 90.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the paternal mind provides the souls of men with conjectural signs <note>original: *coiecturalia signa*; likely referring to omens or symbols of the divine</note>; and a beautiful declaration of this saying: Book 10, Letter **B**, 95.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that man ought not to increase his fate, as if it were in his own judgment to yield or not to yield to fate: Book 13, Letter **F**, 121.

**The opinion of Zoroaster and Plato**: that men endowed with a tempered constitution and educated in divine manners obtain whatever they wish from the gods: Book 13, Letter **B**, 127.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the soul of men somehow draws God into itself when, retaining nothing mortal, it is entirely intoxicated by divine draughts; and many other things on this: Book 13, Letter **B**, 117.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that the soul becomes a splendid fire through the power of its homeland, and other things which follow there: Book 13, Letter **B**, 120.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that there is something intelligible which man must understand with the **flower of the mind**; <term>flower of the mind<gloss>original: *mentis flore*; a technical term from the Chaldean Oracles referring to the highest, most intuitive part of the intellect</gloss></term> where it is also explained what the "flower of the mind" is called according to Plato and Paul: Book 13, Letter **G**, 129.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that man is the masterpiece of a most daring nature: Book 14, Letter **B**, 129.

**The opinion of Zoroaster**: that nothing proceeds or turns from the paternal principle <note>The "Paternal Principle" is a Neoplatonic term for the first cause or God the Father.</note> in an imperfect state: Book 14, Letter **A**, 134.

**The opinion of Zoroaster, Moses, Plato, and Plotinus**: that since the soul precedes the body and rules over it, it does not so much receive a bodily effect from the body, but rather through an effect of this kind, it immerses itself into the body: Book 16, Letter **B**, 172.

---

**The opinion of Zoroaster** concerning the regeneration of the world, which Plato posited would occur at the end of the world’s revolution, by God's command and with demons <note>original: *demonibus*; here meaning guardian spirits or intermediary beings, not necessarily "evil" demons</note> ministering: Book 17, Letter **A**, 177.

**The opinion of Zoroaster and Mercury**: <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> that the soul is sent down as an example from the orbit of the world; and many other things according to the mind of Aristotle which follow: Book 18, Letter **B**, 184.

**P**aul the theologian <note>Saint Paul the Apostle</note> ascended to the three heavens of the celestial hierarchies in a state of divine abstraction: Book 13, Letter **G**, 119.

**P**erfect things are always to be preferred to imperfect things: Book 1, Letter **E**, 5.

**P**eripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> designate divine minds nowhere except where they appropriately govern and move something: Book 15, Letter **B**, 153.

# Index

**Plotinus** was often accustomed to being released from his body: he would change his countenance: then he found certain wonders which he wrote down afterward: he <note>This refers to Porphyry, Plotinus's student and biographer, who wrote the "Life of Plotinus."</note> asserts that he was present at these miracles of Plotinus four times: indeed, he affirms that he himself, when he was in his seventy-eighth year of age, was seized once by the deity while contemplating: and many other things about this: Book 13, letter **B** below 119.

**Possible** is the middle ground between the necessary and the impossible: Book 5, letter **L**, 39.

**Divine powers** subject to themselves whatever does not include a contradiction: Book 2, letter **E**, 19.

**The power** toward non-existence is never found in the soul: because it is immortal: Book 5, letter **B**, 39.

**The Precipice**, which place the Magi <note>Referring to the "Chaldean Magi" or followers of Zoroaster often cited in Neoplatonism.</note> name: and what Zoroaster writes about the miracles that can be performed by the soul: Book 13, letter **B**, 124.

**Rulers** over the world are primarily three: as the Magi believe, namely: God, Mind, Soul: Book 4, letter **G**, 31.

**First principles**, what they are: Book 11, letter **M**, 105.

**The Principle** of things, why it is called by the name of Unity: Book 12, letter **S**, 110.

**Privations** of things are known through their positive states <note>original: *habitus*. In Scholastic philosophy, a "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, understood only by knowing the "habit" or presence of that quality.</note>: Book 11, letter **B**, 105.

**Prodigies**, many: which occurred in the times of Plutarch <note>A reference to Plutarch’s "The Obsolescence of Oracles," which recounts the famous story of the death of the "Great Pan."</note>: namely, that a great demon and many other demons wailed, and thereafter died: Book 10, letter **E**, 82.

**Musical proportions**, how all of them are born: Book 17, letter **I** below 176.

**Beauty** is something different from a beautiful thing: and the same must be said about the other species, which Plato calls Ideas: Book 11, letter **L**, 97.

**Beauty itself** is the measure of all beautiful things: and how beauty is measured: Book 11, letter **L** with the following, 99.

**A point**, according to Pythagoras, makes a line by its motion: a line truly makes a surface: a surface, in the same way, makes depth: Book 15, letter **D**, 146.

**Purgatory**, whether Plato posited it just as the Christians do: and many other vain fictions: Book 10, letter **L** below 179.

---

**Quality**: by its benefit, once gathered into a narrow space, in what way action proceeds from it: Book 1, letter **J**, 2.

**Quality** for which there cannot be a body: Book 1, letter **L**, 2.

**Quality**, according to Plato, is the name for every form divided within a body: Book 1, letter **P**, 2.

**Qualities**, all of them: whose forms are in another; whenever they are generated, they generate forms in another: Book 1, letter **D**, 3.

**Quality**: in what way it becomes prior to quantity: Book 1, letter **G**, 4.

**Quality**: three things are found to be within it, namely: essence, power, and action, which are involved in motion: Book 1, letter **L**, 5.

**Qualities** of bodies act upon one another without deliberation: Book 2, letter **F**, 14.

**Quality**: how it does not generate extremes: Book 3, letter **I**, 25.

**Contrary qualities** do not receive one another: for they alternately both put to flight and are put to flight: Book 5, letter **B**, 42.

**Qualities**, five kinds of which man naturally seeks: namely, red things and green things to the sight; smooth things to the hearing; sweet things to the taste; temperate things to the touch and the sense of smell: Book 11, letter **A**, 101.

**Quality**: that which inheres inseparably in some subject is destroyed once the subject is removed: Book 11, letter **J**, 105.

**Quantity** is nothing other than the extension of matter itself: Book 1, letter **F**, 1.

**Quantity**: division occurs only by reason of quantity: Book 1, letter **M**, 2.

**Quantity's extension**, wherever it is found, prohibits such power and presence that an object extended through quantity cannot be entirely and simultaneously in several places: Book 5, letter **B**, 25.

**Quantity's extension** compels the parts of the body to remain disjointed: Book 6, letter **E**, 51.

**Quantity**: matter itself rather than the soul stands in need of it, or rather matter precedes quantity; yet it is by no means subject to quantity as it arrives: Book 15, letter **L**, 155.

# Of Platonic Theology

...is directed toward its own proper principle: just as the universal order of things relates to one universal principle: Book 6, letter J 10. <note>This entry is a continuation from the bottom of the previous page regarding the order of the universe.</note>

**How manifold** everything may be: Book 4, letter D 32.

**How manifold** essence may be: and whether operation differs from being, just as it is shown to differ from essence: Book 5, letter G 41.

->R<-

**Reason** dictates: that which is named everywhere: is nothing other than the universe of the natures of things: and that it is God: Book 2, letter E 11.

**The strong argument** of Olympiodorus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato who lived in the 6th century.</note> the Platonist: that the mind itself lives: Book 8, letter L 62.

**Universal reason** <note>original: "Ratio vniuersalis"</note> that is in the soul: by which we feel and live: and because of which we are named rational, is the opinion of the philosopher in the book on the habits of animals: Book 15, letter S 149. <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whom Ficino often calls "The Philosopher."</note>

**From Reason itself** order proceeds: reason consists in life: life in a certain indivisible virtue <note>In the sense of an inherent power or quality.</note>: Book 1, letter D 4.

**Rational power** is the very virtue of reasoning: which discerns consequences: Book 11, letter D 105.

**Rationality** in man is nothing other than: immortality itself brought forth into the act of reason: Book 8, letter L 66.

**Regions**: some are more suited than others for exercising the intellect according to Aristotle: although in any region many have shone wonderfully in every art: Book 13, letter L 125.

**Any thing** moves always by the reason of good <note>meaning: for the sake of the good</note>, which is its quality: but not by the reason of greatness or quantity: Book 1, letter K 2.

**A moving thing** lacks a limit of its own accord: since it does not rest in itself: although some stable state is necessary in things: so that even motion itself does not lack a state: Book 1, letter S 6.

**Each thing**, the more powerful it is, the more extensively it operates: Book 1, letter F 8.

---

**Any things** always do something: and at that time more so: when they are better in their own species: Book 2, letter E 13.

**Each thing** does not properly act upon others: nor by any other reason: except to exhibit its own form: Book 5, letter F 36.

**A composite thing**: such as fire and water: perishes then: when it is separated from its form: Book 5, letter E 37.

**Every thing** except God himself is called a "creature" by the theologians: and is necessarily composed of four certain things: Book 5, letter A 41.

**Each thing** operates according to the mode of its substance: Book 10, letter A 88.

**Each thing** rests in its own proper end: and its proper end is its own proper cause: Book 10, letter L 90.

**No thing** ever raises itself above itself: unless it is pulled by a superior: for water cannot fly into the air <note>A classic Scholastic example of "natural place": water only rises if heated or acted upon by an outside force.</note>: Book 12, letter L 107.

**Three orders of things** seem to belong to the human soul: namely: providence, fate, and nature: and what each of these is: Book 13, letter J 120.

**In any order of things**, nature is so arranged: that action is in the highest of that order and without passion <note>In philosophical terms, "passion" is the state of being acted upon or receiving an influence.</note>: passion is in the lowest, deprived of action: and in the middle, a middle composition: Book 16, letter A 166.

**Each proper order of things**: just as it is right to be directed to its own single principle: so the universal order of things is referred to one universal principle: Book 2, letter J 10.

**To Rufus Antius**: while he held Africa: as the day was declining and he walked in the portico: the figure of a woman appeared: larger and more beautiful than a human: who predicted that he would come to Rome: and hold honors, etc.: Book 13, letter F 113.

**A certain countryman**: as the Blessed Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note> relates, in his own times withdrew from noise and knew he was awake: while nevertheless he saw certain wonders with non-bodily eyes: Book 13, letter R 124.

# Repertory

<margin>☞</margin> **A** priest of Calama: <note>original: "Sacerdos calamenhis"; referring to Restitutus, a priest mentioned by St. Augustine in "The City of God" who could enter a trance-like state at will.</note> as Augustine reports, he was accustomed to withdraw himself from his body at his own will: especially when he was soothed by a mournful harmony: and many other things concerning this: Book 13, letter E, 119.

**S**ardanapalus: <note>The last king of Assyria, often used in philosophy as a symbol of extreme luxury and decadence.</note> and the desires of the Persians: Book 10, letter J, 135.

**S**cience, any kind of: according to the philosophers, has its own object: which they call the "known": Book 8, letter A, 65.

**S**eminal powers: <note>original: "Seminarie vires"; these are the "seminal reasons" (rationes seminales), the hidden principles in nature that govern growth and development.</note> whether the powers in the seeds of living things are the highest causes: Book 11, letter G, 94.

**S**empiternity: <note>Everlastingness or eternity.</note> what it is in itself: Book 2, letter L, with the following, 11.

**S**enior: <note>An old man.</note> according to Aristotle, if you provide the eye of a youth to an old man, he will see exactly like a youth: Book 9, letter L, 79.

**S**ense: is occupied with bodies; imagination with the <term>simulacra</term> <note>Images or mental representations.</note> of bodies; <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of processing images into intentions.</note> with the individual intentions of those images; the intellect with the common natures and entirely incorporeal reasons of those individual intentions: Book 8, letter D, 61.

**S**ensing and judging: are acts of the soul: Book 13, letter C, 118.

**S**ingularity: in any individual thing, three things are required: namely, the nature of the species; <term>accidents</term> <note>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like hair color.</note> which are not necessary to the species; and the composite of both: Book 11, letter F, 94.

**S**ocrates: whom Aristotle judged to be <term>melancholic</term>: <note>In ancient medicine, having an excess of "black bile," a temperament linked both to depression and to creative or prophetic genius.</note> through the inspiration of a familiar <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "demonis"; not a "demon" in the modern sense, but a personal guiding spirit or "daimonion."</note> he foresaw many things: Book 13, letter B, 123.

**S**ocrates: when he was fleeing with several others from the attack of enemies: when they came to a crossroad, he refused to flee the same way as the others: because he was deterred by his daemon: and so it happened that those who fled by the other path fell into the enemy cavalry: Book 13, letter C, 123.

**S**ocrates: as long as Aristides, Thucydides, and many others remained near him: even with Socrates himself remaining silent: they made progress in the study of philosophy by the instinct of his daemon: however, the further they withdrew from Socrates, the more inept they became for philosophy: Book 13, letter D, 123.

**S**ocrates: when he was approaching death, he predicted to Anytus: <note>One of the primary accusers of Socrates at his trial.</note> that his son, who then seemed moderate, would become most shameful: Book 13, letter D, 123.

**S**oothsaying dreams: are often difficult to interpret: and often easy: and for what reason this happens: Book 13, letter E, 122.

**S**pecies, natural: by natural reason: because they are everlasting: they cannot come from a mobile cause: Book 8, letter B, 60.

**S**pecies: whether they are implanted in us from the beginning in all persons: Book 11, letter G, 94.

**S**pecies: two kinds of things that cannot perfectly exist together: Book 15, letter A, 154.

**S**pecies: <note>Here referring to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas."</note> Plato commands that they be honored: for in these consist the perfection of the world: and the truth of science: Book 15, letter L, 159.

**S**pirits: some are entirely immortal: others entirely mortal: others are intermediate between these: Book 9, letter N, 81.

**S**pirits: what kind of order the Platonists place among them: Book 17, letter K, 177.

<margin>🞩</margin> **S**phere: the life of the sphere is an angel: and natural fortunes proceed from the ideas of the angelic mind: Book 4, letter B, 28.

**S**pheres: why the 13 souls of the spheres are reduced to 12 principles: Book 4, letter D, 28.

**S**pheres of the world: how many there are according to the ancients: Book 4, letter E, 29.

<margin>☞</margin> **S**pheres, celestial: not only the Platonists: but even the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> confess that they have souls: Book 4, letter J, 31.

<margin>𝔑</margin> **S**pheres of the elements: that they are alive: and while this is clearly established among the Platonists: the ancient Peripatetics did not differ on this: Book 4, letter K, 31.

**S**phere, eighth: <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> its concave surface is the natural place for the sphere of Saturn: and there the convex of Saturn’s sphere touches the concave of the eighth: Book 4, letter A, 33.

**S**phere of fire: possesses a triple quality: namely color: light: and a lightness tending toward the higher regions: Book 10, letter F, 88.

**S**pheres, celestial: according to Plotinus: Porphyry: Iamblichus <note>Three foundational Neoplatonist philosophers who expanded on Plato's cosmology.</note>

# Platonic Theology

Iamblichus, Proclus, Theophrastus, Algazel, Avicenna, Zael, Manilius, Ptolemy, and Albumasar [state that the celestial spheres] are animate: Book 15, letter D, 148.

The Sphere according to Aristotle: just as he moves the sphere, so [he moves it] through desire and will: Book 15, letter A, 152.

To stand: what else is it than to persevere in the unity of one's own nature? Book 3, letter E, 23.

The state of fools: whether by nature, or by chance, or whether it ought to be as with infants, or in another way, and how it is to be spoken of according to the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> and the Platonists: Book 18, letter A, below and above, with several following [pages], 195.

Every subject, according to Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential.</note>, must be bare of the species of that quality which it is to receive: Book 15, letter B, 163.

Substance by nature is prior to quantity and the remaining accidents: <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are properties (like color or size) that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note> Book 1, letter K, 4.

Incorporeal substances, according to the nature of their genus, are more suited to be outside the body than in the body: Book 1, letter F, 5.

Substance in any thing is more excellent than its duration: Book 18, letter D, 182.

To rise and to depart: what else is it than to bring oneself to God in mind, according to that Gospel saying: "Watch and pray, lest the Lord find you sleeping": Book 18, letter C, 194.

**T**he tabernacle of a German craftsman <note>Ficino refers here to a complex mechanical clock or planetary model made by a German artisan, which he used as an analogy for the design of the universe.</note> seen in Florence in Marsilio's time: Book 2, letter G, 21.

Tatius, the son of Mercury <note>Mercury is the Roman name for Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary sage; Tatius is his disciple/son in the Hermetic texts.</note>, having been purged by his father's purifications, exclaimed that he had been transported into a mortal body and beheld and heard wonders: Book 8, letter I, 185.

Touch is proper to two bodies: Book 15, letter B, 146.

The speed of time surpasses the speed of the tongue: Book 11, letter B, 103.

Time is always falsely said "to be," since its being is "not to be": <note>Referring to the philosophical idea that the present is a vanishing point between a past that no longer exists and a future that does not yet exist.</note> Book 11, letter L, 103.

Orphic theology <note>Theology based on the mythical poet Orpheus.</note> immediately calls the "third essence" the seat of rational animals: Book 11, letter L, 95.

The theologian John the Evangelist: when the mind of man reaches anything true, he does not say—as others are accustomed to—that it "sees" some true thing, but that it "makes" the truth: Book 12, letter E, 109.

Consummate theologians call the mind "ignited gold": Book 11, letter F, 109.

The theologian Paul affirms that the mind which contemplates divine things is both daily renewed, and transformed into the same image with God, and becomes one spirit with God: Book 12, letter F, below, 109.

The theologian Trismegistus says: from a pure mind and divinity, a single spirit somehow coalesces; and all the Platonists prove that in contemplating [divine] reasons, the divine reason is touched by a certain substantial touch of the mind rather than by imagination, and that the mind's own unity is joined to the unity of God—the unity of all things—in a certain inestimable way: Book 12, letter F, below, 109.

The theologian, according to Plato, ascends by suitable foundations and steps of demonstration all the way to the principle of the universe, and touches it, etc.: Book 12, letter B, 109.

The theologian, both by acting and by disputing, purges the soul of bodily affects and separates reason from the deceptive projections of sensible things—and many other things concerning this: Book 12, letter B, 109.

In the *Timaeus*, Plato calls theologians "sons of God": Book 13, letter L, 117.

The ancient theologians—namely the Magi, Egyptian priests, prophets, Hebrews, Orphics, Pythagoreans, and Platonic philosophers—who excelled in marvelous wisdom, worshipped God, and not only unrefined men: Book 14, letter D, 138.

Theramenes, Socrates, a certain Rhodian, Calanus the Indian, and Pherecydes the Syrian: why and for what reason they prophesied many things when near death: Book 9, letter E, 72.

# Index

Why the Earth is round according to the mind of Plato: Book 2, letter A, 16.

Why the globe of the Earth is surrounded by water and air, and its own fire, in its own volumes; why the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their mathematical and mystical views on the cosmos.</note> called the sphere of the world one and a certain star: Book 16, letter D, 170.

Plato calls the Earth the most ancient of all the gods who are within the heavens: Book 17, letter D, 170.

Theramenes, Theodorus, Cyrenaeus, Cleombrotus, all the Cyrenaic <note>A school of philosophy that generally emphasized pleasure or specialized ethics.</note> followers of Hegesias, the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked wise men," referring to ancient Indian philosophers known for asceticism.</note>, and the peoples of Thrace: they did not depart from the lands or human life unwillingly, but of their own accord <note>referring to voluntary death or philosophical withdrawal from the world</note>: Book 16, letter A, 173.

A certain Tymarchus, when he had left that banquet where Socrates was reclining: Socrates, with his demon <note>original: "demone"; Socrates' *daimonion*, a divine voice or sign that warned him against certain actions</note> forbidding it, thereafter committed those things for which he was killed; Carneades competed in the Nemean games, with Socrates turning back, and he regretted having competed; a certain branch struck the eye of Crito while he was staying in the country against Socrates' advice; and many other things concerning the wonders of Socrates: Book 13, letter L, 123.

Plato’s Timaeus <note>A character in Plato's dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the universe.</note> relates that God, the craftsman of the world, made all the seeds of things in a certain bowl, and tempered them in turn with musical measures: Book 17, letter B, 177.

According to Homer, Tiresias <note>The famous blind prophet of Thebes.</note> alone is wise among those in the underworld; all the others flit about like shadows: Book 14, letter G below, 136.

Which philosophers and theologians of the ancients denied the transmigration <note>original: "transmigrationem"; the passage of a soul into another body after death</note> of souls into beasts, and who allowed it: Book 17, letter D, with several following [pages], 180.

Men of the Triballi and Illyrians: when they are angry, if they gaze upon a person for a long time and more intently, they kill them; they also have double pupils in their eyes. Certain women in Scythia also do the same: Book 13, letter B, 127.

Hercules and many Arabs excelled in prophecy <note>original: "vaticinio"</note>; they were seized by the falling sickness <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; epilepsy, which in antiquity was often associated with divine possession or prophetic states</note>—

-> <-

—[and were seized] by it: Book 13, letter B, 127.

Albigerius of Carthage so excelled in the appearance of prophecy that, whatever anyone had done or thought, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian.</note> testifies, he would answer by the inspiration of demons: Book 13, letter B, 124.

Natural prophecy, especially of the most excellent minds, cannot go astray according to Plato's opinion: Book 14, letter R, 133.

He affirms that the sensible world was adorned by the Word <note>original: "Verbo"</note> or Divine Reason, which Plato calls the intelligible world: Book 1, letter F below, 8.

Truth indeed is stronger than the deceptive, since truth can exist without it, but the false cannot stand without truth: Book 1, letter B, 13.

What Truth is properly said to be: Book 1, letter B, 8.

There is nothing above Truth: Book 2, letter B, 9.

Truth is not corporeal; otherwise it would not be in incorporeal things, for example, in God, angels, and numbers: Book 8, letter E, 62.

Whether Truth is said to be in the soul: Book 11, letter L, 114.

Truth is the pure integrity and the whole purity of each nature: Book 11, letter M, 105.

The truth of a thing according to Plato consists in this: that it corresponds to its Idea <note>The perfect, eternal patterns of things in the mind of God or the Intelligible World.</note> everywhere; knowledge, however, consists especially in this: that the mind itself conforms to the truth: Book 12, letter A, 107.

From where the True draws its origin: Book 1, letter D, 7.

Sophocles and Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, died suddenly at the news of a tragic victory; a mother expired upon seeing her son returning from the battle of Cannae <note>A major battle of the Second Punic War (216 BCE) where Rome suffered a massive defeat.</note>; and many other things concerning this: Book 13, letter F, 88.

In the act of seeing, a threefold movement concurs: namely, the appearance of color, the brightness of light connecting the other acts together, and similarly in understanding: Book 12, letter F, 108.

That which is violent is neither long-lasting, nor is it always the same and ordered: Book 4, letter A, 29.

# Platonic Theology

LL i

Virtue itself is effective: insofar as it is virtue, it does not include a fixed number of degrees: Book 1, letter B, 11.

A higher virtue must be whatever the lower one is, and something beyond: Book 2, letter B, 15.

Two kinds of virtues are said to exist: Book 8, letter F, 62.

What the discrepancies of the virtues are according to Plato: Book 8, letter B, 63.

What else is speculative virtue <note>The virtue associated with contemplation and intellectual study rather than just moral action.</note> but the clarity of the intellect: Book 8, letter D, 63.

Whether an operation differs from virtue, and virtue from essence and being: Book 5, letter A, 41.

How the life of mortals is joined to bodies: Book 3, letter K, 25.

Humans lead their lives through reason assigned to the brain, through anger to the heart, and through desire attributed to the liver: Book 4, letter F, 28. <note>This refers to the "tripartite soul," a classic Platonic concept where different faculties are localized in specific organs.</note>

How many lives there are, and in what way we use them, and other beautiful things on this: Book 4, letter B with many following, 29.

Bodily life itself is nothing other than a continuous act of the soul infused into the body's temperament, not departing from the soul: Book 15, letter D, 111.

Euripides <note>An ancient Greek playwright (c. 480–406 BC) known for his tragedies.</note> calls human life the dream of a shadow <note>original: "umbre somnium"</note>: Book 14, letter B, 106.

Olympiodorus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and commentator on Plato who lived in Alexandria in the 6th century AD.</note> posits three vices from the mind of Plato: whether they are curable or not, and what each one is: Book 18, letter D, 194.

Unity is called the principle; truth is the reason of the principle; and finally, goodness is the love of the rational principle: Book 2, letter N, 11.

The order of the universe takes its origin from the order of the lowest mind: Book 1, letter A, 3.

The three ways in which Plato uses "vicissitudes" <note>Refers to the cyclical changes or rotations of souls and cosmic states.</note>: Book 17, letter F with following, 177.

When something is offered to the will as good, the will can be inclined toward it, with no natural inclination to the contrary preventing it: Book 9, letter B, 74.

In what way the will differs from the intellect: Book 14, letter L, 122.

The higher face <note>original: "vultus"; here used metaphorically to mean the highest aspect or "countenance" of the soul that gazes toward the divine.</note> of our soul is called the imitation of the divine face by the Platonists: Book 12, letter B, 111.

# ->Table of Chapters<-

## Chapters of the books of theology on the im/mortality of souls by Marsilio Fi/cino the Florentine, divided into 18 books. The first book ascends all the way to God.

### ->Chapters of the first book.<-

**I**f the soul were not immortal: no animal would be unhappier than man: chapter one, letter **A**, page 1 <note>Ficino argues that since humans have the highest desires but often the most suffering on earth, a lack of an afterlife would make human existence uniquely tragic compared to unthinking animals.</note>
**T**he body by its own nature does nothing: chapter 2, letter **B**, page 1
**A**bove the divided form in the body stands an indivisible form, that is, the soul: chapter three, letter **C**, page 3 <note>original: "forma indiuidua." In Platonic philosophy, physical things are "divided" by space, but the soul is "indivisible" because it is a single, unified spark of life.</note>
**T**he rational soul is immobile through its substance: it is mobile through its operation: through its power it is partly immobile and partly mobile: chapter four, letter **K**, page 5
**A**bove the mobile soul is the immobile an/gel: chapter 5, letter **L**, page 7
**A**bove the angel is God. Since the soul is a mobile multitude. The angel is an im/mobile multitude. God is immobile unity: chapter 6, letter **M**, page 7 <note>Ficino uses a "Great Chain of Being" logic: God is the perfect One, Angels are many but unchanging, and Souls are many and move through time/thought.</note>

### ->Chapters of the second book.<-

**T**he second book disputes concerning God, having now been found.
**U**nity: truth: goodness are the same: and above them is nothing: chapter one, letter **L**, page 9
**T**here are not many gods equal among themselves: chap/ter two, letter **M**, page 9
**T**here are not many gods, one above another, with/out end: chapter three, letter **N**, page 11
<margin>X</margin>
**G**od's power is infinite: chapter 4, letter **A**, page 10
**G**od always is: chapter 5, letter **B**, page 10
**G**od is everywhere: chapter 6, letter **M**, page 11
**G**od acts upon all things: and preserves them: and works all things in all: chapter 7, letter **B**, page 13
**G**od acts through his own being in whatever he does: chap/ter eight, letter **E**, page 14
**G**od understands himself first: and also each sin/gle thing: chapter nine, letter **F**, page 15
**G**od understands infinite things: chapter ten, letter **G**, page 16

---

**G**od has a will: and through it he effects all things out/side himself: chapter eleven, letter **L**, page 16
**T**he will of God is at once necessary and free: and it acts freely: chapter 12, letter **D**, page 18
**G**od loves and provides: chapter thir/teen, letter **D**, page 20 <note>This refers to Divine Providence—the idea that God actively cares for and guides the universe.</note>

### ->Chapters of the 3rd book.<-

**T**he third book descends from God: and com/pares the levels of things in turn to the mid/dle level: and this level to the others.
**T**he descent happens through five levels: through which there is also a sacred ascent: which levels are compared to one another and appropriately: chapter one, letter **B**, page 22 <note>These levels usually include Body, Quality, Soul, Angel, and God.</note>
**T**he soul is the middle level of things: and it connects all levels, both higher and lower, into one: while it ascends to the higher ones: and descends to the lower ones: chapter 2, letter **D**, page 24 <note>This is Ficino's famous "Copula Mundi" (Bond of the World) theory, where the human soul is the glue that holds the universe together.</note>

### ->Chapters of the 4th book.<-

**T**he fourth book divides the middle level of things—that is, the soul—into its species.
<margin>+</margin>
**T**here are three levels of rational souls. In the first is the World Soul. In the sec/ond are the souls of the spheres. In the third are the souls of the ani/mals: which are contained in each of the spheres: chapter one, letter **B**, page 26 <note>term: "anima mundi" (World Soul). This is the idea that the entire universe is a living creature with its own spirit.</note>
**T**he souls of the spheres move the spheres through the law of fate: and they move in a circle: because they them/selves are circles: chapter 2, letter **F**, page 31

### ->Chapters of the 5th book.<-

**T**he fifth book. It treats the immorta/lity of the soul through common reasons.
**B**y every reasoning the soul is immortal.
**T**he first reason: because it is moved by itself: and in a circle: chapter one, letter **L**, page 33
**S**econd reason. Because it stands by its own substance: chapter two, letter **E**, page 34
**T**hird reason. Because it clings to divine things: chapter three, letter **F**, page 34
**F**ourth reason. Because it rules over matter:

## ¶ Book 8.

**The eighth book concerning the soul** specifically regarding the intellectual part: since it is indivisible, it is therefore immortal.
**First reason. The soul is an individual form, whole in every part: and it draws no origin from matter; therefore it is immortal, as is shown through the power of understanding.** The soul ascends to the spirit through four degrees: chapter one, letter **E**, page 60
**Second reason. The soul is nourished by truth:** chapter two, letter **E**, page 61
**Third reason. The power of the soul: because it is indivisible, it cannot be a quality of the body:** chapter 3, letter **D**, page 62
**Fourth reason. Species <term>species: in this context, the mental images or "intelligible forms" of things that the mind perceives</term> and intelligible perception cannot be received by a body:** chapter 4, letter **B**, page 63
**Fifth reason. If the mind were a body, it would understand by touching or by running:** chapter 5, letter **A**, page 66
**Sixth reason. The intellect receives according to its whole self: and whatever it takes in, it would not do so if it were corporeal:** chapter six, letter **L**, page 67
<margin>X</margin> **Seventh reason. The intellect, in receiving the forms of things, does not lose its own form. Bodies, by contrast, do:** chapter seven, letter **A**, page 67 <note>When a physical object takes a new form (like wood becoming ash), it loses the old one; the mind, however, can learn many "forms" of things without changing its own nature.</note>
**Eighth reason. Form in the mind is universal. Such a thing cannot exist in a body.** chapter eight, letter **L**, page 67
**Ninth reason. Minds embrace one another. Bodies do not at all:** chapter 9, letter **F**, page 67
**Tenth reason. The mind works through all bodies: and above bodies:** chapter 10, letter **B**, page 68
**Eleventh reason. The mind benefits from stillness. The body from motion:** chapter 11, letter **B**, page 68
<margin>X</margin> **Twelfth reason. Those things that are in matter are not opposites; in the mind, opposites coexist:** chapter 12, letter **L**, page 68
**Thirteenth reason. The mind is not changed by receiving forms:** chapter 13, letter **L**, page 68
**Fourteenth reason. The operation of the body tends toward a composite thing. The mind’s operation toward simple things:** chapter 14, letter **D**, page 69
**Fifteenth reason. The operation of the mind ends in the act itself: the operation of the body in a finished product:** chapter 15, letter **A**, page 69
<margin>X</margin> **Sixteenth reason. A corporeal form does not have infinite power. The mind does:** chapter sixteen, letter **C**, page 70

## ¶ Book 9.

**The ninth book.** That the soul is more effectively immortal: not only because it is indivisible, but also because it does not depend on the body.
It is proven through the power of reason that the soul is not only an individual form, but also does not depend on the body, so that immortality may be more clearly demonstrated. **First reason: because the mind reflects back upon itself:** chapter one, letter **A**, page 71
**Second reason. The more the mind is separated from the body, the better its condition:** chapter two, letter **L**, page 72
**Third reason. The mind resists the body:** chapter three, letter **B**, page 72
**Fourth reason. The soul acts freely:** chapter four, letter **L**, page 73
**Fifth reason. The mind operates without the body:** chapter five, letter **L**, page 76
**Sixth reason. The soul reaches first to divine things, and the best to the blessed:** chapter 6, letter **A**, page 80
**Objection of the Epicureans <term>Epicureans: followers of a philosophy that claimed the soul was made of atoms and perished with the body</term> and the response concerning the tempering of things:** chapter 7, letter **G**, page 81

### Chapters of the Tenth Book.

**The tenth book: That the soul is immortal: with respect to the order of things.**

**First reason:** Just as the last in the order of bodies is incorruptible: so is the last in the order of minds: chapter one, letter E **82** <note>Ficino argues for a symmetry in the universe: if the highest physical heavens are indestructible, the highest part of the human—the mind—must be as well.</note>

# Preface

->¶ The preface of Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the *Platonic Theology* on the immortality of souls, addressed to Lorenzo de’ Medici, <note>Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–1492), known as "the Magnificent," was the ruler of Florence and Ficino’s primary patron.</note> a man of great spirit.<-

Plato, the prince of philosophers, <note>original: "Plato philosophorū"</note> great-spirited Lorenzo, held that just as the sense of sight relates to the light of the sun, so do all minds relate to God. For this reason, he believed that minds can never know anything without the light of God. He rightly and piously judged that since the human mind possesses all things from God, it should likewise refer all things back to God. Therefore, whether we philosophize about morals, the soul must be purified so that, having finally become more serene, it may perceive the divine light and worship God; or whether we investigate the causes of things, those causes must be sought so that we may at last find the very Cause of causes <note>A philosophical term for God as the ultimate origin of all existence.</note> and, having found it, venerate it. Nor does our Plato merely exhort others to this duty of piety, but he himself excels in it most of all. Thus it happened that he himself is called "divine" without controversy, and his teaching is called "Theology" among all nations. This is because, whether he treats of morals, logic, mathematics, or physics, he immediately leads the subject back to the contemplation and worship of God with the highest piety. Because he truly considers the soul to be like a mirror in which the image of the divine countenance easily shines back, he diligently tracks God himself through every footprint, turning aside everywhere into the "appearance" <note>The inner form or nature.</note> of the soul. He understood that the famous oracle "Know Thyself" <note>original: "nosce te ipsum." This was the famous inscription at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note> warns us most of all that whoever desires to recognize God must first know himself. For this reason, whoever most diligently reads these Platonic works—all of which I have long since translated into Latin—will certainly achieve everything, but two things in particular: the pious worship of God through knowledge, and the divinity of souls. <margin>2.</margin> In these two things consist the universal perception of things, the whole conduct of life, and all happiness—especially since Plato’s views on these matters are such that Aurelius Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), a key Church Father who heavily integrated Platonic thought into Christian theology.</note> chose him from among all the philosophers to be imitated, as being closest of all to Christian truth. Indeed, Augustine asserted that **the Platonists would be Christians with the change of only a few things.** <note>original: "platonicos mutatis paucis christianos fore"</note>

I myself, relying long ago on the authority of Augustine and moved by the greatest charity toward the human race, decided to express a certain "image" of Plato that is very similar to Christian truth. To this end, I have labored more diligently than on anything else, and therefore I judged that this entire work should be titled *The Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*. In composing this work, my chief purpose was that in the divinity of the created mind—as if in a mirror positioned in the middle of all things—we might both behold the works of the Creator himself and contemplate and worship his mind. I believe (and not by a vain faith) that it has been decreed by divine providence that the perverse wits of many, who do not easily yield to the authority of divine law alone, might at least find rest in Platonic reasons which strongly support religion. <margin>1.</margin> Furthermore, I hope that those who too impiously separate the study of philosophy from holy religion may eventually recognize that they wander astray, just as if someone were to separate the love of wisdom from the honor of wisdom itself, or true intelligence from a righteous will. Finally, I hope that those who think only of things perceived through the senses of the body—and who unhappily prefer the shadows of things to the true things themselves—might at last be warned by Platonic reason to contemplate sublime things beyond the senses, and happily place reality before shadows. <margin>1.</margin> This, above all, almighty God commands. This, human affairs entirely require. This, the celestial Plato once easily [offered] to his own, with God’s inspi... <note>original: "deo aspi..." likely "deo aspirante" (with God's inspiration/breathing). The text breaks off at the end of the page.</note>

# Preface

...completely accomplished. This at last we ourselves, following our Plato indeed, but trusting only in divine help, have attempted in this laborious work. But would that we have finished it with as much truth as we have treated it with reverence for divine truth; so much so that we wish nothing to be considered proven by us unless divine law <note>original: "divina lex"</note> confirms it. Moreover, I have judged that this work itself should be dedicated to you, great-spirited Lorenzo, above all others, not so that I might open philosophical matters to you—about which you have for so long disputed in such a way

that I seem to be publishing the secrets <note>original: "archana" (arcana)</note> of the ancients not so much for you (who have already perceived these things, having attained them with a certain marvelous genius) as for all others. But also because we, through your kindness, have obtained that leisure <note>original: "ocium" (otium) — This refers to the productive, scholarly peace or "creative leisure" supported by Medici patronage, which allowed Ficino to focus entirely on his translations and writing.</note> by which we might be able to philosophize more easily. And our Plato seems very likely to be grateful for this duty of ours toward you. For what he once most desired in great men, you yourself have joined: philosophy along with the highest authority in public affairs. <note>Ficino is referencing Plato’s famous "Philosopher King" ideal from The Republic, suggesting that Lorenzo embodies the perfect union of wisdom and political power.</note>
