->Book One of Platonic Theology<-

# Book One of Platonic Theology

<margin>a</margin>
Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s *Platonic Theology* on the immortality of souls, dedicated to the high-spirited Lorenzo de' Medici: Book One.

**If the soul were not immortal, no animal would be more unhappy than man. Chapter 1.**

<margin>b</margin>
Since the human race—owing to the soul's ingratitude <note>Ficino likely refers to the soul's tendency to forget its divine origin.</note>, the body's weakness, and a lack of all necessary things—leads a harder life on earth than the beasts, no animal would be more unhappy than man if nature had granted him the same limit of living as she gave to the other living creatures. However, it is impossible for man to be the most unhappy of all, since through worship he comes closer to God (the author of happiness) than all other mortals. Therefore, man can only be made happier after the death of the body. It seems necessary that some light remains for our souls as they depart from this prison. Yet, if human minds do not look back toward their own light, they remain closed in darkness and a "blind prison" <note>original: "carcere ceco"; a common poetic description of the physical body in Platonic and Stoic thought.</note>. For this reason, we are often forced to lack confidence in our own divinity. 

I pray, O heavenly souls desirous of your heavenly homeland, let us break the chains of our earthly shackles as soon as possible so that, lifted up on Platonic wings <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings to ascend to the realm of true Being.</note> and with God as our guide, we may fly freely to the ethereal seats. There, we shall immediately and happily contemplate the excellence of our race. To make it clearly and evidently appear by what means human minds are best able to loosen their mortal barriers, perceive their own immortality, and attain happiness, we shall attempt to demonstrate the following in the discussion that follows: 

Beyond this sluggish bulk of bodies—where the considerations of the followers of Democritus, the Cyrenaics, and the Epicureans <note>These were materialist philosophers who believed the world was composed only of physical matter and atoms.</note> ended—there is a certain effective quality and power; it was toward this that the investigation of the Stoics and Cynics turned. Above quality, however—which is divided along with the dimensions of matter and is entirely subject to change—there exists a certain more excellent form. Although this form changes in some way, it does not admit division within the body. In this form, the ancient theologians placed the seat of the rational soul. Heraclitus, Marcus Varro, and Marcus Manilius <note>Varro was a Roman polymath; Manilius was a Roman poet/astrologer; Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for the idea of constant change.</note> ascended this far. 

Above the rational soul, there exists the "angelic mind." This mind is not only indivisible but also immutable, a level where Anaxagoras and Hermotimus <note>Anaxagoras was the first to propose "Mind" (Nous) as the primary cause of the universe; Hermotimus was a legendary seer mentioned by Aristotle.</note> seem to have rested. Finally, over the "eye" of this mind—which desires and receives the light of truth—presides the Divine Sun itself. Our Plato commanded, taught, and contended that we must direct the purified sharp edge of the mind toward this Sun. 

Therefore, when we have ascended to this point, we shall compare these five ranks of all things: the material bulk of the body, Quality, the Soul, the Angel, and God. Since the genus of the rational soul itself holds the middle rank among these levels, it appears to be the bond of all nature. It rules qualities and bodies, while joining itself to the Angel and to God. We shall show that the soul is properly "indissoluble" <note>Meaning it cannot be broken down or destroyed.</note> because it connects the levels of nature; it is most excellent while it presides over the machine of the world, and most blessed when it introduces itself into things divine. We shall assert that our soul is such and behaves in this way through four types of reasoning: first, through common reasons; second, through specific arguments; third, through signs; and fourth, through the solutions to questions.

<margin>E</margin>
**The body by its own nature does nothing. Chapter 2.**

<margin>f</margin>
According to Plato, the body consists of a certain matter and quantity. Because it is extended into matter, its role is only to be "acted upon" <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic physics, "matter" is passive, while "form" or "soul" is the active principle.</note>; extension and affection themselves are types of passive experiences. As for quantity, it is either nothing other than the extension of matter itself, or if it is something else, it is a thing of such a kind that it is always subject to division. It subjects matter to all subsequent passive experiences and pours nothing out into "foreign" matter. Consequently, the body itself, insofar as it is a body, does nothing at all, but is subject only to being acted upon.

<margin>g</margin>
This same point is also clear from the fact that for the perfection of any natural action...

<meta>catchword: Marsi. Fici.</meta>

He begins his formal proofs by arguing that the physical body is purely passive and incapable of independent action.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the opening of Book I of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." After establishing in the previous page that man’s happiness depends on the immortality of the soul, Ficino now moves into a metaphysical argument regarding the nature of "power" and "action." He aims to prove that the ability to act belongs to incorporeal (spiritual) things rather than physical matter.</meta>

# Platonic Theology Book I

Perfect action requires three things in particular. First: that the acting agent be most powerful in itself. Second: that it be most fit for motion. Third: that it easily penetrates the patient <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, the "patient" is the entity that receives an action or is acted upon by an "agent."</note>, and that the patient itself be most closely united to the agent. Physical bulk <note>original: "moles corporis"</note> seems to be a hindrance to all of these. First: because a body is stretched out into many parts, the acting power <term>virtus<gloss>The inherent power or "virtue" of a thing to produce an effect.</gloss></term> within it is dispersed, distant from itself, and extremely distracted. Power is increased by union, just as it is diminished by dispersion. Therefore, dryness increases the force of both heat and cold because it unites it. Humidity, however, weakens it because it scatters it.

Next: the larger a body is, the more sluggish and unfit for motion it is in itself. Therefore, the more a body increases in size, the more it retards motion and delays action for a long time. Often, a spark of lightness carries upward more quickly than a flame. The force of gravity pulls a piece of wood downward more quickly if it is sharpened than if it is flattened. Finally, since any body fills its own place, and one place is by no means sufficient for two bodies, they cannot migrate into the bodies of one another. Also, by their own solidity and density, they prevent mutual penetration. 

Thus, the distance of parts <margin>A</margin> weakens the power of acting. The magnitude of the mass slows down motion. Thickness prevents the penetration of bodies. Therefore, it is worse if nature constricts the scattered parts of some body to increase power through union, while meanwhile the body itself becomes thicker and more unfit for entry. And if it thins it out to acquire ease of motion and penetration <margin>B</margin>, the power of acting is immediately scattered.

Wherefore, since there ought to be three conditions for perfect action, the body either has three others opposed to them, or by accepting one of them, it does not receive the others. It would be necessary to have smallness, lightness, and rarity at the same time. These three things reduce the body to a certain incorporeal state, so that all power of acting must be referred to an incorporeal nature. Is it not from quantity itself that there is a multitude of parts in the agent, in the patient, and in the space between them? But as soon as that happens, the action is more weakened, because otherwise it would be far more vehement.

---

Because of the second condition, it carries out gradually what should be fulfilled suddenly. Because of the third, it completes late what should be finished quickly. Wherefore, vehement, swift, and sudden operation seems to belong to an incorporeal acting force. Fire shows us the same thing; by its thinness, it approaches a spiritual nature more than the other elements. <margin>C</margin> It is the most effective of all. For it does in a moment what other bodies do over a long time. It does not suffer the mixture of other things within itself as other bodies do. A spark of fire, if given material, will occupy almost the entire world. The remaining elements do not spread themselves so much, so quickly, or so vehemently. But fire, because it is thin, becomes powerful. Because it is powerful, it spreads wide rather than the reverse. It also becomes capable of light, which is called incorporeal, whose action occurs in a moment; even a small amount of air at the top of a vessel sustains the water below, even if it is burdened with the weight of many stones. In lightning and thunderbolts, it is clearly seen how much fire and air are capable of. 

Finally, the less thick the heaven is compared to the other elements, the more wonderful it is in light, motion, and effect. If, therefore, a body becomes more effective for acting the closer it gets to incorporeality, who does not see that the power of acting does not consist in a physical nature? <margin>D</margin> This can also be observed from here: just as the first in nature, which is God, acts on all things and suffers <note>In this context, "suffers" means to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> nothing, so the last, which is physical matter, must suffer from all things and act by itself on another least of all, since there is nothing below it to suffer from it. And if in the highest and infinite unity there is infinite power of acting, in an infinite multitude there is no power <margin>E</margin> of acting, but an infinite nature of suffering. 

The Pythagoreans <margin>F</margin> think that a body is an infinite multitude because it is divided without end. If, therefore, bodies seem to act, it is not from their own mass—as Democritus, the Cyrenaics, and the Epicureans <margin>G</margin> <note>Ficino lists these groups as "materialists" who wrongly believed that the physical size or shape of atoms determined their power.</note> thought—but they operate from some power and quality implanted in them. And not without reason. For where there is opposition of contraries, there the action of natural bodies is produced. That opposition is born <margin>H</margin> in the genus of qualities. Add to this: that matter under all these bodies is one.

<summary>Ficino argues that physical mass is a hindrance to action, whereas incorporeal (spiritual) qualities are the true source of power. He cites the speed and penetration of fire and the heavens as evidence that things are more powerful the closer they are to a non-physical state.</summary>
<keywords>incorporeality, virtus, power vs. mass, fire, elements, Neoplatonism, Pythagoreans, Epicureans, nature of action</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s metaphysical argument from the beginning of Book I. Having previously argued that physical bulk hinders action, he now demonstrates that all "doing" or "operation" in the universe arises from qualities and forms, rather than the raw material or size of an object. This serves as a stepping stone to his eventual argument for the soul's immortality.</meta>

# Theology
# First [Book]
<note>The sigil "A 2" indicates this is the second leaf of the first gathering in the printed book.</note>

...also an unlimited dimension. If therefore action proceeded from matter or dimension, the operation of all things would be one and the same. Now, however, since the actions of different bodies appear different, they do not act through matter or a single dimension, but through their various forms and qualities. Deservedly so, because they act for the same reason that they exist. They exist not through bulk in this or that species <note>The "species" here refers to the specific "kind" of thing an object is, defined by its form.</note>, but through this or that form.

<margin>I</margin>
Therefore they operate through form. Especially since the agent is closer to the patient <note>In this philosophical context, the "patient" is the thing being acted upon.</note> through the qualities of form rather than through the limits of quantity. And the power of form passes into foreign matter more so than does the dimension of quantity; it touches individual points of matter not by dimension, but by quality. Thus, water cools through coldness. Fire heats through heat rather than through bulk. For fire burns not because it is at its largest, but because it is at its hottest. And if all its heat were reduced as if to a single point, it would be most powerful for burning because of that maximum union. Thus, by the benefit of quality—especially when condensed into a narrow space—action occurs. Hence it happens that natural causes produce effects similar to the qualities of the causes, rather than equal to their quantity. And if it happens that equality occurs between the two, it must have appeared first through similarity. It is as if action is completed through qualities, since effects necessarily refer back to their causes in and through them. Therefore, almost all children immediately upon birth are similar to their parents in complexion and appearance; but they are equal in size only more rarely and much later. But who has not seen these things? For if you approach a large body, you do not become large yourself. But if you approach a hot one, you certainly get warm; nor do you perceive any quantity by sense unless quality has first moved the sense. For how can the size of a wall be judged unless color and light have led this very magnitude to the eye? Indeed, the judgment of quantity is lost more easily through sight because of distance than is the judgment of light and color, as if the efficacy of motion lies in the quality.

<margin>K</margin>
From this it is clearly confirmed that any thing moves the appetite <note>The "appetite" is the natural inclination or desire of a thing toward what is good for it.</note> by reason of the "good"—which is a quality—always, and not by reason of the "great" or the "many." Otherwise we would always choose those things which are larger or more numerous. Now indeed, in those things which we think are bad, we choose the smaller or the fewer.

<margin>L</margin>
Quality, however, cannot be a body for this reason: because two bodies cannot be placed together in the same place without mutual interference. Yet many qualities are poured into the same subject equally. For instance, in the matter of honey, the yellow color, sweetness, and scent—three qualities—are found everywhere together. For every little drop of honey is yellow, sweet, and pleasing to the nose.

<margin>M</margin>
Added to this is that every body is by its nature extended into length, breadth, and depth. Quality, however, does not extend its power by its own nature. For there would be no quality that was not extended somewhere [if it were a body]. For certain unextended qualities exist in a point, in unity, in number, and in the virtues of harmony. Quality therefore is not a body. Especially because if extension were natural to it, the wider it became, the stronger it would become. But it becomes weaker by dispersion. Therefore quality, which is in a way <term>indivisible<gloss>Something that cannot be split into smaller parts without losing its essence.</gloss></term> in itself, is divided only within the dimension of a body. Indeed, division happens only by reason of quantity, since division is always led from one into many. Yet quality preserves a certain property of an indivisible nature even in a body.

<margin>N</margin>
For as the Platonists judge: the <term>whiteness<gloss>original: albedo. In scholastic and Platonic thought, "whiteness" is the abstract quality that makes a white thing white.</gloss></term> which is in a part of a white body should not properly be called a "part" of that whiteness which is in the whole body; rather, it is better called "whiteness" than a part of whiteness. Certainly, if you divide a white body into many parts, the same essence <note>original: "ratio," meaning the defining principle or logical nature of the thing.</note> of whiteness remains in each part. In each one, there is also a similar action. Yet the magnitude is not the same or equal; therefore division belongs not properly to quality, but to the body by reason of quantity. Action belongs especially to quality reduced to a small point. This is certainly not a body; and most of all, when it is collected at a point, it becomes incorporeal. From which it follows that through the power of an incorporeal nature, operation does not proceed from the matter of bodies.

<margin>O</margin>
->Above the form divided in the body, there stands an indivisible form, that is, the soul. Chapter 3.<-

<margin>P</margin>
Since therefore we ascend from body to quality—and we call "quality," in the Platonic manner, every form divided in a body—must one stop at this step, in the manner of the Stoics and Cynics? By no means; but Quality...

<summary>Ficino argues that physical bodies act through their qualities and forms rather than their mass, proving that quality is an incorporeal power. This distinction sets the stage for his discussion of the soul as the highest, most indivisible form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book I of his *Platonic Theology*. Having established that bodies act through form rather than sheer mass, he now begins a "ladder of being" argument. He is distinguishing between the "qualities" we perceive with our senses (like heat or color) and the "True Forms" that exist in the divine intellect. This is a crucial step in his proof for the existence of God and the immortality of the soul, as it moves the reader from the physical world to the metaphysical world.</meta>

# Platonic Book
<note>original: "Platonice Liber." This is likely an abbreviation for "Book of Platonic Theology."</note>
<sig>a iii</sig>

is a certain form. The nature of form is simpler:
<margin>S</margin>
effective: agile for acting. Whence form is often called "act" <note>original: "actus." In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the fulfillment or active state of a thing, as opposed to "potency" or mere potential.</note> by the physicists. A nature of this kind is stained in the lap of matter: from simple it becomes divisible and impure; from active it becomes subject to passion <note>original: "passio." In this technical sense, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or being passive, the opposite of action.</note>; from agile it becomes inept. Therefore this is neither pure form, nor true, nor perfect. This cannot be the first form if it is not pure.
<margin>M</margin>
For everything must first exist purely according to its genus <note>A "genus" is a general category or "kind" of thing.</note> before it is stained. Likewise, it cannot be the first form if it is not true. From where, indeed, does the mind argue that this form is not entirely true, if not from the fact that the mind itself discerns some truer form? Compared to that one, this [material] form falls short and is proven to be false in some way. Where then does the mind see this true form? Surely it beholds it either outside itself or within itself. If it perceives it outside itself, there is certainly somewhere in nature a certain true form superior to quality. If the mind looks upon it within itself, the mind is not lacking the true form; therefore, the world is not lacking it. Furthermore, truth is certainly more
<margin>B</margin>
powerful than falsehood, since truth can exist without falsehood, but falsehood cannot exist without truth. For nothing is called false unless it is at least true that the thing is false. Nor does anything have power unless it is true that it has power; nor is something truly understood to be false except through truth. Nor is something called deceptive unless it deceives, and it does not deceive except through an image of truth. If therefore truth is more powerful than falsehood, and this less true form—namely, quality—is something in the order of things, then something much more truly "form" is found in the order of things. Especially since, just as the intellect is more excellent and truer than sense, so much more excellent and truer must the intelligible <term>intelligible: things that can only be perceived by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses</term> form be than the sensible form.

Through these points it has become clear: quality cannot be the first form, both because it is not pure and because it is not true. The same thing is also established because
<margin>L</margin>
it is not perfect. For the first in any genus is the principle <term>principle: the "principium" or foundational source from which other things arise</term> of the whole genus. That which is the principle of others contains the things that follow. Therefore, nothing of its own genus is lacking to that which is first in its genus. Just as the sun, which is first among bright things, lacks no degree of light. Other bright things beneath it, such as stars and elements, do not receive the whole fullness of light. Since therefore the first form embraces the perfections of all forms, and for that reason cannot be imperfect, it is rightly concluded that that form which is called "imperfect" cannot be the first. Add to this: that quality, which so inheres in matter that it expands and divides with it, turns out to be—if I may say so—entirely material.
<margin>C</margin>
And if it were separated from matter, it would be corrupted. For this reason, it does not sustain itself, but is sustained by matter as a subject. But that which cannot sustain itself can much less subsist from itself. And so, since it acts in another, it certainly depends on another. For quality is said to exist "at some time," since it changes and perishes. But nothing that exists "at some time" arises from itself. For that which provides a beginning to the thing generated must precede the thing generated. But nothing precedes itself. Therefore, since quality arises from another,
<margin>D</margin>
and nothing arises except by the power of something superior, it cannot be the principle of nature. But from where does it draw its origin? Surely not from matter? Not at all. Since matter is a common and formless subject and therefore, as far as it is in itself, relates equally to all forms always and everywhere, from where then does it happen that at different times and places it is adorned with different forms, if not from something superior? Which affects it both in different places and at different times in different ways. Furthermore, if matter were to give form to itself, we ask whether it, by its own power, first has that form which it is about to provide to itself, or whether it does not have it. If it does not have it, it cannot even conceive it. But if it has it, it is certainly not "prime matter," but something composed of matter and the power of form. And concerning this power itself, we shall inquire similarly: whether it has it from itself or from another. If it has it from another, it also has form from another. If from itself, does it perhaps have this through another power, likewise its own, and so we shall proceed to infinity? Or rather, does it possess that power not through another power, but through its essence? If this is so, the essence of matter will be the same as the power, or the effective substance of forms. And it will be the source of forms rather...

<summary>Ficino argues that physical qualities are too imperfect and dependent on matter to be the ultimate "First Form" of the universe. He demonstrates that because these qualities are subject to change and division, they must derive from a higher, immutable, and "intelligible" source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book I of his Platonic Theology. Following the previous discussion on the nature of "form" (the essence or blueprint of a thing) versus "matter," Ficino now explores the hierarchy of these forms. He is moving the reader from the physical world—where fire produces fire—to the spiritual world, arguing that physical things are merely "instruments" used by a higher, incorporeal power. This leads into his description of how the human mind naturally "ascends" from observing physical objects to understanding universal truths.</meta>

# First Book of Theology

...is the subject: Rather it will be form instead of matter: and the most excellent form of all. A form impatient of all division: nor will it fluctuate: as happens now with the variety of falling forms <note>Ficino refers to the "falling" or "decaying" forms of the physical world which are constantly changing and passing away.</note>: but through an eternal essence it will be endowed with eternal forms.

<margin>f</margin>
From these things, it is gathered that matter by its own nature does not have any power to procreate forms. Because an unformed subject cannot form itself. Since it can do nothing at all: indeed action proceeds from form: from which being itself proceeds. And even if matter: which is subject to art <note>Here "art" refers to human craftsmanship or skill.</note>: does not lack every form: it is not nevertheless led to the form of the artifact by itself: but by the form of the art: certainly matter: which is subjected to nature: since it is unformed: is led to a natural form not by itself: but by the nature of form.

<margin>q</margin>
Whence therefore will quality <note>In ancient philosophy, a "quality" is a property like heat, coldness, or color.</note> be? Perhaps from another quality: for example: that one fire generates another. Not even that. For quality: because it cannot exist without the nourishment of matter: therefore does not dominate its own matter.

<margin>s</margin>
Much less will it dominate another's matter. Therefore, the quality of some body cannot form another body by its own power alone. A natural body indeed acts not at all through its own mass: which is subject to passion <note>original: "passioni." In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon or being passive, the opposite of "action."</note> alone. Through quality, however, it does not act sufficiently. Nor indeed, since it sometimes lacks the sufficiency of being: it does not provide the sufficiency of operating to the body.

<margin>r</margin>
Certainly because fire was first generated by something before it itself could generate another thing: it happened to it first to be an effect rather than an efficient <note>An "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about.</note> cause. This condition is innate to an effect: that it depends on something else. Wherefore as often as fire operates anything: it acts as an instrument of a higher cause. For if this fire: or that fire were the first cause of generating fire: that is: the highest: since from the first cause of any genus <note>A "genus" is a general category or "kind" of thing.</note> the whole genus flows: it would produce fire everywhere and always. Thus it would make both itself: and any fire: which was before it: and which will be after.

<margin>S</margin>
Since therefore this fire: or that one is not the first cause of such generation: we ask of what cause it is the instrument. Is it of another fire? Not at all. First: because that cause is equal, not superior. Next: because either that fire is already extinguished: from which this one previously flowed: or it is most remote. Or is it perhaps the instrument of other elements? Not even that. For there is not in dissimilar: and contrary elements any reason for generating fire: to which this fire, about to generate another, might be subjected as an instrument. Is it therefore the instrument of the heavens? Not at all. For this fire cannot become the instrument of that most remote body otherwise than through a medium. Indeed these middle bodies are inept. And rather between the heaven: or the sphere of fire: and the dissimilar elements for the purpose of producing this fire on earth: some fire must be interposed which is about to generate this fire as a conversion <note>original: "conuersio." This refers to a turning or transformation in the hierarchy of being.</note>. Similarly, we shall argue in the individual species of natural things.

<margin>D</margin>
On account of which beyond all forms of this kind it is necessary that there be in all things: and preside over them a certain incorporeal <note>Incorporeal means "having no body" or spiritual.</note> substance penetrating through bodies: whose instruments are the corporeal qualities. For in what way would individual qualities: which by their own nature are unstable: and disordered: either preserve a stable order in the succession of generation: unless they were ruled by the stable order of a higher cause: or always return to the same effects: in the established courses of times: unless there were one: and the same cause: which was their leader at any time: and would similarly lead them at established times.

<margin>J</margin>
The human mind daily conveys itself from particular forms to universal: and absolute ones. Likewise it is accustomed to ascend from supernatural forms bound to certain matters—through mathematics for which uncertain matter suffices—to metaphysics: which need neither certain: nor uncertain matter. Furthermore from dimensions: which need both position and parts: to a point without parts: but in a certain way concerning position: again from points to numbers: which indeed need parts: but by no means position: finally from numbers to unity: which needs neither position nor any parts: it raises itself. And beyond individual unity: but accidental <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities like color or size that aren't essential to what a thing is. Ficino is arguing that the mind looks past these to the "substantial" core.</note> it transfers itself to substantial unity—that is, form: the essence of the individual: the foundation of accidents: at the same time as the origin as if to a certain fixed: and remaining in itself, of accidents which are through themselves muta... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "mutabili" (changeable).</note>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from the previous page regarding the nature of forms. Having established that physical matter is passive and requires an external "form" to act, Ficino now argues that there must be a highest, indivisible form—an incorporeal substance—that serves as the ultimate source of all movement and existence in the universe.</meta>

<header>Platonic Theology, Book VIII <note>While the OCR indicates "Book VIII," this text corresponds to the arguments found in Book I of Ficino's *Platonic Theology* regarding the hierarchy of substances.</note></header>
<sig>F iii</sig>

# Platonic
# Theology

...axis, always clinging to the other.
If the human mind possesses such great power for a rational ascent—a mind which is itself a certain image of the universe, even when hindered by the chains of the body—certainly the universe itself possesses a far greater power for this same ascent within itself. 
<margin>A</margin> This is especially true since the order of the lowest mind derives its origin from the order of the universe. Where a greater power for action flourishes, there it is natural for that power to be brought into action more greatly and more swiftly. Added to this is the fact that any kind of thing can be reduced to a certain "one" that is, in its own way, indivisible; it is in the simplicity of this "one" that they consist. For example: motion and time are reduced to the **moment** <note>In medieval philosophy, a "moment" is the indivisible "now" that makes up time, just as a point makes up a line.</note>; natural form is reduced to the **minimum natural degree**; geometric dimensions to the **point** <note>original: "signum"</note>. Numbers are reduced to **unity**. Why then should the genus of substance not also be reduced to an **indivisible substance**? Just as all shapes that share in inequality refer back to the circle (the most equal of all), and the circle refers back to the indivisible center (the beginning of all equality), so too should accidental and divisible forms be reduced to substantial and indivisible forms. Let this kind of form be reduced to a substantial and 
<margin>B</margin> indivisible one. Furthermore, just as there is a substantial and bodily form that is beyond "quality"—which is subject not only to decrease but also to **remission** <note>Term: <term>remission</term>. In medieval physics, "remission" refers to the weakening or loss of intensity in a quality, like water becoming less hot.</note>—and is free from such remission even if the body decreases, so there must be a substantial form above this which neither weakens nor decreases. Thus, the ascent, which progresses toward the better, may reach its perfection in the "best." Such a substance will be **incorporeal**, having this primary trait: that by its nature it cannot be diminished. It is necessary that this substance exists somewhere in nature according to its own proper form. For indivisible and simple things necessarily precede those that are divisible and composite. For each thing must first exist before it can be stretched out or swell up. The composite things need the simple ones, not the other way around. For the composite take their beginning from the simple and are bounded by them. Therefore, if composite things exist in the nature of things according to their own form, it is much more necessary that those simple things—the source of the genus—be 
<margin>C</margin> found somewhere according to their own proper form. Indeed, because nature moves its matter more effectively and better than art <note>Ficino uses "art" to mean human craft or technology.</note> moves its own, we conclude that the primary form in nature has more mastery over its matter than the primary form in art has over its matter. If it dominates more, two things are concluded: first, that it is closer to the matter in its position than art is; and second, that it excels its matter in substance more than art does, and is better able 
<margin>D</margin> to exist by itself without that matter. Moreover, a similar reason moves me greatly: that all qualities—which are forms existing in something else—whenever they generate, they generate forms in something else. For they cannot give birth to something more "free" or "primary" than they are themselves. They generate forms in the "womb" of matter. Now, however, those forms which do not lie within another thing are made and preserved only by a form that itself does not lie in another. For matter does not exist from itself, since it is imperfect and does not act from itself. Nor does it exist from qualities (which matter itself precedes), but from a certain form which precedes matter. Such a form is entirely incorporeal. In the power and operation of such a form are founded the powers and operations of qualities, since the work of the qualities is always founded upon the work of that higher form. But more on this elsewhere.
<margin>E</margin> Now, however, one must remember that matter itself—as **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of wisdom texts (Hermetica) that Ficino famously translated.</note> and **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> believe—is a "not-nothing" without form, something very close to nothing, which is primarily and infinitely "passive." From this, **Plotinus** <note>The primary philosopher of Neoplatonism (3rd century AD), whose works Ficino translated and commentated upon.</note> thinks it follows that the immediate disposition of matter—that is, its dimension and quality—is something most vain; and however small it is, the whole of it is a certain **passion** <note>Term: <term>passion</term>. In this context, it means the state of being acted upon or "undergoing" something, as opposed to "action."</note>. 
<margin>F</margin> For dimensions are nothing other than the extensions of matter itself, while qualities are nothing other than its "affections." These are shadowy and fleeting affections, like the shadows of tall trees in a rushing stream. Finally, he concludes: neither matter (since it is the primary "passive" thing), nor dimensions or qualities (since they are the primary passions of the primary passive thing), can be the primary principles of action. So says Plotinus. Others distinguish this somewhat differently, though toward the same end. They say that matter itself can perform no action. Quantity as well—if it is the passive extension of matter proceeding from something that extends the matter—can do nothing, since it is a perpetual passion of the primary passive thing. But if it is like a form...

<summary>Ficino argues that just as mathematics reduces complex shapes to a single point, the physical world must be reduced to an indivisible, incorporeal "form." He concludes that matter and physical qualities are purely passive, like shadows in a stream, and requires a higher spiritual substance to provide action and existence.</summary>

--- Page 53 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book I of the "Platonic Theology." He is moving from a discussion of how physical matter is passive and how "quantity" (physical dimensions) limits a thing's power, to the necessity of an incorporeal (non-physical) "life" or "soul" that provides order and action to the universe.</meta>

# Theology

...a certain "one": through which the motor cause of matter extends matter, perhaps acting somewhat upon its own matter, since it serves as a medium through which that matter is seen to extend. But in foreign matter, it works nothing at all, because the agent is always forced to be distant from the recipient <term>the patient</term>, which hinders action. However, according to the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who emphasized physical and empirical causes.</note>, **quality** does work something upon matter—both foreign and its own. 

If reason leads us from **matter** (which acts on neither) to **quality** (which in a certain way moves both) via the medium of **quantity** (which operates only in a certain way on its own matter), will we then pass from quality—which in no way moves foreign matter without some medium—to that thing which entirely moves foreign matter? <margin>B</margin> By no means. Moreover, quality is very close to quantity. Therefore, quality is not entirely sufficient for external action. If, then, it "limps" <note>original: "claudicat," meaning to falter or be hindered in its natural function.</note> in acting, it must be directed by a superior substance that is completely powerful. 

Quality rightly falters. For at the very moment it is born, it is spread through the breadth and depth of matter, and is, as it were, drowned in the **River Lethe** <note>A river in the Greek underworld representing forgetfulness; Ficino uses it here as a metaphor for a spiritual form losing its power when submerged in physical matter.</note>. Thus it happens that before it acts at all, it is in a sense overcome by the matter that "infects" it. Therefore, its own power never overcomes matter by itself. For this reason, it will never move anything by itself unless it is strengthened by a higher cause. 

It is indeed strengthened and led by a certain **life**, which produces life and sensation even from non-living mud—as when frogs and flies are generated—and creates various and most beautiful flowers simultaneously from one shapeless matter through various and most beautiful **seeds** <note>original: "semina," referring to "seminal reasons," the hidden blueprints in nature that guide growth.</note>. Since these seeds are often not found in the lowest physical realm, they are necessarily within life itself. It also forces scattered matter into an <margin>D</margin> **order**. Order proceeds from **reason**. Reason consists in **life**. Life consists in a certain **indivisible power**. 

Since death occurs through division and dissolution, [this life] conversely generates fire from the collision of cold bodies. And when the reflection of rays in a mirror, or hot iron, heats wool through the "accidental" quality of fire, that **life** produces the **substantial species** <term>the essential nature or "soul" of a thing</term> of fire in the wool through the vital seeds of fire.

# Book One

Finally, what do we think is within ourselves? That which consumes nourishment not by force, but gently and orderly cooks and digests it? That which so wonderfully restores non-living food to a living form? That which continuously moves heavy things upward and light things downward <note>This refers to the ancient belief that elements have "natural places": earth and water go down, while air and fire go up.</note> without obvious violence, beyond—indeed, above—their nature, as the use of life requires? 

That which reconciles conflicting elements and binds them into one? Surely not the simple heat of fire. Nor any other quality of the conflicting parts. Not a divisible nature. Not a bare property of nature. Rather, it is a certain higher, indivisible, and life-giving power. 

As it is in us, so consider it in the universe. And from these things, conclude: bodily forms do not possess sufficient power of generation from one another, but require a higher cause besides. If this superior cause were itself a form joined to matter in the same way, it would descend again from another superior substance. Finally, so that there is not a progression to infinity, we must arrive at some form which is mixed with no bodies. 

Indeed, so great is the power in the genus of "forms" for this, that they can exist separately from matter. Even if someone were to say that they are joined of themselves, but are joined [to matter] through the contemplation of minds, he would at least be forced to admit from this that the minds themselves are separate, since <margin>K</margin> they separate other things. 

This appears again from the fact that **substance** is prior by nature and dignity to **quantity** and the remaining **accidents** <term>non-essential properties like color or size</term>. And because that which is "prior" can exist apart from that which is "posterior," there can be a certain substance without the division of quantity. If it can exist, it certainly does exist at some time, lest nature lack that perfection, <margin>L</margin> or lest this potential be in vain. For in those things that pertain to the chief order of the universe, it is the case that whatever can exist, either already exists—as the physicists believe, so that no change occurs in eternal things—or at least exists at some time. 

Marsilio Ficino.

<summary>Ficino argues that physical qualities are too weak and "diluted" by matter to account for life and order. He concludes there must be an indivisible, incorporeal "life" or "mind" that directs the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book I of the "Platonic Theology." The previous page concluded that physical qualities are insufficient for action and must be directed by a superior substance. This page moves into specific proofs from authorities like Averroes and Proclus to show that "form" and "unity" must exist independently of physical dimensions and matter.</meta>

# Book of Platonic Theology

...whenever: lest anything be always in vain <note>original: "inane," meaning empty or without purpose.</note>. And if **life**—which by natural origin alone precedes sensation—already exists somewhere by itself without sensation, how much more does **substance**—which surpasses **quantity** in both dignity and origin—now exist in the order of things separate from quantity. Especially since the universe is a perfection: if certain substances are released from the chains of quantity, even if they are certain types of lives devoid of sensation.

<margin>A</margin> **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher, known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>, following the opinion of **Aristotle**, proves that the corporeal and substantial form of the heavens lacks matter. This is because there is clearly no potential there for diverse forms, which is the proper nature of matter. Yet, dimension exists there; he judges such forms to be a middle ground between natural forms and divine forms. For while natural forms exist simultaneously with matter and quantity, and divine forms are entirely absolute from both, the form of the heavens is the middle between the two, so that one does not pass from one extreme to the other without a middle. Therefore, he deems it agreeable that it exists with quantity, yet without matter. From this, we argue in this manner: Since substantial form usually lies in matter rather than in quantity, and has a greater proportion with matter than with quantity according to the order of genus and nature, if it can exist anywhere without matter, it can much more easily exist somewhere apart from quantity.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, as **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino’s thought.</note> suggests, there are three types of bodies. For there are some—to use his words—that are material and composite at once. These are the kinds composed of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. There are further the spheres of the elements: material indeed, but in some way simple.

<margin>C</margin> Finally, there are the celestial bodies: both simple and immaterial at once. He also posits three types of forms, not unlike Averroes. For he wishes the general definition of forms to be this: **Form** is that by which something is distinctly in act and acts. In this definition, however, no dimensions at all are included; yet a subject is perhaps signified in some way when it says, "that by which something [is]," and the other things that follow. Whence he concludes: if any forms exist without subject matter, such as the celestial ones, much more—and many more—can and should be able to exist simultaneously without dimension.

<margin>D</margin> Likewise, **Proclus** and **Syrianus** <note>The teacher of Proclus and a prominent Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> argue toward the same point. That which is always extended by another is necessarily bound by dimensions. But that which extends [others] is not. Therefore, since matter is always extended by another, it is necessarily subject to dimensions. Yet, because each thing is in some way in itself before it is extended, matter can be thought of as indivisible. Therefore, that principle from which it is extended can much more be thought of—and indeed exist—without dimensions.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, every divisible thing is a certain whole made of many parts. Unless these parts had something "one" within them—and that same "one" common to all—they would never constitute that whole. For "one" is not made except by the "one." Again, unless they were participants in **unity**, none of the parts would be one, but would be infinitely many; and any part would be innumerably infinite. That "one" implanted in the parts is not divided individually among the individuals. For it would itself also need another joining [it]. Therefore, it is the same and whole in each part. It is necessary that such a thing be **incorporeal**. Likewise, since every corporeal thing is a certain whole made of parts, what then is the cause of that union?

<margin>F</margin> Does the whole itself unite the parts, or do the parts unite the whole? Or does something higher—which is neither a part of anything nor a whole made of parts—unite the parts to each other and to the whole? The whole follows the parts rather than uniting them. And if it is admitted that it <insert>the higher thing</insert> unites the parts, it will be incorporeal; for if it were [corporeal], it too, being divisible, would need another similarly uniting it. If the parts unite the whole, that is indeed absurd—that a union should be made from a multitude opposed to unity, which ought to be made by unity. It remains, then, that besides the individual parts and the whole, there is something "one" present as the cause of that conspiracy <note>original: "conspirationis," here meaning a harmonious "breathing together" or union.</note>. This must indeed be incorporeal, lest it be forced to also require a bond. And thus we would go on to infinity. Therefore, it is not to be thought that any form divided in a body is the peak of nature and the principle of things.

<summary>Ficino argues that substantial forms and the principle of unity must be incorporeal and independent of physical dimensions to avoid an infinite regress of causes. He cites Averroes and Proclus to demonstrate that celestial and higher forms exist without the limitations of matter and quantity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book I of the "Platonic Theology." The previous page argued that "form" (the essence of a thing) must exist independently of physical matter. Here, Ficino argues that the "First Principle" (God) must be eternal and incorporeal, and introduces the "Rational Soul" as the "Third Essence" which bridges the eternal and the physical worlds.</meta>

<header>Theology One</header>

# Theology

# One

<margin>D</margin>
¶ This is especially true since the principle <note>original: "principium," referring to the first cause or origin of all things</note> of all things must have been eternal in its own power, and must remain so. It must have always existed, for it could never have emerged from itself at some point in time. If it had, it would have existed before itself. Nor could it have come from another, for nothing exists before the first. All other things would never have existed unless the first had existed beforehand. It must also exist forever. For if the principle were extinguished, the entire universe would collapse. Neither the principle itself nor anything else could ever be born again.

<margin>E</margin>
¶ Therefore, an infinite power <note>original: "vis infinita"</note> must necessarily possess that by which it lives infinitely from itself. It cannot have this power if it were a physical body. For if it had infinite dimensions, there would be nothing else in the world except itself. If it had finite dimensions, its power would also be finite.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Add to this what we have shown elsewhere: that neither a body nor a physical form can be a sufficient principle of motion, as they are both unworthy and subject to change; instead, every physical thing is set in motion by something else. Furthermore, the artisan <term>Artisan (Opifex): A term often used by Platonists to describe the divine creator or 'Demiurge' who shapes the world.</term> who is mixed into the work cannot dominate the work; thus, the artisan must be perfect, the primary architect of the worldly work. Therefore, let us transcend physical form and now consider the first form that we encounter next.

<margin>H</margin>
Just as we ascend from the body, as if from the lowest point, to physical form—which is like a middle ground because it possesses something of the body as it spreads through it, yet also lacks something of the body since it is not itself composed of matter and form—so now let us be moved forward from this middle ground to a higher, incorporeal form. This form possesses nothing of the body, but rather distributes qualities to bodies. Because it subsists through itself, it is called "true form" and "essence." I call this the **third essence**, which in its proper place we shall also call the **rational soul**. The irrational soul <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic biological functions and reflexes, rather than reason.</note> accompanies it just as a shadow follows a body.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
That essence is judged by the Platonists to be both true and immortal because it does not require parts into which it might one day be dissolved, and through which its scattered power might be weakened. Nor is it bound to a subject <note>In philosophy, a 'subject' is the underlying matter or thing in which qualities exist; Ficino argues the soul exists independently.</note> from which it might vanish if abandoned. It is not mixed with a contrary form by which it could be infected, nor is it confined by place or time, nor subject to motion, due to the indivisible and self-contained simplicity of its substance.

¶ **C** The rational soul is immobile in its substance, yet mobile in its operation; in its power, it is partly immobile and partly mobile.

<margin>K</margin>
<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
¶ **W**hat shall we say is the nature of this third essence? Is it entirely immobile, or rather mobile? Certainly not entirely immobile, because it is the source of the qualities that flow into matter, which are entirely devoid of rest. Every cause acts according to its own nature. Therefore, it is necessary that some power and image of the cause be preserved in the work. If that essence, which is the cause of qualities, were entirely immobile, then because it would act through its entirely immobile nature, the quality descending from it would retain an immobile nature within itself.

<margin>L</margin>
However, the opposite is true. For in quality, there are three things: essence, power, and action; all of these are involved in motion. Its essence is generated and corrupted. Generation and corruption are brought about through motion. Its power is also intensified or diminished according to its nature—for example, heat burns more or less intensely. Since it does not burn with the same intensity at different times, it is undoubtedly changed. Action suffers the same fate. For the action of fire is heating. It does not heat water in a single moment, but over time. Action occurring in time is called "motion" by everyone; therefore, quality is subject to motion in every respect.

<margin>M</margin>
This is clearly apparent again from this: the state of a body, which is produced through qualities, cannot remain exactly the same and similar through any delay of time. It is always changing, sometimes into a different proportion of degrees, and sometimes for better or worse. Indeed, if anyone should say that a mature state of the body remained the same for an hour, the Platonists would ask him: "When the hour is finished, is the power in that state the same as it was at the beginning of the hour?" If the power is not equal, then certainly it did not stay the same for the hour, since it changed potentially during that hour. If the power is said to be equal, that state will endure for yet another hour. Equally...

<summary>Ficino defines the "Third Essence" (the Rational Soul) as an incorporeal bridge between the eternal, immobile divine realm and the changing, physical world. He argues that the soul must be the source of motion and quality because physical bodies cannot move themselves.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the end of the previous page concerning physical forces and the stability of form. Ficino is moving from the analysis of physical "qualities" (like heat or cold) to the "Rational Soul," which he identifies as the bridge between the physical world of change and the divine world of stability. He then introduces the "Angel" (or pure Intellect) as the next level of being.</meta>

<header>Platonic Theology</header>

...for equal forces produce equal effects. Therefore, if a body has remained in its state for an hour through such force, it will remain for another equal hour through an equal force. Once the second hour is finished, they will ask similarly about that power: whether it is equal or unequal. If it is unequal, the body did not stand. If it is equal, it will also stand for just as long. They will proceed similarly afterward into infinity, and they will show that the nature of that body—if it stood for but an hour or even half an hour—is destined to remain perpetually. 

In truth, the composition <term>Composition (complexio): In Renaissance medicine and philosophy, this refers to the specific "mix" of qualities or humors that make up a physical body.</term> of any body does not flourish perpetually according to itself, since all are soon extinguished and perish; thus, they scarcely endure for a moment of time in the same state. And because they begin and end in that same moment, a completely intact habit of existence is least possessed in the act of beginning and ending. Yet, an intact act of existence is necessary for performing an action; therefore, it seems to be confirmed—as we proved in the previous dispute—that there is no sufficient principle of action within physical qualities. 

But to return to the question proposed here: if action is found in qualities, then as far as they are concerned, every state of motion is in some way lacking. How can they be the immediate cause of a sign when they are separated from the cause by such a great interval that the cause possesses a state entirely devoid of motion? 

If all things pass from extreme to extreme through a middle ground—as one goes from winter through spring into summer, or from summer into winter through autumn—then certainly between a quality that is entirely mobile and an essence that is utterly immobile, something must necessarily be placed that is partly immobile and partly mobile. 

Therefore, that substance which is the immediate parent of qualities cannot be entirely immobile. What then shall we say? Shall we assert that this substance is also entirely mobile? Not at all. For it would either be in the category of physical qualities (and yet we cannot stop our search at that level), or the cause—which is located in a higher category—would not exceed its effect with sufficient perfection if the substance which is the cause of quality wavered no less than the quality itself. 

Wherefore, that substance <margin>B</margin> stands in part, but in part it is moved. It possesses three things within itself: essence, power, and operation <term>Essence, Power, and Operation: A standard Neoplatonic triad. Essence is what a thing is; Power is its capacity to act; Operation is the actual performance of that action.</term>. Which of these shall stand? Which shall be moved? Certainly, the operation cannot stand if the two preceding things are changed. Nor can the essence be moved without the following things being moved. Therefore, the first will stand: namely, the essence itself. The last will be changed: namely, the operation. But what of the middle between them both—the power? It will also stand in part, and in part it will also be changed.

---

->### Chapter V. Above the mobile soul is the immobile angel.<-

<margin>C</margin> **H**itherto we have found a certain form above the composition of the body, which we shall call the **rational soul**. Its essence remains always the same, which is signified by the stability of the will and the memory. Its operation, however, changes because it does not think all things at once, but step by step; nor does it nourish, increase, or generate the body in a single moment, but over time. Its natural power remains, because its natural vigor flourishes perennially, neither being intensified nor diminished. Its acquired power <note>original: "virtus acquisita," referring to skills or knowledge learned over time</note> changes, because it passes from potentiality into act, and from act into habit and conversion. 

<margin>D</margin> Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows."</note>, Varro, and Manilius ascended this far, but one must ascend higher. Indeed, this form cannot be the principle of all nature. For a stable operation—which completes its work most perfectly in a single moment—is more perfect than one which requires time. A life is more intact when it is all united with itself at once, not distant from itself, than a life which is stretched through different moments of time and is, in a way, distracted from itself according to its internal acts and affections. 

Therefore, above this form—whose external operation wanders through time and whose life (that is, its internal operation) is dispersed as if by a certain flow—must be placed another, more sublime form, whose operation is stable and whose life is entirely united at once. <margin>E</margin> For indeed, perfect things are always prior to the imperfect...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul serves as a middle ground between physical matter and the divine, possessing an unchanging essence but changing actions. He concludes that there must be a higher level of being, the "Angel" or pure Intellect, which is entirely stable in both its nature and its actions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical argument regarding the hierarchy of being. Having previously discussed the limitations of physical qualities, Ficino now argues that since imperfect things depend on perfect ones, and moving things depend on the stable, there must be a "Mind" (pure Intellect) above the human soul that is eternally and fully active.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>First Book of Theology</header>

# Theology

# Book One

Perfect things are to be placed before the imperfect. This is because things perfect in any category are those which are such by their very nature; similarly, imperfect things are those which are not such through themselves—otherwise they would be perfectly so. If, therefore, imperfect things are not <margin>f</margin> such through themselves, they are compelled to exist through superior things. Furthermore, <margin>a</margin> whatever moves breaks forth from potentiality <note>original: "ex potentia." In Aristotelian philosophy, "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, while "act" is the fulfillment of that capacity.</note> and rest into act; it seeks some limit of its motion and an end, as if it were less than sufficient for itself, but lacked that toward which it directs itself by its own motion. 

But truly, above that which migrates from rest into act, there always exists something that is full and perennial act. Above that which changes due to a lack, there necessarily exists something that either never lacks anything or is already completely full, and thus is not moved. This is especially true since that which is moved is changed by a desire for perfection; it could not be perfected except by the acquisition of a better and more excellent nature. It does not possess the thing it seeks through motion, but acquires it after the motion is complete. It does not acquire it from itself (otherwise it would not have needed to change), but from something more abundant. For that which lacks a limit by its own nature must be <margin>b</margin> limited by something else more perfect. 

A mobile thing, by itself, lacks a limit because it does not rest in <margin>c</margin> itself. And if such a thing were the principle of all things—namely, that it made everything changeable through its own operation—there would be no stability in the world. <margin>g</margin> But in fact, a certain stability in things is so necessary that even motion itself is not without it. For any thing that is said to be affected in different ways through motion must remain the same in substance for some time; otherwise, it would neither change its characteristics nor vary gradually, but would cease to exist entirely in an instant. Even the most orderly revolution of the heavens around the same center and the same poles—the equality of motions and the return of the stars—participates in a kind of stability. 

And yet, just as that which stands still does so because of unity, and is united in its state (as we shall declare elsewhere), so that which moves is moved for the sake of stability and "stands" within its motion. It is moved, I say, for the sake of stability—that is, for the sake of the stability of the moving power; unless that power remained in its vigor, no order would be preserved in the motion; indeed, the motion would not continue for even a moment. Again, it "stands" in motion—that is, it perseveres in the same, or equal, or similar rule of movement. There are also many things which, while they move according to one kind of motion, do <margin>g</margin> not move according to others; they are partly moving and partly at rest. 

Add to this that since the primary matter <note>original: "prima rerū materia." This is the fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe that underlies all physical change.</note> of things is eternal, even though it is changed through substantial form, it is nonetheless compelled to remain the same through its matter. Therefore, how much more can a thing remain stable—and indeed it must remain stable—in its substance while it changes in quantity, quality, and place? What more can be said? That which in no way remains stable while admitting a state of change is compelled to lose both its existence and its motion at once. If, therefore, there is any stability in things, the principle of things cannot be mobile. Therefore, that which is mobile is not the principle of nature. 

Thus, there is something above the soul. For the soul, which is by its nature indifferent to understanding or not understanding—since it changes from one to the other in turn—is determined toward understanding by the influence of something that is always "in act" <note>original: "in actu." Meaning something that is currently and fully functioning, rather than just having the potential to do so.</note> in that category. Such a thing is that which is always "intellecting," or what is the same, always "intelligible" in act. Furthermore, whatever is "such" <margin>m</margin> according to its parts is only such through that which exists as "such" according to its whole self; just as wood, which is hot in one part, grows hot through fire, which is hot in its entirety. For that which is such by its nature—take "hot" for example—is as much grasped by its own nature as a whole as it is by that quality. Conversely, that which is such only in part is not such through itself. 

Now, that third essence <note>Ficino’s "Third Essence" is the Soul, which sits in the middle of his five-level hierarchy: God, Mind, Soul, Quality, and Matter.</note>, namely the soul, is not a totality of intelligence according to itself. For it has certain other natures besides intelligence that are devoid of intelligence. Therefore, the Mind <term>Mind (Mens): In this context, Ficino uses 'Mens' to refer to the highest part of the soul or the pure angelic intellect that exists above the human soul.</term> in the soul is indeed a part of the soul. It is also a "part" of a Mind, so to speak—of a higher Mind which is entirely and solely Mind. Certainly, if the soul had a mind from itself, the reason for producing a mind would exist within the soul's own substance. Hence, the entire soul would be Mind, and a perfect Mind at that. And every soul would possess a mind...

<summary>Ficino argues that since the soul is changeable and only partially intellectual, it must depend on a higher "Mind" (pure Intellect) that is eternally active and stable. He establishes that motion requires a stable principle to exist, positioning the Mind as a more perfect reality than the Soul.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, Marsilio Ficino, potentiality and act, stability, motion, hierarchy of being, third essence, intellect, soul vs mind</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the hierarchy of the soul. On the previous page, he established that imperfect and moving things depend on a higher, stable reality. Here, he begins to differentiate between the human mind, which is "attached" to a body, and higher angelic minds, which exist independently.</meta>

## Platonic
## Book

...[the soul] would have: because in any soul, the <term>essence</term><note>original: "ratio." In this context, it refers to the defining principle or "reason for being" of the soul.</note> of the soul is found. And just as moving the body—which belongs to the soul by its very nature—is present in every individual soul, so the faculty of understanding would be present in all souls, even those of beasts, if it belonged to the soul by its own nature. 

But since it is necessary that there be some more effective power above a nature that is not fully effective on its own—and since the mind, which is in the soul, neither produces any work outside itself by its own act alone, nor rules over the effective power of its own soul—there must be a Mind above the soul which, by its own act, is the creator of some work and the master of effective power. Just as the mind is the "head" of the soul and its most excellent part, so too is there a "head" for this mind. For the mind within us is not independent; it is attached to the soul. It is not absolute, but drawn down to the soul’s capacity; it is not clear, but obscure and in some way <margin>A</margin> doubtful. Therefore, the "head" of our mind is that Mind which exists in itself: free and bright. 

In this, one truly unravels that <term>enigma of the Magi</term><note>Ficino often references the "Magi"—ancient Persian or Chaldean sages like Zoroaster—whom he believed shared a common "ancient theology" with Plato.</note>: There is a thing that is bright everywhere. There is a thing that is obscure everywhere. There is a middle thing that is partly bright and partly obscure. In the order of bodies, a thing bright everywhere is any star above the moon. The air is obscure everywhere. The moon is the middle thing. Truly, in the order of spirits: the Mind is full of light. The irrational soul is empty. The rational soul holds the middle ground. It possesses a part of intellectual light, and it lacks a part. And that part which it has from God—as the moon has from the sun—it receives differently at different times and changes its "shape." Therefore, there is rightly an angel above it, who, like any star above the moon, is always complete and shines in the same way with the light of its own sun.

Certainly, where a superior nature touches an inferior one, it reaches the highest level of the inferior from its own lowest grade. For example, the lowest part of fire touches the highest part of air. Indeed, intellectual nature is superior to bodily nature; it touches it so closely that the most excellent thing among bodies participates in the intellectual soul. But inferior things—which are the <margin>B</margin> majority—do not participate at all. According to the Platonists, the most excellent bodies are those of the celestial inhabitants, the <term>daemons</term><note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>, and men. 

But are the minds assigned to bodies of this kind the highest of all minds? Not at all. Otherwise, an inferior nature would reach the summit of a superior nature without a middle ground. Therefore, just as there are many bodies lacking mind beneath those bodies endowed with mind, so above the minds implanted in bodies, there are many minds assigned to no bodies. And indeed, these are many more than the <margin>C</margin> species of bodies. For, as we shall show elsewhere, rational souls are established between eternity and time. The excellence of eternity seems to demand that there be, in a sense, more species and perfections within it than there are in time. 

Therefore—as we will demonstrate elsewhere—there is a vast distance between souls and the first, infinite Principle. But the space between souls and matter is finite; so it should seem a wonder to no one that there can be many more grades of angels above souls than there are grades of forms below souls. Furthermore, when one thing is made from two, and one of them (the less perfect one) is found to exist somewhere on its own, separate from the other, then even more so can that other part—which is more perfect and less needy—exist somewhere without the <margin>D</margin> other. 

Now, a living being is made of one intellectual substance (that is, the rational soul) and a body. We see many bodies exist and live without this kind of intellect. What, therefore, prevents there being many minds not united to bodies? Such minds would certainly be above the souls that are united to bodies. Furthermore, minds joined to bodies, insofar as they are such, do not complete the species of a living thing on their own. Instead, they are parts of a composite species; and for the most part, in order to understand, they look toward those things which are <margin>E</margin> sensible <note>original: "sensibilia." Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. For this reason, they are in some way imperfect and act imperfectly. If, therefore, one must ascend from the imperfect in any genus to the perfect (which are prior by nature), it follows that reason leads us from joined minds up to separated minds. These separated minds sufficiently fulfill their own species and, in the act of understanding, [they do not need the senses]...

<summary>Ficino argues for a hierarchy of intellect, placing "separated minds" (angels) above the human soul. He uses the "Enigma of the Magi" to illustrate the soul's middle position between the total light of pure Mind and the total darkness of irrationality.</summary>
