# Theology

...and to those things which are intelligible through themselves: let them look. The mind itself: because through intelligence and will it does not necessarily depend on a body: it naturally separates forms: and is occupied around separate things: and is perfected by rest rather than motion: by nature it is free from the body: and free from motion. Therefore it more suits its nature: to live apart from the body: and free from motion: 

<margin>C ¶</margin>
than to live in a body: and with motion. Many minds in bodies lead a mobile life. Wherefore much more: and many more lead an immobile life without bodies. 

<margin>F ¶</margin>
Who would deny that in a body, it belongs more to the nature of a substance according to its genus: to be outside the body than to be in the body. And therefore more species of that genus ought to be separated from the body than joined to it. For what is more natural to any genus: that exists in it for the 

<margin>G ¶</margin>
most part. Such indeed are the <term>angels</term><note>Ficino uses "angels" and "minds" interchangeably here to describe pure intellectual beings that exist without physical bodies.</note>: who, if they move the bodies of the world: they themselves: while the bodies are moved: are in no way moved. Souls, however: while they transport bodies: are also themselves carried. A motor: which travels together with the moved body: does not keep a perpetual: and stable tenor and order of moving: unless an immobile motor presides over it. Therefore the perpetual order of the mundane 

<margin>D ¶</margin>
revolution testifies: that there are some <term>immobile motors</term><note>original: "motores immobiles." This is the Aristotelian concept of the "Unmoved Mover"—a being that causes motion in others without being moved itself.</note> above souls. Since the elements consist of the fluidity of matter: and always infect one another: they would observe no order from themselves: unless they were ruled by the most orderly law of celestial motion. Since indeed 

<margin>I ¶</margin>
even heaven by itself is perpetually immobile and therefore <unclear>undignified</unclear>: the stable order in its motion does not come from itself: but from a supreme motor that is entirely immobile: and indivisible. For in things so diverse: and mobile, a stable union does not persevere: unless from a most stable: and most unified center: which at last is referred to unity itself: and to a state of rest. Surely just as the mobile relates to the mobile: so the motor relates to the motor. Therefore just as an element: which is moved in a mobile way: relates to heaven: which is moved in a stable way. So the motor of the mobile and varied heaven relates to the stable and unified motor: finally, it reduces the stable: and the unified to the state of rest and unity itself. Indeed, that action which is called "to move" follows the motor: 

<margin>K</margin>
that <term>passion</term><note>In this context, "passion" (passio) refers to the state of being acted upon or "suffering" an effect, the logical opposite of "action."</note> which is "to be moved" follows this action: nor does it happen the other way around. For prior things are not led by posterior things: but the reverse. It is possible, therefore, much more for that action which is called "to move" to be somewhere without that passion which is "to be moved": than for such a passion to be apart from action. Yet such passion is in bodies apart from action. 

<margin>L</margin>
Therefore somewhere there will be action far from passion. So that just as bodies are moved indeed: but do not move others: so angels may move: but not be moved. Concerning whom Zoroaster says: <note>original Greek: "περι κοσμους νοερους κιονας αναπειθει"</note> "He persuades [us] regarding the pillars in the intellectual worlds"; he has two intellectual immobile rulers. Therefore just as entirely mobile qualities precede souls: which are partly mobile: and partly immobile: so entirely immobile angels precede souls. That angels exist: and exist in 

<margin>M</margin>
multitudes, Aristotle proves in the eleventh book of <term>Divine Matters</term><note>Ficino refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, specifically Book Lambda, which deals with the first principles of the divine and the unmoved movers.</note> in this way. The whole continuum of heaven is ordered: and as far as it is in itself: it must be made by a motor that is never-failing: which is moved neither in itself: nor by accident. Since indeed motions of this kind in heaven are many and distinct among themselves: and diverse in species: and virtue: it is necessary that they be made by many motors of this kind: who clearly are not bodies: lest they be forced: while they move: to be moved meanwhile by another: and so it would necessarily proceed to infinity. Nor again are they forms in a body: lest it happen that they are moved together with the moved body. For it is necessary to arrive at a most perfect motor, that is, an immobile one: lest any transgression ever occur in the motions. Motors of this kind are minds: since in forms entirely released from matter, the <term>intelligible</term><note>The object of thought.</note> and the <term>intellect</term><note>The power of thinking.</note> are the same. These are the words of Aristotle. The Hebrews: and later philosophers call those minds angels: and messengers. <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose Neoplatonic interpretation of Aristotle deeply influenced Ficino.</note> Avicenna disputes somewhere that the chief among them are no fewer than ten: but elsewhere he seems to signify many more. Aristotle, however, says they are by no means fewer than the celestial motions: and he confesses to have computed the number by probable reason. But that it is necessary for wise men to humble themselves...

<summary>Ficino argues for the existence of "immobile motors" or angels, which are pure intellectual beings that direct the movement of the heavens and elements without being moved themselves. He synthesizes Greek philosophy (Aristotle and Zoroaster), Islamic thought (Avicenna), and Hebrew tradition to prove that these separate minds are a necessary higher level of reality above the human soul.</summary>

Having established that there are "minds" (angels) that exist independently of bodies, he now argues for their vast, nearly infinite number and explains their mathematical and symbolic organization according to both Christian and Platonic traditions.</meta>

B

<margin>N</margin> As if someone suspected: perhaps those minds should be numbered according to their own primary action—that is, <term>intelligence</term><note>In this context, "intelligence" refers to the direct, non-discursive understanding of truth, which Ficino considers the primary activity of an angel.</note>—rather than according to their common and secondary action, which is motion. Furthermore, since those minds are the ends or goals of motions, he perhaps prophesied that they should not be counted according to the number of motions. And it is possible that there are as many minds as possible which are not distributed to moving physical bodies. For this reason, it is not without justice that we have previously signified that <term>angels</term><note>Ficino uses the term "angelos" to bridge the gap between the "minds" of Platonic philosophy and the celestial beings of Christian theology.</note> are almost innumerable, and we demonstrate it here in this way. If the species of natural things in matter—however narrow they may be in their subject—are distinguished among themselves not by the subject but by themselves, and are expanded into the greatest possible number, then much more so are the substances themselves which live in themselves above matter. They are distinct through <margin>M</margin> themselves, and through a certain marvelous fecundity of their own absolute kind, they are most profusely amplified into almost innumerable species. Furthermore, the <term>intelligible genus</term><note>The realm of things that can be known by the mind alone, as opposed to the "sensible" world known through the physical senses.</note> seems to be more multiplicable by nature than the corporeal genus. Indeed, the dimensions of numbers, figures, proportions, the rarity of bodies, and the velocity of motions are always limited within the bodies themselves; yet in the mind, they are produced without limit at will. Again, things that are particular in matter become universal in the mind. Finally, the intellect thinks of countless other things—both incorporeal and corporeal—at its will, beyond all existing bodies. Since, therefore, the intelligible genus can be amplified so much more than the sensible, and such a good power should not always be empty in the universe, there are undoubtedly already in act species of <term>separated substances</term><note>A technical term for beings like angels or souls that can exist "separated" from physical matter.</note> far more numerous than the species of corporeal things. This is especially true since a more excellent, greater, and prior power in the universe claims its own act for itself before a weaker one. Finally, since the order of the universe is most excellently disposed under the <term>Infinite Good</term><note>A reference to God as the ultimate source of order and being.</note>, it seems to require absolutely that those things which are better within it should be multiplied, as far as possible, beyond the quantity of inferior things—especially since the lower things were established for the sake of the higher. We clearly see this in the spheres of the world themselves: for the nobler a sphere is, the more ample it is. So much so that earth and water, if compared to the higher spheres, are considered to be like a point compared to a circumference. But what is <term>dimension</term> in bodies seems to be <term>number</term> in incorporeal things. Wherefore it is consistent that intellectual substances—inasmuch as they are the best and most perfect, and are the ends of all corporeal things which were created for their sake—are far more numerous than all space, motion, and bodies. <margin>C</margin> <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term><note>A 5th-6th century author (Pseudo-Dionysius) whose "Celestial Hierarchy" was the definitive source for medieval and Renaissance angelology.</note> bears witness to this, saying that there are more separated intellectual species than corporeal ones. Deservedly, the most powerful Creator of the universe both could, knew how to, and wished to render his work most humble to himself. He created that which is most similar to himself not in a corner, but rather expanded the absolute minds—which are most similar to him—beyond the gates of matter into an immense space, so to speak. Hence that saying of the prophet <margin>D</margin> <term>Daniel</term><note>A reference to Daniel 7:10.</note>: <note>original: "Milia miliū ministrabant ei: z decies cetena milia assistebāt ei"</note> "Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." However, in distinguishing the orders of angels, Dionysius primarily uses the numbers three and nine, and sometimes the number seven. Indeed, we also find the number twelve in the mysteries of the Christians. The Platonists <term>Iamblichus</term> and <term>Proclus</term><note>Late Antique Neoplatonists who influenced Ficino's systematic approach to the hierarchy of being.</note> observed the same after Dionysius. For they divide the highest and middle angels by the numbers three and nine, but they divide the following ones by seven. Finally, they partition the last ones by the number of twelve orders. <margin>E</margin> In truth, among the Platonists, the degrees of bodies are the shadows of rational souls. The fourth degrees are the images of angels; therefore, some distinguish the orders of angels according to the orders of bodies and souls simultaneously. But more on these things elsewhere. 

Above the angel is God. Because the soul is a mobile multitude. The angel is an immobile multitude. God is immobile unity.

### Chapter 6.

The Platonists believe the <margin>F</margin> angel to be entirely immobile: in essence, in power, and in action. Since it is always the same, and is what it is able to be. It understands all things simultaneously forever, and wills the same things, and—as far as it is in itself—acts suddenly in whatever it does. These are the views of the Platonists. What others might say, I shall say elsewhere. Reason does not permit us to rest here with <term>Anaxagoras</term> and <term>Hermotimus</term><note>Early Greek philosophers who posited "Mind" (Nous) as the first principle; Ficino argues we must look higher to the "One" or God.</note>, but commands us to ascend higher. Furthermore, the soul, which is mobile, is moved by another...

<summary>Ficino argues that angels (or "minds") are nearly infinite in number, outmatching physical species in variety and quantity because higher realities are more "fecund" than matter. He integrates Christian scripture and Dionysian hierarchy with Neoplatonic number theory to define the angel as an "immobile multitude" positioned between the mobile soul and the "immobile unity" of God.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the nature of celestial intelligences, Ficino now begins a formal metaphysical ascent from the Soul to the Angel (the Mind), and finally to God (the One). He uses the Aristotelian and Platonic logic of "multiplicity" and "unity" to define the hierarchy of existence.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>A</margin> ¶ [The soul] passes into another. Therefore, it possesses in itself both one thing and another. For this reason, it possesses multiplicity; wherefore the soul in itself is a certain multiplicity—a mobile multiplicity, I say. The <term>Angel</term><note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic Christian framework, an "Angel" is synonymous with "Pure Mind" or "Divine Intellect," existing entirely without a body.</note>, which precedes the soul in the first rank: is it not an immobile unity? Since one is a mobile multiplicity and the other an immobile unity, they seem to be separated by a very great distance. For unity is opposed to multiplicity, and the immobile to the mobile. Since, therefore, these things are opposed in every respect, they do not succeed one another immediately, but require a certain middle link to join them. Yet the Angel precedes the soul itself (which is a mobile multiplicity) without any middle. 

<margin>B</margin> ¶ Therefore, the Angel cannot be an immobile unity, lest two extremes be joined without a medium. It is certainly immobile, as we proved above. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, it is not unity. It remains, then, that an angel is an **immobile multiplicity**. Here it now agrees with the soul in that it is itself a multiplicity; but it differs because the soul is mobile, while the angel is immobile. We are certainly forced to place some kind of multiplicity in the angel. And what kind? Such as pertains to the <term>intellect</term><note>Ficino defines the intellect not just as a brain function, but as a spiritual substance whose "multiplicity" consists of its essence, its power, and the various "Ideas" it contemplates.</note>: that is, its essence, its blessed state, its power of understanding, the act of intellection, and the many species of things understood. 

Since, however, the angel is not simple but rather possesses number—and above number there must be Unity, because Unity is the origin of the entire number and does not need union, whereas multiplicity by its nature requires union—it is necessary that above the angel there exists something else, which is not only immobile, but entirely **One** and simple. That indeed is **God**, who is the most powerful of all things because He is the simplest of all. Indeed, union consists in simplicity, and power in unity. Let no one dare to say that God is composed of many parts. <margin>F</margin> Because if He were composed, He would consist of something acting as a subject and something acting as a form. Thus, God would not be most perfect in every way, since in Him one part would be more imperfect than the other, and any part is more imperfect than the whole itself. He would not be the highest agent, because He would not act through His whole self in whatever He does, but through one part—namely, the form. He would not be the most blessed, because He would not enjoy Himself everywhere. For He would not embrace Himself as a whole in 

# [Book] One

<margin>H</margin> every member. Furthermore, there would seem to be something else in Him besides God, since a part and the whole are not the same thing. He will certainly be more blessed if whatever He sees in Himself is His very self; if no part of Himself is missing, but His whole self meets Him everywhere. Finally, that part which was posed as the "subject" in God—because it is conceived as formless in itself—cannot form itself; moreover, the other part which played the role of "form"—since it does not subsist in itself—much less can it exist from itself. Therefore, this "composed" God would be formed by some superior form, and *that* would rather be God. But this is not the first discourse by which we prove that God is above the angel. 

<margin>K</margin> ¶ Furthermore: just as your eye relates to your body, so your mind relates to your soul. For your mind is the eye of the soul. Again: as the light of the sun relates to the physical eye, so the light of truth relates to the eye of the soul. Therefore, just as the eye of the body is not light, but a power capable of receiving light, so the mind (which is the eye of the soul) is not truth, although it receives truth. For your mind seeks truth. Truth, however, does not seek itself, nor does truth admit the false, through which your soul is often deceived. 

¶ Imagine in your mind that your eye grows to such an extent that it occupies your whole body; and with the various types of members removed, the entire body is one single eye. This eye will see nothing else certainly than the same light of the sun which it looked upon when it was narrow. But it will receive that same light more abundantly, and it will behold the colors of bodies within that light from every side. With one single gaze, it will see all things at once; it will not turn here or there to see, but by resting, it will contemplate all things equally. Nevertheless, the light will still be one thing, and the eye another. For if vision is established for the purpose of grasping light, vision is one thing and light is another. And the light has no need of vision, since the light itself has no need to receive light. 

¶ Imagine again <margin>L</margin> that your mind grows so strong over the soul that, with the remaining parts of the soul pertaining to <term>phantasy</term><note>The "phantasy" or imagination was considered a lower faculty of the soul that deals with images of physical things, as opposed to the pure abstract truths of the Mind.</note>, sense, and generation deleted, the whole soul is one single mind, and...

<summary>Ficino argues that while the Soul is mobile multiplicity and the Angel is immobile multiplicity, God must be the "immobile Unity" or the "One" to avoid the imperfections of composition. He uses the analogy of an eye becoming a total body to explain how the Mind relates to the Light of Truth.</summary>

# Platonic Book

...alone. **T**his mind alone: and left pure: will be an <term>angel</term><note>In Ficino’s system, when a human mind is fully purified of bodily concerns, it operates like a celestial Angel—a state of pure, non-discursive intellect.</note>. This, I say, expansive mind will behold the same truth which it had seen when it was narrow. But it will receive that truth more abundantly; and in it, the mind will behold all true things with a single intuition: to speak in the Platonic manner: it will not catch at one thing now, and another then. However, the mind will still be one thing, and truth another. This is what <term>Zoroaster</term><note>Ficino refers to the "Chaldean Oracles," which Renaissance scholars attributed to an ancient Persian prophet, Zoroaster, believing them to be a source of "Ancient Theology" that prefigured Plato.</note> reveals: "Learn the <term>intelligible</term><note>The 'intelligible' refers to the realm of Ideas or divine truths that can only be perceived by the intellect, not the senses.</note>, since it is outside the mind" <margin>B</margin> <note>original Greek: "μάνθανε τὸ νοητόν επει ο νοῦ εκτος"</note>, that is: Know that the intelligible itself exists outside the mind. Indeed, if the mind is designed for perceiving truth, then the mind that is unworthy of truth is one thing, and truth itself is another. Nor does truth itself have need of a mind through which it might grasp truth. And if the mind were the same as truth itself, every mind would be truthful, and every true thing would participate in mind. But as it stands, human minds are deceived, and many things are true in some way that lack a mind. Truth is not only something other than the mind, but also something superior. For the mind needs truth. Truth does not need the mind.

<margin>B</margin> And the empire of truth and mind spreads more widely. For the intellectual <term>Idea</term><note>original: "Are." likely an abbreviation for "Area" or "Archetypus." Given the context of "forms," it refers to the archetypal realm.</note> is found in individual forms. But in formless matter, it is not found at all. Yet matter is truly called the "subject" of all natural things. But if truth is above the mind, and that which is superior does not lack the lower goods, then the clarity of the mind is not absent from truth. Yet these are not two distinct things in truth: namely, clarity and truth. Instead, truth is most simple and is by no means hidden from itself: just as if light, although it does not have an eye distinct from itself, nevertheless is not hidden from itself.

<margin>C</margin> For God is the most clear-seeing truth, and the truest clarity, or rather, "perspective." He is Light seeing itself. Sight shining by its own power; the source of intellectual clarity and light: by whose light, and whose light alone, the clarity of the mind perceives. And just as wood is called "hot" through a certain participation, but fire is "hot" according to its own form, and finally the sun is hot in a more excellent way according to its eminent power and the cause of heat: so the soul is a part of the mind, and the angel is the mind's form—

---

<margin>D</margin> **D**eus is the most effective origin of the mind. And, to speak in the manner of <term>Plotinus</term><note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated into Latin.</note>: God is <term>intellection</term><note>The act of pure thinking or understanding.</note> itself; not in any intellect as if by potential, nor of truth as if it were an object, but existing in itself and of its very self. Just as if vision were neither in any specific eye, nor the vision of an outside light, but remained in itself and were the vision of itself. For wherever the intellect is placed as a kind of power of understanding—even if it understands itself—nevertheless, insofar as it is "intelligible," it is said to be one thing, and insofar as it is "intellectual," it is considered another. For the "intelligible," being prior and more excellent, moves, forms, and perfects the "intellectual" power, which is posterior and inferior. Therefore, some call God the "Intelligible" or "Intellection" rather than by the name "Intellect," even though these names suit God by no means perfectly. But more on these things elsewhere.

<margin>E</margin> Added to this: it is the work of the soul to provide vital motion. Indeed, the soul is a kind of life itself. But the work of the mind is to organize through <term>Forms</term><note>In Platonic thought, "Forms" or "Ideas" are the perfect blueprints of all things in the physical world.</note>. For the mind is a kind of species itself, and it operates through species, as we observe in our own mind. That "vital motion" is poured through all living things. It does not belong to things lacking life. But "organization through forms" belongs even to things that are not living. For these things do not lack order and species. By such a great interval does the mind surpass the soul, as the order of forms is spread more widely than life. But because, beyond the order of forms, there is that primary matter within forms, in which there lie hidden (if I may say so) the seeds of sprouting forms—the duty of the mind, which is bounded by forms, does not embrace these seeds. Nevertheless, matter itself is good in a certain way, because it is a desirer of the Good (that is, of Form), because it is exposed to receive the good, and because it is necessary for a good world. The seeds are also good, because they are the beginnings of good forms. At the very least, Goodness surpasses the Mind by as great an interval as the gift of "The Good" extends further than the gift of "Species."

<margin>F</margin> For the more powerful any thing is, the further it operates. To these are added reasons of this kind: All things desire the Good. But not all things desire the Mind;

<summary>Ficino argues for a hierarchy of existence where Truth (and ultimately God) sits above the Mind, just as the Mind sits above the Soul. He explains that while the Soul provides life, the Mind provides order and form, but God is the source of the "Good" which extends even to formless matter.</summary>

<meta>Continuing the metaphysical argument from the previous page, Ficino is concluding his proof that the "Good" is the ultimate principle, situated even higher than the "Mind" or "Angel." He is transitioning from the end of Book 1 into the beginning of Book 2 of his treatise.</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>
-> Theology, Second [Book] <-

...not all things are capable of everything. Therefore, there are many things which do not seek the mind, lest they seek in vain. If all things, by the act of desiring, are turned toward the good, but not all are turned toward the mind, we must ask: where is the goal of this "turning"? For perfection is found at that goal. Since all things proceed from the good and not all from the mind, it follows that the Good, rather than the Mind, is the primary cause of things. <note>Ficino employs a Neoplatonic rule: a cause must be at least as universal as its effect. Since everything—even inanimate objects—seeks "the good" (survival or utility), but only rational beings seek "the mind," the Good is a more universal and thus higher principle than the Mind.</note> Furthermore, those beings that do possess a mind do not stop there, but still seek the Good. Indeed, it is the very nature of Being to have a certain striving toward understanding. Now, after this striving, the mind finds itself in a state that is either worse, better, or equal. It cannot be worse, because the operation of the mind is itself a kind of perfection. And nothing falls into a worse state except by force or ignorance, neither of which can affect the mind when it is pure and free. Nor can it be equal, for then it would have strived in vain, achieving nothing and adding nothing to what it already possesses. Therefore, it strives in order to be in a better state. Thus, the mind itself is not the supreme Good, for nothing is better than the Good.

In this way, the mind draws goodness into itself through the act of understanding. But it draws it from elsewhere. If the mind possessed goodness inherently, it would not need to labor in order to achieve perfection. That source from which it draws goodness is the Good itself, which stands above the mind, since it pours the "fluid" of its own perfection into it. Furthermore, we seek wisdom and mind only by the impulse of reason; but we seek the Good even before any promptings of reason. All our desire is always toward the good, whereas not all desire is always toward the mind. We desire intelligence for the sake of the good, not the other way around. Therefore, nature values the Good more than the Mind, since it draws us toward the Good earlier, more frequently, and more powerfully.

Because of this, some people in the study of philosophy think they have enough if they merely *appear* to have wisdom, even if they do not. Yet in the conduct of life, they do not feel they have enough unless they truly possess that which they judge to be their primary good. If the Good is judged more precious than the mind by natural instinct, it must also be judged more eminent. This is why the mere act of understanding is not enough for us, unless we understand "well" and understand "the good." Indeed, we often reject knowledge for a time if we suspect it will be bad or troublesome for us; but we can never reject the Good itself. We often prefer pleasure to the abstract study of things, but we can never prefer anything to the Good itself, insofar as it is good.

Nothing is more necessary than the attraction of the Good, since no one can "not-will" the Good itself. Yet nothing is more voluntary than the attraction of the Good. For all things are for the sake of the good; indeed, we want the good in everything and everywhere, so willingly and joyfully that we even wish we were unable to "not-will" it. Since, therefore, in the Good the highest necessity coincides with the highest liberty, and the rule of the Good is both entirely necessary and entirely voluntary for its subjects, it is clear that all things take their origin from here as if from a father, and all things aspire to this place as if to their true homeland.

# The Second Book of the Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls by Marsilio Ficino of Florence, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>

## ¶ Unity, Truth, and Goodness are the same thing, and nothing is above them. Chapter 1.

> **W**e have now
> shown by three
> arguments that
> there is something

> that there is
> above it a most
> simple Unity;
> second, Truth;
> third,

Goodness. These three are one. For the highest Unity is nothing other than the highest simplicity. Because of this simplicity of Unity, any thing is rendered pure and true. For that which is true is that which is purely "one." Thus the truth of things consists in that simple Unity. And because of that same simple and pure Unity, all things are good. For anything is "well" <note>original: "bene", a play on "bonitas" (goodness)</note> when it is united to itself and to its own principle, and when it remains pure and is not [mixed with other] things...

# Platonic

...be mixed with lower things. And if in things, the unity, truth, and goodness of things consist in the same point, then deservedly above these is the First itself: the One, the True, and the Good. That there is a principle of things in these is proven by this argument: that traces of the good are found in all things, as if all things flowed from them; and all things desire these, as they seek their own principle.

<margin>A</margin>
For individual things are both partakers of and greedy for unity, truth, and goodness. Above unity there is nothing else, because nothing is more powerful than unity. Since union provides perfection and power to all. But above it, if you wish, let there be something. Two absurdities immediately follow. For if unity is under some higher principle, it certainly becomes a participant of that higher thing. For lower things always receive something from higher causes. Thus this will not be unity itself, but something composed from a certain unity and a force received from above; and it will be a certain multiplicity, not unity. And also, that which is placed above unity will be a partaker of no unity. For a higher principle receives nothing from a lower one, according to its own nature. Therefore it will either be nothing, or a multiplicity entirely deprived of union, of which no part will be one thing. Neither will the whole multiplicity be one, nor will any communion exist in the parts, either with each other or with the whole.

<margin>B</margin>
Again, above truth there is nothing. For by similar reasoning, this would not be truth itself, but something true composed of a certain truth and a portion of that higher thing. And that which is located above it—since it is neither truth nor the ruler of truth—is entirely false and nothing. Nor can anything be more excellent than truth unless, through the power of truth, it is undoubtedly true that it is more excellent.

<margin>C</margin>
Similarly, there is nothing above goodness. For then this would not be pure goodness, but something good, and a certain goodness contaminated by the mixing of another. And that which is placed before goodness will be entirely evil. For it will not be good, since it is beyond the boundaries of goodness. Nor is it better than goodness, since nothing is better except by a greater portion of goodness.

<margin>D</margin>
However, how evil could exceed goodness, I do not see. Since excess and superiority belong to goodness. For they are desirable <note>In Platonic thought, anything "desirable" is by definition a "good."</note> as goods. Therefore, evil would overcome goodness by the nature of goodness. And goodness would provide the power of command to evil. Furthermore, if there is another principle of things above goodness itself, it certainly imparts some gift from itself to things, just as every cause is accustomed to do. Moreover, goodness itself imparts its gift to all—that is, a certain goodness to each one. We ask then about that gift which descends from the higher principle: whether it is better than the goodness given, or not. It cannot be better. For whatever is called "better" is called so by a greater portion of goodness. Yet it is absurd for the gift of a higher principle not to be better than the gift of a lower cause.

# Book

<margin>E</margin>
It is added that since all things desire the good, if there is another principle above the good itself, we ask: do they desire it, or not? If they are said to desire it, it follows that something is sought beyond and more than the good. If they deny that they seek it, it is a foolish thing to say—that an effect does not desire the first cause by which it is preserved. Indeed, goodness itself would compel it to desire the higher principle, although that is absurd. For every reason for desiring is closed by goodness itself. Therefore, nothing exists above goodness that can be loved. No principle, then, is above it. Wherefore, unity, truth, and goodness themselves, which we have found above the angel <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic hierarchy, the "Angel" refers to the "Intellect" or the Cosmic Mind, which is the first thing created by God.</note>, are, according to the mind of Plato, the principle of all: one, true, and good God.

### That there cannot be several gods equal among themselves. Chapter 2.

<margin>F</margin>
Certainly, there are not several gods, because there cannot be several principles. But let there be, if you like, twin gods: two principles of the whole world, this one and that one. We ask whether this is under that, or that under this? Or are they both equal? If one is under the other, the one that is ahead will clearly be the principle; the other not at all. If they are equal, we ask: do they differ entirely from each other? Or do they agree entirely? Or do they partly differ and partly agree? The first will not be granted. For at least they agree in this: that they both are, they act, and they are called equal principles of things. And if they did not harmonize in any way, there would be no concord in the world-machine <note>original: "machina mundi"; a favorite metaphor of Ficino describing the universe as a complex, divine mechanism.</note>. If the second: we admit that they agree entirely, they are not...

<summary>Ficino argues that the ultimate principle of reality (God) must be absolute Unity, Truth, and Goodness, and that nothing can exist above these concepts. He then begins a logical proof against polytheism, asserting that multiple "equal" gods would destroy the harmony of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Unity, Truth, Goodness, Monotheism, First Principle, God, Plato, World-machine, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the end of Book 1, transitioning into Book 2 of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." Ficino is moving from the general concept of the "Good" to a specific logical proof that the First Principle (God) must be an absolute, simple Unity.</meta>

# Second Book of Theology

**B 2**
<meta>catchword: Marsilio Ficino</meta>

There are two now: but as we desire: one. But if a third thing were granted where they partly agree in nature and partly differ: then surely, because they cannot agree and disagree through the exact same thing, some one common nature exists in both, through which they coincide. There are, moreover, in those two, two specific natures beyond the common nature, through which they differ. Therefore, neither of them will be **simple** <note>In philosophy, "simple" means something that is not made of parts or components.</note>: but both will be **composed** of the common nature and a specific property. Neither will be the **first** principle: because each depends on that which reconciled their different parts into one. Neither is sufficient by itself, since the whole requires prior parts, and one part requires the other. Neither is most powerful, since it is not entirely unified. And yet, that common nature, through which both have this thing equally—namely, that they are equal principles—will be the principle rather than those two. Indeed, that which gave them their common nature despite their different natures will be the principle.

<margin>d</margin>
Soon this one nature—which lies within other things and is hemmed in by the limitations of others—flows from **Unity** itself, which, existing in itself, is narrowed by no limit. Thus, that common and single nature comes to both from elsewhere, and from a higher principle. Furthermore, those two specific natures through which they differ also come to them from the outside. For besides those, nothing remains in both except the common and single nature; if those specific natures which are added were born absolutely from that common nature, they would no longer be different (as the metaphysicians judge), but the property of both would be one and the same, gushing from the same vein. For it would gush forth according to the mode of a purely absolute nature and flow back inward. If, therefore, those two specific properties are in them absolutely, they necessarily arrive from the outside. Wherefore, each receives the property of its own essence from elsewhere. And because each obtains its specific nature from elsewhere, neither exists by itself: but is made by a higher principle.

<margin>☞</margin>
In any genus <note>A "genus" is a category or class of things.</note> of things: that which is the **highest** of that genus is only one. For if there are two "highest lights," each agrees in the fact that it is the highest light: and thus they are one. But if they are two distinct things, they differ by some nature other than their "light." Therefore, some other nature is present...

---

...different from light: by whose contagion the light becomes opaque and ceases to be the "highest." In this same way, there is a **highest heat**: which is only such if it is not mixed with cold or other things. Because if it is mixed, it is certainly hindered, and it could be made more powerful if it were purified. Therefore, the highest in any genus is only one, and consists of only that one nature. Pure, highest light is one, not two lights: and it is light alone, not light and something else simultaneously.

<margin>19</margin>
**God** is the highest of all things. Therefore, God is one and **simple**. Truly, there is one highest unity. One highest truth and goodness: one God. One, I say, according to the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato, whose ideas Ficino is reconciling with Christian theology.</note> for a triple reason. First, because he is the highest unity. For if anything that is "highest" is unique, what is more unique than the highest unity itself? Every specific multitude of innumerable things is reduced to a specific unity. A multitude of innumerable men is reduced to one human species. A multitude of horses to one equine species; and similarly for others. Take then all the specific unities, which are limited to a certain number (that is, the species of things), and collect them into one common unity: that is, God, the prince of species. So that just as the infinite multitudes of individuals are referred to the finite unities of species, so the finite unities of species are referred to the one single unity above all species.

<margin>3</margin>
It is only right that, just as every specific order of things is directed to its own single principle, so the universal order of things should be referred to one universal principle. And just as individual materials refer to one Matter, and all members of the world to one Body, so all the natures of the world refer to one Nature, all the lives of the world to one Life, all motions to one Motion, and all movers to one Mover of the world. Furthermore, when several things that are different from each other in nature aspire to a certain single order and mutual connection, it is necessary that such an order exists in them because of an order which they have toward some one thing—just as the order of the parts of an army among themselves exists because of the order of the whole army toward one leader. For the fact that things which are different from each other obtain this—that they are joined by mutual communion—does not come from their own specific natures, through which they are different. For from those specific natures they would rather be disjoined. Nor even...

<summary>This page presents a logical proof for the existence of a single, simple God (the First Principle) by arguing that any "highest" quality must be unique and unmixed. Ficino uses the Platonic hierarchy of species to show that all diversities in the universe must eventually converge into a single, governing Unity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical arguments from Book 2 of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." Having previously argued that the first principle must be simple, Ficino now addresses why there cannot be multiple "first" principles or multiple gods, using the interconnectedness of the world as evidence of a single designer.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Platonic

# Book

The order of the world arises from various distinct ordainers. Truly, because of their differing natures, in virtue of how they differ, they do not incline toward a single order. And so, that mutual order of many things either happens by chance, or it is established by one first ordainer directing everything toward one end. Indeed, all parts <margin>A</margin> of the world, however diverse, are reconciled by a mutual order because they constitute one body; they lend their natures to each other and are lent to in turn. Lower bodies are moved by higher ones. Higher ones are moved by an incorporeal nature. Nor does this order occur by chance, because it is always the same and similar, and because it always weaves the same web in a similar way. Therefore, the one God is the one ordainer of the one world. He is one, I say, <margin>B</margin> according to the first reason of the Platonists: because He is Unity <note>original: "vnitas"</note>. He is also one according to their second reason: because He is Truth <note>original: "veritas"</note>. For the supreme truth is one. Indeed, if two supreme truths were said to exist, either one of them possesses whatever the other possesses, or it does not. If the first is granted, there is one truth, not two. If the second is granted, neither is supreme; for this one lacks that portion of truth which is in the other, and that one lacks what is in this one. Again, God is one according to the third reason of the Platonists: because He is supreme Goodness <note>original: "bonitas"</note>. Indeed, supreme goodness encompasses whatever good can be found anywhere. Therefore, if you introduce two supreme goodnesses, whatever good is in one is also in the other; otherwise, neither would be supreme. According to the nature of good itself, they are one, not two. Nor is there anything else mixed into them except the nature of goodness; for if there were, they would not be supreme, but tainted. Therefore, <margin>C</margin> they are altogether one. Finally, if there are two gods, and each can equally bring about this whole world, either neither will make the world—and the power in both will be in vain, nor will there ever be a world—or one will create the world, and the power of creating will be in vain in the other. Or both will generate the whole. And so there will be two worlds altogether equal to each other and most similar. One of these will suffice; the other will be superfluous. But if one is capable of the whole, while the other is capable only of a part, the one who is not capable of completing the whole is not God. And he would generate a part of the world in vain, which the other manufactures simultaneously with the whole world. If, however, each has the power to create only half of the world, neither will be the principle of all things. And because those parts concur in one whole toward one end through a communion of nature, it will be necessary for those two gods to be referred to one superior God, so that the movement toward one end, which is performed by two, is derived from a communion of the two, led down from some one higher source. If anyone asserts <margin>D</margin> that two worlds altogether diverse and dissimilar from each other are constructed by twin gods, they will be forced to admit that neither those gods nor those worlds agree with each other in any way. By what agreement, then, is each of them God—living, understanding, and acting—or is each of these one world—a work and a corporeal thing? And so, the twin worlds will agree with each other. But the one nature in which they agree is drawn at last from one principle, not two. Again, if both gods always desire the same end, either one will be from the other, or both from one superior, or at least both will exist in one substance. For unless they agreed in this way, they would not harmonize toward the same end. However it may be, God is one alone. But if one god always wants the same work and the other does not, it follows that the work is simultaneously made and not made, exists and does not exist—provided that the "will" of this god and the "will not" of that one are equally powerful. For only he whose desire always prevailed would be God. But if they now agree and now disagree, and now the effort of this one exceeds, and now that one, then both are mutable. Nor should we agree with the Manichaeans <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that taught a struggle between a Good God of light and an Evil God of matter.</note> or the Gnostic <margin>E</margin> philosophers, who assert that there are two gods, one the author of all good things, the other of evil. For just as the God who is the author of good things is the supreme good, free from all evil; so conversely, a supreme evil would be deprived of all good. This "supreme evil," therefore, would not act at all, nor know, nor live, nor even exist. Since being, living, and knowing are good things and are desirable.

---

¶ There are not multiple gods, one above another or without end.

Chapter 3.

<summary>Ficino argues for the existence of a single God by demonstrating that a unified world requires a single designer. He refutes dualism (Manichaeism) by arguing that "Supreme Evil" cannot exist because existence itself is a "Good."</summary>

--- Page 67 ---
<meta>This page continues the logical defense of monotheism within Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." After establishing that the first principle must be simple and unique, he now refutes the idea of an infinite hierarchy of gods, arguing that without a single "First," the order of the universe would collapse into an incomprehensible and unstable flow.</meta>

## Theology, Book Two

->B 3<-

<margin>¶</margin> **F**urthermore: perhaps someone will object to us: saying that there is a God above an angel, and that God is one, so that there are not many equal gods alongside one another; yet they might argue there is one God above another, without end. Although we believe this has been refuted by the previous arguments, we shall nonetheless disprove it more clearly with other reasons. If the gods were innumerable here, the causes of things would be infinite, surpassing one another in innumerable steps; for since these gods themselves are the causes of things and are innumerable, some are placed above others. If this were so, there would also be <margin>B</margin> innumerable effects in the world. For any cause produces some specific effect in the order of things. And just as the causes surpass one another, so too do the effects surpass one another. Therefore, there would be infinite effects in descending order, failing one after another in an innumerable series, if the causes were infinite and surpassed each other innumerably. And since a higher cause always casts its power further in producing effects than a lower one does, the "reach" of effects would extend into infinity if there were an infinite ascent of causes. Who could fail to see how absurd this is? First of all: if there is no "first" thing among things, there will be no <margin>b</margin> subsequent things at all. For all things are drawn from a first. If this first exists nowhere, there will be no source from which the outflow of things—which flow from elsewhere—might ever begin. Second, <margin>a</margin> we see in things that some are more perfect than others: and the power of perfection increases as one ascends and decreases as one descends. From this, it follows that the natural force of things gradually weakens as it descends. Hence, it is forced to fail entirely at some point, after it has been diminished little by little. Therefore, one thing cannot exist beneath another without end. Thus, there will not be innumerable effects. Consequently, there will not be innumerable causes. If, by the very fact that perfection increases as one ascends, it clearly stands to reason that it will eventually arrive at the <margin>g</margin> highest point. Why do we judge the soul to be better than the <margin>H</margin> body, except because it possesses a closer proximity to supreme goodness? If there were no "supreme" goodness, but one ascended from good to good into infinity, the body would be distant from supreme goodness by an infinite interval. So too would the soul. One infinity is not "more" or "less" than another infinity. <note>Ficino is using a mathematical argument common in Scholasticism: you cannot compare distances to a "top" if the top does not exist or is infinitely far away.</note> Nor would there ever be a ratio or an "ideal measure" <margin>E</margin> through which some things could be preferred over others. Therefore, the soul would be neither closer nor more suited to goodness itself than the body. Thus, it would not be better. Nor would an angel be better than a soul. Furthermore, whatever <margin>M</margin> flows from another thing fluctuates by its own nature. For since it is nothing according to itself, it possesses its "being" through a kind of flow. If there is no "first" thing among things, every thing will emanate from another. All things will therefore fluctuate. For this reason, there would nowhere be unity, equality, similarity, stability, order, or restoration. But in truth, because these qualities are present in things, it is necessary that the flux of things emanating from another be led and restrained by the stability of some "hinge" <note>original: "statu cardinis", referring to a fixed point or axis upon which everything turns.</note> that does not emanate from another. Just as the indeterminate flow of liquid bodies must be terminated—not by another similarly flowing liquid body—but by a solid body. Finally, any higher level acts upon a lower one and receives something from the one above it. If there is no "first" level in things, and no "last," then any middle level will depend on infinite higher levels, and in turn, will produce infinite lower levels. For this reason, it would receive innumerable perfections, since it receives some degree of good from every one of its causes. And it would exhibit infinite gifts to the lower things. For to each it would grant something. Therefore, it would be of immense power and full of infinite perfections. Thus, all things would be equally infinite. One thing would not be more excellent than another; a cause would not be better than its work. Or perhaps every thing would be innumerably finite, because it would be surpassed by an innumerable number of predecessors. Again, every thing would be infinite, because it would surpass an innumerable number of following things. Nor would there ever be any true science <note>original: "sciētia" (scientia), meaning systematic knowledge or certain understanding.</note>, since infinite causes of things cannot be comprehended. Nor would there be anything in the universe to move or stop the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the natural inclination or desire of all things to reach their perfection or goal.</note>, if there were no first principle and no ultimate end. For by the power of this end, every appetite is moved and made firm. Therefore, let there be one <margin>M</margin> principle of things above all. Let it be called **Unity**, because it stands above all things in most excellent simplicity. **Truth**, because by producing things it gives "being" to all. **Goodness**, because by calling things back to itself once produced, it grants them "well-being." And as the theology of John the Apostle <margin>C</margin>—the most divine of all theologians—teaches (which the Platonist Amelius <margin>n</margin> <note>Amelius was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist. Ficino often cites him as a bridge between Platonic philosophy and the Gospel of John.</note> gladly embraces): Call the Principle **Unity**. Call the reason of the Principle **Truth**. Call it, finally, **Goodness**...

<summary>Ficino argues against an infinite chain of causes, asserting that without a "First" principle, the universe would be an unstable flux and knowledge would be impossible. He identifies this First Principle as a triad of Unity, Truth, and Goodness, harmonizing Platonic philosophy with the Gospel of John.</summary>
<keywords>infinite regress, first principle, causality, perfection, Unity, Truth, Goodness, Amelius, John the Apostle, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding the nature of the first principle. Having argued against an infinite hierarchy of gods, Ficino now moves to define the relationship between Unity, Truth, and Goodness, and begins a formal proof that the power of the divine must be infinite.</meta>

# Platonic Book

...the principle, a common love. And this very substance—that is, true good unity—or whether one true goodness be the one good and the true God. But because it is unity, it is therefore truth (because it is true unity), and therefore goodness. In unity, he <note>Referring to God as the First Principle.</note> enfolds all things. He unfolds them in truth. He pours them out through goodness. Indeed, once all things have flowed from that source, they flow back through goodness. They are reformed through truth. They are restored into one through unity.

## The power of God is infinite. Chapter 4.

<margin>A</margin> Just as in the greatest dispersion there is infinite weakness, so in the highest unity there is infinite power. Act <note>In this philosophical context, 'Act' refers to the state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to 'potentiality' or 'passive' capacity.</note> by its very nature does not include a limit; for to be subjected to a limit is a "passion" <note>original: "passio." In the Latin tradition, this means being acted upon or receiving an influence, rather than the modern sense of emotion.</note>, which is the opposite of act. Therefore, act does not suffer a limit, except perhaps by being joined to some subject where some degree of passive potential is present. <margin>B</margin> But the divine act subsists in itself. Effective power itself, insofar as it is power, does not include a fixed number of degrees. For what prevents power itself, as power, from being thought of and existing in a high number just as in any other? For this reason, it receives no limit of degree except either from the passive potential with which it is mixed, or from a limiting cause. But divine power is pure and supreme. Being itself, considered absolutely, is immeasurable, because it can be communicated to infinite things and in innumerable ways, and can be so conceived. Therefore, if the being of anything is finite, it is necessary that such being be limited either by its own cause or by its subject. Neither of these applies to God. Moreover, in infinite being itself, there is infinite power, just as in finite being there is finite power. In pure nothingness itself, there is no condition of being, whether true or imaginary. For who could define nothingness under the logic of being? Therefore, in pure being itself, there is nothing of the privation of being, nor any potential for non-being, by either true or imaginary logic. Therefore, it neither can be compelled nor even thought not to be—which pertains to its eternity—nor can any degree of power be lacking to it which the mind is able to imagine. <margin>D</margin> Otherwise the mind, which is an effect of God, would be able to extend itself beyond God, since the mind is always able to think of some greater degree than any finite number of degrees. Indeed, the mind would have been ordered toward an infinite progression in vain unless some infinite limit were found. And because nothing of the true and the good is lacking to truth itself and goodness, all degrees are present in it—as many as can be understood as true and desired as good. Such degrees are innumerable. <margin>E</margin> Every agent is more powerful the more it leads a potentiality—that is distant from act—into act. Indeed, greater power is needed to heat water than to heat air <note>Air was considered closer to the nature of heat than water, thus requiring less "work" to change.</note>. But that which is nothing at all is infinitely distant from act, nor does it possess any potential to receive the act of being itself; we shall discuss this more clearly in what follows. Therefore, whether God creates something newly from nothing, or continually brings forth and preserves the primary matter of bodies and the essence of minds and souls from no prior subject—always depending on the first (that is, divine) act—He undoubtedly possesses an immeasurable power of acting. Why say more? <margin>F</margin> The motion of this so vast and so complex machine <note>A common metaphor for the universe or the spheres of the heavens.</note>, so consistent through so many ages, teaches us that the governor is untiring, and therefore that His power is infinite. For a finite power is exhausted and falters in infinite time—indeed, even in a long time, however finite it may be. <margin>G</margin> From the infinite power of God, therefore, all intellects receive the ability to always understand firmly; others receive the ability to discourse without end. Matter receives the infinite potential for receiving forms. Motion and time receive the ability to flow without limit. Likewise, the generation of things—as it pleases the physicists—is able to be continued in an alternating and unending succession. For they think that infinite action and motion draw their origin from infinite power. And whatever things are said to be infinite—whether by potential or in any other way—are such and are so judged because of the supreme infinity of existing act. <margin>H</margin> Hence the divine nature is named by Orpheus as <term>the endless end</term> <note>original: "ατελεστε τε λευτη" (ateleutos teleute). Ficino cites the legendary poet Orpheus to show that ancient wisdom agrees with his philosophical conclusion that God is the beginning and the final goal.</note>.

## God is always. Chapter 5.

<margin>I</margin> Any thing is more long-lasting the more powerful the strength is by which it remains and is preserved. God, through His infinite power, remains into the infinite, and preserves all other things...

<summary>Ficino argues that God's power must be infinite because He is "Pure Act" without the limitations of matter or a prior cause. He further suggests that the human mind's ability to conceive of the infinite and the perpetual motion of the heavens prove a divine, inexhaustible source.</summary>
<keywords>infinite power, pure act, creation from nothing, Orpheus, divine unity, potentiality, celestial motion, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

--- Page 69 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of God as the First Principle, specifically focusing on God’s eternity and the beginning of a proof for His omnipresence. It follows the argument that God’s power is infinite because it is pure "act" without "passion" or limit.</meta>

[...preser]ves. Likewise, divine truth precedes the beginning of every thing and succeeds the end of every thing. For even before the beginning of any thing, it was true that that beginning would come to be; and after the end of every thing, it will be true that that end has passed. Whatever, however, is at any time true, is true by reason of Truth itself. If truth itself were said to have begun at some point, long before that, through that very same truth, it would have been true that truth was going to begin. And if one imagines truth to end, even afterward, through that same truth, it will be true that truth has ended. Therefore, truth can be thought neither to begin nor to end at any time.

Again: if God exists entirely above motion and time, He does not undergo temporal change from a "before" to an "after" according to being and non-being. It follows that if God is the highest necessity of essence—which we will show in the following sections—He never was, nor will He ever be able, not to be. Finally, if whatever is born at any time comes from something prior, and whatever is resolved <note>In the sense of decaying or breaking down into constituent parts.</note> is resolved into something older than itself, then that which is first cannot have begun or end.

We often ponder in our minds a certain simple duration, without beginning and without end, and we call it, so to speak, sempiternity; which is indeed God Himself, even if we barely distinguish it as such. For God Himself is simple infinity. Our imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> prevents us from distinguishing this, for it immediately clothes and floods that simple and unchanging sempiternity with a certain multiple flux. Thus it surely deceives us, while it drags toward the accidental flux of time that which is the substantial state of eternity. And so it compels us to think that what God is, is time. Therefore, the eternal God <margin>M</margin> then offers Himself to us, but wrapped in time. No one, however, ought to doubt that God always is, since God is "always" itself; or rather, sempiternity itself is God Himself. And those things which are called sempiternal are properly those which God propagates through Himself and into Himself.

<margin>D</margin> ### God is Everywhere. Chapter 6.

<margin>n</margin> **F**rom the preceding we are able to prove that God is everywhere. Just as a body touches that in which it exists through the dimensions of quantity, so an incorporeal substance touches through its power. Wherefore, just as if there were in nature some infinite physical dimension, it would be everywhere; so, since there is a certain immense power of incorporeal substance, this is necessarily everywhere. And just as a particular cause is present to a particular effect—as fire is present to ignited wood—so the universal cause is present to the universal effect. <margin>O</margin> Wherever, therefore, that which is a universal effect is found or thought to be, there also is God, who is the universal cause. Wherever there is some work which must necessarily be done through one certain cause alone and without a intermediary, there its cause must be. <margin>U</margin> But there is everywhere something which can subsist through God alone by a certain mode of creation. That, indeed, is prime matter <term>prime matter: "materia prima," the most basic, formless substrate of all physical things in Aristotelian and Platonic thought</term> in bodies, and essence in spirits.

It is desirable, as a good thing, to be present everywhere at once, almost no less than to always be; but to the first Good, nothing of goodness is lacking. <margin>Q</margin> God is not prevented by anything from penetrating through all things; for nothing resists infinite purity and power. The nature of God does not suffer a limit of place around itself, just as it does not suffer in itself a limit of dignity. Because if the highest infinity itself suffers nothing finite, it follows that God does not have a finite presence of space, just as He does not have finite power, action, or duration. Nor should it be thought that the Good itself is less present to the whole world than the soul is to the whole body. For the world is less compared to God than the body is to the soul; and the world needs God more than the body needs the soul. Goodness is more extensive than life, because it belongs to more things. <margin>R</margin> It is also more necessary to the world than life. For if life were removed, the world would cease to move; but if goodness were removed, it would cease to be. If, therefore, in the one living body of the world a certain single life is everywhere—which we will show elsewhere—much more is that one Good itself everywhere, even outside the world. If the first passive thing—which is matter and essence—is propagated through all things, much more does the first agent—which is God—propagate Himself through all things and beyond all things. It is not fitting <margin>S</margin> for the machinations of the mind to progress further than the presence of the Good. <margin>G</margin> Indeed, the mind progresses through the immense. And the Platonists <note>The school of philosophy following Plato, which heavily influenced Ficino’s view of God as "The One" and "The Good."</note> think it fitting that the infinite Good, by overflowing through the immense, thus pours itself out whole, so that it leaves no part of the immense—even an imaginary one—whether it be in the world or merely thought...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of God's infinity and sempiternity. The previous page ended with the observation that our imagination often obscures our understanding of God's simple, unchanging nature by imposing temporal and spatial categories upon it. This page moves into the concept of God's omnipresence—His existence both within and beyond the world—and how He sustains all things in being.</meta>

# A Platonic Book #
<meta>Catchword: Anebon</meta>

outside the world: nor does He leave it destitute by His presence. Indeed, if the nature of the good is to amplify itself, then the infinite good amplifies itself infinitely. It is difficult to find <margin>A</margin> where God is, because He is nowhere, in that He is not confined by the limit of any subject or of any place. It is even more difficult to find where He is *not*, because He is that in which all things are, through which they are made, and through which all things everywhere are preserved. God is therefore in all things because all things are in Him; for if they were not in Him, they would be nowhere and would not exist at all. Through God, this very "where" exists and is said to be "everywhere." Through God, acting as both leader and light, whatever anyone does, they do, and whatever they seek, they seek somewhere. Nothing is desired anywhere except the good; nothing is found anywhere except the truth. God is all good; God is all truth.

<margin>B</margin> Add to this that God is amplitude and fullness itself. I do not see, therefore, why He should not amplify Himself through all things and fill every single thing. If visible light—which belongs to something and is within something, and is finite—can spread itself through the whole world, surely invisible light, which belongs to itself and is infinite in itself, amplifies itself through the world and outside the world. For finite light is born from infinite light so that it may shine, and by its power, it shines most intensely, so that it might shine most widely. If, when the light of the sun is absent for even a very brief time, whether through an eclipse or through the night, things fare so poorly, how poorly do we think things would fare if God were always absent from them? Why would they not rather, in the very moment they lost that which is "being" itself, suddenly collapse into nothingness? Orpheus wisely said in the *Hymn to Saturn*: <note>original: "οὐ ναίχοι κατὰ πάντα μέρη κόσμοιο γέναρχα"</note> "You who dwell throughout all parts of the world, prince of generation."

<margin>C</margin> We often contemplate a certain purest capacity which no limits anywhere can contain, which contains whatever is able to exist <margin>D</margin> or can be imagined. Since, in truth, that pure infinity is nothing other than God, when we contemplate that capacity, we are then thinking of God Himself, even if we do not fully perceive it.

For <term>Imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; in this context, the faculty of the mind that deals with sensory images and spatial dimensions, which Ficino argues can distract from pure intellectual truth.</note> soon deceives us with its illusions, suddenly substituting for divine rays a certain stretch of lines in length, width, and depth. Thus, it compels us to see the divine light as a certain dimension or even as a void. It deceives us again when we consider that God fills all things entirely, for then it persuades us that He is somehow "located" within things. But in reality, He is "everywhere" in such a way that the very thing called "everywhere" exists in Him. Indeed, He is the "where" itself, through which He contains Himself and the rest; and those things which are said to be everywhere because of Him are properly those things which He amplifies through Himself and within Himself. Reason dictates that what is called "everywhere" <margin>E</margin> is nothing other than the universal nature of things, and that this is God. Therefore, when we say that God is everywhere, it ought to be understood that He is in Himself, and vice versa. Furthermore, God is absent from nowhere, if that which is called "everywhere" is never absent.

But when <term>Imagination</term> <margin>F</margin> thinks that the nature of things is only this bodily machine, it cries out that what is named "everywhere" is nothing other than the total extension of physical things. Since it considers this extension to be most vast, it doubts that God can fill all of it. Reason, on the contrary, proclaims that the bodily machine is a certain thin and meager shadow, which is divided into innumerable small parts and tiny fragments of parts, possessing an endless smallness and a limited greatness. But Reason asserts that what is truly great is that in which nothing is small, in which whatever exists is the whole, and equally great. And just as He enfolds <margin>M</margin> all that is within, so He unfolds the whole through all that is without. Therefore, God, subsisting in Himself, exists everywhere. Nor is God through the world, but the world extends through God as far as it is able. And just as the world attains the divine power (which is infinite) in a finite way, so it attains His presence (which shines everywhere through the immense) in a certain finite location. The world does not proceed in a straight line to reach God, who is nowhere absent, but it revolves according to its strength around Him—or rather, it revolves *within* Him—only there where the divine law prescribes its location <margin>S</margin> and motion. Anebon <note>A reference to Porphyry's *Letter to Anebo*, a text central to Neoplatonic discussions on theurgy and the divine.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that God is both "nowhere" (transcendent) and "everywhere" (immanent), sustaining the universe like an infinite light. He warns that human imagination wrongly spatializes God, whereas reason understands that the physical world is merely a shadow within the infinite capacity of the Divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into God's presence, shifting from God’s nature to the nature of the "Mind" (both angelic and human) and how it participates in God's infinity. It bridges the previous discussion of God's omnipresence with the soul’s ability to transcend physical space.</meta>

-> # Theology, Book II # <-

<margin>A</margin> Abammon the Egyptian priest <note>Abammon was a name used by the philosopher Iamblichus in his work "On the Mysteries."</note>, as well as Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Julian the Platonists, maintained that not only God, but every mind—whether angelic or animal <note>In this context, "animal" refers to a living soul (from the Latin 'anima') that animates a body.</note>—pours itself out immeasurably. They believed that spirits of this kind exist within each other everywhere without any mutual confusion, just as various habits of virtue exist in a soul, or as diverse images of colors exist simultaneously in the air. These foundations are also supported by the following: <margin>B</margin> Forms that are inferior to the rational spirit, which arise from specific and limited matter, are necessarily confined by that matter. However, rational spirits, which in no way sprout from matter, neither possess a fixed dimension within themselves nor are they bound to any specific dimension. Therefore, since they relate equally to any part of any space, they are either nowhere or they are in the universe. It must not be said that they are entirely absent anywhere, for they truly exist; therefore, they are nowhere absent. Every mind is, in some way, eternal.

<margin>D</margin> That which is eternal, although it is indivisible through time, nevertheless stretches itself through the whole course of time. Similarly, although it is indivisible according to space, it is nonetheless dilated through all space. And just as time relates to eternity, so does the temporal relate to the eternal. But moments of time always encounter a moment of eternity; therefore, the points of a temporal body everywhere encounter a point of the eternal spirit. Just as an eternal thing is always outside of time, so it seems to be everywhere outside of place. Wherever the moments of time flow, they run into the point of eternity. Wherever a line is drawn, it touches a point. Wherever space extends, it finds the eternal thing. <margin>F</margin> What is it, most of all, that can be everywhere? Certainly, that to which the dimension of quantity is not repugnant. Again, what can exist always? Especially that which the action of quality does not overcome. Since quality is much more effective than quantity, whatever can exist always (quality not preventing it) can much more easily be everywhere (dimension not preventing it). Local motion, which is an external motion, appears more perfect in any thing the more the internal nature of the thing is effective. Therefore, to propagate itself through all things, which imitates local motion, requires that there first be within the thing itself a perpetual conserving power. This is called "intrinsic perfection"; and to whatever this intrinsic perfection belongs, there follows an extrinsic <note>meaning 'outward'</note> dilation through universal space. It is more excellent to *always be* (which is intrinsic) than to *be everywhere* (which is extrinsic). Therefore, what can always be can much more easily be everywhere. <margin>L</margin> For it is easier to exceed nearby dimensions than to exceed the effective motion of quality and time. 

The Mind signifies to itself and others, above all else, the nature, counsel, and affection of God; it proceeds, therefore, from God like a word—or rather, like the meaning of a word from a speaker. <margin>B</margin> Since the Speaker is everywhere, the Word follows there too; thus the Mind is everywhere, just as God is everywhere. The Mind is immeasurable in thought and affection, insofar as it wills and considers the immeasurable machine <note>original: "immensam machinam"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a vast, complex mechanism</note>, and it runs through it by its own operation. It cannot shine or operate where it is not, nor can such an operation be broader than its essence. Therefore, it exists in the immeasurable. 

The end <note>The 'final cause' or natural goal</note> of fire is the hollow of the highest heaven <note>In ancient physics, fire's natural place was the highest sphere, just below the moon.</note>. Therefore, any small flame, <margin>M</margin> if nothing prohibited it, would fly all the way there; and when it reached that hollow, if it had sufficient dimension, it would amplify itself through the whole of it, so that it might enjoy all of that which is natural to it. If it were indivisible, it would strive to be whole in every point of it, so that it might enjoy the whole everywhere. 

The target <term>scopos<gloss>the final goal or aim</gloss></term> and end of the mind is Truth itself and Goodness itself—that is, God. Toward this, it runs by a certain essential instinct, like fire, even before it runs by a vital instinct, and by a vital instinct before an intellectual one. Nothing stands in the way of the essence of the mind penetrating all the way to God; for a body does not resist a spirit, and much less does a spirit resist a spirit. <margin>N</margin> And God penetrates all things. Therefore, the mind, through its essential instinct, always reaches God—and indeed everywhere, for it strives toward this very thing. It has no assigned dimension nor a natural need for any specific site that would prohibit it from being everywhere. And because it acts wherever something exists, it follows that it lives and understands everywhere and always.

<summary>This page argues that the rational mind is immeasurable and omnipresent because it is not bound by matter. Using the analogy of fire seeking the heavens, the author explains that the mind's natural "target" is God, allowing it to transcend spatial limits.</summary>
