# Platonic

<margin>A</margin>
Although any minds whatsoever are immense, some seem to direct certain actions toward others more clearly within this vast region: angelic minds do so by governing, and animal <note>The term "animal" here refers to "animating" minds—souls that give life (anima) to a body, including human souls.</note> minds by giving life. This is just as if many candles were lit in the same hall: the individual light of each would fill the whole hall; they are joined together, yet not mixed. For one light can be separated from another; and even if these lights are spread through the entire hall, each is still directed back to its own specific candle. Indeed, it is possible for a mind to think it exists only in the body it rules, even though it is actually everywhere beyond that body.

<margin>B</margin>
Just as our mind, although it is in this whole body, nevertheless thinks itself to be only in the heart according to many philosophers. This is what they say concerning the mind. We, however, shall return to God.

<margin>Chapter VII</margin>
->God acts upon all things, and preserves them, and works all things in all.<-

<margin>B</margin>
**T**hat God exists, and is one, the first, and infinite in power and duration, we have shown through the preceding arguments. From these, that which Parmenides the Pythagorean <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic philosopher whom Ficino and the Platonists viewed as a predecessor to their own metaphysical traditions.</note> said concerning God in his book *On Truth and Opinion* is confirmed: <term>One Being, Immobile, Infinite</term> <note>original Greek: "ον εν ακινητον απειρον"</note>. Next, we shall prove that this God acts upon all things, preserves them, and works all things in all. If God is the simplest unity, and this unity alone exists in nature (because whatever is supreme is one), then whatever exists besides God is multiple and composite. All multitude descends from unity, and all composition descends from simple purity. If God is the supreme truth, and nothing can exist without truth—for how can anything be, unless it truly is what it is said to be, and its very being is true?—then all things proceed from God. If God is the supreme goodness, and this goodness by its very nature communicates itself most greatly, then God imparts Himself to all. Therefore, all things desire the Good; since they were born from the Good, they seek their own origin, so that they may be perfected by the source from which they were made.

<margin>E</margin>
Any things of a certain species always perform some action, and they do so more strongly the better they are within their own species. And those which are in a better 

---

# Book

species act most of all. Each thing works to create things similar to itself according to its strength—similar, if possible, in species. They work for the sake of the good. Therefore, every action in any thing is done from the good, through the good, and toward the good.

<margin>F</margin>
Therefore, the supreme goodness acts because it is goodness; it acts always because it is supreme; and because it is not limited to any one species but is equally common to all species, it acts in everything. Furthermore, since God is not mixed with anything, He is the specific leader of no one thing, but exists as common to all. If He is common, a common duty belongs to Him. Being <note>The act of "existing" or "to be" (esse).</note> itself is common to all things. Therefore, being, wherever it may be, depends upon God. Zoroaster <note>Ficino refers here to the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to the ancient sage Zoroaster, which were highly influential in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> touched upon this mystically: <term>All things are generated from one fire</term> <note>original Greek: "εισι παντα υποο ενοσ εξεφααντα"</note>. Moreover, the lower bodies of the world migrate from non-being into being, and pass from being into non-being. The higher bodies change from one way of being to another, or from one mode of existing to another. Because of this, all these things are by their own nature equally disposed toward being and non-being. If there were nothing else above bodies of this kind, either they would never have received being at all, or if they had received it, they would have ceased to be long ago. They would not have received it because, since they are equally disposed by their nature to being and non-being, they by no means determine themselves toward being. They would have ceased to be long ago because, since they flow away by their own nature, they would have already flowed away into nothingness if they were not held back by something more stable. Therefore, an incorporeal and stable substance presides over the movable bodies of the world. If this substance were also equally disposed to being and non-being like bodies, it would again require another thing to define it. Finally, there must be one certain substance that exists necessarily through itself; this will be entirely simple. Indeed, if it were composed of parts, it would not exist through itself, but through the union of its parts and through that which had reconciled those diverse parts to each other. Rather, it would be just as subject to the dissolution of its parts as it was subject to their connection. Therefore, it would not exist out of necessity, since through dissolution it could, at some point, not be. Such a being is surely God: a simple substance, necessarily subsisting through itself. For this reason, Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and musician, considered by Ficino to be the first of the "ancient theologians."</note> called God "Necessity." <term>For strong necessity rules over all</term> <note>original Greek: "εινι γαρ αναγκη παντα κρατυει"</note>. If...

# Theology [Book] Two

The highest <term>necessity of being</term> <note>In Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, a "necessary being" is one that must exist by its own nature and cannot "not exist."</note> is shown to be God: for that which is the "highest" in any category is unique. No thing besides God will possess such a necessity of being. Indeed, if you wish an angel also to be such a thing—so that there are two "highests" of necessity, God and an angel—you would be forced to explain in what way the angel differs from God. For they would not differ in the necessity of being itself, since in that respect you have posited them to be one and the same. Therefore, there must be something else in the angel besides that necessity by which it is able to differ from God. Because of this, the angel will not be the "highest necessity," since it is not pure and solitary necessity, but a mixture.

<margin>g</margin>
Furthermore, whatever is the highest in any category must possess the nature of that category in its purity, not mixed with other things, lest its power be diminished by the mixture. You would also be forced to answer: from where does the angel have that property added to its necessity? Does it come from its own necessity, or from elsewhere? If the first is granted, then God will have that same property coming from a similar necessity of His own; therefore, the angel is not distinguished from God by that property. If the second is granted, it follows that the angel's own nature arises from somewhere other than the angel, because it acquires the property through which it is distinguished from the outside. That which depends on another is not "necessary through itself." Therefore, neither an angel nor any other thing is the necessity of being, but God alone. If nothing else besides God exists necessarily through itself, then all things must receive their being from God.

By this argument, the false opinion of certain <note>Ficino is likely targeting the "Averroists" or certain "Peripatetics" (followers of Aristotle) who argued for the eternity of the world independent of a creator's continuous will.</note> **physicists** is condemned; they think that matter, the world, and the mind <note>The "Mind" or "Intellect" (Mens) was often treated as an eternal emanation in Neoplatonism.</note> have not only always existed, but also that they do not depend on God in their essence, even though they might depend on Him for their "act"—that is, for their motion. For they admit that all things are moved and operate toward the Good as if toward an end; but they ought to consider that whatever cannot be sufficient for itself in its operation, but requires sufficiency from an external end, is much less able to be sufficient for itself in its essence, seeing as it must have its essence from an external principle. For indeed, if it is the task of the same 

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
power to bring a thing to perfection as it is to bring it into being—and vice versa—then just as all things are perfected by the Good as their end, so they are brought into being <note>The original Latin word "efficiuntur" (brought into being/effected) is split across the page break: "effi-" on page 14 and "-ciuntur" on page 15.</note> by the same as their principle.

# [Book] Second

And since essence is most perfect in its own source, if any of those three <note>Matter, the world, and the mind.</note> were the source of its own essence, the substance of each would be just as perfect as God's. They would not turn toward God, but toward themselves as their own end and perfection. As art relates to nature, so nature relates to God. The works of the arts remain undamaged only as long as they preserve the strength of nature; for instance, a statue stands for a long time through the natural solidity of the stone or the bronze. Similarly, all natural things remain only as long as they preserve the "influx" of God. And just as nature provides motion to its works, so God provides being to nature. The works of nature move only as long as nature moves them. Therefore, nature exists only as long as God preserves it in existence.

Furthermore, this whole universe, the work of God, either always was, or it began to be at some point. If it always was, a "first moment" cannot be assigned in which it received being from God above all other moments. Therefore, either it received being at no moment (which is false), or it receives being from Him at every moment. This is nothing other than being continually preserved by Him. If, however, it began to be at some time, it needs God as a preserver much more than if it were assumed to be eternal. In every case, that which belongs to something according to its own nature 

<margin>M</margin>
comes before that which arrives from elsewhere. But "non-being" belongs to a created work according to itself—since, if a cause did not approach it, the work would not have existed. Existence, however, belongs to it through a cause. Therefore, "not being" comes to it before "being." For this reason, it is more fitting for the work to be preserved by a cause than by itself. And because that which is natural is never lost, the work is always such that, if the power of the cause were removed, it would not persist in being; for from the beginning, it was naturally such that it could not come into being apart from 

<margin>N</margin>
the action of a cause. We properly call God the "Cause," for He alone brings the whole of any thing into being; He is not forced, nor does He need the help of another, nor does He borrow matter from elsewhere. Instead, every thing is compelled to depend entirely on Him forever, as a shadow depends on a body. Indeed, since the Cause creates the effect in its entirety, the effect, if compared to the substance of the Cause, is something imaginary <note>In the sense of being "image-like" or having a derivative reality, like a reflection in a mirror.</note>.

<summary>This page argues that God is the only "pure necessity," meaning He is the only being that must exist by His own nature. Ficino refutes the idea that the world or matter could be eternal and independent, explaining that all things require God's continuous "influx" to remain in existence, much like a shadow requires a body.</summary>

# Platonic Book

<margin>A</margin>
**E**vanescent rather than substantial: in such a case, an effect that is inherently "vain" <note>In this context, "vain" (vanus) means empty or lacking independent reality.</note> requires the continuous support of its cause. And the Cause which made the whole also preserves the whole. If the world is compared to God—the finite to the infinite—it is more "vain" and more like a shadow than a finite shadow of a finite body compared to that body. Finally, the highest of causes dominates things so thoroughly that things do not merely flow from it once, but they depend upon it continuously, just as images are produced by bodies and are preserved within a mirror. <margin>G</margin> Since God acts upon and preserves all things, He therefore operates in all things. That is, the causes of things that follow after God do nothing without divine power and action. If God grants an angel its <term>being</term> <note>Latin: *esse*. In Ficino's philosophy, this is the act of existing itself, which only God possesses by nature.</note> and its act, and preserves them, He also grants the power of acting and the action itself, and preserves them. Thus, whatever an angel performs naturally, it performs by the power of God, acting as an instrument acts by the power of the craftsman. Therefore, God performs not only the angel, but the very work of the angel; indeed, God effects the work of the angel much more than the angel does, since He is the first origin of the action. If this work, which is sacred and comes from the angel, moves anything else, it performs that same power of God through which it was itself made by the angel. For this reason, whatever happens anywhere happens by the power of God, <margin>M</margin> regardless of who does it. This is especially true since all things that act in some way provide their own "being" to their work. By "being," I mean being "this" or "that," or "such" or "so." Thus, all things that act under God concur toward one common effect, which is "being." However, many and diverse agents do not conspire together toward a single work (which is "to be") unless they themselves are one; they are nothing unless they are under the One, and directed toward the One. Therefore, the remaining agents operate by the power of the one first acting God. Do we not arrange the order of causes according to the order of acts? <margin>B</margin> The first and only effect is <term>existence</term>; <note>Latin: *esse*. Ficino argues that "to exist" is the most fundamental effect, preceding specific qualities like being "human" or "hot."</note> for the remaining effects are nothing other than certain determinations and properties of existence itself. <margin>L</margin> For each thing is first "according to nature" <note>original: *secundum naturam*</note>. Then it is "this" or "that," "such" or "so." Add to this that "to be" is the last thing that is lost; for one loses being "such a thing" before one loses existence simply. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, existence itself is the proper effect of that Agent which is the principle and end of all things. And toward that end,

---

the other agents, if they contribute anything, they contribute by the power of the first Agent. And these agents, as inferior beings of a narrower command, do nothing else except distinguish that universal force and action of God which is present everywhere and tends toward the universal. With God helping them at every turn, they induce certain "dispositions" of being rather than the nature of being itself. In fact, the divine power distinguishes itself into various effects through various media, just as the light of the sun—which in itself is equally related to any color—if it penetrates through two glass windows (one of which is red and the other green), it will produce two glows on the pavement: one red and one green. The fact that both are "brightness" comes simply from the light. But the fact that one is red and the other green comes from the light again, but only insofar as it penetrates through such-and-such a glass, forming itself in one way or another. Let us first conclude: that the <margin>D</margin> First Cause acts more vehemently in any effect than the remaining causes do, because the "trace" which is impressed by it—namely, *existence*—is both impressed first and deleted last, compared to the traces of the other causes, as if it were impressed more strongly. Secondly, the other causes fix their own traces upon the trace of the First Cause. Just as they must necessarily found all their works upon the work of the First Cause, so they stabilize their powers and actions within His power and action.
> ¶ God acts through His own being in whatever He does. <margin>Wisdom 8</margin> <note>original: *Sap. viij*. Ficino cites the Book of Wisdom to support the idea that God's power reaches mightily from end to end.</note>
<margin>E</margin> **B**ut lest any <term>Epicurean</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus, who Ficino often targets for believing that God is indifferent to the world or that the world is made of random atoms.</note> should say that if God does many things, He must be troubled by deliberation and burdened by the work, one must remember that God can produce His work through His being alone; He does not require deliberation or choice. For if the divine "being" itself were not of such great value that it could operate by itself, but instead required some "counsel" (which would be different from His being), then He would certainly not perform any work of any thing through His being. But as it stands, <margin>F</margin> the qualities of bodies act upon one another without deliberation. Does not the sun illuminate the world, and fire [burn]...

He asserts that while secondary causes provide specific qualities, the fundamental act of "being" is a direct and constant gift from God.</summary>

<header>Theology [Book] Two</header>

# Theology

<margin>A</margin>
Fire heats; and the soul nourishes the body through choice rather than merely through its <term>being</term> <note>Latin: *esse*. Ficino distinguishes between a thing's mere existence and its active choices.</note>. Accordingly, even those things which act through choice also do something through their own natural being, by a power naturally inherent in that being itself. For instance, although the human soul performs many things through choice, it nevertheless gives life to the body through its very being, without the need for choice.

<margin>B</margin>
Is not choice itself also somehow a work of the soul? And a work of this kind comes from the very being of the soul, without a preceding choice—otherwise, that preceding choice would similarly require another preceding choice, and that one yet another. Thus, any work of the soul would require an infinite number of choices before it could begin to happen; and it would never begin to happen, since one cannot traverse the infinite. Let us conclude thus: If action that is carried out through natural being is present in all things, but action through choice is not (since physical bodies choose nothing); and if the action of choice and deliberation is always preceded by action that occurs through being and nature; then it is clearly established that this action, which occurs through being itself, belongs to the universal and first cause, which is God. Thus, the first and common action belongs to the first and common agent. Action that occurs through being happens without care or labor. In this way, the sun most easily illuminates nearly infinite things with a single act, and generates life through that illumination. Fire most easily heats many things. The soul nourishes the body and thrives within it, doing many things simultaneously without anxiety or labor. Thus God, through His own being—which is a kind of most simple center of all things, from which the rest are drawn out like lines—vibrates whatever depends upon Him with the easiest <term>nod</term> <note>Latin: *nutu*. This refers to a divine command or will that is effortless, like a mere inclination of the head.</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
However, there is this difference between the first agent and all other agents: the first agent is said to operate through being in such a way that He acts through **pure being**; whereas the others act through being—that is, through some natural or, so to speak, essential power.

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, the operation that proceeds from deliberation is preceded by the operation carried out by essential power. This, in turn, is preceded by that which is done by pure being. And just as that which is done by power is easier than that which is done by deliberation, so that which is fulfilled by **pure being** 

# [Book] Two

is easier than that which is done by power.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ God understands Himself first, and also individual things.

<margin>L</margin> <gloss>Chapter 9</gloss>
**T**he intellect would never become capable of understanding a thing unless there were some kinship between itself and the thing itself. Therefore, since there is a kinship between the intellect and the thing to be understood, the same path by which something advances toward becoming intelligible is the path by which it advances toward being an intellect. But a departure from matter is the path by which every thing reaches that limit of being "to-be-understood" and "intelligible"—that is, such that it can properly be understood—because a thing is properly understood only when it is thought of apart from matter and the conditions of matter. Therefore, by that same departure, anyone can reach the point of being an intellect.

<margin>M</margin>
Certainly, if being separated from matter is the reason why any form becomes one with the intellect, then being removed from matter is much more, and more primarily, the reason why a thing is an intellect and a thinking being. Because there is no removal from matter greater than God, no one understands more precisely than He.

<margin>n</margin>
Furthermore, intelligence is desirable as a good; for every thing can enjoy itself and all other things, but primarily the First Good—that is, God, who lacks no good. Add to this that every cause acts through a form. And the more expansive the cause is, the more expansive the form is through which it acts. God is the most expansive cause. Therefore, the most expansive form is in God. But nowhere is a form more expansive than in the mind. Therefore, God possesses a mind. He also proves this from the fact that it is not fitting for minds to be the instruments of a mover who lacks a mind. Yet all minds are the instruments of God.

<margin>O</margin>
This is further supported by the fact that, since in God essence and operation are the same, it follows that His operation belongs to that class which does not pass into external matter, but remains in the agent as its own perfection, rather than the perfection of the matter. Such is knowledge and desire.

<margin>P</margin>
In God, therefore, there is at least knowledge—namely, intelligence—or something even more eminent than intelligence itself. And since the intelligence of God pri...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Divine Mind from the previous chapter. Having established that God acts through His very being, Ficino now explores how God’s knowledge is identical to His existence, arguing that the supreme intelligence must know all things—even the smallest details—within Himself.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

...the [highest] intelligence is: and whatever is first in any genus is pure, alone, and exists in itself. Therefore, in that realm, being and understanding are exactly the same thing; otherwise, if being were one thing and understanding another, we would be forced to place that intelligence in something else—that is, in an <term>essence</term> <note>Latin: *essentia*. Here referring to the underlying nature or "stuff" of a thing, which Ficino argues is not separate from God's act of thinking.</note>. Likewise, if the first intelligence is there, it is certainly the most perfect. It is clearly of such a nature that it is first through that very object which is to be comprehended by it. For in this way, the experience is certain, lacking nothing, and most full. Indeed, that intelligence is closest to the thing to be known through which the intelligent being understands itself. Therefore, the proper intelligence of God is that he understands himself. This is especially true because if God’s intelligence were perfected by some external object, God’s essence (which is the same as His intelligence) would be perfected by that same external object; thus, God would be "made" or completed by another. Who would say that the divine mind follows external things in order to understand, when external things are instead forced to follow the divine mind in order to exist? Who would place the object of the divine mind outside of God? For no power can exceed its own object, yet God exceeds all things immeasurably. 

<margin>B</margin> When we attribute the names of "intellect" and "intelligence" to God, it should be understood in this way: that such titles are applied by way of cause rather than by way of form. For we properly consider an angel to be a "mind." God, however, is above the genus of minds, so that He is the Mind of minds and the Light of lights. God understands whatever He understands in a certain way that is "above intelligence"; and, to come to our point, He understands individual things. For whatever the intellect does, it does by its own nature, and so it acts by understanding. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, whatever He makes, He understands, as is evident in the arts and in human planning. Since God acts through His very being, and that being does not lack intellect—indeed, since being and understanding are the same thing due to God’s supreme simplicity—it is necessary that He works by understanding. His knowledge extends exactly as far as His operation, since in the most simple God, voluntary knowledge and operation are the same thing. His operation extends through all things down to the smallest details. Therefore, God understands all the smallest things. This is especially true because he who knows all the smallest causes of things understands the smallest things. 

<margin>D</margin> God is ignorant of nothing, for He certainly knows Himself. He is the cause of all things. Therefore, by knowing the first and highest of causes—and the cause of all things—He knows them all. He knows them, I say, distinctly and most clearly. 

<margin>G</margin> For while He sees Himself (who is the cause of the angelic nature), He sees the angel most clearly. While He beholds the angel, He beholds through it—if necessary—its works, as if beholding His own through them. Through those works, again, He beholds the results of those works most plainly. 

<margin>E</margin> In this way, He knows the highest cause, the middle causes, and the closest causes of the lowliest things. And therefore He distinguishes them clearly. Although there is no need for God to look outside Himself at subsequent causes to see the ultimate effects, since He Himself is the first origin of their being and the cause of existence for all following things. Therefore, while He inspects Himself, He inspects the total being of any things whatsoever. The total being, I say, plainly and distinctly. For if He knows Himself perfectly, He comprehends His entire power. His power expands through every individual thing. He knows, therefore, individual things. 

Likewise, while He sees His own essence and the goodness to be communicated to things, He sees in how many ways that goodness of His can be shared. Things in nature become as varied as the ways in which the divine essence and goodness are shared. Therefore, through the distinct knowledge of His own goodness, He sees the distinct properties of individual things. 

<margin>F</margin> For no kind of understanding should be missing from the supreme intelligence. For this reason, God possesses intelligence not only of genera and species—as some thinkers have claimed—but also of individual things. For the knowledge of any thing is desirable as a kind of good, and no good is lacking in God. Add to this that a superior power ought to know whatever an inferior power knows, and something beyond it, as appears in our own souls. For those things which the individual senses receive one by one, the <term>phantasia</term> <note>Latin: *phantasia*. In the psychology of this period, this refers to the "imagination" or the internal sense that combines data from the five physical senses into a single image.</note> discerns as a whole; and the intellect sees something even more excellent in one single vision than what the *phantasia* sees in many images. The intellect sees individual things more clearly than even the *phantasia* does; it sees, moreover, the universal reasons of things, which the *phantasia* does not know. In this way, God, by a single power, knows whatever we know through three powers—namely, the senses, the *phantasia*, [and the intellect].

<summary>Ficino argues that because God's being and intellect are identical, God knows all things—including individual, material details—by simply knowing Himself as the cause of all existence. He refutes the idea that God only knows universal categories, asserting that the divine mind must possess every possible form of knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that God’s self-knowledge necessarily includes knowledge of all created things. Having established that God is the source of being, Ficino now addresses the philosophical objection that knowing "lowly" or "base" things would be beneath God’s dignity, using both Platonic (Orphic) and Aristotelian sources to prove God's omniscience extends to every detail and even to the infinite.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>Theology: Book Two</header>

...substance: and we know by the intellect. Therefore, He contemplates universals; and He contemplates individuals in almost all their modes of being, for He sees the origin of being and comprehends the entire nature of its existence. If this is so, He certainly inspects individuals, which are distinguished from one another by various modes of being. Regarding this, Orpheus says: <margin>I</margin> <note>original Greek: "καὶ Διὸς ὄμμα τέλειον ἐπείγως ἀφίκεται ἡμεῖν μοῖρά τε καὶ Διὸς οἶδε νόος διὰ παντὸς ἅπαντα"</note> "The perfect eye of Jove arrives among us with haste; both Fate and the mind of Jove know all things through all." The perfect eye of Jove. For whatever things happen among us, both fate and the mind of Jove inspect them all through the universe. Therefore, let no one give credit to Epicurus <note>Greek philosopher often associated with the idea that gods do not intervene in or care about human affairs.</note> or to Averroes <note>The influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher (Ibn Rushd), who argued that God only knows universals, not particulars, to maintain His simplicity.</note> when they say that the knowledge of the most base things is unworthy of the divine majesty. For God contemplates things not as they are in themselves, but as they are in Him; not through their own images, but through His own <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental "being" of God which serves as the mirror for all reality.</note>. He is not distracted by a multitude of things, but beholds all things as if they were one. He never labors, because He does not have to search for knowledge, but already possesses it. He does not turn away from more important things to consider the trivial, because He sees both the former and the latter with the same gaze—just like the eye, which beholds many stars in the sky with a single glance.

Are you ignorant, impious Averroes, that the goodness of the universal order is more excellent than the quality of any single part? Indeed, even your Aristotle affirms in his <term>Divine Book XI</term> <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, Book Lambda (XII in modern numbering, often XI in older manuscripts), which discusses the Prime Mover.</note> that individual parts are referred to the good of the order which is in the whole as if to their goal. If, therefore, God knows any other noble thing—which you do not deny—He must especially know the order of the universe. An order of this kind cannot be understood unless every precious thing and every base thing are distinguished from one another; it is in their intervals and proportions that the order of the whole consists. Remember also that these very things which are commonly called "most base" were each constructed with a certain most exact art, just as those things which are considered "most precious." Furthermore, while things may seem less beautiful when considered in isolation, within this whole order and in the mind of the Orderer Himself, they harmonize most fittingly with themselves and with all others. Orpheus sang this whole concept in his hymn to Apollo: <note>original Greek: "ἔχεις δὲ τέπειρατα κόσμου παντός σοι δ’ ἀρχή τε τελευτή τεστὶ μέλουσ’ ἅπαντοβαλλος οὐδὲ πάντα πόλον κιθάρα πολυκρέκτωι ἁρμόσεισαι"</note> "You hold the boundaries of the entire world; to you belong the beginning and the end. Through you all things live. You prepare the whole sphere to resonate like a lyre." <margin>K</margin> <note>Ficino provides a Latin transliteration of the Greek here: "Tu thes mudi terminos vniuersi. Tibi cure e pricipiu: atq finis. per te viuesunt oia. Tu sphera tota cithara resonate prepara."</note>

### God understands infinite things. Chapter 10. <margin>L</margin>

True reason teaches us that God knows not only individual and even the lowest things, but also infinite things. If God perfectly knows His own power, He knows distinctly all things to which that power extends. For the magnitude of a power is measured according to the quantity of things it can perform. Since the power of God is infinite, it extends to things beyond number. Therefore, God knows things beyond number. The knowledge of God reaches deeply through all those things which are said to "be," in whatever way they exist or are described. Thus, it is necessary that He clearly understands not only those things which exist in <term>act</term> <note>Things that currently exist in reality.</note>, but also whatever can exist in <term>potential</term> <note>Things that could possibly exist but do not yet.</note>. 

<margin>M</margin> In natural things, there are some that are infinite, if not in act, then at least in potential: for instance, the capacity of matter, the progression of motion and time, the succession of generation, the division of a continuum, and the multiplication of numbers. Therefore, God clearly understands infinite things. <margin>N</margin> Just as Unity, which is the beginning of numbers, would see infinite numbers in act if it could see all those numbers which are within it according to potential—for Unity is potentially every number—so too God sees all things through His essence as if through a certain <term>Exemplar</term> <note>A divine blueprint or perfect model of a thing existing in the mind of God.</note>. Since there is infinite perfection in this essence, innumerable things can be expressed in its likeness, so that they progress little by little toward the better through innumerable degrees of perfection. This is because neither a single created thing, nor any finite quantity of things, can fully exhaust the total perfection of the Exemplar. And so, forever and without end, there remains a new way in which something else can imitate the Exemplar itself even further. God, therefore, through the innumerable degrees of the infinite Exemplar, contemplates innumerable images.

<summary>Ficino argues that God’s omniscience includes even the lowliest particulars and the infinite, refuting Averroes by claiming that the "order of the whole" requires knowledge of every part. He uses the metaphor of Unity containing all numbers to explain how God's infinite essence contains the potential for all created things.</summary>
<keywords>Averroes, Epicurus, Aristotle, Orpheus, divine providence, omniscience, infinity, potentiality vs act, universal order, Exemplar</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of God’s intellect from the previous page, specifically addressing the paradox of how a finite human mind can conceive of infinity while arguing that God’s own intellect must be actually infinite. It transitions into Chapter 11, which discusses the Divine Will and how all forms exist within God’s simple essence.</meta>

# Platonic

# Book

<margin>A</margin>
In God, being and understanding are entirely the same; therefore, just as His being is infinite, so is His understanding infinite. Since the human intellect has the power to know those things which are potentially infinite, it can multiply the species of numbers to infinity, and proceed at its own will in many other things without end. But if the divine intellect does not understand things that are actually infinite, but only gazes upon a certain fixed number, I ask whether He is able to understand further, or whether He is not. If He can, then God does not actually understand all those things which He possesses the power to understand; if He cannot, then the human intellect would be able to know more things than the divine intellect. Both conclusions are absurd. 

<margin>B</margin>
He therefore understands things that are actually infinite. For this reason, since the divine mind is infinite, it is deservedly named by the <term>Orphics</term> <note>Followers of the legendary poet Orpheus; Ficino believed Orphic hymns contained ancient theological truths that prefigured Christianity.</note> *apeiron omma*, that is, the "infinite eye" <note>original Greek: ἄπειρον ὄμμα</note>. From these points, the error of those philosophers is refuted who thought that God sees only finite things, 

<margin>M</margin>
because they believed that whatever is seen by Him must be comprehended, and whatever is comprehended must necessarily be limited <note>Ficino is playing on the Latin *comprehendere*, which means both to understand and to physically grasp or enclose within a boundary.</note>. To these people we respond for the present: that God and the things which are seen in God by Himself are the same. Whoever, therefore, says that these things 

<margin>A</margin>
are comprehended by God, says nothing other than that these things are comprehended by themselves. It would indeed be absurd 

<margin>sr</margin>
for an infinite thing to be comprehended by another. However, to be comprehended by itself is not absurd. This truly is nothing other than for the infinite to extend through itself and to be inwardly equal to itself. Therefore, the infinite God does not limit Himself when He beholds the infinite in an infinite way; rather, He confirms His own infinity. Nor is it absurd for God to discern innumerable things. For He does not discern them by counting them step by step, but by gazing upon them all at once. And just as He sees many things as if they were one—since He contemplates them through a single species with a single act—so He sees an infinite multitude as if it were finite: that is, as a certain thing entirely simple in essence, but in a certain way multiple in its logic. Because He considers His own form, which is truly one, to be "all-formed" <note>the quality of containing the patterns of all possible things</note> by His power and by a certain relationship. It is just as if the light of the sun—the 

---

fount of all colors, which is, so to speak, of a single color—should perceive itself as if it were "all-colored."
**C** God has a will, through which He effects all things outside of Himself. <margin>Cap. xj.</margin>

<margin>C</margin>
**E**very cause acts through some form, and it produces an effect somewhat similar to its own form; therefore, it is necessary that the form of the effect be comprehended by the cause. Since God is the cause of all things, it is necessary that the forms of all things be in Him. 

<margin>D</margin>
God is therefore an "all-formed" essence. Hence that Orphic saying: *Zeus eidos panton*, that is, "Jupiter is the species of all" <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς εἶδος πάντων; Ficino uses "Jupiter" here to refer to the supreme Divine Mind.</note>. Just as in pure potentiality—that is, <term>matter</term>—all natural forms exist according to a certain confused potential, so it is necessary that in <term>pure act</term> <note>A philosophical term for God, meaning He is fully realized and has no unrealized potential or "room to grow."</note>—that is, in God—all forms exist according to a distinct actuality. 

<margin>E</margin>
But are these forms in God distinct according to a certain mode of nature? In the same way that light, heat, dryness, and lightness are in fire, through which it acts by a certain necessity of its nature? Not at all. The first reason: since God makes all things, if He operated through forms of this kind, He would be much more multiple and composite than any other cause, whether those forms in Him were essential or accidental. Yet it is necessary that He be the simplest of all things; therefore they cannot be essential, for no essence would be less "one" in itself than the divine essence. Nor again can they be accidental. For in what way can God receive qualities? Not from elsewhere, since He denies that He suffers anything from anyone. Not from Himself. Indeed, if He received them from Himself, insofar as He gives them, He would play the role of the "efficient cause"; insofar as He receives them, He would play the role of the "subject." But the first agent and pure act, to whom all things are subject, cannot undergo the condition of being a subject.

<margin>F</margin>
Likewise, substance does not depend on an accident, although an accident depends on a substance. What does not depend on another is able to exist separately from the other. Therefore, a certain substance can exist separately from the conditions and limits of accidents. Whatever of liberty and of good can exist, all of that can exist through the power of the highest principle and the Good.

<summary>Ficino argues that God's intellect is actually infinite and contains the forms of all things within a perfectly simple essence. He refutes the idea that God is limited by what He knows, explaining that God's knowledge is a single, unified act rather than a sequential counting of parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of God’s nature from Book II. While the previous page established God’s infinite intellect, this page argues that God does not act out of "blind nature" or necessity (like fire must burn), but through a unified "intellectual nature" that allows Him to order the universe with total freedom and variety.</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>Theology: Book Two</header>

# Theology
## Book Two

<margin>Power</margin>
**It is possible.** For this reason, God is already in <term>act</term> <note>original: "actu"; in philosophy, this means something is fully realized or "actually" existing, rather than just having the potential to exist.</note> that infinite substance: which is able to be, or rather, which is free from <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentibus"; these are qualities like "redness" or "height" that can change without changing what a thing fundamentally is. God has no such external qualities.</note>. This leads to the idea that an effect is found in a more excellent way in its higher causes than it is in itself; and therefore, in the highest cause, it exists in the most excellent way possible. Since the effects of God are themselves substances in their own right, they must not exist in God as if they were merely accidents. However, there are not many substances there. Therefore, they are all there as one certain thing: namely, the very substance of God Himself. Since it is necessary for all things to be found in God in the most perfect way, they must be united to Him, and to each other, most perfectly. They cannot exist in a more sublime way in God, nor be more sublimely united both to God and to themselves, than if they are, in God, God Himself.

<margin>Question</margin>
The forms of things, therefore, are not distinct in God according to the manner of nature. If they were, God would be led to act by a certain natural necessity, no differently than fire is led to burn. This is the second reason. The nature of any thing is one specific form: a power determined toward one specific work in a certain way, doing whatever it does with its whole force, and doing it by necessity. 

<margin>Reason</margin>
For instance, the hot nature of fire does one specific work, namely the work of heat, and it always heats with the same consistency; and as far as it is able, it exercises every degree of heat everywhere. 

<margin>Sequence</margin>
Therefore, if one piece of matter is heated by one degree and another by two degrees, this does not proceed from the planning of the agent (the fire), but from the order of degrees found in the preparation of the materials. Thus, the fire does not "rule" over its entire work. It is not the author of the order of degrees present in the result. If it were to generate two separate heats outside of a subject, it would perform both with its whole self, and they would be equal; indeed, even now, in subjects that are entirely similar, it generates entirely similar and equal heats.

<margin>Power</margin>
**It is possible** for a natural thing to produce different effects either through different media or from different materials. But if the diversity of media and materials is removed, it produces either one single thing or things very much alike. Nor can it fail to act when matter is present. God alone, however, produces <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "materiam primam"; the most basic, formless substance of the universe before it is given shape.</note> for bodies, and many essences of minds and souls, without any medium or underlying subject. These things are indeed very different from one another, and are distinguished among themselves by many degrees of perfection. Rightly then, because God is the first agent, He rules over His entire work to such an extent that He Himself is able to bring about the forms, the orders of the forms, and the distinction of their degrees. If God acted only by the mode of mere nature, He would produce fewer and less varied effects than any other agent; indeed, God would act as only one single thing, since the divine nature is the simplest of all. Therefore, He is not driven to act by a natural instinct. The third reason: if intelligence in us is effective, and in angels more effective, then intelligence in God must be the most effective of all. In God, His nature and His intelligence are the same. Likewise, the mode of natural operation and the mode of intellectual operation are usually the same everywhere. 

<margin>1</margin>
For both nature and intelligence act through form, and produce something similar in form. 

<margin>2</margin>
Therefore, God should not be said to act through "naked nature," nor through a "borrowed intelligence." Rather, He acts through an intellectual nature and a natural intelligence. 

<margin>3</margin>
Because He is the first, common, and most blessed cause, a "natural" operation is appropriate to God, which is prior, more common, and easier than others. Again: because He is the most precious cause, an "intellectual" operation is appropriate, which is prior in dignity within us, even if it is not prior in time. 

<margin>A</margin>
And therefore, it is first in the order of things. And as something precious, it is suitable only for the more excellent species. Therefore, the proper operation of God is both operations together. 

<margin>M</margin>
Furthermore, among the <term>Platonists</term> <note>The followers of Plato, whom Ficino spent his life translating and interpreting as a "pious" philosophy compatible with Christianity.</note>, there is a single unique property of the divine essence, insofar as God is God. Therefore, both are the same operation in God. The fourth reason: naked nature looks toward this specific good or that one. Intellectual nature looks toward the universal good. Therefore, a cause that acts through naked nature is compared to a cause that acts through intellectual nature just as a specific cause is compared to a universal cause, or as a servant is compared to a master craftsman.

<sig>L</sig>

<summary>Ficino argues that God's creative power is not a blind "natural" force like fire, which acts by necessity, but an "intellectual nature" that allows Him to freely create and order a diverse universe from His own simple essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of God as a craftsman, expanding on the previous page's distinction between "natural necessity" and "intellectual action." Here, the author introduces the "Fifth Reason" to explain how God can be a single, simple being while simultaneously containing the blueprints (Ideas) for all the diverse things in the universe.</meta>

<page-num>XI</page-num>
<header>Book of Platonic Theology</header>

## Platonic Theology

<margin>A</margin> The servant compared to the architect. ¶ Therefore, the architect of the world works through an intellectual nature, insofar as he is an intellectual being. **The Fifth Reason.** That specific way of operating suits God above all others: the way by which God neither slips from his own stable state nor from his simplicity. Such an operation is, first and foremost, the work of the mind. A "natural" operation begins from the agent but ends in the object that is acted upon—just as heat moves from a fire into a piece of wood. An intellectual operation, however, keeps both the beginning and the end within the agent itself. ¶ For through this intellectual power, God, while he is occupied with contemplating himself within himself, also directs all external things. ¶ And as

<margin>B</margin> Parmenides the Pythagorean says: <note>Parmenides was an ancient Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging, and motionless sphere. Ficino is blending this with the idea of God as a "still point" around which the world turns.</note> he rotates the moving orb of things while he himself remains motionless. ¶ Furthermore, it is necessary for God to be entirely "uniform" (single-formed), because he exists above the forms of all things. Yet, he must also be "all-form," because he is the shaper of all things. The fact that he can be uniform and all-form at the same time is possible only through an intellectual nature; through this, the form of God, by gazing upon itself, conceives itself as the specific <term>rational pattern</term> <note>original: "rationem"; in Platonic thought, this refers to the logical blueprint or "ratio" that defines what a thing is.</note> of all forms.

He sees in himself what is unique to each thing; he discerns to what degree each thing can imitate the divine form, or where it must fall short. For example, when he understands his own form by way of "life" but not yet by "cognition"—if I may put it that way—he conceives the form and the <term>idea</term> <note>original: "ideam"; here meaning the eternal, perfect archetype or blueprint in the mind of God.</note> of plants. But when he conceives his form as imitable by way of cognition, but not yet of full "intelligence," he conceives the idea of an animal. And the rest follow in the same way. Truly, in all things that happen not by chance but by nature or purpose, it is necessary that the goal of the making be the "form" of the work produced. An active cause 

<margin>M</margin> does not direct its action toward a form for any other reason than through the form dwelling within itself. Nor does it direct itself toward specific forms except by specific forms, or by specific rational patterns conceived within itself. Since, therefore, the marvelous order of the world cannot consist of chance—even in part—it is necessary that in the manufacturing of the world, there is a "form" within the intelligence, according to whose likeness the effect is created. And since the purpose of God 

---

## Book

<margin>D</margin> regarding the universe is the highest order, the primary Idea held by him is the Idea of the universal order. But the logic of the whole order cannot be held unless the specific logic of all the parts, from which the whole is made, is also held. Just as an architect cannot conceive the design of a building unless he first conceives the logic of its parts, the specific patterns of all things are therefore within God. These things do not receive their distinct appearances as species from any other source than from where they receive their very existence. ¶ Nor is the divine simplicity any less simple because of this multitude of Ideas, since God gazes upon them all through a single form and with a single look. Nor is a "Divine Idea" called the "Divine Essence" simply as it is essence, but only insofar as it is the model for this or that specific species. 

<margin>E</margin> For this reason, insofar as many patterns are understood from one essence, they are called "many Ideas." 

<margin>C</margin> These kinds of relationships, by which Ideas are multiplied, are not produced by the things themselves; rather, they are produced by the divine intellect comparing its own essence to the things. Nor are these relationships "real"—so to speak—in the same way as those relationships that distinguish the Persons <note>A reference to the Christian Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), where the relationships are considered "real" distinctions within the one God.</note>; but rather, they are relationships of the intellect. Under one single Idea, many things are both known and created. Some things are even perceived through an Idea by way of contrast: for example, the "habit of evil" and lack (privation) are seen through the Idea of Goodness. And as some think, matter is seen through the Idea of Form. The properties of a substance are also known through the Ideas of that substance. Common qualities, however, are designated by their own specific Ideas. Just as an architect, through the form of the house itself, brings about all the "accidents" (incidental features) that accompany the house from its beginning. But those things which happen to a house once it is already finished—for example, paintings and the like—are arranged through other Ideas. But we have now treated Ideas more diffusely than we intended, having found the opportunity here as if by chance. 

<margin>F</margin> ¶ This, however—even if certain dogs bark to the contrary—is the most certain opinion of our Plato and the Platonists. This is what we touched on above and will declare more broadly elsewhere.

# Theology Book Two

**W**e have proven so far that the First Cause <note>A philosophical term for God, the ultimate origin of all things.</note> carries out its various effects through a complex order of wisdom, rather than through the bare and simple necessity of nature. We shall next prove—God willing—that He does not produce external effects through pure intelligence alone, unless the assent of the **will** is also present; this, indeed, was the purpose of this discussion.

<margin>b</margin>
**The First Reason.** The First Cause directs all things by its own power toward the best possible end through the most direct paths and in the most fitting manner, as we shall show in the following sections. It cannot do this unless it anticipates the end through the intellect, discerns the paths, and measures the proportions between the paths and the end. Then, through the will, it must approve that end and choose such a path above all others.

<margin>c</margin>
Hence, Plato in the *Timaeus*, *Phaedo*, *Philebus*, and the *Statesman* <note>original: "politico"</note> expresses detestation for those philosophers who attribute the causes of natural things either to physical forms or to the necessity of matter or nature itself. He himself considers natural things to be merely instruments of intelligence rather than the primary agents; he everywhere traces individual effects back especially to the final, efficient, and formal causes. <note>In ancient philosophy, the "Final Cause" is the purpose of a thing, the "Efficient Cause" is what makes it, and the "Formal Cause" is its design or blueprint.</note>

<margin>d</margin>
Therefore, if anyone asks why the earth is round, he answers: because it participates in the <term>Idea of Roundness</term> <note>The perfect, eternal concept of a circle in the mind of God.</note>, according to the likeness of which the Wisdom that crafted the world arranged the earth. This was done because it was judged so, and because He willed that the good of the earth would be better if it were held in that shape.

<margin>e</margin>
**The Second Reason.** That which accompanies whatever exists must belong to "being" insofar as it is being. Whatever is of such a nature must be found in that which is the "First Being." But whatever exists has this quality: it both desires a good that is absent and most gladly rests in a good that is present. Indeed, the intellect desires an absent good and embraces a present one; nature, though devoid of sensation, does this through a certain "inclination."

<margin>f</margin>
The senses do this through appetite; the Intellect through the **will**. Therefore, since God is—to speak in the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Referring to the followers of Aristotle.</note> manner—the First Being, who will deny that the Divine Intellect gladly embraces its own present good (which is the sum of all good) through the will?

<margin>E</margin>
Just as in His truth He sees all true things—which become true because He illuminates them—so in His goodness He wills all good things, which are born from His own spreading-forth and become good because He perfects them. Furthermore, a Being creates works by willing them rather than merely by seeing them. For by "seeing," He reflects the forms within Himself. By "willing," He unfolds them outward. By seeing, He regards the Truth, whose nature is purity.

<margin>G</margin>
By willing, He reaches the Good, whose nature is diffusion <note>The idea that goodness naturally wants to "spread itself out" and create more good.</note>. **The Third Reason.** The knowledge of the senses and the intellect—because it is something like an image within created beings—produces no substantial effect unless it is joined by "affect" <note>A movement of the soul or will toward something; a feeling of attraction or drive.</note>, which seems to be something essential; hence, the more vehemently one is affected, the more powerfully one acts.

<margin>H</margin>
This is indicated in a way by the **eye of the ostrich**, which is most greedily fixed upon its egg. <note>A common Renaissance belief held that ostriches did not sit on their eggs to hatch them, but rather used the intense "heat" of their focused gaze and "love" to bring the chicks to life.</note> If God’s intelligence is more effective in creating than the ostrich's gaze is in brooding—indeed, if it is of immeasurable effectiveness, as is clear from the fact that He needs neither a subject, nor an instrument, nor time for creating—we can surmise that the "affect of the will" is most powerful in the Divine Intelligence.

<margin>K</margin>
Add to this that it is also most delightful; for if intelligence is most perfect, and if it always and everywhere enjoys the most whole and perfect object, it must be most sweet. **The Fourth Reason.** Where there is no will (which is the mind’s inclination toward the good), there is no pleasure of the mind (which is the expansion of the will into the good and the resting of the will in the good).

<margin>L</margin>
If there is no pleasure there where the Good itself resides, then there will be pleasure nowhere, since pleasure occurs wherever it does because of the Good. Therefore, in the Good itself, there is both pleasure and will. If such an "affect" in creatures is a byproduct of generation, in the Creator himself it is surely the very origin of creation.

<margin>M</margin>
**The Fifth Reason.** If all agents—whether acting according to nature or according to art—always arrange their works toward an end (that is, toward the good), and by their own goodness...

<summary>Ficino argues that God creates the world not just through cold intelligence, but through a "Will" that chooses the best possible outcomes out of love for the Good. He uses the famous example of an ostrich hatching an egg with its gaze to illustrate how intense focus and desire (affect) lead to creative action.</summary>

...they do: they receive the orders for their operations from the first agent; and that is the Good itself.

<margin>A</margin>
# It is certain that He directs His works toward the best end.
If specific goods, because they are good and because they are ordered by the supreme Good, direct individual things toward some good, how much more will the universal Good direct all things to the universal Good? God, therefore, leads all things to Himself as their goal <note>In Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" or "goal" (Latin: *finis*) is the purpose for which a thing is created.</note>. For no goal of divine action exists outside of God. Because the goal

<margin>B</margin>
is located in the same rank as the one who acts toward that goal. It is itself a kind of good, and it moves the agent cause. Now, nothing is located in the same rank with God except God Himself. God does not serve any good other than His own. For the "Total Good" never serves a "particular good." Furthermore, God is not moved by anything else. If God's goal is His own goodness, then God, in His own way, desires and loves His goodness. Since God is both intellectual and His goodness is intelligible <note>Intelligible (original: *intelligibilis*): That which can be understood by the mind/intellect, rather than perceived by the physical senses.</note>, He loves it with an intellectual love. Such love resides in the **will**. God, therefore, **wills** Himself. He wills Himself, I say, as the end of Himself and of all things. From the will for the end comes the operation regarding those things which are directed toward the end.

<margin>C</margin>
# Therefore the divine will, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*, is the beginning of all creatures.
The same is read very often in Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure associated with a body of mystical and philosophical texts called the *Hermetica*, which Ficino translated and highly valued.</note>. For they believe that the most perfect principle of the universe ought to have the most perfect mode of action; that is, that by His **will** He is entirely the master of the act of making, just as He is entirely the master of the things made—a master disposing of them in His free will. For if He acted by necessity—whether of nature or of intelligence—He would act upon all things at once, and upon infinite things at once. He would also compel individual things and sweep them away in an instant.

<margin>D</margin>
## The will of God is at once necessary and free, and it acts freely.

-> Chapter 12 <-

<margin>☞</margin>
# I believe it has been sufficiently proven that God produces individual things not by the necessity of nature or of intelligence, but by the command of the will.
However, I believe it must now be demonstrated how His will is both necessary and free at the same time. <margin>☞</margin> The First Reason. Let everyone take the greatest care lest they accidentally fall into such reckless impiety as to ever suspect that God is, or operates, in a way that just happens by chance. If it never happens to any natural thing that its being or acting is by chance—for example, it does not happen to fire by chance, but by necessity, that it is hot and that it heats—it follows that for the supreme Being <term>Being (*ens*): the most fundamental state of existence.</term>, it is natural to be, and for the supreme Act <term>Act (*actus*): the state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to just having the potential to be.</term>, it is natural to act. It follows that God, who is the supreme Being—indeed, more than Being—and the supreme Act, exists or acts in no way according to contingency <note>original: *contingentiam*; the philosophical concept that something could either happen or not happen, or occurs by "luck."</note>. If where there is more reason, there is less chance, then in God, who is supreme reason or the fountain of reason, nothing accidental can be imagined. If fortune does not produce reason, since they are opposites (indeed, fortune is a deprivation or defect of reason), how then could it produce either God or any divine action that is superior to any reason? If God is that very rule and kingly orderer of all things, such that He removes all chance from the things that closely follow Him, how could it be that He Himself just happened to be or to act in a certain way? Therefore, God does not exist and act "as it happened," otherwise no order would ever be found anywhere; rather, He exists as it was fitting—or rather, as it is fitting. For what "is fitting" is what "was fitting." He Himself is Beauty <note>original: *decor*; can also mean "fitness," "appropriateness," or "grace."</note>, and it is He from whom and through whom all fitting things are made. Indeed, He is and acts as is necessary. He is necessary through necessity itself. But God is that very Necessity, through whom all other necessary things are necessary, whatever they may be. Therefore, God is as He is. He acts as He acts. And since no necessity stands above Necessity, there is the highest liberty there. Liberty is desirable as a good. In the supreme Goodness, there is whatever can ever be desired as a good. Whoever lives as he wills is free. Goodness itself lives as it wills above all others; every will desires its life, and no will desires anything except through it. God is that which He is, such that He could not have been anything other than what He is...

<summary>Ficino argues that God acts through a free and intellectual will rather than blind necessity or chance, directing all creation toward Himself as the ultimate "Good." He further explains that because God is the source of all reason and order, His existence is characterized by a "necessary freedom" where His will and His being are one.</summary>

# Theology, Book Two
### Signature C 3
<meta>catchword: Marsifici (referring to Marsilius Ficinus)</meta>

...I say: every being and every power; rather, He would not have wished [to be otherwise], because He is all good. 

<margin>b</margin> **To be able**, however, or to wish to possess oneself differently, would be weakness and ignorance tending toward old age—indeed, it would be a rush toward nothingness. **The second reason.** If the motivation for good in individual things is the most necessary and the most voluntary (and spontaneous) of all things, then certainly in the Good itself, the highest necessity of nature concurs with the highest liberty of the will, as we have proved elsewhere. And in that place, the necessity of nature confirms the liberty of the will, and liberty consents to necessity, to such an extent that God is necessarily free and voluntary, and voluntarily necessary.

**The third reason.** As long as something is, so to speak, devoid of the Good itself, it is displeased with itself and seeks something else beyond itself. But when it becomes a participant in the good, it then pleases itself and wills itself; it is then such as it wills to be. The more it attains this, the more it pleases itself, and the more it is such as it wills itself to be. Therefore, the Good itself possesses this above all: that it wills itself most greatly and pleases itself. And it is entirely such as it wills itself to be.

**The fourth reason.** If things become less servile and more <term>self-governing<note>original: "sui iuris". A legal term meaning "of one's own right," used here to describe the autonomy and freedom of a being.</note></term> the closer they approach God, then God is self-governing in the highest degree. Thus, He not only wills to be such as He is by His own nature, but He is entirely such as He wills to be. Furthermore, He does such things as He wills, and for the sake of whomever He wills. No agent would ever be the free principle of its own action, or prescribe the end <note>The "end" or "final cause" refers to the purpose or goal of an action.</note> for its action, unless the principle and end of the universe were the master of His own action and had established the end for His own action. But let us return to the proposition.

**The fifth reason.** In those things in which these three—namely, being, understanding, and willing—differ in reality from one another, there is no absolute liberty. This is because in things of this sort, the mode of willing follows the pattern of understanding, and the understanding follows the condition of being; finally, being follows the one who gave that being. But in God, being, understanding, and willing are the same in reality. For this reason, He is so much the master of His intelligence and His essence through His will that He not only wills as He is and as He understands by His own nature, but He also understands and exists just as He wills.

<margin>B</margin> Perhaps for this reason, the followers of **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino often cites Zoroaster as an ancient authority on "natural magic" and theology who prefigured Plato.</note> hand down the tradition that God, in a certain way, "acts Himself" <note>original: "agere semetipsum". This suggests God is the cause of His own existence, a radical claim about divine freedom.</note>. **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino was his primary translator and commentator in the Renaissance.</note> explained this in roughly the following manner: God is an act, not of another, nor concerning another, but of Himself and concerning Himself. For He is an act remaining within Himself. Since, however, the act is infinitely second <note>i.e., immediately follows from</note> because of the nature of the infinite good, He does not lack an act—that is, an infinite act that is begotten or performed. But since through an internal act something internal is made, and only God is infinite, that which is acted (that is, begotten) therefrom is within God and is God Himself.

<margin>L</margin> God is a vigilant and perpetual act, from Himself, in Himself, and entirely concerning Himself. Therefore, as He acts and is vigilant, so He exists. The entire effort of the divine act turns around itself. And while He leans upon Himself, He in a certain way "acts" Himself—that is, He begets Himself—because if He looked elsewhere, He would lose Himself. Therefore, divine being is an act directed toward itself, whereas not to be divine would be an act directed toward another. God wills Himself. To will, however, and to act—indeed, even to be—is entirely the same thing. Therefore, by willing Himself, He acts (that is, produces) Himself; indeed, He already places or marks Himself in being.

<margin>M</margin> From these things, **Plotinus** wishes to conclude that God does not exist as He perhaps happened to be, or as necessity compelled, but as He Himself is vigilant, acts, and wills. But let God Himself see to these things. We, for our part, wish only to affirm everywhere that which is worthy of God. Such is what we proposed before: namely, that in God, the highest liberty meets with the highest necessity. 

**The sixth reason.** Only divine goodness is the absolute object of the divine mind. For any power can be equal to its object, but can by no means exceed it. But nothing...

<summary>Ficino argues that God's will, being, and intellect are identical, meaning God is "self-governing" and exists exactly as He wills to be. He reconciles divine necessity with absolute freedom, citing Plotinus and Zoroaster to suggest God is a perpetual, vigilant act that "produces" His own being.</summary>

# Platonic

[nothing] is outside of God, for God cannot exceed himself. God wills himself by a certain absolute necessity of will. For all things necessarily will their own ultimate end. The divine goodness is God’s ultimate end, for the sake of which he wills whatever he wills. Therefore, one must either admit that God wills nothing—and thus lacks all "taste" or desire—which is absurd; or one must affirm that if he wills anything, he necessarily wills himself, especially since in God, **to be** and **to will** are the same. By willing himself, he wills all other things; as they exist within God, they are God himself; as they flow out from God, they are images of the divine face.

<margin>a</margin>
And these things are ordered toward reflecting and affirming the divine goodness as their chief end. But indeed, that act of the divine will—which is absolutely necessary insofar as it regards the divine goodness—is called by some "not absolutely necessary" insofar as it regards creatures. For although the will entirely and necessarily wills the end itself, it nevertheless wills those things which are directed toward the end by a certain **conditional necessity**; indeed, sometimes it wills them with no necessity at all, if the end can be possessed without them. However, the divine goodness has no need of creatures. **The seventh reason.** This leads to the point that by willing his own goodness, God wills other goods for no other reason than as images of that goodness. Since divine goodness is immense, innumerable images can be shaped according to its model—innumerable, I say, beyond those that are shaped in these ages. Therefore, if by the fact that he wills his own goodness, he necessarily willed each thing that could imitate it to exist, he would certainly will infinite creatures to exist, representing the divine goodness in infinite ways. 

<margin>ib</margin> <note>original: "ibidem," meaning "in the same place" or "referring to the same author."</note>
If he willed it, they would certainly exist. But in this matter one must remember, as it pleases our **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, the splendor of theology: although the act of the divine will, according to some condition 

---

# Book

or position, can be said to will this or that thing necessarily—namely, after he has once willed it, since the divine will is no less immutable than his essence—nevertheless, by its own nature, it does not have that relationship of **absolute necessity** toward its effects that it has toward itself. **The eighth reason.** If God is the perfect cause of being, and "being" is the proper effect of God, then God's act can expand itself at least as far as the potentiality of being can expand. This is especially true since passive potential must be led by a higher act; and in this kind of potentiality of being is contained whatever is not opposed to the <term>reason of being<note>original: "rationi entis." This refers to the fundamental logic or definition of what it means for something to exist.</note></term>. In the same way, in the potential of a corporeal nature, there are whatever things do not take away that corporeal nature. Nothing can be imagined that is 

<margin>C</margin>
repugnant to the reason of being except its opposite. That is: what is called "non-being." Contradiction alone includes the logic of non-being. Therefore, whatever things include no contradiction—as the <term>Peripatetics<note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they reportedly walked about while debating.</note></term> 

<margin>D</margin>
think—are included in the potentiality of being. And God can bring all those things to pass. This is confirmed by the fact that the mind, once contradiction is excluded, can stretch itself through the entire—indeed, through the immense—breadth of being. The creative power of God ought not to be less ample than the imagining power of the mind. Add to this: if the divine intellect perceives innumerable goods, and his will can turn itself toward all those things which the intellect offers as good, it follows that the will of God is not bound to finite objects. Therefore, his power 

<margin>E</margin>
also stretches to the infinite. To what purpose is all this? So that you may understand that whatever does not include a contradiction is subject to divine power. And since there are many things that do not exist in the nature of things, which nevertheless, if they did exist, would introduce no contradiction—which is especially evident regarding numbers and magnitudes...
