# Second Book of Theology

...and the distances between the stars: and let him know that most things are contained under divine power which, however, are never found in the natural order of things. And since God, of those things which he is able to do, does some and does not do others, he operates such things by no necessity of nature, intellect, or will, but by the free choice of his will. **The ninth reason.** Not without reason is God said to operate certain things by choice, so to speak. Indeed, all agents, whichever act through another and are led to act, must be reduced back to the first agent, which acts through itself in such a way that it leads itself to act. Therefore, it follows that he turns himself entirely toward his own action. Therefore, it follows that he understands and wills to work or not to work, and again to work in this way or otherwise. No one is ignorant that those things which proceed from God in this way proceed by free choice. Yet no wise man is ignorant that choice in God does not differ from his <term>essence</term> <note>In medieval theology, God's "essence" is what He is; because God is simple, His attributes like "will" or "choice" are not separate parts of Him but are identical to His very being.</note>.

<margin>❦</margin>
But lest someone should think by chance that the divine will, if it looks toward created things, brings force upon individuals: it is necessary to remember that the will of God prefers the good of the universe over the apparent convenience of any particular part. For in that universal good, the image of divine goodness shines more expressively; that good is seen to consist in a certain order. Exact order requires that all levels of things be contained in the universe, so that some are stable causes and some are mobile. And those which are mobile produce effects that are moreover more wandering and in a certain variable way. For the effects of proximate causes seem to imitate their own manner rather than that of more remote causes. God, however, wills not only the things themselves to exist, but also the "modes of being" which are required for them as a consequence. Since, truly, it is fitting for certain things—according to the mode of their nature—to be in some way <term>contingent</term> <note>Something is "contingent" if it can either happen or not happen, as opposed to "necessary" things which must be as they are.</note>, God chooses something—as certain theologians say—to happen in a certain way 

according to contingency. Yet nothing so transgresses that it either disturbs the order of the universe or escapes the <term>providence</term> <note>original: "providentiam" — the protective care of God as the spiritual guide of the universe.</note> of the Orderer.

---

### God Loves and Provides. Chapter 12.

<margin>☞</margin>
If God is pleased with himself, if he loves himself, surely he loves his own images and his own works. A craftsman loves his works which he made from external matter. He loves much more a son born, whom he generated from intrinsic matter <note>The author uses a physical analogy: a human father provides the "matter" for a child from his own body, though he originally "received" that matter by eating food from the outside world.</note>, although he received that matter first while he ate from elsewhere. God loves any of his works more ardently, since he did not receive the matter from elsewhere, but he himself created the very same matter which he also formed; by which it happens that he was both the sole cause and the cause of the whole work. If God loves his good works to such a degree, he wills for them that which he truly wills to follow. Therefore he disposes them well, and by his supreme goodness he disposes them most excellently. For just as fruitfulness and the inclination to act is implanted in all agents by the fruitfulness of the first agent, so diligence in guarding works is inserted in each by the primary diligence of the first agent—who is the steward, as it were, of all things as if they were his children. In whom, the greater the fruitfulness is than in others, the more diligent is his providence. Again, God does all things for his own sake: because if he acted for another end besides himself, the action of God would depend on that end. Therefore, the will to act would also depend on that same end. From this it follows that God himself would depend on it, since God and the will of God are one and the same. If he does all things for his own end and he himself is the supreme good, he disposes all things toward the good—as <term>Plato</term> <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BCE) was the Greek philosopher whose cosmology deeply influenced this text's view of a rational, ordered universe.</note> wills in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The "Timaeus" is a famous dialogue by Plato that explains the creation of the world by a divine craftsman (the Demiurge) who makes the world as good as possible.</note>—so that individual things, according to their nature, may grasp divine goodness. Furthermore, since all things desire the good, and the desire for the good is itself good, and therefore is from the first good itself from which all things are good, it follows that, attracted by divine goodness, the divine...

<summary>This page explains that God creates and governs the world through free choice and loving providence rather than out of necessity. It argues that God loves His creation more than any human father or craftsman could, because He is the source of both its form and its physical substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument for divine providence. Having established God’s free will on the previous page, the text now addresses how that will manifests in the physical world, specifically through the governance and harmony of conflicting natural elements.</meta>

# Platonic Book

<page-num>10</page-num>

...they desire goodness. Therefore, although someone might deny that God governs things, since He directs them toward a good end: how else could the <term>elements</term> <note>In ancient and medieval science, these are the four building blocks of the world: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> and the contrary members of the world—which by their very nature, form, or power are at war with one another—come together into one? And how could they remain joined for so long, exchanging their natures and motions with one another, unless they were held together by some more excellent power? Furthermore, if the governance of the world were left to these members that are contrary to one another, they would remain separated in their own places, balanced by their own weights, and would not mix. And even if they were to mix, they would do nothing other than be hot, cold, dry, moist, rare, or dense, and other things of that kind. They would establish no order of forms, figures, or <term>revolutions</term> <note>This refers to the circular movements of the planets and stars.</note>.

<margin>a</margin>
For even in the arts, the material does not create such an order, nor do the tools; only the thought of the craftsman does. And if the heavens in some way rule the elements, they do not rule in such a way that they themselves are not ruled from elsewhere. For such a great diversity of forms, powers, and motions in the heavens does not come from the celestial bodies themselves—which are by their own nature diverse and movable—but is directed into a single, stable order by a certain higher power that is entirely one and stable in itself. Finally, any natural agent—whether elemental or celestial—is both movable (and therefore needy and imperfect, always depending on something else) and acts by a necessity of nature with its whole being; therefore, it receives a measure and a method of acting that reaches a certain end through fixed steps from a certain heavenly ruler. For heat—whether according to its form or its power—simply dissolves everything everywhere; cold, however, condenses. Therefore, that the former dissolves so usefully and appropriately, and the latter condenses by a similar logic, and that they do this continuously and most orderly, they receive not from a simple nature, nor from chance, but from a higher cause. And because the <term>spheres</term> <note>The transparent shells believed to carry the planets and stars around the Earth.</note> depart from their present position by continuous motion and do not rest in themselves, they both exist and are moved by another, in whose power the "end" or purpose lies, for the sake of which they are moved and act. Indeed, the purpose necessarily precedes the motions toward that purpose by a certain intention.

Hence, **Aristotle** in his *Books on Divine Matters* <note>original: "libris diuinorum"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note> says: just as the order of the parts of an army toward one another and toward the whole proceeds from the order of the whole toward a single leader, so the order of the parts of the world toward one another and toward the whole depends on the order of the whole toward God. From this he concludes: just as the order of an army is in the general, so the order of the whole world is in the one God, the only prince of the world.

Furthermore, the parts of the world and any tiny bodies <note>original: "corpuscula"</note> travel toward a certain end through a most orderly path and the most suitable methods—either always or for the most part—in such a way that they perform their works as well as they can possibly be done, just as if they had the arts inside them, and indeed a most perfect art. In fact, they proceed with such wonderful logic that they surpass human art and reason. And since these bodies are themselves ignorant of their own motion, and therefore do not know how to prescribe for themselves the end toward which they tend—not by chance, but by necessity—yet they have a prescribed end (otherwise they would not travel toward this end more than any other), it is clear that a certain end is prescribed for them by another. They desire this end and are led toward it by his wisdom, just as **arrows are directed toward a target by the skill of the archer.**

Where then is this wisdom? If it is in the highest God, then God provides for all things, since He reconciles those things that fight against each other so they do not destroy one another, and He leads all things to the best ends. But if it is in any other thing below God—such as an angelic mind or a soul—know that God moves all things that are below Him. Therefore, if an angelic mind or a certain soul rules the world and leads it toward the good, it certainly does so only because it is led by God and by God’s power. For this reason, God is the first and highest ruler, who can provide for all things, since He can make all things through His intellect, as He is more excellent through His intellect...

Using the metaphor of an archer and his arrow, the text explains that natural bodies move toward purposeful ends not by their own intelligence, but by God's supreme wisdom.</summary>

# Theology

...to act as well as to contemplate: and to preserve what is already made. He also knows how to rule all things, if He was not ignorant of how to make them. Finally, He wills to govern and guard those things which are His own, which He Himself made, to which He does not grudge the gifts of being well, just as He did not grudge the gift of being. 

<margin>C</margin>
Furthermore, He governs everything with a marvelous ease. For He does not handle foreign materials received from elsewhere, but His own, which He makes Himself. He does not touch them from the outside, but moves them from within. For He is present in the innermost parts of all things. Nor does He labor over many things, but through His very being—which is the universal <term>hinge</term> <note>Latin: *cardo*. Ficino uses this term to describe God as the central axis or pivot upon which the entire structure of reality turns.</note> of all things—He turns the subsequent hinges: that is, essence, life, mind, soul, nature, and matter. 

<margin>D</margin>
And as a Platonist might say: through the specific hinge of each order, He turns that specific order itself; likewise, through one essence He turns all essences, through one life all lives, through [one] mind [all] minds, similarly through one soul individual souls, through nature all natures, and through matter all matters. Nothing resists His decree, because He surpasses all things by an immense interval. 

<margin>E</margin>
Divinely did Orpheus sing of the divine nature: "whirling a swift rush with an everlasting hinge." <note>Original: "ἀεναω στροφαλιγγι θοον ρομα δινευουσα" (*aenaō strophalingi thoon rhouma dineuousa*). This Orphic fragment illustrates the universe revolving around a divine center.</note> 

<margin>F</margin>
It is well known that in a living creature there is a certain nerve around the neck; those who pull it move all the animal's limbs at once, so that each part is moved by its own proper motions. Aristotle writes in his book *On the Universe* <note>Historically attributed to Aristotle, though now often considered "Pseudo-Aristotle," this text describes God as a puppet-master who moves the world without effort.</note> that the members of the world are moved by a similar pull from God; there he asserts providence most clearly. He also indicates this in the tenth book of the *Ethics* and in the *Physics*, where he proves that nature everywhere looks toward a certain and optimal end, and that her works are the works of an unerring intelligence. 

<margin>G</margin>
In Florence, we saw a <term>shrine</term> <note>Latin: *tabernaculum*. Here referring to a complex mechanical automaton or clockwork display, a marvel of Renaissance engineering.</note> made by a German craftsman, in which statues of various animals were connected to a single rod; by the movement of that rod alone, they were all driven at once with different motions: some ran to the 

---

# Book Three

right, others to the left; up and down; some rose from a sitting position, others bowed from standing; some crowned others, while others wounded others. The sounds of all kinds of crowds and the singing of birds were heard. And many other things happened there at once, and similar things followed, all by the single impulse of one rod. 

Thus God, through His very being—which is the same in reality as His understanding and His will, and which is a most simple center of all things from which, as we have said elsewhere, the rest are drawn out like lines—vibrates whatever depends on Him with a most easy nod. Therefore, let Lucretius the Epicurean be silent, who wishes the world to be made and carried along by chance. 

<margin>H</margin>
He thinks that the constant habit of a most beautiful order proceeds from an unstable and deformed lack of order, just as if someone thought wisdom were born from folly and light from darkness. Look here, Lucretius: whenever you move by chance without a plan or an intended goal, do you always proceed by a straight path to a certain and identical end? Not at all. You wander here and there. When you handle stones without art and a prescribed goal, do you then construct a building with perfectly ordered and interconnected walls, most beautiful to see and convenient to use? Not at all. Instead, it is a deformed and useless heap. 

Consider the plants and animals, whose individual members are so arranged that one is placed for the sake of the other. One serves the other. Certainly, if one part is removed, the whole structure almost dissolves. Finally, all the members are arranged for the sake of the whole compound. And the compound itself—namely, the plant and the animal—is equipped with suitable instruments for the necessary works of its own nature; food, places, and times are provided for all; the earth and water prepare elements for them. The heavens temper the waters and the earth. Finally, all parts of the world converge toward the single beauty of the whole world in such a way that nothing can be taken away and nothing added. If you were to say all this happened without any plan...

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book III of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." # Platonic Book

...to provide for trees and animals: would you have provided otherwise? Not otherwise, but not nearly so well. Therefore, a counsel better than your own counsel arranges these things. Otherwise, you would daily see many things lacking their own limbs, or their necessary tools missing everywhere. Likewise, you would see dogs born from mares, figs from apples, human limbs attached to lions, or the limbs of donkeys on men; stars falling; and stones ascending. But now, because the individual parts of the world arise from certain seeds, are endowed with distinct shapes, and seek and return to certain boundaries in a straight path, at fitting times and orders, most beautifully and conveniently:

<margin>C</margin>
it follows that they are moved in the same way as those things which are moved by human art and counsel. If in the same way, then they are moved by almost the same art and counsel—and by one so much more excellent as they are ordered more beautifully and stably. By "counsel," I mean not something ambiguous and changeable, but something deeply certain and sudden, acting by intuition rather than by <term>discourse</term> <note>discourse: the process of reasoning step-by-step from one conclusion to another. Ficino argues God doesn't need to "think through" problems; He sees the solution instantly.</note>. For if there is no delay in the work, nor any transgression or retraction anywhere, there is no ambiguity in the maker. We call this kind of intuition "counsel" through a certain metaphor, not because some things are investigated from others there, but because some things are made for the sake of others. Sluggish men are accustomed to deliberate over crafts. But he who perfectly masters an art deliberates no further. Instead, he acts by habit just as nature does by forms. If there is a most perfect art anywhere, it is certainly there from where this miraculous work of the world is arranged. You might perhaps place arts of this kind in a nature devoid of all sense. But I would say you yourself lack sense if you were so alienated from feeling that you did not perceive:

<margin>B</margin>
if even the tiniest earthly beasts feel, it is much more necessary for the whole world and the nature that crafts all things to have sense—a rational sense, I mean—if it orders its works more rationally than human reason. Long-standing habit diminishes our wonder. But if your parents had raised you from infancy with the house closed up on all sides, so that you did not see this miraculous beauty of the world before your thirtieth year: without a doubt, being then a new spectator of these things, you would have wondered so greatly that, however doubtful you were before, you could never doubt afterward that all things are made and ruled by the providence of a single, most wise craftsman. Let us therefore confess that it is necessary: since the parts and effects of the world proceed in a constant order, the world as a whole cannot proceed now, nor have come forth from the beginning, except through constancy and order. Finally, let us confess that the world is neither moved by its own accord without life, nor rolled for so long and so evenly without a most powerful life, nor with such order without a most wise mind, nor so excellently and conveniently without the

<margin>C</margin>
highest good. Rather, a certain single queenly life, excelling in power, wisdom, and goodness, leads the world toward the best, most providently, both from the beginning and continually. This is either the supreme God or the <term>handmaid</term> <note>handmaid: Latin "pedissequa," referring here to the "World Soul," which Platonists believed carried out God's will in the physical realm.</note> of the supreme God. If it is the supreme God, then God certainly provides. If it is the handmaid of God, God still provides, because the first principle acts for its own sake and moves all things. Divinely did Orpheus say of <term>Jove</term> <note>Jove: Jupiter. Ficino frequently uses the names of ancient gods as allegories for aspects of the one Christian God.</note>:

<margin>D</margin>
->**The beginning of all, and the end of all**<-
<note>original Greek: "πάντων μὲν ἀρχὴ πάντων δὲ τελευτή"</note>

that is, the parent, beginning, and end of all things. Therefore, if the life of the world provides, it surely provides having been led by God toward God’s end. Thus, all things are finally directed toward the goodness of God. And since this goodness has care for the whole of its work, it certainly neglects no parts. For the best state and condition of the entire composite consists of the individual parts.

<margin>E</margin>
Orpheus expressed this whole idea thus: 

->**You see all, and you hear all, and you distribute to all**<-
<note>original Greek: "πάντ' ἐσορᾷς καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούεις καὶ πάντα βραβεύεις"</note>

that is, you inspect all things within, you hear all things within, and you distribute all things. Since the entire framework of the world was established to be referred back to the grace of divine goodness, and the parts of the world are applied for the sake of that framework itself, there is in this whole work nothing at all...

<meta>This page concludes the second book of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." While the previous page’s metadata mentioned Book III, this specific leaf contains the closing arguments of Book II, focusing on the reconciliation of Divine Providence with human freedom. Ficino argues that God’s governance does not violate the nature of things but perfects them according to their own character.</meta>

# Theology: Book Two

Perfection should be sought, but only as much as suffices to indicate, according to its capacity, the more sublime perfection of the author. Nor should any specific perfection of a part be demanded in every part of the world; 
<margin>f</margin>
rather, one should look for what harmonizes with the other parts and benefits the whole. Thus, although some small part of the world’s condition may sometimes seem blameworthy when viewed by itself, if it is compared to the state of the whole, we will find that the world could not be better arranged than it is. Truly, the Creator of the universe does not refer the whole to any specific parts, but rather refers the parts to the whole. Deservedly, therefore, those things which in some places seem either evil or deformed regarding the parts, ultimately turn out to be good for the ornament of the whole. For this reason, in the writings of <term>Orpheus</term> <note>Orpheus: A legendary Greek figure credited with ancient mystical hymns that Ficino believed prefigured Christian truths.</note> God is called <term>eternal life and immortal providence</term> <note>original Greek: αίδιοσ ζωη και αθανατοσ προνοια</note>.

<margin>g</margin>
**Mercury** <note>Mercury: referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> says that this providence is the nurse of the human race. And **Plato**, in the fourth book of the *Laws*, says: God contains the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of all things; He encompasses everything and disposes each thing rightly. He is present and favorable to religious men, while He punishes the proud and the impious. Nor does Plato think that the freedom of our <term>choice</term> <note>arbitrij: often translated as "free will," referring to the capacity to judge and choose.</note> is taken away by divine providence; on the contrary, it is preserved. This appears in the fifth book of the *Republic*, as well as in the book *On Kingship* and in the *Critias*. This is because God does not act so much by knowing as by **willing**. Otherwise, He would have made all things at once, and would still be making them, and He would also be the maker of evil. Likewise, just as the future outcomes of things are "written" in the foreknowledge of God, so too are the causes of those outcomes and their modes of acting.

<margin>h</margin>
And just as our works are known to God, so too is our **will**, which is the cause and the free mode of acting of our works. For just as He foresees that you will do a certain thing, so He foresees that you will do it in that way—namely, voluntarily and freely. Therefore, if the divine foresight makes our works "necessary" by the very fact of its existence, it similarly makes necessary—that is, it confirms—the *mode* of acting, which is the freedom of our judgment. Since God, the regulator of all natures, bestows upon each thing, He does not take away the nature which He had given. Thus, while He rules all things, He rules each one according to its own nature: He leads the ascending elements to ascend, and the descending ones to descend. If He rules the movement of animals, because that movement is by its nature progressive, He contributes to their walking.

<margin>L</margin>
If He leads the heavens, which are by nature rotatable because of their roundness, He contributes to the span of their circuit. If He strikes the minds of men, which are freely rotatable upwards and downwards, He strikes them also **freely**, so that He allures them, does not drag them; He does not compel, but persuades. **Zoroaster** <note>Zoroaster: The ancient Persian prophet; Ficino viewed him as one of the "ancient theologians" (prisci theologi) who shared a single, ancient wisdom.</note> testifies to this: <term>the Father does not instill fear, but pours forth persuasion</term> <note>original Greek: πατηρ ου φοβον ενθροσκει, πειθω δε επιχεει</note>. But because the First Mover must prevail and dominate, He draws the minds (as Plato wishes) as if by a "compulsion" toward the good, so that they cannot *not* want the Good itself.

<margin>M</margin>
For all things necessarily will the **Good**, for the sake of which they will whatever they will; just as they necessarily do not want evil itself, for the sake of which they reject whatever they reject. For if the "adequate object" of our <term>appetite</term> <note>appetite: here, the natural drive or longing of the soul toward an object.</note> is the Good itself, then goodness is the very reason for the appetite to desire whatever it desires. Thus, in every thing it desires, it desires the Good no differently than the eye sees light in every color. And even if it desires to desire nothing further, it chooses this very vacation from desiring as something "good." The soul, therefore, is necessarily carried toward the Good. But because God must reserve for the soul its own proper nature, He leaves its judgment free, through which it may consult about things to be done in its own manner, and from many things proposed to itself, judge one to be better than another, and choose that which it deems more fit for attaining the Good.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book III of Ficino's masterwork. While the previous page concluded Book II's discussion on Providence, this section transitions into the metaphysical hierarchy of the universe, specifically the "five grades of being" that bridge the gap between material bodies and the Divine.</meta>

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici: **Book Three.**

## The descent occurs through five steps, just as the ascent was made; these steps are fittingly compared to one another. Chapter 1.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a figure holding a staff</note> We have ascended so far from the body into quality; from quality into the soul; from the soul into the angel; and from the angel into God—the one, true, and good author and ruler of all things. The <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Pythagoreans: Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the ultimate reality and that the soul was immortal.</note> call the body "multiplicity." Quality they call "multiplicity and one." The soul they call "one and multiplicity." The angel they call "one-multiplicity." Finally, God they call "the One." They say this because the body is indeterminate toward any specific form and is by its own nature endlessly divisible; they claim its matter would flow into infinity unless a form stopped it and united it. Quality contributes to defining matter by a specific form; it is in a certain way indivisible in itself, but becomes divisible through its mixing with the body. Another grade [the soul] defines matter by form, yet is divisible neither in itself nor through the contamination of the body, but is a "moving multitude." The angel is the receptacle of the <term>spheres</term> <note>spheres: In the geocentric model of the universe used in the Renaissance, these were the transparent shells that carried the planets and stars around the Earth.</note> and is an "immobile multitude." God is the "immobile unity" above the spheres; they say God is entirely indissoluble in Himself, because He is unity and stability itself.

Bodies, however, being composed of elements, are altogether dissoluble, since in them multiplicity overcomes unity and motion overcomes stability. But the angels, souls, spheres, and stars appear in a way to be dissoluble insofar as they have parts, yet they are actually indissoluble because in them unity and stability surpass multiplicity and motion. Here then is that "divine knot" by which God—as <term>Timaeus</term> <note>Timaeus: The main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name, which describes the creation of the world by a divine craftsman.</note> believes—preserves these things (which are dissoluble in themselves) as forever undissolved.

<margin>B</margin> So powerful is the gift of unity and stability itself that only in the lowest level of the universe does it seem to be surpassed by its opposites. Yet meanwhile, even there it somehow conquers, since it always preserves matter itself—though subject to infinite multiplicity and change—remaining in the unity of substance and permanent order. <margin>C</margin> And certainly God is Unity, as we have proved. He is also immobile, because He is neither moved by another (since nothing is stronger than He) nor by Himself (since He cannot change Himself for the better, as He is Goodness itself). Nothing moves itself toward the worse of its own accord. And if God were said to "flow" from one state to another, we would ask whether He attains anything new, or nothing at all. If He attains nothing new, then He has not changed. If He attains something new, then He did not possess all things before. That which does not possess all things is not God. 

Because God is everywhere, He does not change place; because He is the end of all things, He is not moved toward anything else; because He is most simple, He is immobile even within Himself. For if He were moved within Himself, He would either move one part of Himself toward another, or at least He would join certain new things within Himself to the old. For He would be, in substance, what He was before, while additionally putting on a new form, and thus could not be most simple. Finally, God is Unity itself. Unity is the foundation of stability. Because just as motion proceeds into multiplicity, so stability relies upon unity. For that thing in any nature is said to "stand" [be stable] which possesses a single continuous condition in such a way that it does not depart from the unity of its nature. But who would say the foundation of all stability is mutable? We can confirm these types of reasons through the <margin>D</margin> argumentation of the Pythagorean number. Whatever, it says, is changed according to past and future, has a certain admixture of "privation" <note>privation: A philosophical term for the absence of a quality or the "not-being" of something.</note>; for the future is not yet, and the past is no longer. But in God, since He is the first being and the highest act, there is no privation; He is therefore immutable. The angel is also immobile, since from God [it receives] of all goodness...

<summary>Ficino begins Book III by defining the five-step hierarchy of existence—Body, Quality, Soul, Angel, and God—emphasizing God as the immobile and indissoluble Unity at the summit. He argues that the higher grades of reality are characterized by stability and unity, while the lower material grades are characterized by motion and multiplicity.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysical hierarchy, five grades of being, Pythagorean philosophy, immutability of God, Timaeus, divine knot, stability vs motion, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

--- Page 91 ---
<meta>This page continues Book III, Chapter 1, of Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. Having established the five grades of being (Body, Quality, Soul, Angel, God) on the previous page, Ficino now moves into a technical metaphysical analysis of why the Angelic Mind, while high in the hierarchy, is not identical to God. He introduces the Aristotelian and Platonic concepts of "act" (actuality) and "power" (potentiality) to explain the composition of these spiritual beings.</meta>

# Theology

### [Book] Three

<margin>E</margin> From the fountain of unity <note>original: "enitatis fonte." This refers to the Source of Being or the One.</note>, he draws the good through himself without any intermediary; he is filled from a single point of eternity and remains forever most full of goodness. However, since every effect produced outside of its cause retains something of that cause and yet turns out inferior to the cause, the angel created nearest to God retains something of God and loses something. God possesses both **unity** and **stability**. The angel cannot retain both; for then he would be God himself, not an angel. Nor does he lose both, lest the work closest and first to God should turn out most unlike its maker. What then? Will he retain unity alone, or stability? He cannot have unity alone without stability, for unity itself is altogether immobile. Therefore, he will retain **stability**, but he will fall away from simple unity, so that the angel is an **immobile multitude**. <margin>f</margin> Nor do we assign multitude to the angel without reason. For if there were perfect and most absolute unity, there would be supreme and unbounded power, since virtue consists in unity. Such unbounded power is God himself alone.

Furthermore, if it is the property of a body to receive and to suffer <note>To "suffer" here means to be acted upon or to undergo change (passion).</note>, it is the property of an incorporeal nature to give and to act. In a corporate nature, there is said to be "power"—specifically, as the theologians say, a **receptive and passive power**. <margin>g</margin> In an incorporeal nature, there is **act**, <margin>h</margin> that is, the efficacy for acting. Therefore, quality—which in a certain way is incorporeal in itself—has some force for acting, whence it is also named "act." But because it is received into and divided by matter, and thus becomes in some way corporeal, it is not a "pure act," but is stained by the "passion" (the receiving nature) of the body. It is certain, then, that quality consists of both **act** and **power**.

Although the soul is separable from matter and is thus called an "act" and is foreign to the passion of the body, it is nevertheless not yet a "pure act." For it is mobile. If something moves, it acquires through that motion something <margin>i</margin> which it previously lacked; insofar as it lacked it, it has that power which we call **receptive** and, in a sense, **passive power**.

# [Book] Three

By moving, it achieves something: it is an "act," and while it acquires something, it is also made into an "act." Therefore, the soul is composed of **power** and **act**. <margin>J</margin> But is the angel then a "pure act"? Not at all. Clearly God is, for He is entirely distant from matter, in which there is passive power without any virtue for acting. Thus, God is understood to be **pure vigor of acting**, separate from the nature of receiving and suffering. If God is "pure act," the angel cannot be such. For that which is one in itself never becomes many except through the addition of a foreign nature. The nature and definition of "pure act" is unique; it is in God as the Father. But if it is also said to be in the angel, we must ask: is there something else in the angel besides "act," or not? If there is nothing, then only one "pure act" remains, since the "act" attributed to the angel does not differ from the "act" of God. If nothing is in either besides "act," then the "act" itself is by its own definition one. But if something is added to the angel besides "act," the angel is no longer "pure act," but is infected by mixture—not an absolute act, but rather "this kind" or "that kind." Just as a light that is green or red is not "pure light," but is light and at the same time some quality of the elements through which it becomes red or green. <margin>K</margin> Wherefore the angel is also composed of **act** and **power**.

This is what Plato means in the *Philebus* <note>Plato's *Philebus* is a dialogue concerning the nature of pleasure and the good, where he discusses the "Fourfold Division" of reality.</note> where he says: God is the limit <term>terminus</term> <note>terminus: A boundary or defining limit that gives form to the formless.</note> of all things, devoid of the infinite. All other things, however, besides Him, He composes from the **limit** and the **infinite**. He calls "act" the **limit**, and "power" the **infinite**, which is in itself indeterminate but is limited and formed by the "act." But to come to the point: the power of the angel is in his essence, which in a certain way exists from God before it is formed by God. For in the first moment of his creation, the angel simply *is*; in the next, he is illuminated by his author so that he may be intelligent, and thus he is "formed." Therefore, that essence is in the beginning in some way formless, and acts as a passive subject.

<summary>Ficino explains that only God is "Pure Act" and absolute Unity; the Angel, while stable and spiritual, is a "composite" of actuality and potentiality, which Plato described as the Limit and the Infinite.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Act and Power, Pure Act, Immobile Multitude, Philebus, Neoplatonism, Angelic Hierarchy, Divine Unity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the third book of Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', specifically focusing on the hierarchy of being. Having defined the five levels—God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Body—Ficino here explains the specific metaphysical "ingredients" of the first three. He uses the 'Chaldean Oracles' (attributed to Zoroaster) to provide ancient authority for the idea that the Divine Mind (the Angel) is a 'second' level of reality following the absolute unity of the Father (God).</meta>

# Platonic Theology: Book Five

...is set forth for the act of understanding and for receiving the adornment of forms and ideas, regarding which **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino, like many Renaissance scholars, attributed the 'Chaldean Oracles' to the ancient Persian prophet Zoroaster. These texts were central to his attempt to harmonize Pagan philosophy with Christianity.</note> says:

> **For the Father perfected all things and delivered them to the second mind.**
<note>original Greek: "παντα γαρ εξετελεσε πατηρ και νω παρεδωκε δευτερω." This refers to the relationship between the first principle (the Father/God) and the first created intellect (the Angel).</note>

That is: the Father perfected all things and offered them to the second mind. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, the angel is a **multitude**, since it consists of many things. It is, I say, an **immobile multitude**. In this respect, it is certainly lower than God, because it is not a true unity like God. Yet in another respect it approaches Him, because it is almost—if I may put it this way—immobile like God. Rightly, then, after God, who is **immobile unity**, is placed the angel, who is **immobile multitude**.

After the angel comes the **soul**, which is even further removed from God because it is a **mobile multitude**. It is indeed a multitude, <margin>B</margin> since nothing after God can be a most simple unity. It is in some way mobile because, receding further from God, it becomes close to the qualities of bodies, which are entirely in motion. If it were completely immobile, it would surely be an angel. If it were completely mobile, it would be a quality. Yet there must be some middle ground between the angel and the qualities of bodies, lest the completely immobile angel be too close to the completely mobile quality.

Let the soul, therefore, be partly immobile and partly mobile. Its **substance** will remain stable; it will not change into more or less, nor into this or that. However, its **operation** will flow; it will act now in this way, now in another, differently and yet again differently. **Quality** is lower than the soul, since it is changed both through its essence and its operation. Lower than quality is the **body**. For quality is moved and also moves, for it moves bodies. The body is indeed moved, but it moves nothing.

The angel indeed possesses the fact that it is a certain "one" and that it is an **act** <note>term: act — in Aristotelian and Platonic terms, this refers to a state of being fully realized and active, as opposed to 'potential' which is the capacity to become something.</note> not from itself, but from God, who is truly One and the most pure Act. But the fact that it is manifold, through the power of receiving and undergoing <note>term: undergoing (passivity) — the capacity to be acted upon or changed by a higher force.</note>, it has from itself, insofar as being brought forth outside of God, it falls away from the perfection of its producer. Therefore, multitude is natural to the angel. The soul also receives the fact that it is a single substance and a stable act through its essence not from itself, but from God, the most stable act of union. But that it is manifold and passive, it possesses from itself, because it is located beneath God. Finally, that it is mobile, it possesses again from itself, <margin>C</margin> because it is located beneath the angel.

Therefore, just as unity is natural to God and multitude to the angel, so **motion** is natural to the soul. The light of God produces the angel under God’s "shadow," as it were; the light of God produces the soul under the shadow of the angel. The angel gains stable unity from the single act of God; falling under the shadow of God, it slips into multitude. The soul obtains its state from the light of God; under the shadow of God it finds multitude, and under the shadow of the angel it finds change.

God is the **fountain of unity**. The angel is the **fountain of multitude**. The soul is the **fountain of motion**. God is unity through Himself. The angel is one through God, but manifold through himself. The soul is one through God; through the shadow of God—that is, because it exists simultaneously with the angel under God—it is manifold through itself and mobile. **Quality** possesses the ability to move something through those things above it. It possesses through itself the fact that it is mixed with matter. The **body** possesses the ability to act through quality; through itself alone, it has only the capacity to be acted upon.

Quality exceeds the body by one degree, because it moves the body. It yields to the soul by at least one degree, because it is moved by the soul. The soul exceeds quality by at least one degree, because it is moved by itself. It yields to the angel by one degree, because it is changed; the angel exceeds the soul by one degree, because it remains stable. The angel yields to God by one degree, because it is manifold. God, however, through this "One," transcends all things into the infinite. <margin>D</margin> Regarding this, **Zoroaster** sang thus:

> **So he snatched himself away, and did not shut up his own fire in his intellectual power.**
<note>original Greek: "ωστ’αρ εαυτον εχασεν ουδ’ενει δυν’αμει νοερα χλεασας ιδιον πυρ." Ficino interprets this to mean that God's essence is so transcendent that it cannot be fully contained even by the highest Mind or Angel.</note>

That is: the Father snatched himself away, and did not include his own fire even in the mind that follows him. It is as if he were to say that He has no comparison with the rest. The body is moved only by another; it does nothing of a being by its own nature. Quality moves another and is moved by another. The soul indeed moves another, but is moved by itself. The angel moves others—that is, it acts upon others—while remaining stable itself; but it is not stable through itself. For it stands through the divine <margin>E</margin> unity. For what else is it "to stand"—as we have said—than to persevere in the unity of one's own nature? Which also happens through God.

<summary>Ficino explains the ontological hierarchy where God is Immobile Unity, the Angel is Immobile Multitude, and the Soul is Mobile Multitude. He uses the metaphor of 'shadows' to explain how each level of being loses a degree of perfection as it emanates further from the divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Hierarchy of Being, Marsilio Ficino, Chaldean Oracles, Zoroaster, Neoplatonism, Immobility, Multitude, Soul, Angel, God, Emanation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', Book III, Chapter 2. Having previously established the hierarchy of being, Ficino now focuses on the third level: the Soul. He is specifically defining the Soul as the "first movable" thing, bridging the gap between the eternal stability of God/Angels and the passive sluggishness of physical bodies.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>S</margin>
For by the power of the first act, all agents do whatever they do. God moves and acts upon all things through Himself; He is indeed stable through Himself. Truly, because all things that are such through another are traced back to some first thing that is such through itself—therefore, whatever things are stable and moving through another, we trace back to God, who is stable through Himself and moves through Himself. And whatever things are movable by another—namely, bodies and qualities—we have referred to the **soul**, which is movable through itself. I say "movable through itself" because if you descend from God through the angel, both God and the angel will seem to you to stand still. 

<margin>f</margin>
The first movable thing you encounter is the soul. Whatever is first of its kind in any category is such through itself; for example, that which is primarily bright or hot shines and heats through itself. Thus the soul, since it is the **first movable** <term>primum mobile: here referring to the first thing in the hierarchy of existence that possesses the capacity for change or motion</term> among all things that are movable, is certainly movable through itself. A sign of this is that bodies lacking a soul are moved only by an external impulse, whereas those that have a soul move by their own accord and toward any part of space. 

And since the soul grants to bodies the ability to move in some way toward any part, it follows that the soul itself is truly and primarily movable through itself, the first movable. 

<margin>C</margin>
Since through the soul's presence there appears in the body some image of a self-moving faculty, and since there is motion in every direction, this signifies that the soul is the **fountain of motion**. From it flows a free and universal agitation. 

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>d</margin>
Through these points, I believe that Pythagorean riddle used by **Xenocrates** <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato and the third head of the Academy; his definition of the soul as a "self-moving number" was famous in antiquity.</note> is solved: namely, that the soul is a **self-moving number**. By "number," he means a manifold nature; by "self-moving," he means changeable by its own inherent property. 

<margin>S</margin>
That such a nature must exist somewhere is now made clear to us by many signs, as we have indicated. **First**: because everything that is "such" through another must be reduced to something that is "such" through itself. **Second**: because since there are many things moved by another, if all things were like that, we would either wander into infinity or revolve in the same circle 

<margin>E</margin>

# Book Three

<margin>¶ 4</margin>
—so that the same thing would be both the first mover and the last effect, the cause and the result being identical, and there would be no order in things. Therefore, we are compelled to arrive at some mover who is no longer moved by another. But that mover who immediately precedes bodies (which are moved by another) is not entirely immobile. For these two are too far apart: that which is movable by another, and that which is entirely stable. Between them, there is a **middle**: that which is changeable from within itself. 

**Third**: because if a thing is moved better the closer it is to the mover, and if an "optimum motion" is to be reached, there must be something in which the essence of the movable and the essence of the mover are the same. 

**Fourth**: because if something is to be moved, either the mover must turn toward the movable thing, or vice versa, or both in turn. If nature were granted only angels/God on one hand and bodies on the other, this "turning" would not happen. The former will not approach because they are immutable; the latter will not approach the former because they are naturally sluggish. Therefore, there would be no motion at all in the world. 

It is necessary, then, that there be a certain nature that is changeable of its own accord. By approaching sluggish bodies through itself, it may rouse them; it experiences within itself the same ever-watchful cycles that it produces in bodies. Thus, just as a bodily substance is produced by a spiritual substance, so too is **bodily motion** produced by **spiritual motion**. 

<margin>b</margin>
I believe Plato understood this in the *Laws* <note>Referring to Book X of Plato's Laws, where he argues that self-motion is the definition of the soul and the cause of all other motions.</note> when he says: "If all things now stood still, and a moment later something had to be moved, what would be moved first? Clearly, that which is agile toward motion through itself, being closer to the power of moving; the rest of the things subject to motion would follow its lead." He calls this the **fountain** and the **principle of motion** in the *Phaedrus*. <note>In the Phaedrus, Plato argues that the soul is immortal because it is a self-mover, and a self-mover is the starting point (arche) of motion for all other things.</note> It is a "fountain" because it has motion from itself; it is a "principle" because it pours it into others. 

But here a doubt arises: if God and the Angel move anything, and the soul is subject to them, it is surely agitated by them. How then is it moved by itself? Let us answer...

<summary>Ficino defines the soul as the "first movable" and the "fountain of motion," acting as the necessary metaphysical bridge between the immobile God and passive physical matter. He interprets the Pythagorean definition of the soul as a "self-moving number" to mean a manifold spiritual nature that possesses inherent, spontaneous activity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', Book III, Chapter 2. On the previous page, the soul was defined as the 'first movable' thing. Here, Ficino uses the metaphor of a painter to explain how the soul’s activity occurs in time, even though it is sparked by eternal things.</meta>

# Platonic Book

<margin>A</margin>
...in this manner. When a painter, let us call him Apelles <note>Apelles was the most famous painter of ancient Greece; Ficino uses him as a classic example of human creativity.</note>, undertook to paint a meadow, he attempted to depict it in colors upon a panel. The meadow indeed showed itself to him all at once. And suddenly, the desire of Apelles was ignited. The demonstration of this kind of act and its approach can be called an "act" insofar as it does something. But it is by no means a "motion," because it is not completed bit-by-bit. For **motion** is an act running through moments of time. However, the "act" of painting itself, which occurs in Apelles, is called **motion** because it is carried out gradually: for at one moment he looks at one flower, and at another moment another, and he paints them similarly. The meadow certainly causes the soul of Apelles to see it and desire to paint it, but this happens suddenly. However, the fact that now one blade of grass and now another is seen and expressed through diverse moments of time is not caused by the meadow itself, but by the soul of Apelles. It is the nature of the soul not to look upon and represent various things simultaneously, but rather bit-by-bit. Therefore, of this motion which is in the seeing and the painting, the meadow is both the beginning and the end. For from there the painter's consideration began, and his desire tends toward the same place. But the fountain through which such an act occurs gradually and in time—and is thus called "motion"—is the soul of the painter himself.

<margin>B</margin>
Similarly, among the Platonists, the rational soul thinks of—or rather, divines—God and the Angel by a certain perpetual light, and it desires to paint itself in their likeness, both through contemplation and through morals and action. By forming itself bit-by-bit, it moves itself. This motion flows from the nature of the soul itself, as if from its own fountain of motion—specifically, temporal operation. However, it is incited by higher things...

<margin>C</margin>
...as if from an external beginning and end. The infusion that flows from higher things into the soul is one, stable, sudden, and eternal. And as far as it is within its power, it also works similar things in the soul—that is, sudden, stable, and eternal things. However, the fact that the operations of the soul and its works happen gradually in time and are changed proceeds from the soul's own nature, which is weaker than the higher things. But take this whole matter by means of an example. 

The Sun has light from within itself. It infuses that light into Mercury <note>In the cosmology of Ficino's time, planets were thought to receive their light from the sun; here Mercury represents the Angelic mind.</note> in an instant. Mercury also receives its whole light in an instant and remains thereafter always completely full. The same Sun infuses light into the Moon <note>The Moon represents the human soul, which changes and has phases.</note> in an instant. But the Moon does not receive it in an instant, but over time. For as it turns toward the sun in different ways, it receives light in different ways, and by its own nature, it is varied by the fluctuation of light. The Sun signifies God. Mercury signifies the Angel. The Moon signifies the Soul. What I say about Mercury, understand to be said similarly of all the stars above the Moon. For just as they are referred to the Sun, so the Angels are referred to God. But the soul alone is to God as the Moon is to the Sun. Therefore, nothing prevents the soul from descending from divine things and grasping divine things, while still being moved by its own nature, and being able to always move and live.

The soul is the middle grade of things, and it connects all grades—both the higher and the lower—into one, while it both ascends to the higher and descends to the lower.

### Chapter 3

<margin>D</margin>
**F**urthermore, so that we may eventually arrive at what we desire, let us again collect all things into five degrees: placing God and the Angel at the height of nature, and Body and Quality <term>Quality: in Aristotelian/Platonic philosophy, "quality" (like heat or color) was considered a separate level of reality from the physical body itself</term> at the bottom. 

<margin>E</margin>
Between those highest things and these lowest things, we place the Soul as the middle. Which we rightly name, in the Platonic custom, the **third essence** and the **middle essence**, since it is middle to all things and is "third" from every direction. If you descend from God, you find it at the third degree of descent. Likewise, at the third degree of ascent if you rise above the body; we judge this kind of essence to be exceedingly necessary in nature.

<margin>F</margin>
For since the Angel—as the Platonists say—"truly is" (that is, it stands forever), and Quality "becomes" (that is, it is moved at some time), Quality therefore differs entirely from the Angel: first, because the former is moved while the latter remains; and second, because the former "becomes" at a certain time, while the latter "is" always. Therefore, there is a need for a middle thing, which is partly with the Angel and partly with Quality...

<summary>Ficino explains the Soul's role as the bridge between eternity and time using the metaphors of a painter (Apelles) and the celestial bodies (Sun, Mercury, Moon). He establishes the Soul as the "Third Essence," the central pivot in a five-level hierarchy of existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', Book III. Following the discussion of how the soul acts in time despite its eternal sparks, Ficino now moves to define the soul’s ontological status as the "Third Essence" or the "Center of Nature," serving as the necessary bridge between the eternal divine and the temporal material world.</meta>

# Theology Book Three

...agrees with quality. What of this: does that which is internally the same ever remain so? No. For such a thing is not found. For whatever remains the same internally for any length of time—whether by its own power or by the state of its primary matter—remains so forever. Therefore, there shall be a middle thing: that which is always becoming the same and yet moves. Because this thing exists forever, it is compatible with the <term>angel</term> <note>In Ficino’s hierarchy, an Angel is a pure, immobile intellect existing entirely outside of time.</note>; but because it moves alongside quality, it follows that there must be a **third essence** <note>original: "essentiā tertiā"; this is the Soul, the middle rank of Ficino's five-level reality (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter).</note> which is the middle of these things. This essence is always moved and lives, and by its own motion, it diffuses life into bodies.

<margin>a</margin> It is rightly said by the Platonists: above that which exists in a part of time, there is that which exists through all time. Above that, again, is that which exists through <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "euū" (aevum). For Platonists, this is a state of "ever-present" time, distinct from the linear time of humans.</note>. Finally, above that, Eternity itself exists. But between those things which are solely eternal and those which are solely temporal, the Soul exists as a kind of **bond** between both.

<margin>b</margin> Indeed, in this matter, the parts of the world-body are in some way similar. There are those who place the **empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the physical universe.</note> in eternity because it is entirely immobile. However, they place the other spheres in both eternity and time simultaneously, and finally, composite things in time alone.

<margin>c</margin> Similarly, they place pure intellects in the first rank. But they place the "soul-intellects" in the second rank. Finally, they place the corporeal souls in the third.

<margin>d</margin> But to return to the proposal: every work that consists of many parts is then most perfect when it is so glued together from its members that it becomes one thing throughout; it stands consistent with itself and harmonizes, and is not easily pulled apart. Physical nature clearly demonstrates this in the tempering of the four elements: where earth and fire, which are far apart, are coupled together through the means of air and water.

<margin>e</margin> Much more so in the universal work of God must a connection of parts be established, so that there is one work of the one God. For the <term>Angel</term> and the **Body** are the extremes in nature, and they are most diverse from one another.

<margin>f</margin> The Angel does not bind these. Truly, it is raised entirely toward God and neglects bodies. By right, the most perfect and nearest creature of God becomes entirely divine and passes into God.

<margin>g</margin> Quality also does not connect the extremes: for it declines toward the body and leaves behind higher things. In its abandonment of incorporeal things, it becomes corporeal. Thus far, all things are extremes, and the supernal and infernal things flee from each other, lacking a competent bond.

---

<margin>h</margin> However, that **third essence** placed between them exists in such a way that it holds onto higher things and does not desert the lower. And thus, in it, the higher things are gathered with the lower. For it is immobile, and it is also mobile. On one side it agrees with the higher things; on the other, with the lower. If it agrees with both, it desires both. Therefore, by a certain natural instinct, it **ascends to the higher** and **descends to the lower**. And while it ascends, it does not desert the lower things; and while it descends, it does not leave the sublime. For if it were to desert either one, it would decline toward the other extreme, and it would no longer be the true "knot" or coupling of the world.

<margin>i</margin> Indeed, it does exactly what air does when it is the middle between fire and water. Air agrees with fire in heat and with water in moisture. In the first case, it is always hot with the fire; in the second, it is moist with the water. There it is thinned and becomes clear like fire; here, in turn, it becomes dull like water. Better yet, it does what the light of the sun does. For that light descends from the sun into the air and fills the air, yet it does not desert the sun. It always clings to the sun. It always fills the air. It perfects the air indeed; and though the air is stained, the light is not stained. Similarly, it is necessary for the **third essence** to cling to divine things and fill mortal things at the same time. While it clings to the divine, because it is spiritually united to them—and spiritual union gives birth to knowledge—it knows them. While it fills bodies, it moves them from within and gives them life. Therefore, it is the **mirror of divine things** and the **life of mortals**, the connection of both.

<margin>k</margin> But how is it joined to bodies? Does it perhaps, when it enters a body, touch one specific point of that body? And is it said to be united to bodies in that way? Not at all. For it would then be united to a point, not to a body, and it would not give life to that whole body; instead, only one point would live while the rest of the body lacked life. Indeed, if it always remained gathered into a single point and thus united to itself, it would be the same as an Angel, who is far removed from the body. Or at least, it would cling to divine things in such a way that it would leave bodies behind. Therefore, it would not be the [knot] of the universe... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is the "Third Essence" and "Bond of the World," acting as a necessary intermediary that links the eternal, divine realm of angels with the temporal, decaying realm of physical bodies. He uses analogies of the elements and sunlight to explain how the soul can inhabit both realms simultaneously without losing its divine nature.</summary>

<keywords>third essence, bond of the world, vinculum mundi, empyrean heaven, four elements, spiritual union, microcosm, Ficino, Platonic hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', Book III. Following the previous discussion of the soul as a bridge between eternity and time, Ficino now explains how the soul can be present in the whole body without being physically stretched or divided like a material property.</meta>

# Platonic Book

...is joined at least by a point of the body,
but by many; and thus it fills the parts of the body.
But does it fill it in the same way that **whiteness** fills
white flesh? Not at all, as if a quality
appropriates matter to itself. For then it
would be the same as a quality, and having left behind
divine things, it would sink entirely into the body. Whiteness
is in the whole flesh in such a way that it is equally
extended and divided into many parts along with the flesh.

<margin>a</margin>
And a part of whiteness, according to the **physicists** <note>Ficino refers to the Aristotelian natural philosophers who taught that physical accidents (like color) are divided when the substance they inhabit is divided.</note>,
exists in a part of the flesh. In a larger part of the flesh,
there is a larger part of whiteness; in a smaller, a smaller part.
Thus whiteness is made corporeal. The same would happen to
that essence—which we consider the **third essence** <note>The Soul, which occupies the third rank in Ficino’s five-fold hierarchy of reality (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter).</note>—if it were poured into the body in no other way than that quality.
And thus, dragged down to the other extreme of nature, it
would cease to be the **bond of the world**. Therefore, when it
enters the body, it is present as a **whole** to every single
particle of the body; it is neither divided nor distracted
into any parts, even though it stands by parts of the body
that are distant from one another. For it touches the body
through an **indivisible power**, not through the breadth of
quantity. Therefore, remaining whole and simple, it is
present as a whole and undivided to every single part.
Just as a whole **voice** and its meaning is, in a way,
simultaneously in every single part of a house,
since nearly the whole thing is heard and understood
at once by everyone. Nor is it impossible for this
essence—since it is an indivisible thing existing in itself—
to be present as a whole to the vast mass of the body.
Rather, indeed, because it is both indivisible and not closed
in by space,

<margin>B</margin>
it can, as a whole, penetrate and comprehend the whole of
whatever is in that space. For the **extension of quantity**,
wherever it is found, prevents such power and presence,
so that a thing extended through quantity cannot be a whole
simultaneously in several places. Furthermore, even a thing that
is indivisible, but nevertheless fixed somewhere to the
body's quantity—like a **point** which marks a line as its
boundary—cannot be present as a whole through any parts
of the body. Thus a point that is designated somewhere on a
certain line of a circle is neither in all the other lines

---

nor is it spread through the whole line or the circle.
But the **point** which is the **center of the circle**,
belonging to no specific line, is found in a certain way
in all lines that are drawn from there to the circumference.
And while no point designated on the circumference
regards the whole circle equally, the **center**,
which is properly fixed to no part of the circumference,
looks equally upon the entire circle. Therefore, that thing
which is divisible cannot be present as a whole

<margin>C</margin>
simultaneously in several places; nor can that thing which,
though it be indivisible, has a fixed position in another divisible thing.
But that **third essence** is neither extended
(as a quality would be) nor situated anywhere within extension;
for it would not move by itself and freely if it did not
subsist through itself. Therefore, it is like a certain point
living in itself and entirely absolute from all quantity and position.
Therefore, it equally encompasses every position of the body;
and when it enters the body, because it is not a point
belonging to any quantity, it is not bound to any single
point of corporeal quantity. Indeed, since it is outside the
genus of quantity, it does not limit itself to touching some
point of quantity, but is like the center in all lines
and the whole circle. From this it also follows that
this essence is simultaneously **divisible** and **indivisible**.
Divisible: because through the division of the body it
diffuses its own **vital shadow** <note>original: "vitalem sui vmbram"; the soul's lower functions or influence that animates the physical matter.</note> and communicates itself to
the diverse parts of the body. Indivisible: because it
stands by as a whole and simple. It is divisible, I say,
because its shadow is in the whole divisible body.
It is indivisible because it is itself, in an indivisible
manner, whole in any part of the body. Again, it is
indivisible because it has a stable and united substance.
It is divisible because it is divided into many through its
operation, while it works through motion and time.
Thirdly, it is indivisible because it looks up to higher things,
which are unified. It is divisible because it declines
toward lower things, which are more

<margin>D</margin>
divided. Such a nature is seen to be most necessary in the
order of the world, following after God.

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul (the "Third Essence") is present in the body not as a material quality like color, but as an indivisible power similar to the center of a circle or a voice in a room. This allows the soul to animate every part of the body simultaneously without being physically divided itself.</summary>

# Theology

# Third [Book]

->D 2<-

...and the **angel** <note>In Ficino's hierarchy, the Angel represents pure, static intellect that does not change over time.</note>: who are divided neither according to time nor according to dimension. Above the body and the qualities—which are dissipated by time and dimension—there must be a suitable medium. This [medium] is divided in a certain way by **temporal progression**, yet it is not divided by physical dimension. Neither does it always remain gathered in its own nature like those [the angels], nor is it torn into parts like these [bodies and qualities]; rather, it is at once both **indivisible and divisible**. 

<margin>E</margin>
This is that very essence which **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whom Plato uses as the main speaker in his dialogue, the *Timaeus*.</note> and **Plato** (in the book *On the World* <note>original: "lib. de mundo", referring to the *Timaeus*.</note>) said consists of an indivisible and divisible nature. This is she who inserts herself into mortal things, yet does not herself become mortal. For just as she inserts herself whole and untorn, so she may withdraw herself whole and not dispersed. And because while she rules bodies, she acts as the mistress of divine bodies and not as a mere companion—this is the **greatest miracle in nature**. 

For all other things under God are single individuals in themselves; but this essence is all things at once. She possesses within herself the images of divine things, upon which she depends, and the principles <term>rationes</term> <note>Latin: *rationes*. These are the formal blueprints or "reasons" through which the Soul organizes the material world.</note> and models of lower things, which in a certain way she also produces. And since she is the medium of all things, she possesses the powers of all things. If this is so, she passes into all things. And because she is the true connection of the universe, while she migrates into some things, she does not desert others; rather, she migrates into individual things and always preserves them all, so that she may rightly be called the **center of nature**, the **middle of all things**, the **chain of the world**, the **multitude of all**, and the **knot and bond of the world**. 

We have spoken enough, I believe, regarding the nature of this third essence. That this very essence is the proper seat of the **rational soul** can be most easily seen from this: such is the definition of the rational soul: 

<margin>F</margin>
"Life that understands through a process of reasoning <note>original: "discurrendo", referring to discursive thought that moves from one premise to another, unlike the instant intuition of angels.</note>, while also giving life to the body in time." 

This is the same condition as that of the third essence. For it lives, it understands, and it provides life to the body. That it lives is apparent because we say those things on earth are "alive" which move through all their parts by a certain internal power: upward, downward, forward, backward, to the right, and to the left. Thus plants and animals move. Where, therefore, there is movement that is internal and constant, there is life. Life, I say, is there: the internal power of moving itself. Where this exists, it exists primarily where the fountain and origin of all agitation and the **first movement** is. For internal and common movement is greatest where it is first. But the first movement is placed in that third essence. There, therefore, life is; life, I say, of such a kind that by participation in it, bodies live and move. For it is the life closest to bodies by nature. 

It is also understanding. Indeed, if movement is perfect anywhere, it is certainly most perfect where it is first. No perfection descends into later movements unless it comes from the first. Therefore, the movement in the third essence is the most perfect of all motions. This motion is that which departs as little as possible from its source, which joins most closely to its foundation, which is supremely one and equal, which is sufficient unto itself, and which imitates the most perfect of shapes. Such a motion is a **circuit** <note>original: "circuitus". Ficino uses the image of a circle to describe how the soul "turns" inward to know itself and "revolves" between the divine and the material.</note>, as is evident to everyone; it is also the only one of all motions that is everlasting. Other movements reach a certain limit beyond which they cannot proceed, since no space is infinite. But the circuit, as it repeats the same once, so it repeats it twice, thrice, and four times, by a similar logic; the end and the beginning in it are the same; therefore, when it seems to end, it then begins. 

The **everlasting circuit** is therefore proper to the third essence, such that through movement it is reflected back into itself in a circle. Rightly, if it is moved by itself, it is also moved into itself, so that some end of motion might occur where there is some beginning; especially since the cause of motion itself produces motion, in a way, for its own sake. Therefore that essence, beginning from itself, perpetually revolves back into itself, unfolding its powers from the highest through the middle to the lowest, and again, likewise folding the lowest through the middle back to the highest. If this is so, it turns toward itself and what it possesses within. If it turns toward them, it certainly knows them. It knows them by understanding, while it recognizes its own spiritual essence, which is absolute and free from the limits of matter. For such knowledge is called **intellection**. In ourselves, indeed, we see that knowledge is nothing other than a spiritual union...

<summary>Ficino defines the Soul as the "third essence" and the "bond of the world," positioned between the indivisible divine and divisible matter. He argues that the Soul's primary characteristic is a "circular" self-reflective motion, which allows it to understand itself and give life to the body.</summary>
