...toward some spiritual form. **Vision**, through its own spirit, joined to the spiritual image of colors, sees. Yet, when joined to matter, it perceives nothing; this is evident if anyone places a solid body over the sharp point of the eyes. Our senses also, by a spiritual power united to the bodily appearances and principles <term>rationes</term> <note>Latin: rationes. In this context, these are the formative blueprints or logical structures underlying physical things.</note> of things, understand the things themselves. Similarly, when the **third essence** <note>Ficino’s term for the Soul, which sits in the middle of his five-level hierarchy of reality.</note>—which is indeed spiritual—is joined to itself, it knows and understands itself in a spiritual way by observing itself. It also understands divine things, to which it clings as closely as possible in a spiritual way. It understands bodily things as well, toward which it inclines even against its own nature. It knows, I say, by moving discursively through time, since it is mobile through its own operation. From all these points, a certain definition of the third essence is gathered: namely, it is the **life which vivifies bodies according to nature.** It also knows itself, divine things, and natural things through discourse <note>Discursive reasoning is the step-by-step process of the mind moving from one premise to another, unlike the instant intuition of angels.</note>. Indeed, whoever does not see that this is also the definition of the rational soul, those people lack a rational soul themselves. Therefore, the rational soul has its seat in the third essence; it occupies the middle region of nature and connects all things into one.

<margin>¶</margin>
### **The Platonic Theology of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine: On the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnificent Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Four.**

<margin>¶ B ☞</margin>
**There are three levels of rational souls. In the first is the Soul of the World. In the second are the souls of the spheres. In the third are the souls of the living beings which are contained within the individual spheres.** <margin>Chapter 1.</margin>

<margin>C</margin>
**I**n the beginning, we accepted five levels of reality in ascending order. Then, we compared them to one another while descending. Third, we placed the rational soul in their middle. Now, we shall investigate the levels of this soul, just as the **Mercurial theologians** <note>Ficino refers here to "Hermetic" theologians, followers of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus (Mercury), whom he believed predicted Christian truths.</note> are accustomed to do. Generation is the beginning of nutrition and growth. For nothing can be nourished or increased anywhere without the generation of certain parts. Moreover, we have found it to be proven: where nutrition and growth follow generation, there life and soul are present. Indeed, we see the earth generate countless trees and animate things from its own seeds, and both nourish and increase them. Even stones grow as if they were living things, and herbs grow like hair, as long as they cling to their roots; if they are pulled up and extirpated from the earth, they do not grow. Who would say that the bellies <note>The "ventres" or fertile depths of the earth.</note> of this seed lack life? It is she who brings forth so many offspring of her own accord and feeds them; she who sustains herself; she whose back produces bellies and hair. The same reasoning applies to the body of water. Therefore, water and earth possess a soul. This must be true, unless perhaps someone says that those living things—which seem to us to lack their own seeds—are made by the soul of the earth or of water; that is, they are not born from such a soul but from the **influences of celestial souls.**

<margin>D</margin>
But in truth, the Platonists will deny that those celestial influences—since they are certain **accidents** <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color or heat) that cannot exist on its own, whereas a "substance" is a self-existing thing.</note> far removed from their own vital substances—could generate a vital substance here. This is because an accident cannot generate a substance unless it is subjected as an instrument to a substance—I mean, a proximate substance.

<margin>E</margin>
For an instrument, when separated from the craftsman, does not move toward the form of the art. Thus, that influence of celestial life, if removed from life itself, will not generate a vital form. Justly, the celestial instinct—which is common to any element—is determined toward producing a specific life within that element by the common life of the whole element itself, and is subject to it as an instrument. But it will not generate anything by its own power alone. For since **light** <note>original: "Lum." for "Lumen".</note> extends nothing beyond its own level, an accident can in no way generate a substance; it can only dispose the matter through a certain accidental preparation. Therefore, reason persuades us that this life must be present within the elements as an internal fabricator, because to generate a substance, a substance [is required]...

<summary>Ficino concludes that the rational soul is the "Third Essence" that bridges the divine and material worlds. He then begins Book Four by arguing that the elements of Earth and Water must possess their own souls because they are capable of generating and nourishing life.</summary>

## Theology

...substance is to perform work; and for a perfect action, the perfect presence of the agent itself is necessary. When, however, a bodily substance is applied to another bodily substance for some action, that which is substantial in the agent itself remains outside; that which penetrates inside is altogether accidental. But there is a need for a penetrating substance so that a substance may be formed from it, and formed perfectly. Such a substance is incorporeal and living. Furthermore, natural causes, because they act through their own nature, are therefore directed toward a certain effect in no other way than by the certain principle <term>ratio</term> <note>Latin: ratio. Here it refers to the "formative principle" or "inner logic" that guides natural development.</note> of their nature. Otherwise, they would not incline more toward this effect than toward that one. Thus it happens that, insofar as they are suited to making something, to that extent they operate, and vice versa.

<margin>f</margin>
Therefore, the plants and living creatures that seem to be born in the earth from putrefaction alone <note>Spontaneous generation—the idea that life could arise from decaying matter—was a standard scientific belief during the Renaissance.</note> must arise from their own proper causes no less than those born through propagation. But where are these proper causes? Without doubt, the proper causes of earthly lives are in the **earthly life** <note>Ficino refers to the *Anima Terrae*, or the Soul of the Earth, which he believed animated the planet just as a human soul animates a body.</note>. Even if you attribute these to celestial minds <note>i.e., the intelligences of the stars and planets.</note>, it will still be necessary for those celestial and universal instincts to be drawn down to the earthly and particular souls through the universal soul of the earth. Thus, you may proceed from the celestial and universal to its opposite—the earthly and particular—through a suitable medium: the earthly and universal.

Again, if you place those causes, which are called "proper," in the concurrence of many agents, you will finally be forced to assign one specific cause of a proper order which directs and determines those various causes flowing from here and there toward a specific effect. Therefore, those causes will be in the **soul of the earth**; through a natural idea, principle, and life, it will produce flies through the "principle of flies." It will, I say, make such things in matter previously disposed by the soul itself in this or that way, while it contracts the instincts of the world to dispose that matter.

<margin>B</margin>
Hence, if human art is nothing other than a certain imitation of nature, and if this art fabricates works through certain principles <term>rationes</term> of work, nature itself acts similarly. And it acts with an art that is as much more vital and wise as it acts more effectively and produces more beautiful things. And if an art which produces non-living works possesses living 

## Third [Book] 17

principles, and does not introduce primary or complete forms, how much more must we believe that living principles exist in nature, which generates living things and produces primary and complete forms? What is human art? It is a kind of **nature treating matter from the outside**. What is nature? It is **art tempering matter from within**, as if a woodworker were inside the wood.

<margin>p</margin>
But if human art, although it is outside the matter, nevertheless fits and draws so near to the work being made that it completes certain works with certain ideas, how much more will natural art fulfill this? Natural art does not merely touch the surface of matter with hands or other external instruments—as the soul of a geometer touches the dust when it describes figures on the ground—but rather, just as the geometric mind fashions "phantastic" matter from within <note>Latin: phantasticam. This refers to the *Phantasia*, the faculty of the soul where the mind works with internal mental images or "mental matter" before manifesting them physically.</note>. For just as the mind of the geometer, while it revolves the principles of figures within itself, forms the imagination <term>phantasia</term> from within with the images of figures—and through these, the imaginative spirit as well, without any labor or plan—so in the natural art, a certain divine wisdom, through intellectual principles, imbues the life-giving and motive force joined to it with natural seeds. Through this force, it also 

<margin>g</margin>
fashions matter from within with the greatest ease. What is artifice? It is the mind of the craftsman in separate matter. What is the work of nature? It is the mind of nature in conjoined matter. Therefore, the order of this work is as much more similar to the order which is in natural art, as the order of human artifice is to human art; and as much as matter is closer to nature than to man, and nature dominates matter more than man does. 

Will you then hesitate to place certain principles <term>rationes</term> for certain works within nature? Indeed, just as human art, which touches the surface of matter and fabricates through contingent principles, similarly produces only contingent forms, so it is established that natural art—because it generates or draws forth substantial forms from the depths of matter—operates fundamentally through **essential and perpetual principles**. Many living things, both on land and in the water, [are born] alone...

# Platonic Book

...are born from putrefaction without any bodily seed. Many others come from seeds cast out by animals; later, they grow partly from a certain external heat <note>original: 'fomento'. This refers to a "kindling" or warmth that triggers growth.</note> that ignites them, and partly they sprout without any manifest heat. All herbs and trees are propagated daily either by sowing or planting; nevertheless, in many places, they are born spontaneously every day without seed or bodily germ. I will pass over the fact that many upright men believe that even more perfect animals were created from the earth after the miraculous floods of antiquity.

Yet, it is necessary for certain things to arise from certain specific seeds. Because things pass from potential to act, they must be led into such an act by a cause that already possesses that same state of being within itself—either as an equal or as something more excellent. It should not be thought sufficient if a cause is merely more excellent but removed from the process. Otherwise, the most lowly causes among us could produce the most perfect things through some distant celestial power.

<margin>A</margin> All these things signify that throughout the earth and water, there is a certain artful and vital nature. Within it are the spiritual and life-giving seeds of all things, which it generates by itself wherever bodily seeds are lacking. Furthermore, it fosters the seeds left behind by animals. From a rotten grape-seed—the nature of which is singular and lowly—this power generates a varied, ordered, and precious life by its own precious and varied formative principles <term>rationalibus</term> <note>Latin: rationes. These are the "seminal reasons" or blueprints that Neo-Platonists believed existed within Nature to guide the formation of matter.</note>. This same vital nature leads out the substantial forms of the elements from the very depths of matter, where bodily substances cannot penetrate. Moreover, it takes the elemental qualities—which on their own would only dry or cool—and leads them toward the most beautiful variety of colors and shapes, and toward the vigor of life.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, when fire is created from the collision of cold bodies—where fire did not previously exist except as a certain potentiality, and one far removed from the act itself—Nature generates fire through the most effective "inner logic" <term>rationem</term> of fire. And wherever accidental qualities appear to contribute something to generation, they are never sufficient by themselves without a certain substance suited to the effect; in such cases, Nature itself acts in place of a parent substance. Even mixed bodies—which are by their own nature lazy and lowly due to their earthly or aquatic thickness—are raised by Nature to certain miraculous actions, and even to the power of fascinating or strengthening human souls. This cannot be achieved without the power of a soul, and indeed a more powerful one.

<margin>C</margin> For it is by the power of a more lively and wise nature—which is infused into these very bodies—that the herb **holy-herb** <note>original: 'hierobotanum'. Often identified as Verbena, a plant used in ancient medicine and divination.</note>, as the Magi say, assists in the divinations of doctors. **Agate** <note>original: 'acates'.</note> aids the sight and dulls poison; it provides strength and eloquence. The presence of a **diamond** <note>original: 'adamas'.</note> takes away the power of a **magnet** <note>original: 'magneti'.</note> to attract. **Cornelian** <note>original: 'corneola'.</note> stops the flow of blood and mitigates anger. **Onyx** incites anger and causes terror in dreams. **Coral**, as Metrodorus and Zoroaster testify, removes insane terrors and repels lightning and hail. Certainly, that nature by whose power such things happen reaches our own minds and the very storms. It is necessary that this nature be infused into the lowliest of small bodies, so that these lowest things are elevated, beyond their own natures, to the actions of the higher worlds.

<margin>D</margin> Strato and Chrysippus <note>Strato of Lampsacus and Chrysippus of Soli were influential ancient philosophers; the former a Peripatetic, the latter a Stoic.</note> will admit that such a life is infused into the world, but they will assert that this life is itself the supreme God. The Platonists will deny this. For above that life which belongs to "something else" (and it is fitting that such a life exists within something), there must be a Life that belongs to itself and consists within itself. Indeed, the life of the world is no less familiar to its own sphere than the human soul is to the human body. Therefore, the life of a sphere—whether of a part or the whole—is neither the first life, nor is it God.

<margin>E</margin> For the supreme God is the supreme Unity. According to the Platonists, it is perhaps possible for some multitude to proceed immediately from the supreme Unity, but not such a vast diversity and discord of qualities that corrupt one another. Again, nothing of evil or deformity is close to the highest goodness and beauty; yet many evil and deformed things occur around matter. Furthermore, if God is "Being Itself," he cannot be the form of matter; for such a form is not "Being Itself," but merely a principle of being. And because God is Being—if I may put it this way—so absolute that He is not contained within any specific essence, he is even less contained within matter. Likewise, since God is the first efficient cause, he acts upon all things primarily. However, the form of matter does not act upon all things primarily; for the composite whole acts rather than the individual part. Again, the parts of a composite are in a state of potentiality toward the act of the whole. But in God, there is no potentiality toward any further...

Ficino distinguishes this animating force from the supreme God, arguing that God is absolute Unity and cannot be the direct "form" of material objects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book IV of the *Platonic Theology*. Having established that the Soul acts as a mediator, he now refutes the idea that God or Angels are directly bound to physical matter, proposing instead a hierarchy where each "sphere" of the universe (the elements and the heavens) possesses its own specific soul to govern its physical processes.</meta>

# Theology: Book Four

<sig>D 4</sig>

¶ ...than the previous act is to potential. Therefore, one animal is not made from Him <note>God</note> and matter, as the followers of Amaury <note>original: "almariani". These were followers of Amaury of Bène, a medieval theologian whose pantheistic views—suggesting God was the formal principle of all things—were condemned by the Church.</note> foolishly think. An animal, because it is rational, moves by itself. From which it can be moved and not moved, and moved now faster, now slower. That which is of such a nature will not persevere in perpetual and uniform motion, except by the law of something superior that is in no way changed.

¶ God, therefore, is not the soul of any globe <note>In the Platonic world-view, a "globe" refers to a celestial sphere or a massive body like the Earth.</note>, lest one animal be constituted from Him and the globe, and He be forced to have a leader above Him.

¶ But shall we grant life and an angel to the sphere, and say that natural forms proceed from the ideas of the angelic mind? Not at all.

¶ For just as a body is necessarily prepared for such or such a life through such or such an essence, so it is prepared for such a mind through such a life. Therefore Plato says in the *Timaeus*: God constructed mind and soul for the body. It is as if a clear mind could not be coupled to an opaque body otherwise than through a transparent soul; just as a luminous body is joined to a dense one through a diaphanous—that is, transparent—medium. Thus, that which has light in itself and shows it to others is joined to that which lacks light and blocks light through a middle nature, which, though it lacks light of itself, does not block the entrance of light. 

Thus, if the operation of our mind is perfected through a certain separation from matter, the operation of the angelic mind, which is perfect in the intellectual genus, is far removed from matter. Since the angel itself is nothing other than mind, and by the very reason that it is mind it avoids matter in its operation, in what way would angelic substances inhere in prime matter <term>prime matter (materia prima)</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things.</note>? 

It is fitting that, just as the particular minds of men reach and move their particular bodies through their own souls—that is, their own vital powers—so the common minds of the spheres <note>The great planetary or elemental layers of the universe.</note> embrace and lead the common bodies through souls. For in this way, those spheres will possess an innate life, and the divine minds will by no means be cast down from their sublime state. And above the lives of the spheres, which are simultaneously intellectual and soulful, will be the angelic lives, which exist as solely intellectual. Above these, God will be the "Life of lives." 

Add to this: if the angelic mind is indivisible, immutable, and above place and time, it will in no way fit a divisible, mutable body subject to place and time, nor will it effect such forms in it, unless a soul intercedes. This soul, because it is 

indivisible and above place, is formed or led by the angel; but because it is mutable and has something of time, it accords with matter. It leads the forms received from above within itself toward a mutable and temporal nature, through which they most easily pass into the mutable body as well, and in that body, they now emerge as divisible. 

Thus, it pleases the Platonists that God, through Himself, forms angels; through angels, souls; and through these, finally, matter. And they hold that forms gradually degenerate from the highest life and act, to such an extent that in matter they no longer appear truly alive or effective. Indeed, from God into the angel, they pass from a single essence into multiple qualities. From the angel into the soul, they pass from a state of rest into some effective motion. From the soul into the body, they pass from a vital and active motion into a passive mutation of mortal nature. 

Wherefore, if an innate life exists in water and earth, and yet this is not God (lest the immense act of His most useful power be bound) nor an angel (lest the brightest mind be too close to the darkest nature), it follows that water and earth have souls. By the craftsmanship of these souls, these spheres are adorned with most precious things, just as the little souls of aquatic and terrestrial animals—led, clearly, by the soul of their species—paint and figure their little bodies most pleasingly through innate seeds. 

For the terrestrial globe, one soul suffices, since it is entirely one, with its parts continued into one mass. One soul also suffices for the orb of water. It is necessary, however, for the souls of these two to be twins, differing from each other in species. This is shown by the natures of the bodies themselves, which differ in species, qualities, and effects. If such globes, removed from the purity of the spirit and constricted due to their density, live by their own souls, then all the superior globes live much more so; for they are both purer and much larger, and by their warmth <note>original: 'fomento'. This refers to a celestial influence or "nurturing heat" that triggers generation on Earth.</note> the earth and water bring forth life. Let the air have its own soul, and fire its own, for the same reason that the earth and water have theirs. Similarly, the globes of the eight heavens have souls—for there were eight heavens <note>In traditional astronomy: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Fixed Stars.</note> among the ancients.

<summary>Ficino argues for a hierarchical universe where God and Angels remain transcendent, while specific souls govern the elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) and the eight celestial spheres. This structure explains how divine forms are translated into physical matter through the mediation of the soul.</summary>

Following the discussion that God is not the Soul of the World but its creator, Ficino now explores the hierarchy of life within the elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) and the celestial spheres, arguing that every part of the universe is inhabited by living beings possessing their own souls.</meta>

# A Book on Platonic Theology

<margin>A</margin> On Earth, there are many animals that have their own souls, distinct from the common soul of the Earth <note>Ficino refers to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, suggesting that while the Earth as a whole is alive, the creatures on it have individual souls.</note>, because they move from place to place—which the Earth does not do—and because they live even when separated from the Earth. This is something stones and plants do not do, for they live by the soul of the Earth rather than their own. These animals raise themselves above the earth by flight, by buildings, or by machines. In the water, likewise, there are many animals living by their own souls. If water and earth were favored and adorned by God, why should air and fire not also contain many souls and their own animals, in addition to their common souls?

Argue the same for the spheres of the heavens. Since the stars differ among themselves in size, light, power, and motion, and since each performs its own circuit, they also have souls that differ in kind. Indeed, these stars adorn the heavens just as aquatic animals adorn the water and terrestrial animals adorn the earth. We see those celestial animals clearly because of their vast abundance of light. We also see terrestrial and aquatic ones, which are close to us and show themselves to our eyes by their physical density. But we do not see the aerial and fiery ones, just as we do not see the elements of air and fire themselves. Why should they appear to the eyes of mortals, since they possess neither the benefit of immense light nor the density of 

<margin>B</margin> physical mass? It is necessary that the soul of the Earth itself be rational, since certain animals of the Earth <note>namely, humans</note> are not lacking in reason—especially since the works of the Earth <note>nature</note> are more beautiful than the works of men. If the soul of this lowest globe is not devoid of reason, then the souls of the higher globes are certainly not lacking in reason either. In earth and water, there is such a distinction of parts that some terrestrial bodies are less pure, while others are most pure. The former have irrational souls; the latter have

<margin>C</margin> rational ones. The same is true in the water, where there are irrational fish in the muddy parts of the water. There are also water demons, whom Orpheus calls Nereids <note>original: "nereides". In Greek mythology, these are sea nymphs, but Ficino treats them as "demons" or spirits inhabiting the higher "exhalations" of water.</note>, in certain higher exhalations of the water, such as exist in this cloudy air. Their bodies are sometimes seen by those with sharper eyes, especially in Persia and Africa, as Zoroaster believes. Porphyry adds that those demons are seen only if fire abounds in their bodies alongside the water exhalation, and that this occurs in the East and the South. Furthermore, those are felt who contain a great deal 

---

of earth, such as he says existed among the Tuscans <note>The Etruscans/Tuscans were famous in antiquity for their "discipline" regarding spirits and lightning.</note> in their own times. But in all the globes above the waters, there are no living beings except those who are masters of reason, because those globes are not divided into thick and thin parts. And whatever is there is far purer than watery exhalations.

But let us "chat" a little here with the Pythagoreans. Since every great multitude must be gathered into a small number, and a small number into a few units, and those few units into a single unity, the innumerable crowd of souls living in any sphere of the world must be reduced to a few more excellent souls in that same sphere—namely, twelve princes. But why specifically to twelve 

<margin>D</margin> princes? Because, just as the one body of the world contains twelve "limbs" according to the ancients <note>The twelve parts of the cosmic body often correspond to the zodiac signs.</note>, and these limbs contain many joints, so the one Soul of the World has twelve primary souls. But it contains these primary souls in such a way that it first holds twelve principal ones. Why? Because since the soul of every species was selected from the first "twelve-fold" <note>original: "duodenario". The number twelve was considered a perfect number for governing divisions of time and space.</note> number of souls and adapted to that species, it rightly returns again to the twelve-fold. We have the sign of this number in the first and the last sphere. In the first, we discern 

<margin>E</margin> twelve sidereal animals through the Zodiac. In each of those, there is a certain principal star, acting like the heart of that animal depicted in the heavens. In that heart, the soul of the whole principal constellation lives. There, the twelve divine souls are placed by the Pythagoreans:
* In the heart of Aries: **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>
* In the heart of Taurus: **Venus**
* Of the Gemini: **Phoebus** <note>Apollo</note>
* Of Cancer: **Mercury**
* Of Leo: **Jupiter**
* Of Virgo: **Ceres**
* Of Libra: **Vulcan**
* Of Scorpio: **Mars**
* Of Sagittarius: **Diana**
* Of Capricorn: **Vesta**
* Of Aquarius: **Juno**
* Of Pisces: **Neptune**

In the last sphere too—that is, the Earth—there are twelve lives of men. For men lead their lives through reason (assigned to the brain), through anger (assigned to the heart), and through 

<margin>F</margin> desire (attributed to the liver). If anyone were said to use none of these powers, they would not even breathe. If someone were not moved by reason, they would not be a man. Indeed, it is impossible for a soul joined to a body to proceed by reason alone. Nor can it use the power of anger alone, for this always serves either reason or desire. Nor can it act by desire alone, for this is always strengthened either by a depraved reason or by anger...

# Theology, Book Three

<margin>a</margin> ...strife. Therefore, it is necessary to either proceed through all those powers or through two. First, then, will be the **human life** that uses reason more, anger less, and desire the least. The second is that which uses reason more, desire less, and anger the minimum. The third: that which uses anger more, reason less, and lust <note>original: "libidine," referring here to the lower appetites</note> the minimum. The fourth: that which uses anger more, desire less, and reason the minimum. The fifth: that which uses lust much, reason a little, and anger very little. The sixth: that which uses lust much, anger a little, and reason very little. Thus, from the common use of three powers, six lives are completed. Six others are born from the use of two powers. 

<margin>b</margin> In the first, reason overcomes anger. In the second, the opposite. In the third, reason overcomes desire. In the fourth, the opposite. In the fifth, anger dominates desire. In the sixth, the opposite. If, in the appearance of the world, the number twelve <note>The "duodenary" number, significant in ancient geometry and astrology</note> is observed in the two extremes, it is also observed in the middle. Wherefore, as we began a little while ago, let us reduce the many souls living in any species to the twelve principal souls living in order within that same species. 

<margin>g</margin> Let us again take twelve leaders in any one of the spheres. For among the ancients, there are twelve spheres of the world; let us refer those to the twelve souls who are the companions of those spheres. Furthermore, let us refer the twelve souls of the spheres to the one soul of that single matter itself. Since, indeed, the soul is the leader of the mind, and that which participates in nature must be above nature—being full in itself—therefore the genus of souls is raised up to the **free minds**, and finally, those minds are raised to the **one Mind**. And that one Mind—which is both Mind and the One—must be raised simply to the One, which is not merely "a" one (such as one mind or one soul) but the **One itself**.

<margin>k</margin> This is what <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who saw numbers and harmony as the basis of reality</note> calls the **Universal Apollo**. For he wishes <term>Apollo</term> <gloss>original: "απολλονα"</gloss> to be so named as if from <term>simple</term> <gloss>original: "α π α λοῦ"</gloss>, which signifies "the simple one," and as if from <term>set apart from the many</term> <gloss>original: "απολλῶνυ"</gloss>, which signifies "removed from the multitude." The same name he calls <term>the Good</term> <gloss>original: "τα’γαθον"</gloss>—that is, the Good itself—since the goodness and perfection of anything consist in its unity. Thus, if in things goodness and union are the same, then above things, the First One and the First Good must also be the same. Therefore, the First One and Good presides over the first single Mind; that one Mind presides over many minds—perhaps the twelve leading minds—and by its own twelve-fold order, it presides over those first twelve-fold groups thereafter; and finally, it also presides over the one Soul of the World. The one Soul of the World presides over the twelve souls of the spheres. Those twelve souls preside over twelve sets of twelve souls—namely, the soul of each sphere presides over the twelve most excellent souls in its own species. Finally, those twelve sets of twelve preside over innumerable souls. For in any sphere, those twelve principal souls lead the other souls of that sphere.

<margin>l</margin> This, moreover, the **choir of the Muses** sings and dances perpetually, as <term>Orpheus</term> <note>The legendary poet and musician of Greek myth</note> says, with musical measures at the command of Apollo himself: <term>But you harmonize all of space with your many-sounding lyre</term> <gloss>original: "σὺ δε πᾶντα χολον κιδάρα πολυκρεκτω αρμοζεις"</gloss>—that is, you temper the whole heaven with your tuneful lyre. But we have conversed enough with the Pythagoreans for now. Let us now return to the established Platonic order. We have proved by one reasoning that the spheres of the world are alive; let us proceed to other points. 

Let us see how the spheres of the world are moved, and let us devise some motors for them. Let us know, moreover, that there cannot be one sphere above another, or motors above other motors, without end; we are compelled to confess that there is some sphere that is moved **first**. If it is moved first, it is certainly moved by an internal principle. Indeed, as we touched upon above: that which is first hot or cold is hot or cold by an internal heat or cold. For we have said that whatever is such because of another must always be reduced to something that is such through itself. And if even the smallest tiny bodies <note>atoms or corpuscles</note> of the world have, in some way, the virtues of their own movements and works within themselves—as appears in the parts of the elements, in herbs, and in living creatures—how much more do the vast spheres of the world possess the principles of their own rotations within themselves? Principles, I say, which are most familiar, by which the spheres are more closely joined than our bodies are to our souls. Indeed, motion is more natural and effective the more the thing being moved is joined to the mover. But the motion of the heavens, being more foreign to violence than all others, is more natural and effective.

<margin>M</margin> But what are those principles? Are they not some qualities? For example, just as the parts of the elements are seen to be moved by gravity and levity, and to operate by heat...

Having previously established the existence of the soul, Ficino here argues that the celestial spheres are moved not by mere physical qualities or by God directly, but by an inherent, rational "Celestial Soul." This bridges the gap between the unmoved Prime Mover (God) and the physical matter of the heavens.</meta>

# Platonic

## Book

...with rigor: so do the spheres of the world revolve through qualities of this kind? Not at all. For a **Quality** <note>In Platonic physics, a 'quality' is a physical property like heat or weight, as opposed to a 'soul' which is a self-moving principle</note>, which is arranged by position and parts and is bound to a single specific piece of matter, acts in a limited way and grows weary. Thus, it is unable to move either forever or in the same uniform manner; and every quality performs only a single task and moves toward a single end-point. What does heat produce but heat? What does cold produce but coldness? Lightness pulls only upward, while gravity pulls only downward. Therefore, a quality will never, by its own nature, produce any effect contrary to its principal work. It will never return of its own accord to the place from which it departed, <margin>A</margin> nor will it depart of its own accord from the place where it has naturally brought itself. 

The Heaven, however, moves always uniformly and yet produces various and mutually contrary effects; and to achieve this diversity, it disposes the lower matter in contrary ways. It induces various configurations and has no fixed end-point in its circuit. But whatever point you mark on the "back of the heaven" <note>original: "celi dosum," referring to the outer surface of the celestial sphere</note>, any part of the heaven will approach it and again recede from it with total ease, not through the violence of another force. <margin>B</margin> For that which is "violent" <term>violentum: in Aristotelian physics, motion forced against an object's natural inclination</term> is neither long-lasting, nor always the same and ordered. 

Furthermore, since the heaven revolves with contrary motions at the same time, if it were led by a physical quality, it would certainly have to be moved by contrary qualities. Yet contrary qualities and natures cannot exist there, where there is no conflict and no destruction. Likewise, since nature is determined to one end, and therefore cannot seek an indeterminate and diverse end (which motion is), it moves only for the sake of rest; however, circular motion does not, of itself, lead toward rest. Therefore, the heaven neither acts by a simple nature, nor, if it were ever to rest, would it be stopped by nature. 

Moreover, a quality extended in a physical body is not able to reflect back upon itself, since it is bound to that body. By what means, then, will a quality grant the heavens a revolution back into themselves <note>Circular motion was seen as a physical reflection of the soul returning to itself</note>, when the quality does not possess in itself the power of reflecting upon itself? Likewise, since a body does nothing through its own nature, but through a quality, and a quality does not provide force to a body by its own leadership, but only insofar as it is moved from elsewhere; if some quality moves the heaven, it itself must be moved from elsewhere. <margin>C</margin> What is it that moves the quality? Is it God? Not at all; for the First Cause, since it infinitely exceeds all things, is intimate <term>familiaris: a technical term meaning specifically associated or sharing a nature</term> with no specific body, but is equally common to all and absolute from all. For if God were specifically the primary driver of any one body, He would no longer be the driver of all.

Therefore, so that He may be the driver of all, He is not the specific ruler of any one thing. Nevertheless, as we have said, very intimate "Movers" govern the spheres. And indeed, those spheres that are distinct from one another and are moved by different motions require different specific movers; for there must be a proportion between the mover and the thing moved. Nor should the opinion of those be approved who distribute movers to the spheres in such a way that they assign God to the first sphere and the remaining intellects to the other spheres. For since the distribution must be made according to proportion, just as the spheres agree with one another in nature and order, so God and the Intellect would have to correspond to one another. In that case, God would not surpass the remaining intellects except as much as the first sphere surpasses the others, nor would He be infinite. He would also be composed of a nature shared with others through correspondence and of a specific nature through which He is distinguished.

Furthermore, if God is Goodness itself, and Goodness moves any thing as the desired object moves the desire, then God moves the heaven as an "end" <note>The Final Cause, the goal toward which something strives</note>. But a body is not moved toward an external goal except through some **internal form** that desires that goal and produces the motion. Therefore, there is in the heaven a form that desires the First Goodness and produces motion. This eagerness is neither "blind," like that of stones, nor "irrational," like that of beasts. For how could an eagerness so close to the First Truth and Wisdom be blind and irrational? Especially since it moves its body with greater order than our reason moves ours. Therefore, it is not "Mind" <note>original: "mens," referring here to the transcendent, universal Intellect</note> that moves the heaven primarily, but a certain form proper to the heaven, possessing life and reason, <margin>D</margin> and desiring divine goodness. 

And if anyone should say that the heavens are moved by a certain "mechanical tuning" <note>original: "temperatione," suggesting a structural or mathematical balance</note>, just as the bronze spheres of Archimedes <note>Archimedes was famous for creating a mechanical planetarium or orrery</note> were once turned, he will be compelled to confess that this very tuning is no less substantial, vital, and rational than the "tuning" by which the limbs of earthly animals are moved—since the celestial tuning is closer to the first substance, life, and reason, and appears more uniform both in its nature and its motions. <margin>E</margin> But is that thing an angel? Not at all; for the celestial life itself is most intimate with the heaven and, in a certain way, runs around together with its body. An angel is neither an intimate mover nor is it moved. For surely, above a mobile mover, it is fitting that there be a mo...

<summary>Ficino argues that the circular motion of the heavens cannot be caused by physical qualities or by God directly, but requires an internal, rational, and living soul. He refutes mechanical or purely "natural" explanations, insisting the heavens move out of a rational desire for the Divine Good.</summary>

# Theology
# Fourth Book

<margin>3</margin>
...another [mover] <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the source of motion</note>: who is immobile. On the other hand, an angel is entirely stable. From that which is completely stable, however, such a sudden and varied motion does not proceed. If an angel is entirely stable, and the heaven is moved by another, they certainly require some middle ground: that which is **mobile by itself**. For that which is moved by itself succeeds most closely to the thing that is entirely stable; and to this succeeds the thing moved by another. Indeed, a thing moved **by <gloss>through</gloss> itself**, in that it changes, agrees with <margin>4</margin> that thing which is changed by another. Yet in that it directs itself—because it thus stays within its own nature and does not fall from its seat—it agrees with that thing which remains entirely permanent. What, finally, is that thing moved by itself which turned the primary heaven? It is nothing other than the **soul**. For it is the soul which is both mobile by itself and provides the traces of such motion to bodies. For if it were said that a remote mover moves the heaven in some way, it would nonetheless not give the act of motion to the heaven until it had infused a **motive force** <term>vis motrix: the internal capacity for a body to move</term> joined to the heaven. This kind of force ought not be extended along with the heaven. Otherwise, it would depart from itself; therefore, <margin>5</margin> it would not be able to provide the heaven with the faculty of perpetually returning to itself. Therefore, it shall be **indivisible**. It is not, however, restricted by dimensions like a point, because it would not be able to freely revolve itself and its dimensions from the same [point] into the same [point]. Moreover, it is entirely present everywhere in the whole heaven, so that it may move the whole most effectively. Therefore, that joined force is indivisible, free everywhere, and equal; it is the **rational soul**. By its presence the heaven lives, whose motion is life-giving, since it gives life to all things.

<margin>6</margin>
Finally, since those instruments in animals live through which souls generate living things, who will doubt that the heaven lives? Insofar as it is the instrument of some life for the generation of living things. Is not **spontaneous** motion, so to speak, a sign of interior life wherever it exists? Such a thing is especially present where there is a natural circuit. For what is moved more spontaneously than that which naturally recurs into itself and rolls around a <note>original: "naturalem cardinem," referring to the celestial axis or pole</note> natural hinge and within a natural surface? Therefore, to no body is life more intrinsic than to the spheres of the world. Nor should it be doubted that <margin>D p</margin> **one living being** <term>animal vnum: the concept of the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, where the universe is viewed as a single biological organism</term> is made from the spheres and the divine souls. Because, while it is the property of matter to receive form, it is the property of form to embrace and lead matter; and this happens all the more where both matter and form are more excellent. Who then would deny that from those souls—which are more excellent than ours—and from the spheres—which are simpler and more long-lasting than our bodies—which also contain, draw, and generate us, **one and indissoluble living being** is fashioned? Are those bodies not, on account of their wonderful simplicity and thinness, almost spiritual? Therefore, are they not more easily animated by the presence of spirits than sulfur is kindled by the presence of fire? For in this way, the most excellent matter is joined to the most excellent form—that is, the **intellectual form**—to such an extent that they are never dissolved. <margin>E</margin> If mixed bodies, the further they depart from the imbalance of elemental qualities and approach the temperance of celestial bodies, become so much more capable of life and cognition, then without a doubt the celestial bodies are the **most capable** of life and cognition. The genus of minds is more sublime than the heaven, and is more akin to the heaven than to the earth. Therefore, since there are many minds joined to earthly bodies as forms, it is necessary that minds—both more numerous and prior—are joined as forms to celestial bodies rather than earthly ones.

<margin>I</margin>
Furthermore, the Platonists judge that not only the heavens but even the **elements** live, as we have said. For when they see all the spheres of the world, and many things besides that are connected to these composites, moved by an intrinsic motion without an external pusher, they judge that souls are within them. And if anyone should ask about the ascent and descent of the elements and their composites, the Platonists will respond: that this also happens through the soul. Through the soul, I say, of its own sphere, which—just as a magnet draws iron—so it calls back the particles of its sphere to itself.

<summary>Ficino argues that the heavens must be moved by a rational, self-moving soul that acts as a bridge between the unmoved God and physical matter. He concludes that the universe is a single, living organism (Anima Mundi) and that even the elements possess a form of life that guides their natural movements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 4 of the *Platonic Theology*. Having established that the heavens require a "self-moving" soul, Ficino now explains how this soul directs the natural motions of the elements (earth, water, air, fire) and why the entire universe must be governed by a single, unified World Soul.</meta>

# Platonic [Theology]

Hence it also happens that the motion of a stone falling from on high becomes faster the closer it approaches the earth. Similarly, the motion of a flame ascending becomes more rapid as it gets closer to the heaven. Indeed, since the soul of the sphere <note>The "soul of the sphere" refers to the guiding intelligence of a celestial body (like Earth or the Heavens) that exerts a natural pull on its related elements.</note> draws it more vehemently, the **Soul of the World** <term>Anima Mundi: the vital principle that Platonists believed animated the entire physical universe</term> also pulls it toward the same end. 

<margin>C</margin> And just as if men saw the movement of iron but did not see the magnet, they would think the iron moved by itself while it was actually being pulled by the magnet; so now, those who do not understand the souls of the celestial spheres believe that any little bodies <term>corpuscula: small particles or physical matter</term> are moved by themselves. But since no mind of a craftsman moves his own limbs or tools as correctly as those little bodies are moved in the world, it is necessary that those little bodies are moved and led not by an inert quality alone, but also by a **crafting nature** <note>original: "artificiosa natura"; nature acting with the skill of an artisan</note>.

Furthermore, the natural motion <margin>B</margin> of the elements is that which does not transgress the boundaries of nature and of their natural place: that is, a perpetual circuit within its own place and natural sphere, similar to its own figure. Fire and air circle around, like the revolution of the moon, which is called "long-haired" <note>This likely refers to the "cometary" or trailing appearance of air and fire in the upper atmosphere</note>. Water circles by constantly flowing back. The earth, however—though Hegesias <note>Possibly a reference to Hegesias of Cyrene, though the specific astronomical theory is obscure</note> wished it to move in a circle—most people believe it remains still across its surface. Its parts circle the center of the world in a certain way, as they squeeze together on all sides around it in an everlasting effort. 

<margin>A</margin> But ascent or descent is not properly a "natural" motion. Rather, it is a sudden restoration toward a place and toward natural motion via a straight line. Since this movement is terminated from above and is always directed through a single path, it clearly shows us that the parts of the elements are very little moved by themselves. For if they moved by their own will, they would not always take the same path, and water could sometimes choose not to cool the air it touches, or not to flow downward over a precipice. 

<margin>25</margin> For even if the souls of the spheres always preserve the same tenor, one must not think that the **little souls** <note>original: "animulas"; the lesser vital forces or "motive powers" inherent in elemental matter</note>—that is, the specific powers of the elemental parts—would preserve such an order if they were within those parts as their movers, seeing as our own souls do not maintain such constancy. Indeed, the growth of plants and stones comes from the **Soul of the Earth**. Therefore, they only grow for as long as they cling to the earth. The bodies of beasts and humans, however, live apart from the spheres because they possess their own specific souls. This is indicated by their forms, which are equipped with various instruments <note>original: "instris" (instrumentis); here meaning organs or specialized body parts</note>.

---

# Book [Four]

These forms are utterly dissimilar to the figures of the celestial spheres; their constitution is also most foreign to the constitution of the spheres. As a movable thing relates to another movable thing, so does a mover relate to another mover. Therefore, as body relates to body, <margin>L</margin> so soul relates to soul. Thus, bodies that are separated from one another by position, nature, shape, and quantity also have a separate species and soul. But those that are joined have a joined soul. 

Nevertheless, there is **one single Soul of the World** above the individual parts. For there is one work of life belonging to the one living Craftsman <note>God or the Demiurge</note>. It is not one living thing unless it is through one life. It does not have one life unless it has one soul. Rightly so—even if it is hidden, as many argue—since there is one primary material in all species and one matter within all forms, its soul is also one. 

<margin>D</margin> What else could be the cause that, although the members of the world are contrary to each other, they nonetheless "breathe together" <note>original: "conspirant"; to act in harmony or literal "co-breathing"</note> into one, and communicate their powers to one another? It is because the one soul of this giant animal tempers the humors, however diverse they may be. And it continues the members (which are separated by position) by a "conspiration" <note>A shared vital breath</note> of quality, life, and motion. From where else does it happen that the lower things follow the nods <note>The will or direction</note> of the higher things, and all members of the world (so to speak) suffer together in turn, unless it is from one common nature? And one nature must come from one soul. 

This divine animal <note>The Universe/World</note> must be no less unified than any other animal, seeing as it is the most powerful of all. Therefore, if among all other animals any body you please is governed by its own single soul, how much more must the members of this worldly animal be bound together by a single soul. 

If this soul relates to its body just as ours relates to ours, it is no different: the soul is "entire in any part of the world" just as our soul is entire in any part of our body. Otherwise, it could not perfectly connect, vivify, and move the universe. As nature relates to the body, <margin>E</margin> so the soul relates to nature. Therefore, just as in the universal body the "universal nature" is everywhere, so in the universal nature, the "universal soul" is everywhere. 

Furthermore, that the souls of the spheres are **rational** is shown by the arrangement of the movements of the world, which always proceed toward that which is better and more beautiful. For a motion so swift, free, and long-lasting can only proceed from an innermost life.

<summary>Ficino argues that the orderly movement of the elements and the "sympathy" between different parts of the universe prove the existence of a single, rational World Soul (Anima Mundi). He compares the universe to a giant living animal where the soul is present in every part, ensuring harmony and purposeful motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 4 of the Platonic Theology. Following the discussion of natural motion, Ficino now explains how the orderly movement of the cosmos reflects a "divine art" and introduces the hierarchical structure of the universe as understood by ancient traditions.</meta>

# Theology

Thus there arises so wonderful an order of movement; such a skillful progression proceeds from a most wise art of life itself. For that which <note>original: "species"</note> always directs the same things toward the same end is not some necessity lacking life, as it seems to the common people, but a complete art and a blessed wisdom. Because it does not err in its deliberation—as mortals are prone to do—it does not wander in its motion or its work.

<margin>S</margin>

Finally, the fact that the heaven is moved by a certain intelligence is proven to us by this argument: the body of the heaven, through its motions, so orders the elements and arranges composite things that intellectual souls may be infused into these composite bodies. These souls are indeed far more excellent than the celestial bodies. Therefore, since the corporeal nature of the heaven does not act or arrange anything above its own species by itself, certainly in this very action and arrangement—where it leads to the perfection of the species of the mind—it is led by the divine mind as an instrument by a craftsman. This mind is indeed present in its own soul, since the soul of the most excellent body is the most excellent of souls. 

There are three principal rulers over the world, as the **Magi** <note>The "Magi" refers to the ancient Persian priestly class, particularly the legendary figure Zoroaster, whom Ficino believed anticipated Christian truths.</note> think: Bromasius, Mitrius, and Arimanius; that is: **God, Mind, and Soul**. Unity is proper to God. Order to the Mind. Motion to the Soul. By God alone, that first unity of the parts and the whole is created in the world. From the Mind, through the power of God, comes the order of the unified parts. From the Soul, through the power of those above it, comes the motion of the ordered work. The Soul moves the world changeably through itself. It moves it in an orderly fashion through the Mind. It perseveres always in this one office through the eternal unity of God himself. 

<margin>b</margin>

Thus, these three traces of those three principles are seen in the world, as I have said; which Plato seems to have touched upon in his letter to King Dionysius, a passage which we have explained more fully in our book *On Love*. Let it be added that any natural species has its existence and its unity from God. It has its order from God through the Mind, and it has its perpetuity from both. But from the Soul and the heaven, it has the quality of being manifold through individual instances and of being changeable. For the Mind and the Soul, since they are procreated most closely from an entirely immovable cause through its very substance, turn out to be altogether immutable in substance.

# Book Four

Natural species, however, since they flow from stable causes (that is, God and Mind) through causes that are mobile in their action (that is, souls and the heavens), are also in a certain way changeable in their substance; yet they seem perpetual through the continuous succession of individuals by the gift of their stable causes. For from the same source where the mobile causes have their perpetuity of motion, these effects have their continuous succession of generation.

<margin>m</margin>

That the celestial spheres have souls is admitted not only by the **Platonists**, but by all the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about</term> as well. Aristotle teaches this in the second book of *On the Heavens*. Again, in the seventh and eighth books of the *Physics*, in the second book of *On the Soul*, and the eleventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "divinoz," referring to the Metaphysics</note>. Theophrastus also, the disciple of Aristotle, says so in his book *On the Heavens*. Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>Two of the most influential medieval Islamic philosophers whose works shaped Western scholasticism.</note> confirmed this most strongly. Aurelius Augustine in the book *Enchiridion*, and Thomas Aquinas in the second book of *Against the Gentiles*, hand down the teaching that, as far as Christian doctrine is concerned, it makes no difference whether the celestial bodies have souls or do not have them.

<margin>☞</margin>

Whether the spheres of the elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> actually live is clearly established among the Platonists, yet the ancient Peripatetics discussed nothing regarding them. 

<margin>R</margin>

However, some more recent thinkers are uncertain, because the elements seem to have been established for the sake of composite things, and are as much more lowly than the composites as they are closer to matter. But to this the Platonists will respond that the entire spheres of the elements were indeed established for the sake of the whole world, not for the sake of this or that composite thing. Those particles of the elements which are both separated from the integrity of the whole element and mixed into this or that composite body, are mixed for the sake of such a small body. And although the qualities of these particles are very close to prime matter, the whole elements, because they are numbered in the order of the principal members of the world, are very close: both to the form of the whole world and to the universal pattern and purpose of the Supreme Architect, as well as to the divine influences of the celestial minds and spheres; these influences do not flow into particles and mixed small bodies except through the whole elements. In this way, the globes of the elements become worthy receptacles of the **divine reasons** <term>rationum: here meaning the "seeds" or "blueprints" of creation held in the divine mind</term>.

<summary>Ficino explains the cosmic hierarchy of God, Mind, and Soul, arguing that the heavens are guided by intelligence to create order. He cites a consensus among Platonists, Aristotelians, and Christian theologians like Aquinas that celestial bodies are animated by souls.</summary>

... of rational souls.

<margin>a</margin> Furthermore, there are parts within fire and air which, due to their position and transparency, are suited to the heavens and correspond to the regions of the stars. These parts, through certain direct and mobile influences, are sufficiently prepared to receive minds. However, the thicker parts—namely water and earth—cannot, by the heat of fire and air diffused through them, deserve to separate souls from their own spheres. This is because they lose the dignity of their spheres and, due to the impact of external bodies, do not preserve their own simplicity and purity. But if they are mixed together with care, until through a long-lasting trial of qualities they recover a certain equality similar to the equality of the spheres, they first achieve wonderful operations in these mixtures, then life in plants, then sensation, and finally reason.

<margin>b</margin> If anyone desires to know the names of these divine souls, let him know that the theology of **Orpheus** <note>Orpheus was a legendary Greek poet and prophet; Ficino viewed "Orphic" hymns as a source of ancient, divinely inspired wisdom that prefigured Plato.</note> divides the souls of the spheres in such a way that each power is twofold: one positioned in knowing, the other in the hope of enlivening and ruling the body. Therefore, in the element of earth, Orpheus names the first power **Pluto** and the second **Proserpina**. In water, he calls the first **Oceanus** and the second **Thetis**. In the air, the first is the **Thunderer Jove** and the second **Juno**. In fire, **Phanes** and **Aurora**. In the soul of the lunar sphere, the first is **Bacchus Licnitus** and the second the **Muse Thalia**. Again, in the soul of the sphere of Mercury, the first power is **Bacchus Silenus** and the second **Euterpe**. In the sphere of Venus, <unclear>Iphius</unclear> <note>original: "iphū". This likely refers to a specific Orphic epithet for Bacchus associated with Venus, perhaps Lysius.</note> and **Erato**. <margin>c</margin> In the Sun, **Trietericus** and **Melpomene**. In Mars, **Bassareus** and **Clio**. In Jupiter, **Sabazius** and **Terpsichore**. In Saturn, **Amphietus** and **Polymnia**. In the eighth sphere, **Picionius** and **Urania**. In the soul of the world itself, he calls the first power **Bacchus Eribromus** and the second the **Muse Calliope**. Therefore, according to Orpheus, a certain "Bacchus" presides over each Muse, by which he signifies that their powers are intoxicated with the nectar of divine knowledge. Thus there are nine Muses with nine Bacchuses reveling around the one **Apollo**—that is, around the splendor of the invisible Sun. But let these things said about the names of <margin>d</margin> divine souls suffice. However, let us briefly conclude this whole dispute with this reason: following the custom of the ancients, we must say that those people are utterly to be ridiculed who admit that the impure parts of the elements—from which animals are composed—possess life and reason, yet deny it to the whole, pure elements. It is as if the part were better than the whole. They wish the world to lack life and sense, even though it gives life to plants (which do not come from seed) and gives sense to animals (which are not produced through intercourse). <margin>e</margin> Therefore, we gather three grades of rational souls. In the first, there is the one **Soul of the World**. In the second, there are the twelve souls of the spheres. In the third, there are the many souls contained within the individual spheres. All these things pertaining to the souls of the spheres are narrated from the opinion of the Platonists; they should only be affirmed if they please the council of Christian theologians after being diligently examined. For even **Plato** in the *Epinomis* <note>The *Epinomis* is a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato that discusses astronomy and the religious duties of the philosopher.</note>, where he speaks in his own person, says of these things under this division: "It is impossible for the earth, the heaven, all the stars, and the great masses composed of them to revolve with such exquisite reason through years, months, and days, and to produce all good things for us all, unless a soul were either present to or within each one."

-> The souls of the spheres move the spheres by fatal law, and they move in a circuit because they themselves are circles. <-

### Chapter 2.

<margin>f</margin> **B**y what means do the celestial souls move their spheres? Certainly, as the Platonists believe, it is just as your soul moves your body through appetite; and that appetite is also excited there by thought, and thought there by that fatal law of the soul. Therefore, Plato says in the book *On the Kingdom* <note>Referring to Plato's *Politicus* (The Statesman), which contains a myth about the age of Cronus and the motion of the universe.</note>: "Fate and innate desire move the heaven." This <margin>g</margin> he seems to have received from **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Persian sage. Ficino refers here to the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to him.</note>, from whom all the wisdom of the ancient theologians flowed. For he, when speaking of the heaven, says: <term>It is carried by an eternal will; it always runs by the work of necessity.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀειζώ βουαὶ φέρεται ἀεὶ τρέχει ἔργω ἀνάγκησ"</note>. This we shall clearly understand if we consider the order of things in this way. There is something which is said to be "above all." There is something "below all." That which is "above all" is <margin>h</margin> **God**, who cannot properly be called "all" because He is the simplest unity above number. "Below all" are these individual bodies. It is necessary, therefore, that between that which is above all and that which is below all, there should be something in the middle. That middle thing is the "all" itself, the whole, and the heap of all things.

He concludes by defining the hierarchy of existence from God (above all) to physical bodies (below all), with the Soul of the World acting as the mediating "all."</summary>

## Page 31

... ... ... It will, however, be a triple "All," or rather, the whole "All" is threefold.

¶ **The first All** depends primarily on the very unity of God. For that reason, it must be unified to the greatest extent possible, since it is made to be most like that supreme Unity itself. Now, a thing can be unified in three ways: by essence, by point, and by moment. **By essence**, meaning it is a single substance not composed of multiple substances. ¶ **By point**, meaning it is not dispersed into many parts which would force it to be distracted across many points of location. **By moment**, meaning that whatever it is capable of possessing, it obtains in the blink of an eye, and is not varied through the changing moments of time. ¶ Therefore, that "All" which exists immediately from God is unified in all these ways, making it most like Him. This is the **Angel** <note>Ficino uses "Angel" here as a philosophical term for the "Divine Mind" or "Intellect," the first level of creation below God.</note>. Although it might be called changeable in some sense because it depends on another, nevertheless, because it is first-procreated in the infinite state of God and turns toward Him <margin>b</margin> without any intermediary, it turns out to be entirely stable. 

**The second All follows**, which, because it depends on the One by a secondary intention, now loses one mode of unity while retaining two: it remains one in essence and in point, but it becomes variable in its moments. Such is the **Soul**. 

**The third All** is the matter of the world, which is one substance, but it is not only varied by moments, like the soul, but is also spread out through <margin>g</margin> points of location. But why, in this descent, is time discovered before space? Firstly, because time is the companion of a certain spiritual action, while space is the companion of the body; therefore, time is closer to the spirit and its efficacy than space is. Secondly, because one must descend step-by-step from unity into multiplicity. Whenever the essence of a thing undergoes local multiplicity, its operation also suffers a <margin>K</margin> temporal numbering—but not the other way around. ¶ **For the essence can surpass the operation in unity and perfection, but never the reverse.** 

Finally, any members of the world are not called "The All," but are said to be "under the All." For this reason, the Angel contains within itself the reasons <note>Latin: *rationes*. These are the formal principles or "blueprints" of all things.</note> of all things, in both habit and act simultaneously. The Soul, likewise, contains all things, but in habit and not in act. ¶ **Matter contains all things in poten-**

---

**-tiality**, but not in habit or act; rather, it receives all things through succession. 

It is truly necessary for the soul itself to be, in a certain way, all things. Concerning this, <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>Ficino refers here to the *Chaldean Oracles*, which he believed were written by the ancient Persian sage Zoroaster. They were a primary source for his "Ancient Theology."</note> says: *And the whole of the world encompasses many fullnesses within its bosoms.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὸ πᾶν κόσμου πολλὰ πλήρη μετὰ κόλπων"</note> This means it comprehends many fullnesses of the worldly depths. For if the soul is necessarily the middle between the highest and lowest things, it contains within itself the gifts and images of those highest things, and the powers and models of the lowest. But in that part by which it communicates with the angelic mind, it turns out similar to the angel; <margin>f</margin> in the other part, it is dissimilar. 

Therefore, the souls of the spheres possess all the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Platonic Ideas: the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things.</note> in their minds simultaneously in habit and in act. In their lowest powers, which move the bodies, they possess again the seeds of things to be generated in possession and habit simultaneously, but not in act. <margin>K</margin> ¶ Their middle part—namely, **reason**—follows the mind. Because their bodies are most perfect and lack almost nothing, they are sufficiently ruled by the lowest part of the soul alone. Therefore, the middle part of the celestial souls, which is mobile by its nature, is made stable because it is free from bodily labor and is held fast by the mind. 

In us, however, because of the poverty and need of our bodies, the middle part is also moved like the lowest part, forced by the too-difficult and laborious administration of the body. It also appears that there is some movement, as <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino translated his entire works into Latin.</note> <margin>c</margin> suggests, in the rational part of the celestial souls themselves. For as it flows out from the unity of all things (God), first through its own unity (which is the head of its mind), and then through its own mind (which is the head of reason), it also flows back through its mind and unity into God, the unity of all things. 

Indeed, the soul first naturally desires God himself. Second, it understands Him. Third, it loves Him intellectually. Fourth, it attains Him through a certain amorous union. The Platonists call an action that passes through intermediaries to a certain end "motion." If it passes through **time**, they call it temporal motion; but if it happens in a **moment**, they call it eternal motion. Such is the motion in the reason of the celestial souls. Although...

## Page 16

This middle part, and that portion of those [souls] which is turned toward the mind, may see all the <term>reasons</term><note>Latin: "rationes." In Platonic thought, these are the divine blueprints or "seeds" of all created things.</note> at once. However, the lowest part of them—being most closely related to changeable bodies—is not of such great power that it is able, in a single act, to be carried into all the seeds of the universe. Yet it desires to be carried toward all things in action, so that all things within its potentiality are not in vain. It therefore moves toward them with a manifold effort; at one moment it attains these in action, and at another moment those. But it loses its hold on the former in action when it runs toward others. Therefore, it does not embrace all things simultaneously. It is, however, always <margin>👉</margin> striving toward all things. It runs, therefore, and this sort of running is the **first motion**. Moreover, the interval of this running is the **first time**. Toward that "running," the world runs; toward that "time," the times of the world flow. Now, I believe the soul itself to be as it is in the works of **Orpheus**: like **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape at will. Ficino uses him as a metaphor for the soul's ability to transition between different states or thoughts.</note> changing his forms.

But since those seeds are limited to a certain number, and the soul runs forever, it passes through all things within a certain space of time. Once these are completed, it is either forced to rest (as it seems to us) or <margin>—</margin> to run back gradually through all things again, and to reweave the same "web of generation" in the world, as was pleasing to **Zoroaster**. For Zoroaster thinks that when the same causes eventually return in their entirety, the same effects likewise return. By this same reasoning, both he and many other of his successors confirmed the **resurrection of human bodies**. 

The Platonists have maintained that the interval of the entire circuit is completed in thirty-six thousand solar years; this they call the **Great** or **World Year**. **Mercury** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage whom Ficino believed was a contemporary of Moses.</note> calls the end of this year the "old age" of the world. ¶ **Plato**, in his book on kingship, discusses the restoration of the world. 

<margin>👉</margin> But so that you may more clearly understand the manner of moving the heavens, take this example: **Euclid** thinks of leaving Megara at night to go to Athens to hear **Socrates**. He takes up a **lantern**. First, he prescribes that whole journey in a general thought. From this universal purpose, no actual step is taken unless a particular thought intervenes, designating the first step. Therefore, the lantern first shows the first step; the **imagination** <margin>👉</margin> immediately thinks of this very step, the appetite chooses it, and the feet perform it. In the same way, the lantern shows the second step; soon Euclid thinks of it, desires it, and performs it. He does the same for the third and the others. 

By the same reasoning, they believe it happens in the soul of the sphere. There, the mind and its reason collectively establish as many figures in the heaven—and forms in matter—to be fashioned through the motion of the heaven as it sees ideas and concepts being fashioned in the **Angel** <note>The Divine Mind</note> through the power of God Himself. Thus, the soul itself, according to its powers, produces a worldly work of the same kind that God produces as an angelic work. And so, it imitates the primary Architect. 

However, it does not begin to move the heaven or work upon anything unless the **moving power** (which is its lowest part, like a lantern) brings forth one specific kind of its seeds before the others and offers it, as if to the eyes. As soon as the power of one kind of seed prevails over the others, the **Imagination** itself (which is joined to this lowest power) thinks of that seed, desires it, and unfolds it in the heaven. It formats it in the elements, sows it in the heaven, and brings it to birth in the elements. In the same way, this occurs through a series of successions in the other seeds. 

In this series of fatal succession consists the **Law**; in that thought consists **Desire**. Thus the heaven is moved by fate and innate desire, in almost the same way that in us the spirits and humors are vibrated and formed by intense thought and emotion. Nor should you think that such new effects in the world, or such varied figures in the heaven, are unfolded at every moment except through the new and varied affections of those souls. For from a cause that is entirely stable, the work produced is also stable. Nor should one think that the souls of the heaven are fatigued by moving, if our own soul is not fatigued. For **Movers** who are not extended along with the thing moved are not accustomed to being fatigued—especially if they are very close to the end of all motions in a finite state. 

**Furthermore**, just as the lowest, earthly body is sluggish toward motion, so the sublime body is agile. If a light breeze stirs up dust, and the wind trapped in the bowels of the earth shakes mountains, will you wonder that sublime souls can roll the thinnest of bodies with the slightest nod? Especially since those bodies are oriented toward their natural [state]...
