<margin>o</margin> on a natural axis: and they move in their own orbit: and they themselves are more inclined toward this kind of motion by natural instinct than a terrestrial body is toward falling, even when our path leads its body down a slope. Truly, the body of the heavens is so well-balanced and moves so easily to any position around the center, just as <term>elemental matter</term><note>The basic physical building blocks—earth, water, air, and fire—which are inherently changeable.</note> is inclined toward any form—indeed, much more so. Accordingly, just as the power for moving is appropriate to the soul, so a readiness for motion is appropriate to the body.

<margin>+</margin> For since the body is made from <term>act</term><note>In philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the realization of a thing's potential; Ficino argues that because the heavens are the most "actualized" physical things, they must always be active.</note>, it exists in act and is directed toward act; for that reason, it possesses a nature such that it is always exercised through its forms. Since it possesses both substance and divisible quality, whatever it either does or suffers, it is compelled to do and suffer according to a divisible manner—that is, according to motion. Moreover, the motion of the heavenly bodies and its variety contribute to generation and the diversity of things to be generated. For it adorns the heavens with various patterns and transmits celestial powers more vehemently into the elements. It moves the elements and compels them to mix with one another in many ways. It illuminates and nourishes the globe of the elements everywhere with a certain equal reciprocity. Furthermore, the matter of the world itself cannot hold all figures in the heavens at once, nor all forms under the heavens at once. Indeed, many of these are contrary to one another. Yet, it everywhere desires all of them as if they were the perfections of its own nature. Hence it is made inclined toward perpetual motion, so that what it cannot achieve all at once in a fixed state, it may at least achieve in some way through succession.

But why, specifically, do the spheres rotate in a circle? Although I have just signaled the reason, let us begin from a deeper point. **God** is a single circle: since He is from Himself like a circle and is within Himself, insofar as He has no beginning or end outside of Himself; but beginning in Himself, He ends in Himself. The **Angel** is a double circle: both because he returns there from whence he flowed—while he understands and loves his Author—and because he considers himself. The **Soul** is a triple circuit: because it looks back to God; because it considers itself; and because it descends from the causes of things to their effects and, in turn, ascends from effects back to causes. If these three "heavens" <note>Here, Ficino uses "heavens" metaphorically to refer to the three higher levels of reality: God, Mind, and Soul.</note> go around their own drivers, what is to stop the physical heaven from also being carried in a circuit? And since the heaven imitates these higher causes in its shape and substance, why not also in its motion and operation likewise? The heaven is subject to the noble soul; from there its motion begins. Once one part of the heaven has begun to move, because of its continuity, it pulls another part and pushes another along with it, and they necessarily turn one another back into a circle.

<margin>f</margin> The heaven cannot stand still, since its soul never knows how to rest; yet it does not wish to leave its natural place. Thus it happens that it revolves around the same point and within itself. The heaven is always mobile; indeed, the earth, which is most distant from it, is always immobile. That which is always moved necessarily returns to the same point.

<margin>6</margin> For no straight path of physical things is infinite. Furthermore, **Plato** says in his book *The Statesman* <note>original: "de regno" (On the Kingdom), a title often used for Plato's "Politicus."</note>: "To the most divine of all things alone belongs a state entirely devoid of change." But the world, because it is a body, already falls away from the dignity of divine things; therefore, it cannot be altogether immutable. Since, however, it is closest to the divine, it was fitting for it to be moved by a circular motion, which—since it revolves in the same place, around the same point, according to the same rule, in a similar and perpetual continuity—departs the least from local stability. These are his words. Add to this: that just as among all types of motion, local motion alone (which is as if external to its subject) does not compel the substance or natural quality to change, so the circuit among local motions seems to be called "non-motion," because it alone does not change its place.

<margin>10</margin> If anyone wants the heaven to stand still, let him fix the heaven of **Saturn** on its axis at whatever moment he pleases. Then one semicircle of that sphere stands above our heads, and the other above the heads of the <term>antipodes</term><note>People living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. Since all parts of this sphere are most similar to one another without any natural difference, there is no reason why one part should be here rather than another part there. Therefore, the lower semicircle, which is equally connected to our place as to the region of the antipodes, strives to be here just as it is there; and the upper semicircle...

He argues that circular motion is the closest physical approximation to the eternal stability of the divine.</summary>

Because of this same affinity for that place, it will allow it to be there, just as it was here. From this effort, one part pushes another; any two parts, due to an equal affinity <margin>☞</margin>, will want to be everywhere equally. Indeed, the concave surface of the **eighth sphere** <term>eighth sphere</term><note>In the Ptolemaic system, this is the sphere of the fixed stars, located just beyond the planets.</note> is the natural location of the **sphere of Saturn**. There, the concave part of Saturn’s sphere touches the eighth. Every particle of this sphere—because it matches equally with every particle of the eighth—strives to touch all of its particles. If it were to stand still, individual parts would touch only individual parts, not every part touching all. By running, however, it almost achieves what it could not achieve by standing still: such is the greed of this sphere for that one. Furthermore, the soul of the sphere of Saturn is present in its entirety simultaneously in every point of the sphere. This sphere <margin>☞</margin> is eager to enjoy its soul. Therefore, it runs so that through all its parts it may enjoy the whole soul everywhere. Let it revolve most rapidly so that, as far as possible, it might be everywhere as a whole at once, just as the soul is everywhere as a whole at once. And because it nowhere finds a standing soul, the sphere itself never rests. And just as the soul is constantly revolved around **God** as if around a center, so the body, drawn by the soul, is always revolved around the soul as if around a center. However, the heaven remains in the same order because the soul, through its participation in the **Mind** <note>original: "mentis participationem." In Neoplatonism, the Mind or Intellect is the level of reality above the Soul, characterized by perfect, unmoving stability.</note>, is a participant in a certain rest. All rational souls do this within their bodies. All bodies do this toward their souls, whether we speak of the souls of the spheres and stars, or of demons and men. Although this is less apparent <margin>☉</margin> in this gross body of ours, it nevertheless occurs <margin>☞</margin> in the **ethereal garment** <note>The "spiritus" or "astral body," a subtle vapor that Ficino believed linked the immaterial soul to the heavy physical body.</note> of the soul, which we will discuss elsewhere. This is what **Zoroaster** <note>Zoroaster was seen by Renaissance scholars as a "Primal Theologian" whose ancient wisdom prefigured Plato and Christianity.</note> intended to be constantly revolved within us. Finally, let us conclude this discussion and opinion on the movement of heaven with this thought: neither the movable body of heaven nor the mover—which is moved for the sake of the heaven's movement—is the primary prince and end of this motion, lest labor or transgression occur in such a movement. For motion is always performed and governed toward the stable and around the stable.

# The Platonic Theology of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the Great-Souled Lorenzo de' Medici. 
# Book Five.

<margin>¶</margin> Every rational soul is immortal. The first reason: because it moves by itself, and moves in a circle. **The Fallen.** <note>original: "Lapsi." This likely refers to the "fallen" state of souls into bodies, a key theme in how they regain immortality.</note>

<margin>☞</margin> <insert>W</insert>e place all souls in the order of the **third essence** <term>third essence</term><note>Ficino’s "Five Substances": God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Matter. Being the "third" or middle essence, the soul acts as the bridge (nodus mundi) between the eternal and the temporal.</note>; and for this common reason, we wish them to be immortal: because they are moved first, and because they are moved first, they are moved in a circle; therefore, because they move first, they are moved <margin>☞</margin> always. For there is perpetual motion where there is first motion. For if the fountain of motion were to dry up, nothing else in nature would be moved. Moreover, that which moves first provides internal and external motion to itself. Internal motion is life. Therefore, it supplies life to itself. And because it never deserts itself—since a perpetual love of self exists in every nature—it never ceases to live. For if that which is moved by another moves only as long as it adheres to its mover, much more so does that which is moved by itself—which is one and the same as its mover—never cease to be moved, as it is never deserted by its mover. Furthermore, if one imagines it to perish at some point, it will either cease to exist before it ceases to move, or vice-versa, or both simultaneously. The first is not possible, because motion cannot remain separate from essence; nor the second, because spontaneous motion is the constant companion of that which originates motion for itself; nor the third, since a ruinous change can never break out from within that from which vital and life-giving motion arises. Nor will such a change happen from the outside. For the fountain of motion is not moved from elsewhere. This is the property of the third essence on both sides, and since all rational souls are included in this by a certain common definition, the same property applies to all of them.

# Theology, Fifth Book

E 2

<margin>D</margin>
**T**hey are also immortal because of this: that by the nature of the **third essence** <term>third essence</term><note>In Ficino's hierarchy of being, the Soul is the 'third essence,' sitting exactly in the middle between the eternal (God and Angel) and the temporal (Quality and Matter).</note> and the first motion, they are driven in a circle. For a circle does not scatter its strengths, but gathers each of its own back into itself; and lest it be thought to fail, it renews itself. Thus, we may for now bypass that **Pythagorean** <note>Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher who believed in the transmigration of souls and the mathematical harmony of the universe.</note> reasoning which shows that in a sphere there is no beginning or end. Therefore, that which moves in a sphere has neither ever begun to move, nor does it cease. Moreover, rational souls are certain spiritual spheres, and they perform a spiritual circuit within themselves, rather than the bodies themselves—which are their shadows—having such a shape and motion. So it is that visible spheres and their circuits are the shadows of invisible spheres and circuits; and if the shadows are perpetual, much more will those substances be perpetual, which through a power lacking a limit perform the act of motion without a limit. Nor is there anything contrary to them by which they might be destroyed, just as there is no motion contrary to their motion, which is a circuit.

### ¶ Second reason: because it stands by its substance. Chapter 2.

<margin>E</margin>
**A**nd so the superior reasonings demonstrate the soul to be immortal through its motion. The same is also demonstrated through the state of the soul. When we note the "soul," we wish the genus of **rational souls** to be understood. For we do not properly call non-rational lives "souls," but rather idols and images of souls. If that third essence, about which we have said so much, remains nonetheless through its substance even though it is moved through its operation, it follows that the soul—which is that same essence—is not changed in its substance. That which is of such a nature never ceases to be.

### ¶ Third reason: that it clings to divine things. Chapter 3.

<margin>F</margin>
**I**f two certain things located at the lowest level of nature—namely matter and quantity—are passive, and two others at the highest level are active—namely **God and the angel**—how will the soul and **quality** <note>In Aristotelian terms, a "quality" is a property like "redness" or "heat" that exists within a physical object.</note>, which occupy the middle region between the passive and the active, behave? In this way, certainly, each becomes a participant in passion <note>original: "passio," meaning the capacity to be acted upon or to suffer change.</note>. But quality, because it inheres in things that suffer, receives passions entirely through its operation and essence. The soul, however, which stands further away, receives some bodily passion in its faculty of acting. In its essence, however, it is free from passion. And just as the body, consisting of matter and quantity, renders the quality inhering in itself subject to corruption, so God and the angel, being active, make the soul (which is closest to them and set apart from the body) immortal by their own divinity.

### ¶ Fourth reason: because it dominates matter. Chapter 4.

<margin>G</margin>
**B**ut its immortality appears most of all in this: that it is necessary for the very **prime matter** <term>prime matter</term><note>The fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe that receives physical forms but has no identity of its own.</note> of things—which is moved and formed by the soul—to be perpetual. Art imitates nature. Art performs its works in this order: namely, it imprints different forms one after another upon a certain subject matter, of which the matter possesses none as its own. For clay has no form of any vessel as its own, but receives various ones in turn from the potter; and when the vessel is broken, the clay remains, from which other things may be restored. Therefore, nature itself, the craftswoman of things, has a certain subject matter for itself that is void of all forms and equally prepared to receive all. Because just as God is **pure act** <note>Pure existence without potential for change.</note> at the highest level of things, needing nothing and the maker of all forms, so at the lowest level there must be something that is **pure potentiality**, lacking all things, and being itself formless while capable of receiving all forms. Thus, universal matter is subject to the universal craftsman and to nature, to be formed however he wishes, like an indifferent receptacle. This is called the first of the materials of the elements and of other bodies, equally subject to their forms. And now it receives this form from a natural force, now that; nor does it have any form as its own by its nature. For it would not be the lowest if it had any perfection and faculty of acting natural to it from its own form; nor would it be suitable for another form that was repugnant to its own form. For if coldness were proper and natural to matter, in what way would it receive heat? And if moisture, how would it receive dryness? But observe the mutual commutation of the elements if you desire to find this hidden matter. For when wax...

# A Platonic Book

i 3

...we [have seen]: where previously the species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the outward form or appearance.</note> of earth existed, we cannot say that the form of water appears there later in such a way that it receives the form of water which recently arrived into the form of earth; for these are in a certain way opposite to one another, since earth contains dryness and water contains moisture. Therefore, the form of earth does not "receive" the form of water; rather, as the watery species approaches, the earthly form departs into chaos <note>In this context, "chaos" refers to a state of total formlessness or the dissolution of a specific identity.</note>. However, the form of water cannot exist without a **subject** <term>subject</term><note>The "subject" (subiectum) or substrate is the underlying "stuff" that remains the same even when the outward appearance (the form) changes.</note>, nor did a new subject arrive during the generation of water. Therefore, the same **matter** which had been the subject for the earthly form now undergoes the form of water.

<margin>B</margin> And this is the argument which **Timaeus the Pythagorean** <note>Timaeus of Locri, a character in Plato’s dialogue "Timaeus," was believed by Renaissance scholars to be a real Pythagorean philosopher who taught Plato about the creation of the universe.</note> uses. Likewise, when the sun, by striking the sea with its rays, thins out the water into vapors, it generates air from water; it has certainly drawn some small portion of the watery body out of the element of water. We ask whether that little portion of water was first reduced to nothing and then generated air, or whether it preserved something of the water. If water were reduced entirely to nothing, the intention of nature would be toward evil <note>To the Neoplatonists, "nothingness" or the destruction of being was considered a move toward "evil," whereas "being" and "existence" were "good."</note>, though nature is always directed toward the good, since it is ruled by the supreme goodness of God. And "being" itself, which is the peculiar gift of the eternal God, would sometimes be withdrawn from things by the causes following after God; which <margin>C</margin> cannot happen, since God always preserves by His own influx what He once gave, and no violence from any agent can oppose Him. For things inferior to God, since they do not possess absolute being entirely, but rather "some" specific being—that is, this kind of being or that kind—therefore they do not have the power to take away "being" altogether, but rather to change it from this mode to that. 

It would also follow that the sun would have to generate that new air from nothing, if it had consumed the whole portion of the previous water into nothingness. Natural agents are unable to make something out of nothing. For it is easier to make something from any existing thing than from nothing. However, they cannot generate just *any* thing from *any* seed. Never pears from wheat; never figs from millet; never an eagle from human seed. <margin>B</margin> Much less will they be able to generate something from nothing. By this reasoning it is shown that the sun could not have turned that portion of water taken from the sea into nothing. Therefore, something of its prior nature remains in it. What is that? Certainly that water was cold and moist. The coldness departed, but the moisture remains, as is pleasing to the **Platonists**, because moisture is common to both air and water. If the moisture remains, there also remains some matter subject to that moisture. For moisture is not a form that can exist separated from bodies. 

And so the matter, which previously lay hidden under the cold of water, now lies hidden under the heat of air. Indeed, light <note>The text here follows the progression of elements: Earth → Water → Air → Fire/Light.</note> from air becomes fire; it also loses moisture and accepts dryness. Matter of this kind, which ascends into the form of fire by being thinned out through **rarefaction**, in turn descends through **density**: it swells in the air, then thickens into water, and finally becomes heavy into earth. You see that one matter is clothed in all forms in turn, while it ascends through rarefaction and descends through density. This matter is one for two reasons: first, because one matter suffices for one world; and second, because since it is formless, it has nothing within itself by which it could be distinguished into many parts. But if the whole universe ends in one "formable" thing, it is consistent that it also begins from one single Former <note>The "Former" or "Shaper" refers to the Creator/Demiurge.</note>, and the whole is subject to Him. But of this we have spoken elsewhere and shall speak again. 

<margin>D</margin> This matter is never corrupted <note>In philosophy, "corruption" means to break down or cease to exist.</note> because it is the foundation of all corporal nature; if it were destroyed, the entire machine of the world would collapse. Nor is it ever dissolved into parts, because it is not, by its own nature, constituted of parts. For parts are created through **quantity**. Matter, however, precedes quantity. For it is the subject of both quantity and quality. The subject must always precede the thing which lies within it. Nor can it be killed by the arrival of any contrary quality. Indeed, no quality is contrary to matter itself, since it receives all qualities equally by its nature, and no form—which requires the support of matter—fights against it. For the form would be fighting against itself if it destroyed its own foundation. Nor does matter need some other "seat" or location, which if removed might cause it to fall into the depths. For matter itself is the first support of all things. And if some violence should destroy it, it would either lead it into nothingness or transmute it into something else. The first cannot happen. For whatever acts, does so out of a natural appetite to propagate its own perfection, and is thus induced to act so that it might make another thing like...

This philosophical foundation prevents the universe from collapsing into nothingness and points toward a single Creator.</summary>

# Theology, Book Five

<page-num>35</page-num>

...according to its powers, it generates something like itself: which is clear in the elements, plants, and animals. In these, a natural appetite for the **Good** <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Good" is the ultimate source of all being and value, often identified with God.</note> appears—namely, for life and for existence—and these things are loved, rather than their opposites. This is because the Good has been inserted into all things that follow from it, as we have said. For from wherever things originate, from there they are moved, and toward that place are all things carried. Therefore, every appetite and operation of all things, arising from the Good, returns and reflects back into the Good.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, he who fundamentally removes **matter** <term>matter</term><note>Ficino refers to "Prime Matter," the underlying, formless "stuff" of the universe that receives different shapes (forms).</note> from the midst of things cannot establish his new work anywhere, once the foundation of all generatable forms has ceased to be. Thus, if matter were destroyed, nothing would be generated. For if that which is to be made anew requires matter, it can no longer be made if matter is taken away. If it does not require matter, it is free from it; and that which is free from matter towers above it and is procreated by its author separately from matter.

<margin>f</margin> Thus, its author, while he creates it, does it no violence, since he fashions it as something far older <note>In this context, "older" or "senior" refers to ontological priority—the idea that the soul or higher forms are more fundamental and "earlier" in the chain of being than physical matter.</note> than matter. Nor in its generation does he move matter in any way, for the work to be completed does not need it. Therefore, that which gives birth to a new thing—whatever kind of thing it may be, whether needing matter or foreign to it—does not reduce matter to nothingness.

<margin>D</margin> Or perhaps matter will be changed into something else, so that one part of matter remains while another part perishes?

<margin>G</margin> Not at all. For matter is **simple** <note>In medieval and Renaissance logic, "simple" means not composed of parts. If something has no parts, it cannot be broken down or destroyed.</note>; it is not composed of matter and form, since it is the first and formless potential. Nor does it require a certain mass of parts for its existence, since by its natural origin it precedes the dimensions of quantity. Furthermore, if it were changed such that something remained after the change was complete, what would that thing be? Matter? If it is matter, it seems it has not yet been changed into something else, since it still exists. If it is quantity or quality, that would be absurd, because these cannot remain without matter. If some form remained that towered above matter, what need was there to destroy matter so that this very foreign form might be made—a form that is in no way made from matter and is produced far away from it? Rather, because matter is entirely one thing and form (removed from it) is another, nothing of matter remains through this; because once the form is changed, the matter remains as something separate.

Let us therefore conclude: matter cannot be changed from that which it is in any other way than by being turned into nothing. But nature does not allow anything to be turned into nothing. Therefore, matter does not perish. Much less will that very natural force perish which is the mistress of matter. The mistress of matter is that **efficient power** <term>efficient power</term><note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being—like a carpenter making a chair.</note> which forms it. This, in turn, is formed by that power which first moves. The source of motion is the **rational soul**, to which qualities serve as instruments for moving matter. And every rational soul, by the nature of its essence, stands over the third <note>The "third" essence usually refers to the Soul's position in the hierarchy between the eternal (God/Angel) and the temporal (Body).</note> universal matter. But of this, more elsewhere.

<margin>h</margin> Indeed, God produces and unites matter; the Angel strengthens and orders it (as the Platonists believe); and the immortal Soul moves and forms it. God is the Unity who gives unity to immortal matter; the Angel is the immortal Order who displays order in immortal matter. The Soul is the immortal Life which, by moving, provides life to immortal matter.

### The Fifth Reason: Because the Soul is Free from Matter (Chapter 5)

<margin>I</margin> **F**our causes of natural things are numbered by the physicists: **Efficient**, **Final**, **Material**, and **Formal**.
*   The **Efficient** cause of man is universal nature and man himself.
*   The **Final** cause (the goal) is human happiness.
*   The **Material** cause is the body.
*   The **Formal** cause is the soul.

Whenever something is said to exist "through itself," it is understood to exist without a cause. Whenever it exists "through another," it exists through a cause. God alone exists "through himself" in such a way that he exists through no cause; for this reason, he is entirely "through himself," because he excludes all four kinds of causes from himself. A natural body exists entirely "through another," because it includes all four causes at once.

Below God, nothing can exist that lacks an efficient cause and an end, since the one God is the efficient cause and the end of all things. Therefore, nothing besides God will be found that so exists "through itself" as to not have an efficient cause and an end. Nevertheless, it is not fitting that all things under God exist "through another" in such a way that they are *entirely* "through another." Truly, these two—that which is "entirely through itself" and that which is "entirely through another"—are separated from each other by a very long interval. Therefore, there is need for a **middle** <note>A "mean" or "intermediary." Ficino is arguing that if God is totally independent and bodies are totally dependent, there must be something (the soul) that sits in the middle.</note> between them that is more similar to both. Since an agent acts from its own nature, it is necessary that the work made most closely by it—because it is drawn immediately from the nature of the agent—appears most similar to it.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, specifically Book 5. He is building a hierarchical argument to prove the immortality of the soul by placing it in a middle rank between the purely divine (God and Angels) and the purely material (Body and Qualities).</meta>

# The Platonic Book

<margin>a</margin>
Therefore, that which is established by the first and principal cause—by God, so to speak—does not turn out to be entirely dissimilar to God. Consequently, there are certain things between God and the body that are not said to exist entirely through something else. Such a thing appears to be **quality**; it is not caused by four factors as a body is, but depends on only three causes. A body has **matter** <term>matter</term><note>In this context, matter is the physical "stuff" or potentiality that requires a form to become a specific thing.</note> and **form** <term>form</term><note>Form is the defining essence or shape that makes matter into a specific object, like "chair-ness" or "human-ness."</note> as its efficient and final causes. Quality, however, does not have "form" as its formal cause, for it is itself a kind of form. No form, insofar as it is a form, is formed by another; nevertheless, a quality is produced by some agent and is directed toward a specific end by that agent. It also depends on matter as a cause, since such an offspring is brought into the light from the "pregnant womb" of matter, and it is extended and divided along with the matter itself. For this reason, quality stands one degree above the body, because in a certain sense it exists through itself, as it is not formed by another.

But why should there not also be a **third essence** <note>The "third essence" is Ficino’s term for the Soul, which sits in the middle of the five-step hierarchy of reality: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Body.</note> which is at least one degree higher than quality, just as quality is one degree above the body? It certainly is higher. But why? Not because this essence lacks an efficient cause or a final end (since that belongs to God alone), nor because it does not have a form as its cause (for quality already possesses that trait). It remains, therefore, that it is superior because it does not depend on matter—a condition that does not apply to quality. Thus, it is necessary to proceed by degrees from four opposites into four opposites through three and two. Just as we ascended from the four causes of the body to the three causes of quality, so we should ascend above the three causes of quality into the two causes of the third essence. Therefore, this essence will have only an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause</term><note>The agent or force that brings something into being.</note> and a **final cause** <term>final cause</term><note>The ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note>. It will not have matter or form as internal components.

<margin>d</margin>
Finally, the **Angel** <note>In Ficino’s hierarchy, the Angel is the rank immediately above the Soul, characterized by pure intellect without any "inclination" toward the physical world.</note> surpasses this essence by one degree. This is because an Angel neither depends on matter nor inclines toward matter, being occupied primarily by God. The third essence (the Soul), although it does not depend on matter, is nonetheless made by God at a greater distance, and being close to matter, it inclines toward it in a certain way. Because of this inclination, it is called the **soul**. And although it inclines toward matter, it does not depend on it, which we have demonstrated through many reasons. The first is the one we just assigned.

<margin>ii</margin>
The second reason is that if this essence were immersed in matter, it would never emerge into divine things, which are most remote from matter; and thus it would not be a suitable **knot of the world** <note>original: "mundi nodus." Ficino famously describes the Soul as the "knot" or "center" of the universe because it links the eternal, divine realm with the temporal, physical realm.</note>, as it would not connect the lowest things with the highest.

<margin>a</margin>
The third reason is that since it moves first, it necessarily moves by itself freely in a circuit. If it moves by itself, it operates by itself in both respects. If this is so, it also exists by itself, bound to no bodies. If it moves freely, it is not tied to matter. If it revolves in a circuit, it returns into itself, leaving matter behind. The fourth reason is that if it dominates matter by being the first to move and form it, it does not mix with that matter.

<margin>b</margin>
Through these points, that essence which is the seat of the soul—which Plato also calls the **mixing bowl** <note>original: "patera." A reference to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the Creator mixing the soul of the universe in a large bowl.</note> of souls in the *Timaeus*—appears to have no origin from bodies, nor is it composed of the parts of quantity. Indeed, parts of this kind exist only in bodies and qualities, not in forms separated from the body. Therefore, the soul will not be dissipated by being dissolved into any parts. Clearly, it has no distance between parts, because it is not divided in the body; nor will it ever fail because it is deserted by some support. For that essence, which by its nature is the mistress of bodies, requires no foundation from the body. Nor will it perish because the contrary and mutually clashing forces of the **elements** <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> might sometimes disturb it; for these forces clash only in matter.

<margin>c</margin>
The soul, however, is placed by God above matter, so that the storm of the elements and the injustice of competing qualities do not touch it. Furthermore, it will never be stained by receiving some foreign quality contrary to its nature that might inflict a harmful passion upon it. For the first subject exposed to "passion" <term>passion</term><note>In classical philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon or changed by an external force, often associated with suffering or decay.</note> is matter, through which both the quantity immersed in it and the quality adhering to that quantity are exposed to change.

<margin>d</margin>
Wherefore, that essence which is separated from matter—that is, separable in its power—has no power within itself through which it might receive anything foreign or hostile, and thus be subjected to passion.

### ¶ The Sixth Reason: That it is Indivisible. Chapter 6.

<margin>e</margin>
**Furthermore**, since it is indivisible, it does not receive divisible and corporeal qualities. For only that which is divisible can touch the indivisible. For if it were said that the indivisible is touched by that which is divisible, we would ask: does this divisible thing touch that indivisible thing with a certain **point** of itself, or with some divisible part of itself? If you admit the first, then it is merely a point that touches it...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a "third essence" situated between the divine and the material, functioning as the "knot of the world." He asserts that because the soul moves itself and is indivisible, it cannot be destroyed by the physical decay or elemental conflicts that affect the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 5 of the *Platonic Theology*. Having discussed the hierarchy of reality (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Body), Ficino is now proving why the Soul is immortal by arguing it cannot be "touched" or corrupted by divisible, material things.</meta>

### Theology, Book Five

L 4

...touches; and so it is not this divisible thing, but something **indivisible** that touches that indivisible thing. But if you say that it touches with some divisible part of itself, then we reason thus: if this divisible thing touches that which you call indivisible through some divisible part of itself, it is necessary that it is likewise touched by a similarly divisible part of that thing. For how does the former touch the latter, unless the latter also touches it? And how does it touch through many of its own parts, unless that other thing is also touched through its own parts? Indeed, insofar as the former touches, the latter is touched. Therefore, that thing which you affirmed to be **indivisible** is then forced to be **divisible** for the first time, when it is conceded that it is touched by another divisible thing. 

Thus, that indivisible **essence** <term>essence</term><note>The core nature or "what-ness" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> of the **soul** <term>soul</term><note>Latin: *anima*. For Ficino, the soul is the "center of nature," connecting the eternal divine world with the temporal physical world.</note> is never touched by any divisible quality. It is not touched, I say, by a straight line, nor even by a reflected one. Not by a straight line, because the soul itself does not receive a quality running toward it from the opposite side; and not by a reflected one, because since it is exempt from the body, it is not snatched away by the force and fury of the qualities remaining in the body. And so it is corrupted by nothing. 

Or perhaps it might be corrupted by some indivisible thing which it easily receives? Not at all. For the receiving of indivisible qualities perfects the soul, since that which it receives does not corrupt it. This is evident through those indivisible images of things which are received by the soul—both through the senses and through reason—like reflections in the mirrors of water.

<margin>§</margin> Strictly speaking, there is no other way this thing acts upon that one, except that it offers its own form to it. Indeed, all things are led to act according to the propagation of their own nature. But no corporeal thing can, or even attempts to, generate its own bodily form in the essence of the soul, which is so segregated from matter that corporeal forms have no entry into it. 

But does God or an angel perhaps introduce a new form into the soul by which the soul might be disturbed? Not at all; for if they create some form subsisting through itself, they create it separately from the soul; therefore, the soul is not disturbed by its creation. But if they infuse some power into the soul, a power of this kind is beneficial, since it comes from the best causes which are the preservers of the soul itself. Therefore, the soul does not perish through them, but is preserved.

<margin>¶</margin> **Seventh reason: Because it has its being in its own essence.**

<margin>Chapter 7</margin>

## **W**e call "essence" one thing and "being" another. 

By **essence** <term>essence</term>, we mean the "reason" <note>original: *rationem*. Here meaning the logical definition or blueprint of a thing.</note> of a thing, which is captured by a definition. But **being** <term>being</term><note>Latin: *esse*. Ficino distinguishes between the abstract "what" (essence) and the actual "is" (existence).</note> is the act of that essence and its specific presence in the nature of things. 

Take the example of a **comet** <term>comet</term><note>original: *crinita*, literally "hairy star."</note>: the essence of a comet is this "reason" and definition of it—for instance, "a dry vapor in the air, ignited by fire, circling through the air in an orderly way." This definition is true today even if no comet shines anywhere today. But the "being" of such a comet is said to be this: namely, that such a nature of a comet, which is designated daily through the definition, <margin>b</margin> is now actually shining somewhere. 

This "being" cannot exist without a specific place and time. For that essence does not become present otherwise than *here* or *there*, at *this* hour or *that* one. Therefore, the "being" of natural things requires a certain place and time. Essence, in itself, does not need them. For that definition of a comet is true even if at present no comet is burning anywhere. Indeed, if that definition included a certain time and place—suppose "today, here" or "tomorrow, there"—then in that same hour and in that same region of the air in which one comet exists, all comets would have to exist at the same time. For in every individual comet, there is the same common essence and definition of "comet." But if this definition were restricted to a certain place and time, all comets would be restricted to those same boundaries of place and time. 

Just as the power of reason is included in the definition of "human," it applies to every individual human. Thus, the essence and the being of natural things differ in this way: "being" is restricted to a certain place and time, <margin>g</margin> but essence, as far as it is in itself, relates equally to almost all time and every place. Indeed, **humanity** itself can exist no less in other ages than in our own, or no less in the East than in the West. But **Plato** and **Socrates**, in order to "be" and to live, need this or that place and time. In "humanity," the essence is designated; in each of these individual men, "being" is perceived. Therefore, essence is excluded from the limits of time and place found in individuals. For this reason, for its own preservation through its own nature...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is indivisible and thus cannot be harmed by physical forces. He then distinguishes between "essence" (the timeless definition of a thing) and "being" (its existence in a specific time and place), using the example of a comet.</summary>

# Platonic Book
### B

...it needs no place: nor does it have limits of time by which it might at some point be surpassed: seeing that it is exempt from limits of this kind. Therefore, it thrives everywhere and always. **Essence** <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental nature of a thing that defines what it is, independent of its physical location or state.</note> therefore, according to itself, is called immortal. And such, by its own nature, is the essence of every form. But when the Author of all forms generates essences and brings them into being: He determines some to such a being that they exist in a body: whence the being of such an essence, or such a form, is contracted <note>Ficino uses "contracted" to mean limited or narrowed down from a universal state to a specific, physical one.</note> by the Agent to corporal conditions. When being is contracted to the body, the essence is also constrained by those same limits.

<margin>A</margin> The conditions of natural bodies are these: that they fill a space and are moved in time. For that reason, that form—which through itself would have existed above a certain time and place—now undergoes its own time and place. Because it undergoes time, it therefore begins to be changed little by little and ceases. Because it undergoes place, therefore while the body itself in which it lies receives contrary qualities daily, it is also disturbed by this storm of qualities and becomes mortal. Such are the forms and qualities of bodies. But that Author leads other essences of forms into being in such a way that they do not receive their very being in some other thing or matter, but contain it in themselves. Such are all forms alien to commerce with matter. For they have their being in themselves, not in matter. Whatever is received from something else is usually received according to the capacity of that which receives it and is drawn to its property. But any essence is immortal through itself. Therefore, being—which is received from that essence—since it is received by an immortal thing in an immortal manner, is rendered <note>original: "mortale" - This is likely a scribal or printer error for "immortale" (immortal), as the logic of the sentence "received by an immortal thing in an immortal manner" requires an immortal result.</note> [immortal]. Wherefore, a form that is separated from association with matter is immortal in every way: that is, as much according to its being as according to its essence. Such is the **third essence** <note>In Ficino’s hierarchy, the "Third Essence" is the Soul, which sits in the middle between the eternal (God/Angel) and the temporal (Quality/Body).</note> of rational souls.

¶ Eighth reason: that it has its own being and never departs from its form. <margin>Chapter 8</margin>

<margin>B</margin> **G**eneration and corruption <term>generation and corruption</term><note>The Aristotelian terms for "coming into being" and "passing away."</note> are so opposed to each other that they tend toward contradictory states: generation becomes a certain path toward being, and corruption a path toward non-being. Each thing tends toward being because it receives a certain form; but toward non-being because it is forced to lose its form. In the arts, no work is of this or that kind because of the matter, but because of the form. A bronze horse or a man is not called such because of the matter of the bronze—since bronze is equally prepared to receive the figures of all animals—but because of a certain form of a horse or a man, and a likeness proceeding from the craftsman. This part of the bronze is called a horse; that part a man. Similarly in nature: matter is certainly not that by which Plato is a man, or a fig is a tree. For the same primary matter of the world is common to men, beasts, and trees. And many ages before Plato, and many after Plato, that same matter exists. But Plato himself by no means exists [forever in that matter]. Therefore, Plato does not have the human species because of matter, but because of such a complexion of the body and a soul, which are called forms. 

<margin>C</margin> Similarly one must judge concerning other things; and in summary, it must be concluded: that anything has its own being, nature, and species—differing from others—from its form. Wherefore, whatever ceases to be, loses its very being because it is separated from its own form, just as it had previously begun to be when it had attained its own form. Therefore, a thing composed of matter and form—for instance, fire composed of its mass and natural heat—perishes when it is separated from its form. For the cold of water or earth can sneak into the matter of fire and expel the form of the natural heat of the fire, and once this is expelled, it ceases to be fire. 

<margin>D</margin> Thus that fire, composed of matter and such heat, loses its being because it loses its heat—I mean its substantial form with its properties, which (since it does not have a clear name) we now call "heat" for the sake of the argument. But heat itself, when it loses its being, since it is a form and being comes from form—that is, when it is driven out from that matter... For in composite things, being is naturally attributed to the whole, not the parts. Truly, the being of fire belongs properly to the composite itself, not to the matter alone, nor to the heat. For when heat, in the generation of fire, by a natural agent...

<summary>Ficino explains that essence is inherently immortal, but when a form is "contracted" into a physical body, it becomes subject to time, place, and mortality. He argues that the soul, as the "third essence," remains independent of matter and thus retains its immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 5 of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is contrasting the "common" forms of physical elements like fire—which depend on matter and are therefore mortal—with the "pure form" of the soul, which is self-subsisting and immortal.</meta>

-># Book Five of Theology<-

...drawn forth from the natural seed of matter. On this condition was the **fire** extended through matter: so that it might depend entirely upon it, nor would it have its own heat as its own property; rather, its heat would be the common <note>original: *commune*. Ficino argues that physical heat belongs to the category of "fire" in general, not the specific instance of matter.</note> being of all fire, and by this it would be said to exist. However, that common being ceases when those two parts are separated from each other. When the common being ceases, the **form** <term>form</term><note>Latin: *forma*. The organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> also perishes, which flourished through that common being. Matter, however, does not perish, because it immediately takes up another form through which it may exist; thus, while it loses a certain heat, it loses its "fiery being." While it receives a certain coldness or humidity, it takes on an "earthy being" <margin>E</margin> or a "watery being." Conclude then that a composite thing, such as fire or water, perishes because it is separated from its form. But that form is lost because it departs from the law of the one who forms it. The Sun, which begat the fire, stands as the "former" of fire. By that law, it drew out the heat from the tinder <note>original: *fomes*. This refers to the potentiality within matter that allows it to be ignited.</note> of that matter, so that the heat, lying within that matter, would be contained within the being of the whole composite. <margin>L</margin> It transgresses this law when it departs from that matter. It departs when it is driven away by cold. If, therefore, it departs neither from its own form nor from the law of its former, in what way does it perish? Since the being of each thing depends on its form and is preserved by the law of the one who forms it.

The **soul**, however, on account of the property of that third essence <term>third essence</term><note>In Ficino’s five-tier hierarchy of reality (God, Angelic Mind, Soul, Quality, and Matter), the Soul sits in the middle as the third essence, the "bond of the world."</note>, is a certain pure form; it is not composed of matter and form, nor is it reclining in matter. Therefore, it remains within itself, because whatever is in it is nothing other than form. She <note>Ficino uses the feminine *Anima* (Soul).</note> herself, therefore, by her own essence, does not "form" anything else; rather, she is the form of her very self. That is, she is the form itself. Now, there is nothing that can be separated from its own essence by itself, because nothing departs from itself. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, all things, by a natural instinct and perpetual effort, preserve themselves according to their strength and cling to themselves. Therefore, if the soul is never separated from itself, and is its own form, it is never separated from <margin>S</margin> its own form. Thus, it never ceases to be, since it always draws its "being" from its form. Of its own accord, it is not separated from itself, as we have said. But neither is it forced by external violence to withdraw from itself. For whatever it receives from the outside, it receives in its own specific way. It is clearly **spiritual**, and absolute from place and time. Therefore, in a spiritual way and absolutely, it receives all things. 

Spiritual and absolute things, when they are captured by something, never destroy it. For when spiritual reception occurs in bodies, it does not corrupt those bodies, even though they are dissimilar to it—as is the case with the reception of images in water and in a mirror. Much less will it corrupt a spiritual thing very similar to itself. Furthermore, since that "absolute thing"—which was imagined to be received by the essence of the soul—is eternal, why should the receiver destroy its own? Is it so that it may feed itself from that matter? No, since that which is eternal does not lack nourishment. Is it so that it may propagate itself and generate something similar to itself from that matter? Not at all. For that which always remains the same does not lack propagation. Nor can it generate an everlasting thing from a corruptible thing. Therefore, it does not corrupt anything in order to generate something perpetual similar to itself. 

In no way, therefore, can anything seize the essence of the soul so as to destroy it. Deservedly, it cannot receive anything harmful at all, since it lacks matter, which is said to be the first and proper receptacle of such sufferings <note>original: *passio*. In a philosophical sense, 'passion' means being acted upon or undergoing a change from an external source.</note>. On the contrary, if this essence is its own form, nothing ever comes between it and its form. For if some medium ever fell between itself and its form, that medium would surely become closer to the form than its own essence is. But the essence itself is its very form. Thus, something would become closer to it than it is to itself, which is the most absurd of all things. Wherefore, no medium inserts itself between the soul and its form. If this is so, the soul is separated from its form by no intervening thing. But neither is it separated from its own [form] voluntarily. Wherefore, in no way does it depart from itself and its form. Nor does it depart from the law of its Creator. Indeed, it was created by that law so that it might consist within itself. It always remains so; for it is cast down from that state by no one. Not by itself, for every thing preserves its own species and dignity according to its power. Not by superior causes, because they contain it by the same law by which they produced it; nor by inferior ones. For the superior is not conquered by the inferior.

<summary>Ficino argues that unlike physical forms which depend on matter, the soul is a "pure form" that is identical with its own essence. Because nothing can be separated from itself, the soul is inherently immortal and cannot be destroyed by internal decay or external force.</summary>

Therefore the soul, because it is pure form, and thus departs neither from its own form nor from the law of its former <note>The "former" (Latin: *formantis*) refers to God or the divine architect who gives shape and law to all things.</note>, remains without doubt immortal.

### Ninth reason: Because being belongs to it through itself. Chapter 9.

<margin>A</margin> **W**hat belongs to something through itself <term>through itself</term><note>Latin: *per se*. In medieval philosophy, this refers to an essential quality that cannot be separated from a thing without the thing ceasing to be what it is—like "threeness" to the number three.</note> is never separated from it. Roundness exists in a circle by its very nature. And thus no circle ever exists without roundness. But roundness exists in wood only sometimes; this is not because it is wood (for if that were the case, all wood would be round), but because it receives a circular shape from a craftsman. Because roundness accompanies that shape, the wood is then forced to take on roundness. The wood eventually ceases to be round as soon as it ceases to be circular. Then the wood remains, but it is no longer round. But a circular shape is so necessarily round that if it were to cease being round, it would also cease to be circular. Similarly, heat belongs to fire through itself, moisture to water, and light to the sun. In no other way does **being** belong to **form** through itself. For whatever exists as a certain thing in any species certainly obtains what it is from a proper form that leads it to that species. Since, therefore, proper being belongs to each thing through its own form, it follows that being, commonly and simply, belongs to the genus of form itself. Whence it is necessary that form itself be called the "source of being" and that it exists through itself. 

If someone says it exists through something else, we shall ask: does that something else through which the form is said to exist have the nature of form or of matter? It is not matter, because we see in every composite thing that the being of each does not follow the matter. Therefore, even in this form itself—through which composite things exist—that which it is does not have the power of matter, but of form. Thus the question returns to the same point: whether that other form, through which it is a form, exists through itself or through something else? If through itself, then it stands that "form" ought to be called the source of being. If through something else, then we shall ask as before, and there would be an infinite progression. Therefore, being belongs to form through itself.

<margin>B</margin> But indeed, the creator of forms, for a certain end of the worldly work and for the integrity of the universe, produces forms with such distinction that he determines each naturally to a certain way of being: some to be present in a body, others to be in themselves without matter. A form sunk <note>original: *issa*, likely *immersa* (submerged/sunk). Ficino distinguishes between "material forms" that drown in matter and "subsistent forms."</note> in matter does not properly exist, nor has it its own being; rather, it is said to be that by which the composite itself exists, and the form itself exists only through the "common being" of the whole. If being belongs to form through itself, then certainly this form which is in the body—because it too is a form—possesses this: that being belongs to it through itself. 

But how? Since it depends on matter and is contained under the being of the whole composite? Take note: being belongs to it "through itself." That is, being follows it through itself. I say it follows through itself—that is, according to its nature. For what else does "through itself" mean but "through its nature"? Its nature is such as its maker assigned to it. The maker ordained that it should adhere to matter. Nor is its nature anything without adhering to matter. Being follows it through this nature. Therefore being follows it through itself—I mean, as it adheres to matter. Thus, in a way, it belongs to it to be fixed in matter before it exists. Therefore it exists as long as it adheres to matter; but it does not adhere forever. 

<margin>C</margin> Because matter, being prepared for all forms, often gives place to contrary forms which drive out the previous ones. Therefore, that [material form] does not exist forever. But that form which is so determined toward being by the creator that it consists in itself apart from the body—also because it is a form—has this: that being belongs to it through itself; through itself, I say, meaning through its nature. The nature assigned to it is to adhere to itself. Therefore its being follows it as much as it adheres to itself—that is, its existence follows it, not sprouting from a subject <note>In this context, "subject" refers to matter. Physical forms sprout from matter like plants from soil; the soul does not.</note>. And as often as you say, "being follows it through itself," you say, "being follows it as it adheres to itself." Nothing departs from itself. For what could fall between "itself" and "its very self" to separate it from itself? If it exists insofar as it adheres to itself, and because it adheres to itself forever, it exists forever. Such a form indeed is the soul. Therefore, it is immortal.

But someone might object to this reason thus: that just as fire, which is hot through itself, is always hot as long as it exists, yet it does not exist forever, and since it does not exist forever, it is not always hot...

<summary>Ficino argues that since the Soul is a "pure form" and being is the essential property of form, the Soul must always exist. He distinguishes between material forms that depend on matter and the soul, which is determined by God to "adhere to itself" and thus remains immortal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology'. While the previous page was noted as Book 6, the header here indicates 'Theology Book Five'. Ficino continues his metaphysical proof for the immortality of the soul by distinguishing between forms that require matter (like fire) and the soul, which is a "separate form" existing through its own essence.</meta>

-># Theology Book Five<-

absolute and always. So too is the soul’s essence: which is properly and truly a form <term>subsisting in itself</term><note>Latin: *in seipsa subsistens*. This means the soul does not need a physical body to "hold" its existence; it stands on its own.</note>: therefore it exists through itself: and because it exists through itself: therefore it is: and always: namely, while it is. Yet it is not always. Therefore it is not always. This objection is judged ridiculous for two reasons. First, it contradicts itself when it is constructed thus: "That form exists through itself; therefore it is always: namely, while it is; but it is not always." For there are four statements here: the second of which—which says "Therefore it is always"—contradicts this later one which concludes "But it is not always." Then, an objection of this kind abounds in superfluities when it adds: "Namely, while it is." For this phrase "while it is" cannot be said to be anything other than "it is." Especially in the first part where it is said: "it is always." For if it were so, there would be in the same thing a double "is" and a double "being," and it would not exist as one certain thing, but as two. From this it follows that the "is" which is posited when one adds "namely, while it is," should be the same as that which had already been posited when it was previously said "It is always." Things that are the same must be treated with the same logic. Therefore, if the first "is" is uttered absolutely, then the second "is" ought to be uttered absolutely without that phrase "namely, while." Therefore one ought to say "It is always: it is, it is," but one must not add "namely, while it is." Or if you add to that first "is" another "namely, while it is," you must also add to this second "is" that which follows afterward, "namely, while." Again to that "namely, while it is," you add a third "is." Again "namely, while it is." And so on into infinity. Nor will you ever find the first root of being, through which it happens that the thing is, and is always. That which has no root of being is nothing at all. 

Now, come, stop your pace. That separate form, such as the soul, exists through itself. Therefore it is always. Indeed, if "to be" and "to be hot" were the same thing, when you construct it thus: "Fire, because it is hot through itself, is always hot," you would immediately add: "to be healthy and to be is the same thing: therefore it is, and always." But now you cannot conclude in that way. Because "to be" is not the same as "to be hot." Otherwise, whatever things exist would be hot. And whatever ceases to be hot would cease to be. Since that does not happen, fire therefore is always hot *while it is*. Because in a certain way "to be" comes first, and afterward "to be hot." And because "to be" is prior to "being hot" and is something different from "being hot," heat is seen to belong to the essence of fire through something else that acts as a medium; so that first the essence of fire is posited, second its being, and in the third place its being hot. 

Indeed, the essence of fire obtains "being" through that which adheres to matter. For in a certain way it first lies hidden in the womb of matter before it is brought into the light. And just as it lay hidden before it existed, so also it adheres afterward, so that it does not cease to exist. It also obtains "being hot" through the fact that it possesses "being." For this reason it ceases to be hot when it ceases to be; and it ceases to be when it ceases to adhere <note>original: *inherere*. This refers to the way a physical form "sticks" to matter to have a physical presence.</note>. But the soul’s essence, since it is a released form <note>Latin: *forma soluta*; a form not bound to or dependent upon matter for its existence.</note>, obtains being through itself. And in it, being itself is the first and proper act of the essence; nor is there any bond through which being is connected with the essence, which, if loosened, would cause dissolution. And although both "being hot" and "being" belong to the essence of fire through some condition, yet "being" does not belong to the soul's essence through any condition, but absolutely. Therefore, although fire exists and is always hot only under a certain condition, the soul nonetheless always is, absolutely.

### Tenth reason: Because it is referred through itself to God.
<margin>Chapter 10</margin>

<margin>✋</margin> **I**f, however, there should seem to be any condition by the virtue of which the soul is always, it is not in respect to bodies (the help of which it does not need), but in respect to the **First Cause** <note>The "First Cause" is a standard philosophical term for God, the origin of all existence.</note> from which it descends. But even a relation of this kind, since it is completed through the soul's nature itself, does not prevent the soul from being always, through itself, absolutely, and without condition. We shall investigate this by the following reasoning: since all things depend on the first cause of things, individual things remain in their being to the extent that they are referred back to the first cause. But they look back to that cause insofar as they bear some likeness of it. That Cause is the **purest act** <note>Latin: *actus purissimus*. In Scholastic philosophy, God is "pure act," meaning He has no unfulfilled potential and is perfectly realized existence.</note>, most foreign to every property of matter. Inferior things are judged similar to this act not from their matter, but rather from their form, which exists as a certain "act." Whereby...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', specifically Book 6. The text follows a sequence of metaphysical arguments proving the immortality of the soul. The previous page discussed the soul as a self-subsisting form; this page expands on how the soul relates to the "First Cause" (God) and why its lack of material composition prevents it from decaying.</meta>

-># Platonic Book<-

It happens that through their form, all things look back to the first cause. Therefore, whatever things are composed of matter and form—such as the elements and things mixed not through themselves—look back to the first cause not through their whole nature, but only through that part of themselves which is called form. Argue in this manner: As things are referred to the first principle, so they exist. But they are referred through something else. Therefore, they exist through something else. Those things that exist through something else are not stable. For if left to themselves, they vanish into nothingness. In themselves, therefore, they are nothing; those things which exist through something else are whatever exists. Such indeed are natural bodies. But as for corporal forms, <margin>B</margin> they are certainly similar. For a form implanted in bodies has lost its specific excellence and has turned entirely corporal, since it has now undergone all the conditions of the body. <margin>B</margin> There are two conditions of the body: extension according to space and change according to time. But the form immersed in bodies expands with the width of the body and changes when the body is changed. Since, therefore, it has become entirely corporal and stripped of its former excellence, it exists very little through itself (as we have said elsewhere) and has no being of its own. Instead, it is so joined with matter that there is one being for the whole. If, therefore, it does not exist through itself, it certainly does not act through itself. Thus, if it refers back to the first cause, it will refer through something else: namely, through that by which it exists. But it exists <margin>C</margin> through another, more sublime form, free from matter, upon which it also continuously depends within the matter, just as the image of a man's face depends on a mirror. Through this higher form, it is also continually referred back to the first causes. If the corporal form exists entirely through something else, since it even refers back to the first principle through something else, what then is that through which both the natural body and its form are referred to the first? It is surely that <term>third essence</term><note>Ficino identifies the "Third Essence" as the Rational Soul, which acts as the middle ground or "node of the world" connecting the eternal divine realm to the temporal physical realm.</note> which we placed long ago above the qualities of bodies. An essence of this kind refers the qualities of bodies to God in the same way it produces them in matter. But it produces them by its own operation. Its operation is mobile. Therefore, it generates through agitation. Through agitation, it also refers back.

---

And so it refers wonderfully. From this it follows: that natural bodies and their forms, because they refer back to God through something else and through motion, neither exist through themselves nor are they stable, but they waver entirely and perish. But the <term>third essence</term>, because it is its own form—or rather, is form itself—and a form free from matter, is therefore referred to God through itself. As it refers, so it is. Therefore, it also exists through itself. It is referred through its own essence, and that essence is stable. Therefore, having been referred to the stable God through <margin>C</margin> its own stable essence, it remains stable. Truly, this essence is the cause of its own relation and the reason for its perfection. It never deserts itself; therefore, it never ceases to refer itself, never ceases to perfect itself by referring. God, indeed, always overflows; that essence always drinks. Therefore, both on the part of the drink and the drinker, it always drinks in being itself and thus remains immortal.

### The eleventh proof: because it is not composed of any potentiality into which it could be dissolved. Chapter 11.

<margin>D</margin>
**J**ust as generation occurs through the joining of form with matter, so <term>corruption</term><note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the process of decay, breaking down, or ceasing to exist as a unified thing.</note> occurs through the separation of form from matter. Where there is no joining of these things, separation does not happen. But such a composition is not in the soul. But let us pursue <margin>E</margin> this reasoning further. In the corruption of any thing, the <term>act</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "act" (actus) is the reality or fulfillment of a thing, while "potentiality" (potentia) is the capacity to be changed or dissolved.</note> of the thing itself perishes. But after that, something remains which was beneath that act, such as some receptive potentiality, so that corruption does not result in nothingness, just as generation does not come from nothing. Indeed, a thing composed of form and matter is resolved into matter. Also, that form which had been drawn out from the spark of matter is led back into the spark of matter. In the soul, however, its act is its very being. Its essence and substance is that very potentiality which underlies the act of being. For in absolute forms, there is almost no other composition than that of essence and being, or similar. Essence holds <margin>F</margin> the place of matter and potentiality. Being holds the place of form and act. If the soul is corrupted, its being perishes entirely. But surely not its essence? By no means. <margin>G</margin> For no thing is resolved into nothing. Because a thing that is so simple that it is not otherwise resolved...

<summary>Ficino argues that while physical bodies are unstable and perish because they rely on external forms, the soul (the "third essence") is a self-subsisting form free from matter. He concludes that the soul is immortal because it is not a composite of matter and form that can be separated or dissolved into nothingness.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, First Cause, Third Essence, form and matter, corruption and generation, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, metaphysics</keywords>
