<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the soul's immortality from Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology'. It builds on the previous argument that the soul is a self-subsisting form by exploring its "simplicity"—meaning it is not composed of parts that can break across space or time—and its direct relationship to God as its creator.</meta>

# Theology

# Fourth [Book]

...it is so simple that it cannot be broken down except into nothingness. Moreover, it is of such a nature that it was made by God through creation out of nothing. Being of such a nature, it is subject only to its author, God. Furthermore, the flow of vitality and beneficence from God does not destroy anything.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, if the soul is destroyed—that is, if it were to lose its <term>being</term><note>Latin: *esse*. In scholastic philosophy, this refers to the act of existing.</note>—it still remains in its <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental "what-ness" or nature of a thing.</note>. This is evident from the fact that the nobler a thing is, the nobler the matter and the nobler the form it possesses. Souls are far more excellent than bodies. Therefore, beneath their "being" (as if beneath a form and an <term>act</term><note>Latin: *actus*. The realization or completion of a potential.</note>), there lies a certain "matter" and <term>potentiality</term><note>Latin: *potentia*. The capacity to become something or receive a form.</note>, if any such thing lies hidden there at all. This is more excellent than the form and the being of any body whatsoever. That which holds the place of prime matter and potentiality in souls is their very essence. Thus, their essence is more eminent than the matter of bodies. The matter of bodies is incorruptible. Therefore, why is it a wonder if that essence of the soul can be incorruptible? From this it follows that if the soul should ever imagine it is losing its "being," its essence and substance must necessarily still survive. If this survives, it certainly exists. If it still exists, then its "being" has not yet been lost. Thus, if the soul is said to be corrupted, it necessarily survives even after that corruption.

<margin>I</margin>
Indeed, it also lives. For the "being" of the soul is nothing other than "living." But lest anyone say that the soul's "being" is broken down into its essence, and that the essence then ceases to exist because it is without "act" (even if the "potential" remains somewhere), one must remember that this essence cannot be reduced back into physical matter or the potential of matter.

<margin>C</margin>
This is because the soul does not consist of matter as a part of itself, nor does it sprout from the potentiality of matter. Furthermore, it cannot be broken down into the potential power of any other active cause, except perhaps into the power of God, who alone created the soul. Yet the soul does not die because it is "broken down" into the First Life <note original: "primam vitam">Referring to God as the source of all life.</note>. It would only die if, upon being led back into God, it ceased to be a soul. But just as a wax figure impressed by a seal—which is perfectly matched to the seal—is not destroyed, but rather is perfected in its specific shape, so too the essence of the soul, if ever it is moved toward the <term>Idea</term><note>The divine archetype or pattern in the mind of God.</note> through which God disposed it into a certain species of being, is confirmed in its original being. This is especially true since a subsequent act is strengthened by the first act. For how can God be the "end" toward which corruption tends, since He is the *efficient* end from whom all creation and generation are derived? Or in what way does God, who is <term>Pure Act</term><note>A theological term for God, meaning He is fully realized existence with no unrealized potential or "matter."</note>, concur in the composition of the soul as it is born? It is not as if a physical form is made from the potentiality of matter plus an added act of potentiality—where the act of the form is eventually broken back down into that potentiality. It is not as if the soul is made from some "potentiality of God" with an added act, only to be broken back down into God's potential as if into matter.

<margin>K</margin>
For He who is the First Act never plays the part of matter. Someone might assert that the essence of the soul is broken down neither into matter nor into God, but that it immediately withdraws into itself once its prior "being" is taken away. But just as physical matter cannot exist without a physical "act," so too spiritual matter cannot exist apart from a spiritual one. Therefore, the essence (which is the "matter" of spiritual things) and its spiritual "being" (which is like its "act") are never separated—I mean from its spiritual "being." Unless, perhaps, someone says that the essence of the soul puts off one "being" to put on another, and that this essence varies its spiritual "being" in turns, just as matter varies its forms. But that is an absurd thing to say. First, because the essence of spiritual things is more stable than the matter of physical things. Second, because the essence of the soul, since it is the very definition of the soul itself, does not look toward one thing and then another entirely; rather, it looks only toward "being a soul" according to a specific type of soul.

<margin>L</margin>
Common matter <note original: "Materia quidem communis">General matter that can become anything, like clay.</note> can exist without this or that specific act. But a specific matter cannot exist without its specific act. Therefore, the essence of the soul, which exists in such a species of souls, will never take on the act of another species of souls. Nor will the essence migrate within the same species from this soul into that one, lest it be as unstable as the matter of physical bodies. Indeed, if the matter of the heavens is always content with the same form (as most philosophers believe), what wonder is it if the spiritual matter of the soul is always content with the same "act of being"? That essence is life; this "being" is living. Therefore, it lives forever.

<summary>This page argues that the soul is an indestructible spiritual essence whose "being" is synonymous with "living." Ficino contends that because the soul is a simple, non-material creation of God, it cannot be broken down into parts or reduced to physical matter, ensuring its eternal existence.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, essence vs being, act and potency, divine creation, simplicity, incorruptibility, Marsilio Ficino, scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the soul’s immortality. While the previous page discussed the soul's simplicity and its direct creation by God, this page introduces the "twelfth argument," which focuses on the philosophical concept of "potentiality." It argues that because the soul is a pure form rather than a composite of matter and form, it lacks the inherent capacity—or "potential"—to stop existing.</meta>

->Platonic [Theology]<-
->Book VI<-

<margin>a</margin>
<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
### Twelfth argument: that the soul does not have in itself the potentiality for non-being.

<margin>b</margin>
**N**o thing is ever destroyed unless it possesses within itself a <term>potentiality for non-being</term><note>Latin: *potentiam ad non esse*. In medieval philosophy, this is the "capacity to cease to exist." If a thing is "pure being," it has no "room" in its nature for its opposite, non-existence.</note>. For if it were unable to "not be," it would never cease to be. The soul has no such potentiality. Among the Platonists, the soul is nothing other than a <term>simple form</term><note>Latin: *forma simplex*. A "simple" thing is not made of parts; therefore, it cannot be broken apart or dissolved.</note> subsisting through itself: perfect and complete in its own <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note>, and serving to bring about the appearance of a living creature. The <term>act of existing</term><note>Latin: *actus existendi*. The reality of actually being alive or present, as opposed to just being a concept.</note> is present there within the soul itself—that is, within the complete and perfect form. Indeed, it is through the integrity of its form that each thing exists. Therefore, the primary subject of "being" in that case is the soul's own form and essence. 

Where, then, could there be a potentiality for non-being (which is the opposite of "being" itself)? Could it be in "being" itself? But how can one thing have the power to receive its own opposite? Or is it in the essence itself? Not here either. For if the essence, by virtue of being a simple and complete form, is the proper subject of "being," how can it hold a potentiality for non-being, which is said to be its opposite? For in what way can the proper substance of fire—which is the proper subject of heat—possess any potentiality to receive cold, such that it might accept the cold and yet remain fire? 

And yet, even in these physical and mortal substances, there is no potentiality for non-being insofar as they are complete substances in their own species and endowed with form; for it is according to this form that they exist. Rather, they have this potentiality only insofar as <term>prime matter</term><note>Latin: *materia prima*. The most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe that can become anything but is nothing specific on its own.</note> underlies them—matter which never rests under any single form. This matter, however, is absent from the soul. Therefore, no potentiality for non-being is found in the soul. It is, therefore, immortal. 

But let us explain this argument more clearly. In those things composed of form and matter, it happens that the matter in some sense precedes the work itself. For who would doubt that matter exists in some way before it is formed? I take this matter as preceding the work to be made, and I ask: is it necessary that the work come from the nature of this matter, or is it impossible? Or perhaps is it possible, but not necessary? If the power of the matter immediately gave necessity to the work by itself, it would not need any more excellent thing to form it; but as it stands, it does need one, because that which is unformed cannot form itself. Therefore, as far as the matter is concerned, the future work is not "necessary." Is it "impossible"? Not that either. For if it were, the matter would be so unsuitable for that work that it could never be led toward that form and effect. If, then, the work to be done is neither necessary nor impossible in regards to the matter, it remains that it is "possible." For this is the middle ground between those two.

<margin>c</margin>
I say it is "possible" to be and not to be. For if by the nature of matter it were only possible *to be*, it would without doubt be necessary. If by its nature it were only possible *not to be*, it would also be impossible. Therefore, since by the nature of matter the work itself is equally possible to be and not to be, it is clear that in the matter itself, regarding the work to be made, there is a potentiality to be and not to be equally. Since, indeed, simple matter is not composed of many natures, the same nature of matter is the potentiality for being and for non-being. Because it is indifferent to both, it is not limited to either one by itself. It requires a <gloss>higher agent</gloss><note>original: *Superiori agente*. Referring to a creator or a forming force like the World Soul or God.</note> to determine it toward "being" by forming it. It receives from that agent the form of a lion, for example; thus, a lion is made. And the very matter of the lion, which previously held in itself the potentiality to be a lion and not to be a lion, is now determined toward being a lion.

<margin>d</margin>
But does that same indifferent potentiality for both outcomes still remain in the prime matter? If it did not remain, the nature of matter would immediately cease to exist, and nothing would ever be made from matter; it would be established that as soon as something is made, prime matter is deprived of its nature and perishes. Therefore, since it remains even after the lion is born, that same potentiality exists in the matter—not the matter "near" to the lion (the secondary matter), but the "prime" potentiality, I say, to be and not to be equally. Thus it happens that just as the lion began to be at some time through that potentiality (having not existed before), so too through that same potentiality it ceases to be at some time after it has existed. 

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because it is a "simple form" lacking "prime matter," the element that gives physical things the potential to decay or cease to exist. Because the soul is its own essence and not a composite, it contains no internal "potentiality for non-being."</summary>
<keywords>immortality, simple form, prime matter, potentiality, essence, non-being, Aristotle, Plato, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 125 ---
<meta>This page continues the "twelfth argument" regarding the potentiality of the soul. While the previous page established that the soul lacks an internal potential for non-existence, this page explores the source of the soul's existence: God. It argues that because the soul's "potential to be" is rooted in God's own eternal nature, its existence is as stable as its source.</meta>

# Theology, Book Five

...since <term>potentiality</term><note>Latin: *potentia*. In this context, it refers to the "capacity" or "possibility" for something to happen or exist.</note> is indifferent to either extreme: it is either turned toward neither, or it is turned equally and alternately toward both. <margin>E</margin> And just as it was turned from non-being toward being, so it is turned alternately from being back into non-being. From this follows the corruption of physical bodies. But the rational soul, since it is a <term>simple form</term><note>Latin: *forma simplex*. A philosophical term for an entity that is not made of parts and therefore cannot be broken down or decomposed.</note>—from which motion arises in composite things—could not have been made from any preceding matter followed by a form. And since it is a form subsisting in itself, not leaning on matter (since it proceeds both above and below matter in its reasoning), it is not composed of any "potentiality of matter" (as if it were a beginning of a soul) with an added "potential act" (as if it were the soul's perfection). Therefore, it neither consists of matter nor stands apart from it. If it is such a form, it proceeded from nothingness into the light of existence. Therefore, God alone is its author, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere. 

Yet, if this soul could not have been made, it surely never would have been. Therefore, a <term>potentiality for being born</term><note>Latin: *nascendi potentia*. The capacity or "pre-condition" that allows a soul to be created.</note> preceded our soul. Where was that potentiality? Not in the soul itself, which did not yet exist; not in a part of the soul, which is simple and is created as a whole all at once, not in parts. It was not in any matter, since the soul does not depend on matter. It was not in "nothingness," for the potentiality of being is not founded upon nothing. For how could one opposite be the foundation of its opposite and its contradiction? <margin>F</margin> Indeed, "being" and "non-being" are contradictory. 

It remains, then, that this potentiality is founded in God alone, the author of the soul. Therefore, the potentiality for being—through which the soul is brought into existence—is God himself, who alone is immortal and stable. Moreover, the "act" corresponds to the potentiality according to its fitness. Therefore, the <term>act</term><note>Latin: *actus*. The fulfillment or realization of a potential; here, the soul's actual existence.</note> corresponding to that divine potentiality is stable through its essence. Such an act is the soul. And just as in God there is the same power by which God can make the soul and the soul can be made, so in the soul there is the same act—that is, the same "striving"—by which the soul subsists in its own nature and God maintains it within that nature. Thus, it happens that God maintains the soul in its nature with no less desire than the soul itself remains beneath that nature.

Since the soul is subject to God alone, if it is to be destroyed by anyone, it must be destroyed by Him. But from Him it cannot be. For how could an <term>effective and preservative cause</term><note>Latin: *causa efficatrix et conservatrix*. A cause that both brings something into being and keeps it in existence.</note> also be its destroyer? Or in what way is the "Good" itself harmful to anyone? <margin>B</margin> Or is the "First Life" and "Infinite Life" the source of death? 

Someone might say that God does not destroy the soul by applying some new force, but by taking away the force previously granted to it—that is, by withdrawing His <term>influence</term><note>Latin: *influxum*. A Neoplatonic concept where existence "flows" from a higher source (God) into lower beings.</note> through which the soul lived. Just as one who creates his own image in a mirror by looking into it ceases to create that image by withdrawing his face. But this cannot happen here, as we showed shortly before. Again, if God pours life into the soul now, but later does not, a change occurs there from "pouring" to "not pouring." I ask whether the soul ceases to <term>draw life</term><note>Latin: *haurire vitam*. Literally "to drink" or "drain" life, suggesting the soul is a vessel for divine energy.</note>, or God ceases to pour it. 

The soul does not cease to draw it. Indeed, the infusion of life happens within the essence of the soul. For life is the "first act" of essence as soon as it receives being. <margin>S</margin> The soul's essence is immobile, because it depends without intermediary on the stable God; it is perfected by standing still and being at rest. It is disturbed by motion. It reaches for stable things. It rules over falling things. It halts moving things. It collects scattered things. It reconciles conflicting things. Nor is there in the soul that potentiality to "be and not be" simultaneously, such as exists in bodies, which is the beginning of all change. 

Therefore, the essence of the soul never ceases to receive the act of life, nor does God cease to pour it. For God indicated that He would only cease to pour His power into those things in which He implanted from their origin that tendency toward non-being. Furthermore, God, the founder of nature, never takes away from a thing that which is the thing’s <margin>P</margin> own. ¶Life is the soul's own property—I mean <insert>perpetual life</insert>—because insofar as it is rational, even without instruction and experience, it generates life within itself daily through the power of its own nature.

<summary>This page argues that the soul's existence is guaranteed by God, its only cause. Because the soul's "potential to be" is rooted in God's eternal nature rather than material components, it cannot naturally decay or be withdrawn by the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, potentiality, divine influence, simple form, Marsilio Ficino, essence, Neoplatonism, stability of God</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book Five regarding the hierarchy of existence. The previous page established that the soul is a simple form created by God. Here, Ficino begins to place the soul—the "Third Essence"—into a specific ladder of being, distinguishing it from God, Angels, Qualities, and Bodies.</meta>

<page-num>38</page-num>
->Platonic Book<-
<meta>Folio number 3 in top right corner</meta>
<sig>E iii</sig>

# Platonic Book

Therefore, it is primary and fundamental—so to speak—that in the plan established by God, the soul does not turn out to be most unlike God. There are, therefore, certain things between God and the body which are not said to exist entirely through something else. Such a thing appears to be <term>quality</term><note>Latin: *qualitas*. In Platonic philosophy, qualities (like heat or color) are seen as a step above raw matter because they provide form, but they still depend on a body to exist.</note>, which is not caused by its own genus—as a body is—but depends instead on only three causes.
<margin>A: The body has matter and form as its causes, as well as an efficient cause and an end; quality does not have form as a formal cause. For quality is itself a kind of form.</margin>
For quality itself is a certain form. Truly, no form, insofar as it is a form, is "informed" by another; nevertheless, quality is produced by something (an efficient cause) and is directed by that agent toward a certain end. It also depends on matter as a cause, since such an offspring is brought into the light from the pregnant womb of matter, and is extended and divided along with it. For this reason, quality is one degree above the body, as it is in some way "of itself," since it is not formed by another. But why should there not be a **third essence**, which is higher than quality by at least one degree, just as quality is one degree above the body? Certainly there is. But why? Because this essence lacks an efficient cause or an end, since this belongs to God alone? No, that is not it; nor is it because this essence lacks a form as its cause. For quality also possesses that trait. It remains only, therefore, that this essence does not depend on matter—a thing that quality certainly cannot claim. Thus, it is necessary to proceed by degrees from four opposites into four opposites through three and two. Just as we ascended above the four causes of the body into the three causes of quality, so we should ascend above the three causes of quality into the two causes of the third essence. Therefore, this essence will have only an efficient and a final cause. It will not have form or matter. Finally, the
<margin>B: The angel surpasses this essence by one degree.</margin>
<term>angel</term><note>Latin: *angelus*. In the Neoplatonic hierarchy, angels represent pure intellects that are entirely separate from the physical world.</note> surpasses this essence by one degree. Since the angel neither depends on matter nor leans toward matter, as it is primarily occupied by God.
The **third essence**, although it does not depend on matter, nevertheless, having been made by God at a distance and being close to matter, it leans in a certain way toward it. Because of this leaning, it is called the **soul** <note>Latin: *anima*. Ficino is defining the soul as the "middle" of the universe, connecting the divine and the material.</note>. And although it leans, it does not depend on matter, which we have demonstrated by many arguments.
¶ The first is that which we have assigned. The second is that
<margin>C: The second is... The third is...</margin>
if this essence were immersed in matter, it would never emerge into divine things, which are most remote from matter; and thus it would not be a suitable "knot of the world," for it would not connect the lowest things with the highest. The third is that since it moves first, it necessarily moves by itself freely in a circuit. If it moves by itself, it certainly operates by itself. If this is so, it exists through itself, enslaved to no bodies. If it moves freely, it is not tied to matter. If it revolves in a circuit, it returns into itself, leaving matter behind. The fourth is that if it rules over matter by moving it primarily and by forming it, it does not mix with matter. ¶ Through these points,
<margin>B: Plato names the bowl of souls in the *Timaeus*.</margin>
that essence which is the seat of the soul—which Plato also calls the <term>bowl of souls</term><note>Latin: *animarum pateram*. A reference to the "Crater" or mixing bowl in Plato's *Timaeus* (35a), where the Creator mixed the ingredients of the World Soul.</note> in the *Timaeus*—is shown to have no origin from bodies, nor is it constituted from the three dimensions of quantity. For parts of this kind belong only to bodies and qualities; they are not in forms separated from the body. Therefore, the soul will not be dissipated on the grounds that it might be dissolved into parts. Indeed, it has no distance between parts, since it is not divided within the body; nor will it ever fail because it is deserted by some support of its own. For that essence, which by its nature is the master of bodies, needs no physical foundation. Nor will it perish because the contrary and mutually clashing forces of the elements might eventually disturb it; for these
<margin>C: The soul truly is above matter from God.</margin>
clash only in matter. The soul is truly from God above matter, so that the storm of the elements and the unfairness of battling qualities do not reach it. Again, it will never be stained by the fact that it might sometimes receive some foreign quality adverse to its nature, which might bring a harmful passion upon it. For the first subject exposed to passion is matter, through which both the quantity immersed in it and the quality clinging to that quantity are exposed to passion.
<margin>D: Wherefore that essence...</margin>
Wherefore that essence which is separated from matter—that is, separable in its power—has no power in itself through which it might receive anything foreign or hostile, from which it might be subjected to passion.

### ¶ Sixth reason: that it is indivisible. Chapter 6.

<margin>E</margin> **F**urthermore, since it is **indivisible**, it does not receive divisible and corporeal qualities. For that which is divisible does not touch the indivisible. For if the indivisible were said to be touched by that which is divisible, we would ask: does this divisible thing touch that indivisible thing with a certain point of itself, or with some divisible part of itself? If you admit the first, then it is only a point which [touches] that thing...

<summary>Ficino defines the soul as the "Third Essence" in the cosmic hierarchy, positioned between angels and physical qualities. He argues that the soul is immortal and indivisible because it does not depend on matter for its existence and acts as the "knot" connecting the divine and material worlds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book 5. Following the previous discussion of the soul as the "Third Essence" situated between the eternal and the temporal, Ficino here argues for the soul's immortality by proving it cannot be "touched" or corrupted by physical, divisible things, and by distinguishing between a thing's universal essence and its specific existence.</meta>

<page-num>36</page-num>
<header>Theology Fifth</header>

# Theology
# Fifth [Book]

it touches: and so it is not this divisible thing, but something indivisible that touches that indivisible thing. But if you should say that it touches by some divisible part of itself, then we reason as follows: if this divisible thing touches that which you call indivisible through some divisible part of itself, it is necessary that the other thing be touched similarly through a part of itself. For how could this touch that unless that also touches this? And how does this touch that through several of its parts, unless that also touches through parts of itself? Indeed, to the extent that this touches, to that extent that is touched. Therefore, that thing which you affirmed was indivisible is then first forced to be divisible when it allows itself to be touched by some divisible thing. Therefore, that indivisible essence of the soul is never touched by any divisible quality. It does not touch, I say, by a straight line, nor even by a reflected one. Not by a straight line, because the soul itself does not receive a quality occurring from the opposite direction; not by a reflected line, because since it is exempt from the body, it is not snatched away by the force and fury of the qualities raging in the body. Therefore, it is corrupted by nothing. Or perhaps it will be corrupted by some indivisible thing which it easily receives? Not at all. For the reception of indivisible qualities <term>perfects</term><note>In Platonic thought, "perfection" means making a thing more complete or bringing it closer to its ideal form, rather than "improving" it in a modern sense.</note> that which receives them; it does not corrupt it. This is evident through those indivisible images of things which are received by the soul—as if by a mirror of water—both through the senses and through reason.
<margin>S</margin>
In a strict sense, one thing does not act upon another for any other reason than that the former offers its own form to the latter. Indeed, almost all things are led to act by the propagation of their own nature. But no corporeal thing can, or even strives to, generate its own corporeal form within the essence of the soul, which is so segregated from matter that corporeal forms have no entry into it.
<margin>B</margin>
But do God or an angel never induce a new form into the soul by which the soul might be disturbed? Not at all; for if they create some form subsisting through itself, they create it separately from the soul; therefore, the soul is not disturbed by its creation. But if they infuse some power into the soul, a power of this kind is beneficial, since it comes from the highest causes which preserve the soul itself; therefore, the soul does not perish through them, but is preserved.

¶ Seventh argument: that it has its being in its essence. <margin>Chapter 7.</margin>

<margin>H</margin>
# **W** e call one thing "essence" and another "being."
We say "essence" is the <term>ratio</term><note>Latin: *ratio*. Here meaning the "defining logic" or "inner formula" of a thing.</note> of a thing, which is grasped in a definition. "Being," however, is the act of that essence and its presence in the nature of things. Take the example of a **comet** <note>original: *crinita*, literally a "long-haired star."</note>: the essence of a comet is this logic and definition of it—for instance, "dry vapor in the highest air ignited by fire, circling through the air in order." This definition is true today even if no comet shines anywhere today. But the "being" of such a comet is said to be this: namely, that such a nature of a comet, which is daily designated through the definition, now actually shines somewhere. This "being" does not happen without a certain place and time. For that essence does not become present otherwise than here or there, at this hour or that. Therefore, the "being" of natural things requires a certain place and time. But "essence" does not require them. For that logic of a comet is true even if at present no comet is burning anywhere. Indeed, if that definition included a certain time and place—say, "here today" or "there tomorrow"—then in that same hour and same region of the air in which one comet exists, all comets would exist at once. For in individual comets there exists the common essence of "comet" and the same logic. But if this logic were restricted to a certain place and time, all comets would be restricted to those same boundaries of place and time. Just as the power of reason, since it is included in the definition of "man," belongs to every individual human being. Therefore, the essence and the being of natural things differ in this: that "being" is restricted to a certain place and time. Essence, however, as far as it is in itself, relates equally to almost all time and all place.
<margin>I</margin>
Indeed, humanity itself can exist no less in other ages than in ours, or in the East no less than in the West. But **Plato** and **Socrates** require a place and time in order to "be" and to live. In humanity itself, "essence" is designated; in each of these individual men, "being" is perceived. Therefore, essence is excluded from the individual limits of time and place. Wherefore, for its own preservation through its own nature...

# Platonic Book
### B3

needs no place; nor does it have limits of time by which it might at some point be surpassed, since it is exempt from such limits. Therefore, it flourishes everywhere and always. Every essence, therefore, is in itself victoriously immortal. Such by its very nature is the essence of every <term>form</term><note>In Platonic philosophy, a "form" is the ideal blueprint or essential nature of a thing.</note>. However, when the Author of all things generates the essences of forms and brings them into being, He determines some for such a being that they exist in a body; thus the being of such an essence or form is contracted by the Agent <note>The "Agent" refers to the Creator or God.</note> into corporal conditions. When being is contracted to a body, it also constrains the essence within those same limits.

<margin>A</margin> The conditions of natural bodies are these: they fill a place, and they move in time. Therefore, that form which by itself would have existed beyond a certain time and place now undergoes its own time and place. Because it undergoes time, it begins to change little by little and then ceases to be. Because it undergoes place, it daily receives contrary qualities while the body itself in which it lies exists. It is also disturbed by the storm of such qualities and becomes mortal. Such are the forms and qualities of bodies. But that Author produces other essences of forms in being so that they do not obtain their being in some other thing or matter, but contain it within themselves. Such are all forms alienated from any commerce with matter. For they have their being in themselves, not in matter. Now, whatever is received from another is usually received according to the capacity of that which receives it, and is drawn toward its properties. But any essence is immortal through itself. Therefore, the being which is received from the essence itself—since it is received from an immortal thing in an immortal way—is rendered immortal. For this reason, a form that is separated from the association of matter is immortal everywhere—that is, as much according to its being as according to its essence. Such is the <term>third essence</term><note>Ficino identifies the soul as the "third essence" because it sits in the middle of a five-level hierarchy: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Matter.</note> of rational souls.

<margin>Chapter 7.</margin> The eighth reason: that [the soul] has its own being and never departs from its form.

<margin>B</margin> **G**eneration and corruption <note>original: "generatio & corruptio" — these are the technical terms for "coming into existence" and "decaying/dying."</note> are opposed to one another in such a way that they tend toward contradictions: generation is a certain path toward being, while corruption is a path toward non-being. Each thing tends toward being because it receives a certain form; it tends toward non-being because it is forced to lose its form. In the arts, no work is of such a kind or another because of the matter, but because of the form. A bronze horse or a man is not called such because of the matter of the bronze—since bronze is equally prepared to receive the figures of all animals—but because of a certain form of a horse or a man and a likeness proceeding from the artist. This part of the bronze is called a horse; that part a man. Similarly in nature, matter is not that by which Plato is a man, or a fig is a tree. For the first matter of the world is common to men, beasts, and trees. Indeed, that same matter existed many centuries before Plato and will exist many after Plato. But Plato himself does not. Therefore, Plato does not have a human <term>species</term><note>Here, "species" refers to the specific nature or identity of a human being.</note> because of matter, but because of a certain <term>complexion</term><note>The specific physical and spiritual makeup or "weaving together" of a person.</note> of the body and the soul, which are called forms.

<margin>C</margin> We must judge similarly regarding other things and, in summary, conclude: that anything has its own being, nature, and species—different from others—from its form. Therefore, whatever ceases to be, loses its very being because it is separated from its own form, just as it had previously begun to be when it had obtained its own form. Thus, a thing composed of matter and form—for instance, fire, composed of its mass and its natural heat—perishes when it is separated from its form. For the coldness of water or earth can steal into the matter of fire and then expel the natural heat, which is the form of fire; once that is expelled, it ceases to be fire. Thus that fire, composed of

<margin>D</margin> matter and a certain heat, loses its being because it loses its heat—I mean its <term>substantial form</term><note>The core identity that makes a thing what it is.</note> with its properties—which we now call "heat" for the sake of the discussion, since it does not have a well-known name. But that heat itself loses its being because it is a form, and being comes from form; specifically, when it is driven out of that matter. For in things that are composed naturally, being is granted to the whole, not specifically to the parts. Truly, the being of fire belongs to the composite itself, not to the matter alone, nor to the heat. For when heat in the generation of fire by a natural agent...

He explains that a thing's identity (like Plato being a man) comes from its "form," not the universal matter it is made of.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument in Book 5 of the Platonic Theology. Having established that the soul is not a composite body, he now contrasts the "being" of elemental things (like fire) with the "being" of the soul. He argues that while physical forms depend on matter and can therefore perish, the soul is its own "form" and "essence," making it inherently immortal.</meta>

# Platonic Theology
### Book Five

->Theology: Book Five<-

...was drawn out from material seed: it was in such a condition that it was extended through all the matter of fire, so that it depended entirely upon it. Nor did it have a heat proper to itself; rather, through the fire itself, it was said to have a certain being that was the common heat of the entire fire. However, that common being ceases when those two parts are separated from one another. When the common being ceases, the **form** also perishes, which was flourishing through that common being. But **matter** does not perish, since it immediately receives another form through which it may exist; thus, while it loses a certain heat, it loses its "fiery being." When it receives a certain coldness or humidity, it takes on an "earthly being" <margin>E</margin> or a "watery being." Conclude then that a composite thing—such as fire or water—dies when it is separated from its form. But that form is lost because it departs from the <term>law of the former</term><note>The "law of the former" refers to the metaphysical principle or "Agent" (like the Sun or God) that gives a specific shape and nature to matter.</note>. The Sun, which generated the fire, exists as the "former" of the fire. By this law, it draws out heat from the <term>tinder</term><note>Latin: "fomite." In this context, it refers to the material substrate that "ignites" or takes on the form of fire.</note> of that matter, so that, lying within that matter, it is contained within the being of the whole composite. It transgresses this law when it departs from that matter. It departs when it is chased away by cold. If, therefore, it departs neither from its own form nor from the law of the former, in what way does it perish? Since the being of each thing proceeds from its form and is preserved by the law of the formers.

The <term>Soul</term><note>Latin: "Anima." For Ficino, this specifically refers to the rational human soul.</note>, however, because of the property of that "third essence," is a certain pure form; it is not composed of matter and form, nor is it "reclining" in matter. Therefore, remaining in itself, whatever is in it is nothing other than form. It is not, therefore, formed by anything else through its own essence, but it is the form of itself. That is, it is the form itself. Now, there is nothing that is separated from its own essence by its own power, because nothing departs from itself. Indeed, all things, by a natural instinct and perpetual effort, preserve themselves according to their strength and adhere to themselves. Therefore, if the soul is never disjointed from itself, and it is its own form, it is never <margin>F</margin> disjointed from its own form. Thus, it never ceases to be, since "being" is always drawn from form. 

Certainly, it is not separated from itself by its own will, as we have said. But neither is it forced by external violence to withdraw from itself. For whatever it receives from the outside, it receives in its own specific way. It is clearly spiritual, and absolute from place and time. Therefore, it receives all things in a spiritual 

---

and absolute manner. Now, when spiritual and absolute things are received by something, they never destroy it. For a spiritual reception, even when it occurs in bodies, does not corrupt those bodies, even though they are dissimilar to it—as seen in the reception of <term>images</term><note>Latin: "simulacrorum." Ficino uses the way a mirror or water reflects an image without being physically changed by it as an analogy for how the soul receives information.</note> in water and in a mirror. Much less will it corrupt a spiritual thing that is very similar to itself. 

Furthermore, since that "absolute thing" which was imagined to be received by the essence of the soul is eternal, why should its receptacle be destroyed? Is it so that it may feed itself from that matter? No, for that which is eternal does not stand in need of nourishment. Is it so that it may propagate itself and generate something similar to itself from that matter? Not at all. For that which always remains the same does not need propagation. Nor can it generate something perpetual from a corruptible thing. Therefore, it does not corrupt anything so that something perpetual and similar to itself might be generated. In no way, therefore, can the essence of the soul receive anything by which it might be destroyed. Rightly so, it cannot receive anything harmful at all since it lacks matter, which is said to be the first and proper receptacle of such <term>passions</term><note>In classical philosophy, "passions" (passio) are things that happen to a substance—external influences or sufferings that change it.</note>. 

On the contrary, if this essence is the form of itself, nothing will ever fall between it and its form. For if some "middle" were to fall between the essence and its form, that middle would surely become closer to the form than the essence itself is. But the essence itself is its very form. Thus, something would become closer to it than it is to itself, which is the most absurd of all things. For this reason, no "middle" inserts itself between the soul and its form. If this is so, it is disjointed from its form by no intervening thing. But it is also not separated by its own will. Therefore, in no way does it depart from itself and its form. Nor does it depart from the law of the former. Indeed, it was created by that law so that it might consist in itself. It always remains so. For it is cast down from that state by no one. Not by itself, for every thing conserves its own species and dignity for itself according to its power. Not by superior causes, for those causes contain it by the same law by which they produced it. Not by inferior things; for the superior is not conquered by the inferior.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a "pure form" that is identical to its own essence, unlike physical objects like fire where form and matter can be separated. Because the soul receives experiences spiritually rather than physically, and because it is its own source of being, it cannot be destroyed by external force or internal decay.</summary>

# Platonic Book
->Page 58<-

<margin>12</margin>
For this reason, the soul—because it is pure <term>form</term><note>In Platonic philosophy, 'form' is the essential nature or blueprint of a thing, rather than its physical shape.</note>—consequently departs neither from its own form nor from the <term>law of the former</term><note>The 'law of the former' refers to the divine or natural principle that gives a thing its specific essence.</note>; it undoubtedly remains immortal.

### Ninth reason: Because it belongs to the soul to exist through itself. Chapter 9.

<margin>13</margin>
**Q**uat which belongs to something <term>through itself</term><note>Latin: "per se." This means an essential quality that cannot be removed without the thing ceasing to be what it is.</note> is never separated from it. Roundness is present in a circle by its very nature. And thus, no circle is ever without roundness. On the other hand, roundness is sometimes present in wood, but not because it is wood—for if it were, every piece of wood would be round. Rather, it is because the wood receives a circular shape from a craftsman, which roundness then accompanies; thus it is forced to take on roundness at that time. The wood eventually ceases to be round when it ceases to be a circular object. Afterward, the wood remains, but it is no longer round. But a circular figure is so necessarily round that if it ceased to be round, it would also cease to be circular. Similarly, heat belongs to fire through itself; moisture to water; light to the sun. In no different way, <term>being</term><note>Latin: "esse." In this context, it refers to the very act of existing or the state of existence.</note> belongs to form through itself. For whatever exists within any species certainly attains that which it is from a specific form that leads it to that species. Since, therefore, "being" belongs to each thing through its own specific form, it follows that "being," commonly and simply understood, belongs to the very <term>genus</term><note>The broader category or class.</note> of form. Hence, form itself must be called the <term>fountain of being</term><note>Latin: "fons essendi." Ficino views "Form" as the source through which existence flows into the material world.</note> and must exist through itself. If one were to say that form has being through something else, we would ask: does that thing through which form is said to exist have the nature of form or of matter? Not matter, because we see in individual <term>composites</term><note>Things made of both matter and form, like a person or a tree.</note> that the specific being of each thing does not follow from the matter. Therefore, even in this very form through which composite things exist, that through which the form itself exists does not have the power of matter, but rather of form. Thus the question returns to the same point: Does that other form, through which the form exists, exist through itself, or through something else? If through itself, then it stands that "form" ought to be called the fountain of being. If through something else, then we shall ask as before, and there will be a progression into infinity. Therefore, it belongs to form to exist through itself.

<margin>B</margin>
But the founder of forms produces them into being for a certain end of the worldly work and with an integrity of forms with this distinction: that he determines each one naturally toward a certain way of being—some to exist in a body, others to exist in themselves without matter. A form that is merged with matter does not exist in the proper sense, nor does it have its own being; rather, it is called "that by which the composite itself exists," and it exists through the common being of the whole. If being belongs to form through itself, then certainly this form that is in the body—because it is also a form—possesses this quality: that to exist through itself belongs to it. But how? Since it depends on matter and is contained under the being of the whole composite? Consider this: to exist "through itself" belongs to it; that is, being follows it through itself. It follows it, I say, through itself—that is, according to its nature. For what else does "through itself" mean than "through its own nature"? Its nature is such as its maker assigned to it; and the maker decreed that it should adhere to matter. This, then, is its nature: to adhere to matter. Being follows it through this nature. Therefore, being follows it through itself—I mean, following it as it adheres to matter—so that, in a certain way, it belongs to it to be fixed in matter before it belongs to it to exist. Wherefore, it exists only as long as it adheres to matter; and it does not always adhere.

<margin>C</margin>
Because matter is prepared for all forms, it often gives a place to contrary forms which drive out the previous forms. Therefore, such a form does not always exist. But that form which is so determined toward being by the creator that it consists in itself apart from a body—because it is form—also has this: that to exist belongs to it through itself; through itself, I say, through its nature. Its assigned nature is to adhere to itself. Therefore, its being follows it as much as it adheres to itself; that is, its existence follows it as something that does not sprout from a <term>subject</term><note>Latin: "subiecto," referring here to a material base or substrate.</note> at all. And every time you say "being follows it through itself," you are saying "being follows it as it adheres to itself."

<margin>D</margin>
Nothing, however, departs from itself. For what could fall between a thing and its very self that would separate it from itself? If it exists insofar as it adheres to itself, because it always adheres, it always exists. Such a form is the soul. It is, therefore, immortal. But someone might object to this reasoning thus: just as fire, which is hot through itself, is always hot as long as it exists, yet it does not exist forever, and therefore is not always hot...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that existence (being) is an essential property of 'form.' He concludes that because the soul is a form that exists independently of matter, it can never be separated from its own existence, thereby proving its immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Ninth Reason" from page 37, where Ficino argues that the soul exists "per se" (through itself). He is currently refuting an imaginary opponent who claims the soul only exists "always" as long as it actually exists, which Ficino finds logically absurd.</meta>

# Theology, Book Five

->Page 38<-

...absolutely always. Thus also the <term>essence of the soul</term><note>Latin: "anime essentia." The core nature of the soul that makes it what it is.</note>: which properly and truly is a <term>form</term><note>In this context, a "form" is a non-material blueprint or essence that gives life and structure.</note> subsisting in itself; therefore it exists through itself; because it exists through itself, it therefore exists, and exists always: namely, as long as it exists. Yet [an objector might say] it is not always. Therefore it is not always. This objection is judged ridiculous for two reasons. First, it contradicts itself when it is broken down as follows:

<margin>a</margin>
"That form exists through itself; therefore it is always—namely, while it exists—but it is not always." For there are four statements here: the second of which, saying "Therefore it is always," contradicts the last one, which concludes "But it is not always."

<margin>b</margin>
Secondly, an objection of this kind is full of superfluity when it adds: "Namely, while it exists."

<margin>c</margin>
Indeed, this phrase "while it exists" cannot be said to be anything other than "it exists." For if it were otherwise, then in the very same thing there would be a double "it is" and a double "to be"; thus the thing would not exist as one, but as two.

<margin>d</margin>
From this it follows that the "it is" which is posited when one adds "namely, while it exists" must be the very same "is" that was already posited when it was said earlier "it is always." Things that are the same must be treated by the same logic.

<margin>e</margin>
Therefore, if the first "is" is uttered absolutely, then the second "is" must also be uttered absolutely without that phrase "while." Therefore one ought to say: "It is always: it is, it is," rather than adding "namely, while it exists." Or, if you add to that first "it is" the later "namely, while it exists," you must also add it to this second "it is" that follows, and again to the third, and so on to infinity. You would never find a primary root of being through which it is granted to the thing that it exists, and that it exists always. Whatever does not have a root of being is nothing at all. 

Now, stay your foot. That <term>separate form</term><note>Latin: "forma separata." A form that can exist independently of physical matter, such as the soul or an angel.</note>, such as the soul is, exists through itself. Therefore it exists always. Furthermore, if "to be" and "to be hot" were exactly the same thing, when you composed the argument: "Fire, because it is hot through itself, is always hot," you would immediately add: "To be hot and to be is the same thing; therefore it also exists always." But now you cannot conclude in that way. For "to be" and "to be hot" are not the same thing. Otherwise, everything that exists would be hot, and whatever ceased to be hot would cease to exist. That does not happen; and so fire is hot always *while it exists*. For first, in a certain way, it exists, and afterwards it is hot. And because "to be" comes before "to be hot," and is something other than "to be hot," therefore through something else—which seems to be the medium—the heat dwells in the essence of the fire. Thus, first the essence of fire is posited, second its being, and in the third place its heat. 

Indeed, the essence of fire receives its "being" through that which adheres to matter. For it lies hidden, as it were, in the lap of matter before it is brought forth into the light. And just as it lay hidden before it existed, so it also adheres afterwards, so that it does not cease to exist. It also receives "to be hot" through that which 

<margin>D</margin>
possesses being. For this reason, it ceases to be hot when it ceases to be; and it ceases to be when it ceases to be attached [to matter]. But the essence of the soul, since it is a <term>detached form</term><note>Latin: "forma soluta." A form released from the constraints of physical matter.</note>, receives its "being" through itself. And in it, "being" itself is the first and proper act of the essence; nor is there any bond by which "being" is connected to the essence, which, if loosened, would cause dissolution. And although both "being hot" and "being" belong to the essence of fire through some condition, "being" belongs to the essence of the soul not through any condition, but absolutely. Therefore, although fire exists and is hot always under a certain condition, the soul nonetheless always exists absolutely.

### Chapter 10.
### Tenth reason: Because it is related to God through itself.

**I**f, however, there should seem to be any condition by virtue of which the soul exists always, it is not through any relation to bodies—whose help it does not need—but through a relation to the <term>First Cause</term><note>The "First Cause" refers to God, the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic and Christian thought.</note> from which it descends. But since a relationship of this kind is fulfilled through the very nature of the soul itself, nothing prevents the soul from existing always through itself, absolutely, and without condition. We shall investigate this by the following reason: since all things depend on the First Cause of things, individual things remain in their being to the extent that they are referred back to the First Cause. They look back to it insofar as they bear some likeness to it. That Cause is the <term>purest act</term><note>Latin: "actus purissimus." A philosophical term for God, meaning a being that is fully realized and has no unrealized potential or material change.</note>, most foreign to every property of matter. Lower things are judged to be similar to this Act not from their matter, but rather from their form, which exists as a certain act. By which...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s arguments for the immortality of the soul. On the previous page, he concluded the "Ninth Reason" by refuting an opponent's logical fallacy regarding the soul's "always" existing. Here, he transitions into a discussion of how the soul relates to the First Cause (God) compared to physical bodies, leading into the "Eleventh Reason."</meta>

# Platonic Theology: Book Five

->Page 38<-

It happens that through their form, all things look back to the <term>First Cause</term><note>Latin: "primā causam." In Ficino's Neoplatonism, this is God, the source of all existence.</note>. Therefore, whatever things are composed of matter and form—such as the <term>elements</term><note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and mixtures—look back to the First Cause not through themselves, nor through their whole nature, but only through that part of themselves which is called "form." Argue in this manner: Just as they refer back to the first principle, so they exist. But they are referred back through something else. Therefore, they exist through something else. Things that exist through something else are not stable. For if left to themselves, they vanish into nothingness. In themselves, therefore, those things which exist through another—whatever exists—are nothing. Such indeed are natural bodies.

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, bodily <term>forms</term><note>The "form" of a body is the blueprint or essence that makes it a specific thing, like "treeness" or "waterness."</note> are certainly similar. For the form implanted in bodies has lost its excellence and has turned entirely bodily, since it has now undergone all the conditions of the body. There are two conditions of the body: extension according to space, and change according to time. But the form immersed in bodies expands with the breadth of the body and changes when the body is changed. Since, therefore, it has become entirely bodily and stripped of its former excellence, it exists in no way through itself—as we have said elsewhere—and has no being of its own. But it is so joined with matter that there is one single "being" for the whole. If, therefore, it does not exist through itself, it certainly does not act through itself. Therefore, if it is referred back to the first cause, it will be referred through something else: namely, through that by which it exists.

<margin>G</margin> It exists, however, through another more sublime form free from matter, on which it continually depends within the matter, just as an image in a mirror depends on a man’s face. Through this [higher form], it is also constantly referred back to the first cause. If the bodily form exists entirely through another, since it also refers to the first principle through another, what then is that through which both the natural body and its form are referred to the First? Surely it is that <term>third essence</term><note>Latin: "essentia illa tertia." Ficino’s specific term for the Soul, which sits in the middle of his five-level hierarchy of reality: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter.</note>, which we have long since placed above the qualities of bodies. Indeed, an essence of this kind refers the qualities of bodies to God in the same way it brings them about in matter. It brings them about by its own operation. Its operation is mobile. Therefore, it generates through <term>agitation</term><note>Latin: "agitationem." A term for the active movement or "stirring" of the soul's power.</note>. Through agitation, it also refers them back.

Thus it refers them back wonderfully. 

From this it follows: that natural bodies and their forms, which refer back to God through something else and through motion, neither exist through themselves nor are they stable, but they waver entirely and perish. But the third essence—because it is its own form, or rather it is the form itself, and a form free from matter—is therefore referred back to God through itself. As it refers back, so it exists. Therefore, it also exists through itself.

<margin>C</margin> It is referred back through its own essence, and that essence is stable. Wherefore, having been referred back to the stable God through the stable essence of itself, it remains stable. Indeed, this essence is the cause of its own relation; the reason for its perfection. It never deserts itself; therefore, it never stops referring back to itself, and never stops perfecting itself by referring back. God indeed always overflows; she <note>The soul is traditionally feminine in Latin (anima).</note> always drinks. Therefore, both on the part of what is drunk and the one drinking, she always drinks Being itself, and thus remains immortal.

### Eleventh reason: because it is not composed of any potentiality into which it could be dissolved. Chapter 11.

<margin>D</margin> **J**ust as generation occurs through the joining of form with matter, so corruption occurs through the separation of form from matter. Where there is no joining of these things, separation does not happen. But such a composition is not in the soul. 

<margin>E</margin> But let us pursue this reason more extensively. In the corruption of any thing, the <term>act</term><note>Latin: "actus." In Aristotelian terms, "act" or "actuality" is the finished state or existence of a thing, as opposed to "potency."</note> of the thing itself is lost. But after that act, something remains which was beneath it: such as some receptive potentiality, lest corruption become nothingness, just as generation does not come from nothing. A thing composed of form and matter is indeed dissolved into matter. That form also, which had been drawn out from the "tinder" <note>Latin: "fomite." Ficino uses this metaphor to describe matter as the "kindling" from which physical forms are sparked or drawn out.</note> of matter, is led back into the tinder of matter. 

In the soul, however, its own "act" is its very "to be" [existence]. Indeed, its essence and substance is that very potentiality which underlies the act of being. For in absolute forms <note>Forms that exist independently of matter, like the soul.</note> there is hardly any other composition than that of essence and "to be," or something similar. 

<margin>F</margin> Essence holds the place of matter and potentiality. "To be" [Being] holds the place of form and act. If the soul is corrupted, its "to be" is lost entirely. But surely not also its essence? By no means. 

<margin>G</margin> For no thing is dissolved into nothing. Because a thing that is so simple that it cannot be otherwise dissolved... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because, unlike physical bodies, it is a form free from matter that relates to God through itself. He also begins a new argument stating that because the soul is not a composite of matter and form, it cannot be dissolved or corrupted.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the soul's immortality in Book Five of his Platonic Theology. Following the discussion on page 38 regarding how things relate to the First Cause, Ficino now examines the unique metaphysical "simplicity" of the soul—arguing that because the soul is a direct creation of God from nothing, its "essence" and "being" are uniquely protected from the natural decay seen in physical objects.</meta>

# Theology

...to such an extent it is simple: that it cannot be resolved in any other way than into nothingness. It is also such that it was made by God through creation out of nothing. Because it is of this nature, it is subject only to its author, God. Moreover, God’s vital and beneficial influence destroys nothing. Therefore, if the soul were to be destroyed, it would lose that which belongs to <margin>b</margin> its being, yet it remains in its essence. This is evident from the fact that the more noble a thing is, the more noble <term>matter</term><note>Ficino uses "matter" here in a metaphysical sense, referring to the underlying "stuff" or potential of a thing, rather than physical atoms.</note> and more noble <term>form</term><note>The "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> it possesses. Souls are far more excellent than <margin>c</margin> bodies. Therefore, beneath their "being"—as if beneath their forms and acts—there lies a certain "matter," and a "potency" if any lies hidden there. This is more excellent than the matter found under the form and being of any body whatsoever. 

However, that which holds the place of <term>prime matter</term><note>The most basic, formless substrate of existence.</note> and potency in souls is their very essence. Thus, their essence is more eminent than the matter of bodies. The matter of bodies is incorruptible. Therefore, what wonder is it if that soul-essence can also be incorruptible? From this it follows that if ever the soul should imagine it loses its "being," the essence and substance must necessarily still survive. And if it survives, it certainly exists. If it still exists, "being" has not yet been lost. Thus the soul, even if it were said to be "corrupted," necessarily survives even after such corruption. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, it lives. For, to the soul, "to be" is nothing other than "to live." 

But lest anyone say that the "being" of the soul is resolved into its essence, and that the essence further ceases to exist because it would be without "act" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is what makes a potential thing real and active.</note>—even though the potency might perhaps survive somewhere—one must remember that this essence cannot be reduced back into physical <margin>E</margin> matter or the potency of matter. This is because the soul does not consist of matter as a part of itself, nor does it sprout from the potency of matter. Furthermore, it cannot be resolved into the power of any other acting cause, except perhaps into the power of God, who alone created the soul. But the soul does not die simply because it is resolved back into the "First Life" <note>A Neoplatonic name for God.</note>. It would only perish if, having been brought back into God, it ceased to be a soul. 

Yet, just as a figure in <margin>f</margin> wax impressed by a seal—because it is perfectly matched to the seal—is not destroyed but is reintegrated into its own likeness, so too the essence of the soul: if it ever approaches the <term>Idea</term><note>The divine blueprint in the mind of God.</note> through which God had disposed it into a certain species of being, it is confirmed in its original being. For a <margin>g</margin> subsequent act is most greatly strengthened by the first act. 

---

# Quartus 39

For how can God be the end-point toward which corruption tends, since He is the <term>efficient end</term><note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being. Ficino argues God only builds; He does not function as a "grave" for existence.</note> from whom every creation and generation is derived? Or in what way does God—who is "Pure Act"—concur in the composition of the soul when it is born? 

In bodies, a corporal form is made from the potency of matter when "act" is added to that potency, and the act of the form eventually resolves back into that potency. Should we then say that the soul is made from some "potency of God" with an added act, only to eventually resolve back into God's potency as if into matter? <margin>H</margin> No; for He who is the "First Act" never plays the part of matter. 

Someone might argue that the essence of the soul is resolved neither into matter nor into God, but that it immediately withdraws into itself once its prior "being" is taken away. But just as bodily matter cannot exist without bodily act, so spiritual matter cannot exist apart from spiritual act. Therefore, the essence—which is the "matter" of spiritual things and is related to spiritual being as if to an act—is never segregated from being; I mean, from spiritual being. 

Unless, perhaps, someone says that the essence of the soul, while it exits one "being," puts on another, and that <margin>K</margin> this essence alternates its spiritual being in the same way that matter alternates its forms. To say this is indeed absurd. Firstly, because the essence of spiritual things is more stable than the matter of physical things. Secondly, because the essence of the soul, since it is the soul's own proper definition, does not look toward "being something else" at all; rather, it looks only toward being "animated" according to the specific <margin>L</margin> species of the soul. 

Common matter <note>General physical matter that can become anything, like clay.</note> can exist without this or that specific act. But "proper matter" <note>Matter already designated for a specific purpose or form.</note> can by no means exist without its proper act. Therefore, the essence of the soul, which exists in such a species of souls, will never receive the act of another species of souls. Nor will the essence migrate within the same species from this soul into that one, lest it be as changeable as the matter of bodies. Indeed, if the matter of the heavens is always satisfied with the same form (as most philosophers agree), what wonder is it if the spiritual matter of the soul is always satisfied with the same act of being? That essence is life; to be is to live. Therefore, it always lives.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a "simple" substance created directly by God, making its essence more stable than physical matter. He concludes that for a soul, existence and life are identical, meaning the soul's essence cannot be separated from its living state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book III. Having previously discussed the soul's relationship to the divine and its inherent simplicity, Ficino now introduces the "Twelfth Reason" for the soul's immortality. He focuses on the metaphysical concept of "potency" (potential), arguing that because the soul is a "simple form" without "prime matter," it lacks the inherent capacity to stop existing.</meta>

Platonic [Theology] Book III

### Twelfth reason: because it does not have in itself the potential for non-being.

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
**N**o thing is ever destroyed unless it possesses in itself the potential for non-being. For if it were unable to not exist, it would never cease to be. The soul has no such potential. This is because, among the Platonists, the soul is nothing other than a <term>simple form</term><note>In Platonic philosophy, a "simple form" is a basic, indivisible reality. Because it has no parts, it cannot be broken down or "decomposed" like physical objects.</note> subsisting through itself: perfect and whole in its own essence, and also serving to bring about the form of a living creature.

<margin>A</margin>
**T**he act of existing is present there in the whole and perfect form itself. Indeed, it is through the integrity of the form that each thing exists. Therefore, the proper subject of "being" itself is the soul's own form and essence. Where, then, will there be the potential for non-being, which is the opposite of being? Surely not in being itself. For how does one thing have the power to receive its own opposite? Or is it in the essence itself? Not here either. For if it is the essence—since it is a simple and whole form—it is the proper subject of being; how then could it have the potential for non-being, which is said to be its opposite? For in what way does the proper substance of fire, which is the proper subject of heat, have any potential to receive cold? How could it receive cold and still remain fire? Yet even in these bodily and mortal substances, there is no potential for non-being insofar as they are complete substances in their own species and endowed with form; for it is according to this form that they exist. But it is insofar as <term>prime matter</term><note>Ficino refers to "materia prima," the most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe that can become anything but is nothing specific on its own. It is the root of change and decay.</note> underlies them, which never rests under any one form. This matter, however, is absent from the soul. Therefore, the potential for non-being is never found in the soul. And thus it is immortal.

<margin>B</margin>
But let us explain this reasoning more clearly. In those things composed of form and matter, it happens that the matter in some way precedes the work itself. For who would doubt that matter exists in some way before it is formed? I take this matter which precedes the making of the work in some way, and I ask: would that work be necessary, or impossible, according to the nature of this matter? Or perhaps possible, but not necessary? If the power of the matter immediately gave necessity to the work by itself, it would not need any higher forming power; but in fact, it does need one, because that which is unformed cannot form itself. Therefore, as far as the matter is concerned, the future work is not necessary. Is it then impossible? Not that either. For then the matter would be so unsuited to that work that it could never be brought to its form and completion. If, as far as the matter is concerned, the work to be done is neither necessary nor impossible:

<margin>C</margin>
it remains that it is "possible." For this is the middle ground between those two. I say it is "possible to be" and "possible not to be." For if by the nature of the matter it were only possible to be, it would without doubt be necessary. But if by its nature it were only possible not to be, it would also be impossible. Therefore, since by the nature of the matter the work itself is equally possible to be and not to be, it is clear that in the matter itself, as far as making the work is concerned, there is a potential to be and not to be alike. Since prime matter is simple and not composed of several natures, that same nature of matter is the potential for both being and non-being. Because it is indifferent to both, it is not limited to one or the other by itself. It requires a superior agent to determine it toward being by forming it. It receives from that agent the form of a lion. From this, a lion is made. And that matter of the lion, which previously had in itself the potential to be a lion and not to be, is now determined toward being a lion.

<margin>D</margin>
But does that same indifferent potential for both still remain in the prime matter? If it did not remain, the nature of matter would immediately cease to exist, and nothing would be made from matter; and it would be established that when something is made, prime matter perishes by its very nature. Therefore, since it remains even after the lion has been born—that same potential in terms of its kind, I say, the potential to be and not to be alike—it exists not in the matter specifically belonging to the lion, but in prime matter. It follows that just as it began to be a lion at some point through that potential (since it had not been one before), so it may at some point cease to be, after it has been.

Therefore... <note>original: "Quor", likely an abbreviation for "Quocirca" (Therefore), used as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because it is a "simple form" lacking "prime matter." Since decay and non-being only exist where there is a material potential to change, the soul’s lack of matter means it has no potential to cease existing.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, simple form, prime matter, potentiality, non-being, Marsilio Ficino, metaphysics, Platonic Theology</keywords>
