<meta>This page continues the discussion on the immortality of the soul from Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. While the previous section may have been from an earlier book, this page is headed "Book Five" and focuses on the metaphysical relationship between "potency" (the potential to be) and "act" (actual existence). Ficino argues that because the soul's potentiality rests in God rather than in unstable matter, the soul is inherently immortal.</meta>

# Theology Book Five

<page-num>40</page-num>

<margin>E</margin>
...since potency <term>toward either extreme</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "indifferent potency" means a capacity that could go one of two ways—for example, a piece of wood could either be a chair or be burnt to ash.</note> is indifferent: it is either turned toward neither, or it is turned equally and in turn toward both. And just as it is turned toward being and non-being, so in turn, having "being" is turned into "non-being." From this follows the corruption of physical things. 

However, since the rational soul is a <term>simple form</term><note>A "simple form" is a reality that is not made of parts. Because it cannot be broken down, it cannot "decay" or "de-compose" in the way a body does.</note>—from which motion arises in composite things—it could not have been made from some preceding matter and a subsequent form. And since it is a form subsisting in itself, not leaning upon matter—because it proceeds both above and below matter in its power of judgment—it is not composed of any potentiality of matter, such as an "incomplete soul," with "act" added later as the soul's perfection. Therefore, souls neither exist nor emerge from matter. If this is its nature, it proceeded into the light out of nothing. Therefore, God alone is its author, as we shall show elsewhere. 

But if this soul could not have been made, it certainly never would have been made. Therefore, a "potency" or potential for our soul to be born preceded its existence. Where then was that potency? It was not in the soul, which did not yet exist; it was not in a "part" of the soul, which is simple and is created as a whole all at once, not by parts. It was not in any matter, since the soul does not depend on matter. It was not in "nothingness," for the potency of being itself is not founded upon nothing. For in what way can one opposite be the foundation for its own opposite and contradiction?

<margin>F</margin>
Being and non-being are indeed contradictory. It remains, then, that this potentiality is founded in God alone, the author of the soul. Therefore, the "potency of being," through which the soul is produced into existence, is God himself—the only one who is immortal and stable. 

Furthermore, <term>act</term><note>In this context, "act" (actus) refers to the realization or the "doing" of existence. If "potency" is the blueprint, "act" is the finished building.</note> corresponds to potency according to congruence. Therefore, the act corresponding to that divine potency is stable by its very essence. Such an act is the soul. And just as in God there is the same power through which God can make the soul and the soul can be made, so in the soul there is the same act—that is, the same "striving"—through which the soul subsists in its own nature and God maintains it in that same nature. From this it follows that God has no less a desire to maintain the soul in its nature than the soul has to subsist in it.

Since the soul is subject to God alone, if it is to be destroyed by anyone, it must be destroyed by Him. But it cannot be destroyed by Him. For how can the cause that brings a thing into being and preserves it also be its corrupter? Or in what way is "Goodness itself" ruinous to anyone? Or how can the "First Life" and "Infinite Life" be the origin of death? 

Someone might say: "God does not destroy the soul by bringing in some new force, but by taking away the force previously granted to it—that is, by withdrawing His influence, through which the soul lived." This would be like a person who creates his own image in a mirror by looking into it, and then ceases to produce the image by withdrawing his face. But this cannot happen here, as we showed just a moment ago. Again, if God infuses life into the soul now, and later does not, a change occurs in Him from "infusing" to "not infusing." I ask: does the soul cease to draw in life, or does God cease to pour it out? The soul does not cease to draw it in, for the infusion of life happens within the very essence of the soul.

<margin>G</margin>
Since life is the "first act" of essence, it begins as soon as the essence receives being. The soul’s essence is immovable <note>original: "immobilis"</note>, because it depends without any intermediary upon the stable God; it is perfected by standing still and being at rest. It is troubled by motion. It reaches out to stable things. It rules over falling things. It anchors moving things. It gathers what is scattered. It reconciles things that conflict. Nor is there in the soul a potency that is equally toward being and non-being (the kind of potentiality found in bodies, which is the beginning of all change). Therefore, the essence of the soul never ceases to receive the act of life. Nor does God cease to pour it in. For God has indicated that He will only cease to pour His power into those things in which He implanted, from the beginning, a leaning toward non-existence.

<margin>H</margin>
Furthermore, God, the institutor of nature, never withdraws from a thing anything that is "proper" to that thing. Life is proper to the soul—I mean, perpetual life. Because the soul is rational, even without formal schooling or practice, it generates life within itself daily through the power of its own nature alone.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is immortal because its potential for existence (potency) resides in God rather than in matter, and as a "simple form," it lacks the internal capacity to decay or cease to be.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the immortality of the soul from Book Five of his "Platonic Theology." Building on the previous page's definition of the soul as a "simple form" that does not depend on matter, he now explores the soul's direct relationship with God and the eternal "Ideas."</meta>

### Platonic Book

<margin>A</margin>
**Absolute species** <note>In Platonic thought, "species" or "forms" are the perfect, non-physical blueprints of things in the world.</note>: through which one goes most closely to the eternal **Ideas**. If it is natural for the rational soul to ascend to the **Ideas**, then it is natural for it to find rest in those **Ideas**. Just as the soul naturally lived through them, so it should naturally live in them. One who works according to nature constantly toward eternal things should, at some point, work according to nature eternally among those eternal things. And because every **Idea** is eternal life, anyone who can reach those **Ideas** through the nature of an **Idea** can also attain everlasting life through an eternal mode.

->Thirteenth reason: that the soul receives its being from<-
->God without a medium.<-

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
Although **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> and **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major late Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> and several other Platonists believe that the soul is created by an angel, I more willingly follow **Dionysius the Areopagite**, **Origen**, and **Aurelius Augustine**—the most excellent Platonists—who believe the soul is procreated by the one God. Indeed, I am confident this can be demonstrated by the following reason. The soul is a <term>simple form</term> <note>A reality not made of parts, and therefore indestructible.</note>, and so free that it is neither composed of many parts nor extracted from the "innards" of matter. Therefore, when it is made, it cannot be generated from any previously existing things. For it is not fashioned from diverse things placed far apart and then forced into one, since it lacks parts; nor is it fashioned from a spark of matter that was previously unformed and then given shape, since the soul is above matter. Therefore, it is made **from nothing**. To make something from nothing is the unique property of **God** alone. For from the order of works, the order of causes is investigated. Effects are matched to their causes. Therefore, it is necessary that we trace specific effects back to specific causes, and that which is found to be common in all specific effects, we must refer to the common cause of all things. Thus, since among all things—beyond the specific conditions of each individual—**being** <note>original: "esse"</note> itself is found to be common to all, we must assert specific causes for specific conditions and qualities. However, for **being** itself, which is one thing common to all, there must be one cause common to all. 

<margin>D</margin>
The cause common to all is the one **God** himself. Therefore, God is truly the cause of **being**. However, for being "this" or "that," or being in "this way" or "that way," there are certain other causes besides God. Thus, you have being from God alone. But you have being "as a man" even from a human father; you have being "as hot" from a fire. God will give **being** to his works; other causes, differing among themselves, will give different **modes of being**, and even then, they do so by the power of God. Indeed, that **being** which follows after "nothingness" is called <term>absolute being</term>. For immediately after "nothing," there follows being, simply. After "being, simply" follows being "this" or "that," or being "such and such"—for example, being a man, or a horse, or being white, or black. For nothing can become "this" or "that" or "such" unless it first exists so that it may become "this" and "that" and "such." For this reason, being "such" and "this" and "that" does not follow immediately after nothingness, but follows after **being** itself, simple and absolute. Since, therefore, it is God's own property to grant this common and absolute **being** to all things—and since that **being** precedes all "modes of being" after nothingness—it will be the office of **God alone** to lead something out of nothing into **being**. 

<margin>F</margin>
So, the first thing given to all, namely **being** itself, comes from the **First Cause** <note>i.e., God</note>; from the subsequent causes come second or third gifts. Certainly, that which participates in some nature cannot produce that nature in its absolute form. Because that which is "such a thing" by <term>participation</term> <note>The idea that things in our world "participate" in or reflect a higher, perfect form without being that form themselves.</note> necessarily follows that which is "absolutely such." Indeed, whatever it is, it exists through that absolute; if the participant were to beget the absolute, certainly that which is later would beget the thing prior to itself, and would even beget its own cause. It would beget itself for you! Therefore, **Ariston** <note>The father of the philosopher Plato.</note>, who is not "Man" in the absolute sense but "this man" established in such-and-such matter, did not beget **Humanity** itself in the absolute sense, but only "this man." 

Since, truly, as far as it pertains to the nature of being, everything under God is a **participant** in being itself and does not have being simply, but only "such-and-such being" determined in a certain essence and species, it follows that no thing subject to God produces **being** itself. But rather some such "mode" of being...

<meta>catchword: being</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is created directly by God "ex nihilo" (from nothing) rather than by intermediary angels. He distinguishes between "absolute being," which only God can grant, and specific "modes of being" (like being human or being hot) which can involve secondary causes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Ficino began discussing why the human soul must be created directly by God rather than by an intermediary like an angel. He is now explaining the fundamental difference between how God creates and how nature or art works.</meta>

# Theology [Book] Five
<margin>f</margin>

...bestows a mode of being upon such matter. Thus it happens that for its work, it always requires a prior foundation. Moreover, whatever both art and nature do, they produce into act from a certain potentiality. A sculptor makes a statue out of stone that has been so prepared for the statue that it possesses the statue, in a way, in potentiality; a man generates a man from seed, in whose power the man exists. That matter from which art and nature make something is sometimes very obedient and fit for the work, and at other times more unfit, so that the potentiality of the matter is sometimes less and sometimes more distant from the actualization of the work being fabricated. The potential of air is only a small distance from the effect of fire, but the potential of water is far from it. <note>original: "aeris potentia ab ignis effectu... aque potentia." Ficino refers to the Aristotelian elements; air is "hot and wet" and thus easily turns into fire, which is "hot and dry," whereas water is "cold and wet."</note> From this it appears that the one who acts must be as much more powerful as the interval is wider between that potentiality and the act into which the work is to be led. 

But the distance between nothing and being is infinite; both because in nothingness there is no proportion to being, and because no distance can be, or even be imagined, greater than this. Only that power which has no proportion to other powers and has no end <note>i.e., is infinite</note> can transcend a distance that lacks proportion and limit. God alone is a power of this kind. For all other things fall short of God’s power. Therefore, God alone leads something from nothing into being.

<margin>3</margin>
Furthermore, every thing besides God himself is called a "creature" by theologians, and is necessarily composed of four certain things. For this reason, the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras; Ficino often attributes the idea of the "fourfold" structure of reality to them.</note> place four elements not only in bodies, but also in a certain way in spirits. For both consist of **essence**, **being**, **power**, and **action**. Indeed, in them, **essence** is one thing and **being** <note>original: "esse"</note> is another. For being is the "act" of essence. If there were no essence there for such an act to adhere to, it would be "pure act" and infinite, because it would not be circumscribed by anything. But this is God alone. Again, "being" itself would be absolute, without any participation in another. Every such thing is unique in its nature. Therefore, this belongs to God alone. Rightly, the creature is not its own being, because it cannot be its own act. 

<margin>K</margin>
Since the creature has not a little "passive potentiality" mixed within it—because it is subject to God—and potentiality is opposed to act. Since, indeed, **operation** <note>Meaning "action" or "functioning."</note> differs from essence even more than "being" itself does—for the essence exists before it operates—therefore, where there is a distinction between essence and its being, there is a much greater distinction between operation and essence. Operation is the act of an essential **power**, just as being is the act of **essence**. Because a created essence is not its own act, it is therefore not its own operation. Otherwise, such an operation would be self-subsisting and entirely absolute from every limit of a participant. We have said that such a thing exists as unique and infinite. 

<margin>L</margin>
But does operation differ from being just as it is shown to differ from essence? Undoubtedly. For operation is twofold: one flows out beyond the operator, like heating; the other remains within, like cognition and will. That which flows out undoubtedly differs from being, which does not flow out from yourself. That which remains within also differs for this reason: because the "being" of a creature is enclosed within a certain species of things <note>The creature is limited to being a "human," a "stone," etc.</note>, but such an operation wanders through many genera—indeed, intelligence and will wander through infinite things. For the object of the former is truth itself, and of the latter, the good itself. Truth and good are at least as widely open as that which is called "existence" itself. Operation, however, draws its form from its object. Therefore, such an operation is clothed in all the forms of all things. 

But does operation differ from power, and power from essence and being? 
<margin>M</margin>
Certainly. First, because the act is always opposed to potentiality; therefore operation, which is an act, differs from power and essence, which are certain potentialities; and power differs from "being," which is an act. And it differs from essence because potentialities are distinguished by their acts, since a specific potentiality regards a specific act. The act of **essence** is **being**. The act of **power** is **operation**. Therefore, essence and power differ from each other as much as being and operation differ. To what purpose are all these many points? <meta>This page continues the argument that only God can create the human soul. The previous page established that the distance between "nothingness" and "being" is infinite, requiring an infinite power (God) to bridge it. Here, Ficino argues that creatures only "operate" (act upon existing things) rather than "create" (bring into being from nothing), and explains why the soul is superior to other forms of life.</meta>

# Platonic Book
<note>This is a volume of Marsilio Ficino's "Platonic Theology," specifically discussing the immortality of the soul.</note>

<margin>14</margin>
The operation of any creature depends on its <term>power</term> <note>Latin: virtus; in this context, it refers to the specific capacity or "faculty" an object has to act</note>; this power belongs to its essence. No creature acts directly through its own substance, but through an operative power which is a quality or an "accident," since it is distinct in every way from the substance itself. Whenever, therefore, something acts, it produces certain qualities. It bestows a mode of being such as it possesses itself—that is, something always "clinging" to another. Such things require a prior foundation. Those things that require a foundation cannot be created out of nothing. Therefore, no creature creates anything, and rightfully so. For its operation and its power cling to something else; and whatever clings to another does not remain free and whole but is received according to the capacity of the recipient, limited by the boundaries of its subject. Creation, however, requires an infinite operative power. 

<margin>A</margin>
Thus, the soul is created by God alone. But perhaps someone will think that the soul is made by God in such a way that He acts through an angel as a medium—that God is the craftsman in that creation, and the angel is the instrument. This opinion seems absurd because an instrument has this nature: it is moved by another so that it may move something else. It must affect some subject and translate the form of the principal agent into that subject over an interval of time. Creation, however, requires no subject, nor does it happen through motion or time. Furthermore, if the work of creation requires immense power, what is more absurd than to suggest that the power which is infinite in God should first be "limited" within an angel (whose nature is finite) in order to execute that work? And then, to have that work—which belongs to infinite power—be performed by the angel?

<margin>B</margin>
From what has been said, it is concluded that the soul is procreated by the highest God without any intermediary. Why, then, are the angel and the soul not equal in perfection, since both depend on God without a medium? It is because God produces the angel under one <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints or "Forms" of things existing in the divine mind</note> and "reason," and the soul under another. He produces the angel under a higher Idea, and the soul under a lower one. In the same way, a man and a horse painted by the same painter are not equally beautiful. For the figure of the man is more beautiful than the horse because the painter expressed the painting of the man according to a more beautiful model in his mind than that of the horse. 

<margin>a</margin>
But let us now put an end to this reasoning. If the essence of the soul is made directly by God, nothing falls between the soul and God (its preserver) to separate it from that preservation. And if it needs God alone to be made, it also needs God alone to remain. 

<margin>α</margin>
And because God preserves created things by the same power through which He created them, just as the soul proceeded from the infinite goodness of God out of nothingness into being, so it remains in being far from nothingness through that same goodness. Thus, a life closest to God is most similar to the divine life. This will be the case if the soul either lacked a beginning and an end like God, or, if it had a beginning, it shall at least have no end.

<margin>C</margin>
It is the opinion of the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, dealing with the creation of the universe</note> and of Plato that the Architect of the world procreates His works through <term>Ideas</term>—that is, through exemplary and absolute "reasons." Therefore, whatever is created directly through such an Idea (or Ideas) always persists in that state. That which is created further down the line, however, does not necessarily persist forever, but only for a time. For it is necessary that an effect produced directly by a cause should emerge most similar to it. A more remote effect is less similar, and as they proceed, they always become more dissimilar. 

Thus, an Idea is a power that is simultaneously in itself and eternal. The power that comes from it directly does not exist in itself—rather, it exists in something else—but it exists forever. However, that which comes later neither exists in itself nor exists forever by its own nature, nor does it persist as the same or similar. Since the rational soul is made directly through the "Idea of Life" without a medium, by such a power of direct origin, it is a form that is always living. The irrational soul <note>The "lower" part of the soul associated with animal instincts and biological functions</note>, however, since it proceeds from there through the rational soul, is only "living for a time" according to its own nature. For that which is created by an Idea alone through action is made entirely stable by that action and possesses a stable essence from it. But that which is born from an Idea through the soul as a medium is begotten by a mutable action, and is thus compelled to derive a nature that is mobile according to itself. By "according to itself," I mean that it considers the life impressed by the soul upon the ethereal vehicle—as if in an eternal mirror—to always accompany the impure soul. <note>The text ends mid-sentence, discussing the "ethereal vehicle," a Neoplatonic concept of a subtle body that carries the soul.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul must be created directly by God because creation from nothing requires infinite power, which no creature or angel possesses. He further explains that because the soul is created directly from the divine "Idea of Life," it is inherently immortal, unlike the souls of irrational animals.</summary>

# Fifth [Book] of Theology

For one should consider that the <term>ethereal body</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "ethereal" or "astral" body is a subtle, celestial vehicle that connects the immaterial soul to the heavy, physical body.</note>, which is nearest to the soul, is perpetually animated by the substance of the soul, which lives forever. Indeed, the elemental body receives some life from the soul through that ethereal vehicle; but more on these matters elsewhere.

### Fourteenth argument: because it is life in itself.

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
<margin>D</margin> **A**nima is essence; it is also life. In the previous arguments, we showed that the soul is immortal because it is an essence existing through itself. At present, we show its immortality through the fact that it is life living through itself. Furthermore, the soul is life from its very essence: for everything that is in it is life. For if there were anything in it that was not life, that part would not belong to the soul; rather, one would call the whole thing "something animated" <note>Something that has been given life by another source.</note> rather than the "soul" itself. Let us admit, therefore, that the entire essence of the soul is life. If it is entirely life, it must certainly be called life by its very self, according to its <term>form</term> <note>Latin: *forma*; the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>. For that which lives through something else—not living by its own self—is composed of two parts: namely, from its own nature which is not alive in itself, and from that life received from elsewhere. Conclude thus: If that thing which lives through another is not entirely life, it follows that a thing which is entirely life lives by its own self. Therefore the soul, which is entirely life, lives by its own self, especially since it moves by its own self; if this is so, it is life by its own self. Therefore, the essence of the soul is life. A sign of this is that to whatever thing it comes, it provides life, as if it were essentially the very thing it grants to another. Hence, when the soul departs, <margin>E</margin> the body ceases to live. And while it is present in the body, it does not cease for a single moment to exercise the works of life by giving life to the body. Therefore, the soul's perennial act is <term>vivification</term> <note>Latin: *vivificatio*; the active process of bestowing or maintaining life.</note>. 
<margin>C</margin> A perennial action is the proper action of a thing. Therefore, the proper action of the soul is to give life. To give life, however, is the property of life itself, just as to heat is the property of heat. Therefore, the essence of the soul is life. Take again another deduction: since the body is prepared, the soul immediately gives it life. Therefore, it gives life either by its very being, or by desire, or by knowledge, or by deliberation. If the soul gave life to the body through knowledge and deliberation, everyone would know what the soul creates and nourishes in the guts at every moment, and what the arrangement of the internal work is like. And unless the soul knew these things, they would not happen. But does it give life by desire? <margin>f</margin> Not even this; otherwise, as long as the soul willed to be in the body, it would remain there. And he who hates the habits of the body would depart from the body immediately. It remains that the soul gives life to the body by its very being—that is, by a natural power. If it gives life by its very being, it is life, or a living thing, through its own essence. Just as that which heats by its very being is heat, or a heating thing, through its essence or power. Conclude then that the essence of the soul is a certain life. If it is not pleasing to call it life living through itself—just as one calls the sun heat heating through itself—at least through the arguments above you are forced to admit that the soul is a substance made vital by its own life, just as you say fire is a substance made hot by its own heat. Whichever of these you accept, I care very little. For from both, the same thing follows which we seek. But I am led by the previous arguments to call the soul life through itself; life, I say, that is natural, and a vital form. <margin>g</margin> To life or a vital form, death is said to be contrary in a certain way, or some almost deadly quality. Just as cold is contrary to heat, and dryness to moisture. Truly, such is the nature of contrary forms, that none of them accepts the other; as heat does not receive cold. Nor does a substance, to which one of these forms is proper, receive another form contrary to its own nature. As fire, to which heat is proper, does not accept cold, so as to be both fire and cold at the same time. But rather both the heat and the fire depart or are lost when cold arrives, sooner than either the heat or the fire should become cold. Therefore both are, so to speak, <margin>h</margin> "un-chillable," since they cannot end up as a partaker of cold. Similarly the soul, since it either is natural life itself or has life as its <term>natural attendant</term> <note>Latin: *pedisequam*; literally a servant who follows close behind, meaning life is an inseparable companion to the soul's essence.</note>, it does not admit death, its contrary. If it does not admit death, it is thus essentially immortal, just as fire is essentially hot, because it does not receive cold.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul’s essence is life itself, proven by the fact that it animates the body automatically rather than through conscious will or thought. Because life is the soul's defining "form," it can no more admit death than fire can admit cold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the immortality of the soul. # Platonic Book

...fire <note>The text begins mid-word with "-gus," likely completing *ignis* (fire) from the previous page.</note> is incapable of being chilled. If "incapable of being chilled" were the same as "indestructible," then fire would not only never grow cold, but it would also never be destroyed. As it stands, however, fire is destroyed rather than becoming cold. ¶ Since "immortal" is the same as "indestructible," the soul—which is called immortal because it does not admit death—is also indestructible. Therefore, when death arrives, the soul departs; it is not destroyed. The entire preceding discussion is summarized in these words of Zoroaster <note>Ficino refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, which were attributed to Zoroaster in the Renaissance.</note>: <margin>B</margin> **"It remains immortal and is the master of life."** <note>Original Greek: *ἀθανάτους τε μένει καὶ ζωῆς δεσπότης ἐστὶ*.</note> That is, it remains immortal and is the lady of life. It is as if he were to say that it remains immortal because it has life as its constant attendant, just as the sun has light, or a comet <note>Latin: *crinita*, literally "hairy star."</note> has its tail. Here, Strato <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek philosopher who proposed a naturalistic view of the soul.</note> or some Epicurean <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the soul was material and dissipated at death.</note> will argue thus: "Certainly the soul does not 'receive' death, because when a death-bearing quality arrives, the soul departs and ceases to exist. If it ceases to exist, it certainly receives nothing." But we, O Epicurean, are not so foolish as to be ignorant of the fact that death cannot be "received" by anything. First, because death is nothing <note>In this philosophical framework, death is seen as a privation or absence of being, rather than a positive substance.</note>. That which is nothing cannot be "held" or "taken." Second, because neither the living nor the dead "take" it. The living do not, because as long as they live, they are away from death; the dead do not, because if they no longer exist (as you think), they receive nothing. And if they survive (as our people hold), they are also away from death. Let us stop playing with words. Hear what we mean when we say the soul does not receive death: we mean that it does not admit into itself any death-bearing quality through which it would cease to live. ¶ Indeed, contrary qualities do not receive one another. They both drive each other out and flee from each other. Therefore, heat by its very nature not only does not receive cold, but does not even come near it in space. For those things which differ by nature by the greatest interval drive each other away and flee to the furthest distance. Since these <term>forms</term> <note>The essential qualities or "blueprints" of things.</note> are such by their own nature, if they existed in their pure and solitary nature—and were opposites as they are now—they would never approach one another. Nature would keep them apart, and no middle mediator would be present to reconcile them. They would truly be such if heat existed in itself, separated from <term>matter</term>, so that it had nothing mixed with it except heat. The same would be true for cold. ¶ As it is, heat lies within matter, which by its own nature is no less ready for cold than for heat; it opens its lap to the approaching cold. Once coldness has entered, it thrusts out the heat. The heat, thus driven out, is extinguished, since it was produced by its author on the condition that it would remain only so long as it was cherished in that "lap" of matter. For this reason, forms that are sustained by matter, although they do not "receive" forms contrary to themselves, are nevertheless destroyed by the force and approach of those opposites. However, those things which remain in themselves—even if they sometimes seem to cling to matter—sustain that matter rather than being sustained by it. They cannot admit a force contrary to themselves. Furthermore, if any force comes to the bosom of matter, it stains the qualities and forms that are bound to matter. But it does not touch that Form which stands above matter. Such is the soul—I mean the **rational soul**—which, since it is the source of motion and the mover of bodies, cannot be changed from its state by bodies. Since it has life innate to its own <term>species</term> <note>Its specific category of being.</note> as its own property, it lives always without the labor of living, especially as long as it lives within itself. But when approaching a body, it pours out from itself an **irrational** life (to speak in the Platonic manner) like a shadow. The soul itself is truly the soul and the source of animal life; it not only supplies such life to the body for a time, but much more so to itself forever. It never deserts itself, nor is it forced to desert itself by the body, whose quality does not pass into an incorporeal form. Again, it is not forced to do so by other souls, whose office it is to give life, not to destroy it. Without doubt, the rational soul is judged to be such. The <margin>D</margin> **irrational** [soul], however, is not a true soul, because it is neither a true essence nor a true life. It is not a true essence because it does not exist through itself, since it does not act through itself; indeed, it does nothing without the instruments of the body. It is not true life because it is deprived of the freedom of motion. For it is not moved by itself, but is drawn by force by those things which are offered to the senses. Therefore, many Platonists say that the rational soul is the [only] soul, and the soul...

<summary>Ficino argues that the rational soul is indestructible because it is the source of life, unlike physical qualities like heat which can be extinguished when matter "chooses" a contrary quality. He distinguishes the rational soul, which exists independently, from the "irrational" soul, which is merely a shadow dependent on the body's senses.</summary>

...[substanti]al <note>The Latin "alam" is the conclusion of *substantialem* (substantial) from the preceding page.</note> and a subsisting life; and giving life to the body from itself. <margin>f</margin>

### The fifteenth argument: that life is more excellent than the body. Chapter 15.

<margin>h</margin>
**The rational soul is the essence of natural life.**
True life is, by itself, the shaper and ruler of the body. Therefore, it is far more excellent than the body. Although the body may turn into various qualities, or be divided a thousand times into parts, it never ceases to be a body. For the nature of a divisible body always remains, since parts may be divided into smaller particles without end. Therefore, much more so the rational soul—which is the true life of the body—no matter how much it changes, never 
<margin>i</margin>
ceases to be life. We judge the force of this argument to consist primarily in this: that the "third essence" <note>Ficino identifies the Soul as the "Third Essence," the middle point in his five-tiered hierarchy of reality (God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter).</note>—which is the seat of rational souls—possesses three gifts because it occupies the middle point of all things. **First, that true images of divine things shine back in it.** **Second, that it shapes and contains the entire bodily machine.** **Third, that it reconciles divine and bodily things to each other.** All these gifts show the soul to be eternal. First, because if some things in the genus of bodies are eternal (in which there are only shadows of divine things), then much more so are the rational souls, the most excellent of all souls, in which the eternal images of divine things exist. For in divine matters, life exists before splendor, since their splendor is both a reflection and an outpouring of life. Therefore, the immortality and abundance of life flows into the soul from that source before the splendor of divine images does. **Second, because if the rational soul is the principle of shaping and containing, it can lose neither its own form nor its natural constancy.** Truly, since the whole genus of "living being" is more excellent than the whole genus of "body," and in all the members of the world there are some bodily things that are eternal, it is probable that in all these there are eternal souls. For who would deny that the genus of souls has a perpetual head (in which the rational souls are), given that the bodily world has certain perpetual members everywhere? Third, because if the soul is the source of universal reconciliation 
<margin>R</margin>
and the "bond" <note>Ficino famously calls the soul the *copula mundi* or "bond of the world."</note>, it cannot be pulled apart or dissolved. For if the bond of all things were undone, what further thing would you bind? We shall now confirm these Platonic inventions by the opinion of **Aurelius Augustine**. If the rational soul perished when the body passed away, it would necessarily change when the body changed. But it is not changed by the body. For it is itself the principle of motion. Therefore, when it seems to be changed by the body, it is then changing both itself and the body, and it leads itself as it commands. If the soul moves itself so that the body does not remain immobile, much more—from the fact that it sustains and contains the body—does it sustain and contain itself. For that which stands most firm in moving another can stand forever by leaning on and containing itself. For who does not know that when a body, whether one's own or another's, is moved by the soul, that very motion...

<meta>This page continues the logical proof of the immortality of the soul, specifically refuting the idea that the soul is merely a "harmony" or a result of the body's physical balance (temperament). It focuses on the mind's ability to grasp immutable mathematical truths as evidence of its non-physical nature.</meta>

# Theology, [Book] Five
### F 4

In which subject it exists inseparably. Moreover, since the harmony of the humors is a certain composite accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change or be lost without the subject ceasing to exist. Augustine argues the soul cannot be an accident of the body.</note>: if the **soul** were either that harmony, or dependent upon it: it would in no way know, affect, or grasp the <term>ratios</term> <note>original: "rationes". This Latin word means both "reasons" and "mathematical ratios." Augustine uses this dual meaning to show that logic and math are the same kind of eternal truth.</note> of substances and invisible things. In addition, those things which the mind understands when it has turned away from the body are certainly not corporeal: and yet they exist—indeed, they are the things that most truly exist. For they always remain the same: and nothing more absurd can be said than that the things we see with our eyes exist, but the things we perceive with our intelligence do not; for it would be the mark of a madman to doubt that intelligence is incomparably preferred over the eyes. Now these things which are understood—which remain always the same—since the mind gazes upon them without any [physical] instrument, they show clearly enough that the mind is joined to them in some wondrous and equally incomparable way: namely, not according to physical location. For either they are in the mind, or the mind is in them, or both subsist by themselves. If the first is true, the mind is not the harmony of the body, nor is it enslaved to harmony. For whatever is of such a kind cannot be separated from the body as its subject. Therefore, whatever is in that [subject] is bound to the body just as the subject itself is.

But the human body is mutable. Therefore, those ratios of things which are in the contemplating mind would be mutable if the mind were bound to a mutable body. But those ratios cannot be mutable. For it is always true in the same way that two and four make six; or that whatever comparison exists between two and four, the same exists between four and eight; and many other things of this kind. Ratios of this sort are inseparably in the mind, which uses them always and immediately at its will. In these consists the <margin>D</margin> **art of reasoning**: which is not at all separated from the rational mind. For if that artful reason, or rational art—which is a certain [order] of ratios—were separated from the mind, it would either be nowhere, or in something non-living, or in something living. It must not be said that perpetual and immutable ratios exist nowhere. It is also impossible for true ratios to be in a non-living thing, since life is the foundation of reason. If, however, artful reason passes from life to life [from person to person], it never does so more conveniently than when it teaches others. But in truth, that does not happen. For no one forgets by teaching others; no transition of the art takes place. Therefore, **Art** is inseparably in the mind. It would also be in the body if the mind were the harmony of the body. Wherefore, both the reason itself and the mind would be mutable, just like the body. But since such reason is immutable, and therefore the essence of the mind (in which reason exists as its subject) is also immutable, the mind is not the "temperament" <note>original: "temperatio," referring to the specific balance of bodily fluids or "humors" that ancient medicine believed produced health and consciousness.</note> of the body.

And let it suffice to have argued this from that first part of the previous division: in which it was granted that ratios exist within the mind. Furthermore, if someone admits the second part, namely that the mind exists within those [ratios]: the same conclusion follows. For in what way is the mind the temperament of the body, if it exists in the ratio of things which is separated from the body as a subject? Since the temperament of a body cannot be anywhere but in the body. If you grant the third part of that division—namely, that both the mind and the ratio of things are substances subsisting by themselves—the mind will subsist by itself, and will not be bound to the temperament of the body. Finally, whichever part of the division you take, this one reason strongly persuades us: that the mind does not lie within the physical composition of the body as its origin; for it mixes itself with immutable ratios so greedily, easily, and constantly when we philosophize, setting aside the mutable body. Nor would it be better off when it is within those [ratios] than when it is in the body [unless it were a different kind of substance]. But it is so much better in them than in the body, as it lives more excellently in them than in itself. And it lives so much more excellently as it operates more perfectly.

Indeed, it operates more perfectly in them, because it understands more truly, desires more peacefully, and enjoys more sweetly, fully, and securely. And since often, while the body is sounding in harmony with itself, the mind itself is out of harmony with it, both in its speculation and in its morals. And on the contrary, [the mind] thrives <note>original: "pronet" - likely "provenit" or "prolet," suggesting the mind thrives or grows.</note> in a disharmonious body; who has not seen the mind...

<summary>Augustine argues that the soul cannot be a mere physical harmony of the body because the mind perceives immutable mathematical and logical truths (ratios) that the changing body cannot contain. Since these truths are eternal and the soul grasps them directly, the soul's essence must be distinct from the body's physical temperament.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the nature of the soul. Having argued that the soul is not a mere "harmony" of the body, Augustine (Aurelius) now addresses the concern of whether the soul could ever be degraded or transformed into a physical body.</meta>

# Platonic
# Book

[that the soul] does not consist in the harmony of the body: this idea is discordant with the truth. But to return <margin>B</margin> to Aurelius <note>Aurelius Augustinus, better known as St. Augustine (354–430 AD). The text refers to his dialogue "On the Magnitude of the Soul" (De Quantitate Animae).</note>: here perhaps a certain question arises. Whether, just as the **mind** does not perish, it likewise cannot be changed into a lower essence. For it might seem to someone—and not without reason—that this has been established: that the mind cannot come to nothing. Yet, perhaps it could be turned into a body. For if that which was previously a mind were made into a body, it would certainly not cease to exist entirely.

But this cannot happen unless either the mind itself wills it, or it is compelled by another. Yet it does not immediately follow that the mind—whether it desired it or was forced—could actually become a body. For it follows that if it *is* a body, it must have willed it or been forced. But it does not follow that if it wills it or is forced, it *becomes* one. Moreover, the mind will never will this. For all its <term>desire</term> <note>original: "appetitus". In this philosophical context, it refers to the soul's natural inclination or drive toward an object.</note> regarding the body is either to possess it, to give it life, to fashion it in some way, or to care for it in some manner. None of these things can happen if the mind is not better than the body. But if it were to be a body, it would surely not be better than a body. Therefore, it will not will to be a body; nor is there any more certain proof of this matter than when the mind asks this of itself. For it easily finds that it has no desire except for acting, knowing, perceiving, or at least living as far as its power allows.

If, however, it is compelled to be a body, by whom is it compelled? By just anyone? Surely by something more powerful. Therefore, it cannot be compelled by a body. For in no way is any body more powerful than any mind. But a more powerful mind does not compel another toward anything except that which is subject to its power. Nor is a mind subject to the power of another mind in any way except through its own <term>cravings</term> <note>original: "cupiditatibus". Augustine argues that the soul only loses its freedom when it allows itself to be enslaved by its own desires for lower, worldly things.</note>. Therefore, the one who compels does so no more than those cravings allow.

It has been said, however, that the mind cannot have a desire to be a body. It is also manifest that it reaches no fulfillment of its craving while it loses all craving—and it loses it while it becomes a body. Therefore, it cannot be compelled to become one by that which has no power of compulsion except through subject cravings. Furthermore, any mind that holds another mind in its power would necessarily prefer to keep it in its power rather than have it become a body—either to care for it through goodness or to rule over it through malice. Therefore, it will not wish for the other to become a body.

Lastly, this compelling mind is either a living being or it lacks a body. But if it lacks a body, it is not of this world; and if that is so, it is supremely good <note>Augustine is referring to God or perhaps angelic intellects, which being "supremely good," would never force a soul to degrade into matter.</note>. It could not wish such a shameful transformation for another. If, however, it is a living being, then either the one it compels is also a living being, or it is not. But if it is not, nothing can be compelled by another. For it has nothing more powerful than itself if it is in the highest state—that is, one who is free is not compelled. 

If, however, it is in a body, it is again compelled by one who is in a body, through the body, toward whatever it is compelled. But who could doubt that such a great transformation of the mind could in no way happen through the body, as if the body were more powerful than the mind? Although whatever it is that the mind is compelled toward through the body, it is not truly compelled by the body, but by its own cravings, about which enough has been said. Now, that which is better than the rational soul—as all agree—is the divine. This [divine power] certainly cares for the soul. And therefore, the soul cannot be compelled by it to turn into a body.

If, then, the soul suffers this neither by its own will nor by the compulsion of another, by what means could it suffer it? Should we fear that, because sleep often overcomes us against our will, the soul might turn into a body through some such failure? As if, because our limbs grow limp in sleep, the mind therefore becomes weaker in any part! It is true that it does not perceive sensible things. Because whatever causes sleep is of the body and operates in the body. For it lulls and closes the bodily senses in a certain way; yet it does so such that the soul yields to this bodily change willingly, because such a transformation is according to nature, refreshing the body from its labors. However, this does not take away from the mind either its perception <margin>C</margin>...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of the soul, specifically addressing the impossibility of the soul's transformation into a physical body. It explores the soul's role as a mediator between eternal truths and physical existence, drawing on concepts from Augustine's "On the Magnitude of the Soul."</meta>

# Theology Fifth

...the mind's power: or of understanding. For it even has at hand the images of sensible things with such an expression of likeness that at that very time they cannot be distinguished from those things of which they are images. And if it understands anything—whether it be while sleeping or waking—it is true. For example: if in sleep one seemed to oneself to be disputing, <margin>B</margin> and having followed true reasons in the dispute, learned something, these same things remain unchangeable even for the person when awakened, although the rest are found to be false—such as the place where the dispute seemed to happen, the person with whom it was held, and the words themselves which belong to the dream and by which one seemed to dispute, and other things of this kind which are felt by the senses and acted upon by those who are awake. For these things pass away, nor do they in any part attain the eternal presence of <term>true reasons</term> <note>original: "verarum rationum". These are the stable, intelligible principles or "ideas" in the mind of God that do not change, unlike physical reality.</note>. From which it is gathered that by such a change of the body, which is sleep, it is not the power of the soul itself that is diminished, but the life of the body. Lastly, although space is occupied by the body, the soul nevertheless is not joined locally to those highest and eternal reasons which remain unchangeably, nor are they contained by any place. The soul is affected by them before the body; and not only before, but even more so. For it is as much prior as it is closer to them: and for the same reason, it is affected as much more as it is better than the body—nor should this closeness be called a closeness of place, but rather of the <term>order of nature</term> <note>The hierarchy of being, where the spiritual is "closer" to God than the material.</note>. By this order, it is understood that <term>form</term> <note>original: "speciem". In this context, it refers to the essential quality or "Idea" that gives a thing its being and shape.</note> is granted to the body by the <term>highest essence</term> <note>God.</note> through the soul, by which the body exists as much as it exists.

<margin>L</margin> Therefore, the body subsists through the soul, and it exists for the very reason that it is animated: whether universally, as the world, or particularly, as each individual animal within the world. Wherefore it followed that a body would be made through the soul by means of the soul, and it could not be otherwise. But because this transformation does not happen—since the soul remains in that which is soul—the body subsists through it; because the soul gives form and does not take it away, it cannot be changed into a body. For if it does not hand down the form which it receives from the <term>highest good</term>, the body is not made through it; and if it is not made through it, either it is not made at all, or it receives form as closely as the soul does. But it does not become a body [in that way], because if it received form so closely, it would be the same thing as the soul. Is the soul not better for the very reason that it receives form more closely? And the body would receive it just as closely if it did not receive it through the soul. For with nothing placed in between, it would surely receive it just as closely. Nor is there found any fitting medium between the highest life—which is wisdom and unchangeable truth—and that which is the last thing to be given life (that is, the body), except the life-giving soul. But if the soul hands down form to the body so that it becomes a body as far as it is, it certainly does not do so by surrendering its own form. However, by transforming the soul into a body, it would be taking away that form. Therefore, the soul does not become a body, neither through itself—because the body is made through it, and the body is only made through it while the soul remains a soul—nor through other things, because the body is made through the soul only by the transmission of form; and by the removal of form, the soul would be converted into a body, if it were to be converted at all. This can also be said of the <term>irrational soul</term> <note>original: "irrationali anima". The life principle found in animals, which possesses life and sensation but lacks human reason.</note> or life: that the rational soul is not converted into it. For it too, unless it were subjected to the rational soul in a lower order, would receive form equally and would be like it. Therefore, more powerful things hand down the form received from the <term>highest beauty</term> to weaker things in the natural order. And certainly, when they hand it down, they do not lose what they are; rather, those things that are weaker exist as they are through the form that is handed down to them by the more powerful. These more powerful things are also better. This is granted to those natures which do not have more power over smaller masses by having a larger <term>bulk</term> <note>original: "mole". Physical size or mass.</note>, but without any swelling of local size, they are more powerful by the same form by which they are better. In which class the soul is better and more powerful than the body. Wherefore, since the body subsists through it, as was said, the soul can in no way be converted into a body. For no body is made except by receiving form through the soul. But for the soul to become a body, it would not be receiving form, but losing it. And therefore, it can in no way happen.

<summary>This page argues that the soul cannot be transformed into a body because it serves as the essential mediator that transmits "form" from God to matter. If the soul became a body, it would lose the very form that allows the body to exist, creating a logical and metaphysical impossibility.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from a general discussion of the soul's relationship to eternal truths into a specific investigation of the human soul. It marks the beginning of Book Six of Ficino's masterwork, shifting from a philosophical dialogue to a systematic classification of historical theories regarding the soul's nature.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Six. The reduction of opinions about the soul into five categories. Chapter One.

<margin>A</margin>
**T**hese things I once discussed in the Roman countryside at the home of Giovanni Cavalcanti, our unique friend, on the <term>Kalends of March</term> <note>The first day of March.</note> under a laurel tree. Three of our most intimate companions were present for these discussions: Cristoforo Landino, Bernardo Nuthi, and Giorgio Antonio Vespucci—men most renowned for their integrity and learning. After Giovanni had heard these things with the greatest attention, he said: "Marsilio, it could not be said how much I was delighted by the previous discussion. But I desire this in addition: that since you have discussed the common immortality of rational souls, you would next, if it pleases you, discuss the immortality of our own soul more carefully with its proper reasons."

I indeed agree that there are five levels of things, just as you arranged in the previous discussion, and that the third essence occupies the middle of these—which is released from matter and is perpetual. Furthermore, I do not doubt that celestial souls are placed in the level of that essence. I also think it is probable that our own mind is placed there. However, I believe this can hardly be fully affirmed until all the opinions of philosophers regarding the human soul are reduced to five heads—and four are refuted, while the last is upheld.

<margin>B</margin>
For either the soul is some very thin <term>little body</term> <note>original: "corpusculum". Ficino is referring to the materialist view that the soul is made of physical atoms or subtle matter.</note> spread through this thicker body. Whether it be fiery, as Democritus, Leucippus, and Hipparchus think. Or airy, as Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, and Critias. Or watery, as Hippias. Or earthy, as Hesiod and Xenophon. Or whether it consists of fire and air, as Boethus and Epicurus. Or of water and earth, as Xenophanes. 

Or the soul is something better—that is, not the mass of the little body itself, but some quality of it spread through the parts of the body, such as heat, or a warm <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio". In Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific balance of bodily humors that determines an individual's physical and mental state.</note>. <margin>C</margin> This is what Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Antipater, and Posidonius seem to have wanted. 

Or it is something purer, like a certain luminous point assigned by a quality from elsewhere to a more powerful part of that quality and the little body—for instance, the heart or the brain. <margin>D</margin> Residing there, it governs the remaining limbs from that spot, as is found in Chrysippus, Archelaus, and Heraclides Ponticus. 

<margin>E</margin>
Or it is something even more free, like a certain point fixed to no part, but secluded from every determined location, and present as a whole to every part of the body. But such that it is dependent on the very nature of the body. I say "dependent" in two ways: either because the body's <term>complexion</term> generated it, or because, although the complexion did not generate it, its generator—whoever that may be—led it out from the potentiality of matter and its inner workings—that is, from some seed, or beginning, or proportion of matter itself he brought it into the light and assigned it entirely to matter as if to a natural womb. This is the opinion followed by Xenophanes of Colophon, Asclepiades, Aristoxenus, and Critolaus. According to these men, the soul is either a certain power of the body agile for movement, or a harmony of the corporal parts. 

<margin>F</margin>
Or finally, the human soul is something divine—that is, something indivisible, standing as a whole in every part of the body, and so produced by an incorporeal author that it depends only on the power of the agent, and not on the beginning, capacity, or nourishment of matter—as the ancient theologians Zoroaster, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius", referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, Orpheus, Aglaophemus, Pythagoras, and Plato teach us, whose...

<summary>This page introduces Book Six of Ficino's treatise, framed as a dialogue at a villa near Rome, where he begins to categorize historical philosophical views on the soul into five distinct types. These range from purely materialist "little bodies" to the Platonic view of the soul as a divine, incorporeal entity.</summary>

...[In this opinion] the great natural philosopher Aristotle follows the tracks. Besides these five opinions, no others are found. ### Common philosophers, not persuaded by any reason but deceived by corrupt habit, posited that the soul is corporeal. Chapter 2.

<margin>❦</margin>
**I**n the first place, I consider that the common philosophers, who judged the soul to be corporeal and followed one of those four opinions, were not persuaded by any reason, but were driven to this view by a certain long and most unfortunate habit. <margin>❦</margin> There seem to be three principal functions of our soul. In fact, it acts in the body, it acts through the body, and it works through itself. In the body, it acts through that power which the <term>Peripatetics</term> call "vegetative"; but our <term>Platonists</term> call it the "nature" which generates, nourishes, and increases the body. Through the body, it acts according to sense: both the exterior sense, which sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches; <margin>f</margin> and the interior sense, which revolves within itself the images (like leftovers of the senses) of those bodies it perceived from without. It acts through itself when it neither touches bodies through the exterior senses nor gathers the images of bodies through the interior sense. But by the very pure and incorporeal force of the soul, it investigates and finds something incorporeal, which is neither a body nor the image of any body. This action we indeed call **intelligence**. <margin>3</margin> You have, therefore, natural action, sense, and intelligence. The soul uses natural action in the fetus itself, immediately upon entering the body. It uses sense a little later, namely, as soon as the human is born. Pure intelligence is only achieved with difficulty once the body is adult; indeed, a great part of men almost never achieve it, especially those who are still children even in their thirtieth year of life. <margin>k</margin> If you ask that natural power what the soul is, it will undoubtedly answer that it is a body. For it touches almost nothing other than the body. If you ask the exterior sense, it will likewise answer "body." The eyes will ascribe a certain figure and color to the soul. The ears, a voice. Smell, an odor. Taste, a flavor. Touch, weight, solidity, heat, and the like. But if you should inquire of the interior sense (which feeds on the rest of the external senses) concerning the soul, it too would paint the soul as a likeness of bodies. For it has nothing else it can use. Our unhappy youth, nourished here under unlearned teachers, forces us to feel foolishly about the soul throughout our whole life, while we suppose it to be corporeal, having been taught by these masters who perceive only bodily things. <margin>2</margin> Especially, however, this error seems to have arisen—or rather, to have been confirmed—from this: that if ever, having altogether dismissed these three teachers like <term>Sophists</term> <note>Here used to mean deceptive or superficial instructors, referring to the lower senses.</note>, we flee to that mind, the mistress of wisdom, and ask of her what the soul is, she answers that it is such as she herself sees. But what kind does she see? How foul? How miserable? Certainly not such as it once was when it descended from heaven. But that power...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book Six of his Platonic Theology. Having dismissed physicalist views of the soul, he now explores how the soul’s perception is clouded by its residence in the body and why reason must correct the errors of the senses to recognize the soul's true, incorporeal nature.</meta>

# Platonic [Theology]

The soul perceives itself as the natural builder of the body, yet it sees itself submerged in the corruption of the <term>four humors</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, these were blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, thought to govern physical health and temperament.</note>, polluted by their decay and suffocated by the heavy fatness of the limbs. It observes the external <margin>A</margin> senses everywhere declining toward physical bodies—acting through the body and, in a way, suffering because of bodies. It even sees the internal sense, which they call <term>phantasy</term> <note>Also known as the "imagination," this was considered an internal faculty that processed sensory data into mental images.</note>, covered with the various shapes and qualities of diverse bodies, as if it had drunk them in through the senses. 

Therefore, while the soul sees itself wrapped in a bodily garment and notices its own appetite is inclined toward physical things, it surely concludes that it is itself corporeal. This is no different than if a newborn child had been so smeared with mud that he was covered by a shell of clay throughout his entire childhood; if he were then asked, <margin>B</margin> "O boy, what is your little body like?" would he not answer that it is made of mud? Wash the body, boy! Wipe the flesh clean of the clods! Then you will see that you are made of flesh, not mud. 

O miserable ones, dismiss the senses—those most impious teachers! Question only the pious mind, but on this condition: that you show the mind a soul that is pure, just as you received it—not enslaved to the body, nor stained by the spots of vice. Then, and only then, will the mind respond that the soul is not merely incorporeal, but divine. 

You are a great thing, O soul, if small things do not satisfy you. You are the best of things, if evil displeases you. You are most beautiful, if you shudder at the base. You are eternal, if you hold temporal things of little value. Since you are such a being, if you desire to find yourself, I pray you, seek yourself there where such things exist. For truly great things are found only where no location imposes a limit or boundary. The best things are where nothing adverse occurs. The most beautiful are where nothing is out of harmony. The eternal are where there is no failing. 

Seek yourself, therefore, outside the world. Turn yourself, so that you may both seek and find yourself outside; fly outside! Indeed, look outside. For you are outside even while you embrace the world itself. But you think you are in the lowest place of the world because you do not perceive yourself flying above the heavens, but only see your shadow—the body—in the depths. It is as if a boy standing over a well thought 

---

# Book [Six]

that he was at the bottom of the well, because he does not turn his gaze toward himself, but sees his own shadow in the depths. Or as if a bird flying in the air believed it was flying on the ground while seeing its shadow on the earth. Therefore, leaving behind the narrowness of this shadow, return into yourself. For thus you return into vastness. 

Know that in the spirit there is immense breadth, but in the body there is (so to speak) infinite narrowness. One may perceive this from the fact that numbers, which are close to the spiritual nature, lack physical position; they measure and count both incorporeal and corporeal forms, being nothing other than certain repetitions of unity itself. Unity is incorporeal, because everything corporeal is made of many parts. These numbers, I say, which are spiritual, increase without end, yet they do not decrease without end. Magnitude <note>In this context, "magnitude" refers to physical size or geometric space.</note>, on the contrary, has a limit to its growth, even if it has no limit to its decrease through division. 

O unhappy ones, why do you value the judgment of the senses so highly? They deceive us with false images <margin>C</margin> so that the sight judges the sun—which is far larger than the earth—to be scarcely two cubits wide. It sees that which runs most rapidly as if it were standing still. In water, it sees a straight object as broken or crooked. It perceives the shore to be running while the ship itself is moving. Hearing often signals that a voice is coming from somewhere other than its source. Taste frequently finds sweet things to be bitter, and there are infinite errors of this kind. 

Who corrects the errors of the senses? Reason. But that which amends and perfects is more noble than that which is perfected. Therefore, reason is more diligent and more truthful than the senses. Reason judges that something incorporeal can be found, and reason is always occupied with such things. It is therefore true, by the judgment of reason, that something incorporeal exists somewhere, just as it is true by the judgment of the senses that many corporeal things exist in the world. However, the judgment of the senses fails in this: it affirms nothing except the body. Likewise, the judgment of reason would fail if it were to assert that there is nothing corporeal in things. But as it stands, reason is so far from being false that even those things which appear false...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul misidentifies itself as physical because it is "mired" in the body, using the metaphor of a mud-covered boy or a shadow in a well. He asserts that reason, which is superior to the fallible senses, reveals the soul's true nature as an infinite, incorporeal, and divine essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book Five of the Platonic Theology. Following the discussion of how the soul is often deceived by its physical vessel, Ficino now explains how the human reason must overcome the conflicting and limited testimonies of the five senses to recognize the existence of incorporeal (non-physical) realities.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
<header>Theology, Book Five</header>

# Theology
# Book Five

...fallacy, I might correct the sense. For the powers of sensation are so deceptive that they are not only corrected by reason, but they are even condemned by one another. If you entrust yourself to sight alone, you will say there is nothing else in the world except what is seen in the light. You would think voices, odors, and the rest—which are not seen—simply do not exist. If you trust only your ears, you will deny that colors exist. If you trust smell, you will think there are only odors in the world. And so it must be thought of the others. Just as each sense denies that anything else exists anywhere except what belongs to itself—and yet through another sense we condemn one by the other and find that something else exists beyond what is proper to a single sense, and we find this rightly—so all the senses conspiring together deny that anything can exist in nature that is not a body. Nevertheless, reason, refuting them all, prophesies <note>original: "vaticinat". Ficino uses this word to suggest that reason has a divinely inspired or intuitive foresight into truths that the physical body cannot grasp.</note> that there is also something incorporeal; and it prophesies truly, and much more truly than the senses, which are both condemned by each other and refuted by reason.

<margin>e</margin>
For what is more foolish than to grant that we surpass the beasts in reason, and to confess that those things we perceive by sense exist (which even some beasts sense more acutely than we do), yet to contend that what we behold with the eye of reason is nothing?

<margin>f</margin>
For no animal would be more foolish than man if that power of the soul which is proper to man were to deceive him more than the sense which is common to the beasts. It is a crime, however, to say the king of animals is the most insane of all.

<margin>g</margin>
But he alone will be most insane who does not confess that the object of the mind is as much more excellent than the object of the sense as the mind is more excellent than the sense; and for that reason, incorporeal natures are found in a more excellent kind of substance than corporeal ones. Especially since, if the objects of the mind move the mind just as the objects of the sense move the sense, those very objects of the mind must have some substance in themselves so that they are able to move the mind. But if it should be said that the intellect is not at all moved by its objects, it will already be sufficiently proven that the intellect itself is an incorporeal nature, since while it constructs its own [thoughts], it is not moved by another, and it constructs incorporeal buildings.

Indeed, one ought to remember how a boy born blind hardly believes in the variety of colors and the existence of light, even though nothing is clearer than light to other men. So the soul, recently surrounded by the shadows of the body, can hardly be led to believe that some incorporeal light exists, even though nothing in the order of things is more manifest than that light is to the angels.

<margin>h</margin>
Plato complains of this at length in the seventh book of the *Republic* <note>This refers to the "Allegory of the Cave," where prisoners see only shadows and cannot believe in the sunlit world outside.</note>. Aristotle confirms this in the second book of "divine matters" <note>original: "diuinorum". This refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, which was frequently titled *Theologia* or *De Rebus Divinis* in the Renaissance.</note>, saying that the human intellect relates to those things which are by nature most manifest in the order of things no differently than the eye of an owl relates to the light of the sun. Therefore, let the "puny philosophers" <note>original: "minuti philosophi". A derogatory term borrowed from Cicero to describe materialists who cannot see beyond the physical world.</note> finally come to their senses—those who, relying on the judgment of the senses, cannot conceive of the soul being incorporeal and divine. Let it be noticed that from long habituation with the body, they have become so corporeal themselves that they deservedly know nothing except the body or things born from the body. Let them become pure, and they will perceive pure things. Let them at some point experience this within themselves.

For they can [perceive] as much as they wish in the world, which they have long desired in the universe; they certainly perceive composite things, and they perceive many forms within those composites. Furthermore, they desire certain forms separated outside of the composites. They themselves are composed of soul and body. They have life handed over to the body from the soul. They also have the life of the soul itself flourishing within itself. Therefore, let them look down upon the former life and look up to the latter; let them lead an intellectual life separated from the body. Once separated, they will immediately reach separated forms.

<margin>i</margin>
And they will soon prove the Socratic opinion <note>The "Socratic opinion" here refers to the Theory of Forms, suggesting that perfect archetypes exist independently of physical objects.</note> by the thing itself: that above the forms which lie within formed subjects (since these are imperfect), there are forms in themselves and perfect, from which unformed subjects are given shape. And there is one single way not only to reach the incorporeal but even to possess it: namely, to make oneself incorporeal. That is, to call back the mind from motion, sense, emotion, and corporeal imagination as much as one is able. For thus, the experience itself will be established.

<summary>Ficino argues that reason must correct the deceptive and limited nature of the senses to recognize incorporeal realities. He concludes that the only way to perceive the soul's divine nature is to detach the mind from physical sensations and bodily habits.</summary>
