<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book Five of the Platonic Theology. Having established that reason can correct the deceptions of the senses, Ficino now moves to a deeper exploration of the soul’s nature. He uses a famous thought experiment from the Islamic philosopher Avicenna to prove that the soul’s awareness of its own existence is independent of the body.</meta>

# Platonic
# Book

**F**irst, indeed: what the pure <term>soul|animus: the rational part of the human spirit</term> is like—that is, reason living within itself and eagerly turning toward the light of truth. Second: what an angel is like—that is, pure <term>intellect|intellectus: a higher form of knowing that does not require step-by-step reasoning</term>, already rejoicing in the infused light of truth. Third: when the soul itself, like an angel, will rejoice in the full light of truth, it will perceive that God exists; then it will perceive truth itself shining and rejoicing in itself; then it will perceive the Light itself rejoicing in its own truth; and finally, it will perceive Joy itself shining in its own truth.

<margin>A</margin>
We shall begin to understand somewhat that the error of the common people <note>original: "plebeorum errorem". Ficino refers to those who rely solely on physical senses rather than philosophical contemplation.</note> arises from a habit of focusing on the body, if we consider an opposite kind of upbringing, such as the one **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a 10th-century Persian philosopher. This refers to his famous "Floating Man" thought experiment.</note> devised in the sixth book of his *Natural Sciences*. Imagine, says Avicenna, a person created by God suddenly and placed in a state of physical perfection, but so arranged that he cannot perceive anything through any of the five senses. The mind of a person in such a state would still think. Since he is in an adult state, his physical structure does not disturb his intelligence, nor is he occupied by the works of the senses, which normally hinder the mind's operation. Furthermore, there is something present that can be understood: the very substance of the soul is present to the mind. Therefore, the mind, disturbed by nothing, will think upon the substance of the soul present to itself. But what kind of soul will it imagine? Will it be colored? Long? Or wide? Not at all. For the sense of touch does not perceive such things here. Will it be sounding, or sweet-smelling, and the like? Not even these.

<margin>E</margin>
For he has not yet received such qualities through the senses, so he cannot assign such a nature to the soul. Therefore, that soul will not be able to attribute anything corporeal <note>non-physical or bodily</note> to itself. What, then, will it assert about itself? Certainly, at least that which is offered to its first intuition: its own essence. For this reason, it will affirm that it exists, yet it will not perceive anything bodily within itself. Thus, it will affirm that it is entirely <term>incorporeal|without a physical body</term>. It will not even be able to imagine that it is a body, just as the souls of the common people—created and educated differently—are now unable to consider themselves as incorporeal.

If someone were to say that the soul would not affirm any of these bodies we perceive through the five senses, but rather some other body of a different nature, that would be quite vain. For if even now, when we have perceived so many various bodies, we cannot devise anything new that is not either in these things, or composed of them, or drawn from them, how could a soul ignorant of these bodies imagine the nature of a new body? Moreover, even if it were possible for the soul to imagine some member of its own body, it would in no way think that member belonged to its own proper substance. Therefore, that soul will affirm its own existence, yet it will not affirm anything corporeal. These two things are different: that which is affirmed, and that which is not affirmed at all. Therefore, the essence of the soul in that consideration will be something beyond the body. We believe the judgment of that consideration would be true because it would follow the completely pure nature of the soul, not images received from the outside.

It would, therefore, be a very natural judgment and thus most true. And so, if the soul were later to "wake up"—as we are now—and begin to feel, it would not be (as we are) totally unfit for the investigation of spiritual things. Instead, it would have a more convenient path by which it could eventually return to the consideration of itself and declare that it is something beyond the body. Miserable souls now lack this path, for through nature and the senses, they touched bodies (both their own and others') before they ever considered themselves. From this arises that miserable and progressed error: that they cannot see themselves apart from the stain of the body. Let it suffice to have recounted this imaginary education from Avicenna thus far.

<margin>B</margin>
Next, let us briefly touch upon what kind of education our **Plato** describes in the seventh book of the *Republic*. Imagine, he says, a certain cave under the earth. In it are people nurtured from childhood, with their necks and hands tied behind their backs, and their feet...

<summary>Ficino uses Avicenna's 'Floating Man' thought experiment to argue that if a soul were stripped of all sensory input, it would instinctively know it exists as a non-physical entity. He contrasts this with 'miserable souls' who are so habituated to the body they cannot imagine existing without it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book Six of the Platonic Theology. Following the discussion of Avicenna’s thought experiment on the soul’s self-awareness, Ficino now turns to Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave from the Republic to illustrate how the soul is imprisoned by the senses and must be liberated to see the truth.</meta>

## Theology

<margin>B</margin>
...bound by certain chains: so that they can move nowhere, nor see anything except what appears from the part of the cave placed before their sight. Behind their backs, however, let a **lamp** <note>original: "lampas". In Plato's original Greek, this is a fire; Ficino uses the term lamp or torch.</note> be lit from above; and between the lamp and those who are bound, let many others walk about, talking among themselves and carrying in their hands various likenesses of trees and animals. Those who are thus bound will truly never see either themselves or the other things we have described; rather, they see only their own **shadows** or the shadows of others, which are cast onto the opposite part of the cave because of the fire lit behind them. For this reason, they will think they are nothing other than their own shadows, and they will believe other things to be nothing but the shadows of those objects; nor will they imagine the light itself to be anything other than that meager reflection which appears there. But if one of those who are bound should by chance be released, and suddenly be forced to look back toward the lamp and the other things under it that follow behind his back, he will immediately be **dazzled** <note>original: "caligabit". Literally to have be misted over or darkened, describing the temporary blindness caused by looking directly at a bright light after being in darkness.</note> and feel pain; and because of the splendor, he will be unable to look upon those things whose shadows he was seeing just a moment before. And this misfortune would happen to him much more severely if he were suddenly dragged upward from the cave toward the celestial and daylight. Therefore, he must be led forth not suddenly, but gradually by appropriate steps from the shadows of things to the things themselves. Likewise, he must be led from the image of the light to the light itself, so that he may first see those things that are in the cave among them reflected in water before he gazes upon them in themselves. Again, regarding those things which are outside the cave among us: first let him look at the moon in the water at night in the same way; then at these earthly things in themselves; and similarly let him gaze upon the celestial things in the heavens at night. Afterward, truly, by day, let him look upon the sun itself and the things seen under the sun—first in the water, then in themselves—and finally let him look up at the **sun in the heavens**. By this method especially, he will distinguish each thing clearly and easily; and he will consider that he had been blind, deceived, and wretched when he was occupied by the meager shadows of things while bound under the cave.

<margin>☛</margin>
Accordingly, whatever comparison exists between that cave and this world, which we call **visible**, the same comparison exists almost exactly between this world and that one, which we call **invisible and divine**. Since here the wretched souls are enclosed in the darkness of the dying body and in a blind prison, they never see themselves, nor any other things truly, nor the true sun, but only the shadows of themselves and others, and a certain faint image of the true sun. For indeed, the **minds**, the true things themselves, and the true sun are only in the invisible world; if we attempt to gaze upon these suddenly without the steps of a suitable education and disciplines, we are immediately dazzled and feel pain. But when we are led through the appropriate steps of character, doctrine, and time, we discern clearly and judge that those are blind and wretched who are deceived, occupied, and weighed down by the false shadows and images of this world. Nevertheless, when the soul descends from the immense light of the invisible world into the dark body to rule and move it, overwhelmed by new darknesses contrary to its own nature, it is compelled to be blind for a long time and to stumble. Add to this that, on account of the sudden and greatest change for the worse, it is compelled to be sick for a long time, and to be affected almost like those who are mocked and distressed by false images due to **frenzy**, <note>original: "phrenesiz". Referring to a state of delirium or mental agitation.</note> sleep, or drunkenness. Or certainly, it is no different than if someone were suddenly cast down from the light of the sun into that cavern we described. For indeed, he will be so overwhelmed by the new darkness that he can distinguish those shadows we spoke of either not at all, or only with great difficulty under that meager light of the cavern. Furthermore, because of that sudden change for the worse, he will fall into various diseases of both the senses and the body. These things are from **Plato** in the seventh book of the *Republic*. But let us return at last to those things we had established from the beginning.

## Sextus

<margin>☛</margin>
**Emerge**, I beseech you, souls of mortals now immersed in bodies; for you will immediately find your own nature above the limits of the body. For the body is long, wide, and deep. But no soul is a body, for it is infinite. Therefore, without the boundary of depth, the soul is a surface, not a depth. You already have a long surface...

<summary>Ficino recounts Plato's Allegory of the Cave to explain the soul's transition from sensory deception to intellectual truth. He argues that the soul, imprisoned in the body, is initially blinded by the "light" of divine truth and must be gradually educated to perceive reality beyond physical shadows.</summary>
<keywords>Allegory of the Cave, Plato, Republic, soul, shadows, divine light, visible vs invisible world, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, enlightenment</keywords>

--- Page 152 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book Six of his Platonic Theology. Having just discussed the soul's ability to turn inward away from the body (using the cave allegory and Avicenna's "floating man" thought experiment), Ficino now uses mathematical and physical analogies—geometry, light, and mirrors—to prove the soul's existence as an incorporeal "unity."</meta>

# Platonic

...just like a body, but lacking depth; and from this one part rising toward the incorporeal. The finite width of a **surface** <note>original: "superficies". In the geometry of this period, a surface or plane is understood as having length and width but no thickness.</note> also ends at a long line, having neither depth nor width. You have a **line** <note>original: "linea". A one-dimensional object.</note> approaching the spirit by two parts. But since this very length of the line is finite, it is led to a **point** <note>original: "punctum". A zero-dimensional location, representing the final boundary of physical space before reaching the purely spiritual.</note>, which is deprived not only of depth and width, but also of length. You have a point turning toward the incorporeal nature by three parts. But because this is the boundary of a line, it has a fixed position in the body; yet it is neither the whole body, nor does it give life. 

Separate this point from the line, if you please. It can at least be separated from the line by thought, since it is the boundary of the line; and it exists in itself in some way before it terminates the line. That which comes first may be separated from that which comes after. You have the point, in a certain way—that is, released from the line by thought—now descending from the body by a fourth degree. In this very release, it achieves a state where it looks upon all parts of the body equally. It is founded through them all and moves them; here the **irrational soul** <note>original: "irrationalis anima". The part of the soul responsible for basic biological functions and sensory perception, which Ficino situates at the level of the geometric point.</note> has its seat. 

And since rational thought does not fail as it ascends, just as it finds a point free from the body through thought, so in truth it will find a "point"—that is, an individual something—released from the body in actual reality. This would not only fill the body and move it, but move it freely, and be raised to the things above; this is what he now calls by the name of **unity**. Here the **rational soul** <note>original: "rationalis anima". The higher human intellect.</note> flourishes, at the fifth step, alienated from the mass of the body. 

If a thing is more impure the more it is in need and the more it suffers, then the body is more impure than the surface. For the body needs more dimensions—and is divided into more parts—in order to exist. The surface, by a similar reasoning, yields to the line; the line to the point; and finally the point to **unity**, which needs neither dimensions nor position. If substantial unity is the most perfect of these, and because it is the most perfect, it is therefore the most powerful and most true; and if these other things are "something" and exist, who would deny that unity truly exists? What, then, prevents the soul from being something, and indeed something great in power, even if it is not something great in quantity? 

# Book

Consider a **fiery form** <note>original: "igneam formam". Ficino often uses fire as a metaphor for the soul's active, purifying nature.</note>, which in your three-cubit body is three cubits long; gather it all into the center of the heart. From this point, let it grow as much in power as it has grown through its union. It is not unlike the rays of the sun collected in the center of a concave bronze mirror; these are strengthened to such an extent that, leaping back from there, they suddenly set fire to and consume even the hardest objects. Subtract that small portion of the heart by which that form of fire is pressed down. Let there remain the individual form: agile, warm, and glowing, but in a different and more wonderful way than before. Because it is individual and agile throughout its whole self, it illuminates the whole body equally. Because it glows incredibly, it becomes vital and life-giving. Because it shines miraculously, let it perceive. Let it moreover understand, if it reflects upon itself and lifts itself upward. 

Thus far, by proceeding step-by-step through things that are touched, you have found the soul, when you proceeded from the solid body to something like a completely free point. Now, examine the soul again through things that are seen by the eyes. Why, I ask, do you doubt <margin>a</margin> that there is something spiritual in nature, when you see a spirit, in a certain way, with your very eyes? You know that the light of the sun, manifest to the eye, is therefore not a body, because it pours itself into everything in an instant. Once infused, it does not break bodies, nor is it stained. Behold, you see a spirit. Why do you deny it? 

Or will you perhaps deny that something exists because you do not see it? If that is so, then since the spheres of air, of fire, and of the heavens are more excellent than water and earth, you will say they are nothing because they are not seen. Thus the greatest and most excellent part of the world will be nothing, because it is not visible. But let us return to light. You would deny that light exists in the sphere of fire <note>The "sphere of fire" was believed in pre-modern cosmology to be a transparent layer of the atmosphere below the moon.</note> because it is not perceived by the eyes. But even the brightness of the sun would exist even if it were not seen, since it exists now and is not seen by **owls** <note>original: "noctuis". A classic philosophical trope: the human intellect is to divine truth as an owl's eyes are to the sun.</note>; and some of its splendor, mixed with vapors, is seen by us; but we infer from this splendor that the sun itself exists somewhere. So also, we infer from the light of the stars (which is its image) that a spiritual light exists within celestial souls. Or do you not know that the action of light is nothing...

<summary>Ficino uses a geometric hierarchy—from 3D bodies down to a dimensionless point—to argue that the soul is a "Unity" that exists independently of physical space. He then uses the instant movement and purity of light to prove that spiritual, invisible substances are more powerful than visible, material ones.</summary>

<keywords>geometry, dimensions, point, unity, rational soul, irrational soul, light, sun, mirrors, fiery form, incorporeality</keywords>

--- Page 153 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book Six of his Platonic Theology. Having just described the soul as a dimensionless point released from the body by thought, Ficino now transitions into an analogy of light and geometry to explain how the soul (the invisible "center") relates to the celestial and human bodies (the "circumference").</meta>

# Theology

...to be nothing other than to shine? And to glow even more clearly the further it is separated from dense bodies. Separate it from all matter and it will glow more miraculously. Indeed, it will then live most fully, if it is ever to truly live. Where the activity increases, life also increases. Especially since all these things live by its heat. It will also perceive (so to speak) since all these things perceive through its rays. Yet it will be perceived least of all. For by its thinness it will escape the sharp edge of the eyes, and by the abundance of its intelligible brilliance, it will overcome the capacity of earthly sight. <margin>C</margin> It is enough [to observe] in the spheres of the elements <note>The four elements: earth, water, air, and fire, arranged in concentric spheres around the Earth.</note> that the lowest fire declines so far toward the nature of the highest air, and the highest air conversely is raised up toward that fire, so that the fire seems to be almost nothing else than thin air, and that air a thicker fire. So much so that whoever sees that air could affirm without lying that he has seen fire. 

The same comparison applies to the lowest mind—which is the rational soul—in relation to the sublime body, which is the heavens. Therefore, the soul is in a certain way a "thin heaven," and the heaven is a "thicker soul." And he who looks up at the heavens gazes upon the soul. Consider a certain geometric point; because it looks toward every part of the space surrounding it, if it ever moves, it moves in a circle through every part. Hence, what was a point is seen to escape into a circumference. In this sense, a circumference is a point running around and unfolded outward. A point, truly, is a circumference folded together on a certain stable hinge. 

Think again of a certain spark of invisible light; because it exists above every place, it pours itself equally into any part of space, and while it moves in a circle, it results in a flaming orb. An orb, I say, manifest to the eyes. In this case, the spark is a compressed flame. The flame is a spread-out spark. A spark of this kind is the soul. The flame is the ethereal body <note>original: "corpus ethereuz". The celestial or "astral" body that Neoplatonists believed clothed the soul as it descended from the heavens to the earth.</note>. And as great as the variety of spiritual light is in rational souls, just as great is the variety of visible light in their precious and celestial bodies. And that light follows spiritual light just as the pale <margin>D</margin> orb in the clouds follows the light of the moon. 

But there is this difference among rational souls: the souls of the fixed stars and the planets are surrounded only by a lucid <note>shining or transparent</note> body; all other souls are surrounded by twin bodies: one lucid and one opaque, or at least one very bright and the other less bright. It seems to be the same light which, while it remains a spark, perceives but is not perceived. When it unfolds into a flame, it is then perceived, but it perceives nothing further itself. And just as anyone would lack sense who, seeing a flame, denied he was seeing a spark, so too will he lack soul who, while looking up at the ethereal globes, does not perceive that souls are within them as centers of their circuits. Nor would he concede that souls are globes of light folded inward, while the globes are souls unfolded. <margin>E</margin> This is what Heraclitus meant: <margin>The dry light is the wisest soul <note>original Greek: αυγη ξηρη ψυχη σοφωτατη</note></margin>. 

From this it follows that nothing is more pleasing or more miraculous to the soul than light. Nor can it dwell anywhere else than in the light of spirits while it inhabits the earth. Here you have found, therefore, that the soul is like an invisible light: life-giving, perceiving, intelligible, and intelligent. And a little before, it was like a point free from the body, agile by its own power, hot, life-giving, perceiving, and capable of higher things—which is called a "substantial unity." And so this first excursion is made, as a kind of prelude, by which that unhappy disagreement may be removed which leads the minds of the common people very far away from the confession of spiritual things.

> ¶ The soul is not a body, or a form divided in the body, as is shown through the natural power of the soul. Chapter 4.

<margin>F</margin> **T**he order of the proposed question requires that in the first part of the following dispute we show, through the natural power of the soul, that the human soul is primarily not a body, and partly also that it is not a form divided within a body. In the second part, we shall show the same thing through the power of sensing: namely, that the soul is an indivisible form; and we shall add further that it is not [subject] to any craftsman <note>The argument continues to the next page, establishing the soul's independence from physical construction.</note>.

Marsilio Ficino

He begins a new chapter to prove the soul is neither a material body nor a divisible physical form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, specifically Book 6. In the preceding text, Ficino used the analogy of light and geometric points to argue for the soul’s incorporeal nature. Here, he transitions from abstract analogies to formal logical proofs, beginning a series of "reasons" (rationes) to demonstrate that the soul cannot be a physical body.</meta>

->Book on Platonic Theology<-

...to be attached to a specific member of the body; rather, it is poured out as a whole through every individual part. In the third part, let us confirm these same points through the power of understanding: namely, that the soul is an indivisible <term>form (an organizing principle rather than a physical shape)</term> that is whole everywhere; and let us add that it draws no origin from matter. For in this way, the soul of man will belong to that third essence—which is eternal—and will be rightly judged immortal. Now indeed, having invoked the divine power, let us approach the first part of the discussion in this manner.

<margin>A</margin>
### ¶ First reason: because the soul is the principle of nourishment, and of operating in any other way. Chapter 4.

**Living beings** and green plants are bodies. Logs and rocks torn from the earth are also bodies. Those [living bodies] grow and knit together; these [rocks and wood], however, do not. But what is the principle of nourishment in the living ones? It is not bodily matter, because if it were, other bodies would also be nourished, since such matter is common to all of them. Therefore, since that power through which they grow is something other than bodily matter, and that power is nothing other than the <term>nutritive soul (the basic life-force shared by plants and animals)</term>, it follows that such a soul is not a body. 

But if someone were to object: "On the contrary, the soul is indeed a body—not just any body, but a specific kind, disposed in such a way as is proper to the nature of plants and living beings, and certainly not common to dry wood." We will ask him about this "certain kind of body" which he calls the soul: does it contain two things within itself—namely, a physical mass and, in addition, a certain <term>quality (or 'affection,' meaning a specific state of being)</term> through which it is so named and becomes a specific, individual body—or does it have nothing beyond the matter common to all bodies everywhere? 

If he answers that it has nothing besides this common mass, then his objection was entirely empty. He had claimed that not every body is a soul, but only a "specific" body disposed in a "certain way." Yet a body cannot be "specific" or "disposed in a certain way" except through a quality itself—a certain specific property added to the body through which it is not only a body, but a *particular kind* of body that differs from every other body. 

Therefore, if there is nothing there except the mass alone—the common property of a body—and since that mass is present even in dry logs and rocks, then these would also have a soul through which they are nourished. Because this is clearly false, it is necessary that this "specific body" (which the opponent called the soul) contains not just the matter of the body, but also a quality or some form. 

And that thing is not called "soul" because of the matter of the body, because matter belongs even to bodies lacking life. It remains, then, that it is called soul because of the form—the life-giving form, I say. For that is what is proper to the soul. We shall call that life-giving form itself the "soul." As for the matter to which it is joined, we shall call it "animated" (since it becomes a sharer in life), but we shall call it neither the soul nor a part of the soul. 

This present reasoning is most strongly confirmed by the opinion we introduced at the start: when we argued that a body, by itself, can do nothing. Indeed, we see that when the soul is added to bodies, many operations proceed from them which happen not at all before the soul's arrival or after its departure. Therefore, we conclude that the soul, which is the source of such operations, is not a physical body.

<margin>B</margin>
### ¶ Second reason. The soul is neither an animated body, nor an inanimate one. Chapter 5.

**What kind** of body do you wish the soul to be: an animated one, or an inanimate one? You will not say "inanimate," for the soul is that which grants animal life to another. How could the soul bring life to bodies if it were itself an inanimate body? Nor can you say it is an "animated body." For if the soul is called an "animated body," then surely that body—since it is called "animated"—must be said to be animated by *another* soul. 

Regarding that [second] soul, I ask again: is it a body or not? If it is a body, it is either animated or inanimate. If you answer "inanimate," it is an absurdity. If you say "animated," I will again ask about the soul by which *that* one is said to be animated. And so you would be forced to proceed into infinity <note>A logical fallacy where an argument requires an endless chain of causes, never reaching a primary source.</note> as long as you assert that the soul is a body. And you will always be compelled to answer absurdly. And indeed, without... <note>Original: "Citraque enim," the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because life-functions like nourishment require an organizing "form" that matter alone lacks. He further demonstrates that calling the soul a body leads to a logical infinite regress.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, Aristotelian form, nutritive soul, bodily matter, logical proof, infinite regress, Marsilio Ficino, Platonic Theology</keywords>

--- Page 155 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book 6 of the Platonic Theology. In the previous page, he argued that the soul cannot be a physical body because the principle of life (the soul) must be distinct from the matter it animates. Here, he addresses the logical absurdity of the soul being "animated" by something else and examines whether the soul could be a "subtle" body like fire or air.</meta>

It seems like absurd reasoning to say that you <note>the soul</note> are an animated soul, just as you are in a soul. This is like saying of wisdom: that it is both wise and unwise. Or of light: that it is both illuminated and dark. For if light is not dark—because it illustrates other things—nor is it illuminated by another—because it is itself the **primal light**—then in the same way, the soul is neither inanimate (since it gives life) nor is it animated through something else. This is because the soul is properly the very thing through which anything is truly animated. 

Furthermore, if you refer the soul to something else through which it might be animated, I will likewise refer that other thing back to something else, and that other to another, and I will never stop. Or, if I do stop, I will certainly rest at the point where I say: either that very thing which I first proposed, or some subsequent thing, is neither animated nor made living by another, but is itself properly the thing which, through itself, animates and gives life to another. The soul is something of this kind, and I shall properly call it "life," or whatever else you wish. 

Perhaps you—in order to avoid that infinite regress and those absurd responses, and yet still asserting that the soul is a body—will claim that it is a body, not indeed an "animated" body <note>original: "animatum"</note>, but a "living" body <note>original: "corpus animale"</note>; not "made alive," but "living." If this is the case, you have revolved back to the same point. Indeed, I will ask: is it a soul by that reason through which it is a body, or by some other reason of some new addition through which it is called "living" and "animal"? Certainly not by the reason through which it is a body. For if that were so, all bodies would be souls and would display the operations of life. It follows, therefore, that there is something else there in its nature, beyond the nature of being a body, through which that body is called "living" and "animal." That thing, I shall properly name "life" and "soul."

<margin>¶</margin>
### ## Third reason. It is neither a gross body nor a subtle one. <gloss>Chapter 6.</gloss>

<insert>I</insert>s the soul perhaps a **gross body**, such as water, or earth, or similar things? Or is it rather **subtle** and rare, like fire and air? The first cannot be said. Since the duty of the soul is to penetrate bodies very easily, to fill them, and to move them, gross bodies are entirely unsuited for this operation. The second option might perhaps seem more probable: that the soul is a rare body like fire or air. But if it is said to be fire, is it the soul by the reason that it is fire? Or by some other reason? If it were said to be a soul because it is fire, then surely any fire would be a soul, and all ignited things would be living. Therefore, it must be by another reason. The same must be asked and concluded regarding air: the soul must always be sought **beyond the nature of the body**. 

Nor should anyone bring up some "fifth" <note>This refers to the "quintessence," a hypothetical fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire, often used by ancient physicists to explain celestial or spiritual movement.</note> and most thin little body, beyond the four elements, which might be the soul of those grosser infused bodies. For the same question will return: whether that little body is the soul through its own matter, or through some power added to its matter. If the first: then either all bodies will be souls (since matter underlies all of them), or if the second: we will have already achieved what we desire—that the soul must be referred to some <term>incorporeal power (a force that does not have physical dimensions or weight)</term>. 

Certain brief persuasions of this kind are asserted here by some:
If the soul is said to be **divisible**, it is asked whether its parts live as the whole does, or not. If they live, the whole soul is in each of its individual particles. From this it follows that it does not require quantity, since it is not diminished through division. If they do not live, then life would consist of non-living things, which is impossible. 

Again, every body can become known to the five senses; the soul can be known to none of them. Every body is circumscribed by some shape or boundary; the soul is not at all. Every body necessarily performs its operation through an interval of time. While light is not divisible in its essence, it is much more so in its action. The soul often operates in a **moment of time** <note>Meaning it acts instantaneously rather than moving through physical space over time.</note>. 

A body is in a place because of its quantity rather than its essence, because it fills a place through quantity. The soul is present to the body through its essence. Just as light is present to the eye, it gives it "being." It gives "being" through its essence, just as one is wise through "wisdom"; therefore, it is present through its essence. A body is in another thing in such a way that it is contained by that in which it is placed, and is exceeded by it. The soul is in the body not as something "contained," but as something **containing** <note>Ficino argues the soul holds the body together, rather than the body holding the soul like a cup holds water.</note>. For she herself perfects, contains, and leads the body. Finally, the soul is more excellent than any body, and more excellent than the whole body. For this reason, she is more excellent than the lines and points which are in bodies as if in a subject. The indivisible is more excellent than the divisible.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body (neither dense nor subtle) because it is the source of life, whereas matter is merely the recipient of life. He concludes that the soul is an incorporeal essence that contains and governs the body rather than being contained by it.</summary>
<keywords>incorporeal soul, divisibility, primal light, four elements, subtle body, essence vs quantity, Marsilio Ficino, Platonic Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument for the incorporeality and immortality of the soul, likely from Book 6 of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology. Having previously argued that the soul cannot be a physical body because it is the source of life, Ficino now uses the Aristotelian concepts of "matter" and "form" to prove that the soul must be a "substantial form" rather than a physical object or a mere byproduct (accident) of the body.</meta>

# Platonic [Theology]

...is more excellent. The mind, therefore, is more indivisible than either a geometrical line or a point.
¶ The fourth argument: the body is composed of matter and form.
->Chapter 7<-

<margin>A</margin> A natural body is composed of matter and form. A <term>living being</term> <note>original: "animal." In this context, Ficino uses the term to mean any creature with a soul, including humans.</note> is a natural body. Therefore, matter and form are both within it. It consists, moreover, of a soul and a body. The body is certainly not a "natural form," because a natural form is the form *of* something and exists *within* something as if in a subject—that is, in a thing being formed. A body, however, is the form of nothing; nor does it exist within a subject, but rather within a place. It remains, then, that the soul is the form, primarily because it is the proper and internal principle of operations and motions. Indeed, the soul is even the principle of being for the living creature. All of this <margin>C</margin> pertains to the nature of "form." Therefore, the soul is a form.

But if the soul itself were also a body, there would still be a need for another form for both the soul and the physical body, through which both together might be called a single "living being." This other form we would then more properly call the "soul." For through the soul—acting as a form—the body, which previously was living only in potential, becomes living in actuality, and becomes a <margin>B</margin> living creature in actuality. Therefore, the soul is form alone.

This is especially true because if the soul had two parts—namely, matter and form—three absurdities would follow. First, the soul would not form the body according to its whole self, because it would not form the body through that part of itself which is matter. However, it is necessary that a "proper form" perfects its own matter according to the whole of its essence. Second, that part of the soul called the "form" would be the perfection of two different matters of the same kind <note>i.e., the matter of the soul and the matter of the body</note>, which nature does not allow—just as nature does not allow two forms of the same kind to shape the same piece of matter. Third, because the soul in the body would change into these lower material things and vice versa if it shared a common matter with them. This is forbidden <note>original: "nephas," suggesting a violation of natural or divine law</note>, because if a mutual exchange of bodies and souls could occur, then it would be even more likely that any soul could transmute into any other soul, and any body into any other body. Let the soul, therefore, be form alone.

---

# Book [6]

A form, I say, that is not accidental, but substantial <note>A "substantial form" makes a thing what it is (like the "human-ness" of a human), while an "accidental form" is a non-essential quality (like being tan or tall).</note>. For since the soul itself is the ruler and <margin>C</margin> mover of the body—holding it together, making it stand, and turning it—it is more excellent than the body. The body is a substance. But no "accident" <note>a secondary quality</note> is more noble than a substance. Again, a mover, insofar as it is the principle of motion, does not depend for its existence upon the thing that it moves. Therefore, the soul itself, which is truly the mover of the body, does not depend on the body as if it were the body's **servant** <note>original: "pedissequa," literally a footman or female slave who follows behind a master.</note>. Thus, it is not an "accident" of the body.

Furthermore, whatever remains the same substance while receiving opposite qualities in turn is a substance. The soul, while remaining the same, receives now this opinion and now that (which are contrary to one another), as well as knowledge and ignorance, and conflicting emotions. The soul, therefore, is a substance. A substance, I say, acting as a kind of substantial form. But a form is not a body, because every body is defined by some form. Form, however, by the very reason that it is form, cannot be "formed" <note>meaning form cannot be the recipient of a shaping principle, as it is the principle itself</note>. From this it follows that the soul is not a body.

I offer these arguments at present to show that our soul cannot be an accident; for if it were attached to a subject by some necessity, it could not resist that subject, nor could it ever reflect back upon itself. Nor could it rise above the category of "accidents" to the category of "substance," nor could it properly define substance, or distinguish it from accidents, or rightly measure the vast distance by which it surpasses accidents.

¶ The fifth argument: The body by its nature is dispersed.
->Chapter 8<-

<margin>D</margin> The body by its nature is entirely dispersed. First, because it suffers from a distance between its parts, such that one part is always in a different place than another. Second, because it is continually being changed. For if it is subject to time, then just as various moments follow one another in time, so the conditions in the body vary with every single moment. Indeed, while this variety occurs in the heavens, it occurs much more so in the elements here below, driven by the motion of the heavens. Third, because it is subject to contrary qualities—to heat, to cold, and similar things. From this it follows that it is against the nature of the body to unite into one...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a "substantial form" rather than a physical body or a mere accidental quality, asserting that the soul must be a singular, non-material substance to serve as the body's ruler and mover. He further posits that if the soul were material, it would be subject to constant change and physical dispersion, preventing it from exercising higher functions like self-reflection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VI of the *Platonic Theology*. Having established that the soul is the "form" of the body, he now argues that the physical body is naturally unstable and requires the soul as an internal "binding substance" to maintain its unity and existence.</meta>

# Theology [Book] Six
->B 3<-

<margin>e</margin>
...to remain similar to itself and to be consistent. For the very <term>extension</term> <note>The quality of taking up physical space.</note> of a body's quantity forces its parts to remain separate. Perennial motion compels it to change its nature: not to hold its properties all at once, but to lose one and seek another. The conflict of opposing qualities drives them to flee from one another; through this flight, the composite body itself is scattered. Although it appears from these facts that a body, by its own nature, can in no way stand firmly in unity, nevertheless any body is somehow bound together in its parts, with all parts conspiring into a single connection of the whole body.

<margin>f</margin>
There is, therefore, something in the body beyond the nature of the body itself: something that unites, stabilizes, and contains it. It unites the distance between parts. It stabilizes the perennial flow. It contains the discordant qualities of the body through its own simple harmony. What is this thing? Is it a body? If it is a body, it similarly requires another thing to connect it. What is that other thing? Is it a body? If it is a body, it also needs another. For this reason, it must be admitted that there can be no unity in bodies, no constancy, and no harmony, unless there is some <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Existing without a physical body; spiritual or mental in nature.</note> power within them. Therefore, if the soul were also said to be a body, it would itself require some bond. However, we shall assert that this kind of binder is the soul—or the power of the soul—rather than the thing being bound. Let us see that it is the soul's own work to bind together contrary fluids and diverse limbs into the single frame of a living creature; when the soul departs, everything flows apart. Therefore, the soul is not a body, but the inner bond of the body, or the **binding substance**. Nor is it a "form" divided through the body. For such a form, as the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, whom Ficino synthesized with Christian theology.</note> believe, loses the nature of simplicity and constancy when in a body. Thus, such a form would—just like the body—need another container that remains one within itself and is not at all scattered by the division of the body.

<margin>h</margin>
If anyone should ask from where stones and wood obtain the union of their parts, the Platonists will respond: as long as they are attached to the earth, they receive both unity and growth from the **soul of the earth**. But after they have been torn away, they no longer receive growth, but they retain unity.

## Sixth reason. Two bodies are not in the same place.

### Chapter ix.

<margin>g</margin>
**T**wo bodies cannot be completely equalized with one another in the same place. For if they must be entirely in the same place, they must first be divided into parts. Then, their parts must be joined to each other's parts in turn. If these parts are <term>indivisible</term> <note>Smallest possible units that cannot be split further, like geometric points.</note>, then those bodies have been resolved into indivisible points. And since they were composed of the same things and are not dissolved, it would follow that the magnitude of the body grew out of certain indivisible points. This could not happen because indivisible points gathered together never produce a physical size. But if those parts were divisible, each would be a body in its own right, and each would then have its own place separate from the other. Therefore, there would not be two bodies in one place; rather, there would be many tiny bodies in many tiny places. If, then, two bodies cannot be equalized in the same place, the soul—which pours itself everywhere into the living body and extends itself through every point of the body—is not a body.

<margin>i</margin>
That it is everywhere in the body is evident for the present reason: nothing is more intrinsic to an <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of a thing; what it is.</note> than "being" itself. Therefore, the **form**—through which <term>substantial being</term> <note>The core existence of a thing, rather than its secondary characteristics.</note> is granted both to the whole body and to the parts—is most intimate to the whole and the parts.

<margin>k</margin>
And because as a thing relates to "being," so it relates to "one" (unity): the soul, which of itself gives being, is united of itself without a middle-man to the entire body. That it grants substantial being is evident from this: that when the soul is removed, all the limbs change their <term>species</term> <note>In this context, their "kind" or "essential form"; for example, a dead hand is no longer truly a "hand" in the functional sense.</note>. Since being flows from essence, and operation flows from power: the soul, which grants being and operation to individual limbs, also communicates its own essence and power to each one. For it provides being and operation in the same way that it is united. Therefore, if it provides these to each part, it is united to each part. Now, if any natural body lacking a soul is a single thing through a single form existing in the whole and the parts, how much more will an animated body be one through a soul present to the whole and the parts. But if the soul were in only one limb...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul must be an incorporeal "binding substance" because physical bodies are naturally prone to decay and division. He also demonstrates that the soul cannot be a body because it occupies the same space as the physical body, a feat impossible for two physical objects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VI of the Platonic Theology. Having previously argued that a body requires an incorporeal bond to remain a unified whole, he now demonstrates that if the soul were merely another body, it could not provide this unity without causing physical damage or constant pain.</meta>

->Platonic [Theology]<-
->Book [Six]<-

...it will be the form of only one part. The others will have different forms; from which a natural body, truly one, would not be composed of all members, but rather a certain collection, just as a house is made from walls.

Nor would there be in any part of the living being a consensus and harmony with any other part, as there is now, unless the various members were glued together by one soul. Just as all joints do not contract at the pull of a nerve unless the same nerve is in all of them. Add to this: that in any portion of the body, however small, life is present, and in most, motion and sense. These are the inner powers and operations of the soul. An inner power and action does not exist without the substance of the agent. Therefore, the soul is in those parts, if it thrives and acts in them. When the soul moves in its own way, it does not dissipate the body; for no pain arises from the soul’s movement through the body. However, perpetual pain would occur in the body if its parts were dissipated and disturbed by the movement of the soul. They would undoubtedly be dissipated if the soul were a body, since the soul itself is moved through the body by its own certain perpetual motion.

In what way will the soul be a body, which is everywhere through the body and fills and penetrates the whole from every side without any injury to the body? Furthermore, if it were a solid body, either it would not fill the whole body, and thus the whole would not live; or if it did fill it, it would break the body by penetrating it, and be broken itself, and perpetual pain would reach us. 

But if <margin>7</margin> <margin>11</margin> the soul were a fluid and slipping body, it would neither bind the body of the living being nor firmly solidify it; but it would itself need some other bond, as we said above, by whose stability it would be strengthened, ruled, and moved. We shall more willingly call that bond the soul, or rather the power of the soul. 

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, the power of the soul in the body is almost the same as the power of rennet <note>original: "coaguli." A substance used to curdle milk into cheese; Ficino uses it as a metaphor for the soul's ability to bind the "fluid" body into a solid form.</note> in milk, which solidifies from it. Or the force of a magnet in iron, which is drawn and suspended by it. Or the <term>tuning</term> <note>original: "temperatio." The balanced arrangement of parts.</note> of art in a clock, which is governed, moved, and sounds in a wonderful order. Yet the soul itself is not a power or a temperament of humors. But it is a certain substantial form: simple, indivisible, which through power and natural art tempers the <term>spirits</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were thin, vaporous substances that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note>, humors, and members.

<margin>C</margin> ### Seventh ratio. A body is not whole in many places at once.

#### Cap. x.

Neither bodies nor forms divided through bodies can be entirely present in many parts or places at once. The <term>seminal power</term> <note>original: "vis seminaria." The generative force or blueprint contained within a seed.</note> is whole in any small particle of seed. For into however many particles the seed is divided, just as many animals arise, which is most apparent in the eggs of fish. If a whole animal sprouts from any tiny drop of seed, the whole seminal power lies hidden there. But this is the instrument of the soul, serving generation. Therefore, the soul is much more whole in any particle of the seed and the body. Since the whole power of the soul is in each part, is not the vegetative power whole in any part of a plant's seed? since it produces a whole plant from any part. 

<margin>D</margin> The vegetative soul is first held in a tiny root or bud; then, as the tree grows, it pours itself through all the branches. Finally, when the branches are dried or cut off, it contracts itself back into the root. <margin>E</margin> Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Two foundational Neoplatonic philosophers whose works Ficino translated and reconciled with Christian theology.</note> believe this soul lacks quantity, as it is equally enclosed in the smallest things and fills the largest.

<margin>F</margin> ### Octava ratio. The soul is life, or the source of life.

#### Cap. xi.

We think the soul is a certain nature which is either a certain life, or has life as a companion and attendant. Since bodies obtain life through the soul, a body is necessarily divided into many parts. In one case, a body is composed of several elements. In another, an element is not gathered from other elements, but is constituted from form and matter. If we ask whether the soul is a body constructed from several elements, would each of those elements have life on its own apart from the others? Or none of them? Or do they produce life when gathered together? Or does one certain element among them possess life? If each of them has life by itself, there are as many souls there as elements. Nor is there one soul there...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VI of the Platonic Theology. Having just argued that the soul cannot be a physical body that merely fills space, he now explores why the soul cannot be a composite of physical elements or a single element, focusing on the soul's ability to govern "contraries"—opposing physical forces—which a simple body cannot do.</meta>

<page-num>52</page-num>
<header>Theology, Sixth [Book]</header>

# Sixth [Book] of Theology

<margin>a</margin>
[The soul is not] formed from many parts: for if many souls were inhabiting the same seat, and if none of those parts possessed life on its own, they would never create life through their mutual meeting. And if life were to be born from their meeting, it would certainly not be by their own power—since they themselves lack life—but rather by the power of someone ordering that meeting would that life be born. Especially since it must be admitted that even if life consists of a meeting of many things, it does not happen simply by them meeting in any old way. Rather, if they meet by a certain reason and way, life is produced in them. Thus, the soul itself will certainly be the internal orderer of that meeting, providing life in its own way to the things flowing together. But if you say that one among the many elements has life, then that part alone will be the soul itself, and there will be no need for other elements besides it for a soul to be generated.

<margin>b</margin>
Wherefore the soul is in no way to be thought of as a body constituted from several elements.

<margin>c</margin>
Nor is it a single element. Because any element is composed of matter and form. If that element lived, it would not live through its matter, since formless matter <note>Ficino uses the Aristotelian concept of "prime matter," which is pure potentiality without any qualities or life until "Form" is applied to it.</note> cannot provide life either to something else or to itself. Therefore, such a thing would live through its form.

<margin>d</margin>
The soul, therefore, would be the form. Furthermore, if the soul is a body—whether it be an element, or something similar, and whether simple or composite—it will certainly be affected in a specific way: namely, it will be hot or cold, dry or moist, light or heavy, rare or dense, fluid or solid, white, black, or the like. If it is hot, it will only heat. If it is light, it will seek the heights; and generally, whatever kind of body it is, it will act according to its own nature, and will never perform an effect opposite to its nature.

<margin>h</margin>
For the cold does not heat. However, the nature and form of any body is fixed and determined, just as its place is bounded, its time is certain, and its power is finite. Therefore, the operation of each body is determined and does not extend to contrary effects. But the soul seems to have power over any contraries whatsoever. For both in the diverse bodies of animals and in the same body, it effects many things that are mutually exclusive <note>original: "repugnantia" – here meaning contradictory or opposing forces.</note>. It stops, moves, contracts, extends, thins, thickens, sharpens, blunts, opens, closes, melts, and solidifies. It imparts contrary odors, tastes, and colors, and opposite powers and shapes to the fluids and limbs; it moves light spirits <note>In Renaissance physiology, "spirits" were subtle vapors that acted as the bridge between the soul and the physical organs.</note> downward to the feet and leads heavy fluids upward to the head. This happens against the nature of bodies. It agitates the body in every direction: upward against the weight of heavy elements, downward against the high-striving nature of light ones, sideways, and in a circuit against every faculty of the body. Since, therefore, it produces almost all effects that are contrary to each other and is so capable of opposing motions that it moves beyond the natural order of bodies, who will be so mad as to admit that the soul is either a body, or a quality of a body, or something belonging to a quality?

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>12</margin>
->Ninth reason. The body does not move itself.<-
->Chapter 12<-

<margin>3</margin>
**T**hat which is truly and primarily mobile through itself—so that it is entirely the same thing, acting as both the source and the recipient of motion—must be mobile through itself according to its whole self. This appears in all other things which are said to be such-and-such primarily and through themselves: just as that which is clear is clear throughout its whole self. What is good is entirely good. What is understood is entirely intellectual. For the essence that first pours out a quality, and first embraces and receives it—because it perfectly performs both—effects both through the whole.

<margin>K</margin>
Moreover, there must be found in nature an essence that is mobile through itself or from itself in that way; and the soul is such a thing, as we demonstrated in the previous books. But even if a body is imagined to be mobile through itself and primarily, it still could not be such a thing according to its whole self. For it would be necessary for every part of it to be moved by itself, and the parts of the parts, and the tiny particles. For if there were even one particle in the body that did not move itself, that body would not be self-moving according to its whole self. And thus it would not truly and primarily be such, but rather [the motion would come] from some other...

<sig>b 4</sig>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because bodies have fixed, singular natures (like heat only heating), whereas the soul can govern opposing physical states. He concludes that the soul must be an incorporeal form that is "self-moving" in its entirety, unlike a physical body which can only be moved in its parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VI of the Platonic Theology. Having argued that the soul cannot be a simple element or a composite of elements, he now addresses the physics of motion, arguing that a physical body—being divisible—cannot be the primary source of its own movement.</meta>

### A Book on Platonic [Theology]
A

<margin>A</margin> ...participation in such a way and by presence. Wherefore, for this [the body] to be perfectly <term>per se mobile: something that moves by its own nature or power, rather than being moved by an outside force</term> self-moving in its own right, it would have to be granted that any of its small parts are moved by themselves. These parts are divisible into infinity; thus, there would be innumerable particles that would move themselves. That which moves, acts; that which acts, exists in <term>actu: "in act" or "actuality," a state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to mere potentiality</term> actuality. There would therefore be infinite parts in actuality, each driving themselves, and infinite movers within whatever body of the world we consider. Indeed, those parts would not even belong to another body, because they would exist by their own act; rather, each would stand by itself as a whole, and there would be a certain infinite multitude of little bodies existing in actuality. But it is impossible for such a multitude to exist in nature <note>Ficino follows the Aristotelian principle that an "actual" infinity of physical things cannot exist in the natural world.</note>. Therefore, since the parts of a body cannot be infinite in actuality—indeed, they cannot truly exist as separate things at all, since they have no existence of their own but are contained under the existence of the whole composite—it follows that the parts of a body do not move themselves, nor are they forced to exist in actuality or be entirely infinite for this reason. We conclude, therefore, that a body cannot truly be 

<margin>B</margin> primarily self-moving in its own right, since this cannot belong to the whole itself if its parts are unable to achieve it by moving themselves. 

Let us proceed toward the same point by another path. When someone asserts that a body moves itself, they are compelled to confess one of four possibilities: either one part of the body is moved by another; or the whole is moved by a part; or a part is moved by the whole; or the whole is moved by the whole—that is, all parts are moved by all parts. 

If the first is affirmed—since one part is one thing and the other is another—the same thing will not be moving itself, but rather one thing will be moving another. Nor will that composite body truly move itself from this, since it is made of parts that do not move themselves, but it will have two distinct things within it, one of which moves the other. 

If you take the second branch of that division—namely, that the part moves the whole—or the third, that the whole moves the part, that composite is still not truly driving itself. For we mean the part to be one thing and the whole to be another. Furthermore, that part which moves the whole would certainly move all the parts. Therefore, in the count of the other parts, it also moves 

---

itself. Simply put, if the whole is said to move a part, it moves that one part through all the parts. Therefore, it drives only one part, in a certain way, through itself. 

I see in these two branches of that division that it cannot be said that the whole moves itself, except by virtue of that one part of it which drives itself, and not at all because of the other parts. And so, the whole will not truly be self-moving in its own right, but perhaps only that part of the whole—which would then not even be a "part" of it, 

<margin>C</margin> since it would be operating by itself. 

But if you grant the fourth option—that the whole is moved by the whole—since the whole is perhaps nothing other than all the parts together, you will be admitting that all the parts are moved by all. In this case, that composite ought not be said to move itself for any other reason than that every single part of it drives itself. Wherefore, you are always forced to retreat to the "part" if you wish to affirm that a body is self-moving. 

We condemn this primarily because that composite body will not properly be self-moving in its own right, after it has "borrowed" this from something else—namely, from its parts. For it is called self-moving only by reason of its parts. Even if it is established that the body is, in a way, all its parts at once, it nevertheless seems to borrow this kind of motion from the individual parts, just as it receives its substance from the individuals. 

I ask you to answer concerning that part (or those parts) by reason of which the whole is asserted to move itself: are those parts <term>indiuidue: indivisible; used here to describe something that cannot be cut into smaller physical pieces</term> indivisible? If they are, then surely that which moves itself is not a body, but something indivisible within the body, by whose impulse the body also appears to be carried of its own accord. 

But if they are divisible, we shall divide that part in the same way we have already cut the whole. And by the same reasoning, we will find that it can in no way be affirmed of those parts that they are moved by themselves, except by reason of the smaller particles that move them. We shall investigate the particles in the same way. Since these are distributed into infinity, we will always find new and more numerous movers, and we will never arrive at a single one, since by dividing we always have many. Nor will we ever reach the "first" movers or the "first" mover, since we divide infinitely in the same way. Nowhere...

<meta>catchword: Nowhere...</meta>

<summary>Ficino argues through a logical proof that a physical body cannot be the primary source of its own motion. Because bodies are infinitely divisible, attributing self-motion to matter leads to an impossible infinite regress of movers, suggesting the true source of motion must be an indivisible, non-physical entity (the soul).</summary>
<keywords>self-motion, infinite divisibility, actuality, Aristotle, physics of the soul, movers, parts and wholes</keywords>

Having established that the body is not self-moving in the previous section, Ficino here identifies the soul as the primary internal mover and argues that this mover must be incorporeal and self-moving by its very essence.</meta>

# Seventh Book of Theology

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, there is one within the substance of the body: and it is its first <term>motor: a "mover" or source of motion</term>. For this reason, the body has no origin of its own motion within itself, through which it could truly be asserted to move by its own power; rather, we are compelled to arrive at something indivisible. From this, the origin of all bodily agitation arises.
<margin>D</margin>
The internal agitator of the body, however, is the soul; when it is present, bodies are moved in a certain way of their own accord and into all parts. But when the soul is absent, they require an external mover. If the soul were also a body, it would itself require a mover—an internal mover, I mean—since every living thing is moved without external impulse. That innermost motor will be the soul itself, which must be moved <term>per se: by itself or through its own nature</term>, since bodies eventually appear to have the power of moving themselves through the soul. But every such thing must be reduced to some nature that is truly the agitator of itself. Thus, the soul properly moves by itself; by participating in this, other things obtain the faculty so that they move, in a certain way, by themselves.
<margin>E</margin>
This, therefore, is not a body, nor is it even a form <gloss>dispersed or scattered</gloss> within a body. <margin>C</margin> For even such a form, according to the higher reasons, is not able to move itself, being subject to the same conditions as the body, as has appeared. Here, that <gloss>sophistry or quibble</gloss> is excluded, by which some strive to show that a certain body moves by itself, saying it is so composed of matter and form—or of the four elements—that a certain other nature arises beyond the matter, form, and four elements, which is the <term>integrity of the whole: the "wholeness" of a thing that is more than the sum of its parts</term>, which moves itself; for it has this through form, that it moves, and through matter, that it is moved. Such an objection has no weight against the Platonists, both because the root through which it moves will be in one essence, and that through which it is seen to be moved will be in another. Nevertheless, one must reach some essence which is both the fountain and the receptacle of motion and of life, just as one reaches that which is the root and foundation of light and heat simultaneously. Furthermore, that nature which is the "integrity of the whole," if it is extended by quantity, will no more be able to move by itself than the bulk of the body

---

itself, as we have shown above. If, however, it is indivisible, we have already arrived—as we desired—at an incorporeal nature in which the power of agitating itself resides. Not that it acts and suffers <note>original: "agat & patiatur," referring to the philosophical distinction between the agent (actor) and the patient (one acted upon).</note> upon itself. For motion in it does not signify a transition from the agent to the patient, but a natural <term>vicissitude: a regular change or succession of states</term> of that essence, by which it varies the turns of its affections, and thus runs through itself without another agitating it; just as fire is hot by itself, with no other thing heating it, nor one part of itself pouring heat into another. Therefore, since the origin of a living creature is not from the body—which is by its nature lazy <note>In this context, "lazy" (piger) refers to the Aristotelian idea that matter is inert and lacks its own initiative.</note>—nor from the composite alone—in which there will be no power of moving if it is composed of such parts in which there is no power for motion—it is necessarily from the soul. If the soul grants the power of migrating from leisure into act to the animal, it does so much more to itself before it grants it. For whatever good or vital act is translated from a cause into an effect is first unfolded in the cause. For thus heat is hot and boils within itself before it heats other matter; and animated bodies swell with seeds and conceive offspring within themselves before they bring forth young. Therefore, while the soul unfolds the vital progression from <term>potentia: potentiality or the capacity to be something</term> into <term>actu: actuality or the state of being active</term> within itself, it is said to be moved by itself.
<margin>F</margin>
The Platonists properly name motion in the soul "action," since it is in its own fountain, and it fosters and agitates the body. But in the body, they name motion "passion" <gloss>suffering or being acted upon</gloss>. And since it is necessary for the corporeal mass and the universe to be moved by another, they conclude that the motion of the entire body is a "passion" resulting from the motion of the higher soul, as if from a certain action of those [souls]. And just as in any genus they always reduce imperfect things to perfect ones, so they refer the imperfect motion of the body to the motion of the soul as the perfect form in that genus of motion.
<margin>G</margin>
Furthermore, when it is asked by what motion the soul is chiefly moved, they respond: not by a corporeal one, for it is incorporeal; not by an imaginable one, for it lacks shape. Not by a cognitive one—for it would be ignorant of itself <note>Ficino likely means that discursive, step-by-step reasoning is not the primary motion, as that implies a lack of immediate self-knowledge.</note>—but by a motion according to its vital essence. For just as the act of essence is "to be," and the act of the intellect itself is...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is the "primary motor" of the body, possessing an inherent, incorporeal power of self-motion that distinguishes it from inert physical matter. He defines the soul's movement as "action" (internal vitality) and the body's movement as "passion" (being acted upon).</summary>

# Platonic Book
### On the Immortality of the Soul

<margin>A</margin> Just as understanding is an act of the intellect, so living is the act of life. For the soul does not possess life as something added from the outside, but from within itself. To use the words of the Platonists: the soul is life generating and producing itself. Indeed, all life is motion. Therefore, if everything that lives is moved, and even that which lives by itself is moved by itself, then that which lives always is also always moved—not in an <term>intellectual way: referring to pure thought</term>, but in a <term>vital way: referring to the lived experience and movement of the soul</term>. For this reason, it is always moved, but not always in the same manner. For while the mind exists in a state of potentiality, life exists in a state of <term>actuality: the state of being active or fully realized</term>. Finally, its essence always lives, and it exercises an internal, perpetual motion, since essential life is always mobile. However, the powers and acts that happen concerning both life and the intellect can sometimes be interrupted or go astray. But let us return to where we digressed.

<margin>B</margin> This same conclusion is persuaded by the third following reason, involving all these types of motion: **Alteration**, **Generation**, **Corruption** <note>original: 'corruptio'; in this context, the breaking down or ceasing to be of a thing</note>, **Increase**, **Decrease**, **Condensation**, **Rarefaction**, and **Progression** <note>these are the traditional Aristotelian categories of change</note>. 

Does a body move itself according to *alteration*? Not at all. If it ought to heat itself, it must already possess the heat which it would grant to itself. Yet, it must also *not* have that heat if it is only now about to receive it. For no one receives what they already possess. Therefore, to heat something, it is already hot; but to be in the process of becoming hot, it is not yet hot. It would be a ridiculous statement to say something has a quality and does not have it at the same time. Unless, perhaps, someone says that water has a certain "coldness" by its <term>virtue: an inherent power or capacity</term> which it retains even after it has been heated by a fire; through this power, once removed from the fire, it returns to a state of actual coldness. 

To this, the Platonists will respond: either that water is made cold by external elements, or, if its quality—which leans somewhat toward an incorporeal nature—buds forth from that internal "productive quality," then that power is much closer to an incorporeal nature. It follows that a power of this kind must spring from a certain substance that exists as entirely incorporeal. Such a substance will be the principle of motion 

---

<margin>C</margin> within the body. Therefore, no body moves itself by *alteration*. But neither does it *generate* itself. Whoever generates something gives "being" through that generation. Therefore, the creator already possesses the "being" which it grants to the thing created. But that which is being generated receives its "being" from elsewhere, as it does not yet possess it. Nothing, therefore, can give "being" to itself. For it would have to possess it and not possess it at the same time. And since the creator must precede the created, if something were the creator of its own limited nature, it would be both prior to and posterior to itself at the same time—which, in a finite nature, no one could imagine. 

Furthermore, a body does not *corrupt* <note>destroy or dissolve</note> itself. Since every thing generates its offspring from its own nature, and therefore produces something compatible with itself rather than contrary, it follows that the natural instinct of every thing—which is a kind of "offspring" of its essence—cannot rise up against its own essence and being. Therefore, no thing leads itself to "non-being" by its own instinct, nor by its own power, nor by the power of any other part of itself. On the contrary, since the effort of every thing is directed toward preserving itself, it will not turn toward its opposite. 

Neither does a body *increase* or *decrease* itself. <margin>D</margin> For these things cannot happen without *alteration*, and even a kind of *generation* and *corruption*. For we grow and shrink through the alteration of qualities. While we grow, new parts of the body are generated within us. While we shrink, the old parts are corrupted. If, therefore, increase and decrease require alteration, generation, and corruption, then a body—which cannot move itself through alteration, generation, or corruption—cannot move itself by increasing or decreasing. Nor does it *condense* or *rarefy* itself, since these also do not happen without alteration. 

Someone might say: at least a body changes its *place* by itself, through traveling or turning in a circle. <margin>E</margin> This also is impossible to claim. If it is powerless regarding those superior motions which are internal, it will be much more powerless regarding external ones. I call "external motions" the circuit and the transit, which tend toward boundaries further removed than internal motions. Therefore, if a body is not strong enough to move itself toward its own internal limits, in what way can it move toward 

<summary>Ficino argues that physical bodies are incapable of self-motion because any change (heating, growing, or being born) would require the body to already possess a quality it is currently lacking. He concludes that all physical motion must originate from an incorporeal substance, which is the soul.</summary>
