<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section concerning the nature of the soul. While the previous page discussed the soul as the source of life, Ficino now moves into a specific proof involving the different types of motion. He transitions from physical mechanics to the 'intellectual motions' of the soul, arguing that because the soul moves itself in ways a body cannot, it must be incorporeal.</meta>

-># Theology Book Six<-

...us as strangers. <note>original: "nos alienos"; this completes a sentence from the preceding page regarding the soul's relationship to the body.</note> Therefore, let us now conclude in this way. No other motions appear in bodies besides those eight already numbered. <note>These eight motions (generation, corruption, increase, decrease, alteration, condensation, rarefaction, and progression) were a standard part of Aristotelian physics.</note> They do not act through any of those by themselves. Therefore, in no way are bodies moved by themselves.

<margin>§</margin>
It is moved then, as is evident to everyone, by a certain nature agitated from within, and without external impulses. 

<margin>g</margin>
<margin>§</margin>
No one would deny that this is the Platonic soul, which can be moved by itself because within it certain other motions of a different nature are found, besides those eight. As far as the part that governs the body is concerned, there is found in the soul a temporal succession of <term>seeds: the "rationes seminales" or formative principles that guide biological growth</term> emerging in it at different times to generate bodily things. As for the part of the soul concerned with cognition, there is within it a temporal <term>discursive movement: the step-by-step process of reasoning from one idea to the next</term> from one thought and affection to another. From the final effects of nature, there is a space of ascent through middle causes to the principles above. And conversely, from the supernal principles through middle causes, a descent to the final effects. These discursive movements are certain motions, and proper to the nature of the mind, as we have declared elsewhere. For they do not suit God or the angels, who possess and see all things simultaneously. <note>Ficino follows the tradition that divine beings see all truth at once, whereas humans must "move" through logic to reach it.</note> Nor do they belong to bodies, which do nothing by themselves, nor to bodily forms, since they do not move incorporeal things. Indeed, discursive movements of this kind, leading us to divine things, raise us above the nature of the body. But neither a body nor anything else is able to be carried above its own nature by itself. Therefore, such revolutions, which are alien to bodies but are nonetheless in the soul, remain as proof that the soul cannot be a body or a form divided in the body. Especially since the soul is agitated according to those motions through itself—that is, through its own nature and power. Therefore, it is moved by itself, which a body cannot do.

<margin>§</margin>
Furthermore, there appear in the soul the <term>archetypes: the original patterns or mental blueprints</term> of bodily motions. Of **Generation**, when it clings to divine things; of **Corruption** <note>original: "corruptionis"; here meaning the dissolution of a state or passing away</note>, when it clings to mortal things; of **Increase**, when it remembers; of **Decrease**, when it forgets; of **Alteration**, when it varies its states of affection; of **Condensation**, insofar as it suddenly gazes upon something or collects itself; of **Rarefaction**, insofar as it wanders or is distracted by many things. 

<margin>§</margin>
Of **Linear progression**, when it first touches external things. Of **Circular motion**, however, when it either resolves the effect into the cause within the things themselves and deduces the effect from the cause, or is reflected back upon itself to consider itself.

<margin>§</margin>
It seems to move in a straight line again when it leans toward the body and the senses. In an oblique line, when it reflects the angel back into itself. In a circle, when it moves toward God, its beginning and its end. Upward toward universals; downward toward particulars. Also to the right and the left—namely, into the opposite <term>differences of a genus: the specific traits that distinguish species within a category</term>. Finally, forward and backward, when it turns toward natural causes or effects. 

<margin>h</margin>
Who would deny that the soul is the source of motions, since within it are its own motions and the archetypes of bodily motions? In these, contrary to the nature of the body, the soul generates itself in a certain way, or (as I might say) as if it corrupts, increases, and diminishes itself, and transfers the rest. Rightly, therefore, through its presence, living bodies acquire this faculty so that they may alter, nourish, and increase themselves, while generating something from themselves within themselves. And again, so that they may walk by themselves, wherever they judge they must go. None of these things are accomplished by those who do not live, as if spontaneous motion were proper to life.

### The Tenth Reason. The soul does not grow according to the increase of this body. Chapter 13.

<margin>§</margin>
**I**f you say the soul is a body: it is certainly this body which you see as solid. So that it may live as a whole, the soul itself would have to be a thin and agile body, as the speed of the mind indicates. Therefore, if you divide the body of an animal into members—just as all parts of a body are themselves bodies—so those tiny bodies that remain in the severed members would be souls. Especially since the soul is whole in every part, so that it may love different things. Therefore, the arms and legs separated from the body would live, move, and feel for a time. And the soul, which remains in the rest of the body—which often lives for ten years after the arms and legs have been amputated—will be much smaller than it was before; therefore it will be small-souled, dull, and forgetful. Indeed, let us argue thus: if the soul is a body, it is evident that it completely equals the magnitude and quantity of this body and grows... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as it moves to the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is the source of all motion because it contains the mental archetypes of physical movements (like growth or walking) and performs "discursive" intellectual movements that a physical body cannot. He concludes by beginning a rebuttal against the idea that the soul is a material substance that grows and shrinks with the physical body.</summary>

He argues that if the soul were material, it would change and flow away as the body does, making memory and identity impossible.</meta>

<note>original: "te ipso crescet:decrescere decrescet"</note> [The soul] will grow as you grow, and as you decrease, it will decrease. Within a
vast body, it would be more magnificent and a more divine
soul. And in the same man: when
 the body matures, the soul would also mature; it would be
necessary that it matures by the addition of a body
similar to itself. Does nourishment of this kind

<margin>C</margin> into the nature of that which is being nourished.
Therefore, many souls would perish daily from nature

fleeing away. From where would it compel new souls
to always join it, through which the soul
might be continually renewed? But in what way
does a "recent" soul agree with the previous one?
How, if something is continuously flowing out from

just as we see happening in the flesh—does the

opinion, the same knowledge, and the perpetual memory

<margin>D</margin> that same soul which had received and judged them?
In what way does it preserve them if it is not itself preserved? By what
reason, if the soul does not stand still, will images and knowledge stand still?
Nor should anyone say that the soul stands for a long time if it
were a body. For what body under heaven can remain

so swiftly? Likewise, if any body is of such a kind that
it remains for a while, nevertheless subtle and

diffused through the internal organs, it might easily vivify all things. Therefore,
bones and nerves would last longer than the soul;
indeed, even flesh, which nevertheless falls away in a short time,

---

and is renewed daily. Moreover, the soul would be
like some state that is utterly unstable and
vanishing at every single moment. Wherefore, not even
for a single day would it preserve the knowledge of things and
images. It would also suffer the same thing if the soul
were a <term>quality: an accidental property rather than a fundamental substance</term>, or some <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</term> of the humors and
members. For quality and humor flow in the same way.
And in the act of nutrition itself, the soul would flow out and flow back
just like the body; nor would the living being consist more in its form
than in its own matter. Neither would the immeasurable unity
of the living thing be preserved, nor the continuous
motion of nourishment or growth.
Nor would there be in the living thing any power to order
these motions, which would so stand over itself that it
imposes both the order of proceeding and the limit

or increased. For it is necessary that that ruler
consist in himself, he who orders and halts moving things.
Perhaps someone will object: "we see in our body
the same figure remaining for a very long time,
although the flesh falls away and flows back.
Similarly, what prevents the same
images of known things from remaining in the soul,
even though the substance of the soul changes from old to new?"
We respond: neither does the exact same figure remain,
nor is it entirely the same; rather, the former figure frequently
departs as the flesh departs, and in the recent flesh, a new figure,
in a certain way similar to the former, is remade.
And that is done by a certain very stable <term>artisan: the "faber" or internal maker, identifying the soul as the active formative power</term>
building from within; who, since he
always remains the same and has in himself the <term>rational principles: the "rationes," or blueprint-like patterns</term>
and seeds for disposing the members of a familiar body,
is able—while new humors flow in daily—
to hand down a complexion similar to the previous ones,
and to provide the recent flesh with a figure similar to the old.
It is not otherwise than a face which, looking down
upon a river from above, paints the flowing waves
and the new ones at every moment with new images
of itself, so that the same face seems to persist
in the various waters. But that innermost
builder of the body and the stable thing is the
soul. If it were to flow itself, certainly it would
neither carry similar representations and figures
of the body for long, nor would the soul
retain similar knowledges. Because then it would
neither hold them by its own power, nor would
anyone be present to it who either stabilizes
them in the soul or makes them similar to the previous ones.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a material body or a byproduct of physical humors because it maintains a stable identity, memory, and knowledge while the physical body constantly changes. He famously compares the soul's formative power over the body to a face reflected in a flowing river.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Book VI to the beginning of Book VII of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. Having previously argued that the soul cannot be a mere "complexion" or mixture of physical parts, Ficino concludes those arguments and begins a new section focusing on the soul’s power of perception to prove its immaterial nature.</meta>

...would generate others. For it must not be said that when a soul possessing the image of a thing flows out, it insinuates that same image into the soul flowing in. This is because no quality can pass into a new subject from an old one. Nor does that vanishing, prior soul figure another image, or even a similar one, in the incoming soul. To "figure" or shape something, being a perfected action, requires a perfected agent. But while that soul is perishing, it is failing; it cannot then bring a new soul to perfection. Furthermore, a new soul cannot form itself, especially at the very moment it is born, because it is then still imperfect. Therefore, in no way can the soul hold the images and knowledge of things it once knew in its memory if it flows out and in gradually, like the body and its physical qualities.

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence, on the Platonic Theology regarding the immortality of souls, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de’ Medici. Book Seven.

### The soul is not a body, nor a form divided within the body, nor some point of such a form; but it is a form that is whole in every part of the body, as is shown through the power of sensing. First argument. A body does not receive images suitable for sensing. Chapter 1.

<margin>B</margin>
**I** do not know how it happened that in the previous argument we fell into the second part of this discussion, in which we are about to prove our proposition <note>The proposition being the immortality and immateriality of the soul.</note> through the power of sensing. Let us therefore proceed further in this way. If a body ever receives anything, it receives it in a bodily manner; that is, the parts of the thing are received in its own parts. Nor can it receive a thing larger than itself, just as wax receiving a shape from a seal never accepts a shape larger than the wax itself. If the wax had the sense to judge the magnitude of the shape, it would clearly judge it to be only as large as itself. Nor can it receive another shape in turn unless it either loses the first or confuses both within itself so that they can hardly be distinguished from one another. 

In the same way, if the soul were a body, it would receive the images of bodies through the eye in a bodily manner, such that the image of Plato in the eye of Socrates <margin>C</margin> would be no larger than Socrates' eye. Thus, Socrates' soul would think Plato to be no larger than his own eye—or certainly no larger than the brain into which the image is transferred from the eye. Finally, he would think Plato no larger than the magnitude of the Socratic body. For the soul of Socrates, if it is a body, is not larger than its own body. Therefore, if it receives the whole image of Plato into itself, it receives an image no larger than itself. For this reason, it would never think anything to exist that is larger than the Socratic body. 

Furthermore, when the soul receives the images of Xenophon, Alcibiades, and Phaedrus <note>Ficino uses these names of famous students of Socrates to illustrate how the mind holds multiple distinct ideas at once.</note>, it would then either lose the image of Plato or would thereafter have them all so confused that it could not distinguish one from the other. You may also conclude this: the soul is either a solid body or a fluid one. If it is solid, it is hardly shaped by other bodies, and thus its teachability and sharpness perish. Once one shape of one thing is received, it either does not receive another, or if it receives others one after another, they all become obscured by each other. If it is a fluid body, it holds no shapes and has no memory at all. 

Moreover, is it not clear that the same thing looks small in a tiny mirror and larger in a larger one? If you look at your own face in my pupil, then in a mirror, you will pronounce it tiny in the first and huge in the second. In these cases, bodies are judged as larger or smaller according to the size or smallness of the mirrors themselves. In the human soul, the images of almost all bodies shine forth, through which the soul judges how large those bodies are. There is no body so vast, so immense, that the soul cannot either gaze upon it or conceive <margin>D</margin> of it, and it can always conceive of another body even larger than the one imagined. From this it appears that there is no prescribed limit to the soul's magnitude...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino begins Book VII by arguing that the soul cannot be a physical body because, unlike physical objects like wax or mirrors, the soul can perceive and imagine things far larger than itself and maintain distinct memories without confusion.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, perception, immateriality, Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Socratic dialogue, memory, cognition</keywords>

--- Page 166 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book VII, Chapter 1, where he explores how the soul perceives physical reality. He has just begun arguing that the soul cannot be a physical body because it would then be limited by physical dimensions, which would prevent it from perceiving the vastness of the universe.</meta>

...limit of magnitude: both regarding those things it is meant to encompass, and regarding the soul's own substance. For if the soul had its own physical magnitude, it would primarily be as large as the magnitude of its own body. Consequently, in such a tiny <term>animal mirror</term><note>Ficino uses "animali speculo" to refer to the living, physical organs of perception, like the eye or brain, which act as "mirrors" for the world.</note> things so varied, so clear, and so immense could not shine forth, since things usually appear larger or smaller according to the different sizes of mirrors. 

However, we should not think that the spiritual images of colors are either created by bodies or merely reflected in mirrors and the brain. For they are nothing other than the splendors of light striking bodies. Although this visible light shines out in bodies, it is nevertheless created and preserved by the invisible light of celestial souls. This light overflows from an immense abundance, escapes outward, and becomes visible. It is not, however, attached to any physical bodies. Nevertheless, it can be joined to the light of our own <term>spirit</term><note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "spirit" (spiritus) is a fine, vaporous substance that connects the immaterial soul to the physical body.</note>, which depends on our soul, and offer its splendors to it. 

Furthermore, the meanings of voices reaching our hearing—which are themselves also spiritual—are neither created by the body nor fixed in the body. Instead, they are transmitted from soul to soul and are created and preserved by the power of souls. 

But let us briefly conclude the previous discussion with this division: If the soul were something corporeal, either the images of bodies would touch its surface, like a mirror, or their qualities would penetrate into the deep substance of the soul, like flavors and odors into water. If the first were to happen, we might perhaps perceive bodies while they are present, but we would not be able to think about them when they are absent, for we would not preserve the images. If the second were to happen, the senses would always function gradually and only through the <term>passion</term><note>In this context, "passion" (passio) refers to a physical change or "suffering" an effect from an external stimulus.</note> of the body; similarly, memory and qualities would be confused with one another without any power of discernment.

### Second reason. The five senses must be led to one center. Chapter 2.

---

<margin>B</margin>
**S**ight reaches colors, but not voices. Hearing reaches only voices. Smell reaches odor, and so on. The mind compares color, voice, and odor with one another, or judges that a color is one thing and voices are another, and judges other things similarly. That power through which the mind thus judges and knows both colors and voices—and other things which it compares to one another—is a single power. For how could it say that a color is something other than a voice unless it knew both at the same time? Is this power sight? Not at all; for sight does not recognize voices. Similarly, it is not hearing, which is ignorant of colors, nor is it any other of the five senses at all. For each of them reports only one specific thing and is not able to compare several things together. 

That is certainly a single internal power of the soul, to which, as if to a center, various reports are brought from all sides by the instruments of the five senses arranged around it. That single power judges all the objects and operations of those five senses. 

And do not say that there are two or more internal powers of the soul through which the soul makes that comparison. Let there be a pair of powers if you wish. Answer me then: whenever the soul is about to compare a color to a voice, does it perceive both—namely, both the color and the voice—through both powers, or does it perceive one through one and the other through the other? If each power perceives both, what need is there for a pair of powers, when one is sufficient for the work of comparison and one does as much as both? Nature does not fail in necessary things, <margin>B</margin> nor does it abound in superfluous ones. But if it knows only one through one power, it will not compare both to each other through either power. Nevertheless, it does compare them through some power. There is, therefore, some other power besides those two previously imagined ones, through which the soul compares those many things to each other. 

Is that one power indivisible? Or is it divided into several parts like a body? Suppose that power is like some indivisible point, marked by <gloss>voice</gloss>, or a certain line drawn from <gloss>a.</gloss> to <gloss>b.</gloss>? If you say that it is a line from <gloss>a.</gloss> to <gloss>b.</gloss> such as <gloss>a.b.</gloss>, I will ask you in this manner: whenever the soul is about to compare a color to a voice through a line of this kind, it is certain that both touch that line at its endpoints.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul must be immaterial because it can perceive immense and varied concepts that a physical organ could not contain, and concludes that a single, indivisible internal power (the "common sense") must exist to synthesize data from the five distinct senses.</summary>

**T**herefore, does color only reach the "head" or start of the line (point *a*) and not arrive at point *b*? And does the voice only touch the end of the line (point *b*) and not pass over to *a*? Or rather, do both color and voice come to both points simultaneously—that is, to both *a* and *b*? If you grant the first option—that only one reaches one end of the line and the other reaches the other—then truly those two endpoints would be two distinct powers, each of which would recognize what is its own but remain ignorant of the other. Therefore, the mind would not be able to compare the two through either power. But if you grant the second—that both meet at both ends so that the power at each end perceives both—then one of them is sufficient. The other is redundant, since two powers do nothing more than one. In fact, these two powers would be entirely indivisible. Thus, we are forced to confess that this single power of the soul, which judges through many channels, is not divisible into parts. Therefore, that power which is the <term>master of the senses</term><note>Ficino refers here to the "Common Sense" (sensus communis), a faculty theorized by Aristotle to reside in the soul, which coordinates and compares the data from the five individual senses.</note> is neither a body nor a quality spread through a body. If the power of the soul is such, what prevents the soul itself from being so? Unless perhaps the parts of a substance could be more noble in power than the substance itself.

# Third Reason: The narrower the sense, the more perceptive it is.
<margin>Chapter 3</margin>

<margin>C</margin>
**S**urely it is necessary for the visible image of a body to be collected into something indivisible. This occurs even in the pupil of the eye itself. Otherwise, we could not discern massive bodies and even the sky itself through such a tiny pupil. If this <margin>D</margin> pertains to the eye—that to see more sharply, there is no need for a larger size—then indeed a greater quantity of matter is not required. In fact, very small eyes often look more keenly than the largest ones, such as the eyes of an eagle compared to those of an ox; in the latter, the great size of the sight not only fails to help but actually hinders. If, I say, the external sight does not require size to perceive, what shall we say of that interior sight and the <term>common sense</term>? Since it is more excellent and sharper than the individual senses, it ought to be even more self-sufficient; it will be more sufficient if it requires no physical quantity of the body. Finally, the substance of the soul itself will be the foundation of the senses, more sufficient than any individual sense, if it does not lack for quantity.

<margin>E</margin>
**W**ho would say that the soul requires the dimensions of physical quantity? For the size of the body neither contributes to the soul’s gifts, nor would it hinder them if size were a necessary factor. If size were helpful, a bee would not be more skillful than a sheep; a fox would not be craftier than a pig; a monkey would not be more clever than a donkey or bolder than an ox. If size were necessarily harmful, an elephant would not be wiser than a horse, nor would a <note>original: "Lenis"</note> gentle creature be more sagacious than a lamb. But if physical quantity is of no value to these powers of the soul that deal with the size of bodies, it must be thought to be worth much less to that power of the soul which transcends the quantity of bodies entirely—namely, to <term>Reason</term><note>Latin: "ratio". For Ficino, Reason is the higher faculty that deals with universal truths and abstract concepts, rather than just physical sensations.</note>, which we will discuss in its proper place.

# Fourth Reason: If the sense is divisible, the sensible image within it will be divided.
<margin>Chapter 4</margin>

<margin>F</margin>
**L**et it be, if you wish, that that innermost sight is stretched out within a physical mass; attend to what follows from this. When it receives an external color, it conceives it as an image and receives it in its own way—which would be a physical way. An image of this kind would be divided through the parts of this sight: one part of the sight would look at one part of the color, and another part at another. There would be nothing within us that could grasp the visible color as a whole. Yet it is necessary for a single comprehension of a single thing to be made by a single perceiver. And if you say that the perceiver itself is a certain form of the whole composite, common to all the parts, we will then ask whether it is divisible—whereupon the same question returns—or indivisible, in which case we place the power of comprehension in an indivisible force. It is necessary, therefore, for the sense to be devoid of physical magnitude. This is especially true because if the sense were large, it would not fit a small part of an object, nor would the whole sense feel it, but rather only that part of the sense which is equal to the small part of the object. If the sense were small, it would not contain large things; if it were middle-sized, it would not match the extremes. But if you wish to divide the sensible color along with the sense, in what way will you distribute it? Will you fit equal to equal? But you cannot. For the sense is not equal in size to every object being felt. Into how many parts will you distribute both? Into certain parts, finite in number, and naturally very small? But if...

He points out that physical size does not correlate with intelligence or sensory sharpness in animals, further suggesting that the soul is independent of bodily magnitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, specifically Book VII. Ficino is in the midst of a logical proof regarding the nature of the soul. Having previously argued that the "Common Sense" cannot be physical, he now addresses the absurdity of viewing the senses as divisible, mathematical entities, and begins Chapter 5 on the soul's omnipresence within the body.</meta>

...you will not find a single comprehension of a single thing. But rather, in the manner of mathematicians, I think you have partitioned it into all the parts they possess. You will therefore cut both the sight and the color into infinite particles, and each individual part of the sight will perceive individual portions of the color. Thus, there will be innumerable "sights" there. Innumerable colors seen. Innumerable visions. And so, a single color could never strike the sight without an infinite number of sights seeing infinite colors infinitely at that same moment. This cannot even be imagined. 

Perhaps to avoid these monstrosities, we might suggest that the whole of that sight perceives, while its parts do not. But this is also reckless. For in what way will things that lack sensation generate a sensing substance? In no way. Therefore, those parts will not perceive, nor will those devoid of sensation constitute the sensation itself. Or shall we say that the individual parts of the sight perceive, but through the same single and complete vision of the whole sight—and that they perceive the whole <term>species</term><note>In Renaissance philosophy, a "species" is not a biological category, but a formal image or "likeness" of an object that travels through the air to the eye to allow for perception.</note> as well as the parts along with the whole? No. First, because the species is not what is seen; rather, the color itself is seen through the species. Second, because an operation that results from the gathering of distinct parts also results from the gathering of moments in time, and is completed gradually. Sensation, however, happens suddenly, which signifies that the power of sensing is indivisible. 

Finally, if each part of the sight is sufficient by itself for seeing, what need is there for many parts? If it is not sufficient, does a sensing thing arise from a non-sensing thing? Unless perhaps those parts are gathered into one by some higher sensing power. But that would be the soul rather than the sense. Therefore, we will never escape "delirious" responses as long as we affirm that the sense is divisible. Let the sense, then, be impartible. And let the soul be such as well—the fountain and subject of this indivisible power.

### Quinta ratio . Anima sentit ubiq tota. Cap.v.
### Fifth Reason: The Soul senses as a whole everywhere. Chapter 5.

<margin>pointing hand symbol</margin>
**A**re you unaware that a part of any body cannot be equal to the whole? And therefore, a form of such a kind that it is extended through different parts of the body is unable to exist as a whole in any part of the body; otherwise, the part would be equal to the whole. I admit these things. What then? Surely the soul is present as a whole to any part of the body, because the whole feels the <term>passion</term><note>Here, "passion" refers to a "passive experience" or an impression made upon the body, such as pain or touch.</note> of any bodily particle. For if the foot should feel pain by some accidental injury, immediately the eye is turned there; the hand is moved instantly. The mouth cries out and the other members do almost the same. This certainly would never happen unless that which belongs to the soul, which is in all parts of the body, also felt in the foot. 

Furthermore, the soul could not feel what has happened there if it were absent. Nor should we believe that this happens by some "messenger"—as if the event occurs without the reporter themselves feeling it—because that which does not feel cannot report. Nor can a suffering that occurs through the mere continuation of physical mass always reach the other parts of the soul located elsewhere, for pain does not always occur everywhere. But the soul feels as a whole that which occurs in a tiny part of the foot, and it feels it only there where it happens. Therefore, the whole is present to each individual part at once, since the whole feels at once in each part. 

<margin>B</margin>
However, in the case of physical forms spread through the body—take "whiteness," for example—the same thing happens to them as happens to the body: namely, that the suffering of one part does not necessarily change all the other parts. For what prevents one part of the body and its whiteness from being stained or darkened while the other parts remain unpolluted? But nothing happens in even the smallest particle of a living creature without it immediately pertaining to the whole soul. 

Our [Saint] Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a primary authority for Ficino in blending Christian theology with Platonic philosophy.</note> confirms this Platonic mystery thus: "The soul is extended through the whole body which it animates, not by local diffusion, but by a certain <term>vital intention</term><note>Latin: *vitali intensione*. This means the soul is present through its life-giving power and attention, rather than filling the body like a liquid fills a vessel.</note>. For it is present as a whole through all the particles at once. It is not smaller in smaller parts, nor larger in larger parts; but in some places it is more relaxed, and in all it is the whole, and in each individual part it is the whole. For otherwise, it would not feel whatever happens in the body as a whole, even if the event does not happen in the whole body. For when some single thing is touched in the flesh with a tiny point, although that spot is not only not the whole body but is scarcely seen in the body, it is nevertheless not hidden from the whole soul. Nor does that which is felt run through all the parts of the body; rather, it is felt only there..."

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that the soul and its senses must be indivisible because perception happens instantaneously rather than in mathematical increments. He concludes that the soul exists entirely within every part of the body simultaneously, citing St. Augustine to support the idea of "vital intention" over physical extension.</summary>

it is felt where it is. How then does the sensation reach the whole soul immediately, if the soul is not present in the whole body? Nor does it abandon the other parts to be entirely present in that one spot; for those other parts remain alive because of the soul’s presence, even when no such sensation occurs there. But if two sensations were to happen at the same time in different places, both would equally be known to the whole soul. Thus says Aurelius <note>Aurelius Augustine (354–430 AD). Ficino frequently draws on Augustine’s *De Quantitate Animae* (On the Magnitude of the Soul) for these specific arguments.</note>. 

But perhaps you will say that the soul is indeed stretched out through the entire body in such a way that one part of it is in the foot, another in the leg, another in the thigh, the chest, the neck, and the highest part in the brain—which you might consider the <term>principal seat of judgment</term><note>The "iudicium principale" or "hegemonikon," a concept often associated with the Stoics, referring to the commanding part of the soul.</note>. In this view, a pain in the foot is not judged by the power of the soul sitting in the brain because that power is also present in the foot, but because one part of the soul, in a kind of succession, announces the suffering of the foot to the next part, all the way up to the brain. 

Surely you will not deny that these "lower parts" of the soul feel, since it clearly appears that suffering is perceived in those limbs. For if the suffering of the foot must be reported to the brain, it is reported either because the intermediate limbs suffer step-by-step, or because, even if they do not suffer, they nevertheless feel the pain of the foot and report it to the brain. Certainly, the whole body does not always suffer equally, nor is the agony in the intermediate limbs the same as that in the foot; rather, there is a certain troublesome "perception" of that agony. Therefore, in all the parts, there is a certain trouble and a sense. 

Notice what follows from this: the part of the soul in the foot would feel the agony of the foot; the part in the leg would feel the trouble not of the foot, but of the leg. For it feels only where it is, and it feels only the <term>passion</term><note>From the Latin "passio," meaning an experience or something acted upon the body, often translated as "suffering" or "affection."</note> that runs into it. Similarly, the part in the knee would only perceive the suffering present to itself, and so on for the rest. After all these, that judiciary power of the brain would only notice the trouble present to itself. The parts of the soul from the foot to the brain—just like the parts of the body—are almost innumerable, if the soul itself is bodily. Therefore, when a foot is struck against a stone, there would not be one single and sudden act of sensing, but many gradual acts; and almost innumerable pains would occur just as there are innumerable perceptions. Finally, after all these parts—which is an absurdity—that part in which the principal sense resides would feel. It would feel not the suffering of the foot, but only its own.

---

Nor would it ever judge where the injury is located or where help is needed. Nor would the limbs of the body be turned toward the foot by the soul's command. To avoid these absurdities, one must confess that the entire judiciary power of the soul, together with the entire substance of the soul itself, is present to each individual limb. Thus, whatever happens anywhere, the whole soul immediately perceives it without a messenger; the whole soul suffers with itself and brings all the powers of the soul and all the parts of the body together by a sudden command to provide a remedy for the injured part. 

And so, whatever and however much of the soul is in any limbs, it is not absent from any other limb; for in any part, any power can be moved toward any other. A body and the form that supports it <note>Ficino refers here to "form" in the Aristotelian sense—the organizing principle of a physical thing.</note>, like a geometric point, are not the sort of things that can be in many places at once as a whole, nor can they suffer and act together with themselves in their own parts without delay. Therefore, the soul is far different from these. 

<margin>D</margin> Let it not disturb us that there are many animals <margin>E</margin> whose bodies, when cut, have pieces that both move and feel. It is as if the soul were as long as the body, and so, when the body is cut into bodies, the soul also seems to be cut into souls. <margin>F</margin> For the soul is not divided first, but rather it departs as soon as that specific composition of the body to which it was assigned is dissolved. However, new souls are suddenly created from the "Life of the World" <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, a central Neoplatonic concept: a universal spirit that animates the entire cosmos.</note> within those fragments that are still fit to receive a soul. For the nature of those fragments is the same as the nature of the whole. And because such souls <note>Meaning the souls of simple creatures like worms or insects.</note> are so lowly that they have very few powers and operations, they require very few instruments. Thus, the remaining body suffices for them, even if it is not equipped with various complex organs. This does not suffice for more perfect souls <note>Such as the human soul.</note>, which for this reason live in every individual limb. 

If a piece of wood is cut at a point, even though this point is indivisible, it nonetheless perishes, and two new points appear at the ends of the two fragments. Or, if you break a mirror in which the image of your face was appearing, the image is not cut first; rather, it vanishes, and two images are recreated by you in the two mirrors instead of one. <margin>G</margin> If this name "Lucifer"—in which the voice holds the place of the body and the meaning holds the place of the soul—were divided into two...

What then <margin>B</margin> prevents reptiles from having an indivisible soul according to the Platonists, even though their divided members continue to live? <note>Ficino is arguing that just as a word's meaning remains "whole" even if the letters are split, the soul’s essence remains whole even if a creature like a worm is cut in two and the parts continue to move.</note>

### Sixth Argument: The Soul Does Not Necessarily Suffer While Perceiving. Chapter 6.

<margin>C</margin> The soul itself—as true philosophy teaches—since it is most pure, is joined to this thick and earthly body (which is far distant from its nature) only through a certain very thin and very bright little body, which we call the <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine and philosophy, the "spirit" was a subtle, vaporous substance—halfway between matter and soul—produced by the heat of the heart to carry life and sensation through the nerves.</note>. This spirit is generated by the heat of the heart, diffused from the thinnest part of the blood, and from there spread through the entire body. The soul, easily insinuating itself into this spirit which is most akin to it, first pours itself through this whole spirit, and then, by this medium, through the body in its entirety. It first grants life and motion to this spirit, making it vital, and through it, the soul governs and moves the body. Whatever flows from the body into this spirit, the soul—being constantly present to the spirit—perceives immediately. This perception we call "sense." Then, the soul notices and judges this perception. This "noticing" we define as the <term>imagination</term> <note>Original: *phantasia*. This is the faculty that translates raw sensory data into a mental image that the mind can then judge.</note>.

What is the point of this? When a doctor cuts the outermost skin of the body, the flesh is broken, and the spirit is dissolved and contracted. The sense of touch, which is present to the soul throughout all the limbs, feels all these things; the sense judges them, and the imagination <term>suffers along with it</term> <note>Original: *condolet*. Ficino distinguishes between the physical damage to the flesh and the mental "suffering" or "shared pain" in the faculty of imagination.</note>. How can the flesh be cut without the spirit poured within it being partly dissolved with the loosened flesh, and partly contracting by fleeing into itself? Furthermore, how can the dissolving and contracting of the spirit be hidden from its own soul? And if it is not hidden, why should the soul not take the destruction of its own work poorly? For the spirit and the body are the work of the soul. Indeed, everyone loves their own work. <margin>D</margin> In the flesh, there is the <term>passion</term> <note>In the philosophical sense, "passion" refers to "undergoing" or being affected by an external force.</note>; in the spirit, there is the torment; in the touch, there is the sense; and in the imagination, there is compassion and shared suffering (if I may put it that way).

To summarize briefly: in both the flesh and the spirit, a certain destructive loosening or contraction occurs that corrupts the substance; let us call this a harmful injury. Does such an injury also pass into the soul? Not at all. For such an injury destroys substance. Thus, it would destroy the power of that substance itself. Consequently, it would destroy the operation of that power. Therefore, in any injury of the flesh and spirit, however slight, the substance of the soul present to them would be similarly injured. Its power would be injured much more, <margin>E</margin> and its operation would be injured as well. But "sense" and "imagination" are powers of the soul. "To perceive" and "to judge through sense" are the actions of these powers. Therefore, if that division passed into the substance of the soul, we would neither perceive the injury, nor judge its nature, nor know from where and how to bring help. It would either be entirely hidden from the soul, or it would be perceived only minimally and judged falsely.

And since the soul is whole everywhere, if it suffered in one part of the body that was cut, it would suffer as a whole. Yet that same whole soul, which is there, is also throughout the entire body. Therefore, it would suffer throughout the entire body. If it suffers everywhere, it cannot perceive or announce that the suffering is in one part of the living being more than in another. Furthermore, since the suffering is one thing and the judgment of the suffering is another—and suffering is always indicated by something else—if the suffering were present in the judgment itself, there would be a need for yet another judgment by which the suffering judgment could be judged. If that were also suffering, another would be needed again. Therefore, one must finally arrive at a certain judge who is free from the suffering. This judge, while it judges the sufferings of the body, if it receives any physical quality from them, it undoubtedly "suffers." If it does not receive a quality, it is not formed by the body. Therefore, the judge must be such that it receives neither sufferings nor forms from bodies. The soul could not be such a judge if it were either a body (even the thinnest one) immersed in this body, or some affection of this body, or some point of affection. Thus Augustine follows these Platonic views: <margin>F</margin>

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul is linked to the body via the "spirit" (a subtle vapor) and argues that the soul itself does not undergo physical damage because it must remain an unaffected "judge" to perceive and respond to bodily injuries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book VII. Having previously used the analogy of words and meanings to argue for the soul's indivisibility, Ficino now moves into a physiological and metaphysical explanation of how the soul interacts with the body through "spirits" without itself being changed by physical sensations.</meta>

# Theology Seventh [Book]

Plotinus and others confirm this. It seems to me that the soul, when it senses, does not "suffer" <note>original: *pati*; in this philosophical context, to "suffer" means to be passively acted upon or changed by an external force</note> anything from the body, but rather acts more attentively upon the body's own "passions" <note>original: *passionibus*; the passive states or changes occurring in the physical organs</note>. These actions—whether they are easy due to harmony or difficult due to disharmony—do not escape the soul's notice. And this whole process is what is called "sensing." But this sense—which is present even when nothing is being sensed—exists as if through a bodily instrument. This instrument is managed by the soul with such a "temperament" <note>A balanced mixture of physical qualities</note> that it is prepared to act with attention toward the body's affections, so that it might join likes to likes and repel what is harmful. 

Furthermore, the soul acts like an opinion: something luminous in the eyes; something airy, most clear and mobile in the ears; something misty in the nostrils; something moist in the mouth; and something earthy and, as it were, muddy in the physical act of touch. It performs all these things in peace, provided that those things which are in the living being cling together in a unity of health through a certain natural consensus. But when those things are applied which affect the body with some (so to speak) "otherness," the soul performs more attentive actions, adapted to their specific locations or instruments; and then it is said "to sense." To these actions, it willingly joins what is congruent and troublesomely resists what is incongruous.

<margin>☞</margin>
I believe the soul exhibits these operations to the body's affections when it senses, without receiving those same affections itself. When the airy spirit of the ear is struck by sound, the soul—which before such a percussion was nourishing the body of the ears in silence—then nourishes it more attentively. To do this is not to be acted upon. This operation of attention does not escape the soul as it works. For "not to escape notice" is to sense. In short, sensation is either the observation of that attentive operation, or a judgment of the bodily affection and quality, excited by that action of the soul's attention.

<margin>☞ Chapter 7.</margin>

### Seventh Reason. Specific reasons concerning the natural and sensitive power of the soul: that the soul does not become a divisible form, because the work of a quality is singular.

<margin>b</margin> Although in the previous reasons we have proved not only that the soul is not a body, but also that it is not a form spread through bodies, we nevertheless think it should be shown through specific arguments regarding this part. And so that we may speak more conveniently about this matter, we shall call such a form—as we have said—sometimes a "quality," sometimes an "affection of the body," after the manner of the Platonists. If the soul were a bodily quality, it would either be a simple quality, or a <term>complexion</term> <note>original: *complexio*; in ancient and Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific "temperament" or mixture of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that make up a body</note>, or a form bound to these. It cannot be simple. For any simple quality, or a form following it—as we have declared elsewhere—performs only one specific thing and does not extend to opposites. The soul does very many and contrary things. Nor will it be a complexion, or a form following a complexion. Because in such a mixture, one certain quality always dominates over the others, and its operation thrives in the body before all others. But the soul is bound to no single quality and no single specific motion.

<margin>Chapter 8.</margin>

### Eighth Reason. The complexion acts through the power of qualities.

**T**he action of a complexion and its form is always carried out through the qualities from which it is <margin>J</margin> woven together; therefore, a complexion never performs anything so sublime that the powers of its qualities do not extend to it. The work of heat is to penetrate and dissolve. However, the soul's nutritive power, using heat as an instrument, does not only dissolve food—which is the proper work of heat—but also cooks and digests it, leading it to the form of living flesh and the human figure. Indeed, this action of the living being cannot proceed from heat as its primary cause. For it does not happen except through nourishment, and it is led to a certain limit of size and a certain figure. Heat, however, if it were the source of matter, would spread itself without a certain limit or figure. Since it is necessary <margin>L</margin> for the limit and figure to be prescribed to the work by the principal agent, it is clear that heat cannot be the principal craftsman of growth; rather...

<summary>Ficino argues that sensation is an active power of the soul rather than a passive reception of physical stimuli, and he distinguishes the soul from a mere "complexion" (physical temperament) by showing that biological growth and form require a higher guiding principle than simple physical heat.</summary>

Having argued that the soul's sensing is an act of the soul rather than a passive reception by the body, Ficino now begins a series of logical "reasons" (rationes) to prove that the soul is a substance in its own right, rather than a mere byproduct or "accident" of the body's physical makeup.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
->Platonic Book [Theology]<-

Indeed, no other accidental form <note>original: *accidentalem formam*; a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, such as being tan or tall</note> can do this if color—which is the most excellent of all—cannot. Yet growth is achieved by the soul. From this, he concludes that the soul is not an accidental form, a point we must prove very often. It is also concluded that the soul is not composed of accidental forms, because such forms could not rationally organize qualities—which wander without a certain limit, degree, proportion, or figure—into these very structures. Finally, it is concluded that souls are not some substantial form of an element or a mixture. For the movement of such a form is directed toward a single end, as we have said. But growth is extended equally into every part.

<margin>A</margin>

# Ninth reason. Complexion is an accidental form. Chapter 9

**T**emperament <term>complexio: the specific "blend" or "mixture" of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that makes up a physical body</term> is a certain nature constituted from contrary qualities in a specific way, which holds a sort of middle ground between them. From this it follows that it cannot be a substance, because it does not subsist in itself, but in that body which is the subject of those contrary qualities. Because these qualities fight against one another, they do not receive each other; but once received by matter and mixed together, they generate the "complexion" or temperament. Therefore, this temperament is not a substance, both because of what I have said, and because it has something contrary to itself—namely, an excess of some foreign quality that results in its own dissolution. Furthermore, it admits of "more" and "less." For the nature, power, and operation of a temperament is intensified and relaxed. 

But a substance has no contrary proper to itself, since it exists in a different category than the contrariety of these qualities—that is, it exists in the category of substance, not quality. Nor is a substance intensified toward "more" or relaxed toward "less" in its own nature, such that this or that substance becomes now more, now less of what it is. A stone is not "more" or "less" a stone than another. Since 
<margin>B</margin>
therefore a temperament is not a substance, and the soul is a substance, the soul is not a temperament. That the soul is a substance is also evident from this:

---

it is through the soul that a living being receives its specific and substantial nature of species and genus, as well as its name. Through this soul, this thing is indeed a dog. Through that soul, that thing is a horse. Through another, that thing is a man. That quality which is an "accident" comes to its subject after that subject is already perfected in its own species. But the soul itself crafts its own body for itself; it preserves it once made, and while it fails, it repairs it; it binds the fighting elements into one. When the soul departs, the body falls away, and neither the previous temperament nor the species is retained. Such a soul is necessarily the "nutritive" soul <note>The most basic level of soul responsible for growth and survival, shared by plants and animals</note>. Nor should it be said that the soul which is solely nutritive constructs the body so that later, once perfected, a "sensitive" soul <note>The level of soul responsible for movement and sensation</note> arrives as a sort of accident. For a body suitable for a sensitive soul must have the instruments for sensing and moving forward. The nutritive soul, insofar as it is that alone, would only make instruments for nutrition. But the soul will make other instruments because of those powers whose use the instruments serve. Nor are there two separate souls in the same body, one of which crafts instruments for the other. For the one that nourishes is the same as the one that senses. Indeed, disturbances of the senses hinder or increase the work of nourishing. For the sadness of the imagination weakens it, while joy strengthens it, as if there were one single soul in man whose duties both are. Therefore, it is a substance, because it is the master-craftsman of the body, not its servant. Thus, it is not a temperament.

<margin>C</margin>

# Tenth reason. The harmony of the temperament does nothing to the body. Chapter 10

**N**or should it be permitted for Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist who argued the soul was merely the "harmony" of the body's physical parts</note> or other musicians to dream that the soul is a certain harmony produced from the temperament itself. For in that case, the soul would likewise not be a substance, but an accident. Does not a harmony draw all its power from the strings? It does not exist at all through itself, nor is it capable of effecting anything in the strings. Indeed, it does not move the strings itself; rather, when the strings are moved from elsewhere, the harmony is born. Therefore, if the soul were a harmony...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is a substantial form rather than a mere "complexion" or physical mixture of qualities, proving this by showing that the soul acts as the architect and sustainer of the body's unity.</summary>

<sig>n 3</sig>

...of humors composed in a certain way: [the soul] will depend entirely on them; nor will it move them, but the soul will arise from them when they are moved by something else. Nor will it rule them; rather, they will rule and sustain it. Therefore, there will be no movements in the body besides the condition of the humors; no works beyond their command. Just as they are now, as we described in previous chapters. Neither skillful shape nor arrangement [would exist]. The mind would never resist bodily passions; nor would it reflect upon itself or, separated from bodily things, join them together; nor would it operate anything through itself if it did not exist through itself <note>original: *per seipsun*; existing independently as a substance rather than a quality of something else</note> in any way. But we have spoken of this elsewhere and will speak of it again.

### Eleventh reason. In every composite body there is harmony. <margin>Chapter 11</margin>

<margin>E</margin> In every body composed of many things, there is some harmony of its parts, through which they harmonize by mutual agreement. Thus, if harmony itself were the soul, any composite bodies would live and grow together. Perhaps you will say: the soul is indeed a harmony—that is, an elegance <term>concinnitate: a structural beauty or fitness of parts</term> and a consonance—but not just any harmony: rather, one tempered in a certain and proper way. You see that the definition of the soul and of consonance are not the same. For it is not merely because a thing is a consonance that it is also a soul, but because it is arranged in a certain way. This specific mode of arrangement does not draw its elegance from its own nature, because then it would be present in any elegance. Therefore, does it come from somewhere else, from an external principle? Indeed, it does. But this external thing is not enough. For that which is outside the harmony does not move and temper it continually and naturally. Therefore, there lies hidden in the consonance of the humors a certain superior power, the temperer of bodily consonance, which, by tempering the humors in its own way in the bodies of living things, makes their elegance definite and different from other bodies; this proper consonance is the vital harmony produced by a life-giving spirit latent within.

### Twelfth reason. Harmony is understood as either the composition of the members itself, or some ratio of the composition. <margin>Chapter 12</margin>

<margin>f</margin> **W**hen someone asserts that the soul is a consonance, one might think they mean two things: either the composition of the humors and members itself, or some ratio of that composition. The soul is certainly not the composition. For every part of the soul would have to be a composition of some parts of the body. How this could clearly happen, we cannot assign. The composition of the body is manifest to physicists, but the soul is unknown. And how it could be composed from its powers—namely, intellect, sense, appetite, and the rest—is difficult to know. It is most difficult, again, to see how the individual powers are composed. Furthermore, composition is nothing other than the union of many; but many things are not united except by one thing. <margin>G</margin> By one, I say, which is within the many, so that they are glued together by an internal bond <note>original: *coagulo*; literally a rennet or curdling agent, used here metaphorically for a unifying force</note>. Therefore, that single power implanted in the members, from which the union of the members arises, is the soul itself rather than the union proceeding from it. Nor is it the ratio of the composition itself. For since different ratios and proportions of composition exist in different members of the body, the individual members would possess individual souls. Indeed, the bone would have one soul, the nerve another, the flesh another, and similarly for the rest. Since these members are composed among themselves by different proportions. But we could by no means assign a single life to one living being unless we attributed a single form to it—to one author and ruler, that is, one soul. We also see that the ratio of consonance <margin>J</margin> belongs more to the qualities of the body than to the soul. Health is the consonance of humors. Strength is the consonance of bones and nerves. Beauty, in a certain way, is the consonance of members and colors. But as for sense and intellect, which are simple acts, I do not know what kind of harmonies they could be. When we know the substance of a thing, we can easily judge its accidents <note>original: *accidentibus*; properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like hair color</note> from there. Therefore, because the proportion of the humors or members is known, we easily judge those things which pertain to health, strength, and beauty. It is clear that these three consist in the proportion of those things. But truly...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a mere "harmony" of the body, as harmony is a passive result of arrangement, whereas the soul is an active principle that governs and unifies the body's various parts.</summary>

...since even if such a proportion is found, we still do not clearly discern the powers, affects, or habits of the soul; it is clear that the substance of the soul does not consist in that proportion at all. For who, having found that [proportion], would immediately boast that they had discovered the nature of sensing and understanding? Aristotle understands the nature of these things better than Hippocrates. Yet Hippocrates considers the proportion of the [humors] more diligently. Chapter 13.

<margin>B</margin>
**Thirteenth reason. The harmony of humors perceives nothing without matter.**

Whatever produces something must be more excellent than what is produced by it. The more a thing is free from matter, the more sublime it is. Therefore, the cause must always be freer from matter than the effect. No effect can be freer from matter than its cause. The power of nourishment is quite free from matter, as it has been shown elsewhere to operate upon many things above and beyond the order of the elements. The power of sensing is even more free from matter, because in its very act of sensing, it receives the forms of things without the matter of the things themselves. For sight does not receive the color along with the wall, but it reaches a <term>spiritual image: an "intentional" or non-physical representation</term> of the color. Much more so does the intellect do the same, as will appear in what follows. Since, therefore, these powers of the soul are greatly free from matter, they cannot proceed from a cause that is either matter itself or immersed in matter. Humors are entirely corporeal. <margin>E</margin> For this reason, humors can in no way procreate such powers by their own mixing or consonance. Much less can they create the soul itself, which is the source of such powers. Indeed, if the soul had its substance in the qualities of the humors, it would receive whatever it perceives through the <note>original: *affectiones*; the physical dispositions or states</note> of the humors. But through these, only corporeal forms are received. For through heat and dryness, it would not receive a spiritual image of fire, but the corporeal substance of fire. Again, through cold and dryness, it would receive the earth itself. The earth itself, since it would receive in the same way, would also sense in the same way as the soul. A stone and other things would do the same.

---

<margin>B</margin>
**Fourteenth reason. That which harmonizes more is more of a harmony. Chapter 14.**

**H**armony consists in the concord of many things in such a way that when strings harmonize more, there is more harmony; when they harmonize less, there is less. The soul of a wicked man harmonizes with itself very little. Sensation disagrees with reason. Appetites also fight one another. The soul of a virtuous man harmonizes in every respect. If the soul were a harmony, the soul of a virtuous man—which harmonizes more—would be "more" of a harmony. Therefore, it would be "more" of a soul. Since the soul is life, it would be "more" of a life. Thus, the soul of a virtuous man would be more alive, bolder, and more robust than that of a thief. Nor would the thief’s soul digest food as well as the just man's. Nor would it generate offspring. Nor would it sustain or move the limbs of the body. Nor would it discover things sharply, remember firmly, speak elegantly, or act boldly. Nor would it breathe as long, and so forth.

<margin>C</margin>
**Fifteenth reason. Harmony admits nothing dissonant. Chapter 15.**

**T**rue harmony—to proceed more correctly—admits nothing dissonant while it remains harmony. If it is harmony, it sounds in concord; if it sounds dissonant, it is not harmony. Yet do we not see our soul constantly distracted by dissonant opinions and affects? And nonetheless, it remains a true soul and equally vital. Do not object that the discord of affects does not destroy the soul, while the discord of elements and humors does. Furthermore, if the soul cannot perish from its own intimate dissonance, nothing else can. That intimate and proper dissonance of the human soul is that which belongs to <margin>D</margin> every soul alone: that is, the disagreement of opinions and affects, which does not touch bodies lacking life, yet strikes all the souls of mortals. Such disagreement does not cast them out of life or the state of sensation. Therefore, the discord of humors—which is more foreign to the soul—will much less dissipate the soul's own natural state. Surely, if the soul consisted in the concord of humors, it would be dissipated by even a slight dissonance between them. Wherefore nothing stands in the way [of the fact that] beyond the soul's and the bodies' [long...] <note>The text breaks off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul cannot be a mere harmony of bodily humors because the soul's intellectual powers are non-material, and because a soul remains a soul even when internal conflict or "dissonance" (vice) is present. He concludes that if the soul were a physical harmony, virtue would make one "more" alive and vice would make one "less" a soul, which contradicts the reality of living beings.</summary>

...[the body] might be dissonant, and yet the soul nevertheless persists as a true and living soul. Harmony <note>Referring to the theory that the soul is a "musical" balance of the body's physical humors</note> does not allow for this. ### Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Eight.

The soul is an indivisible form, whole in every part, and draws no origin from matter; therefore it is immortal, as is shown through the power of understanding. The mind ascends through four stages to the spirit. First argument. Chapter One.

<margin>E</margin>
We shall now approach the third part of our disputation, which proves our proposition through the power of understanding—provided we first explain how our mind, according to the opinion of the Platonists, ascends from the body to the spirit through four stages of knowing, the last of which is intelligence. For it ascends through **sense**, **imagination**, **phantasy**, and **intelligence**.

Through **sense**, indeed, Socrates sees Plato. In this act, he reaches an incorporeal likeness of Plato, free from Plato’s physical matter, through his eyes. This occurs, however, on the condition that the eye does not see Plato unless Plato’s body itself is present. 

Next, even when Plato is absent, through internal **imagination**, Socrates thinks upon Plato’s color and the shape he had seen. Likewise, he recalls that sweet voice of Plato’s which he had heard, and the rest of the things he had received through the five senses. Imagination of this kind rises above matter more than sense does: both because it does not need the presence of those bodies in order to think of them, and because it alone performs whatever all five senses do together. Yet it is not entirely pure, because it perceives <note>original: *sapit*, meaning to taste or to have a sense of</note> nothing other than what the sense has received or conceived. Sense revolves around bodies; imagination revolves around the images of bodies received or conceived through the senses. 

A little later, through **phantasy** <note>Ficino uses *phantasia* to describe a higher "judgmental" power that organizes sensory images into meaningful concepts</note>, Socrates begins to judge this whole likeness of Plato which imagination itself had collected through the five senses, in this way: "Who is this with such a tall body, broad forehead, wide shoulders, fair complexion, gray eyes, high eyebrows, aquiline nose, small mouth, and [this] voice? This is Plato: a beautiful man, a good disciple, most beloved." 

<margin>F</margin>
You see how much Socrates's phantasy excels his imagination. Imagination itself collected such an image of Plato. But *whom* it designated, or *what sort* of person that image was, the imagination did not know. Phantasy now discerns that this is the image of this man who is called Plato: a beautiful image of a good man and a friend. 

Therefore, in these things it now has some sense of substance—as some think—and of beauty, goodness, and friendship. 

<margin>G</margin>
The Platonists, however, deny that substance is truly known by phantasy, since they [the powers of phantasy] do not recognize the definition <note>original: *rationem*, the underlying essence or logical principle</note> of substance. Imagination does not even suspect the substance of a thing, but only the surface and outer "picture" of the thing. Phantasy at least divines the substance when it pronounces to anyone it meets: "That man is a certain person, Plato." 

And it even seems to dream of incorporeal things in a way, while it judges Plato to be beautiful, good, a friend, or a disciple. For beauty, goodness, friendship, and learning are incorporeal; they are subject neither to the senses nor to imagination. Certain concepts of phantasy of this kind are called, in a way, incorporeal <term>intentions: the mental "pointers" or meanings that represent an object without being the object itself</term> of bodies. 

But the mind does not yet fly entirely above matter: both because phantasy does not recognize that these "intentions" are incorporeal, and because Socrates's phantasy specifically inspects *this* man Plato—namely, in this specific place and position, at this specific time, and at this hour of the day.

<summary>Ficino begins Book VIII by outlining the "ladder of cognition," explaining how the mind moves from physical sensation to the more abstract powers of imagination and phantasy. Using Socrates's perception of Plato as an example, he argues that the mind begins to grasp incorporeal qualities like "goodness" and "friendship" even before reaching pure intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of the previous page regarding the hierarchy of knowledge. this beauty: this goodness: and the rest in the same way. In this state, the phantasy <note>In Renaissance psychology, the "phantasy" is the faculty that creates and stores mental images based on sensory input.</note> depicts Plato within itself under the same conditions in which he exists in matter. But while the phantasy wanders among the singular conditions of this specific man, the **intellect** conceives of **universal principles** <note>original: "communes rationes"</note>; and both faculties execute their work simultaneously. For in this way, the intelligence reasons. What kind of man Plato is, such also is Antisthenes; such also is Xenophon: they are similar in appearance, equally beautiful, and good friends; they are disciples in the same way. Therefore, in these three there is one common **humanity**, through which they are equally men; there is one nature of beauty, and one of goodness, through which they are equally beautiful and equally good. This humanity itself, which is common here, also exists as common to countless others who are, were, or will be—at whatever time and in whatever place they are born. The same applies to beauty and the rest. 

But why do I speak only of humanity? Consider the same said of all other things. If, therefore, humanity communicates itself equally to individual persons, places, and times, it is restricted to no single person, no place, and no time. A nature of <margin>a</margin> this kind is seen to transcend the individual conditions of bodies. It is, therefore, according to itself, in a certain way **incorporeal**. It infuses itself into individual bodies, and because of this, it exists both in "the other" <note>i.e., in the physical person</note> and in "the many." Yet above that which exists in another, there must be that which remains in itself; and above that "one" which exists in many, there must be the "One Itself" which subsists in itself. Therefore, above all bodies there exists a certain principle and **Idea** of humanity itself, <margin>B</margin> through participation in which—or through a certain similarity to—human beings are made, whoever are humans. 

Indeed, that nature which is common to individual persons does not occur by chance, because it is always ordered in a similar way; nor <margin>c</margin> does it subsist through itself, since it cannot stand alone within itself. For it requires the foundation of matter <note>Ficino is arguing that the "humanity" we see in people needs a body to exist, so the "Universal Humanity" must come from a higher source: a Divine Idea.</note>. It is therefore created by a certain cause. Yet it is not created by matter (which does not form itself), nor by a single person (who cannot work upon all people, for whatever a person does, they do as an individual, not as something common to the rest). It is not created by all persons together; for as much as they differ among themselves, they do not produce a common thing, but diverse things. Insofar as they agree, they agree through this very nature—indeed, they exist through it, and it is prior to them to the same degree that it is simpler than they are. For various properties happen upon this nature, as something prior, in order to distinguish the individual persons. 

Yet this nature is produced by a single form, since it is one. What form could be above the multitude of persons? We must ask this lest that form also be produced by another, and that by another, without end. Thus we ascend to the **Divine Idea**, which is necessarily above all things, so that it may act equally upon all and reconcile them in a common nature. If we must rise from the part (which is beneath the whole) to the whole, and from the whole to that which is above the whole, we rightly rise from individual persons (who exist in specific parts of place and time) to the nature that is common to them in itself. That nature exists as if through all place and all time; from there, we rise to the **Principle** <note>original: "rationem"</note> which exists above all place and time, which Plato calls an **Idea**. 

Next, the intellect looks up to the Divine Idea itself, <margin>A</margin> whether it finds it within itself or existing in the Divine Light. For reason dictates that **natural species** <note>The essential forms or "blueprints" of natural things</note>, because they are eternal, <margin>B</margin> cannot come from a "mobile" <note>i.e., changing or physical</note> cause. Otherwise, having been produced through motion, they would eventually fail. Yet they were indeed created, because they are parts of the universe, which is composed of elements from elsewhere; and they all come from a single cause. Indeed, they are so ordered among themselves that they lead into a single nature, a single work, and a single end. Hence the human intellect concludes that above the changing world, within the immobile Mind that moves the world, there exist the **archetypes** <note>original: "exemplaria"</note> of the natural spheres. These do not exist in a corporeal or animal nature, for then they would be subject to change; rather, they exist in an intellectual—or rather, an **intelligible**—nature. For intelligible things must be placed within the Supreme Intelligible. 

However, a necessary reasoned argument is not always required for the intellect to reach these common principles of things. Rather, just as the phantasy by its own nature judges things individually, <margin>C</margin> so the intellect, by its natural power, acts immediately without any step-by-step discourse. As soon as that singular image of Plato is depicted in the phantasy, the intellect suddenly—having set aside this specific man—thinks out that human nature and Idea which is common to all. Once beauty and goodness are depicted as images, the intellect immediately thinks of the universal nature of beauty and goodness, and the principle in no...

<summary>Ficino explains the process of abstraction, where the human intellect moves from perceiving individual people (like Plato or Xenophon) to understanding the universal "Idea" of Humanity. He argues that these universal Ideas must exist eternally in a Divine Mind above the physical world of change.</summary>
