# Theology Book Eight

---

...a certain matter: placed in no specific location or time: but either in all matter, or absolute from matter, subsisting simply in itself <note>original: "absolutam a materia in seipsa simpliciter subsistentez." Ficino is arguing that the highest form of reality exists independently of physical substance.</note>. 
<margin>D</margin> For this reason, the senses are occupied with bodies. The imagination is occupied with the images <note>original: "simulacra"</note> of bodies. The phantasy <term>Phantasy|The mental faculty that processes and interprets sensory images.</term> is occupied with the individual intentions of those images. The **intellect**, however, is occupied with the common natures of those individual intentions, and with reasons that are entirely incorporeal. One must remember, indeed, that the intellect knows not only universal nature but also the particular; otherwise, it would not be able to compare the two with each other. Furthermore, it knows all the powers beneath it and their actions when it compares them all to itself. However, almost all agree that the universal nature is known by it before the particular nature. For it acts primarily according to the nature of the intelligible form. Since that form is conceived through a certain abstraction, it is "absolute" <note>In this context, "absolute" means "set free" or "unconnected" from physical constraints.</note>; hence it refers primarily to a universal nature. It acquires this power from the virtue of the intellect in which and from which it exists, because the intellect itself is absolute. 
<margin>E</margin> From the image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note>, however, which is in the phantasy, only the particular is represented. Both the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy.</note> and the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> mostly judge that this particular is seen by the intellect only through a certain reflexive act. To the extent that the intellect—after it has suddenly and by a direct path gazed upon the universal through its "species" <note>A "species" in this philosophical sense is the mental form or "look" of a concept.</note>—it reflects upon itself in a sort of discourse, looking back at the image by which the conceived species had been prompted, and thus it now perceives the particular. Therefore, the movement toward incorporeal and absolute things is most natural to the mind, since it betakes itself toward them first, suddenly, and directly. Here it appears that the power of understanding is altogether incorporeal. If, therefore, through the works of nourishment, and again through the works of sensing—the first of which occur in the body, and the second through the body and concerning bodies—we have shown that the soul is not divided within the body, how much more should it be thought that the same is revealed through the works of understanding? And furthermore: that the soul neither derives its origin from matter, nor is it mortal. For it executes the work of understanding by itself, in which it leaves matter behind entirely, and ascends to incorporeal and eternal reasons. Come then, let us see by what way we can find what we seek through the works and affections of the intelligence.

### Second reason. The soul is nourished by truth. 
### Chapter II.

<margin>F</margin> **A**liment <note>The decorative initial 'A' begins the word 'Alimentum'.</note> is taken for this reason: so that it may pass into the substance of the thing that is to be nourished, just as bread is eaten so that it may become flesh. Therefore, the food must be very closely related to that which is to be nourished, so that it can easily pass into its nature. Thus, aquatic creatures are fed by aquatic nourishments; terrestrial ones by terrestrial; aerial ones by aerial. Similarly, bodies are nourished by corporeal things, and incorporeal things by incorporeal things. For a body does not pass into a spirit, nor does a spirit migrate into a body. This is because there is no common matter underlying them through which and in which they might be exchanged with one another. It is clear that the soul is not nourished by bodies. It is clear it is nourished by incorporeal things. It follows, therefore, that the soul is incorporeal. If the soul were to feed upon any bodies, it would feed most especially upon those that nourish its own body. For since the body is most suited to the soul, its own nourishments would also be the most suited among all corporeal things—provided those nourishments are so thinned and purified that they suit that "small body" <note>original: "corpusculo." Ficino is mocking the idea that the soul is just a very thin or subtle physical substance.</note> which is commonly thought to be the soul. If this were true, the soul would be stronger in a fat body than in a thin one. It would be sharper in discovery, firmer in remembering, and more prompt in acting. It would be more continent in overcoming the base allurements of the body. There would be magnanimity <note>Greatness of soul or courage.</note> in a large body, and small-mindedness in a small one. As the body grows, the mind would mature, even if it learned nothing and were exercised by no study of things. As the body and its strength decreased through age, its wisdom, judgment, and constancy would perish. After feasts and wines, the genius would be sharper and more sublime. All these things would happen if the mind were made to grow by corporeal foods. Yet now the opposite of these things occurs. Therefore, the mind is not fed by corporeal nourishments. What then? By nothing? If so, it will be eternal if it lacks any need for nourishment, which is what we most desire. Or perhaps...

<summary>Ficino argues that the intellect's ability to abstract universal concepts from physical images proves the soul is incorporeal and immortal. He further contends that the soul cannot be material because it is nourished by incorporeal truth rather than physical food, noting that physical health does not equate to spiritual or intellectual wisdom.</summary>

## Platonic [Theology]

<margin>A</margin>
...it feeds on spiritual feasts. Indeed, it feeds on no others at all: a fact that is not doubtful to a wise man, for he who is nourished by such things is made all the wiser by them. Nor should we agree with the <term>Epicureans|Followers of the philosopher Epicurus who believed the soul was material and died with the body.</term>, who imagine that the soul grows together with the body because they see greater strength in older children than in infants, and that adolescents and grown men surpass them in strength day by day, until the strength is again diminished as the body grows old. For the relationship of the soul to the limbs is the same as that of an **art** to its **instruments**. An art often remains the same and unchanging, yet it moves its instruments with more ease at one time and more difficulty at another. This is because these instruments are sometimes more fit, and at other times less fit for movement. Thus, although the power in the soul is always the same, the limbs—due to excessive softness or dryness—neither stand as firmly nor bend as easily. And that very power which seems to exist in the body does not follow the weight of the flesh so much as it follows the natural proportion and <margin>B</margin> artistic harmony of the limbs. These two qualities belong to the **spirit** <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the "spirit" is a thin, vaporous substance that acts as the bridge between the physical body and the incorporeal soul.</note> rather than to mere physical mass. Furthermore, the power that exists in the soul is not acquired through the growth of the body. This is evident in those who are sluggish and lazy; in them, even as the body grows, the mind makes no progress. Instead, mental power is acquired through the soul's own industry, through character, practice, and devotion. Who would deny that the body's strength is gained over time? Yet to the soul, strength is often granted in a single moment, either when reason reveals something and commands a magnificent deed, or when a sudden "fury" or passion provides the weapons. Often a small man overcomes a larger one. And he who does not grow in body often grows in the virtue of the soul. Indeed, while we decrease in body, we often increase in soul. The soul very often acquires knowledge and magnanimity <note>original: "magnanimitateq3." This refers to "greatness of soul," a classical virtue involving high-mindedness and courage.</note> suddenly. The body, however, can neither give <margin>C</margin> nor receive anything except over time. Finally, the virtue of the soul is a certain "equality" <note>original: "equalitas." Ficino uses this term to mean a state of balanced harmony or consistency.</note>, as the masters of wisdom teach, through which the soul is in harmony with itself, with truth, and with the good. In the same way, if a square line were made into a circular one, it would become more perfect—not because it became longer, but because it became more equal. Again, if a lyre is tuned, it will be more perfect—not because it becomes

---

## Book [3]

larger, but because it becomes more harmonious. Thus, when a young person grows in virtue, the soul does not grow in quantity, but advances through a certain spiritual equality and harmony. Nor should anyone object by saying that when the body is neither burdened by the weight of excessive feasting nor weakened by hunger, but is moderately nourished, the soul is similarly fed and becomes stronger in that state. They argue the opposite is also true. For while it is true that the soul is strongest in such a human state, this does not happen because it is nourished in the same way as the body. Rather, it is because the soul by its nature rules the body. When the body is sick, the soul is so weighed down and occupied in caring for and ruling it that it cannot be intent on seeking the truth. However, when the body is quiet, the mind speculates freely, and then it feeds most especially on its own proper food. But what shall we say is the food of the soul? None other than that for which it always hungers and thirsts; which, once obtained, it rejoices in exceedingly; and which, once consumed, causes it to grow and be filled. Every soul, at every age and continuously, desires **truth** above all else. Craftsmen seek this in every art, and in every matter people ask what the reality of the thing is; even infants ask questions out of curiosity. They do not seek it once or twice or three times a day like bodily food, but at every single moment, investigating it in all affairs. Therefore, out of the zeal for acquiring truth, we frequently neglect the nourishment of the body. We spare neither time nor money, nor do we fear exhausting the body through labors; for when the body is weakened, the soul often becomes more vigorous <note>original: "neruosior," literally "more sinewy" or "stronger."</note>. The soul itself desires this truth, not the body. For truth does not increase the body; in fact, the pursuit of it is often harmful to the body. Furthermore, the soul seeks truth for its own sake, not for the sake of the body. For what does truth contribute to the body? If truth ever seems to benefit the body, it does not happen because of the truth itself, but because of some bodily convenience that occurs once the truth is known. Indeed, the soul, even if it gained nothing in...

He concludes that the soul's true nourishment is not food, but the constant pursuit of truth.</summary>

<header>Eighth [Book] of Theology</header>

# Theology
# Eighth

...utility follows: [the mind] studiously searches for truth; and while the body is full with its own food, the mind still hungers and thirsts for truth. When truth is found, it exults—not just for a time, as happens with the needs of the body, but it rejoices forever. It is illuminated, it grows, and it becomes so magnificent that, because of its own greatness, those things which usually seem very large to a hungry little soul appear very small. By this nourishment, the soul also becomes invincible, temperate, just, a governor and master of men, higher than heaven, equal to the angels, and similar to God. Who, therefore, would doubt further whether truth is the natural food of the human mind? All minds seek this same food. Every mind seeks it always. <margin>G</margin> This stable agreement in seeking truth signifies that minds agree with one another in a marvelous way, and that every mind remains stable in its own nature; for their appetite does not vary or change like the appetite of the senses, which differs according to the diversity of bodies and is subject to the changes of the body, as if the senses simply followed the movements of physical matter. <margin>¶</margin> Recognize the stability of divine things. <margin>¶</margin> For the soul eats the nourishment of the body, yet it also feeds on the same food as the celestial and eternal minds. <margin>¶</margin> This food is truth. But truth is not corporeal; otherwise, it would not exist in incorporeal things. <margin>☛</margin> Now, however, truth exists in God, in angels, and in numbers—which are both incorporeal and true. And since incorporeal things are as much truer than bodies as they are purer and firmer, it follows that truth is found in them rather than in bodies. Indeed, what is more: truth is not properly found in bodies at all. For in these <margin>☛</margin> there are two things: matter and form. Truth is not in matter. For through matter, nothing truly exists as a specific kind of thing; a human is not truly a human because of matter, nor a horse, and so on. Nor does truth lie in the physical form of a body, since a form whose power is "infected" <note>original: *inficitur*. Ficino uses this to mean that the pure, ideal form is diluted or weakened when it is mixed with physical matter.</note> by matter is not a "true" form. <margin>☛</margin> This is also testified by the mathematicians, who do not find true geometric figures in bodies.

For a circle <note>The OCR reads "Clerus," likely a typo for "circulus" (circle).</note> placed on a true plane rolls continually; reason compels this to happen, since that circle touches the plane at only a single point. But a physical body cannot rest on a single mathematical point. No one has ever seen these perfect things in physical bodies. Therefore, true figures are not in bodies, because perhaps there are no true principles of figures there either—at least as far as the senses can perceive—such as points, lines, and surfaces. <margin>and</margin> Reason shows that a true point ought to lack length, a true line lack width, and a true surface lack depth. But such things are never found by the senses in matter. Since truth must exist somewhere, and yet it is absent from bodies and the senses, it is without doubt located in spirits. It is, therefore, incorporeal. The same is clear from this: truth exists most where science <note>In this context, *scientia* refers to certain, demonstrative knowledge.</note> exists. This knowledge truly deals with the universal <term>rationes|The "reasons" or "rational principles"—the abstract essences and definitions of things.</term> of things. Someone knows what goodness itself is, what justice is—concepts common to all individual good and just actions and duties—and similar things. Reasons of this kind are incorporeal, since they are not enclosed in any one particular body but are common to many. <margin>☛</margin> The rational principle of a body or a circle is found in its entirety in the smallest circle, just as it is in the largest. The principle of length, or width, or depth is found in its entirety in the shortest line or shallowest surface, just as in the greatest. Finally, the principle of quantity itself is equal as a whole to the quantity of any thing. <margin>☛</margin> For this reason, the principles of the body, figures, dimensions, and even quantity itself are not corporeal or extended. Much less can higher principles be corporeal and extended. Furthermore, the principles of things are immutable; for they cannot be otherwise than they are. But all corporeal things are mutable. <margin>b</margin> Therefore, since science deals with these immutable things, it is incorporeal. Thus, truth too is incorporeal. From which it follows, regarding the truth of things: what it is, by what reason it consists, and how it is found...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that truth is the soul's natural "food," proving the soul is incorporeal because it grasps universal, immutable principles (like those in geometry and ethics) that do not exist in the physical, mutable world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the human soul is incorporeal and immortal because it feeds on "Truth," which is an eternal and non-physical substance. The previous page established that truth is the natural food of the mind; this section explores the consequences of that nourishment and introduces a new argument regarding the indivisibility of virtue.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

...what is closer to it, or more remote, no sense but only reason judges; and then most of all when it withdraws itself from the senses and the deceptions of the body. Therefore, truth is incorporeal. Such especially is the truth and knowledge of divine things. In this, the soul takes chief delight and is nourished. How, then, can the soul be corporeal, which is harmed by corporeal foods but nourished by spiritual ones? Whenever it delights in all truth, especially the truth of divine things, it is nourished and grows. Or how can it be mortal if it feeds on immortal truth? Since a corruptible stomach neither desires nor receives incorruptible food, nor does incorruptible food pass into a corruptible body. Truly, truth is immortal and is the continuous food of the soul; whether it is converted into the soul, or the soul converts itself into truth, it makes the soul immortal. Since, while it feeds on this familiar food, it is filled with such pleasure that it has no pain mixed in, nor does it turn into disgust or pain, it is clear that the mind is never fatigued, nor disturbed by the opposition of any darkness, nor can it be corrupted into any contrary.

<margin>B</margin>
Again, since nothing is more naturally desirable to the mind than truth, and truth is obtained through a certain separation from mortal things, nothing is more natural or familiar to the mind than to be segregated from mortals. From that which is most natural, no slackening of life follows, but rather an intensification. Therefore, the mind will live most especially when it has departed from here.

<margin>C</margin>
<term>Indeed, we can confirm this argument of ours with a certain argument of Olympiodorus the Platonist</term> <note>Olympiodorus the Younger was a 6th-century philosopher in Alexandria; his commentaries on Plato were essential for Renaissance thinkers like Ficino.</note>, which he wove together here, partly from Pythagorean and partly from Platonic mysteries received from the *Phaedo* and *Gorgias* <note>Two of Plato's famous dialogues; the *Phaedo* focuses on the soul's immortality and the *Gorgias* on ethics and rhetoric.</note>. The mind, by its natural greed for truth, continually separates itself from the body and separates forms from matter; it desires and strives to live separated in this way, even though the body and the senses daily twist it back in the opposite direction. It naturally seeks that life separated from the decaying body as something naturally good—that is, truly good—especially since such a life is entirely dedicated to truth and goodness. If a life of this kind is good, it is therefore also possible. For what is impossible is also useless. But the good should not be called useless. Likewise, if impotence <note>In the sense of "lack of power" or "inability."</note> belongs to evil, power belongs to good. Therefore, everything good is possible by its own nature. From this, it follows that the natural desire for good is a desire for a possible possession. And even what *appears* good is possible; certainly, the truly good itself is most powerful, and true goods are possible for those who seek them truly and well.

### ¶ Third Reason. The virtue of the soul, because it is indivisible, cannot be a quality of the body. Chapter 3.

<margin>D</margin>
**W**hat is indivisible cannot be a quality of the body. For if it were posed as a quality of it, we would ask: does it touch some divisible part of the body, or some indivisible point of the body? If the first is granted, surely a quality of this kind will be divisible, since it touches in a divisible manner. And thus, it would not be an indivisible quality of an indivisible thing, but a divisible quality of something divisible. If the second is granted, then certainly that quality is only a quality of that point which it touches, not of the body. For which reason, that which is individual <note>Original: "individuum." In this philosophical context, it means "indivisible" or "unable to be split into parts."</note> will never be a quality of the body. Now, the indivisible virtue of the human soul is a quality. Therefore, the soul is not a body. A demonstration of this kind will be thought sufficient if we show those two things more clearly.

<margin>E</margin>
Namely, that virtue is a quality of the soul, and that this virtue itself is indivisible. The first is most evident to everyone, since by the presence of virtue, such and such a soul becomes and is called wise, prudent, just, brave, and temperate. And virtue can be absent from the soul while the soul remains. Such is the condition of qualities.

<margin>F</margin>
Furthermore, we show the second point—namely, that virtue is indivisible—as follows. There are two kinds of virtues. Some are in the intellect. Others are in the appetite, whether rational or irrational. The former are called speculative virtues. The latter are moral...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 62 regarding the soul's relationship with truth. Having established that truth is the soul's immortal food, the author now distinguishes between the different types of virtues—speculative and moral—and argues that they are "indivisible," meaning they exist in the soul as whole units rather than physical, divisible parts.</meta>

# Theology

[...natu]ral virtues. The former are speculative: because by speculating and comparing, they are engaged comparatively in the act of contemplation. The latter are moral: because they are acquired by habit and custom; and once acquired, they consist in the exercise of character and actions. In the first category belong the <term>wisdom of divine things</term> <note>sapientia: usually refers to knowledge of the highest, most eternal causes</note>, the science of natural things, civil prudence, and the art of human works.

In the second category are justice: which gives each his due <note>Original: "suum cuique tribuit," the classic Roman legal definition of justice</note>. Fortitude: which, for the sake of honorable deeds, casts away from us the obstacle of fear. <margin>B</margin> Temperance: which repels the softness of lust, which is the other obstacle to honorable deeds. These are indeed Plato’s observations on the virtues. If there were any bodily size in these virtues, then the larger a person was, the wiser and more just they could become. Nor could small men surpass or equal great men in virtue. Furthermore, <term>science</term> <note>scientia: certain knowledge gained through demonstration</note>, which is the knowledge of the largest bodies, would be broader and clearer than the science of smaller things. However, we know many things whose magnitude we cannot equal. The whole mind perceives a great thing just as easily as a small one.

<margin>h</margin> To speak briefly, what else is speculative virtue but the clarity of the intellect? What else is moral virtue but a steady heat of appetite kindled by that same intellectual clarity? That clarity does not happen bit by bit, although we may arrive at it step by step. Just as after a long investigation following many tracks, a <term>hare</term> <note>The "hare" is a favorite metaphor in Platonic philosophy for the sudden moment of discovery after a long intellectual "hunt."</note> is suddenly sighted, so anyone will notice in themselves after a long search that, in a single moment, they behold what is true regarding the matter they sought. The light of truth suddenly—as Plato says—shines out in the soul; not suddenly struck out from things, but through a certain long discussion, as a spark is struck from a stone often hit. Similarly, by long habit, youth is disposed toward character. Until even the smallest bit is missing to light that stable and moral fire of appetite, it is not yet sufficiently kindled, and moral virtue is not yet held; but by repeated inspiration, at last the heat of the appetite suddenly blazes up sufficiently for virtue. Why say more? When a mirror is turned toward

# Eighth Book

the sun, the light is reflected in the mirror in a single moment. If wool is placed under that mirror, as soon as it is ready, fire is kindled in it. Therefore, both a sudden splendor occurs in the mirror, and a sudden fire in the wool. In no other way is there a sudden clarity of truth in the intellect, and from there, a sudden burning in the appetite. Let us summarize it again in this way: Speculative virtue is a certain knowledge of truth. If it were fused together bit by bit, one would have a part now, and a part would be missing and sought after. Insofar as one held a part of the truth, one would know; but insofar as it was missing, one would be ignorant. Thus, one would both know and not know the same thing at the same time. Not even a drunkard would dream of such a thing! Therefore, speculative virtue does not progress step by step from one part of itself to another, but the whole shines out at once from its very footprint. <margin>g 3</margin> Moral virtue, likewise, is a certain constant will to choose whatever reason dictates. If it had many parts and happened gradually, part of this will would be present, and part would still be absent. Insofar as the part is present, we will it; insofar as the part is absent, we do not will it. Thus, we would both will and not will the same thing at the same time through the same power of the soul. This is akin to a monster.

Since, therefore, virtue is created in an indivisible moment, it is itself also indivisible, provided that each nature follows its own origin. This is especially true since it has an indivisible end. For why should something whose birth and end are indivisible not be indivisible itself? <margin>K</margin> What is the end of virtue? The end of moral virtue is to purge and separate souls from the divisible body. The end of speculative virtue is to comprehend the incorporeal and universal reasons of things, which are placed far from divisible bodies. You see that the end of both virtues—just as their origin—is something indivisible. And so, they show that the virtues themselves must be judged as indivisible. Both virtues of this kind demonstrate their nature most especially in this: that many sciences are in the intellect at the same time, and many moral virtues are in the appetite at the same time. Nor do they confuse each other by their number, but rather they increase and illuminate one another.

<summary>This page argues that virtue and truth are indivisible and incorporeal, entering the soul not piece by piece, but in a sudden flash of insight or "blaze" of will. The author uses analogies of mirrors and sparks to show that while preparation is gradual, the arrival of virtue is an instantaneous event that transcends physical dimensions.</summary>

# Platonic

And we perceive the conception of one science within ourselves separately from another, so that we can think of one without considering the other. Therefore, we have such <term>ideas of the arts</term> <note>ideas of the arts: these are the mental archetypes or "blueprints" for skills like building or medicine</note> in the mind: I say they are equally united and yet so distinct that we can speak according to the pattern of one idea and manufacture something specific to it, even if we do nothing according to the pattern of another conception. These <term>intelligences</term> <note>intelligences: here refers to individual units of understanding or specific concepts</note> cannot be bodies. They remain in the same bosom of the soul in such a way that they neither push each other out nor drive each other away, nor do they confuse themselves through mutual mixing. The same reasoning applies to the moral virtues. Furthermore, since there are many intelligences in the soul of a wise person, each of them is found whole in every part. Indeed, 
<margin>a</margin>
he who is skilled in geometry or theology possesses the first proposition of that faculty, then the second, the third, and the rest. And from the knowledge of one, he proceeds to the knowledge of another. If the first teaches the second, and the second the third, and whoever teaches something possesses within himself what he teaches, it follows that in any preceding proposition all subsequent ones are contained. Moreover, in any subsequent one, the preceding ones are similarly present. Indeed, we are often accustomed to search for the preceding things by the evidence of the following. Nor is this done wrongly. Since the images of causes shine forth in their effects, it happens through this series of things that a wise person, having thought out any single proposition, runs very swiftly into many others. And thus they see many—indeed, all—in one. Therefore, any intelligence is in every other, and each one is contained as a whole in the individual parts. The same happens in the moral virtues. For once one of them is acquired, all are immediately possessed. For who would destroy justly, if he either fears threats or serves lust? Who will bravely overcome fear if he is softened by lust? Who will tame desires if he succumbs to dread? Finally, who will lead an honest life unless, through <term>prudence</term> <note>prudence: the virtue of practical wisdom or right reasoning</note>, he has established the best end of life and chosen the more direct paths to that end? Or who will look upon things prudently if the sharp edge of the mind is clouded by the darkness of vices?

# Book

Therefore, those virtues are so connected to one another that all are in one, and any virtue is grasped as a whole in the individual parts. Just as the entire faculty of geometry lies hidden in its chief proposition—indeed, in any of them—since through the sagacity of a skillful mind, all are drawn out from any single proposition. A divisible quality cannot be present as a whole in many things at once. Certainly, if it is in only one thing—that is, one body—it extends its other parts through the other parts of the body; its entire quantity is not present in the individual parts of the body. Therefore, those intelligences and characters are entirely <term>indivisible</term> <note>indivisible: something that cannot be cut into parts, like the number "one" or a perfect circle in the mind</note>. For this reason, the soul can be neither a body nor a form divided throughout a body, since it is itself the subject of indivisible qualities. Therefore, just as he is delirious who either asks how large science or justice is, or thinks that geometry is smaller than the body of the geometer, so too is he foolish who either asks how large the soul is or thinks it is smaller than the body. For it is in no way corporeal. For it not only receives incorporeal things, but also 
<margin>cII</margin>
makes many things incorporeal within itself, while it conceives the species, reasons, and habits of things, especially when it fashions the definitions of incorporeal things. But who would say that she who is the cause of incorporeal things is herself corporeal? Or that she is mortal, who is the subject of the virtues, since the duty of the virtues is to resist mortal things? For speculative virtue flees those things, and moral virtue puts them to flight. However, a quality cannot resist its own subject. Rather, that must necessarily be immortal which is the natural receptacle of those qualities whose nature it is to oppose and command mortal things. The force of this reason consists mostly in this: that the soul is not only the subject of such qualities, but also their principle <note>original: "principium," meaning the source or origin</note>; therefore, they derive from the soul that nature which resists mortal things.

# Theology, Book Eight

L

[...to] confirm by the opinion of the Arabs <note>referring to medieval Islamic philosophers like Avicenna and Averroes, whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Renaissance debates on the soul</note>. The intellect does not understand a specific thing—for example, a human being—unless it acquires a certain universal form representing humanity, which they call an **intelligible form** and a **species**. Having acquired this, it judges what the nature of a human is: "A human is a rational animal." This judgment is called both a concept and a **conception of the mind**, as well as the essence and definition of the thing to be known. This is also what we are accustomed to call **science** <note>original: "scientiam"; in this context, it means systematic knowledge or certain understanding</note>. 

If the intellect were extended across the breadth of a physical body, then both the intelligible form and the conception would be attached to that physical breadth. In this very breadth, two things must be considered: specifically, a **point** and the **extension** of that breadth. Therefore, the seat of that form and conception would be either a single point of the body or its extension. But if neither can be allowed—as we have demonstrated—it follows that the intellect is not extended within a body at all. 

Let us first show that a point cannot be such a seat. 
<margin>a</margin>
First, it must be noted that a point does not exist by itself; rather, it is so fixed to the measurement of a body that it is always its boundary. If it receives something according to its own nature, it certainly never receives it except as a certain boundary of some magnitude that is contained within that physical measurement of which the point is the boundary. Just as a physical measurement receives the magnitude of an incoming object, so the boundary of that measurement receives the boundary of that magnitude. Therefore, whatever is said to be received by a physical point is not free from magnitude. Thus, if a point were the receptacle of an intelligible form, it would be impossible for that species not to be **divisible**, having its boundary in the physical point and its remaining parts in the breadth of the body. However, we shall prove in what follows that this form is indivisible. 

Furthermore, if it were argued that the point receives that form in such a way that the point alone is its seat and foundation—and that through this, the form remains separate from the breadth of the body—then it would be necessary for the point also to be separated from the 

<margin>c</margin>
breadth. This is especially true since nothing belongs specifically to the <term>accident</term> <note>an "accident" is a quality or property that exists only within a subject, such as color in an apple</note> of a certain subject unless it specifically exists in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "actu"; meaning fully realized existence rather than just potential</note>. Such a point would be separated from the line; it would be neither a part of the line nor the boundary of the breadth. And the line would be bounded by some other point adjacent to this first one. 

Again, that other point would similarly exist in its own right in actuality, by which it too could become a seat for the accidental form, and it too would be separated from the line. This is especially so since the same logic applies to all points. The result would be that there is no point actually in the line—than which nothing is more foolish to say—for the lines would then lack boundaries. Or else, the length of a line would be composed of points, which is a ridiculous thing to say, because a point added to a point does not increase length. 

This is seen by the following logic: if three points are imagined succeeding one another, we shall ask whether that middle point forces the two end points to be so distant from each other that they do not touch one another, or if it does not prevent the end points from meeting. If it forces them to be distant, it certainly does not touch one of them with the same part of itself that it touches the other; otherwise, it would not keep them separate. But if it faces one of the endpoints with one part of itself and the other endpoint with another part, the point itself is made of two parts, and is thus not a point at all, since it would be divisible. 

Therefore, we are forced to admit that a middle point does not prevent the others from meeting. And so all things will be in all things, nor will they produce any length by their meeting, since no interval is recognized between points by means of a middle point. If a physical length is not composed of points, no point is found in it which could ever exist so independently in actuality as to become the subject of an intelligible form. 

Perhaps someone might say that a point is in a body not in **actuality**, but in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to exist or be acted upon, as opposed to "actu" (actuality)</note>, and through that very potentiality, it becomes the subject of the intelligible form. Although that has already been refuted, it is refuted again as follows: Such points—both because they exist only potentially and not actually, and because they are infinite—can in no way be distinguished from one another such that one of them rather than another should receive that form. All...

...and so they receive it. Therefore, the intellect
<margin>A</margin>
would either receive the infinite forms of every thing to be understood simultaneously in act, or it would understand the same thing at infinite points at the same time. Both
<margin>B</margin>
are impossible: both that there are infinite forms in act, and that there are infinite acts of understanding at the same time. Through this, it is manifest that a point of a body cannot be the seat of an **intelligible species** <note>the mental representation or "image" of a concept that allows the mind to recognize a universal truth</note>. But could the very continuation of points, or the extension of a body, be the seat? By no means. For every form that is received in a divisible subject becomes divisible itself, just as the whiteness of snow is divided by the division of the snow. Therefore, if that species is received from the width of a body, it becomes wide and divisible. However, it is impossible for it to become such a thing, which I shall demonstrate as follows. If a species is cut into parts, those parts must be said to be either entirely similar to one another or dissimilar. But neither of these can be admitted. It cannot be admitted that they are entirely similar; for if they are so similar that the complete **ratio** <note>the logical essence or defining principle</note> of the whole species is in any given part—just as the complete ratio of the whole of the water is preserved in individual drops of water—certainly the intellect would behold the whole in any part whatsoever. Thus, one part of the species would suffice for the understanding of the whole thing, and the others would be superfluous. Furthermore, through such a species—which is entirely similar to itself everywhere and deceives the intellect led from there toward knowledge—the judgment of the intellect would be utterly confounded in discerning the parts from the whole, both in any thing constituted of parts and especially in that thing which is composed of various natures. Nor would it be able to discern the parts from the parts, or from the whole. Yet, in truth, the ratio of a part is one thing, as it is a part; the ratio of the whole is another, as it is a whole; and this is always affirmed through the judgment of the mind, since neither the whole itself can be a part, nor the part a whole. Therefore, we think it must be denied that the parts of a species are entirely similar. This is chiefly for the reason that since the mind understands the parts of a thing as they are parts, and understands the whole as it is a whole, and truly distinguishes the whole from the parts, it could not truly distinguish them unless there were some natural distinction within them.

---

It follows that the parts of an **intelligible species** <note>the mental concept</note> must have parts in some way, and they must differ from one another and from the whole by some natural variety. Another reason is added: namely, that parts which are entirely similar to each other and to the whole, when they produce some whole by mutual meeting, do not complete the whole except by an increase in number or magnitude. We see this in grains of wheat and drops of water. For where the form is not varied and yet some change occurs within, an increase or decrease happens there in a certain way. Therefore, if that species of the mind grows together from such parts, it will be some number, or something numerical, either a heap or something continuous. Consequently, through that, we will understand only numbers and numerical things, or certain magnitudes and figures. And the species would belong to the **imagination** and **phantasy** <note>the faculty of the mind that deals with physical images and sensory data</note> rather than to the **mind** <note>the higher intellect</note>.
<margin>B</margin>
From these points, it is concluded that an **intelligible form** <note>the essential concept of a thing</note> is by no means divided into parts that are similar to one another. Perhaps then it is cut into dissimilar parts? Just as the body of an animal is divided into bones, flesh, and nerves? Not at all. For the mind knows what the **substance** <note>the underlying essence</note> of a thing is through this form, as we have said. The substance of a thing is understood most of all by its **definition**. A definition consists of a **genus** and a **difference**; for example, the definition of "man" consists of "animal" and "rational." "Animal" is the **genus** <note>the broad category</note> through which man has something in common with the other animals. "Rational" is the **difference** <note>the specific trait</note> through which he differs from animals lacking reason. Therefore, if there were any diversity of parts in that form, it would be primarily through the genus and the difference. Let these two be, if you wish, the parts of the understanding form. Let them be extended through physical width. Listen to what follows from this. Because the parts of a body can be divided unto infinity, both the genus and the difference will be cut without end along with them. Thus, in one definition, there will be innumerable genera and innumerable differences. Nor will it truly be a definition, because it would not be grasped by the intellect if it were infinite...

...it will neither be bounded by its own limits, nor—what is even more absurd—will we either replicate the same <term>genera</term> <note>the broad categories of being, such as "animal"</note> and the same <term>differences</term> <note>the specific qualities that distinguish a species within a genus, such as "rationality"</note> infinitely, or we will ascend by resolving a genus into a higher genus unto infinity. For true reason finally reaches the primary genera of things and the ultimate differences, beyond which it is not permitted to proceed. Indeed, <term>substance</term> <note>the most basic category of something that exists in itself</note> is the supreme genus in man, which is not resolved into any other genus. This error increases above all others because if a genus and difference exist in a thing, they will be infinite in effect. For those things which lead to the essence of a thing pertain to the natural order; they exist in nature in effect and in reality, and are not merely fashioned by human thought. But nature does not suffer any such multitude to be in the thing itself, or to be innumerable in effect, especially in a body; in which, however, there would be an innumerable multitude if innumerable genera and innumerable differences were cut equally through the parts of the body, for there would be just as many portions of the body itself. Again, we question the
<margin>C</margin>
**Epicureans** <note>materialist philosophers who believed the soul was made of physical atoms</note>, who divide the <term>species</term> <note>the specific definition or "form" of a thing</note> in the intellect just like a form in a body. They place its parts in different locations: one in one part of the mind, for instance, the genus in the right part of the mind and the difference in the left. Why should the right part suit the genus better, and the left the difference? Is not any part of the mind equally "mind"? Otherwise, a mind would be made of mindless parts. Therefore, any small particle of the mind regards both equally: both the genus and the difference. Thus, any part captures both. But if any part receives both, and both are in each part, it follows that they are not separated from one another. But, as the Epicureans want, chance brings it about that one of those two falls on the right and the other on the left. But let them answer us: whether they then remain distinct in this way, or whether they are mixed together? If they grant the first, it follows that knowledge is not born from it. For no <term>definition</term> is made from a genus and difference separated from each other. In neither of those placed apart is perfect knowledge of the thing itself held; it is necessary for them to be joined into one, so that one knowledge of one thing can be held by one mind through one definition at one time. It is certainly necessary for both to be in the whole mind so that they may be truly understood. For what is in a part of the mind is not yet fully understood. For action belongs to the whole thing, not to a part. Therefore, they must confess that those things are mixed. But from where are they mixed? Is it by chance or by the mind? By chance, they say. This is a most wicked thing to say. For such a mixture would happen very rarely; and when it did happen, only then would they concede that those things so united are **incorporeal** <note>original: "incorporalia"; not made of physical matter</note>—which is what we desire. Finally, they will concede that those things are mixed by the mind. From this concession we will immediately infer two things. First, that the mind is incorporeal if it leads the forms it has received into an incorporeal habit, which is an opinion that opposes the Epicureans. Second, that this mixture made by the mind would not otherwise be true unless there were some such union in the things themselves. For what is fashioned by the mind contrary to the nature of things is a fiction rather than knowledge. It is altogether necessary for genera and differences to be joined to one another by nature, or to be disjoined, and not by a fiction of the mind or by physical location. For if it were done by a fiction of the mind, we are in error, not learning. But if it is by location—so that the genus is in the right part of the mind and the difference in the left—surely the mind may resolve these common elements; that
<margin>R</margin>
mind will divide them. By this very division, they will be cut in a bodily manner. And one half of the genus will be left in one half of the right part, and the other half will be left in the other. The same will happen to the difference. It will be possible to divide them again. From this, a tearing apart will follow, not a logical resolution; and while we tear the common elements to pieces, we will destroy knowledge. But if those common elements were not mangled by division, but the genus in any...

Here, the author examines how parts of a concept relate to the whole and critiques the Epicurean materialist view.</meta>

<sig>b.iii.</sig>
-> # Platonic Theology <-

...remaining whole in every part; and similarly, the **difference** <note>the specific quality that distinguishes a species, such as "rationality" for humans</note> will no longer be corporal because they do not require a specific physical quantity. Furthermore, anyone who divides in such a way will find innumerable <term>genera</term> <note>broad categories of being</note> and just as many differences. And the multitude of these things will not exist by nature but will be born from the machinations of the mind.

Perhaps the **Epicureans** <note>followers of Epicurus who believed the soul was made of physical atoms</note>, to avoid these objections, will no longer grant that the **intelligible species** <note>original: "speciem illam intelligibilem"; the mental "image" or concept we have of a thing</note> is composed of a genus and a difference, but of other parts. However, we shall ask: does any part of a species, whatever it may be, differ from the whole species or not? If it does not differ, then it will not truly be a part (since it is the same as the whole), nor will that species be a composite (since it lacks any diversity of parts). Therefore, they must admit that the parts of a species differ from the species itself. 

We, however, will ask them: in what way does it differ? If it is not like a genus or a difference—as we have already shown—perhaps it is like one species differs from another, such as a shape differs from a color? But this cannot be admitted. For such a species does not exist within another species. Shape is not contained under the category of color. Yet a part is within a whole and is contained by it. Perhaps, to prove that this species and mental conception has parts contained under it, they will flee to numbers; they might infer that a species is discerned from its parts just as four is discerned from two, or two from one. Although we have refuted this above, we shall strike it down again thus: do they want those parts of the species—and of the conception they call **knowledge** <note>original: "scientiam"</note>—to be "knowledges" themselves? If they do not, they will be creating knowledge out of ignorance, as if they were trying to construct **whiteness** out of geometric shapes.

<margin>E</margin>If they *do* want them to be knowledges, we argue against them thus: it is well-established among philosophers that any knowledge has its own object; it revolves around something, which they call the "known." Let them explain to us: if those knowledges which are parts of a single knowledge must not lack an object, is the specific "known" thing of each part the same as the "known" thing of the whole, or is it something else? If they answer that it is the same, then none of those will be a part, but each will be the whole, since it is equal to the whole. For where the objects of study are equal, the knowledges are also equal. But if they admit it is something else, then this absurdity follows: that the knowledge of the whole "known" thing will exist apart from the knowledge of the parts, and the whole will not be known from the cognition of the parts, since the individual knowledges do not converge into a universal knowledge.

Furthermore, let us proceed again. The mind, for the most part, understands the **reason** <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning the essential definition or blueprint</note> of things as something single and universal—for example, **goodness** itself, which is equally common to many good things. This kind of reason, insofar as it is one and universal, is also simple. Likewise, the "reason" of God or an angel, whenever it is truly known, is judged to be indivisible. These are called **intelligible essences** <note>realities that can only be grasped by the intellect, not the senses</note>. Our mind would never know them unless it held their forms within itself like images. For if the mind performs an act in the process of knowing, it cannot act unless it is "in act" <note>active or realized</note>, and it only acts in the way that it is "in act." It becomes active through a **form**. Thus, it never contemplates essences unless it is adorned with the forms of those very essences. 

Such forms, although they are sometimes called "intelligible," ought more properly to be called **intellectual**, while the essences themselves are called **intelligible**. This is the custom of the ancient **Platonists**. If such a form—an image of such an essence—were scattered into parts in our mind, then those parts would either be such that none of them relates to the essence itself, or some would relate to it and others would not, or all of them would. If the first is granted, then the whole form will not relate to the essence in any way, since there is no relationship in the parts. For just as the whole form consists of parts, so the relationship of the whole is gathered from the relationships of the parts. If it does not look toward the essences at all, it will not be their image, nor will it contribute to the understanding of them. If the second is granted, then the part which does not relate to the essence has nothing to do with the **intellectual form**, since it does not look toward the **intelligible essence**. But if the third is conceded, we shall immediately ask: does each part have the same outlook, or do different parts have different outlooks?

If it is answered that they <note>the parts of the mental image</note> possess the same [essence]: they cannot possess the same essence except if each part represents the essence in its entirety. Certainly, no part of them would then be a part of the intellectual form; rather, any one of them would be the whole. One part would suffice for the act of knowing. The others would be superfluous—and indeed, they would be infinite in actual number if they were cut by the division of a physical body—and they would contribute nothing further to the action of the mind. 
<margin>28</margin> If, however, they were to have one aspect and then another—and this cannot happen unless individual parts of the form gaze upon just as many parts of the essence—it would follow (since the intellectual must be equal to the thing being understood) that the essence itself is divisible. Yet, true reason concluded that essence is simple <note>original: "simplicem"; in philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts, indivisible</note>. 
<margin>B</margin> The mind could not judge the essence to be simple unless it intuited it with a simple gaze. With a manifold gaze directed at diverse parts, it would instead judge the essence to be manifold. We believe that they <note>likely the Epicureans or other materialists</note> 
<margin>29</margin> fell into this error because they observed that certain sciences deal with composite things. Such is the science of **man**, who is composed of **animal** and **rational**, as if from his <term>genus</term> <note>the broad category, like "animal"</note> and <term>difference</term> <note>the specific trait that sets a species apart, like "rationality"</note>. Such is the science of the **septenary** <note>the number seven</note> and the **denary** <note>the number ten</note> and other numbers, which are gathered from numbers or units. 

We, however, believe that a man, insofar as he is a man, is a single and simple thing, because his form <note>his essential nature</note> is one. The proof of this is that he is not divided into multiple "men." For whether you divide him according to his species into genus and difference, neither of those is a "man." Or whether you divide him according to his individual parts into head, chest, and thigh, none of those is a "man." You may indeed cut the body, because you tear it into limbs, which are themselves bodies. But you do not cut the "man," because you do not cut him into "men." Whatever is such a thing in itself, and is not divided into several such things, is certainly—insofar as it is that thing—indivisible and simple. 

The **denary** <note>the number ten</note> likewise, insofar as it is the denary, is not divided. It is exactly one species and one form, which we cannot partition into several "tens." If we do partition it, we partition the number (because we divide it into other numbers), but we do not partition the "ten-ness," because we do not distribute it into multiple "tens." 

Nor is it an obstacle that the genus and the difference seem to be included in the species. For there are not two forms in the species, but only one. For although "being an animal" is one thing in the order of nature and "being rational" is another, in a human being they are the same. And (to speak in the Platonic manner) the very nature of man is a certain **rationality**. 
<margin>C</margin> Rationality, moreover, is nothing else in a man than **animality** 
<margin>D</margin> itself brought forth into the act of reason. Such a simple form is the foundation of a simple being: a species that does not scatter itself into individual men, but communicates itself as a whole to each individual; through this form, individuals are "one." They differ, however, through other things that are added externally and do not belong to the species at all. This indeed signifies the simplicity of the species—as does the fact that a species does not admit of "more" or "less." It stands at a certain fixed degree of nature, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away without the species itself changing. 

The species of numbers testify to this. The **septenary** <note>the number seven</note> is a certain species of number. Add one to it, and you will create a new species, namely the **octonary** <note>the number eight</note>. Subtract one, and you have the **senary** <note>the number six</note>, a new species of number again. Since true science is not properly about individuals or genera, but about species—for individuals are innumerable and ever-changing, and can neither be fully grasped nor held firmly; and genera are not perfectly discerned in themselves due to their confusion—I say, since science is about species, and species are simple, then science of them is also simple, provided that science is the attainment of truth. Truth is the alignment <note>original: "adequatio"</note> of things with minds. 
<margin>E</margin> Let neither the multitude of words nor the variety of manifold thoughts disturb us, from which science might seem to be composed. These are merely preparations for science, or its attendants. The act of science—or its habitual state—is unique. It is, I say, a simple touch of a simple form. An indivisible intuition of indivisible truth. A sudden light of intelligence. 
<margin>F</margin> But their error is even more evidently refuted by the fact that there are many sciences concerning things that are undoubtedly indivisible. Who would not divide unity? Who likewise [would not divide] simplicity, and...

Having previously established that if the mind were a physical body, it would be divisible and thus unable to grasp unified truths, he now invokes Plotinus and begins his sixth major reason for the soul's immortality.</meta>

<sig>I 3</sig>

<margin>a</margin> ...will know. It will apply parts that are, in a certain sense, infinite. For the mind would have parts if a physical width existed within it. Thus, in a short time, it would understand any portion of that body in an almost innumerable way; and it would apprehend the body itself according to its nearly infinite particles, known innumerably, through what I might call infinite turns.

<margin>b</margin> ¶ But let us briefly conclude this argument with a certain noble thought of our Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino regarded as the primary interpreter of Plato.</note>. Whatever things are understood are either <term>simple</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "simple" (simplex) means something that is not made of parts, being indivisible and pure.</note> by their very nature, or at least they are understood when they become simple through the process of resolution <note>Resolution is the logical process of breaking a complex idea down into its most basic, indivisible components.</note>.

<margin>c</margin> ¶ Because, in truth, indivisible things are captured only by things that are themselves indivisible, that power within us which captures such things must be indivisible. If, therefore, the mind is said to be bodily, it will not capture those things by its width, but rather by something <term>impartible</term> <note>original: "impartibili"; something that cannot be divided into parts.</note>. If it captures by this alone, it understands by this alone. Only this impartible [element], then, will truly be the mind. What need is there for the remaining parts for it to be the intellect? Since other parts are not necessary for the act of understanding once that one impartible thing suffices.

<margin>d</margin> ¶ This one thing, then, is the mind; hold fast to this. Separate all the rest, and you have thereby attained the simple mind. Its simplicity is also apparent from this: that it accepts a point without length, a line without width, a surface without depth, numbers without physical position, and beauty without any mixture of ugliness. For it discerns these things separately through consideration, nor does it consider them otherwise than it receives them. However, a bodily form does not receive these things separately in such a way.

<margin>e</margin> ¶ If it clearly shows that the soul is simple and indivisible because it comprehends simple and indivisible things, it declares this much more clearly: that whatever things might be simple or indivisible in themselves, yet because they are joined with others, they turn out to be composite and divisible, the soul separates them from their opposites and renders them entirely simple and indivisible. It could not restore a simple and indivisible nature to them unless it were itself simple and indivisible. Finally, if it restores purity to things that are stained <note>original: "infectis"; referring to things "infected" or "stained" by their immersion in material, divisible bodies.</note>, the soul itself is outside and above the stain.

---

<margin>C</margin> ### Sixth reason.
The intellect receives whatever it captures according to its whole self, which it would not do if it were bodily.

<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
# **N**o body contains anything in itself except through that equality of quantity by which it, as a whole, encompasses the whole thing, and part to part. And with its larger part, it contains a larger part of the thing contained; with a smaller part, a smaller. The intellect does not capture things in this way. For it captures whatever it receives as a whole. Indeed, it captures in the same way it understands. But it understands whatever it understands as a whole. To be sure, if someone says that the intellect has two bodily parts, one of which captures and understands a thing while the other does not, we will refute him by asserting that the intellect is truly only that part which captures and understands the thing. Indeed, the "intellect" is named from the act of "understanding." That which does not understand is not the intellect. Therefore, that nature which is truly the intellect captures and knows as a whole whatever is to be understood. If, therefore, it understands a human body, it understands the members of that body as well; it knows the whole human body as a whole, and it knows any one of its members as a whole. For he who compares any member to another, and refers any members to the whole, must necessarily know the individual members just as he knows the whole body. Nor should you posit two parts in the intellect, one of which knows one member and the other another. For that comparison could be made through neither of them. If it captures just as it knows, it certainly captures both the whole body and the individual members of the body as a whole. No body, however, and no bodily form can capture something in this way. Nor can one body be made equal to all bodies alike. How will the body of a dog be equaled to the body of an ant, a horse, an elephant, or the sun? But the mind is equalized to all bodies, both the greatest and the smallest, since it comprehends all things similarly by understanding them. Nor is it [equal] to these alone, but also, in a certain way, it equals itself to the highest equality. While it perceives all things as more or less equal through their approach [to equality]...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind must be indivisible because it can grasp concepts that have no physical dimensions, such as points or mathematical numbers. He also posits that the mind perceives things as a whole rather than as a collection of physical parts, proving it is not a material body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book 8. Having argued that the mind is indivisible because it can grasp indivisible truths, Ficino now moves through his seventh, eighth, and ninth proofs for the immortality and incorporeal nature of the soul.</meta>

...rightly measures according to the highest equality. In this state, the mind places itself as a middle point between any two things and equality itself, the ruler of things. Because if things are made most nearly equal to the highest equality, they are not struck by any of the injustice <note>In this context, "injustice" (iniquitate) refers to a lack of mathematical or philosophical proportion or "unevenness."</note> found in unequal qualities.

<margin>B</margin>
# ¶ Seventh Reason. The intellect, in receiving the forms of things, does not lose its own; bodies, on the contrary, do. Chapter 7.

Bodies are accustomed to lose their own forms when they receive the forms of other bodies. For how would water take on the heat of fire unless it cast off its own coldness? But if the original form remains when a foreign one is received, an imperfection occurs: as when sweetness remains in wine, even the water poured into it becomes sweet, and the flavor is thereby made weaker. The Mind, however, receives the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas"; in Platonic philosophy, a "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> of all things while it recognizes them all and revolves these known things within itself; yet by receiving them, it does not lose or weaken its own form. Indeed, since a habit of form is always designated by its operation, and the operation of the intellect is intelligence, it follows that the form of the intellect is itself—if I may put it this way—a natural <term>intellectuality</term> <note>original: "intellectualitas naturalis"</note>. This is judged to be most perfect when its operation, intelligence, is most perfect. Furthermore, it is not less perfect the more forms of things it touches. Rather, it becomes more sublime, faster, and clearer. For this reason, the intellect, by receiving the forms of all bodies, not only does not lose or diminish its own, but—contrary to the nature of a body—it is perfected to the highest degree. It penetrates their substances and perceives all things within individual things; while in simple things it sees mixtures through composition, in mixed things it beholds simple things through resolution. Therefore, the mind is seen to be in all things in such a way that it is all things within each individual thing. Again, it is outside and above all corporeal things. Otherwise, it would not be able to separate these from incorporeal things, nor discern those from these. If it is in all corporeal things, it is all things; and being also outside all things, it rules all things by its nature. Therefore, it is cast down from its state by the violence of no body.

---

<margin>C</margin>
# ¶ Eighth Reason. Form is universal in the mind. Such a thing cannot exist in a body. Chapter 8.

<margin>C</margin>
The body and the form extended through the body are so—to speak thus—material and bound to a particular site and time that they have no universal power. For the closer a thing approaches to corporeal matter, the narrower it is; the further it departs, the more ample it becomes. Therefore, if the intellect were a body, or a form diffused through a body, all forms received by it—even if they were universal in themselves—would turn out to be entirely particular and material within it. For forms in a subject <note>A "subject" is the thing in which a quality or form exists.</note> that is bound by the passions of matter have no power to represent anything universal. Thus, the intellect would think of whatever it considered through a material form, bound by singular conditions. Since, truly, the operation of any thing follows the form of the thing operating, the intellect operating—that is, thinking—through such a form would operate only in a singular way. Moreover, as the operation is, such is always the work. Therefore, the intellect thinking in a singular way would think only of <term>singulars</term> <note>A "singular" is a specific, individual object (like "this specific dog"), whereas a "universal" is a general category (like "the concept of a dog").</note>; it would not know anything common or universal. It would revolve in itself one man—say, Socrates or Plato—but it would not at all recognize the human nature common to them both. Nor would it establish universal rules in morals and arts for many things, nor would it ever establish a law regarding the many acts of men. If the mind, without choice and by daily use, produces universal forms within itself, it follows that the mind itself is their natural source and natural receptacle. Forms of this kind are not at all bound to any specific matter; therefore, the mind is neither bound to matter nor will it ever be destroyed. For corruption <note>Ficino uses "corruption" to mean the process of breaking down, decaying, or dying.</note> proceeds from the traps of matter.

<margin>E</margin>
# ¶ Ninth Reason. Minds embrace one another; bodies by no means do. Chapter 9.

<margin>F</margin>
Where corporeal things are concerned, they cannot contain one another in a mutual embrace. For that which contains another by way of quantity is larger than that which is contained. One body cannot be simultaneously larger and narrower than another single body. Thus the sphere of Saturn surrounds and contains the sphere of Jupiter, but not vice versa. Other...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino presents three arguments (7-9) for the soul's immortality, emphasizing that the mind is perfected by knowledge rather than changed by it, and that the mind's ability to grasp universal concepts proves it is not a physical, material entity.</summary>

--- Page 190 ---
<meta>This page continues the Eighth Book of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology. Following the previous discussion on the intellect's ability to measure equality, Ficino concludes his ninth argument regarding how minds contain one another and begins his tenth argument, focusing on why the mind must be incorporeal because its operations transcend the limits of physical bodies.</meta>

...one mind contains another: and is equally contained by the same. <margin>A</margin> My mind indeed considers yours; yours considers mine. Thus our minds, by considering each other in turn, capture each other; by capturing, they understand; they embrace by understanding. And what is greater: one mind embraces all, when it considers the nature of all minds. Therefore, if any mind gazes upon any mind—which it can certainly do if it turns its attention—any mind is enclosed by any other mind. But any body cannot be enclosed by any other body. If any species of things is immortal, it follows that a singular substance, which equates itself to its own species, is immortal. But any mind, if it happens to, looks within any other, and in individuals, it perceives the species of all things. In this, through a <term>reflexive act</term> <note>original: "actum reflexum"; the mind's ability to turn back on itself to contemplate its own nature or the concepts it holds.</note>, which is cognition, it equates itself to its own species. Therefore, also through a <term>direct act</term> <note>original: "actum rectum"; the primary, outgoing activity of a thing's life.</note>, which is life, it previously equated itself to the same. If this is so, it follows that any mind has always been, or will be, just like the species of minds itself; or at least it will be forever, as that is.

<margin>B</margin>
# Tenth reason. The mind operates through all bodies, and above bodies. Chapter 10.

**S**ince the form of acting is the principle, each thing acts according to its own kind; from which all things can, in their own way, generate offspring similar to themselves in species. But nothing acts beyond its own kind. Nor indeed do these lower things operate beyond their species. A dog never generates a sheep, and much less do they operate in any way above their own species. For how would a dog procreate a human? Thus it happens that a body cannot extend its power of acting beyond its own kind, and much less above its own nature. Therefore, it will never reach, attain, or produce either any body [as a whole] or incorporeal things. 

If the intellect were a body, it would certainly be a specific body within some species of bodies. From this, two absurdities would follow. First: that it would neither receive nor conceive the forms of many bodies. It would not receive the forms of bodies similar to itself, since it would already have them. For how would fire receive the form of another fire? It would by no means conceive or give birth to the forms of dissimilar bodies. For any nature gives birth to what is similar to itself. To understand this, however, it is necessary that it first receive the form of the thing to be understood. Then from that, it must conceive the definition or the reason of the thing. Only then is intellection perfected. 

Therefore, the intellect would know very few bodies if it were a body, since it could receive the form of no similar body and conceive the form of no dissimilar body, and it cannot understand unless it both receives and conceives equally. But if it could somehow happen that a corporeal thing receives or conceives any form, it would surely effect this in no other way than according to its own nature. If it receives a form from elsewhere, it will pull it into its own nature. If it conceives from itself, it will give birth according to its own nature. Therefore, through any form received by it, or even conceived, it would always apprehend a certain specific type of body suitable and congruent to itself, and it would not consider the diversity of corporeal kinds. But from this we see that the mind not only notices whatever bodies exist, but also imagines infinitely more and varied ones as it pleases. 

<margin>G</margin> The second absurdity would follow if the intellect were a body: namely, that it would not transcend the order of bodies. Since bodies almost never operate beyond their species, and certainly never above their kind. Therefore, the mind would never know incorporeal things. Which of these do you judge to be more excellent? The substance? or the action? The substance, certainly, which is the cause of the action itself. We must take care, therefore, that we do not at some point admit the operation to be more sublime than the substance. But the operation of the mind would be more sublime than its substance if its substance were merely a certain body, while its intelligence comprehended both every body and incorporeal things. Therefore, it is not a body, since it apprehends even incorporeal things beyond any bodies. And yet, it is also not a form mixed with a body; for just as a mixed form becomes divisible through the division of the body, so it becomes whatever sort it is through the quality of the body. Therefore, the mind would contract to itself a certain quality from the body—

<sig>J 4</sig>

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind's ability to encompass all other minds and grasp incorporeal truths proves it is not a physical body. If the intellect were material, it would be limited to its own specific physical nature and unable to perceive the infinite variety of forms and non-physical realities it clearly understands.</summary>
