[...cor]poreal [organ] through which it would be determined toward a specific kind of physical things: so that it would only know a specific kind of physical things, just as sight is drawn toward colors through the eye. And it would not grasp forms most similar to itself—as we have said—nor those most dissimilar. And this opinion of Aristotle is approved by the Platonists. But the Platonists add that if the mind were mixed with the body, it would neither grasp incorporeal things—because that which is mixed does not comprehend pure things—nor would it desire to reach anything separated from the body. Otherwise, it would desire to be separated from the body and dissolved. Nor would it know in any other way than by being moved, as is the habit of material power. But now, it does not act as it is moved, but as it produces species for itself; thus it abstracts, it discourses, and it reflects itself into itself as if without end. Nor should any **Epicurean** <note>original: "epicureus"; a follower of Epicurus. In Ficino's time, Epicureans were often criticized for believing the soul was material and died with the body.</note> noise in our ears here, denying that the intellect grasps incorporeal things. Indeed, it always desires those things and grasps only those with the greatest pleasure, as being most similar to itself. Nor does it only desire and grasp those things, but it also produces them. For what else are we striving for now in these disputations, if not to fashion with the "hands of our mind" (so to speak) some thing most foreign to the body? Which we have already fashioned, and are fashioning, and handle with those very hands of the mind. And before we fashioned it, we foresaw it was to be fashioned. Surely, when we first determined to show the soul to be <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "incorporealem"; meaning it has no physical body or mass.</note>, we already saw somewhere some level of incorporeal nature to which we wished to lead the soul. What do we do daily in disputing? As often as we asserted some thing to be, which indeed exists, but has no length, width, depth, or any quality or figure. Then we certainly create a certain spirit with the mind above the body and the passions of the body. There indeed our mind is, where it gives birth; it gives birth, I say, to an offspring very like itself, in no way more sublime than its own substance. Therefore our mind towers over bodies and the conditions of bodies. For which reason it is neither closed by place, nor circumscribed by the limits of time. Therefore it can be everywhere and always. For that reason, nothing prevents it from being eternal.

---

### ¶ Eleventh reason. The mind progresses by standing still, the body by motion. Chapter 10.

<sig>B</sig>
**N**ever does a body receive a new form except through motion. For through alteration (as the physicists say) form is induced into matter. The mind, however, neither receives forms through motion, nor is it moved in receiving them. Indeed, the more it acts in rest from all motion of disturbances and business, the more it progresses in <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "speculando"; the intellectual act of "seeing" or meditating on truth.</note>. Where also its eternity appears: because by its own nature it desires only the contemplation of truth, and thus a state of rest, without which contemplation is not perfected. But the body progresses by motion, because it is born through motion. Therefore, what progresses by standing still depends on rest. And thus it has a stable and perpetual substance.

### ¶ Twelfth reason. Things that are opposites in matter are not opposites in the mind. Chapter 12.

<sig>C</sig>
**T**he forms of opposite elements, which are in matter, are contrary among themselves, as they drive each other out and destroy one another. In the mind, they are not contrary. Because there, not only do they not drive each other out, but they also help each other; for indeed our mind holds the forms of opposite elements, since it considers the elements at the same time. It also simultaneously comprehends good and evil, useful and useless, beautiful and deformed, light and darkness, voice and silence, sweet and bitter, and the rest. And from the knowledge of one opposite, it judges the other more inwardly. Therefore, it is not corporeal. <margin><sig>D</sig></margin> Nor is it properly corruptible. For that which decays, for the most part, decays because of its opposite. But what can be contrary to the mind? Which has such great power over opposites that it takes away their contrariety and reconciles enemies into its own peace. Nor, again, is it corruptible since it would be separated from its preservers. For if it reconciles foreign and opposite things to foreign and opposite things, much more does it move itself toward its own causes and preservers.

### ¶ Thirteenth reason. The mind is not changed by receiving forms. Chapter 13.

<sig>E</sig>
**S**ince the form of any body is received from another body, it makes it entirely such...

Here, Ficino continues to argue for the mind's incorporeal nature by showing it can grasp opposites and move beyond time and space.</meta>

[...] the thing which receives it becomes like the body from which the form is given. <note>original: "illud quod suscipit ipsum quale est corpus illud a quo forma tribuitur"</note> Just as when a flame of fire is received from wood: it makes the wood hot and fiery. But that flame, shining in a distant mirror, does not make the mirror hot or fiery; for it does not truly receive from the flame, since due to the distance it is not prepared for the true flame of fire. Indeed, that little flame—that is, the image of the flame—since it is spiritual, is not fixed in the body of the mirror, but in the spiritual light of the sun, which surrounds the surface of the mirror. <note>Ficino uses "spiritual" here in the philosophical sense of "incorporeal" or "non-physical," rather than strictly religious.</note> Furthermore, images of such things are not made by these bodies whose images they are. For a body does not create anything incorporeal; rather, they are made by the spiritual light poured around the bodies. This light itself is not born from the globe of the sun, but from the sun's soul. Although its light is invisible within itself, when poured out further it becomes visible, in which the soul itself also becomes conspicuous. For, as it pleases the **Orphics** <note>Followers of the legendary poet Orpheus, associated with mystical teachings.</note> and **Heraclitus**, light is nothing other than visible soul; hence, all things come back to life through this. But the soul is invisible light. 

But let us not wander too far: forms or images of bodies are not in the mirror. <margin>e</margin> For when the mind receives the forms of all bodies, when it judges concerning bodies, does it not receive them truly? Certainly, for as it receives, so it judges. It certainly judges; therefore, it certainly receives. It receives from itself (as the Platonists arrange it) when, excited by the likenesses of bodies, it brings into the light those forms which lie hidden at the entrance of the mind. <note>This refers to the Platonic theory of "innate ideas," suggesting the mind already contains the "blueprints" of reality and only needs external stimuli to remember them.</note> It follows that where a form is more perfect, it is also more true. We have declared elsewhere, and will declare again, how much more perfect the form of bodies is in the mind than in the bodies themselves; and it is clear from this: that human nature in **Plato** or **Socrates** belongs only to Plato and only to Socrates. <margin>f</margin> But that human nature which is conceived by the mind, when it considers the conditions of men under a single definition of "man," has power over all individual men, since it encompasses all. 

Furthermore, if the truth of any thing consists in its pure integrity—or integral purity—and a form in matter does not retain its integral power because of the mixture of suffering <note>original: "passio"; here meaning the state of being acted upon or modified by external factors.</note> and is surrounded by external accidents, then every thing is found more truly in the mind. There, the <term>Idea</term> <note>The perfect, eternal pattern of a thing existing in the mind or a higher reality.</note> of the thing, naturally implanted, produces a notion of the thing, including all that is necessary while entirely excluding all that is superfluous. Therefore, the mind captures the forms of bodies so truly that it possesses them even more truly than the matter of the bodies does. 

Therefore, if the mind were something corporeal, it would be rendered entirely like physical bodies. If it were water, it would be water when it understands water; and fire when it understands fire. And because it understands color and cold at the same time, it would become opposites simultaneously. Yet now it receives the forms of all things and is not cast down from its own state; rather, it is perfected by receiving them. From this, it appears that the intellect is not corporeal. <margin>f</margin> It appears that it is not mortal. 

Indeed, the mind receives whatever it receives in the same manner in which it exists. Its being is intellectual as long as it lasts. Therefore, it does not receive anything except in the manner of understanding. Through this kind of reception, it not only does not fail, but actually progresses. It receives nothing from elsewhere that might change or destroy it; what is more, it gains so much in receiving all forms that it even seems to gain from evil things. If it turns out to be more perfect the more things it knows, then it is certainly more perfect if it discerns the changes, defects, and evils of things than if it were ignorant of them. Therefore, those things which are evil and harmful in themselves are good and healthy in the mind; so far is that nature from being destroyed by evil and harmful things, that it converts evils into goods such that all things are good to it.

<margin>g</margin> ### Fourteenth Reason: The operation of the body tends toward composite things; the mind’s toward simple things.
### Book 8, chapter 14.

<margin>h</margin> The operation of any thing always follows the "being" of that thing, so that the operation belongs to the one whose being it is; and the mode of acting is the same as the mode of being; and the work which the operation completes is similar to the one who acts. In things composed of matter and corporeal form, "being" does not belong properly to the matter or the form, but to the whole <term>composite</term> <note>A thing made of multiple parts; here, the union of a physical body and a soul.</note> created from the union of both. Therefore, the operation also belongs to the composite itself. For this reason, it acts in a composite way and produces a composite work. We observe this in elements, plants, and animals, which produce composite works just as they themselves are. If the intellect were some body composed of matter and form, since its operation is intelligence, this intelligence itself...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind must be incorporeal because it can hold universal truths and contradictory concepts (like fire and water) simultaneously without being destroyed. He concludes that the mind's ability to turn the knowledge of "evil" into a "good" (understanding) proves its immortality and superior nature over physical matter.</summary>

<header>Book on Platonic [Theology]</header>

[...the mind] would always terminate in something composite. Whence it would never understand anything except composite things. But in truth, our mind so greatly excels natural composition that it resolves composite bodies into matter and form, and thinks of each separately. Yet each of these, by itself, is simple. And in this especially its excellence is seen: that those things which in matter are in some way false, it grasps as true—such as geometric figures and the principles of figures. Those things which are impure in matter, it discerns as pure. <margin>13</margin> For qualities which are mixed together in matter and infected by their opposites, the mind judges by their own proper definitions <term>rationes</term> <note>original: "rationes"; here referring to the essential, rational structures or archetypes of things.</note>. Things which are many in themselves, it beholds as if they were one—as when it sees infinite individual men under a single species. Those things which are mobile in themselves, it contemplates as stable; for it collects together the parts of time which flow within themselves, and joins the past and the future to the present. Those things which are distant in themselves, it very often looks upon as if united, since it sees the whole world in a single point. Neither the intervals of time nor the spaces of place restrain the mind's gaze. It treats things which are (so to speak) dead as if they were living. Indeed, the mind possesses stones, which lack life, as living things within itself, because it relates them to that primary Life from which they were made. It treats corruptible things as if they were perpetual, because by its own gaze it exempts from place and time those individual bodies which are subject to place and time. From all these points, it is gathered that the intellect is not a corporeal thing—since it operates far differently than bodies—nor is it impure, infected, dispersed, mutable, or corruptible. Especially since, by its own power, it frees even those things which are of such a nature from these kinds of sufferings <term>passiones</term> <note>original: "passiones"; in classical philosophy, this refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing change from an external force.</note>.

# Fifteenth Reason. The action of the mind ends in action; the action of the body ends in a body.

## Chapter ->XV.<-

<sig>a</sig> <margin>a</margin> **N**o action of a body properly ends in the action itself, but rather passes over into external matter. For if it were to end in the action, that action would remain within the one performing it, where it would operate upon itself; for example, fire would heat itself. This cannot be done by a body. Because if a body does not act from itself, it also does not act upon itself. Again, if whatever a body does, it does by moving, then certainly—since it is denied that a body moves itself—it cannot act upon itself. However, we see that the operation of the mind itself—namely, the act of understanding—ends in itself, and does not of itself do anything externally, unless perhaps it sometimes moves the will; then, when the arms are moved, the will produces some work outside <margin>13</margin> such as had been first conceived in thought. But we say that the senses, in a certain way, flow outside themselves. Because the sense is moved from elsewhere, it looks at things belonging to another. It operates for the sake of an external goal, nor is it conscious of itself. The mind, on the contrary, moves itself freely and inspects its own contents. It operates for its own sake. Therefore, in Plato's view, essence is called a "statue" <note>Ficino refers to the stable, foundational nature of "Being" or "Essence," which remains fixed like a statue until enlivened.</note>, because if it were without life, it would be sluggish. Life is motion, since it is then in a state of act. Mind is reflection, because without this life <margin>z</margin> it would flow out into an external work. But the mind, just as it contains the vital motion of essence within itself, reflects that motion back into the essence through a certain self-awareness <term>animadversione</term>. It also draws all other things to itself, considering them more as the mind itself is, rather than as the things exist outside. This is also called "infinite reflection," because the human mind is not terminated in its operation just once, but truly in innumerable ways: as when it notices that it understands something, and then recognizes that it notices. And when it wants to will something, and wants that it wills, and wants to will that it wills, and so on by the same reasoning. In this process, either one operation is terminated by another infinitely, or the same operation is folded back upon itself innumerably. From this it is clear <note>original: "pȝ" (patet)</note> that the intellect is not only incorporeal but also immortal. For indeed, through itself and its own operation, it always forms itself and always perfects itself by understanding and willing. This, moreover, is nothing other than to either make, preserve, or renew itself continually; which indeed the Apostle Paul called by the name "daily renewal" <note>referring to 2 Corinthians 4:16.</note>. Thus it happens that the mind never falls away or is distant from its own perfecter or preserver, since it can never be absent from itself; and therefore it is always being formed and perfected. Furthermore, if the goal of natural generation is a certain kind of immortality, much more so is immortality the goal of intellectual generation <margin>C</margin>. But because nature especially begets outside itself, its immortality is fulfilled in succession <note>i.e., through the survival of the species via offspring rather than the individual.</note>...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind's ability to abstract pure forms from messy matter and its capacity for self-reflective thought (infinite reflection) prove it is a spiritual, self-sustaining, and immortal entity. Unlike physical bodies that act on external things, the mind acts upon itself, allowing for a continuous "daily renewal" of its own being.</summary>

<header>Theology: Book Nine</header>

...birth. Because the mind truly generates within itself—both itself and other things—since it conceives the underlying reasons <term>rationes</term> <note>original: "rationes"; in Platonic thought, these are the rational blueprints or archetypes of things.</note> of both itself and all other things whenever it understands itself or others, it follows that by the immortality of this power, it preserves itself in the mind which is its own generator. <margin>D</margin> In this there also lies hidden a certain argument of this kind: It is more excellent to *be well* than simply *to be*. Therefore, whatever provides "well-being" to itself is much more able to provide "being" to itself. The intellect is seen to give well-being to itself when it forms itself through its own creative shaping <note>original: "fictitiam"; referring to the mind's power to "fashion" its own intellectual and moral character.</note>, both in contemplation and in morals. Therefore, it can also provide being to itself according to its form in such a way that it never ceases to exist. <margin>E</margin> I set aside what he says without doubt: for since the mind is the principle of its own generation, it so generates and vivifies itself that it possesses its essence from itself. In short, concerning every indivisible substance existing in its own essence, he affirms that it both produces and contains itself. However, concerning every divisible substance and even the heavens themselves, he says they are necessarily produced and contained from elsewhere. But let him [Plato] see to that. Besides, another argument of this sort lies hidden: When the intellect comprehends and loves its own operation first, and thereafter its own power and substance, then it undoubtedly acts upon itself. Therefore, it acts through itself. For nothing—not even the intellect itself—is placed as a medium between them. Add that just as the body, because it does not act from itself, therefore does not operate within itself, <margin>a</margin> so the intellect, because it operates within itself, is therefore judged to operate from itself. If it acts from itself upon itself, then it also acts through itself. For if both ends of the action are within it, then the middle point is also there. What, then, prevents the intellect, when separated from the body, from operating and living? Especially since its operation—which is fulfilled from itself, upon itself, and through itself—necessarily occurs and resides within itself. But this will be explained more clearly as follows: If the operation of the mind is properly terminated in the mind itself, the mind itself is in some way the goal of its own operation. Indeed, the goal <note>original: "finis"; meaning the "end" or purpose.</note> of every thing is the same as its principle <note>original: "principium"; the source or starting point.</note>, since all things desire their own origin and set it before themselves as the goal of their motion. <margin>f</margin> Therefore, the substance of the mind is the principle of its own operation. Therefore, it operates through itself. This is what our Plato calls "to be moved by itself." As it operates, so it lives. For life is an interior operation. It lives, therefore, through itself. As it lives, so it also *is*. For "to be" is the first act of existence. And therefore, similarly, it exists through itself. What hinders it from existing forever, seeing as it is its own cause? A cause, I say, not an efficient cause <note>A cause that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a chair.</note>, but a formal cause <term>causa formalis</term> <note>The essential nature or pattern of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>, by whose power being is granted and preserved. A quality or a life whose entire operation flows out into other things necessarily fails in four ways according to its nature. First, because by flowing out it wavers and requires external support. Second, by spreading out it is weakened. Third, while it flows into other things it is defiled by foreign elements. Fourth, because of need, weakness, and defilement, it is sometimes forced to fall away from its nature. If this is so, it follows that the rational life which flows back into itself sustains itself, is not weakened, is not defiled, and does not fall away. Justly, as life which is forced to flow entirely outside of itself tends toward and is consumed by death as it departs from life; so life which overflows back into itself matures and is perfected into life. Finally, if a more abundant motion is a sign of a more abundant life, the rational life—which exercises, fulfills, and terminates every kind of motion—also fulfills every kind of living. And therefore, neither the privation of life nor any condition subject to death is mixed with it. But we have declared elsewhere that the mind exercises all species of motion in the body, fulfills the archetypes of all motions in itself, and terminates all motion in itself and its own principle through the reflections of the mind itself.

# Theology: Book Eight

...born power: insofar as it works equally upon all things. This also seems to me to demonstrate the infinite power of the mind (so to speak) above all else: that it happens upon infinity itself; it defines what it is and of what quality it is. Since cognition is perfected through a certain balancing <note>original: "equationem"; the Scholastic idea that truth is the "equation" or correspondence of the mind to the thing known.</note> of the mind with things, the mind is equated in some way to the infinity of the thing known. However, that which is equated to the infinite must itself be infinite. And if time, which measures motion by a certain succession, must be infinite if motion were infinite, how much more must the mind be infinite, which measures not only motion and time in a stable state <note>original: "stabili natiõe"; suggesting the mind stands still to measure things that are moving.</note>, but also measures infinity itself. 

<margin>C</margin>
For it is necessary that the measure have a proportion to that which it measures. But there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. This is also clearly shown from the fact that the mind passes from considering non-being into being, and vice versa. Now, being and non-being are separated from each other by an immense interval. Indeed, the power that traverses an immense space must itself be immense. Moreover, the mind performs that "running" whenever we comprehend, with the most certain reasons, creation—which happens from non-being to being—and destruction—which happens in the opposite direction. And we describe the nature of both extremes, and by the intellect we attain the power of being itself <term>esse commune</term> <note>original: "esse communis"; "common being" refers to the universal existence shared by all things before they are specified into types.</note>, which communicates innumerable modes of being to things that are born from its progression. Finally, to speak briefly, that which could serve as testimony to us that there is a certain infinite power in the mind is this:

<margin>D</margin>
that the hunger of the body and sleep are satisfied quickly and by a small amount. The fire of the mind is never extinguished, whether it looks toward human things or divine things. If it craves human things, what heap of riches or what greatness of empire bounds it? If it craves divine things, it is filled by no knowledge of created and finite things. It rightly never rests unless it takes hold of the infinite God, who may fill its infinite capacity, which was provided by Him. If the mind were finite, it would either be filled by some finite thing, or at least its thirst would be quieted. But now, by the removal of any finite things, its thirst is not only not extinguished, but it burns more ardently. For the more it takes in, the closer it comes by a certain comparison to the infinite God; it burns more as it is made closer to its own fire, and it runs more rapaciously, now close to the infinite end of its own motion. This is what the element of fire does when it retreats into its own sphere. <note>In ancient physics, fire was believed to move upward toward its "natural place" or sphere, accelerating as it got closer.</note> A stone does the same thing even more clearly when it descends from on high; the closer it is to the earth, the more vehemently it is carried toward the earth. Who would say the mind is an elemental body, or anything corporeal, if it possesses infinite power? I mean a power of persevering and receiving, as well as of departing and traversing; whether it has this power of itself or (to speak more truly) by a certain divine amplification. That is to say, insofar as the absolute infinity of God inserts an intellectual and vital infinity into minds and souls—which depend primarily upon Him—and preserves them continually, and calls them back from the infinite beginning to the infinite end. For if a similar communicated quality is usually wont to flow everywhere from an absolute quality, what wonder is it that a certain infinity flows out somewhere from absolute infinity? And it flows especially into minds and souls, through 

<margin>E</margin>
which the Platonists think that an infinite succession of time and generation also proceeds in the world. Who, therefore, will be so mad as to wish that the mind should have some limit in its endurance, when in its power (so amplified) and in its operation it has no limit? As if it could have a limit outside itself which it does not have within itself. If life precedes intelligence in origin, and intelligence exceeds life in value <note>original: "precio"; meaning worth or dignity.</note>, and the human soul is gifted with such great dignity that a certain infinite power of understanding and willing was granted to it, then much earlier and more greatly ought an infinite power of living to have been granted to the same soul.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind possesses an infinite capacity because it can understand the concept of infinity and is never satisfied by finite material gains, finding rest only in God. This infinite power of thought and desire suggests that the soul must also possess an infinite power of existence (immortality).</summary>

Platonic Book

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Nine.

## It is proved through the rational power that the soul is not only an individual form, but also that it does not depend on the body, so that its immortality may be more clearly demonstrated. First reason: because the mind reflects upon itself. Chapter 1.

<margin>a</margin>
**T**hus far we have proved through the rational power that the soul is an individual <note>original: "individuam"; in this context, it means "indivisible" or something that cannot be split into parts.</note> and immortal form. Next it must be proved that it does not depend on the body; from this, its immortality is properly concluded. Divisible things are least of all able to reflect <note>original: "reflectuntur"; Ficino uses the image of a line bending back to touch its start to describe self-consciousness.</note> into themselves. But if someone should say that a certain divisible thing is revolved into itself, we shall immediately ask: does one part of this thing turn into another part? Or a part into the whole? Or the whole into a part? Or rather, does the whole turn into its whole self? If the first is granted, the same thing is not being turned into itself, since the parts are distinct from one another. If the second or third is granted, the same result follows, for a part is one thing and the whole is another. Only the fourth way seems to remain: that the whole is turned into the whole. This happens in no other way than if all the parts are turned into all the parts. Suppose this is so. Finally, after such a conversion has been made, we will ask: does any part remain outside of another or distinct from another? Or none? If another part remains, it will be in this position or that mode. And thus, having been turned toward each other, they will not yet be "one." If no part remains distinct, then certainly no part in that thing will be distant or different from another part. That which is such a thing is entirely indivisible <note>original: "individuum"; Ficino is arguing that true self-reflection requires a point-like unity that matter, which always has "side-by-side" parts, cannot achieve.</note>. It is so constituted that it consists neither of quantitative parts, nor of matter and form. Therefore, either a thing does not reflect into itself, or if it does reflect, it is indivisible.

<margin>B</margin>
We have stated elsewhere that the soul is revolved into itself in four ways: namely, through the intellect into its own nature, when it seeks, finds, and considers itself; through the will into that same nature, when it desires and loves itself; through the intellect into the very act of understanding, when it understands a thing and understands that it understands; and through the will into the act of the will, when it wills something and wills that it wills. These four "wholes" Plato attributed to the chariot of the soul <note>A reference to the allegory in Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is depicted as a charioteer with two horses.</note>; and I judge this to be that fourfold fountain of perpetual nature which Pythagoras said was granted to the souls of men by Jove. If no divisible thing returns into itself, then surely this rational four-horse chariot of ours—which recurs into itself through all four ways—and the very intimate fountain itself—which flows back into itself through four whirlpools—is simple and utterly indivisible. Indeed, a conversion of this kind is not from body to body, but is from soul to soul. This has been proved both from many other points above and here from the fact that it returns into itself. Therefore, such a conversion is free from the body, since it neither begins from the body nor returns into it. Much more is the substance of the soul free from the body if the conversion, which is its motion, is free from the body. Thus the rational soul in no way depends on the body in its being, just as it does not in its moving or its operating. Likewise, if it reflects into itself through its operation, it also reflects through its essence. Thus the conversion of the soul's essence into itself occurs. From whence the conversion of any thing occurs, from there also is its perfection, and vice versa. Therefore, the soul, which turns into itself, is from itself. It is from itself, I say, in three chief ways. First, according to its form, because it is not formed by another form; otherwise it would not recur to itself, but to that other. Second, according to its foundation, because it is not sustained by another. For this form, which leans upon itself when it strives toward itself, does not lean upon another. Third, according to its simplicity, because it does not consist of parts. For in what way can that form be spread out through a surface of parts if it is folded back entirely into its own center? Since this is so, it exists always from itself. For whatever ceases to be, does so either because it is abandoned by its forming cause, or because it is deserted by its foundation, or because it dissolves into parts.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul must be indivisible and independent of the body because it is capable of self-reflection, a movement that material objects cannot perform. He links this self-turning nature to Platonic and Pythagorean allegories of the soul's fourfold powers of intellect and will.</summary>

On the previous page, Ficino began arguing that the soul must be immaterial because it can "reflect" or turn back upon itself—a property that physical, divisible matter cannot possess. This page concludes that thought and proceeds to the second and third reasons for the soul's independence from the body.</meta>

<page-num>72</page-num>
<header>Theology: Book Nine</header>

That which indeed turns back upon itself, because it is indivisible, is not dissolved; because it is its own form, it is not abandoned by the forming cause; because it remains in itself, it is never deserted by its foundation.

### ¶ Second reason. The more the mind is separated from the body, the better it fares. Chapter 2.

<margin>C</margin>
**I**f the soul drew any origin from the body, then the more closely it clung to the body, the better it would fare. For every single thing is preserved and perfected by its own origin. But now, the opposite occurs. The most excellent parts of the soul are the intellect and the will. When we are occupied with bodily matters, the intellect either perceives nothing at all, or it does not discern clearly, being deceived by the senses and by imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; in Ficino's psychology, this is the faculty that processes sensory images, which can often "cloud" pure intellectual thought.</note>. The will is afflicted while it is vexed by many cares from that source. On the contrary, when it despises bodily things and the senses are lulled—the clouds of mental images having been driven away—if it contemplates anything through itself, then the intellect discerns clearly. This is most evident in those who, through the quiet of sleep or any other alienation from the body, prophesy.

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, as Plato says in the *Crito* and the *Apology*, some people predict future events when they are near death, as if they then see those things prescribed among the heavenly powers. To these powers the soul is joined by its own nature, provided the body does not hinder it.

<margin>E</margin>
Hence Socrates, when dragged into court by false accusers, first predicted to the judges their future repentance, the ruin of his accusers, and sedition for the city. Then, in prison, he pre-marked the day of his own death, which had been shown to him by a divine power during rest. Likewise, when Theramenes <note>A Greek statesman and one of the "Thirty Tyrants" of Athens; he was forced to drink hemlock by his rival Critias.</note> had been cast into prison and was drinking the poison, he prophesied the approaching death of his adversary Critias, which followed shortly thereafter. A certain man of Rhodes, as the Stoic Posidonius writes, named six of his peers as he was dying and stated who among them would be the first to die, who the second, and so on in succession.

<margin>F</margin>
Aristotle also writes that Eudemus of Cyprus, his close friend, fell gravely ill when he came to Pherae, a town in Thessaly. In a vision, a youth of extraordinary beauty appeared to him and said that he would soon recover, that Alexander the tyrant of that town would perish in a few days, and that Eudemus himself would return home five years later. Shortly thereafter, Eudemus recovered, the tyrant was slain, and after five years had passed, Eudemus died—and thus his soul "returned to its fatherland."

§ For Calanus the Indian <note>An Indian gymnosophist (ascetic) who accompanied Alexander the Great and famously committed ritual self-immolation.</note>, when he was just about to die, announced a swift death to King Alexander. And Pherecydes of Syros, while dying, prophesied a victory for the Ephesians against the Magnesians. Many other things of this kind are read. Truly, not only does the intellect perceive many things clearly while we live apart from the contagion of the body, but the will is also fulfilled and is not afflicted by any disturbances. Instead, it rejoices exceedingly in divine things, as if in things most similar to itself. From this it follows that the body is not the origin of the mind, if the further the mind departs from it, the more perfectly it conducts itself. It also follows that if the more the mind is immersed in this body, the more it fails, and the further it departs, the more it is perfected, then the mind will be most perfect when it has flown entirely away from this body. Moreover, that from which the highest perfection comes is not the cause of destruction; rather, it is the cause of a complete life, even to the point of being eternal. For by what change will the soul ever fail, since it does not perish when departing from the body—a change than which none can be greater for it?

### ¶ Third reason. The mind resists the body. Chapter 3.

<margin>G</margin>
**N**o thing can, of its own accord, resist its own origin; otherwise, it would be carried by its own will toward its own destruction, which necessarily follows once the origin is lost. Furthermore, whatever an effect performs, it does by the power and help of its origin. If, therefore, it fought against its causes, in that struggle the cause would be opposing itself.

<margin>H</margin>
The soul resists and is opposed to our body—indeed, to all bodies. Therefore, it does not derive its origin from any body. It has two principal duties: to contemplate and to deliberate. In both, it resists bodies. First, let us see how it resists in the act of contemplating.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's independence is proven by its improved function during sleep or near death, and by its natural opposition to bodily impulses. He concludes that if the soul reaches perfection upon leaving the body, it must be immortal rather than destroyed by death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book Nine, Chapter 2. Having previously established that the soul is superior to the body because it can reflect upon itself, Ficino now moves to show how the higher Reason (ratio) must correct the errors of the lower Imagination or Fantasy (phantasia). This sets the stage for a ladder of contemplation leading from the material world to God.</meta>

# Platonic Theology

Daily, external bodies, arranged in various ways, move the instruments of our body assigned to the senses in such a way that they deceive us for a time. Reason, however, emends and corrects this deception, as we have explained more fully elsewhere. In cases where reason judges differently than either an external body suggests or one's own body reports—and it often judges in a contrary way—it condemns the affection of its own body as much as that of others. 

<margin>¶</margin> Let us set aside for the moment the investigations of all other things. Let us take up the highest contemplation of the Highest, so that we may recognize how much the mind, by its own nature, refutes bodily things. 

<margin>¶</margin> Fantasy <note>original: "phantasia"; in Ficino's psychology, this is the faculty that translates sensory data into mental images. It is "lower" than pure reason because it is still tied to the physical world.</note> follows the external senses. The senses follow the disposition of their own body and of other bodies. Therefore, we attribute the judgment of the senses and of fantasy to the disposition of bodies, and we say that this judgment becomes "bodily" according to the affection it receives. 

When our soul—desiring to find out what God is—asks teachers of this kind, Fantasy (an overly bold sculptor and craftsman) fashions a certain statue out of five materials: those which the external senses have presented to it as the most beautiful of all things received from the world. It does this, however, in such a way that it makes those materials somehow more excellent than those it received from the world through the senses. 

Fantasy therefore offers us a light so bright that no other could seem more radiant; so vast that none could be larger, diffused almost through the immense void; adorned with innumerable colors and revolving in a circle. 

<margin>¶</margin> Because of this revolution, let it resonate with the sweetest melodies, both filling and soothing the ears. Let it smell of the most pleasant odors. Let it also abound in every flavor, fashioned to be the sweetest of all. 

<margin>21</margin> To the touch, let it be wondrously soft, delicate, smooth, and tempered. Fantasy proclaims that **this is God**. The body of the world gives us nothing more beautiful. The bodily sense neither reaches anything better nor reports anything more excellent. Fantasy, the friend of the senses, fashions nothing more sublime. But meanwhile Reason, looking down from the highest watchtower of the mind, cries out against the plays of Fantasy in this way:

---

"Beware, little soul <note>original: "animula"; a term of endearment for the soul, famously used in a poem by the Emperor Hadrian.</note>; beware the tricks of that empty sophist. Do you seek God? Receive a light as much brighter than the light of the sun as the sun's light is brighter than darkness. If the sun's light were compared to this, even if it were a million times brighter than it is, it would seem to be a shadow. 

And also, receive it as something so subtle that it escapes the sharpness of sight. Do not spread it through the void, lest it consist of parts and thus require a location to support those parts. Gather it all, if you can, into a point, so that from this infinite union it may be infinitely powerful. Then, if you like, let it be present everywhere—not scattered by location, but whole in every place, standing by each thing. Nor should it be stained by a manifold variety of colors. For pure light is more splendid than colored light. Nor should it revolve or make a sound. For I do not wish that light to be moved, or struck, or broken. And I judge a state of rest to be more perfect than motion. 

Take away also the odors, flavors, and tangible softness, lest it be composed of a coarser nature. Here shines what space does not hold; here sounds what time does not snatch away. Here smells what the breeze does not scatter. Here is tasted what greed does not diminish. Here it clings, and satiety does not pull it away." 

Do you desire to look upon the face of God again? <margin>¶</margin> Behold the whole world full of the sun’s light. Behold the light in the matter of the world, full of all the forms of all things, and in motion. Subtract, I pray, the matter from the light. Leave the rest. Suddenly you have the **soul**: namely, an incorporeal light, containing all forms, but changeable. Remove again from this soulful light its changeability. You have now attained the **angelic intellect**: namely, an incorporeal light, containing all forms, and unchangeable. 

Subtract from this that diversity by which any form is different from the light and is infused into the light from elsewhere. Do this so that the essence of the light and of every form is the same. Let the light itself form itself, and through its own forms, let it form all things. This light shines infinitely. Because it shines by its own nature, it is not stained or contracted by the mixture of anything else. 

<margin>¶</margin> It is through all things because it is in nothing. It is in nothing, so that it may shine abundantly through all things. You wish...

<summary>Ficino describes how the imaginative faculty (Fantasy) mistakenly tries to picture God as a beautiful physical object, while Reason corrects this by describing God as an immaterial, infinite, and unchangeable light. He provides a hierarchical "ladder" of light leading from the physical world to the soul, the angelic mind, and finally to the pure essence of God.</summary>

Let us speak next of how much it resists in deliberation. Often, when the stomach is hungry, or the lungs are thirsty, or the brain is heavy with sleep, or the genital members are swelling with seed, the sense—the companion of the body—invites one to food, drink, sleep, and intercourse. It incites, I say, or rather it announces the body's incitements to the soul. But Reason, for the sake of contemplation or virtue, judges that one must abstain from these; and as it commands, we frequently abstain. When an insult or injury is felt in the heart, the blood is inflamed toward vengeance. Then the motive power of the soul—the companion and guest of the body—moves the feet and hands to take revenge. Reason, sometimes for the sake of peace and quiet, commands one to stop, and restrains them; often, it trembles at the dangers presented. When Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato known for his extreme self-discipline and asceticism.</note>, the beloved disciple of Plato, and Origen <note>An early Christian theologian who, according to tradition, castrated himself to ensure his chastity.</note>, their follower, burned away their virility so that they might utterly extinguish the fires of lust, was not the unconquered mind declaring war on the members of the body? Therefore, let no 
<margin>H</margin>

...nevertheless, the struggle itself would be: which is in us continual, to show that the soul fights against the body. If there were no other nature in us but the corporeal, we would rush forward immediately whenever a bodily affection drew us toward something, just like <term>brute animals</term><note>Ficino uses "bruta" to refer to non-human animals that lack rational choice and act only on instinct.</note>. Nor would we have any concern, nor would we deliberate whether that thing to which the body allures us ought to be done. For nothing fights with itself. Yet there is almost always a struggle in us, brought upon us by the whole body.

<margin>A</margin>
There is, therefore, something in us besides the body itself, removed from its lineage. Removed, I say, both from the nature of all <term>humors</term><note>The four "humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) were believed in medieval medicine to determine a person's physical health and temperament.</note> and elements, by which it can resist all their inclinations and transcend them through thought and affection; and also removed from every celestial nature infused into these humors by the heavens themselves and led to their specific property. By this, it is also able at times to oppose celestial inclinations—a point which the <term>astrologers</term><note>Even in the 15th century, astrologers often conceded that while "the stars incline, they do not compel" the rational soul.</note> themselves concede to us.

<margin>☾</margin>
And it always devises and cherishes a certain substance far more excellent than the heavens. I add: that whatever is produced through the corporeal and mobile power of the heavens is both corporeal and entirely subject to change. Nor can it surpass a corporeal and mobile nature. Therefore, the soul can live separately both from elemental nature and from the celestial nature infused into the elements.

<margin>☜</margin>
But if any of the <term>Platonists</term><note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, particularly those in the Neoplatonic tradition like Plotinus or Proclus, whom Ficino translated.</note> should say that the soul is always in a <term>celestial vehicle</term><note>original: "celesti vehiculo"; a subtle body or "astral chariot" that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited as it descended from the stars to the earth.</note>, we shall respond: it is not the soul that depends on the vehicle, but the vehicle on the soul; and among the Platonists, the eternal soul always gives life to the eternal vehicle. But let us return to the established order. Nor should it disturb us that the soul often obeys the body, for it does not obey by force, but by love: by which it is moved toward the body living through it, as if toward a son and its own work.

<margin>𝔐</margin>
A mother loves her son as her own work. The little son desires food beyond measure. The mother commands him to abstain. He lies there and cries—if he has been well-educated. If poorly, he screams and disturbs the house. The mother, who loves him too much, feels pity for the wailing son. Nevertheless, she consents that he take food only so far as she first judges by deliberating with herself that he can taste something without detriment to the body; or if some harm is brought upon him, it can easily be helped through medicine. Only then does the child receive food. The mother is not forced by the little son. Rather, the love of her own work allures the mother to obey the son. She complies at last just as she deems she ought to comply. Often she judges truly. Sometimes she is deceived, because being too desirous to comply, she does not examine the outcome diligently enough. Such is the similarity of the soul to the body.

<margin>☾</margin>
Therefore, if it were natural for the soul to succumb to the body, every soul would always yield to the senses. Since it does resist frequently by deliberating, if ever it does consent, it obeys not by nature or violence, but by love. By this, the highest power of the soul affects the middle power. The middle affects the lowest. The lowest affects the <term>vital complexion</term><note>The "vital complexion" or "temperament" refers to the specific physical balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that sustains life in a body.</note>. The vital complexion affects the body. Indeed, the Platonists think that from the substance of the rational soul, as if from a sun, an irrational bodily life is poured out like light; and that the soul is moved toward this life as toward its offspring. To receive this offspring, as the <term>Timaeus</term><note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the world and the nature of the physical universe.</note> teaches, the body is prepared through celestial souls.

<margin>B</margin>
What then shall we say to this: when some soul kills its own body, whether it does so by deliberation, or by indignation, or by fear, or by grief? How would it ever undertake this if the body were the origin of the soul? Since no appetite in nature can rise up against its own nature. No beast kills itself of its own accord. Because no stimulus can arise in their souls, which sprout from the body, against the body. In man, however, although he is a more prudent animal, he often does this. <term>Prophesying</term><note>original: "Vaticinans"; Ficino suggests the act of suicide, in some philosophical contexts, is a misguided or desperate "intuition" of the soul's survival after death.</note>, as I believe, that he will survive after the body, and that he is unloading a burden from the body rather than losing himself.

->R 2<-

No action arises from a general consideration alone, unless some particular <term>estimation</term><note>Latin: "estimatio." In Renaissance psychology, this is the faculty that judges the usefulness or harmfulness of specific sensory objects.</note> intervenes. This is because motions and actions occur regarding particular things. For example, when someone considers in a general sense that physical exercise is useful, even though they consider it so, they do not yet exercise until they first consult how many modes of exercise there are and which might be more beneficial. But when they have chosen one particular exercise above the others, then they begin the work. If they choose walking, they walk; if riding, they ride. 

The intellect, by its nature, is occupied with the conception of universal reasons. Therefore, for some action to arise from its apprehension, its universal conception must be deduced toward certain particulars. However, a universal notion contains many—indeed, infinite—singular things by its own power, just as the common category of "exercising" contains innumerable ways of exercising. Therefore, that universal notion can be derived equally toward various singulars. From this kind of derivation follows the <term>judgment</term><note>Latin: "iudicium." Here, the intellectual decision-making process that precedes a choice of the will.</note> regarding things to be done. Consequently, a different judgment can follow. Thus, the judgment of the intellect regarding things to be done is not determined by its nature to any single thing. It is, therefore, free.

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, some things lack freedom of judgment because they have no judgment at all, such as plants. Others, although they have judgment, have it determined by nature toward one specific thing, such as <term>brute animals</term><note>Ficino uses "bruta" to refer to non-human animals that act solely on instinct rather than rational choice.</note>. For by a natural estimation, a sheep judges a wolf to be harmful to itself and flees. Nor can it *not* flee, as nature impels it. By a natural instinct, swallows are carried to build their nests, bees to their hives, and spiders to their webs. For this reason, all animals of the same species always build their works in the same way; they never learn at any point, nor do they ever vary, because the natural blueprint by which they are led is present from the beginning and remains the same. 

Humans, however, learn and always vary their works, yet they possess a single nature from the beginning. They are not, therefore, dragged by nature into acting, but they themselves, by their own <term>counsel</term><note>Latin: "consilio," referring to the deliberate process of weighing options before making a choice.</note>, move themselves sometimes one way, sometimes another.

---

For why do we think it happens that trees and beasts never err in certain of their motions, arts, and choices, while man errs very often? Certainly not because a more perfect intellect is in them—for indeed, no intellect is in them at all. 

<margin>E</margin> Rather, it is because they are drawn by the Divine Intellect, which never errs. Man, however, is led by his own intellect, which can err. Even if at times he takes a rest from his own actions for a while, then he too is led by God and does not err—which is made clear through prophecies and miracles. And if he were always led in this way, just like the others, he would err so much less than they do, insofar as he would be a more perfect instrument. Conversely, if the others led themselves as man does, they would err so much more, insofar as they have been allotted a less perfect species. 

<margin>F</margin> Since, therefore, man does not have a judgment regarding things to be done that is determined by nature to one thing, he is necessarily free. Moreover, we gather that he judges freely from the fact that he leads himself to the act of judging. That he leads himself is shown by the fact that he reflects upon his own judgment. That he reflects is shown by the fact that he knows he is judging and defines the judgment itself. The intellect obtains this very liberty by its own power. For the intellect does not only apprehend "this" or "that" good, but the <term>common good</term><note>Latin: "commune bonum," also known as "good in general." Ficino argues that because we can conceive of the very idea of Goodness, we aren't "locked in" to any one specific physical pleasure.</note> itself. 

Since the intellect moves the will through the form it has apprehended, and in all things the mover and the mobile correspond to each other in proportion: 

<margin>G</margin> the rational will is not determined by nature except toward the common good itself. Beneath that common good, all individual goods are contained. Therefore, whatever is offered to the will as a good, the will can be inclined toward it, with no natural inclination in the opposite direction prohibiting it. 

This is indeed signified by what we said above: that man chooses many things contrary to the use and pleasure of the physical body. He very often prescribes for himself a way of life that is harmful to the body; he hates the body, thins it out, and kills it. Beasts never do this, for their every impulse and action serves the utility of the body. It is worthwhile to consider certain things from the philosophers...

<summary>Ficino argues that human freedom arises from the intellect's ability to conceive of universal concepts and "the Good" in general, unlike animals which are driven by fixed natural instincts. This capacity for self-reflection and choosing against bodily needs serves as evidence for the soul's higher, non-material nature.</summary>

## According to Platonic Wisdom

According to <note>original: "Platonice sophis"</note> Platonic wisdom, some things are necessary, some are impossible, and some are "middle" things—which are called "possible." Among possible things, some happen for the most part, some happen more rarely, and some happen almost equally either way <note>These "equal" occurrences are what philosophers call "contingent" events.</note>. They believe this order is most suitable for the universe. They affirm, moreover, that some things are natural, while others are voluntary. They add further that there would never be any power capable of turning toward either of two <term>contingents</term><note>Latin: "contingentiū." Events that are not predetermined and could happen in multiple ways.</note> equally unless that power resided in voluntary agents. For natural agents are "determined" (fixed) rather than voluntary. Finally, they prove that the natural duties of any being cannot be in vain. Now, the duty of a human being is <term>deliberation</term><note>Latin: "consilium." The process of weighing options before acting.</note>. Yet deliberation would be in vain if it were directed toward opposites in a situation where neither could be chosen or enacted, as the process of weighing options <margin>A</margin> suggests. Our soul's freedom will be found especially if we look more clearly at how the souls of beasts are moved. When a brute animal is hungry, if food is placed before its eyes, its soul judges that such food is suitable for it. Its <term>appetite</term><note>Latin: "appetitus." The drive or instinctual desire.</note> craves it and moves its limbs toward it. We must ask: where does that movement of the limbs come from? Without doubt, it is from the appetite. Where does the motion of the appetite come from? From the judgment. For because it judged the food to be suitable for itself, it immediately desired it. Where does the judgment come from? From such a form (the appearance of the food) appearing to its eyes, and from the internal need of such a body. For as often as such a body is hungry and such an apple is shown to its sight, so often does that soul judge the thing to be suitable for itself and desire it. You see that the <term>principle</term><note>Latin: "principium." The starting point or governing cause.</note> of that motion is not in the soul, but in the body—in the body, I say, of the food so arranged, and in the body of the beast so affected. Therefore, that soul does not properly lead the body, nor does it properly move from itself; rather, the nature of the food and the nature of its own body "drag" the soul. And by this dragging, the <margin>B</margin> limbs are also snatched away. We shall offer four signs of this fact. First, that when such a situation is presented and the body is so affected, the soul immediately judges and desires. After it has looked upon the shape of the food, it does not delay its judgment or its desire for any time at all, not even the shortest moment. It is as if that soul contributes almost nothing from its own power to the process; rather, once the cause of judgment is placed there, the effect of judging follows immediately.

## Book [Nine]

And not without reason. For the "form" <note>In this context, the "form" is the essential quality or appearance that triggers a reaction.</note> is the principle of acting, just as the heat of fire is the principle of heating. Now, some forms are impressed by nature, like heat and lightness in fire; some are apprehended, like the species of food through sight. The movement of fire follows an impressed form. The judgment and appetite of a beast so affected follows that apprehended form of the food. Therefore, the principle of this motion is the food and its form. And just as fire is not moved by itself—because it cannot *not* ascend, and when nothing stands in its way it cannot *not* burn when something to be burned is present—so the beast does not move by itself, because it cannot *not* be carried toward those things which are offered in this or 그 way. The second sign is that the irrational soul never judges, desires, or pursues anything except what pertains to the use of the body. In every one of its actions, the goal is the comfort of the body. Now, the final "end" (goal) in things is almost the same as the "principle" (origin). The principle of fire is the <term>concave of the moon</term><note>Latin: "lune concauū." In medieval/Renaissance cosmology, the "sphere of fire" existed just below the sphere of the moon; fire naturally moves upward to reach this home.</note>. The concave of the moon is the end goal of the motion of fire, because every cause acts and moves toward its own end. Therefore, in a brute, the principle of actions is the nature of the body, or the soul—not the <margin>C</margin> soul alone, but the "bodily" soul. And as it perceives the whole of nature and the "natural craftsman" <note>A reference to the "Archeus" or the guiding vital force in nature.</note> of life, the goal of acting is the preservation of nature and the bodily life. The third sign is that beasts never "repent" of having acted in this or that way, nor do they retract or correct anything. This signifies that there is only a single principle of acting there, since there is no conflict. Certainly, the bodily life moves them as its own proper goal. Therefore, nothing else is present there besides the bodily life to move it. Fourthly, as we said above, there is no diversity in the works of beasts of the same species. One spider does not weave its web differently than another. All swallows likewise make their nests similarly, and each one in the same way every year. Just as all fire heats similarly; every stone descends similarly; every plant sprouts similarly according to its species. For the nature of each thing is a single, fixed thing.

<summary>Ficino distinguishes human free will from animal instinct by arguing that animals are "dragged" by bodily needs and external stimuli, whereas humans possess the power of deliberation. He provides four proofs that animals lack freedom, including their lack of regret and the uniformity of their actions across a species.</summary>

# Theology

...its own form and certain [principles] implanted from the beginning. Through which alone, and always in a similar way, there is always one work and a similar one. Therefore, the soul of beasts, following the instinct of nature, preserves the tenor familiar to its species. <margin>b</margin> The same happens to us as often as reason is sluggish and we live according to the nod of the senses and the imagination. But when reason is awakened and intent, we deliberate for a long time in matters to be done, and we condemn the nod of the imagination; we act otherwise than the nature of external bodies or of our own limbs might demand. And if we ever indulge in these things, we repent and try to amend, and we often tame and subject the nature of the body.

For we act not only through those images received or conceived from the objects of bodies, but also through universal species and reasons of things, which partly are innate in the soul, and partly are produced by its own peculiar power. Where the principle of acting is our own form, not that of the body. It is produced by us, not received from the body; created according to the mode of the soul rather than the mode <margin>c</margin> of bodies, and it is common to infinite modes of acting. Therefore, we are not bound to a single way of acting, but we wander freely through all. For we have in our mind a certain common exemplar of good things, to which, comparing individual things, we either reject them or approve them more or less—not being dragged by the things themselves or the body, but rather dragging the things themselves to the exemplar, and the body to the mind.

Therefore, even while the disposition of things and the body remains the same, we often choose differently at different times. And while it may be different, we often choose similarly; indeed, in almost the same moment, because of various conjectures and reasons proposed, even while bodily conditions remain the same, choices are made variously and, in a certain way, contrarily. For by deliberation <margin>d</margin> it happens that we do not subject the soul to things, but rather things to our soul; surely, as <term>Plotinus</term><note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> often says and <term>Proclus</term><note>A later Greek Neoplatonist (412–485 AD) who systematized Platonic thought.</note> confirms, we have evidence of this in the sciences and in morals. 

In the sciences, it works in this way: when we are content with the speculation of truth alone, communicating nothing at all with the body, nor affecting to do anything outside ourselves. Who would not see that our contemplation is entirely, in no way, dependent on the body? In morals, again, it works in this way: when we direct all right studies to our soul so it may be adorned with morals, who would not understand then that the end of our duties is the soul, and therefore the soul is the principle of those same duties? 

# Ninth [Book]

The principles of these actions are not the <term>humors</term><note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient and Renaissance medicine believed determined a person's temperament and health.</note>, because the humors do not invite one toward something against their own body and above bodies. Nor are they the heavens <note>Ficino refers to the stars and planets, which were thought to influence human temperament via the humors.</note>, which move through the humors. For the body of the heavens is far removed, and it does not move our four humors before it moves the four elements. Nor will it move the soul unless the humors are agitated. But the mind opposes the agitation of the humors, while it despises their impulse by the intention of speculation, restrains it by the study of morals, and breaks it by the industry of the arts. 

No one was more naturally inclined toward love than <term>Socrates</term>, or toward lust and drunkenness than Alciphones the Megarian <note>Likely referring to a figure from the history of philosophy known for overcoming natural vices through discipline.</note>; yet no one emerged more continent than they through study. Did not Xenocrates, Demosthenes, and Cleanthes repel the impediments of nature by their diligence? If we resist the humors, we also resist the elements and the heavens; indeed, if we are not subjected to the heavens, much less are we submitted to other bodies. 

That the soul of man is not subjected <margin>K</margin> to the heavens appears from this: first, because it foresees future events by knowledge. Then, it either avoids them by prudence or thinks nothing of them by magnanimity—as if they do not pertain at all to the man himself (who is the soul itself), but rather to the soul’s prison <note>The "prison of the soul" is a classic Platonic metaphor for the physical body.</note>. Added to this is that he uses prosperous fortune happily because of temperance, and adverse fortune best because of tolerance, so that both equally profit him toward virtue and salvation. 

In what way does he follow a chance event who precedes it? Or does he necessarily undergo what he avoids by diligence? Or does he dread nature, which he often despises? Or is he conquered by good things, when he directs those things toward his own happiness? Or is he overcome by evils, when he converts evils into goods? Or by some necessity...

# Platonic
# Theology

...by which it is compelled: he who, while he freely consents to the divine will out of piety, makes even those things that are necessary and appear terrifying into things that are voluntary and light. We demonstrate the same point again through the intellect and the will. First, here, through the intellect: The celestial body <note>Ficino refers to the planets and stars as "celestial bodies."</note> possesses a corporeal, <term>singular</term> <note>Meaning specific to one individual time and place, rather than universal.</note>, local, and temporal form. However, the form through which the mind understands all things is incorporeal, universal, and absolute. Therefore, this mind is not born from the heavens. For a form that is enclosed within a specific place does not generate an <term>absolute</term> <note>A form that is free from physical limitations or specific material conditions.</note> form. Therefore, the heavens do not generate any form within the intellect.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ Does intelligence perhaps arise within it by chance? By no means. For the intellect does not follow physical form. Therefore, that which cannot provide the form will not provide the intelligence. In general, no body understands anything through its own physical form. For such a form is entirely singular. Much less will it generate intelligence in another. Since, therefore, the intellect has neither its own action nor the principle of its action from the heavens, it is not subject to the celestial body. This is especially true because our soul—according to that power by which it is joined to those things said to be above the heavens—is not only not subject to the heavens but presides over them. Here, moreover, insofar as it understands the truth, it is joined to the angels who preside over the heavens. For it understands only insofar as it receives intellectual light from that source. Thus, it is clear that the intellect is not subject to the heavens.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ In the same way, it will be clear that the will is not subject to them. Truly, those things that happen by nature are led to their end through determined means. They almost always arrive in the same way. For a thing is determined toward one specific end. But the choices of men tend toward an end through diverse paths, both in morals and in the arts. Furthermore, in natural actions, things of the same species do not differ among themselves. For just as every swallow, as we say, builds its nest in a similar way, so every intellect understands in a similar way those first principles of the arts and morals which are known to everyone by nature. And every will similarly desires the good itself, because the will desires the good according to its nature.

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, such is the nature of man that just as the intellect relates to the principle of speculation <note>The pursuit of theoretical truth.</note>—which is that which is everywhere manifestly true—so the will relates to the principle of action, which is the good itself; and all of us necessarily assent to both. But choice is a certain action following the human species, just as the discourse of reason is. For these two are not the only things proper to man. Therefore, if men reasoned by natural instinct, the opinion of all men regarding individual things would be the same; likewise, if they chose by the guidance of nature, there would be one choice for all. But as it is, different people choose different things in different ways, just as they judge variously by reasoning. For this reason, the heavens do not move our will by natural instinct. However, they do influence the body. The movement of the body follows this influence, and the senses report it. From this, the will is often enticed. Yet this incitement is not a necessary cause of choice, because the will sometimes assents to it and at other times not at all. Nor is it only by celestial bodies that the human body or sense is moved. For even Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the famous ancient astronomer and geographer.</note>

<margin>D</margin> himself concedes that particular effects regarding matter by no means follow the celestial things absolutely—which are universal and remote causes—but follow insofar as intermediate causes grant it, and insofar as the changeable disposition of matter (subject to contrary causes) receives it differently at different times and places. Indeed, we prove this daily by experience itself, especially in those who, although born at the same time, follow the nature of their species, individual character, place, nourishment, and habit, so that they behave differently despite having the same moment of birth. Justly, therefore, does Ptolemy instruct astrologers to offer a general and possible judgment rather than a distinct and necessary one. He adds that wise men can resist the stars when they threaten or favor them when they promise. Therefore, one must not believe the

<margin>E</margin> assertors of fate <note>original: "fatists" or "fate-tellers"</note> who say that individual things proceed from determined causes, and that once the cause is set, the effect necessarily follows. First, indeed, from a remote cause, however necessary it may be, the effect does not necessarily follow unless the [intermediate] cause...
