<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book Nine of the Platonic Theology. In the previous section, Ficino argued that the human intellect is not subject to the stars because its forms are universal and incorporeal, while the stars are physical and particular. Here, he explores the logic of causality to further prove that the soul remains free from celestial determinism.</meta>

# Theology

# Ninth [Book]

...even if the influence is necessary through intermediate causes. ¶ Just as in logical arguments: from a <term>necessary major premise</term> <note>A statement that must be true, like "All men are mortal."</note> and a <term>contingent minor premise</term> <note>A statement that might be true but isn't necessarily so, like "Socrates is running."</note>, a necessary conclusion does not usually follow. But between celestial causes and earthly effects, the intermediate causes are the <term>elemental virtues</term> <note>The basic qualities of the four elements: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>—whether simple, mixed, active, or passive—which are indeed contingent and changeable, and very often can hinder one another. Furthermore, it is not necessary that even if a specific and sufficient cause for an effect is present, the effect follows immediately. This is because it can be hindered by the meeting of another cause. For often a cause here is sufficient to produce <term>yellow bile</term> <note>One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament; bile was associated with heat and anger.</note>, but from another side, a cause is sufficient to produce <term>phlegm</term>; thus, they can hinder each other. Finally, we cannot assign specific causes for everything. ¶ For if you are white, you have a specific cause for that. Likewise, you have another specific cause for being a grammarian. But for the fact that whiteness and grammar happen to meet in the same person, you have no specific cause. For if the meeting of these two things I mentioned arose from a common, determined cause, they would certainly have some natural order between them. We say, therefore, of any effect among us, that it does not necessarily proceed from its own cause, because it could be hindered by some other cause meeting it by accident. And although someone might trace a coinciding cause back to a higher cause, nevertheless, no one can trace the *coincidence* itself—which causes the hindrance—back to a specific cause so as to prove that such a hindrance proceeds from some celestial principle. Therefore, if those things pertaining to the body do not necessarily follow the stars, much less are our minds and their actions subjected to the stars.

<margin>☩</margin>
¶ Nor should anyone dare to say that the minds of men are moved by <term>Supernal Minds</term> <note>Higher spiritual beings, such as angels or the "intelligences" that move the planets.</note> through the heavens as if through some instrument or medium. ¶ For minds are more compatible with other minds than they are with bodies. Therefore, the heavens are not placed between those higher minds and our own. Rather, our minds hold the middle ground between those higher minds and the heavens. ¶ For that reason, the heavens should be moved by the divine spirits *through* the minds of men, rather than our minds being moved by the divine through the heavens. Perhaps someone might say: our minds are moved by those higher minds without any medium. If that is so, let them move us—or rather, let them lead us. For in this way, the minds of men will be divine, if they are moved directly by the divine. For they will be closest to them by nature. Otherwise, if they were moved through a medium, other things would be naturally closer to the divine than they are. They will certainly be closer to the divine than the sphere of heaven is, since they are moved by the divine without the heaven's help. If they believe the heavens to be perpetual, why should they not also believe the human soul to be eternal, since it is closer to the divine? ¶ Furthermore, the infusion that passes into lower minds from higher ones and the angels should be called "illumination" rather than "motion." For while the higher minds give in their own way, the lower ones also receive in their own way. Both, indeed, are intellects. ¶ Therefore, that which is given and that which is received is <term>intellectual light</term> <note>A metaphor for spiritual truth or understanding that clarifies the mind without forcing the will.</note>. One [light] of this kind does not prevent our soul from turning toward that light in its own way—using it according to its own nature, and through it, reasoning and choosing freely. This is especially true because our soul sometimes turns itself toward the worse side in its deliberations. However, the instinct of the Divine Minds would always pull toward the best. Therefore, the human soul, by the inspiration of the divine powers, acts according to its own nature. From that source, indeed, it descends as something stable. The soul itself makes that influence "mobile" <note>Meaning "changeable" or "active."</note>, since the soul itself is mobile and subsequently acts in a mobile way. Thus, nothing stands in the way of the soul's action being free, since it is not subject to being moved by anything else's specific nature.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who greatly influenced Ficino.</note>, and in his wake Avicenna <note>An influential Persian philosopher and physician (c. 980–1037) who synthesized Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism.</note>, argue that celestial motions are not the causes of lower things, but rather instruments obeying the Divine Movers as if they were craftsmen. They argue that the various thoughts of these Movers are indicated to us through the celestial bodies, shapes, and motions, as if by their eyes and nods, and that they portend the future. They add that the concepts of the divine are unfolded in celestial arrangements like letters in a book. And just as birds, by their flight and chirping, provide signs to <term>augurs</term> <note>Ancient priests who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the behavior of birds.</note>...

# Platonic

...and just as <term>augurs</term> <note>Ancient Roman religious officials who observed natural signs, like the flight of birds, to interpret the will of the gods.</note> are believed to show not what they themselves do, but what they signify; so too the heavens—through their configurations and movements—signify to us daily what is happening elsewhere. <margin>A</margin> Astrologers demonstrate this when, in judging someone's <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genesi"; a birth chart or horoscope used to predict a person's life based on their birth.</note>, they bring forth many details regarding fathers, grandfathers, brothers, wives, friends, and enemies—people whose fortune does not depend on the birth of another, but is only signified by it. Therefore, if corporeal things (as we also proved above) are not properly or entirely subjected to the heavens as instruments of the <term>higher movers</term> <note>The spiritual intelligences or angelic beings that Ficino believed moved the celestial spheres.</note>, much less is the mind itself subjected. Its habits and arts, if they are ever predicted by astrologers, are presented through signs rather than through causes. Indeed, the higher movers not only contemplate those things of which they themselves are the causes, but they also think within themselves of those things for which our minds will be the future causes; and they often demonstrate these things through celestial signs. 

Our mind and will declare most clearly that they are not subjected when the mind is so elevated that it almost wishes to exist for itself alone. For then it is in a way liberated from other creatures and is nearly content with itself. Again, [this is seen] when it reflects back upon its own act in a circle. For a <term>spiritual circuit</term> <note>The act of the mind thinking about its own thinking; a self-reflective loop that Ficino considers a sign of immateriality.</note> does not serve an external limit. 

Furthermore, when it wills one thing not just because of one conjecture, or refuses another for another reason, but also wills that it may be equally able to will or not to will. In this matter, the soul appears indifferent to both willing and not-willing, and is bound by nothing at all. Likewise, it shows this when it chooses the highest <term>vacation</term> <note>original: "vacatione"; here meaning a state of being empty or free from external desires, a contemplative stillness or cessation of striving.</note> of every desire. <margin>α</margin> For then it dissolves the pull of every specific object. This power, which puts an end to every act, serves no object of its own. 

But let us explain all of this more clearly. Whenever some good is proposed to us, the soul can reason in this way: "Because liberty is the greatest good, I wish to experience it within myself at some point. Therefore, I prefer to remain master of myself by retaining the act of choosing, rather than serving this or that thing by willing it." Yet, it still chooses liberty as a good, which at other times it might postpone for the sake of other goods. Therefore, we do not 

# Book

choose any of these goods by necessity, even though we necessarily desire the Good itself <note>Ficino follows the Scholastic idea that while humans must desire "Happiness" or "The Good" in general, we are free to choose which specific objects we think will lead us there.</note>. Finally, either motion is nowhere free, or it is free where it is first. It is first in the soul. Now, the first must be free, if indeed whatever is "first" of its kind is so by its own nature. For who can doubt that the motion of action begins its descent from the point where the motion of inquiry ends its ascent? It ends in the command of the mind itself: I say that I do this for the sake of that, and that for the sake of the other. That, because I want to. To want, because it pleases me. 

To please me, and moreover, to want that which pleases. I add that it is even asked: what if I happened to want <margin>B</margin> to not-want? Plato often calls this "being moved by oneself" <note>original: "per se moueri"; a core Platonic concept where the soul is defined as that which has the power to initiate its own motion.</note>, that is, acting through oneself and freely. Here the soul wishes to achieve this: that he who acts freely, lives freely. So that he who lives freely is not subjected to the impulse of any particular thing, whether good or evil; so that he who is not struck by violence may never be lost.

### ¶ Fifth argument. The mind operates without the body. Chapter 5.

<margin>C</margin> **T**he mode of operating follows the mode of existing. Therefore, if the soul exists in some way through the body, it never acts without the body or the body’s help. But now the opposite happens. Therefore, it does not exist through the body. 

Let us first hear Plato's mind regarding the way the human soul operates in the act of knowing. Since the soul is much more excellent than the body, and that which continually forms something is more excellent than the thing formed, therefore no bodies—whether they be outside us or within us—paint their own forms or images in the soul. Instead, with certain qualities, powers, or images, they strike that warm and vital vapor which is, in a sense, the <term>knot</term> <note>Ficino uses the term "nodus" (knot) to describe how the spirit binds the soul to the body.</note> of the body and the soul, and which is called "spirit" <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle, gas-like substance that served as the intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note> by the physicians. For if those bodies share the same matter as this spirit, but do not share it with the soul, it is more rational that the spirit is formed by them rather than the soul, which is so far removed that, rather than being formed by the body, it actually

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book Nine of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is transitioning from discussing the soul's relationship to celestial signs to a deeper exploration of how the soul functions as an independent "form" that governs the body without being determined by it.</meta>

# Theology

...it becomes both the **form** of the body and its **former** <note>original: "formatrix"; the active principle that gives shape and organization to something.</note>. It is indeed the former of its own body by nature, but of other things only in part. The rational soul, then, which is the source of bodily movements, actually moves bodies but is not moved by them. It would be moved by them if it were formed from them. But the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; in Ficino's philosophy, this is not a "ghost" but a subtle, vaporous substance that acts as a physical bridge between the immaterial soul and the material body.</note>, which runs ahead of the soul, is struck by various bodies. This kind of striking <note>original: "pulsatio"</note> does not escape the soul's notice. Insofar as such an affection or agitation of the spirit does not escape the soul, we are said to **sense**. 

Immediately from this sudden act of sensing, the inner power of the soul is stirred to another work similar to this one. For when it touches colors through the spirit of the eye, sounds through the spirit of the ear, and other things through other spirits, it does so by its own power—a power through which it presides over bodies and possesses their seeds, no less in the power of knowing than in the power of nourishing. <margin>C</margin> Soon it either conceives within itself the entirely spiritual **images** <note>original: "simulacra"</note> of colors, sounds, and the rest, or it brings forth what was conceived long ago and gathers them into one. This we have called **imagination** in previous sections. Afterward, we placed **phantasy** slightly above this, which wanders in almost the same way through the images of bodies. Finally, we placed the **intellect** at a far more eminent distance, as we have declared. 

<margin>D</margin> When the soul senses anything, according to the **Platonists** <note>The followers of Plato, whom Ficino synthesized with Christian theology.</note>, it is said to operate "through the body," not because the soul and the body sense together; for just as the soul is the source of living (as Plato says), so it is the source of sensing. Furthermore, objects are often present to the eyes or ears. If, however, the soul is agitated by something within itself, those objects are not sensed until the soul turns back to them; this shows that not these limbs, but the inner nature of our soul itself possesses the power of sensing. Yet this power of sensing does not sense unless the bodily spirit is agitated by bodies. 

When the soul acts through imagination or phantasy, it is said to operate "with the help of the body," because it revolves through individual images. These images were conceived individually through the impulse of the bodily spirit caused by bodies. And also because the kinship between these internal images and the spirit is so great that a vibration of the spirit itself always follows the internal revolution of images; and conversely, a revolution of images is usually triggered by a vibration of this spirit. When the soul contemplates and chooses something through the intelligence, it is said to operate both "without the body" and "without the aid of the body." This is because it sees and chooses something entirely foreign to those images, even without that impulse of the spirit and without the images collected from it.

<margin>E</margin> For the moment, I pass over the fact that the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who traditionally met in the "Peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum in Athens.</note> place all powers of sensing in the soul according to their origin, but in the **composite** <note>original: "composito"; the unified entity formed by the union of body and soul.</note> according to their form. They place the power of understanding in the soul alone. In this way, they believe that sensing powers act through the body, but the intellect acts even without the body. Nevertheless, they believe the soul naturally turns itself toward the images of bodily sense for as long as it naturally inhabits the body. 

However, the following signs will show us that this last operation (understanding) sometimes happens without bodily support, while the former ones always happen with the help of the body. First, the very power of the soul that uses the body, whatever it may be, does not perceive its own instrument. For who tastes their own tongue with the sense of taste? Who, through imagination or phantasy, has ever known the nature of spirits and images? Such things are hardly recognized even after long discussions of the mind. Yet it would be open and easy to everyone if the soul knew them through imagination and phantasy. 

The second sign: the **reason**, as we said, knows both itself and its own action through the body. If sight properly perceived that it was seeing by the very fact that it sees, we would always notice that we are seeing whenever we look at something. But this does not happen. For we often see a person present before us with open eyes, but because the inner power of the soul is focused on something else, we do not notice at all that we are seeing. It is as if an act of this kind is perceived not by sight, but by some inner power when it is unencumbered. Furthermore, acts of seeing and similar acts are, in a certain way, incorporeal. Sens...

He uses the example of "blind sight" (seeing without noticing) to prove that sensing is actually an internal power of the soul rather than a purely physical process.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book VIII. Ficino is contrasting the "lower" powers of the soul (senses, imagination, and phantasy) with the "higher" power of the intellect. He argues that the lower powers are bound to the body and its material conditions, while the intellect is independent and immaterial.</meta>

# Platonic Book

...through their own [organs], those senses know only bodily things. If they are ignorant of their own actions and powers, they are also ignorant of themselves. For what else is a specific power but a principle [operating] in a specific way and in its own proper manner? Therefore, he who does not know the operation does not know the mode of operating either. He also does not know the specific principle of operating in this way. 

<margin>A 2</margin>
Thus, the five senses are ignorant of themselves. But neither do imagination and **phantasy** <note>original: "phantasia"; in Ficino's psychology, phantasy is a higher faculty than basic imagination, responsible for processing and judging the images received by the senses</note> know themselves. For although everyone always uses these two powers of the soul—and everyone does so very easily—everyone would easily know their nature and powers [if they were self-aware]. 

<margin>B 3</margin>
But in fact, hardly anyone knows these things except those who have sought them through a long examination of the mind. The **third sign**: when something intense is presented to these powers, it occupies them by shaking them quite violently, so that they cannot perceive weaker things well—neither at that same time nor for a while afterward. Our eye, when sometimes staring directly at the rays of the sun, cannot see other colors, neither then nor for some space of time afterward. The same happens to the ears from a loud noise and thunder. The same with the other senses. The same also for imagination and phantasy whenever they are occupied by certain horrifying images. This shows that the act of these powers coincides with a vibration of their **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu"; in Renaissance medicine, this is a subtle, airy substance that transmits signals between the soul and the bodily organs</note> and vice-versa. It is just like the senses and movement of a **spider** staying in the middle of its web: the tension of the threads follows the flying flies everywhere, and the vibration of the web is felt throughout; conversely, the movement of the spider follows the vibration of the web. This certainly shows that these powers are close to matter, since they are often, as it were, overcome by the object. And the remnants of bodily passions remaining in the spirit for a time confuse them. 

The **fourth sign**: from a more powerful object, not only is the act of discerning confused, but injury and distress occur in us, as if the bodily spirit were damaged; through a certain mutual use of these powers, some offense also occurs. 

The **fifth [sign]**: they do not apprehend a quality or image that is natural to them. For example, the eye does not see its own brightness or its own image through itself. Touch does not indicate its own heat. Indeed, if some external heat becomes naturalized to the body, the sense does not feel it. This is common in those suffering from a **hectic fever** <note>original: "ethica febre"; a chronic, consuming fever that becomes part of the body's habit (hexis), making it harder for the patient to perceive</note>, whose touch no longer perceives the fever. Imagination and phantasy are also completely ignorant of their own power, habits, and the images they have conceived. For reason hardly finds such things. 

The **sixth [sign]**: after the seventh or eighth **seven-year cycle** <note>original: "septenarium"; Ficino refers to the "ages of man" theory where the body changes significantly every seven years, here meaning around ages 49 to 56</note> of age, when the bodily temperament begins to decline gradually toward an earthy quality, as the spirits are either dissipated or too thickened and cooled, sight grows dull, hearing is blocked, smell is obstructed, taste becomes stiff, and touch withers. The usual speed of imagination and phantasy is slowed down. 

<margin>B</margin>
The **seventh [sign]**: the longer they work, the more the senses are weakened and perceive things worse and more confusedly. For if you stare at something fixedly for an hour, your vision will dim; as the spirits are dissipated or darkened, the qualities of sensible things and the images you sense do not appear clearly in them. 

<margin>C</margin>
The **eighth [sign]**: they reach only a certain kind of things, not all kinds. Each sense has its own specific type of quality, as is evident. Imagination and phantasy have the specific conditions of these qualities. These and other such things usually happen to the powers of the soul that use the body. 

But the **opposite** happens to the **intellect**. Therefore, the intellect does not use the body. <margin>D</margin> Note how the opposite things happen to the mind. Those [sensory] powers are ignorant of themselves. <margin>☩</margin> But the mind knows itself. For it finds that it exists, what species of things it is in, and what power it has. Those powers have certain instruments [organs] and are ignorant of them. The intellect has no instrument; and if it had one, it would know it, since it knows both itself and other things. And it would place that instrument between itself and other things. If anyone says the mind has an instrument, we will ask whether it is bodily or otherwise. If he answers that it is bodily, he is refuted by **Peripatetic** <note>original: "peripateticam"; referring to the school of Aristotle, who argued the intellect must be "unmixed" with the body to know all things</note> argumentation. Every bodily instrument is contained in some species of body through some form specific to itself. If the intellect were to use such an instrument, it would not [know] bodily things purely...

<summary>Ficino provides eight "signs" or arguments to prove that the senses and imagination are material and dependent on the body, whereas the intellect is immaterial and self-aware. He uses metaphors like the spider's web and medical examples like hectic fever to illustrate how material conditions limit perception.</summary>
<keywords>intellect, senses, phantasy, imagination, hectic fever, spirit, spider metaphor, Peripatetic philosophy, aging, self-knowledge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in the Platonic Theology regarding the nature of the mind (intellect) and why it cannot be a physical body. On the previous page, he argued that physical senses are limited by their organs and cannot know themselves. Here, he explores why the mind must be immaterial to perceive truth and universals.</meta>

# Theology Book Nine

...would hold that opinion. For whatever is perceived through such an instrument is **infected** <note>original: "infectum"; in this context, Ficino means the perception is "colored" or distorted by the properties of the tool used to see it</note> by its quality. It will not appear entirely as it really is, but as the instrument is; for example, to red eyes the air appears red, and to yellow eyes, yellow. Because of this, the pupil [of the eye] lacks all color so that it can receive all colors purely. Thus, the mind's instrument ought to lack every bodily quality so that it might discern all things purely through itself. However, it would not lack every quality if it were a body; it would necessarily possess some. But whichever quality it possessed, it would not perceive. Thus, the mind would not know qualities similar to that [inherent] one through it. Just as the sense of touch, whose instrument possesses a certain degree of heat, does not feel an identical heat. But neither would it purely discern qualities dissimilar to it, because they would be "infected" by the instrument's own quality before the mind could notice them. Finally, through an instrument that was a body—which would belong to some certain category of bodies, being something individual and limited by place and time—the mind could not know anything more excellent than a body.

<margin>+</margin> Not even all of those things, but only a certain category of bodily things. Just as each individual sense perceives individual types of bodily things through individual instruments <note>For example, the eye sees color but cannot hear sound</note>.

<margin>D</margin> Lastly, the mind would not grasp anything **universal** <term>universal: a general concept or "essence" (like the concept of "Circle") as opposed to a specific, physical example (like a hoop or a coin)</term> through an individual, physical instrument. Yet we experience that we know universals through the mind. We judge that diverse things sometimes agree in a single nature. This happens when we reduce individual things into one **species** <note>original: "speciem"; the shared form or category that defines what a thing is</note>. When we compare a singular and specific thing with a common one, we judge that the universal differs from the particular. We cannot compare these two with each other except through a single power that encompasses both. Whenever by right reason we separate a certain class of the truest things from every kind of body—so that we see nothing bodily in it—at that point, we reject whatever can be called bodily. However, we cannot reject all bodily things through a bodily instrument, because at the very least that instrument itself cannot be rejected by the same instrument. And when we behold an abstract species and live through it, focusing on abstract forms and reasons, a bodily instrument would be a hindrance placed in the way rather than a help. For a body is most different from those abstract things, being much lower; it brings about distance rather than union. Since these things are so, the mind cannot use any bodily instrument. But does it use some other kind? Absolutely none. For if the mind joined any other instrument to itself, we would ask: can it understand anything without it, or nothing? If it can, it does not need an instrument. But someone might say it cannot. We, on the contrary, assert that it can. For now, everyone will admit that the intellect knows itself—and in this knowledge, it uses no instrument. For if it used something else to grasp itself, that thing would certainly stand in the middle between the mind and the mind's own essence. Thus, something external would be closer to the mind than the mind's own essence. And when the power of the mind reflects back upon its own power, or its act reflects upon its object, no instrument is placed in between.

<margin>E</margin> For a **medium** <note>original: "Medium"; a bridge or middle-man between two things</note> is usually adopted to create a connection between two extremes. But no instrument is more compatible with a power and its action than that power and action are with each other.

Everyone will also admit that the intellect—even if it had an instrument—is not ignorant of that instrument. For we are accustomed to saying that the intellect knows its instrument primarily because we assume the instrument exists and add that it serves the intellect. Furthermore, if the intellect knows itself and also external objects, it is necessary that it also sometimes knows the instrument through which it passes from itself to the objects it understands. Moreover, when the intellect turns itself toward its own act by way of objects already known, and through that act toward its own power and substance, is it not forced in this very "turning back" to also encounter its own instrument, if it has one? For that instrument would be the medium between the mind's act and its power. In that case, the mind would be forced to recognize its own instrument.

<margin>F</margin> But the mind hardly recognizes its instrument through another instrument; nor, if...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind must be immaterial because a physical organ would "color" or limit its perception, preventing it from grasping universal truths and self-knowledge. He concludes that the intellect needs no physical "instrument" because it can reflect directly upon itself and abstract concepts.</summary>

Ficino is in the middle of a series of proofs ("signs") demonstrating that the human mind (intellect) is an immaterial substance, distinct from the body and its sensory organs. He is currently arguing that because the mind can know itself and does not require a physical "instrument" to function, it must be simple and immortal.</meta>

# Platonic Book
<note>original title: "Platonice Liber"</note>

<margin>a</margin>
...through something [else]: I ask about that other, and then about another again to infinity. If it knows through nothing [external], then it does not need an instrument for knowing, since it knows itself without an instrument. In that case, what is called an "instrument" is rather a certain object and a medium. And if the mind passes from this to another in the act of knowing, it does not run from a medium to an object, but from a prior object to a posterior object. But perhaps someone might say: the instrument is known by the mind through some instrument, but [specifically] through that very same instrument. I, however, would ask: is it through the essence of the instrument, or through its image? Not the first, because the mind would then always know it, since it is always similarly present to it. But if it happens through an image, then that which was called an "instrument" is an object that is known, rather than an instrument through which something is known. And the image itself can be known with no intervening instrument, since the image necessarily precedes [the act of knowing] insofar as it is the medium between the object and the soul. 

Now, therefore, the intellect knows both itself and what is outside of itself without any instrument. 
<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, from the very fact that we can conceive of truly simple things and true simplicity <note>In Platonic philosophy, "simplicity" refers to being non-composite—not made of parts like a physical body</note>, the Platonists conclude: that which thinks within us is neither constituted by an intellect and an instrument, nor composed of a soul and a body; rather, the mind is simple and exists alone. Therefore, the mind operates through itself, and in this way, Plato says it is "moved by itself." Therefore, it lives by itself, and lives forever. 

Let us proceed to the third sign. Those [sensory] powers are confused by a powerful object <note>For example, a bright light can blind the eyes, or a loud noise deafen the ears</note>, so that they cannot discern weaker ones. The mind, on the other hand, when it sees magnificent and difficult things, then both within them and after them it discerns smaller and lighter things more clearly and easily. This is because the mind is great, and it is nourished and grows more [by great things]. 

Let us proceed to the fourth [sign] and those that follow. Other powers are harmed by a potent object. Is the mind's consideration harmed by any thing, even an immense one? Certainly, it is as if it were not subject to a certain "proportion of humors" <note>Physical health was thought to depend on the balance of four "humors" or bodily fluids; Ficino argues the mind is not limited by this biological balance</note>. Indeed, it finds the greatest truths more slowly because it does not investigate them while it is entangled in foreign [bodily] things. But when it is free, it finds them more quickly; and once they are found, it then shines more intensely, as if it were thoroughly prepared for them; then it is filled with incomparable pleasure, as if it had reached the things closest to it. Who does not see here that the power of the mind is in some way infinite, since it is not overcome by any finite object? 

Furthermore, these [sensory] powers are ignorant of the qualities and images familiar to them. But what "familiar thing" could the mind be ignorant of? It even defines familiarity itself, and it sees itself by understanding its own act, as well as the <term>species</term> <note>original: "spēm" (speciem); here meaning the mental form or concept</note> through which it understands, and its habit, and its virtue. Therefore, the mind dwells with itself. It is its own domicile. Any thing is preserved in its natural place. Therefore, the mind is preserved by itself, and remains forever unharmed. 

It follows that those who are physically stronger, as far as natural operations and often sensory ones are concerned, fare better than others. But as for intelligence, this is neither always nor often the case, as if intelligence were not a companion of the body. Add to this that the nature of the senses fails in operation through old age; but the eye of the mind then sees more clearly, once the clouds of youthful vices have been chased away. For Plato said divinely: 
<margin>B</margin>
The virtue of the soul does not flourish unless the virtue of the body withers. The sharpness of the mind is not sharpened unless the sharpness of the body is blunted. Then the wisdom of divine things flourishes, human prudence is perfected, and equity and constancy prevail. 
<margin>C</margin>
And what is greater: not even the power of sensing itself, which is in the soul, is lost by old age or disease, although its act may be interrupted when the eye is damaged. This is because the objects are no longer represented clearly enough. For even when a pen is broken, the act of writing ceases. But the **art of writing** remains whole in the soul. That the art suffers no loss from this is clear: for the mind writes within itself, and once the pen is restored, it writes at its own will. The same would happen if the tongue of a speechless man were cured, or the foot of a lame man. It is as if the damage were in the body, not in the soul. For often, once the eye is cleansed, we see immediately. This would either not happen, or would happen late even with the body healed, if the power of living itself had failed, which restores a certain...

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind is immaterial because it can know itself without physical tools, grows stronger when contemplating difficult truths, and often reaches its peak clarity as the physical body declines in old age. He concludes that sensory impairment is a failure of the bodily "instrument" (like a broken pen) rather than the soul's underlying ability.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book IX of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is in the middle of a series of proofs demonstrating that the human mind (intellect) is an immaterial substance, distinct from the physical body. He is arguing that the mind's apparent decline in old age or illness is not a failure of the soul itself, but rather a result of the body becoming a poor instrument or a distraction.</meta>

<page-num>79</page-num>
-> Theology <-
-> Book Nine <-

...as the time of its operation would require; after the body has completed its own time. Aristotle wisely said: <note>original: "Scite Aristoteles"</note> if you were to provide an old man with the eye of a youth, he would see exactly like a youth. If the senses, which are assigned to certain parts of the body, lose their power neither through injury to those parts nor through old age, then the **Mind**, which is assigned to no specific part, will never fail—not even when the whole body is injured. Here that reasoning comes to our aid which Socrates brings forward in the tenth book of the *Republic* <note>Plato’s Republic, Book X, contains a famous argument for immortality based on the "specific evil" of a thing.</note> by Plato: that the rational soul cannot die through any member of the body. 

<margin>C</margin>
In what way, he asks, will it perish by a disease of the body, when it does not perish by its own proper disease? Indeed, our body does not perish by another's disease, but by its own. 

<margin>D</margin>
For if it dies from a defect in food or the corruption of the air, it does not perish because of these things until they lead to its own proper disease, by which it is properly dissolved. And if it did not perish by its own proper disease, it would never perish by another’s. For if it is not harmed by a fever, it will not be harmed by unwholesome food or air. But the soul does not perish by its own proper flaw—that is, by **injustice**. For an unjust soul is no less a soul, and no less vital, than a just one. Therefore, it does not perish by a disease of the body. 

Furthermore, a disease of the body does not bring upon the soul the specific vice of the soul itself. Since the soul does not become more unjust when the body is sick, but often corrects itself and makes progress in the pursuit of character. Therefore, a disease of the body not only fails to destroy the soul, but does not even corrupt it. And if at any time the mind seems to be harmed while the body is sick, it is not actually so. 

<margin>E</margin>
Perhaps the mind is at leisure there, either acting within itself or occupied with human affairs; it is not harmed. When Socrates was either playing with his children or caring for them, he did not lose the habit of his more sublime philosophy, even though he was not philosophizing at all in those moments, or at least not philosophizing excellently, while his intellectual activity was distracted by the consideration of lowlier things. 

Our soul often "plays" with the body in the body's pleasures. In its illnesses, the soul governs and cares for it. In both states, that sublime consideration of reason is either interrupted or relaxed; it either rests for a time or is too anxiously occupied with baser matters. But when things are peaceful, it rises again. For it is so arranged by nature that we are not sufficiently capable of diverse works at the same time—as far as human strength is concerned. Guests intent on a feast do not hear the melodies of the lyre well. While the soul is heavily digesting food in the stomach, it relaxes the duty of human contemplation. Therefore, it then seems to be dulled. While it speculates more intensely, food is digested with difficulty. Hence, philosophers are often physically weak, yet they are not weak in soul; rather, they excel in intelligence as much as they fail in body. 

Therefore, why is it a wonder if the soul, while the body is feverish, ceases from contemplation because it is most intent on sustaining and curing the sick body? Or if it uses the intellect less while it is very occupied in sustaining the body of a decrepit old man? And when dark vapors <note>In Renaissance medicine, "vapors" were gases or fluids produced by the body that could cloud the mind or cause hallucinations.</note> occupy the spirit of the brain, and the soul is strained by their vibration and moves horrible things in the **imagination**, do you wonder if it should meanwhile interrupt the work of contemplation? Eventually, when the vapors are cleared, that work is restored. Often, even while the vapors are boiling, reason itself is wide awake and refutes the illusions of images; this happens in those who suffer from vertigo, whose reason denies that the sky or earth is falling, even though the senses report it. 

<margin>F</margin>
Again, those who are incited by the madness of a rabid dog, or who are rushing into human fury, sometimes notice the impending insanity even in the very onset of their rage. And those who are terrified by horrific things in dreams often cry out against the fantasy, saying they are dreaming. Therefore, the mind does not always need the lower powers, for it is often at leisure when they are active, and it is active when they are at leisure. It judges their shortcomings and commands them to be silent. 

If someone says the mind needs those powers to be awakened, and therefore can do nothing at all without them, I respond as follows: since the soul always occupies itself with the body's survival while it inhabits the body, it is distracted by many things far removed from divine matters. Therefore, it does not turn toward the intuition of divine things unless it is awakened to them by grasping certain more expressive likenesses of them through those lower powers which it uses most. But after it has turned enough, and has been prepared by frequent turning for the infusion of divine things, it no longer needs their service for that contemplation.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's immortality is proven because the mind is independent of bodily organs. Using examples of illness, old age, and distraction, he demonstrates that the soul is not damaged by physical decay but is merely preoccupied with bodily maintenance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book IX of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is addressing counter-arguments regarding the soul's immortality, specifically explaining why the mind's functions appear to decline when the physical body is ill, injured, or aging, and how individual differences in intelligence arise.</meta>

# Platonic Book
-> B <-

...needs. Rather, the mind lulls the senses to sleep as much as it can so as not to be hindered by them. Indeed, it would always gladly persevere in that state if the necessity of caring for the body did not press upon it. This signifies that the mind can continue its speculation by itself; and when it is no longer pulled back from this by the care of the body, it will speculate freely by itself without the service of the other powers—for which it was previously enough simply not to be hindered by them. But as long as it is enclosed in the body, because of that service of the senses by which it is prepared for its turning <note>original: "conuersioni" — the process by which the soul turns its attention toward or away from material objects.</note> toward things, it happens that when the body is injured and the **spirit** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" (spiritus) was a subtle physical vapor that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the heavy physical body.</note> is clouded, objects are neither clearly represented, nor is the perception in the senses and the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes sensory images before they reach the intellect</term> clear. Consequently, the mind is not easily aroused from there to true speculation. 

It also happens that some people appear more talented than others because of the diversity of these spirits. Although I believe the difference among men in learning the arts should be attributed not so much to a difference in natural talent as to a difference in will. For anyone attains the greatest things if they strive studiously. It happens, moreover, that some are called "insane," who either do not use their mind or misuse it. This is because the entire attention of the soul in these people is too occupied with the more violent illusions of the imagination.

<margin>B</margin>
But once the bile—whether black <note>Melancholy</note> or yellow <note>Choleric humor</note>—which provides the cause of the illusion is emptied, they suddenly regain their senses, as people who never actually lost their mind. 

Add to this what **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian who theorized the pre-existence of souls.</note> and **Plotinus** <note>The primary philosopher of Neoplatonism.</note> argue: that human souls are, in a way, minds fallen from their own purity; namely, they fell into bodies when they slipped from the attention of the mind toward the **Ideas** <term>Ideas: the eternal, divine blueprints of reality in the Platonic tradition</term> to the attention of the life-giving power of bodies. And the more some souls are attentive and deeper turned toward matter than others, the less (as they say) they retain of intellectual light. From this arises a great diversity in talents and characters among souls. To this also contribute the ethereal bodies of souls <note>The "astral body" or "starry garment" that the soul was thought to pick up as it descended through the celestial spheres.</note> which are adapted to the various configurations of the sky and stars. Finally, the variety of **geniuses** <note>original: "geniorum" — guardian spirits or guiding daimons.</note> brings about a variety of talents. 

If anyone does not grant that souls existed in time before bodies, yet wishes to follow the Platonists in some measure, he might perhaps be able to say that souls—at least at that very moment they are created and joined to the body—are affected and disposed almost as Origen and Plotinus argue. Truly, some angelic minds have fallen further to lower things, others least of all; and among those who fell, some more, others less. But the minds of men, as the lowest of all, by a natural instinct as soon as they are created, incline toward natural parts and bodies; and some merge themselves deeper than others into the **river Lethe**—that is, into matter. <note>In mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness; Platonists used it to symbolize the soul forgetting its divine origin upon entering a body.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
And in this way **Pamphilus** <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea, a 3rd-century scholar who wrote a defense of Origen.</note> seems to have corrected Origen as much as he could. But about these things, we shall speak elsewhere. Now, therefore, let us return to the proposal.

<margin>C</margin>
If someone seems to lose their memory because a certain part of the head is injured, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> will answer that the images of things which are retained in the spirit of the brain are confused. But the forms <note>original: "species"</note> which are in the mind are not properly harmed; rather (so to speak) they are idle. For it is necessary for the mind, as long as it inhabits the body, to look upon the forms of bodily things only through the images of those bodily things.

<margin>D</margin>
The Platonists will add that insofar as the soul's attention is more intensely occupied with the healing of the injured limb, to that extent its cognition and memory are weakened and interrupted.

<margin>E</margin>
**Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali** <note>Arabic philosophers whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance Latin thought.</note> will say that the mind, when turned toward lower things, is diverted from a certain **Divine Mind**, upon which they think the act of all understanding continually depends. 

However, because **Lucretius** <note>Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher who argued the soul was mortal and material.</note> distrusts immortality for this reason—especially because at the approach of death, the powers of the soul seem to fail—it must be noted that the life of the body consists in the balance of moisture and heat. Therefore the body dies when either heat dissolves the moisture or moisture extinguishes the heat. Since moisture is the food of heat, and heat is the vehicle of the spirit, and the spirit is the bond between the soul and the body, it happens that when the moisture in the limbs of the body is gradually dissolved, the soul also leaves the limbs gradually. And because it is then less occupied with ruling the body than it usually is, it collects itself into its own mind; it perceives secrets <note>original: "aranea" is likely a transcription error for "arcana" (secrets/mysteries), which fits the context of prophecy.</note> and presages the future. Let the Lucretian suspicion be far from us—namely, that the soul is going to die with the body—which, even as the body is weakened...

<summary>Ficino explains that mental deficiencies and individual differences in intelligence result from physical obstructions or the soul's "descent" into matter, rather than a failure of the soul itself. He refutes Lucretius by arguing that as the body dies, the soul actually becomes more independent and prophetic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the immortality of the soul in Book IX of his Platonic Theology. He is currently enumerating specific "signs" or logical proofs that the soul (animus/mens) is a distinct, incorporeal substance that does not perish with the body.</meta>

# Theology
# Ninth [Book]

<margin>p</margin>
...is strengthened. Since union is the furthest thing from dissolution <note>original: "dissolutioni," referring to the breaking apart of the physical body into its elements</note>, the soul must be thought to be furthest from dissolution when it most gathers itself into itself. Having set aside its lower animal nature, it rises into the mind. This clearly happens in death which occurs through "resolution." However, in a death that occurs through the extinction of the vital force, the soul’s power is intent on curing the humors and swellings; the senses are occupied with judging pains; the **imagination** <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes sensory images into mental pictures</term> is occupied with looking at the phantoms stirred up by the vapors of the humors. For this reason, reason remits its duty for a time, just as it often does in sleep, so that it may resume after the tumult of death, just as it is accustomed to wake after dreams. The fact that it by no means loses its powers and gifts at that very time is proven by the fact that many who are recalled to life from imminent death by the diligence of doctors either never recover their bodily strength, or do so only very late. Yet, as soon as the humors are purged, the light of the mind returns, as if the bodily powers had been extinguished, but the light of the mind had been hiding like fire under ashes rather than vanishing. Who would say that the exit of the body and the soul from life is the same, since their return is not the same? For the body returns with difficulty and late; the soul returns easily and suddenly. Nor does it lose anything of itself at that time, since it suddenly brings its natural and acquired gifts back into the light no less than it was accustomed to before—inasmuch as it had then collected its belongings which it had previously scattered, and had been prepared like a servant about to strip off old clothes. It is destined to exit those gates into the light living and whole, no differently than when it once struggled from the mother’s womb into the light. Thus, the wise man understands that when he leaves the body, he is not being deprived of a part of himself, but is being freed from a most troublesome burden. So much for the 
<margin>†</margin>
sixth sign. Now receive that seventh sign. The senses are fatigued by daily work, but the mind never is. The longer you look at something, the more dimly you will see; yet the longer you investigate with the intellect, the more clearly you will understand. Every work of the body and the senses is exhausted by use, 

but the soul's work is strengthened. It is true that the head is often weighed down by long-standing thought and the eye grows misty, but this is because the movements of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasie"</note> and the vibration of the **spirit** <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance that Renaissance thinkers believed connected the physical body to the immaterial soul</term> frequently accompany the exercise of the mind. The latter is caused by injury to the brain or the eye. But the edge of the mind itself becomes lighter and sharper. It would certainly remain directed upward without any interruption, were it not that, out of pity for the body entrusted to it, it interrupted its own work for the sake of refreshing the body. This is clearly seen in those who, while contemplating something quite attentively, are pained to find the body fatigued. In them, the mind ceases from work in a way that is reluctant, while the body and senses cease most willingly—as if it were not the mind that is exhausted by working, but the body. That which is tireless is also immortal. The eighth sign is that other powers are assigned to some specific class of things, but the mind to none. For what is there in the number of things that are said "to be" toward which the edge of the mind cannot be directed? It grasps the essence, nature, and power of that which is called **being** <term>ens: a technical philosophical term for anything that exists</term> through its definition. Under this "being," all things that exist are contained. It also finds the difference between being and non-being; thus it knows both. It divides being into its parts and particles, as it distributes all various kinds and species under the category of being. And what is greater: it ascends "above being" and descends "below being." It ascends when it establishes "The One" itself and "The Good" itself above being; it places matter or the privation of things below being. The mind is bound to no single genus of things if it encompasses all things. It has nothing outside itself by which it might be destroyed, since it encloses all things, in a sense, within itself. Let us conclude the dispute in this way: if the human soul existed through the body in some way, it would do nothing without the body's instrument or aid. But it acts without the use of the body in understanding and willing, as we have shown through eight signs. Therefore, it does not exist through the body. It exists, therefore, either through itself or through divine things. If through itself, it never deserts itself; if through divine things, then it is eternal through eternal causes.

<summary>Ficino presents arguments for the soul's immortality, noting that the mind thrives while the body fatigues and that the intellect can contemplate "Being" as a whole, placing it above physical limitations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, specifically Book IX. In the preceding sections, Ficino has been detailing various "signs" or logical proofs for the immortality of the human soul. He is currently transitioning into the "Sixth Reason," which focuses on the soul's intermediate nature—sharing qualities with both the divine and the animal kingdoms.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

<margin>Book 9. Chapter 6.</margin>
# Platonic [Theology]

$\P$ The Sixth Reason. The soul corresponds partly with divine things and partly with beasts.

<margin>A</margin>
**I**f the human soul sprang from matter—the river they call **Lethe** <note>original: "letheuz," referring to the mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld; Ficino uses this to symbolize the material world which causes the soul to forget its divine origin</note>—it would never be joined in its activity with divine things, which do not spring from that river. However, we shall show that the soul corresponds with them in activity, and indeed in essence and life, in the following way.

<margin>B</margin>
Since we see that all things act most intensely when they are mature and perfect in their kind, we are forced to assert that God, who is the most perfect of all, is not idle, but is active, since **activity** <term>operatio: the actual exercise or functioning of a power, as opposed to just having the potential</term> is the sign of perfection. Indeed, we ourselves would not do anything unless he acted, he by whom we are moved, just as by his making we exist, and by his breathing we live and draw breath. But what is the activity of God? It cannot begin from elsewhere or tend toward some other thing, lest God be forced to depend on something else. Therefore, the activity of God is a certain perpetual turning-back into himself, through which he enjoys himself and rejoices. Thus, he contemplates himself; by contemplating himself, he sees his own power. Gazing upon this, he discerns all that he is able to do.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, he views himself and his entire work simultaneously in a single act. By observing, he conceives all things within himself. By conceiving, he brings forth outside of himself whatever he wills. The activity of his holy ministers and celestial spirits is almost the same. For they too observe themselves and their own works. They also observe God and divine works. Certainly, **contemplation** <note>original: "speculatio," the act of mental looking or philosophical vision</note> is the only activity suitable for them, because it is the most perfect of all activities. This is also apparent in us. It does not require external matter, as craftsmanship does. Nor does it require bodily instruments, as the senses do. Nor is it moved from elsewhere, or tend elsewhere, like other activities. It does not give shape to foreign matter, but cultivates and adorns the mind. It is not limited by anything else, but ends in itself; nor is it quickly exhausted like others, but remains tireless. It is not troublesome or needy, as those others are, but easy, full, and bathed in in-

<margin>D</margin>
comparable joy. If, therefore, any of these activities within us is to be attributed to the higher powers, contemplation must certainly be attributed

---

# Book

to them as the happiest of all activities. From these points, it is clear that the human soul corresponds with divine things in contemplation. We do not doubt that it also corresponds with beasts in nutrition, sensation, and the affections of the body. Certainly, activities require specific and appropriate powers and substances directed toward objects suited to them. And whatever the proportion of one object is to another, the same is the proportion of one activity to another. The comparison of power and essence to another power and essence is the same. Thus, just as in us, regarding the use of the body, there is an activity common with the beasts toward an object common with them, so a nature common with them appears. This is the activity and power of nourishing and sensing, and the physical temperament of the body, which in us are almost as **perishable** <note>original: "caduca," literally falling or transitory; refers to things that decay and die</note> as they are in beasts.

<margin>E</margin>
It is necessary, then, that there be found in us a power and a substance common with those celestial beings, from which that activity is born which we have in common with them, directed toward an object common to us and them. For this reason, just as the nature of nourishing and sensing and the bodily temperament are in a sense perishable in us (since they deal with perishable things and are common to perishable beings), so the power of contemplating will be immortal, since it deals with immortal things and is common with immortal beings. For the same activity cannot proceed except from the same nature and power. Who would doubt that our contemplation is very similar to the higher kind? Since through it, the soul—just like those celestial beings—considers itself and its works. It also investigates higher causes and their effects. Likewise, it ascends from lower effects through intermediate causes all the way to the Supreme Cause, and in turn returns in a circle from the Supreme Cause down to the lowest outcomes. Here, it seems to embrace the entire sequence of the divine work by no other power than a divine one, and to survey it like some god. Not only does the soul have an understanding in common with the divine spirits, but also a will, since it desires their happiness. Furthermore, it has a similar way of acting, insofar as it acts freely and commands its own body almost as they do.

<margin>F</margin>
From all these points, it is gathered that our soul [is one] with the celestial [beings]...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul occupies a middle ground between the divine and the animal. Because the soul is capable of contemplation—a tireless, self-contained, and joy-filled activity shared with God and angels—it must possess an immortal nature similar to theirs.</summary>

Having previously discussed how the soul's activity mirrors God's, Ficino now argues that the soul’s essence and life are also linked to the eternal heavens, leading into a rebuttal against Epicurean materialists.</meta>

<sig>L</sig>

...to agree in essence with the celestial beings. If our essence shares a common and close bond with them, and those beings have no origin in matter, it follows that our soul likewise has no such origin. Furthermore, if those divine powers are everlasting—the ones who move the spheres of the world in the same order forever and never grow weary—it follows that the essence of the mind is everlasting. For a limited and changeable life can in no way be "next" to an unlimited and unchanging life. Moreover, the soul corresponds with them in the immortality of life, the understanding of truth, and the desire for happiness, just as life itself comes before understanding or will. And if the will is the striving of the intelligence, and intelligence is the highest peak of a growing life, the mind is directed toward a right will only through true intelligence. So too, it reaches this intelligence only through a true and mature life. It possesses a right will when it directs itself toward the first and total Good. It possesses true intelligence both when it is not deceived (insofar as it is intelligence) and when it possesses within itself the true **inner patterns** <term>rationes: the formal principles or blueprints of things that exist in the mind</term> of all things. We shall demonstrate this elsewhere. Therefore, it is necessary that the soul possesses a true and mature life. Such a life is one that is not subject to death. 

<margin>B</margin>
That famous saying of **Origen** <note>original: "Origenis"; an early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) whose views on the soul's pre-existence and nature heavily influenced Ficino’s Neoplatonism</note> greatly supports this argument of ours: "All natures that share in the same principle are similar to one another." Just as eyes are all similar because they all share in light, since they are all naturally turned toward light in the same way; yet, according to their different participation in light, one eye is sharper than another. All rational substances share in God, since they all turn toward God. Therefore, they are similar, both to one another and to Him. Thus, just as the higher beings are immortal, such as the angels, so too are the lower ones, such as souls. Indeed, all are immortal because they are very much like the immortal God. This similarity is shown by that very turning toward God—the angels turn toward Him like the higher stars turning toward the sun. The soul, however, turns toward Him like the moon; although the soul may be changed by a certain "waxing and waning" of the divine light, and thus receives it in a changeable way, it nevertheless perceives it through **inextinguishable reason** <note>original: "inextinguibili... ratione"</note>. For the soul comprehends through certain logical proofs both that this Being is inextinguishable and the reason why it is so.

<margin>I</margin>
### The objection of the Epicureans: and the response concerning the tempering of things. Chapter VII.

**R**eluctance will be shown by **Dicaearchus** <note>original: "dicearcus"; a Greek philosopher who argued that the soul was merely a "harmony" of the body's elements and thus died with the body</note> or some Epicurean, as if this idea were like a monster—namely, that a single thing could be partly incorruptible and partly subject to corruption. But we shall affirm that the order of nature cannot be preserved without this. There are some bodies entirely removed from all corruption, such as the heavens, of which neither the sphere itself nor any small part is corrupted. There are also bodies entirely opposite to these: namely, those that are completely perishable, like wood, stones, metals, and other things composed of the four elements. Indeed, some small parts of wood eventually rot. Then, the whole piece of wood itself ceases to be wood—even though anything composed this way is at least superior to the incorruptible and the corruptible because it holds within itself **prime matter** <term>materia: the underlying "stuff" of the universe that Ficino considers eternal even as it takes on different temporary forms</term> which is perpetual, even if its form is mortal. Therefore, the joining of mortal things with immortal things is neither impossible nor rare. But let us return to the established order.

<margin>J</margin>
There are also "middle" bodies: namely, the four spheres of the elements, which are partly incorruptible and partly corruptible. The whole sphere of an element itself preserves its type, its position, and its continuity. Yet some of its particles are led away from here or restored from there. Since bodies were established either by spirits or for the sake of spirits, the order of bodies must proceed from the order of spirits, or at least imitate the order of spirits. There are, therefore, some spirits who are entirely immortal, such as angels, whose entire substance is never changed, nor is any power, nor even any activity. There are others who are entirely mortal, as is the common opinion: namely, the souls of **brute animals** <note>original: "brutorum"; non-human animals lacking rational souls</note>, whose power and activity are changed, and whose entire substance is changed as well. There must also be spirits that are "middle" between both, so that there may be one single, uninterrupted weaving together of all nature. <margin>Z</margin> These through all...

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence: Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.
## Book Ten.
### First Reason: Just as the last in the order of bodies is incorruptible, so too is the last in the order of minds. Chapter 1.

<margin>L</margin>
Since the order of physical bodies is situated beneath the order of intellects, and depends upon it, the order of the body follows the orders of the intellects in no other way than a footprint follows the foot itself, or a shadow follows the body. Therefore, we ought to imagine that the order we see among physical bodies is nearly identical to the order found among minds.

<margin>di</margin>
In the order of bodies, we see a "sublime body"—namely, the highest heaven—which contains within its nature all the powers of all the active **forms** <term>forms: the essential blueprints or organizing principles of things</term>. Through these powers, which are active and effective, it prepares lower bodies to receive various forms. Therefore, through the various virtues of its nature and the various configurations of its motion, it moves and shapes the lower bodies in various ways.

<margin><note>manicule: a hand-drawn pointing finger used to highlight important passages</note></margin>
Thus, it can rightly be said that the highest heaven encompasses the forms of all other bodies, either in actuality or through an active power. We can assert that the bodies following it are so subject to it that they possess those same forms in a certain **receptive potentiality** <term>potentiality: the capacity to become or receive something, as opposed to "actuality," which is being it already</term> (as it is called) and a passive state, and they receive those forms from the heaven in actuality.

<margin>f</margin>
Truly, such an order is maintained so that the more sublime a body is beneath that highest heaven, the more active power it possesses and the less passive power. For that which is closest to the "First" receives and undergoes action from that single First source, yet it acts upon many things. That which is placed on the next level undergoes even more action and acts less. Since it undergoes action from two sources—namely the first and the second—it pours out what it has received into the things that follow. This continues until 

<margin>H.</margin>

---

<margin>6 37</margin>
one comes to a certain "lowest matter." Since this matter receives from all things above it, it gives to none. Therefore, in its passive potentiality, it indeed possesses all forms, which it receives through a succession of actions from the things above it; however, in terms of effective power, it possesses none. Imagine the same thing occurring among minds. God, the principle of these minds, possesses all **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the conceptual versions of things as they exist in the mind</term> in a single and unique act; He distributes to all and receives from none.

The minds following Him receive everything from that source, and they relate to one another in such a way that a higher mind distributes those **ideas** <note>original: "ideas"; the eternal, divine patterns of all things</note> and light, as it were, to a lower one. Therefore, the higher a mind is, the fewer things it is subject to and the more it presides over. It undergoes action from fewer sources in its "receiving" and acts upon more in its "distributing." Finally, the lowest mind must be such that it is the opposite of that first principle: it receives from all and gives to none. According to its nature, it possesses those ideas in passive potentiality, but none in active power, since it does not pour ideas into any intellect placed beneath it. Indeed, in the First, there is only the active power of ideas. In those that follow, there is an orderly mix of active and passive. In the lowest mind, there is passive power.

Therefore, God holds the rank of the first heaven. The middle minds take the place of the intermediate bodies. The lowest intellect holds the place of the lowest matter. By its nature, this lowest intellect receives all intelligible principles in a certain succession in actuality—that is, it "sees" them—though it does not gaze upon all of them at once in actuality. This is just as matter receives the forms of bodies by succeeding from one form to another.

<margin>,,</margin>
¶ This matter, which is not made from any preceding matter, requires an infinite creator. For this reason, it is created by—or flows from—God alone.

<margin>2 7</margin>
¶ It is only right that a simple potentiality should be made by a simple **act** <term>act: the state of being fully realized or active; here, God is "Pure Act"</term>. Since God, by His action, surpasses the actions of all other agents, He alone makes "matter," which holds the final rank in nature. ¶ If God alone creates matter, which is the lowest of physical things, He alone creates that mind which is the lowest of intellects. If the least work of divine works is that which is most remote from God, and the intellectual race is the closest, and if matter is made separately from the mind, it can much more...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Marsilio Ficino is establishing that the human mind (or "ultimate intellect") must be incorruptible because of its position in the cosmic hierarchy. He is comparing the role of the mind in the spiritual world to the role of matter in the physical world.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

<margin>☩</margin>
...the mind must exist separately from matter. If the **ultimate intellect** <term>ultimate intellect: the lowest level of purely rational or spiritual mind, which Ficino identifies as the human soul</term> holds such a place in the category of intellectual things as **matter** <term>matter: here referring to 'prime matter,' the underlying substance of all physical things</term> holds in the category of natural things, and if matter cannot be created from any natural thing, it follows that the lowest intellect cannot be created from any species of intellect that exists within that category. <margin>a</margin> And if an intellect of this kind does not depend on any intellect of the same category (or even a much more excellent one), it is even less to be thought of as depending on the natural category, and much less still on matter. From this it follows that the lowest mind is not drawn out from matter. It also follows that it is incorruptible. For since the order of minds is more excellent than the order of bodies, and the order of physical things eventually descends into eternal matter—since that matter is never corrupted, however far removed it may be—who would be so far gone as to concede that the order of minds, which is more stable and more divine than bodies, should end at last in a corruptible mind? Therefore, the ultimate intellect must be eternal. It relates to **intelligible forms** <term>intelligible forms: the abstract, eternal truths or ideas that the mind perceives</term> in the same way that prime matter relates to sensible forms. Matter is not destroyed by any sensible form through physical corruption—for it is shaped by them—nor is it destroyed by any intelligible species, for it is perfected by them. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, the ultimate mind is not destroyed by any intelligible species through spiritual corruption, for it is perfected by these; nor does it perish through physical corruption by any sensible form. For the mind stands above and is not subject to physical forms. Nor does physical corruption pass into the mind, just as spiritual corruption does not pass into matter. Indeed, if spiritual violence does not pass into the mind, much less will physical violence pass into it because of the density of bodies. Furthermore, if the corruption of physical things does not reach the matter underlying them, much less will it pollute the higher mind dwelling there.

<margin>B</margin> Let it be granted then that the ultimate intellect is eternal. But what is this intellect? It is, I say, the human intellect. Who would doubt that there is an intellect within us? To doubt it would be impossible, since we cannot even argue about intellects except through the power of the intellect. And just as the eye does not capture the light of the sun except through a certain internal light of its own, so our soul neither investigates nor contemplates divine intellects except through its own intellect. But what is the nature of this intellect of ours? I care for nothing further: for whatever its nature may be, it will be eternal. For the higher intellects are undoubtedly eternal if even the lowest is eternal. <margin>C</margin> I truly believe that our mind is the "last" or "lowest" for this reason (as was pleasing to many of the ancients): because it does not act upon its objects all at once, but turns the forms over within itself in succession, like **Prometheus** <note>In Ficino's allegory, Prometheus represents the human soul's struggle to "steal" divine knowledge and process it through time and reasoning.</note>, and understands by proceeding from one thing to the next. <margin>C</margin> Just as the moon, which is the last of the stars, changes its light in turns while the others do not change, so let our mind be the last. And let it be eternal. Because it is eternal, it always gasps for eternal things; and as often as it is not disturbed by the body, it reaches them instantly, rejoicing in them as if they were its own and familiar to it. For the "natural birth" of any thing is that which happens immediately once an obstacle is removed. It moves toward a goal most similar to itself; and because it is the "last" of the spiritual things, it loves the nature of bodies as if they were kin, approaching them, giving them life, and governing them.

### The objection of Epicurus and the response regarding the series of things. Chapter II.

<margin>D</margin> **H**ere again, **Epicurus** <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was an ancient philosopher often associated with the view that the soul is mortal and the world is made of atoms.</note> rashly exclaims: "Could it be possible for the divine to be bound to mortal things?" He says this as if he does not see that mortal things cannot exist without the companionship of the divine and the stable. <margin>E</margin> I think it escaped him that the **series of things** <term>series of things: often called the "Great Chain of Being," the idea that all levels of reality are connected in an unbroken chain</term> must be so arranged in its parts that, since there are many and varied orders of things in nature, the lowest parts of every higher order are always coupled in some way to the highest parts of the lower order that follows immediately after. <margin>E</margin> This is taught to us by the kinship of the **ether** <term>ether: the "fifth element" that makes up the heavens, considered more refined than earth, water, air, or fire</term> with the nature of the elements. Indeed, the moon is the lowest part of the ether and the first thing above the elements; it has something of an elemental power, both through the frequent change of its shape and by the very variety of its bright and dark body. Conversely, fire—the highest element—imitates the heaven closest to it, since it moves and shines in the manner of the heavens. This same thing is shown by the natural arrangement of the four elements among themselves.

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect is the "lowest" of the spiritual minds and must be eternal, using the analogy that it occupies a similar foundational role in the spirit world as matter does in the physical world. He then begins to answer Epicurus's objection by explaining the "Great Chain of Being," where every level of existence is linked to the one below it.</summary>
