...I thirst. Where the lowest part of fire is more humid: and it grows lukewarm, almost like air. The highest region of air is thinned out and almost boils: just like fire. There, the air is fiery, and the fire is airy. And so they are joined into a single structure. The lowest region of air and the highest region of water do the same thing. Where the air is clouded over, it turns to liquid like water. Conversely, water that has been thinned out by heat exhales as vapors: just like air. Again, the higher earth is rich and slippery, like water. The bottom of the water swells into earth and is often frozen: just like earth. Beyond the elements themselves, the thick vapors and smoke are already composite bodies, but they remain very close to the elements. Later, they are glued together a little more solidly and become certain spongy and porous stones, which are near neighbors to the vapors. Afterward, stones are found that are truly hard and beautiful, such as metals.

<margin>§</margin> Among the metals, iron and lead are close to stones. Silver and gold are closer to plants. For their shine and splendor reflect white and purple flowers. In plants, the red color exceeds that of metals because a plant is more clearly nourished and grows, though only a little, because it does not have a complex arrangement of different parts. The most active trees are close to "brutes" <note>original: "brutis," referring to non-human animals</note>. They have roots in place of a mouth. They have branches like legs, arms, and the like. Some trees even have both sexes: masculine and feminine. When planted near each other, they sprout more abundantly. Among the animals, 

<margin>§</margin> oysters surpass plants by only one degree, because they possess the sense of touch. But they are fixed to the earth and nourished almost like trees. Furthermore, adult beasts are born spontaneously without mating, just like herbs <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief in "spontaneous generation," where life could arise from decaying matter.</note>. 

<margin>b</margin> There are also monkeys, dogs, horses, and elephants, and other beasts that are very similar to humans in certain shapes, gestures, and skills. There are dull and lazy men—as it appears—who are also very close to these animals. On the other side, there are heroic men, leaders of others, who are most closely related to the higher divinities. Again, it is necessary that there be spirits <note>original: "spiritus," here referring to "daemons" or intermediary beings in the Platonic hierarchy</note> joined to humans in close familiarity; <term>Plato</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC), whose works Ficino translated and harmonized with Christianity.</note> maintains that through their instruction, the miracles of the magical arts were discovered. Just as some animals, through the instruction of humans, become closer to us and often perform wonders beyond their own species. And so these daemons or heroes are so close to us in affection as they are in nature and even in their placement, so that they are affected by certain human disturbances. Some favor certain people and places, while others are opposed to them. Indeed, <margin>ll .</margin> the Egyptians—whom <term>Origen</term> <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who incorporated Platonic ideas.</note>, <term>Numenius</term> <note>A philosopher who bridged Platonism and Pythagoreanism.</note>, and <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who organized the works of Plotinus.</note> follow—say there are many daemons who raise minds to higher things, and many also who twist them toward lower things. They say the worst daemons are in the West. In the Northern region, they are also evil. The good ones are in the South. The best of all inhabit the Eastern region. Among them, superior beings preside over the lower daemons; over these, in turn, are others whom they call angels. Likewise, <margin>X and Augustine</margin> <note>A reference to St. Augustine, who also discussed the celestial hierarchy.</note> the Platonists place archangels above angels, and principalities above archangels. Above the principalities, however, are certain "intellects" who are called "gods" by a certain participation, being always full of the Highest God and drunk on divine nectar.

If we confess that in all <margin>ll .</margin> kinds of things, the lowest parts of a preceding order are joined with the highest of the succeeding order, and are in some way blended together, why should we not admit that the lowest intellect <note>Ficino's term for the human mind, the bridge between the physical and spiritual.</note> is so joined with the highest of the sensitive souls <note>The part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement in animals.</note> that even though the latter is mortal, it has some image of intellect? This is manifest in the most sagacious beasts. The last intellect, <margin>M movement</margin> although it is divine, also has a certain sensitive and "brute" nature, through which it appropriately leans toward earthly bodies. Especially since it is fitting that not only the human mind, but all others which are in some way "impure," should harmonize with purer bodies. "Impure" minds are all those rational souls which, although they are pure souls, are nonetheless "impure minds" because they are animal-like minds <note>original: "mentes aiales," minds that animate a body.</note>. I say they are minds so <margin>ll .</margin> dedicated to moving bodies that they imprint their vital and animal traces upon those bodies. <margin>ll .</margin> Pure minds, however, are those that are minds only; they do not pour forth from themselves animal-like images immersed in governing bodies. According to <term>Plato</term>, the pure bodies are the twelve <margin>i 2 .</margin> [parts] of the world itself...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino describes the "Great Chain of Being," arguing that all levels of reality—from the four elements to metals, plants, animals, humans, and celestial spirits—are interconnected without gaps. He places the human mind as the crucial bridge between the physical world of "brute" animals and the divine world of pure intellects.</summary>

# Platonic

<margin>A</margin>
There are eight spheres of heaven, and four elements beneath the heavens. Furthermore, there are certain most precious parts within each of these spheres. Therefore, rational souls are present in all the spheres, arranged step by step according to their dignity. But Plato calls the single soul of the single world-machine "Jove" <note>original: "Ioem," referring to Jupiter or Jove as the World Soul</note>.
<margin>22</margin>
Moreover, he calls the souls of the twelve spheres the twelve gods who are the followers of Jove. In a similar way, he assigns souls that participate in the Mind to the purer parts of the spheres: namely, to the stars and the planets, which he also calls gods. To the parts of Fire, he assigns demons and fiery heroes. To the parts of clear Air, he assigns airy demons. To the parts of misty Air, he assigns aquatic demons and heroes. Finally, he joins minds to the purer parts of the Earth, which are called men living on the ground.
<margin>27</margin>
Sometimes, demons and heroes are also placed on the earth. He locates a great multitude of demons and heroes not only under the moon, but also in the heavens beyond the stars. But in all the spheres, beyond the leading demons and heroes, he places "particular" souls—whether they be demonic, heroic, or human—which do not always follow eternal things like those leaders do, but instead follow eternal and temporal things by turns. These souls change their bodies and their lives, sometimes ascending toward the better, and sometimes descending toward the worse. Accordingly, for as many stars as there are, just as many crowds of demons, heroes, and souls are subject to them. Under Saturn are those of Saturn; under Jove, those of Jove; and under Mars, those of Mars. And so on in succession. He adds that
<margin>B</margin>
he believes all things are in all things. But in the earth, they are in an earthy way; in the water, in an aquatic way; and similarly in the air and the fire. In heaven, they exist according to a celestial nature. All things are in the moon according to a lunar nature, and in the other spheres in the same manner. So much so, that any sphere is an entire world in its own way and by its own proper quality. But to conclude what was proposed: there will be some spirits outside of a body and perpetual. Likewise, there are some opposite to these, within a body and mortal. Therefore, there must be intermediate beings which are either outside a body and mortal—which is impossible—or they are indeed in a body, but are immortal. Those first ones are the supernal minds, which they call the purest angels, who are distinguished among themselves by very many ranks. Opposite to them are the souls of beasts <note>original: "bestiarum," meaning non-rational animals</note>.
<margin>3</margin>
The rational souls will hold the middle ground, which

# Book

are like certain inferior angels. Nor is it absurd for a spirit in some body to be immortal, since some immortal body is found: namely the heaven, and any entire sphere of the universe itself. Indeed, it is fitting for perpetual spirits to be present in all the principal bodies of the world as if they were their forms. For since (as most believe) matter is perpetual in all things,
<margin>L</margin>
it is necessary for matter to be overcome everywhere by certain forms. That opinion of the Egyptians, confirmed by all the Platonists and especially by Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino deeply</note>, leads to the same point: namely, that for the perfect harmony of the world, there must be not only certain rational and immortal animals, and conversely, animals that are both irrational and mortal, but also many intermediate things between these which are rational but mortal—not only on the earth, but also in the other elements. Therefore, it is not only humans who have everlasting souls in a mortal body, but also many demons, some near to us and some far more sublime. Their bodies may be born and pass away, although they live step by step much longer than ours. For they do not think it fitting to descend suddenly from celestial animals—which are rational, everlasting, and most happy—to earthly animals, which are rational but most unhappy and have the shortest lives. Rather, one descends through certain levels of rational animals that are happier and longer-lived than humans, yet not everlasting in body, nor most blessed in soul. Plutarch and his associates—the philosopher Demetrius and the rhetorician Aemilianus—affirm the same thing.
<margin>E</margin>
For he testifies from many wonders that happened in his own time that the great demon Pan <note>A reference to the "Death of Great Pan" story in Plutarch's *De defectu oraculorum*</note> and many other demons first wailed and then died. Therefore, the fellowship of an everlasting mind with a human body, however frail, is not so absurd as Epicurus and Lucretius <note>Epicurus and Lucretius were famous for their materialist philosophy, arguing the soul dies with the body</note> believe. Especially since our mind is the last of the minds, just as the moon is the last of the stars. And just as the moon is related to the sun, so our mind is related to God. The moon revolves around the sun in such a way that it shines differently at different times and is shaped in various ways. Never is it of total light...

# Book Ten

We believe, however, that our bodies are suitable lodgings for the mind: both because of our upright posture—not looking at the ground, but gazing upward and recognizing the heaven as its own proper homeland—and because of the altogether wonderful beauty of our various limbs. Also, because the purest elements, fire and air, are most powerful within us, which is indicated by the agility of the body, its tall stature, and its upright gaze. ¶ Most <margin>2 👈</margin> <margin>H.</margin> especially, this is because of our most balanced temperament <term>complexionem</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which determined health and personality.</note>, which is signified by the delicate, smooth, firm, and bright softness of the flesh; this does not occur except from the most exact tempering of the elements. The eagle surpasses man in sight. ¶ Many birds in hearing; the dog in smell. But none of the animals surpasses man in taste or touch. It is not clearly seen from this why men plunge themselves into feasts, drinking, and sexual matters more immoderately than brutes, although they are sometimes restrained by reason. It is only fair, for they embrace those pleasures which they perceive more greedily and more sharply than the beasts. <margin>3</margin> Those three superior senses <note>Sight, hearing, and smell were considered "superior" because they perceive objects from a distance, whereas taste and touch require contact.</note> are most unencumbered when the brain is dry. God did not grant this dryness to man, whose brain never rests. Lest, perhaps, if it were dry by nature, it might be dried out sooner than is fitting by being parched by continuous activity. <margin>Gust:</margin> Taste is nothing other than a kind of touch of the tongue. Since touch is a universal sense—belonging to every animal and to the whole body—where it is sharpest, it declares the best temperament to be present in the body. ¶ This is chiefly because touch occurs in the nerves; when the nerves are drier, they feel poorly, but where touch is sharp, it signifies that a softness is present which tempers the dryness of the nerves. ¶ Furthermore, the instruments of the senses should never actually possess those qualities which the sense is about to perceive. ¶ For the pupil lacks colors. Hearing lacks sounds. Smell lacks odors. The tongue lacks flavors. Since touch deals with the four qualities of the elements <note>Hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, it is necessary that it lacks them entirely (which is impossible in a composite body) or that it is far removed from any excess of them, so that no single quality appears to dominate in its instrument...

...threaten: but as if a certain harmony produced from expelled qualities. Yet, a great deal of earth and water was necessary: to exist within us according to our mass: so that the abundance of the mass of water and earth might temper the far more vehement force of fire and air. <margin>a</margin> We were also given a larger brain and a hotter heart than other living creatures. The former, indeed, so that it may supply various instruments for speculation. The latter, however, so that many and bright spirits <term>spiritus</term> <note>In Renaissance physiology, 'spirits' were thin, vaporous substances that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> might be present for the brain. The head is also suspended high, lest the filth of heavy humors descend to the brain and pollute the purity of the spirits. Furthermore, the vehement coldness and humidity of the brain, as well as the heat and dryness of the heart, temper both each other and all the members. <margin>b</margin> Therefore, in man there appears to be the most temperate complexion <term>complexio</term> <note>The 'complexion' refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which determined a person's physical and mental constitution.</note> of all. If it were earthy, as with the horns, teeth, claws, beaks, and hides of almost all beasts, we would be covered with rough, hairy skin or scales. But now, on the contrary, the human body is so affected that it is neither rough from an excess of heat and dryness, nor rigid or sluggish from too much cold. Neither is it fluid or slippery from superfluous moisture, but equally delicate and solid. This is also understood from the nourishments which we constantly eat: airy, sweet, ground, thinned, liquefied, cooked, and most temperate. <margin>c</margin> Beasts, however, eat the opposite. For as the complexion is, so it desires such food; and such as the food it uses, so it turns out. Let us conclude, therefore, that man was born for contemplation, as Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously stated that the purpose of life is the investigation of the sun, moon, and heavens.</note> says. Since both the brain and the rest of the body were so constituted in him that they may continually serve the duty of contemplation. This requires both a softness of the brain and a temperate complexion of the body: the former lest it dry out too much from speculating; the latter lest it be turned away from contemplating by the tumult of the humors. Since, however, the moderation of our body is so great and so sublime that it imitates the temperance of heaven, <margin>d</margin> it is no wonder if the celestial soul inhabits this house, so very similar to heaven, for a time. Nor is it first infused into the flesh, but is led by suitable intermediaries, as the Magi <note>Ficino often uses 'Magi' to refer to the ancient followers of Zoroaster or the 'Ancient Theology' (Prisca Theologia) which he believed prefigured Plato.</note> teach most perfectly. First, indeed, in the descent itself, it is enveloped in a celestial and airy body. Then comes the spirit generated from the heart, which in us is most temperate and most clear, like heaven. This is enclosed by the thicker body of the intermediaries. And it becomes equally close to all these, although it pours itself through one into another. Just as the heat of fire adheres most closely to air and water, although it is drawn through the air to the water. And rightly the immortal soul joins that immortal, ethereal body to mortal bodies. <margin>e</margin> It indeed always cherishes that perpetual one. To these mortal things, it belongs for a short time; so that the mind ought rightly to be called a certain god, or a star surrounded by a cloud, or a demon <note>original: 'demon' - used here in the classical sense of a 'daimon' or guiding spirit, a being between the human and the divine.</note>; <margin>D</margin> not an inhabitant of the earth, but a guest. Guest, "know thyself." Know that you are a citizen of a celestial fatherland. Since you were born to contemplate celestial things. Remember, if your end is contemplation, your life is increased and perfected by contemplating. Since, however, from this very thing the life of the body in some way slackens, it follows that in the very detriment and death of the bodily life, your life does not decrease but grows.

# Theology

...on the other hand, we are driven to ascend without end. For nowhere will there be a **mixed act** <note>original: "actus mixtus"; in Aristotelian philosophy, an "act" is the realization of a potential. A mixed act is one limited by the matter it inhabits.</note> if nowhere there is a **mixed potential**. Again, nowhere will a **pure act** be found if nowhere a **pure potential** can be discovered. And since action has its beginning from pure act, and passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive impressions, rather than emotion.</note> from pure potential, then actions and passions would exist nowhere. Therefore, it is necessary that there be **simple matter**. This simple matter, which is subject to the form of an element, is called **prime matter** <term>materia prima</term> <note>The most basic, formless reality that underlies all physical things; it has no qualities of its own but can receive any form.</note>. Indeed, the Artisan of Nature himself <note>A reference to God as the Creator or "Demiurge."</note>, in the fabrication of bodies, takes this naked matter as a beginning. He then clothes it with the qualities and forms of the elements. Then he leads the elements into the appearance of humors. Next, he arranges the humors into the forms of members. To the members, he adds the species of nourishment; to this, the form of sensation; <margin>5.</margin> and to this finally, the form of understanding.

But the **intellectual nature** is twofold. One is so alien to bodies that it provides no life to them; therefore, it is not called the form of matter or of a body, and that order of bodies does not terminate in this nature of the mind as its own proper form. According to Plato, the sublime **angels** occupy this rank. <margin>6.</margin> But there is another nature of the mind which, joined to the body as if by a certain treaty, breathes together with it; into this mind, the progression of bodies ascends as if to the ultimate form of matter.

There are two boundaries of this progression: **matter** is the lowest, and this **mind** is the highest. If they are most distantly separated from each other, they possess conditions opposite to one another. <margin>A.</margin> Therefore, just as prime matter is mere matter—by its own nature entirely devoid of form, yet subject to all forms and materials—so that ultimate form, namely the mind, is **mere form**; that is, entirely devoid of matter, presiding over all forms and their materials. Likewise, just as prime matter is most distantly removed from the "First Being" <note>God</note> and is closest to nothingness— <margin>B.</margin> whence it is placed between "being" and "nothing" by Plato—so the ultimate form is most distantly removed from nothingness and is closest to the **First Being**. <margin>I. 2</margin> From this, three things follow. First, that the ultimate form does not spring in any part from matter.

## Book Ten

<margin>3.</margin> Second, that it is made by God alone. Third, that it will be able to remain **immortal**. The first of these is concluded from the first comparison we introduced; the second from the second; and the third follows from both the first and the second.

<margin>1. similarly [...]</margin> From the first, it follows thus: If it is entirely devoid of corporeal matter—which is the beginning of destructive change—it is far from destruction. And if it is the head of changeable things, it neither succumbs to changeable things nor undergoes any other change except a **vital** one <note>i.e., the "change" of thinking or living, which does not destroy the substance.</note>.

And from the second, it follows thus: <margin>~</margin> If the boundary closest to nothingness <note>prime matter</note> does not tend toward nothingness, is it any wonder that the boundary furthest removed from nothingness and closest to the First Being is neither ever thrust out from being, nor pushed into nothingness? Again, the nature of **form** is more perfect than that of **matter**, since matter is perfected and adorned by form. Therefore, <margin>5.</margin> just as in descending from matter to matter we arrive by degrees at the eternal prime matter of bodies, so also in ascending from form to form, we are carried forward little by little into the **ultimate form** of bodies, which is eternal. This is so that the ascent is not more imperfect than the descent, and the highest boundary is not more imperfect than the lowest.

<margin>form [...]</margin> It is fitting that this intellectual form—toward which, as if to a goal, the entire striving of universal nature tends—be so absolute and consummate that it is far from death. <margin>R. [...]</margin> However, it is not necessary for the **intermediate forms** <note>The souls of plants or irrational animals.</note> to be immortal. For nature seems to bring those forth not so much for their own sake, but rather chooses them for the sake of the ultimate form. In this regard, they certainly seem <margin>X.</margin> to exist as certain preparations of matter for receiving the ultimate form, rather than as principal forms themselves. Through them, as if by a path, the motion and impetus of nature itself passes. In that ultimate form, nature halts its motion. Rightly, therefore, those intermediate forms will pass from being into non-being. But that ultimate form will rest in being, so that the goal of nature may remain without end.

<margin>Z.</margin> We say, moreover, that the entire striving of universal nature is directed chiefly toward this: that an **intellectual animal** may be created from the fact that the intellect is present in the body; but as for the intellect being in itself, that is strictly a divine action...

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by placing it at the pinnacle of a cosmic hierarchy, mirroring the permanence of "prime matter" at the bottom with the "ultimate form" (the mind) at the top. He concludes that the human mind is the goal of all natural processes and, being closest to God, is immune to physical decay.</summary>

# Platonic Book

...to be able to contribute. And since it depends solely upon eternity itself, it shall be eternal. But what shall we say of the **intellectual animal**? The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and sages, like Zoroaster, whom Ficino regarded as part of an ancient lineage of wisdom (*prisca theologia*).</note> do not doubt that it also would have remained in its own tempered state, as Plato writes in the *Charmides*, if only the soul had remained in its own—that is, its divine—temperance. For from the soul itself proceeds every harmony as well as every dissonance of the body. The Mosaic <note>The Law of Moses or the Pentateuch.</note> and the Christian law teach exactly the same thing. But that the entire order was once lost because of the disordered motion of the soul, yet will finally be restored to order as order itself prevails: on this not only Moses, but Zoroaster, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, and Plato agree. 

<margin>Moses Zoroast.</margin>

But of these things, elsewhere. Now let us conclude what was proposed. Let the boundaries of the bodily order, therefore, both be perpetual: the lowest and the highest. Indeed, the ancient theologians thought that the **rational soul** was the supreme boundary and the ultimate form. 

<margin>Aristotle: soul</margin>

Aristotle agrees with them in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "de diuinis"; Renaissance scholars frequently referred to Aristotle's *Metaphysics* as his "Books on Divine Matters."</note>. Where, disputing about efficient and formal causes, he says: moving causes certainly precede matter, but forms not at all. But if some form remains after matter, it must be investigated. For in certain cases nothing prohibits it. As if the soul is such a thing—not the whole soul, but the intellect. He says the same in the second book of the *Physics* <note>original: "de naturalibus."</note>. The investigation of the natural philosopher extends all the way to that form which is simultaneously separate and yet in matter. He indicates there that this is the human soul, and all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> explain it thus. We, however, think that both the ancient theologians and Aristotle converged on this opinion for the following reason.

Just as a **tempered constitution** <term>complexio</term> <note>The specific balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that allows the soul to inhabit the body.</note> is the end toward which all natural motions and constitutions are directed, so the rational soul, which a tempered constitution underlies, is the end of all natural forms. Again, this is the condition of the ultimate form: that it be neither entirely absolute <note>completely detached or independent from matter</note> nor entirely immersed in bodies. If it were entirely free, it would not operate through the body at all, and thus would not be the form of the body. 

<margin>C</margin>

If it were entirely overwhelmed, it would do nothing without the body, and would not be the ultimate form. For there would be a form beyond this one: whichever one was found to be such that it was joined to the body in part, but not joined in part. Surely there must be such a form, so that between that angelic substance—entirely severed from the body and acting in no way through it—and another form entirely joined to the body, through which it performs all actions (such as the soul of beasts), there might be a certain middle form: partly joined to the body, and partly separate, so that it may effect something through the body and something through itself. 

<margin>A</margin>

Such is every rational soul, because it both rules the body and contemplates. The human soul is undoubtedly such a thing; it carries out the works of nourishing and sensing through the instruments of the body. But the act of **understanding** and **choosing** it performs through itself. Thus the angel is separated from matter both in substance <note>what a thing is in its essence</note> and in operation <note>what a thing does</note>, and is entirely in eternity because it is entirely in a state of constancy. The souls of beasts are joined to matter in both ways, and are entirely in time, because they change in both ways. Rational souls, because they must be partly joined and partly separate, could not be separate in any respect if they were joined in substance; therefore they are necessarily separate—or separable—in substance, because they clearly have no origin from matter or from bodily agents and instruments. They are, however, joined through their operations—not indeed through all operations, but the lowest ones—and this not by violence, but by love. Whence, according to the Chaldeans <note>The sages of ancient Babylon; Ficino refers here to the *Chaldaean Oracles*.</note>, they exist on the **boundary of eternity and time**. In substance they are indeed in eternity, but in operations they are in time. For the former remains, while the latter change. 

<margin>D</margin>

It is fitting, then, that between that which is entirely eternal and that which is utterly temporal, there be something that is partly eternal and partly temporal. And between that which always *is* and that which is *made* at some time, there be something that is *always being made*. Such a thing is the heavens: both a substance remaining always and yet mobile. Again, such is the matter of the world itself, and even (if I may say so) corporeity itself. Furthermore, the soul is almost such a thing: which flows...

<summary>Ficino argues that the rational soul is the "middle form" of the universe, existing on the boundary between eternity and time. He uses this dual nature to explain how the soul can both manage the physical body through "love" and contemplate divine truths through its independent intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Book 10 of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. Ficino is establishing the soul's status as the "ultimate form"—the highest point of the material world and the starting point of the divine world. Having previously discussed the permanence of the soul's substance, he now explores how the soul interacts with the body while remaining essentially independent of it.</meta>

->Theology [Book] Ten<-

...always in disposition and in act: because the substance remains. From there it <term>declines</term><note>Meaning it stoops or reaches down toward the material world.</note> toward bodies that flow over the substance. Such indeed is the soul: namely, the **ultimate form** of the body: which indeed forms and rules the body. Yet it so nearly exceeds the nature of the body that it exists in the light itself, and having stepped just a little beyond the limits of the body, it is entirely ready to leave it behind. Certainly, it is much more separated than it is joined. For it communicates to the body a part of itself—or rather a lower power—which it holds in common with brute animals and plants. 

<margin>The nature of the rational soul is remote from the body both in essence and in action.</margin>

But its principal part, which is most similar to the divine and in which the whole **reason** of the rational soul consists, it keeps remote from the body both in essence and in action. And as often as it operates through the intellect, it first, by a natural instinct, betakes itself to "separated reasons" <note>This refers to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas"—the eternal, abstract blueprints of things that exist independently of matter.</note>, a fact which all the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle, named after the "colonnades" (peripatoi) where they walked and talked.</note> confess. 

<margin>A</margin>

But toward individual and joined forms <note>Forms that are currently "joined" to physical matter.</note> it turns itself not primarily or directly, but by a certain second and oblique act, insofar as it reflects upon the **images** <note>original: "simulacra"; these are the mental representations or phantasms created from sensory experience.</note> from which it produced the intelligible species. Who, then, does not see that the rational power is more separated than joined? Since indeed it turns toward separated things directly and primarily, but toward joined things obliquely and by a subsequent act. It attains what it wants most especially when it departs furthest from the body. 

Conversely, when it descends through the senses to bodies, it is then deceived and disturbed by countless passions. It cannot, however, be similar to mortal things if it is deceived and troubled by their presence. Rather, it is indeed similar to divine things, as Plato teaches in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the soul's immortality and the death of Socrates.</note>: because the more closely it adheres to them, the more it shines and rejoices. Now, any thing whatever rests in its own natural place, but is distressed in a foreign one. 

Hence, among the Platonists, it appears that the natural seat of intelligence is not in mortal bodies, insofar as they are mortal. Therefore, it is only a very little way from being the case that the rational soul is primarily separated from the body. It is, therefore, the **ultimate form**, 

<margin>Form</margin>

since above it there is no other form of the body. Below it, however, there are many forms so arranged that, by approaching this soul step by step, they are raised up, as it were, above matter.

# **The objection of Epicurus: and the response concerning forms**
## **most similar to God.** <margin>Chapter 3</margin>

<margin>B</margin> **E**picurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) often associated with the view that the soul is material and mortal, composed of atoms that disperse at death.</note> says we are dreaming when we assert that forms exceed in any way the matter by which they are sustained. He thinks they are absorbed by matter to such an extent that it is impossible for any form, however excellent, to operate at all beyond matter. 

<margin>Plutarch, Aristotle</margin>

We, however, judge that all the works of nature (just as Plato writes in the *Philebus* and Aristotle confirms) are perfected by a certain divine intelligence. Which, indeed, revolving and urging on the heavens as its own instruments—just as Plato speaks of the **celestial chariot**—from there forms this lower matter of the elements. And as in the craft of a work, the form has a triple degree: 

<margin>3 - forms</margin>

First, it is in the mind of the craftsman. Second, it is in the instruments moved by him. Third, it is in the matter formed from there. So too the forms of things, which God generates or creates here—either by translating them or preparing them through the motion of the heavens—are first in God himself; then in the heavens, as if in channels or seats; and finally in this lower matter. 

<margin>Thus the form in the 3rd degree: divided by number.</margin>

It is necessary, however, that this matter, since it is so moved by the divine intelligence, should receive and display a most exact form of that divine intelligence. This we see happening both in nature and in the arts. For the vital nature of the soul, through natural heat <note>original: "calor naturalis"; in Ficino's time, this was considered a subtle, life-giving heat that served as the primary instrument of the soul within the body.</note> as its instrument, moves the matter of the food we have taken and makes it vital. This life attributed to the food does not imitate the form of that heat, but of the soul. For heat does not generate life of itself. 

A painter also, through his instrument, the brush, marks a certain form on a wall; it is not similar to the brush, but rather to his own mind, which had conceived it in himself beforehand and later brings it forth. Therefore, according to both nature and art, the form of the work 

<margin>J</margin>

reflects the agent. But in this we find a triple degree. We see one form closer to the matter than to the agent; another closer to the agent than to the matter; and a certain one in the middle. Take first an example in nature. For the soul, through its instrument—namely, that natural heat—acts upon the food...

To the finest parts, however, it mostly applies the form of <term>spirit</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle, vaporous substances produced from the blood that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>; for it recreates spirit from those. For by its own nature, heat only burns and dissolves; but it is tempered to works of this kind through the power of the soul. The form of bones is most remote from the soul and closest to matter. For there is no sensation in bones. The form of flesh and nerves is closer to the soul than that of bones. For sensation occurs through these. Sensations in the human race never yet depart very far from the body, since they never act except in the presence of external bodies. Finally, the form of the spirits is closest to the soul; since these already serve the more excellent powers of the soul—imagination and <term>phantasy</term><note>The mental faculty responsible for processing and storing sensory images.</note>—in a certain way.

<margin>Jor:</margin>
You have an example in nature. Take, in addition, an example in the arts. Indeed, the instruments used by craftsmen have only a certain nature and shape of their own; yet they do not possess the beauty of the craftsman's own intelligence.

<margin>3</margin>
Truly, through these, the mind of the craftsman carries out three types of things. Some are closest to itself, others most remote, and others in the middle. Indeed, the works of the craftsman which pertain to sight or hearing declare almost the whole genius of the craftsman. Those which pertain to the three remaining senses, very little. For in the mixing of scents and flavors, or the preparing of beds and baths, the intention of the craftsman appears little or hardly at all. In paintings and buildings, however, the counsel and wisdom of the craftsman shine forth. Furthermore, the arrangement and, as it were, a certain shape of his own mind are inspected. For the mind expresses and shapes itself in these works just as the face of a person looking into a mirror shapes itself in the mirror. But most of all in speech, songs, and sounds, the skillful mind brings itself into the light. In these, the whole arrangement of the mind and the will are most clearly

<margin>3</margin>
designated; and whatever the emotion of the craftsman, his works tend to excite that same emotion in us: a mournful voice often compels us to mourn, a furious one to be enraged, a wanton one to be lewd. Therefore these works, looking to both sight and hearing, are closest to the craftsman's mind.

<margin>3</margin>
Others, which pertain to the three remaining senses, are, as we said, most remote. Those middle operations are those which pertain to bodily exercises, whether for play or for war.

<margin>7</margin>
From where are art and nature so tempered for the arrangement of their works, if not from God, the founder of nature and the arts?

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore God similarly tempers his works in bodies, so that He Himself generates a triple grade of forms in the matter subject to Him: namely, forms that are primary to Him, those that are most remote, and those in the middle.

<margin>3</margin>

<margin>H.</margin>

<margin>or <unclear>???</unclear></margin>

Surely it would be more similar if it were always similar; that is, if it rose up immortal. Therefore, some form in matter becomes immortal.

<margin>7</margin>

# Theology

<margin>$\delta$</margin>
...rather than the principal forms and species. This is because any of these <term>qualities</term><note>In Aristotelian and Platonic physics, "qualities" are the properties like heat or cold that characterize the four elements.</note> belongs to many species; they are often intensified or diminished. Yet it is certain that species (as the natural philosophers agree) do not change in this way. Qualities often arrive and depart while the species remain. Who would deny that heat and cold are common to many species of trees and animals? And these qualities vary in living beings according to a degree of "more" or "less," while the same species of the living creature remains. Therefore, there are materials that are very similar, which, like a basic substance, are subject to many species; nor do they distinguish the species of things from one another by their presence alone. Therefore, let them be called the "affections" and "preparations" of matter for receiving species.

<margin>L 766.</margin>
Therefore, matter—through the extension of quantity familiar to it and common to many things—opens its bosom to qualities of this kind. Once prepared by these qualities to receive species, it immediately receives the forms and species of the elements from the Divine Mind, the architect of the entire world. It receives the species of **fire** when it has been prepared by heat, dryness, <term>rarity</term><note>original: "raritas". In this context, it refers to the thinness or lack of density characteristic of fire, as opposed to the "spissitudo" (density) of earth.</note>, and lightness. It receives the species of **earth** when it is prepared by cold, dryness, density, and weight. And the others each by their own reasoning. These forms of the elements surpass those preparations of theirs because the forms are the ends [goals], and they are what distinguish the proper species and remain in a more stable way. For the coldness of water is seen to change more quickly than the species of water itself; and similarly in others. There are, however, things deeply immersed in matter that do not resolve into other species or principal forms. But soon, once matter is affected by qualities, they are brought into the lap of formless matter nearby. Hence, because of the passive nature of matter, they are scarcely capable of a single action.

What else does fire do except burn? Nor do they perform anything except insofar as those preparations of matter assist them, which do nothing beyond what heat, cold, dryness, and the rest can do. Furthermore, they have a single motion and a single position. Yet there is some order among the forms of the elements. For the form of fire—which is freer from matter than the others because of its wonderful rarity—is more effective in acting and more remote from the infection of passion <note>In the philosophical sense, "passion" refers to being acted upon or undergoing change from an external source.</note>.

Then the Mind gathers these four elements into one: and from their various <term>temperaments</term><note>A "temperament" is the specific ratio or mixture of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</note> it creates various species of stones and metals, as well as those things called "compounds." The forms of these excel the forms of the elements in this: they are resolved back into other primary forms, nor are they made unless the matter is more diligently elaborated; and they perform something to which the forms of the elements and those dispositions of matter are not sufficient.

<margin>B</margin>
For it is not through the elemental qualities that **Jasper** induces labor. **Sapphire**<note>original: "Zaphyrus", likely a variation of "Sapphirus".</note> drives away harmful phantasms, checks sweat, and contributes to grace. **Emerald** extinguishes lust. **Amethyst** calms drunkenness. For many other things that have similar qualities would produce the same effect [if it were just the elements]. Instead, they do these things from a certain power granted to such species by the <term>souls of the spheres</term><note>Ficino believed that gemstones acted as "batteries" or conduits for celestial energy emanating from the souls that inhabit the planetary spheres.</note>. But they are not far removed from matter, because such power is corporeal and is channeled through the bodies of the spheres. And although they perform some operation, such as we have described, no work perfected by such power remains after them. And these have one motion and one place, according to whichever element prevails in their mixture.

<margin>b</margin>
Generally, however, among these forms, those are more effective in whose mixture the purer elements dominate the coarser ones. The **forms of plants** follow after these and are superior to them for this reason: because they perform a living work through the qualities of the elements used as instruments, which the previous forms cannot do. They propagate plants like themselves in species, which is not granted to the forms of those compounds. By nourishing themselves, they carry out motions into all parts of their location, contrary to the nature of the heavy elements that excel in their mixture. They have obtained a body distinguished by different members: branches, shoots, a trunk, and roots; as if there were many powers in these forms, for the fulfillment of whose duties many and various instruments are needed. They also display a likeness to certain celestial powers and motions. They reflect powers insofar as they perform certain actions for which the elements do not...

<summary>Ficino describes the hierarchy of being from simple elements to gemstones and plants, arguing that higher forms use elemental qualities (like heat) as mere tools to perform complex, life-sustaining, or celestial functions.</summary>

<margin>2</margin>

Next come the souls of brute animals, which are more excellent than the souls of plants because they are similar to celestial nature, not only in movement but also, in a certain way, in knowing.

<margin>3</margin>
Those celestial <term>virtues</term><note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the powers or spiritual intelligences associated with the stars and planets.</note> know all things. The souls of beasts also know something; they possess a <term>spiritual operation</term><note>original: "operationem... spiritalem". For Ficino, "spiritual" refers to a refined, subtle substance that bridges the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>. For the act of the senses and the imagination is spiritual, occurring through the spiritual images of objects themselves. Nor do they perform the act of sensing through any quality of the elements. For when they sense something, they do not sense it by heating it or by cooling it.

<margin>17</margin>
Yet these forms are still occupied with matter because they exercise the acts of the senses through bodily instruments; they perceive nothing except what is corporeal and particular, and they always obey the needs of the body. Finally, the human soul towers over all of these; it is similar to the celestial minds not only in knowing, but even in its very *kind* of cognition. For the human soul understands, just as those minds do. In this operation, neither the qualities of the elements nor any bodily instrument composed of them plays a part. This signifies, above all else, that the nature of this mind is excluded from the chains of matter, since it has been granted an operation free from any commerce with matter.

<margin>na</margin>
Indeed, matter hinders the power of knowing. This is evident from the fact that the forms of elements, mixtures, and plants—which are close to matter—know nothing. And in animals, those parts serve more senses where the thicker matter ascends less, such as the head; there, the sense is sharper where the instrument is purer and the <term>spirit</term><note>original: "spiritus". This refers to the "pneuma" or "animal spirits," a subtle vapor that Renaissance doctors believed flowed through the nerves to carry sensory data.</note> is most abundant. Hence sight, because it is purer than the rest, senses more swiftly and sharply. It imprints the marks of things more deeply within us.

Therefore, through those things which pertain to sight, we recognize anything more clearly after a long time than through the evidence of the other senses.

<margin>D</margin>
And indeed, things seen offer themselves to us in sleep more often than things heard. Not only does matter hinder the power of knowing, but also the object to be known itself. For this reason, when the very mass of things presses upon the sense, we feel it either not at all or with great difficulty.

<margin>E</margin>
The forms of things also offer themselves to us first, and through them, we "under-stand" the matter, as it were. Furthermore, we necessarily conjecture regarding <term>privations</term><note>A philosophical term for the absence of a quality, like "darkness" being the privation of "light."</note> through habits, and regarding matter through a certain relation to form. Yet we do not think of all forms through a relation to matter. This signifies that matter depends on the genus of forms, and that there are some forms free from matter.

<margin>X</margin>
Again, we know things most clearly and firmly when we think of the very <term>reasons</term><note>original: "rationes". These are the essential definitions or divine blueprints of things, similar to Plato's "Ideas."</note> of things without the conditions of matter. If matter is an impediment to both the power and the object of cognition, it follows that the soul which senses and imagines anything is not composed of matter; indeed, it is not even a form divided by <term>quantity</term><note>original: "quantitate". This refers to physical extension or size. Ficino argues that if the soul had "size," it couldn't hold the "forms" of things properly.</note>. For in cognition itself, there is a mutual and miraculous union and penetration between the form apprehended and the power apprehending. The dimension of quantity would completely prohibit this. And if we conclude from lower forms of cognition that the soul is not made of matter, we can certainly conclude through the highest cognition—namely, through the intelligence—that the soul is not from matter.

<margin>2</margin>
So that, just as that which knows without matter exists without it, so that which comprehends apart from the conditions of matter exists far from the passions of matter. For if the human soul were such a form that it was referred to matter as if to its own origin, it would not know any forms except through some relation to matter. But now, as the mistress of matter, the soul subjects matter to forms while it refers matter to forms; and like a being similar to God, it refers the subsequent forms back to the first re... <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("refert"), likely continuing on the next page.</note>

He concludes that because the mind can grasp things apart from physical constraints, the soul itself must be immaterial and immortal.</summary>

# Theology, Book Ten

...bears the form, and God himself. And yet in this very thing it rises above matter most especially because it lifts matter above itself; it also becomes closest to God because it leads all forms back to <margin>D</margin> God. From these things it is clearly established: what we have long sought, namely that the rational soul, out of all the forms of the body, emerges as most similar to God, to such a degree that <margin>C</margin> no other can be made more similar. This is because no further form can be made in <margin>E</margin> matter, since the soul stands out at the very furthest boundary of the body. Indeed, it was necessary for some form in nature to be expressed that was most similar to God, provided that the divine craftsman was to overcome matter, as Plato taught in the <note>original: "Timeo". Reference to the *Timaeus*, Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> *Timaeus*. He intends for such a thing to be the <term>Mind</term><note>Ficino uses *mens* (Mind) to refer to the highest, most divine part of the human soul.</note> which is in the body, derived from the Mind which is outside of bodies—like a certain face of that [Divine] Mind shining back in the higher mirror of matter.

<margin>F</margin> Consider to what degree of similarity to itself fire lifts matter, and by what steps. The sphere of fire possesses a triple quality: color, light, and <term>lightness</term><note>original: "levitatem". In ancient physics, "lightness" (levity) was the actual physical force that caused things like fire or air to rise upward, the opposite of gravity.</note> tending toward higher things. That sphere moves the lowest and thickest bodies; it pours only color into the most unsuitable bodies, as occurs mostly in stones. Into purer bodies, it pours heat and light, which it does easily in wood. Finally, into the thinnest bodies, beyond heat and light, it also pours that lightness which draws them toward the heavens. This it does in paper and linen, so that it immediately takes their substance into itself, as if they were most similar to it. Therefore, the form of fire in a stone is dark and unsuitable. In wood, it is unsuitable but clear. In linen, it is both clear and agile.

In almost the same way, the Divine Mind provides only life to the lower bodies, just like heat. To the more excellent ones, it provides sensation, like light. To the most excellent ones, it adds intellect, like that lightness through <margin>G</margin> which the soul rises into God. Thus, that divine ray penetrating all things is indeed in stones, but it does not live; in plants it lives, but it does not shine; in brute animals it shines, but it is not <term>folded back into itself</term><note>original: "replicatur in seipsum". A key Neoplatonic concept where the mind "reflects" or turns inward to recognize its own existence and its source.</note>, nor does it return to its source. In humans, it is present, it lives, it shines, and it folds back into itself. First, through a certain turning of the soul toward itself. Then, it reflects back into God, its source, by happily recognizing its own origin.

However, just as the ascent of fire has a certain fixed end which it can reach—and this is rest in its own sphere—so the ascent of our mind, perpetually directed toward God, has a determined end. It will eventually take possession of this, and this end will be nothing other than rest in God, which the soul, having departed from here, will attain in no small measure.

## The Objection of Lucretius: and the response that the mind can operate without the body. Chapter VI.

<margin>Lucretius</margin>
Two impious men, Lucretius and Epicurus, will disturb our discussion, as is their custom, not with any reason, but with a shout. We indeed assert two primary things here: first, that God creates souls similar to <margin>lu d' ani mrg</margin> himself in matter. Against the first, Lucretius will object: if the mind is so divine, first, it is against its nature to be joined with a body to complete the species of an animal; and second, even if it is joined, why does the mind never contemplate anything unless the <term>imagination</term><note>original: "phantasia". The faculty that processes sensory images.</note> is thinking?

Against the second point, <margin>Epicurus</margin> Epicurus will object here: if God creates the soul in matter, then he creates it *from* matter, and therefore it is mortal. <margin>epic d' m arg</margin> We have responded to the first objection, and we will respond more diffusely elsewhere. Now, briefly, in this manner: Since the final power of understanding in the universe is awakened to its own proper contemplation through the operations of the senses and the imagination—and since the senses and the imagination act through corporeal spirits—it follows that it is not against the nature of the mind to be united to this body to complete the human species on earth. Especially since our mind is not called a simple mind, but an "animal mind," the last of the minds and the life-giver of bodies. And even if in the general definition of "mind" there is no inclination toward bodies, nevertheless, in the specific definition of the "last mind," such an inclination is in a certain way included as natural to it; namely, insofar as the mind, created at the boundary of minds and souls, has emerged as an animal mind, and from there toward the...

<margin><unclear>scribble</unclear></margin>
...inclined to bring life to the nearest bodies. And **every thing operates according to the mode of its own substance**: the substance of the human mind is indeed entirely incorporeal, but it is united to matter. From this it happens that it understands incorporeal things; yet, while it inhabits the body, it often views them in some way together with something corporeal—that is, with an **image of the imagination** <note>original: "simulacro phantasie". In Renaissance psychology, the "phantasia" or imagination was the faculty that processed sensory data into mental images.</note>. Therefore, it frequently requires an image of this kind. Truly, when it has been led back into itself after laying aside this body, it will understand within itself. 

But this mind relates to the images of the imagination in one way before it conceives a universal <term>species</term><note>original: "spem" (species). Here meaning a universal concept or form, like the "idea" of a tree rather than a specific tree.</note> within itself, and in another way after it has conceived it. Before, it needs them so that it may be stirred by their prompting to give birth to the universal species. <margin>B</margin> Afterward, however, if it needs them at all, it needs them (as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who generally argued that all human knowledge must begin with sensory data.</note> think) as a foundation or as a companion to the species. And often, by the command of the intellect, a new image is formed in the imagination that matches that universal species, in which that universal species of the mind shines forth, just as a model shines in its likeness. 

<margin>C <note>original: "plat." Reference to the Platonic school.</note></margin> Nevertheless, perhaps the mind does not need the image of the imagination, as the **Platonists** believe, once it has produced and retains its own species after being prompted by that image. But such is the nature of the twin eyes fixed in the same root, or hanging from a single hinge, that they open and close at the same time and look at the same thing. So the **Mind** and the **Imagination**, which are the twin eyes of the same soul and very close to each other, open together and view things in the same <unclear>way</unclear>. 

<margin>D</margin> <margin><unclear>scribble</unclear></margin> And while the imagination thinks of *this* specific man, the mind thinks of the *universal* man, and vice versa. This is a natural coincidence. Yet, just as one eye can look without the other by the use of a hand, so too by a more burning study, the mind is no less able to turn toward universal species while the imagination ceases—just as it often happens through some disturbance that the imagination wanders more intently through corporeal things while the mind ceases. Furthermore, when the soul considers itself, it can then look upon its own act, power, and essence without an image of the imagination. Especially so when the soul

**Column 2**

### Book

notices that it understands, and again understands that it notices, and is folded back upon itself in a similar way without end. This is especially true if (as some think) it notices its own intelligible species and its own act through that very species or act itself. In that case, it certainly would need neither an image nor an instrument. It can even judge the nature of an image itself without another image. 

If someone argues that the understanding requires images of natural things when it considers their principles, we shall perhaps grant this for the sake of argument. This is because, just as a connection to individual men accompanies "humanity" itself, so the understanding of humanity accompanies the thought of this or that man. However, we will not easily grant this in **divine matters**; we are not forced to look at corporeal images every time we contemplate angelic essences. Because just as such essences do not decline toward this or that matter, so our speculations—by which we are made equal to them in a certain way of knowing—are not necessarily bound to corporeal images. For the knowledge of them is not borrowed from bodies by souls, but from <term>Ideas</term> (when the soul returns to itself) or from **infusion** (when it rises above itself). 

But who would say that minds, in the exact contemplation of divine things, need the help of images? For by the meeting or intervention of images, the mind is vehemently hindered from such speculation and is often deceived. If it does not wish to be deceived, it is compelled to scatter those images like clouds. 

<margin>E</margin> Perhaps when the soul departs from itself through the senses, it reaches only sensible qualities. When it returns to itself through the imagination, it reaches the intangible "intentions" <note>The mental representation or "meaning" of a physical object.</note> of sensible images. When it returns into itself through **Reason**, it reaches intangible principles that decline toward intangible intentions. When it rises above itself through the **Mind**, like an angel, it reaches intangible principles already separated from imaginary intentions. Whatever the philosophical mind views in the universe and in itself is a certain **angelic knowledge**, even a divine one, free from images. First, he proves...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book 10. Having established that the mind uses images from the imagination while in the body, Ficino now argues that the mind's highest functions actually move away from these images toward pure abstraction. He transitions from answering Lucretius to addressing Epicurus regarding the origin of the soul.</meta>

-># Theology, Book Ten<-

<margin>Symbol of a cross within a circle; hand icon pointing right</margin>
¶ He proves that such a cognition must exist; he describes within himself of what sort it is, of what quality, why, and how it occurs. And he also attains it according to form and experiences it by describing it.

<margin>Hand icon pointing right; letter "A."</margin>
¶ Truly, a description of this kind is a certain conception of the soul that is free from every **image** <note>original: "simulacro". In this context, a *simulacrum* is a mental "picture" derived from the senses. Ficino argues higher thought doesn't need these pictures.</note>. For it is not through an image that he gazes upon or defines a cognition that is itself free from images. Then, in such a conception, the soul turns back upon itself; while it recognizes itself, it realizes it has already received the concept in this way. This turning <term>conversion</term> <note>Latin: "conversio". A central concept in Neoplatonism where the soul "turns back" from the external world to look at its own inner nature and its source in God.</note> is much more absolute and free from images. Finally, in this turning, it turns back upon itself again and again, and always flies further away from images step by step, as the mind dismisses individual things to look upon not only the most specific species, but also the subordinate types, the general categories, the most universal genera, and finally the **transcendental** concepts <note>The most universal categories of being, such as "Truth," "Goodness," and "Unity."</note>; it divides, composes, defines, and argues. In these activities, the soul certainly not only strives to bypass images but is compelled to do so.

It is worthwhile to notice further that the lowest power of the soul is joined more to the body than the middle power, and the middle more than the highest. When the highest reasoning power of human intelligence and will gathers itself firmly into itself, then the lowest power is largely separated from bodily labor; for then the function of governing, moving, nourishing, digesting, and purging usually loses half its strength, or even more. If this is so, it is necessary that the middle power is then moved away from matter to a much greater degree. This is evident in men who are in **abstraction** <note>A state of deep contemplation where the person becomes unaware of their physical surroundings.</note> while contemplating; they feel nothing at all. From this it follows that the highest power may occasionally leave bodily things entirely during this very act, and by its virtue, the remaining powers leave them more and more. Indeed, that which grows can eventually be fully completed, specifically when that which was increasing along with it is consumed. Therefore, the soul's abstraction from the body, which grows more powerful as the intensity of speculation increases, is also fully realized when that intensity is fulfilled. It is fulfilled when, having set all other things aside,

the soul loves and thinks upon only the **First True and Good** <note>That is, God.</note> with the greatest mental fervor. Then abstraction is completed, and the goal of this abstraction—which separates us from mortal things—will at last be not a separation from life, but the attainment of the **First Life**. For those things which accompany each other on the journey also accompany each other at the destination. Therefore, the same port receives the soul fleeing the body that receives the one contemplating. This port is Truth itself. It is eternal clarity; indeed, it is eternity itself. These things were said in response to **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and Epicurean who argued for the mortality of the soul.</note>; let us proceed to **Epicurus** <note>Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who taught that the soul was made of atoms and perished with the body.</note>.

<margin>Handwritten mark "Ec" (for Epicurus)</margin>
¶ The objection of Epicurus, and the response that God does not make the mind except from himself and through himself.

### Chapter Seven.

<margin>Hand icon pointing left</margin>
**I**n what way, asks Epicurus, does God produce this soul in matter, if not from matter? But we ask him: in what way does the sun produce light in the air, yet not from the air? Or a face produce an image in a mirror, yet not from the mirror? Or the mind of a speaker produce the meaning of a voice in the air, yet not from the air? Just as the sun produces heat in the air from the air, but produces light not from the air itself (though it is within it); and just as the mind of a speaker produces sound from the air, but produces the *meaning* of the sound not from the air itself (but in it); so too God draws other forms from the "bowels" of matter. 

<margin>Handwritten note: "vltia form" (The final form)</margin>
But the **Intellect**, which is the **final form** <note>The highest and most complete stage of being in the material world.</note>, He spreads over the face of matter; He does not draw it from its womb.

<margin>Handwritten mark "1b"</margin>
Epicurus ought to have considered that matter itself has no power of its own to form itself. For nothing forms itself into a form. Yet matter has a power and a preparation for being formed, which we call the "incipiency of forms" and the ancient theologians called **Ancient Chaos**. 

<margin>Handwritten "J"</margin>
To this matter, as **Timaeus** <note>A character in Plato's *Timaeus* who explains the creation of the world by a divine Craftsman (Demiurge).</note> teaches, God applies a formative power—not as something belonging to matter, but as an instrument of God himself. He provides a celestial and elemental influence for this power to use in forming. Truly, the divine influence flowing from God, penetrating through the heavens, descending through the elements, and ending in the lower matter, is that very formative power which Plato calls the **reason of the divine intelligence** <note>original: "divine intelligentie rationem" (the Logos).</note>, through whose infusion the machine of the world **is made bright.** <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "clarifici," meaning "to be clarified" or "made bright."</note>

<meta>catchword: clarifici. (is made bright)</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains how the soul achieves divinity through mental abstraction from the body and refutes Epicurus by arguing that the human intellect is infused into matter by God rather than being born from matter itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's *Platonic Theology*. In the preceding sections, Ficino discussed the soul's ability to transcend sensory images. Here, he moves into the metaphysical origins of different types of souls (rational vs. irrational) and how God acts as the direct creator of the human intellect, contrasting this with the way physical forms are "drawn out" of matter.</meta>

# Platonic

# Book

Everything consists of necessity: secondly, from the mind—that is, from matter <note>original: "ex materia". Ficino follows the Platonic tradition of identifying 'Necessity' with the recalcitrant nature of matter.</note> necessary for bodies; and from forms representing the divine mind and goodness in a most beautiful order. <margin>A</margin> This formative power the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked while discussing philosophy.</note> call sometimes the instrument of God, sometimes nature, and sometimes the "seminal power." To this formative power, the formable nature of matter is subject. Therefore, God, through a formative power of this kind spread through the "machine of the world," fits those forms to the formable power of matter itself—specifically those forms we have placed as "proximate" to matter and those we have placed as "middle" forms.

Here, any Platonist will observe a certain order <margin>B</margin> in four levels: both of the forms and of the subjects. <margin>Rational soul:</margin> **Rational souls** are ignited through the sole and pure ray of God upon the pure face of indivisible matter. **Irrational souls** are expressed into the light through celestial and animal influence applied to that divine ray, and they are formed in matter that is not yet extended <note>Ficino is discussing the "point" at which a soul enters matter, before it takes on physical dimensions.</note>. <margin>Forms</margin> **Forms of the elements** and those familiar to mixtures are drawn out from the bosom of matter that is already extended—extended into that which lacks finished dimensions. **Foreign forms** of those same things are rescued from the womb of matter that is already extended through certain finished dimensions.

<margin>A</margin> These forms (except for rational souls), we believe, are bound to matter; therefore, we judge that they have no operation whatsoever in which the nature or instrument of the body does not concur in some way. They always propose the use of the body as their end, inasmuch as they depend on the body, while they are fitted to the formable power of matter through a celestial or elemental formative instrument. A sign of this is that none of them "turn back" toward God <note>original: "in deum convertitur". In Neoplatonism, "conversion" is the soul's ability to look back at its source; physical forms cannot do this.</note>, as if God were not their proximate cause, but rather a distant one. <margin>Non-rational soul</margin> But we conjecture that the **rational soul** is made by God without instruments, chiefly from the fact that it turns most proximately toward God, as <margin>C</margin> we shall declare in what follows. Therefore, instruments concur not for the production of the human soul, but for the preparation of the matter which the human soul will inhabit. But God, through Himself, produces that soul once the matter is prepared.

<margin>D</margin> Plato teaches this in his book on nature <note>Likely the *Timaeus*, which deals with the creation of the world and the soul.</note>, where he intends that the rational soul is granted by the sole Maker of the world, while irrational souls are granted also by his "ministers" who assist in this work. <margin>E</margin> Aristotle also, secure in this, follows his master in the second book of *On Animals*, saying: "When a man is generated, the **intellect** is infused from without and is alone divine; its operation is not fulfilled through anything corporeal." Because it is not "squeezed out" from the innermost bosom of matter, as he thinks other forms are squeezed out. Therefore, God himself infuses this soul without an instrument. 

You have an example in the light of the sun and in the soul. The light of the sun clears the air through heat as a medium, by dissipating the clouds. But it illuminates the clear air through itself. The soul, through natural heat, prepares food by "cooking" it for the form of life. Once the food is cooked and prepared, the soul grants the form of life not through heat, but through itself. Again, the soul breaks the air through the tongue as an instrument. The broken air sounds. By sounding, it signifies. That sound is like a certain "animal" composed of broken air as its body, and <margin>F</margin> from the **meaning** itself as its soul. This meaning, like a soul, lies hidden in words; it is like a certain life of the heard voice that is not itself heard. From where is such meaning given to sound? From the soul of the man speaking. But does the soul give meaning to the voice through the tongue? Not at all. For the tongue <margin>G</margin> is a body, and it performs only a corporeal and sensible task; it gives no meaning through itself, just as when someone speaks by chance when the mind is not attending to the matter. Meaning is an **incorporeal** and **insensible** thing. Otherwise, whoever heard a voice would immediately know what is signified by that voice. Therefore, meaning, which is something insensible, becomes like a soul in the voice—that is, in the "broken air" as the body. I say it is created by the thought of the soul alone, not through the service of the tongue. And thus, while you pronounce the name "Plato," that broken air is divided into many parts: Pla-to. Which, through three moments of time...

<summary>Ficino argues that while physical forms and irrational souls are produced via natural "instruments," the human rational soul is created directly by God and infused into prepared matter. He uses the analogy of speech to show how a physical medium (air) can carry an incorporeal soul (meaning).</summary>
