<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument from Book 10 of his *Platonic Theology*. Having previously established that the rational soul is distinct from physical forms, Ficino here uses the analogy of "meaning" (signification) versus "sound" to explain the soul's relationship to the body and its divine origin. He also addresses a common Stoic objection regarding hereditary traits.</meta>

# Theology, Book Ten

...run through. However, **meaning** <note>original: "significatio". Ficino uses the linguistic concept of a "word" to explain how the soul exists within the body.</note> is not divided into parts: because in the mind of the speaker it is conceived in an indivisible moment before it is even pronounced. It often signifies the most immense things, whose mass it cannot equal in physical magnitude. It also signifies motions, and often time, without having motion or time itself. And when it is pronounced as a sound, while the sound itself is being uttered, the greater part of it is not yet grasped by the listener, nor is it perceived little by little; rather, only when all the syllables have been spoken is the meaning of all of them understood in an instant. This meaning often remains perpetual in the listener's intellect, even as the syllables perish, just as it had been in the speaker's mind before they spoke.

<margin>H</margin>
Therefore, **signification**, produced without a medium from the speaking soul, is incorporeal. The "soul" of the voice is likewise simple and, in a certain way, immortal. Sound, however, manufactured through the medium of the tongue, is dissipated into parts and perishes. If the sun and the soul can effect something in matter without an instrument, how much more will God be able to hand over some form to matter with no intervening instrument? And that form will be, above all, the **rational soul**, which thinks and chooses many things without any physical instrument. This would never be possible if the soul were manufactured through the operation of an instrument. If it is made by God through no intermediary, it is made by him only through himself. God is Eternity itself; let the soul, therefore, be made through Eternity itself. That which is made through Eternity is eternal. And that which is closest to the highest state is so stable that it is most remote from mortal change—for death is the ultimate change. Justly, as in other categories of things, besides that which is "such" by itself, there are others which are "such" through another; so in the order of eternity, beyond God (who is eternal by Himself), there are many things which become eternal through Him. **Timaeus** <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, where the Demiurge creates the immortal part of the human soul directly.</note> teaches that those things which are procreated by God without a medium are of such a nature. The human soul, therefore, will be both immortal and inserted into this body just as meaning is inserted into the air by God the Speaker. If anyone observes this "meaning," he will understand the mind of the Speaker.

---

### Objection of Panaetius: and the response that the soul exists from God without a medium. Chapter VIII.

<margin>IK</margin>
Perhaps **Panaetius** <note>Panaetius of Rhodes (c. 185–109 BC), a Stoic philosopher who argued that since children resemble their parents in character as well as body, the soul must be born and die with the body.</note> objects to us that something can be created by God in matter without a material instrument, but he will not concede that our soul is made this way unless we show this again by some clearer sign. For he thinks that the soul of a newborn is generated from the soul of the parents, just as the body is from the body, because children are often born similar to their parents in both body and character. But the conjecture of Panaetius seems to have little weight. This is because children are often born unlike in body, and very often unlike in soul. And where they do follow their father's morals, they drink them in through **habit** <note>nurture</note> rather than through **birth** <note>nature</note>. Even if some do not acquire these traits by practice but still imitate them, they do not imitate them because the soul is born from a soul, but because from a tender age the soul flatters its own body, in which certain similar impulses are formed due to the physical constitution <term>complexionem: the specific balance of physical humors or elements inherited from the parents</term> of the parents. But as they age, their morals change by their own judgment—not only for the worse, but for the better. Therefore, the conjecture of Panaetius must be cast aside. 

Since he would demand a sign from us by which it might be shown more clearly that the soul comes from God, our sign shall be of this kind: The rational soul, whenever any thing occurs to it, investigates not only what that thing is and of what sort, but also what its **origin** is. Nor does it ever cease until it has found its cause. Yet it does not stop its step at just any cause, but always searches for the cause of the cause, so that it does not rest until it has attained the **Supreme Cause**. Every thing rests in its own proper end; and its proper end is its proper cause.

<margin>L</margin>
For it is there that a thing is perfected; and all things naturally desire perfection as their end. If they seem to seek a common end, they do not adopt it unless it is congruent and accommodated to them, becoming their own. It becomes such when it receives its end in a proximate cause ordained by a higher power. Air does not seek Venus or Jove—even though it may draw its origin from there—but it seeks the concavity of fire, where its own principle and domestic place reside. Other things also follow a similar reasoning...

He refutes Panaetius's Stoic argument that souls are inherited from parents, asserting that the soul's drive to find the "First Cause" proves its divine origin.</summary>

Here, Ficino shifts to the soul's ultimate goal: its return to God, which he argues happens directly rather than through intermediaries.</meta>

<meta>Catchword: -tas (indicating the start of the next page's first word)</meta>

# Platonice

All things seek their own cause. Indeed, no things would stop until they were transformed into God, who is the first principle of all. Or, if they were never transformed into God, they would be moved in vain and by chance. Therefore, things do not seek just *any* cause, but rather their **proximate cause** <note>original: "causam propinquam". The most immediate or direct cause in a chain of events.</note>. It is enough for each thing to preserve its own species uncorrupted and whole. This species is preserved by its own proper cause, which is sufficient and ordered above it. However, the **highest cause** <note>God</note> would change the species of a thing far removed from it into a more sublime nature. In that case, the thing would cease to be what it was and would perish; but things do not desire this. Instead, they desire to remain unharmed in their own state. Insofar as they remain in that state, they also achieve a likeness to the first cause.

What is the point of this? It is so that you may understand that any thing rests as soon as it has reached its proximate cause, and does not search further. And therefore the **mind** <note>original: "mentem"</note>, which rests in nothing except the First, has no proper cause except the First Cause. The sign of this is that the human 

<margin>a</margin>
mind is turned toward God **without a medium** <note>original: "sine medio". This means there is no intervening step or "middle-man" between the soul and God.</note>. For things return to their cause in the same way they proceeded from it. Those things that proceeded through a medium return through a medium. Those that proceeded without a medium also return without a medium. The soul is reflected back into God without a medium when it looks upon God not in any creature, nor in an image of the senses or the imagination, but as absolute and naked above all created things. It looks upon Him as such when it argues that God is so infinite that He towers over everything that can fall into thought by an infinite interval. In this state, nothing created is placed between God and the soul. In what way could the soul's gaze be fixed on God without a medium, unless the power of seeing had also proceeded from Him without a medium? 

Now, if it seems the soul requires certain mediums for this—because it ascends to God through the disposition of the world and the orders of angels—know that the soul does not use these mediums to look at God *within* them, or *through* them (as if looking at the sun in water or through glass). Rather, it uses them like **steps** <note>original: "gradibus"</note>, so that the soul itself, which once fell below itself, may return through these steps into its own **citadel** <note>original: "arce sua". A metaphor for the highest, most refined part of the intellect.</note>. Once it has returned there, it sees God without a medium. Furthermore, through the world's 

# Liber

disposition, the soul is invited to return to its own **reason** <note>original: "rationem"</note> by letting go of its care for the body. Through the investigation or inspiration of angels, it is warned to leave behind the usual discourse of reason and betake itself to a light divinely infused into it. Once reflected by this light, it now looks upon God through the light of God itself, like a man who, by means of a sunbeam, no longer looks at the colors of bodies, but looks at the sun itself. Regarding this, **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino often cites Zoroaster, whom he believed was an ancient sage and a precursor to Plato.</note> says: 

<margin>b</margin>
*You must hasten toward the light and toward the rays of the Father, from where the soul was sent to you, having been clothed in much mind.* <note>original Greek: "Χρη σε σπευδειν προς το φαος και προς πατρος αυγας ενθεν επεμφθη σοι ψυχη πολλυν εσσα μενη νουν."</note> 

That is: You must ascend to the light itself and the rays of the Father. From there, your soul was infused into you, surrounded by the great light of the mind. We infer that the mind eventually reaches this state because it separates itself from the thought of every created thing to such an extent that it asserts the divine peak stands above every concept of any created thing—no matter how sublime—by an infinite distance. While it describes God in this way to the best of its strength, it holds God as its head. Therefore, it has some power capable of receiving God without a medium. 

But this power is granted by God alone. For He who alone forms, He alone disposes. He who fills, He himself amplifies. Just as a ray of sight receives every day from the sun's light that internal and innate power by which it sees the sun's light most closely, so too that power capable of God requires no medium beyond God to look upon God. Just as a ray of sight needs no medium to receive a solar ray, because the ray comes from a ray, so the power capable of God comes from God with no medium interposed. 

Thus far we have proved our proposition chiefly through the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectum"</note>. Now we prove the same thing chiefly through the **will** <note>original: "voluntatem"</note>. 

<margin>c</margin>
Every appetite is filled by the possession of its cause. For the same thing that ignites a thirst by acting upon it also extinguishes that thirst by completing it. The will can be filled only by the possession of the **infinite good** <note>God</note>. For the will affects the good only as far as the intellect offers the good to it. The intellect finds the common nature of good itself, separated from all the constraints of participation in specific things...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is unique because it connects directly to God without any intermediaries, using the world and angels only as steps to return to its own "intellectual citadel." He supports this by citing the "Chaldean Oracles" of Zoroaster and comparing the soul's vision of God to the eye perceiving a sunbeam.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument from Book 10 of his *Platonic Theology*. Having established that the mind seeks a cause beyond the physical world, he now explores why only an infinite God can satisfy the human intellect and will, concluding that the soul must have been created directly by God without any intermediaries.</meta>

# Tenth Book of Theology

...and because of this very thing, it remains **infinite** within itself. ¶ It is also poured out into the infinite, since goodness can be communicated to innumerable things through infinite modes. ¶ If the **will** <note>original: "voluntas"</note> desires a good to the same extent that the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus"</note> offers it, ¶ and the intellect here offers an infinite good and infinite goods, ¶ it follows that the will desires just as much. Therefore, the will is filled only by the possession of the infinite good. <margin>D</margin> ¶ To this end: just as the object of the intellect is **being** <term>Being (ens): In this context, everything that exists, considered as a whole.</term> itself under the aspect of **truth**, so the object of the will is being itself under the aspect of **good**. Because any power can be satisfied only by that in which the complete nature of its object is found, it follows that the intellect and the will can be satisfied by God alone, in whom alone is the complete nature of truth and goodness. And because the intellect always moves from one truth to others, and the will is carried from some goods to others, the reason is clear that rest can come to them only from that which embraces all such things. <margin>E</margin> ¶ For a **habit** <note>original: "habitus". A stable disposition or state of being.</note> stops motion, and an infinite, unbounded habit in some way stops motion. ¶ Finally, a legitimate intellect is one that understands things as they are. A legitimate will is one that desires things as they are desirable. However, things are as they are ordained by God. Truly, they are desirable as they are ordained toward God. Therefore, neither the intellect nor the will can find rest in things themselves. But the former resolves back into God, and the latter refers back to God. ¶ To the former, God alone is proposed to be seen by a natural instinct. To the latter, God alone is to be loved. ¶ If only infinite goodness is able to fill the capacity of the will, then surely only infinite goodness procreates the nature of the will. This is especially true since the will itself sometimes bestows itself upon infinite goodness **without a medium** <note>original: "sine medio". Directly, without any intervening step or secondary cause.</note>. It does this most evidently when the intellect no longer proposes this or that specific good to the will, but instead shows either the sum of all goods together or the very source of goodness itself, from which the harvests of such a sum have sprouted. <margin>F</margin> ¶ Finally, no effect extends beyond its cause. 

---

¶ The human soul transcends any finite thing; for whatever finite truth or good you offer, the intellect can understand more, and the will can desire further. ¶ Therefore, no finite thing is the cause of the soul. This seems to be confirmed most strongly by the fact that a particular cause and mover cannot produce a power or an inclination that tends toward the **universal** <note>original: "universale". The concept of the "whole" or "all things," rather than just one specific thing.</note>. ¶ And because there is a power in the intellect for universal truth and an inclination in the will for universal good, it is plainly evident that the intellect and the will are not made or moved by any created thing. ¶ For whatever is created is truth and good only to a **certain extent** <note>original: "duntaxat". Only or merely.</note> or in a particular way. Can the soul not reject any particular good, even though it cannot reject the universal good? What does this signify, if not that the soul is subject to the action and command of the universal good alone? ¶ Let us conclude, therefore, through the acts of the intellect and the will and the turnings of man, that the soul has come forth into the light from nothingness, created by God with no medium interposed. ¶ And that infinite power of God, by which the soul was so produced, is in a certain way inserted into the soul itself, so that it becomes as if the soul's own and natural power, through which the soul, as often as it wishes, turns itself toward God. <margin>G</margin> ¶ The **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, whom Ficino synthesized with Christian theology.</note> think that no less than an infinite power is needed for someone to bestow themselves upon the infinite God, and to recognize and love the Infinite under a certain aspect of infinity. Just as God, by His infinite power, created the soul out of nothing, so by the same infinite power of God, the soul reaches that same infinite power of God which procreated it from nothing. <margin>H</margin> ¶ This infinite power—whether it is infused into the soul once or rather is continually infused and preserved by God—demonstrates that the soul is a participant in infinite power and (so to speak) is capable of it in such a way that through this power the soul reaches the infinity of God. We know that the infinity of God is all at once and whole. The infinity of time, because it passes away continuously, is also continuously renewed. It has flowed...

<summary>Ficino argues that because the human intellect and will can never be satisfied by finite things and always seek the "universal" truth and good, the soul must have been created directly by an infinite God. He concludes that the soul possesses a spark of God's infinite power, allowing it to turn back toward its Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's argument from Book 10 of his *Platonic Theology*. He is discussing the soul’s relationship to time and its direct creation by God, concluding that the soul’s capacity for the infinite proves its divine origin and immortality.</meta>

# Platonic [Theology]

...partly: and partly also fleeting; nor having at any time in the present anything but a moment. A moment is surpassed innumerably by a whole infinity. From which it happens that the infinity of God surpasses the infinity of time by an infinite distance beyond counting. The soul reaches that [God's infinity]; therefore, it stands far above this [time]. For which reason it exceeds all boundaries of time and lives perpetually. This is most strongly confirmed by this: that if God does not make the soul through angelic and celestial powers, much less does He do so through material seeds. Therefore, it does not undergo a deadly change. If, then, you desire to worship your parent: worship only the Good itself. You seek a parent: the nature of the body is not a parent to you, O soul. For you are so much better, the more you obey your parent. Moreover, you are so much more excellent, the more you oppose the body. It is entirely good for you to be with the father. It is in a certain way bad for you to be with the body.

<margin>A</margin>
No particular spirit <note>original: "animus"</note> begat you, O soul. Through the help of a spirit, reason is mobile. If, therefore, you had been made through it, you would have an entirely changeable substance. Therefore, you would come to a halt within that very changeability of the spirit. You would neither demand a stable nature nor think of anything above the spirit. No multiplex intellect created you. For [if it had], you would not reach supreme simplicity. And the attainment of that intellect itself would suffice for you. But now, by understanding and loving, you ascend toward life itself, toward essence itself, toward absolute being itself, above any intellect; nor is intelligence enough for you, unless you understand both "well" and the "Good." Indeed, the Good itself is undoubtedly enough for you. For you do not seek anything for any other reason than that it is good. Therefore, your procreator is the Good itself, O soul. Not a good body. Not a good spirit. Not a good 

<margin>B</margin>
intellect: but the Good: the Good itself, I say: which exists in itself, infinite beyond the limits of any subject; and it grants you infinite life: either from age to age <note>original: "ab euo in euum"; from eternity to eternity</note>, or 

<margin>C</margin>
at least from a certain beginning into eternity.

# Book

¶ Third reason. As the object is, so is the power. Chapter nine.

<margin>B</margin>
**F**our things—**essence**, **power** <note>original: "virtus"; the inherent capacity or strength of a thing</note>, **operation**, and **object**—have this order: that from essence flows power, and from this, operation. Operation seeks the object. And a certain kind of essence, through a certain kind of power—that is, its own power—operates in a certain way around an object suitable to it. It is not to be thought that any power flows from an essence other than one familiar to it. Nor is any operation produced by a power other than a natural one; nor does an operation concern itself with any object unless it is similar, fitting, and convenient. For why does that natural power of the essence, in its operating, desire one such object rather than another? Is it not because such a thing is more familiar, more apt, and more convenient to it? For unless it agreed more with one certain thing than another, it would either desire nothing or seek all things equally.

<margin>C</margin>
Thus the innermost ray of the visual power gazes upon the colored rays of the sun's brilliance. The innermost air of the ears, through the external air, drinks in "broken air," that is, sounds. Smell, produced in the misty vapor of the air, perceives the fragrant vapor in an apple through a similar vapor diffused from the apple in the thick air. Taste, submerged in the moisture of saliva, reaches flavors that are either naturally liquid or already liquefied there in the mouth through the dissolving of food.

<margin>D</margin>
Touch, adapted to the earthy nerves, easily feels earthy and solid things, and specifically physical qualities. You see that objects always agree with natural operations and powers. You are compelled to confess the same in the mind: that the mind is free from matter, since its object is free from matter. Such is the universal reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> and **Idea** of any thing.

<margin>E</margin>
The Platonists and Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about the Lyceum.</term> call an object of this kind "primary," because it presents itself to the first and direct gaze. But the "adequate object" is the whole of being...

<margin>A</margin> ...it encompasses both ways. Especially because a <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental "form" or "concept" of a thing</note> cannot have an absolute power of signifying if the mind—which is both its subject and its source—is not itself absolute. Since every subject, by its own nature, receives qualities, and a fountain pours its own flavor into the streams flowing from it, two things follow: First, that the substance of the mind is not drawn out from the hiding places of matter. Second, that it is immortal because it is one with that species and with universal <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratione"; the underlying logical principle of a thing</note>, which, insofar as it is universal, escapes both place and time. Let us argue toward the same point again in this way: The <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibile"; an object that can be understood by the mind rather than perceived by the senses</note> itself is the proper perfection of the intellect. For the intellect in action and the intelligible in action are one. Indeed, as long as the intellect is only a potentiality, it is not yet joined with the thing that is potentially to be understood; but when it is actually understanding, it is joined with the thing already actually understood.

<margin>B</margin> They are joined, however—as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</note> would have it—because the form of that thing inheres in the mind. Things that share one form are themselves one. Therefore, a single unit is made from the understanding mind and the thing understood, since the form of this thing, as such, shapes the mind. Whatever, therefore, applies to the intelligible (insofar as it is intelligible) applies to the intellect (insofar as it is intellect). Because the perfection and that which is perfected are of the same kind, they are always bound to one another in a mutual relationship.

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, the intelligible, insofar as it is such, is necessary and perpetual. Certainly, in the act of contemplation, we do not consider things that can decay. We do not believe we "know" anything unless we grasp the certain and necessary reason of the thing; those things which are necessary are perfectly comprehended by the intellect. <term>Contingent</term> <note>original: "contingentia"; things that are not guaranteed to happen or can change, like the weather or human actions</note> things, however, are comprehended imperfectly. For when the intellect makes affirmations about contingent things, it is often deceived. If it does not wish to be deceived, it doubts; and both acts—being deceived and doubting—are imperfect. Rightly so, when it thinks of contingent things, it is accustomed to doubt, lest they change in the meantime, and it must judge them differently at one moment than at another. For they change in every single moment. For example, when we say "Plato is sitting," he may, in the meantime, have stood up.

<margin>D</margin> Universal definitions of things, however, are perpetual; for instance, **"Man is a rational animal."** <note>original: "homo est animal rationale"; the classic scholastic definition of humanity</note> Also, the properties of the <term>species</term>, which are properly defined, are everlasting; for instance, **"Every rational being is able to reason."** For such definitions and properties are always equally true, even if no human being were breathing on the earth. The intellect has clearly declared these; it holds them firmly and asserts them without error or doubt. And if it understands any contingent things, it comprehends them primarily under these universal reasons. Where it thinks of corruptible things, it does so not as they are corruptible, but as they are eternal. Therefore, the intellect is perpetual, for it is united to everlasting reasons and perfected by them alone. If the intellect grasps them, and that which it grasps has some proportion or harmony with that which is grasped, then certainly the intellect will have harmony with these reasons; these have neither beginning nor end. And if the mind had a beginning or an end, it would have no proportion with them, since it would be distinguished from them entirely by opposite conditions. Therefore, the mind either always was and will be, as they are; or, if it began to exist at some point, it will nonetheless never cease to be.

### The objection of the Epicureans and the response regarding the union of the mind with absolute species and everlasting reasons. Chapter 2.

<margin>E</margin> **N**or should some **Epicurean** <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the soul was made of atoms and died with the body</note> thrust himself in here, objecting that while the light of the sun is received by the eye, the eye dies while the sun's light survives unharmed. Similarly, he might say that the universal species (that is, the thing signifying universally) and the everlasting reason are grasped by the intellect, but the intellect perishes while the species or reason remains. We respond that the light of the sun is not "received" by the eye in the same way, since it is not even held by it for a moment; when the sun sets, the sight loses the light instantly. If it had received any of the light into itself, it would surely retain some part of it, if only for a little while—just as water retains heat for a time after the fire is removed. Thus, we can say the light is *present* to the eyes, but not that it *inheres* in them or is *received* by them. The mind, however, is said to "receive" that species and the universal reason of "man" and other things because it retains them in memory even when the human object is absent. However, that universal <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the mental "form" or "concept" of a thing</note> of "man": the very fact that it is universal, it does not possess from the individual persons of men, in whom whatever exists is particular. Yet that universal is in the mind. Therefore, it has its universality from the mind.

But in what way is this especially so? As it pleases <term>Aristotle</term>. <margin>C</margin> Our mind has two powers: one that is active, and another that is receptive. The active power is that which produces universal forms; the receptive power is that which receives those forms once they are conceived by the active power.

When, therefore, the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty that holds mental images of sensory things</note> looks upon a likeness of a specific man within itself—such as <term>Socrates</term>—the light of that active power <margin>☞</margin> immediately strikes that likeness, no differently than a ray of the sun strikes water. And just as this ray of the sun, reflected from the water, produces a bright and trembling circle on the opposite wall: so the light of the active power itself strikes the particular image of a man conceived by the imagination. And from that image, reflected into the receptive <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "intellectus"</note>, it then gives birth to a certain form within it. This form no longer represents "this Socrates" located in this specific place and time, but rather the nature of "man," which is equally common to all individual persons and is freed from the certain limits of place and <margin>3</margin> time. In this state, both the form itself is universal, and the nature which is represented through it is universal.

In this, the marvelous power of the intellect appears. <margin>B</margin> Namely, it is that which creates a form freed from matter, place, and time; and because it apprehends something that is, in a way, eternal and similar to its creator, why should it not itself be freed from those same physical constraints and be perpetual? Finally, those things which the intellect reaches are thus "separated" <note>meaning separated from physical matter</note>; if they are such by their own nature, then the intellect is also such. For when it reaches separated things, it is then present where they are; therefore, it too is separated. But if those things are by nature bound to physical suffering and change, yet the intellect by its own power sets them free, it is much more the case that the intellect itself is free, so that it may free the others.

# Eleventh [Book]

Tell me then, why can the form of any thing not become one with the intellect before it is entirely separated from matter? It is because the intellect itself is, much earlier and more significantly, separated from matter. In what way the intellect and that form become one is shown by that comparison we introduced regarding the ray and the water. Indeed, that bright and trembling circle born from them does not truly unite with the wall, because the nature of that brightness and the wall are surely different. But if it falls upon a mirror, it will be more closely united. Finally, if that same light returns to the light of the sun—from which the ray had been sent down to produce the bright circle—it would be gathered together entirely into one.

What, then, are those "forms" among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> which the intellect has produced, if not a certain "spark" <note>original: "scintilla"</note> of that likeness which the imagination had gathered from things, and of that active power through which the mind produced it? And what is our mind, if not a certain spark of the higher Mind? Therefore, that form is infused into our mind just as a spark of things is joined to the spark of the higher mind; and just as that bright circle is joined to the light of the sun from which its ray was produced.

Therefore, from the mind and the form, one thing is made, just as one union is made from two sparks, or one flame; or as one light is made from the rays of many candles; or as one splendor is made from that bright circle and the light of the sun. Because the mind is thus united to eternal things through this form, let it be without controversy that the mind is eternal—especially for the reason that the intellect, in the act of understanding, is perhaps not only joined with the eternal thing understood, but is also itself the very eternal thing which is understood. For it is the same ray, in a way, which strikes the water from on <margin>g</margin> high, which shines in the water, and which is reflected back through the air. There, if it were turned back into itself and gained the power of seeing, it would immediately see its own splendor which had overflowed from the water. It would do the same if it bounced back from gold or silver. For it will always see its own splendor, although affected in various ways according to the variety of objects from which it was reflected. If a more convenient example regarding those two powers of the intellect and this union [is needed]...

<margin>A</margin> we desire. Let us consider in the eye that which is almost in the eye: just as in our mind there are two powers. There is in the eye a glassy transparency: and a spark. The former is scarcely capable of acting, while the latter is the active force. This spark flashes outward at night; it draws the image of this color or that from the bodies placed opposite to it. It imprints that image upon the transparent power. Through this, the eye perceives the object. Indeed, perhaps it does not so much perceive the opposite body as its own ray, which has been extended and then reflected back. And when it was reflected, it leapt back into the eye already "painted" with the image of the body. Therefore, although the eye seems to discern now this color, now that, it is nevertheless always discerning itself, in a way; but in a varying way, as it shines back from various colors. What prevents that active power—which is the ray of our mind—from being reflected back into itself from various different mental images <note>original: "phantasie simulacris"; images held in the imagination</note>, flashing out in one way and then another, and thus seeing itself affected in different ways according to the diversity of the images? In this case, that mental form <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the conceptual "form" or "category" of a thing</note> or reason by which we understand something as absolute and eternal, is perhaps nothing other than the ray of the intellect reflected back into itself. It notices itself most easily when it directs itself toward these mental images, just as a face does not see itself unless it looks into a mirror. From this, it is also reflected back differently according to the variety of the mirrors themselves. Just as the ray of the mind is reflected back into the mind in different ways from images according to their diversity; but we shall speak of these things more completely in what follows.

<margin>E</margin> ### The objection of Epicurus and the response that ideas are innate to the mind. Chapter 3.

<margin>B</margin> **N**egating this, perhaps <term>Epicurus</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who argued that all knowledge comes from the senses and that the soul is mortal.</note> will say that those forms which the intellect conceives daily are not eternal, because they begin to exist when they are born (conceived), and they cease to exist when they are committed to oblivion. First Reason: Indeed, sensing and understanding, which are vital operations, proceed from an intrinsic and vital principle.

# Book

<margin>C</margin> That is, from an active principle. For there are certain operations common to both living things and those lacking life: such as generation, alteration, and change of place. Those things that lack life suffer these kinds of operations rather than performing them. For they do not in any way generate themselves, or alter themselves, or change their own location. But living things act upon themselves in these matters. For by nourishing and increasing themselves, they alter themselves and generate something within themselves. And by judging and desiring, they change their location. If nature ought to equip living things better for their own specific actions than for common ones—and that which is active is better equipped than that which is passive—and since nature granted an active principle to them for common operations, how much more so for their own specific actions: namely, sensation and intelligence. Thus, nature disposed them so that they might act through these powers rather than merely being acted upon.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, neither the mind nor even the senses—as it seems to many <term>Platonists</term>—perceive anything from external physical forms. Instead, just as the life-giving part of the soul alters, generates, nourishes, and grows through implanted "seeds," so the interior sense and the mind judge all things through formulas that are indeed innate, but are excited by external things. Nor is this judgment anything other than the transition of a formula from a certain potentiality into act. For no operation of an agent ought to transcend its own limits. Therefore, a vital operation that remains within is not caused by an external principle lacking life; rather, it takes its beginning from that which composes, divides, reasons, and by its own affection turns the body into contrary qualities.

<margin>E</margin> The proof that the mind is supremely effective is taken from <term>Boethius</term> <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" was a key text for Ficino.</note> against the <term>Stoics</term>: because the mind, going beyond those things which the sense perceives, devises universal rules beyond the nature of the objects themselves. It descends by composing and ascends by resolving. And by referring itself back to itself, it refutes false things with true ones. Finally, since different powers of the soul judge the same thing differently—for the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> judges in one way, and reason judges in another—it is consistent that the judgment itself follows the form and nature of the judge, not the thing being judged. And because the judgment exists as an act of the one judging, it is probable that every judge performs his work not from an external power, but from his own power through...

Having argued that the mind is like a light or a spark, he now moves to his "Second Argument" to prove that our universal concepts—like the idea of "Man" or "Beauty"—cannot be simple copies of physical objects, but must be generated by the mind’s own internal power.</meta>

# Theology
# Book Eleven

leads to perfection. **The Second Argument.** But let us return to the mind: just as singular images <note>original: "simulacra"; the mental "pictures" of specific things</note> are not imprinted on the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty that holds sensory images</note> by physical bodies—as we have already proven elsewhere—so too the "species" <note>original: "species"; the universal forms or concepts of things</note> of universals are not stamped into the mind by these singular images. Instead, the mind creates those species through its own power, just as the imagination fashions images by its own efforts. For in what way could a mental image (which is also called a *phantasm* <note>original: "phantasma"</note>) create something freer and more expansive than itself? A phantasm is singular to itself and is bound by the conditions of matter; a species, however, is universal, and therefore freer and broader. If this species—which is also called a universal—does not come from mental images, it certainly does not come from external things, which cannot shape the mind through any medium other than those images. Furthermore, for a single and spiritual species, there must be a single spiritual cause, or at least one that is unified and ordered in a spiritual way. But the individual things that exist outside us are many and corporeal. And none of those things, taken by itself, can produce an incorporeal species that signifies a common nature, since each is merely corporeal and limited to its own nature. Nor can all singular things joined together achieve this. For they are scattered; they do not possess an order such that, when connected to others, they form a single chain of causes. Therefore, just as a heap of stones does not become a single simple object but remains a pile, so too a crowd of singular things might produce a confusion of images, but it will not produce a single, simple species.

<margin>☛</margin> Furthermore, in any singular individual, three things are found: the nature of the species, the "accidents" <note>original: "accidentia"; non-essential qualities like color or height</note> which are not necessary to the species, and the individual itself composed of both. For example, in Socrates, there is "humanity" (which is called the nature of the species) and there is a certain whiteness and a certain shape (which are called the accidents of the species and are considered "additional"). The person of Socrates is composed of both. Now, is that common species—which is the equal likeness of all men—imprinted on the mind by these persons? Certainly, it is not imprinted by the accidents of these persons. For that would reflect the accidental traits of a man, not his substance. Nor is it imprinted by that "nature" which underlies the accidents. For that nature is not the whole person of any man, but only a part of him. Therefore, such a nature is not predicated of any man. Who would say, **"Socrates is humanity"?** Instead, we say that Socrates is a man. Therefore, "Man" is predicated of Socrates—of the whole Socrates, I say—not of humanity alone or of his accidents. The same applies to the whole of Plato, and to all others. Here it appears that "Man" himself—whom our mind commonally predicates of every whole person and conceives within itself—is much broader than the specific nature of this or that person. Because that which comprehends is something different and broader, it cannot be made by that which is comprehended and is narrower; especially since that "nature" becomes singular in individual men. But that which has been made singular does not create a universal.

<margin>15</margin> But is that species perhaps brought into us by the sum of all whole persons? Not at all. Indeed, that species regards an infinite number of persons equally. But we have never inspected infinite persons, nor have we received that species from only a few persons, since the species comprehends infinitely many others besides. Nor can anyone safely enough write down a common rule from a few singular cases; for whoever attempted that would be deceived. It would be just as if someone, considering only land animals and seeing that they breathe, concluded that every animal breathes <note>This is a classic critique of "induction"—assuming a universal rule based on limited observations</note>. Since, therefore, the species is generated neither from singular persons nor from their images, it remains that it is produced by the intellect. The intellect does not generate it *from* the phantasm or *within* the phantasm. For the phantasm—because it is singular both in its being and in what it signifies—if it were to become the "matter" or the "place" of the species, it would likewise make the species singular. However, there is a doubt as to whether the intellect generates the species *through* the phantasm, as if using the phantasm as a "middle cause" between the intellect and the species to be generated. We believe this cannot happen for this reason: a middle cause and a primary cause usually share more in common with the effect than does a remote cause. As in the generation of a human: because the sun generates a human through a human medium, it is more...

<summary>Ficino argues that universal concepts (like the idea of "Man") cannot be derived from physical objects or sensory images because the universal is broader and more spiritual than the singular, material things we perceive.</summary>

# Platonic Book
## a

a man generating <note>original: "homo generans"; referring to a father</note> is more consistent with the man born than the sun itself is. If, therefore, the mental image <note>original: "phantasma"; the specific picture of a thing held in the imagination</note> were the primary cause of the universal concept <note>original: "species"; the general idea of a thing</note>, the concept would be born more similar to the mental image than to the intellect. From this, two absurdities would follow.

**One:** that a concept born in this way would immediately adopt the mental image itself and the imagination—being more closely related to them—as its natural seat, rather than adopting the intellect.

**The other:** that if the intellect received the concept through such a mental image, it would understand a specific, individual thing <note>original: "singulare"</note> more clearly and sooner than it would understand the universal. Indeed, that concept would report the individual thing first, because of its kinship with the individual mental image.

Nor should we listen to those who place the mental image between the intellect and the concept as if it were some kind of instrument. Does not the active power of the mind agree more with the receptive power <note>original: "capace"; the part of the mind that receives knowledge</note> than a mental image does? In what way, then, will the active power form the receptive part through an "extraneous" <note>external or foreign</note> mental image? For it is necessary that an instrument of formation be placed between the formatter and the thing being formed. A mental image, being extraneous, cannot be placed between those two powers which are, in turn, kindred.

Therefore, when the intellect creates that form, it produces it neither **from** the image, nor **in** the image, nor **through** the image. Perhaps, instead, it inserts a certain ray or power into the image of the imagination, through which the image itself—acting as a "formatter" for the mind—generates a form of this kind, which we call an **intelligible species** <note>original: "speciem intelligibilem"; a concept that can be grasped by the reason</note>? But we do not think this can happen either. Surely that power, once received by the image, would be bound by the same material conditions as the image itself. Thus, it would not generate an intelligible form, which is absolute <note>free or detached</note> from those conditions.

And if someone should say that the form is captured in an absolute way by the intellect, even though the imagination did not create it as something absolute, we shall conclude from this very fact what we desire most: that the intellect is not subject to the imagination like a thing being formed is subject to a formatter, since the intellect possesses forms in a more excellent way than the imagination is able to grant.

From this it follows that if the intellectual form is born, it is born from the intellect alone, and without a medium. For if the mind generates that form, and in generating it receives it into itself without a medium, it certainly gives birth to it through itself, and gives birth with no other thing intervening. From all these points, it is concluded that the **intellect forms itself**. And since it could not form itself if it were entirely formless, it is necessary that—before those forms or notions which it gives birth to within itself almost every single moment throughout one's life—there must lurk in the inner recesses of the soul other forms that are natural to the soul. These are equal in number to the species of created things in the world, and through them, the soul is able to give birth to the intelligible forms of those species.

**The Third Argument.** Certainly, things require specific "seeds." Nature does not make anything out of just anything, nor does it make something from nothing. Therefore, the essence of the soul—which is one, and regards almost all things equally—cannot produce many and various types of forms, some at one time and others at another, unless it does so through many internal "formulas" <note>original: "formulas"; innate patterns or blueprints</note> that differ in kind. By these, it may give birth to or bring forth certain forms at certain times rather than others.

**The Fourth Argument.** That is to say, the soul often brings things to light suddenly, with no previous consultation or will, but by a certain natural instinct alone. Now, effects that happen in a natural order display the same kind of form that their causes possess. For hot things are produced by a fire that is itself hot. Because the soul, out of its own being, naturally produces something, it produces an effect—albeit in a lower way—that is like itself.

I see, therefore, that the soul, which naturally generates the universal concepts of all things through its own being, seems also to have obtained the universal species of all things within its own essence from its origin, so that like may be generated by like. For if there is one efficient cause of those species (namely, the intellect) and one subject (the same intellect), no reason can be assigned as to why many different types of concepts are made, unless the intellect brings them forth as distinct through various "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning inner logical structures</note> natural to itself. For the diversity of mental images is not enough to produce this variety; those images contribute nothing to this construction other than providing a certain **occasion for working**, while through their presence the mind is excited to bring forth its concepts. This, however, is nothing other than making those idle reasons more ready. Re... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Reasoning" or "Ratio"</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that human concepts are not derived from sensory images but are generated by the intellect using innate "seeds" or formulas already present in the soul. He concludes that the mind is self-forming and contains natural blueprints for all things in the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 11 of the *Platonic Theology*. Having previously argued that the human mind does not simply copy external objects like a mirror, Ficino now begins a series of numbered arguments (the Fifth through the Eighth) to prove that the soul is born already "full" of divine ideas and formative principles, rather than being a blank slate.</meta>

# Theology, Book Eleven

### Fifth Argument
Therefore, if the divine mind—which is full of all <term>Ideas<gloss>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the mind of God</gloss></term> through its own essence—creates the soul directly and without any intermediary, it is necessary that the soul flow forth from that source full of Ideas. Truly, since God is hindered by nothing at all in the making of a soul, He makes it as perfect as it can possibly be made within that kind of being. 

Certainly, the soul comes forth more perfect if it descends into these regions already full of such difficult notions than if it were empty. From its very beginning, the soul is capable of holding these notions in that part of itself where it matches the nature of the angels. For just as the soul has a temporal aspect, which allows it to run through thoughts in a continuous search, it also has an eternal aspect, allowing it to possess knowledge from the start. 

This is especially true since the soul is closer to God than <term>prime matter<gloss>The most basic, formless substance of the physical universe</gloss></term> is. Therefore, if matter receives all its forms from God and receives them as soon as it is prepared, it is necessary that the soul also receive them all. Indeed, the soul is "prepared" to receive all things as soon as it receives its being from God. Because its essence is simple and stable above the flow of time, it cannot be increased or made "more ready" over time.

This is what <margin>B</margin> **Zoroaster** <note>Ficino refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, which he attributed to the ancient sage Zoroaster.</note> sang: **the paternal mind sowed symbols in souls** <note>original Greek: "σύμβολὰ πατρικὸς νόος έσπειρε ψυχαῖς"</note>. And **Orpheus** said: **for he placed all things in the first nature** <note>original Greek: "πάντα γὰρ πρώτει πρώτῃ φύσει έγκτέθηκεν"</note>, which means that the First Cause implanted all things in the primary nature. <margin>C</margin> **Orphic Theology** calls this "third essence" <note>The soul is often called the "third essence" in Neoplatonism, sitting between the indivisible divine and the divisible material world.</note> the seat of rational souls. **Archytas of Tarentum** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician.</note> also says in his book *On Wisdom*: "Man is born the wisest of all living creatures because God infused the Ideas of all things into him; through these, the mind is able to produce notions of things in the same way that the mouth, by means of the tongue, creates the names of things."

### Sixth Argument
<margin>D</margin> To speak in the Platonic manner: in matter, the beginnings of all forms lie hidden. In nature, through which matter is moved toward taking on forms, the "seeds" of those forms lie hidden. Just as the seed is enclosed within the natural makeup of a tree to propagate a similar tree, the entire tree-to-be is contained within that seed. The same occurs in the natural makeup and seed of a living animal. 

Therefore, in that lower part of the soul which nourishes the body and acts as an instrument of nature to move and shape matter, there must exist—in a much more excellent way—the <term>reasons<gloss>Latin: "rationes"; here meaning the formative principles or inner blueprints</gloss></term> of all forms. For example, from the "reason" of a head that exists in the soul, that specific seed for a head is born in physical nature. From this seed, the visible form of the head sprouts in matter. The same happens for the chest, the arms, and all other members. 

Now, if this lowest part of the soul is second-to-none and shapes bodies—rather than being shaped *by* bodies—and contains the principles for generating forms, would the **mind**, which is the highest part of the soul, be sterile? Would it only be shaped by bodies? Would it lack the principles for producing the various <term>species<gloss>The mental concepts or universal forms of things</gloss></term>? By no means! Rather, just as the lowest part of the soul (which is primary in relation to individual bodies) gives birth to individual physical things through principles implanted in it from the start, so the mind (which is primary among both bodies and pure spirits) possesses principles inserted into it from its origin. Through these, it produces those concepts that are independent of the physical impressions of bodies.

### Seventh Argument
The soul will only hold the middle place between divine and bodily things if it appears to share in both. It must possess within itself the principles of both types of forms: both the **intelligible** <note>things known by the mind</note> and the **sensible** <note>things known by the senses</note>.

### Eighth Argument
It is not right for the soul to be in a worse condition than physical bodies. Therefore, if bodies possess natural qualities before they acquire accidental ones, the soul has its own internal formulas in the mind much more so before it receives "foreign" ones from the outside. 

<margin>E</margin> There are two types of commonality belonging to matter: **natural** and **accidental**. The "natural" is that nature in which individuals of the same species agree with one another—such as "humanity," in which all individual men agree. This commonality, as many believe, is perpetual and more excellent than any individual. The "accidental" is that universal notion that the mind thinks up regarding that natural commonality, setting aside all individuals. 

This universal notion is accidental (or "adventitious") not only regarding matter, but also regarding the mind. If matter possesses one type of natural commonality before this accidental one, then the mind—which is better than matter—similarly possesses a common form before the accidental one. For a common form must exist in a more excellent way in the mind than it does in matter. 

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is created "full" of innate ideas and formative principles by God, serving as a vital link between the divine and material worlds. He uses authorities like Zoroaster and Orpheus to claim that the mind contains the "seeds" of all knowledge from its very beginning.</summary>

Here, he continues a numbered list of "reasons" (arguments 9 through 14) to prove that human knowledge is a process of "recollecting" or uncovering truths already planted in the mind by God.</meta>

# Platonic Theology

...natural perfection is greater than that which is accidental. Therefore, it is necessary for <term>common forms<gloss>Universal concepts, like the idea of a 'circle' or 'justice,' that apply to many individual things</gloss></term> to exist within the mind before those obscure forms which the mind fashions from physical things. Truly, we often gaze upon these **innate forms**, but through our lack of skill, we believe we are seeing external or visiting objects. It is just like those who—whether in sleep or due to some disease of the brain or an affliction of the eyes—think they see certain things flying here and there outside their eyes, when in fact those things are both moving and being seen internally. 

### A New Reason
Why is it that <term>brutes<gloss>Non-human animals</gloss></term>, having inspected individual things, do not think up a common notion? Man, however, does this by his very rational nature, which distinguishes him from the animals. This is because his nature possesses a **seal** of such figures. For if nature produces forms and its own species, it certainly produces them through a "form-making" nature. Who would say such a nature lacks its own identifying marks? 

### The Tenth Reason
Furthermore, when we construct perfect **demonstrations** in the sciences, we usually demonstrate certain properties of species starting from principles that are more excellent and broader. However, among those notions which are newly fashioned by the soul, the broader a notion is, the further it is from the actual substance; for instance, the notion of a "species" (like 'human') is closer to the substance than the notion of a "genus" (like 'animal'). Because of this, among those mental constructs, the one that is less general is judged more excellent. Therefore, there must be other notions in the soul besides these—notions that are simultaneously broader and more excellent—from which a true demonstration is made. Since a demonstration is formed not only from universals, but from universal causes...

<margin>A</margin>
...to proceed from these; however, the notions innate to the mind are not effects produced by causes. Again, since forms in physical bodies cannot be universal, it follows that beyond the forms found in bodies and those in our minds, we must seek other forms in the **Divine Mind**—the creator of all things—which are the universal causes of everything. The human mind possesses the "formulas" of these, so that through these formulas (as likenesses of the causes), it may refer its conclusions to those causes as effects through the process of demonstration. But more on Ideas elsewhere. 

### The Eleventh Reason
And this very demonstration always introduces things less known to us from propositions that are better known. It leads back to others in turn, until the mind reaches certain...

# Book Eleven

...principles that are **known through themselves** to the mind, shining out to the mind’s gaze by the very nature of the mind. This is so that the progression does not wander fruitlessly into infinity, nor turn back into a reckless circle from the same points to the same points. In the various branches of knowledge, specific demonstrations are made for individual types of things based on their own principles. Therefore, according to the various species and various faculties, there are present in the mind different principles of teaching, known by the natural light of the mind. Indeed, all following steps are contained within those very principles. From this it follows that the soul, by its very nature, abounds in all teachings.

### The Twelfth Reason
Just as trees and living creatures—and their limbs—sprout from their own **seeds**, so too should the sciences arise from internal beginnings. This ensures the mind is not more sterile than nature, which brings forth its offspring from implanted seeds and does not merely pour them out by chance. 

### The Thirteenth Reason
When we search for truth among ourselves by questioning and answering, how could the reasoning reach a conclusion? It could only do so if something were granted beforehand. But could anything be rightly granted if it were not already known? Thus, this reasoning (as <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian philosopher whom Ficino synthesized with Platonic thought.</note> **Aurelius Augustine** says) would find nothing already known within us to lean upon to lead us to the unknown; we would discern nothing at all through it. Therefore, there is within us, prior to the act of reasoning, a certain <term>intelligence<gloss>A direct, intuitive grasp of truth that precedes logical step-by-step thinking</gloss></term> from which reasoning takes its starting point.

### The Fourteenth Reason
Is not our reasoning mobile? While it seeks the truth, it descends from one thing to another, and when it examines something it has found, it ascends from one thing to another. But every movement starts from rest—or from something stable—and tends toward stability. Movement of this kind is a "weaving together" of notions. Every single thing has its own beginning and its own end. For this reason, because reasoning is a progression of notions, it is led back to notions. Because it is mobile, it is led back to certain stable notions, so that by their impulse it may seek what it desires; by their evidence it may find what it sought; by their light it may examine what it found; and in the firmness of what is found, it may rest. From there, therefore, it began its search.

<summary>Ficino presents a series of logical arguments to prove that human knowledge relies on innate "seeds" or "formulas" of divine truth already present in the soul. He argues that scientific demonstration and human reasoning would be impossible if the mind did not already possess stable, self-evident principles provided by God.</summary>

# Theology
## Book Eleven

The same point returns upon examination. Therefore, there are in the mind certain stable and perpetual notions which are both the principles and the ends of reasoning.

### The Fifteenth Reason 
<margin>B</margin>
These notions are necessary not only for reasoning, but indeed for understanding in any way whatsoever. For just as the senses—which perceive through external forms that are called <term>accidental<gloss>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like its color or size, which can change without the thing becoming something else</gloss></term>—always perceive accidents (as the Platonists believe), so conversely the mind, which defines the essence of things, understands through <term>essential forms<gloss>The core "blueprints" or definitions of what a thing truly is</gloss></term>. And because the sense, which trusts in the deceptive and suddenly vanishing images of things, is often deceived and does not distinguish an image from a true thing (requiring the judgment of reason for this), the mind must therefore rely on "essential reasons" (if I may call them that) so that it too is not deceived and does not require the judgment of some higher power.

### The Sixteenth Reason
Furthermore, if we know angels, we are not able to know them through <term>species<gloss>Mental concepts or forms</gloss></term> drawn from the senses; for since those species depend on bodies, they do not reflect angelic forms, which do not decline toward bodies. It follows, then, that we know them through **innate species**. For by what means could we judge angels to be natures that do not tend toward bodies, unless it is through species that are entirely independent of bodies?

### The Seventeenth Reason
Finally, intellectual cognition is the middle ground between divine cognition and sensory cognition. Therefore, it also possesses middle-ground conditions. God knows through His own immobile essence. The sense knows through mobile qualities—that is, "visiting" species. For this reason, the mind must know through immobile qualities, which are called **innate species**. 
<margin>C</margin>
Ultimately, the order of the universe requires that, just as pure minds <note>Ficino refers here to angels or higher intelligences</note> look into themselves, while senses look only at other things, the soul—as a participant in both mind and sense—should look not only at forms outside itself, but also at those within itself. 
<margin>D</margin>
Now, where we are accustomed to say in the manner of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle argued the mind is a blank slate (*tabula rasa*) that creates concepts from sensory experience</note> that the mind "procreates" new species, we can say more accurately in the manner of **Plato** that innate species are "drawn out" from the inner sanctuaries of the mind. It is the nature of "sister powers" to accompany one another in operation just as they do in existence, and to mutually awaken one another to action. Smell and taste are sister powers; thus, the soul is often invited to taste through the sense of smell. The power of desire and the nature of anger are sister powers; thus, we are easily provoked to anger by lust. Even the "sisterhood" of the eyes causes both to turn toward the same object at once. The sisterhood of sense and imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> ensures that when the sense is working on something, the imagination works on it as well. Because of a similar sisterhood, when the imagination brings its own species into action, the mind also leads its own into the light. The mind's species are not strictly "generated" then, but those which were narrowly compressed now spread out more widely and flourish; those which were lukewarm now boil; those which were shining by themselves only in the "peak" of the mind now glitter from a distance and shine out in the **reason** (which follows the mind) once it has been made more serene.
<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, what Aristotle would call a "creation" of species, Plato would name a **coruscation** <note>A sudden flash of light or brilliance</note>, through which the "eye of reason," having been awakened, is irradiated by the species of the mind. That first "flashing" in the mind is intelligence itself; the subsequent irradiation is the actual discourse of reason. Through intelligence, the essences of things are defined. Through reason, those defined essences are combined and arguments are constructed. The mind cannot fabricate true definitions of essences through the accidental "shadow-images" of things; rather, it builds them through the <term>reasons<gloss>Formative principles or divine ideas</gloss></term> infused into it from the origin of all things.

### The Eighteenth Reason
"Infused," I say, by the reasons of things which God possesses. These are, in fact, in God the very essence of God, understood by God Himself under various "reasons" <note>This is a standard Scholastic and Platonic idea: God is one, but contains the ideas of all different things within His one essence</note>. Therefore, the forms of all things are in God, where they are nothing other than the essence of God itself, and all exist there as both "habit" and "act" <note>Meaning they are both eternally present and eternally active/knowable</note>. All forms are also in an angel; they are not the essence of the angel itself, but certain "essential reasons"—that is, those which always accompany its essence. There, they all flourish as both habit and act, because an angel understands all things simultaneously in act. Furthermore, they are all...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind relies on innate, immobile "essential forms" rather than just sensory data, using a Platonic framework to explain how we understand non-physical realities like angels. He reconciles Aristotle and Plato by suggesting that what looks like the "creation" of a new idea is actually the "flashing forth" of an idea already latent in the soul.</summary>

# Theology Eleven

...that would indeed be absurd. First, because by the same thing, something would be both greater and smaller. Next, it would place something of one species into another; for instance, defining "greater" or "smaller" through the species of a "head." It is better to name a "headed" thing by its head than to use it to define "greater" or "smaller." Finally, it is absurd to call something "greater" by means of something "small." Therefore, if a <term>formal cause<gloss>A philosophical concept where a thing is what it is because it 'participates' in an ideal blueprint—for example, a chair is a chair because it follows the 'form' of a chair</gloss></term> must be asserted, what is "greater" is known through Greatness, and what is "smaller" is known through Smallness. Similarly, we will not call the number ten "more" than the number nine specifically because of the "unit" <note>original: "vnitate"</note>—since we name a single thing from a unit—but rather we shall say it is "more" because of **Plurality**, and another is "fewer" because of **Paucity**. Likewise, we shall assert that the dual number (the number two) is made not by the division of one into two (which could also be claimed to happen by the joining of one thing and another), for one should not say that the same effect is produced by properly opposite causes. Therefore, we will instead assert that the dual number is made according to the **Form** through the participation in **Duality** itself. 

But let us set aside these lighter matters and proceed to more serious ones. If color or shape were Beauty itself, by what means could any color or shape be ugly? Likewise, for what reason would many subjects participate in one single Beauty as a common thing, unless a single common nature of Beauty existed which both dwelt within each individual and presided over them—so that the beauty within depends on the Beauty that presides? Therefore, **Goodness** itself is one thing, and the things that become good by the participation in goodness are another. 
<margin>C</margin>
**Beauty** is one thing, and beautiful things are another; and it is similar for all the other species, which Plato calls **Ideas**. For beautiful bodies are many, but Beauty itself is one. Or rather, 
<margin>D</margin>
everything that is primary and supreme in any class of things is only one. Again, these beautiful things have two natures: both the corporeal matter, which becomes a participant in beauty, and the quality of beauty itself. But Beauty itself is nothing other than Beauty. Is not whatever is primary in any genus nothing other than itself? Furthermore, these bodies are partly beautiful and partly ugly. For they are judged deformed because of their very matter, which is something other than Beauty. 

But Beauty itself does not admit ugliness. If opposites by turns flee from one another, then beautiful bodies also change: at one moment they are beautiful, at another the opposite. But Beauty is **immutable**; it is nothing other than Beauty, and insofar as it is Beauty, it does not change. For in this way, it is neither turned into its opposite, nor is it ever deprived of its foundation and support, since it sustains itself. Add to this that any corporeal things can seem beautiful to some, but not beautiful to others. But Beauty itself cannot be thought of as lacking beauty. Moreover, beautiful bodies are divisible; but Beauty is indivisible and not "small" (for then it could not form large bodies) nor "large" (for then it would not fit small bodies). Finally, it is not corporeal, since it would not be suitable for spiritual things. It is also not temporal, because it would not exist in eternal things. 

However, it exists much more in souls and minds than in bodies; yet it is not primary even in them. This is both because souls are deformed in themselves unless they are formed by the **Good** (whose splendor is Beauty), and because they seek Truth as something beautiful. But Beauty does not seek itself. Finally, it is because it is simply and commonly lovable not merely to be an animal or an intellectual being, but to be well and to be good. Since the Good attracts us most highly, it is the highest Beauty. Therefore, the **Idea** of beautiful things is above bodies, souls, and minds. It is one, simple, pure, immutable, 
<margin>E</margin>
indivisible, incorporeal, and eternal. And the nature of all Ideas is the same, which we prove here by another example. When this man begets that man, he does not, strictly speaking, beget the "Specific Humanity" itself which is considered commonly in both. For if he beget it, he would also beget himself, who exists through that humanity. Furthermore, a finite nature cannot beget an infinite nature. Therefore, "this man" is not the cause of Humanity existing simply, but only the cause of it being propagated in that specific matter. It is necessary, however, that there be a common cause for the common human nature, and one that acts through itself. 

->Marsilio Ficino<-

He demonstrates that these Ideas must be non-physical, unchanging, and the true source of definitions for things like numbers and biological species.</summary>
