<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 11 of the *Platonic Theology*. Following the previous discussion on how we recognize universal truths (like "Greatness" or "Duality") through Forms rather than just physical observation, Ficino now moves to explain the hierarchy of these Forms and how they relate to the human mind, the angelic intellect, and God.</meta>

<page-num>98</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

<margin>A</margin> This is shown by its most orderly and stable composition. For this reason, above the specific agents acting within particular <term>species<gloss>In this context, a "species" is the essential form or blueprint that makes a thing what it is, such as the "human" species</gloss></term>, there must exist a universal agent that looks toward the species and directs it. This is also apparent in those things that are generated without manifest seeds, as we have demonstrated elsewhere. Many Platonists argue further from the objects of the mind in this manner: Since our intellect naturally takes in forms and understands <term>reasons<gloss>The Latin "rationes" refers to the underlying principles or logic behind things</gloss></term>—either separated from matter or by the process of separating them—it follows that these common principles of things, being separate from matter, are the intellect's natural objects. 

Because objects of this kind move, form, and perfect the intellect, they are established in a more excellent and truer grade of the universe. They are very far removed from fictions; otherwise, the mind—which is the judge of truth and the corrector of the senses—would be further from the truth than the senses themselves are. For this reason, those principles are deservedly considered more sublime, truer, and more effective in nature than the intellects that are formed by them. But should those principles themselves be called "intellectual"? Not properly. Indeed, rational souls are "intellectual" by participation <note>Meaning they share in the power of intellect rather than being Intellect itself</note>. Angels, however, are intellectual according to their <term>form<gloss>Their very nature is pure intellect</gloss></term>. Finally, those principles and <term>Ideas<gloss>The eternal, perfect archetypes in the mind of God</gloss></term> are "intellectual" according to their cause, but they are **intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibiles" — meaning they are the objects that can be understood by a mind</note> according to their form.

<margin>B</margin> For the "intellectual" relates to the "intelligible" almost as the desiring and mobile relates to the formative, or as that which can be formed relates to the desirable mover and former. But where are they? The Platonists place the less common Ideas within more common Ideas. And finally, they place all categories of Ideas in **Being** itself—the first, most common, and most perfect of all things. They call this the "Supreme Intelligible." It is "intelligible" by its form, but "intellectual" by its cause. Next to this, they place many minds that are intellectual by form, but intelligible only by participation.

<margin>C</margin> Below these, they place rational souls, which are intellectual by a certain participation, but are not "intelligible" at all <note>meaning a soul is a thinker, not a pure object of thought like a mathematical principle</note>. Furthermore, they judge that **Being** itself and the **Intelligible** are the same thing, because being is natural to and perfectly matches the intellect, which is why it is the object of the intellect. Moreover, they place the Intelligible itself under the first principle of all things. For the Intelligible is such that it can be comprehended in some way. But the First Principle cannot.

<margin>D</margin> They properly call the First Principle **Unity** itself and **Goodness**. And because Unity implies an eminence and a light set far apart from all things, while the "Intelligible" refers to a light already adjusted to the intellects in a certain proportion, they believe that Unity is something different and higher than the Intelligible. Again, because minds desire both to understand and to reach the Intelligible—not simply, but *well* and as a *good* thing—and they desire the Good simply for its own sake, they place the **Good** (that is, the Supreme God) before Being itself. 

Add to this that the Intelligible regards the intellect, while the Good regards the **will**. Thus, the Good is not only different from the Intelligible but more excellent. For indeed, that which ravishes the will is more excellent than that which is merely understood by the intellect. Therefore, they believe that "Being" is perceived by the intellect as much as it is able, but that the "Good" draws souls toward itself through the will, and once they are drawn, it pours itself into them. If the soul touches the Good at all, it is touched properly through the "head" or peak of the mind's unity, which God—who is the Prince of the Unity of the universe—inserted into us from the beginning.

<margin>E</margin> But to return to the point: in the Good itself, the Ideas exist only by way of cause, as <margin>NB</margin> "relatives" distinguished from one another only by certain relationships. In the **Intelligible** itself, however, they exist properly through form, and are distinguished from each other as absolute, distinct forms. In the minds that follow—whether separated from the body or joined to it—they exist by participation and are more and more distinct by degrees. In nature, however, there are certain "lowest seeds" of forms infused from the Ideas. <margin>F</margin> Finally, in matter, there are only shadows. 

Plato, in his letters, names the Good itself "God the Father," and the Intelligible itself "God the Son." Plotinus also calls it "God of God," "Light of Light," "Reason," and the "Word of God" <note>original: "verbumq; dei" — Ficino is explicitly linking the Platonic "Intelligible" to the Christian concept of the Logos or the Second Person of the Trinity</note>.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of reality, moving from the "Good" (God the Father) down through the "Intelligible" (the realm of Ideas/God the Son) to human souls and finally physical matter. He argues that the Good is higher than Being because it appeals to the will and draws the soul back to its creator.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Plotinus, Ideas, Intellect, The Good, Being, Trinity, Unity, Intelligible, Will, Forms</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion from Book 11 of the Platonic Theology. Having established that universal principles must exist as objects for the intellect, he now draws on the authority of Plato and later Platonists like Plotinus and Proclus to explain the hierarchy of these Forms (Ideas) and their presence in the Divine Mind.</meta>

<header>Eleventh Book of Theology</header>
<sig>n 2</sig>

## ## Eleventh Book of Theology

<margin>☞</margin> **A**gain, Plato in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue often attributed to Plato in the Renaissance, exploring the relationship between astronomy and wisdom</note> affirms through divine reasoning of this kind—or the Word, which he calls the "intelligible world"—that the sensible world was decorated. For while <term>Ideas<gloss>The eternal, perfect blueprints of all things in the divine mind</gloss></term> are in the first principle as a single form, in the second principle they exist as many forms. For they do not believe that absolute diversity of forms exists within the first form. Therefore Plato, having contemplated how colors exist in light around a lamp, or how lines exist in a circle around the center, says in his letters that the multiform Ideas, which are absolutely distinct, exist around the first principle of things rather than within the first itself. Similarly, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, he says that the Idea of the Good—that is, the Good itself, in whose form all Ideas are a single form—is the cause of the beautiful Ideas; namely, of those which in the subsequent stages are multiform and absolutely different from one another. Plotinus and Proclus confirm the existence of Ideas with these higher reasonings; and they place them in God (as they say) in one way in the first principle, and in another way in the second. Some others <margin>b</margin> proceed toward the same point in this way: In the lowest matter, a shadow of the Ideas is reflected. But above matter, the face of all the Ideas shines. Their fountain is God, the author of things, as Plato's *Timaeus* most clearly teaches, along with the tenth book of the *Republic* and the *Parmenides*. For if the Mind and Nature are full of forms and act through them—as is apparent in natural things and man-made <term>artifacts<gloss>Objects created by human skill or art</gloss></term>—then God, who is the former of both Nature and Mind, ought not to be formless. Therefore He acts through the forms which we call "Ideas."

<margin>☞</margin> Plotinus and Proclus call these not only "exemplary" forms <note>Patterns or models used for creation</note> but also "essential" forms. For they believe that an imperfect maker of the world would use consultation or deliberation while fabricating the world. Such an operation would be imperfect. For he who deliberates about completing a work has first conceived the work in himself as something imperfect in a way, and then proceeds toward its completion. This is alien to a perfect mind. Likewise, if He disposed the universe only by a changeable discourse of providence, nothing would be stable anywhere, nor would the motion of the world be perpetual and stable. Therefore, God makes and disposes the universe through His own being. This is especially true since an action of this kind is the first, most common, and easiest of all actions. Therefore, it is performed by a first cause that is most common and most blessed, wherever it occurs, and it is most fitting to Him in the first place. Moreover, every cause that acts by its very being produces an effect in the following grade that is similar to what the cause is in the first grade. Therefore, since the world is a collection of all the spheres, it follows that the world's maker is, in a way beyond what can be thought, a more excellent collection of all the spheres, and possesses the exemplary forms of all things, which are (to use their way of speaking) essential to Him.

They confirm this again in this way: If art imitates nature and produces works through the <term>reasons<gloss>The Latin "rationes" refers to the underlying logic, blueprints, or formative principles of things</gloss></term> of those works, then nature also possesses the reasons for its own works. Again, since nature lacks reason in itself, yet is moved and perfected by God, it receives its reasons from the Ideas of the divine mind itself. And by as much as the internal reasons of nature are more internal to nature itself than the reasons of art are to art, by at least that much the divine reasons must be more internal to God than the reasons of nature are to nature itself. They add that sensible forms are not entirely or truly such as they are named. Indeed, equality and similarity everywhere participate in inequality and dissimilarity. Truly <margin>12</margin> beautiful form cannot exist in a subject that is in itself deformed and formless. Likewise, the true Good cannot exist where there is defect and a leaning toward evil. Furthermore, they do not believe that a true line, surface, center, or the point of the poles exists in the celestial bodies. For those things whose definition is <term>indivisible<gloss>Latin: "impartibilis," meaning it cannot be broken into smaller parts</gloss></term> cannot exist in a divisible thing. But our soul possesses and generates true forms, through which it refutes other false forms, noticing how much they differ from the true ones. On which account, the Soul of the Universe much more possesses and generates the true reasons of forms. For where is there greater power and intelligence? Where is there a more express conception and birth of forms? Finally, the maker of the world generates more certain and perfect forms in Himself; and (to use Proclus’s words), while He generates Himself by noticing Himself, He generates all things in Himself at the same time. To this is added that since the members of the universe remain in a certain perpetual order...

<summary>Ficino argues that the Divine Mind contains the "Ideas" or perfect blueprints of all things, asserting that God creates through His very being rather than through labor or deliberation. He draws on Plato, Plotinus, and Proclus to show that these internal "reasons" are more real than the imperfect physical forms we see in the material world.</summary>

**Left Column**

...they conspire among themselves; they harmonize and rule not by chance, but by <term>Reason<gloss>Latin: *Ratio*. For Ficino, this is the divine logic or "Word" that structures the universe</gloss></term>. That Reason which orders all things cannot be ignorant of itself. Otherwise, the supreme Reason would be irrational if it possessed no reason of its own self. It is a rational reason which embraces itself by knowing itself, rather than one which deserts itself by remaining ignorant. It understands itself, therefore, as the reason that orders all things. From this it follows that it always understands by what reasons and modes individual things are disposed. Wherefore, in the supreme Reason of all things are the "reasons" <note>Here *rationes* refers to the eternal blueprints or "Ideas" of everything that exists</note> of all things. 

Did God, then, know all things because he was going to make them? Certainly not. Otherwise, he would refer his essential operation and his very turning toward himself to external things, and would depend on something else. <note>Ficino argues that God's knowledge is self-contained; he doesn't "look" at the world to know it, but sees the world within his own creative thoughts</note> Therefore, just as the sun by shining in itself illuminates all things, so God, by understanding and willing himself, both knows and effects all things. Who would not see that if by seeing himself he sees and makes all things, it follows that in his substance there are substantial forms which are the patterns and causes of all things? 

For always in the very order of nature, it is such that the external action proceeds from the internal. And the work itself is very similar to the action. Just as "to illuminate" comes from "to shine," and the thing "illuminated" is similar to the "illumination" and the "light" itself. 

Furthermore, plants and animals are generated from seeds. It is necessary, however, for "reasons" to be in the seed in some way, since the living thing is then rationally procreated from it. For these are not in the seed as bodily powers—for the seed is uniform and almost formless, while that which is born from it is multiform and beautiful. Also, if a seed is divided, several whole things are born from it, as if the whole things that are produced were hidden in the parts. 

Hence it is clear that the <term>seminal power<gloss>Latin: *vim seminariaz*. The invisible life-force or "program" within a physical seed</gloss></term> latent in the seed itself is, in some way, incorporeal. In this power is the principle of this motion and generation. It is necessary, however, that the multiple "reasons" of a complex living being be in the multiple seminal power which we call Nature. For the same thing, insofar as it is the same, could not generate such great primary diversity. Furthermore, it is necessary that this exists in <term>actuality<gloss>Latin: *actu*. A state of being fully realized, as opposed to "potentiality"</gloss></term>. For that which is such only in potentiality—being as it were imperfect—cannot be produced into something that is actually such, except by something that is already actually such and more perfect. There are,

**Right Column**

<margin>B</margin>
therefore, individual reasons for the parts of individual living things that differ in species, by which they are procreated in their own individual time, place, and order, and once stirred up, are recreated as often as possible. 

But are the seminal powers in the seeds of living things the supreme causes? Not at all. For the <term>species<gloss>The "form" or "type" of a thing (e.g., the concept of "Human" rather than a specific person)</gloss></term> itself is not made by any of those, but rather something particular under the species; and each of those takes its origin from another under the same species. Therefore, one must flee to universal Nature, in which the universal reasons of all their species exist. To the nature of the Earth, I say, the procreatress of earthly things. Especially since bodily seeds are often lacking for plants and animals that are born spontaneously <note>Ficino refers to the ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," where some creatures were thought to arise from mud or decaying matter without parents</note> here and there. Whereby it happens that for their production, incorporeal seeds are needed. 

<margin>C</margin>
And so that we may proceed in a convenient order, let us refer the individual earthly species to the universal nature of the Earth; and similarly in the other <term>elements<gloss>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</gloss></term>. Then, we refer the natures of the four elements most closely to the nature of the Moon, in which are the reasons for all elemental things. The nature of the Moon to the nature of the superior sphere, and so on in turn. Finally, all natures are referred to the Nature of the Universe itself, in which the reasons of all natural things and all natures necessarily exist—reasons, I say, that are both exemplary (the patterns) and effective (the movers), so that it may direct and lead all natures by certain rules to certain ends. 

Nature, however, cannot be the supreme reason and cause of things, both because it is irrational in itself—which is clear in our own nature, for it knows neither itself nor other things—and because it is a cause mixed with the effect, just as if a carpenter, poured into the wood, were to handle the wood. <note>This is a classic Platonic metaphor: Nature is like a craftsman who is stuck inside the material, whereas the Divine Mind is a Craftsman who stands apart and sees the whole plan</note> For such a cause was necessary, so that those things which are moved by another external and common thing might possess a certain familiar and intrinsic power from a separate cause. Indeed, since these things are not properly, distinctly, and appropriately led except through a power proper, distinct, and appropriate to them; and finally, the most excellent cause, which is to rule purely and absolutely over the work, must be separate from the work itself in terms of essence, being, and power. Just as in the air we see heat from the sun above...

<summary>Ficino argues that the complex order of living things proves the existence of "seminal reasons" (incorporeal blueprints) within nature, which in turn must be governed by a higher, separate, and self-knowing Divine Intellect. He describes a cosmic hierarchy where individual physical seeds are linked to the Universal Nature of the Earth, the Moon, and ultimately the Mind of God.</summary>

# Theology

<margin>B</margin>
...to be made: Not at all. It is necessary, however, for nature—even if it is <term>irrational<gloss>Latin: *irrationalis*. Here, it means nature acts by instinct or physical law without "thinking" about it</gloss></term> in itself—to possess the "reasons" of bodily things. By these, it can inwardly and rationally order, move, and form individual things in ways that are congruent with a fitting end. Since nature is irrational in itself, it must be led by that which is rational by its very nature, and it must be formed by those "reasons." Indeed, it is irrational to commit the order of the universe to a nature that is irrational by itself. Therefore, in the superior Cause, it is necessary that things exist so rationally that the Cause itself takes notice of itself and its own things, and possesses a certain "reason" for both itself and its own <term>reasons<gloss>Latin: *rationes*. These are the divine blueprints or "Ideas" that govern the structure of reality</gloss></term>.

<margin>C</margin>
It would certainly be absurd if, while we possess the reasons for ourselves, for our works, and for the universe, the Cause of the universe should have no reasons for itself or for its own works. For this reason, if the founder of the world knows all things, he certainly did not look toward other things in order to perceive them; for his knowledge undoubtedly precedes those other things, having been produced by that very knowledge itself. For who does not know that an external work follows an internal action?

<margin>D</margin>
Thus God, looking into himself, knows all things. From this it happens that the <term>Ideas<gloss>Latin: *species*. The eternal archetypes or forms of all created things</gloss></term> of all things are in Him, through which He may know and create all things. And (to speak briefly) just as in this material world all matters are finally reduced to one most inward matter, so—and much more so—in the <term>formal world<gloss>The realm of pure spirit and perfect Ideas, as opposed to the physical world of matter</gloss></term>, all forms are necessarily reduced to one most inward form. This can be argued from the following: every life generates its own offspring within itself before it does so externally; and the more excellent the life is, the more inwardly it generates its offspring within itself. 

Thus, the vegetative life—both in trees and in animals—generates a seed (which is like a tree or an animal) within its own body first, before it either acts outside or produces a tree in matter as an external product. Likewise, the sensitive life—which is more excellent than the vegetative—gives birth through the <term>imagination<gloss>Latin: *phantasia*. The faculty of the soul that stores and manipulates sensory images</gloss></term> to a likeness and an "intention" of things within itself, before it fashions them in external matter. But that first "offspring" of the imagination, because it is in the soul itself, is therefore closer to the soul than the offspring of the vegetative life, which is not in the soul but in the body. Likewise, the rational life—which is more 

# Eleventh

excellent than the sensitive—gives birth within itself to the "reason" both of things and of itself as a kind of offspring, before it brings them into the light either by speaking or by acting. That first offspring is closer to the soul than the offspring of the imagination. For by that offspring, the rational power is reflected back upon its own birth, and through that, back upon itself—which the imagination does not do. 

Likewise, the angelic life produces notions of itself and of things within itself before it brings them forth into the matter of the world. This offspring is more internal to the angel than reason is to us, because it is neither incited by external things nor is it changed. For this reason, the divine life—the most eminent and most fertile of all—generates this entire machine of the world within itself as its own offspring before it gives birth to it externally. It is necessary, moreover, for an offspring of this kind (which Orpheus calls **Pallas**, <note>original: "Palladez". In Greek mythology, Pallas Athena was born fully formed from the head of Jove (Zeus), which Ficino uses here as a metaphor for the Divine Mind's internal creation</note> born from the head of Jove) to be more inward, so to speak, to God than the notion of an angel is to the angelic mind.

<margin>E</margin>
In an angel, since being and understanding are different things, the "notion" which is generated by understanding is something other than the essence of the angel itself. In God, however, because being and understanding are the same, the notion which God begets by understanding himself—as the most exact image of himself—is the same as God himself.

<margin>F</margin>
Since pleasure accompanies generation, Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "timeus Platonis". A reference to Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> that God is wonderfully delighted by his own work. In that most inward offspring of God, which is the universal seed of the world, there are present the specific "seeds" of all the members which are begotten as his external offspring in this world. Those seeds agree with one another in essence, so that God is not a "multiple" substance; yet they differ in "reason," so that whatever is made in the world is not a single thing without any variety. Come then, proceed further. Since God has infinite power, and all things that follow Him are finite, the divine power is not limited solely to nourishing those things which finite things can provide; rather, He is able to perform innumerable and incorporeal works even without them. Does it not seem necessary to you that the forms of these works—which He can make without instruments or specific subjects—are at least so distinct in their relationship to Him that they possess their own "reason" there? For since from the one...

He uses a hierarchy of life—from plants to angels—to show that higher forms of life generate their creations more inwardly and perfectly than lower forms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 11 of the Platonic Theology. The previous page established that God knows and creates through internal "reasons" or blueprints. Here, Ficino argues that these Ideas are not separate from God but are the multiform expressions of His single wisdom, serving as the measure for all created things.</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>
<sig>E iij Theology</sig>

# Platonic

He is entirely one without any medium; certainly, multiple things do not arise from a specific subject: there is no reason why such forms could emanate from God in a manifold way, unless it is through the—if I may say so—manifold and in some way multiform wisdom of God. Furthermore, whatever the remaining causes <note>Secondary causes, such as nature or human agents</note> perform, all of it is operated as if they were instruments of the First Cause. They act in such a way that they are tempered by that Cause. They are tempered and led in such certain ways to generate certain forms in matter, through nothing other than the specific "reasons" <note>original: *rationes*; the divine blueprints or Ideas</note> of the forms which exist in God. Just as the instruments of art and nature are directed toward forms by the forms of the agent.

And just as forms—both those of art and those of nature—are more clearly present in the agent than in the work or the instruments, so the forms of the whole world are, in their own way, more expressive in God than <margin>A</margin> in the subsequent causes and in matter. For this reason, <term>Mercury<gloss>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage whom Ficino believed was a precursor to Plato</gloss></term> thinks that the world is the "all-formed" image of the "all-formed" God. And <term>Plato</term> says in the <term>Timaeus<gloss>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the universe</gloss></term> that when the divine power, by the grace of His own goodness, wished to make the world as beautiful as possible, He decreed to shape it according to that exemplar which is the most excellent of all. Therefore, He made the world in His own likeness, just as the parts of the world correspond to the Ideas of His own forms.

From these points, the "madness of certain dogs" <note>A harsh Renaissance metaphor for critics or those who misinterpreted Plato, likely referring to those who claimed Ideas existed independently of God's mind</note> is condemned, who barked that Plato placed the Ideas outside the divine intelligence. The single, starry heaven, full of light, shapes the "torrents of the night" <note>The darkness of material chaos</note> with the images of its own stars. These images are indeed not the stars themselves, even if they seem to be present in the moments; nor do they remain, but are continually renewed as the water flows, although the common people think they remain. Similarly, God—the one <margin>B</margin> overflowing fullness of Ideas—constantly shapes the fluctuating matter with the likenesses of the Ideas. These likenesses are certainly not true "species" <note>The formal essences of things</note> according to the Platonists (though some physicists think they are true), nor do they ever rest, as <term>Heraclitus<gloss>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the doctrine that "everything flows" (*panta rhei*)</gloss></term> says, because matter is constantly slipping away—even if those who are ignorant think they are at rest. And this is the way through which temporal things, as the Pythagorean <term>Parmenides<gloss>A philosopher known for his work on being and eternity; here Ficino links him to the Platonic tradition</gloss></term> wishes, become participants in the eternal Ideas. Indeed, just as eternity, which

# Book

is only one moment—remaining always the same—measures all time (which flows through innumerable moments) by its own stillness; and just as a stable center measures the points of a running circumference: so each Idea, remaining one and the same in eternity, measures all those temporal things which, within the same species, are participants in one and the same Idea. What I say of one Idea must be understood of all.

Beauty <margin>C</margin> itself is the measure of all beautiful things. Because by approaching the first Beauty or receding from it, subsequent things are judged to be more or less beautiful. That which falls away from all beauty, falls away from all essence <note>original: *essentia*; being or existence</note>. And that which possesses total beauty, possesses total essence. This is because the primary essence and the primary beauty are the same. Whatever a human judges in any species, he judges by referring it to the [ideal] species: for example, when he judges the sun or fire to be beautiful, he then refers two beautiful things to one absolute species of beauty. And when he pronounces the sun <margin>C</margin> to be more beautiful than fire, he refers them to the same Idea—not absolutely, but by comparison. In each relationship, he measures the beautiful sun and the beautiful fire through the same Idea. But in the first case, he measures both through the whole Idea. In the second, he measures the one through another degree of the Idea.

Nor should certain <margin>D</margin> "barbarians" <note>Likely referring to scholastic thinkers or skeptics who argued that the infinite cannot be a measure for the finite</note> be listened to, who think that beautiful things cannot be measured by their proximity to the pure "act" <note>God as *actus purus*, pure being without potentiality</note> of beauty, because that act is infinite, and therefore other things cannot move closer to it. They want such a measure to be devised by the distance away from the pure privation of beauty. But they are seen to err in this because if pure act is infinite in its affirmation, pure privation is similarly infinite in its negation. Moreover, the comparison of beautiful things is not made to the divine essence as it is entirely infinite, but to the *Idea* of beauty itself. Which is, in a certain way, finite insofar as it regards the creature; for it is a certain determination of divine perfection, made indeed by the divine mind and confirmed by His will. They approach [this Idea].

<summary>Ficino explains that the "Ideas" or blueprints of creation exist within God's multiform wisdom. He argues that all temporal things are measured by their participation in these eternal Ideas, using the analogy of a circle's center to define the movement of time and beauty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 11 of the Platonic Theology. Having established that divine "reasons" or Ideas exist in the mind of God, Ficino now argues that the human mind possesses internal "formulas" or reflections of these Ideas. These internal standards allow us to judge physical objects, which are always imperfect imitations of the true Ideas.</meta>

<header>Theology Eleven</header>
<sig>n 4</sig>

...approach it more closely: those which reflect its likenesses more purely. On the other hand, those which do the opposite recede. Rightly, therefore, the measure of beauty in beautiful things is taken from the source from which beauty itself is perceived. This beauty, however, is derived from the Idea, not from a pure privation <note>Privation refers to the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present, like darkness being the privation of light.</note> of beauty. Finally, what is more foolish than wanting to distinguish the possession of beauty by its privation, when both nature and reason compel the opposite to occur? For this reason, let us confess without doubt: that human minds refer beautiful things <margin>E</margin> to the very "reason" <note>original: *rationem*; here meaning the conceptual essence or blueprint</note> of beauty.

<margin>☞</margin> **Since**, indeed, that which measures is superior to that which is measured: the human mind—insofar as it measures all temporal things contained under those Ideas through their relations to the Ideas—is more excellent than those things. And thus it is closest to the Ideas, because it measures whatever follows from them. Inasmuch as it falls in the middle between the fountain of Ideas and the streams flowing from it.

But although it measures according to the Ideas, it does not, however, measure through the Ideas themselves as if through its own and immediate mediators. For universal Ideas are not the specific instrument of this or that human mind; nor do universal Ideas fall in any way as mediators between an individual mind and other individual things. Because, however, the soul cannot measure the individual images of universal Ideas otherwise than through the "formulas" <note>original: *formulas*; innate concepts or mental blueprints that bridge the gap between abstract Ideas and physical things</note> of the Ideas proper to the soul—and as it were inclining <margin>☾</margin> toward individuals—it is necessary for the formulas of Ideas to be inherent in the mind, through which it may compare the images <margin>☞</margin> to the Ideas. 

Those that agree with the formulas, it approves; those that do not agree, it rejects. But from where do these formulas come to the mind? Do they come from the images? Or from the soul's fiction? Or perhaps from the Ideas? Not from the images. For through these formulas, the soul measures the images. Hence the formulas precede the images and are more excellent insofar as they are closer to the Ideas. Moreover, if they were created from the images, they would not truly <margin>☞</margin> measure them, but would rather be measured by them. 

For a measure is an equalization. A cause equals the effect. An effect does not equal the cause. Nowhere in bodies do we find the perfect "reasons" of unity, goodness, and beauty. For it is necessary that these be not mixed with their opposites. In bodies, however, unity is mixed with a multitude of parts, goodness with vice, beauty with deformity; nowhere have we inspected the straight "reasons" of figures <note>Geometrical forms like perfect circles or lines</note> in the matter of bodies, yet we hold them ourselves. Otherwise <margin>2.</margin> we could neither speak of them, nor through them—as if by a standard <note>original: *examen*; literally the needle of a balance, used here as a standard of judgment</note>—rebuke the defect of bodily forms. Therefore, it does not seem that we received them from bodies, for they would be inferior to them. 

Nor should it be said that they exist nowhere, because the mind cannot understand through itself that which is nothing at all. For it even thinks of privations as possessions <note>For example, the mind understands 'blindness' through its concept of 'sight'.</note>, and false opinions do not arise in us because we think of that which is absolutely nothing, but because we either join things together or separate them contrary to the natural order. Nay, indeed, if the objects of the senses exist anywhere, the "reasons" are also objects of the mind—provided that the mind is more noble than the senses, and that which is absolutely nothing neither moves the sharp edge of the soul, nor draws it, nor defines it. 

Therefore they are not fashioned by the soul. Truly, fictions do not measure real things <margin>b</margin>. The fictions of the soul follow the things themselves more confusedly even than shadows follow bodies. Bodies are not discerned through shadows. Who, then, through a fictitious and external image of beauty, smell, taste, or heat, will inspect the essential definitions and hidden properties of these very things? Furthermore, a fiction of the soul is inferior to the soul itself. But those formulas are more excellent than the soul for this reason: that through them the soul even judges and corrects itself. 

Certainly, through the "reasons" of unity, goodness, and beauty, the soul often judges of itself what it is: either multiple in its parts or wavering <note>original: *diffidens*; lacking confidence or unstable</note> in its affections. Likewise, it judges how much it may fail by nature or be depraved by vice. Again, how much it was either born deformed or has turned out foul. Does it not, through the seal of beauty, pronounce itself to be more beautiful than bodies? And this part of itself than those, and this habit [more beautiful] than that...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind possesses innate "formulas" or mental standards of beauty, goodness, and unity that allow it to judge the material world. He concludes that these standards cannot come from the senses or from mental fiction, as they are more perfect and certain than the physical objects they measure.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, formulas of the mind, epistemology, beauty, measure of the soul, Platonic Theology, judgment of the self</keywords>

--- Page 252 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from Book 11 of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology. Ficino is explaining how the human soul possesses internal "seals" (sigilla) or "formulas" (formulae)—mental blueprints that act as absolute standards for judging beauty, truth, and even the nature of angels and eternity.</meta>

# Platonic

...to be more beautiful. Indeed, they even seem to be more sublime than the angels. This is because our mind designates the very angel through a "seal" <note>original: *sigillum*; here referring to an internal mental imprint or archetype used as a standard for judgment</note> when it affirms that the soul is more beautiful than one angel, or one angel than another, and the angels than God. Yet, the mind does not measure God; rather, it leaves Him as the measure itself, beyond all measure.
<margin>B</margin>
For if wisdom itself is not "wise" <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the source of a quality (like Wisdom) doesn't "have" the quality; it IS the quality, and thus is beyond the description of the adjective.</note> and motion itself is not moved, then the first measure is not itself measured. Therefore, insofar as those formulas measure the angels—like rules expressed by the Ideas existing above the angels—they are certainly more sublime than the angels. And the soul, in this very act by which it measures the angels, is more excellent, so to speak, than the very nature of the angel which it designates within itself through measurement. Although the angel also measures the soul through rules that are, in a sense, more "straight," and by that very act the angel exceeds the soul more than the soul exceeds the angel through its own mental act. But in what way are these seals—which we also call formulas—fashioned by the soul if they are higher than the soul and the angels? Rather, they are in the soul before every mental invention. For the soul compares all its own inventions to such seals. Indeed, it discerns by the seal of truth
<margin>C</margin>
which things are true inventions, which are truer, and which are false. Likewise, whatever the soul fabricates through its new and specific acts is entirely mobile <note>original: *mobile*; meaning changeable or shifting</note>. For what is made by motion is undoubtedly also mobile. But such seals are immobile. For they adhere immovably to the soul. Since whatever occurs to the soul at individual moments, or is made by the soul according to our judgment, we refer back to those seals as things firmly inherent within us.
Furthermore, if those seals also wavered, they would have to be referred to other things, and those to others again, and there would be no principle of judging within us. The seal through which we pass judgment on the state of this thing, or the state of that, or even on eternity, cannot be mobile. Indeed, in the seal is expressed the "reason" <note>original: *ratio*; the essential logic or blueprint of a thing</note> of that which is signified by it. But the reason of "state" <note>original: *status*; referring to a condition of rest or permanence</note> itself and of eternity is most foreign to the reason of motion. Moreover, we define the stable and the eternal in no other way than under the reasons of permanence and eternity.

# Book

Of this kind of reason, all are free from change. This is because permanence precedes motion. What is prior in nature is independent of what comes after. And yet we have these reasons—through which we define such things—within us. For the mind does not speak through things foreign to itself. If they were outside of us, we would still need other reasons, and we would draw out those reasons as if through middle-grounds, through which we would speak about permanence and eternity. In that case, those reasons would be immobile because they would be the reasons of immobile reasons. Therefore, wherever we walk, we shall arrive at the immobile reasons innate within us. <margin>B</margin> Plotinus says skillfully when he disputes concerning eternity: "Do we speak of these things concerning eternity as if testifying about external things? And as if dealing with things foreign to us? Not at all. For we do not understand unless we touch, nor do we touch things that are foreign." <note>Plotinus, *Enneads* III.7. Ficino uses this to show that we can only understand eternal truths because they are already part of our inner being.</note> Therefore, we are participants in eternity; thus, these seals are immobile. Indeed, even the seal of motions is immobile. For when we judge the motions of things, we compare them to the eternal Idea of motion through the seal of motions implanted in us. If this seal were also a motion, or mobile, it would have to be compared through another seal. For motion is not bound to eternity except through a competent medium. Which is neither
<margin>C</margin>
motion, nor mobile. Likewise, if it were mobile, we would not rightly judge motions through it. For motion is judged correctly only when it is referred to boundaries and spaces that remain permanent. For if these do not remain, no motion occurs, nor is the progression of motion discerned. Even time itself—which is a certain property and duration of motion—is not measured otherwise than if it be preserved through a stable memory and circumscribed by a stable moment of eternity. If the seal of motion is stable, much more stable are all the seals of the rest. From all these things, two things are concluded equally: namely, that such seals are both inserted into the soul by the Ideas, and they adhere to the soul immovably.

### Confirmation of the above through signs.

He concludes that these mental standards are more "sublime" than even the angels and are directly implanted in the soul by divine Ideas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book 11 of the Platonic Theology regarding the soul’s innate knowledge. On the previous page, he established that the soul uses internal "seals" or archetypes to judge the perfection of things like truth and even the nature of angels. He now moves into specific "signs" or proofs that these internal standards exist within everyone from birth.</meta>

# Theology
# Eleventh [Book]

Chapter 5.

**W**e have found many signs of this matter. The first is that simple country folk—who have never thought anything about <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things, existing in the divine mind rather than the physical world.</note>—as well as young children who have heard nothing of them, refer beautiful bodies to these Ideas in two ways as soon as they encounter them through their senses, provided they are using their reason. The first way is when they affirm that a thing is "beautiful." They only do this because the shape of that body matches a <term>seal</term> <note>original: *sigillum*; Ficino uses this to mean an internal "stamp" or blueprint of beauty imprinted on the soul.</note> of beauty that was born within them. The second way is when they affirm that "this thing is more beautiful than that," or "that thing is more beautiful than this," judging by how much closer one thing comes to that internal seal than the other. 

They did not acquire such a seal through being taught, nor through their own invention, for they had neither thought about it nor heard of it before. Nor do they "collect" the idea of beauty at that moment by looking at individual beautiful bodies. Indeed, it is by using this unerring internal seal that they are able to point out the deceptions and defects of individual physical objects. Nor is this seal derived from some "common nature" found within the objects themselves. For whatever lies within deceptive, physical things becomes deceptive itself and produces only a deceptive notion. 

Furthermore, when people think carefully about this seal, they find that it either is, or refers to, something that is "one above many," existing consistently within itself. For above that nature which is somehow "one *in* many" <note>This refers to the shared characteristics we see in groups of objects.</note>, there must be a nature that is "one *before* many," so that it may be equally common to all those many things. Because such a seal is in no way confined by the multitude of individual things, it is in no way gathered from that multitude. Nor is it conceived by the mere mechanical contrivances of thought. For through this seal, we discover that above the shifting and manifold beauty of any individual soul, there is a single Beauty that remains constant within itself. Therefore, the seal raises its power higher than our individual souls. Yet the inventions of the soul cannot produce anything more excellent than the soul itself. 

If, therefore, when we first use our reason, we refer many things to seals of this kind—which we neither learned beforehand, nor gathered or fabricated in the moment (especially since the standard of comparison must always exist before the things being compared)—it follows that we possess these seals before any use of reason. 

The second sign is that both types of these judgments happen suddenly, often without any prior intention of the will or long process of reasoning. This signifies that the soul does not have to acquire this rule of judgment from the outside or just recently; rather, it has been possessed internally for a long time, and the soul can use it at will whenever it turns its attention toward it. 

The third sign is what everyone experiences within themselves: whenever they wish to find the definition or the cause of any thing, they try nothing else but to penetrate into the inner depths of the mind, removing all the obstacles of the senses and the <term>phantasy</term> <note>In this context, "phantasy" refers to the faculty of the mind that stores and manipulates sensory images.</note>. What they are hunting for first shines forth most clearly to them only when they have entered the secret sanctuaries of the mind—as if the treasures of knowledge were hidden away inside. It was of this that Pythagoras sang:

<margin>D</margin>
-> But take heart, for the race of mortals is divine, <-
-> to whom holy nature, bringing forth all things, <-
-> shows each thing clearly. <-
<note>original Greek: αλλά συ θάρσει επει θείον γένος εστί βροτοίσιν οις ιερά πρόφειρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν έκαστα.</note>

That is: "But you, have confidence, since the race of men is divine. To them, sacred nature shows all things by bringing them into the light." 

<margin>E</margin>
Shall we then wonder that Homer, Didymus, and many others—who were blind either by nature or from infancy—wrote in such a way that they seem to have clearly seen everything? Shall we wonder that Zoroaster and other discoverers of wisdom produced the knowledge of all things through long solitude and the turning of the whole soul toward the mind alone? 

The fourth sign is taken from our "approval" or natural disposition. A bodily <term>complexion</term> <note>original: *complexio*; the balance of "humors" (blood, bile, phlegm) believed to determine a person's health and personality.</note> that abounds in blood requires certain tastes and uses of things; a person of bile requires others, and one of phlegm still others. When each temperament is offered what belongs to it, its nature adopts that thing just as fire catches a sulfurous fuel. Hence, the "sanguine" person praises sweet things; the "choleric" praises sharp and bitter things; the "melancholic," sour things; and the "phlegmatic," soft and tasteless things. What we say of the sanguine person must be applied similarly to the others. The sanguine person does not know why...

<summary>Ficino argues that human beings possess innate divine "seals" or archetypes that allow them to judge beauty and truth without being taught. He cites the internal reflections of the blind and the natural preferences of different bodily temperaments as evidence that knowledge is discovered within the soul rather than through the senses.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, Platonic beauty, archetypes, human divinity, Pythagoras, Homer, Zoroaster, four humors, internal judgment</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book 11 of the Platonic Theology, where he provides "signs" or proofs that the human soul possesses innate knowledge and divine archetypes. He has just finished discussing how even uneducated people judge beauty based on internal seals; he now shifts to the role of natural instinct and the innate presence of the "arts" within the soul.</meta>

# Platonic

<margin>A</margin>
...judges sweet things; he commends them not by deliberation, but by the natural instinct of his <term>complexion</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual.</note>. Indeed, through this natural instinct, he seeks five types of qualities: Red and green for sight; joyful things for hearing; sweet things for taste; and tempered things for touch and smell. If he desires and approves of these five qualities through his complexion, it is necessary that within the very framework of that complexion, there exist five "seeds" or "kindlings" <note>original: *fomites*; used here to mean the latent sparks or triggers of sensory inclination.</note> for these five types of approval. For just as one of those five qualities is distinct from the others in its nature, so too are they approved by the complexion according to different reasons. Therefore, in every human being, there are five natural seeds for five qualities corresponding to and approved by the five senses. And because the complexions of the humors differ in different people, the kings of physical desire are diverse among men. However, because there is but one human species among all, since there is one species of mind, there is a shared approval among them for those things that pertain to the mind.

<margin>B</margin>
Every mind praises a round figure as soon as it is considered in objects, yet the mind does not know why it praises it. Similarly, in buildings, it praises a certain squareness of the halls, or the equality of walls, the arrangement of stones, the alignment of angles, and the shapes and placement of windows. Furthermore, in the same way, it praises a certain fixed proportion of human limbs, or of numbers, and the harmony of voices. It commends moral gestures and habits as being decorous. It commends the light of wisdom and the intuition of truth. If every mind adopts all these things always and everywhere, and yet does not know for what cause it adopts them, nor can it fail to adopt them, it must adopt them by a necessary and natural instinct. But because the underlying reason for these desired things differs, they must be sought by the mind through various reasons of its own nature—acting as seeds—and they must be approved by the mind as if by "formulas" and rules, so that their opposites are rejected by these same rules. Indeed, when their opposites are first presented to us, they offend us by their very nature, even if we do not know the reason why. Therefore, the reasons for these similarities are innate to the mind.

# Book [Eleven]

The fifth sign is taken from the definition of art. Every art, because it orders a work by a certain reason toward a certain end, is a rational faculty. If a rational faculty is implanted in every irrational nature, it is much more implanted in every rational one. The elements seek their proper place with "artful" precision. With what great geometric art do they maintain a straight line in their ascent and descent? With what great architectural industry does the rain restrain itself into spherical droplets? With what great sagacity does the air come to the aid of the nature of things, so that no vacuum is left within it? Does not the complexion of plants and animals use a marvelous skill of the medical art in preserving its natural state or in recovering it? Even the souls of

<margin>C</margin>
brute animals exercise specific arts within their specific species. Silkworms weave woolen webs; spiders weave linen ones; swallows practice the art of pottery; swans, the art of music; bees, architecture; storks, civil life; lions, the art of war; and finally, foxes practice the art of hunting. Who, then, considering these things, would say that rational nature alone was idle, and was constituted as irrational from the beginning out of that idleness? On the contrary, if the seat of reason ought to receive a rational art much earlier and more fully than an irrational seat, it is necessary that all arts be born into the rational species of men, since individual arts are innate to the individual species of irrational creatures. For almost all these arts are gathered together in the whole genus of brutes. But while the different species of arts are dispersed through the different species of animals, they are all collected in the single rational species of humans, even if they are divided among individuals. These arts are found again in the unity of the angelic species, though they are divided there according to <term>forms</term> <note>In this context, Ficino refers to the Platonic idea that angels possess knowledge through direct spiritual archetypes or "Forms" rather than through learning.</note>. For an angel is multiform. Finally, all are found in the one unique God, and in one way—specifically, the Form of God. Therefore, arts are divided among themselves in the genus of brutes according to <term>habit</term> and <term>act</term> <note>original: *habitum atqz actū*; "Habit" refers to the internal possession of a skill, while "act" refers to its outward performance.</note>. Since no species of mute animal either exercises all arts in act, or possesses them all as habits; rather, any species of them uses and possesses a single art. Therefore, the arts must be divided 

<margin>D</margin>
in the species of men according to *act*, because different people study different things; however, they are not divided according to *habit*, because individuals possess them all. Indeed, in any angel, there is a union of all...

<summary>Ficino argues that human taste, aesthetic judgment, and technical skills are not learned from scratch but are triggered by innate "seeds" or "formulas" within the soul. He compares human capability to the "natural arts" seen in animals (like bees or spiders), concluding that humans must possess all arts potentially because we are a rational species.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, natural instinct, five senses, geometry, architecture, animal intelligence, rational faculty, Marsilio Ficino, Platonic Theology</keywords>

--- Page 255 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the "Signs" of the soul's immortality and its innate divinity. Having discussed how the soul judges beauty and sensory input through internal standards, he now moves to the sixth sign: the way human beings acquire knowledge and the "arts" (disciplines like medicine or agriculture) through internal recollection rather than external instruction.</meta>

# Theology, Book Eleven 102

<margin>¶</margin>...all [the arts] are held both in potential and in practice. For any one of them [souls] meditates on any of these arts, but they are divided by their execution, since different souls govern the world in different ways. Thus, in all who are working, as the theologian <term>Paul</term> <note>original: "theologus Paulus"; a reference to the Apostle Paul, specifically 1 Corinthians 12:6, "it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone."</note> says: He works all things in all. The sixth sign is derived from the acquisition of the arts. These are mastered not only by those who lack a teacher, but even by those who are said to have had masters, books, or men to guide them. For even <margin>E</margin> those <margin>a</margin> who learn by reading do not draw a spiritual and living <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning a deep, structured understanding of a subject.</note> from physical, lifeless letters; rather, being provoked by the letters, they give birth to it within themselves. And those who learn by hearing do not truly learn until they reflect upon what was heard, examining and approving it within themselves. <margin>f</margin> Moreover, no examination or approval of truths occurs unless the rule of truth has shone from within. Those who are said to "teach" do not at all pour the same knowledge they possess into another person. For if they did, by teaching others they would themselves become ignorant. The quality of knowledge would pass from one mind to another as if moving from one subject to another, which does not happen with such qualities. Nor do they generate a similar kind of knowledge in the student through their own. Such generation belongs to physical qualities, not to human knowledge, whose action is closed within <margin>☞</margin> and perfects the one who is working rather than <margin>B</margin> something external. In what way, then, does a master instruct a disciple? There are two kinds of arts. Some are those whose matter—the stuff they work with—possesses no internal principle for producing the work, such as clay or stone. <margin>a</margin> These are subject to the potter and the sculptor in such a way that they merely wait for the hand of the craftsman; by their own nature, they have no power to produce the work. But there are other arts whose matter, through a certain form, possesses a movement toward the work; such a work should be called natural rather than artificial. In this way, the earth is subject to the farmer, and the human body to the physician. Indeed, the fertility of the soil contributes greatly to the farmer in producing crops, as does the <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific internal balance of a person's physical and mental constitution.</note> of the human body to the physician in recovering health. This goes so far that often a field produces crops without cultivation, and the complexion of our body drives out diseases without the work of a healer. This signifies that the seeds of the crops exist in the field by nature, and the seeds of health exist in the complexion. Therefore, in the first kind of art, the craftsman is called the master and lord of the matter. But in the second kind, he is called the awakener of nature and its <term>minister</term> <note>original: "minister"; meaning a servant or assistant to a natural process rather than its primary cause.</note>. That the art of teaching belongs to this second <margin>b</margin> kind can be proven by this testimony: the mind, which appears to be the matter subject to the teacher, sometimes senses what is to be heard before it hears it, and after it has heard, it renders what was heard more fruitful and better. Often, even if it does not hear, it gives birth from itself. Indeed, the mind possesses the seeds of knowledge no less than a field possesses the seeds of crops. Thus, he who teaches is an assistant rather than a master. For this reason, <term>Socrates</term> in <term>Plato's</term> book on knowledge, the <term>Theaetetus</term>, says that he is the son of a midwife and very much like a midwife himself. For in educating men, he does not "induct" knowledge, but "educates" or leads it out, just as midwives bring out the offspring already conceived. Therefore, when a teacher strives to demonstrate something to a listener through many arguments, the listener is not shaped bit by bit—like clay by a potter or stone by a sculptor—but after many signs, he suddenly beholds the truth, even in the absence of the teacher, once he has been sufficiently provoked. Just as a field cultivated by a peasant, after his long labors, brings forth fruit in its own time while the farmer does nothing. Who taught the eyes to see? Who taught the ears to hear? A physician does not grant sight to the eyes; he either clears away the mist poured over them or directs them toward an object. In the same way, a teacher does not pour knowledge into the mind, but clears its vision or directs it. No one grants the sagacity of the hunt to dogs. No one grants the power of running to horses, nor warlike strength to elephants. Yet often men [awaken] these same virtues which are latent and sleeping in the mind...

<summary>Ficino argues that teaching is not the "pouring" of information into a blank mind, but a form of "midwifery" that helps the soul give birth to innate knowledge. He compares the teacher to a farmer or doctor who merely assists a natural, internal process already present in the "seeds" of the soul.</summary>
<keywords>innate ideas, Socrates, Plato, Theaetetus, midwifery, education, seeds of knowledge, Saint Paul, nature vs art</keywords>

--- Page 256 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that human knowledge is not merely learned from the outside but is "recalled" from within the soul. He focuses here on the method of Socrates and the divine origin of the "arts" or branches of knowledge, tracing a lineage of wisdom back to God.</meta>

# Platonic Book 101

<margin>A</margin> ...they [books] compel us to wake up from our habit of sleep. He [Plato] does the same thing regarding the concepts held in the mind, as Plato teaches in the seventh book of the *Republic*. ¶ For the mind possesses its own power—which is the <term>intuition of truth</term> <note>original: "veritatis intuitus"; the direct, immediate "seeing" of truth with the mind's eye.</note>—no less firmly and naturally than the senses and animals possess theirs. Socrates, acting as a leader of teaching, provokes these [internal truths] by inquiring. The soul, when questioned correctly, answers with the truth. It could not answer with truths unless it had already known them. Furthermore, because things themselves are interconnected, the underlying reasons for things are joined together in turn. From one [reason], a transition is easily made to many; thus it often happens that from a single "footprint" pointed out by a <margin>C</margin> teacher, a sagacious mind hunts down many things in a long sequence using its own "scent." Add to this that the mind’s gaze for seeing the truth is no weaker than the feet's power for walking. Socrates leads an infant with an outstretched hand so that the child may walk. He questions a youth so that the youth may learn. He does not provide the infant with the power of walking, but provokes it and leads it more safely to its destination. He does not bestow understanding upon the youth, but brings about an effect proportional to his own effort. However, if Socrates himself is ever said to have attained his own knowledge, he attained it as if it were something new, either through discovery or through instruction. If he discovered things by himself, he would never have used the discovered things unless he had already known the way to use them; but one who does not hold the nature of a thing cannot hold the method for using it. If he heard it from another, he did not conceive knowledge from what was heard until he knew whether the reasons of the teacher agreed with the truth. No one understands this unless they are looking at the truth itself. Therefore, before they find anything or hear anything, <margin>B</margin> they are in possession of the truth. And Archelaus, who taught Socrates, either found it by himself or received it from Anaxagoras. Whatever the case, he knew it beforehand. And even if Anaxagoras received it from Anaximenes, and he from Anaximander, and Anaximander from Thales—even then, Thales, or whichever Egyptian priest or <term>Persian magus</term> <note>original: "persicus magus"; Ficino refers to the "Ancient Theology" (*Prisca Theologia*), a lineage of wisdom including Zoroaster and Hermes Trismegistus.</note> you like, lacked a teacher. He who lacks the instruction of a man learns from nature as his teacher. Or rather, he knows it because God has been teaching him for a long time. For this reason, Socrates says in Plato's book on wisdom, the *Theages*: "No one ever learned anything from me, even though many became much wiser through my company, both by my exhortation and by the inspiration of a <term>good daemon</term> <note>original: "bono demone"; Socrates' *daimonion*, a divine inner voice or guiding spirit.</note>." You too will profit much in a short time if God favors you. ¶ Furthermore, Socrates recounts in the same place how some were greatly improved by his company; they would draw near to him and, even while he was silent, they would become sharper. Yet upon leaving, they would suddenly become duller again. It was as if that power of genius belonged to a certain divine influx from God, penetrating through the <term>Genius</term> <note>original: "genium"; a protective or guiding spirit assigned to a person at birth.</note> and mind of Socrates into the souls of his associates. And Orpheus <margin>C</margin> says the <term>Muses</term> <note>original: "musas"; the nine goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note> are the daughters of Jupiter and Memory. This is because knowledge lies hidden in deep memory, having been granted to us by God long ago. Indeed, he [Orpheus] handed down these things concerning <term>Memory</term> <note>original: "memoria"; here personified as the goddess Mnemosyne.</note>: <gloss>that is</gloss> [Memory] who holds together the customs which are familiar to the souls of mortals, [she who] reminds [them]; and you, [who are] the awakening of the mind of all things which each person always holds fixed within their thought according to all things <gloss>in all</gloss>, that is, containing the whole mind, familiar to human souls. You [Memory] call to mind all things whose notion everyone always hides within the borders of the soul; you rouse the mind in all people. We shall now conclude the present discussion, if we first remind ourselves that when we hear that the "arts" are in us by nature, we should not understand them as being impressed by a celestial or bodily nature, nor as flowing from the mere essence of the soul. For if indeed <margin>D</margin> they were impressed by such a [physical] nature, the beasts would have them. If they flowed from mere essence, God alone would possess them. Instead, let us understand that the forms of things and the rules of the arts were infused into our minds immediately upon being born from God—as Plato teaches in the *Timaeus*—no differently than they are poured into angelic minds. There is, however, a threefold difference between us and the beasts <margin>E</margin> regarding the arts. First: we receive them from God without a medium [intermediary]. They [beasts] receive them through the mediation of celestial nature. Second: each of us receives all of them. Each species of beast receives only one. Third: beasts are compelled at a certain time to the use of their arts by a certain necessary impulse of nature. We, however, by the free judgment of reason, [choose] the use of one art or of many...

we choose. Moreover, we coincide—as far as the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the Platonic Ideas or the essential blueprints of things.</note> of things and the rules of the arts are concerned—with the angels and with God. We agree with them in many other respects, but especially in this: that these things exist within us through an <term>absolute</term> <note>original: "absolutum"; meaning independent of matter or unconditioned.</note> and clear mode, much as they do in them. Therefore, the divine ideas have impressed their absolute and distinct images upon us as if upon mirrors; but they have impressed only certain more confused shadows of corporeal nature upon us. 

Just as we, in the light, paint a clear image of our body in a mirror, but cast a shadow against the wall: so it is here. Where the Idea shines through an absolute and clear mode, it does not merely shine brightly, but almost in its entirety. For all the properties of the Idea—which we recounted at the beginning of this discussion from the mind of the Platonists—consist primarily in this: that it is universal and unbound. That not merely shadows of the ideas, but clear images, are within us is most evident from this: that we distinguish their shadows from their images by right reason. For the "formulas" of those ideas planted within us represent the ideas themselves clearly to us and turn us toward them; whereas the shadows of the ideas found in physical bodies do not refer back to the ideas until they are purified and reformed by the formulas of our mind. 

Finally, if they shine in our minds through distinct images and in a complete and unbound way, they also shine in a manner that is entirely immortal. If the natural subject of an immortal thing is itself immortal—for if the subject is destroyed, whatever was attached to the subject is lost—then without a doubt the human mind is immortal, since it naturally and firmly receives the forms of immortal ideas in an immortal way.

### ¶ Second Reason. The Mind is the Subject of Eternal Truth. Chapter 6.

<margin>☞</margin>
**A**urelius Augustine, a man of divine genius—than whom no Latin author has more accurately expressed Platonic majesty in both wisdom and eloquence—constructed arguments of the following kind once the foundations mentioned above had been laid by Plato. A "true thing" is one thing; "truth" itself is another; just as a "chaste person" is one thing and "chastity" is another. Truth is more excellent than a true thing, since every true thing is true because of truth. When something called "true" perishes, truth itself does not perish. Just as if a chaste person dies, chastity itself does not die. 

If this world remains forever, it is true that it will always remain. If it does not remain, it is true that it will not always remain. What if the world perishes—if it is destined to perish—will it not then be true that the world has perished? For as long as it is not true that the world has perished, it has not perished. It is therefore a contradiction to say the world has perished but that it is not true that the world has perished. But nothing can be true where truth is not. Therefore, truth will exist even if the world perishes. 

What if truth itself should die? Would it not then be true that truth had died? But I do not think anything can be true if truth does not exist. Therefore, truth will in no way die. Thus says Augustine. 

But where exactly is truth? Not in physical bodies, for it would change when the bodies were changed. Since truth is eternal, there follows that Platonic <term>paradox</term> <note>original: "paradoxon"; a statement that seems contradictory but reveals a deeper truth.</note>: that bodies do not truly exist, because truth does not remain in them.

<margin>§</margin>
Therefore, what we call gold—if it is not "truly" gold—is false gold. If so, it is not even gold at all. The same applies to all other species of corporeal things. Furthermore, a condition of the body does not remain entirely the same for even two points of time, as we have shown elsewhere and show now in this way. 

Just as stable and simple eternity is the measure of stable and simple things, so flowing and varied time is the measure of moving and multiple things. The points of time never remain the same, but always creep up on one another, one succeeding another. The body of the world, being mobile, has time as its own specific measure. If this is so, the arrangement of the heavens fits with the flux of time’s change. Thus, the arrangement of the heavens cannot be entirely the same in two moments of time. For if it remained the same for two moments, in that very interval, time would have flowed from one moment to another, but the heavens would have rested in one. But flow does not at all agree with rest. And what does not agree, it does not measure. For how...

Does motion measure rest, or does a flowing thing [measure] through two points while one thing remains still? For this reason, in that small pause, time would not have measured the heavens. But in truth, time always measures the heavens, just as <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "eternitas"; in Platonic thought, eternity is a simultaneous whole, whereas time is a moving succession.</note> measures those things that are above the heavens. Therefore, just as those higher things remain in eternity continuously without any change, so the heavens run through time continuously without any rest. If the configuration of the heavens remains in no way the same, much less do the small bodies which are under the heavens and are swept away by the heaven's speed. For it is necessary that these things be continuously varied through influx and efflux, <term>condensation and rarefaction</term> <note>The physical process of matter becoming more dense or thinner.</note>, the intensifying or relaxing of qualities, and the harmony or dissonance of their <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific balance of humors or qualities in a body.</note> and other motions. 

Plutarch and Proclus demonstrated this abundantly. And before them, Heraclitus said: "Just as we cannot enter the same water of a torrent twice, or touch the same part of a running wheel twice in the same way, so we are unable to grasp a completely similar disposition and complexion of a body that persists through two points of time." If no state of a body persists as exactly the same and similar through two moments, then such a quality begins and ends in that same moment. That which begins in nature does not yet possess the <term>absolute act</term> <note>A state of fully realized existence or completion.</note> of existing or operating; that which ends no longer retains such an act. Therefore, at that point in which that quality is said "to be," it can also be said "not to be," since it has not yet completely departed from non-being, and is already slipping back into non-being. And because 

<margin>B</margin>
the speed of time surpasses the speed of the tongue, while you pronounce that it "is," it escapes you as you are speaking, before you have finished uttering this very word. And as Timaeus <note>A reference to the character in Plato’s "Timaeus," who discusses the creation of the world.</note> says, it deceives the speaker, nor is anything ever truly pronounced or perceived regarding this flux. It cannot be called "being" any more than "non-being," since it is and is not at the same time while it is being uttered. Truly, since things which are continuously changed "become" only insofar as they change, and things which are "becoming" (while they are becoming) truly *are* not, therefore whatever is changed and "becomes" in this way is not so much said "to be" as it is "to seem to be."

<margin>C</margin>
But what shall we say of time? It is always falsely said "to be," since its "being" (if I may speak thus) is "not being." Indeed, of any present moment it is truly said: "this is not time," but rather the <term>limit of time</term> <note>original: "temporis terminus"; the 'now' is seen as a boundary between past and future rather than a duration of time itself.</note>. For it is only regarding the past or the future that it is affirmed to be "time." Indeed, we think that a certain continuous succession is signified by time. But the past and the future *are* not. Therefore, we place the "being" of time, in a way, within "non-being." The moment, however, which is 

<margin>D</margin>
the limit of time, even as we pronounce that it "is," turns into "not being," and compels the speakers to have lied. Moreover, what we demonstrate regarding time must also be judged regarding temporal things: namely, that they have their "being" in "not being," so to speak. With this agrees that 

<margin>E</margin>

Only once will you say of the whole: "this is the man." Hence, regarding the elements: 

<margin>F</margin>
Timaeus, in making a distinction, thinks there are two parts of an element: matter and form. He thinks that a thing is not called "fire" or "water" because of its matter, but because of its form. Therefore, it is fire only according to a part. He says, therefore, that this is fire only according to its part, and that is water according to its part. And in truth, this is not "fire," but "fiery"; that is not "water," but "watery." Add to this that a thing is "truly such" which is "purely such," just as pure wine is that which is "mere wine." But the nature of any species, when it is in matter, first possesses a mixture with the potential for non-being, as we proved in the fifth book. Then it suffers many additions, and often contrary ones. Indeed, in the air there is often something fiery; there is always some position or state outside the nature of air. In this or that man there is often some complexion contrary to his nature. There is always some habit, or affection, shape, or position, beyond the necessity of the human species. The remaining species of natural things behave similarly.
