# Theology, Book Eleven

<margin>¶</margin> [Timaeus believes] they are entirely and purely such things. Timaeus thinks that above the stained and defective forms of **matter**, there exist other forms that are pure, whole, and separate. He places the greatest confidence in the strength of the reasoning argued here: **Forms** <note>original: "formae"; the essential shapes or qualities that make a thing what it is.</note> which exist in another thing—namely, in matter—also come from another source. Yet they do not come from the formless nature of matter; rather, form must come from form, and ultimately from a form that subsists by itself. Thus, a single formable matter is eventually reduced to a single **Maker** <note>original: "formatore"; the divine craftsman or demiurge.</note>. For even if he had introduced many makers, many things (insofar as they are diverse) would never have a mutual order among themselves or contribute to a single work, unless they were led by the one Maker of all. Therefore, it is necessary that forms are given to matter by a certain **Mind** that is full of forms. To you, these forms are the very essence of that Mind. And therefore, they are the true **Species** <note>original: "species"; here meaning the ideal, perfect versions of things.</note>. But because that Mind is the primary "Being," while matter is very close to "nothing," and the Mind is **pure act** while matter is **pure potential** <note>In philosophy, "act" is the finished, perfect state of a thing, while "potential" is the raw possibility of becoming something else.</note>, it follows that matter is almost infinitely inferior to the Mind.

<margin>b</margin> Furthermore, whatever is received by something passes into the nature of the receiver. For this reason, forms immersed in matter are so much inferior to the species in the Mind that they are **shadows** of them rather than images; they retain the name of those forms (and a false name at that) rather than their true nature. Just as **artifacts** are likenesses of natural things, so natural things are likenesses of divine things. However, artifacts come closer to the truth of natural things (because they share the same kind of matter) than natural things come to the truth of the divine. If, therefore, a **painted horse** falls so far short of a natural horse that it is not a "true" horse, how much more does a **natural horse** fall short of the **Divine Horse**—that is, from the **Idea** <note>The perfect, eternal blueprint of a horse in the mind of God.</note> and the true definition of a horse? It must be said to represent a shadow of the horse itself rather than its true form. And if the true definition and nature of a man or a horse is the Idea itself, and matter (being so far distant) does not preserve this, we reach the conclusion of **Socrates** in the *Phaedo* and in the *Republic*: namely, that true men and true horses are not found in matter. Matter deceives our little souls with these shadows of Ideas, so that like people **dreaming**, we see the likenesses of real things and think we are looking at the things themselves. This harmonizes with the paradox of our **Proclus** <note>A late ancient Greek philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino.</note>.

<margin>¶</margin> Things composed of the elements possess neither eternity nor stability. **Pure minds** possess both, and they grasp all their contents simultaneously. In the middle of these are things that have their own kind of eternity within a certain motion. **Souls**, being closest to Minds, admit motion only into their operations. But the souls that follow are, in a way, also subject to motion in their power. Finally, the entire **machine of the corporeal world** <note>original: "mūdi machina"; a common metaphor for the universe as a complex, functioning system.</note>—being inferior to the essence, operation, and power of souls—has acquired an essence so changeable that it is entirely temporal. And just as a thing that is totally eternal remains always whole in the "One," so this world-machine, which is entirely temporal, flows out from the divine world at every moment of infinite time. It constantly flows away and flows back, not unlike how some think **light** is poured out from the sun: in every moment, it is poured out as a whole, and as it spreads, it suddenly vanishes and is replaced.

<margin>¶ K</margin> Surely, that which is measured by **indivisible eternity** must itself be indivisible. Therefore, that which has a divisible essence—constituted both of parts and of many natures, such as the machine of the world—is not compatible with indivisible eternity. Rather, it is compatible with **divisible time**, by which it is measured and with which it perpetually slides along. Furthermore, it is assigned a power and action that is divisible by motion. For this reason, the mass of the world begins to be and ceases to be in every single moment; it is reborn again just as in motion and time (to which it is entirely subject), where moments flow through individually and are replaced. This is further confirmed as follows: The perpetual motion of the heavens requires **infinite power**. Since the limited body of the world can neither have this power from itself nor receive it all at once from another, it must receive it from the **Maker**...

## Platonic

...by its own mover, and little by little, to drink in every single moment. I say "to drink in" that which is momentary and suddenly vanishing. Indeed, a temporal essence is received entirely in a temporal way; and a limited nature is not capable of eternity, which possesses an infinite and total power all at once. Certainly, the nature of the world cannot receive infinity all at once. And eternal infinity, since it is indivisible and stands as a whole all at once, can be received by nothing "little by little."

<margin>A</margin> Here **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers and a key figure in Neoplatonism; his work deeply influenced Renaissance thought.</note> distinguishes in this way: He says that immobile essences are indeed from God in a certain way "once and for all," but they are preserved by themselves through their own power. For since they are there without motion and all at once, they are able to persist as stable things through themselves; and by their own power, they can proceed from certain of their capacities into their acts. For this reason, he calls such essences "self-subsisting" and affirms that they, in a way, produce themselves.

But he calls the **corporeal machine** <note>original: "machinā vero corporeā"; refers to the physical universe as a complex, moving system.</note>—which follows the motion of the soul and time, and flows along with that motion and time—nothing stable. It has no power to preserve itself. Therefore, he names it not "substantial" or "true," but entirely "shadowy" and "false," in the manner of the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that viewed the material world as inherently evil or illusory.</note>; it is perpetually slipping away and stands in total need of being renewed by a perpetual influence from above, just like the shadow of a body in very fast-flowing water.

<margin>B</margin> Hence we say, following that famous passage in the **Timaeus** <note>One of Plato's most influential dialogues, dealing with the creation of the universe.</note>, that the "intelligible world" always *is* and never *becomes*, but the "sensible world" is certainly always *becoming* and never *is*. Here Proclus adds that the former world always exists as the same in number, while this physical world is not properly "one," nor is it ever the same in number; rather, it is "one" and the same in number only by being continually recreated. Insofar as it is a body, it is always *becoming* and beginning; but insofar as it depends on the **Divine Mind**, it has always *been made* and immediately attains its end. 

But let this paradox now have an end. Since, therefore, the entire sensible machine is a kind of vanity—and a cause of vanity for the senses every day—therefore **Solomon** exclaimed: 
> **Vanity of vanities; and all is vanity.** <note>original: "Vanitas vanitatum: & oia vanitas"; a famous quote from the biblical Book of Ecclesiastes (1:2).</note>

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, truth is not in sensible things. But is it perhaps in

## Book

the soul? Perhaps it is in the soul. Yet it is not as **Protagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for saying "Man is the measure of all things," often associated with relativism.</note> and **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the senses are the only reliable source of knowledge.</note> believed it to be in that part of the soul which is "sense"—the part which looks outside itself, is compelled to feel through a certain passion, and is deluded by frequent sensible trifles. 

For this reason, **Xenophanes**, **Parmenides**, **Zeno**, **Melissus** <note>OCR reads "Belissus," but the text refers to the Eleatic philosopher Melissus of Samos.</note>, and **Stilpo** said that nothing of the truth is grasped by the senses. **Anaxagoras** felt the same, and it pleased **Empedocles** and **Plato**. For even if someone were to say that there are some sensible things that always remain in the same way—bringing up the question of the sun and the stars, where one cannot easily be convinced that they deceive us with rapid change—there is certainly no one who is not forced to admit this: there is nothing "sensible" that does not have a "false double" so similar that they cannot be distinguished. 

For to omit other things (as **Augustine** says), regarding all things that 

<margin>D</margin> we feel through the body: even when those things are not present to the senses, we nevertheless experience **images** <note>original: "imagines"; mental phantoms or representations.</note> of them as if they were entirely present, whether in sleep or in a "fury" <note>original: "furore"; can refer to madness, delirium, or prophetic trance.</note>. When we experience this, we are completely unable to discern whether we are feeling the things themselves with our senses or whether they are merely images of sensible things. If, therefore, there are false images of sensible things that cannot be distinguished by the senses themselves—and nothing can be "perceived" unless it is distinguished from the false—then no judgment of truth has been established in the senses.

<margin>E</margin> And it may perhaps happen that the sense perceives some things truly, as **Aristotle** pleased to think. Yet the sense never discerns whether it perceives truly or the opposite. Since the truth of natural things consists in their agreement with the **Reasons** <note>original: "rōnibus" (rationibus); the divine blueprints or logic behind creation.</note> of the Divine Mind—just as the truth of artifacts consists in their agreement with the ideas in the craftsman's mind—the sense does not recognize this kind of agreement, and therefore it has no "test" for truth. 

Furthermore, since the truth of a knowing power arises when that power agrees with the things to be known, and is perfected when the sense is made equal to the "ideas" of things: the sense, which notices neither that agreement nor that equality, lacks a judgment of truth. Add to this that the sense does not grasp the **innermost parts** <note>original: "intima"; the essential, hidden core of a thing.</note> or the pure substance of a thing, nor in what order any thing is arranged in nature; all of which belongs to the truth of the thing itself.

# Book Eleven of Theology

<meta>Catchword: clarii fici (likely a continuation of the author’s name, Marsilio Ficino)</meta>

<margin>Truth</margin> ...truth. But it is lured by a sudden impulse toward pursuing or fleeing a quality; in this, it indulges the comfort of its own body rather than the truth of things that must be understood. Therefore, the judgment of truth is not established in the senses. It is, however, established in reason.

<margin>Privations</margin> For the privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness being the privation of sight.</note> of things are known through their positive states <note>original: "habitus"; in classical logic, this refers to a stable quality or possession of a faculty.</note>. Darkness is known through light. Silence is known through voices. The privation of truth is the false. Our reason proves the falsity of sensible things and the senses themselves—which it could not do except by an examination of the presence of truth. Again, reason describes truth itself in this way: 

<margin>Definition</margin> **Truth is the pure integrity and the integral purity of each nature.** <note>This Neoplatonic definition suggests that truth is the "wholeness" of a thing as it exists in its perfect, essential form.</note> Truth is not defined except under the natural and proper account of truth. Truth is within that very account of truth. Therefore, truth is in the soul that defines truth, just as it is in the soul that refutes the false. Moreover, it is in the soul that describes any thing whatsoever. Indeed, the definition of a species <note>original: "speciei"; referring to the "Form" or essential blueprint of a thing.</note> encompasses the very essence of the thing: at once pleasing and separated from external, accidental things. If, therefore, the truth of things is in the species themselves, and the species is understood by a definition, and the definition by the mind: who does not see that truth is in the mind of man? 

If truth is immortal, it clearly declares that the mind—to which it inheres inseparably—is incorruptible. For a quality that inheres inseparably in some subject is destroyed if the subject is removed. That truth inheres in us inseparably can be proven by this testimony: that either continually, or at least suddenly at our own judgment and by the collection of the mind into itself alone, we both condemn many false things and define certain common natures, whether of natural things, or moral things, or of the arts. Indeed, the same conclusion is drawn from what we showed above: that the clear and stable accounts <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the rational structures or "Logoi" of the Ideas.</note> of the Ideas inhere in the mind. In these accounts, the truths of all things are understood.

<margin>Rationality</margin> Beyond the rest, the power of reasoning itself declares this most highly; it is no less natural to man than flight is to birds or barking to dogs. Through this, "**Socrates is a man**"; through this, man is distinguished from other species of animals. We call "rational power" in this context the very virtue of reasoning which discerns consequences—that is, it notices step-by-step what follows from what, and runs in order from preceding things to those that follow. This is a certain "natural dialectic" <note>An innate, logical ability to argue and reason that all humans possess regardless of education.</note>—that is, the art of discourse implanted in men from their origin. Through this, children and even the most unlearned <margin>Natural logic</margin> defend their positions by whatever conjectures and assertions they can. And all human speech, the entire action of life, and every consultation is nothing other than a kind of argumentation. For no one is so insane that they do not infer some things from others while arguing. And so, the mind argues from images to images, just as a healthy mind runs from things to the things themselves. Therefore, this rational power is never separated from man.

<margin>Necessity</margin> Now, if truth is not separated from this power, truth will never be separated from the soul. In this virtue of discourse, two necessities exist: one according to its subject, and the other according to its use. The first necessity is that the faculty of discourse itself is so implanted in the whole human species that it cannot be separated. The second necessity, which is seen in its use, is twofold: absolute and relative. 

Absolute necessity appears in three things: in the principles of disciplines, in definitions, and in properties. Principles <margin>Principles</margin> are of this sort: **Whatever exists, exists either through itself or through another.** **Contraries by their nature repel each other.** **Every whole is greater than its part.** **To each must be given his due.** These and many such things are necessarily so, just as they are necessarily known. For they can never be otherwise, nor can they be ignored by anyone, however unlearned. 

There is also necessity in definitions, such as when a circle is defined: <margin>Definitions</margin> **A circle is a figure in which all lines drawn in a straight path from the center to the circumference are equal.** Although such a conjunction of words in the mouth or such a drawing in the dust may be contingent <note>Meaning the physical drawing or spoken words are temporary and can change.</note>, that truth is nonetheless necessary and eternal, because that is the very nature of the circle. A similar necessity exists in properties: that is, that the circle is the most spacious of all figures. And <margin>Properties</margin>—to omit other things—is it not so in numbers from a... 

clarii fici.

# Platonic Book <note>The full title of this work is *Platonic Theology*, written by Marsilio Ficino in the 15th century to reconcile Christian doctrine with Platonic philosophy.</note>

...from necessary truth into necessary truth without end? Two times two is four. Three times three is nine. Two times four is eight: and those that follow. We do the same in the compositions and the comparisons of figures <note>referring to geometric shapes and mathematical proofs</note>. But if the definitions and properties in the principles flow forth—those which flow out from the principles—then the principles are necessarily always present in the power of reason, so that reason may continually calculate concerning any matter. Thus, these three necessary truths—all of which are called **absolute**—are contained within the natural logic <term>dialectics: the art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical argumentation</term> of human beings.

There remains **relative necessity**, which is divided into three parts. One <margin>A</margin> is in **position**, another in **condition**, and another in **demonstration**. 

The first is of this sort: No thing can not-be while it is. An animal, while it lives, necessarily lives: and similar things which are affirmed regarding the present time. From these, necessity is held for the past and the future: what has been done cannot be undone; what is to be, cannot not-be. 

The second is of this sort: If a body lives, it necessarily exists. If an animal runs, it is moved. 

The third is of this kind: Every part is smaller than the whole. The head of a human body is a part. Therefore, that head is smaller than the human body. This conclusion is entirely necessary because the two preceding propositions, when joined together, are necessary. For it is necessary that the head be smaller than the body, both because a part is smaller than the whole, and because the head itself is a part of the body. 

Wherefore, in these three as well—position, condition, and demonstration—there are three necessary truths. And if these three are in human reason when it disputes, then these three necessary truths are also within reason itself. And <margin>B</margin> because reason disputes always—even while we are silent, and even while we sleep (for the whole life of a human is a certain perpetual reasoning)—therefore those truths are always in reason. Reason is always (so to speak) both **truth-telling** <note>original: "veridica"</note> and **truth-making** <note>original: "verifica"</note>. It is truth-telling in the first three truths, which are necessary in themselves even if reason has done nothing. It is truth-making in the three others, which reason imposes upon them by a certain necessity through positions, conditions, and demonstrations, or through any other modes of arguing. 

For it happens that this animal lives; but it does not just happen while it lives, it is *necessary*. It happens that this man is moved; but it is not a mere happening if he runs; rather, it follows necessarily. It happens that this head is smaller than this body; but once those two prior propositions have been set by the mind, it is *necessary*—even if in the specific form of a head or a body that fact were never a matter of chance. 

If reason captures necessary truth in some things, and in others it creates and captures it always, who will deny that perpetual truth is in reason? Indeed, who will deny that reason itself is necessary? For it accepts those things which are necessary in themselves just as they are, without changing them. But those things which are not such in themselves, reason makes necessary by its own power. And reason is much more "necessary" when all things that are made necessary by positions, conditions, and arguments are made so by reason itself. 

Therefore, reason itself is almost **absolutely necessary**, just like those principles of the sciences, and those perpetual definitions and properties. Wherefore human reason either was always necessary and will be as those things are, or at the very least it will always necessarily be. For what prevents reason from being perpetual? Its perennial action is nothing other than to provide for any temporal or contingent things from an absolute eternity—firmly remaining within—by a relative eternity, and <margin>C</margin> to arrange a single series, both necessary and perpetual, out of things both necessary and contingent. If it will exist always, it will also live always. For reason does not exist except as a living thing, and within a living thing.

<margin>Objection of the Sceptics and the response:</margin>
### Chapter Seven.

<margin>D</margin> Nor should the **Sceptics** <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> be listened to if they deny that truth exists in our souls because they seem to doubt every single thing. For the soul does not doubt all things, as has appeared in all the necessary truths we have related, and similar ones. I know that this seems white to me. I know that this smells pleasant to me. I know that I touch this sweetly with my taste. Who does not know that the **Highest Good** exists, than which nothing is more excellent? And that it exists either in man or outside of man? And if it is in man, it is either in the soul, or in the body, or in both? Who does not know for certain that God either exists, or does not exist?

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind is the seat of eternal truth by demonstrating how reason creates and perceives logical and mathematical necessity, even during sleep. He concludes that because the mind handles eternal truths, it must itself be eternal, and refutes Scepticism by pointing out the certainty of basic perceptions and logical axioms.</summary>

# Eleventh Book of Theology

<margin>D</margin>
**A** [The mind establishes] that it must be one, or many; and if many, then either a finite or infinite number. It establishes that God must be either corporeal or incorporeal; and if he is not corporeal, he is necessarily incorporeal. Likewise, the mind declares that many rules of astrology <note>In the 15th century, astrology and astronomy were often treated as a single science of celestial influence and calculation.</note> and medicine have certain effects, not to mention arithmetic and geometry, than which nothing is more certain. And what is greater: when the mind doubts any particular thing, it is at that very moment certain of many things. For it does not doubt that it is then doubting. And if it holds this as certain—that it is doubting—it holds this certainty from a specific truth. Indeed, he who understands that he doubts, understands something true. And concerning this thing which he understands, he is certain; therefore, he is certain of the truth. Thus, everyone who doubts whether truth exists has the truth within himself, from which he might not doubt. Nor is any truth "true" except by Truth itself. Therefore, it is not necessary for him to doubt truth who was able to doubt everything else, as **Augustine** says. <note>original: "ut Augustinus inquit." This refers to Augustine's *De Vera Religione*, a key source for Ficino's argument that the ability to doubt proves the existence of truth.</note> Especially since he does not only understand that he doubts, but notices that he understands this; and
<margin>g</margin>
having noticed it, he acknowledges it, and so on into infinity. He discerns, moreover, the doubting soul from the undoubting one. Nor is it hidden from him how much better it would be not to doubt, and how ardently he desires the truth. He compares certainty with doubt. By which it happens that he is certain of both. He is, furthermore, certain that he investigates, feels, lives, and so forth. For he has no doubt that he who lives, feels, and investigates, exists. He is also certain that he is not the **supreme truth**, <term>supreme truth: God, or the ultimate source of reality which cannot err or doubt</term> since that truth would not doubt itself. He knows that such truth is not entangled in doubt or error. He knows that in judging, he must either be deceived or not be deceived. He knows that whether he is deceived or not, as long as he judges, he is undoubtedly alive. Finally, he is not ignorant of the fact that there is something else in nature outside his own soul which brings doubt upon him. Certain truths of this kind are perceived in doubt itself.
<margin>E</margin>
By this we are warned not to fear **Aristo, Pyrrho, and Herillus**; <note>Aristo of Chios, Pyrrho of Elis, and Herillus of Carthage were ancient philosophers associated with Skepticism, the view that human beings cannot reach certain knowledge.</note> for while they are of the opinion that nothing true is known by us, they themselves undoubtedly know that this opinion of theirs must be either true or false. They know that if it is true, something true is indeed understood by man. They know that if it is false, the opinion opposite to theirs is true—namely, that something true is known by man.

<margin>f</margin>
-> The objection of the Peripatetics, and the response that truth dwells familiarly in the soul. <-

### Chapter Eight.

<margin>S</margin>
**B**ut should we fear the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who argued that knowledge is not innate but must be acquired through the senses</term> who deny that truth dwells familiarly in the soul, because so few seem to be skilled in it, and whoever does know it was unlearned for so long a time since infancy? Certainly, they are not to be feared, as **Augustine** testifies where he explains the mind of **Plato**: Either there is something in the soul which is not in its present thought, or the art of music is not in the musical soul when it thinks only of geometry. But the latter is false. Therefore, the former is true. For the soul does not perceive that it possesses anything except what has come into its thought. It is possible, therefore, for something to be in the soul which the soul itself does not perceive to be in it. How long it remains there, however, makes no difference. For if it has been occupied with other things for a long time, so that it cannot easily reflect its attention back to what was previously thought, it is called "forgetfulness" or "ignorance." But when we perceive truths concerning the liberal arts—either by reasoning with ourselves or by being well-questioned by another—we find the things we discover nowhere else but in our own soul. For because of this very fact, the soul must withdraw into itself, leaving behind external things, in order to find these truths. Nor is "finding" the same as "making" or "begetting." Otherwise, the soul would be begetting eternal things through a temporal discovery. For it often finds eternal things. For what is as eternal as the **ratio of a circle**? <note>original: "circuli ratio." The mathematical principles defining a circle, which Platonists argued exist eternally regardless of whether a physical circle is drawn.</note> Or if anything else of this kind in the arts is understood never to have not-been, nor ever to cease to be. From this it is manifest that the human soul is **immortal**, and that all true reasons <note>or "proportions"</note> are in its secret depths; although, through either ignorance or forgetfulness, it may seem either not to have them or to have lost them. Suppose someone has forgotten something, and you wish to recall it to their memory. They say, "Is it this?" or "Is it that?" offering various similar things. You, however, do not see the thing you desire to remember, and yet you see that it is *not* what is being suggested. Does it not seem to you, when this happens, that your [memory] is still intact?

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul contains innate truths, proving this by showing that even the act of doubting requires a certain knowledge of truth. He counters Aristotelian skepticism by citing Plato and Augustine, asserting that the soul's ability to "find" eternal mathematical laws proves its own immortality.</summary>

<keywords>immortality of the soul, innate ideas, skepticism, Augustine, Plato, Peripatetics, mathematical truth, certainty of doubt, reminiscence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument for the soul's innate knowledge, transitioning from the psychology of doubt to the Platonic concept of recollection (anamnesis). It concludes the eleventh book and begins the twelfth book of Ficino's "Platonic Theology," dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

...forgetfulness? By no means. For that very discernment by which the mind does not admit what you might falsely suggest is itself a part of **recollection**. Such people, therefore, do not yet see the truth; however, they cannot be misled or deceived, and they know well enough what they are seeking. But if someone were to tell you that you laughed a few days after you were born, you would not dare to say it is false. And if the person telling you is trustworthy, you are not going to **remember** it, but rather **believe** it. For that entire time is hidden from you by a most powerful forgetfulness. 

This state, therefore, differs greatly from that other kind of forgetfulness; this is a middle state. For there is another kind that is closer and nearer to recollection and the revisiting of truth. It is similar to when we see something and recognize for certain that we have seen it before, and we affirm that we know it. But as to where, or when, or how, or in whose presence it came to our notice, we struggle to repeat and recover. As might happen with a person: we ask ourselves where we have known him. When someone reminds us of the circumstances, suddenly the whole matter pours into the memory like a light, and no further labor is required to remember. 

<margin>g</margin>
Such are those who are well-educated in the **liberal arts** <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy) were considered the essential path to higher knowledge in the Renaissance.</note>. Indeed, through learning, they undoubtedly unearth those arts which were buried within them by forgetfulness and, in a sense, they dig them out. Yet they are not satisfied, nor do they restrain themselves, until they can gaze most broadly and clearly upon the whole face of Truth, whose splendor already glimmers subtly within those arts. 

But in these arts, certain false colors and forms pour themselves into the thoughts like a mirror; they often trick and deceive those who are inquiring, leading them to think that what they already know—or what they are seeking—is the whole of it. In themselves, these images must be avoided with great caution, for they are found to be deceptive; they vary as the "mirror" of thought varies, while that "face" of truth remains one and immutable. For example, let the thought paint for itself a square of one size or another and hold it as if before the eyes; nevertheless, the inner mind, which wishes to see the truth, turns instead toward that **Idea** <note>original: "ideā" – Referring to the Platonic Idea or Form, the perfect, unchanging blueprint of a thing that exists beyond the physical world.</note> according to which it judges all those things to be squares. 

What if someone should say to us that the mind judges according to the same idea it is accustomed to seeing with the eyes? Why then does the mind say—if it is truly educated—that...

---

...no true plane can be touched by a point? <note>This is a classic geometric paradox: a mathematical point has no dimension, and a true plane is perfectly flat; in physical reality, a "point" (like a pen mark) always has some width.</note> What such thing has the mind ever seen with the eyes? Or what can it see, when nothing of this sort can be fashioned even by the imagination of thought? Do we not prove this when we describe a very small circle in the mind through imagination and draw lines from it to the center? For when we have drawn two lines, between which one could scarcely prick a needle, we can no longer, in that same imaginary thought, draw others <margin>C</margin> in the middle so that they reach the center without any mixing together. Yet **Reason** cries out that innumerable lines can be drawn, such that in every interval between them, another circle could even be written. 

Since the phantasy <note>term: "phantasy" <gloss>The faculty of the mind that creates mental images based on sensory input.</gloss></note> cannot fulfill this, and the eyes themselves fail even more—since it was infused into the soul through them—it is manifest that phantasy differs greatly from the truth; and while the soul sees this truth, it does not see the image. The same thing happens when reason divides a line into infinity, which neither the senses discern nor the phantasy attains. From all these things, **Augustine** concludes <margin>A</margin> what **Plato** also teaches in his *Letter to the Syracusans*: that the truths of things themselves dwell familiarly within our mind and show that their familiarity is perpetual.

## Many reasons and signs. The human mind is formed by the divine mind in the act of understanding. Chapter 1.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of Platonic anamnesis (recollection). Here, he uses the specific example of a "circle" to illustrate how the soul ascends from physical sensory objects to divine Ideas, and compares Platonic thought with the views of Arabian philosophers like Avicenna.</meta>

# Twelfth Book of Theology

...we should judge by all these things. Our soul is frequently reminded of the knowledge of a **circle** through hearing: both when it hears this name, "circle," and when it hears a description of a circle of this kind: "A circle is a curved figure which is everywhere equidistant from its center." It is also reminded through sight: when it sees a circle made on a lathe from wood or one drawn on a wall. This latter is not a **true circle**, because it is not perfect; rather, it is an image <term>idolum: a physical representation or "idol" of a higher reality</term> and a likeness of the true one. Reminded by these three things, the soul, greedy for truth, draws out into active thought the **formula** of the circle that is innate to it. Through this formula, as if through a character or stamp, the soul directs its sharp gaze toward the very **Idea of the circle** flourishing in the divine mind. This directing of the gaze is the true knowledge of the circle.

Plato shows in that letter <note>Ficino refers here to Plato’s "Seventh Letter," which describes the five stages of knowing: the name, the definition, the image, the knowledge (or formula), and the thing itself (the Idea).</note> that the soul, enclosed in the body, cannot rise to the Idea without those four steps. Because it is necessary for the soul, which has long ago fallen below itself, first to return to itself through those three external things. Then, through the formula which it holds within itself, it must ascend above itself to the Idea. For just as the forms of things are transmitted from the divine mind into matter through the lowest power of the soul—that is, through the "seeds of forms" infused into this power—likewise, there is no passage from the perception of bodily forms into the Ideas of the divine mind except through the highest part of the soul—that is, through the **innate formulas** of the Ideas.

This allows the soul to transcend from the forms of the body (which are entirely temporal because they change in both essence and quality) into the eternal forms of the divine mind (which do not change in any part). It does this through the forms of the human mind, which are partly eternal and partly temporal: they are eternal in that they remain in their essence, but temporal in that they turn from a state of potential <term>habitus: a settled disposition or latent knowledge</term> into an act of thought, and back again. 

Rightly, then, does the craftsman who is about to shape matter first prepare himself. Therefore, that sublime Mind, which is daily about to form our minds through Ideas, long ago prepared them for this formation through the "characters" <note>original: "caracteres" — here meaning stamps, imprints, or distinctive marks engraved in the soul.</note> of the Ideas. As the prophet sings: *He has sealed the light of his countenance upon us* <note>A reference to Psalm 4:6. Ficino interprets "the light of God's face" as the innate intellectual light given to humans.</note>, so that we might see light in His light. That is to say: through a formula timely awakened, the Idea is kindled in the mind no differently than fire is kindled in wood by sulfur, or as light is kindled in the air through its clear and serene nature. And because just as nature relates to its own matter, so almost does God relate to His.

Heavenly nature (as some believe) decorated its matter once and for all with all forms. Elemental nature <note>The world of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire, which is subject to constant change.</note> decorates its matter at every single moment. Therefore, it is probable that God also filled "angelic matter"—so to speak—once and for all with all Ideas, but fills "animal" <note>meaning "ensouled" or human</note> matter daily. In one respect, the opinion of **Avicenna** and **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algantelis." Ficino refers to the influential Persian philosophers Ibn Sina and Al-Ghazali.</note> seems similar to this Platonic mystery.

<margin>E</margin>
For they are of the opinion that both elemental and intellectual matter beneath the moon are subject to a certain divine mind as if to a "form-giver." They believe that the instruments for disposing elemental matter are the bodily forms, but the mind itself finally imprints the substantial forms upon the prepared matter. Similarly, they believe the human mind is often so disposed by the images of bodies received through the senses and the imagination <term>phantasia</term> that it turns itself toward that divine intelligence. And to the extent that it turns, it is daily formed by it. Nor is that which we call "understanding" anything other than being formed by the divine intelligence. Furthermore, what we call "remembering" is simply having already contracted a "habit" <note>A learned ability or readiness.</note> by which we may easily turn toward the divine mind at will.

<margin>F</margin>
But let us leave the Arabs for now, however much they are friends to Plato. Let us return to Platonic matters. Plato seems to have persuaded himself by these reasons that we cannot truly know things unless we are formed by Ideas. 

**First:** The **name** of a circle is changeable. For as the use of language varies, it can be called something else. If this is so, the **description** (definition) is also changeable, since it is composed of names. The **image** <note>original: "idolum"</note> is also changeable. For a wooden circle can be destroyed, and a painted one can be erased. The **formula** in the soul is also changeable, because it migrates from potentiality or habit into act, and from act back into habit. But that which is grasped through the *science* of the circle is entirely unchangeable, because it is both universal and cannot be otherwise. Therefore, an unchangeable **Idea** is necessary to comprehend the unchangeable reason of the circle.

**Second:** A circle that is made on a lathe or painted is not "pure," because it contains something of a straight figure mixed in. Similarly, the imagination which follows the sight of it does not attain the pure reason of the circle, which is entirely opposite to that figure produced by...

<sig>S 3</sig>
<meta>Catchword: ...craftsmanship [artificii]</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the Platonic path to knowledge, using the circle as an example of how the soul moves from physical objects to innate "formulas" and finally to divine Ideas. He also compares this process to the psychological theories of Arabian philosophers like Avicenna regarding the "form-giving" divine mind.</summary>

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Platonic Book

...separated. Reason also, if it listens to the imagination, is deceived; it is necessary, therefore, that it recur to the pure Idea, through which it may perceive what is pure. **Third**: The true knowledge of the circle consists in this: that it knows what the circle is. But those four <note>Referring to the first four stages of knowledge mentioned on the previous page: the name, the definition, the image, and the mental formula.</note> signify quality rather than substance, since they themselves are qualities. **Fourth**: A clear <note>The original Latin "Clerus" is likely a transcription error for "Clarus" (clear).</note> and perfect mode of knowing follows the mode of being. Therefore, just as the circle, as well as the remaining species of things, are conceived and produced by the divine mind through the Ideas of Ideas, so they are seen to be known by subsequent minds through those same Ideas.

<margin>A</margin> This is so that all sciences might imitate the primary science to the best of their power. The truth of a created thing consists in this: that it responds to its own Idea in every way. Knowledge, however, consists chiefly in this: that the mind corresponds to the truth. But it cannot fit the truth of the thing itself unless it also fits the Idea, in whose congruence the truth is situated. So that in this way, through the Idea—which is the cause of the thing—it may know the thing; since indeed true knowledge is knowledge through the cause. For this reason, the theology of John the Evangelist <note>St. John the Apostle, whose Gospel begins with the "Logos" or Word.</note>, which calls the Idea the "Divine Reason," calls that same Reason "Truth." Because through it, things both truly exist and are truly known. **Fifth**: The intellect understands and judges all created things in their own absolute reasons. And just as, for the most part, the same sensible things are present by their nature to all who sense them, and are not changed when those people change, so the same intelligible reasons show themselves everywhere and always to all who reason; and they remain stable in themselves, while the souls of those who reason approach them more or less. Reasons of this kind are more excellent than all created things, not only because all created things are tested or rejected by them as if by rules, but also because they are prior both due to their amplitude and due to their simplicity.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore they are in God himself, through which He himself both discerns and disposes individual things. When, therefore, the intellect apprehends reasons of this kind, then it apprehends in a certain way both God, in whom they are, and the things of which they are the exemplars <term>exemplaria: the divine "blueprints" or original patterns of all things</term>; yet first, according to a certain natural origin, it apprehends God in a certain way (in whom those reasons are), rather than the things (in which they are not present, even if they are near to them). Nor should it seem incredible to anyone that any corporal things are known through incorporeal exemplars, rather than the reverse. For we perceive sensible bodies through spiritual images of sensible things—whether they are in the senses or in mirrors—and not the other way around. But what wonder is it if we are so deceived in this matter that, while we gaze upon the spiritual exemplars of things, we often think we are only gazing upon the corporeal natures of things? Since infants, when they see incorporeal likenesses of bodies in mirrors, and dreamers, when they think of spiritual images, believe they see actual bodies.

But about this more clearly in what follows. Add to these arguments two signs: one through the intellect, the other through the will. Through the intellect in this way: in the knowledge of a natural species, such as beauty, first we devise some description of beauty common to individual beautiful things. We add some properties of beauty derived from the description to these natures; we will perhaps concede that these notions can be devised through a **formula** <term>formula: an innate mental concept or "inner rule" that allows us to recognize things</term> of beauty innate to the mind. But when we linger longer in this very consideration, we find that the nature of beauty which we have defined—which is pure—is infinite. And because it is infinite, it is God. No one of sound mind would concede that an infinite nature, and God himself, could be apprehended through a finite formula existing at a very long—indeed, incomparable—interval below God. Therefore, the mind, through its formula drawn from potentiality into act, connects itself by a certain preparation to the divine Idea.

<margin>C</margin> Having been connected to it, the mind rises above itself. For no thing ever raises itself above itself unless it is drawn by something higher. For in what way does water fly into the air, unless it is elevated by the heat of the air? Moreover, by a certain easy and natural instinct, the formula itself—since it is a ray of the Idea—leaps back into the Idea, and carries the mind up with it, into which this ray was infused; and when it is led back into the Idea, it flows back into it as if into a fountain, like a ray reflected back to the sun; and through this, a certain "one thing" is made from the mind and God. Hence the divine theologian Paul <note>St. Paul the Apostle, quoting 1 Corinthians 6:17.</note> says, "He who adheres [to the Lord is one spirit with him]."

<summary>Ficino explains that human knowledge of physical things is actually a recognition of divine Ideas. He argues that our ability to conceive of infinite concepts like "Beauty" proves that our minds are being drawn upward by God, as a finite mental formula cannot encompass an infinite truth on its own.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of how the soul achieves union with divine truth. Having previously discussed the stages of knowledge and the role of the Ideas, he now moves into the necessity of divine illumination—comparing God to the sun—and integrates the teachings of Plato and Socrates with the theology of St. John the Evangelist.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
<header>Theology Twelve</header>

...I pray: let there be one spirit. This is a sign through the will. And the mind, in the clear knowledge of truth, is bathed in such wonderful pleasure that it exceeds every limit of human pleasure. The will desires such a state of life for its own sake alone, and other things only for the sake of that state. For a state of this kind exists in the highest summit of nature, beyond which nothing remains to be desired.

<margin>D</margin>
By these reasons, and others nearly similar, Plato seems to have persuaded himself that nothing can truly be learned unless God is the teacher. Therefore, in the same letter <note>referring to Plato's Seventh Letter</note> he says: "Divine mysteries cannot be taught with words." But if anyone dwells for a very long time with divine things and leads a life similar to theirs, suddenly at last, as if from a sparking fire, the light of truth shines forth in the soul and then nourishes itself. He writes that this very thing happened to him. Rightly also in his letter to King Dionysius <note>Plato’s Second Letter</note> he had written that every care of the mind is occupied in the investigation of divine things. Socrates thinks that this investigation will at last attain whatever it desires through the purification of the mind. Therefore, having sometimes sent ahead the solitary solitude of inquiry, he flees to moral philosophy; so that by its benefit, the clouds of the body having been dispersed and his mind made more serene, he might suddenly grasp the light of the divine sun always and everywhere. This Socrates himself first, then Plato by imitation of Socrates, seems to have achieved. But let us return to the established order.

<margin>E</margin>
Plato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, when he had called God "Goodness itself," added that it can scarcely be perceived. But if this is ignored, nothing can be truly known or rightly done, whether publicly or privately. Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle</note> affirms that Socrates and Plato learned this from the Indian philosophers. Socrates declared this most aptly to Theages <note>Referring to the Platonic dialogue *Theages*, which discusses the "daimon" or divine voice of Socrates</note>: namely, that these things, like others, are learned from God alone, as we narrated in the previous book. In the sixth book of the *Republic*, Plato compares God to the sun, as we explained in the *Book on Love* <note>original: "libro de amore"; Ficino's famous commentary on Plato's Symposium</note>. Just as the highest thing in the category of sensible things <term>sensibilia</term> <note>things perceived by the five senses</note> relates to the senses and the objects of sense, so the highest thing in the category of intelligible things <term>intelligibilia</term> <note>abstract realities understood by the mind rather than seen by the eye</note> relates to the intellects and the things understood. The sun creates both the eyes that will see and the visible colors. It grants to the eyes their generation, their power of seeing, and the act of seeing itself. For without light we see nothing in act. Again, it gives to colors their generation and the power by which they can move the eyes, and the act through which they move them. So God—as Plato writes—grants essence to minds. Then He grants the virtue of understanding. Finally, He infuses the understanding itself. He also provides essence to intelligible things: the power to move the mind, and the act through which they move it. Therefore, God joins the act of the mind

<margin>F</margin>
with the act of the intelligible things, just as the light of the sun joins the act of the eye with the act of colors. And just as in seeing there is a triple act: namely, the rising of the color, the gaze of the eye, and the brightness of the light connecting the other acts together. So it is in understanding. There, the act of the intelligible things is called "Truth" by Plato. The act of the mind is called "Knowledge." The node <note>the binding point or connection</note> of both, according to Plato, is God: who brings it about that the mind understands knowingly and the thing is truly understood; indeed, He makes it so that He Himself is understood. For this reason, John the Evangelist <note>St. John, author of the fourth Gospel</note> says: the mind of God is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. And that no one proceeds to God except through it. For it is the Truth of things to be understood; the Life of the understanding mind; and the Way through which the things themselves flow into the mind,

<margin>G</margin>
and in which the mind meets the things. Therefore also elsewhere he said: those alone can see the Spirit of Truth <note>original: "veritatis spm" / spiritum</note> with whom and in whom God is. For if good things move the will under the aspect of goodness, and therefore goodness itself moves the will through goodness toward goodness—nor do we desire anything else but goodness itself in individual things—it follows that for those things which truly move the intellect under the aspect of truth, truth itself moves the intellect through truth toward truth itself; nor does the intellect understand anything other than truth itself. No one doubts that goodness and truth itself are God. Glowing eyes see glowing things by a common light; airy ears hear airy things by common air.

<margin>H</margin>
Truth-telling minds understand true things by truth when they understand and pronounce them. The [will]... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "Uo/" indicates the next word is "Voluntas" (Will).</note>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that human intellect relies entirely on divine illumination. Having previously established that God is the source of truth, he now illustrates this by comparing God to the sun and quoting both Christian scripture (St. John) and the "ancient theologians" (Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus) to show that philosophy and piety are inseparable.</meta>

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

...wills also, being good, are affected by that same common goodness toward good things. And just as the eye, illuminated by the light of the sun, looks upon colors and shapes in those bodies; nor does it truly see anything else but the light itself, although it seems to see various things, because the light infused into it shines with various splendors—that is, it is reflected into the sight from various bodies. And indeed, the eye perceives this light reflected in bodies, but it cannot endure the light itself in its own source. In the same way, our mind, illuminated by a ray of God, understands in that very ray the reasons <term>rationes; original: "rõnes"</term><note>In Platonic thought, these are the "Logoi" or the blueprint-forms of all things existing in the divine mind.</note> of all things, of which God is the source and which are God himself. Therefore, it understands through the light of God and knows only the divine light itself. Yet it seems to see diverse things, because it understands that light under the diverse ideas and reasons of things flowing from it.

However, although we know all things daily through the light of God, and we gradually perceive that same light shining under this or that figure of things, we shall not see the pure light of God—absolute and free from all ideas, and utterly infinite in its source—until we attain that state of the purest mind in which we may behold the light itself in a single gaze, shining with the splendor of all ideas at once. <margin>A</margin> Then, as that distinguished herald of truth, John the Evangelist, says: *we shall see God as He is* <note>original: "videbimus deum sicuti est"; a reference to 1 John 3:2</note>, because we shall know God as God. For now, formed by this idea or that, we see Him as if through this or <margin>B</margin> that species of things.

Although even in this life, according to the theologian John, they may be children of God, because they are daily reformed through divine ideas; the series of these ideas is called by him the **Reason of God**, the **Life of all things**, and the **Light of minds**—not only of angelic minds, but also of human ones. I say of all human minds, because He *lighteth every man that cometh into this world* <note>John 1:9</note> in such a way that whatever a person understands, he understands in Him and through Him; although dark minds do not comprehend Him, because they do not recognize that they see all things through Him. This voice of the divine spirit is heard indeed wherever it wills to breathe, but they do not know where that voice comes from or where it goes.

When the ancient theologians <note>Ficino refers to the "Prisca Theologia," a lineage of ancient wisdom he believed led to Plato and eventually Christianity.</note> knew these things, they always joined the study of philosophy with religious piety. <margin>C</margin> In the beginning, the philosophy of *Zoroaster*, as *Plato* testifies, was nothing other than wise piety and divine worship. The discussions of *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Mercurij trismegisti"</note> also all begin with prayers and end in sacrifices. The philosophy of *Orpheus* and *Aglaophemus* is entirely concerned with divine praises. *Pythagoras* used to begin his philosophical studies with a morning song of sacred hymns. *Plato* commanded that in every single thing one should begin from God, not only in speaking but also in thinking; and he himself always began from God.

But I return for a moment to *Pythagoras*. When he had discovered that the longest side of that triangle which they call right-angled was equal in power to the two remaining sides joined together <note>The Pythagorean theorem</note>, he prayerfully sacrificed a hecatomb <note>A massive sacrifice of one hundred oxen</note> to God. He did this as one who understood that nothing of the truth can ever be seen without the light of the light of truth. Hence, finally, *Minerva*, the goddess of wisdom, is imagined to have been born from the head of *Jove* alone. Hence also this saying: *From Jove is the beginning of the Muse; all things are full of Jove.*

### First question concerning the ascent to God: how the mind is raised to the divine Idea. Chapter 2.

<margin>D</margin> Three questions arise here. First, in what way the mind is raised to the divine Idea. Second, for what cause we do not at all notice that we see God in that state. Third, in what way God constantly infuses this same understanding into us, which Plato affirmed in the preceding sections.

To the first, we respond for the present as follows. When the imagination <term>phantasia</term> is excited by the shape of some man drawn in through the sight, it is formed into a human likeness; then the formula of the human species, which lay hidden in the secrets of the mind, flashes forth when prompted. It forms the edge of the mind or reason into an act, which it had previously formed only as a habit. Such a formation is either a certain ambiguous intelligence or the birth of intelligence. After it has been sufficiently formed in this way, the "Idea" of man is formed—that is, by that Reason through which God generates man. Thus, the mind through the formed Idea of man matches the human, just as wax which has been shaped by a ring...

# Theology, Book Twelve

<margin>E</margin>
...is diligently moved toward the ring: it fits its own exemplar. That very "squaring" <term>quadratio</term><note>Ficino uses the geometric term "squaring" to describe the perfect alignment or fitting of the human intellect to the divine archetypes or "ideas."</note> is the true and distinct intelligence of man. Therefore Plato says in the *Symposium* <note>original: "in conuiuio"</note> that the soul, a lover of divine beauty: when it reaches divine reasons <term>rationes</term><note>In this context, "reasons" refers to the divine blueprints or "Logoi" that exist in the mind of God.</note>: then it no longer gives birth within itself to images of things: but to true things: and it nourishes what is born: it becomes familiar to God: and immortal above others. But no one seems to have revealed this secret more clearly than John the Evangelist: who, when the mind of man reaches something true: does not say, as others are accustomed to, that it "sees" something true, but that it "works the truth." <note>original: "facere veritatem"; a reference to John 3:21, where doing the truth leads to the light.</note> Because, namely, it follows in fact that God, who is truth itself: is made, as it were, its form. For then the mind, having put on the "idea," becomes the very truth of that thing: which is created through such an idea. This is what all contemplators do: whom John says receive from the fullness of divine reason: because, namely, whoever truly contemplates some species of things: has already received into himself one from the number of ideas: of which the fullness is divine reason itself.

<margin>F</margin>
Moreover, the consummate theologian calls the mind "ignited gold" <note>original: "aurũ appellat ignitum"</note>: which just as gold takes on the form of fire, through which it is heated, rarefied, and shines: so that mind, having put on the ideas of the divine mind through them: then shines with the light of truth, and burns with the fuel of goodness. Paul the Apostle also affirms that the mind contemplating divine things: is both renewed daily: and transformed into the same image with God: and becomes one spirit with him. Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage whom Renaissance scholars believed was a contemporary of Moses and a forefather of Plato.</note> similarly says that from a pure mind and divinity, a single spirit somehow coalesces. And all the Platonists prove that in contemplating reasons: divine reason is touched by a certain substantial touch of the mind, rather than by imagination: and the unity of the mind is joined to God—the unity of all things—in a certain inestimable way. Which Plato confirms in the *Phaedrus*: and in the *Epinomis*: and often elsewhere. Especially when in the *Phaedrus* he says the contemplator of divine things is segregated from the rest. He is utterly purified, clings to God, is filled with God: and in the *Epinomis*: the soul perfected by contemplation comes out entirely as one with the divine unity. He judges the same in the books on the Republic.

### ¶ Question two: For what reason do we not notice that we see God in that state. Chapter 3.

<margin>G</margin>
¶ To the second question we can answer thus. Just as the eye sees color through a species <term>species</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental representation or "look" of an object that allows the mind to perceive it.</note> formed by color. But it does not discern the "species" through which it sees: so perhaps the intellect is somehow formed by an idea: through this it immediately understands the natural species itself which was made through such an idea. However, it does not yet clearly behold the idea itself: indeed, it does not recognize it, even though it beholds it. Perhaps this indeed happens at the beginning of contemplation and "squaring." But when it proceeds in contemplating and fits together better: it also receives the idea itself more clearly, and recognizes it: but where it might behold it, it does not yet discern. For just as children, while they look at their own shapes in that brilliance of the sun which surrounds the surface of water: they think they see them not in the extrinsic light, but in the bottom of the water: so the mind, while still unrefined 

<margin>D</margin>
when it sees the reasons of things on high in God: thinks it sees them in itself, or in other things. Especially since the reason of a natural thing in God—for example, the reason of air—does not reflect God entirely as God, and as the loose and free principle of the universe: but as the exemplar of air: which results in the mind, when it is surrounded by that very reason of divine air: understanding God not as God, but as "airy." For it sees the "airy" God—that is, circumscribed to the nature of air. But the angels, who are formed by all ideas at once: through that very gathering of all ideas, they behold the source of all nature. For thus they insinuate themselves into the divine substance not from a certain part of it like us, but almost entirely. Therefore they notice where they see those things. The same will happen also to us: when we are fully reformed into God. But now we are deceived in this matter in no other way than the common people: who, when late at night looking at the moon...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of divine illumination. Having previously discussed how the mind "squares" itself with divine truth through the Gospel of John and the "Logos," Ficino now uses a solar metaphor to explain how humans often mistake God's light for their own, before transitioning into a specific commentary on Plato's Republic and the hierarchy of the One, Mind, and Being.</meta>

# Platonic Book

...[they] see: they say they see by the light of the moon: even though it is actually the light of the sun: by which they see even at night. Thus ungrateful men claim they behold truths in their own private and natural light: which they [actually] behold in the common and divine light. Because if the orb of the sun itself did not exist: or if it set: or if it were never seen by us in its actual shape: no one would know where this light it sends into the air comes from—the light by which we see all things. It is just the same with the light sent down into the mind: by which we discern all things: for God, from whom that light descends, is hidden. 

It descends, however, in such a way as to be the beginning, the middle, and the end of our intelligence. It is the **Beginning**: because just as the vision of the eye is produced by external light as a universal cause, and by a certain internal spark <note>original: "scintilla... interiore"; the Neoplatonic concept of a "spark of the soul" that allows for divine connection.</note> ignited from it as a particular cause: so in us the act of understanding depends on both the vast mind of God and our own. It is the **Middle**: because in it we discern the eternal reasons <term>rationes</term><note>The divine archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note>: which exist only in eternity. Finally, it is the **End**: because we seek to know nothing but God himself. For the eternal reason of any thing: is nothing else in its essence but eternity itself within that very eternity. Here is revealed that divine mystery of our Plato: which is read in the seventh book of the *Republic*. He says that the theologian <note>Ficino often refers to Plato as a "theologian" or "the philosopher-priest."</note> ascends by suitable foundations and steps of demonstration all the way to the principle of the universe, to touch it and to hold it. He always clings to those things that cling to the principle. Indeed, he does not strive toward it by any bodily steps of sensible things: but relies on the species <term>species</term><note>Ficino uses "species" here to mean the formal "types" or "Ideas" that structure reality.</note> themselves, moving through them toward the species themselves as if toward a harbor: until he reaches the species that is the end of the universe. A brief explanation of these words follows.

<margin>B</margin>
The theologian, both by acting and by disputing, purges the soul from bodily affections. He separates reason from the deceptive conjectures of sensible things. He invites the mind to carry itself by such steps toward the truth. By **species**, I mean the formulas implanted in us from our origin; **through species**, I mean through the formation that comes to us from the Ideas; **to species**, I mean to the Ideas themselves and the consideration of the forms of natural things. He says these forms "cling" to God, the principle of the universe. For He is the source of the Ideas: and the mind of the theologian "clings" to them. That is, the mind works its way into them to be formed: by which "working in," he says, one "touches" God. That is, one is formed by the divine mind. He also added "to hold" God for two reasons, as I think. First, because once the mind has begun in this way, it perhaps never entirely ceases that state of life; and second, because after our mind has been formed by the divine mind in many parts through long contemplation: it begins to be wise so far above man, that it no longer knows how to contemplate itself except through God, and of God, and in God.

<margin>C</margin>
Furthermore, he calls God here by many names: **Principle, End, Species**. He is the **Principle** because all things are from Him, and because intelligence takes its start from Him. He is the **End** because both intelligence and all things are terminated in Him. He is the **Species** <note>In this sense, "Form" or the "Act of Being."</note> because He is the very act who forms and makes all things while they proceed from Him as their principle: and He reforms and perfects those same things while they turn back toward Him as their end. Also, every mind is "formed" by Him while it understands the truth. He added a fourth name for God: namely, the **Good** itself, or **Goodness** itself. It is characteristic of the Good that it diffuses itself: that it allures things: and that it perfects them. God diffuses Himself by producing things; He allures them by turning them back [to Him]; and He perfects them by forming those things proceeding and reforming those things returning. However, he places the Good itself above the Mind and above Essence. It is **above Mind**: which is the invisible eye capable of truth and greedy for goodness. For God is not said to be "capable" of truth, nor "desirous" of goodness. Rather, He is Truth and Goodness themselves. Yet, in a more excellent sense, He can be called Mind: both because divine truth is not ignorant of itself, and because many minds flow out from a certain exuberance of divine goodness.

<margin>D</margin>
God is also placed **above that essence**: which is the subject of "to be" <term>esse</term>. Indeed, He is even placed above that "being" which is the act of essence. For such an act, because it is mixed with passive potentiality, is impure and finite. Nevertheless, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> locate "being" <term>esse</term> there, insofar as it is pure and absolute act, through which all essences receive the act of being.

<margin>E</margin>
Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism.</note> and Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist.</note>, however, place the "One" and the "Good" itself above Being for these reasons: the influence of the One and the Good propagates itself more widely than the influence of Being.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic commentary. While the previous page used the metaphor of solar light to explain how God illuminates the mind, this page moves into a metaphysical hierarchy. Ficino argues that "the One" and "the Good" are the highest principles, sitting even above "Being" (existence) itself. He relies heavily on the authority of Dionysius the Areopagite and the later Platonic commentators to justify why unity is more fundamental than existence.</meta>

## Theology

<margin>F</margin> Indeed, **matter** and formless potentiality should be said to participate in the **One** and the **Good** more than in **Being**. For while being comes through form, and matter is formless, matter is nevertheless said to be "greedy" for the good. <note>Ficino is referencing the Neoplatonic idea that matter, though it lacks "being" in the sense of defined form, still possesses a fundamental drive toward the Good.</note> And he seems to have taken this argument from **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>original: "Dionysio areopagita"; a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose works were central to Ficino's attempt to reconcile Plato with Christianity.</note>. Furthermore, just as a multitude is not the same thing as nothingness, so Being itself is not the same as the One. Nor, however, are Being on one side and the One on the other placed as equals, lest two separate principles of things be foolishly established. Nor, again, is Being above the One; for if it were, the One would become a participant in Being, and would no longer be simply the One, but two: that is, it would be the One and Being at the same time. It follows, therefore, that the **One is above Being**. Finally, as much as "Unity" signifies something simpler than "Being"—in which both essence and existence are enclosed—so much more does it suit the first principle of all things. Nor do they allow existence to be separated anywhere from essence, lest the actual act be separated from its own potentiality. Nor do they want it to seem strange to anyone that they name the principle of things **Unity**. 

<margin>G</margin> For they distinguish it thus: It must be named Unity, or Multitude, or a composite of both. But it cannot be a composite, lest it be forced to depend on some higher power that reconciled those diverse parts into one. It cannot be a Multitude devoid of unity, because then both the principle itself would lack all power, and the universe would lack all cohesion. Again, in the principle of all things, there ought to be all power. Therefore, if the principle were Multitude itself, things would become more powerful the more they fell into being a multitude. But since things are actually stronger the more they approach unity, it follows that the principle of things must properly be called **Unity**. Finally, since individual things are properly created and preserved by a certain union, who cannot see that Unity itself is the cause that makes and preserves all things? 

<margin>D</margin> Likewise, all things simply desire the **Good**. But they do not desire Being simply, but only **well-being** <term>bene esse</term> <note>original: "bene esse"; the distinction between merely existing and existing in a state of flourishing or goodness.</note>. <margin>H</margin> Even the Forms, if they did not desire well-being at all, would not even desire to exist, as **Olympiodorus** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote commentaries on Plato.</note> proves. For they desire existence for the sake of the good. Since the Good is the ultimate end, it is surely the first principle of all.

## Book Twelve

If it exists above Being, it exists much more so above Life and Mind. When they say "the One" and "the Good," they always mean the same thing. <margin>J</margin> For just as in the order of things well-being consists in union—since evil joins through discord and division—so also above the order of the universe, the One and the Good are the same. <margin>K</margin> The splendor of this is **Beauty**, which is nothing other than the rational order of many forms reflecting from there into the mind, the soul, nature, and matter. They prove that the One is above this beauty because beauty is composite. Again, they prove the Good is above beauty because all things always desire the good, but only those things that possess knowledge desire beauty, and only after they have come to know it. Likewise, we desire beauty for the sake of the good, hoping it will be beneficial to us. Finally, we want to possess the Good in reality. Yet often it satisfies us if we only seem to have a false beauty. Thrice blessed are those whom the beauty of the universe—the splendor of the Good itself—transforms into the Good through love. Especially since, while it transforms them into the Good, it likewise reforms them into the One. And thus it joins them to the Good itself in unity. 

Indeed, the **One** and the **Good** are as if the same thing: they are spread equally through all things, above and below; and they are equally desired by all things, even without knowledge, by a natural desire. Nor can they differ between themselves as two equally placed things, lest there be two principles of things; nor can the One be above the Good, lest something be called better or more desirable than the Good. Nor, again, can the Good be above the One, lest that which is called good should cease to be a single, unified good. <margin>L</margin> **The One and the Good are therefore entirely the same**, because they are equally desired; just as division and evil are equally fled as if they were the same thing. Blessed is he who is united to the Good. But he is not united by intellectual virtue properly. For since this [intellectual virtue] is manifold and placed below the intelligible <term>intelligibile</term> <note>The realm of pure ideas or forms that can be understood by the mind.</note> realm, it neither suits Unity nor can it reach that which towers over the whole of Being. Add to this that since the One and the Good [are reached] by a certain instinct that precedes...

<summary>This page argues that the "One" and the "Good" are identical and represent the highest principle of reality, sitting above Being, Life, and Mind. Ficino explains that while all things desire to exist, they specifically desire "well-being," which is only found through unity and the pursuit of the Good.</summary>
