<meta>This page follows a discussion on the hierarchy of the "One" being above "Being." Here, Ficino explores the mystical union between the soul and the Good, transitioning into an explanation of how God continuously provides light and knowledge to the human intellect through "divine formulas."</meta>

...is sought by the understanding: it follows that it is reached by a certain touch above the intelligences; a touch, so to speak, that is **unifying**. This occurs through our own unity, which surpasses the intellect and joins the soul to the very unity and goodness of all things—not through an imaginary bond of the intellect, but through a true union of substance itself. From this follows not some light, external, or partial joy (as if one were merely seeing or hearing the Good), but a powerful, internal, and universal pleasure. It is like a taste or a touch superior to the intellect, a tasting and touching of that sweetness which is higher than the intelligible, now experienced deep within. 

Indeed, a natural thirst seeks liquid before we even recognize through our senses that we are thirsty; and after we recognize it, we seek it again. The appetite that follows the senses is imaginary and more distant from our substance. But the appetite that precedes them is intimate to our substance. For this reason, when we attain liquid through taste, we embrace it and perfectly transfer it into our substance—not primarily by the power of the appetite that follows, but by the power of the appetite that precedes. Similarly, it is not so much the desire that follows the action of the mind, but the desire that precedes it (as the beginning of motion), which enjoys the end of the motion while it completes the substantial union. Therefore, this alone fills the whole being from deep within.

### ¶ Third Question. In what way God continually infuses intelligence into us. Chapter 4.

**B**ut let us now descend from here to the third question. I believe this to be the sense of **our Plato** <note>Ficino frequently refers to "our Plato" to indicate his role as a translator and devotee, often harmonizing Plato's voice with Christian theology.</note> when he writes that knowledge is infused into the intellect, and truth into intelligible things, by the **Good** itself. This means that the beneficent and life-giving act of all things, which is God, always surrounds His works and inserts Himself into the universe. 

Most especially, by shining in the secrets of the mind, He constantly purges, sharpens, illustrates, and sets its gaze on fire. At the same time, He gives life to the **innate formulas** <note>original: "formulas"; these are the "seeds" of knowledge or latent ideas present in the human soul from birth, which require divine light to be "activated."</note> within the mind. Thus, whenever we apply a mind free from cares to the investigation of truth, those formulas—having been made more vivid by God's life-giving power—burst forth more readily into the open. Then, the gaze of the mind, set ablaze by God’s irradiation, looks upon them more clearly and ardently. In this process, God stands in relation to the act of understanding itself as the **primary and common agent**. The **Formula** acts as the proper and secondary agent. The **Image** <note>original: "Simulacrum"; a sensory stimulus or symbol that triggers the mind.</note> acts as the incitement. The **Mind** holds the place of "matter" <note>In this context, "matter" means the receptive potentiality that receives the form of knowledge.</note>.

But let us consider this matter by an example, so that we may see more clearly by what means the act of understanding descends into us from God. If God, in order to create the ideas of the mind, tempers our thriving mind within Himself by procreating it, He configures it most closely to Himself. And just as motion and sound are drawn from one lyre to another if they are tuned together, is it any wonder that when the **Divine Mind** sounds in its understanding, the mind of man resonates? 

Imagine a craftsman who makes a thousand mirrors. Once they are made and arranged in order, he presents himself before them. In a thousand mirrors, a thousand images of the craftsman result. The craftsman also moves himself in such a way that he turns his eye to look at his other limbs, and he turns his limbs toward his eye as much as possible. The images in the mirrors imitate these movements. At the movement of the living eye, all the imaginary eyes move. At the movement of the living limbs, the imaginary limbs move. In a like manner, God procreates souls. Then He presents Himself to them as if to mirrors; through this presentation, images of God are made in each one. These images are the **minds** of the souls themselves. Thus, your minds are as many as there are souls in which they exist, yet they are all one insofar as they refer back to the one God. 

The mind, however, refers back to the **Ideas** <note>The eternal "blueprints" of all things existing in the mind of God.</note> through the power of understanding (the power of God who conceives Ideas). Through the **formulas**, however, it refers back to the Ideas themselves. From this, that prophetic saying which we touched upon above is also opened:

> The light of your countenance, O Lord, is sealed upon us; and in your light we shall see light. <note>A combination of Psalm 4:6 and Psalm 36:9, frequently used by Neoplatonists to explain divine illumination.</note>

Truly, through His second power—by which He conceives Ideas through discernment—God provides and preserves for the mind the power by which it may reach Ideas through understanding. Again, God impresses and preserves for the mind the **formulas** of Ideas through the Ideas themselves, which are already conceived and distinguished by reason.

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul's union with God is a "unifying touch" deeper than mere intellectual understanding. He uses metaphors of mirrors and tuned lyres to illustrate how God's light activates innate "formulas" of knowledge within the human mind.</summary>
<keywords>unifying touch, divine infusion, formulas, innate ideas, mirror metaphor, lyre metaphor, Marsilio Ficino, divine illumination, Psalm 4:6</keywords>

# Theology [Book] Twelve

<margin>☛</margin>
...minds. To the motion of God—that is, to the continuous act of God—there is a continuous motion in our minds. In what way? The power that is in God, as it conceives of the Ideas <note>Ficino refers to the Platonic Ideas—the eternal, perfect blueprints of all things existing in the mind of God.</note>, in a certain way turns itself toward those very Ideas. Therefore, our minds reflect back to that power in return. Meanwhile, through a certain harmonious temperament, it happens that the power of understanding in the human mind—if it is unhindered and directed toward God—turns itself toward the <term>formulas</term> <note>Latin: *formulae*. These are the mental reflections or "inner stamps" of the divine Ideas within the human soul.</note>, and the formulas turn back to the power of understanding. 

<margin>☛</margin>
And so, the acts of the mind perpetually imitate the acts of God with a wonderful harmony. But because a face in a mirror, when it seems to look at the face from which it flows, is actually seen rather than seeing, the Apostle Paul 
<margin>B</margin>
says: *“Since you have known God, or rather are known by God.”* <note>original: "Cum deum cognoueritis: imo cogniti sitis a deo." From Galatians 4:9. Ficino uses this to show that our knowledge of God is actually a result of God's primary knowledge of us.</note> Thus, this imitation of the divine countenance by the higher countenance of our soul is named by the Platonists. It goes so far that Plotinus, Theodorus of Asine, and Iamblichus <note>Three major Neoplatonic philosophers who influenced Ficino’s view of the soul's divinity.</note> believed that the human mind—which is not merely human, but divine—lives and operates continuously in the **intelligible world** through a constant intuition of the Ideas. Two reasons in particular moved Plotinus, Theodorus, and Iamblichus to this conclusion. First, the soul's supreme mind, because it is an intellectual essence in itself, understands by its very essence—just as fire is hot by its essence and water is cold—even though the power of the soul lower than the mind does not understand by essence. Therefore, just as fire is always hot, so the mind is always understanding. The objects of this intelligence are the eternal species of things themselves. 

<margin>☛</margin>
And in the act of understanding, the intellect does not cling to the deceptive images of objects; rather, so that it may truly understand, it is united with the objects themselves. Therefore, the mind 
<margin>C</margin>
is always united with the eternal species. Thus, it follows that it diligently dwells in the halls of eternity. 

<margin>☛</margin>
This is the point of Iamblichus’s saying: *“The being of our intellect is nothing other than the understanding of the divine.”* <note>original: "Intellectus nostri esse non est aliud quam intelligere numina."</note> For he thinks that just as it is the same act by which the sun illuminates the moon and the moon is illuminated and looks back at it (forming itself in the likeness of that light), so it is the same act by which the divine mind creates and illuminates our mind, and our mind is created and illuminated by it, and is turned back toward it by a certain natural intuition.

Similarly, an image in a mirror looks back at a face by the same act by which it is seen by the face. And just as it comes to be through that "looking," it is preserved by that "looking back." The soul’s likeness to God is the same. The second reason is this: the rational soul comes from the divine mind and is joined to the body. It holds the middle ground between the Mind and the body. If it clung only to the Mind, it would not grant life to the body. If it clung only to the body, it would understand nothing. Therefore, it clings to the Mind and the body at the same time—just as a line touches the center and the circumference simultaneously, or as the light of the sun is joined to the sun and diffused through the air at once. But as the rational soul relates to the body, so the Mind relates to the rational soul. 
<margin>D</margin>
Yet corporal life itself is nothing other than a continuous act of the soul infused into the complexion of this body, without receding from the soul. Therefore, the intellectual life of the soul is nothing other than the perennial act of the divine intellect attached to the soul, not separated from God. And just as the soul inserts the seeds of things to be generated into corporal life, so God ignites the sparks of things to be known in the soul. Corporal life is a shadow-image <note>original: *simulacrum*</note> of the rational soul. The intellectual life of the soul is a shadow-image of the life and mind of God. The lowest part of the soul, which is the power of nutrition, presides over corporal life. If this lowest part, which is joined to the body, acts always and operates in a certain way by its very being, then much more does the supreme power—which is stronger because it clings to its source and is closer to it—operate always, and operates in a certain way through its very being. It acts upon the Mind, from which it most closely flows. For from the Mind, only mind flows. Moreover, the Mind that is above us, because it is pure intellect, feeds upon the purely intelligible—that is, it enjoys pure truth. Our own mind feeds upon the same constantly; it reclines at the banquet of the higher Mind. And not without reason: we place an essential and perpetual intelligence in the soul because it exists in the soul from that which accords with the perpetual causes of its essence. And just as a perpetual and essential appetite for the Good is innate to the soul, so too is the nature of Truth itself...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect is a divine "mirror" that perpetually reflects and participates in God's eternal ideas. He compares the soul's relationship with God to a mirror reflecting a face or the moon reflecting the sun, asserting that our higher mind is constantly active and united with divine truth.</summary>

# III Platonice Liber

<note>This heading, "The Third Platonic Book," likely refers to a specific volume within Ficino's *Platonic Theology*.</note>

...and the essence within: or rather a deep drawing forth, to use the words of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's need for divine ritual and connection to the divine.</note>. This act, I say, of all mental cognition and discourse is higher and more excellent. Furthermore, the divine Iamblichus confirmed such an opinion by this reasoning: that just as we reach temporal and contingent things through temporal and contingent knowledge, so it is necessary to reach determined and necessary things through an essential and perpetual notion. This notion does not fail <note>original: "labitur"</note>; it precedes our conscious cognition and even the state of death. 

Secondarily, however, the thinking of these things follows in such a way that, like a connecting effect, it follows motion and time. They think <margin>G</margin> that the divine act of the mind itself—which occurs through a certain divine touch—is not interrupted by inferior actions. Indeed, it remains in itself, though as far as our conscious attention <note>original: "animadversionem"</note> is concerned, it may be interrupted in the lower powers. And the act of the rational intellect, or of intellectual reason, which occurs through discourse <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to the step-by-step process of logical reasoning, rather than direct intuition.</note>, is usually interrupted because of lower operations, and vice versa. 

But why do we not notice such a wonderful spectacle of our own divine mind? Perhaps because, through the constant habit of seeing it, we have ceased to wonder at it or even notice it. Or perhaps because the middle powers of the soul—namely Reason <term>ratio</term> and Fantasy <term>phantasia</term> <note>In Renaissance psychology, *phantasia* was the "middle" faculty that processed sensory images before they reached the higher intellect.</note>—since they are mostly inclined toward the business of life, do not perceive the works of that higher mind with any loud clamor. It is just as when the eye looks at something while the fantasy is occupied with other things; it does not recognize what the eye sees. 

But when the middle powers are at rest, a spark of that intellectual speculation flows down into them as if into a mirror. From this, true reasoning is born from true intelligence, and human intelligence from divine intelligence. Nor is it a wonder that something happens in that mind which we do not perceive at all. For we notice nothing except what passes into the middle powers. Therefore, although the power of desiring <note>original: "vis concupiscendi"</note> often hungers and thirsts, we do not notice this until the intention of such a passion passes into the fantasy. Does not the power of nutrition act constantly? Yet we hardly perceive its constant action. 

---

Therefore, neither is the perpetual intelligence of the mind weaker because we do not recognize that we are understanding. On the contrary, it is rather more intense. For often while we sing or run, we do not think about the fact that we are singing and running. And because of this, we perform the work more attentively. For conscious attention <note>original: "animadversio"</note> distracts the soul's intention and diminishes the action. 

<margin>⚜</margin> Beginners <note>original: "tirones"</note> in any art cannot perform the works of that art without focused attention. But veterans, even if they do not pay attention, operate by a certain habit and, as it were, by nature. What prevents the perpetual intelligence of the mind from being like this? 

Since <margin>A</margin> light joined to light conspires into one without confusion, so that both are everywhere and one can be distinguished from the other, it follows that the minds of men, joined to the divine mind, become one in a certain way with the divine mind, and one with each other. Yet they are not confused among themselves, no differently than many lines reflected from a circumference to a center touch the middle point of the circle through their own points. There, the point of each line becomes one, in a certain way, with the middle point of the circle. Each point also becomes one with the others. And though location or time does not distinguish them, reason itself distinguishes them; just as many notions in the mind are joined both with each other and with the mind without any confusion. 

Indeed, just as smaller spheres within a larger sphere touch the center of the larger one with their own centers, so minds—like smaller spheres of the intelligible world—are contained under the divine goodness as if under a larger sphere. Revolving under it, they join themselves through their own centers and through their own unities—which are more excellent than their intellects—to the divine unity as if to the center of the universe. <margin>A</margin> And if by chance the circles are separated, the centers are also separated, since they had been united rather than confused. But <margin>C</margin> Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism, who taught that the soul never entirely leaves the divine realm.</note> never wants the eternal spheres of minds to remain less united with their highest sphere than the temporal spheres of the visible world remain with the larger sphere. But let him see to that himself. We, however, return to our purpose...

It uses analogies of circles, spheres, and master craftsmen to explain how the human soul remains distinct yet united with the divine mind.</summary>

Ficino is moving from the general nature of the soul to a specific metaphysical proof: that the human mind functions as "matter" to the "form" of God's ideas, creating an unbreakable, eternal bond.</meta>

## Theology

->Let us return to the order.<- From all these things which we have drawn from the fountains of Plato and Plotinus, it is concluded: that the human mind, in its very act of understanding, is compared to the divine mind in almost the same way that matter <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "matter" is the potential or "stuff" that receives "form," which gives it identity and purpose.</note> is compared to form. Indeed, if our mind is formed daily by the divine ideas of the [Divine] Mind, and through those ideas it performs its own proper work, who would not see that our mind undergoes the divine just as matter undergoes form? Nor does it relate otherwise to the divine forms than pure matter relates to natural forms. Whence it is said to be no less immortal than matter is; especially since the purer the mind is—being simpler than bodies and souls, and for this reason possessing more unity—so much more tightly does a union come forth from those two minds <note>The human mind and the Divine Mind.</note> meeting as one than is usually the case, whether from any bodily things mixed together, or from souls meeting each other, or from a soul joining with a body. <margin>z</margin> ¶ The knot of this union is increased by the fact that God is unity itself and goodness itself. And since by the power of unity the bond of all things is unified, and by the power of goodness an attraction and nearing happens everywhere, no truer union ever occurs than where the mind conspires with divinity. Likewise, if God—into the mind that emanates proximately and perpetually from Him—flows into it through the thinness of His purity, and fills it through the amplitude of His power, He connects the "joints" of the mind from within like a nerve. He binds Himself to the whole essence like an intimate knot; therefore, He is more interior to the mind than the mind is to itself. What wonder is it then, that God is united to the mind in its act of understanding as its form? <margin>D</margin> ¶ Furthermore, in essence and life, it is already united as more than a form. The chief sign of that union is this: that through true understanding, the intimate substance of a thing is always inspected, as if the mind has penetrated deeper into the "Idea" <note>For Platonists, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things existing in the mind of God.</note> of the thing than sight penetrates into the appearance of color, or imagination into the image of color; for sense and imagination only touch the surfaces of things. <margin>E</margin> ¶ Therefore Mercurius <note>Mercurius is Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage believed by Ficino to be a contemporary of Moses and a precursor to Plato.</note> says: "From the conspiracy of divinity and mind, one spirit coalesces." And the theology of John <note>Referring to the Gospel of John, specifically themes of union with the Word or Logos.</note> teaches that those who contemplate divine reason are so consumed into one with it, just as it is united to God.

---

## Book Twelve

Truly, if in the genus of bodily things there is such a great union that matter—which is the lowest limit of them—makes one thing not only with all intermediate things but even with the supreme member of the bodily genus, who will deny that there is at least an equal union in the genus of intellectual things? Thus the human mind, although it is the lowest limit of those intellectuals, nevertheless becomes one thing with all intellectual forms and even with the Supreme. However, this does not result in a third nature composed of the soul and God (from some third component joining them both and directing them toward a third act), as happens in the composition of natural things. ¶ But because in the contemplating soul God is both the first mover and the ultimate former <note>God provides both the "spark" to start the thought and the "shape" the thought takes.</note>, therefore the whole act is God: by which act He Himself is always God, and the soul becomes, at least sometimes, divine. ¶ And just as Nature, through natural motion, hands over the order of forms to matter, so God, through a divine and immortal life, hands over the clear possession of forms to the mind. ¶ So that a divine and immortal life belongs to the same being to whom divine and immortal understanding is granted. ¶ And just as matter flows under inferior forms, yet always rests under sublime forms (as some think), so the mind of man, although it flows through sensible and imaginary forms, can nevertheless rest forever under divine forms. <margin>B</margin> ¶ Which it does even now, as Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Theodorus <note>Theodore of Asine (c. 275–360 AD), a student of Porphyry and a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> wish. Just as the immeasurable dimension of quantity always perfects matter, so the immense power of divine amplitude perfects the mind; by this light on earth, the mind is continually formed for this end by eternal ideas. And because every formation is produced through congruity <note>The idea that the mind must be "like" the thing it is being shaped by.</note>, this subject which is continuously formed by eternal forms cannot be mortal. ¶ Primary matter is incorruptible, into which certain forms penetrate eternally; although matter itself does not penetrate into them, will the mind not also be immortal? For the mind is not only penetrated by those forms, but it also penetrates them by knowing, and reflects back into them by recognizing them.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that the human mind is immortal because it acts as the "matter" that receives the "form" of God's eternal Ideas, creating a union more perfect than any physical mixture. He cites Hermes Trismegistus and Neoplatonists to show that the mind's ability to grasp the essence of things—rather than just their surfaces—proves its divine and eternal nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the immortality of the soul from Book 12 of Ficino's Platonic Theology. Having established the mind's relationship to the divine in the previous page, Ficino now explores the hierarchy of Being, Life, and Mind, and begins a series of proofs based on human perception and judgment.</meta>

# Platonic
# Book <note>Likely Book 12 of the Platonic Theology.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
Furthermore, where the first mind is, there the first life is found. For the mind is the reflection of life back into its own being. Where the first life is, there also is the first being. For life is the first and innermost movement of being itself. Assuredly, God—insofar as he exists through himself and is truly that which exists—perpetually remains; he is called "Being" <note>original: "panem," likely a typo in the OCR for "ens" or "esse" meaning "Being."</note> by many. Insofar as he does not grow numb in idleness, but works diligently within himself, he is called "Life." Insofar as the act of reason, which does not flow outward, flows back into itself, he is called "Mind." For by that reflection, he takes notice of himself.

<margin>B</margin>
But since that which is highest in any category has nothing of an opposing category mixed into it or even near it, it follows that the first Mind suffers nothing mindless either within itself or near itself. Nor does the first Life suffer anything mortal. Nor does the first Being suffer anything thrust into nothingness. Nor does the first Unity suffer anything dissolvable. Nor does the first Goodness suffer anything subject to disease. Therefore the mind—which is the highest of minds—just as it reserves nothing of mindlessness in that union, so it admits nothing mortal, or perishable, or dissolvable, or subject to disease. This is because through the first mind it is also joined to the first life, and to the first being, and to a similar unity and goodness. Is it any wonder if the intellectual life remains immortal on account of its union with the first life? For even the celestial bodies—as the Platonists maintain—are indeed dissolvable through themselves,

<margin>C</margin>
because they are both mobile and composed, whether of many natures or parts. Yet they endure undissolved because they are joined to the immortal soul with no other body coming between them. Those things, however, which are dissolved do so through another medium. Such are the bodies composed of many elements, which receive the immortal soul—as the Magi <note>Ficino often refers to the "Magi" or "Ancient Theologians" (Prisca Theologia) like Zoroaster or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> teach—through the medium of a celestial body.

### ->Chapter 5.<-
### ->First confirmation of the above reasoning through sight.<-

<margin>D</margin>
**T**hat the souls of men migrate from bodies into [other] bodies, and that they remember the arts of a previous life in subsequent ones, was a theme Plato did not treat as his own conviction, but recounted from the opinion of certain Egyptians. Aurelius Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> rejected their opinion. However, that the soul of man descends from its own Creator marked with the forms of things—and though it does not sufficiently comprehend the substances of things through these [innate] forms, it is able to comprehend them once reformed by the Ideas <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things in the Divine Mind.</note> through these forms as preparations—this, I say, Plato seems to have often affirmed from his own mind, and Augustine highly approved. Therefore, following in the footsteps of Augustine, let us strive again toward the confirmation of the previous sentiment. Let us proceed by a triple path: Experience, Hearing, and Reason.

<margin>E</margin>
First, by Experience <note>original: "Usu," meaning use or practical experience.</note> in this manner: The soul, by which bodies live, is more powerful than all bodies, because it gives life to bodies. Certainly, that which possesses sense perception is more excellent. But in the human soul there is something more outstanding—I do not mean that by which it senses sensible things, but that by which it judges sensible things. Now, it is easy to see that the thing judging is more excellent than the thing about which it judges.

<margin>F</margin>
Moreover, the rational life judges not only sensible things, but also the senses themselves. For instance, why an oar must appear broken in the water when it is actually straight; and why it is necessary for it to be perceived so by the eyes. For the sight of the eyes can report the fact, but it can in no way judge it. Therefore, the rational life stands above the sensual life. Thus, if reason judges according to itself, then no nature is more excellent. But because it is clear that reason is changeable—since it is found now ignorant, now skilled—it judges better the more skilled it is, and it is more skilled the more it participates in some art, or discipline, or wisdom.

<margin>G</margin>
The nature of that art itself must be sought. Nor do I wish "art" to be understood here as that which is noted by experience, but that which is tracked down by reasoning. For surely we must ask: why does it offend us if, when two windows are placed not one above the other but side by side, one of them is larger or smaller, when they could have been equal? Yet if they are one above the other, even if both are unequal by half, that inequality does not offend us so much. And why do we not care much how much one of them is larger or smaller, provided that there are two? <note>Ficino is exploring the soul's innate sense of symmetry and mathematical proportion as evidence of its divine origin.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind's ability to judge the senses (such as correcting the optical illusion of a broken oar in water) proves its superiority over the physical body. He aligns Plato with St. Augustine, shifting away from reincarnation toward a theory of innate divine "forms" that allow the soul to recognize truth and beauty.</summary>

# Theology [Book] Twelve

...they are. In three things, however, the sense itself seems to seek this: that they are not unequal, or that between the largest and the smallest there is a middle ground such that it exceeds the smaller by as much as it is exceeded by the larger. For in this way, at first, nature itself is consulted, as it were, as to what it approves. Here it is most especially to be noted how that which, when seen alone, was less displeasing, is rejected when compared to something better. 

<margin>b</margin> 
Thus it is found that **common art** <term>Common art (ars vulgaris): The practical skill or craft of making things, based on experience and memory rather than theoretical understanding.</term> is nothing other than the memory of things experienced and found pleasing, joined with a certain use of the body and its operation. If you were to lack this physical ability, you could still judge the works, which is a much more excellent thing, even if you cannot produce the artistic works yourself. But since in all things **fittingness** <term>Fittingness (conveinentia): A central concept in Renaissance aesthetics referring to the harmony, proportion, and "coming together" of parts into a beautiful whole.</term> pleases—by which alone all things are beautiful—and since fittingness itself seeks equality and unity, whether through the likeness of equal parts or the gradation of unequal parts, who is there who could find highest equality or likeness in physical bodies? Who would dare to say, after diligent consideration, that any body is truly and simply *one*? For all things are changed, either by passing from form to form or from place to place, and consist of parts occupying their own locations, through which they are divided into different spaces.

<margin>f</margin> 
Furthermore, that true equality and likeness, and that true and primary unity, are perceived not by any sense, but understood by the mind. For from where would any kind of equality be sought in bodies, or how would it be proven to differ by a vast distance from perfection, unless that which is perfect were seen by the mind? And since all things that are sensibly beautiful—whether produced by nature or elaborated by the arts—are beautiful in certain places and times (like a body and its movements), that equality and unity known only to the mind (according to which judgment is passed on bodily beauty through the sense as a messenger) is neither swollen by place nor unstable with time. 

<margin>g</margin> 
For it cannot rightly be said that a round temple is judged according to this law, but that a round vessel or a round coin is not. Similarly, in the timing and motions of bodies, it is ridiculous to say that equal years are judged according to it, but not equal months. But whether something moves harmoniously through these spaces of time, or through hours, or through shorter moments, it is judged by that same one and unchangeable equality. 

But if smaller and larger spaces of shapes and motions are judged by the same law of parity, or likeness, or fittingness, then the law itself is greater than all these things in power. However, in terms of the space of either place or time, it is neither larger nor smaller. For if it were larger, we would not judge smaller things according to the whole of it; if it were smaller, we would not judge larger things according to it. 

Now, however, since a square hearth and a square stone are both judged by the entire law of "squareness," and again, if by the entire law of equality the movements of the feet of a running ant and a walking elephant are judged to agree with one another <note>The author is referring to the rhythmic proportion or "equality" of their strides, regardless of their actual size.</note>, who could doubt that this law is neither larger nor smaller than those intervals of space and time? For in power, it surpasses all things. 

Since this law of all arts is altogether unchangeable, while the human mind (to whom it is granted to see such a law) can suffer the mutability of error, it is clear enough that the law which is called **Truth** is above our mind. Nor should it now be doubted that the unchangeable nature which is above the rational soul is God; and that there is the first life and first essence, where the first wisdom is. 

<margin>l</margin> 
For this is that unchangeable truth, which is rightly called the law of all arts and the art of the almighty craftsman. Therefore, when the soul feels that it judges the form and motion of bodies, and not according to itself <note>That is, the soul does not use itself as the ultimate standard, but uses the higher Law.</note>, it must at the same time acknowledge that its own nature is superior to the nature it judges. But it must also acknowledge that the nature according to which it judges—and which it can in no way judge—is superior to itself. For I can say why the limbs of any body ought to correspond to each other on both sides: because I am delighted by the highest equality, which I behold not with eyes but with the mind. Therefore, I judge those things which I discern with my eyes to be better the closer they are, by their own nature, to those things which I understand with my spirit. Why those things are so, however, no one can say; nor would anyone soberly say they *ought* to be so, as if...

Ficino (quoting Augustine) concludes that this unchanging law of Truth is superior to the human mind and is synonymous with God, the ultimate artist.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into how the human mind acts as a judge of the material world by comparing physical objects to divine, immutable standards. It transitions from discussing the hierarchy of being to the specific "Eternal Law" that governs both ethics and aesthetics.</meta>

# Platonic <margin>G</margin>

...they could not be otherwise. For this reason, either they please us—and we should love them most vehemently when we understand why—or no one, if he understands these things rightly, will dare to say [they are not so]. For since all our **rational souls** <term>Rational souls (animae rationales): In this context, the highest part of the human spirit capable of logic, reason, and perceiving divine truths.</term> judge lower things correctly according to the truth, so truth itself alone judges us when we cling to it; but concerning truth itself, not even the Father judges. For it is not less than He. And therefore, what the Father judges, He judges through the truth itself. For all things that seek **unity** <term>Unity (unitas): The state of being one or undivided; for Platonists, the closer a thing is to absolute unity, the more "real" and "perfect" it is.</term> have this rule, or form, or exemplar: because it alone has fulfilled the likeness of Him from whom it received its being. The mind <note>original: "Sens[us]"; here referring to the interior sense or higher intellect</note> judges all things, because it is above all things when it is with God. It is with Him, however, when it understands most purely, and loves what it understands with total charity. Thus, as much as that law itself is able, it becomes that very law through which it judges all things, and concerning which no one can judge. Just as in these temporal laws, although men judge them when they institute them, yet once they have been instituted and established, it will not be permitted for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but rather to judge *by* them. Nevertheless, the framer of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that very **eternal law** <term>Eternal law (lex aeterna): The unchanging divine reason or will of God that governs the universe and serves as the foundation for all just human laws.</term> which no soul is given the right to judge: so that through its immutable rules, he may discern what is to be commanded or forbidden for a particular time. It is lawful, therefore, for pure minds to recognize the eternal law; it is not lawful to judge it. Indeed, according to it, we can judge concerning the soul and the body: "this action is less than it should be," or "this is less bright than it should be." But concerning the law itself, no one judges in any way. For who would say that eternal things ought to be preferred to temporal things, or that seven and three should be ten? No one says it *ought* to have been so. Rather, it simply *is* so; the one who recognizes it does not correct it as an examiner, but rejoices as one discovering it. But for many, the end is human pleasure, and they do not wish to strive toward higher things so that they might judge *why* these sensible things please them. Therefore, if you ask a craftsman, when he has constructed one arch, why he labors to build another similar one on the opposite side, he will answer, I believe: "So that equal parts of the building may correspond to equal parts." Furthermore, if I proceed to ask why he

# Book

chooses this, he will say that this is "beautiful," or that "it delights those who see it"; he will dare say nothing more. For he rests with his eyes cast down, and he does not understand where that [beauty] hangs from. But I will not cease to remind the man who sees with an internal eye and sees invisibly to ask why these things please him, so that he might dare to be a judge of human delight itself. Thus he is carried above it, and is not held by it, while he judges not *according* to delight, but judges delight itself. And first let him ask: whether things are beautiful because they delight, or whether they delight because they are beautiful? Here it will be answered to me without hesitation: they delight because they are beautiful. I will ask then: why are they beautiful? And if he wavers, I will suggest: is it because the parts are similar to one another, and are reduced to a certain **harmony** <note>original: "uniam convenientiam"</note> by some bond of connection? When he finds this to be so, I will ask: whether they fulfill this very unity which they are proven to seek, or whether they lie far below it and, in a way, "lie" about it? For who, if prompted, does not see that there is no form, nor any body at all, which does not have some **trace of unity** <term>Trace of unity (vestigium unitatis): A philosophical concept suggesting that even physical objects reflect the absolute oneness of God in their structure and symmetry.</term>? Nor can even the most beautiful body—which necessarily has one part here and another there due to the distances of space—ever attain that unity which it follows. I will wait for him to answer where he sees this unity, or from where he sees it. For if he did not see it, how would he know what the form of bodies was imitating, and what it was unable to fulfill? Now, when he speaks to bodies: "We would indeed be nothing unless some unity held us together; but again, if you were unity itself, you would not be bodies," he speaks rightly. From where, then, do you know this unity according to which you judge bodies? For unless you saw it, you could not judge that they do not fulfill it. But if you saw it with these bodily eyes, you would not say truly that, although it is held by its trace, it is nevertheless far distant from it. For with these eyes you see nothing but corporal things; therefore, it is seen [inwardly] that we see it. But where do we see it? If it were in this place where our body is, one who judges bodies in the East in this manner would not see it. It is not...

# Theology Twelve

...therefore He is contained in this place. And while He is present everywhere to the one judging, He is nowhere by the dimensions of physical space: and yet through His power, there is nowhere He is not. The light of the soul is stirred up and disturbed here and there by many illusions of phantasms <term>Phantasms (phantasmata): Mental images or sensory perceptions that do not necessarily represent reality; in Augustinian thought, they are distractions from higher truth.</term>; and yet the soul recognizes these to be false. Where then is the Truth, which is perceived by the mind? That light is the true one, by which you know that all these things are not true; through this light you see that "One" by which you judge that whatever else you see is a single thing. Nor would you be this [One], because what you see is changeable. Furthermore, seek in the pleasure of the body what delights you: you will find nothing else but harmony <note>original: "convenientiam," meaning a fittingness or agreement of parts</note>. For if resistance or discrepancy produces pain, harmony produces pleasure. Recognize therefore what the highest harmony is. <margin>C</margin> Do not go outside. Return into yourself. **Truth dwells in the inner man.** And if you find your own nature to be changeable, transcend yourself. But remember, when you transcend yourself, you are transcending a soul that reasons. Aim, therefore, for that place from which the light of reason itself is kindled. Where does every good reasoner arrive, if not at the Truth? Truth itself does not arrive at itself by reasoning, but is the very thing that reasoners seek. And when we both see in a debate that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true: where, I ask, do we see this? Certainly, I do not see it in you, nor you in me, but we both see it in that unchangeable Truth which is above our minds. There, truly, we behold with the mind's eye the very form according to which these temporal things have been made. And from there, we possess the truth of things we have conceived and knowledge of them, like a "word" <note>original: "verbum"; here Augustine refers to the concept of the inner word or the Logos</note> within us. Behold there the harmony, than which nothing higher can exist, and harmonize yourself with it. Confess that you are not what it is. For Truth does not seek itself. You, however, have come to it by seeking—not through the space of physical locations, but by the movement of the mind—so that the inner man may meet with his Inhabitant in spiritual pleasure. Or, if you are not certain of what I say, and you doubt whether it is true: see at least whether you do not doubt that you doubt. <note>This is a precursor to the famous "I think, therefore I am" argument, establishing certainty through the act of doubting itself.</note> And if it is certain that you are doubting, seek where that certainty comes from. It comes from the light that illuminates every person coming into this world <note>A reference to John 1:9</note>. This cannot be seen with these physical eyes, nor with those by which phantasms are imagined, but with those eyes by which it is said to the phantasms themselves: "You are not what I seek, nor are you that by which I order you." And if some foulness among you should occur to me, I reject it; what is beautiful I approve, since that light is more beautiful from which I reject and approve. For this reason, I approve this light more, and I prefer it not only to you [phantasms], but to all those physical bodies from which I drew you. Where this is seen, there is light without the space of locations or times, and without any phantasm of such spaces. <margin>D</margin> Can these things be corrupted in any part, even if every reasoner should perish? For reasoning does not create such things, but finds them; therefore, before they are found, they remain in themselves. And when they are found, they renew us. In this way the inner man is reborn, and the outer man is corrupted from day to day <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:16</note>. Between our mind—through which we understand that Father and the Truth, that is, the inner light through which we understand—no creature is interposed. Therefore, let us venerate the Truth itself, which is in no way dissimilar in Him and with Him, which is the form of all things that have been made by the One and are led back to the One. From this it appears that all things were made through this form, which alone fulfills what all things desire.

In harmonious sounds there is a certain number <term>Number (numerus): In classical and medieval philosophy, this refers to rhythm, proportion, and mathematical order which reflects divine structure.</term>; this certain number is also present in the act of sensing. For a sound full of numbers is sensed numerically. There is also some "number" in the very nature of sense. For otherwise, the sense would not be soothed by the harmony of sound or offended by absurdity. Therefore, whatever it is by which we either agree or shrink away by nature (and not by reason) when something sounds, I call it the "number" of the sense itself. Not...

<meta>This page continues Augustine’s investigation into the nature of music and the soul. Having previously argued that truth resides within the "inner man," he now applies this to the perception of rhythm. He distinguishes between the transient sounds we hear and the permanent "judicial numbers" within the soul that allow us to judge whether a sound is harmonious or beautiful.</meta>

# Platonic Book

## Platonic

For it then happens in my ears when I hear a sound: this power of approving and disapproving. For indeed, ears lie open to good sounds no differently than to bad ones. See rather that these two things must not be confused at all. For if any verse is pronounced now more quickly, now more lengthily, the span of time must necessarily not remain the same, even if the same logic of feet is preserved. Therefore, that power which makes the ears be soothed by its very kind is that by which we accept harmonious things and reject absurd ones. But whether it perceives it in a shorter time—when it is uttered more quickly than when it is uttered more slowly—makes no difference, except for how long the ears are touched by the sound. Therefore, this affection of the ears when they are touched by sound is in no way the same as if they were not touched. 

Just as hearing differs from not hearing, so hearing this voice differs from hearing another. This affection, then, is neither stretched beyond nor confined within the measure of the sound that produces it. It is one thing in an iamb <term>Iamb (iambus): A metrical foot in poetry and music consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one.</term>, another in a tribrach <term>Tribrach (tribachus): A metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.</term>. There is prolongation in the prolongation of the iamb; shortening in the shortening; a bubble in silence <note>original: "bulla in silentio" – Augustine uses the metaphor of a bubble to describe the fleeting, hollow nature of sensory impressions compared to the lasting nature of the soul.</note>. 

If this happens in a rhythmic <note>original: "numerosa," literally "numbered," referring to text or music that follows a mathematical meter.</note> voice, it must also become rhythmic; nor can it exist when its producer, the sound, is absent. For it is like a footprint pressed into water: it is neither formed before you press a body into it, nor does it remain once you have removed it. But that natural and judicial <note>original: "iudiciaria," referring to the soul's innate power of judgment or evaluation.</note> power which is present in the ears does not cease to exist in silence; sound does not insert it into us, but rather the sound is received by it to be approved or disapproved. 

Who would deny that there is a power of numbers in the soul? <margin>21</margin> Since the soul enacts these numbers which we find in the pulse of the veins and in reciprocal breathing. When I pronounce a verse either more shortly or more lengthily—as long as I observe the law of times by which feet arrive from a single to a double proportion—I offend the judgment of your sense with no deception. And that sound which is emitted in shorter and, as it were, more fleeting syllables, cannot occupy more time than it sounds. But those judicial numbers, if they were held by the bond of time in only as much space as those sounding ones are arranged, they could not aspire to the judgment of those sounding ones which are poured out slightly more lengthily under the same iambic law.

## Book

Therefore, that delay of times does not hold us who preside in judging. But if they were held by nothing, no matter how much more lengthily I uttered iambic sounds (with fitting intervals and mutual responses), they would nevertheless be applied for judgment. Now, however, if I were to utter one syllable for as long a delay as it takes to walk three steps—to say the least—and another for double that, and thus arranged iambs so long in their single and double proportions, that law would nonetheless be preserved. But we could not apply that natural judgment to approving those dimensions. 

Therefore, even those judicial numbers are held by certain boundaries of temporal spans, which they cannot exceed in judging; and whatever exceeds these spans, they do not attain for judgment. Yet they temper individual actions. For that which restrains and inhibits us from uneven steps while walking, or from uneven intervals of strokes when striking, or from uneven movements of the molars when eating, or finally from uneven strokes of the nails when scratching—and which silently commands a certain equality in any attention of doing something through the members of the body—it is that very "I-know-not-what" judicial something. It is what causes men to have a sense and choice of beauty and decency <note>original: "decoris," referring to aesthetic appropriateness or grace.</note> more than beasts, who are driven headlong to whatever their incitements for the sake of calming bodily passion. They are not enticed by the grace of beauty, but by greed. 

Thus horses do not choose a more beautiful mare to love, but are drawn to any at all with equal fury. But that judicial power suggests God as the creator of the animal. Whom it is certainly fitting to believe is the author of all harmony <note>original: "convenientie," meaning a fittingness or agreement of parts.</note> and concord. Furthermore, numbers—both those in sound and those produced in sensing—are offered to and judged by those judicial numbers only insofar as memory can preserve their intervals. For this number, which consists of intervals of time, cannot be judged by us in any way unless we are aided by judicial memory. Of any...

He explains that while sounds are fleeting like footprints in water, the soul's ability to judge them is a permanent gift from God, though it relies on memory to function.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Saint Augustine's deep dive into the philosophy of music from Book VI of "De Musica." Having established that sounds are fleeting physical events, he now explores how the human soul uses "numbers" (rhythms and proportions) to process and judge these sounds. He uses his own famous hymn, "Deus creator omnium," as a primary example to show the difference between simply hearing a rhythm and intellectually judging its beauty.</meta>

# Theology XII

For even a short syllable, since it both begins and ends, the beginning sounds at one time and the end at another. Therefore, in hearing even the shortest syllable, unless memory aids us—so that at the very moment when not the beginning, but the end of the syllable sounds, that motion which was made when the beginning itself sounded remains in the soul—we could say we have heard nothing. This is why it often happens that when we are occupied with another thought while speaking, we seem to have heard nothing. For this reason, those **judicial numbers** <term>Judicial numbers (numeri iudiciales): The innate mental standards or "rhythms" the soul uses to judge whether a sound is harmonious or discordant.</term>, which cannot judge numbers situated in intervals of time unless memory offers them up like a servant, must they not be thought to stretch through a certain space of time? For although we see the smallest spaces of time in them, they are nonetheless only applied to judge those things which exist in spaces of time—and not even all of those, but only those that can be articulated by memory. When that verse is sung:

-> **God, creator of all.** <note>original: "Deus creator omnium" — One of the four hymns certainly written by St. Augustine; it is written in iambic dimeter.</note> <-

We hear the numbers of the verse itself through sensory numbers, and we are delighted through judicial numbers. And I do not know by what other numbers we evaluate this delight, which is like the verdict of those judicial ones, when we can provide a broader but certainly truer verdict through others above these. 
<margin>B</margin>
For it is one thing to be delighted by sense, and another to evaluate by reason. Indeed, it is one thing to agree or disagree with rhythmic motions—which happens in the delight of harmony or the offense of the absurdity of such motions—and it is another to evaluate by reasoning whether they delight rightly or otherwise. And if it seemed right to us that the sense of delight itself could in no way agree with equal intervals or reject disturbed ones unless it were within certain numbers, it can also rightly seem that the reason which is placed over this delight can in no way judge concerning the numbers it has beneath it without certain more "lively" numbers. Now, if you please, let those which had risen up for us to obtain the leadership be called **sensual** numbers; and let the name of **judicial** numbers—since it is more honorable—be taken by those which were found to be more excellent.

Come now, observe the force and power of reason, as much as we can perceive from its works. For reason itself—to speak specifically of what pertains to undertaking this work—first considered what **good modulation** <term>Modulation (modulatio): In ancient music theory, this refers to the "measuring out" of rhythm and movement, rather than the modern sense of changing keys.</term> itself is. And it perceived it to be in a certain free movement, turned toward the end of its own beauty. Then it saw that in the movements of bodies, one thing varied by the brevity and length of time (insofar as it was more or less long-lasting), and another by the striking of local spaces in certain degrees of speed and slowness. Having made this division, it followed how that which exists in the delay of time—articulated by a moderate interval and accommodated to human sense—produces various numbers, and their types and order, even to the modules of verses. Finally, it attended to what the soul (of which reason is the head) does in moderating, working, sensing, and retaining these; and it separated all these **animal numbers** <note>Augustine categorizes "numbers" or rhythms into hierarchy: physical sounds, the soul's reaction to them, the memory of them, and the rational judgment of them.</note> from bodily ones. It recognized that it could neither notice, nor distinguish, nor certainly count all these things without certain numbers of its own. 
<margin>C</margin>
It placed these above the others of the lower order by a certain judicial estimation. And now, with its own delight—by which it weighs the moments of time and exhibits its approval in modifying such numbers—it acts thus: What is it that we love in sensible numerosity? Is it anything besides a certain parity and equally measured intervals? Does the **pyrrhic** <term>Pyrrhic: A metrical foot of two short syllables.</term>, or the **spondee** <term>Spondee: A metrical foot of two long syllables.</term>, or the **anapest** <term>Anapest: Two short syllables followed by one long.</term>, or the **dactyl** <term>Dactyl: One long syllable followed by two short.</term>, or the **proceleumatic** <term>Proceleumatic: A foot consisting of four short syllables.</term>, or the **dispondee** <term>Dispondee: A foot consisting of two spondees (four long syllables).</term> delight us in any other way than by comparing its parts to the other part in an equal division? What beauty do the **iamb** <term>Iamb: A short syllable followed by a long one.</term>, the **tribrach** <term>Tribrach: Three short syllables.</term>, or the **trochee** <term>Trochee: A long syllable followed by a short one.</term> have, except that they divide their larger part equally into as many units as their smaller part? Furthermore, do feet of six beats sound more charming and festive from any other source than that they are partitioned by either law? Namely, as possessing three beats in two equal parts, or as one single part from any side and the other double—that is, as

<meta>While the previous page discussed Saint Augustine’s musical theory, this page shifts focus to a Neoplatonic commentary—likely by Marsilio Ficino or a similar Renaissance philosopher—interpreting Plato’s "Republic" and the nature of divine light. The numbering "Theology XII" from the header is inferred, though the source text identifies this section as the "Platonic Book."</meta>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Platonic Book

...they say they see by the light of the moon, although that is actually the light of the sun, by which they also see at night. In the same way, ungrateful men claim that they perceive truths by their own natural light, whereas they actually perceive them in a common and divine light. For if the disk of the sun itself either did not rise and set, or were never looked upon by us in its own form, then no one would know from where this light is sent into the air, by which we see all things; just as one now knows from where the light is sent down into the mind, by which we discern all things, because God, from whom it descends, is hidden. 

Moreover, it descends in such a way that it becomes the beginning, middle, and end of our intelligence. It is the **Beginning**, because just as the vision of the eye is produced by an external light as a universal cause, and also by an internal spark ignited from within as a particular cause, so in us the act of understanding depends both on the vast mind of God and on our own. It is the **Middle**, because in Him we discern the eternal reasons <note>original: "rationes" — in this context, the divine archetypes or ideas upon which reality is modeled.</note>, which exist only in eternity. Finally, it is the **End**, because we recognize Him alone. 

<margin>A</margin> For the eternal reason of each thing is, in its essence, nothing other than eternity itself within that eternity. Here is revealed that divine mystery of our **Plato**, which is read in the seventh book of the *Republic*. <note>Refers to Plato's "Allegory of the Cave" and the analogy of the Sun in Republic VII.</note> He says that the theologian <note>original: "theologum" — likely referring to the philosopher-king or the soul seeking divine wisdom.</note> ascends through suitable foundations and steps of demonstration until he touches and holds the very principle of the universe, always adhering to those things which adhere to that principle. Indeed, he strives toward this not by any corporeal steps of sensible things, but relies more upon the forms <term>Species: In Platonic thought, these are the "Ideals" or "Forms" that represent the true essence of things, rather than their physical appearance.</term> themselves, through the forms, and toward the forms, until he reaches the very form that is the end of the universe. 

A brief explanation of these words is as follows: The theologian, both through action and through disputation, 

<margin>B</margin> purifies the soul from corporeal affections. He separates reason from the deceptive conjectures of sensible things. He supports the mind so that it may proceed by steps toward this kind of truth. By "Forms," he means the formulas implanted in us from our origin; "through forms," he means through the formation that comes to us from the Ideas; "to the forms," he means toward the consideration of the Ideas themselves and the forms of natural things. He says that these forms "adhere" to God, the principle of the universe. For He Himself is the fountain of Ideas, and the mind of the **Theologian** truly "adheres" to them—that is, he allows himself to be formed by them—and through this "insinuation," he says, the theologian "touches" God—that is, he is formed by the divine mind. 

He adds that the theologian "holds" God, for two reasons, I believe. First, because once the mind has begun in this way, it perhaps never entirely ceases this state of life; and second, because after our mind has been formed for a long time by contemplating the divine mind from many sides, it begins to be wise so far beyond the human level that it no longer knows how to contemplate itself except through God, and God, and in God. 

<margin>C</margin> He identifies God here by several names: **The Beginning**, **The End**, and **Hope**. He is the **Beginning** because all things come from Him, and because intelligence takes its start from Him. He is the **End** because both intelligence and all things are terminated in Him. He is **Hope** <note>original: "Spem" — a unique Neoplatonic attribution where God is the object of the soul's ultimate expectation and the power that draws things back to their source.</note> because He is the act who forms and makes all things while they proceed from Him as their principle; and He reforms and perfects those same things while they are turned back toward Him as their end. It is also because every mind is formed by Him while it understands the truth. 

He added a fourth name to God: **The Good itself**, or goodness itself. It is characteristic of the Good that it diffuses itself, that it allures things, and that it perfects them. God diffuses Himself by producing things; He allures them by converting them back to Himself; and He perfects them by forming those that proceed and reforming those that have turned away. Furthermore, he places the Good itself above mind and above essence. It is above **mind** (that is, the mind which is the invisible eye capable of truth and greedy for goodness), for God is not said to be "capable" of truth or "desirous" of goodness; rather, He is truth and goodness itself. Yet, in a more excellent sense, He can be called Mind, both because divine truth is not ignorant of itself, and because many minds flow out from there by a certain exuberance of divine goodness. God is also placed above **essence**, which is the subject of "being." 

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, He is even placed above that **Being** which is the act of essence. For such an act, because it is mixed with a passive potentiality, is impure and finite. Nevertheless, He is placed by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who defined God as "Pure Act" (Actus Purus).</note> as "Being" insofar as He is pure and 

<margin>E</margin> absolute act, through which all essences receive their act of being. However, **Plotinus** and **Proclus** <note>Famous Neoplatonists who argued the "One" or "The Good" is even higher than "Being."</note> place the One and the Good above Being for these reasons: the influence of the One and the Good itself spreads more widely than the influence of Being.

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic concept of God as the "Sun" of the intellectual world, providing the light by which the mind understands eternal truths. It interprets Plato's Republic to describe the soul's ascent through "Forms" to reach God, who is defined as the Beginning, End, Hope, and the Good above all Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of divine principles, shifting from the metaphor of light discussed on page 109 to a metaphysical analysis of the "One" and the "Good." The author draws heavily on Neoplatonic sources to argue that these principles exist above the level of "Being" itself.</meta>

<header>Theology Twelve</header>

<margin>F</margin>
Indeed, matter—as a formless potential—should be said to participate more in the **One** and the **Good** than in **Being**. This is because being <note>original: "esse" — the act of existing</note> occurs through form, yet matter is formless; nevertheless, even matter is said to be "desirous of the good." It appears that he [the author] received this line of reasoning from **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose work synthesized Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine.</note>. Furthermore, just as a multitude is not the same as nothingness, so "being itself" is not the same as the "One." Nor are Being and the One positioned as equals—one on this side and one on that—lest two separate principles of reality be foolishly established. Nor, again, is Being placed above the One; for if it were, the One would merely participate in Being, and it would no longer be simply "One," but two—that is, the One and Being together. It follows, therefore, that the **One** must stand above **Being**. Finally, since "Unity" signifies something far simpler than "Being" (in which both essence and existence are enclosed), it is all the more fitting for the first principle of all things. Nor do they allow existence to be separated from essence in any place, lest the actual deed <note>original: "actus" — the realization or manifestation of a thing</note> be separated from its own proper potential. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that they name the first principle of things **Unity**.

<margin>G</margin>
They distinguish it in this way: the first principle must be named either Unity, or Multitude, or a composition of both. But it cannot be a composition, lest it be forced to depend upon whoever reconciled those diverse parts into one. Nor can it be a Multitude devoid of unity, for such a thing would lack all power and the whole would lack all cohesion. Again, in the beginning of all things, all things must exist in potential. Therefore, if the principle were Multitude itself, things would become more powerful the more they fell into that multitude. However, because things are actually stronger the closer they approach Unity, the opposite follows: the principle of all things must properly be called **Unity**. Finally, since individual things are properly made and preserved by a certain union, who cannot see that Unity itself is the cause that makes and preserves all things? Likewise, all things simply desire the **Good**. But they do not desire Being simply; they desire "well-being" <note>original: "bene esse" — a state of flourishing or perfection beyond mere survival</note>.

<margin>H</margin>
Even forms, if they were to lack well-being entirely, would not even desire existence, as **Olympiodorus** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonic philosopher known for his commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.</note> proves. This is because they desire existence for the sake of the Good. Therefore, since the Good is the ultimate end, it is undoubtedly the first principle of all things.

If it exists above Being, it exists much more so above **Life** and **Mind**. When they speak of the One and the Good, they always understand them to be the same thing.

<margin>I</margin>
For just as in the order of things "well-being" consists in union—since evil joins things through discord and division—so too, above the order of the universe, the **One** itself and the **Good** are the same. **Beauty** is the splendor of this Good;

<margin>K</margin>
which is nothing other than the rational order of many forms reflecting from the Mind, the Soul, Nature, and Matter. They prove that the One is above this Beauty because Beauty is a composite thing. Again, they prove the Good is above Beauty because all things always desire the Good, whereas Beauty is desired only by those things that can recognize it, and only after they have known it. Likewise, we desire Beauty for the sake of the Good, hoping that it will be beneficial to us. Finally, we wish to possess the Good in truth; yet often it is enough for us if we merely seem to possess a false beauty. Too happy are they whom the beauty of the universe—the splendor of the Good itself—transforms into the Good itself through love! Especially since, while it transforms them into the Good, it equally reforms them into the One. Therefore, it joins them to the Good itself in unity. For the One and the Good, being the same, expand through all things—above and below—and are desired by all, even without conscious knowledge, through a natural instinct. They cannot differ from one another as if they were two equally disposed things, lest there be two principles of reality; nor can the One be above the Good, lest something be said to be better or more desirable than the Good. Nor, again, can the Good be above the One, lest that which is called "good" should cease to be "one" (and thus cease to exist). Therefore, the One and the Good

<margin>L</margin>
are fundamentally the same, just as they are equally desired; in the same way, division and evil are equally fled from as if they were the same thing. Blessed is he who is united to the Good. However, one is not properly united to it by intellectual virtue. For since the intellect is manifold and is situated below the "intelligible" <note>original: "intelligibile" — the realm of pure ideas that can be understood by the mind</note>, it neither suits Unity nor can it reach that which towers above the whole of Being. Add to this that the One and the Good are preceded by a certain instinct...

<summary>This page argues that the "One" and the "Good" are the supreme, identical principles of the universe, residing above Being, Mind, and Beauty. Using Neoplatonic logic, the text explains that all things strive for unity and goodness as their source of strength and preservation.</summary>
<keywords>The One, The Good, Being, Beauty, Matter, Neoplatonism, Dionysius the Areopagite, Olympiodorus, Unity, Metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the soul relates to the highest principle—the One or the Good—moving beyond mere intellectual understanding to a direct, substantial union. It transitions into Chapter 4, which explores how God continuously illuminates the human mind.</meta>

<header>Book on Platonic Matters</header>

...if the Good is sought by the tooth of intelligence <note>original: "dente intelligentiam" — a metaphor Ficino uses to describe the sharp, grasping power of the intellect as it "consumes" knowledge</note>, it follows that it must be reached by a certain "touch" that stands above intelligence. This is a unifying touch, so to speak, achieved through our own internal unity. This unity surpasses our intellect and joins the soul itself to the unity and goodness of all things—not through some imaginary intellectual connection, but through a true union of its very substance. 

From this, there follows no light, external, or partial joy (as if one were merely seeing or hearing the Good), but rather an intense, intrinsic, and universal pleasure is produced. It is as if a "taste" or "touch" of something superior to the intellect were occurring, as the soul deeply tastes and touches that very sweetness which is higher than anything understandable. 

Indeed, a natural thirst seeks out liquid before we even consciously recognize through our senses that we are thirsty. Once we recognize it, we seek it again. The appetite that follows the senses is imaginary <note>based on mental images</note> and more distant from our substance. But the appetite that precedes awareness is intimate to our very being. Therefore, when we attain a liquid through taste, we embrace it not by the power of the later, conscious appetite, but by the power of that original, preceding appetite, and we transfer it perfectly into our own substance. In the same way, it is not so much the desire that follows the action of the mind, but the desire that precedes it—as the very principle of motion—that enjoys the end of that motion when it achieves a substantial bond. Therefore, this union alone fully satisfies the soul's prayer.

### ¶ Third Question. In what way God continually pours intelligence into us. Chapter 4.

But let us now descend to the third question. I believe this is the meaning of our Plato when he writes that both knowledge is infused into the intellect and truth is infused into intelligible things by the Good itself. This means that the beneficent and life-giving act of all things, which is God, always encompasses His works and weaves Himself into everything. 

Wishing to shine most powerfully in the secrets of the mind, God continually purges, sharpens, illuminates, and ignites its gaze. He also vivifies the patterns <term>formulas; innate concepts or "seeds" of knowledge placed in the soul by God</term> implanted in the mind. Thus, whenever we apply our minds, free from cares, to the investigation of truth, those patterns—made more lively by God’s vivification—break forth more readily into the open. Then the gaze of the mind, set ablaze by God’s radiance, sees more clearly and ardently. 

In this process, God stands in relation to the act of understanding as the "primary and universal agent." The innate pattern acts as the "proper and secondary agent." The likeness <note>the external object being studied</note> acts as the stimulus. The mind itself holds the place of "matter" <note>the receptive surface</note>. 

But let us consider this through an example so we may see more clearly how the act of understanding descends into us from God. If God, in order to create the ideas of the mind, tempers our mind while procreating it, and shapes it most closely to Himself—drawing tempered motions and sounds from one lyre to another—is it any wonder that when the Divine Mind "sounds" in the act of understanding, the mind of man resonates? 

Imagine a craftsman who makes a thousand mirrors. Once they are made and arranged in order, he presents himself before them. In a thousand mirrors, a thousand images of the craftsman result. Sometimes the craftsman moves himself in such a way that he turns his eye to look at his other limbs, and he turns his limbs toward his eye as much as he can. The images in the mirrors imitate these movements. At the movement of the living eye, all the imaginary eyes move. At the movement of the living limbs, the imaginary limbs move. 

In the same way, God procreates souls. Then He presents Himself to them as if to mirrors; through this presentation, images of God are made in each soul. These images are the "minds" of the souls themselves. Thus, minds are many (because the souls they inhabit are many), yet they are all one (because the God they reflect is one). Every mind, through its power of understanding, reflects the power of God conceiving the Ideas. Through its innate patterns, it reflects the Ideas themselves. This also explains that prophetic saying which we touched upon above:

> The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us; and in your light we shall see light. <note>A combination of Psalm 4:7 and Psalm 36:9</note>

Truly, God—through His fruitful power by which He conceives Ideas by discerning them—provides and preserves a power in the human mind through which it may reach Ideas by understanding. Again, God—through those very Ideas already conceived and distinguished by reason—imprints and preserves within the mind the patterns of those Ideas.

<summary>This page explains that the soul reaches God not through the intellect alone, but through a "unifying touch" of its core substance. Ficino uses the metaphor of mirrors to illustrate how human minds are reflections of the Divine Mind, continually illuminated and "vivified" by God's presence.</summary>
