<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s relationship with the divine from Book 12. It moves from the soul’s desire for the "Good" to a technical explanation of how the human mind continuously participates in divine thought through a mirror-like reflection of eternal Ideas.</meta>

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>Twelfth Book of Theology</header>

# Twelfth Book of Theology

...of souls. Toward the movement of God—that is, toward the act of God—there is a continuous movement in minds. In what way? The power that is in God, conceiving the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideas" — the eternal blueprints or archetypes of all things in the divine mind</note>, turns itself in a certain way toward those very Ideas. Therefore, they mutually reflect that power back. Meanwhile, by a certain harmonious attunement, it happens that the power of understanding in a person's mind—if it is unhindered and directed toward God—turns itself toward the **formulas** <note>original: "formulas" — the internal concepts or "inner blueprints" that exist within the human mind as reflections of God's Ideas</note>, and the formulas turn toward the power of understanding. And so, the acts of the mind imitate the acts of God in a marvelous harmony. Because, truly, when a face in a mirror is seen looking at the face from which it emanates, it is actually being looked at rather than looking; for this reason, the Apostle <margin>B</margin> Paul says: *When you have known God, or rather, have been known by God.* <note>A reference to Galatians 4:9, used here to suggest that our "knowing" is actually a result of God looking at us first</note> Thus, this "upper face" of our soul is called an "imitation of the divine face" by the Platonists. This goes so far that Plotinus, Theodore of Asine, and Iamblichus <note>three major Neoplatonic philosophers</note> judged that the human mind—which is not merely human, but divine—lives in the **intelligible world** <note>the spiritual realm of pure thought, beyond the physical world</note> and works there continuously through a perpetual gaze upon the Ideas.

Two primary reasons moved Plotinus, Theodore, and Iamblichus to this view. First, the supreme mind of the soul, because it is an **intellectual essence** <note>meaning it is thinking by its very nature, just as a heart is beating by its nature</note> in itself, therefore understands by its essence, just as fire is hot by its essence and water is cold—even if the power of the soul lower than the mind <note>such as the senses or the imagination</note> does not understand by its essence. Therefore, just as fire is always hot, the mind is always understanding. The objects of this understanding are the eternal **species** <note>the Forms or perfect patterns of things</note> themselves. And in understanding, the intellect does not cling to the deceptive shadows of objects; rather, to truly understand, it is united with the objects themselves. Therefore, the mind is always united with the eternal species. Thus, it diligently dwells in the home of eternity. This is what Iamblichus means when he says: *The being of our intellect <margin>C</margin> is nothing other than to understand the divine powers.* For he thinks that just as it is the same act by which the sun illuminates the moon and the moon is illuminated by it (and it looks back at the sun through the likeness of light), so too it is the same act by which the divine mind creates and illuminates our mind, and our mind—being a creature—is illuminated by it and is turned there by a certain natural gaze.

Similarly, an image in a mirror looks back at a face by the same act through which it is looked at by the face. And just as it is made by being looked at, so it is preserved by looking back. Such is the similarity of the soul to God. The second reason is as follows: the rational soul is made by the divine mind and joined to the body. Thus, it occupies the middle ground between the mind and the body. If it only clung to the mind, it would not provide life to the body. If it only clung to the body, it would understand nothing. Therefore, it clings to the mind and the body at the same time, like a line that touches the center and the circumference simultaneously, or like the sun's light is both joined to the sun and diffused through the air. But as the rational soul relates to the body, so the mind relates to the rational soul. <margin>D</margin> However, bodily life itself is nothing other than a continuous act of the soul infused into the composition of this body, without receding from the soul. Therefore, the intellectual life of the soul is nothing other than a perennial act of the divine intellect joined to the soul, not separated from God. And just as the soul inserts the seeds of things to be generated into bodily life, so God ignites the **little sparks** <note>original: "igniculos" — a favorite term of Ficino's for the innate "seeds" of knowledge God places in the human soul</note> of things to be known within the soul. Bodily life is the shadow of the rational soul. The intellectual life of the soul is the shadow of the life and mind of God. The lowest part of the soul—which is the power of nourishing—presides over bodily life. If this lowest part, which is joined to the body, acts always and operates by its very being, how much more does the supreme power, which is stronger because it clings to its source, operate always and through its very being. It acts around the Mind, from which it flows most closely. For only mind flows from Mind. But the Mind that is above us, because it is pure intellect, feeds on the pure **intelligible** <note>that which can be grasped by thought alone</note>; that is, it enjoys pure truth. Our own mind is fed continuously if it sits at the feast of the higher Mind. And not without reason do we place an essential and perpetual intelligence in the soul, because it exists in the soul from that which agrees with the perpetual causes of its essence. And just as a perpetual and essential appetite for the Good is inborn in the soul, so too is the nature of Truth itself...

It uses the authority of Neoplatonists like Plotinus and Iamblichus to assert that the soul's highest part lives perpetually in the spiritual realm of Ideas.</summary>

Having established that the soul imitates the divine face, he now uses the authority of the Neoplatonist Iamblichus to explain why this divine connection remains constant even when we are not consciously aware of it.</meta>

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>III Platonic Theology</header>

# Platonic

Through these points, it must be asserted that there is a unity, or rather a higher <term>touch</term> <note>original: "tactus" — a Neoplatonic term for the direct, non-discursive contact between the human mind and the Divine</note>; or rather, to use the words of Iamblichus: an act, I say, prior to and more excellent than all cognition and <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>original: "discursu" — the step-by-step process of logical thinking, as opposed to instant intuition</note>. The divine Iamblichus confirmed a sentiment of this kind with a specific reason: Just as we reach temporal and contingent things through temporal and contingent cognition, so it is necessary to reach necessary and eternal things through an essential and perpetual notion. This notion precedes our inquiry in the same way that the stable state of the mind precedes its movement. Indeed, temporal cognition follows inquiry in such a way that the joined effect follows movement and time. Moreover, they think that <margin>c</margin> this divine act of the mind—which is made one through a certain divine touch—is not interrupted by inferior actions. Indeed, within itself, it is never interrupted, even if it is interrupted in the lower faculties as far as our conscious observation is concerned. And while the acts of the <term>rational intellect</term>—or of intellectual reason—which occur through discursive thought, are usually interrupted because of lower operations (and vice versa), why do we not observe such a wonderful spectacle of our own divine mind? Perhaps because we have grown unaccustomed to wondering and noticing due to the continuous habit of seeing it. Or perhaps because the "middle powers" of the soul—namely, **reason** and <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: "phantasia" — the faculty of imagination that processes sensory data</note>—since they are for the most part more inclined toward the business of life, do not clearly perceive the operations of that higher mind. Just as when the eye looks at something in full view, yet the imagination is occupied with other things, the mind does not recognize what the eye sees. But when the middle powers are at rest, those sparks of intellectual speculation flow down into them as if into a mirror. From this, true reasoning is born from true intelligence, and human intelligence from divine intelligence. Nor is it a wonder that something happens in that mind which we do not perceive at all. For we observe nothing except that which passes into the middle powers. Therefore, although the power of desiring often hungers and thirsts, we do not notice this until the intention of such a passion passes into the imagination. Does not the power of nutrition act constantly? Yet we hardly

# Theology

perceive its constant action. Therefore, neither the perpetual intelligence of the mind, nor the fact that we do not recognize our own understanding, makes that intelligence weaker. On the contrary, it is all the more powerful. For often while we sing or run, we do not think at all about the fact that we are singing or running. And because of this, we perform the work more attentively. For the conscious observation of an action distracts the intention of the soul and diminishes the action. Apprentices in any art cannot perform the works of that art without intense attention. But masters, even if they do not pay attention, operate by a certain habit and, as it were, by nature. What prevents such from being the continuous intelligence of the mind?

<margin>ac</margin> Truly, because light joined to light breathes together into one without confusion—wherever both are, and one can be discerned from the other—it follows that the minds of men, joined to the divine mind, become one in a certain way with the divine mind and with one another, yet they are not confused among themselves. This is no different than many lines reflected from a circumference to a center, which touch the middle point of the circle through their own points. There, the point of each line becomes one in a certain way with the middle point of the circle. Each individual point also becomes one with the others. And though location or time does not distinguish them, reason itself distinguishes them; just as many notions in the mind are joined both to each other and to the mind without any confusion. Surely, just as smaller spheres within a larger sphere touch the center of the larger one with their own centers, so minds—like smaller spheres of the <term>intelligible world</term>—contained under the divine goodness as if under a larger sphere and revolving under it, couple themselves to the divine unity (as if to the center of the universe) specifically through their own centers, which are their unities, more excellent than their own intellects.

<margin>c</margin> And if by chance the circles are disjoined, the centers are also disjoined, since they had been united rather than confused. Indeed, Plotinus never wishes them to be disjoined, lest the spheres of eternal minds remain less united with their highest sphere than the temporal spheres of the visible world remain with the greater sphere. But let him see to that himself. We, however, return to our purpose...

<summary>Ficino explains that the human mind is constantly connected to the divine through a "touch" that transcends logic. He argues that we often ignore this divine activity because our lower faculties (reason and imagination) are distracted by daily life, similar to how we breathe or walk without thinking.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the human mind's immortality in Book 12. Having previously discussed how the soul imitates the divine, he now moves into a technical argument based on the relationship between "matter" and "form," drawing heavily on the Neoplatonic tradition to prove that the mind is a vessel for eternal divine ideas.</meta>

# Twelfth Book
# of Theology

Let us return to the order of our argument. From all these points which we have drawn from the wells of **Plato** and **Plotinus**, we conclude the following: in the very act of understanding, the human mind is related to the divine mind in much the same way that **matter** is related to **form**. Indeed, if our mind is daily formed by the ideas of the divine mind, and performs its own proper work through them, who cannot see that our mind is subject to the divine—just as <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia" — the basic "stuff" or potential of the universe that requires a "form" to become a specific thing</note> is subject to <term>form</term> <note>original: "forma" — the organizing principle or essence that gives something its identity</note>? Our mind relates to these divine forms no differently than <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materiā primam" — the most fundamental, formless substance in Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy</note> relates to the forms of nature.

For this reason, the mind ought to be no less immortal than matter itself. This is especially true because the purer the mind is—being simpler than bodies and even lower souls, and thus more unified—the tighter the bond becomes when these two minds (the human and the divine) meet. This union is closer than any that occurs in physical things mixed together, or between souls meeting one another, or even the union of the soul with the body.

The "knot" of this bond is strengthened because God is Unity itself and Goodness itself. Since the bond of all things is unified through the power of Unity, and since a "pull" and a drawing-near occurs everywhere through the power of Goodness, no truer union occurs than when the mind harmonizes with divinity. Likewise, if God—who is closest to the mind and perpetually flowing from it—glides within it through an infinite thinness of purity, He fills it completely with the magnitude of His power. He connects the parts of the mind like joints, acting as an internal "sinew" connecting them to each other and to the whole. He binds the entire essence together like an intimate knot; therefore, He is more interior to the mind than the mind is to itself. What a wonder: God is united to the mind in its very act of understanding as if He were its **form**.

<margin>D</margin> After He is already united in essence and life, He is even more than a form. The primary sign of this union is that through true understanding, the mind always looks into the "inner substance" of a thing, because it has penetrated deeply into the **Idea** <note>original: "ideam" — in the Platonic sense, the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing in the mind of God</note> of that thing. This is far deeper than the way sight reaches a color, or the way the imagination reaches an image of a color; for the senses and the imagination only touch the surfaces of things. 

<margin>G</margin> For this reason, **Hermes** <note>original: "Mercurius" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage thought to be a contemporary of Moses</note> says: *From the harmony of divinity and the mind, one single spirit coalesces.* And the theology of **John** <note>original: "Ioānis" — likely referring to the Gospel or Epistles of John the Apostle</note> teaches that those who contemplate divine Reason are so brought to fulfillment into "one" with it, just as that Reason itself is united to God. 

Surely, if in the realm of physical things there is such a union that matter—which is the lowest limit of things—can become a single thing not only with all intermediate things but even with the highest physical element, who would deny that an equal union exists in the realm of intellectual things? Thus, the human mind—even if it is the lowest limit of the intellectual realm—can become a single thing with all intellectual forms, and even with the Highest. 

However, a "third nature" is not created out of the soul and God (as if there were some third component joining them and directing them toward a third act, as happens in the composition of natural things). Rather, because God is both the **Prime Mover** and the **Final Former** in the contemplating soul, the entire act is God. By this act, God himself is always God, and the soul becomes, at least for a time, divine. 

Just as nature, through natural movement, hands down the order of forms to matter, so God, through a divine and immortal life, hands down the clear possession of forms to the mind. Thus, a divine and immortal life is fitting for the same mind to which a divine and immortal understanding belongs. And just as matter may flow under lower forms, yet (as some believe) always finds rest under sublime forms, so the human mind—though it may flow through the forms of the senses and the imagination—can nonetheless eventually find eternal rest under divine forms. 

<margin>G</margin> This is what the mind does even now, according to **Plotinus**, **Iamblichus**, and **Theodorus**. Just as an indeterminate dimension of quantity always perfects matter, so the immense power of divine magnitude continuously forms the mind with eternal Ideas—leading it through His power, into His light, and toward His end. 

Because this formation is achieved through a perfect fit, this subject (the mind) cannot be mortal, for it is continuously formed by eternal forms. **Prime matter** is incorruptible, and eternal forms always penetrate it, even though matter itself does not penetrate them. Shall the mind not also be immortal? For the mind is not only penetrated by those forms, but it also penetrates them by knowing them, and reflects back into them by recognizing them.

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by comparing the human mind to "prime matter" that is uniquely capable of being "formed" by God's eternal ideas. He concludes that because the mind can actively grasp and unite with these eternal divine forms, it must share in their immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the immortality of the soul from Book 12. Following the previous discussion on the mind as a vessel for divine forms, he now explores the metaphysical structure of the "First Mind" and begins a "confirmation through sight" to prove the soul's superiority over the material world.</meta>

->Platonic<-
->Book<-

<margin>A 2</margin>
**F**urthermore, where the first mind is, there is also the first life. For the <term>mind</term> <note>original: "mens" — in Ficino's philosophy, the highest part of the soul, which connects directly to the divine</note> is the reflection of life into its own <term>being</term> <note>original: "esse" — the fundamental act of existing</note>. Where the first life is, there is also the first being. This is because life is the first and most intimate motion of being itself. Indeed, God—inasmuch as He exists through Himself and is truly that which exists and remains perpetually—is called "First Being" by many. Inasmuch as He does not sit idle in leisure but operates unceasingly within Himself, He is called "Life." Inasmuch as the act of <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" — the processing power of the intellect</note>, which does not flow outward but flows back into Himself, He is called "Mind." For by that reflection, He observes Himself.

<margin>B</margin>
Truly, because that which is supreme in any given category has nothing of a contrary nature mixed into it or even near it, it follows that the first mind suffers nothing of <term>madness</term> <note>original: "demens" — literally "away from mind" or lack of reason</note> either in itself or near itself. Nor does the first life contain anything mortal. Nor does the first being contain anything that will fall into nothingness. Nor does the first unity contain anything dissolvable. Nor does the first goodness contain anything subject to disease. Therefore, the mind that is joined to the first mind—just as it retains nothing of madness in that union—admits nothing mortal, or perishable, or dissolvable, or subject to disease. This is because, through the first mind, it is also coupled to the first life, to the first being, and to a similar unity and goodness. Is it any wonder if the intellectual life remains immortal because of its contact with the first life? For even the celestial bodies—as the Platonists maintain—are by their own nature dissolvable, 

<margin>C</margin>
since they are both movable and composed either of many natures or parts. Nevertheless, they endure without dissolving because they are coupled to an immortal soul with no other body coming between them. Those things, however, which are dissolved do so because of some other medium. Such are the bodies composed of many elements which receive an immortal soul through the medium of a "celestial body," as the <term>Magi</term> <note>original: "magi" — referring here to the ancient Persian or "Hermetic" sages like Zoroaster whom Ficino admired</note> teach.

### First confirmation of the above reasoning
### through sight. Chapter 5.

<margin>D</margin>
**T**hat the souls of men transmigrate from bodies into other bodies, and that they remember the skills of a previous life in subsequent ones, is a topic **Plato** did not treat as his own personal view; rather, he recounted it from the opinion of certain Egyptians. <margin>original: "egyptiorū"</margin> **Aurelius Augustine** rejected their opinion. But as for the idea that the human soul descends from its very Creator marked with the <term>forms of things</term> <note>original: "formis rerū" — the essential blueprints or archetypes of all objects</note>, and that through these forms it does not yet fully grasp the substances of things, but can grasp them once it is "re-formed" by the <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ideis" — the eternal, divine truths in the mind of God</note>—this, I say, Plato seems to have often affirmed from his own mind, and Augustine seems to have highly approved. Therefore, walking in the footsteps of Augustine, let us strive again toward the confirmation of the previous sentiment. Let us proceed by a triple path: through sight, through hearing, and through reason. First, through sight, in this manner: 

<margin>E</margin>
The soul, by which bodies live, is more powerful than all bodies because it gives life to them. Surely that soul which possesses <term>sensation</term> <note>original: "sensum"</note> is more excellent. Yet in the human soul there is something even more outstanding—I do not mean that by which it senses "sensible things" <note>things perceived by the physical senses</note>, but that by which it judges those sensible things. Now it is easy to see that the thing which judges is more excellent 

<margin>F</margin>
than that which is being judged and does not itself judge. Not only does the rational life judge sensible things, but it also judges the senses themselves. For example, why an oar must appear broken in the water when it is actually straight; and why it must necessarily be perceived that way by the eyes. For the sight of the eyes can report the fact, but it can in no way judge it. Therefore, the rational life stands above the sensual life. Thus, if reason judges according to itself, then no nature is more excellent. But it is clear that reason is changeable, since it is found to be sometimes unskilled and sometimes skilled. It judges better the more skilled it is, and it is more skilled to the extent that it participates in some art, or discipline, or wisdom. The nature of that "art" must be sought. And I do not want "art" to be understood here as that which is learned by trial and error, but that which is tracked down by reasoning. 

<margin>G</margin>
Certainly, we must ask: why does it offend us if, when two windows are placed not one above the other but side by side, one of them is larger or smaller, when they could have been equal? Yet if they are one above the other, even if both are unequal by half, that inequality does not offend us so much. And why do we not care much how much one of them is larger or smaller, provided there are two?

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind achieves immortality by being joined to the "First Mind" of God. He begins a sensory proof of the soul's superiority, noting that Reason's ability to correct optical illusions (like a broken oar in water) proves it is higher than physical matter.</summary>

# Theology, Book Twelve
### P

...they are. In three things, however, the sense itself seems to seek that they are not unequal: either that they are not disparate, or that there is a middle between the maximum and minimum such that it precedes the smaller as much as it is preceded by the larger. For in this way, nature itself is first consulted, as it were, as to what it approves. In this, it is especially to be noted: how a thing which, when viewed alone, was less displeasing, is rejected when compared to something better. Thus it is discovered that <margin>b</margin> common <term>art</term> <note>original: "artem vulgarem" — referring to mechanical or manual skill rather than the "liberal arts" of the mind</note> is nothing else than the memory of things experienced and found pleasing, with a certain use of the body and operation added; if you were to lack this skill, you could still judge works, which is much more excellent, even if you could not perform the artistic operations yourself.

But since in all arts <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "conuenientia" — a sense of "fittingness" or proportion where parts suit the whole</note> is what pleases, by which alone all things are beautiful—and this harmony itself seeks equality and unity, either through the similarity of equal parts or the gradation of unequal parts—who is there who can find supreme equality or similarity in physical bodies? Who would dare to say, after careful consideration, that any body is truly and simply <term>one</term> <note>original: "vnum" — the philosophical concept of unity; in Platonism, physical things are never "one" because they are made of parts and are always changing</note>, since all things change either from form to form or by moving from place to place, and consist of parts occupying their own places, through which they are divided into different spaces?

<margin>f</margin> Furthermore, that true equality and similarity, and that true and primary unity, are perceived by no sense, but are seen by the mind when it understands. <margin>g</note> For from where would any kind of equality be sought in bodies, or from where would it be proven that they differ greatly from perfection, unless that which is perfect were seen by the mind? And since all things that are sensibly beautiful—whether produced by nature or elaborated by the arts—are beautiful in space and time (such as a body and the motion of a body), that other equality and unity known only to the mind (according to which we judge physical beauty, with the sense acting as a messenger) is neither swollen by space nor unstable in time. 

For it cannot rightly be said that a round temple is judged according to that law, but a round vessel or a round coin is not. Similarly, in terms of time and the motions of bodies, it is ridiculous to say that equal years are judged according to it, but equal months are not. But whether something is moved harmoniously through these spans, or through an hour, or through shorter moments, it is judged by the same one and immutable equality. 

But if smaller and larger spans of shapes and motions are judged by the same law of parity, or similarity, or harmony, that law itself is greater than all of them—not in size, but in power. For the law is neither larger nor smaller than the space of place or time. If it were larger, we would not judge smaller things according to the whole of it; if it were smaller, we would not judge larger things according to it. As it stands, since a square forum and a square stone are both judged by the whole law of "squareness," and if the motions of the feet of a running ant and a walking elephant are judged by the whole law of equality to harmonize with themselves, who could doubt that this law is neither larger nor smaller than intervals of space and time? For in power, it surpasses all things. 

Now, since this law of all arts is entirely <term>immutable</term> <note>original: "incommutabilis" — unchanging and eternal, a key attribute of divine truth</note>, while the human mind (to which it is granted to see such a law) can suffer the changeability of error, it is clear enough that the law which is called Truth is above our mind. Nor should it now be doubted that the immutable nature which is above the rational soul is God; and that the "First Life" and "First Essence" are there, where the "First Wisdom" resides. For this is that immutable <margin>IK</margin> truth, which is rightly called the law of all arts and the art of the almighty craftsman. 

Therefore, when the soul perceives that it does not judge the form and motion of bodies according to itself, but according to something higher, it must simultaneously acknowledge that its own nature is superior to the nature of the thing it judges; but that the nature according to which it judges—and which it can in no way judge itself—is superior to the soul. For I can say why the members of any body ought to correspond to each other with similarity on both sides: because it delights with a supreme equality which I behold not with my eyes, but with my mind. Therefore, I judge those things which I discern with my eyes to be better the closer they are, by their nature, to those things which I understand with my mind. But why those things are so, no one can say; nor would anyone soberly say they "ought" to be so, as if they could be otherwise.

# Platonic [Theology]

...might not be so. Therefore, either they should please us—and we should love them most vehemently when we know better—yet no one, if they understand these things rightly, would dare to say this. For just as all our rational souls judge lower things correctly according to truth, so does that same truth alone judge us when we are joined to it. Indeed, not even the Father judges concerning the Truth <note>original: "de ipsa v[er]o nec iudicat pater" — here "Truth" refers to the Divine Logos or the Son, through whom the Father acts</note>. For it is not less than He is. And therefore, whatever the Father judges, He judges through it. For all things that seek <term>unity</term> <note>original: "unitatem" — the principle of being "one," which in Platonism is the source of all existence and beauty</note> have this as their rule, or form, or exemplar; for they fulfill their purpose only by the likeness of that from which they received their being.

The mind judges all things when it is above all things, which occurs when it is with God. It is with Him, however, when it understands most purely and loves what it understands with total charity. Thus, as much as it can, it acts through that truth, and becomes the very thing through which it judges all things, and concerning which no one can judge. Just as in these temporal laws, although men judge concerning them when they establish them, yet once they have been established and confirmed, it will not be permitted for a judge to <margin>A</margin> judge *them*, but rather to judge *by* them. The maker of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that very <term>eternal law</term> <note>original: "eternam [legem]" — the unchanging divine order that governs the universe</note>, which it is granted to no soul to judge, so that he may discern what should be commanded or forbidden for a particular time according to its immutable rules. Therefore, it is lawful for pure minds to recognize the eternal law, but it is not lawful to judge it. Truly, according to that law we are able to judge concerning the mind and the body: that this action is less [than it should be], or less vehement than it ought; or that this is less bright than it ought.

But concerning the law itself, no one judges in any way. For who would say that eternal things ought to be better than temporal things, or that seven and three ought to be ten? No one says it *ought* to have been so; rather, it simply *is* so. One who recognizes this does not correct it as an examiner, but rejoices in it as a discoverer. But for many, the end is merely human pleasure, and they do not wish to strive toward higher things to understand *why* these sensible things please them. And so, if you ask a craftsman, after he has constructed one arch, why he builds another equal to it on the opposite side, he will respond, I believe: "So that equal members of the building may correspond to equal members." Furthermore, if I continue to ask why he chooses 

---

# Book

this, he will say that this is "beautiful," or that this "delights those who see it," and he will dare to say nothing more. For he has leaned down [toward his work] with his physical eyes and does not understand that which hangs above. But I will not cease to remind a man who is inwardly "eyed" <note>original: "oculatu[m]" — having the "eye of the mind" or spiritual insight</note> and who sees invisibly, to ask why these things please, so that he may dare to be a judge of human pleasure itself. First, [the mind] is carried above that pleasure and is not held by it, as long as it does not judge *by* pleasure, but judges the pleasure itself. 

I will ask first: whether things are beautiful because they delight, or do they delight because they are beautiful? Here, it will be answered to me without hesitation: that they delight because they are beautiful. I will then ask: why are they beautiful? And if he wavers, I will suggest: is it because the parts are similar to one another and are brought into a single harmony by some bond of connection? When he finds this to be so, I will ask: whether they perfectly fulfill this very <term>unity</term> <note>original: "unitatem"</note> which they are proven to seek, or whether they fall far below it and merely <margin>B</margin> mimic it in a certain way? 

If this is so, who—unless they are out of their mind—would not see that there is no form, nor any body at all, that does not possess some trace of unity? And no matter how beautiful a body is, since it occupies space, it necessarily has one part here and another there; therefore, I will think it cannot achieve that unity which it follows. I will ask him to answer: where does he see this unity, or from where does he see it? For if he did not see it, how would he recognize what the forms of bodies were imitating and what they were unable to fulfill? Now, indeed, he says to the bodies: "We would be nothing unless some unity held us together; but again, if you were unity itself, you would not be bodies." This is rightly said. 

From where, then, do you know this unity, according to which you judge bodies? Unless you saw it, you could not judge that the body does not fulfill it. But if you saw it with these corporeal eyes, you would not truly say that although the body is held by its trace, it nonetheless stands far apart from it. For with these eyes, you see nothing but corporeal things. From where, then, do we see it? And where do we see it? If it were in this place where our body is, one who judges bodies in the East in this same way would not see it.

# Theology [Book] Twelve
D 2

Therefore, He is contained in this place. And since He is present everywhere, to the one who judges He is nowhere by spatial dimensions; yet by His power, He is nowhere absent.

<margin>C</margin>
When the soul is stirred by many illusions of phantoms <note>original: "phantasmatum" — mental images or sensory impressions that can be deceptive</note> disturbing it from all sides, and yet it recognizes these to be false, where is the truth that is seen by the mind? That is the true light by which you know that these things are not true; through this light, you see that "One" by which you judge that whatever else you see is a single thing. Yet you also see that what you perceive is not this One itself, because whatever you see is changeable. Furthermore, if you seek pleasure in the body, ask what it is that delights you; you will find nothing other than harmony <note>original: "conuenientiam" — a fittingness or agreement of parts</note>. For if resistance or discrepancy produces pain, harmony produces pleasure. Recognize, therefore, what the highest harmony is. Do not go outside. Return into yourself. Truth dwells in the <term>inner man</term> <note>original: "interiore homine" — a central concept in Augustinian thought referring to the soul's intellectual and spiritual core</note>. And if you find your own nature to be changeable, transcend yourself. But remember, when you transcend yourself, you are transcending the reasoning soul. Reach out, therefore, to that place from which the light of reason itself is kindled. For where does every good reasoner arrive, if not at the Truth? Truth itself does not reach itself by reasoning, but it is the very thing that those who reason are seeking. And when, in a discussion, we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true—where, I ask you, do we see this? Surely I do not see it in you, nor do you see it in me, but we both see it in that unchangeable Truth which is above our minds. There, certainly, we behold with the vision of the mind the very form according to which these temporal things were made. And from there, we hold the truth of things we have conceived and the knowledge of them as a "word" within us. See there a harmony so great that none could be higher, and harmonize yourself with it. Confess that you are not what it is. For Truth does not seek itself; but you have come to it by seeking, not through spatial distance, but through the affection of the mind, so that the inner man might meet with his inhabitant in spiritual pleasure. Or, if you are not certain of what I say and doubt whether these things are true, see at least whether you do not doubt that you are doubting. And if it is certain that you are doubting, seek to know why it is certain. It is from the light that "enlightens every man coming into this world" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:9</note>. This light cannot be seen with these physical eyes, nor with those by which phantoms are imagined, but with those eyes by which it is said to the phantoms themselves: "You are not what I seek, nor are you that source from which I order you." And when I encounter something among you that follows a pattern, I reject what is ugly and approve what is beautiful, since that source from which I reject or approve is more beautiful still. For this reason, I approve that source more, and I prefer it not only to you phantoms, but to all those physical bodies from which I drew you. Where is this seen? There is the light without spatial location or time, and without any phantom of such spaces. 

<margin>D</margin>
Can these things be corrupted in any part, even if every reasoner were to perish? For reasoning does not create such things, but finds them; therefore, before they are found, they remain in themselves. And when they are found, they renew us. Thus the inner man is reborn, and the outer man is corrupted day by day. Between our mind, through which we understand that Father, and the Truth—that is, the inner light through which we understand—no created thing is interposed. Therefore, let us worship that same Truth, which is in no part unlike Him, in Him and with Him; for it is the form of all things that were made by the One, and which strive toward the One. From this, it appears that all things were made through this form, which alone fulfills what all things desire.

For otherwise, it would neither be soothed by the harmony of sounds nor offended by absurdity. # Theology [Book] Twelve

-> D 3 <-

...for even a short syllable, since it both begins and ends, has its beginning at one moment and its end sounding at another. In hearing even the briefest syllable, unless memory aids us—so that at the very moment when it is no longer the beginning but the end of the syllable that sounds, that motion which occurred when the beginning itself sounded remains in the soul—we could say we have heard nothing. This is why it often happens that when we are occupied with another thought while speaking, we seem to have heard nothing. 

Therefore, those judging rhythms <note>original: "iudiciales illi numeri" — Augustine identifies five types of 'numbers' or rhythms: sounding, sensory, advancing, memory, and judicial. 'Judicial' refers to the mind's innate ability to judge whether a rhythm is harmonious</note>, which cannot judge rhythms arranged in intervals of time unless memory offers them up as a servant, must they not themselves be thought of as extending through a certain space of time? For although we see no spaces of time within them, they are nonetheless not employed except to judge those things that occur within spaces of time; and indeed not all of them, but those that can be articulated by memory. 

When that verse is sung: **God, creator of all.** <note>original: "Deus creator omnium" — A famous hymn by St. Ambrose, used by Augustine to illustrate his theories of time and perception</note> We hear the rhythms of the verse itself through sensory rhythms, and we are delighted by the judicial rhythms. And I do not know by what other means we think about this delight, which is like the verdict of these judicial rhythms; though through others <note>meaning other types of rhythms or mental faculties</note> we can perceive a broader, or certainly a truer, verdict.

<margin>B</margin>
For it is one thing to be delighted by sense, and another to estimate by reason. Indeed, it is one thing to agree or disagree with rhythmic motions—which happens in the delight of harmony <note>original: "conuenientie" — fittingness or agreement</note> and the offense of absurdity in such motions—and another thing to estimate by reasoning whether these things delight rightly or otherwise. And if it has seemed right to us that unless the sense of delight itself were imbued with certain rhythms, it could in no way have agreed with equal intervals and rejected disturbed ones, it can also rightly seem that the reason which is placed over this delight can in no way judge the rhythms it holds beneath itself without certain more vigorous rhythms. Now, if you please, let those rhythms which rose up for us to obtain the leadership be called "sensory," and let those take the name of "judicial"—since it is more honorable—who have been found to be more excellent.

Come now, receive the force and power of reason, as much as we can behold from its works. For reason itself—to say that which pertains most to the undertaking of this work—first considered what <term>good modulation</term> <note>original: "bona modulatio" — the skill of rhythmic and melodic proportion</note> itself might be. And it perceived it to exist in a certain free motion, turned toward the goal of its own beauty. Then it saw in the motions of bodies that there was one thing that varied by the shortness and lengthening of time (according to whether it was more or less lasting) and another thing in the percussion of local spaces in certain degrees of speed and slowness. 

Having made this division, it followed how that which was in the delay of time, articulated by a modest interval and adapted to human sense, produced various rhythms, their types, and their order, even up to the measures of verses. Finally, it noticed what the soul—of which reason is the head—did in moderating, performing, sensing, and retaining these; and it separated all these "animal rhythms" from "corporeal" ones. It recognized that it itself could not have noticed, distinguished, or certainly numbered all these things without certain rhythms of its own. It placed these above the others of the lower order by a certain judicial estimation; and now, with its own delight, by which it weighs the moments of time and exhibits its approval for the modification of such rhythms, it acts in this way:

<margin>C</margin>
What is it that we love in sensible rhythm? <note>original: "numerositate" — the quality of being rhythmic or numerical</note> Is it anything other than a certain equality and equally measured intervals? Does a <term>pyrrhic foot</term> <note>a metrical foot of two short syllables</note>, or a <term>spondee</term> <note>two long syllables</note>, or an <term>anapest</term> <note>two short, one long</note>, or a <term>dactyl</term> <note>one long, two short</note>, or a <term>proceleumatic</term> <note>four short syllables</note>, or a <term>dispondee</term> <note>four long syllables</note> delight us otherwise than by comparing its parts to the other part in equal division? Truly, what beauty do the <term>iamb</term> <note>one short, one long</note>, the <term>tribrach</term> <note>three short</note>, or the <term>trochee</term> <note>one long, one short</note> have, except that they divide their larger part equally into as many parts as their smaller part? Furthermore, do feet of six beats sound more charming and festive from any other source than that they are divided by both laws? Namely, either into two equal parts possessing three beats each, or into one single part on one side and a double part on the other, as...

# Platonic Book

-> e ii <-

...greater: it should have twice the lesser: and in that way be divided by it: four beats being measured out equally into two parts in a binary division: and thus cutting it. And in all other things by a similar reasoning. And we are delighted by equality to such an extent: that we establish it not only in the intervals of voices: but even in the spaces of silences. Reason therefore asks: and the carnal soul's delight—which claimed the judicial <note>The "judicial" part of the soul is the faculty that passes judgment on whether a rhythm is harmonious or discordant.</note> parts for itself—questions: since equality soothes it in the rhythms of temporal spaces, whether any two short syllables it hears are truly equal: or if it might be that one of them is uttered more lengthily—not quite to the measure of a long syllable—but by some tiny amount by which it nonetheless exceeds its partner. Can it be denied that this might happen: that this delight of yours might not perceive it: and might rejoice in unequal things as if they were equal? What is more foul than this error and inequality? From this we are warned: to turn our joy away from these things which merely imitate equality—and whether they truly fulfill it, we cannot grasp. Indeed, perhaps we realize they do *not* fulfill it: and yet, insofar as they imitate it, we cannot deny they are beautiful in their own kind and in their own order. That equality, which we did not find to be certain and permanent in sensible rhythms <note>original: "sensibilibus numeris" — Augustine uses "numbers" to mean rhythmic proportions perceived by the senses.</note>, but which we recognized as shadowed and passing away:
<margin>☞</margin>
the soul would surely never seek it unless it were known somewhere else. But this "somewhere" is not in the spaces of places and times—for the former swell and the latter pass away—nor in the forms of bodies, which we can never call truly equal. Nor is it in the intervals of times, in which likewise we are ignorant if something passes by slightly more lengthily or briefly than it should, escaping our senses. Indeed, I seek that equality: where do you think it is? Gazing upon it, we desire certain bodies or the motions of bodies to be equal: and considering them more diligently, we do not dare to trust them. I think it is there: where that which is more excellent than bodies reigns. But let us seek whether it is in the soul itself, or even above the soul. This rhythmic art—or metrics—which those who make verses use: we think it possesses certain rhythms <note>original: "numeros"</note> according to which they fashion verses. Whatever these rhythms are, they do not pass away with the verses: but remain. It must be agreed, therefore, that from some remaining rhythms, passing ones are fashioned: and we do not think this art is anything other than a certain disposition of the artist's mind. What if someone who never learned is questioned about all things pertaining to rhythms? Do you not think he can know this art? These rhythms will not pass from the one who teaches into the one who learns: but the learner will move himself inwardly in his own mind toward something from which these rhythms may be impressed upon his mind, creating that disposition which is called "art": and he will understand that the things he is asked are true, and he will answer. Because these rhythms, about which we inquire, are unchangeable: therefore they are eternal, nor is there any inequality in them. From where, truly, is it to be believed that what is eternal and unchangeable is granted to the soul, if not from the one eternal and unchangeable God? Therefore, he who learns while another questions moves himself inwardly toward God, so that he may understand the unchangeable truth.

### ¶ The third confirmation through the mind according to Augustine. Chapter 7.

<margin>B</margin>
**S**ufficiently have we investigated our proposition through the evidence of sight first, and then through the admonitions of hearing. Now let us investigate through the evidence of reason. Every man declares his own mind in one way by speaking, attending to what is happening within himself. But he defines the human mind in another way by specific or general knowledge. And so, when he speaks to me of his own mind—whether he understands this or that, or does not understand it, and whether he wants or does not want this or that—I believe him. But when he speaks the truth concerning the human mind specifically or generally, I recognize and approve it. From which it is manifest: that one thing is what each person sees in himself, which another person believes when he speaks of it, but does not see. But another thing is in Truth itself, which another person can also behold—one of which is changed through time, while the other subsists in unchangeable eternity. Both, however...

# Theology, Book Twelve

-> 116 <-

...with bodily eyes; we see many minds by a general similarity we collect: <margin>c</margin> or by a specific knowledge of the human mind. Instead, we behold an inviolable truth. From this truth, we define as perfectly as we can: not what the mind of each individual man is, but what it ought to be according to eternal reasons <note>original: "sempiternis rationibus" — the divine archetypes or ideas in the mind of God.</note>. <margin>d</margin> Furthermore, when the wicked think of eternity, they rightly rebuke many things and rightly praise many things in the conduct of men; by what rules, finally, do they judge these things? It is not in their own selves that they see how each person ought to live, even if they themselves do not live in that same way. Where do they see them? For they do not see them in their own nature, since it is certain that these things are seen by the mind, and it is well known that their minds <margin>❧</margin> are changeable. Yet anyone who is able to see this sees that these rules are *immutable*; nor do they see them in the disposition of their own mind, <margin>e</margin> since those are rules of justice, while it is certain that their own minds are unjust. Where then are these rules written? Where does even the unjust man recognize what is just? Where does he perceive that something ought to be possessed which he himself does not have? Where then are they written, <margin>f</margin> if not in the book of that light which is called Truth? From there, every just law is transcribed and transferred into the heart of the man who works justice—not by migrating into it, but as if by being imprinted. Just as an image passes from a ring into the wax, yet it does not leave the ring. <note>This is a famous Augustinian metaphor for "Divine Illumination," where God imprints knowledge on the soul without losing anything of Himself.</note> However, he who does not act, yet still sees what ought to be done, is the one who turns away from that light by which he is nevertheless touched. But he who does not even see how one must live sins more excusably, because he is not a transgressor of an unknown law. But even he is sometimes touched by the splendor of the everywhere-present truth when, having been admonished, he confesses. Finally, this preceding Aurelian <note>original: "aureliana" — referring to Aurelius Augustine (St. Augustine).</note> discussion is concluded by four <margin>☞</margin> ends. <margin>g</margin> Namely, that the mind does not rise to the highest things unless it is drawn by the instinct of that which is highest. That it would not use eternal reasons for judging by its own choice unless it were able to equal itself to eternity. <margin>h</margin> And it would not apprehend immutable things by an immutable reason unless it touched the very rule of immutability itself. That a multitude of souls—

---

—would not thereafter grasp the truth unless there were either one single human intellect in many—which is impossible—or at least that many human intellects immersed themselves in the same fountain of truth. It is as if some people are going to understand the order of a craft best when they have penetrated the single principle <note>original: "rationem ipsam unam" — the singular logic or plan.</note> through which the craftsman had constructed the work. This opinion of Augustine is confirmed in two principal ways. First, through the common power of arguing. Second, through the common notions of truth, goodness, and the rest. <margin>a</margin> Every intellect apprehends a necessary consequence <note>original: "consequentiam" — a logical 'if-then' relationship.</note> in things, whether they are contingent or non-existent. For this consequence is necessary: "If Plato runs, Plato is moved," <note>A standard example in medieval logic used to show that the relationship between two ideas remains true even if the person (Plato) is currently sitting still or is dead.</note> even though Plato, the running, and his motion are all contingent things. Indeed, even this is necessary: "Plato once spoke while he was debating," although neither Plato, nor his disputation, nor his speech exist in the present. Therefore, such a necessity of consequences is not founded in those temporal things—which either do not exist in any way or are contingent—nor is it founded in the thoughts of the soul alone. Otherwise, it would not be a true necessity, but a fiction; indeed, it would not even be immutable, since our thinking is changeable. It is founded, therefore, in the eternal and necessary series of things, which the divine mind, as the ordainer of all, contains within itself, where it grants to things their mutual relationship. For this reason, it kindles every light of true reasoning from the first truth, and it is reflected back into the same. <margin>b</margin> Since every necessity of consequence is founded in the highest necessity of all nature. The common notions of truth and of goodness of the intelligence itself also teach this, which we proved in the sections above to be within the minds of all, from the fact that one continually compares true things and good things. <margin>c</margin> But if truth itself and goodness is God, it follows that God shines into the minds of men as often as we judge true and good things through God as a norm. The same teaches that the notion of Him is innate in all. For all men judge: that this thing in no way exists; but that this other thing exists, though in an imperfect way; and that this exists in a more perfect way. Such a gradation in being, however, neither happens nor is known...

It posits that logical rules (like those of Plato's motion) and moral laws are imprinted on the soul by God, much like a seal in wax.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of how the human mind connects to the divine. Building on the previous discussion of eternal rules of justice and truth, Ficino now moves into a more metaphysical argument: that our very ability to recognize "being" in anything requires an innate connection to the "Source of Being," which is God.</meta>

### Platonic Book

<margin>A</margin> It is known: only through access to the **highest being** <note>original: "esse summum" — the ultimate state of existence, identified here with God.</note>, which is what God is, and from there by a return. Indeed, no one can see the access to Him and the return from Him unless they see Him. However, wiser men see Him in an additional way: namely, when they resolve all the subordinate types of things into the most general classes, and those all the way up to Him; for He is **simple being** <note>original: "ens simplex" — a philosophical term for a being that is not made of parts, an attribute of the divine.</note> and absolute. Such a being is either a false fiction, or it is God. But "being" itself cannot be false, if indeed anything among things is truly real. If that comparison of the grades of things and this resolution does not happen except through that highest and absolute power of being, then it certainly happens through God. Formed by Him, the intellect compares and resolves.

<margin>B</margin> To this it is added: that "being" itself shines so clearly that it cannot be thought not to exist. For just as the thing called "nothing" occurs to us as being entirely devoid of existence, so "being" occurs to us as being entirely devoid of "not-being." Thus, through its very nature, that power does not at all tend toward non-existence, nor does it have any defect of being. From the first part, it is **eternal**. From the second, it is most full of the entire perfection of existing. That is God. For this reason, being occurs to us most evidently; and to those who consider it rightly, it occurs as God.

<margin>C</margin> This is confirmed by two further reasons. First, that "being" is so manifest that in every single thing people know, "being" itself is also always known. He who affirms that Plato runs, affirms that he **is** running. For he who calls someone a man or white, says that he **is** in the species of man, and **is** white. Finally, in every single mode of existing through which individual things remain, he understands "being" itself in the same way that he understands "animal" in all species of animals. Indeed, in cognition—which happens through that intuition—what is called "non-being" is known through "being." Potential being is known through actual being. Actual being is known through the **act of existing** <note>original: "actum existendi" — the pure state of being alive or present in reality.</note>. Such an act is Being itself. If through "being," which is the act of any entity, any entity is recognized, it follows that through Being—which is the act and origin of all existing things—all existing things are known. And if one places above "potential being" and "actual being" the concept of "being" simply—which is neither potentiality nor act—it 

<margin>D</margin> will either be a fiction, or it will be God, or a certain signification of God, as the Platonists prefer. But God is the **act** of all things and the author of all existing things; through the excess of His action, He moves the mind more vehemently and more divinely than the rest of the things that offer themselves. Rather, by His power, the rest move the mind. Therefore, **absolute being** itself—namely, the pure act and maker of all existing things, which is God—is the first thing that offers itself to minds in a certain wonderful way: that which glides in, that which shines forth, that which reveals all other things. Although we possess His forming notion in us in a certain perpetual way, through which and in which we know all other things, we nevertheless do not notice this; just as the eye does not consider that it continuously sees the light of the sun through which and in which it sees everything else; nor does the reason notice that it is continuously reasoning, even though it reasons almost always. 

<margin>E</margin> We are not usually accustomed to noticing things that have been familiar for a long time. For who considers that he is breathing? Where the Platonists call God "the highest," they want it to be understood that He is "Being"—not the being that exists within an essence, but that He is the **principle of being**; namely, that He conceives "above-being" <note>original: "super esse" — a Neoplatonic concept where God is beyond the category of 'existence' as we understand it.</note> in a certain proper way of existing, and comprehends it with a certain notion. For they call the highest Truth—the property of 

<margin>F</margin> unity and goodness, following God from God, and light from light—by the name of "Being," derived from the first Unity into three. Namely: **Essence, Life, and Mind.** And because in any of these three they are present in their own way, they lead the other three into a total of **nine** <note>original: "novenarius" — the number nine, often representing the nine orders of angels or celestial spheres in medieval thought.</note>. From this it arises that in the angels, the number nine is to be observed, and a similar grade in the "happy animals" <note>likely referring to celestial beings or souls.</note>. Indeed, they say the contemplating mind is formed by the highest God through the "head of the mind" (Unity), but by the following God through the intellect. But let them see to these matters; for us, it is sufficient that the soul is formed by divinity.

<margin>G</margin> From all the above, he concludes: that human reason, in considering the order of things, always turns around the **divine reason**, the ordainer of all things, no less than the sphere of the world turns around the center point of the world. But if a revolution that naturally and constantly circles a perpetual center is itself perpetual, then our reason must be perpetual. Since by understanding through God and in God without an intermediary, it reflects back into God...

<summary>Ficino argues that God is "Absolute Being" and the primary light through which the human mind perceives all other truths, often without realizing it. He concludes that because human reason naturally orbits this eternal divine center, the soul itself must be immortal.</summary>
<keywords>Absolute Being, divine illumination, Platonism, Trinity of Essence-Life-Mind, Ninefold Order, immortality of the soul, pure act</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the soul's immortality, specifically focusing on the relationship between the human mind, reason, and eternal truth. Ficino is drawing heavily from St. Augustine’s "Soliloquies" and "On the Immortality of the Soul" to prove that the mind must be eternal if it can grasp eternal things.</meta>

<header>Theology, Book 13, Page 117</header>

# Theology

...it testifies that it has proceeded from God without any intermediary <note>original: "sine medio" — a philosophical term meaning the soul is created directly by God, not through a secondary cause like the stars or nature.</note>. 
<margin>f</margin> Who indeed would deny that what arises directly from eternity will itself be eternal? Furthermore, the soul sees the eternal form in God—for example, it concludes by a certain logic that a form is eternal. Indeed, it sees in such a way that it receives something from that sight; it follows, therefore, that it receives perpetuity by way of that reception. And because it receives according to its own nature—if indeed it captures things through its own nature—it follows that the soul itself is perpetual, since it receives in a perpetual manner. Now this reason of ours is nothing other than **intellectual life**. Therefore, it will always live; indeed, it will always understand, if it is to exist always.

But it is helpful here, as we often do, to wander a bit more widely with **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), whose early philosophical works on the soul are the primary source for this specific argument.</note>. When we reason, it is the soul that acts. For it does not act 
<margin>g</margin> except through what it understands. Neither does the body understand, nor does the soul understand with the body’s help, since when the soul wishes to understand, it turns away from the body. For that which it understands is always of the same kind <note>i.e., universal truths like 2+2=4 do not change</note>, whereas nothing of the body is always of the same kind. Therefore, the body cannot help the soul as it strives toward understanding; it is enough if the body simply does not hinder it. If the soul reasons through itself and reaches the truth by reasoning, it has certainly reached the truth through itself. For this reason, it clings more closely to **Truth** itself (through which all true things exist) than it does to either sensible things or their images—which it does not reach through itself, but through instruments <note>the sense organs</note> and other intermediaries. For the soul could not contemplate Truth through itself without the greatest union with it. 

<margin>h</margin> Those things captured by the senses are felt to be outside of us and are contained in specific places. For this reason, it is even argued that they cannot truly be "perceived" <note>In Platonic thought, "perception" often refers to certain knowledge, which the changing physical world cannot provide.</note>. But those things which are understood are not understood as if they were placed elsewhere, because the soul that understands is there itself. For they understand simultaneously that these truths are not contained by a location. Therefore, this junction of the gazing soul and the truth it beholds must be one of three things: 
1. Either the soul is the "subject" and Truth is *in* that subject; 
2. Or conversely, Truth is the "subject" and the soul is *in* that subject; 
3. Or both are independent substances. 

Of these three, if the first is true, the soul is as immortal as that truth, because the highest reality—which adheres inseparably to the soul—cannot exist unless the soul is alive. The same necessity exists in the second case. For if that truth which reason speaks of has nothing changeable about it (as is apparent), then nothing in which it exists as a subject can be changed. 

The entire struggle, therefore, remains with the third option. For if the soul is a substance and the Reason to which it is joined is also a substance, someone might not absurdly think that it is possible for the soul to cease to exist while Reason remains. But it is manifest that as long as the soul does not separate from Reason but clings to it, 
<margin>i</margin> it is necessary for the soul to remain and to live. 
<margin>3</margin> By what force, finally, can it be separated? By the body? Its power is weaker, its origin lower, and its rank more distant. Not by any means. By another living soul, then? But that is what the soul already is. Could some other more powerful soul, whoever it may be, be unable to contemplate Reason 
<margin>13</margin> <margin>k</margin> unless it separates the other soul from it? But Reason is never lacking to any contemplator, even if everyone contemplates it at once. And since nothing is more powerful than Reason itself—because nothing is more unchangeable—in no way will a soul that is not yet joined to Reason be more powerful than one that is already joined. 

It remains, then, that either Reason itself separates itself, or the soul separates itself from Reason by its own will. But there is nothing of envy in that divine nature to prevent it from offering itself to be enjoyed by souls. Furthermore, the more a thing is "being," the more it causes whatever is joined to it to "be"; and the opposite of "being" is destruction. As for the soul being separated from Truth by its own **will**, who would say such a thing, since the soul never desires anything more greedily than to be joined to Truth?

What then? Must we now conclude that the soul is immortal? Or even if it cannot be separated, can it perhaps be extinguished? But indeed, 
<margin>Ex</margin> that power of Truth affects the soul by its very union; for it cannot fail to have an effect. It affects the soul in such a way as to grant it "being." For Truth itself is "being" in the highest degree, where the highest unchangeability is understood. Therefore, whatever Truth affects from itself, it compels to "be" in some way. Thus, the soul cannot be extinguished unless it is separated from Reason. But it cannot be separated. Therefore, it cannot perish. 

To be sure, one doubt inserts itself: that a foolish soul *seems* to be separated from Reason, and thus exists in a certain state of "defect," whereas a wise soul exists in a more certain and fuller essence. But if (as is doubtful to no one) the soul is then most wise when it gazes upon Truth—which is always the same way—then...

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by demonstrating its inseparable union with eternal Truth. He posits that since Truth is unchangeable and the soul must be joined to it to understand, the soul must share in that unchangeable nature.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the Augustinian argument from the previous page, asserting that the soul's existence is derived from eternal Truth. It then begins Book 13, shifting from purely logical "reasons" for the soul's immortality to "signs" or observable effects of the soul’s power over the body.</meta>

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>A Platonic Book</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...it remains unmoving, joined by divine love. From that essence <note>referring to God or the Supreme Truth</note> all things exist, in whatever way they exist. That essence exists in the highest and greatest degree. If something else exists, it either exists through that essence or through itself. But if it exists through itself, since it is its own cause of being and will never desert itself, it never perishes. If, however, it exists from another, we must carefully ask: what thing could be contrary to it, so as to take away from the soul the fact that it is a soul? For it is Truth that provides this. What is it then? Perhaps falsity? Because that essence is Truth? But it is manifest and readily apparent that falsity can harm no soul. For it can do nothing more than deceive, and no one is deceived unless they are alive. Therefore, falsity cannot destroy the soul. If falsity—which is the contrary of truth—cannot take away from the soul that being which Truth gave it, then Truth is truly invincible. What else can be found to take from the soul that which makes it a soul? Surely nothing. For nothing is strong enough to take away what is given by its contrary. But if we seek a contrary to Truth, let us look at it not just as truth, but as that which is in the highest and greatest degree. To the extent that a thing exists, it is life; indeed, we call those things "true" which are "truly souls." To the extent that they exist, they are true. I would by no means avoid this point, which supports me so evidently: no essence, insofar as it is an essence, has a contrary. Much less does that primary essence, which is Truth insofar as it is essence, have a contrary. For it is the "First True." Every essence is an essence for no other reason than because it *is*.

<margin>B</margin>
Now, **to be** has no contrary except **not to be**. Thus, nothing is contrary to essence. Therefore, in no way can any thing be contrary to that substance which is greatest and primary. If the soul has its very existence from that source—for it cannot have it from elsewhere, since it does not have it from itself—it must come from that thing which is superior to the soul itself. The soul has its being from nothing other than Truth. If indeed it receives its well-being from Truth alone, it follows that there is no thing that can take that being away. Because no thing is contrary to that thing from which the soul holds its being, and because of this, it does not cease to exist. As for **Wisdom**, because the soul possesses it through "turning toward" <note>original: "conuersionies" — the Platonic and Augustinian idea that the mind finds truth by turning its gaze inward or upward toward God</note> the source from which it comes, it can lose it through "turning away" <note>original: "auersione" — the root of the word 'aversion'</note>. For turning away is the opposite of turning toward. But that which the soul has from that to which nothing is contrary, it has no way to lose. Therefore, it cannot perish.

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence: Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and Ficino's primary patron.</note>.
## Book Thirteen.
### Chapter 1: How much the soul dominates the body is shown by many signs, and first from the affects of the imagination.

<margin>C</margin>
**H**itherto we have demonstrated the divinity of the soul by logical reasons. Hereafter, we shall confirm the same thing in nearly the same way by **signs** <note>Ficino here moves from abstract logic to "empirical" observations of human behavior and psychology</note>. Four affects follow the **Imagination** <term>Phantasia: in Ficino's psychology, this is the faculty that processes sensory images and can physically influence the body</term>: Appetite, Pleasure, Fear, and Pain. When these are at their most vehement, they suddenly affect one's own body entirely, and sometimes even the body of another. What great fires does the desire for revenge stir up in the heart? Or the lust for pleasure in the liver? <note>In traditional Galenic medicine, the liver was the seat of the "concupiscible" or desiring soul.</note> It even shows in the pulse; from the change in which the physician **Erasistratus** <note>A famous Greek anatomist (c. 304–250 BC)</note> recognized that **Antiochus** was captured by love for **Stratonice** <note>A famous ancient medical anecdote: Antiochus was dying of a mystery illness until the doctor noticed his pulse jumped only when his stepmother, Stratonice, entered the room.</note>. Again, how often does the desire to harm, through a frequent gaze, bewitch <note>original: "fascinat" — referring to the "Evil Eye"</note> children and others who are more soft and vulnerable? How clearly does the longing of a pregnant woman infect the tender fetus with the mark of the thing she thought of? What various gestures and figures do parents imprint upon their children—and how different from themselves—on account of the vehement imagination of diverse things by which they are affected, by some chance, while they are conceiving. This is why human beings are much more diverse among themselves in figure, gestures, and character than the individuals of any other species of animal. How often is a malicious will said, by common report, to have harmed men, cattle, and plants by its curses and sorceries...

<summary>Ficino concludes an argument that the soul's existence is granted by an eternal Truth that has no contrary, making the soul's being indestructible. He then begins Book 13, discussing how the soul's "Imagination" exerts powerful physical effects on the body, such as changing a pulse or marking a fetus.</summary>
