It specifically focuses on how imagination, emotion, and empathy manifest as physical symptoms.</meta>

<page-num>115</page-num>
**Theology of the Spirit**

# Theology

<margin>E</margin> ...Moreover, some gluttons, by thinking too eagerly of certain feasts, infect their own saliva with a similar taste. Children as well, and pregnant women—on account of an excessive longing for forbidden food, or rather a sheer greed for it—melt away, dissolve, and fall into ruin <note>The author is likely referring to the historical belief that intense cravings or "maternal impressions" could physically alter the body or a developing fetus</note>. The appetite achieves these and many similar things. Intense joy produces no less a result; it can suddenly destroy the body, yet often it lifts the burden of disease.

<margin>F</margin> Did not **Sophocles** and **Dionysius**, the tyrant of Sicily, die suddenly, both upon receiving news of a victory in a tragedy competition? <note>Sophocles was a famous Greek playwright; Dionysius I of Syracuse reportedly died after drinking heavily to celebrate winning a prize at the Lenaea festival</note>. A father, upon seeing his son returning from the battle of **Cannae**, suddenly expired. <note>The Battle of Cannae (216 BCE) was a disastrous Roman defeat by Hannibal; according to legend, some mothers and fathers died of joy when children reported dead actually returned</note>. On the other hand, no one is ignorant of what grief can do. Even the mere distress caused by a foul sight infects the sense of taste and provokes nausea by the look of it alone. Children, and even older people, when they see a bitter potion being offered to someone else, immediately feel a bitter saliva in their own mouths, moved by a powerful imagination.

<margin>G</margin> Sometimes, by such a thought, the bowels are even loosened. And what is more marvelous: for some, the teeth feel "blunted" or numb, triggered by certain sights and sounds. What of mercy, which is a kind of pain? Does it not sometimes affect the body of the one feeling pity so badly that they feel as if their own body were the one afflicted? This is shown by those who, at the sight of human blood, immediately fall into a faint as their spirit fails them, and those whose own elbow hurts while they see or hear of another's elbow being wounded.

<margin>H</margin> What of fear? Do we not often grow dizzy with dread and tremble when looking down to the ground from high windows? Sometimes we even fall. Those who are afraid suddenly grow pale, just as the bashful blush. With sudden fear, the heart pounds, the hair stands on end, and the **voice sticks in the throat**. <note>original: "Vox faucibus heret," a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid</note>. Life itself may fail, or long-lasting illnesses may follow. Yet, sometimes fear cures certain diseases, such as hiccups and **quartan fever**. <note>term: quartan fever; a form of malaria where paroxysms occur every fourth day</note>. However, when the most intense fear meets with the most intense desire, a marvelous effect sometimes occurs.

<margin>I</margin> Hence, as told in **Herodotus**: when a certain Persian wanted to kill King **Croesus**—

---

<margin>K</margin> —the son of **Croesus**, who had previously been mute, suddenly loosed his tongue because of his immense fear of his father's death combined with his desire to cry out. He shouted with a great voice: "O man, do not kill Croesus!" From then on, he was able to speak. For this reason, those four "affections" <note>the four classical passions: joy, desire, fear, and grief</note> rule the body completely, since they change it in every way. Moreover, these are the movements of the soul itself. For as much as the soul judges a thing to be good or evil, so much does it desire, rejoice, fear, or grieve. From this, it follows that the nature of the body is entirely subject to the movements of the soul. Hence it happens that the human face bears both clear signs of the soul's inclinations and the most certain evidence of individual emotions. The former are understood only by **physiognomists**, but the latter even common people understand. Who would not easily recognize a soul that is desiring, fearing, angry, rejoicing, or mourning? Thus it happens, again, that man alone laughs and man alone weeps, because the movements of the soul have the greatest command over the body. From the fact that the body is entirely subject to the movements of the rational soul, we infer two things. First: that this soul is a most excellent form, subsisting through itself, because a form that exists only through a body could not dominate that body. Second: that the human body yields most easily to its soul.

<margin>L</margin> It does not yield easily because it is solid or hard (due to an abundance of the element "earth"). Therefore, if our body is compared to other animals, it possesses the least amount of earth, and even that is of a subtle kind. It possesses a great deal of the more "sublime" elements. For this reason, it is a **celestial receptacle** for the soul.

<margin>M</margin> Proof of this matter can be found in the fact that the most ingenious men are often soft of flesh, slender, and sickly; their bodies are altered by even the smallest of their own movements. We read this concerning **Aristotle**, **Pyrrho**, **Speusippus**, **Carneades**, **Lysippus**, and **Plotinus**. <note>A list of ancient philosophers known for their intellectual vigor despite physical frailty or sensitive temperaments</note>. **Plato** sensed this when he said that God could have made the human body so solid that it would be minimally harmed by external things <note>but chose instead to make it delicate to better serve the soul</note>.

...is introduced, it is a controversy rather than a destruction. For nothing is destroyed by itself.

### Concerning Philosophers. The Second Sign from the Dispositions of Reason. Chapter II.

<margin>E</margin> We have sufficiently narrated how our soul is the mistress of the body through the dispositions of the imagination. We read that the same is indicated, in part, by the dispositions of reason. Let us pursue this part more extensively. In this category, we place philosophers, poets, priests, diviners, and prophets. <margin>F</margin> They say that **Epimenides of Crete** slept for fifty years; that is, in my opinion, he lived withdrawn from the senses. Similarly, it is said that **Pythagoras** remained hidden for ten years, <margin>G</margin> and **Zoroaster** for twenty. **Socrates** (as **Plato** writes) stood from one sunrise until the next, unblinking and motionless in the same tracks, with his face and eyes directed toward the same spot, deep in thought and abstracted from his body. When Plato, through the intensity of frequent contemplation, had long withdrawn himself from the body, he finally departed entirely from his bodily bonds during that very state of abstraction. His disciple **Xenocrates** was abstracted from the body for a full hour every day. **Archimedes of Syracuse**, intent on his geometric figures, did not even notice the tumultuous destruction of his falling homeland or the enemy looming over his head. **Porphyry**, the disciple of **Plotinus**, writes that Plotinus was often accustomed to being released from the body, causing his facial expression to change. At such times, he discovered certain wonders which he would later write down. Porphyry asserts that he himself was present for these miracles of Plotinus four times. He also affirms that once, while he was in his sixty-eighth year, he himself was seized by the divine during contemplation. We read that **Heraclitus** and **Democritus** did the same many years before them. Both withdrew into solitude. One, through the intensity of his study, appeared somewhat mournful in his look. The other, when he began to call his mind away from the senses and found himself hindered by his eyes, blinded himself. <margin>H</margin> Why say more? Whoever has discovered anything great in any of the more noble arts did so especially when, having departed from the body, they fled into the <term>citadel of the mind</term> <note>original: "arcem animi," a Stoic and Platonic concept referring to the highest, most rational part of the soul where it is safe from physical distraction</note>. Hence Plato writes in the *Phaedrus* that the minds of philosophers especially recover the wings by which they fly to divine things, because they are always devoted to the divine. Elsewhere he calls them "divine men," and in another place "sons of God," because they are in a sense reborn from God. For this reason, **Aristotle** writes that all men who have excelled in any art were <term>melancholics</term> <note>Ficino refers to the famous pseudo-Aristotelian "Problem 30.1," which asks why all great philosophers, statesmen, and poets are melancholic</note>, <margin>J</margin> whether they were born as such or became so through constant meditation. I believe this happens because the nature of the melancholic humor follows the quality of the earth, which is never spread out widely like the other elements, but is more tightly contracted into itself. Thus, the melancholic humor both invites and helps the soul to collect itself within itself. Conversely, if the soul frequently collects its spirits within itself in this way, the subtle parts of the humors are dissolved by the continuous agitation, making the <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in the body</note> of the body much more earthy than it was initially—especially since the soul, by collecting itself, makes the physical condition more compressed. <margin>K</margin> Such is the nature of the earth. I pass over the fact that such is also the nature of **Mercury** and **Saturn**; while they collect the spirits into the center, they recall the sharp edge of the mind from external things to its own, fixing it in contemplation and directing it toward penetrating the centers of things. Nevertheless, the planets or humors of this kind do not act as the <term>efficient causes</term> <note>An "efficient cause" is the primary source of a change or effect; Ficino is arguing that biology and astrology provide the opportunity, but the soul itself does the work</note>, but rather provide the occasion or repel hindrances. The mind itself, both invited and unhindered, accomplishes such things. Truly great is the empire of the mind, which by its own power is released from the shackles of the body. Vast is the wealth <margin>3</margin> of the mind, which, as often as it desires the precious treasures of God and nature, digs them out not from the bowels of the earth, but from its own bosom. This is most clearly seen in how much reason dominates the body in those who, having led a shameful youth, suddenly, before old age itself, either through the inspiration of God or...

<margin>A</margin>
...by the exhortation of a man, they change their morals in such a way that from being intemperate, they emerge as temperate or self-controlled. **Polemo** <note>A wealthy Athenian youth known for his profligacy who was converted to philosophy after stumbling into a lecture by Xenocrates while drunk.</note> is said to have done this immediately on the same day he heard **Xenocrates** disputing about modesty. Likewise, **Diogenes** did the same when he heard **Antisthenes** discoursing on liberty. Nature is accustomed to abolish only over a long time whatever she has built up over a long time. Therefore, to shatter in a single moment a habit strengthened by long-standing custom is not a power of a physical nature, but of a higher and divine one.

### On Poets.

<margin>B</margin>
**F**urthermore, consider the poets, whom **Democritus** and **Plato** assert are seized by a certain <term>divine frenzy</term> <note>original: "divino quodam furore"; a state of inspiration where the soul is "possessed" by a higher power, transcending normal human reason.</note>. This is shown by two of Plato’s dialogues: the *Phaedrus* and the *Ion*. He brings forward three signs of this. First, that individual men barely master individual arts over a long time without God’s help. Yet the "legitimate" poets—among whom he includes **Orpheus**, **Homer**, **Hesiod**, and **Pindar**—inserted certain clear signs and proofs of *all* the arts into their works. Second, that while in their frenzy they sing many things—and wonderful ones at that—which they themselves do not sufficiently understand shortly after their frenzy cools down. It is as if they did not speak the words themselves, but God cried out through them as if through trumpets. Third, it is not the most prudent or those most highly educated from an early age who turn out to be the best poets. On the contrary, some who were rather childlike—as is well known of **Homer** and **Lucretius**—or those quite unrefined—as **Hesiod** testifies of himself and as Plato writes of **Ion** and **Tynnichus of Chalcis** <note>OCR reads "Lyrnicuz," referring to Tynnichus, whom Plato calls the creator of the "loveliest of all lyrics" despite having no other talent.</note>. These men, despite having no training, suddenly emerged as wonders in poetic matters. He adds that certain very inept men are seized in their minds for this reason: because divine providence wishes to declare to the human race that noble poems are not human inventions, but celestial gifts. He offers this sign of it in the *Phaedrus*: that no one, however diligent and learned in all the arts, has ever excelled in poetry unless he was joined by that more fervent stirring of the mind which we feel when <note>original: "Est Deus in nobis agitante: calescimus illo. impetus ille sacre semina mentis habet." A quote from Ovid's *Fasti*.</note> "God is within us; when he moves, we grow warm. That impulse holds the seeds of a sacred mind." Let us come to the priests.

### On Priests.

<margin>D</margin>
**T**he writings and deeds of his disciples show that the theologian **Paul** <note>St. Paul the Apostle.</note> ascended the three celestial hierarchies—namely the heavens—during a divine <term>abstraction</term> <note>original: "abstractione"; the state of the soul being "drawn away" or separated from the physical senses and the body.</note> of the mind. Likewise, long ago, some men of Galilee <note>The Apostles.</note> suddenly, by God’s inspiration, turned from fishermen into the highest theologians. All antiquity testifies that many priests before these times were accustomed to be driven into a frenzy by the instinct of spirits and to utter certain wonders. **Aulus Gellius** writes that **Cornelius**, a most chaste priest, was moved in his mind by a sudden awe at the very time **Caesar** and **Pompey** were clashing in Thessaly; he saw both the time, the order, and the outcome of the battle. **Pliny** also relates that the soul of **Hermon of Clazomenae** was accustomed to wander, leaving its body behind, and to announce many true things from far away—until his enemies (who were called Cantharidae) burned his body and thus took away the "scabbard" from his returning soul. **Maximus Tyrius**, the Platonist, and **Herodotus** write that the soul of **Aristeas of Proconnesus** used to do the same. **Aurelius Augustine** mentions a priest
<margin>E</margin>
of Calama who was accustomed to call himself away from his body at his own will, especially when a plaintive harmony soothed him. "He lay there," he says, "very much like a dead man, without breath; and when he was burned or cut, he did not feel it." Once awakened, however, he said that he had sensed nothing during that abstraction except the melody itself and the voices of people speaking. This signifies that the soul was not then working within the body—since there was no movement, nor sense of touch, nor breath—yet it was doing something within itself, since it pondered the harmony heard earlier and perceived voices. And if that **Cornelius**, **Hermon**, and **Aristeas**, whom I mentioned above, had seen nothing distant after they had withdrawn themselves from the body, then the soul would not live more freely and wander more widely when it is released from this little body. Nor would the priest of Calama’s soul have withdrawn itself from the body by its own will and acted as something separate if it were entirely the handmaiden of its body. So much for these matters. Plato...

# Theology

<margin>F</margin>
...these words appear to be confirmed in the *Phaedrus* <note>original: "phedro"; one of Plato’s dialogues concerning the soul and beauty.</note>. He says that he who makes correct use of divine meditations, and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, alone truly emerges as perfect. Withdrawn from human pursuits and always clinging to the divine power, he is perceived by the common people as if he were out of his mind; yet, being full of God, he remains hidden from the common crowd.

->**On Soothsayers and Prophets.**<-

<margin>G</margin>
**H**aving spoken first of philosophers, poets, and priests, let us now speak of soothsayers and prophets. I would be forced to be more long-winded if I were to commemorate <term>augurs</term> <note>priests who interpreted the will of the gods through the flight of birds</note>, <term>haruspices</term> <note>diviners who inspected the entrails of sacrificed animals</note>, <term>auspices</term>, <term>mathematicians</term> <note>original: "mathematicos"; in this context, it refers to astrologers who calculated planetary positions to predict the future</note>, and magi. The minds of those most skilled in these matters indicate their works. Indeed, those divine presages <note>original: "præfagia"; omens or forewarnings</note> indicate such things above all others, as Plato argues in the *Phaedrus*: those which occur without art or deliberate counsel. Such are the things which Plato relates concerning the <term>Mantinean prophetess</term> <note>original: "votina vate"; likely a reference to Diotima of Mantinea from Plato's *Symposium*</note>, and Socrates, and Epimenides. Or what **Varro**, along with Plato, relates regarding the <term>Sibyls</term> <note>original: "syllabis"; a common Renaissance spelling for Sibyllis, the female oracles of antiquity</note>; what historians narrate regarding the Pythian oracles, and what almost all philosophers—especially the Platonists—confirm. These are things which everyone experiences regarding dreams, and which the Hebrews hand down concerning the divine prophets. At those times especially, their minds surveyed many places and embraced three times in one <note>past, present, and future</note> whenever they separated themselves from the body. Therefore, when the soul of a man is entirely separated from the body, it will comprehend every place and every time, as is the belief among the Egyptians. Indeed, the soul is already almost of such a nature in its own part—everywhere and always—that it may look around at many and most remote places. And so that it may recall the whole of past time and anticipate the future, it is not now forced to go outside of itself; but, having left the body and returned into itself, it attains this precisely—either because by its own nature it is everywhere and always (according to its own choice), or because when it receives itself back into its own nature, it is immediately joined to the divine power, which comprehends all boundaries of places and times. For the rest, let us repeat from a deeper source how it is that a presage falls into the soul.

<margin>H</margin>
Three orders of things appear to belong to the human soul: <term>Providence</term>, <term>Fate</term>, and <term>Nature</term>. Providence is the series of Minds. Fate is the series of Souls. Nature is the series of Bodies. In the beginning, under God, we place those Minds entirely released from the body according to Plato, whom **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who organized the hierarchy of angels</note> calls the purest angels: the Intellects. We add a lower grade of Minds, namely those which are already united to bodies and appear to be like certain angels, obtaining in a way the lowest grade of angels. In their number are all rational souls, whether of the world <note>the World-Soul</note>, or of the mundane spheres, the stars, <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demonū"; in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note>, and men. In the third place are the globes of the heavens, of the elements, and of the humors. Accordingly, God is the head of the angels; He, sending out His ray—endowed with the reasons for creating all things—through all the angels, forms all things step by step, so that in each individual He describes the universal figure of the world. Thus He alone adorns those sublime Intellects and purest angels, but also through them (as intermediaries) He leads the same ray into the minds of rational souls
<margin>I</margin>
as if into certain "lowest angels." This ray is endowed with those same "reasons" <note>the divine blueprints or forms</note>. This disposition of things, and the divine law inscribed on minds, is called **Providence**. Fate follows.
<margin>K</margin>
For rational souls not only have that power of understanding by which they are angelic and are numbered in the order of Providence, but also that life-giving and governing power of the body, which nourishes the body within the body, perceives physical things through the body, moves the body through space, and rules it in its place. The Platonists call this power the <term>idolum</term> <note>original: "idolu.i. simulacrū"; an image or "shadow-soul" that acts as the interface between the rational mind and the physical body</note>, that is, the "image" of the rational soul. In this "image" are the seeds of all motions and qualities which are unfolded from the soul into the body.
<margin>L</margin>
Therefore, rational souls have both those powers which are above us—the divine powers of understanding—and these life-giving, governing faculties of bodies. **Nature** follows. For in any animated body there is a certain specific affection, or an effective and vital "complexion," which the life-giving virtue of its soul grants to the body. This is what the Platonists want "Nature" to be in bodies: as it were, a certain vestige <note>trace</note> of the soul in the body, or a shadow. It is divisible along with the division of the body...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's metaphysical architecture. Having discussed the "divine madness" of prophets and poets on the previous page, he now transitions into a technical explanation of how the universe is linked together—from the highest God down to the lowest physical body—through a series of "chains" or "ladders."</meta>

# Platonic Book

...and full of <note>The text continues from the previous page describing a soul filled with divine inspiration.</note> it: and the life of the body flowing from the life of the soul. Let us resume in this manner. All minds—whether they be sublime and positioned above souls, or inferior and instilled within souls—are so connected to one another that, beginning from God who is their head, they proceed in a long and continuous series. Whichever minds are superior distribute their rays to the inferior ones. Let us see what arises from this. When someone taps the very top of a straight piece of wood lying on the ground with their finger, the vibration—even the slightest—resonates all the way to the other end of the wood. The same occurs in a stretched string. If its tip is touched, the whole string trembles and sounds. If you tune two strings on a lyre to the same interval, when one is plucked, the other trembles as well. If you tune two separate lyres to the same tension of strings, when one sounds, the other echoes back. What is the purpose of this? It is so we may understand that here, from the mutual and harmoniously tempered connection of all minds, the same thing occurs: sparks from the highest minds shine into the middle ones, and from the middle into the lowest, until they shine through entirely; and from the last, they are reflected back through the middle ones <margin>A</margin> into the sublime again. This mutual connection of theirs, and this infusion of sparks continually flowing down from the superior to the inferior, we call **Providence**.

Let us set aside "minds" for the moment. Let us consider the <term>images</term> <note>original: "idola"; in this Neoplatonic context, an "idolum" is the lower "shadow" or "image" of the soul that directly animates and governs matter.</note>, that is, the likenesses of souls. Let the head of all be the **Image of the World-Soul**. To this are connected twelve images of the twelve souls that move the twelve celestial spheres. Since there are not many souls in any one sphere, let the images of these be bound back to a single image of a single and common soul which rules that entire sphere. <margin>B</margin> And thus all images of rational souls hang from one supreme image through a certain mutual harmonious alignment <note>original: "conspiratio"; literally a "breathing together" or resonance.</note>. This is arranged so that any nod or impulse of the first image passes into the middle ones, and from the middle into the lowest; and the seeds of all corporeal things are sown by the first images into the images that follow. This kind of harmonious alignment and the transfer of seeds we judge to be **Fate**.

By the same reasoning, let us proceed through bodies. The complexions—whether they be affections or the twelve natures of the twelve spheres—are coupled to the one supreme nature of mundane matter itself.

---

Indeed, the individual nature of every small body adhering to any sphere is similarly referred back to the universal nature of its own sphere. This dependent series is called the **Natural Chain**. In this chain, the instinct of the superior natures is poured into the inferior natures. Thus, all minds are like lights directed toward one Mind as the Source-Light. All the images and likenesses of souls are directed toward one image of the Universal Soul. <margin>C</margin> All the natures of bodies, being like shadows of souls, are led back to the common nature of the one Body, just as shadows are led back to a single soul.

Our soul is connected to the superior minds through its own head—that is, the **Mind**. Through its lowest power—that is, the **Image** by which it rules the body—it aligns harmoniously with the images of the superior souls. Through the nature of its own body, into which the image insinuates itself, it is reconciled to the nature of the mundane body. The nature of this body follows those higher ones. Therefore, we are tied to the whole machine of the world by these three, as if by three ropes: Mind to Minds; Image to Images; Nature to Natures. It is not unlike how a fetus in the womb is connected to the entire maternal body through continuous ligaments. Wherefore, the soul perceives the passions of the maternal soul, body, and spirit through its own soul, body, and spirit.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, the soul, by way of its Mind, is **above Fate**, existing only in the order of Providence; it imitates the celestial things and governs the lower things together with them. For the soul itself, as a participant in Providence, rules itself, its home, the city, the arts, and animals according to the model of divine government. By way of its Image, it is similarly in the order of Fate, but **not under Fate**. Insofar as it is our soul, its Image concurs by its own nature with the superior images to form and move the body. However, by way of its Nature, the body is **under Fate**. The Soul, acting *in* Fate, moves Nature.

Therefore:
*   The **Mind** is above Fate, in Providence.
*   The **Image** is in Fate, above Nature.
*   The **Nature** is under Fate, above the Body.

Thus, the soul is placed within the laws of providence, fate, and nature, not merely as a passive recipient, but as an active agent. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, Plato says in the tenth book of the *Republic*: *The virtue of the soul is not servile;* and again, he calls the *Daimon* <note>a guardian spirit or guiding inner voice</note> the leader of life, and yet again, the fortune of life...

<summary>Ficino explains the "Great Chain of Being," describing how the human soul acts as a bridge between divine Providence and physical Fate through its three levels: Mind, Image, and Nature. He uses analogies of vibrating lyre strings to illustrate how influence resonates from God down to the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Providence, Fate, Nature, hierarchy of being, World-Soul, Mind, Image, celestial spheres, Plato's Republic, resonance analogy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s technical analysis of the soul's structure. Following his discussion on the "chains" of Providence that link all minds together, he now moves into the specific anatomy of the human soul—dividing it into the "Mind" (angelic), "Reason" (human), and "Idol" (animal/bodily)—to explain how we possess free will despite the existence of Fate.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>f</margin> ...that a just choice is made by us, and not by a demon or by fortune. The fault belongs to the one choosing, not to God. Zoroaster also understands it this way: **Do not increase your fate.** <note>original Greek: "mē t' augeas tautas ekarpenthēkēs." Ficino attributes this quote from the *Chaldean Oracles* to Zoroaster. It suggests that while some things are predestined, we should not add further burdens to ourselves through poor choices.</note> This is as if to say it is within your own judgment to yield to fate or not to yield. While we are bound by three of these parts—partly to the order of things <note>Ficino refers to the physical laws of the universe.</note> and partly not—it is through the fourth part especially that we are set free and are entirely our own masters. This is the act of "Decreeing," which we place in the middle between the **Mind** (the head of the soul) and the **Idol** (the foot of the soul). For the "Mind" exists within the soul, not insofar as it is strictly "soul," but insofar as it is "angelic" and occupied by higher minds. That **Idol** <term>Idolum: in Neoplatonism, this refers to the lower "image" or reflection of the soul that governs the physical body and its instincts.</term> of the soul—that is, the power that governs the body—is not the pure office of the soul, but belongs to the soul when it is already leaning toward the body. 

**Reason** is placed in the center. Here are found certain properties of true souls, through which one runs through universal concepts, moving from the principles of things to conclusions in a sequence of time. They resolve effects back into causes, and lead causes back again into effects. They run through particular concepts as well, following the pattern of universal discourse. But in the first part, where the process is truly "intellectual," it should be called discursive thought. In particular discourse, Reason acts as the "thinker" and the "opinion-maker."

<margin>B</margin> However, that **Mind**—which is the head and the charioteer <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as a charioteer driving two horses.</note> of the soul—imitates the angels by its own nature. It achieves what it desires not through a sequence of steps, but in a single moment. Indeed, through a certain "habit"—as Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism and Ficino's primary philosophical influence.</note> wishes—it contains all things simultaneously in act. And rightly, after this stable Mind of the soul which imitates the angels, there follows the mobile **Reason** which is the soul's own characteristic. Following after Reason are those brute powers of sensing which are in the "Idol": namely, the "confused phantasy" (which follows natural instinct) and the "imagination" (the gatherer of the five senses). Nature follows as the servant of the Idol. 

Philosophers compare our **Mind** to our own private sun; our **Reason** to the light of this sun; the **Idol** to a ray of this light; and **Nature** to the reflection and splendor of the ray—or to speak more correctly, to a "Platonic shadow." And so that it may return to the power of the rational, they often say that Reason relates to the Mind just as—

---

<margin>B</margin> —speech seems to relate to the soul; it exists in perpetual and free motion. Finally, that rational faculty, which is the true and proper nature of the soul, is not determined toward any single thing. For it wanders up and down with free movement. For the "first motion" is that which is located in the soul’s own nature, of which the soul itself is the "third essence," <note>Ficino famously defined the soul as the "Third Essence" or "Center of Nature," the knot that ties the divine/eternal world to the physical/temporal world.</note> and its power is self-moving. This "first motion," however, is not just this specific movement or that one. It is not carried only here or only there; it is a universal motion, flowing freely like a fountain of movement, gliding through all parts at every moment.

<margin>E</margin> For this reason, while the soul is in a way subjected to the common order of things through the "Mind," the "Idol," and "Nature"—specifically under **Providence** through the Mind, under **Fate** through the Idol, and under **Universal Nature** through its own particular nature—you, through our **Reason**, are entirely under your own jurisdiction. We are, as it were, set loose, following now these parts, now those. For Reason clings to the Mind when it rises into Providence. Yet it is covered by the Idol and Nature when it submits to Fate through a certain love of its own, while, trusting in the senses, it is distracted here and there by the encounter with sensible things. Sometimes, leaving other things aside, it withdraws into itself, where it either investigates other things through arguing, or examines its own self. To such an extent is this middle power both the soul's own and free, yet restless. 

And whenever something falls upon our extremes—say, into the Mind, the Idol, or Nature—it is possible for the soul to perceive it immediately in some way. However, it does not "notice" that it is perceiving it until the perception passes into the **middle power** (Reason). Since the middle power is that by which we are human—indeed, it is what we *are*—whatever pertains to it most evidently pertains to the human being. Colors often move the eyes, or voices move the ears. Immediately, sight and hearing fulfill their office. This person sees, and that one hears. Yet the soul does not yet notice that it sees or hears unless our middle power directs itself toward this. This is clear in those who do not perceive people they pass on the street while they are thinking intensely about something else.

<margin>Et</margin> Thus, the superior minds are always in motion.

# Platonic Book

# Platonic Theology

...our mind is joined to them. Yet we do not notice an impulse of this kind because the "middle path" <note>Reason, which sits between the higher Mind and the lower Idol</note>, wandering through lower things, turns away from higher ones. By the same logic, the **idols** <term>Idolum: The "shadow" or lower reflection of a soul that governs a body. Ficino believes even celestial bodies have these.</term> of superior souls are always striking <margin>A</margin> our own **idol**. We hardly recognize this influx when that middle part is gazing more firmly at something else. Similarly, the natures of larger bodies <note>The elements and the heavens</note> continually provoke the nature of our own body. We by no means notice this instinct for the very same reason. We have an example of this thing in the body. For often, provoked by no external thing, we <margin>B</margin> grow angry within ourselves. Troubled by no evils, terrified by no news or portents, we become sluggish, we grieve, and we tremble; soothed by no good things, we rejoice within ourselves and sing. From where do these things come? For certainly such new effects must have a new cause. This is surely the various affection of the body at different times: whether yellow bile boils in the gall or liver, or black bile seethes in the spleen, or the heart rejoices in bright blood. These types of bodily affections and natures—since they are nearest to the life-giving power that is contained by the **idol** and which the **idol** itself contains—incite it with various pulses, providing occasions so that the **idol** acts upon the temperament of the body to be enlivened in a way different than usual. This operation, having been rendered into a stir of the power of feeling (since it is contained by that same **idol**), especially tickles the sense of touch or secretly pricks the **imagination** of that same **idol**, just as the stomach is pricked by a natural lack. That pricking and hidden tickling does not pass to the middle part of the soul [Reason] when it is gaping after something else. However, it does pass when it is at leisure. Then, through the thinking reason, we suddenly grow angry in a certain way, or we grieve, or we rejoice. The intellectual reason notices these things. Hence, it sometimes gives its assent. Sometimes, through counsel and remedies, it flees from them and puts them to flight. In summary, we are often struck by these affections in a long order <margin>B</margin> descending into us from universal natures through our own nature, and we are utterly ignorant of where they are being thrust upon us. If this is so, why...

# Book

...should the superior minds joined to our mind not also always strike it? We may notice the impulse very little when our middle part is so occupied with actions that the influx of the mind does not pass through to it. Truly, when it is vacant, what prevents some angelic thought from creeping into the rational powers? And we might not see from where it creeps in. This is indicated by those who, without a teacher, from the mere intention of a vacant reason or even from tranquility, have often found many and most excellent things even while they were not seeking them—as if the light of the sun spontaneously pours itself into the air. And although the disposition of the world—which exists all at once in the minds and reasons of the supernal souls—offers itself all at once to our mind through a certain perennial continuation <margin>C</margin> in time, yet the sequence of "worldly seeds" <note>the causal principles or blueprints of events</note> follows itself just as it does gradually in the **idol** and the natures of those [higher] souls. In a similar succession and continuation, it descends through the **idols** of all souls and the natures of all bodies down to the **idol** of our soul and the nature of our body. Thus, the logic of rain that will happen tomorrow rightly reigns today in the **idols** of celestial souls and the natures of the heavens. The same flows down through the **idols** of the elementary souls and the natures of the elements, until the moisture strikes the **idol** of our soul and our nature simultaneously. The striking of our **idol** is done by those higher **idols**; the striking of our nature is done by those higher natures and our own **idol**. When that influx finds our middle reason idle—or rather, the mind being vacant—it shows to it something of those things which pertain to the universal and eternal knowledge of things, or to the government of the world. Thus, it may foresee either the law of God and the orders of angels, or the restorations of the ages and the mutations of kingdoms. When the instinct of the **idols** and natures strikes the reason and imagination while they are entirely vacant, it portends something to it regarding the changes of the times and the disturbances of the elements—so that it may foresee future rains, earthquakes, and similar things.

<summary>Ficino explains how the human soul receives "impulses" from both higher angelic minds and lower physical natures, though we only perceive them when our active reasoning mind is at rest. This process allows for the "spontaneous" discovery of truths and the ability to foresee future events like weather changes or political shifts.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, psychology, Neoplatonism, prophecy, humors, Reason, Mind, Idolum, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

He is now moving into a detailed physiological and metaphysical explanation of how celestial influences and bodily humors combine to create mental images, leading into his famous discourse on the "seven types of withdrawal" (vacatio) where the soul can detach from the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>322</page-num>
<header>Theology</header>
<sig>Q 2</sig>

# Theology

<margin>D</margin>
**B**y what path does this occur? Because the wheel of the heavens is destined to bring forth rains from those higher **idols** <term>Idolum: A "reflection" or lower power of a soul. Here, Ficino refers to the celestial influences that govern the elements.</term>, and the air is made damp. This moist air moves our **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"</note>, which is an aqueous humor. The phlegm then moves the **spirit** <term>Spiritus: In Renaissance medicine, a thin, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the immaterial soul.</term>, specifically in that part where the spirit itself is watery. Since the spirit is a vapor of the blood, and four humors exist within the blood, the powers of the four humors and elements also exist within the spirit. Therefore, that watery power of the spirit, irritated by the phlegm, goads the life-giving power of our soul in that specific part where the life-giving force possesses the "seeds" of aquatic things. Then, this soul-power stirs up those images which, in the resting **phantasy** <term>Phantasia: The faculty of the mind that stores and combines sensory images.</term> and reason, pertain to phlegm; thus we suddenly think of rivers, rain, snakes, eels, fish, and similar things. In the same way, the power of the higher beings destined to produce heat and summer-glow moves the **choler** (that is, yellow bile) within us through appropriate means, as well as the choleric spirit. This spirit then moves the life-giving power, and this power stirs the fiery images lying hidden in the phantasy and reason, so that we imagine fires and red or yellow colors.

### The Seven Kinds of Withdrawal

<margin>E</margin>
**B**ut when are we at leisure in such a way that we notice these kinds of influences? There are seven kinds of **withdrawal** <note>original: "vacatio." This refers to the soul "taking a holiday" or withdrawing from its duties of governing the physical body.</note>. We withdraw by: sleep, fainting, the melancholic humor, a temperate complexion, solitude, wonder, and chastity. Since the soul fulfills its operations of moving and sensing in this denser body through the spirit which is nearest to it, it follows that when—either because of the exhaustion of the spirit in the outer senses, or because those passages of the brain are filled with vapors and humors through which such spirits (fit for sensation and movement) are usually transmitted to the limbs—then the soul collects itself in a certain way. It is then occupied neither in sensing bodily qualities, nor in ruling and moving the limbs of its body, nor in handling external business; this happens easily in sleep. Moreover, the more the external act is relaxed, the more the internal act is intensified. The internal acts are the visions of the phantasy and the discourses of reason.

<margin>F</margin>
But most often the phantasy—at whose nod we perform many things—acts in such a way that it revolves its own images within itself with a very sharp gaze. Those revolved images shine back even more sharply toward that **common sense** which, in the Platonic manner, we call **imagination** <term>Imaginatio: Ficino uses this specifically for the "internal sense" that receives images from both the external world and the internal phantasy.</term>. From there, they reflect into the lower senses and the spirit. Indeed, an image reflecting in the senses and the spirit is usually asserted to be a "real thing." For waking men say they "see" when they turn themselves toward the image of a man flashing in their senses. Similarly, those who are sleeping affirm they "see" men when the image of a man shines back from the phantasy (which preserves it) through the imagination into the sense and the spirit. However, those images shine out more than others toward which the phantasy is more affected—whether a previous thought or disturbance causes this, or the present tumult of the dominant humors. And these **insomnia** <note>Ficino uses the Latin term for "vain dreams" that carry no prophetic weight.</note> are empty and offer nothing of prophecy; for they are born either from the remnants of waking life or from the turbulence of the body. Men devoted to a life of pleasure are usually deluded by such dreams, as they are vehemently affected by things that move the senses; their phantasy fixes upon these things most sharply, either to be accepted as good or rejected as evil. The result is that the remnants of these things disturb the phantasy in sleep. Furthermore, those weighed down by excessive food or drink never have an unhindered phantasy in sleep.

<margin>G</margin>
For because of the immoderate redundancy of humors and vapors, those images are often moved in the phantasy which present foul spectacles. In these people, because the heat of wine incites the power that expels the reproductive seed, images of a loved person (which the phantasy preserves) are moved, from which an embrace is imagined.

<margin>H</margin>
From these reasons, Plato concludes in the ninth book of the *Republic* that reason is often so occupied in sleep that it does not freely perceive higher influences. He says, however, that the soul will perceive the truth whenever it is not disturbed. There are also many who despise a life of pleasure but are nevertheless studious of civil matters...

<summary>Ficino explains how celestial influences interact with the body's humors to create specific dreams and introduces the seven ways the soul withdraws from the body to gain higher knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's withdrawal from the body during sleep. He is specifically categorizing different types of dreamers based on their temperaments—from the worldly and ambitious to the contemplative philosopher and the "vacant" pious man—and explaining how these states affect the accuracy of divine or natural premonitions.</meta>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>
<sig>I 2</sig>

...or the impious and those greedy for glory. In these people, while they are sleeping, even the **phantasy** <term>Phantasia: The mental faculty that processes and stores sensory images.</term> is sometimes lulled to sleep. But then **reason** <note>original: "rō" (ratio)</note> treats both private and public business, and is very occupied with them. 

There are some who are despisers of both pleasures and human glory, but are devoted to the investigation of divine and natural things. In their sleep, sometimes not only the phantasy ceases, but also the anxious consultation of the **active reason** <note>The practical part of the mind concerned with worldly actions and moral choices.</note>. However, that accustomed investigation of the **speculative reason** <note>The higher part of the mind concerned with the contemplation of universal truths and theoretical knowledge.</note> rises up again, so that the soul seems either to measure the heavens, or to divide the elements, or to count the species of animals. 

**Prophecy** <term>Vaticinium: The ability to foresee future events or hidden truths, often through divine or natural inspiration.</term> does not commonly happen to any of those we have listed, unless these last ones—who are truly philosophizing—reason even while sleeping. From this, they sometimes find what they had sought for a long time while awake but had not found, because **reason** is then more tranquil. 

<margin>A</margin> Something like this happened to **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose works Ficino integrated into his medical and philosophical theories.</note>, who writes that when he was sick around the diaphragm, he dreamed that he would be freed if he let blood from the vein that is between the thumb and index finger; and having drawn the blood, he recovered.

Nor are there lacking some—though very few such are found—who, having tamed their pleasures and neglected civil affairs, so order their lives that they burn with a desire to attain the truth. Yet they distrust that truth can be investigated by human tracks, by which the ambiguous mind of natural philosophers is mostly accustomed to consider things. Therefore, they give themselves over to **God**. They themselves attempt nothing. With open and purified eyes, they wait for what is shown to them most divinely. 

<margin>B</margin> This is what **Socrates** <note>The foundational Greek philosopher, whom Ficino viewed as a precursor to Christian saintliness.</note> is said to have both commanded and done. These are called pious and religious men; their soul is "vacant" in wakefulness more than others. In sleep, it is entirely vacant. Therefore, the heavenly impulse easily directs it. 

But there are two types of these men. <margin>C</margin> Some admire this **temple of God**—that is, the world’s machinery—more frequently. Others more intensely venerate the **deity** <note>original: "numen"</note> of this temple. For the former, when the soul is quiet in sleep, the "passions" (or events) of the world are shown, and especially those to which the soul is more inclined. Thus one might see future rain, war, plague, and similar things. We have stated the manner and order of these demonstrations above.

Moreover, the interpretation of a dream is often difficult, and often easy. <margin>E</margin> It is difficult when, after the future rain has been expressed in the phantasy, the power of the phantasy does not entrust the image of the rain to the memory with enough attention. Instead, being too swift and versatile—once it has been struck—it runs glibly through similar and subsequent images. For instance, from rain it might be stirred toward thinking of winds; from winds, to the highest mountains; from mountains, to clouds. Thus, having passed through these, the person wakes up; and having awakened, they remember the last things seen more than the rain. Hence, they predict future snow, not rain. 

Therefore, the interpreter of dreams must be a most **sagacious hunter** <note>Ficino uses this metaphor to describe the intellectual skill needed to trace a series of mental associations back to their original "scent" or source.</note>, so that he knows how to run back from the nearest track to the remote one, and from that one to another more remote, and sees what follows primarily from each, until they arrive at the first. 

<margin>F</margin> This is what we usually observe in daily conversations: when we have crossed from one topic to another and then another, at last we do not have the original topic proposed ready at hand. Then we consider the newest words, and from which words they could have most likely followed, and again from which ones those came, until we recall the first words very clearly.

<margin>G</margin> This "hunting" skill requires a swift and versatile wit, while the prescient faculty requires a mind that is clear, peaceful, and quiet. Therefore, as if these were repugnant qualities in the same person, they do not easily coincide. For this reason, for the most part, the same people are not both clear **prophets** and **interpreters**. And often those who prophesy do not know what they are prophesying; especially those who interpret are more likely to err swiftly in foreseeing. 

<margin>D</margin> This is what **Plato** signified in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the cosmos, where he distinguishes between the inspired 'mantis' (prophet) and the rational 'prophetes' (interpreter).</note> when he said that some are prophets and others are interpreters of prophets. 

But to return to the matter: the dreams of those who, because of **choleric** <note>Associated with the fire element and yellow bile, making the mind restless and fast.</note> and fiery spirits, run more swiftly through the course of the phantasy, stand in need of an interpreter. But in those in whom—because of a temperate or **melancholic** <term>Melancholic: A temperament associated with earth and black bile; Ficino believed a "tempered" melancholy was the mark of genius and deep, stable contemplation.</term> complexion of spirits—the phantasy proceeds more maturely, the foreseen things adhere firmly to the memory, and are not confused by new and various images. Therefore, the prophecies of these men...

<summary>Ficino categorizes dreamers by temperament, explaining that while philosophers and pious men receive more accurate divine insights, the interpretation of dreams often requires a 'sagacious hunter' to trace mental associations back to their source. He distinguishes between the inspired prophet and the rational interpreter, noting how bodily humors like choler and melancholy affect the stability of mental images.</summary>

# Theology

<margin>☞</margin>
They do not need interpretation. And these are the premonitions of dreams which belong to those of a religious nature, who admire and are struck with awe by this divine temple <note>Ficino often refers to the universe or the human body as a "divine temple."</note>. It is recorded that such things happened to **Hippocrates**: when he went to treat **Democritus**—who was commonly rumored to be insane—he received word from a god during a time of rest that it was not **Democritus** who was insane, but the common people. By the same reasoning, **Socrates** predicted the future excellence of **Plato** from a dream. Enough on these matters. Truly, for those of a religious nature who instead adore the divine power <note>original: "numen"</note> of this temple, this happens when they rest in sleep: their mind, being greedy for divine majesty, is violently struck by the divine power, and such a thought of God occurs to their mind as it is most accustomed to desire while awake—for instance, it might desire to know the seat and the operation of God. To the resting reason, an infinite and invisible light occurs, which is everywhere as a whole, exists within itself, and sees itself through itself without the need of an eye. Here, if the **phantasy** <term>Phantasy: The mental faculty that handles sensory images and imagination.</term> is slower to move, the notion remains clear and transparent; once the soul is awake, it reveals this notion to men as immaculate as it had received it. But if the phantasy is swifter, it immediately begins its own work after the reason, as is its custom. It turns over its accustomed images and, having imitated the reason to the best of its ability, it fashions an immense light of the sun, flashing everywhere before the eyes of all, and revolving back into itself in a perpetual circuit. Here, therefore, there is a need for an interpreter, such as **Joseph** was, <margin>F</margin> and **Daniel**, who interpreted the dreams of kings. **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed.</note> excelled in this divination, as shown by his book on the power and wisdom of God, which was translated by us from the Greek language into Latin. This species of prophecy indeed suits those of a religious nature most of all, as we have said. Sometimes it also happens to others, if ever by some providence or chance they lie sober and free from cares in a state of prosperity. <margin>G</margin> Hence, an oracle showed a herb to King **Alexander** while he was sleeping, with which he might cure **Ptolemy**, who had been gravely wounded. This happens especially near the rising of the sun, when the crowd of vapors and external cares has calmed down a little. Although what is commonly said—

---

that morning dreams are truer—does not happen for that reason alone, because we are more sober. For we often go to sleep sober, yet clear visions do not happen then; rather, it is also because the prophecy is strengthened by the approach of the Sun and the prophet **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the god of prophecy and the sun.</note>, and because the bloody and fiery spirits dominant at that hour contribute by their own clarity to a clear vision; and because what we see, we do not confuse with a crowd of following images, since we wake up immediately. These things said about sleep are confirmed here by the verses of **Orpheus**. <margin>D</margin> <note>The following is a translation of the Greek Orphic fragment: "O messenger of things to come to mortals, greatest singer of oracles: for you, coming as a messenger to those lulled by the silence of sweet sleep, speaking to the souls of mortals, you yourself stir the mind. And you yourself send the thoughts of the blessed ones to those deep in sleep, speaking of things to come in silence to silent souls: to those, I say, whose virtuous mind journeys according to the divine will."</note> Messenger of future things, greatest of prophets for mortals. You approach souls soothed by the kin of sleep: and addressing them, you rouse the mind. You insert the thoughts of the blessed divinities into them through sleep. Silent, you announce the future to silent souls: to these souls, I say, whose mind employs the divine worship most rightly.
<margin>☞</margin>
<margin>J</margin> We have said enough concerning that withdrawal of the soul which occurs through sleep. Next follows the withdrawal which occurs through **syncope** <term>Syncope: A sudden loss of consciousness or fainting; here used to describe a near-death state where the soul partially detaches from the body.</term>, that is, through the fall of a half-dead body, when, due to a failure of the heart, the spirits are not sent to the limbs, and those which are in the limbs are withdrawn to protect the weakened heart. In this state, just as in sleep, prophecy occurs. In this, <margin>K</margin> **Hercules** is said to have excelled, as well as many Arabians who were seized by the **comitial disease** <term>Comitial disease: An old term for epilepsy, so named because the Roman assemblies (comitia) would be dismissed if someone had a seizure.</term>. Hence **Plutarch** says in his first book on the soul: "Enarchus," he said, "recently falling ill, was left by the doctors as if already dead; and a short time later, having been brought back to himself, he said that he had been dead, and was restored again into the body, and would not die from that disease." He also said those [doctors] were vehemently rebuked...

...three times by their master those spirits: who led his soul. For they were sent to Michandas, not to himself. Michandas, however, was a tanner and not unknown in the gymnasium; at the time when Enarchus <note>Likely referring to Hermotimus of Clazomenae or a similar figure from classical lore whose soul was said to leave his body.</note> came back to life, Michandas fell into a very high fever and died suddenly. But this man [Enarchus] lives, survives, and stays most happily with us.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ The **third mode of withdrawal** <term>Vacatio: A state where the soul "vacates" or withdraws from the body's external senses to focus inward.</term> occurs from the contraction of the **melancholic humor** <note>In medieval medicine, "black bile" or melancholy was thought to focus the mind and, when balanced, lead to genius or prophecy.</note>, which calls the soul away from external business; thus, the soul is at leisure while the person is awake, just as it usually is when sleeping. Certainly, just as the most suitable tool must lack its own independent motion—lest perhaps, when the craftsman decides to move it to the right while working, it should meanwhile be carried by its own motion to the left—so it is necessary for that mind, which divine providence has decided to use for prophecy, to be quiet like such a tool. Melancholics are often like this; but when they are seized by a divine spirit <note>original: "numine"</note>, they become so much more stirred up than others, just as dense bodies, if they are set on fire, burn more fiercely than thin ones. 

<margin>B</margin>
By this reasoning, **Socrates**—whom **Aristotle** judged to be melancholic—foresaw many things by the inspiration of his **familiar spirit** <note>original: "demonis familiaris." In the Platonic tradition, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or personal guardian, not an evil "demon."</note>. Witnesses to this fact are **Plato**, **Xenophon**, **Antipater the Great**, and **Apuleius**. Indeed, when **Timarchus** had left that banquet where Socrates was reclining, the spirit of Socrates forbade it; Timarchus went anyway and committed those deeds for which he was 

<margin>C</margin>
executed. **Charmides** competed at Nemea <note>The Nemean Games, one of the four Panhellenic festivals of Ancient Greece.</note> against the warning of Socrates, and he regretted having competed. Against Socratic advice, a certain small branch struck the eye of **Crito** while he was staying in the country. This same Socrates, while he and several others were fleeing the attack of enemies, when they came to a crossroad, refused to flee by the same path as the others because he was deterred by his spirit. Then indeed those who had fled by the other way 

<margin>D</margin>
fell into the enemy cavalry. **Aristides**, **Thucydides**, and many others, as long as they stayed near Socrates, profited greatly in the study of philosophy even while Socrates himself remained silent, 

<margin>18</margin>
by the instinct of that spirit. However, the further they receded from Socrates, the more they were rendered unfit for philosophy. Likewise, when he was near death, as **Xenophon** writes, he predicted that the son of **Anytus**—who seemed modest at the time—would become most wicked; and so it happened.

<margin>E</margin>
¶ There is also a **fourth mode of withdrawal** from a **balanced temperament** <note>original: "temperata complexione." A physical state where the four humors are perfectly balanced.</note>. Indeed, such a constitution brings no turmoil from any dominant humor that might agitate the **phantasy** <term>Phantasy: The internal mental faculty that processes sensory images and imagination.</term> toward any particular image. Such men are also moderate in their passions and actions. Therefore, they live with a mind so tranquil that even while awake they are subject to higher influences. 

<margin>F</margin>
This is said to have happened to **Pherecydes the Syrian**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plotinus**. I admire Plotinus above the others because, as his disciple **Porphyry** relates, he sensed the characters, errors, and outcomes of men. And when Porphyry himself was thinking of making a journey <note>Likely referring to Porphyry's period of suicidal depression, which Plotinus "divined" and cured by suggesting he travel to Sicily.</note>, Plotinus foresaw it divinely and prevented it. For this reason, as the younger **Pliny** writes, while **Curtius Rufus** was governing Africa and walking in a portico at the end of the day, the figure of a woman appeared, larger and more beautiful than a human. She predicted that he would come to Rome and hold high offices, and would even return to that same province with supreme power, and die there. All these things were done.

<margin>G</margin>
¶ The **fifth withdrawal** seems to occur from **solitude**. Here the mind is distracted by no cares of human business; by a slight movement of the divine powers <note>original: "numinum"</note> or the heavens, it daily thinks the same things that the celestial powers intend to do. **Zoroaster**, the prince of the 

<margin>H</margin>
Magi, is said to have achieved this through twenty years of solitude. There, he wrote and did many things concerning every art of divination. The writings of **Orpheus** to **Musaeus** declare that Orpheus performed similar works in the deserts of Thrace.

<margin>I</margin>
¶ The **sixth withdrawal** comes from **awe** <note>original: "admiratione"</note>. The **Sibyls** and the **Pythian** priests, when they withdrew into the cave of Jove or Apollo, believed the divine power itself was present there. They thought of the majesty of the divine power with such a stupor of awe and veneration that their senses...

He supports these claims with anecdotes about Socrates' guardian spirit, the prophecies of Plotinus, and the solitary meditations of Zoroaster.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 13 of the Platonic Theology, concluding the discussion on the seven types of prophetic withdrawal (vacatio) and beginning a new argument for the soul's immortality based on human artistry and technology.</meta>

imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes sensory images</term> and reason would immediately cease their own acts. Then the mind, exposed to the divine power alone—whether that power was God or a spirit <note>original: "demon"</note> above us—perceived his promptings, especially those pertaining to the business they had recently deliberated. Aulus Gellius reports that the priest Cornelius of Padua was affected in a similar way. And Orpheus introduces certain Corybantes <note>Priests of the goddess Cybele, known for their ecstatic, dancing trances.</note> of this kind. <margin>K</margin> Albigerius of Carthage excelled in this species of prophecy. By the inspiration of spirits <note>original: "demonuz"</note>, he answered almost whatever anyone had done or thought. Aurelius Augustine affirms that he was often present at these divinations.

<margin>L</margin> **T**he seventh—and the most excellent of all—is that alienation of the soul which occurs through the purity of a mind devoted to God, just as Orpheus teaches Musaeus in the *Hymn to All the Gods*. For such a mind is not just a temple of God for a time, like the others, but is almost always a peaceful one; whose door, as John the Theologian <note>John the Apostle, traditionally the author of the Gospel and Revelation.</note> says, God knocks at first. Once opened, he enters immediately; he dwells there diligently, and in it, he feeds the man with ambrosia. Through this state, as Aurelius Augustine relates, a certain peasant in his own time used to withdraw from his body; he knew he was awake, while yet seeing certain wonders with eyes that were not of the body. Through this, John the Theologian, the most divine of all, saw the entire order of the ages on Patmos. Through this, Ezekiel looked upon a field filled with the bones of the dead, and the bones later rising again. Through this, Isaiah saw God sitting, surrounded by the Seraphim. But all these men, just like those who dream, immediately covered whatever they perceived in the mind with the veils of imagination, so that the visions of the mind, obscured by the shadows of imagination, required an interpreter.

<margin>M</margin> Let us now conclude, through these seven types of prophecy, that the excellence of the human soul over matter is so great that—when the body is mastered, or asleep, or half-dead—it sees much more clearly and acts much more excellently than when the body is active, as if it does not require the assistance of the body to achieve any magnificent thing. Here it appears how great is the soul's harmony with celestial things, and how great its kinship with God; for as often as it returns into itself, it becomes a partaker of celestial secrets and divine providence.

### Third sign. From the industry of arts and government. Chapter 3.

<margin>N</margin> **O**ther animals either live without art or each by one specific art, to the use of which they do not apply themselves, but are drawn by a law of fate. A sign of this is that they make no progress over time in the industry of their work. In contrast, humans are the inventors of innumerable arts, which they carry out by their own judgment. This is shown by the fact that individuals practice many arts, change them, and become more skillful through long-term use. And what is wonderful is that human arts produce by themselves whatever nature itself produces, as if we were not servants of nature, but its rivals. <margin>O</margin> Zeuxis painted things so that birds flew toward them. Apelles painted a mare and a dog so that passing horses neighed and dogs barked. In a certain Indian temple, Praxiteles expressed a marble Venus so charmingly that she could hardly be kept safe and modest from the lustful gazes of passers-by. Archytas of Tarentum made a dove from wood using mathematical discipline; he balanced it and breathed life <note>original: "spiritu"</note> into it by God so that it flew. The Egyptians, as Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> relates, constructed statues of gods such that they spoke and walked. Archimedes of Syracuse made a bronze heaven <note>An early planetarium or orrery.</note> in which all the movements of the seven planets were most truly enacted, just as in the sky, and it turned just like the sky. <margin>P</margin> Mention also the pyramids of the Egyptians, the buildings of the Romans and Greeks, and the workshops of metals and glass. In short, man imitates all the works of divine nature and perfects, corrects, and mends the works of the lower nature. Therefore, the power of man is almost similar to divine nature, since man—through himself, that is, through his own counsel and art—rules himself, not at all circumscribed by the limits of physical nature, and rivals every work of the higher nature. <margin>Q</margin> And he lacks the support of lower nature so much less because he was allotted fewer bodily protections.

<summary>Ficino concludes his survey of the seven types of prophecy, arguing that the soul's ability to see divine truths while the body is dormant proves its immortality and kinship with God. He then begins a new argument: that human ingenuity and the "rivalry" with nature shown in art and technology reveal a nearly divine power within humanity.</summary>

<keywords>prophecy, imagination, John the Theologian, Isaiah, Ezekiel, human arts, Zeuxis, Apelles, Archimedes, divine nature, immortality of the soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from Book 13 of Marsilio Ficino's Platonic Theology. The previous page concluded the discussion on the seven types of prophetic withdrawal. This page begins a celebrated Humanist argument: the immortality of the soul is proven by man's unique ability to master nature, create art, and act as a "vicar of God" on earth.</meta>

# Platonic
## Book [13]

[Man] is [weaker] by nature than the beasts; but he himself, from his own abundance, constructs food, clothing, bedding, dwellings, furnishings, and weapons. Therefore, since he supports himself by his own faculty, he supports himself more richly than nature supports the beasts. From this arises an unspeakable variety of pleasures, even those that delight the bodily senses, which we ourselves devise for ourselves by our own ingenuity. <margin>A</margin> Beasts are confined within very narrow enclosures of nature. Our soul looks out not only for the body’s necessity—like the beasts, who are enslaved to nature’s command—but for various delights of the senses as a kind of food for the imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty that processes sensory images</term>. Not only does the soul flatter this imagination with various charms, soothing it daily with different games as if in play, but sometimes serious, calculating reason <note>original: "cogitatrix ratio"</note> acts; and, eager to propagate its own offspring, it shines forth and clearly demonstrates how much genius it possesses through the various weaving of wool and silk, paintings, sculptures, and buildings. In composing these things, the soul often regards no bodily convenience and no sensory charm—since it sometimes voluntarily suffers inconvenience and trouble from them—but rather looks toward the enlargement of its own eloquence and the approval of its virtue. In these crafts, one may observe how man handles the materials of the world everywhere and in every way, as if they were all subject to him. He handles, I say, the elements, stones, <margin>B</margin> metals, plants, and animals. He translates them into many forms and figures, which beasts never do. Nor is he content with one element, or a few, like the beasts, but he uses all of them as if he were the lord of all. He treads upon the earth. He furrows the water. He ascends into the air with the highest towers—to say nothing of the wings of Daedalus or Icarus <note>In Greek myth, Daedalus built wings of wax and feathers to escape Crete; his son Icarus flew too close to the sun and fell.</note>. He kindles fire and uses the hearth familiarly, and he alone, above all others, takes delight in it. Justly so, for only a celestial animal is delighted by a celestial element. By celestial power, he ascends to heaven and measures it. By a super-celestial mind, he transcends heaven. Man does not only use the elements, but he also adorns them, which no beast does. How wonderful is the cultivation of the earth throughout the whole world! How stupendous the structure of buildings and cities! <margin>C</margin> How ingenious the irrigation of waters! He acts in the place of God <note>original: "vicem gerit dei"</note>, who inhabits all elements and cultivates them all; being present on earth, He is yet not absent from the upper air.

---

And indeed, he uses not only the elements, but even all the animals of the elements. He uses those of the earth, water, and air for food, convenience, and pleasure. He uses the higher and celestial things for learning and the wonders of magic. Nor does he only use the beasts, but he commands them. It may happen that, by certain weapons received from nature, some beasts may occasionally make an attack on man or escape man’s attack. But man, having taken up arms from himself, both avoids the attacks of wild beasts and puts them to flight and tames them. Who has ever seen any men held under the <margin>D</margin> empire of beasts? Whereas we see everywhere herds of the most savage beasts, as well as mild ones, obeying men throughout their entire lives. Man does not command the beasts only cruelly, but he also governs them, nurtures them, and teaches them. The universal providence of God, who is the universal cause, is his own. Man, therefore, who provides universally for all things, both living and non-living <margin>E</margin>, is a kind of god. He is undoubtedly the god of the animals, for he makes use of them all. He commands all and instructs many. It is also established that he is the god of the elements, for he inhabits and cultivates them all. Finally, he is the god of all materials, for he handles, turns, and shapes them all. He who rules over so many and such great things in the body, and acts in the place of the immortal God, is undoubtedly immortal. 

But although arts of this kind may shape the matter of the world and command the animals, and thus imitate God, the artisan of nature, they are nevertheless inferior to those arts which, imitating the divine kingdom, undertake the care of human governance. Individual beasts are scarcely sufficient for the care of themselves or their few offspring. But one man abounds with such perfection that he first commands himself—which no beasts do. Then he governs a family. He administers a republic. He rules nations and commands the whole world. And as one who was born to rule, he is entirely impatient of servitude. Add to this that for the sake of the public good he undergoes death, which beasts do not do.

<summary>Ficino argues for the soul's immortality by highlighting man's unique status as a "god on earth" who masters the elements, creates complex art, and governs both himself and society. Unlike beasts, man's ingenuity and desire for dominion prove his divine origin and eternal nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the soul's immortality from Book 13 of the Platonic Theology.
