# Theology 13.

<margin>f</margin>
As one who despises these individual mortal goods, trusting in the firmness of the common and eternal good. Furthermore, arts of this kind might seem to some to belong to the present life; however, such great care is not necessary for the present life, but rather looks toward imitating divine providence <note>Ficino argues that the liberal arts are too complex and taxing to be merely for survival; they exist to show our likeness to God's creative power.</note>. Let us therefore consider those arts which are not only unnecessary for bodily sustenance but even harmful, such as all the liberal sciences <term>liberal sciences: the "artes liberales," subjects like grammar, logic, and music considered worthy of a free person</term>, the study of which weakens the body and hinders the conveniences of life. The subtle calculation of numbers, the curious drawing of figures, the most obscure movements of lines, the superstitious harmony of music, the long-term observation of the stars, the inquiry into natural causes, and their long-lasting investigation; the eloquence of orators and the frenzies <note>original: "furores," referring to the Platonic concept of divine inspiration or poetic madness</note> of poets. In all these, the human soul despises the ministry of the body, as one who can—and even now begins to—live without the body’s help.

<margin>g</margin>
One thing above all must be noted: that anyone cannot discern the work of a skillful craftsman, constructed artistically—by what reason or in what manner it was built—except for one who possesses the same artistic genius. For no one would discern by what path Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE), the Greek mathematician known for his mechanical inventions, including a famous planetarium or orrery.</note> constructed his bronze spheres and gave them motions similar to the celestial movements, unless he were endowed with a similar genius. And he who discerns these things through a similarity of genius could certainly construct the same things once he has understood them, provided that the material was not lacking. Since, therefore, man has seen the order of the heavens—where they move, where they proceed, and by what measures, and what they produce—who could deny that he is of almost the same genius (if I may speak thus) as that Author of the heavens? And that he could, in a certain way, make the heavens if he obtained the instruments and celestial material? Since he makes them even now, although from different material, yet very similar in their order.

<margin>h</margin>
### Four endowments of man in the arts.

# In the human arts, four most excellent endowments of our soul shine forth:
The swiftest facility for perception; a most ample and completely indelible memory; a most sagacious prediction of the future; and the use of innumerable words. How divine a sharpness do you think flourished in Homer? Who, though both blind and poor, perceived so many and such great things, and sang so excellently, that Plato asserts all arts, both human and divine, met together in him.

<margin>K <insert>Humanity</insert></margin>
How divine [this light was] in Didymus of Alexandria <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian who lost his sight at age four yet mastered mathematics and grammar.</note>, whom Jerome writes was blinded from childhood, yet afterwards drank in logic, physics, and theology beyond all others. And what is marvelous, he turned out to be a wonderful geometer, and was accustomed to describe and teach geometric figures, and also composed excellent works of theology. Certainly, a divine light infused these men at their birth and revealed to them as seekers things that would have been impossible to find through human studies alone.

<margin>L</margin>
And although Plato and Aristotle write in their books on civil institutions that some regions are more suited than others for exercising the genius, yet we have found it true that not only in the East and South, but also in the West and North, many men have frequently flourished wonderfully in every art. If the diversity of regions and ages necessarily causes a great difference in the habit of bodies, but a minimal difference in geniuses—and we correct even this through counsel and study—who does not see that the human genius is not, by its nature, subject to places and times? From this follows that indelible memory, in which many have excelled.

<margin>M</margin>
Mithridates, king of twenty-two nations, used to administer justice to each without an interpreter. Cyrus and Lucius Scipio knew the names of all their citizens. Fabius Maximus and Lucullus held the histories of all nations in their memory. Seneca says that he repeated two thousand names in the same order they were recited. He also recited two hundred verses pronounced by his students in reverse order. Augustine writes that there was a certain man in his time who had read many things and had never forgotten anything of what he had read. There was another in Rome who committed an entire comedy to memory while it was being recited. So great is the capacity for so many and such vast things in those who have received them...

<summary>Ficino argues that human mastery of the liberal arts and the ability to understand the heavens prove that the human intellect is nearly identical to the divine intellect. He cites extraordinary examples of memory and genius, such as Homer and Didymus the Blind, to show the soul's independence from physical limitations.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>
...the ability to be comprehended in a narrow corner of the brain: and its fluid and fleeting matter cannot preserve it; rather, it requires the most ample and stable receptacle of a divine soul. There is also that prediction of future things, in which the <term>Chaldeans: ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers</term> and Egyptian <term>mathematicians: here referring to astrologers or those who calculate celestial movements</term> excelled. Certainly, that substance does not fail in the future whose presaging power anticipates the whole future in the same way its memorial power recalls the whole past. Moreover, this substance is eternal, as it gathers the fleeting intervals of time into an eternal moment. Finally, the use of speaking and writing, which is unique to man, indicates that a certain divine mind is within us, which beasts lack. Without speech, we could live just as beasts do, or like "walls of men" <note>original: "homines murum"; a metaphor for being mute or inanimate</note>. Therefore, speech was granted to us for some more excellent work: namely, as the interpreter of the mind, the herald of infinite inventions, and an infinite messenger. Nor should <note>Epicurus: a Greek philosopher often criticized by Ficino for his materialist views on the soul</note> **Epicurus** dream that beasts possess reason just as we do, but simply lack
<margin>B</margin>
the use of speech and hands through which they might signal the reason lurking within. For nature does not fail in necessary things, nor does she abound in
<margin>has</margin>
superfluous ones. She did not give feet or arms to trees, for their earthly body is fixed in the soil and is nourished everywhere by earthly food. To the bodies of beasts, as they are less "earthy," not all earthly food is sufficient everywhere. Therefore, they are equipped with feet to seek more convenient nourishment. Their imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> holds only a few and confused concepts, and only those necessary for the use of the body, which can be sufficiently expressed through lowing, barking, neighing, chirping, snarling, growling, or nods.
<margin>ha:</margin>

<margin>The Mind</margin>

Indeed, nature would have given these same things to beasts as well if that same interior craftsman <note>The "inner craftsman" refers to the rational intellect</note> were present in them to use such instruments.
<margin>N.</margin>
**T**herefore, the mind conceives as many things within itself through understanding as God creates in the world through His understanding. It expresses just as many in the air through speaking. It writes just as many on paper with a pen. It figures just as many in the matter of the world by manufacturing.
<margin>C</margin>
Wherefore, it is clear that anyone is out of his mind who denies that the soul—which is the rival of God in the arts and in governing—is divine.

### The fourth sign from the effect of miracles. Chapter 3.

<margin>D</margin>
**N**ot only in the forming and figuring of matter through the reason of art, as we have said, does the human mind claim a divine right for itself, but also in the transforming of the species of things through command. This work is indeed called a **miracle**, not because it happens contrary to the nature of our soul (since the soul becomes the instrument of God), but because, since it is a great thing and happens rarely, it produces wonder. Hence we marvel that the souls of men dedicated to God command the elements: they summon winds, they drive clouds into rains, they dispel mists, and they cure the diseases of human bodies and the rest. The poets sing that these things were openly done in certain ages among various nations; historians relate them; and the most excellent of our philosophers do not deny them.
<margin>3</margin>
Especially the Platonic theologians of old testify to this—**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius"; refers to the legendary Egyptian sage</note> first of all, and **Orpheus**—and later theologians also confirm it by word and deed. You will perhaps marvel if I seek out the reasons for miracles. But listen. In the first book, it was discussed that the "third essence" <note>The Soul, placed in the middle of Ficino's hierarchy of five being: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, Matter</note> is below the angel and above the whole matter of the world. It is formed by the Divine and, in turn, forms matter. It receives spiritual forms from the Divine and gives corporal forms to matter. In the third
<margin>3</margin>
book, it was also established that the third essence is nothing other than rational souls, both our own and those superior to ours. Hence it is concluded among the Platonists and the followers of <note>Avicenna: a Persian polymath whose views on the soul's power over matter influenced Ficino</note> **Avicenna** that every rational soul, through its essence and power, is above the whole matter of the world; it can move and form the whole—namely, whenever it acts as the
<margin>H. E</margin>
instrument of God for these things. Nevertheless, such is the order of things. All rational souls have, as we said, an intellectual head, a rational middle, and a lowest life-giving part. This middle way is the property of the soul. But the intellectual power is...

<header>Theology</header>

# Theology

A certain ray of a higher intellect is sent down into the soul: and it reflects itself back again toward that higher intellect. The life-giving force is also an act of the soul overflowing into the body: and resulting from there back into the soul. Just as the light of the sun in a cloud is, according to its own nature, a splendor—as a ray looks back to the sun—but as it fills the cloud, it is a paleness <note>original: "pallor"; here referring to the way pure light becomes dimmed or diffused when it enters a material medium like a cloud or body</note>. The intellect looks up at the intelligible <note>that which can be understood by the mind alone, separate from the senses</note>: and remains within itself around that very intelligible. Reason runs: but within itself. The life-giving force runs beneath itself until it reaches something else: until it fills the body. Because, however, through this lowest part of itself—or its shadow—souls depart furthest from their own dignity by approaching bodies, it has happened that these governing forces of bodies have, in a way, been relaxed or interrupted in that amplitude of dominion which the soul possesses over the whole universe of bodies. Instead, they are distributed individually to individual bodies; while they are bound to these, they take private care of their own bodies and, within themselves, they do not neglect the concerns of others.

<margin>☛</margin>
What binds them to these bodies? As **Plato** intends: Love. That is, the affection of an exuberant life more prone to vivifying those things nearest to itself. Moreover, diverse species of bodies are closely matched to the diverse species of rational souls. From this, he maintains, it happens that some rational souls harmonize with some bodies and others with others. Some with the celestial spheres. Some with the stars. Some with others still. Finally, others harmonize with the bodies of men. And from certain internal dispositions of the <term>seeds: "seminal reasons" or the formative principles of life</term> established by providence, some human souls are more suited to governing some human bodies than others.

<margin>3</margin>
And to speak summarily: that life-giving force of every rational soul, because it belongs to the <term>third essence: the Soul, which acts as the middle link between the eternal Mind and the material world</term>, has equal power toward any body whatsoever. But through a certain amorous instinct, some souls accommodate themselves to moving certain bodies, with divine tempering clearly contributing to this; and when one such instinct ceases, that life-giving force emerges free, so that by a new affection or instinct it may, in a certain way, rule and move another body.

<margin>.)</margin>
If these lowest parts surpass all the natures of bodies, how much more do the middle and the highest? The highest,
<margin>mind</margin>
<margin>middle</margin>
that is, the mind, stands so far above that it never tastes anything corporeal, being greedy only for divine things. It is stable in its nature. Its intelligence is sudden. The middle, that is, the faculty of reasoning, also stands out more than the lowest part; and now indeed, as we have said elsewhere, it ascends into the mind when, having received principles from the mind, it seeks the universal reasons of natural things through the process of demonstration and argument. At other times, however, it declines toward the life-giving power: when it trusts in the phantasy <note>the faculty of imagination or mental images</note>, listens to the senses, and flatters the body.

<margin>ß</margin>
It ascends into the mind through the love of grasping higher things. It descends into the lowest power through the love of governing lower things.

<margin>{</margin>
Rightly, since it is the middle between both, it loves both. And as it is more eminent than the lowest part—while the lowest rules only one body—reason itself moves and governs many. For while the governing faculty of your body nourishes only your body and serves the sustenance of your body through sense and desire, your reason takes care of both your body and those of others; and it fashions works of art in external matter. This reason also, although it is equally able to handle any material whatsoever, nevertheless at different times it attacks different materials to be worked upon, wherever love snatches it. When the love ceases through which it carved this stone, it suddenly abandons the statue. When love draws it toward earthen vessels, it takes up the craft of the potter. When we speak of the handling of bodies, we set aside for a moment that mind which is a total contemner of bodies, and we speak more of reason and the governing power. Although both of these, on account of the common nature of the third essence, have equal power toward any bodies of the world, they nevertheless act most powerfully upon that which they are most affected by, provided that the divine tempering of the seeds does not prohibit it.

<margin>3</margin>
The affections of those souls which are above us are more stable than ours; and they always weave the same order, proceeding always with their accustomed tenor: because in them, both the highest and the middle power turn upward, dwelling upon eternal contemplation. Only the lowest force varies its works, yet it acts through successions, and those indeed are most orderly; so that in that very change...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul governs the body, specifically focusing on how the power of imagination—or "phantasia"—can physically alter one's own body and even influence other bodies from a distance, including through the mechanism of "fascination" or the "evil eye."</meta>

# Platonic Book

...seems to be stability: as long as the same tenor <note>original: "tenor"; a consistent course or character</note> is observed: and the same things are similarly rewoven. But however it may be: the forms of things implanted in those three powers of souls are the causes of the forms: which are expressed in worldly bodies. And, as I might say: fatal imaginations: which arise step by step in the images <note>original: "idolis"; here referring to the mental images or reflections within the soul</note> of those souls: just as the most vehement feelings of pregnant women express whatever they imagine for themselves in their own spheres: and in the following things as if in their offspring. Our soul also, being affected toward this body: according to the order of its own seeds <note>the "logoi" or rational principles that guide development</note>, shapes this body out of its very power as the ruler of the body. What provides this body with a certain "complexion" <note>the unique balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines health and personality</note> of the four humors? What gives the colors of the face: and its features? except the soul? The soul also, against the nature of a heavy body, drives it upward: and overcomes four opposites in turn. Nor does anyone marvel at this miracle.

<margin>phantasia</margin>
How much that same power, through <term>phantasia</term> <gloss>the faculty of imagination that creates mental images and mediates between the senses and the intellect</gloss>, can achieve in shaping the body through more vehement feelings: we have spoken of in the preceding sections. Indeed, according to the diversity of feelings, it produces diverse qualities in the limbs. Thus from anger: redness: a bitter taste: and a flow of the bowels. From fear: coldness: and paleness; from sorrow: the moisture of sweat: and a bluish-white color. From anxiety: dryness: and blackness. These qualities are indeed authored by the feelings of the soul themselves: which often move us to some such qualities contrary to our previous complexion. And as **Hippocrates** <note>the famous Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> teaches: and **Galen** <note>an influential Roman physician and philosopher whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years</note>: a long-standing feeling changes the prior complexion of the body: and draws it into its own nature. This is the work of phantasia. What reason, however, performs in the arts: and in governance: we have declared elsewhere. Accordingly, what is done in one's own body by the ruling power of the body through the life-giving virtue: and the feelings serving it: we have explained here. Furthermore, something is done by it in the bodies of others: which are near it: sometimes through natural heat it cooks food: and warms those touching it. The maternal soul also acts upon another's body: when it nourishes the fetus in the womb. By the same power it completes this from the continuous bonds: by which the fetus is tied to the maternal body. Nor does it shape only a nearby body: but sometimes a remote one.

<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, once the seed is placed by the man into the womb: and long after, with the man being absent: the "formative power" <note>original: "virtus formatrix"; the biological force believed to shape an embryo according to the soul's blueprint</note> left in the seed thrives there: and takes the place of the paternal soul in the seed: and fashions the human body. Or when someone throws a stone far off: the "expulsive power" sent into the stone by the thrower, as long as it reigns in the stone: so long does it drive the stone: specifically by that blow of the air: and toward that mark: which and to which the thrower had directed it. If the part of the soul suited for governing the body works something upon another's body and a remote one through the life-giving power: why not also through the "sensitive power" <note>the faculty of the soul responsible for sensation and perception</note> which is more eminent? Namely, through the feelings of phantasia?

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, phantasia, in the likeness of the life-giving virtue, also shapes its own body: as we have said: whenever it is agitated by sharper feelings. It also shapes the body of another through "fascinations": and "evil deeds" <note>original: "maleficijs"; often used in a legal or theological sense to mean harmful magic or sorcery</note>. Nor is it a wonder: that the soul should do such things by its feelings: if certain herbs do so: or stones by their vapors: with the celestial breaths of the soul nevertheless inspiring them. Nor is there a lack of a continuation of mediums for the soul: through which it may pass its action into another's body. Indeed, the phantasia of a "sorcerer" <note>original: "venefici hois" (veneficus); literally 'poisoner,' but in this context, a worker of harmful magic or the "evil eye"</note> hostile to the tender little body of an infant, affects the boy with a fever. The imagination of fever vibrates the "febrile spirits" (that is, the choleric ones). Just as the imagination of sexual union vibrates the seminal spirits: and the genital members. That "driven spirit" <note>original: "spiritus ille pecullus," likely "perculsus"; the spirit being struck or impelled by the will</note> rouses the choleric and fever-inducing spirits, the foul and feverish vapors: if any are in the body of the sorcerer. These, as soon as they are stirred up: together with the spirit, rush forth like arrows: toward that place where the wicked phantasia had intended as if at a mark. Most especially they flash forth from the eyes of the elderly: through which they pass into the eyes of the child as if through glass materials: and through the glass materials they infect the rays and spirits of the child: and his humors. To these

<margin>D</margin>
evil deeds, those are most powerful of all: for whom, at their birth, a malignant aspect of **Saturn** <note>the planet Saturn was traditionally associated with melancholy, old age, and malevolence in astrology</note>: and the "terrestrial seed" of parents: and a similar diet, have forged a "complexion" abounding in foul vapors: and <term>melancholy</term> <gloss>an excess of "black bile," one of the four humors, associated here with dark psychic powers and harmful influence</gloss>.

# Theology

### Theology

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, the savage power of Mars has placed the fire of bile <note>Bile, or "choler," was associated with the planet Mars and the element of fire, believed to cause anger and heat in the body.</note> beneath the eyes. When these people are in their old age—the earthly and <term>melancholy</term> <gloss>the temperament associated with black bile, earth, and old age</gloss> stage of life—they are exceedingly morose. Whatever happens, they flare up in the sharpest anger and curse with a most hostile mind.

<margin>D</margin> Certainly, because of the "earthy humor" <note>Referring to black bile, which is cold and dry like earth</note>, they fix their <term>phantasia</term> <gloss>the faculty of imagination that forms mental images</gloss> more stably and effectively upon their desires. Once this humor is set ablaze, it burns most vehemently and is slow to be extinguished, just like a fire in thick logs or hard wood. Malignant vapors are also present, which are hurled at an adversary like poisoned arrows. If you do not wonder that the body of one person can be defiled by the soul of another, why then do you wonder that a soul can be harmed by a soul, especially when we soak up the vices of others through close association? You do not wonder that your body is easily infected by the vapor of another diseased body. This is proven by epidemics, leprosy, the itch, dysentery, pleurisy, and the redness of eyes.

<margin>f</margin> Among the Western Ethiopians, it is said there were beasts called *catoblepas* <note>A legendary creature mentioned by Pliny the Elder, said to kill anyone who looked into its eyes</note> which could kill men with a mere glance. The same is said of the <term>basilisk</term> <gloss>the "king of serpents," legendary for killing with its breath or gaze</gloss> in Cyrene. So great is the force in the vapors of the eyes! Why should your body be less subject to another's soul than to another's body? Why not even more so? Since the soul is more powerful, and there is no lack of media through which it may act.

<margin>g</margin> We read that certain people among the Illyrians and Triballi used to do this; when they were angry, if they looked at a person long and intently, they would kill them—these people were said to have "double pupils" in their eyes. It is said some women in Scythia did the same. Such is the power of imagination, especially when the vapors of the eyes serve the passions of the mind. For that wonderful attention of the imagination increases the power no less than the eye of an ostrich fixed upon its egg <note>The ancients believed ostriches hatched their eggs simply by staring at them with intense heat and focus.</note>. Indeed, while one passion seethes, another grows cold.

<margin>a</margin> Therefore, during the intense focus of a "malefic" <note>evil or harmful</note> imagination, the natural affection of the soul—by which it is bound to its own body—is momentarily relaxed. Once it is made somewhat freer from its own body, it begins to transform new matter in which it has recently taken an interest, just as it would its own body. If a malefic

---

imagination has such power, do you not think a "benefic" <note>kind or healing</note> one will have at least twice as much power? Both because reason surpasses imagination, and because goodness surpasses evil. Therefore, when reason is fixed upon some benefit with the soul's entire intention directed toward God, it sometimes affects the body it is concerned with—whether its own or another’s—with a benefit.

<margin>b</margin> Those among the Platonics excel in this gift who, by a certain divine favor, are endowed with a more <term>tempered complexion</term> <gloss>a perfectly balanced mixture of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) resulting in ideal health and character</gloss> than others. They are also nourished by pure and moderate food and educated in honest and divine habits. These people are often the "physicians of the human race." If they ardently desire good things for a body with pious prayers directed toward God, they grant them immediately—especially if the person about to receive the benefit is open to it. On this subject, Zoroaster says:

<margin>I</margin> **"If you apply the burning mind to the work of piety, you shall also save the flowing body."** <note>original Greek: ἐκείνας πυρίνου νόου ἔργον εὐσεβείας ῥευστὸν καὶ σῶμα σαῶσαι.</note>

If you stretch the burning mind toward the work of piety, you will preserve the fragile body. Philostratus narrates that such miracles were performed by the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana. Again, many Pythagoreans affirm that similar things were done by Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Philolaus. Furthermore, Iamblichus writes that the Pythagoreans, whenever they told of miracles, were quick to believe that those things were done by God through divine souls. And in such matters, they always had these verses of Linus <note>A legendary musician and poet of Greek myth</note> on their lips:

<margin>K</margin> **"All things must be hoped for, since there is nothing that cannot be believed. All things are easy for God to complete, and nothing is impossible."** <note>original Greek: ἔλπιστά χρὴ πάντά ἐπεί οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδέν ἄπιστον. ῥᾴδια πάντά θεῷ τελέσαι καὶ ἀνήνυτον οὐδέν.</note>

That is, all things are to be believed. For nothing is incredible. All things are easy for God. Nothing is impossible. But let us return to those souls through whom God performs miracles as if through instruments. What does a tempered condition of the body contribute to this excellence? So that their reason may be more unimpeded, undisturbed by any tumult of excess humors. Why a moderate and pure diet? So that the soul is not weighed down like a heavy burden by its own body. Why that honest and pious education? So that it may be inclined to help people with good things as is proper, and so that, being in a certain way like God, it may be helped by God—or rather, be led by God as His instrument. Finally, since...

# Platonic Theology, Book 13

### The Power of Reason and the Divine Soul

Reason is more eminent than <term>phantasia</term> <gloss>the faculty of imagination</gloss>. When reason gives itself entirely to God for the sake of performing a benefit, that prior natural affection by which it is joined to its own body relaxes considerably. <margin>cl</margin> Being loosened from the body, it acts upon what is outside of it. Indeed, the soul can easily be led by God like a tool toward these things; for by its nature, the soul is above all bodies, even if some specific affection once snatched it away to govern just one body. This is no different than if a most wise and powerful king, under whose providence and <margin>E</margin> jurisdiction all the vast parts of his kingdom equally fall, should neglect the rest because he is enticed by the beauty of one particular high place. Yet, once his love for that part cools, he turns himself to governing the others.

Our Plato seems to have touched upon all these things. I recall both that "tyranny" of the imagination and, conversely, that "holy empire" of reason in the *Timaeus*, where he discussed the power of the soul over the body. In the *Phaedrus*, however, he hints at something even more wonderful when he says that every soul has care for the whole of the <term>inanimate world</term> <gloss>the "universal body" or the physical cosmos</gloss>. He says that our soul, when it is free, wanders through the entire heaven and governs the world together with the celestial spirits, moving in various circuits and forms. <margin>H</margin> When it becomes such a soul, he explains in the *Epinomis*, where he affirms that the "necessity of the mind"—that is, the soul joined to the mind—surpasses all other necessity, and every such decree is fated. Furthermore, in the tenth book on justice <note>Referring to Book X of Plato's *Republic*</note>, he called the intellectual soul "Necessity," between whose knees a spindle is turned, around which the spheres of the world revolve.

What is the point of this? To help us understand that it is possible at some time for the human soul, through the total intention of its reason, to be turned toward the Mind and its own desire. This is just as it is sometimes turned toward the imagination and toward its lower reasoning, as we have already said. What kind of soul does these things? It is the one that commands the imagination to be silent; the one that, burning with desire for the supreme divinity, does not trust in the usual wanderings of natural reason. It lives by the mind alone; it becomes an **angel** and receives God into its whole chest. <margin>B</margin> Zoroaster signifies this where he says:

->The soul of mortals will in some way draw God into itself;<-
->having nothing mortal, it is entirely intoxicated by God with harmony.<-
<margin>3</margin> <note>original Greek: "ψυχὴ μέροπων θεὸν ἄξει πωσ ἐν ἑαυτῇ οὐδὲν θνητὸν ἔχουσα ὅλη θεόθεν μέμεθη σται ἁρμονίασ"</note>
->You boast secretly around the mortal body.<-
<note>original Greek: "ἀυχείσ κρυφη περὲ σωμα βροτει"</note>

This means the soul of men draws God into itself in a certain way: when it retains nothing mortal, it is completely intoxicated by divine draughts. Then it also exults in the harmony of the body. The theology of the divine John says that a soul of this kind is "born again" from God. Indeed, the influence of the highest God, flowing down through the angelic minds to the soul of man, daily goads the soul that is submerged in the body, urging it to strip off its fleshy covering and set aside its animal powers and operations, so that the soul may become an angel. 

Just as a ray of the sun thins out vapors, draws them upward, and converts their nature into fire, so the person who commits himself entirely to this divine inspiration ceases to be a mere soul. <margin>E</margin> Through God's regenerating power, he becomes a son of God—an angel. Therefore, Plato called the theologians "sons of God" in the *Timaeus*. If the soul, by its own nature, exceeds the machine of the world and performs wonders through its lower powers—even in the bodies of others—what do we think it will do when it has risen to its own "head" and emerged as angelic? This must be possible at some time, after it has been frequently purified from the allurements of the senses. And the inspiration of God ought not to be less powerful than the allurements of the senses. 

At that time, therefore, the soul will no longer merely bewitch or heal one tender person or one sick man; rather, it will command the spheres of the elements. As long as it is addicted to this body, it agitates the elements of this "small world"—that is, the four <term>humors</term> <gloss>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</gloss>. It induces in them heat, cold, moisture, dryness, and all colors and flavors, as was shown above, both in the act of living and in the affections of the imagination. Therefore, when it emerges loosened from this body and is filled with God, it moves the humors of this "greater animal"—that is, the four elements of the greater world—as if they were its own. Indeed, it has now effectively become the **Soul of the World**—specifically that part of the world toward which it is most inclined. 

Just as the same human soul that had ruled the tiny, one-cubit-long body of an infant later rules a body of two cubits, then three, then four; and ten cubits again, as is said of the giants; so, if it grew to a hundred, it would rule two hundred just the same. Because indeed...

# Theology

In the order of nature and in dignity, the soul precedes all the mass of the body; it can fill—and move—no less the whole of that mass than any individual part of it. <margin>A</margin> If the life-giving power of the rational soul in the spheres of the world comes from God Himself, then it also possesses power <margin>D</margin> over the reason and mental dispositions of those spheres. Therefore, by its disposition alone, the soul can summon the winds to fly at God’s command, bring clouds into a clear sky, and force them to turn into rain. Conversely, it can calm the winds and make the air clear again. That this is possible—and has indeed been done—is confessed by **Hippocrates of Cos** <note>The famous Greek physician</note>, as well as by the Moorish and Arabian theologians. Among the Moors, their prince **Avicebron** <note>The Latinized name of Solomon ibn Gabirol, a Jewish philosopher</note> affirms this, as does **Avicenna** among the Arabs. <margin>E</margin> Add to this the belief of the Egyptians and Platonists that disturbances of the elements and storms often happen due to the conflicts of demons or the "falling" of souls into bodies. **Plutarch**, **Porphyry**, and **Proclus** discuss this matter with great diligence. It is certainly the opinion of Plato and the Platonists that all the regions in the spheres from heaven to earth were <margin>F</margin> distributed from the beginning to different deities or spirits. Thus, when the disposition in a region of the earth dedicated to certain spirits is heightened—either through celestial influences or especially through the affections of the mind—miracles fitting for such spirits are often performed, either by the spirits themselves or by the souls in that place occupied by those spirits. But more on these things elsewhere.

<margin>G</margin> Let us now refer to a certain **Magical** opinion. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages often associated with the occult</note> believe that something else quite wonderful can be done by the soul: namely, that by rays poured out into its own body, it can surround itself with light and, by the lightness of those rays, lift itself on high. Some report that their father, **Zoroaster**, did this very thing. <margin>H</margin> For my part, if any reason can be assigned for such a miracle, I think it is perhaps this: The First Light is in God; and there it is such that it surpasses the intellect. Thus, it cannot be called "intelligible light." But when that light of God is infused into an angel, it immediately becomes "intellectual light" and can be understood. When it is infused into the soul, it becomes 

-> rational <-

rational; and it can be not only understood, but even thought upon. From there, it migrates into the soul’s <term>idol</term> <gloss>the "image" or lower shadow of the soul that governs the physical body</gloss>. There it becomes "sensitive," though not yet corporeal. From there, it passes into the <term>ethereal vehicle</term> <gloss>a "spirit-body" made of light that carries the soul</gloss> of the idol. There it becomes "corporeal," though not yet clearly perceptible to the senses. Finally, it enters the elemental body—whether it be simple and airy, or composite—which is the small vessel of the ethereal vehicle, in which the light at last becomes clearly visible. And I believe this is that **Golden Chain** which **Homer** saw hanging from heaven and reaching down even to the earth; once grasped, men can lift themselves up into the heavens.

Truly, celestial souls abound with such great light from God that a huge supply of radiance overflows from them into their bodies—the very light we see in the stars. If the soul of a human should ever fix its gaze so intensely upon God that it is filled with divine light and <margin>A</margin> "snatched away," it then shines with equal brilliance and pours out most abundant rays into its vehicle; and through that vehicle and the airy body, it pours light into this body which is visible to our eyes. Because it then glows with that fullest abundance of rays, the body is refined and lifted up—the ethereal vehicle and the airy body assisting in this, like kindling lifted up by a flame. By such a "fiery chariot," the Magi and the Platonists would say that **Elijah** and **Paul** were snatched up into heaven. <margin>B</margin> And finally, after the judgment of the world, the body—which our <margin>C</margin> people call "glorified"—will be snatched up in a similar way. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, **Zoroaster** gives this command: <note>The following is translated from the Greek of the Chaldean Oracles</note> "Since the soul is a bright fire by the power of the Father, let the immortal depth of the soul be the master in you; and lift all your eyes upward. Then do not leave the dregs of matter behind at the precipice." <margin>E</margin> That is to say: Since the soul, through the power of the Father, becomes a <margin>F</margin> splendid fire, let the immortal depth of the soul rule within you, and lift all your eyes together on high. Then, you will not leave even the body itself—which is the dross <margin>G</margin> of matter—behind at the precipice. <margin>H</margin> He calls his light **Fire**; God overflows with this by His own nature, and the soul, having been turned toward the Father, abounds with it through the Father's power. And because God...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from Book 13 of his "Platonic Theology," where he examines the soul's capacity to transcend the body and perform miracles. # Theology

I believe this happens through that center of the soul, which we called a little earlier the "unity" bestowed upon the soul by God. Through this unity, the soul is reconciled to God, the center of all centers and pure unity itself. Through this, it reconciles not only the elements of this body, but even those of the world. He <note>Ficino refers here to the "Chaldean" wisdom or Zoroaster</note> revealed that God can be reached only through this unity, as Zoroaster said: "There is something intelligible which you must perceive with the flower of the mind" <note>original: <term>εστι τι νοητόν ο χρη σε νοείν νοου ανθεί</term></note>. Zoroaster calls the very center of the soul the "flower of the mind." Plato calls it the "head of the mind." This opinion of ours seems to be confirmed by that statement of Paul, the divine theologian, who said that a soul snatched up to God was neither clearly in the body nor outside the body <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2-4, where St. Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven"</note>; evidently because it did not inhabit the body through its spirit-image <term>idolum</term> <note>In Ficino's philosophy, the "idolum" is the lower part of the soul that mirrors the body and governs its functions</note>, but was present through its center. The soul performs these wonders as long as it remains così abstracted. Yet it remains so only for a short time, because a certain natural affection for its lower power pulls it back to the care of the body. Just as a stone thrown upward is said to remain for a moment in the air between its ascent and descent.

<margin>☞</margin>
But does the human soul throw the order of the world into confusion by performing miracles? Not at all. For, to speak in the Platonic manner, such miracles are prescribed in the universal law of things and through a certain perpetual series of causes converging toward the same end. The providence of the minds that continuously breathe together under God—all the way down to our own mind—leads to this very result. Toward this same end flows the divine fate of the spirit-images <term>idolorū</term> from the first soul down to the image of our soul. Toward this same end flows a certain divine disposition of all natures, from the affection of the first nature down to the temperament of our own nature. The celestial signs often foretell these same things to us; through them, as if through cups or the nods of the divine powers, thoughts are signified. "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of His hands" <note>original: "Celi enarrant glorias dei: 7 opera manuū eius annūtiat firmamentuz." This is a quote from Psalm 19:1.</note>. Therefore, it is not that whenever that angelic soul desires to accomplish some wonderful work—such as summoning the winds—the higher causes immediately favor this wish and desire something new just because the soul has affected something new. On the contrary: because the celestial beings have decreed that very thing, the soul desires it. In what way? The providence regarding future winds resides in the higher divinities. A disposition of this kind—as we have said elsewhere—runs down through those three series directly to our souls: primarily through providence into the mind, in a certain way through fate into the spirit-image, and through nature into the temperament of our body.

But the disturbed souls of men do not receive these impulses. A peaceful soul, however, receives these heavenly impulses from every side. Whence it begins to think secretly the same things that the higher beings think, and to will and nill the same things. For it is inclined by a natural—that is, a divine and intimate—instinct. All thoughts and affections follow for this soul according to its prayer, and whatever it asks from the higher beings, it receives. Indeed, it asks for those things which they were already going to give; and because they were going to give them, they provoked the soul to ask. Just like a mother who holds out an apple in her hand before the eyes of her son so that, being thus invited, the son asks for the apple. The son sees it, asks for it, and receives it; he receives it, I say, not only because he asks, but he asks also because he was about to receive it. Nor does the mother wish to give it only after the son wishes to receive it, but rather the reverse. We, indeed, mostly proceed not by natural or divine desires, but by those which daily chance kindles; for as different things encounter our senses, we are affected in one way or another. And so, occupied by contingent things, we rarely achieve what we desire, because we rarely (and then only by chance) concur with the will of the higher beings.

But the angelic soul both consents with them—because it lives peacefully—and commands the world, because it is released of its own accord from this little body (which is a tiny part of the world) and has returned into its own most ample nature.
<margin>☜</margin>
God foresaw that the soul would be such; such, I say, not only by higher help but also by its own will. This will acts most freely when, having dismissed external actions, it turns back into itself to contemplate and love its own origin.
<margin>☜</margin>
God also chose such a soul to perform wonders. That its prayers are not in vain, even concerning public changes in the world, **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian polymath and philosopher</note> affirms in his *Metaphysics*...

->Marsilio Ficino<-

He uses the analogy of a mother prompting her child to ask for an apple to show how the soul’s desires are inspired by the divine gifts it is already destined to receive.</summary>

Here, he concludes that discussion by citing Proclus and Iamblichus before beginning Book 14, which focuses on the soul's innate desire to become God.</meta>

->Platonic Book<-

...sacrifice; and Proclus and Iamblichus <note>Influential Neoplatonic philosophers who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine</note> argue this in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue regarding the creation of the world</note>. For they prove that the vows <note>original: <term>vota</term>, referring to the focused prayers or spiritual desires</note> of a most holy man—especially if the vows of the people also concur with him—wonderfully join souls to God in such a way that, in a certain sense, a single operation of God and the soul is formed. But this occurs as if by a craft: either of the soul, or as a divine instrument. Regarding those miracles which God performs by Himself without an instrument, which are far greater, we are not treating them at present. 

Are miracles of this kind natural to the soul? They are natural in a certain way, as the Platonists believe, and again they are not natural. They are natural insofar as the soul returns into the mind and becomes the attendant <note>original: <term>pedissequus</term>, a servant or follower</note> and instrument of the highest God. They are non-natural insofar as the soul serves only the use of a single body; captured by the love of that body for a time, it neither unfolds the breadth of its own power nor becomes a participant in the divine. However, as often as the soul unfolds itself and becomes a participant, it shows that it will not be dissolved by any blow to the bodies. Indeed, the soul in some way stands before all things and twists all things according to its will. Now, the individual points we have discussed concerning miracles from the Platonic perspective, in conjunction with the mind, let them be affirmed by us in such a way as they are approved by Christian theologians.

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls to the Magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Fourteen.

## That the soul strives to become God: we show by twelve signs according to the twelve gifts of God. Chapter 1.

<margin>
In the beginning of the discussion, twelve foundations of signs pertaining to the immortality of the soul. In one part, he treats how much the soul rules over bodies, through which signs we pass. In the other, he discusses how the soul strives to become God. Concerning this, we shall treat through twelve signs according to the twelve gifts of God. In this, the wondrous greatness of the soul will appear.
</margin>

It would not be enough for the soul to emulate God in these wondrous ways we have mentioned, unless it also became God. Here Zoroaster <note>A legendary ancient Persian prophet whom Ficino believed anticipated Christian and Platonic truths</note> thus exclaimed: **O man, craft of a most daring nature.** <note>original Greek: <term>ω τολμιροτατης φύσεως ανθρωπε τεχνασμα</term></note> It is agreed among all theologians that God is Truth itself and Good itself. That He is all things. That He is the author of the universe. Above all. In all. Always providing for all. Administering justly. Persisting strongly in His own state while He administers. Treating things temperately and sweetly. Living most opulently and most joyfully. Beholding, wondering at, and worshipping Himself as so blessed—to which twelve gifts of God all theology among all nations attributes everything. 

Whatever men do everywhere, they refer to the possession of these things; nor do they seek or strive for anything else than to acquire gifts of this kind for themselves most fully. God alone is the most full possessor of these. Therefore, the entire effort of our soul is that it may become God. Such an effort is no less natural to men than the effort to fly is to birds. For it is present in all men, always and everywhere. Therefore, it does not follow a contingent quality of some particular man, but the very nature of the species itself. 

Now, a natural movement directed toward some end is determined toward this end rather than another for no other reason than a certain affection of its nature, through which it agrees with such an end rather than another. Because of this agreement, it loves. And because of the same, it can attain what it loves. Just as air, by its lightness, agrees with the hollow of fire <note>In the ancient and medieval conception of the cosmos, the element of fire occupied a sphere just above the air; air "strives" to rise toward it</note>. Through this same thing, it exerts itself and is moved toward it. Through this same thing again, it can reach it, and rest in it after it has reached it. Therefore, the human struggle intent upon God can be fulfilled. For who inserted this into our souls, except that same God whom we seek? Who, since He alone is the author of species, inserts a proper appetite into those species. For from the first principle of things, as if from the first good and desirable thing, all nature...

<summary>Ficino concludes his discussion on how the soul performs miracles by acting as God's instrument and begins Book 14, arguing that the soul’s ultimate natural desire is to become God. He outlines twelve divine attributes that the human soul naturally strives to possess, asserting that this "daring" ambition is a fundamental part of human nature implanted by God Himself.</summary>

# Theology

<margin>E</margin> We are led by a natural appetite <note>original: <term>appetitus</term>, referring to an innate drive or spiritual hunger</note>. The First Mover is also the ultimate end. Indeed, the order of ends follows the order of agents; just as the supreme agent moves the agents that follow it, so too the ends of all other agents are directed toward the end of the supreme agent. For whatever a first agent does, it does for its own sake. Now, the first agent leads and performs all the actions of every subsequent thing by moving them all toward their own actions, and therefore toward their own ends. From this, it follows that the ends of all inferior agents are ordained by that first agent toward its own proper end. This first agent is God. The end of the divine will is His own goodness. For this reason, all subsequent things are necessarily ordained toward God as their end. This is especially true because nothing tends toward anything as an end except insofar as that thing is good. Thus, it happens that the "good" is the end, by the very reason of it being good. Therefore, that which is the highest good is the greatest end of all.

<margin>D</margin> Add to this that the first good is the cause for all things being good. Therefore, He is the cause of them being desired. If, however, He is the one for whose sake all things are to be desired, it follows that He is the greatest of all and must be desired by all. He is therefore the end of all things—yet with this distinction: that for minds, He is the end according to the "form" <note>meaning a direct, intellectual realization</note>, while for other things, He is the end according to the "shadow" <note>meaning an indirect or physical reflection</note>. Therefore, He exists as the end for humans according to the form, since nothing else satisfies them. In this way, humans desire the form of God because such an appetite has been granted by God Himself. Nor is the appetite by which we desire God any less a gift from Him than the physical appetite enticed by objects presented to the senses. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, it is even more so, as the supreme good is more powerful in drawing us than the smallest goods. Truly, as I discussed in my book *On Love* <note>original: <term>De Amore</term>, Ficino’s famous commentary on Plato’s Symposium</note>, the splendor of the supreme good itself shines in individual things; and where it shines most appropriately, there it chiefly allures the beholder, excites the thinker, ravishes and occupies the one who approaches it, and compels him to venerate this kind of splendor above all others as if it were a divinity. He desires nothing else except that, having laid aside his prior nature, he may become that splendor himself. This is evident from the fact that a lover is not content with the mere sight or touch of the beloved, and often cries out:

"This person possesses I know not what, which burns me; and yet I do not understand what it is I desire." <note>This "I know not what" (the *je ne sais quoi*) is a recurring theme in Renaissance philosophy, describing the divine spark that attracts lovers to one another.</note>

It is clear here that the soul is using a divine radiance, which sparkles in a beautiful person as if in a mirror; and by this, the soul is secretly snatched away as if drawn upward by a hook, so that it might turn into God. <margin>E</margin> God would be—if I may speak this way—an unjust tyrant if He commanded us to attempt things which we could never fulfill. Yet He commands that we seek Him, and He inflames human desire for Himself with His own little sparks. He would also be an unskilled and overly reckless archer if He directed our desires toward Himself like arrows at a target, but failed to add feathers to the arrows <margin>12</margin> by which they might eventually reach that target. Finally, He would be unfortunate if His own effort, by which He pulls us toward Himself, never achieved its end. For this reason, our soul can at some point "become God," since it naturally strives toward this goal while God urges it on. It does not become God except by putting on the "form" of God. Just as nothing becomes fire unless it receives the form of fire. Therefore, just as the matter of air—which was previously characterized by the moisture and heat of air—casts off its moisture through the power of fire, keeps the heat, and, having accepted dryness, is transformed into the form of fire; so the essence of the human soul—which now possesses a mind and inferior powers—is stripped by God. It casts off the inferior powers and the mind—or rather, the human "head" of the mind <note>The "head" or "unity" of the mind is the highest point of the soul that connects directly to the divine.</note>—while the unity is preserved. It puts on the divine substance as if it were a new form, through which it almost becomes God, and through which it then performs all operations as if it were a certain God rather than a soul.

It is necessary that this be able to be fulfilled at some point, lest the human species seek in vain—or rather, lest God draw us in a reckless manner. <margin>S</margin> While surrounded by the dark dwelling-place of this body, the soul releases its inferior powers either never, or hardly at all, and then only for a moment. Therefore, that wonderful work is not fulfilled in this body, and is hardly ever even tasted by anyone. But natural desires must be fulfilled in many, and not through a fleeting moment, but through a stable habit, which is what they truly seek. For if the mind is raised higher to contemplate spiritual things, it departs further from corporal things. Now, the supreme limit which the intellect can reach is...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul’s natural desire for God is proof of its destiny to be transformed into a divine state. He uses the metaphor of an archer and the physical transformation of air into fire to illustrate that God would not give us a desire for the divine if it were impossible to achieve.</summary>

<meta>This text is from Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology," specifically Book VI, Chapter 2 (despite the previous page's label of Book 14, the content here transitions into the "Fifth Sign of Immortality"). Ficino is arguing that the human soul’s drive for universal truth proves it is immortal because only an eternal being could have an infinite appetite for the ultimate cause (God).</meta>

...divine substance follows: so that then at last the mind may be able to enter the divine substance, when it has been completely alienated from mortal senses. Therefore, the soul, exempt from the bonds of this body and departing pure, by a certain reasoning becomes God. Moreover, God and God’s eternity are the same. Therefore, by a similar reasoning, it becomes eternity; or rather, it becomes eternal. Which state indeed John the Theologian <note>The Apostle John; Ficino likely refers to 1 John 3:2: "we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is."</note> calls becoming like God; but Paul <note>The Apostle Paul; referring to 2 Corinthians 3:18: "are being transformed into the same image."</note> calls being transformed into the image of God.

¶ The fifth sign of immortality: from that which the soul desires—the first truth and the first good.

### Chapter 2.

<margin>a</margin>
This superior reasoning will at last make us more certain about immortality: if, running through those twelve gifts of God one by one, we show that the soul, in seeking these things, naturally tries in a certain way to equal itself to God. Our [mind] conceives a common <note>Meaning "universal" or "transcendental"</note> reason of truth and goodness. Through this, it seeks universal truth and desires universal good. In universal truth, all true things are contained; in universal good, all good things are contained. Thus it happens that the soul naturally seeks all truths and naturally desires all goods. This is evident from the fact that once the truth of any one thing is known, we do not rest, but we seek another, and again another, as long as we think some truth remains to be known. The same is observed in the gathering of goods.

<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, every truth and every good is God Himself, who is the first truth and the first good. Therefore, we desire God Himself. But what do we desire most in Him? To become like Him. For all things, according to the capacity of their nature, tend toward Him as their end, and they desire in their own way to become like Him. Bodies lacking life [tend toward Him] according to being alone. Living things, according to life. Sentient things, according to sense. Rational things, according to intellect. We cannot, however, be made like God through the intellect unless by understanding God. Indeed, the intellect becomes like whatever other things it understands, when it transforms itself into their images through the act of understanding. Our end, therefore, is to see God through the intellect, and to enjoy the seen God through the will; because our highest good is the highest object of our highest power, or rather the most perfect act concerning that object.

Now, our highest powers are the mind, the "head" of the mind, and the will. The highest object of these is universal truth and the universal and whole good. That is God. Nor should any of the Arabs <note>original: <term>arabum</term>; Ficino refers to Islamic philosophers like Avicenna or Averroes, who argued that the human mind connects to a lower celestial "intellect" rather than directly to God.</note> object to us that it is enough for us to enjoy some angel. For a natural desire is in us always to find the cause of every effect. Nor does the inquiry cease until one reaches the first cause. Since, therefore, we wish to see the causes of every known effect, and our intellect knows "being" itself universally, it follows that we naturally desire to know the cause of being itself, which is God. Nor are we said to have reached the ultimate end unless the whole natural desire is at rest. Wherefore the ultimate human end consists in the knowledge or possession of God alone, which alone terminates the natural appetite. This is clearly apparent from the fact that the attainment of one's own end delights everyone exceedingly. Yet the soul rejoices in the possession of no thing so vehemently, so purely, or so firmly as in even the slightest taste of divine speculation; through which, if it is ever truly perceived, both every other possession and the whole world and life itself are held in contempt. For whoever lives piously at any time with God, cries out that he was only then truly alive, and lived removed from evils, and tasted something of the good—as if he had only then finally retreated into his own harbor.

<margin>D</margin>
To this tends that saying of Plato in the book *On Knowledge* <note>The *Theaetetus*, 176a-b</note>: "Evils cannot be altogether avoided. For it is necessary that there always be something contrary to the good. Among the gods above, however, it is impossible for evils to exist. But they necessarily revolve around mortal nature and this lower place. Wherefore one must flee from here to there as quickly as possible. To flee from here to there is nothing other than to make oneself like God as far as possible. Justice and holiness with wisdom make one like Him." Thus he rightly teaches. For where the Good of all goods flourishes, there alone is found the medicine for all evils. Nor do we believe...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's infinite drive for universal truth and goodness proves its immortality, as this hunger can only be satisfied by union with God, the First Cause. He cites Plato, St. Paul, and St. John to support the idea that the soul's ultimate goal is "divinization" or becoming like God.</summary>

We must [not] yield <note>The Latin *cedendum est* is implied here; Ficino is refuting Panaetius.</note> to Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who doubted the immortality of the soul.</note> when he says: we certainly desire divine things, but we shall never attain the summit, because the full possession of divine things and a quiet life do not belong to the souls of men, but to the angels. ¶ Nature itself teaches us the opposite. ¶ Indeed, the elements, which by their natural desire seek their proper places, are moved all the more rapidly the more they approach their own locations and boundaries. ¶ Therefore, Aristotle in his book *On the Heavens* shows that natural, straight motion cannot wander into infinity; otherwise, in its progress, it would not be now slower and now faster. For whatever is such that it tends more vehemently toward something later than it did before does not wander into infinity, but carries itself toward something certain. ¶ Moreover, we experience this in the very desire for knowing. For the more someone understands, the more ardently he burns for what remains. Therefore, the natural desire for knowing is directed toward some determined end. What is this end? The **Cause of all causes**; when this is found, all natural investigation of them is terminated. Nature gave to heavy bodies an appetite and an inclination by which they desire lower places. It further provided them with weight and coldness as a medium through which they might descend to the desired location. It gave to subtler things an appetite for a higher place, and joined to them lightness and heat, through which media they might attain the desired end. It gave to brute animals an appetite for food and sex. It added members prepared for eating and for sex. To the soul, the universal leader and guide of nature gave a vow for the whole of truth and the good. Indeed, this is more natural than the appetite for food and sex, insofar as it is more continuous. The body demands to eat only rarely. It demands sex even more rarely. <margin>f</margin> But we desire the **truth** and the **good** at every single moment. For we are always desirous of new things, imaginations, and reasons. We always open our eyes to whatever presents itself, and we are exceedingly delighted by the longest and widest prospect. Indeed, we are satisfied only by the immense. We always prick up our ears to hear whatever it may be. This is what infants do, and adults. The learned and the ignorant alike. And all craftsmen in any art do so, with nature as their guide. Add to this that the libido for sex can be tamed, and the voracity for eating can be diminished. But the will for the truth and the good cannot be diminished; rather, while the former decrease with age, the latter increases. Add further: that those bodily things are desired for the sake of something else, but these for their own sake. Therefore, as much as the desire for truth and the good is more natural than the desire for food and sex, so much more has it been provided for by the guide of nature that it should attain its own end for its own sake. Indeed, it is more natural for this very reason: that it is more prepared to acquire its end. ¶ Surely, if the property of any species is necessary and has been prudently arranged by its author, it follows that the rational species is able to attain what it strives for—that effort which is directed toward the possession of the whole good as if it were the end. Indeed, if the attainment of the ultimate end were impossible, then the entire species and the action of the species would be contingent, fortuitous, and vain. Sometimes the eye of the species rests in a graceful sight. The ear rests in melody. And each sense is satiated and filled by its own objects. Nature has gifted the senses with such great happiness. But shall the **queen of these senses** <note>The human soul or intellect.</note>—who, although she is lower than the angels, is nonetheless superior to the brutes—<margin>6</margin> be so unhappy and so neglected by the Artificer of nature that she wanders forever and never rests? Certainly not in this life. Nor should any of the Arabs <note>Ficino refers to Averroes and his followers, who argued for a single, collective "Active Intellect" shared by all humanity rather than individual immortal souls.</note> be listened to here, imagining that the human intellect cannot attain its end in individuals in this life, but at least does so in the whole of humanity. First, because there is not one intellect in all people (which are utterly repugnant to each other), as we shall show elsewhere. Then, because the soul never attains an exalted state in all men at once. And while it is blind to divine things in individual men, it is similarly blind in almost all of them together. Finally, it is not permitted to imagine that we can comprehend the very substances of divine forms from natural substances according to our wish. <margin>✠</margin> For these [natural] substances incline toward matter. But those [divine ones] do not at all. Moreover, the human intellect, insofar as it inhabits this body, to that extent leans toward corporeal things in its knowing. ¶ Furthermore, natural effects cannot equal or demonstrate the powers and substances of divine causes. Add that divine forms [are separate] from nature...

He refutes the Averroist "Arabs" who claim the intellect is a single collective entity rather than an individual soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the soul’s immortality from Book VI, Chapter 2. He is transitioning from the physical arguments of the previous page to an epistemological and theological argument: that because the human intellect seeks the "whole" truth and not just fragments, its ultimate fulfillment (and thus its survival) must lie beyond the physical body.</meta>

# Platonic ## Book

[things] are much more distant from natural things than natural things are from each other. Therefore, if colors are not known through voices—as is apparent in the case of a **blind man** <note>original: "cecio", likely a transcription of *caeco* (blind man)</note>—much less are divine things grasped through natural things, as Plato writes to Dionysius of Syracuse. This is because the divine substance and power, being infinite, cannot be perceived by us according to our desire until we are absolutely formed by that power itself. This indeed cannot be perfected in a soul joined to a body affected in this way.

<margin>A</margin>
But to return to the argument of this chapter: the capacity of reason and its appetite requires not just certain true things or certain goods, but all of them in their entirety. Here on earth, it seems it never achieves this, for as Plato says in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue often attributed to Plato in the Renaissance, focusing on astronomy and the soul’s journey.</note>: the intellect is always ambiguous and the will is always anxious. Therefore, the soul will attain these things when it is stripped of the body. If it attains the universal good, it will by no means lack **immortality**; for immortality is as much a good as death is an evil, since death deprives one of all goods. Furthermore, the mind, which will see all true things, would enjoy no goods if it suspected it were going to die. Therefore, so that the attainment of the end may be secure and tranquil, it is necessary for the mind to be certain of the eternal possession of that end. 

This is confirmed by **Aurelius Augustine** in the thirteenth book of *The Trinity*: "All wish to be happy; and for that reason, they do not wish to perish and be consumed, because they are happy. Nor can they be happy unless they are living. They do not wish, therefore, to perish while they live. Whoever is truly happy, or desires to be so, wishes to be immortal. However, he does not live happily who does not have what he wants. In no way, therefore, can life be truly happy unless it is eternal." Thus he says.

<margin>B</margin>
But so that the **Panaetians** <note>Followers of Panaetius, a Stoic philosopher who argued against the soul's immortality.</note> do not further doubt that a truly happy life is suited to man, we conclude thus: Since it is the property of an intellectual nature to "taste" every good through cognition, it is certainly its property to "feed" upon every good—that is, the whole good—through affection. **Beatitude** <note>A state of supreme, divine happiness.</note> is therefore proper to the intellectual nature. However, according to the kind of intellect one has, such is the beatitude one can achieve. If one has a **true and formal intellect**, one achieves a true and formal happiness. But if one has a **shadowy intellect**, one achieves a shadowy happiness. 

Although the human soul is a certain image of a more divine intellect, it nevertheless possesses the true **form of a mind** within itself. This is proved by three signs. The first is that it understands many true things according to their true nature. The second is that it understands the true nature of truth itself. The third is that if our soul possessed only a shadow of an intellect, it would never understand or define the form and substance of the intellect, but would only view its "accidents" <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are secondary qualities (like color or size) rather than the core essence of a thing.</note> in a confused way. Since, therefore, the soul possesses a power of understanding that is not merely **shadowy** <note>original: "vmbvatilem" (umbratilem), meaning reflecting like a shadow rather than being the solid thing itself.</note>—like that of certain more clever beasts—but is truly expressed and **formal**, it can therefore eventually attain a truly happy life. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that I posit one intellect as shadowy and another as formal.

<margin>L</margin>
Indeed, the Platonists (as **Proclus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Ficino's hierarchies of being.</note> discusses) distinguish all classes of things in this way: first **Unity**, then **Mind**, then **Soul**, and then **Nature**. But let us set these aside for the present. Let us see by what reasoning **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian who blended Greek philosophy with scripture.</note> confirms the above in his books *On First Principles*. When Origen considered that God, the craftsman of all things, consulted not only necessity and utility (both private and common) in each thing, but also studied beauty and the admiration of those looking upon them everywhere, he concluded that just as a human craftsman builds the most beautiful works so that those looking might be enticed to consider and admire the **genius** <note>The guiding spirit or innate power of the creator.</note> by which he built them, so God built the most artistic structure of the world. 

From this, he wishes it to be understood that the "reasons" <note>The underlying divine blueprints or logic of things.</note> by which all things excel by instinct were inserted into our minds by the very reason of God, the craftsman of all, and from there the mind is daily prompted. Thus, our mind desires these reasons through nature no less than the eye desires colors or the sense of taste desires food. He adds that God has [placed] us in such a condition...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human intellect is "formal" (substantial) rather than "shadowy," proving that humans are capable of achieving eternal beatitude. Citing Augustine and Origen, he asserts that our natural craving for universal truth and beauty reflects a divine design that requires an immortal soul to reach fulfillment.</summary>

<margin>☞</margin># Sixth sign. Because the soul 
# strives to become all things.
->Chapter III<-

<margin>E</margin>**I**t has been shown that our soul, in all its acts, acquires that first gift of God according to its strength: that is, the possession of the whole truth and the whole good. But does it seek that second gift? Does it strive to become all things, just as God is all things? It strives in a wondrous way. Indeed, it lives the life of a plant, insofar as it indulges the body by nourishing it. It lives the life of a brute beast, insofar as it flatters the senses. It lives the life of a man, insofar as it deliberates on human affairs through reason. It lives the life of heroes, insofar as it investigates natural things. It lives the life of demons <note>original: "demonum"; in the Platonic tradition, "daemons" are intermediary spirits or rational beings between humans and gods, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>, insofar as

---

<page-num>132</page-num>
<header>xiv. 132</header>

it contemplates mathematics. It lives the life of angels, insofar as it inquires into divine mysteries. It lives the life of God, insofar as it performs all works by the grace of God. <margin>Symbol</margin> Every human soul experiences all these things in itself in some way, though some differently than others. And thus the human race contends to become all things, since it lives the lives of all. 
<margin>Symbol</margin> Not without wonder, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure to whom a collection of mystical and philosophical texts (the *Hermetica*) was attributed; highly revered by Ficino.</note> says: "Man is a great miracle, a venerable and adorable animal, who knows the race of demons as if kindred by nature, and who passes into God as if he were God himself." Furthermore, whatever things exist, insofar as they exist, they are true. Insofar as they have obtained some power, order, and use, they are good. We have shown above that the soul seeks all true things and all good things. Therefore, it seeks 
<margin>☞</margin>all things. What else does it seek? Except that it might know all through the intellect, and enjoy all through the will. In both ways, it strives to become all things. Just as a sense—
<margin>//</margin>take sight—does not discern colors unless it puts on the forms of the colors, and becomes one from the power of seeing and the act of the visible form. Or as one is made from air and light. So the intellect does not know the things themselves unless it is clothed in the forms of the things to be known, and becomes one from the power of understanding and the act of the intelligible form. A single action accompanies their union. For there is one operation of understanding for both. Who, likewise, would deny that one thing is made from corporate matter and the form granted to it? Since from that composite a single act and a single motion proceeds. 
<margin>G</margin>But it is much more necessary—as is pleasing to the Platonists and Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>—that a certain unity be made from the power of the intellect and the form of the thing to be understood, because often a more stable composition results from these. For often they remain as one longer than corporate matter and its form. <margin>)</margin> Moreover, the intellect itself is a certain form. A form, I say, gaping <note>original: "inhians"; suggests a longing or opening up toward something.</note> toward a further form, just like matter. Therefore, it agrees more with the form to be received than corporate matter agrees with its own form. 
<margin>Symbol</margin> For the forms given to the matter of the world descend from the supreme mind. Wherefore, they agree much more with our mind than with matter.
