<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book VI. In the previous section, Ficino discussed the soul's desire for the universal good. Here, he explores how the human intellect and will allow the soul to "become" all things and ultimately strive toward a divine state.</meta>

# Platonic Book

<margin>{</margin>
Finally, just as the mind is more excellent than matter, it more effectively takes up and unites with the form <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "form" is the ideal essence or blueprint of a thing.</note> it desires for itself. Nor should one believe that the soul unites itself less to what it grasps than the body does. For the body, through the soul's power of digestion, turns even the most diverse foods into its own substance. So too the soul: what it receives—or rather, conceives—it turns into itself, and much more so. Since the physical dimensions of bodies impede their mutual union, <margin>B</margin> spiritual things are far more suited to union. Therefore, the "reasons" <term>rationes: the formal principles or internal logic of things</term> of things understood pass more into the substance of the intellect (as **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note> maintains) than food passes into the substance of the body.

Through these points, it is clear that our mind and the form of the thing to be understood become a single thing. However, that which undergoes the form of something in such a way that it produces a unity from that form and itself, almost becomes the very thing whose form it has undergone. Who does not know that the matter of air, when it has received the form of fire, becomes fire or something fiery? Therefore, the intellect almost becomes that thing which it understands. I say it becomes that thing *in act* <note>original: "actu"; in Aristotelian terms, "in act" means actually or fully realized, as opposed to "in potential."</note>. For both in potential and in a certain habitual way, it was already the same thing before it understood it, as **Plotinus** thinks. Surely, the intellect then understands a "circle" when it itself becomes, in act, the "reason of the circle" <note>original: "ratio circuli", the essential definition or conceptual blueprint of a circle.</note>. Indeed, this very "becoming in act" is the act of understanding itself. Moreover, the intellect was that same reason of the circle even before, both according to potential—as far as it pertains to the substantial Idea of the circle—and according to habit—as far as it pertains to the formula of the Idea familiar to us. Now, the clarity of individual things consists in the firm "reason" <term>ratione</term> of those things. And so, the mind becomes any true thing when it understands those things by converting itself into their eternal reasons. But more on this elsewhere. It suffices for us at present that since the intellect seeks to understand all things, and by understanding clothes itself inwardly in their forms, it follows that it seeks to "become" all things. From this, it strives to become God, in whom all things exist, while it strives to become all things. Enough regarding the intellect.

<margin>Note</margin>
Our will desires the same thing, because it always affects to enjoy all good things. By enjoying things, it unites itself to the things it enjoys. But there is a difference between the intellect and the will. Both are "all things." The intellect is "all true things"; the will is "all good things." But the intellect is united to things by transferring them into itself. The will, on the contrary, is united to things by transferring itself into the things. In what way? Surely, our intellect understands things in its own mode rather than according to the nature of the things themselves. It understands the forms of bodies—which are particular, immersed in matter, divided, confused, tainted, and changeable—in a certain universal, absolute, simple, distinct, pure, and stable way. But it comprehends God and the angels—who are stable and simple—mostly through a changeable and manifold discourse <note>The process of reasoning step-by-step rather than grasping truth all at once.</note>. Thus, our intellect perceives both those things which are below it and those above it in its own particular way. For this reason, it is said to transfer all things into its own nature. <margin>D</margin> From this, that saying of **Plato** also seems to be confirmed: that the mind understands through innate forms, since it understands according to the mode of its own nature. 

The will, however, does not first remain within itself like the intellect, but moves the soul and body to act, so that they may approach the desired things. Furthermore, it does not desire things in that specific mode by which they exist in the soul, but rather as they exist in themselves. For the intellect wishing to know gold, that universal and incorporeal species of gold is sufficient. But for the will, that is not enough. For as far as it regards human life, it wants *this* particular and corporeal gold, just as it is in itself. <margin>C/</margin> Let us conclude that our soul, through the intellect and the will, possesses those "twin Platonic wings" <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where he describes the soul's wings which allow it to soar toward the divine.</note>. It flies to God for this reason: because through them it flies to all things. Through the first [the intellect], it applies all things to itself. Through the second [the will], it applies itself to all things. And so the soul desires, endeavors, and begins to become God, and it makes progress every day. For anyone who is directed toward a certain end begins that which is primary. He proceeds, then intends little by little, and makes progress; eventually, he is perfected. For he intends by the same faculty with which he began. He later makes progress by the same faculty with which he was intending. Finally, he perfects by the same faculty with which he made progress. For which reason, our mind will one day be able to become all things in a certain way, and emerge as a "certain god." <margin>}</margin>

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul has a divine potential because the intellect transforms all things into itself, while the will moves the soul toward the reality of things. Through these "twin wings," the soul strives to become all-encompassing and ultimately attain a god-like state of perfection.</summary>
<keywords>intellect, will, Plotinus, Plato, wings of the soul, forms, divinity, potentiality, actuality, union with God</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology', specifically from Book XIV. In the previous section, Ficino discussed the soul's capacity to become all things through the intellect. Here, he provides further "signs" of the soul's divinity, focusing on its desire to emulate God’s creative power, universal sovereignty, and eternal presence.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
¶ The seventh and eighth signs: Since the soul strives to do all things, and likewise to overcome all things.

<margin>E</margin>
Other divine attributes follow: the third is being the author of all things, and the fourth is being above all things. Our soul also hunts for these. We have said elsewhere how, through various arts, the soul emulates all the works of God and thus, like God, produces all things. We have also said that man always struggles to rule over himself and all others—both men and beasts—and that he is impatient with all servitude. Even if he is forced to serve, he hates his master, since he serves against nature. Moreover, he strives resolutely to overcome in any matter, and is ashamed to be overcome even in the smallest things and the lightest games, as if that were against the natural dignity of man. Indeed, the feelings of shame and modesty, which are unique to the human race, signify a certain hidden majesty within us which it would be a sin to violate and which is most worthy of veneration.

<margin>F</margin>
I have spoken of this elsewhere. But as far as the desire for victory is concerned, one can clearly see the immense magnificence of our soul from this: that the empire of this world would not be enough for it if, having conquered this world, it learned that another world remained which it had not yet subdued. Hence, when **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), often used by philosophers as an example of boundless human ambition.</note> heard <term>Anaxarchus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher of the school of Democritus who accompanied Alexander on his campaigns.</note> arguing that there were innumerable worlds, he exclaimed, "Alas, miserable me, for I have not yet gained possession of even one!" Thus, man wants neither a superior nor an equal, nor does he suffer anything to remain excluded from his empire. This status belongs to God alone. Therefore, he seeks a divine status. We can clearly infer this from the fact that many philosophers and princes have sought divine honors for themselves. It was not enough for them to be considered good men; they had to be considered

<margin>G</margin>
divine. Indeed, they wished to be worshipped as gods. While countless men have attempted this, among philosophers <term>Empedocles</term> <note>A Greek philosopher who, according to legend, jumped into Mount Etna to prove his divinity.</note> and among princes **Alexander of Macedon** are said to have especially craved it. In short, all people affect the same desire, and if they hoped it would succeed, they would attempt it, as if they were claiming divinity as their own by right.

<margin>Chapter 5</margin>
¶ The ninth and tenth signs. That man strives to be everywhere, and likewise to be always.

<margin>J</margin>
**M**an desires to be everywhere. He uses the four elements, as we have said. He measures the earth and the sky, and searches through the deep hiding places of the underworld <note>original: "tartari"; in this context, the deep abyss of the classical afterlife.</note>. To him, the sky does not seem too high (to use the words of **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus, which Ficino translated.</note>), nor the center of the earth too deep. Intervals of time or place do not stop him, since he runs through all things that exist in any times or places. No wall blocks or pushes back his gaze. No boundaries are enough for him. He strives to rule everywhere and to be praised everywhere. And thus he strives to be as God is: everywhere. He also strives to be always, like God. He seeks this in two ways. First, he struggles so that all future time might remain "in the mouths of men" <note>An idiom for being remembered and spoken of by posterity.</note>. He grieves that he could not be celebrated in all past ages, nor be honored in future ones by all nations of men and ranks of the blessed. All people—youths and adults, the unlearned and the educated—strive for this with all their might and zeal. And they desire it more ardently the more they excel in talent. Now, that which all men—and especially the most outstanding—appetite, is desired by them as a "good" by natural law. Therefore, it is not sought in vain, for there is no rashness in the law of nature. It would be sought rashly and in vain as a good if it were to be of no profit to those seeking it. But praise is of no profit if it is not felt. Therefore, the human species prophesies that it will not lack sensation in future ages. For men often despise even their present life so that they may be celebrated by posterity. He also has the greatest care for his own descendants, both throughout his life and at the end of it, believing that future ages pertain to him. We do not see this happen with beasts, as if their nature prophesies that there is nothing in them worthy of veneration or endowed with eternal sensation. But the natural prophecy of the most excellent minds especially does not go astray.

<margin>K</margin>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul's infinite ambition to rule the world, its desire for divine honors, and its craving for eternal fame are "signs" of its innate divinity and immortality. He contends that nature would not instill such universal desires if the soul were not truly capable of surviving death to enjoy them.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, divine emulation, Alexander the Great, Empedocles, natural law, desire for glory, Neoplatonism, human dignity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of the soul's divine nature. In the preceding section, Ficino explored how the human soul emulates God’s creative power and desire for universal rule. This page transitions to the soul’s natural desire for immortality, using the "desire for being" found in all nature as a proof for the soul's eternal existence.</meta>

# Platonic Book [XVIII]

...can. Just as **Plato** writes in his letter to **Dionysius** <note>Plato’s Second Letter, which discusses the soul’s concern for its reputation and state after death.</note>. From this, he intends to show that for the souls of men, a sense of human affairs survives. He also confirmed this in the *Laws* as being within the order of divine providence. There is another way: by which our soul desires to be always—indeed, even to live, since for the soul, "to be" is the same as "to live"—and such a desire is clearly evident. The human soul—and indeed every soul—at some point thinks of eternal life. Once it has thought of it, it immediately affects it and always desires to exist.

<margin>A</margin>
In every way, the desire for being is natural, for it is present in all things as soon as they are born, and it is continuous. It does not arrive by deliberation, because it is present in things immediately upon birth. Nor does it happen by chance, because it is in all things and is continuous. Indeed, the elements, through the power of their natural qualities, resist things attempting to corrupt <note>In this context, 'corruption' refers to the physical breaking down or decay of a substance.</note> them, lest their "being" be taken away from them. Again, they seek out places suitable for themselves most greedily and repel things blocking their movement, so that they may preserve their being. This desire for being is called "natural" because it follows their natural qualities. Plants also, by the instinct of their vital constitution, suck up more healthy moisture, spreading their roots very far for this purpose, so that their being may be preserved. Likewise, they turn away from shadows by pulling back their little branches, and they entwine themselves around supports with certain hooked twigs, lest they lose their being. This desire we call natural because it follows the natural constitution of life. Brutes <note>A common philosophical term for non-human animals.</note>, through natural desire, adopt those things which preserve their being. They repel destructions through natural anger. In these creatures, the desire for being is likewise natural, because it follows not deliberation or chance, but natural and innate powers. However, since the natures of these things do not have any power through which they can provide eternal being for their own proper subject and body, none of these desire to always exist in their own proper substance; they would strive in vain. Yet they do desire, according to nature, to be eternal in their species. For this, their natural powers serve sufficiently. Hence they generate things similar to themselves in species, so that by propagation, the species of such things remains perpetual in the world. This appetite exists not only in elements and plants, but also in brutes, and it lacks knowledge. Certainly, the power of generating which serves this purpose has no knowledge.

<margin>B</margin>
If indeed there are any bodies whose principles are sufficient for being eternal in their own substance, those things desire to be eternal according to nature—not only in species, but truly in their own proper substance. Such, perhaps, are the bodies of the stars. Let us return to our own concerns. Our soul desires to be.

<margin>C</margin>
But is a desire of this kind natural? It is, without doubt, no less natural to our soul than the desire for being is to all other things. But indeed, it desires to exist *always*. Is this desire for "always being" just as natural as the desire for "being"? It clearly is.

<margin>D</margin>
Nor let any **Epicurean** <note>Followers of Epicurus (341–270 BCE), who argued that the soul is composed of atoms and dissolves at death; they are Ficino’s primary intellectual opponents regarding immortality.</note> object to us that, although the soul naturally desires being itself—even as if it did not know it—it nonetheless desires to exist forever *beyond* nature, perhaps because it first knew that eternity and then desired it. That knowledge does not prevent the greed for eternity from being natural. For our senses also recognize foods which they nonetheless desire according to nature. The wolf desires the lamb and the dog the hare after they have seen them; yet they desire them naturally.

<margin>E</margin>
Since from their natural constitution they are immediately driven to desire such that they cannot *not* desire. And just as it is natural for the eyes to perceive such objects before them, so it is natural for the power of desire to long for such things once they have been inspected. By the same reasoning, it is natural for the intellect to know clear objects. To the **will** <note>The 'voluntas', or the rational appetite. Unlike the 'animal' appetite, the will is guided by the intellect's understanding of what is good.</note>, those things which are judged good are offered by reason; the will desires them naturally. Whatever is clearly offered, the intellect naturally recognizes. Whatever is offered under the reasoning of "the good," the will naturally desires. Therefore, it is natural for the intellect to know "eternal being." Once known as a good, it is natural for the will to seek it. And just as the irrational appetite follows the senses, so the will—which is rational desire—follows the intellect.

<margin>F</margin>
Therefore, if the appetite for food is natural because it is sudden and not born of deliberation, so the will for immortality is natural because it is a sudden act following the pure intellect...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human desire for immortality is a "natural appetite" similar to how plants seek water or animals seek food. He contends that because the intellect can conceive of eternity, the will naturally and inevitably desires it, which serves as evidence that the soul is meant for eternal existence.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, natural appetite, being vs. living, intellect and will, Epicureans, Plato, species preservation, eternal substance</keywords>

Here, Ficino transitions to the human mind's specific desire for "eternal being," arguing that since this desire is universal and natural, it must be attainable.</meta>

->Theology<-
riiij.

# Theology

...and the nature of the will. For as soon as **eternal being** is presented to the mind, the mind judges it as something to be sought after without any discursive reasoning <note>discursio: the process of step-by-step logical deduction. Ficino argues we recognize the goodness of eternity instantly, like a reflex.</note>. And it is desired with no prior deliberation. Because if it were desired either <margin>a</margin> by chance or by deliberate choice, then not everyone would desire the same thing, nor would they desire it always, nor in the same way; instead, this desire would vary according to circumstances and the diversity of those deliberating. But as it stands, all people necessarily and suddenly adopt this desire, driven by nature.

In the same way, we necessarily will "the good" itself, but we do not necessarily or by nature will *this* or *that* specific good. Thus, we do not naturally desire to be "this way" or "that way," or to be "here" or "there." But to **be** itself, in an absolute sense—where no privation <note>privatio: the absence or lack of a quality. Here, the lack of existence itself.</note> of being is mixed in—is what we desire by the pull of nature. And just as we always dread the eternal privation of life by a natural impulse, <margin>c</margin> so we love eternal life by a natural attraction.

The Artisan of nature <note>nature artifex: a Platonic way of referring to God as the Creator or "Demiurge" who crafted the world.</note> tempered essence with knowledge, knowledge with desire, and desire with the attainment of the end. Therefore, just as a brute animal knows "being" only as something temporal <note>i.e., existing only within the limits of time and physical life.</note> according to the capacity of its nature, and according to its nature desires temporal being, <margin>d</margin> so our soul, by the magnificence of its own nature, knows **eternal being** and naturally desires it. For "being" itself is naturally desirable. Indeed, it is naturally desirable in the same way that it is naturally knowable.

Therefore, just as "being" is known by the nature of a brute animal only as something temporal and present, so it is similarly desired by that animal according to its nature. But by human nature, just as <margin>e</margin> "being" itself is known as something perpetual, so it is naturally sought after by that nature as something perpetual. Thus, that which is known according to one's own intellectual nature is naturally sought after according to that same nature. Furthermore, we shall attain what we desire according to that same nature. For it is reasonable that we reach the goal through the same faculty <margin>g</margin> by which we reach it in knowing and in willing. Thus, the natural end of a motion belongs to the same thing to which the motion itself is natural.

Therefore, I do not see why one who reaches eternal life through knowledge and will should not also reach it through life itself. Indeed, by the virtue of that life which overcomes temporal things, both the intelligence and the will (which depend upon it) carry themselves beyond the transitory toward the eternal. Furthermore, since a natural desire is not in vain, <margin>h</margin> it follows that the human soul naturally attains the perpetual being it longs for. I say "perpetual being," not just in the species <note>Ficino distinguishes between the "species" (mankind surviving through children) and the "individual substance" (the specific person surviving death).</note>, but in its own proper substance. For it desires this.

Rightly do bodily things—because they are born through propagation—strive for perpetual being through propagation. But the mind seeks the perpetual being of its own substance because each mind subsists in itself; and since it comes from God, it does not lie within any <margin>i</margin> subject of generation, nor is it produced by succession.

Who, according to nature, desires <margin>j</margin> the impossible? For who desires to fly, or to cross rivers with dry feet? A vain child might occasionally, by some chance or moved by a sensory whim, wish for the ability to perform such miracles. But even children do not often desire such things, and grown men never think of or desire them. Yet we all desire **eternal life**, and we desire it always, even when we are not consciously aware that we are desiring it. Therefore, <margin>k</margin> the attainment of this is not impossible.

But I think this should be noted above all: that life is more natural than knowledge. For life is prior to, more internal than, more continuous with, and more substantial than knowledge. Truly, therefore, the appetite for true life is more natural than the appetite for true knowledge. **True knowledge** is that which is so far removed from its opposite (that is, ignorance) that it no longer has ignorance actually mixed in through fallacy, nor can it ever fall into it through forgetfulness. **True life**, likewise, is that which is neither mixed with any death-dealing quality in its action, nor liable to death by any downward inclination.

Since, therefore, the desire for true (that is, eternal) life is much more natural than the desire for true knowledge, it follows that the attainment of eternal life is far more natural and possible than the attainment of true knowledge. Indeed, since life accords much more with eternal life than do intelligence and will, if we attain it by understanding and willing, we shall certainly attain that life much more so by living.

<summary>Ficino argues that the universal, natural human desire for eternal existence proves that immortality is possible and intended by God, as nature does not create any natural desire in vain. He distinguishes human desire for individual immortality from the animal instinct for mere species survival.</summary>

<keywords>immortality of the soul, natural desire, eternal life, Marsilio Ficino, teleology, human nature vs animal nature, substance vs species, Artisan of Nature</keywords>

# Platonic Book
### B

...we follow the eternal. Indeed, if this eternity communicates itself to the later acts of the soul—that is, to the intellect and the will—then it has surely communicated itself even earlier to that life which is the primary act <note>act: in Scholastic and Platonic philosophy, an "act" (actus) is the realization of a potential. Ficino argues that if our thinking and wanting (later acts) seek eternity, then our basic life-force (primary act) must already be rooted in it.</note>. Otherwise, the Author of nature would not so forcefully drive us every day toward a hunger for this thing, just as He does not drive us toward anything impossible. For Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster: the ancient Persian prophet, whom Renaissance Platonists like Ficino viewed as a "pious philosopher" who anticipated Christian truths.</note> spoke divinely:
> **For nothing proceeds or revolves imperfectly from the paternal source.** <note>original: "ου γαρ απο πατρικης αρχης ατελεστ τι τροχαζει." Ficino provides the Latin: "Nihil a paterno principio progreditur aut voluitur imperfectum."</note>

->**Signs 11, 12, 13, 14. That we desire to attain the four virtues of God. Chapter 6.**<-

<margin>B</margin>
**T**here are four other certain gifts of God pertaining to the four virtues. For we have called Him provident, just, brave, and temperate. Who would deny that God surveys every single thing? That He governs through dutiful and natural orders? That He remains immobile in His own state while He does these things, and never tires? That He is tranquil, and handles each thing gently and with moderation? Look at the human soul, the rival of <term>divine prudence</term> <note>prudentia: often translated as "wisdom" or "foresight"; the ability to govern and plan effectively.</note>. How diligently it recalls the past—not only private or personal matters, but all public and worldly affairs! How intensely it investigates the present, even things foreign and external! How anxiously it gapes at the future! How carefully it anticipates future ages! What heavier insult can a man hear than to be called ignorant or improvident? From this it follows that no one willingly confesses to ignorance of any matter or art. Since nature shows the way, people judge that ignorance of anything does not belong to man. Rather, they feel that a skill for almost all things belongs naturally to man, just as it does to God.

<margin>C</margin>
**O**ur mind also hunts for <term>divine justice</term>. Under how many laws does it subject its own body? How does it govern a household? How does it temper a city? How does it moderate even kingdoms? With how many punishments does it rage against sinners? How many good people does it affect with rewards? How heavily are we indignant at the most wicked? How ardently are the most upright men loved, even by the bad? Finally, with what great order—almost a celestial one—is human society arranged? And in every form of government, is not everything directed toward one elder and wiser person, just as the whole world is directed toward the one God? Indeed, even unjust men and thieves, if they inflict any injury, they think they inflict it justly: either as a way of avenging injuries received, or removing harmful men from their midst, or stealing those things which they themselves need while others have in abundance. They wish to be seen as carrying out every single thing most justly. In all these things, it is apparent that the human race wishes to claim for itself no less justice than God Himself possesses.

<margin>D</margin>
**W**e also labor to attain <term>divine fortitude</term>. Indeed, the fortitude of God is an "immobile state" <note>status immobilis: a condition of being unchanging and unaffected by external turmoil. To Ficino, true strength is not physical power, but the soul's ability to remain steady regardless of fortune.</note>. The wisest men prepare this state for themselves as much as they can, because they live content with the goods of the soul; they make nothing of the advantages or disadvantages of the body and fortune, as if these things have nothing to do with themselves, who are the souls. Those who neglect these shifting things remain immobile in soul. The less wise desire the same stability of life, but they approach it by another path, thinking the matter will succeed more easily for them that way. What then? They fight and subjugate everyone they can, anyone who seems to be able to eventually drive them from their seat and dignity.

<margin>E</margin>
**W**ho, moreover, would not desire <term>temperance</term>? The wise strive to moderate the movements of the soul so that they do not clash in any part. The unwise try to arrange both their body and their affairs so that they do not disturb the soul. Both seek the complete harmony of their own soul. For the wise man, the matter succeeds eventually; for the unwise, not at all. Finally, just as with all other things, the highest "reasons" <note>rationes: here, the Platonic "Ideas" or perfect blueprints of the virtues as they exist in the Divine Mind.</note> of these four virtues are in God. So much so that God is the supreme Prudence, the supreme Justice, and the rest. And men who are students of these virtues...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul's universal desire for prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance proves its divine nature, as it instinctively seeks to emulate the perfect versions of these virtues found in God.</summary>

Here, he describes the "ladder" of virtue that leads from earthly life to God and introduces a new "sign" of immortality: the human craving for infinite wealth and pleasure, which Ficino argues is actually a misplaced desire for God's own abundance.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>Theology, Book 14</header>

# Theology

seek the highest expression of these virtues; for they wish for nothing to be lacking that pertains to their own perfection. All men desire this, even if different people set out upon different paths. <margin>¶</margin> All, therefore, seek God. But those seek God by the most direct path who first, through the <term>civil virtues</term> <note>These are the social and political virtues (like honesty and fairness) used to manage everyday life and moderate basic emotions.</note>, prune away the secondary "affections" (or passions) of the mind. Second, they pull them out by the roots through the <term>purgatory virtues</term> <note>Ficino uses this term not for the afterlife, but for "cleansing" virtues that help the soul detach from the physical body’s demands.</note>. In the third place, through the virtues of the purified soul, they further moderate the primary passions. Once these are tempered, they are finally shaped by the <term>exemplary virtues</term> <note>original: "virtutibus exemplaribus." These are the "blueprints" or archetypes of virtue that exist within the mind of God.</note> which exist in God. Indeed, we can undoubtedly be shaped by these exemplary virtues at some point. For the preparation or "disposition" for such forms looks toward a permanent state of being, and a specific disposition leads to a specific state. For this reason, whatever prepares a subject more and more, step by step, prepares it for this purpose: to bring in a substantial and excellent form. And that subject—according to the common order of nature—insofar as it shares in that preparation, can likewise be made capable of the principal form. <margin>¶</margin> God, who is archetypal virtue itself, affects the "species" (the essential nature) of the human soul from the beginning with certain seeds and incitements of virtue. Through these, we enjoy human fruits—that is, the civil virtues. Once we are purified by the purgatory virtues, we are suitably prepared for the exemplary and divine virtues. We infer that these three kinds of human virtues are preparations for the divine because they are implanted in us and stirred up by divine things. Their images are so clear within us that the divine virtues may be recognized through them. We approach those divine virtues more and more by degrees. They affect us in such a way that we do not find rest in the human versions, but are moved toward the divine ones. Therefore, God must at some time form the nature of the soul with the immortal state of divine virtue, and the nature of the soul is capable of being so formed.

<margin>¶</margin> **The Fifteenth Sign. The soul seeks His supreme wealth and pleasure. Chapter 7.**

# H
It follows that we are capable of seeking the most opulent and most joyful life of God. For <margin>¶</margin> He alone is supreme wealth and supreme pleasure, He who is the fountain of all goods and in need of nothing. If, therefore, all men seek supreme wealth and supreme pleasure, they are seeking to become gods. No fixed possession of certain things or any particular kind of pleasure suffices for a human being—as it does for the other animals. Instead, a person thinks he has achieved very little in these things as long as even the smallest thing remains to be acquired. For this reason, the wise, considering the wealth and joy of God to consist truly in the treasures of intelligence and integrity alone, desire these things only, but they desire them to the highest degree. However, foolish men, imagining that the divine majesty also flows with physical goods, seek physical things to the extreme as well. It is clear that they do not seek such things merely for the sake of bodily necessity or convenience. For even if they judge that they have enough to live, and enough to live joyfully and in abundance, they still do not cease to pile up treasures and diligently seek out the most exquisite delights. <margin>I</margin> Midas, Sardanapalus, and Xerxes demonstrated this. The first <note>Midas, the mythical king who wished that everything he touched would turn to gold.</note> accumulated treasures to an immeasurable degree. The others <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king, and Xerxes a Persian emperor; both were used by ancient writers as symbols of ultimate luxury and excess.</note> offered the highest rewards to those who could invent new pleasures every day. These men do not serve the body; they harm it. Nor are they ignorant of the physical damage they cause. They are not following the body's lead; rather, out of a sort of "envy" for divine happiness, they strive to seize for themselves an immeasurable abundance of both things and pleasures. And to achieve this, they betray their own bodies, afflict their minds, and throw their lives into disorder. In the end, neither the wise (though they come closer) nor the foolish attain those vast treasures they desire in this life. Therefore, they never find rest here. But any thing rests when it is in its own place and its natural state. How vigorously the <margin>K</margin> elements <note>Earth, air, fire, and water.</note> seek their own places! How firmly they cling to them! How greedily a plant adopts the soil and the setting that suits it! How stably it remains there with all its strength! It is the same with brute animals. For the mole seeks the depths of the earth; the herds and flocks seek the surface of the land; the fish seek the water. They seek these places most greedily and linger in them most willingly. Finally, all these things (to be brief) <margin>L</margin> find rest once they have obtained their natural place and state. And the body also indicates this...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul's inability to find satisfaction in earthly virtues, wealth, or pleasure proves its divine origin; the soul is "restless" because its natural home is with God's infinite attributes.</summary>

# Book

our body: when it is doing well. It is beautifully fed and reclines softly according to its desire. Then, neither its physical constitution nor its companion, the senses—which is the <term>beast</term> <note>Ficino often refers to the lower, sensory part of the human soul as "the beast," which shares the same biological drives as animals.</note> within us—demands anything further. 

Yet meanwhile, either the <term>intellectual reason</term> <note>The "king" or highest faculty of the soul, capable of understanding universal truths.</note>, our king, studiously inquires into causes and anxiously deliberates on actions to be taken, or the <term>cogitative reason</term> <note>original: "ratio cogitatrix." The faculty that moves between sensory images and abstract thought, often responsible for "daydreaming" or planning earthly pleasures.</note> fashions and demands new pleasures. It is stung by repentance and unsettled by suspicion. This sort of anxiety is unique to man himself. Indeed, it arises from the soul’s own powers which are proper to man, and not from the physical elements of the body, nor from the powers of the beast which, as we have said, find their fulfillment in us. 

For this reason, man alone in this present way of living never rests. He alone is not content in this place. Man alone, therefore, <margin>A</margin> wanders as a pilgrim in these regions; and he cannot rest upon this journey so long as he sighs for his heavenly homeland. We all seek this homeland, though because of the variety of our opinions and plans, we set out upon different paths. 

If, therefore, those things which are lower than us find rest once they have attained their natural state and their ancestral home, it is necessary that we too—as we have said elsewhere—be able to eventually reach this state and find rest. In this present life, it is not granted to us. For we rightly desire, as if it were our natural state and our end, that "Good" which possesses three primary conditions: namely, that it be pure, whole, and stable. 

In this life, however, the possession of the Good is not pure. For a certain natural affection of the soul toward the body, and the very first movements of the senses, distract and disturb the minds of even the most excellent men. Nor is it whole. Indeed, it is necessary that everything which naturally possesses a potential for certain acts should strive to reach those acts completely if it is ever to find rest. Since, therefore, there is within the human intellect a natural capacity and a striving to perceive and possess the forms of all things, it will only have attained its natural end when it has acquired them all. But because in this life it never acquires such a state, it never possesses the "whole" good here, <margin>B</margin> nor a stable one. 

For our good consists in an action that is unhindered, secure, and continuous. However, every action of men living on earth suffers some hindrance, danger, or interruption. Furthermore, those things which require a longer time for growth usually endure longer once they are mature. But man strives laboriously until extreme old age to acquire the state of happiness, which he finally perceives only in part, and possesses in this life for the briefest time. 

Therefore, so that the state which is acquired only in part may one day be fulfilled, and that which grew for the longest time may endure for the longest time, it is necessary for the soul to survive the body. Because the soul here <note>original: "italiam sequitur fugientem." A literary reference to Virgil’s Aeneid, where Aeneas is constantly pursuing the "fleeing" coast of Italy; Ficino uses it to describe the soul's elusive search for peace on earth.</note> "follows a fleeing Italy" and does not reach its fatherland’s port, it is troubled, it grieves, and it does so constantly. 

Furthermore, what is truly remarkable is that as often as we are idle, we fall into sorrow like exiles. <margin>C</margin> Although we may not know the cause of our sorrow, or certainly do not think about it. From this it happens that man is unable to live alone. For we think we can dispel this hidden, perpetual sadness through the society of other men, and moreover, through a manifold variety of delights. 

But alas, we are too much deceived. Truly, in the midst of pleasures and praise, we sometimes sigh; and when the games are over, we depart even sadder. The same thing happens to us as to those who, sleeping with a hungry stomach, eat in their dreams; they are not satisfied, because the stomach does not crave the image of food, but the food itself. 

We too, when the mind is thirsting for <term>nectar</term> <note>Ficino uses "nectar" to symbolize the joy of the "vision of the Father" (God), contrasted with the "waters of Lethe" (forgetfulness/earthly distraction).</note>—that is, the joy of the Father's vision—offer it the deadly waters of the river Lethe, while we provide the shadowy games of bodily pleasures. These are false pleasures, not only because they are very brief and full of anxiety, but because they are mixed with pain. Indeed, a craving that is unfulfilled is a kind of pain. Moreover, the pleasures of the body are perceived only as long as the lack and the craving remain. Rightly, therefore, earthly delights do not fill the soul, but merely tickle it. For the soul affects the things that are truly real...

<summary>Ficino argues that human anxiety and the failure of earthly pleasures to satisfy the soul prove that humans are "pilgrims" on earth whose true fulfillment lies in a post-mortem union with God. He characterizes bodily pleasures as mere shadows or "dreams" that cannot quench the soul's thirst for the divine.</summary>

He now moves to the Platonic and Pythagorean idea that our current life is essentially a dream or a state of spiritual sleep compared to the true reality of the soul.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>C</margin>
...and true joys. However, physical things are merely shadows of real things, and their allurements are but shadows of joy. For this reason, if neither any single temporal thing nor the sum of all temporal things can quench the thirst of the mind, then the mind does not thirst for a temporal liquid, but for an eternal one. And if a thirst ignited by the <term>celestial sun</term> <note>Ficino uses the sun as a metaphor for divine truth and the source of the soul's longing.</note> must eventually be quenched, and yet it is never satisfied by the <term>Lethean river</term> <note>original: "letheo flumine." In mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; here, it represents earthly pleasures that make us forget our divine origin.</note>, then it shall one day be satisfied by a draft of eternal nectar. But it is helpful to confirm what has been said with the mysteries of the ancient theologians that I shall now relate.

<margin>D</margin>
For <term>Plato</term> <note>The "ancient theologians" Ficino refers to are primarily the Platonists and Pythagoreans.</note> asserts that souls doze within bodies, and that whatever we seem to do or suffer here is nothing other than dreams. He argues that the <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "logirationes."</note> of souls separated from bodies differs far more from the thoughts of souls joined to bodies than the thoughts of those awake differ from the delusions of those sleeping. The same is true of their respective pleasures. This is proven thus: we experience in ourselves not only daily, but almost every hour, that as soon as a tiny bit of vapor—somewhat thicker and more humid—exhales from the lower parts of the body, seeks the head, and fills the passages of the brain, we are immediately weighed down by sleep,

<margin>E</margin>
and soon we are even mocked by dreams and phantoms. We also occasionally experience that if some vapor of <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "bilis atre." Historically known as "melancholy," one of the four humors thought to govern human health and temperament.</note>—which the Greeks call <term>melancholy</term>—occupies the citadel of the body and captures it, our "queen" herself, namely <term>Reason</term>, is immediately (so to speak) cast down, and men are seized by manifest insanity. If a tiny smoke has such power over us, and if so light a movement changes us so much, how much more must we think the celestial and immortal soul is changed? From the very moment it falls from that purity in which it was created—that is, when it is shut within the dark prison of the earthly and dying body—then, as the Platonists say, it is moved from its true state. For then it is weighed down not by just one usual vapor of some humor, but by all the new vapors of all the humors together, and moreover by the incoming mass of the limbs and fluids. Furthermore, it is submerged in that formless matter (which is the total opposite of the mind's most beautiful form) as if in the <term>river Lethe</term>.

<margin>F</margin>
For this reason, the Pythagoreans and Platonists believe that for the whole time the sublime soul spends in the lowly body, our mind is tossed here and there, up and down, like a sick person in perpetual restlessness; it is always dozing and delirious. They believe the individual movements, actions, and passions of mortals are nothing other than the dizzy spells of the sick or the dreams of sleepers—the ravings of the insane. Thus, <term>Euripides</term> <note>An ancient Greek playwright.</note> did not wrongly call this life "the dream of a shadow." Therefore, while all are deceived, those are usually less deceived who, in the meantime, occasionally suspect (as sometimes happens in sleep) and say to themselves: "Perhaps the things appearing to us now are not true; perhaps we are dreaming at present." Whoever is so disposed among the dreamers is certainly to others as <term>Tiresias</term> <note>The blind prophet of Thebes who retained his wisdom even in the underworld.</note> is said by Homer to be among those in the underworld. "He alone," Homer says, "is wise. All others flit about like shadows"—or rather, they *are* flitting shadows.

### The Sixteenth Sign: How We Honor Ourselves and God.
### Chapter 8.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
**I**t remains for us to speak of that twelfth gift of God, through which He loves and honors Himself. Humans claim this for themselves in two ways. First: because all people—not just in the way all other creatures do—love and protect themselves, but they also greatly honor themselves and worship themselves as if they were certain deities. Prudent men do this insofar as they subject external and bodily things to the mind as if to a prince. They hang entirely upon the mind as if upon God. They consider it a sacrilege to defile the august majesty of their mind (like a divine statue) with base thoughts and earthly filth.

<margin>I</margin>
Indeed, this natural notion has bred <term>shame and modesty</term> <note>original: "pudorem verecundiamque." Ficino argues that our natural sense of dignity comes from the soul recognizing its own divine nature.</note> in the human race, so that we revere the "face of God"—which Pythagoras commanded—not only in the sight of other excellent men, but also in the privacy of our own conscious mind, which continually goads us when it is aware of misdeeds.

<summary>Ficino explains the Platonic view that life in the body is a state of spiritual sleep or "delirium" caused by physical vapors, contrasting our earthly "shadow" existence with the soul's true intellectual life. He concludes by arguing that human self-respect and conscience are evidence of our innate recognition of our own divine nature.</summary>

...even if we did not fear punishment. Indeed, the memory of good deeds is delightful. It is as if the <term>celestial soul</term> <note>Ficino identifies the human soul as "celestial" because of its divine origin and immortal nature.</note> always shrinks from the earthly stains of vice. The unwise do the same in some manner, but they are surpassed in the completion of this work by the wise. Again, the most foolish of men act in the same way, but differently: to the extent that they please themselves too much, they persist most stubbornly in their own opinions. They hold onto their own judgment <margin>B</margin> with their teeth <note>original: "mordicus tenent." A Latin idiom meaning to hold tenaciously or stubbornly.</note> as if it were a divine decree. Finally, all men honor the most excellent souls—those who have deserved best of the human race in this life—as divine. They worship them once they are released from their bodies as if they were certain gods most dear to the highest God, whom the ancients called <term>heroes</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "heroes" are semi-divine beings or souls that bridge the gap between humanity and the gods.</note>. Such great reverence toward oneself and one’s own kind is not seen in beasts; not only in the viler ones, but not even in the greater ones. And this is the first way in which men imitate divine worship: namely, that <margin>B</margin> they honor themselves as gods. There is also a second way: for we alone of all living beings worship God; we alone honor God with affection, gestures, words, shrines, and sacrifices. 

Regarding this, Plato in the <term>Protagoras</term> <note>One of Plato's dialogues; Ficino is referring to the myth of Prometheus where humans receive a share of the divine lot.</note> wishes for the greatest proof of our divinity to be that we alone—as if sharers in the divine lot because of a certain kinship—recognize God. We desire Him as our author; <margin>C</margin> we call upon Him and love Him as a father; we venerate Him as a king and fear Him as a lord. For just as the sun is not perceived without the sun, and just as the air is not heard without the air—and the eye, full of light, sees light, and the ear, full of air, hears the resonating air—so too is God not known without God. But the soul full of God is directed toward God only insofar as it recognizes God, being illustrated by divine light, and thirsts for Him, being kindled by divine heat. 

<margin>C</margin> Through this, the soul is made a temple of God, as <term>Sextus the Pythagorean</term> <note>original: "Xistus pythagoricus." Referring to the *Sentences of Sextus*, a collection of moral aphorisms popular in the Renaissance.</note> believes. Indeed, he considers that the eternal temple of God will never fall into ruin. The human mind ponders God daily. The heart burns for God. The breast sighs for Him. The tongue sings of Him. The head and the hands adore Him, as do the knees. The crafts of men reflect Him. If God does not hear these things, perhaps He would seem ignorant. If He does not 

---

listen, perhaps He will appear ungrateful. He would be cruel, in a way, if He compelled us to cry out daily to someone who would not listen. Nor should anyone dare to say that God despises human affairs as if they were trifles. Truly, a comfortable dwelling moves the builder as a goal, acting as a cause, so that he devises a certain specific form for the house. Because of this form, he again seeks out specific material. Thus the <term>end</term> <note>original: "finis." In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, the "end" or "final cause" is the purpose for which something is made.</note> moves the agent, the agent moves the form, and the form moves the matter. The same thing happens in civil and military deliberations. Thus it happens that the end is the "cause of causes." Therefore, <margin>D</margin> it precedes all other causes. 

Moreover, all natural things are established for the sake of some certain end, since individual things seem to lead toward specific uses. For example, the <term>vine-shoot</term> <note>original: "vimen palmitis."</note>, which they call a <term>tendril</term> <note>original: "capreolum." In Latin, *capreolus* literally means "little goat," named so because the vine's tendrils climb and cling like a goat.</note>, was born for this purpose: to bind the vine to the nearest small tree. This act of binding is the reason why the shoot came into being. Because that which does not exist in any way cannot be the cause of existence for any effect, nor can it move all other causes, it is necessary that a purpose of this kind existed even before the shoot, and before all the other causes of the vine. However, it did not exist in physical bodies except most recently. Therefore, it existed in a certain incorporeal nature that rules over bodies long before it existed in the vine-branch. 

Indeed, that nature—the craftsman of the vine—for the sake of such an action, shaped the form in such matter through its own "form" of the shoot. But did this kind of purpose exist in that nature according to the mode of nature, or according to a proposal of the will? Surely according to both. From the former, it was the same as a certain form of the agent and a model of the effect itself. From the latter, it was the "end" or goal. But where there is a proposal of a skillful will, there is Mind. For this reason, a **Divine Mind** presides over all bodies. It embraces the forms of all bodily things in an intellectual way, and like an **archer**, it directs individual things toward their own ends. Finally, it directs all things toward the One. This **Divine Farmer** cultivates the foliage, the tendrils, and the roots. For from where else do the leaves turn toward the sun to avoid the shade? Or from where do the tendrils, like hands, stretch out especially toward that part where a support is closer?

<summary>Ficino argues that human worship and the purposeful design of nature (teleology) prove the existence of a Divine Mind. He uses the example of a vine's tendril to show that purpose must exist in a higher intellect before it manifests in physical matter.</summary>

The understanding of the worldly order is, by that very fact, more excellent than the order itself. For an order of this kind was made through intelligence and is governed by it. If our mind is more outstanding than the world through its knowledge, it shall also be more outstanding through its life. By the power of this life, which is separable from the body, the soul possesses the ability to be separated from the body through its operation, and to transcend the world itself by a **super-worldly**
<margin>F</margin> power of life, so to speak. How much intelligence surpasses the order of the world is apparent here: for such an order is dispersed in time, while intelligence possesses the whole simultaneously and in a stable manner. Again, the order follows its cause, but does not attain it; intelligence attains the cause of the order when it finds God, its architect. There, it receives such ample things from God that it thereafter regards the world as a mere shadow. No **King** <note>Referring to God as the sovereign of the universe.</note> scorns such a great thing, unless he conceives of even greater things. If the human soul is so vast, why should it be neglected by God, the provider of even the smallest things? If the soul perceives God, why should God not also perceive the soul? Especially since God Himself gave this very power and action of perceiving to the soul, and He preserves and leads it. Hence, **David** asks: *Does He who planted the ear not hear? And does He who formed the eyes not consider?* <note>A reference to Psalm 94:9.</note> Furthermore, if the soul ascends to God, why should God not, in some way, descend to the soul? And since the mind asks for just things from God—while it seeks its **paternal inheritance**—why should God not hear it? What does this most dutiful son ask from his most indulgent parent? **Eternity**. He shall certainly obtain it. For the eternal God can grant it, and the life of the mind can receive eternity, which its knowledge and will already grasp. For it does not will unless it knows, nor does it know unless it lives. Indeed, eternity ought to be given to the mind, which both transcends time and, for the sake of the eternal God, despises temporal things. This is done not only by the more religious, but also in some way by the impious. For those whom the love of God does not allure, at least the fear of Him terrifies. Those whom fear does not frighten, at least suspicion makes anxious. Thus men—many in all things, all certainly in very many things—cast away the comforts of temporal life for the sake of the love, suspicion, or fear of God. God, therefore, ought to grant eternal things in exchange for temporal ones. None of the remaining animals refrain from present goods because of a greed for future ones. From which it follows that man would be the most foolish of all animals, and the most miserable, if he enjoyed neither the present life nor the future one. And this miserable folly and foolish misery would arise from the fact that he trusted himself to the most wise and most happy God. For as he says: just as nothing can become extremely cold by proximity to fire, so the man who alone cleaves to the most wise and most blessed God cannot, from this, turn out to be the most foolish and most miserable. Rather, for this very reason, he becomes
<margin>S</margin> most blessed, because he joins himself to the Most Blessed One. He joins himself to Him by despising temporal things and desiring eternal ones. If he becomes blessed by despising temporal things, he is made so in no other way than by the attainment of eternal things. Furthermore, if God is the first and highest life, the animal that cleaves more closely to Him lives longer. However, we do not live longer in the body. If God is the highest wisdom, man is so much wiser than the other animals as he cleaves more closely to God. In this approach...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book 14. Following the argument that God’s providence governs all things, Ficino now explores why the human soul’s innate desire for immortality and its unique capacity for religion are proofs of its eternal nature.</meta>

<header>->Platonic<-</header>

...by its proximity [to God], the soul judges itself immortal. Because a judgment of this kind is true—occurring when the soul is at its wisest compared to other animals and men—it is true that the soul is eternal. If the **First Truth** <note>original: "prima veritas." In Platonic thought, this is God, the source of all reality and logic.</note> cannot deceive, then the hope of immortality will not be a deception. This hope is so deeply implanted in us by that very **First Immortality** <note>God as the source of eternal life.</note> that we retain it even against our will and despite all the arguments of those we live among. If the First Goodness is not malicious, then the "greed" for that Goodness which He infused in us does not deprive us of temporal goods except to grant us eternal ones. If an opinion is truer the better it is—and better because it makes those who hold it better—then the belief in immortality is the truest of all, because more than any other belief, it produces the best, most excellent, and therefore the happiest of men. Who is ignorant of the fact that whatever leads most to human perfection must be the truest thing in human nature?

If the nature of the intellect loves God as Truth and Goodness itself, and God in turn loves the intellect—especially the pious one—as something most akin to Himself, and loves those who love Him in return, it follows that there is a certain natural **friendship** <note>original: "amicitia." Ficino uses this to describe the reciprocal relationship between the human mind and the Divine.</note> between them. The goal of friendship is the sharing of life.

<margin>☞ a</margin>
Therefore, the life of God can be communicated to the intellect, specifically by the same reasoning that He is loved by it; for the end of friendship is equal to the friendship itself, and vice versa. Truly, He is loved and desired as a perpetual being. This seems to be confirmed by the fact that, since it is the property of the **Good** to draw all things to itself and to communicate itself to all, it is necessary that the Infinite Good (which is God) draws and communicates infinitely. Therefore, He communicates Himself to each according to their desire, because it is the same God who communicates as He who drew the soul to Him. Now, the intellect by its nature desires the perpetual life of God no less than it desires a certain understanding of Him. Finally, if God is beneficial—indeed, if He is Beneficence itself—He cannot lack the duty of gratitude. He cannot be grateful toward one who loses their present life out of love for divine worship unless there is a life after this one.

### ¶ That Religion is the most proper and truthful characteristic of the human race. Chapter 9.

<sig>B</sig>
That man is more excellent than the brutes is most clearly evidenced by his works. **Aristotle** <note>Referring to *History of Animals*.</note> shows this in the twelfth book of the *History of Animals*. Let us ask, therefore, by what specific gift man is most excellent. He certainly seems to excel in the genius of the arts and of governance, especially because (as we have declared elsewhere) humans vary their crafts, being themselves the masters of the craft and not merely the tools of another craftsman. Beasts, however, do not vary their works, because they are instruments of a skillful nature rather than possessing the skill themselves.

But although we surpass other animals in the genius of art and governance, we still share this industriousness with the brutes. It is necessary, then, that the human species—having been distinguished from the brutes—possesses some distinct and proper perfection in which no beasts participate in any way. Is it speech? But beasts imitate speech with gestures, cries, and song. Is it **reason**? <term>ratio: the capacity for logical thought and discourse.</term> Certainly, reason. Yet not every operation of reason is unique to us. For active reason has certain "footprints" in beasts through the evidence of their crafts and governance. Even the reason that speculates on natural things seems to have a certain imaginary presence in beasts. For they treat their own diseases through the selection of certain foods and remedies, and they offer signs of future storms as if they were foreseeing the future; they change locations to avoid coming seasonal dangers, although they are led to this by nature rather than leading themselves.

<sig>C</sig>
What remains, then, that belongs entirely to man alone? The **contemplation of things divine**. For brutes show no sign of religion; thus, the lifting up of the mind to God, the King of Heaven, is as proper to us as the upright posture of the body toward the sky. Divine worship is almost as natural to humans as neighing is to horses or barking to dogs.

<sig>D</sig>
But if some curious person should assert that certain beasts also venerate celestial things—which I do not believe for a moment—the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists like Plotinus and Proclus, whom Ficino translated.</note> will respond: such beasts are either doing something else when they seem to honor the heavens, or if perhaps a man...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human desire for immortality is a divinely implanted truth and identifies the "contemplation of the divine" (religion) as the unique, defining characteristic that separates humans from animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*, Book 14. Having argued that the soul’s desire for immortality is a natural instinct, Ficino now moves to prove that religion—the unique human trait—must be true, otherwise man would be the most miserable of creatures. He also introduces the necessity of divine law and "prophets" (divine messengers) to sustain human society.</meta>

<header>Theology 14. 138</header>

...they do not know what they are doing. Or if they do know, they too must be participants in intelligence and immortality. But truly, to return to the purpose: the most perfect **living being** <note>original: "animal." In this context, Ficino uses the term for any ensouled being, including humans.</note> is most powerful in that specific property of its perfection when it is distinguished from lower beings by that which joins it to the most perfect—that is, to divine things. Again, if man is the most perfect of mortal animals by virtue of being human, he is the most perfect of all chiefly by that gift which he holds as his own, not shared with other animals. That gift is **religion**. Therefore, through religion, he is most perfect. If religion were empty, he would conversely be the most imperfect of all through it. For because of religion, as we were explaining just before, he would be the most insane and most wretched. It is impossible for a being to suffer such opposites through the same part of itself—that through religion it should be at once supremely perfect and supremely imperfect.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, religion is true. Are we ignorant of that **prophetic sign** <note>original: "vaticinium." Ficino is comparing human religious instinct to the natural instincts or "omens" seen in animals.</note> which is produced by an entire species of animals and is true? Many reptiles crawl out from the depths of the earth when the sun rises, and a darkening of the air is foretold. A great crowd of crows flies from a certain quarter of the sky in the evening, and a wind is announced in advance. By the common "prophecy" of men, religion is likewise true. For all people, always and everywhere, worship God for the sake of a future life. It is true, therefore, that there will be another life. This is so if the most perfect species of animals possesses the truest judgment in that which is most natural to it of all things. That such is the nature of the claim of religion appears not only from the fact that it belongs to man alone, but also from the fact that all human opinions, affects, and customs change—except for religion.

<margin>F</margin> When I say "religion," I mean that very instinct common to all nations, which I understand to be natural. By this instinct, a certain **Providence** <note>The guiding care of God over the universe.</note> as the queen of the world is everywhere and always conceived and worshiped. We are certainly led to this piety by three principal causes. First, by a certain natural (so to speak) sagacity infused in us by Providence itself. Second, by philosophical reasons proving the providence of the Architect from the very order of the building. Finally, by prophetic words and miracles. Regarding what I just said about the **prophet**, it is worthwhile to confirm it next with arguments that both **Plato** <note>Greek philosopher (c. 427–348 BC) whom Ficino translated and specialized in.</note> in the *Protagoras* and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Metaphysics" influenced Western Scholasticism and Ficino.</note> in his *Metaphysics* bring forward.

<margin>h</margin> Man (as they say) is a naturally social animal. For he necessarily lacks many things which individuals cannot provide for themselves. But when all are gathered into one, they provide mutual services to one another in turn. Furthermore, speech indicates that he is social, acting as a kind of interpreter of the human mind from one person to another; nature would not have given this to man unless he were intended to live in a community. For this reason, congregation is natural to man. But if they come together without law, they will shortly be scattered by mutual injuries; once scattered, they will perish from the lack of many things, and being effectively unarmed, they will be torn apart by wild beasts. Therefore, so that they may live, and live well, it is necessary for them to be gathered together.

But again, to remain in a community, there is an absolute need for law. I mean a law of such great authority that no one trusts that he can or should transgress it by either violence or deceit. Such a law cannot exist unless there is a **legislator** who is esteemed to be divine. Finally, for him to be such, and to be held as such, he must be sent to men by divine providence with certain manifest miracles.

<margin>i</margin> Such a prophet and divine leader of the human race is so named by Plato and Avicenna. <margin>J</margin> This is the point of that Platonic saying in the book *On Kingship* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue "The Statesman" (Politicus).</note>: Just as beasts cannot be led happily by a beast without a human, so neither can men be led by a man without God. Again, in the *Protagoras*, he says that men could not live together without law. Nor could they receive laws sufficient for this from **Prometheus** <note>In this allegory, Prometheus represents a "created" or lower form of providence/foresight.</note>—that is, from a certain created providence. But **Jupiter** <note>Representing the supreme God, the Creator.</note> himself, the creator of all, sent **Mercury** <note>Representing the prophet or messenger who interprets the divine will.</note> to men along with the law—that is, some prophet and interpreter of the divine will, and a giver of both divine and human law. <margin>K</margin> That God sends prophets to this office in certain ages we can show together with Avicenna in this way: If God...

## Book [14]

...they should never hesitate or distrust. Avempace <note>Ibn Bajja (c. 1085–1138), an Andalusian philosopher known for his work on the soul and intellect.</note> writes that this happened to him. They do not distrust because they are excellent in genius or learning, but because they are suspicious and fearful due to an **earthy humor** <note>original: "humorem terreum." This refers to black bile or melancholy, which in medieval medicine was thought to be cold, dry, and heavy like the earth.</note>. For even unlearned and dull little men sometimes distrust if they are weighed down by that same humor. Conversely, distinguished men often hope for the best if they are not vexed by such a humor. Although one who is troubled by it from an early age—provided they have not been entirely poorly educated—can easily cast aside vain suspicions and follow the natural instinct of religion. So great is the force of

<margin>A</margin>
nature itself; so great its stability. This is what Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Varro, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus or Pythagoras.</note> followed above all others. Therefore, those suspicions have no weight in signifying the death of souls, since they arise neither from genius nor from

Furthermore, those people are often quite sharp in whose birth **Saturn and Mercury** <note>In Renaissance astrology, Saturn governs deep thought and melancholy, while Mercury governs the intellect and communication.</note> have the greatest power. For these stars invite contemplation because they draw the spirit toward interior things. When these planets are **direct** <note>Moving forward in their orbit from the perspective of Earth; considered a positive and strengthening position.</note> and best disposed, they increase genius; they do not diminish religion. But if they are **retrograde** <note>Appearing to move backward; considered a weakening or "perverting" influence in astrology.</note> and poorly disposed, they make a man thoroughly fearful and suspicious everywhere because of their earthy quality, which is not sufficiently tempered by the aspect of other stars. Thus it happens that he hesitates and distrusts not only in religion, but in other matters as well. Moreover, it must be remembered that such an opinion or affection does not possess sufficient

<margin>M</margin>
authority <note>original: "fidei," here meaning credibility or weight.</note> if it follows either a melancholic, sick genius that is in a way contrary to life, or an unseemly and harmful position of the stars. Such a position perverts the human **complexion** <note>The physical and mental temperament resulting from the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile).</note> and brings a defect with it, not only regarding confidence in life, but also regarding the

<margin>C</margin>
governance of human affairs. Hence these men are for the most part either extremely idle, as **Epicurus** <note>Greek philosopher often criticized by Christians and Platonists for his atomism and focus on pleasure/peace as the highest good.</note> is said to have been; or shameful, like Aristippus; or insane, like their follower **Lucretius**. While Lucretius was being stirred to madness by **black bile** <note>original: "atram bilem."</note>, he first attempted to destroy his own soul with words in the third book of *On the Nature of Things*, and then he destroyed his body with a sword. Therefore, just as a sick person is not to be believed regarding the taste of wine, but rather one who is in good health, so too one should believe a healthy and sound genius regarding the end of human life, rather than an insane one.

<margin>D</margin>
I call the **sanguine** <note>The humor of blood, associated with the element of air and a cheerful, balanced personality.</note> and most tempered complexion the healthy and natural one for man. The sanguine is "airy," consisting of vital heat and moisture. The tempered complexion is similar to heaven; it does not disturb the judgment of truth. Such human complexions are for the most part suited to a sound genius and to prudence. These do not exactly "bring" us religion—for religion is divinely infused into the mind, since by the grace of the divine it commands us to neglect all else—but they certainly do not impede it, nor do they cast vain suspicions into the soul. What is found in the majority and in the most perfect individuals is judged to be **natural**. What is found in a tiny few and in the sick is considered **monstrous**. That which is natural is truthful, while the monstrous is usually deceptive.

<margin>E</margin>
Judgment against religion is found to be deceptive in the majority of serious men. Only in a very few and very superficial men is the contrary found. Sometimes others are infected by their example. Yet in those few, this is not a judgment of reason, but a disease of the soul and a fearful suspicion arising from a depraved complexion of the body. This is clear from the fact that such men often possess reasons of the mind that favor the eternity of the soul. Nevertheless, they are suspicious—just like those whose reason judges that wine should not be drunk, yet their lungs thirst for it anyway. Or like one whose reason judges that there is nothing in the path that might hurt him, yet his senses shudder in the darkness. Not only a faulty complexion contracted from parents or stars, but also a quality induced by habit—as we indicated from the beginning—leads the human race away from religion. For men who are

<margin>F</margin>

Plato writes about this in the *Theaetetus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of knowledge.</note> against those who said that nothing in reality ever stands still.
