<margin>A</margin>
...thinking that everything revolves around their own solution, while they themselves are the ones being turned. Thus, it is no wonder if men who are over-curious in the arts sometimes clearly lose their minds, both in religion and in other matters. Their insanity is revealed both by their very frivolous behavior and by their excessively ridiculous opinions on many subjects, as well as the contradictions within those very opinions. Therefore, religion does not arise from a corruption of the **complexion** <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person’s health and temperament</term>, but rather impiety is born from it. Nor does impiety arise solely from a depraved complexion, but also from
<margin>B</margin>
depraved morals. ¶ Plato, in his letters to the Syracusans <note>referring to Plato's *Seventh Letter*, a famous autobiographical epistle</note>, asserts this by saying: one must always believe the ancient and sacred oracles which assert that the souls of men are immortal, that they have judges, and that they suffer the greatest penalties once they have been separated from the body. For this reason, it should be considered a lesser evil to suffer the gravest injuries than to inflict them. A greedy man, or one destitute of mind or devoted to pleasures, might either not hear these things or is accustomed to mock them; being effectively blind, he does not see
<margin>C</margin>
that the greatest evil—impiety—always follows him as he is conquered by it, and that a miserable migration <note>original: "misera demigratio"; referring to the soul's journey after death</note> awaits him after death. ¶ All these things are found there. Similar things are also found in the *Gorgias*, in the tenth book of the *Republic*, and in the *Laws*. There, he adds this opinion concerning the soul: that it is necessarily proven by **adamantine reasons** <note>original: "adamantinis rationibus." In the Renaissance, "adamantine" meant unbreakable or diamond-like in its strength</note>.
<margin>D</margin>
Cleombrotus was so persuaded by this that he deprived himself of this life out of love for the other <note>Cleombrotus of Ambracia was a philosopher who reportedly leaped into the sea after reading Plato's *Phaedo* on the soul's immortality</note>. Demosthenes also said: it is better to die honestly than to live basely, after he had heard Plato and Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato and the third head of the Academy</note> debating the immortality of souls.
<margin>E</margin>
Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that the greatest cause of impiety is usually attributed by the Platonists to the lowest kind of demons. These demons, through a certain silent persuasion, do not fail to push men with all their might—either toward a false religion because of ambition, or toward no religion at all because of envy.

### Second objection and solution.

<margin>F</margin>
**W**e have refuted the first objection of the **Lucretians** <term>Lucretians: followers of the Roman poet Lucretius, who argued in *De rerum natura* that religion was born of fear and ignorance of natural laws</term>, by which it was said that the worship of God happens because of a depravation of human nature. In that discussion, it appeared that it is the Lucretians themselves who are depraved, for they judge the nature of humans to be at its worst precisely because it is joined to the best God. But what of the second point they bring forward: that the veneration of divine things arises from the planning of men and from civil institutions? It cannot be denied how quickly human inventions are changed, even the true ones, let alone the false and faked ones. All human institutions are changed in a short time into contrary institutions. Contrary laws are also different among various nations at the same time; what are judged shameful by some are considered honest by others. But what is more ancient than religion? Or what is more widespread? The founders of laws did not invent this just to restrain the common people. For
<margin>L</margin>
religion flourished in the world before cities and homes. Even scattered and wild men worship God, and the very makers of laws themselves feared the divine powers. Plato confirms this in the *Protagoras*, saying that even before they gathered together, or spoke, or practiced any arts, men from the very beginning—because of a **natural kinship** <note>original: "naturalem cognationem"—Ficino's idea that humans are naturally "related" to the divine</note>—adored God and made altars and sacrifices. ¶ Therefore, men would have eventually rejected such a hard yoke of religion (which is sometimes contrary to so many of life’s comforts) if it were a fiction and did not stand upon the stability of truth. But perhaps Protagoras <note>A famous Greek Sophist known for the saying "Man is the measure of all things"</note> will say: religion is not natural, but only seems to be so because we drink it in **from our tenderest nails** <note>original: "a teneris unguiculis," a Latin idiom meaning "from early childhood"</note>. We will answer Protagoras thus: he also learned to speak and to drink from infancy. Nevertheless, speech and drinking are still natural. Men speak and drink everywhere and always because it is natural. Yet, at different times and places, they speak and drink in a different order, because the order of the action consists in opinion rather
<margin>M</margin>
than nature. Similarly, among all nations in all ages, God is adored because it is natural, even if not with the same rites and modes. Speech, because it is natural, reaches its end: that is, to make the will of one person clear to another. Drinking also reaches its end: to restore the body’s moisture. I do not see why religion should not also reach its end. Its end is to enjoy God. Its prayer is to enjoy Him forever.

<summary>Ficino refutes the idea that religion is a social construct, arguing that it is a natural human instinct older than civilization itself. He uses the analogy of speech and drinking to show that while the *forms* of religion vary by culture, the *impulse* is universal and points toward the soul's ultimate goal: union with God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the natural origin of religion. In the previous section, he argued that religious doubt stems from physical illness or moral failure rather than intellectual logic. Here, he addresses the "Third Objection"—the claim that religious belief is caused by the influence of the stars—and begins a beautiful meditation on why loving God is superior to merely knowing Him.</meta>

# Platonic Book

### ¶ Third objection and its solution.

<margin>A</margin>
**D**o the stars lead men to religion? This is the third objection raised by the impious. ¶ Not at all. To be sure, the stars support the bodily **humors** <term>humors: the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that medieval medicine believed determined a person’s health and temperament</term>. Religion, however, is a foe to the desires of the body. Nor can the heavens instill a desire higher than the hope for celestial things <note>Ficino refers here to the physical "heavens" or the stars themselves</note>. Yet the religious man even scorns these physical celestial things. Add to this that religion condemns fate and asserts freedom. By what logic, then, would religion receive from fate the power to resist fate? ¶ Furthermore, a certain conjunction of planets provides fertility, while the opposite brings scarcity. This brings plague, while that brings health; likewise war and peace. We see how quickly the gifts of the heavens change into their opposites. Therefore, if a certain position of the stars forced men to worship God, then in a short time, a contrary position of the stars would have to erase divine honors from human memory. Yet never and nowhere has there been an interruption of religion, although God may have been honored differently at different times and in different places. This variety has followed the choices of human minds, which are by no means subject to the stars. For the human mind, by its own divine nature, leads us to sense, worship, and fear God, just as its nature leads us to love the good and avoid evil. <margin>B</margin> Nevertheless, through the free choice of its own deliberation, the ritual of worshiping God varies, just as one walks toward the good by various paths according to one's own will. From the previous discussion, it is gathered that this common religion of all nations toward one God is entirely natural to the human species and is man's proper—and therefore most excellent—virtue. <margin>C</margin> There are indeed two most excellent human acts: namely, those which occur in the highest part of the soul and are directed toward the most excellent object. These are the **knowledge** and **love** of God in our mind. In this life, human love for God is superior to human knowledge. This is because no one truly "knows" God <note>original: "deum nemo vere cognoscit"</note>. But those who truly love God—in whatever way He is understood—are those who scorn all things for His sake. Again, just as it is worse to hate God than to be ignorant of Him, so it is better to love Him than to know Him. Add to this that by searching for God for a very long time, we accomplish very little. <margin>D</margin> By loving Him, we accomplish the most in the shortest time. For this reason, love joins the mind with divinity faster, more closely, and more firmly than knowledge does, since the path of knowledge consists more in making distinctions, while the path of love consists more in union. Moreover, it is more pleasing to God Himself to be loved than to be scrutinized. For we grant nothing to God by looking at Him. But by loving Him, we grant Him whatever we are and whatever we possess. To those who love, God gives Himself back more than to those who merely investigate. Furthermore, we can use knowledge of God badly—namely, for the sake of pride. We cannot use the love of God badly. And by loving God we receive a far greater pleasure than by searching, and we are made better by loving than by inquiring. Indeed, just as it is not the one who sees the good, but the one who *wills* it, who becomes good; so the soul becomes divine not because it considers God, but because it loves Him. It is just as matter does not become fire by merely receiving light from it, but because it is transformed by the fire’s heat. Hence that saying of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>: "The soul, by seeking God, makes itself pure; by imitating God, it becomes God." <note>original: "Animum deum inquirendo purum efficit; Deum imitando fit deus."</note> This was certainly accepted by Plato himself when he said that divine light is not acquired by us little by little through inquiry, but by a perfect joining of life it is finally and suddenly kindled within us by divine power. Furthermore, by knowing God, we contract His vastness to the small concept of our own mind. But by loving Him, we amplify our mind to the immense breadth of divine goodness. In the former, we bring God down to us; in the latter, we lift ourselves up to God. For we know only as much as we can grasp. But we love both what we see and however much more of the divine goodness we intuitively sense <note>original: "vaticinamur," suggesting a prophetic or spiritual intuition</note> remains beyond our sight. Nor is love content with human knowledge, for that is created and finite. <margin>E</margin> The will rests in the first and immense good alone. Since religion consists entirely in this very love, man has nothing more divine than religion (as Plato testifies in the *Epinomis*) <note>The *Epinomis* is a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato or his circle, exploring the relationship between astronomy and religion</note>. It is as much further from falsehood than other human pursuits as it joins us more closely to God, who is supreme truth. Therefore, its intuition is truer...

<summary>Ficino argues that religion is a natural human instinct that transcends astrological influence and fate. He concludes that loving God is superior to intellectually knowing Him because love expands the soul and creates a direct union with the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul and divine justice. Having previously argued for the natural origin of religion, he now demonstrates why the soul must be immortal to receive the infinite rewards or punishments that divine justice demands.</meta>

# Theology

...than the opinions of other faculties. Indeed, the foreknowledge of religion promises worthy rewards to the good, while it threatens others with punishments. A worthy reward is owed to the integrity of a most holy man. Integrity, once confirmed by the highest **habit** <term>habit: from the Latin *habitus*, meaning a permanent disposition or state of character formed through repeated action</term>, is an indelible good. Even if such a man lived for thousands upon thousands of years, he would always act in the same way. Therefore, no reward is worthy of such integrity unless it is likewise indelible and eternal. This is especially true since the most fitting reward for holiness—that for the sake of which holiness performs every action—is that which can fully satisfy its desire. Such a reward is that in which the whole essence of the Good resides. Therefore, its reward is the eternal possession of an infinite good.

The religious soul shall live forever, so that it may receive a worthy reward. The impious man shall also live forever, so that he may suffer the punishments of his impiety. He who sins infinitely—whenever he forgets the infinite God for the sake of finite comforts—contracts a malignant and indelible habit. Because of this, he would continue to sin for thousands upon thousands of years if he were to live forever; he has once and for all resolved to sin for as long as he lives. To Divine Justice—to whom future ages are present as though they were now—he has already offended for as long as he was destined to sin if he had lived. Therefore, an infinite punishment is due to this man who is already sinning infinitely. 

Add to this that if the reward of true virtue is eternal—for virtue looks toward Him upon whom it depends as its beginning, as if He were its end—it follows that for vice (which falls away from the Eternal), the punishment must be as everlasting as the reward of virtue and the principle of life itself. No such balance exists in this briefest span of life. It must, therefore, exist in the future. In this way, the adversity that strikes the good in this life and the prosperity that happens to the wicked are seen to be compensated, lest piety be a loss to the good, or as it is read in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul, original: "Phaedo"</note>, lest impiety be a gain for the wicked. 

Indeed, good ought to be beneficial, and evil harmful. Yet in this life, piety is harmful, as it compels one not only to despise present goods but even to undergo labors and death for the sake of God and honor. Conversely, impiety often profits a man greatly. Therefore, so that a place for justice is not lacking, the sentence must be delivered elsewhere. Nor should it be thought that this part of justice, which regards human affairs, does not pertain to God, to whom the administration of the whole world belongs. If, in this world, God creates each thing by understanding and loving it (as Plato maintains), it follows that in the act of creating, He understands and loves each individual thing. And in caring for the whole, He does not neglect the parts, for if the parts are not cared for, the whole is not cared for. Plato writes this in the *Laws* <note>Plato’s *Laws*, Book X, where he argues that God cares for the small details of the universe as much as the large</note>. 

From this, it follows that the human species is no small part of the world, being itself an administrator of justice. If, therefore, Divine Justice—as they sing in the Orphic hymns—distributes the elements to their proper places, and if it assigns small gifts to even the tiniest things according to their nature, why should it not also assign places, rewards, and punishments to men according to their merits? God frequently leaves the good without reward or the wicked unpunished in this life to show us by these signs that another life remains, in which justice, which cannot be deceived, may be fulfilled according to merit. Sometimes, however, He punishes crimes—especially the most serious—even in this life, so that we may recognize His providence through this. There are many present examples of divine providence.

<margin>b</margin>
Philo Judaeus <term>Philo Judaeus: a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy, particularly Platonism</term>, the Platonist, writes in his book *On Providence* that laws existed among the ancients decreeing that the sacrilegious should be burned, thrown from a cliff, or suffocated. When Philomelus, Onomarchus, and Phayllus <note>General-kings of Phocis who plundered the Temple of Apollo at Delphi during the Third Sacred War (c. 350 BC)</note> had plundered the temple, after a few days—without the work of any human judges—they fell by a certain divine chance into these three specific punishments. 

Plato commands in the *Laws* that we should never doubt divine providence just because unjust men often seem to depart from here unpunished. For we do not know by what reason and in what place—as it benefits the order of the universe—each thing is repaid to each individual. Again, in the final book of the *Republic* <note>Referring to the Myth of Er at the end of Plato's *Republic*</note>, he proves that the soul becomes like God through virtue and thus becomes His friend. For this reason, it is so cared for by God that whatever happens is eventually led toward the good. Whether the soul is placed in poverty, in sickness, or in some other calamity, each thing will eventually lead to good, either in this life or in the future one.

<margin>j</margin>
Nor, for this reason, should divine goodness be called harmful because it permits sins to be committed...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that divine justice requires the soul's immortality to provide eternal rewards for virtue and eternal punishment for vice, as the brief span of earthly life often allows the wicked to prosper and the good to suffer. He cites Plato and Philo Judaeus to demonstrate that God's providence governs both the whole universe and its individual human parts.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s fourteenth book on the justice of God and the necessity of the soul's immortality for reward and punishment. ...and punishes what has been committed. Indeed, in the kingdom of God, rational nature holds its own rank: to this nature, free movement is suited. <term>To motion</term> <note>original: "Ad motum"</note> of this kind it is granted that it may progress toward the better: and to the good of its nature, it may add furthermore the good of its will, its actions, and its ultimate attainment. Thus, a nature of this kind is not only made good by another—as a passive recipient—but also makes itself good as an active agent. Moreover, it is granted to such movement that it can transgress toward the worse: not that it strips off its own nature, but that it puts on an alien one, and a lower one at that. Punishment follows this infection, whether it be harmful or purgatorial. It follows, I say, by a certain necessary and divine law, leading the sinner inwardly toward things similar to himself. And as Plato says in the tenth book of the *Laws*: <term>To the principle of motion in the soul belongs</term> <note>original: "Ad motionis principium in anima est"</note> the power by which it makes itself such or such according to its own choice. But after it has become such, it is soon transferred—not so much by its own choice as by a certain fatal law of God—into such a condition and place. He adds what is said by the divine mouth of David: <margin>A</margin> "Whether you penetrate to the center of the world, or fly to the surface, you cannot escape the divine law." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 139:7-8: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? Or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there..."</note> To this point tends that passage in the tenth book of the *Republic*: Since you can neither hide from nor escape the divine eyes and hands, take heed above all lest you think you can appease Him with prayers—that is, lest you ever become more dissimilar to God. For He hates souls that degenerate far from His likeness. Nay more, even if you obtained the ring of Gyges <note>A mythical ring mentioned by Plato that granted the wearer invisibility, testing whether they would remain just even when they could not be caught.</note> and the helmet of the underworld, flee far from injustice. But let us return <margin>B</margin> to the *Laws*. It says in the same place: The world is full partly of good things, and partly of evil. And God has set over us certain gods and daemons like shepherds for guarding sheep. By whose providence we may both avoid evils and pursue goods. He adds that those who, having unjustly seized much, trust they can appease the gods with gifts, err just as if wolves, preying on sheep, thought they could win over the shepherds by giving back a few limbs of the sheep to them. Finally, everywhere Plato repeats both that we sin by choice and that after the sin we must necessarily suffer. But now let us return to the established order. <margin>C</margin>

What then? If God both permits sin and punishes it. In permitting it, the wonderful excellence of the human race shines forth. In punishing it, the power and immense goodness of God shine. If He did not permit sin, how would it be seen that men are masters of themselves, of their own right, and by their own judgment act one way or another? If God punishes crimes, He establishes the good of justice within the very evil of the crimes. This justice would have no place here unless there were transgressors. And a certain part of justice—or if I may say so, the administration of justice upon injustice—would seem to be missing in the kingdom of God. Whose power and infinite goodness shine forth here, while against the nature of evil He makes good out of evils so that all of nature is wonderfully ordered. In this, the abundance of good is so great that it shines in both the good and the bad; and it demonstrates how much it prevails in both. Such too is the observance of order, that the soul which seems to deviate from order by sinning, still walks within the order of free movement; and while it deviates, it immediately returns into the order of justice by suffering, for because of the habit of transgressing, it suffers such things as are appropriate to that habit. These things I had to say concerning immortality insofar as it pertains to the testimony of signs; but next, we must most diligently solve the doubts that compel one to lack confidence in immortality.

***

# ¶ The Platonic Theology of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Fifteen.

## ¶ Five questions about the soul follow. First: whether there is one intellect for all men. [Answer]: No. Chapter 1.

<margin>D</margin> We have already refuted many things usually brought against the soul in the preceding discussions. Five doubts remain, I believe, to be clarified. The fourth: why do they depart upon a mere glance? <note>Referring to the sudden departure of the soul in death or ecstasy.</note> The fifth: what is the state of the soul before it enters the body? And what is it after its departure? Averroes, a Spaniard, an Arab in his native tongue, was devoted to the doctrine of Aristotle, yet he was ignorant of the Greek language. And what is most important: the very Greek words of Aristotle cry out against Averroes.

<margin>F</margin>
Plethon himself says: Aristotle held without controversy that the minds of men are many and everlasting. He adds that he does not wish to pervert Aristotle's words, even if Aristotle perverted the words of Plato and the other philosophers. So says he. Nevertheless, <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who argued the soul was mortal.</note> seems to have perverted Aristotle’s meaning regarding the soul where he says that Aristotle judged the soul to be mortal. <term>Themistius</term> <note>A 4th-century commentator who took a middle ground between Alexander and Averroes.</note> explained Aristotle more fairly, saying that he thought the <term>active intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that produces universal thoughts.</note> was indeed unique, but the <term>receptive intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that receives and stores information.</note> was manifold, and both are perpetual. However, Alexander declares what he himself thinks in his *Natural Questions*, where he says: Medicine, though it is a science, appears as an art in its practice. In the same way, the soul, though it is immortal, appears to be mortal when it is submerged in a mortal body. And again he says: The Maker of the world wished to bind the divine and celestial souls of men to earthly bodies without a certain suitable <term>medium</term> <note>A connecting link or bridge between spirit and matter.</note>. He names this medium a "spirit" and a "vehicle" in the manner of the Platonists. But Proclus affirms that not only the Platonists, but even Aristotle, posited the soul as immortal.

---

<margin>{ </margin>
Themistius asserts that he posited it for the same reason that Plato did. And after he proved in the third book of *On the Soul* that both intellects—namely, the active and the receptive—are perpetual, he added only this: namely, that the "mixture" of the two is [mortal]. <margin>1</margin> But the passive reason—that is, the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>—is not perpetual at all. For this reason, he concluded that we do not remember human things after death, because the recording of these things usually happens through a turning toward mental images and because of an affection for bodily things. And therefore, he says, we do not remember. Thus, Themistius wants this added to indicate that souls live after death, and that there are many souls, but that it is no wonder if they do not remember bodily things. For if he had thought that souls perish, no reason would have needed to be assigned as to why they do not remember. But let us return to Averroes.

## ¶ An account of the opinion of Averroes.

<margin>3</margin>
When Averroes read frequently in Aristotle that the intellect undoubtedly has nothing of a bodily nature and is not mixed with the mortal, he understood it in such a way that he concluded three things. First, the intellect is not a body—that is, it is not composed of matter and form. Second, it is not some quality divisible along with the body, and it is in no way dependent on the body. Third, it is not a form of such a kind that it can perfect, vivify, and rule the body—and thus be so attached to the body that from the matter and the substance of the intellect one single composite being is made, whose existence is one. We grant the first and second points to Averroes. But if we follow the <term>ancient Peripatetics</term> <note>The traditional followers of Aristotle's school.</note>, we in no way concede the third. He denies that the substance of the intellect can be the perfecting form of the body and its vivifying act. <margin>ll</margin> His first argument is of this kind: If the intellect were such an "act" of the body, one composite would be born from it and the body, and the existence of the composite would be one. But one thing cannot be made from its meeting with the body unless the intellect itself becomes a participant in the body. The mind does not admit this participation, since reason shows its existence to be absolute and free from bodies. The second reason: If the mind were the form of the body, in the same way each...

For that which is the form of a physical body receives nothing without its own matter. ¶ Indeed, whatever matter receives, it receives in a divided way. From this, the forms of things divided within matter become temporal and particular <note>In Aristotelian thought, "particular" refers to a specific, individual thing (like "this dog"), whereas the intellect seeks "universals" (the concept of "Dogness").</note>. The intellect would also grasp things in such a way. Therefore, it would never comprehend any universal nature through its forms. The third reason: ¶ Matter does not recognize the forms it possesses. Thus, if the mind were joined to matter and, through its fellowship, received things in the same way matter does, it would recognize nothing at all. The fourth reason: It is impossible for there to be an infinite power in a body by any reasoning. ¶ However, the power of the mind is, in a certain way, infinite. From this, he [Averroes] wants to conclude that the mind has no commerce <note>Meaning no shared substance or direct interaction.</note> with matter. Since there are many species of mind in nature, he wants one specific species to be the human mind—namely, that which contemplates the order of things within us. Indeed, in all humans, the mode of understanding is the same according to its species, and the soul is the same in its species, through which there is one life and one form in all humans according to their species. Because the human mind is one in its species, it must also be one in number; that is, unique and singular, not divided among individuals. For a form, which is one in itself according to its species, is not cut into many parts except by the addition of matter. But how could the human mind, existing as one in itself, be divided into many, since it is a participant in no matter? Furthermore, if there were one intellect in me and another in you, it would be necessary that the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem"; in this context, the mental image or representation of an object.</note>—which is the likeness of the thing being understood—would be one in number in me and another in you, even though they are the same according to their species. For since the species of things to be understood exist in the mind as if in a subject, it must be that in other minds there are other and distinct species. I say distinct in number, just as the minds themselves are distinct in number. But species or forms that are many in number but one in species are particular forms, which cannot contribute to true understanding, because that which is truly understood must be universal. It follows that when one person teaches another, the teacher seems to pour his own knowledge into the student. Therefore, he either

hands over to the student the exact same knowledge that he himself had, or another knowledge that is different in number but the same in species. If he hands over knowledge that is the same in species but different in number, he would be generating knowledge in the same way that nature is accustomed to generate its own work. Indeed, that which acts through nature produces its form in another, agreeing mostly in species but differing in number <note>Like a fire starting another fire: the "heat" is the same kind (species), but they are two distinct instances of heat (number).</note>. ¶ But this belongs to those things that agree with one another in matter. ¶ Truly, the soul of both the teacher and the student is above matter. And knowledge itself is not an active quality, like heat or similar things. It remains, therefore, that he communicates to the student exactly the same numerical knowledge that he himself possesses; this can never happen unless there is a single intellect in both of them, so that the same quality of knowledge does not pass from one subject to another, and so the teacher is not forced to lose his knowledge by teaching it. <margin>8</margin> Add this: if the notions of known things in our minds were diverse in number but agreeing in species, then these notions would agree in species but differ in number. But those things which, beyond their diversity, agree in some species, certainly agree in some common notion. Both my intellect and yours will see a common notion of this kind, to which it will collect those diverse notions. Thus we will both conceive a notion of this kind: I one, and you another, also differing in number but agreeing in species. Therefore, we would reduce them again to another common notion in the same way. And so on to infinity. But it is absurd to introduce an infinite progression in ordered things. And in the species of things, an order is necessary.

# Theology, Book 143

...whom we see: he <note>Averroes</note> believes that the human is composed of this body and a **sensitive soul**, as he calls it. But by no means of an intellective soul. Instead, he holds this **sensitive soul** to be the most perfect of all such souls, differing in species from those of the beasts. There are as many of these [sensitive] souls as there are human bodies, and they arise and perish along with the bodies. He calls the highest power of this soul the **cogitative power** <note>original: *virtutem cogitatricem*</note>, which the Greeks call **phantasia**.

<margin>B</margin>
He adds that he believes the souls of beasts possess a certain **estimative power** <note>The instinct that allows an animal to "estimate" if something is dangerous or useful without reasoning.</note>, through which, by natural instinct, they judge what is good or bad for themselves, and they suddenly pursue or flee from it. But our [human] soul possesses that **cogitative power** which is not carried along by the guidance of nature, but searches things out by reason; it deliberates by a certain counsel and chooses as it has consulted. However, it perceives nothing **universal**, but ranges only through **particulars** <note>Meaning it can think about "this specific apple," but not the abstract concept of "Apple-ness."</note>. For this reason, he calls it **particular reason**, while he calls the Intellect **universal reason**. He locates this particular reason in the middle part of the brain, between imagination and memory.

<margin>☞</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
For he is of the opinion that in the first part [of the brain] is the **common sense**, which collects within itself the operations of the five senses. In the second part is the **imagination**, the preserver of those images which the common sense had collected. In the third part is the **cogitative power**, the judge of those things which the imagination has preserved. In the fourth part is **memory**, the guardian of the judgments which the cogitative power produced.

Therefore, the cogitative power—the queen of the middle part—is, above all other lower things, closest to the Mind; so much so that the Mind is present to it everywhere, and fulfills its own understanding through its assistance. This happens while the likenesses of things shining in the cogitative power move the Mind toward understanding. And this is the only communion the human has with the Mind—not because the intellect is a part or the life-giving form of this human (who is composed only of a body and a cogitative soul). For the intellect is separated from the human both in essence and in being. But [it is connected] because the intellect is present everywhere to the thought of this human. And from this **particular thought**, that [Intellect] draws out the **universal species**.

The human provides the occasion for the intellect to speculate, just as a colored object provides the occasion for light to see. Nor does he claim that one single being is made from this human and the Mind; rather, one single operation happens. Namely, one single act of understanding, which nevertheless is not in the human in any way, but in the Mind alone—in the Mind, I say, when it is "struck" by human thought. Nothing from that Mind passes into the human; instead, the whole act is completed in the Mind. A human does not "understand something through the mind," but the Mind understands *within* my human. And within that Mind itself are the habits of the arts and sciences. The cogitative soul is united to a boy from his first origin.

<margin>D</margin>
The Mind, however, joins much later, when the likenesses in thought are so pure that they move the intellect.

<margin>E</margin>
The Averroists <note>The followers of Averroes’s philosophy.</note> affirm that there are not only two powers, but two **substances** from which the intellect is composed. Indeed, they say the **active power** <note>original: *intellectus agens*</note> is one substance, and the **capable power** <note>The potential or passive intellect.</note> is another substance. And they say the former is by its nature luminous and form-giving, while the latter is entirely dark and formable. By their eternal coupling, they forge one soul according to its being, just as from **matter and form** a single composite is made in nature. They call the former the **Agent Intellect**, and the latter the **Formable** or **Capable Intellect**.

<margin>F</margin>
They judge that the Agent Intellect, because it is an act existing through itself, always understands itself by itself; thus, by looking at its own essence, it sees itself, and through itself, it also sees the higher minds. They believe such an act of understanding is its very essence. If, then, its essence is always joined to the Capable Intellect, they think it follows that through this same intellectual essence, the Capable Intellect always understands the Agent Intellect, whose understanding is its very essence. It would even understand the superior minds. They claim this understanding exists in the **Universal Intellect**, or the Soul, as a single, stable, and eternal act. They also claim there is another intelligence in its formable part: one that is indeed sempiternal, but variable, temporal, and multiple—which it borrows from us. And because it clings more closely to the Agent Intellect than to the phantasy, and because of its conjunction with the temporal phantasy, it acquires a temporal...

# Platonic Book
<a>

...knowledge: they think what we said a little earlier is clear: namely, that through its conjunction with that eternal intellect, [the human soul] possesses eternal understanding. This understanding is clearer the more the **agent intellect** <note>The "active" part of the mind that processes information.</note> is more familiar to it than the **phantasia** <note>The faculty of imagination or mental images.</note>.

<margin>a</margin> In us, however, he [Averroes] thinks that we hunt for a doubtful and changeable knowledge bit by bit. For example, he would say that while Pythagoras was alive, he gathered that "Pythagorean knowledge" through the images of things shining in Pythagoras's own thoughts. But when Pythagoras died—that is, when those images ceased—the Intellect lost the **species** <note>Mental concepts or forms.</note> it had received from them, along with the knowledge itself. For he believes those **species** are created and preserved by the images.

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, even while Pythagoras was alive, the Intellect would stop its action within Pythagoras whenever his thought ceased to be active. It would receive a concept, then forget it, then receive it again. 

<margin>B</margin> He claims it worked the same way in Plato, and daily in every individual in the same manner.

<margin>D</margin> [The Universal Intellect] is imbued everywhere and always, in various ways through the various souls of men. In a way, it "feeds" on them; it receives as many **species** as there are images within us, just as a mirror receives images from bodies, and it produces just as many acts of understanding.

<margin>E</margin> It also develops various habits of the sciences based on the diversity of human studies. And because an innumerable multitude of men daily study the knowledge of all things, the Intellect "learns everything" from this. Through these very **species** drawn from our images, the capable Intellect knows not only lower things but finally—both in all men and in the wisest men—it knows itself. On one side is the **agent intellect**, and on the other are the superior minds. 

They believe that a wonderful connection of things consists in this: for there are forms entirely absolute from matter, namely the **angels**. Among them, there are not many individual angels within one "angelic species," but as many angels as there are, there are just as many species of angels <note>Ficino is referencing the Thomistic idea that each angel is its own unique category.</note>.

<margin>a</margin> He believes there are also forms that are entirely corporeal and numerous within the same species—for instance, the souls of animals and forms lower than them. Between these two, he places this "composite" made of the human and the Mind: a single Mind for many human souls. It is like a certain huge monster composed of many legs but only one head. In this arrangement, the absolute form joins with the corporeal, and the corporeal with the absolute in turn. And as a part of the whole, that which is absolute remains one within itself. That which is corporeal is multiple, while the one Mind suffices for innumerable souls. 

They call that composite of the Mind and any one of us the **intellectual man**. But they call each of us, separated from the Mind, the **cogitative man**. They affirm that the "first man" <note>the intellectual composite</note> understands something because his part—that is, the Mind—understands. This is just as we are accustomed to calling a man "snub" simply because his nose is snub. But the "other man" <note>the individual human</note> understands absolutely nothing.

## Refutation of Averroes. That the mind is the form of the body is clear first from the order of nature. Chapter 2.

<margin>B</margin>
There was once a great controversy among the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> concerning the mind of man, and the dispute is still before the judge. **Dicaearchus** said it was the form of the body and was itself corporeal. He called it the form of the body because it gives life to the human body; he called it corporeal because it is drawn from the "bosom" of the body.

<margin>C</margin> **Averroes**, on the contrary, said it was neither a corporeal form nor even the form of the body. **Avicenna**, the prince of Arabian theologians, and **Algazel** followed a middle path. They asserted that the mind is indeed the form of the body, but not a corporeal one. 

Thus, between forms that belong to the body and are corporeal, and forms that are neither corporeal nor belong to the body (as these are most different), there should be certain "middle forms" which agree partly with the former and partly with the latter. Rightly, between forms that are entirely divine—which are so separate from matter that they cannot be joined to it—and forms that are entirely natural—which are so joined that they cannot be separated—there are placed middle forms. These are partly natural and partly divine; they are separate enough that they *can* be joined, and joined enough that they *have the power* to be separated. This is shown by their powers and actions...

Finally, it is not without reason that we distinguish between **sense**, which exists in the form of the body and requires a physical instrument; the **angelic intellect**, which is free from both <note>That is, free from being the form of a body and free from needing physical organs.</note>; and the **human intellect**, which is indeed the form of the body, yet requires no physical instrument for its specific work. For the forms in bodies are nothing other than images of the **divine ideas**, just as the figures impressed upon wax by a gold seal are images. If a confused impression were made in all the pieces of wax, you would call the one who pressed it so clumsily "unskilled." In the same way, the **Divine Mind**, which is eager to impress its own likeness when moving matter, would perhaps seem unskilled if it never achieved its desire. But this desire will never be fulfilled unless forms of this kind appear in bodies—forms which rule over their own bodies almost exactly as God rules the world. Thus, through their intelligence, they are reflected back into themselves and into God, just as God turns back into Himself. Truly, by agitating matter through the motion of the heavens, the Divine Mind is said to generate or produce something—indeed, all things—even though it does not

<margin>E</margin> produce every form or draw every form out of matter itself. Because the first starting point from which this universal generation or production takes its beginning is the Divine Mind itself, the final goal in which such generation concludes must also be a certain **divine mind**. The final goal of generation exists in that which is born, and it is the "form" of that thing. Therefore, it is necessary that there be some divine mind which is the form of matter. For if the generation caused by fire ends in the form of fire, and that caused by a man ends in the form of a man, why should the generation or production arranged by the Divine Mind not end in a **mind**? Generation does not end except in a form, which is the specific and innermost perfection of the thing generated. If art, through its instruments, finally grants to matter a form most similar to the form contained in the mind of the artist; if the nature of the human body in generation moves the seed first to the form of milk, then blood, thirdly flesh, and finally a man; if fire moves wood first to be warm, then hot, and thirdly ignited—what stands in the way of the Divine Mind moving the matter of the world first to the forms of elements, secondly to compounds, thirdly to plants, fourthly to beasts, and fifthly to the form of **Itself**? That is, to a Mind which is the form of the generated body, so that in the most noble of offspring, the face of the parent may shine forth. Yet it moves matter toward the lower forms by drawing them out <term>eduction <gloss>the process of drawing a form out of the potential of matter</gloss></term> from matter itself through change. For if it were "drawn out," it could not be a Mind. It belongs to the divine order that, whereas the higher forms <note>Such as angels.</note> are neither drawn out nor brought in, and the lower forms are both brought in and drawn out, the rational soul itself should be **brought in** but not **drawn out**. And if the form of a compound is of such value that it possesses the power and action of the elements; and if the form of plants is so strong that it does whatever the lower forms do; and likewise the form of beasts—who could deny that the Mind has the power and act of the lower forms? Thus, its very essence, while it understands, also feels through the body and nourishes the body. Surely, since a superior nature both includes and exceeds the entire power of an inferior nature, and would perform the same work as the inferior as long as the same instruments were supplied to it, it is necessary that the mind which flourishes within us be able to carry out the work

# Platonic Book

<meta>catchword: order</meta>

Our bodily constitution’s spirit is a sufficient instrument for the mind to perform its service of understanding—as the <term>Averroists</term> <note>original: "auerroici"; followers of the philosopher Averroes who believed the human intellect was a single, separate power shared by all mankind.</note> believe. It will serve the mind's substance even more for sensing and nourishment. And since nature does not abound in superfluous things, there is only one primary soul in us, just as there is only one primary form in other bodies, since higher forms contain the lower ones within themselves.

<margin>A</margin> We conclude that the human mind is the lowest of all minds both because it moves from idleness into action (and vice-versa), and because it receives the opportunity for understanding from physical bodies. In this way, it is closest to bodies, which are brought from potentiality into action because of matter, and are moved by external forces, and take their opportunity for operating from the outside.

If it is the last of the minds, it is therefore joined to the highest body <note>The human body, considered the most refined and balanced of all physical compositions.</note>. Because of this proximity, the mind itself draws its "rest" and external motion from bodies; it is necessary then that the human body—the most noble of composite bodies—when joined to a mind, receives two things back from the mind: namely, action and internal motion. Action is received from the **form**, and interior motion from the soul. Therefore, the lowest mind becomes the form of the highest body, and thus the **soul**.

<margin>B</margin> Just as matter (which is the ultimate boundary of physical things) is not any specific body, so the human mind (which is the ultimate boundary of minds) is not some "separate mind," but is naturally joined to the body. Because it requires the senses to begin the process of understanding—perceiving bodies through the senses and "drinking in" their forms—nature decreed there should be the greatest possible kinship between sense and intellect, so that this "drinking in" happens as easily and perfectly as possible.

There could be no greater kinship, nor could it be done more easily, than if both mind and sense were present in the same substance of the soul. <margin>C</margin> Consider the **oyster**: these are the lowest of all sensing creatures, yet they are so close to trees (which are the highest of things lacking sense) that they are partly attached to the earth like trees, and partly use the sense of touch like animals. In the same way, the human intellect, the lowest among minds, is so joined to the nature of those forms which are highest among physical things that it partly forms the body (like a physical form) and partly understands (like the higher minds).

Just as **air** sits between fire and water (which are most distant from each other), being hot like fire and moist like water, so the **rational soul** <note>original: "rõnalis anima"</note> is placed between angels and brute animals, which differ greatly. It understands like the former and forms a body like the latter. If a form is closer to matter, it is its "shadow"; as the vegetative soul is to the sensitive, or the sensitive to the intellective. It follows that the intellective soul joins to matter through its "shadow," that is, through its life-giving act.

<margin>D</margin> A **principal agent** moves the agents that follow it. A **principal end** compels the remaining ends. **Principal matter** supports other matters. Therefore, a **principal form**, as much as possible, forms all other forms. Since the mind is the principal form in natural things, it must in some way form the other forms and take the place of all of them. But it never does this unless it first forms matter that has been suitably prepared through lower forms. When those lower forms cease, the mind experiences within itself the powers of the forms that follow.

Furthermore, if natural motion reaches its end, and there is such an ascent in the types of forms that they gradually strive to transcend matter, it is necessary that at least the final natural form achieves this. It must not only form matter but also, through some part of itself, entirely exceed matter. In that part where it exceeds the body and time, it is joined to spirits and eternity through understanding.

<margin>E</margin> The <term>Platonists</term> call such a form both "natural" and "divine," because it is the boundary between natural and divine forms. The minds that govern the heavenly bodies are distributed such that each moves one body primarily, and does so from within and without a medium <note>That is, directly, without an intermediate tool.</note>. Much more so must the human mind move its one primary body and stir it from within without a medium, since it is even closer to the body. Hence it seems to be against the order of nature for that sublime mind to be joined to the body without a medium, while the lowest mind [is joined] through a "thinking soul."

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, the **order**...

Using analogies like the oyster and the elements, he explains how the soul is uniquely both the form of the body and a divine substance capable of transcending time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the "Great Chain of Being." On the previous page, he established the mind's unique position as the bridge between the physical and the spiritual. Here, he provides the formal metaphysical structure for that hierarchy, moving from God down to the lowest forms of life, and introduces support from the Persian philosopher Avicenna to reinforce his Platonic worldview.</meta>

# Theology

The order of nature is as follows: there is pure Good, and there is intellectual Good. There is pure Intellect, and there is animal intellect. There is pure Soul, and there is corporeal soul. The first is God. The second is the Angel. The third is the **rational soul**. The fourth, however, is the irrational soul. <margin>§</margin> Therefore, unless there exists somewhere a form that is partly intellectual and partly life-giving, the order of nature would be thrown into confusion. This order consists in this: that God is pure Good. The Angel is indeed an intellectual good, but a pure intellect. The rational soul is an animal intellect, but a pure soul, because it sustains itself. The irrational soul is an "impure" soul <note>original: "impura"; here Ficino means 'impure' in a technical sense—not sinful, but dependent upon and mixed with material bodies.</note> precisely because it requires the support of a physical body. Thus, because "being in itself" precedes "being in another," and because that which exists in itself overflows by its own perfection into something else, the sequence is: Good in itself; Good in the mind. Mind in itself; Mind in the soul. Soul in itself; Soul in the body. Just as the body of the highest heaven exists in itself, while all other bodies exist within it.

Not only is the entire genus of "soul" more excellent than the entire genus of "body," but the genus of soul must be more expansive than that of body. Thus, the lowest part of the soul-possessing genus exceeds the highest part of the physical genus. For this reason, in a wonderful way, the highest part of the soul-possessing genus vastly exceeds the highest part of the physical genus. Consequently, the rational soul does not merely enter the depths of the body by nourishing it, but also transcends the heights of the body by the act of understanding. This is rightly so, because that which is more excellent ought to depend less on that which is inferior than vice versa. Just as the lowest souls are, in a sense, contained by bodies, and the middle souls are both contained by and contain bodies, so the highest souls entirely contain their bodies. They do not contain the body unless they both penetrate it from within and surround it from without. And just as the soul receives intellectual life from on high by moving away from the surface of the body, so by penetrating the innermost parts of the body, it grants animal life to the lowest parts.

<margin>§</margin> When the soul rises toward what is granted by God, it obtains the **active intellect** <term>active intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectũ sortitur agẽtem"; the power of the mind that actively creates concepts.</note>; when it resides within itself, it possesses the **receptive intellect** <term>receptive intellect</term> <note>original: "capacẽ possidet intellectũ"; the capacity of the mind to receive and store knowledge.</note>. When it penetrates the body—as it weaves itself into the vital spirits—it feels and moves; as it immerses itself in the bodily fluids, it nourishes and sustains. 

But let us return to the universal order of things: We can say that God is the Form that neither adheres to matter, nor is formed by another, nor acts as a forming agent of matter. The irrational soul, by contrast, is formed, forms the body, and adheres to it. But the Angel is indeed formed by God, yet neither adheres to matter nor forms matter. Therefore, between the Angel and the irrational soul, we shall place the **rational soul**, which is endowed with such a nature that it does not adhere to matter, yet it is formed by God and forms the body.

<margin>☞</margin> Furthermore, that Platonic distinction found in the *Metaphysics* of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: "metaphysicis Auicenne"; Ficino frequently cites the Persian philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina) as a way to bridge Aristotelian logic with Platonic spirituality.</note> seems highly commendable: namely, that in the intelligible world, one must proceed from the highest intelligible being toward many intellects, as if from a "Former" to the powers that are capable of being formed. First, from that Absolute One to absolute intellects, which in no way decline from their source. Second, to intellects that turn slightly toward sensible things—that is, only to govern them from the outside, so that such a duty appears to happen to them externally. Third, to those intellects which, as much as is possible in an intellectual nature, naturally decline toward sensible things—that is, to govern them from within through life and motion. <margin>¶</margin> For in no other way is the sensible world perfectly connected with the intelligible world, and the lower things disposed according to the most beautiful and best pattern of the higher things. 

From this follows a fourth degree, though a shadowy one, as some believe: a kind of "knot" of minds with bodies—namely, the species of irrational lives. These, as the Platonists believe, follow the minds like shadows proceeding through bodies. 

<margin>g</margin> But let us return again to divine matters. No one denies that God exists; however, the "being" of God himself is not determined by any certain species of being, through which he would become "this" or "that." Nor is God composed of a common nature of "being" and some added difference (that is, a property of being). <margin>§</margin> Therefore, Being itself is absolute, circumscribed by no limits. That which exists is utterly infinite. It is the immense root that contains and procreates all those things which have a specific "being," whether this kind or that. For all composition flows from a simple source. Therefore, angels have "being," but that which belongs to them is "this" or "that" being—that is, with this or that property in one species of angel or another...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s metaphysical mapping of the universe. # Platonic Theology

...things. Therefore, the **being** <note>original: "esse"; in this context, it refers to the act of existing.</note> of an angel is not infinite, like the divine being. For it no longer contains the complete fullness of the whole of being, nor does it exist as all of being. Instead, it is enclosed within one specific **species** <term>species: here meaning a specific "kind" or "form" that defines what a thing is</term> of thing, through which it is determined to a single mode of being. For it is right that the divine being—which precedes the Ideas (that is, the species) and through those species distributes being to the things flowing from Him—should hand over this very being within the species. And thus, different species have different modes of being.

Accordingly, angelic being is limited within the angelic species. However, the angelic species—which we also call the **essence** <note>original: "essentia"; the fundamental nature of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>, which is the foundation for such a being—is in a certain way infinite: not indeed as God is, but because it remains within itself and preserves the entire integrity of its species; nor does it receive anything into itself beyond its species and the properties of that species. This is because it is close to no inferior nature whose contagion might infect it.

But if this angelic essence did not differ from its being, its being would also be called infinite. For it would then subsist in itself and through itself; however, to be infinite in both directions—and to exist through itself—is the property of God alone. Likewise, if its being did not differ from its essence, since being is an **act** <note>original: "actus"; the state of being real or active as opposed to just having the potential to exist.</note>, the angel would certainly be pure act alone. Since participation in being does not occur through potential alone, the angel would participate in nothing else, and would be in every way most simple: a condition that can belong to God alone.

Thus God is completely infinite, because He exists as being alone, and as being in its whole and its entirety. The Angel is finite according to its being, but infinite according to its essence. Add also that it is infinite, in a certain way, according to its power and operation. For it is hindered by no obstacle, care, or anxiety of a lesser thing from always exercising its whole power, however great that may be, in its work.

<margin>A</margin>
The form of a body, such as the **rational soul** is: because it exists in a certain species just like an angel, it also has a finite being, but an essence that is partly infinite and partly finite. It is infinite indeed, because it never loses anything belonging to its species; for its nature is a vital and rational act, which act it never gives up nor interrupts. It is finite, however, because it admits something beyond the species (that is, beyond the principles of the species): namely, this or that affection toward a specific disposition of the human body. Through this, it becomes the life-giving form of the body and is numbered according to the quantity of bodies. 

The essence of this soul, insofar as it is infinite, exceeds the capacity of the body and leads an intellectual life. Insofar as it is finite, it has a proportion with the body, and with the body it leads a corporeal life. In the former, infinite power and operation flourish; in the latter, by contrast, they are finite. 

Finally, the corporeal form is finite in every way—according to being, essence, power, and action. According to being, because its being is certainly circumscribed by the limits of a species. According to essence, both because it receives into itself many accidental qualities beyond its species, and because it does not preserve its own vigor at all. Likewise, because its nature is an effective or vital act, yet it undergoes passions <note>passiones: here meaning "undergoing external influences" or "suffering change," rather than just emotions.</note> and death within the body. According to power and action: since its power increases and decreases, and any operation extends only as far as the quality of its physical instruments and subjects allow. 

Such are all forms inferior to the rational soul. It is necessary that these four grades of things exist in nature, so that we may descend little by little from that which is entirely infinite, through intermediaries and mixtures, to those things that are entirely finite. This gradation cannot be continued unless—just as in the intelligible world there is the infinite and the finite (namely God and the Angel)—so in the sensible world there are images of those things: namely, something that is in a way infinite (the rational soul) and something entirely finite (any inferior form). The soul is the form *of* a body, but it is not corporeal itself. The lower form is both *of* a body and is itself corporeal. Let us descend by these steps again:

<margin>B</margin>
God possesses being from Himself, in Himself, and for Himself. The Angel possesses being not from itself (since it is from God), but in itself and for itself. The form of the body, such as the rational soul, has being neither from itself (since it is created by another) nor does it keep its being only for itself (since it communicates it to the body); yet it has being in itself, because its being is grounded in its own essence, and is the proper act of that essence.

# Theology

<margin>D</margin>
According to the Platonists <note>original: "secundum Platonicos"</note>, it shines in itself and illuminates only others; yet in such a way that it does not lose its own light. But corporal <term>corporal: related to the physical body</term> form does not have **being** <note>original: "esse"; the act of existing</note> from itself, nor does it hold it for itself, as the soul does. Nor, again, does it exist within itself. For it is so dedicated to matter that a composite is made from it and matter; in this composite, being itself is properly founded, and its being is an **act** <note>original: "actus"; the realization or fulfillment of a potentiality</note>. However, its form is not the proper foundation of being itself.

Nature must not lack this order. Yet it would lack it, unless there were some form of the body that was not itself bodily. Our Proclus’s <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who greatly influenced Ficino’s hierarchy of the universe.</note> distinction seems similar to this. He says that the **Divine** itself is to be called the "Intelligible." Then there is **Pure Intellect**, which belongs to itself and is within itself. Next is the **Animal Intellect** <note>original: "intellectus animalis"; the "soul-intellect" or rational soul</note>, which belongs both to itself—since it possesses its being in its own essence—and to another, because from its own rational life it diffuses another life lacking reason (as if an image) into the body. After these comes **Nature**, that is, the vital complex; like a shadow because of the life infused by the soul, it is supported by the body and must be judged as belonging only to another—that is, to the body—with which it is extended and divided. Finally, the **Body**, on account of its diverse and utterly dissipatable condition, is properly
<margin>E</margin>
called "the other." Here it appears that in the very order of things, the animal intellect (or the intellectual soul) holds the middle place.

<margin>f</margin>
Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a student of Plotinus and a major figure in the preservation of Platonic thought.</note>, following the mind of Plato in his commentaries on the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world.</note>, seems to assert a similar order, distinguishing the whole universe into six grades in this way: <margin>G</margin> He proves that some things only **are** <note>original: "esse"</note>; some only **become** <note>original: "fieri"; to come into being or change</note>; others both **are and become** at the same time; and others **become and are** at the same time. Furthermore, he proposes that something stands above all things, and becomes; he also supposes that something lies beneath all things, and is placed in becoming. He says that "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note> refers to the whole breadth of minds, whether they are minds in themselves or minds within souls. <margin>H</margin> On the contrary, he wishes "becoming" <note>original: "fieri"</note> to be the breadth of sensible things, whether they are elementary or celestial. The "being and becoming" at the same time is the genus of souls. And conversely, "becoming and being" is the very nature of the universe that gives life to the whole; this is indeed the summit of those things that "become." And insofar as it is distributed through bodies, it is said to "become." But insofar as it is not at all bodily in itself, it is said "to be." Finally, he places **The Good** above all things and **Matter** beneath all. Why are these things so? So that we may understand that the order of the universe cannot be continuous unless there are intellectual forms that are simultaneously the life-givers of bodies. For to these alone can it belong to be said to "be and become" at the same time. They "are" through their utterly indivisible substance and the sudden intuition of their own intelligence. They "become" through the temporal discourse of their remaining actions.

<margin>B</margin>
This Pythagorean reasoning persuades us that there must be such a form. As it pleases Timaeus of Locri <note>A character in Plato's dialogues, often treated by Renaissance scholars as a real Pythagorean philosopher.</note>, God the Father broods over Matter the Mother, about to generate forms as if they were offspring. In the Father, there is an effective fertility of all forms. In the Mother, there is a receptive fertility, especially of corporal forms. In the Father is the effective **act** of forms; in the Mother is the receptive **potential** <note>original: "potentia"</note> of forms. Many offspring similar to the mother are born—namely, those forms that emerge from the depths of matter and are finally submerged back into the same. Just as the shape of a golden vessel comes from gold and returns into gold. Again, it is necessary that some offspring be born very similar to the Father, provided that the Father has more power than the Mother in this union. Of this kind will be the forms leaping out from the act of the Father onto the face of matter, and then leaping back into the act of the Father. Just as brightness goes from the sun into gold, and back to the sun. Those forms more similar to the mother lie hidden, in a way, in the internal organs of matter, like the shape of the vessel in the gold; they also lie hidden in the powers of souls and mundane bodies, which are the instruments of the Divine Craftsman. God draws them out from the bosom of matter through the movements of the world and leads them into being according to the capacity of matter. But to what does such a "being" properly belong? To that composite body which is finished from this generation. Why? Because the instrument through which they are generated by God is a composite. If, therefore, the first cause is composite, and the effect is usually very similar to the nearest cause—

# The Platonic Book

It follows from the matter that what is properly generated is that which is **composite** <term>composite: a thing made of both matter and form, like a physical object</term>. Truly, "to be" properly belongs to that which is generated. Therefore, that specific **being** <note>original: "esse"; the act of existing</note> belongs to the composite. For it does not come from form alone, nor from matter alone, but from the composite itself. It happens that such forms of matter are, in a certain way, inherent in potentiality <term>potentiality: the capacity to become something, as opposed to already being it</term> before they achieve actual being. They are brought forth in the **womb of matter** at the very moment when the being of the composite is completed. Because they truly come into existence and receive their being by inhering in the power of matter itself, they retain their being by adhering to that same matter in **act** <note>original: "in actu"; in reality or completion</note>; they exist only as long as they cling to it. Therefore, they do not exist through their own being after they are made, nor do they stay or remain by themselves, but through the being of that composite of which they are parts, which is the endpoint of the process of generation. And rightly so, since they do not have their own being, they possess no power or operation of their own. Such are the forms that seem more like the **mother** <note>Ficino uses "mother" to refer to Matter—passive and receptive—following ancient philosophical metaphors.</note> than the father. But those which are more like the **father** <note>The "father" represents Form or the Divine—active and organizing.</note>—such as rational souls—are brought forth from the pure act of God. Therefore, they are suddenly brought to the act of being. Because they possess being in themselves first, they are only afterwards joined to matter. The soul has being before it clings to the body; and before the body, in the very order of nature, souls retain being, and after the body, they have their own being within themselves. They have a certain choice within themselves that is not shared with the body. In one respect, they impart their being to the body; they perform some operations in the body, and some through the body.

### ¶ How the mind approaches the body. Chapter 3, Book 3.

<margin>A</margin>
**B**ut in what way do they impart their being to the body? Is the mind mixed with it? Not at all. For that which is mixed is destroyed and confused. Or do they touch the body? By no means.

<margin>B</margin>
**T**ouch is proper only to two bodies. Are they perhaps enclosed within it? Not that either. For nothing is enclosed by a location except a body. What, then, do these forms do to the body when they communicate their being to it? They **penetrate** it everywhere with their essence; they dedicate the power of their essence to it. Since being is drawn from essence, and operation flows from power, they impart being by joining their essence to it. By dedicating their power, they communicate operations. Thus, from the meeting of soul and body, one being of a living creature and one operation emerges. This being indeed belongs to the soul itself through its essence, but through **participation** <term>participation: the way a lower thing shares in the qualities of a higher thing</term> it becomes the body's being as well. The soul does not submerge its own being into the body, but rather **lifts the body up** to itself. Nor does the body take in the whole breadth of that essence, but it touches something of it according to its own nature; it does not sustain the essence, but is sustained by it.

<margin>2</margin>
How a form without physical extension can fill the mass of a body will be clearly understood by anyone who considers that even an extended form relates to a body in such a way that any part of it relates equally to any part of the matter, and vice versa. Thus, we can imagine that any part of this form is in individual portions of matter, and forms them in such a way that the whole is present at any single point. But let us take away extension from this form, while meanwhile leaving it the office of forming the body.

<margin>3</margin>
For we are able to do this: to "form" is something different and more excellent than to "be extended." Thus, if matter is indeed extended, but does not form, then some form of matter can "form" without being extended. In this way, we will see an **indivisible form** <note>original: "individua"; a form that cannot be split into pieces, like the soul.</note> forming the whole matter all at once, and every part of it equally.

<margin>4</margin>
And if that **Pythagorean** <note>Pythagoras (6th c. BC) and his followers believed that the physical world was built upon mathematical and geometric principles.</note> principle is true—namely, that a point by its motion creates a line, a line a surface, and a surface by a similar motion creates depth—we can easily imagine that the same point, by its motion, spreads its whole, indivisible self through length, breadth, and depth. From this, it happens that wherever you divide it, or touch it, you find the point.

<margin>5</margin>
If this point were merely an accident <term>accident: a non-essential property, like color or shape</term>, it would necessarily be sustained by the mass. But if it were a **substance** <term>substance: a thing that exists in itself</term>, like a soul subsisting in itself, it would be present to the mass, yet remain perpetually within itself, separate from the mass.

### ¶ How the mind is present to the body. Book 4.

<summary>Ficino explains that the rational soul, unlike physical forms, possesses its own independent existence (being) granted by God and "lifts" the body up to share in its life rather than being absorbed by the body. He uses the analogy of a geometric point to show how an indivisible soul can be present throughout a physical, extended body.</summary>
