<header>Theology XV.</header>
<sig>Z 3</sig>

# Theology

<margin>E</margin>
Is this soul, so excellent, joined to unformed matter without a medium? <note>original: "sine medio"; meaning without an intermediary or middle step</note> A more perfect form always contains the less perfect forms within itself: just as a square contains a triangle. If the rational soul possesses the power of understanding, which is the most excellent of all, it also possesses the powers of sensing, of nourishing, and of ruling. Therefore, within the power of the rational soul, the sensitive and nutritive souls are enclosed. It is also the form of mixed bodies <note>In ancient physics, "mixed bodies" are those made of a combination of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire).</note> that lack life. The rational soul approaches matter endowed with all these aforementioned forms: through its own form—or power—which acts in place of the forms of lifeless mixed bodies, it clings most closely to unformed matter. And in that matter, it creates the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific "recipe" or balance of the four elements in a body</term> of the four elements, while it binds the parts of matter into one and tempers the elements.

¶ Through its own form, which possesses the power of plants, it clings to the body composed of matter and its element-balance. To that balance of elements, it grants movement in every direction; this movement is called **life**. ¶ Through the form proper to animals, it adapts itself to these elements and creates the **spirit** <term>spirit: a subtle, vaporous substance that Renaissance thinkers believed acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term>, which is the instrument of the senses. ¶ Through the rational form, it commands the rest. Thus, through its lowest power, it is the form of matter; through the second, it is the form of the mixed body; through the third, it is the form of the plant; through the fourth, it is the form of the animal; indeed, it is the **form of forms**. From this it follows that the rational soul forms bodies more than other forms do, because it forms them through more powers; and it forms them more purely, since it touches unformed matter up close with its **foot**, but looks out from afar with its **head**. <note>Ficino uses "foot" and "head" as metaphors for the lowest and highest faculties of the soul.</note>

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Just as fire, out of its four proper degrees of heat: ¶ First, it pours heat into cold wood. Second, into wood that is already lukewarm. Third, into wood already made hot by two degrees. Fourth, it adds to those three degrees a further one, through which it shines from above; so too the essence of the rational soul is filled with four certain degrees: the mixed, the vital, the sensual, and the intellectual. First, it applies itself to matter; second, it applies the second degree to the first; third, it adds the third to the second; and fourth, it adds the fourth to the third. In this way, it is seen to form matter according to its whole essence as well as according to all its degrees. It is true that it forms matter in the same way according to its whole essence, but in different ways according to all its degrees. ¶ For the first is the form of matter. The second is the form of the mixed body.

<margin>B</margin>
The third is the form of the vital form. The fourth is the **form of all forms** among bodily things. Through three degrees, the particular soul emerges; through the fourth, it remains absolute <note>original: "absoluta"; meaning independent, detached, or perfected in itself</note>, and capable of receiving absolute forms. Is it any wonder if, in this most excellent degree, some power and operation appear that are very similar to the divine? For this degree is closest to the divine because it is furthest from matter. Since in many forms of mixed bodies—on account of a certain balance agreeable to the celestial bodies—some power and action may result that is foreign to the elements of which the subject of that form is composed, but in harmony with the celestial things to which it is similar in its balance. Nor should it seem strange that the soul, although it is the form of the body, nevertheless possesses some power not shared with the body. For angels are not drawn out of matter, neither according to their essence nor according to their preparation for essence. But irrational souls are drawn out through both. For rational souls, which are in the middle, there must be a **middle condition**. They cannot spring from matter by essence. Yet, they may spring from matter according to their preparation. <note>Ficino means the body is prepared by nature to receive the soul, but the soul's actual being comes from God.</note> Therefore, they will indeed flow forth according to preparation, but not at all according to essence. If power follows essence, then no power of an angel is shared with the body. However, every power of beasts belongs to the soul and body together, because it is drawn from matter along with the essence.

<margin>D</margin>
But the power of the rational soul is in its essence alone, since it descends from on high. And because a soul of this kind exceeds the proportion of the body, it is not "in" the body, but rather the body is "in" it; the body does not grasp the soul's entire power. Yet it does reach some small part of its power, because the soul—which according to its preparation depends in a certain way on matter—affects the body to such an extent...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the soul as a "form of forms" that contains all lower biological functions (vegetative and animal) within its rational essence. He argues that while the soul organizes the body's matter, its highest intellectual power remains independent and divine, effectively containing the body rather than being contained by it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s investigation into the metaphysical "middle ground" of the human soul. Having established that the soul possesses the powers of lower life forms, he now argues that the soul must exist as a logical bridge between purely spiritual beings (angels) and purely physical beings (animals), and begins to explore the specific physical-spiritual mechanics of how the soul "fits" inside a body.</meta>

->Platonic<-
->Book<-
<sig>L</sig> <note>This letter L refers to the signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in order.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
...so that it may accommodate its internal powers to the body with a certain proportion, and through that proportion, it may act freely within it. Nor should it be thought absurd for a rational substance to be joined to matter, because the order of nature cannot be preserved otherwise. For there is a certain spirit that is separated from matter, rational, and incorruptible—such as an angel. There is also a spirit that is connected to matter, irrational, and corruptible—such as the soul of beasts. These two are very far apart. Certainly, they are within the same genus of "spirit," yet they differ from each other by three distinctions. 

What, therefore, is the medium <note>original: "medium"; the middle point or bridge between two extremes</note> between these? It cannot be a spirit that is only "separated," for such a thing cannot exist without also being rational and immortal. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "rational," for such a spirit must additionally be either connected or separated. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "incorruptible," since it is necessary for such a spirit to also be rational. It cannot be a spirit that is only "separated and rational," because one must also posit that it is incorruptible. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "separated and incorruptible," for if it has these two, it also has reason; since it exercises neither sense nor nutrition, it would exist in vain unless it had the operation of reason. 

It cannot be a spirit that is only "connected and irrational," for such a thing is also mortal. Nor can it be a spirit that is only "connected and immortal," for that which has an immortal life in common with the angels also has intelligence in common with them. Nor can it be a spirit that is "connected, rational, and fleeting <note>original: "caducus"; meaning subject to decay or falling</note>," because if it has intelligence in common with the angels—which is a certain reflection of its own life back into itself—it also has life in common with them. 

Therefore, it is necessary that there be some spirit in the body that is the middle of these extremes, which is both rational and incorruptible. Let it agree with both because it is a spirit. Let it differ from the angel because it is "connected." Let it differ from the beast because it is "rational." It specifically agrees with the angel because it is immortal. It specifically agrees with the beast because it is connected. Indeed, since there must be a medium between those extremes that is in some way equally distant from both and equally a participant in both, it is necessary that there be a spirit that is partly separated, rational, and eternal, and partly connected, irrational, and subject to decay. Such, above all, is the human soul. In its highest part, those first three conditions 
<margin>B</margin>
exist. In its lowest part are the following three. In the middle, all six are mixed together and, as Plato says, tempered with musical scales <note>Ficino refers to the "Timaeus," where Plato describes the World Soul being constructed according to harmonic ratios.</note>.

### How the mind is in the body. Chapter 5.

<margin>C</margin>
**H**ere, in what way is the rational soul joined to the body? It is not as a solid body is joined to a solid body. For these solid bodies, which are joined only by touch, are neither entirely together, nor do they act together; whereas the soul and the body are entirely together and act at the same time. Furthermore, it seems most absurd of all to compare the soul—the most effective origin of vital motion—to the densest of bodies. For the more things are said to have "corporeal properties," the less they seem to possess "natural action" and "vital motion." Indeed, if they are divided, they remain scattered, and they do not immediately return to their union as purer things are accustomed to do. 

On the contrary, things which have the least corporeal thickness, when they seem to be struck by more solid things, avoid the blow very easily; when they penetrate, they penetrate most effectively. When they are divided, they return to their unity so swiftly that they seem not to have departed from it at all. Therefore, as we were saying, the soul is not joined to the body as a solid is to a solid.

<margin>D</margin>
Again, it is not like water in wine. For these soft bodies lose their prior power through mutual mixing and cease to be what they were. Since the soul is incorporeal <note>original: "incorporea"; not composed of matter</note>, and has no matter in common with this body, it cannot be mixed or confused with the quality of this body. 

Is it perhaps like the heat of fire in water? This is a better way, since heat is not a body; therefore, it is more similar to the soul. But even this does not satisfy us. For a part of the heat is in a part of the water, not the whole heat in the whole water. Perhaps it is like a voice in the air? For a voice is perhaps one and the same whole in any part of the ear, if the whole is heard in every part. It moves the ears. It announces something to the intellect. In the same way, the soul is whole in any small particle of the body. It rules the body and understands at the same time. But I do not know what fragile quality the voice has, and it passes...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul is the necessary "middle" between angels and animals, possessing traits of both. He explores various metaphors—solid contact, liquid mixing, and sound—to explain how the soul exists entirely within every part of the physical body without being divided by it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul’s relationship to the body in his *Platonic Theology*. Having previously discussed the soul as a bridge between the spiritual and material worlds, he now employs various analogies—specifically sound, the pilot of a ship, and the light of the sun—to explain how the soul can be "whole in the whole" of the body while remaining distinct in its essence.</meta>

# Theology

<note>original: "soni"; the OCR "fioni" is a common misreading of the long 's'</note> ...subject to sound. It is born in the breaking of the air and is pushed back by a light breeze. But I have, in the meantime, a better analogy: namely, the image of color in the air coming to the eyes. This is spiritual <note>in the sense of being incorruptible or non-material</note>. It travels in a moment. It reaches far. It occurs as a whole everywhere. It does not suffer from any forceful impact. It paints the air. It shapes the vision. This is indeed very similar. But it differs in this: that it does not rule or govern the air as the soul does the body. But look: a pilot governs a certain ship. And he is in the ship. In the same way, does the soul relate to the body? No: because the pilot does not fill the ship; he is not present to the whole of it; he does not move it by himself alone, but through the rudder. But now, I have found the soul in this rudder. For since the sailor rules the ship through it, the art of navigation <note>the 'ars gubernatoria' or skill of the pilot</note> is not only in the sailor, but it also passes into the rudder. It exists as a whole in the whole of it, and it rules it. This is the very "soul" of the rudder. But this art contributes nothing of its own nature to the substance of the rudder; it merely moves it, being itself moved from the outside. The soul, however, contributes something to the body and moves it by its own nature.

Please, philosopher, lift your eyes to the heavens: you seek a celestial soul on the earth or the sea. Look up at the light of the sun. This light is one and indivisible: it is, so to speak, whole in any part of the air. It illuminates the air and heats it. It takes nothing from the air, nor does it suffer any violence anywhere. Nor is it stained by any filth. The air fluctuates with the winds; the light remains, as Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism, a major influence on Ficino</note> maintains. It comes from the sun and passes into the air in a moment. Again, it is not separated from the sun; it is reflected back into the sun as well. Without light, the air is dead, since it is cold and dark, destitute of any form. Light has two qualities: brightness and heat. It exercises brightness in the air, yet it does not bestow it permanently to the air <note>meaning the air does not keep the brightness once the source is gone</note>; however, it does bestow heat. Hence, when the sun sets, 
<margin>E</margin>
the light is not extinguished, as Plotinus thinks, but all the light suddenly withdraws together with the sun. Traces of heat are left behind deep into the night, as if the air had become a participant in the heat, but not the brightness. But if you please, let us say it does not grant brightness. And indeed, what is it for that light to shine other than "to be light"? Without that light, the air does not shine. Without the air, 

---

the light still shines. If indeed the opinion of Plotinus is true: light does not depend on anything transparent in any way, but depends continually on the sun alone; and light always accompanies the sun, as it were, as its own perpetual act. But let us proceed to the rest. Light approaches the air; the light shines there just as it did before in itself. The air shines, which did not shine before; but that light shines through itself. The air shines through the light. Is the "shining" of the light something different from the "shining" of the air? Not at all; otherwise, the air would remain bright when the light departs. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, it is one "shining" by which both shine. But it belongs to the light by essence, while it belongs to the air by participation <note>a key Platonic concept where a material thing "shares in" the quality of a higher spiritual reality</note>. Therefore, a single "being" in a certain way belongs to both. And light is not "in" the air, although people commonly say so; rather, the air is in the light. In this way, that which is more narrow and subject to greater passion <note>here meaning "being acted upon" or affected</note> is contained in that which cannot be acted upon. 

Similarly, the soul of a human is sent down from God into matter. It passes into it suddenly, yet does not depart from God. But it acts in both ways at once. It rules the body, and it also reaches the truth itself of all things—which is God himself—in a certain miraculous way, as Plotinus discusses, through the intellect. Again, just as light reflects in the sun, so the soul reflects toward God through the will, insofar as it always desires the goodness of all things, which is God himself. It fills the body without hindrance, as light fills the air; and similarly, it is present as a whole to the whole. While the body suffers, the soul does not suffer, but it senses and judges those sufferings <note>Ficino argues the soul observes the body's pain without being "damaged" by it</note>. It does not flow away as the body falls away, but remains constant. It has two principal powers: the Judicial and the Vital. It does not hand over Judgment to the body, but carries it out itself. It lends or bestows Life to the body, insofar as it communicates a certain "imaginary" <note>reflected or derivative</note> force of its own life to it. Hence, the soul alone judges, not the body. However, both the body and the soul "live." For this reason, when the soul departs, the senses leave immediately; yet traces of life seem to remain for a time—namely, heat and motion. For the soul, "to be" is "to live," since the essence of the soul is life, through which the body formally lives. To be a living being is nothing other than to live. Yet, "to live" itself is not the same as the soul being coupled to the body. <margin>G</margin> The "living" of the composite thing <note>the body-soul unit</note> is something else. Rather, it lives through one and the same life—that is, the essence of the soul.

<summary>Ficino uses analogies of light and heat to explain how the soul can be present in the body "whole in the whole" without being corrupted by matter. He concludes that the soul is the source of life and judgment, while the body only participates in life as long as the soul is present.</summary>
<keywords>soul and body, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, analogy of light, participation, essence, Marsilio Ficino, judicial power, vital power, immortality of the soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that the soul is not merely a passenger in the body, but a governing form that encompasses it. Having previously used the analogy of a pilot and a rudder, Ficino now transitions to the "Platonic" view that the body exists within the soul, rather than the soul being "trapped" inside the body.</meta>

# Platonic Book

<margin>A</margin>
...both, but the soul lives through its own power, and the body through another's. Most people judge that both live through one thing only, and they call them "living things": the body through the soul, but the soul through itself. As we touched on above, the soul is not "in" the body, though it appears so to those who see the body but do not see the soul, and who therefore think the soul is hidden in the body as if in a small vessel. <note>original: "tanquam vasculo"</note>. But those who look closely at the soul see it entering the body from within, surpassing it from without, embracing and sustaining it; and moving this tiny bit of dust <note>the physical body</note>, they conclude that the body is actually contained within the soul. Who could doubt that the soul is larger than the body? Since it equals the body with one part of itself—that is, the vital power—but exceeds it with another—the faculty of judgment. Therefore, the body, being narrower and prone to change, exists within the soul, which is larger and stable, just as a thing contained is within that which contains it. Thus, although the whole soul is present to the body, the body is not present to the whole soul, but only to its lowest part: the vital power.

<margin>B</margin>
This is confirmed by the fact that since the soul is far greater in power than the body, and since motion and growth proceed from power, it is necessary that the soul is not only present to the whole body but also, according to its presence, exceeds the body, as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the soul's relationship to the divine</note> believes. And because the soul is indivisible, wherever it is, it is there as a whole. The body, however, just as it does not equal the full power of the soul, does not equal the soul's total presence. <term>Plato</term> perceived this in the <term>Timaeus</term> <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> when he said the Maker of the world placed the body within the soul. Again, in the tenth book of the <term>Republic</term>, where he says the body of the world is turned between the knees of Necessity <note>an image of the cosmic spindle governing the fates and the rotation of the heavens</note>; that is, it is ruled and moved by the lowest part of the celestial soul. In the <term>Phaedrus</term>, he also affirmed that souls lift their heads above the heavens. Indeed, although the soul thus exceeds the body, it should not seem impossible to anyone that the soul draws matter to itself to such an extent that it creates a single composite being.

<margin>E</margin>
For since it is the nature of forms to perfect and bind matter to themselves, and to join the parts of matter together, the more excellent a form is and the more it dominates matter, the more perfectly it can achieve this. Even the lowliest forms do this. What prevents the sublime forms from doing the same? Provided they naturally desire it. If angelic minds <note>spiritual beings that do not have physical bodies</note> do not do this at all, it is because they have no inclination to complete the form of any living creature by joining with it. But all the Platonists and the ancient Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> believed this was done by the celestial minds.

<margin>D</margin>
For none of them are found who did not affirm that the celestial spheres are animated by rational souls. Among the Platonists, <term>Plotinus</term>, <term>Porphyry</term>, <term>Iamblichus</term>, and <term>Proclus</term> <note>The major figures of the Neoplatonic tradition</note> testify to this above all. Among the Peripatetics, <term>Theophrastus</term>, <term>Avicenna</term>, and <term>Al-Ghazali</term> <note>OCR "alganteles" likely refers to the philosopher Al-Ghazali, known in Latin as Algazel</note>. In this matter, <term>Ptolemy</term>, <term>Albumasar</term>, <term>Zahel</term>, and <term>Manilius</term> <note>Influential ancient and medieval astronomers and astrologers</note> and other leading authors of astronomy seem to agree with us. They clearly affirm that the celestial bodies are endowed with divine souls and minds, and like certain divine animals, they obey God himself, the ruler of all. And this is not done without reason. Indeed, when they saw that many things pertaining to the soul are foretold by the stars, they thought this could only happen if the stars were alive and could see the future actions of humans, indicating them in a way with their nods. Furthermore, just as the rays of those celestial bodies flow into our bodies, so the rays of their souls flow into our souls. All things are sent from those most orderly causes in an orderly and good fashion. However, they can be distorted by the diverse mixing of many causes around us and by the defects of matter, so that the prudence of Mercury turns into malice, the magnanimity of Mars into ferocity, and the love of Venus into lust. The same applies to the rest. Just as the rays of the sun are sent from there in a gentle way, but here they are often received as scorching. But let us leave these things aside for now as they are superfluous to our current point. That the mind is the form of the body is clear from human opinions and actions. The first reason: because man is a rational animal.

### Chapter 6.
<margin>E</margin>
**N**ot only does the order of natural things demonstrate that the soul which contemplates and the soul which senses in man are one and the same—as we declared above—but so too do the opinions of wise men and human operations. All those who practice philosophy have agreed on this opinion...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul is larger than the body and encompasses it, using Plato's "Timaeus" and "Republic" as evidence. He also asserts that celestial bodies are animated by rational souls, explaining how stellar influences like those of Mars or Venus can be distorted by earthly matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the human soul’s nature. Following the previous discussion on how the soul contains the body, Ficino now argues that human rationality—our defining characteristic—must come from an internal "mind" or intellect that is part of our very essence, rather than an external or separate force as some philosophers suggested.</meta>

# Theology XV

Man is a certain species of things, whose proper difference—the specific quality by which he differs from the beasts—is rationality itself. Now, one must always derive a thing's proper difference from its intrinsic form; for nothing differs from another in species except through its interior nature. This rationality is not derived from the "cogitative soul" <note>original: "anima cogitatrice"; referring to the faculty that handles specific, sensory-based thoughts</note> alone, because in that faculty there is only a particular kind of reason. Man, however, operates according to universal reason, acting with a view toward the common good and with beauty in both his words and deeds. Therefore, his defining difference is taken from this universal reason. This reason resides in the mind <note>original: "mens"</note>. Thus, the mind is that form through which every one of us is placed within the human species. If, however, the mind were separated from man in its being, a single species could not be formed from the mind and the man together. Indeed, man would then be more properly called "fleshy" because of his internal flesh than "rational" because of an external reason.

<margin>f</margin>
Nor should **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" theory suggested all humans share one single, separate intellect—a view Ficino is attacking here.</note> say that man is something assembled from a "cogitative animal" and a "mind," and that the whole is called "rational" because of one of its parts—just as a body might be called "snub-nosed" because the nose itself is snub. For, first of all, a nose is physically continuous with the body, whereas the mind is by no means continuous with the faculty of thought. Furthermore, the mind in this scenario would be one kind of species existing apart from the "cogitative animal," and this animal would be a species in itself, separate from the mind. A name derived from a defining difference does not simply pass from one species to another separate one. And just as Averroes does not say the "cogitative" and "sensitive" mind are rational or intellectual because they are near a "thinking soul," so too the "thinking soul" should not be called rational or intellectual because of a separate mind. Nor, again, will the name of that difference pass into a third thing created from them. For one specific difference requires one specific species, and vice versa. Those two <note>the mind and the animal</note> do not create one species, because they do not meet in one essence or one being. 

It is entirely ridiculous to suggest that man receives the difference by which he is human from a single, separate mind. In that case, many individual persons would be but one single man, though they remain many animals. The nature of the species would remain universal to him, while the nature of the genus <note>the broader category of "animal"</note> would have already become particular. 

It is no less ridiculous to place the human species in such a "heap." Because just as he would not be one thing in a simple sense, he would not be (so to speak) a "being" in a simple sense. He would not be a substantial species of thing, but a "contingent pile" <note>original: "contingens aceruus"</note>. This is especially true because one thing is not truly formed from two things that each exist in act as perfect species in their own right; rather, it would be a "false one," held together only by something else binding them. A thing that can exist entirely on its own does not throw itself into the lap of another, nor does a thing that is self-sufficient admit another nature into its interior. On the contrary, since every thing is distinguished by its own acts, and "act" is the principle of separation, things that exist in act resist being joined. Both the mind and the animal exist in act; therefore, they cannot be coupled by another, as we shall show in what follows.

<margin>ß</margin>
Furthermore, **Aristotle** teaches in his *Ethics* <note>original: "libro de moribus"</note> that universal reason exists within the soul—the very soul by which we feel and live—and that we are called "rational" because of it. In the first book, he says that the mind is in the soul just as sight is in the eye. He also says there are two parts of the soul: the irrational and the rational. The first he divides into two: the nutritive part, which never obeys reason, and the sensitive part, which sometimes obeys it. The other part he likewise divides into "active reason" and "speculative reason." He places the moral virtues in the will and the appetite (which obey reason), and the principles of the moral virtues in active reason. He places the speculative virtues in speculative reason. He does the same in the sixth book, where he asserts that the rational power is a part of the human soul. He says this power does two things: it knows and it governs human affairs through prudence and art; and it contemplates natural and divine things through wisdom, which is comprised of intelligence and science. In the book of *Problems*, he says that Nature—the parent and author of all things—has implanted two instruments within us, by whose labor we are able to use external tools. He gave the hand to the body, and the mind to the soul. For the mind is also to be numbered among the things granted to us by nature, truly performing the role of an instrument. Thus far Aristotle.

# The Platonic Book

## The Second Reason: Because Man Understands
### Chapter 7.

<margin>A</margin> **A**ristotle maintains that man is a living being composed of a body and a mind. Significantly, in the first book of his *Ethics* <note>original: "de moribus"; referring to the Nicomachean Ethics</note>, he establishes a discussion on the happiness proper to man, which consists in man’s own proper operation. In the tenth book, he says that the proper operation of man is understanding, which occurs according to the mind—which is more properly "us" than the senses are. This is the supreme part of the soul. He adds that we either *are* the mind, or we are *mostly* the mind, even though he still wishes us to be composites <note>Referring to the "hylomorphic" composite of body and soul.</note>. It is as if the mind were the most natural form of man. In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, he says: it should rather be said that man understands through the intellectual soul, than that the soul itself understands. Here, **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century commentator on Aristotle who argued all humans share one single, separate Mind.</note> admits that understanding properly belongs to the whole composite, just as sensation does. Furthermore, everyone experiences within themselves that they understand something. Nor do they do this except through the intellect. How could we ourselves, at this present moment, investigate the nature of the intellect unless we ourselves were understanding? And since we use the intellect more by our own will than we use the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty that processes sensory images</note>—which often forces itself upon us—the intellect is more familiar and more natural to us than the imagination is.

<margin>B</margin> If the Averroists are asked what it is that "properly" understands when Aristotle and Averroes say "man properly understands," they will respond that it is not the mind. For, in their view, the mind is not the man, nor is the "cogitative animal" <note>The human animal using only basic sensory reasoning.</note> the man, as it lacks the power of understanding. Rather, they say man is a certain "heap" <note>original: "acervum"; a pile or unorganized collection</note> made of the mind and this kind of animal. They say the action of the mind—which is understanding—is attributed to the whole because the action of a part is often ascribed to the whole. That is indeed foolish. First, because such a "heap" does not exist in any single species or single genus; nor does it possess that union through which it might agree in a single operation, such as understanding is. Furthermore, the action of a part is only ascribed to the whole when that part is either continuous with the other in one essence—just as we say a man "sees" because the eye sees—or when one is inherent in the other, as when we say "fire heats" through the heating that comes from the heat and the form <note>In Aristotelian thought, "form" is the organizing principle that makes matter into a specific thing, like fire.</note>. For such a part of the fire forms the other part of the fire (the matter) so that it is brought into a single state of being. Or, it is ascribed when they work toward a single effect of movement, such as when we say the soul, together with the arm, "vibrates the sword," because such motion passes from the soul into the sword through the arm. But the mind, according to those Averroists, is neither continuous with the animal in one essence, nor does it result in a single state of being (as is evident), nor does it result in a single effect of movement. This is because understanding never leaves the mind so that it could be communicated to anything other than the mind, nor is it completed through any instrument. 

<margin>C</margin> From this, they are forced to admit (contrary to their leader, Aristotle) that it is "properly" said that the mind understands. It cannot be said that "man understands" except very improperly and absurdly. Nor should they bring up that common example of the heavens—that the heavens are sometimes said to "move themselves" because one part of them moves another. Thus, they say man understands because a part of him understands. This example does not fit. For motion passes from the mind of the heavens into the heavens themselves. Understanding, however, neither passes from the human mind into the animal, nor vice versa. But they will bring forward another equally ridiculous point: that the heavens are affirmed by some to "understand," even though only a part of them understands. Although one rarely hears that the heavens "understand," yet always hears it of man, whoever said such a thing would be speaking falsely and foolishly—unless perhaps he thinks that specific mind of the heavens shares a single species with the heavens themselves. Accordingly, those who say all men understand through a single mind, and that mind is separated from men, are no less delirious than those who would say all people see individual things through the same single eye, removed from all of them. Finally, when they are asked why *we* are said to operate based on the fact that a separate mind operates, they respond: because although that mind is not the "form" from which we have our being, it is nevertheless that from which we have our operation. This response is ridiculous because it tries to prove the same thing by the same thing. The Averroists bring up a certain "connection" <note>original: "copula"</note>, as they think of it, between the mind and the imagination of this animal, through which a man becomes "one" and "understanding." Because the mind "draws" the species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental concept or "inner form" of an object</note> through which it understands from the likeness <note>original: "simulacro"</note> which the imagination has formed for itself through the senses. For if the "species" is the form of the mind, and the "likeness" is the form of the imagination, they believe it follows that...

<summary>Ficino argues against the Averroist view that humans share a single, detached intellect. He asserts that for "man" to be said to understand, the mind must be an intrinsic, essential part of the individual, not a separate entity linked by mere mental images.</summary>

# Theology
## E

whenever the <term>species</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a 'species' is a mental representation or image through which the mind knows an object.</note> is coupled with a <term>simulacrum</term> <note>A sensory image or 'phantasm' stored in the imagination.</note>, the mind likewise conspires with the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination.</note>. This coupling occurs as often as the species depends on the image. Truly, this happens whenever a human contemplates something. We do not believe such a coupling is sufficient. For in what way can an intelligible species be the knot by which the phantasy is bound to the mind? For the nature of this species is such that as long as it inheres in the images of the phantasy—as if in particular foundations—it remains particular and separate from the mind. And as soon as it is made universal in the mind, it is already far removed from the images of the phantasy. Therefore, the phantasy will never bind our mind to itself, because the species cannot exist in both [the mind and the phantasy] at the same time. The act of understanding is indeed in the mind alone; this no one denies.

But the mind is accustomed to understand that of which it holds the species and likeness within itself. Therefore, from this very fact—that the mind receives the species (through which it is to understand something) from the images of the phantasy—it in no way follows that the phantasy understands anything. Rather, it follows that the phantasy itself, or its images, or its objects, are being understood. Therefore, whoever claims to join the mind with the phantasy, professing to constitute one single "understanding thing" out of these two, achieves nothing more than trying to make a single "understanding thing" out of the thinker and the thing understood outside of the mind. This is just as if one were to make a single "seer" out of the sight and the thing seen.

Unless, perhaps, someone wishes to argue as follows: just as from the heating fire and the air heated by it, one "heater" is made when the ignited air heats a hand; so too from the understanding mind and the phantasy—either understood or somehow agitated through the intelligence—one single act of understanding is produced again, by which both understand the thing positioned outside the phantasy. If that were to happen, then that sublime and separate mind would have communicated its intellectual power to the phantasy, just as fire communicates heat to the air before the external act of heating. Indeed, even more so. Because the act of understanding is always enclosed within the intellect. Nor does it migrate outside; thus, nothing can be handed over by the 

intelligence without the mind. And in this way, the mind would be within the human body as its **form** <note>The 'form' is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is; Ficino is arguing that the mind must be the actual form of the body, not a separate entity.</note>; which is what we are currently investigating. 

Nevertheless, that connection cannot happen. Because intelligence is not completed through a physical instrument. Finally, to prove that intelligence is common to that entire "heap" <note>The 'heap' refers to the composite of body, senses, and soul.</note>, they bring forward another connection: that when the phantasy conceives some image of things, that same image is immediately received in the mind; in the phantasy it is called a "phantasm" and appears particular and multiple, but in the mind it is called an **intelligible species** and appears entirely absolute and one. 

Since it is, however, one and the same form—because it forms the mind and the phantasy simultaneously—it is established that one composite exists from both, which is called **man**. Because the act of intelligence follows the intelligible species, and the species is the form of the composite, intelligence is properly assigned to the composite.

They show an example of this connection in the eye. In the eye, there is the **visual spirit** <note>original: "spiritus visivus"; a medieval physiological concept of a subtle fluid that travels through the nerves to enable sight.</note>. Light, colored by the image of a color, works its way into the visual spirit. And the spirit, in turn, penetrates the light. Where the image of the color—which is in the light—shines exactly the same in the spirit. Therefore, from light and spirit, it makes one thing. 

But we will deny that it can happen that the exact same form is received simultaneously in an eternal subject and in a corruptible one. For all forms have modes of being as diverse as the subjects by which they are received. Therefore, the form will have a far different existence in the mind than in the phantasy. Where there are two existences, and very different ones, there will also be two and very different forms, which are the principles of being. Nay, even if we were to grant that the form is the same in both, even so, intelligence would not be common. Indeed, intelligence is only there where the proper and intrinsic principles of understanding are. These are two: the **intellectual power** and the **intelligible species** in an entirely absolute mode. In the phantasy, however, there is neither the intellectual power, nor the absolute mode of the intelligible species. Nothing

He contends that because the mind deals with universal truths and the imagination with particular images, they remain distinct, using an analogy of the eye's visual spirit to illustrate his point.</summary>

# Platonic

Therefore, that knot <note>Ficino refers to the "knot" or bond that links the mind to the body via the imagination, discussed on the previous page.</note> serves this purpose: that man may understand. Just as the image of a color—even if it is the same in the light and in the spirit—does not cause either the light or the composite of light and spirit to see. For only that **visual spirit** <term>spiritus visiuus</term> <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, this was a subtle substance thought to travel from the brain to the eyes to enable sight.</note> sees, in which alone exists both the power of seeing and the image of the color according to the mode of the senses. Nor should they further object to us that the composite <note>The human being as a combination of body and soul.</note> understands for the reason that the **phantasy** <note>The faculty of imagination.</note> offers to the intellect whatever it is about to understand. For in a similar way, a certain animal is constituted from light and spirit, which one might call a "seeing animal," and the whole will be said to see because the light offers to the spirit what it may see. Let the followers of Averroes <term>Auerroici</term> <note>Followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), who famously argued that all humans share one single, eternal Intellect, rather than having individual souls that think.</note> finally come to their senses and agree with their own Aristotle. 

<margin>A</margin> That by which something exercises its own proper action is its own proper form and the producer of its species. Truly, the proper action of man is **intelligence** (understanding), through which he differs in his operation from the actions of brute animals. And therefore, through the intellect—as if through the intimate form of the species—he differs in his being from the souls of irrational creatures. Does not Aristotle show from this 
<margin>B</margin> that the soul is a **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is; the soul is the "form" of the body.</note>, because through it the animal lives and feels? But it does not understand except through the intellect. Therefore, in that question where he investigated the principle by which we understand, he finally handed down the nature of the mind, saying: "The intellectual part of the soul is that by which we understand." He does not use the plural number; he shows it is not some separate thing, but that we, properly speaking, understand. And in the human soul itself, he places both the **active** and the **capable** (passive) intellect. In the second book 
<margin>C</margin> *On the Soul*, he says this definition is common to every soul: "The soul is the act of a physical, organic body having life in potentiality." <note>original: "Anima est actus corporis physici: organici: potentia vitam habentis."</note> Or: "The soul is the principle of living, sensing, moving according to place, and understanding." Again: "The soul is that by which we first live, and by which we feel and understand." From these two descriptions, he concludes the first as if through a **syllogism** <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>. Since, however, a syllogism ought not to be made from equivocal terms, it follows that the word **act** <note>original: "actus"</note> signifies the same thing everywhere: that is, the natural act of the body, which he himself immediately reveals when he adds the division

# Book

of substance into matter and its form, and that which is composed of them. And he says that every soul is that form which is the other part of the composite. Again, where there is the power of understanding, there are also the powers of sensing and nourishing. And just as a triangle is within a quadrangle, so the **vegetative soul** <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic biological growth and nutrition.</note> is in the **sensitive** <note>The part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement.</note>. And these are in the **intellectual soul**. And although he says the power of understanding is "separated"—that is, distinguished—and is separable from others as the eternal is from the fleeting, he nevertheless says further: the intellect is distinguished from the others either by its "subject" (as the ancients thought, who seemed to attribute reason to the head, anger to the breast, and lust to the liver), or it is distinguished rather by a certain "reason," just as the concave is distinguished from the convex on the same surface. Furthermore, he praises those above others who judge the soul of man to be indeed incorporeal, but still "something of the body"—that is, such an act in such a certain subject. Hence, in the third book *On the Soul*, he says: "Since the intellect is not separated from the body, it will have to be examined elsewhere whether it can understand forms separated from the body." Most evidently, however, in the second book of *The Physics* <note>original: "libro naturaliū secundo"</note> he opens this up, where he wishes the soul of man to be a **natural form**. And it is both separated from matter and joined to it: he says it is joined because it is the "goal of human generation." Truly, I judge it is called "separated" on account of intelligence. But these things can be rightly understood neither regarding a "thought-centered" soul nor regarding a single, universal mind. 

<margin>D</margin> Also, in the twelfth book of *Metaphysics* <note>original: "de diuinis"</note>, where he denies that forms precede their matter, but follow after matter, he concedes only that form which is the intellectual soul; he clearly declares our soul to be the form of the body. It begins with the body, yet does not end with it. Nor can those words be understood regarding the Averroistic mind, which would be numbered among "moving causes" rather than "formal causes," and which precedes the human body. Nor is it joined to our body from the very moment of birth. This is against that order which Aristotle uses in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, where he applies the intellect to us from our very origin, even if it comes from without.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino uses Aristotle’s definitions of the soul as the "form of the body" to argue that the intellect is an individual, internal part of each human being, rather than a single universal entity as the Averroists claimed. He emphasizes that just as the soul provides life and sensation, it also provides the individual capacity for thought from the moment of birth.</summary>

# Theology Book XV.
# 151

...descending. **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle and his successor at the Lyceum.</note> also and **Themistius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> confess that from the beginning the intellect is joined to us and is implanted in our soul. But if one reads in Aristotle that whatever is born will be subject to corruption, this pertains nothing to the soul, which is not born through motion but created in a moment. <margin>E</margin> Nor does everything that began according to Aristotle become corruptible, provided that its nature is such that it may be preserved forever by the power of God, because it proceeded from God without an intermediary; this entire view was discovered by **Pythagoras** and approved by **Plato**. If the generation of humans were eternal, there would now exist an innumerable multitude of souls, provided they are in the same species. Truly, species cannot be infinite. However, some **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> indicate that those things which are both spiritual and of the same species can be innumerable from the fact that innumerable images are produced in the air from color and light. There are, however, some philosophers who think that the generation of humans has not always existed. I pass over for now that Pythagorean "generation"—namely, the eternal and certain number of souls changing bodies <note>A reference to metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls.</note>.

### Third Reason: Because man moves himself freely.
### ->Chapter VIII<-

<margin>G</margin> The **Platonists** and all the **Peripatetics** agree that man moves himself and that human actions are so arranged that the man himself who acts is the master of his own operations. To act rationally is to act in a certain way by reasoning before one executes the act. First, one accepts a universal rule. Second, one joins to it a particular opinion. Third, one draws a conclusion in this manner: *Every good thing is to be chosen. That food is good. Therefore, that food is to be chosen.* The first part of this kind of argumentation belongs to the mind alone. The second can also belong to the **phantasy** <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that processes sensory images and "particular" (specific) information.</note>. And the third likewise. And just as the universal rule for judging the good is in the mind alone, so in the mind alone is the universal will for desiring the good. In the phantasy there can only be a particular opinion and a particular desire.

When they affirm that man moves himself freely, they do not mean only the mind—in which "to move" is to act rather than to be moved. Nor do they mean only the animal <note>The physical, biological aspect of a human.</note>—in which "to be moved" is to be compelled to work rather than to be led freely—but they mean both together. Now, if both together produce a certain species and one human person, the mind will be the life-giving **form** <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> of the body. Otherwise, there will be found nowhere anything that freely moves itself; instead, a certain mind close to the animal would compel the animal to motion, just as a force applied to a stone by a thrower drives the stone upward. And thus the name of "liberty" would be a fiction, just as the "person" of a man would be a fiction. 

<margin>D</margin> Moreover, if we assume a single mind for all—as **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century philosopher who argued that all humans share one single, collective Intellect.</note> wants—whatever you answer to these questions will be either absurd or perhaps suitable to us, but not at all to Averroes. For if that mind moves us by nature, it will certainly move us continuously and uniformly, just as an intelligence moves the heavens. For they apply that mind to us just as they apply intelligences to the heavens—either by will, or it will compel us through that will, and thus we will never be free. There will be nothing in the order of things that is moved freely or by persuasion. If this is admitted, you might ask in what way "I"—namely, the cogitative animal—perceive that persuasion, which I cannot reach except through the intelligence. And thus it will appear that the intelligence is my own property. 

Especially since it is necessary, if I am moved freely, that it be the same substance that persuades and moves, and the same that is persuaded and moved. Otherwise, the name of liberty will be empty. But let us proceed again toward the same point by a different path. Since we have found that this living body is moved by the mind very often—especially in those operations which, with preceding counsel, lead in the most ordered ways to a rational end—we ask whether the mind moves through a natural joining of its substance to the substance of the body, or only through command. It does not seem to do this through command alone. Because it would do this in no other way than by persuading or by instructing the phantasy...

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul must be the individual "form" of the body to account for human free will, refuting the Averroist idea of a single shared intellect. He uses the logic of rational choice (syllogism) to show how the mind interacts with the body's imagination to produce free action.</summary>

Having previously argued for the individuality of the human soul against the Averroist view of a single collective intellect, Ficino here focuses on the soul’s internal unity—arguing that the higher mind (intellect) and the lower functions (like sensation and movement) are parts of a single substance, which allows for free will and immediate control over the body.</meta>

...so that it may move the very members of the body. And it will indeed move them, provided they consent. Yet now, time and again, the intellect drives the body against the inclination of the <term>phantasy<note>The faculty of imagination or the ability to form mental images from sensory data.</note></term> and the feeling of the senses, even while the appetite of the senses resists. Therefore, it moves the limbs through a certain natural union of its substance, and by its very being rather than by a mere command. Furthermore, if the mind frequently halts or moves the limbs against the leaning of the phantasy—without the phantasy being persuaded at all—and does this from within and in the same order in which the phantasy is accustomed to move them, who does not see that that <term>cogitative soul<note>In medieval and Renaissance psychology, the 'virtus cogitativa' was often seen as a specific faculty that processed individual intentions; Ficino argues here that it isn't a separate soul, but a function of the single mind.</note></term> then ceases from its work and is superfluous? For the mind usurps its functions. But does the mind move after the manner of a **natural form**? Certainly, for nature is the internal principle of motion and rest. And since the mind produces external motion in the limbs, it can much more easily produce internal motion in the <term>humors<note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow and black bile) believed to regulate health and personality.</note></term>, which are more easily stirred. By stirring the humors, it will temper their qualities for the works of nutrition. Again, how much more easily can it vibrate the <term>spirit<note>In this context, "spirit" refers to 'pneuma'—a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note></term>, which is moved by even the lightest breeze? As an internal leader, the mind will temper the spirit and exercise the senses within that spirit. Why then do we need twin souls—one intellectual and one cogitative—when one is sufficient? The mind is no less able to both understand and feel than the cogitative power is to feel and nourish; indeed, the mind can even nourish, since even the <term>vegetative power<note>The lowest level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note></term> can not only nourish, but also carry out the motions and actions of the elements. There is surely in us a certain power which weighs **being** itself—or "the existent"—and reason itself, and a certain perception of what is sensible or insensible; it can, at its own judgment, compare any intelligible thing to any sensible thing—indeed, individual and all intelligible things to individual and all sensible things. From this it follows that this same power 

<margin>jupiter ☌</margin> knows all these things. Since the senses do not reach insensible things, nor perceive anything more general than the entire genus of sensible things, and the phantasy knows nothing beyond them, that power alone will be the **mind**. Therefore, in the substance of the mind, there will be a power that discerns all sensible things, just as there is in the phantasy. This could certainly be called an "excellent phantasy" or an **intellectual sense**. Where there is a power of sensing, let there also be an act of sensing, provided the spirit is not lacking—in which either the passions of the body are expressed or the images of qualities shine forth. Moreover, a lucid spirit is subject to the mind, sufficient for the duty of sensing. Therefore, that "excellent phantasy" which resides in the substance of the mind thinks when infused into the spirit of the brain, and sees when infused into the spirit of the eyes, while it pours out many powers from a single source. Indeed, if in the view of **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued that humans share a single "Active Intellect." Ficino is using Averroes' own logic to refute him.</note> the corporeal phantasy offers service to the intellectual substance for the act of understanding, why should the spirit not also serve the same substance of the mind in our view—joining the corporeal phantasy to it—to carry out the act of that phantasy which joins with the intelligence? And if the earthly members of the body receive motion from the mind and transmit it to the outside, what stands in the way of the fiery spirits—illuminated by the presence of the mind—offering the occurring images of bodies to the mind's phantasy? For this reason, the power of understanding, sensing, and nourishing is located in the same substance of the mind. In this substance also consists the entire power of acting and moving freely. For when we are 

<margin>B</margin> about to do something through **reason**, that "reasoning" <note>original: "ratiocinatio"</note> which we described above necessarily precedes within us. If this reasoning were scattered through many substances—as if through different people—it would not result in action. For it is necessary to reduce every effect to one principal cause, in which the entire faculty and reason for acting is gathered. But the "reason" of human action consists in that process of reasoning. Therefore, the whole of it is concluded within the nature of the mind. This nature will indeed be a sufficient principle for human action, both because the entire reasoning is in it, and because the members of the body obey it alone. The eye, the tongue, the hands, the feet—they perceive and follow nearly every nod of the mind so easily, so quickly, and so constantly that it is incredible to think the mind is not their own proper form and familiar ruler.

### Fourth Reason: Because the powers of the soul hinder and move each other alternately.
### ->Chapter VI<-

<margin>C</margin> **A**s often as a single thing having different powers of acting is too intently [occupied] in the act of one...

<summary>Ficino argues for the functional unity of the human soul, asserting that the mind (intellect) is the single source of reason, sensation, and even physical nourishment. He concludes that the body’s immediate obedience to the mind proves the mind is the body's direct, individual ruler, refuting the idea of a shared universal intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the *Platonic Theology*. On the preceding page, Ficino argued that the mind (intellect) must be naturally united with the body because it can directly command physical movement. Here, he expands this argument to show that all psychological functions—from basic nutrition to high-level contemplation—must belong to a single, unified soul because they compete for the same "energy" and influence one another's states.</meta>

# Theology XV.

...[the soul] almost ceases from the act of one power due to the act of another. This is why diners can scarcely listen intently to the <term>lyre<note>A stringed instrument; here used as a general example of intellectual/aesthetic focus.</note></term> and taste their feast at the same time. If the most intense tasting did not hinder the hearing, we would affirm these two powers to be not of one substance, but of two different substances. However, the most intense acts of **nourishing** and **sensing** hinder the human **intelligence**, and the intelligence hinders them. This signifies that the intellect is a power of that very same soul of ours to which the power of nourishing and sensing belongs.

The followers of <term>Averroes<note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century philosopher whose followers argued that the higher human intellect was a single, universal entity shared by all humans, rather than part of each individual soul. Ficino is arguing against this.</note></term> will respond to this by saying that sensation and **phantasy** are two powers of our soul, and for that reason they hinder one another. They claim that the act of the mind is weakened when the act of phantasy is relaxed due to an excessive focus on the senses—not because the mind is in the same soul as the phantasy or the senses, but because the mind needs the service of the phantasy to create and perceive **images** <note>original: "species"; in this context, the mental forms or representations used in thinking.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> Yet, it does not belong to the Averroists to say that the phantasy is relaxed because of the focus of the senses, for they think that phantasy is a motion produced by the senses. Nor is it likely that the phantasy is much weakened by the effort of nourishing; nevertheless, let us set aside nutrition and sensation for now.

¶ Let us instead consider the **phantasy** and the **mind**. I certainly explore this within myself: when the phantasy is too intent, human intelligence or reason is relaxed, and vice versa. Indeed, the mind or reason is mostly idle when the phantasy is too busy—even if it is a healthy and sober phantasy—and likewise in reverse. Just as the sense, even if it is healthy, distracts the phantasy when it is more attentively occupied with external things, and vice versa. 

Again, in those who are **dreaming, drunk, angry, in love, insane,** or **frenzied**, when the phantasy rolls its images around with the soul's entire attention, is not all judgment of the human mind or reason put to sleep?

¶ When, however, in those who are **contemplating**, reason fixes its burning gaze on considering divine things, does not the phantasy fall completely silent? And if it interrupts at all, it is immediately commanded by reason to be still. Nor is it permitted to be carried away too much by affections, or to wander more widely through its accustomed labyrinths. Who, then, will deny that the mind and phantasy are powers of the same soul, since they weaken each other by their respective intensity?

Furthermore, let us grant the Averroists that there is as much alternation of motion between the mind and the phantasy as there is between the <term>common sense<note>The 'sensus communis', a faculty theorized to sit in the brain and unify the data from the five individual senses.</note></term> and the particular senses. Just as the image of a thing shining in the eye then reflects into the common sense, and similarly the act of seeing overflows from the eye into the common sense, so too do both the likenesses and the acts continually reflect from the phantasy into the mind.

¶ Although, it seems to me that there is a greater alternation between the mind and the phantasy than between the internal and external sense. For from the mind into the phantasy, both likenesses and acts reverberate. But how that might happen from the internal and common sense back into the eye, I do not clearly see, nor do they explain it themselves. If they should claim that this sometimes happens in dreamers, so be it.

I shall find yet another thing in which the alternation of the former exceeds the alternation of the latter. For between the mind and the phantasy, there is a mutual exchange not only of **images** and **acts**, but also of **affections** and **habits**. This never happens between the one [the eye] and the other [the common sense].

¶ Since, therefore, the mind has a much greater kinship and a more indissoluble bond with the phantasy than the common sense has with another sense—and yet both this sense and that are in the same soul—why are not the mind and phantasy also in the same soul? Why is the eternal mind almost always affected toward the temporal phantasy to such an extent that it obeys it and flatters it? And when the phantasy grieves or rejoices, why does the mind grieve and rejoice with it (so to speak), unless a foundation of the same nature and substance underlies both?

¶ Since the finite power of phantasy often accompanies the somewhat infinite power of the mind in its acting—so that as far as the mind speculates, so far does the phantasy itself think—unless the same substance made them equal? There is never a sudden, easy, and complete exchange of qualities between any two things unless a common matter underlies them. For this reason, neither would the intellect ever so easily become **phantastic** [driven by images], nor would the phantasy turn out to be **intellectual**. Neither would the former sometimes be made irrational, nor the latter rational, unless a common subject lay beneath both.

<summary>Ficino argues that the mind and imagination (phantasy) must be part of the same individual soul because they compete for energy and mirror each other's emotional states. He uses the interference between eating, sensing, and thinking to prove that these faculties share a single underlying substance.</summary>

# Platonic Book
<margin>A</margin>
¶ For just as one wheel moves another because they both rely on the same **machine**, so too those two appetites—namely, the **rational** and the **irrational**—move each other in turn very easily, as much by impulse as by judgment, because they exist in the same substance of the soul. Hence that <term>Aristotelian<note>Referring to Aristotle, the Greek philosopher whose works on the soul were foundational to medieval and Renaissance thought.</note></term> saying in the third book of *On the Soul*:

¶ "Just as a sphere moves a sphere, so desire moves the will." <note>original: "Quemadmodum sphera mouet sphera: sic concupiscentia voluntatem."</note> But desire cannot move the will unless it were either like a superior sphere pulling an inferior one—which no one would ever say—or a sphere connected to the same mechanism to which the mind is also joined.

¶ **The fifth reason.** Because the separated mind does not need <term>phantasy<note>The faculty of the soul that creates and stores mental images (phantasms) based on sensory data.</note></term>.

## Chapter 10.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ According to <term>Averroes<note>Ibn Rushd, a medieval Islamic philosopher who argued that the higher intellect was a single, eternal substance shared by all humans, rather than a personal faculty.</note></term>, the nature of the mind does not share a common existence with the body, nor does it communicate its own existence to the body. It does not take its origin from the body, neither in its essence nor in its preparation for existence. It does not form any single species with the body, nor is it numbered according to the number of bodies. Therefore, just as it has a way of being entirely separated from this "animal" state, so it will have a mode of cognition that is entirely segregated from the body. Consequently, there is no reason why it should be forced to draw its forms from the images of the phantasy, or why it should require a temporal and mobile process of reasoning to reach the knowledge of things, especially **eternal things**. Indeed, the mind will be most similar to the **supernal minds** <note>Angelic or divine intellects.</note> and much closer to them than to the qualities of bodies. Therefore, it will understand those higher beings and their ways even more than it understands these physical things. This, however, contradicts the leader of the Averroists, Aristotle, who writes that this mind understands nothing without <term>images<note>original: "simulacris"; the mental representations used by the intellect to process sensory information.</note></term>. Yet these images belong to bodies, not to minds. But since the primary and familiar objects of the human intellect are the common natures of natural things—principles that are indeed joined to bodies but are separable from them—it is possible for us to argue from the proportion of the power to its object that the human intellect is such that it is both joined to the body and able to be separated from it. And because it is joined, it almost always turns itself toward images. Indeed, because it is joined, it turns to things that are joined. And because it is joined in a **separable way**, it turns to them in a separable way—that is, by abstracting and separating them. However, those minds which are not only separable but are actually **separated** behold things both in a separated manner and as separated entities.

¶ Hence, to speak briefly: nothing seems to me to better demonstrate that the nature of the human mind is a **mean** <note>A middle point or bridge between two worlds.</note> than its natural inclination toward both directions. For whether through the intellect it begins from bodies, it soon transfers itself from there to incorporeal things; or if it occasionally begins in incorporeal things, it slides back in turn to the images of bodies. Whether through the **will** it chooses eternal things, it is meanwhile deflected by an affection for temporal things; or on the contrary, if it desires temporal things, it is often restrained in turn by a reverence for the eternal. But let us now return to the Averroistic question.

<margin>C</margin>
The Averroists will respond that this intellect indeed understands supernal minds without the images of the phantasy, but it does not understand the natures of bodies in that way. To this we shall reply: In those supernal minds, there are **incorporeal forms** of bodies, through which they judge of bodies. Therefore, if our intellect understands those minds, it receives the knowledge of bodies from them. There is, then, no need for it to receive that knowledge from bodies. Furthermore, they assert that this intellect is the lowest in its own self-subsistence, but it is attached to us. Insofar as it subsists in itself, it is compared to the higher minds as a transparent or glassy body is compared to light, and it perceives them. Insofar as it adheres to us, it draws its forms from images and understands corporeal things. To this we will say, first of all, that it is superfluous for an intellect that always gazes upon bodies in the **causes of bodies** <note>The divine or higher principles that create physical things.</note> to also see the same things in images. And it is redundant for that which it possesses in eternity to be borrowed daily from time. Furthermore, it does not receive forms from images *because* it adheres to us; rather, it adheres to us *because* it captures them from here.

<margin>D</margin>
For as Averroes thinks, the intellect is joined to us only because it is formed by the species received from us. Therefore, the intellect must be considered as being prepared first, through a certain power, to receive these kinds of forms, before it adheres to us. It is not, therefore, through its adherence to us that it is [prepared] for these kinds of... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind acts as a middle ground between the physical and spiritual worlds, capable of moving between temporal images and eternal truths. He rejects the Averroist view that the intellect is a separate entity, arguing instead that its ability to process both sensory images and divine forms proves its unique, dual nature.</summary>
