# Theology

...prepared species of this kind: unless perhaps he <note>Referring to Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> thinks that it clings to us insofar as nature looks to proximity—that is, that the nature of that intellect is close to our soul by some degree. If it is so, nothing further follows than that a mind of this kind moves and forms our soul. For a more worthy degree, when it approaches a lower one, does not receive from it, but bestows upon it. The sphere of the moon moves the sphere of fire; it is not moved by it. <margin>Etc.</margin> Why then does this mind borrow knowledge from the soul rather than lend it? Indeed, if it is superior and as much more excellent as Averroes thinks, it ought to be wise solely through itself, while the soul is wise through it. Especially since this mind is joined to the body in the same way as the celestial mind is to the heaven, as Averroes wants. Therefore, just as that one takes nothing from the heaven, so this one takes nothing from the body. Nor should the Averroists object to us that, just as the celestial body is full of its own forms, so its mind is full of its own, but our mind always receives new forms, just as our body continually varies its own forms.

This objection achieves nothing. Indeed, that action of a craftsman takes its manner from the instruments which is performed through instruments, such as cutting and the like. But that which remains in the mind of the craftsman alone, such as the deliberation for arranging the work, does not take its manner from the instruments. Therefore, it is not fitting to give a manner of understanding from the body itself, through which understanding is not fulfilled. We shall next ask Averroes: whether the mind, while it understands in us, becomes more perfect, or more imperfect, or neither. If neither, this perpetual agitation will be in vain, profiting nothing by its operation. In fact, it will not even operate, for there is no motion toward an indifferent end. If more perfect, it will depend on things that are not eternal. <margin>E</margin> That which is imperfect will always be perfected by that which is more perfect. Especially since they do not want it to be moved and formed by our <term>phantasy<note>The faculty that produces mental images from sensory data.</note></term> any differently than a mirror is by a body. But if it becomes more imperfect, how does it always move toward the imperfect? By what appetite does it assiduously strive toward a defect?

---

And what is weaker, by what force does it always infect that which is more excellent? Does not Averroes himself, where he disputes about separated minds, say that since they know eternal things through their own essence, they know no temporal things? Otherwise, as he says himself, and to use his own word, they would **become cheapened** <note>original: "vilescerent"</note>. If this is so, it follows that, according to Averroes' opinion, temporal knowledge brings a defect where knowledge is eternal. Since therefore the human intellect (as he himself asserts) always knows eternal things, not only is it said in vain to understand temporal things—since it would not emerge more perfect from this—but it would even become more imperfect. I certainly judge that that mind, the observer of eternal things in us, would be more imperfect for this reason: because here it is always mocked by false images and disturbed by cares. And I judge this intelligence of its to be superfluous in the nature of things, because it contributes nothing, nor is it instituted for the sake of any end.

What does it bestow of its own upon ours? Does the human soul have a particular power of reasoning by its own nature, through which it instructs that mind, as Averroes thinks? <margin>f</margin> On the contrary, it often mocks and disturbs it. But the soul has no universal discourse from itself, nor does it receive it from the mind. For the particular and mortal soul is not capable of universal and eternal reasons. For if it received them, it would certainly understand, and it would be an intellect, and it would be everlasting. Therefore, a <term>link<note>original: "copula"—the union between the human soul and the separate Intellect.</note></term> of this kind confers nothing upon our souls, unless perhaps you think the presence of a mind is useful to us because it drags us against our nature, unwillingly, and entangles us in false fables, while it deprives us of the pleasantness of present goods by a deceptive hope for divine ones. But neither is it of use to the mind, as we have said. Since the mind is divine, it is not to be referred to this human being as if to an end—a human being, I say, who is separated from its being. Again, since through its essence it sees the supernal causes of things, in which all middle causes and any effects are contained, and therefore it perceives all corporal things through those causes, it needs none of our phantasms or senses to discern corporal things. Especially because there is within it, according to Averroes, that **agent intellect**, which, since it is in eternal act, through which...

He concludes that such a connection would be useless or even harmful to both the human soul and the divine intellect.</summary>

# Book of Platonic Philosophy

nature can provide an intelligible <note>Something that can be understood by the mind, as opposed to "sensible" things perceived by the senses.</note> quality to individual sensible things; it can do even more: it can fill a pure and capable intellect with that same intellectual splendor. And in that intellect, it can both offer the species <note>The mental "forms" or concepts of things.</note> of heavenly things that are innate to its capacity, and then, through its own most effective power, derive those universal species into particular concepts. For if it can fashion universals from contingent particulars, it can also conceive any particulars from universals—whether they are innate or seen by divine light. This is especially true since the essence [of the soul] is capable of containing superior things. And it has always fulfilled this task from eternity. Nor, again, should it be said that the mind and the animal are joined because of a composite of both. For they are not joined in such a way that one true thing is actually made from the two of them. Nor is it fitting to refer true parts to a false whole as if to an end. Perhaps they will say that this bond contributes to the beauty and ornament of the world. But I do not think the world is adorned by this superfluous fiction; rather, it is a monster, which has a single head; and that head, although it is divine, nevertheless like a chameleon changes colors according to the variety of objects. Furthermore, it has innumerable legs. The head remains. The legs are always cut off and sprout again. Nor shall we tolerate them if they say: this monster contributes to the connection of both superior and inferior things. For in what way will it connect the rest, when it is not only not one thing in itself, but does not even receive any connection from elsewhere? There must be one certain form in the world that binds the superior forms to the inferior ones. For it is the duty of form and unity to connect. And in that form it is necessary <margin>A</margin> that the properties of all forms meet, so that the superior forms are in a way relaxed and cast down to the inferior ones, while the inferior ones are intensified and raised up to the superior ones. But in that Averroistic monster, neither is one common form found, nor do the extremes migrate into each other; but while individuals keep what is their own, they remain scattered.

---

Finally, if they say that the intellect is everywhere beneath the moon, they place it in vain where there are never any humans, such as in the highest air, the unnavigable sea, and the uninhabitable land. For there, the intellect never achieves anything, nor does it move anything. The <margin>B</margin> Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> truly never designate divine minds to be anywhere except where they fittingly rule and move something. But if they say that it is only present where there are humans, two absurdities immediately follow. First: that the whole will be in two humans separated by a very long distance from each other, yet it will not be in the middle, which nature does not allow. Second: that as humans die, the intellect itself will also be moved. However, the Peripatetic sect is not accustomed to admit that such a substance—which is neither a body nor the specific form of a body—can be moved either by itself or by accident. Furthermore, what reason can explain why such a divine mind would follow a wandering little man—who very rarely uses his mind—everywhere like a servant? By natural necessity? But the mind is superior; and it seems to need the man neither for its being nor for its well-being. But it is not permitted to imagine it follows by violence or by counsel. Nor is it permitted to assert that it is moved when the man is moved because it is naturally adapted to the human species. For they do not adapt it to the human in any other way than they adapt the [celestial] mind to the heaven. Yet they do not think the celestial mind moves along with the heaven. Finally, if they say that the mind does not move when the man moves, they will be compelled to admit both that the mind sometimes lives far from the man, and the man far from the presence of the mind.

### ¶ The sixth reason. Because both intellects are powers in the soul. Chapter 11.

As for the fact that they affirm the active intellect and the capable [passive] intellect to be two distinct essences <margin>C</margin> from which the single identity of the intellectual soul is constituted: this is indeed superfluous and absurd. It is superfluous because one essence is sufficient if it is equipped with two powers, so that through one power it forms the species, and through the other it receives them. Just as the phantasy <note>The faculty of imagination or forming mental images.</note> draws certain intentions from images and receives those very things it has drawn. And the eye...

# Theology

...eyes of animals <note>original: "oculi animalium." The word "li" at the start of the page completes "oculi" from the preceding page.</note>: which see at night: in the same essence it possesses twin powers. ¶Through one, they draw out the image of colors. ¶Through the other, they receive them. Light itself also both creates and receives certain colors in the clouds or in water.

<margin>B</margin>
In what way, then, is a double power—both productive and receptive—founded in the same essence? Clearly from different principles or relations. Indeed, light, insofar as it comes from the sun, creates colors; insofar as it exists as if in itself outside the sun, it receives them. So also the soul, insofar as it is from God in most pure act <note>In philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to something being fully realized or active, whereas "potentiality" refers to the capacity to become something.</note>, is allotted the power to manufacture species <note>The mental forms or concepts of things.</note>. But insofar as it is in itself below God, it turns out to be passive, as it were, and is formed by receiving species. From this it follows that that Averroist fiction is superfluous. It is also absurd.

<margin>D</margin>
Because from two essences, both of which exist in act, a single substantial being is not constituted. For two acts of existing are two "beings," not one. That the "active intellect" <note>The part of the mind that processes sensory data into abstract thoughts.</note> is a certain substance in act for them, since it does something, is not in doubt, nor do we fight against it. But what they add—that the "receptive intellect" <note>The part of the mind that receives and stores knowledge.</note> is also another substance, and such that it is pure potentiality <term>potentiality</term> <note>Pure capacity or "possibility" to become something, without yet being it.</note>, no differently than prime matter <term>prime matter</term> <note>The basic, formless "stuff" of the universe before it takes any specific shape or identity.</note>—this we do not approve of. Otherwise, if the receptive mind were pure potentiality, it would not be distinguished from prime matter. And wherever matter existed, intelligence would exist, such that even stones themselves would think. It is indeed certain that prime matter is pure potentiality. But there cannot be more than one "pure potentiality" in nature, just as there is only one "pure act," and vice versa. For if all things said to be "in potentiality" are such through one common reason, and all those "in act" likewise, it is necessary to arrive at a single source of potentialities and a single source of acts. Again, if the primary and common distinction or composition in things is that which occurs through potentiality and act, and many things do not come from one except through a certain order of some to others—and similarly one does not come from many except through this kind of order, in which one is related to the other as potentiality to act—it follows that the multitude in things takes its origin from the very mixture of potentiality and act.

Thus it happens that neither pure act nor pure potentiality can be multiple. ¶Since neither potentiality (except through a mixture of act) nor act (except through a mixture of potentiality) enters into number <note>i.e., becomes a distinct, countable thing.</note>. From these things it is concluded that the mind cannot be pure potentiality. And if it is said that the mind is also a simple potentiality no less than matter is, and yet differs from it, we shall ask by what reason it differs from matter. Clearly not insofar as it is potentiality—both because they agree in this very thing, and because through potentiality confusion and chaos reign; distinction occurs through act. Something beyond potentiality will therefore be added to the mind, through which it differs from the potentiality of matter; and this will indeed be some act. And if this act is infused into the lap of the mind, it will cause the mind not to be pure potentiality, since it has an act mixed in. But if it hangs over it from the outside, it will not make the mind differ from the potentiality of matter (insofar as it is that potentiality) until, by acting through its own agreement in the mind, it grants some internal act to the mind, through which it may differ from pure potentiality insofar as it is potentiality. 

<margin>G</margin>
For such a discrepancy does not occur except through some act, insofar as it is an act. And so again the mind will not be pure potentiality. The Averroists will imagine that the mind differs from matter for this reason: because the mind regards <note>Refers to or is oriented toward.</note> a different act—namely <term>namely</term> <note>original: "f." (abbreviation for scilicet).</note>, the absolute and universal. Whereas matter regards another—namely, the concrete and particular. As if indeed those very "regards" were not themselves some kind of acts! For if the mind's regard is nothing other than the mind's potentiality itself, it will not provide a difference. But if it is something else, it will be an act. ¶Furthermore, if the mind and matter exist before they regard the forms they are to receive, and they regard them as they are in themselves, then surely they regard different acts because they are already different from each other—not the other way around. Nor should it be thought that the mind regards a more perfect act than matter itself regards, except for the reason that the mind is more perfect than matter. If this is so, it stands further away from nothingness and approaches more closely to the highest act <note>God, as the ultimate reality and "Pure Act."</note>, from which all perfection comes. Therefore, the mind is not merely potentiality. ¶Accordingly, if matter holds a middle place between act and nothingness: and that which in...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind cannot be "pure potentiality" like prime matter, because it possesses an active, divine-given power to create and process thoughts, which distinguishes it from the formless nature of physical matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s technical refutation of Averroism—a school of thought based on the philosopher Averroes which argued that the human intellect is a single, separate substance shared by all people. Ficino is arguing here that the human mind (mens) must have its own inherent "actuality" and cannot be mere "potentiality" like physical matter.</meta>

# Platonic Book

...considers <note>original: "infra eam considerat." The text likely continues from a discussion of levels of being below the mind.</note> below it: it is nowhere: because the act exists above it, or is itself in act. We ask where we should place the essence of the mind. Surely, if it is something, it will not be placed below matter. Or perhaps it should be placed in the same degree of perfection as matter? By no means. For it would then possess nothing more excellent than matter. 

Add to this that just as things which are equal in quantity are "one" in respect to that quantity, so things which are equal to each other in their level of perfection are "one" in perfection. Perfection resides in the form; the <term>species</term><note>The specific "kind" or "essence" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> exists through that form. Those things, therefore, which are one in perfection are one in form and one in species. From this it follows that two different species of things cannot be equally perfect as one another. 

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, the mind, which is a different species than matter, will not be located at the same level of perfection as matter. It must therefore be in a more excellent degree. If it is placed above matter, it will be an "act," or at least "in act" <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "act" (actus) refers to something being fully realized, active, or alive, whereas "potentiality" (potentia) refers to a raw capacity to be changed, like a block of marble that is "potentially" a statue.</note>. And it is much more "in act" than other natural forms, insofar as it is removed from matter by many degrees and is closer to the Divine Act. 

If it is "in act," and is not categorized among sensible <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> things, then it is certainly above the acts of sensible things; in the genus and species of <term>intelligibles</term><note>Things that can only be understood by the intellect, such as math, logic, or divine truths.</note>, it will have an intellectual act according to a specific species, or an intelligible one. Furthermore, in the genus of things, it will have a vital act by which it gives life to sensible things. 

But if someone were to say that the mind relates to intelligible forms in the same way that matter relates to sensible ones—this comparison might be true in some sense, but it does not force the essence of the mind to be entirely devoid of "act." 

Perhaps some <term>Averroist</term><note>A follower of the 12th-century philosopher Averroes, often criticized by Christian Platonists for denying the individual immortality of the soul.</note> will think he can escape the previous arguments if he concedes this: that the nature of "mere potentiality" is not restricted to a single point, but has a certain range in which it can be stronger or weaker, so that its natural perfection is more intense in the mind but weaker in matter. 

But he cannot escape this way either. 

<margin>B</margin>
For just as "pure act" is the highest act, so "mere potentiality" is the highest potentiality. Whatever holds the highest place in any category is fixed (so to speak) and has a limit beyond which that category does not extend; anything short of that limit is not yet the "highest," nor is it the mind.

Indeed, a quality does not fall away from the summit of its kind except through some mixture of an opposite kind. Furthermore, if the nature of potentiality is more "perfect" in the mind than in matter, then the mind is not "pure potentiality," because of that extra perfection added to it. If it is more perfect by its own nature, then that potentiality is more intense in the mind and weaker in matter. 

This must be true either in terms of "quantity" (having more of it) or "quality" (being better). If we say it has more potentiality, then matter would no longer be the "extreme" or lowest potentiality, since there would be something else with even more. If we say it is "better," then it will not be pure potentiality, because whatever is "better" participates more in the Highest Good. And the Highest Good is pure act. 

Since, therefore, the mind is not mere potentiality, there is in it not a "substantial" potentiality, but an "accidental" one. And because potentiality and act must agree with one another, the mind will be subject to an accidental act, but never a substantial one. Therefore, a third "substance" cannot be created from the mind's own substance and the act of the <term>active intellect</term><note>The "Active Intellect" was thought to be the "light" that allows the mind to turn sensory images into abstract thoughts.</note>. 

<margin>C</margin>
For potentiality "in a certain respect" (as the <term>metaphysicians</term><note>Philosophers who study the nature of reality beyond the physical world.</note> say) does not receive a simple act. 

<margin>D</margin>
The Aristotelians think that the "capable intellect" <note>The "Passive" or "Possible" intellect that receives information.</note> understands the universal reasons of natural things only when it has received their absolute and intelligible forms. But because these forms are not like that in themselves (being tied up in physical objects), and cannot become "actually intelligible" except through an intellectual nature and some efficient Active Intellect, they introduced a "creator of absolute forms." 

If this nature of the Active Intellect is actually a "status" or quality inherent in the same essence in which the innate capable power also exists, what need is there for that Averroistic heap of two separate substances? 

But if it is some other, more excellent substance that pours intellectual power through the substance of the capable mind all the way down to the images of the imagination (<term>phantasie</term>), and grants those images the power of intelligible forms—as the Averroists believe—it would much sooner and more greatly bestow that same power on the substance of the capable mind itself. That higher substance would bestow it in a stable way, and this mind-substance would receive it in a stable way, since both are eternal. Therefore, the very same substance, which [has] the capable power...

He concludes that the "Active Intellect" and "Passive Intellect" are two powers within the same individual substance, rather than separate substances as the Averroists claimed.</summary>

<margin>E</margin>
it will have both and be effective. Nor will there be a need for two separate substances for those two duties of the mind <note>The two duties are "receiving" information and "acting" upon it to produce thought.</note>. Hence the error of Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle who argued that the higher "agent" intellect was divine and external to individual humans.</note> is also refuted; he, through a forced interpretation of Aristotle, would take all divinity away from the human race. He asserted that minds in us are indeed "capable" <note>Potential or receptive.</note> and distinct in number, but that the "Agent Mind" <note>The <term>intellectus agens</term>: the active part of the intellect that makes thinking possible.</note> is outside of humans and is a single entity, in which alone the whole divinity of the mind resides. He claimed this was the universal cause of all intelligible species <note>The mental "blueprints" or concepts we use to understand the world.</note>. However, since in all natural things there are certain powers that produce their own movements, it is a sin to believe that the substance of the human mind—the most excellent of all natural things—is deprived of an effective power. And because an operation proceeds from a power, the universal mind does not grant our mind the act of understanding before it grants it the effective power of intelligence itself. Furthermore, if a universal cause is strictly opposed to a particular effect—namely, as a cause to an effect and as a universal to a particular—it is necessary to interpose a particular cause between these two as a middle ground. For example, the universal power of the sun does not produce *this* specific man (who is a particular effect) except through another man acting as a particular and proper cause. By the same reasoning, that universal agent mind will not produce this or that effect of a concept or an understanding in the "capable mind" without some particular agent mind that lives within us. For just as we use the "capable mind" at our own will for understanding, as if it were a familiar form, so too do we manufacture concepts through the effective mind as we please, as if by our own innate art. Skilfully, Aristotle 

<margin>F</margin>
never called the agent and capable minds "two essences," nor did he place them above the soul; rather, he called them parts of the soul and said they were two different powers within the soul. If anyone, however, calls the "Averroistic mind" the soul, he is abusing the word "soul." <note>Averroes (the 12th-century Islamic philosopher) argued there was only one "Intellect" for all of humanity; Ficino argues this contradicts the very definition of a personal soul.</note>

<margin>G</margin>
### ¶ Resolution of the Averroistic arguments concerning the separate mind. Chapter 12.

**F**rom all that has been brought against Averroes, we conclude two things. First: that the soul in man which gives shape to bodily things is the same soul that is shaped by incorporeal things. For only by this middle ground are the rays of divine things transmitted all the way to the lowest things—if that which is illuminated by the higher things also illuminates the lower. Indeed, by this same middle ground, the lowest things are reflected back to the sublime—if the same thing that rules the lowest 

<margin>H</margin>
is ruled by the highest. We also conclude the second point: that human minds are numbered according to the number of individual men, so that they are distinguished from each other either by species <note>As the Magi (ancient Persian sages) believed.</note> or certainly by number, as the later theologians assert. For as many as there are bodies of men, there are just as many vital complexes <note>The unique physical and spiritual makeup of a person.</note>. Just as many life-giving souls. Just as many minds of souls. For almost as complexes are distributed according to the distribution of bodies, and lives according to these complexes, so minds are distributed according to the number of souls to be given life—for minds are the powers of souls. This distinction of the incorporeal substance and power does not, however, arise from the distinction of the body as if from a cause, but proceeds from the incorporeal Creator himself. Those arguments of Averroes, with which he denied from the beginning of the question that the intellect is the "form" of the body, have no power against us. For they only prove that it is not a "bodily form" <note>A form that cannot exist without a body, like the shape of a piece of wax.</note> lacking its own being and depending on the body for its essence. We, however, do not wish it to be such a form, but rather one subsisting in its own being and ruling over matter. Furthermore, to repel certain little traps with which the Averroists strive to catch the Platonists: one must remember that it is not against the nature of the human soul to be joined to a body. Rather, it is natural for this everlasting soul to always be with an everlasting and celestial body, and to be with a temporal and earthly body for a time. Just as it is natural for any planet to always be in its own sphere, but for a time to be under this or that zodiac sign. After...

He concludes that human souls are as numerous as human bodies and are created by God to rule over matter.</summary>

# Platonic Book

[When the soul] has departed from the body: it is natural for it to be reconciled once again, so that it might remain separate from the body while still possessing a certain affection <note>In this context, "affection" refers to a natural inclination or attraction toward something.</note> for returning to that same body; just as a stone, even when placed up high, remains intact, yet in the meantime sinks toward lower things with all its might. And a planet, departing by its natural order, eventually returns to the same sign. 

<margin>A</margin> 
Indeed, the soul will one day return to the dwelling of the same body, lest that natural affection of the <term>wandering</term> <note>original: "vagi"</note> be in vain forever; the Egyptians agreed with the Platonists on this. Otherwise, something violent <note>Meaning "unnatural" or "forced."</note> would be eternal. ¶ The soul does not exist in itself through its own power but through the act of God; it exists in the body through the qualities of its <term>complexion</term> <note>In early medicine and philosophy, "complexion" refers to the specific physical balance of humors and qualities that make up an individual body.</note>. Since the act of God remains eternal while the complexion is dissolved, the soul ceases at some point to be in the body, yet it does not cease to exist in itself. It subsists in its own being after it has been separated from the body. It subsisted similarly while it was present in the body, though it did not communicate its being then in the same way it does now. Nor should it seem miraculous that the soul, which inhabits the body for a time, can remain separate from the body without decay, especially since the thing being moved depends more on the mover than vice versa. Now, the soul is the true mover, and the body is what is moved. Therefore, if certain bodies separated from the soul remain somewhat undecayed—such as bones, nails, nerves, and hair, which seem to endure for a very long time, as do wood and stones—

¶ and especially balsam, honey, and oil, which almost never rot—will not the soul, the governor of the body, be able by natural order to remain forever without 

<margin>B</margin> 
the corruptible body, remaining itself undecayed? ¶ This clearly shows that in the progression of this life, the soul is not corrupted by the decay of this or that body, since it remains the same throughout every age; it sheds old matter and puts on new, while the body is continually renewed through the "outflow" and "inflow" of matter. But let us proceed to the rest. ¶ When the soul approaches the body, a living creature is born through the generation of the bodily complexion and the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>The "vital spirit" was thought to be a subtle substance that acted as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>. ¶ When it departs, once the complexion is dissolved and the spirit is released, the living creature is dissolved. Nor is this creature born from some random event, but from the ordered convergence of all natural causes; and in the same way, it dissolves. 

¶ However, <term>Plotinus</term> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated and championed.</note> proves that this evil of dissolution does not pertain to souls, because the soul did not mix itself with the body. Instead, remaining within itself, it created a single irrational animal beneath it—not out of itself and the body, but out of the body and a certain "vital image" <note>original: "simulacro"</note> of its own. But he shall see to that himself. Whether the soul approaches matter through the mediation of "quantity" <note>Physical dimensions or extension.</note>, it is not necessarily extended, just as a surface on a deep body does not become deep, nor a line in a wide space become wide, nor a point in a long space become long; nor does the meaning of a word or the image of a color become vast when in the vast air. 

<margin>C</margin> 
¶ For matter itself, rather than the soul, requires quantity. Or if the soul precedes quantity, it is by no means subject to quantity when it arrives. Indeed, since the reception of qualities happens through potentiality and not through act, quantity is received in the matter, not in the soul. ¶ I say quantity is at first indeterminate because of the infinity of the matter itself. Then, it is determined toward a certain figure because of the presence of the soul, which certainly provides the beginnings of a specific form. No one doubts that matter, by a certain natural order, precedes quantity. Natural causes, because they are subject to place and time, act locally and temporally. Thus they complete their work bit by bit—one part at one time, and one part in one place after another. Therefore, a work of this kind cannot be completed anywhere except in extended matter. 

But God, because He surpasses all division of both place and time, acts in an entirely indivisible manner and can grant an individual form to matter itself, at the very stage where matter precedes quantity. Just as with other forms, a determined quantity may accompany this form, residing not in the soul, but in the matter. Let there be a single common form of the whole in a human, which is the chief form—

<margin>D</margin> 
<gloss>that is, the rational soul.</gloss> 
Let there also be, as many people believe, many particular forms of the parts that are distinct in kind and obedient to the soul: the forms of the flesh, the bone, the nerve, and the rest. From these, a certain composite is made, which becomes the subject of the bodily figure, of division, and of suffering. Let the soul be present to the figured body...

# **Theology**

[The soul] is not shaped. Indeed, it is clear from this that the soul itself is not the subject of such a shape: because such a shape of the body precedes the soul and outlives it. When Light is questioned concerning the being of the whole, some respond: that through the substantial being of the soul itself, the substantial being of the whole is formed. This results from the joining of parts. For they say that the being of the soul is that by which the being of the whole exists, and by which the soul itself exists in its own right. 

And this soul is not fixed in the foot when it is at rest, but it stays in the hand when it is moved; it moves, and yet perhaps it is not moved. For just as in a physical body the soul does not "undergo" place <note>To "undergo place" means to be physically contained or limited by a specific location.</note>, but is present above place and within place; so in the movement of another body, it does not undergo the movement, but is in a certain way immovably present within the motion. And if it runs with running minds, it runs by transferring others, not by being transferred itself. Therefore, when the hand is moved at the same time the foot is resting, the soul—which is whole in both—is not forced to move entirely and rest entirely at once. 

But let the soul be moved in the hand, if you like. <term>Duns Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Medieval scholastic philosopher.</note> responds: What compels it to rest in the foot meanwhile? Can it not be moved in the foot while you yourself are moved? Although, just as it is not impossible for the same whole man to be moved by contrary motions at once—while he is carried by a ship toward the rising sun, yet meanwhile is pushed toward the west by another, or runs himself within the ship—so it would not be absurd, according to <term>Thomas Aquinas</term>, for the soul to be at rest and in motion simultaneously in different parts, according to the state or motion of the other. 

The whole soul is in the arm; it is whole in the hand. If the hand is amputated, the soul is not cut off; it does not remain in the air, nor does it condense itself into the remaining arm, nor does it flee in time. For all these "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to physical modifications or things that happen to matter.</note> belong to bodies. Instead, the soul, which previously gave life to both the arm and the hand, now gives life to the arm alone. It ceases to be where it was, not through movement, but in a moment it ceases to work where it used to work. 

Just as if a small portion of air is broken in the west, and the light vanishes—which is whole in the east, as <term>Plotinus</term> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism, who often used light as an analogy for spiritual presence.</note> maintains, and whole in the west—it is not broken along with that portion in which it was whole. Instead, it ceases to illuminate the portion it previously illuminated; it does not condense into itself by a temporal flow, just as it had not extended itself from east to west by a temporal flow of thinning itself out. For in a moment it had made itself present; in a moment it makes itself absent. 

If the soul is whole everywhere throughout the body, and it alone understands, then it understands everywhere. Yet it does not understand in any specific member, because it is not *in* the members, but rather the members are *in* the soul. Yet it seems to the common people that it understands in the brain, because the <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "phantasia". The faculty of imagination that processes sensory images before they reach the intellect.</note> very much accompanies intelligence. 

This imagination, in turn, is accompanied by the agitation of those <term>spirits</term> <note>In medieval physiology, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried life and thought through the body.</note> which are in the brain; the affections of the imagination accompany the agitation of the spirits which are in the heart or liver. The spirits of the heart follow the affection of anger. The spirits of the liver follow the affection of lust. 

If anyone asks what it is that feels or understands, the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> will answer, but in different ways. For they will say that feeling is an act of the "composite" <note>The human being viewed as a single unit composed of both physical matter and spiritual soul.</note>: first, that the power of feeling is in the composite itself, made of matter and form mixed with the soul. Then, they say it is also an act of the soul, since the sense is produced by its power. 

They also say intelligence is an action of the whole composite. Although intelligence exists in the soul alone—and thus can remain in a separated soul—nevertheless, while the soul is the "form" of the composite in such a way that it concurs in a single common being, that whole (to which that being belongs) is said to operate through the form, just as it is said to exist. 

This is the aim of that <term>Aristotelian</term> saying: "The intellect is the act of no organ." And rightly so. For it is not in the body like a sense, but in the soul. Nor, as <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> thought, should it be considered separate from the human being, but rather separate from the organ. Nor, again, should it be explained in the manner of <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (fl. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>—as if individual senses were allotted individual instruments, while the whole body becomes the instrument of the intellect itself. For we see that the most noble powers do not use just any instrument, but only the most noble. Thus touch uses almost anything [any part of the body]. The imagination uses a single and distinct one. Therefore, the entire body will not suffice for the mind. Nor is it the case that a single harmony is produced from the conspiracy of all instruments to be used by the intellect as an instrument. For if it were so...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul and the intellect, transitioning from how the soul inhabits the body to a specific refutation of the theory that all humans share a single mind.</meta>

Platonic Book

If the case were otherwise: the intellect would need all instruments: and it would be the most organic and mixed of all powers. Furthermore, that <term>Aristotelian</term> principle would no longer stand. <note>Referring to Aristotle's "De Anima," where he distinguishes the physical senses from the immaterial intellect.</note> Sense, indeed, is not without the body: but the intellect is separate: and unmixed: using no organ whatsoever. For if it used organs, it would turn out to be this or that kind of thing: and it would no longer be able to know all things. Nevertheless, it is not so separate that it does not vivify the substance of the soul in which the body exists. Otherwise, they would not say that a human being understands. For it is separate because it is not in the composite <note>The "composite" is the human being as a union of body and soul.</note> as the sense is, but in the substance of the soul itself, which is separable from the composite. Nor does it use an instrument in the act of understanding. This is indeed what he confirmed in the book *On Animals and on Sound and Vigilance*, <note>original: "de animalium & ſono & vigilia"; Ficino is likely conflating or referring to Aristotle’s works "History of Animals" and "On Sleep and Waking."</note> saying: Those things which have actions, have also the powers of acting. Since, however, sensing happens through an instrument, but understanding does not, for that reason the power of sensing belongs to the composite, while the power of understanding can be the soul’s own property.

### Solution of the Averroistic arguments concerning the
### single mind. Chapter 3.

<margin>a</margin>
**W**e have already solved the arguments of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Andalusian philosopher who famously argued that there is only one shared "Active Intellect" for all humanity.</note> and the Averroists, by which they thought it could be demonstrated that the substance of the mind cannot be the vital form of the body. Let us now solve those arguments by which Averroes attempts to show that there is only one mind. He says that the number <note>In this context, "number" refers to the plurality or multiplicity of individuals within a species.</note> of forms under the same species comes from matter. But the mind lacks matter. Although this is the opinion of certain <term>Peripatetics</term>, <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>
<margin>B</margin>
nevertheless, the majority of the <term>Pythagoreans</term> and **Platonists** think that the nature of a species is poured into many individuals not because of external matter, but because of certain modes innate to the form itself. Once the form is brought into act through these modes, it turns out to be this or that individual. For they say that in any angel, the angelic species is drawn down to the angelic individual without the mixture of matter. But so that we may follow for the present partly the Peripatetics and partly some of the Platonists, we will perhaps concede that the number of forms comes either from matter, or on account of matter, or rather on account of the composite of matter and form. Indeed, just as corporal forms draw their essence in a certain way from matter, so too they draw their number placed under the same species. But forms that are not corporal, yet are "of the body"—such as rational souls—since they do not have their origin from matter, they do not have their number from it either. Because Divine Providence established them not only for the contemplation of divinity, but also for the governance of bodies, just as He willed the number of various bodies (that is, of composite humans) to be fixed for the adornment of His work, so He ordains a fixed number of souls. But to speak as <term>Plotinus</term> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> does:
<margin>E {</margin>
What then distinguishes the soul of **Plato** from the soul of **Socrates**? It is that Divine Concept: which first tempered the vivifying power of the Platonic soul for a certain "garment" <note>Neoplatonists often referred to the lower parts of the soul or the subtle body as a "garment" (indumentum).</note> of the celestial bodies, and through this, accommodated it for the generation and rule of a specific temperament of the elemental body. So too He did for the soul of Socrates toward its own specific things. Thus, He distinguished the vivifying powers of souls on account of matter; or rather, on account of the composite for the sake of the world’s adornment. But He distinguished the intellectual powers of these same souls for the sake of the distinction of the souls themselves. But for what reason? On account of one or another gaze upon divinity.
<margin>{ </margin>
We are able to enjoy the Divine Mind under various ideas. We can track it through various footprints. We can progress toward this end by various paths. Surely Infinite Goodness willed to communicate itself in infinite ways (so to speak) not only to bodily eyes, but also to spiritual eyes; and to show the innumerable countenances of itself to almost innumerable eyes. And so He tempered the intellectual eyes and affections of various souls in different ways: so that by a different path we might set out toward the different possessions of the manifold divine goods.
<margin>D 2 {</margin>
**Proclus**, <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher who systematized Platonic thought.</note> following the mind of **Plato** who says in the *Timaeus* that God assigned the souls of men to different leaders and stars, proves that the differences of souls do not come from bodies or from inclinations toward bodies, but from that essential assignment made by God to different leaders and stars. From this, the difference of inclinations and actions also arises, both toward eternal life...

Theology 15.

<margin>to be given: as much for governing temporal things.</margin>
Furthermore, as <term>Duns Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) was a major Franciscan medieval philosopher who argued for the "haecceity" or individual "thisness" of things.</note> and his followers argue: Every nature except for the first—which alone is pure act—possesses a certain potentiality that is in some way formless in itself and capable of receiving form from elsewhere. This potentiality relates to many singular modes of existence just as matter relates equally to many forms. Therefore, just as with the human species or the horse species, so too <margin>.</margin> can any intellectual species—whether of angels or of souls—be derived into many individuals. Moreover, the number of minds within the same species contributes to the complete fulfillment of the order of the universe. Indeed, that order is full in which the higher things are ordered toward the lower, and these back toward those in turn, and equal things are likewise ordered among themselves. We clearly perceive an order of this kind in <margin>Z</margin> corporeal things. But if incorporeal <margin>7</margin> things have a fuller order, we are compelled to think of a similar, triple order within them as well. Now, there cannot be any order among equals unless many individuals are contained under the same species. Furthermore, a number of many minds in the same species leads to their more perfect happiness. For they <margin>a</margin> congratulate themselves, as they—so to speak—rush into one another through a mutual and equal recognition and familiarity, as naturally tends to happen. Finally, the universe is far more beautiful if there is a multitude everywhere below the species, just as there is above the species. Above, certainly, in a generic and specific variety; but below, adorned with a certain numerical variety. Nor do they think the number of angels leads only to this: that the species itself is preserved. For even in bodies, there are everywhere far more individuals than are necessary for the preservation of the species. Furthermore, <margin>E</margin> we see that nature in individual species does many things not entirely for the sake of survival, but for the sake of ornament. We see this manifested in colors, shapes, features, and in a most highly ordered arrangement. Finally, the principal end for which God wants all things to exist is not properly that they simply *exist*, but rather that they exist *well* and are in a good state. And if they exist primarily for this reason—whatever they may be—they certainly exist for the same reason, however many they may be. For this reason, God did not want there to be many minds in the same species simply so that the species itself might exist and be preserved, but rather so that it might exist well and be in the best state. Indeed, a blessed state of this kind consists in an ornament that is everywhere diverse and in an action that is everywhere varied in its modes. But if anyone should argue that the multitude of human souls contributes to the health of the species, we will grant it in this way: namely, that such a number is necessary not properly for the species of the soul itself, but for preserving the species of the "composite" <note>The "composite" refers to the human being as a union of body and soul.</note> human being. <margin>h.</margin> For God wants there to be many men perhaps because the human species is not preserved in a single individual. However, many men cannot be made unless there are also many souls. The number of souls seems to serve not so much the number of bodies or of composites, but the order of the whole universe. Nor should anyone think that souls differ among themselves solely because they regard different bodies. For they are first different in themselves before they regard the body with a different <margin>and 12. m</margin> rationale. These are their arguments. Let us now return to the proposal. As for what <term>Averroes</term> <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued that all humans share one single, eternal intellect.</note> adds: "if my intellect and yours differ in number, the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental image or intelligible form of a thing being studied.</note> of things to be known will similarly differ and will be particular. Yet it is necessary that the things to be understood be one." This is solved as follows. It is not so much singularity that is opposed to understanding, but the collection of bodily accidents. Indeed, individual intellects and their individual conceptions can be understood most conveniently. Add to this that just as the image of a color in the eye is not that which is properly seen, but that *through which* the color itself is seen, so the species and likeness of things in the mind is not that which is properly understood, but that *through which* the universal reasons <note>original: "rationes rerum vniuersales"; the underlying logic or definitions of things.</note> of things are understood. Nor is that species in the mind so singular that it prevents the use of the understanding of reasons. For if a statue, which is singular and corporeal, represents to us in some way the common figure of men, how much more so does that species represent a common nature? Since it exists in the mind, which is released from all bodily passions. Therefore, the species itself is free from them. Thus it represents to us a thing not enclosed in a certain place.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ nor in time. ¶ **It is necessary to remember** that this order in the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciebus." In this context, "species" refers to the mental forms or "concepts" that the mind uses to understand the world.</note> is established by many: that in angels they are universal, both in how they relate to things and in how they exist; in brute animals, they are particular in both ways. In human souls, they are singular in how they exist, because they exist within entirely singular essences. They are, however, universal in how they relate to things, because they exist in essences that are free from the limits of matter. But let those thinkers see to this themselves. Furthermore, he <note>Averroes</note> brought up something regarding the knowledge that a master hands down to a disciple, which is easily solved by what we have discussed elsewhere regarding <term>innate species</term> <note>Ideas that are born within the soul rather than learned from the outside.</note>.

<margin>, ,</margin>
But indeed, that argument of <term>Averroes</term> <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" theory—that all humans share one single, eternal intellect—Ficino is refuting here.</note> is easily turned back against him. Surely, if the knowledge of the teacher does not pass into the student, nor does it generate another knowledge in him, one of two things follows: Namely, that the same intellect which is in both possesses the same <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitum." In medieval philosophy, a "habit" is a stable quality or learned skill, like knowing geometry.</note> in both; or, from the habit which it possesses in one person, it generates another habit in the other person within itself. Neither can happen according to Averroes. Not the first, because since that "single mind" of his would daily master all the arts in all men, and since some would be teaching others in a perpetual succession of teachers and students, it would follow that the habits of all sciences would always be exactly the same in that mind—which Averroes clearly rejects.

Nor does the second follow, because then knowledge would be an "efficacious quality" <note>An active force that produces effects.</note>. He denies this, and furthermore, innumerable qualities similar to one another in species would exist in the same subject at the same time, which he would also by no means admit. For if anyone does not see how far such a fortuitous and superfluous heap of qualities is from the purpose of nature—especially in a substance that is eternal and divine—he is himself straying from the purpose of nature.

<margin>Aver.</margin>
Finally, Averroes reasoned: If there were two singular species in two singular minds, it would be possible to reduce them to a universal one. Then each mind would reduce them to its own. And in each mind, again, each species would turn out to be particular. Therefore, it would be possible to collect both again into another without end <note>This is a "reductio ad absurdum" argument where Averroes claims that having multiple minds leads to an infinite, impossible chain of logic.</note>. That is indeed a vain argument. First, because the gaze of the mind is clearly stirred by the species, but it does not stop at the species as if it must look at it as the final object; rather, through the species, it looks at the universal <term>reason</term> of the thing. Two minds behold this reason as one and the same, and they do so through two species. Just as the eyes of two men see the same thing through two distinct images of it. Therefore, minds do not intend to reduce their species to other species, but to see the reasons of things through them. Even if some did intend this, they would not proceed to infinity. Since these species have universal power and meaning, it is not necessary to always resolve them into other, more common ones as if they were merely singular things.

<margin>B</margin>
But let them proceed without end, if you like. For what prevents the mind, which possesses a somewhat infinite power, from wandering without end, provided it never actually completes this infinite course? A similar argument can be made regarding notions and concepts, and the response is very much the same.

<page-num>82</page-num>

[The mind] does not need matter to act: since it is able to work from within and from internal things. Therefore, since there is in the <term>agent</term><note>The "Agent Intellect" in medieval philosophy is the active power of the mind that makes abstract thought possible.</note> a power that is both effective and sufficiently prepared for understanding, the joining of a "receptive capacity" to a single mind to create a substance out of two parts is superfluous. But suppose it is so: let the receptive power be joined to the agent. This power, linked to the agent within the mind, would recognize both eternal and temporal things. Nor would knowledge in the universal mind be redundant on the part of this receptive capacity, provided it were not lacking in the other. Furthermore, this receptive power, formed by human <term>simulacra</term><note>Latin: *simulacra*. These are mental images or "phantasms" derived from the senses which the mind uses to form concepts.</note> in us, knows temporal things which it already knew in the agent. From this it follows that this third type of knowledge is likewise superfluous. If the power of seeing, through some "agent sense" joined to it, always saw individual things, it would be said in vain that the eye lacks the power by which it might be moved and formed by external things. Just as a redundancy arises in these three types of knowledge from the words of <term>Averroes</term><note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century philosopher whose "monopsychism" theory claimed all humans share one single, eternal intellect.</note>, so it arises in the three ways they are formed. If the receptive intellect is formed by the agent once through its essence (as he thinks), it is superfluous for it to be formed again continually through the images of all men at once; it is also superfluous for it to be formed daily through the images of wise and happy men. All these redundancies follow from the sayings of Averroes, which we have reviewed from the beginning. This clearly shows us that his opinion ought to be rejected as useless. Therefore, let him boast that he has discovered a "divine mind" which, while it is wise in itself, is always raving <note>original: "delirat"</note> in us. And since every day innumerable men consider the same thing and often fail, that mind considers the same thing a thousand times and a thousand times over at every single moment—and is often deceived. If the mind itself never notices this redundancy and the fallacy cast upon it by these fantasies, it is forever ignorant of itself. We experience the opposite in ourselves whenever we refute our own errors. If it does notice them, yet does not turn its attention away from these ambiguities when it could, it is always weak and always lacking self-control. But 

---

the eternal mind can forever turn its sharp gaze away from the trifles of temporal fantasies. Indeed, the temporal soul often withdraws itself for a time from the trifles of the senses. Nor can an affection for individual things (which are below humans) delay that mind in those errors and turmoils; that mind is not even so affected toward human nature that it would conspire with it to manufacture a <term>species</term><note>An "intelligible species" is the mental form or concept of a thing.</note>. In what way, therefore, will it concur with this "animal" in its innermost operations, unless it first joins with it in its very being? For even the form of fire communicates the heating itself to external matter—which is an external operation—even if it has not communicated its own being. However, "to be hot" through itself—which is an internal operation—it communicates only after it has communicated its being.

# Theology

They are in act, not just in <term>habit</term><note>Latin: *habitus*. A "habit" in this philosophical sense is a permanent disposition or an acquired capacity that allows a person to perform an action easily, like knowing a language even when not speaking it.</note>. If the <term>species</term><note>In Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, a "species" is the mental form or conceptual "blueprint" of a thing that exists in the mind.</note> remain in the interior sense for a long time—proceeding into action even if they are not actively being preserved—and are triggered by the exterior senses, how much more must these forms remain in the mind without the need for <term>simulacra</term><note>Latin: *simulacra*. These are "shadow-images" or sensory phantasms derived from the physical world.</note>? The mind should not be compared to the exterior senses, which lose forms once the physical objects are absent. For those senses do not possess true forms, but only images; nor do they possess the power within themselves to manufacture those images.

<margin>C</margin>
The mind, however, possesses "true reasons" (rational principles) through which it comprehends the true substances of things. And it fashions these for itself. Therefore, it is able to preserve them by the same power with which it fashioned them. But if the mental forms depended on sensory images in the same way that shadows depend on bodies, they would have nothing in themselves more excellent than the images themselves. If there were something more sublime in them, it would be the gift of the "agent power," by which they would be preserved even when the images are removed. Furthermore, the fact that they do not emerge from images like shadows is proven by the way they are rooted so deeply as to imprint a completely indelible habit. Nor should it be said that these forms have a meager essence because they refer to something beyond themselves, or that they always require the foundation of sensory images as their preserver. First, because they contain and reflect more, better, and more essential qualities of things than the images do; therefore, they possess a nobler and fuller essence. If anyone should belittle the concept of a "genus" <note>A general category or classification.</note> because of its perceived confusion or definition, or the concepts of individual things because of their "shadowy" nature, we would easily disagree. Plato commands us to honor these <term>species</term>. For in them rests the perfection of the world and the truth of science. Individual things are related to these forms as parts are to a whole, and even as a thing is related to its goal. Furthermore, even if they required a preserver because of their dependent condition, it is the <term>agent intellect</term><note>The active power of the human mind that "lights up" sensory data to turn it into abstract thought.</note> that will preserve them most of all, since they derive their nature from it. Nor do we believe this form needs sensory images simply because it signifies a nature existing in individual things. For if it signifies nature as something absolute, it regards the thing apart from individuals rather than within them—namely, the eternal reason of things which has its essence in the Divine Mind. Secondly, it exists through "middle participations" in the minds that follow God. Finally, it exists according to a certain final likeness in physical bodies. Warned by the images of these bodies, the intellect—which is an absolute participant in divinity—immediately either conceives the form or recognizes the Idea within itself once more. Thus, by the very condition of the form, it is clear that it is not some utterly unstable shadow of an image, but a certain excellent and stable nature. We can guess the same thing from the nature of the mind. Certainly, wax and dust preserve the shapes of things for a time, even after the
<margin>D</margin>
objects themselves depart. The brain also (as <term>Averroes</term><note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life.</note> believes) guards the images of bodies when those bodies are absent. But the mind itself, which is stable because of its eternity and stands above motion—will it not, by its own nature, receive forms stably and above motion? Will it not eternally preserve what it has received into its eternal womb? Is not the intellect a power superior to sense? And therefore more unified? For this reason, the intellect alone
<margin>E</margin>
can do all the things that the multiple powers of the senses accomplish. Just as the <term>phantasia</term><note>The "imagination" or the faculty that processes sensory data into mental images.</note> alone knows whatever the five senses perceive because it is superior to them, so the intellect alone will both judge the forms and preserve them.

<margin>F</margin>
Perhaps judging the images and preserving them is not the duty of the imagination alone (as Averroes thinks), but judging belongs to the imagination while preserving belongs to memory. These two duties are distinguished in those lower powers.

<margin>G</margin>
But they must be joined in the mind, even though according to the Platonists, the imagination also possesses its own memory. This is proven by the strengthening of habits and the free wandering from one image to another, which often happens through the effort of recollection. That the mind is "mindful" (possesses memory) is shown by the fact that when we first learn something, we apply ourselves with great difficulty and effort. But after long use of thought, we meditate most promptly at our own will upon those things we once received, as if they had now become our own and were stored deep in the mind. After our mind has once formed within itself certain definitions...

Having previously argued that the mind preserves information differently than the physical senses, he now focuses on how the mind holds onto abstract concepts (species) and dispositions (habits) through its own internal light, rather than relying on sensory images (simulacra).</meta>

# Platonic Theology
# Book IX

of rare things: whether of numbers, or of virtues, or of angels, which succeed each other in order; [the mind] can hardly recall the first without taking up the second and the third. Just as in the beginning, when it first found them, it could barely weave them together; so when it happens upon them again, it can barely unravel what it had previously woven. And it returns from some <term>species</term><note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental "forms" or "blueprints" of things—the conceptual essence of an object held in the mind.</note> to others much more easily and quickly than the interior sense is accustomed to doing, even though the sense itself returns to previous images by remembering them step by step.

This clearly declares that memory exists in the mind much more than in the sense. If anyone should say that the mind does not preserve the formed species and definitions themselves, but rather the <term>habit</term><note>Latin: *habitus*. A philosophical term for a stable disposition or an acquired capacity that allows one to act or think in a certain way without effort.</note> of reforming them, we will respond that the power of the mind is the same: it both contracts and preserves the habit (which is now almost converted into its very nature) 
<margin>B</margin>
and draws the species into its innermost self and preserves it. Indeed, the habit is founded upon the species, and the species are contained within the habit. Therefore, if the habit comes from the mind, the species, and the act, it must obtain its stability from one of these, and not from the mind alone. Otherwise, the mind could also attribute stability to the *act*—but it does not, for the act has no stability. It must therefore come from the species. Thus, the species remains stable. Nor is it necessary, whenever we look at the same thing, to receive new forms from the "agent" power while the previous ones suddenly vanish. This is true as long as that "agent power" has delivered the forms according to its nature, just as the "receptive power" has received them according to its own. 

The nature of both [the agent and the receiver] precedes the mobility of bodies. New images are rightly always being recreated in the sight, because they are created by an external light. In the mind, however, the species remain by that same internal light which, having first flowed out from the mind, illuminates them firmly. This is especially true because if they were created from that light, and because the nature of the thing to be known is separate from the passions of changeable matter, they rightly remain immobile. Thus, the substance of the mind becomes a completely stable transition into an <term>accident</term><note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature (like the color of a shirt compared to the shirt itself).</note>—the intelligence itself is inherently unstable, but it is made stable through an accident, namely, the species. Where substance is always "in act," the species migrates from act into habit, and vice versa. 

Intelligence [can go] from absence into non-existence, and vice versa. Nor do the species need <term>simulacra</term><note>Latin: *simulacra*. These are sensory images or "shadows" of physical objects produced by the imagination.</note> in order to be preserved. Indeed, while they [the opponents] admit the existence of <term>phantasms</term><note>Phantasms are mental images derived from sensory experience, stored in the imagination.</note>, and although we may need specific images to understand the common natures of bodies, we nevertheless do not use specific images to contemplate divine forms; rather, we use the natures themselves, which the images merely accompany. 

Here it is apparent: the notions of divine things in the mind do not come from images that flow in by accident, but are preserved by the mind itself, having already been prepared through previous speculation. Furthermore, we are connecting that Platonic series of Ideas in which we place certain "middle" species before the "final" species, and again sub-alternate <term>genera</term><note>Plural of "genus," referring to broad categories or classes of things.</note> above those, until we ascend through many steps to the widest categories. Let us also transcend the genera, arriving at that nature which encompasses all categories from the outside; then, surely, we are compelled to leave images behind, as they wander only among the final species. Those images cannot accompany that ascent, unless perhaps we were to arrange a universal order within each individual image. That, indeed, cannot truly happen. And if it is imagined, it is not imagined by the <term>phantasia</term><note>The "phantasia" or "imagination" is the faculty that deals specifically with sensory images.</note>, but by the mind. The mind sometimes renovates notions beyond notions, and if it pleases, into the infinite—but it does not renovate images in this way. Nor does anything prevent that which pertains to the mental nature from flying forth forever, naked of images. 

Sometimes, as the mind resolves narrower things into broader ones, it paints images in the imagination that correspond in some way to the species. In this case, the species themselves—because they come first—create and preserve the images, not the other way around. We perceive that the imagination is formed by the mind because many things suddenly shine within it that it had never received from the senses nor even thought out. The mind also divides and composes images, not without a certain logic. It progresses toward infinity in its imagining; indeed, it is imagined by the mind without end. It also receives rational habits and durations. The imagination is formed by the mind much more than it forms the mind. For if it ever forms the mind, it does so only by means of the senses, and...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind possesses its own internal light and memory, allowing it to preserve abstract "species" and "habits" independently of physical sensory images. He describes an intellectual ascent where the mind leaves behind sensory "simulacra" to reach higher, more universal divine truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is arguing against the Averroist concept of the "Universal Intellect," asserting instead that the human mind has its own internal power to generate and store knowledge independently of the physical body and its senses.</meta>

# Theology
# Book XV

...struck by the power of the mind. Nor can it [the imagination] deliver forms without number. However, the Mind fashions the imagination from within itself and does so without end. Sometimes, without its own emotion—or rather, by a certain divine inspiration—it can be provoked to understand without the need for <term>simulacra</term><note>Original: "simulacris." These are mental "idols" or images derived from sensory experience. Ficino argues the mind can function without them.</note>. This signifies what we have often sought: that even while present in the body, the mind sometimes operates without the body’s help. Consequently, when it departs from the body, it will operate much more effectively by itself. 

If the <term>Averroists</term><note>Followers of the philosopher Averroes, who argued for a single, shared human intellect. Ficino strongly opposes this, defending individual immortality.</note> argue here that those who possess a particular bodily <term>complexion</term><note>Latin: "complexionem." In medieval medicine, this refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) which determines temperament.</note> tend to excel more in intelligence and memory—on the grounds that intellectual notions continually depend on the senses—we can respond in the <term>Peripatetic</term><note>The school of Aristotle. Ficino uses Aristotelian logic to counter the Averroists.</note> fashion. 

<margin>B</margin>
A specific bodily condition serves the senses by its very nature, but it serves the mind only incidentally. This is because, while the mind is joined to the body, it fashions its own <term>species</term><note>Mental forms or conceptual essences.</note> out of sensory images in a certain way; and as often as it turns toward its own species—which it has created and preserved itself—it almost always turns back toward those images. I say "turns back" partly because of a certain kinship between them, and partly because of a habit formed by the soul's condition of being joined to the body. And although we see sharpness and memory daily in every type of temperament—from which we are forced to admit these come from a higher principle—it nevertheless happens that a "dry" nature (for example) is more capable of memory. 

<margin>C</margin>
Dryness is the cause of memory in the sense-organs by its own nature, but in the mind only incidentally. This is not only because the memory of the sense itself serves the mind in a way, as we said, but also because the dryness of the <term>spirits</term><note>The "pneuma" or subtle vapors that were thought to carry signals through the nerves.</note>, by contracting toward the interior, does not hinder the soul from recollecting itself. Thus, through intense and constant thought, the intellect is sharpened and memory is strengthened. 

<margin>D</margin>
Humidity, however, does the opposite. 

To these points, the Platonists would say there are as many armies of souls as there are stars, and that they take their nature and names from them. Hence, souls are called "Saturnian," "Jovian," "Martial," "Solar," and so on. They receive various gifts regarding sharpness, memory, will, character, arts, and fortune from these sources. All these gifts are good insofar as they come from there, even though they often degenerate here due to a confluence of multiple causes. Furthermore, souls receive spiritual gifts from the souls and deities of their own stars—who both lead and follow them. From the physical bodies of the stars, however, they receive bodily and sensory gifts. 

Therefore, if Saturnian or Mercurial human souls obtain aids for sharpness and memory from that source, they simultaneously receive a specific condition in the body from the physical bodies of those same stars. This condition is not the *cause* of the intellectual gift, but its companion. Finally, a great excellence of sharpness and memory arrives mostly from the intensity of the will and constant attention. 

<margin>But let us not...</margin>
But I must not digress further here. To what end is all this? It is so that we may reject that <term>Averroist</term> opinion which asserts that the absolute forms of the divine mind depend upon the bodily images of temporal imagination, just as shadows depend upon physical bodies. 

Let us rather place our faith in Plato, who says that what has truly been understood can never be committed to total oblivion; instead, the hope of the thing grasped is transformed in the eternal mind into a perpetual <term>habit</term><note>A stable state of knowledge or being.</note>. For it has no contrary whose approach might destroy it. Nor does it ever abandon its subject. 

<margin>Averroes</margin>
Therefore, if the Averroist mind were said to draw out the forms of all things at every moment through the imaginations of all men, from which it understands all things—and if this mind lacks a beginning and human generation has always existed—then surely all forms and habits would have existed not once, but countless times, thousands of years before us. Indeed, it never received the first forms from anyone, if there was never a "first" thinking human. Thus, it did not fashion its forms through anyone’s mental images; rather, its forms are itself, or come from its very essence. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle would not have conceded this. But [the mind] received the forms, and has long since received them all. Moreover, it preserves whatever it receives immovably, provided it receives them intellectually—that is, according to an intellectual reason. If it acquired these things individually long ago, and is infinite and full of all things and overflowing, why does it seek further? What does it want for itself?

<summary>Ficino argues that the human mind operates independently of the body and critiqued the Averroist view that human thought is merely a shadow of a single universal intellect. He also integrates Neoplatonic astrology, suggesting that intellectual traits like memory and sharpness are spiritual gifts aligned with specific stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is in the middle of a sustained polemic against the "Unitary Intellect" of Averroes—the idea that there is only one mind for all of humanity. He is currently arguing that if the mind were truly a single, external entity, our individual experiences of learning and thinking would be impossible to explain.</meta>
