B
<meta>Catchword: one:</meta>

<margin>Gold:</margin>
...is this reception of forms endless and redundant? For if the mind receives nothing from us, then the mind understands nothing in us. Perhaps <term>Averroes</term><note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was an Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle led to the theory that all humans share a single, eternal "active intellect." Ficino considers this a threat to the idea of the individual soul's immortality.</note> will respond: if the mind already possesses the <term>species</term><note>Latin: "speciem." In medieval philosophy, a species is a mental "form" or concept that represents an object (like gold) in the mind.</note> of a certain thing—for instance, gold—it does not receive a *new* species of gold from my <term>imagination</term><note>Latin: "phantasia." The faculty that processes sensory images before they are understood by the intellect.</note> when I think about it. Instead, that very species of gold, which was in a sense "sleeping" in the mind so far as I am concerned, "wakes up" because of the mental image of gold I am currently picturing. Thus, the mind looks toward my imagination and understands "gold" within me, just as it previously understood it within someone else. If this were the case, the active intellect would no longer create any species, nor would the potential intellect receive any, since all species would have been possessed for a long time. 

<margin>through</margin>
This, however, is repugnant to Averroes and his followers, who want new species to be created and received every day. It is also repugnant to the <term>Peripatetic</term><note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle. They famously described the mind at birth as a "blank slate" (tabula rasa) upon which experience writes.</note> school, which is accustomed to the idea that the intellect is like a **blank tablet** upon which nothing is written. Averroes, in defending his opinion, will never be able to explain this except in an inept and ridiculous way. For us <note>The Platonists.</note>, however, this is not dissonant; following the lead of **Plato**, we believe the intellect does not have to generate a new species of "man" every time the imagination presents us with different images of different men. Instead, a concept previously conceived is simply "awakened." Just as the imagination of **Socrates** does not fashion a new image of **Alcibiades** every time he sees Alcibiades walking toward him on the same day; rather, the image lying hidden within is brought into action. The eyes would do the same, if only they could preserve images.

### Third Argument: Because whenever two people understand the same thing, absolute absurdities follow. Chapter 17.

¶ My imagination is currently thinking of gold. Yours is also thinking of gold. If the Mind of Averroes, excited by our mental images, gives birth to a <term>species</term> of gold within itself and understands "gold," we must ask: does it now hold one single species and one single act of understanding gold for both of us? Or a pair of species and a pair of acts of understanding? Or perhaps one species but two acts? Or vice-versa? Many followers of Averroes follow the first part of this division. 

---

But they are refuted by reason. If the diversity of our individual mental images creates no diversity in the Mind, then they prattle too rashly when they assert that the Mind understands gold "in me" and "in you"—or rather, that "I" and "you" understand gold. For in that case, only the Mind itself would understand, and it would do so within itself while we are merely thinking. This would be like **Xenocrates**<note>A student of Plato and head of the Academy. Ficino uses him here as a model of the "objective observer."</note> seeing the common and consistent truth within himself while listening to **Speusippus** and **Polemon**<note>Other members of the early Platonic Academy who often disagreed on terminology.</note> as they dissent from one another in a dispute out of ignorance. Furthermore, if the Mind understands gold through the same act of understanding in me and in you, then as soon as it stops considering gold in your case, it must also stop considering it in mine. Yet we experience the opposite. 

The Averroists will deny that this follows. They say that just as in our bodies the same soul gives life to the arm and the hand, and if the hand is cut off, it stops giving life to that part but not to the arm; so too the Mind, ceasing its work on your mental image, continues to consider mine alone, though it previously considered both together. This example is not suitable. The act of giving life "passes into" the physical body. The act of understanding, however, does not "descend" into the mental images. Therefore, in two different limbs, two different acts of living are received. But in the one Mind, the act of understanding remains one. 

This example would be more fitting: just as a soul lived through one life in both limbs and then, afterward, lives in one limb through that same life; so the Mind considered gold in both of us through the same act of understanding, through which it later looks at gold only in one of us. But even this example is not quite right. For we can correctly say that living happens "here" and "there" <note>In different parts of the body.</note>. However, we cannot say that understanding happens "here" or "there," since understanding is separated from physical location. 

Again, consider the eye: with a single glance, it sees both the right and left sides of a small surface simultaneously. If the left side is removed, that very same glance which saw both remains entirely intact, but it is now limited to the one side, whereas before it was limited to both. In this same way, the Averroists claim the same act of understanding looks at the mental image...

<summary>Ficino argues against the Averroist theory of a single shared human intellect by pointing out the logical absurdities of shared thoughts and the Aristotelian "blank slate." He uses Platonic "recollection" (innate ideas) to explain how the mind recognizes concepts without needing to create them from scratch every time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book XV of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is refuting the Averroistic theory of the "Unity of the Intellect"—the claim that all of humanity shares a single, collective mind. Here, he argues that a single mind cannot hold contradictory judgments (like loving and hating the same piece of gold) at the exact same moment.</meta>

# Theology

one: <note>Continuing from the previous page: "how could the mind be one if it looked at two things at once?"</note> he who had looked at two things? In that respect also the argument is dissonant. ¶ First, because the eye does not properly "cease to see" while its vision remains intact; rather, it is that part of the surface which is <term>refracted</term><note>Latin: "frangitur." In this optical context, Ficino refers to the way light or sight is broken or interrupted by a surface.</note> that ceases to be seen. But suppose the eye does cease to see. What then? Is that gaze directed toward specific local parts of a surface, so that it can be said with reason that it sees both "here" and "there"? And therefore, perhaps, it might sometimes cease to see here, but not there. <term>Understanding</term><note>Latin: "intelligentia."</note> however, does not stretch itself toward localized <term>images</term><note>Latin: "simulacra." These are the mental pictures or "phantasms" derived from the senses.</note>, but toward a <term>rational principle</term><note>Latin: "rationem." The essence or definition of a thing, which is universal rather than tied to a specific place.</note> excluded from any location. Wherefore it is not rightly said that the mind perishes "here" and not "there"; rather, it must either cease nowhere, or cease entirely everywhere. What, then, is the meaning of that rash response: "The understanding now looks at two images, now one"? It is not because it finds the images themselves—for it looks higher than them—and not because it moves them. For the mind does not properly understand because of these images; rather, it affects the images in such a way that they either "understand," or they move something else to understand. Or is it perhaps because the mind is moved by the images? If this is so, why did they not say the mind is "looked at" by the images rather than the mind looking at them? But suppose they did say that. What would it mean for the mind to be "looked at" by them? Does it mean that the <term>species</term><note>Latin: "species." The mental "form" or concept of a thing.</note> of the mind depend on images just as shadows depend on bodies? Truly, this itself is the "magnificent" invention of <term>Averroes</term><note>Ficino is being sarcastic here, mocking Averroes’ idea that human thoughts are merely temporary "reflections" or shadows cast upon a single, eternal Intellect.</note> himself. Nor does it follow from this that the mind understands within the images any more than hearing hears within a voice, or smell smells within an odor. Rather, having dismissed the images of gold, the mind itself—within its absolute and single species of gold—unites and absolutely works its way into the rational principle of gold. The result is that the mind understands separately from us within the <term>Idea</term><note>The "Idea" is the perfect, eternal archetype of a thing in the Platonic sense.</note> itself through a unique act. And if ever it ceases to understand, it ceases there entirely at once and in a moment. But those who affirm that species are the "shadows" of images, and then claim that one species emanates from two different images—and further, that the same species which previously flowed from your image alone later flows from mine as well, even as you stop thinking—they are as delusional as those who would claim that a single shadow flows from two different bodies, or that the shadow of one body is preserved by a second body after the first has been removed. Add to this: that in the same

---

moment, that one mind—through one species and one act of understanding regarding the same piece of gold—is so at odds with itself that in *me* it judges that gold should be scorned and rejects it, but in *you* it judges it precious and desires it. Such a great repugnance in judgment and desires cannot proceed from a single principle, insofar as it is one. They claim there is no diversity in the species or the understanding. Does it then come from the diversity of the images? Not at all. Surely a diversity of images would produce a difference in the species and the acts of understanding *before* it produced a difference in judgments and desires. Who, then, would agree that a single act of understanding could end in contrary judgments and clashing desires? It would be as if the same motion could proceed toward two opposite goals at once. Some of them fly to this excuse: that those two images create one species in the mind, but that this species, insofar as it proceeds from two images, gives birth to two distinct acts of understanding which are directed toward conflicting goals. But who would say that a variety of images—which is closer to the species than to the acts of understanding—would fail to create different species, yet somehow create diverse acts of understanding? Furthermore, if that species is given to the mind with different relationships to different things, it is not given as something entirely absolute, nor is it a sufficient principle for understanding. If it is not given as something differing, it will not give birth to a difference in the acts of understanding. Add this: no one of sound mind would ever concede that a single power of acting or knowing, through a single form at a single time, could produce multiple operations that are numerically different regarding the same object. Just as a single eye, looking at the same thing through a single image, does not produce two different "visions" at the same time. For one vision is enough. And they cannot be different unless they come from different principles. Whence, if all men used the same eye to see by means of a single image of the sun, they would have only one vision of the sun at the same time. Similarly, one intellect, through one species of gold, has only one act of understanding gold in a single moment. Nor do those two images bring any difference to this.

# Theology

[comes forth]. <note>This completes the word from the previous page, likely "provenit" (comes forth/results).</note> But let it be so: suppose those forms look toward the **images** <note>original: "simulacra." Ficino uses this to refer to the mental pictures derived from the senses.</note>; and suppose they differ by their **gaze** <note>original: "aspectum." This refers to the intentional relation between the mind's form and the sensory image it is considering.</note>. Certainly they do not differ by a simple gaze, but by a double one. Therefore there will be two gazes in two forms. They do not differ in **species** <note>original: "specie." In scholastic logic, things of the same "species" share the same essential nature (like two different humans both being "Human").</note>, to be sure, since they refer to the one nature of the species of gold. Therefore, they differ only in number. 

But through what do they differ? Not through themselves; otherwise they would disagree in their essential nature. Not through a **subject** <note>In philosophy, the "subject" is the underlying thing in which qualities exist—in this case, the mind itself.</note>, for they are both located in one single mind. Nor should they be said to be doubled for this reason: that they are placed in twin forms. For it was granted that the forms themselves are doubled by gazes rather than by something added from without. Otherwise, we would again have to add gazes to gazes, and we would dispute about the later ones just as we did about the prior ones. 

Again we ask: are those relations founded in the forms or in the images? If in the images: the forms will be looked at by the images rather than the forms looking at the images. If in the forms: they neither pertain to the essence of the forms themselves—since that would mean the forms differ in их essential nature—the essences of the forms are added externally by the makers of the images of those forms. From which it follows: forms of this kind are particular because of that very singularity of the bodily images. How much this hinders the purity of intelligence, no one of sound mind is ignorant; indeed, since the images are compared to the forms as external agents, they will never cause one form to be distinguished from another, unless individual images apply certain conditions to the individual forms emanating from them. In that case, the forms will not differ from each other any differently than the images differ among themselves. Thus, the forms will not be **absolute** <note>Meaning "unconditioned" or universal. For Ficino, a true mental concept should be a universal truth, not tied down to one specific, messy physical object.</note> while they are contracted by the narrowness of the images. 

Moreover, it is entirely incredible that two absolute forms are found in the same subject differing only in number. For by that very fact—that they differ neither by reason and essence, nor by subject—they will be forced to differ from each other through "foreign" qualities. Hence they will not be absolute. However, it is not impossible for them to be in two separate subjects [minds]. For they will be distinguished from each other at the same time because they will form distinct subjects, and they will remain absolute. For they will not be "shaped" by the subjects, provided the subjects are simple and free from impurities.

### ¶ Fourth [Reason]. Because either the knowledge of many men would be the same, or there would be superfluous qualities in the same thing.
<margin>Chapter 18.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
All qualities, whether defined by their endpoint or by an external absolute preserver, which are of one species: if they concur in the same subject, they also become one in number. For those things which agree in species also agree in form. If, moreover, they agree in matter because of the subject, they are entirely one. For this reason, in one drop of wine, sweetness and redness are present at the same time, which are two qualities different in species. Yet there are not two separate sweetnesses there, nor two rednesses. 

And if images and radiances of qualities can exist in the same thing differing only according to number—like the images of two eggs in the eye and the imagination, or also the two lights of two candles in the same air—this is because they depend continually on external things; and therefore they follow the number of those things of which they are either images or lights, rather than the subject. However, those qualities which truly exist and follow the nature of the subject rather than the object, become one in number through the subject if they were of one species. 

The absolute form of the mind is therefore a true and stable quality of it, because it is not an image or shadow or radiance of "foreign" accidents. But it is the offspring of an intellectual substance, the exemplar of substances. It is a rule of truth depending on the intellect, not on external things. For this reason, there are not certain absolute forms in the mind differing among themselves only in number. At this point, one may rightly despise that **Averroistic** <note>Refers to the followers of Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the Medieval Islamic philosopher who argued that all humans share one single, eternal Intellect.</note> objection.

<margin>C</margin>
They say that the **image** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> is the principle [the starting point] of the intelligible form. Therefore, they say, as many images as occur at once, so many forms are made. Because any one of the images, separate from the others, can sufficiently produce the form. We, however, have said that the image is neither the principle of the form...

[written]: <note>This completes a word from the previous page.</note> if indeed the universal form exists: neither is the preparation of the capable mind for receiving the form prior in the mind to the form itself; or certainly it is more like the mind. But it is a certain occasion for the inciting of the active power. This it will never effect if the power is in one substance and the form in another. But if they are in the same soul—as they certainly are—how it provides the occasion, we have declared elsewhere. 

Does the **image** <note>original: "simulacrum." In this context, a mental picture derived from the senses.</note> of gold offer itself? If the mind has never before received the form of gold, it produces it itself, having found an occasion for producing it. But if it has produced it at other times and possesses it, it does not produce another, but leads the one it possesses into **act** <note>original: "actum." Transitioning from having knowledge stored to actually thinking about it.</note>. It produces and leads out only one, even if a thousand images of the same species occur. 

Do you not notice when you see a thousand men with your eyes in the theater, and later recall a thousand images of these same men together in your **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia." The faculty that stores and manipulates sensory images.</note>, that the mind meanwhile considers them thus: "Man is a beautiful animal, rejoicing in society, skillful, and religious"? Here the mind does not pronounce this regarding any one of those thousand, but regarding the one common nature of them all; regarding the common substance of the rational animal; regarding the common definition of society, skill, and religion. 

The mind cannot make this one judgment regarding the one nature of all men or virtues more conveniently than through one **species** <note>original: "speciem." The universal "form" or "essence" of a thing, as opposed to an individual instance.</note> and likeness. Here it appears that from a thousand images of men, they have drawn only one species of man. And it does the same always in all images of the same species, however diverse they may be. From all the images of horses collected together, one equine species is formed. But the mind does not form one species from the images of a horse and a man; it forms two. Anyone who ever understands anything experiences this in himself. 

Wherefore when a hundred men see a horse, they collect a hundred images of the horse in their imagination. But if the Mind is one for all: being provoked by a hundred images, it conceives one species of horse. Through which one **intellection** <note>The single act of the intellect understanding a concept.</note> is defined. Therefore, there will be one single act of understanding among a hundred men.

In what way then, when one man's act of understanding ceases, does the other man's act not also cease? Certainly, innumerable men succeeding one another could understand through that same act of understanding remaining in itself. From this it would follow that the contemplation of temporal things would be eternal. This is something Averroes will not grant. 

The mind does not consider the horse insofar as *this* horse exists, but simply according to the universal **reason** <note>original: "rationem." The logical definition or concept.</note> of the equine species. A reason of this kind is one, even if there are a thousand horses, and even if there are a thousand images in the soul of one man or many. Therefore, there will be one consideration of the horse in many men. From such consideration, the **habit of science** <note>original: "scientie habitus." A 'habit' in scholastic terms is a permanent quality or learned skill—in this case, "knowledge."</note> is contracted in the mind. 

In the mind, I say: not in the imagination; if indeed the act of understanding is a preparation for a habit, and where the preparation is, there the form—that is, the habit—is made. A universal habit arises from universal acts and forms. But in the imagination—since according to Averroes it is bound to matter—neither an act nor a habit can exist in a universal mode. 

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, there will be one and the same habit of knowledge, as far as it pertains to the consideration of the equine species, in a hundred men. Indeed, since the intellect preserves species and habits, any one of us who understands through this intellect—and whose intelligence is that very same intelligence of the shared mind—already now understands everything whatever that present men and past men have known. 

Averroes will respond: we understand through the intellect only insofar as it is joined to us through our own individual images. And since the images are not the same among all people, nor affected similarly, therefore one person does not necessarily know whatever another knows. 

Such a response does not satisfy. For when the mind is already actually endowed with species, it can meditate through itself, as Aristotle confesses. From this we see that we can meditate as often as we wish on that which we have already learned, and we are not hindered by the absence of images. For if images are the "way" to the species, what need is there for the way after we have arrived at the goal? # Theology

X 3

[...preparation: after they have attained the highest **habit** <term>habit: (Latin: habitus) a stable, acquired state of knowledge or character</term>; which is so far from needing **images** <note>original: "simulacris." Sensory-based mental pictures.</note> as means of preservation, that it does not even seem to require further those proper acts by which it was most recently and specifically created, once it has been confirmed. Surely, when it is already mature, it thrives in the intellect by its own nature; it no longer depends on images, nor does it look back at them.

If this is so, the habits which are already perfected in the Averroistic intellect are equally one; since they are already absolute, they do not look out more toward this person than toward that person. Therefore, **Aristippus and Socrates** were equally learned and equally good. And when **Plato** and **Xenophon** learn grammar at the same time, they both acquire a habit of grammar very similar to themselves. Of the most similar grammar, there is but one rational principle. Therefore, its habits, wherever they may be, are of the same species. Such a habit in Plato and a similar habit in Xenophon are one in species.

But if the intellect, in which they exist as in a subject, is one, they are also one in number. For if any forms become one because of the unity of the <margin>B</margin> subject, such a habit is especially one, since it passes into the nature of the subject—indeed, it usurps the nature of the subject for itself; it maintains a certain inclination, and, being itself immobile, it moves the subject. Therefore, if the mind is one, either the knowledge of two people will be entirely the same—two will think as one, and as one they will cease to think—or innumerable qualities of the same species will exist in the same subject. And every day the intellect will receive many qualities of the same species as those it already has. It would be as if honey, at every single moment, received one sweetness after another, each very similar to itself. 

And in this, the opinion of **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century philosopher whose "unity of the intellect" theory Ficino is refuting.</note> will greatly oppose itself. <margin>B</margin> For in his books *On the Soul*, he repeated three times, following the opinion of **Aristotle**, that every subject must be bare of the species of that quality which it is about to receive. 

Furthermore, since we experience in ourselves that the mind not only understands, but also notices *that* it understands, and very easily transfers itself in a moment from one thought to another—often a similar one, often even an opposite one—and connects many things into one. Indeed, it even catches many notions of a person it is disputing with through the expression of just one; and what is greater: it often perceives what another has in their **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia." The faculty that processes sensory data.</note>, which is further from the mind. Beyond doubt, it is a wonder if the Averroistic mind—unique, eternal, indivisible, uniform, equally present to all—does not notice that what it understands in you, it never understands in me, and what it understands in you, it notices there. It never joins what it perceives in one person with those things it observes in another. It never, through itself, divines in one person what it is thinking in another; nor is it permitted to flee to the diversity of images which are outside and below the mind. For many things are understood at a certain time without an image then intervening, or accompanying it by itself and properly.

### Chapter 19.

<margin>C</margin> **C**ontradictories oppose each other even more than contraries do, in proportion as there is a greater repugnance between **being** and **not-being** than between being "of this sort" and being "of that sort." Therefore, if contraries cannot meet in the same subject, much less can contradictories. Thus it happens that each of us experiences in ourselves that our mind never entirely affirms and denies a thing at the same time, nor does it both wish for and not wish for it at once, even if many images of that same thing are in its imagination. 

And let the Averroists not now bring forward the argument that the image of whiteness and blackness are in the eye and the imagination at the same time, and again that their species are in the mind at the same time—in which there are also simultaneous cognitions of contraries. For forms of this kind, which are contrary outside the soul, are not contrary in the soul for this reason: that they lose their own nature. They are transferred into a certain quality of the soul, and an imaginary one at that. But **to assent** and **not to assent**, **to will** and **not to will**, retain their contradiction, because they are essential rather than imaginary, and they signify being directed toward the same act or affection of the soul...

# Platonic Book

->E iii<-

...and it is not handled differently; although the **species** <term>species: mental representations or forms of things perceived by the mind</term> of whiteness and blackness in sight are not contraries, nevertheless, the vision of some object as white and the simultaneous vision of the same object as black oppose each other in such a way that they cannot occur together. This is because the visions themselves depend continuously on different species and objects. 

In the same way, in the mind, the affirmation of the **divine Trinity** and its simultaneous negation cannot agree, even if they are said to depend on different **images** <note>original: "simulacris." Mental pictures derived from sensory experience.</note> and species. Truly, a diversity of agents does nothing to prevent contrary effects from opposing one another and expelling each other. 

What then causes the **Averroistic intellect** <note>The "Averroistic intellect" refers to the theory of Averroes that all humans share a single, communal mind.</note> to assert in **Plato** that the **One itself** is above essence and the **Good itself** is above the mind, yet in **Aristotle** to reject it? Certainly, no variety of images brings this about. For such contemplation is only correctly performed after images have been set aside. Or what causes that intellect to affirm in Plato that the heaven is fire, yet simultaneously deny it in Aristotle? 

Would the diversity of two images achieve anything—perhaps—if the mind judged within the images, or through the images, or about the images? But now, having taken the opportunity from them, the mind withdraws into itself and judges within itself through a common species regarding the common nature of the heaven and of fire. It leaves the intuition of images to the **imagination** <term>imagination: (Latin: phantasia) the faculty that processes and stores sensory images</term>, which is weakened all the more as the speculation of the mind is strengthened, and vice versa. This indeed is the final argument for what we were treating above: namely, that the species is neither created by the image nor preserved by it. 

Could it be that different species, conceived in the mind by the occasion of different images, give birth to those different opinions? Not at all. For one mind receives species from two images of the same heaven. But for the sake of argument, let it receive two. Granted those two exist, they are the power through which conflicting opinions seem to be able to proceed into the mind. Nevertheless, there are not certain parts or paths

---

in the mind, or proper forms, in which discordant opinions can be received. Instead, they are gathered toward a single and indivisible center of intelligence. There, a single and most simple judge pronounces the judgment. A mind cannot so manifestly contradict itself at the same time. 

A duality of species can do nothing more than provoke a wavering mind, provided they are themselves varied. But the intellect, having neglected the weaker species, brings forth only one judgment through the power of the one prevailing species. Just as the imagination, although it is stirred by various conjectures through various senses, nonetheless produces a single judgment and affection. Indeed, anyone can experience themselves doing the same thing amidst various conjectures within themselves. 

But if that one mind were to waver through two species in two different men, being carried here and there, yet because it is conscious of itself within itself, it would not be ignorant of what it wavered about; and having weighed the conjectures, it would incline to one side or the other in a brief moment. 

If it is absurd to say that heat and cold are received at the same time in the same subject—even if these two are brought in by different causes, namely fire and water—will it not also be ridiculous for contrary opinions to fall into the mind, even though they are sent in from different causes? For whatever is received is received according to the disposition of the subject. The same subject cannot be disposed in contrary ways at the same time to receive forms that are simply contrary. 

Furthermore, the argument will be stronger if we reason about contrary habits. For since a **habit** <term>habit: (Latin: habitus) a stable, acquired state of knowledge or character</term> confirms, it no longer depends on images; and since they are now absolute—and what is more—even from their own actions, the Averroists cannot say that contrary habits can occur together because of certain contrary agents (that is, the images). 

As for their claim that minds clothed in two species perform the role of subjects through which contradictions are grasped: we do not admit this, because it does not pertain to them to be trusted with species alone...

# Theology

...to see: those who think of these species as if they were shadows encircling the surface of the mind. Furthermore, because among those thinkers, **species** <term>species: here meaning the mental forms or representations of things that the mind perceives</term> hold the place of a foreign and contingent action, belonging to an external substance and subject. However, two subjects do not come into being because of two adventitious <term>adventitious: non-essential or coming from the outside</term> forms. 

Nor is anything received by reason of the forms themselves, but rather by reason of the **subject** <note>subject: the underlying substance (the mind) that "holds" qualities or thoughts.</note>. Therefore, one mind is one subject, even if it receives two different species; and whatever arrives is received by reason of the mind itself, not by reason of the species. How, then, an entry could be open to contradictions cannot even be imagined—unless perhaps they were to add that minds relate to species just as matter itself relates to quantity. 

Therefore, just as matter, when extended through quantity, receives contrary qualities <note>For example, a single piece of wax cannot be both hot and cold in the same spot, but if it is large enough, one end can be hot and the other cold.</note>, so your mind would receive repugnant opinions through these species. This example is hardly suitable, because they consider quantity to be inseparable from matter. But they consider the <margin>C</margin> species to be entirely foreign to the mind. 

Furthermore, matter does not receive contrary forms through quantity unless it is first cut into different parts by extension. If **Averroes** <note>original: "Auerrois." A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose followers argued that all humans share one single, eternal mind.</note> were to grant that minds are "cut" into various other minds through those very species, perhaps we would admit his point. Therefore, just as matter—even if prepared by quantity—does not receive contrary qualities in the very same point, so the mind does not admit contradictions, even if it were affected by various species. 

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, it is the nature of contradictions that they cannot dwell together. Nor can they be together even if something in the middle attempts to reconcile them. Add to this that if repugnant things are to be received through certain "preparations," those preparations themselves must be repugnant. Insofar as preparations contribute to certain **habits** <term>habits: stable dispositions or states of mind, like "knowledge" or "virtue"</term> and agree with them in some proportion, they simultaneously impede different habits and are dissonant with their preparations. 

And if preparations for repugnant things are received by the same subject through other intermediate, discordant affections, we shall wander into infinity. But if no affection intervenes, that is indeed absurd: as if repugnant habits could be received without a medium, just like affections. 

For this reason, if our mind is to be disposed toward the repugnant acts and habits of contradictions, it must first be disposed toward mutually opposing species and discordant discourses; then, those conflicting species would excite opposing principles <margin>E</margin> of reasoning, and through these dissonant means, the mind would arrive at contradictory conclusions. This entire mass of repugnance, which pulls the mind toward contradictions, cannot be received by the mind without a medium, just as the contradictions themselves cannot. If a medium is sought, it will be sought without end.

Just as we have disputed concerning contradictory assertions, we may also discuss contradictory **affections** <note>affections: emotions or desires.</note>. For instance, consider when that one mind, in the case of **Plato**, wills a certain universal object, yet at the same time, in the case of **Aristotle**, does not will it. Insofar as the affection does not belong to the **phantasms** <note>phantasms: sensory images in the imagination.</note>—which no more reach a "universal" thing in desiring than they do in thinking—we see contrary affections in the mind when <margin>F</margin> two men desire two universal objects that are mutually discordant. 

And we see it when, in the case of incorporeal things, some people rejoice while others simultaneously grieve. Finally, the same mind would be virtuous and wicked at the same time; wise and ignorant; certain and ambiguous; happy and miserable. What will they say to this? That from repugnant acts and affections, repugnant habits will coalesce in the same mind—namely, both contraries and contradictions. 

But this is the most absurd of all, since a **habit** is not some imaginary thing, but takes the place of a natural form. A natural form and its natural inclination is destroyed by the arrival of an opposite form and inclination. Perhaps we have disputed longer than was proper about the <margin>G</margin> mind with these people, who deprive themselves of a mind when they segregate it from the human species. This mind is so familiar to the human species that we cannot accept the mind without a mind, nor can they reject the mind without a mind. 

We believe that in the preceding arguments, we have not only refuted Averroes, but also those who think there is only one **soul** <term>soul: Latin "anima," the animating principle of the body</term> for all. For if there is a distinction between minds, there is a much greater distinction between souls.

He concludes that mental and emotional diversity proves that each individual must possess their own distinct soul and intellect.</summary>

...diversity of things: then, because human minds are more united with one another, in that they are more excellent than souls are with each other; and finally, because if one soul were sufficient for governing our bodies, how much more would one mind suffice for grasping the truth. 

Wherefore, we must not believe those counterfeit <note>original: "adulterinis"</note> 
<margin>A</margin>
Platonists who assert that all living things live through a single world-soul; for then we would not be led by free motion and a variety of counsel, but would be carried along by a sudden impulse like arrows. Furthermore, if we all breathed through a single world-soul, we would likewise all behold the world through only one mind. Indeed, the very diversity and distinction of worldly bodies signifies a distinction of natures. The distinction of natures follows the distinction of souls. The distinction of souls implies a distinction of minds. And the minds implanted in souls retain the same number as the souls themselves. 

One may also 
<margin>B</margin>
laugh at a certain barbarian, David of Dinant <note>A 13th-century philosopher condemned for pantheism, who argued that God, mind, and matter were the same substance.</note>, and at the Manichaeans <note>Followers of a dualistic religion who believed human souls were literal fragments of the divine light trapped in the darkness of matter.</note>, who wanted our souls to be certain "portions" of God, or even God Himself. That this cannot be so is sufficiently declared by those five "degrees of things" established in our first book. Nor can God be dispersed into many souls, since the highest unity cannot be divided; nor can He become the "matter" of many souls, lest He be less noble than the souls themselves, or lest the Highest Act take on the role of a passive subject. Nor can He, while remaining in His own form, be changed so frequently within us—since He is the stable center of all moving things—turning from truth into falsehood, from good into evil, or from joy into grief, and vice versa. Finally, if God were the soul of all things, there would be one mind in all things—a concept which was 
<margin>C</margin>
refuted in the previous sections. 

However, since Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle who attempted to reconcile different philosophical schools.</note> asserts that Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus held a single opinion regarding the mind, if we wish to conclude this Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they walked while debating.</term> dispute with a happy ending, let us gather the Platonic and Peripatetic truth—dispersed through many interpreters—into one. Let us accept from Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note> that the "receptive intellect" is immortal. Let us accept from Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, an influential commentator who argued that the capacity for thought was a natural power of the human soul.</note> that the powers of the receptive intellect are naturally implanted in our souls, being as many in number as there are souls. Let us conclude that the souls of men are immortal. And this is the conclusion of the Platonists, the Christians, and the Arab theologians, which is most in harmony with the Peripatetics.

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine’s Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.
# Book Sixteen.

### The second question follows: Why are souls enclosed in earthly bodies? Chapter 1.

<margin>D</margin>
After we have answered the first question and shown that the divinity of the mind belongs to our souls, let us respond to the second: let us show why souls, if they are divine, are enclosed in such lowly, earthly bodies.

### First Reason: So that they may know individual things.

<margin>E</margin>
The essence of God—if indeed it should be called an essence—is not one specific genus <term>genus: a general category or classification of things.</term> of things. Otherwise, He would only act upon things of His own kind, just as water makes things wet but not dry, or fire generates dry things rather than wet. But since God effects all genera of things through His essence, and since that which effects must remain above all things that are made, God is in no single genus of things, but is above all genera. Therefore, when He gazes upon His own essence—the origin and archetype <note>original: "exemplar"</note> of all—He beholds every genus of things, every species, and every individual thing. For the essence of God is the beginning, middle, and end, not only of general principles, but also of the individuals wandering under any given species. Truly, the divine essence, since it has nothing of matter in itself...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine and angelic intellects from the beginning of Book 16. In the previous page, Ficino argued against the idea of a single "World Soul" or the pantheistic notion that human souls are literal pieces of God. Here, he transitions into how God and Angels perceive the world.</meta>

# Theology

...which is accustomed to overshadowing knowledge: He is light and the highest perspicacity. Therefore, God, through His own essence properly as if through an effective light that distinguishes between individual things, perceives each one. And since the essence of God is entirely absolute—not only from all matter and the properties of matter, but also from every specific condition and respect toward this created thing or that—and since it is infinite, for that reason He behaves indifferently (so to speak) toward all things. Therefore, He either knows nothing besides Himself, or He knows all things. But to say He knows nothing is a wicked thing to say, since He is the supreme principle <note>original: "ratio summa"</note> of both those who know, of the things known, and of knowledge itself.

<margin>E</margin>
Nor should Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval thought; he argued that God only knows universal truths, not lowly particulars, to maintain His dignity.</note> object to us that God becomes "base" if He considers lower things. Truly, He who knows Himself to be the principle of all things that are below Him therefore knows what it is to be "lower." Therefore, He understands the way in which they fall short. Yet while He acknowledges the very reason for their defect, He Himself suffers no defect.

<margin>G</margin>
But if God, in considering the very foundation of imperfection (which is the thing most foreign to Him), does not become more imperfect Himself, certainly much less will He end up "filled" by thinking about other things, even the most imperfect. What more? Knowledge of oneself and of others is desirable as a "good." For it is a certain possession of oneself and others. However, one mode of knowing can be less desirable than another. Indeed, the mode by which the external sense knows is imperfect. Less imperfect is that by which the internal sense <note>In the psychology of this period, the "internal senses" included functions like imagination and memory.</note> knows. Less still is that by which reason knows. Finally, the least imperfect is that by which the angelic mind knows. Thus, that mode of knowledge by which God distinguishes individuals, since it is infinitely many degrees more perfect than the angelic mode, certainly encompasses no imperfection; rather, it encompasses every perfection entirely. Such indeed is the mode of divine knowledge, which becomes infinite through its own perfection. Finally, just as it is better for us finite beings to know certain finite things than to be ignorant, so it befits the infinite God to see infinite things rather than nothing or only finite things. Truly, He knows individuals everywhere distinctly, if only because He who perfectly possesses the cause of causes also possesses all and individual causes most perfectly. And distinct perspective, as a perfection...

---

...is much more to be desired than confused perspective. But lest we wander too far, let us proceed to the rest.

<margin>F</margin>
The Angel also beholds all the works of God, and each one individually. For if the object of our mind is being itself and common truth, and therefore the human mind directs itself gradually toward all existing and true things, it is fitting that the mind of the angel, which is more excellent than ours, should grasp all things—and as the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists like Plotinus, whom Ficino translated into Latin.</note> maintain, all things at once. But where does the angel look in order to see all things? Does he direct his gaze toward physical bodies? Not at all. Because the mind of the angel is stable and perceives all things simultaneously. Therefore, he cannot learn those things from bodies, which, having been changed more often by their own course, show themselves now one way, now another—just as the mode of acting follows the mode of being. The Angel, who is entirely free from the body in his being, will also be free in his understanding. Nor will he be formed by bodies, he who is more excellent than bodies and has no commerce with them. Or perhaps he will turn his intuition toward the angelic essence? He will indeed. But in the angel, he will perceive only "angel." For he will see in the angelic nature only as much as it extends itself. That nature is only in the angelic genus. He will therefore see "angel" in it.

<margin>G</margin>
He will hardly discern the other genera of things clearly. Indeed, if matter hinders knowledge, and a created essence has something similar to matter—unformed and dark <note>original: "fuscum"</note>—it follows that no created mind, insofar as it looks upon a kind of naked gloom in itself, can attain clarity of vision. It is just as if the moon looked at itself before being illuminated by the light of the sun. Therefore, just as the eye does not discern colors except through the forms of the colors themselves, so the mind does not clearly see the genera of things except through their forms, since form is the principle of acting. The essence of the angel is the form of the angel alone, and that essence is in a certain way dark. But God's essence—or rather, His truth and goodness—is the form of all things, the purest light, the root, the reason, and the exemplar. Through this alone, as if through the sun, can all things be seen.

<margin>H</margin>
Does the angel therefore discern all things through the very essence of God?

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of how divine knowledge is transmitted from the unity of God down through the hierarchy of angelic intellects to the human soul. On the previous page, Ficino argued that God knows all things through His own essence. Here, he explains the "medium"—the Divine Light—that allows finite angelic minds to grasp that infinite essence.</meta>

# Platonic Theology: Book 16

...know? Certainly not through the absolute essence of God without a medium. For in what way could an infinite essence fit into a finite mind as its form if no preparation came between them? It is necessary, however, for the mind itself to have some form within it through which it acts in the process of understanding. Therefore, an angel receives the forms and patterns <note>original: "exemplaria"</note> of things from the essence of God. Just as the eye receives the forms of colors through the light of the sun (which is the source of all color) and thus sees those colors, so the mind of an angel receives the <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" are not biological categories but "intelligible forms" or mental images that represent the true nature of a thing.</note> of all things through the divine light (which is the producer of all things) and thus understands them. It is only right that God should form "spiritual matter" <note>Ficino uses this term to describe the raw potential of an angelic intellect before it is "filled" or "formed" by God’s light.</note>—which is primary to Him, namely the angelic minds—more early and fully than He forms the physical matter of the world, which is most distant from Him.

<margin>A</margin> But there are many levels of minds—far more than there are levels of bodies—as **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels; Ficino viewed him as a bridge between Plato and Christianity.</note> teaches. For the Greatest Craftsman willed to establish more levels in His most excellent works than in His lowlier ones. Just as a city is more magnificent if it contains more levels of nobles and free citizens than it does of laborers and servants, such is the comparison of minds to bodies. We have discussed enough regarding how many principal orders there are in the angelic levels, following the mind of Dionysius, both in our book on religion and in our discussion on the "Rapture of Paul."

<margin>B</margin> We have also indicated elsewhere how the Platonists divide these into nine orders. Specifically, since angels are certain types of intellects gazing upon the Supreme Intelligible <note>The "Intelligible" is the ultimate reality or God, who is the object of the intellect's gaze.</note>, they behold within Him **Essence**, **Life**, and **Intelligence**. But there, in the realm of Essence, both Life and Intelligence exist in the *manner of essence*. Again, in Life, the other two exist similarly in the *manner of life*. Likewise, in Intelligence, the other two—Life and Essence—exist in the *manner of intelligence*. Therefore, in that realm, each single "Intelligible" is divided into three. Through these three, it then multiplies into nine.

<margin>C</margin> In this same order, the intellects who contemplate Him are distributed into nine orders. In this way, the Platonists divide the angels who are devoted solely to contemplation. However, those who also govern the world are divided by some into groups of twelve and seven, primarily according to the twelve signs of the Zodiac and the seven planets. To these, they add certain other armies of angels, depending on the number of stars, who apply themselves to specific duties in each sphere of the world. They also add as many crowds of demons and heroes <note>In the Platonic tradition, "heroes" were considered semi-divine spirits or elevated souls that acted as intermediaries between humans and gods.</note> who are obedient to the angels, and finally, just as many orders of particular souls who accommodate themselves to the higher divinities.

But let us set aside for now the demonic and heroic armies; it is enough to understand that the Platonists placed innumerable minds above us. In naming these, **Iamblichus** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated elaborate hierarchies of spirits and rituals into Platonic thought.</note> accepts from our traditions the names not only of angels, but also of archangels and principalities. He believes the divine light descends to us through all of them as if through panes of glass. For this reason, through almost innumerable levels of intermediate spirits, that divine ray—the "shaper of minds"—descends all the way to the lowest minds, which are the souls of human beings.

<margin>D</margin> Four things, however, must be considered here. First, that divine ray itself. Second, the species of things within it, which we call the "reasons" for creating things, or **Ideas**.

<margin>E</margin> Third, the minds themselves. Fourth, the powers of those minds. The ray, insofar as it consists in the most simple unity of God, is entirely one and most simple. It offers a single Idea to the divine eye: namely, the one essence of God. But that essence is communicable to the things to be created through many "modes of being." According to Plato, these modes are the very **Ideas** of things which are to be produced through such modes. Thus, the one essence of God is the "one Idea of all ideas," acting in place of all of them; and through this single Idea, God looks out upon all things.

As that ray flows out from God, the further it proceeds from the divine unity, the more manifold it becomes. What had first offered a single Idea to the eye of God now offers many, then more, and finally very many to the eyes of the angels. This is just like a line drawn from a center-point: where it was indivisible at the center, the further it moves away, the more it extends into multiple parts. Or indeed, just as a ray of sunlight represents a single form of light within the sun itself, but represents many forms in fire, and even more in the air.

<summary>Ficino explains how God's singular essence is transmitted through a "divine ray" that multiplies into diverse Ideas as it descends through a hierarchy of nine angelic orders. He aligns Christian angelology with Platonic philosophy, describing angels as "glass" through which divine light reaches human souls.</summary>
<keywords>angelic hierarchy, Dionysius the Areopagite, Iamblichus, Divine Light, Ideas, Essence, nine orders of angels, Neoplatonism, emanation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book 16 of the Platonic Theology, where he describes how the "Divine Ray"—the light of God's knowledge—descends through the hierarchy of being. Having established that God knows all things through His own essence, Ficino now explains how this knowledge is refracted into multiple "ideas" as it moves away from the divine Unity toward more complex minds like those of angels and humans.</meta>

<page-num>166</page-num>
<header>Theology</header>

### Theology

...and water. On the earth, there are very many. <note>This sentence finishes a list of species or forms from the preceding page.</note> Just as that <margin>🔳</margin> divine ray exists in itself, so it is in the minds into which it is poured. For the closer a mind is to the divine unity, the more unified and simple it is. Conversely, the more remote it is, the more complex it becomes. Each mind receives the incoming ray according to its own nature. Those minds which are wiser receive it through a simpler <margin>t</margin> mode; the rest receive it more multiply. Thus, only a few ideas are "painted" by the ray in a sublime mind. In the next mind, there are more; and subsequently, the most. Since indeed, the simpler and more unified a thing is, the more powerful it is, the power of understanding flourishes more sharply in the higher minds, while it is duller in the following ones. Thus it happens that through those very few ideas, the higher minds see no fewer things than the rest see through many ideas. Just as a most skilled physician foresees the future outcomes in a sick patient by a single sign, while the unskilled needs many signs to judge, and the most unskilled needs very many. Or as a <margin>f✝</margin> sagacious servant understands what the master commands by a single nod, while the slower ones require many words. Therefore, both because of the simplicity of the perceived ray and because of the unity of sublime minds and their marvelous sharpness, in the "angelic citadel" <note>original: "arce angelica," referring to the highest orders of angels like the Seraphim.</note> there are very few and very universal ideas; more numerous and more specific ideas follow in order. 

Take an example similar to the truth, as I judge it. The most common thing of all for the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle; Ficino is using Aristotelian logic to explain Platonic metaphysics.</note> is "Being" itself. This is divided into two parts: one exists <margin>3</margin> by itself, and the other clings to another. The former is <term>Substance</term> <note>A thing that exists in its own right, like a tree or a person.</note>; the latter is <term>Accident</term> <note>A quality that exists only within a substance, like the color green or the height of a person.</note>. Substance, in turn, is twofold: one is corporeal, the other is incorporeal. Similarly, one accident is "quantity," and another is "quality." Likewise, Body is twofold: animate and inanimate. Spirits also: some are separated from bodies, while others are joined to them. Each is divided thereafter through <term>genus</term> down to the final <term>species</term>. Finally, any species contains infinite individuals. 

God understands all things through a single idea of His own being—or of the Good—which is the very nature of God. The first angel, for the sake of example, might have two ideas: one of substance and one of accident, through which he understands all types of substances and accidents. This is because that divine ray—which in God was formed through a single idea of His own being or goodness—already divides itself into twin "formulas" <note>original: "formulas," meaning mental patterns or blueprints.</note> in the first angel as it departs from the One, and is clothed with the ideas of substance and accident. The second angel, with the variety of the ray doubled again, receives four ideas from it: two pertaining to the genus of substance and two to the genus of accident—namely, one idea of corporeal substance, another of incorporeal substance; then one idea of the accident which is quality, and another of the accident which is quantity. Through these four ideas, he understands all categories of things that are contained under common substance and common accident. 

The third angel, through the ray being doubled again and divided <margin>B</margin> manifoldly, receives eight ideas, through which he understands as many things as the first and second. Here it appears that to higher minds there belong more universal ideas, and to <margin>12</margin> the following ones, gradually less universal ideas. Indeed, one idea in the higher minds contains as much beneath it and signifies as much as several ideas do in the lower ones. For in descending, one is always doubled into two. And so it is doubled step by step, until the lowest order of minds—such as the **rational soul** <note>The human mind.</note>—receives a divine ray as manifold as it can possibly become in spirits. It can be divided in them down to the "ultimate ideas" of things, so that it presents as many formulas as there are species of things created by God; for instance, it has one idea of the human species, <margin>hb</margin> one of the equine, and similarly for others. However, that ray does not easily or to just anyone show the distinct figures of individual men and horses. For since the ray is entirely absolute, it presents formulas in a primarily absolute way. Indeed, the **Platonists** believe that just as the celestial minds contain the ideas of material and generable things in an immaterial and ungenerable way, so too they possess only universal ideas of particular things. Let us imagine the soul of a man now first flowing out from God, not yet clothed in a body...

<summary>Ficino explains how divine knowledge descends through the angelic hierarchy, doubling in complexity at each level. Higher angels understand the universe through a few universal ideas (like "Substance"), while lower minds like the human soul require many specific ideas to grasp the same reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Divine Ray" and the hierarchy of knowledge. While the previous page was noted as Book 16, the current header and text indicate Book 9 of the Platonic Theology. Ficino is transitioning from how higher minds (angels) perceive things to how the human mind, being the lowest in the intellectual hierarchy, functions through a combination of divine reception and sensory experience.</meta>

# Platonic Theology, Book IX

<margin>A</margin>
...free from the occupation of the body, the soul should direct its entire attention toward its own mind. There, according to its nature, it should at least receive the influx of that <term>ray</term><note>The "Divine Ray" refers to the light of God's wisdom that illuminates all intellects.</note> which is perpetually present and inspiring it. What will the soul naturally grasp through a ray of this kind? As many <term>ideas</term><note>In the Platonic sense, "ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints of things in the divine mind.</note> as there are <term>species</term><note>The "form" or "kind" of a created thing.</note> of created things. It will grasp one idea for each species. Through the idea of "man," what will it understand? Only the nature common to all human beings. It will not see individual men under that idea. It will do the same through the idea of "horse," and so on for the rest. Therefore, the soul's knowledge will be left in a state of confusion, since the distinct progression of species into individual things remains hidden from it. Its natural appetite would thus be empty and always restless—a state of being that wishes to lack no truth and no good. But why is the human soul unable to clearly see individual things beneath the species in these ultimate ideas, in the same way it sees the species themselves? Why can <term>angels</term> see genera, species, and individuals in their ideas, while we cannot? Because, as we have discussed elsewhere, in every order of things, nature is arranged so that <term>action</term> at the highest point of that order is devoid of <term>passion</term><note>original: "passio"; in this context, "passion" means "receptivity" or "being acted upon," rather than emotion.</note>. At the lowest point, "passion" is deprived of "action." In the middle, there is a balanced composition of both. It is established that our souls are the <term>lowest minds</term><note>Ficino places humans at the bottom of the "intellectual" ladder (minds) but at the top of the "physical" ladder.</note>. Therefore, as far as intelligence is concerned, God alone acts; the angel both acts and receives; the soul, by the nature of its mind, only receives and does not act. Indeed, God pours out ideas to others and draws them from nowhere else. The first angel receives two—so to speak—types of ideas: those two broadest categories of things, in the reception of which it is somewhat passive. However, once those are received, the angel penetrates into the very "innards" of those categories through its own power. It clearly beholds all the subsequent species within them. 

<margin>C</margin>
The angel then constructs for itself its own concepts of whatever species it wishes, which it even directs toward individual things. And this is no longer "passion" but "action." The second angel does the same, and so do the others. Yet, a later angel always receives more ideas from above by being passive, and will construct fewer concepts of species for itself by acting. Consequently, "passion" (receptivity) gradually increases, while "action" decreases, until one reaches the "lowest mind," which acts not at all. Instead, it is nourished by the ideas it receives. It creates nothing new. Its intelligence is nothing other than the reception of ideas that does not escape its own notice. And because 

<margin>B</margin>
ideas are universal by nature, no mind can lead them down to distinct concepts of individual things without its own "action." Therefore, the human soul—which, insofar as it is a mind, is the last among minds—understands only by being passive; it does not distribute universals into individuals. Nevertheless, in the respect that it is divine, through its own center—as if it were a stamp of the truth—it possesses some "action" by which it produces or draws out species. But it does not divide them. Furthermore, in the respect that it is a soul (since it is not the lowest of souls), it is capable of animal and bodily operations. Moreover, by divine providence, the human soul is placed at such a rank that just as it follows immediately after the minds, so it immediately precedes earthly bodies. Because of this kinship 

<margin>C</margin>
it is drawn toward these lower things and inserts itself into them with a certain loving affection. Thus, when joined to earthly bodies—the most excellent of all earthly things—it certainly rules them, and through its vital power, it brings vital "passions" to them from within. 

<margin>D</margin>
Through the <term>senses</term>, however, it judges the "passions" (impressions) brought upon the body from the outside. Since the human body consists of the four elements and is located in the middle of the world, it experiences the impulses of all elements and all surrounding things through the five instruments of the senses. The soul discerns these impulses, brought in from all sides by individual things, specifically through the senses. The soul itself, by its own power, fashions the images of these things within itself through the <term>phantasy</term><note>The "phantasy" or "imagination" is the faculty that translates raw sensory data into mental images.</note> and preserves them in the memory. Thus it happens that in a short time, the phantasy is full of individual forms for almost every individual thing. From here, <term>reason</term> is provoked. First, it brings forth universal species, and through them, it receives common notions with a simple gaze. 

<margin>E</margin>
But soon, from this direct gaze—moving from the act of understanding toward the intelligible species—it reflects back upon the <term>simulacrum</term><note>An "image" or "likeness" stored in the mind.</note> through that species, and through the simulacrum, it looks upon the individual. At first, this individual is vague and indeterminate—for instance, "some honey"...

<summary>Ficino explains the human soul's position as the "lowest mind," which is purely receptive (passive) to universal divine ideas, but active in ruling the body. He describes how the soul bridge the gap between universal truths and individual sensory objects through phantasy, memory, and reason.</summary>

--- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Book IX of the Platonic Theology. Having previously discussed how the soul receives divine light, he now explains how the human soul uses its experience in the physical body to learn how to connect specific sensory details (like the taste of honey) with universal truths (the definition of sweetness), a skill it will keep even after death.</meta>

# Theology

### xvj. 167

...then it is determined: namely, this honey or that. But after shorter acts of this kind, the soul is accustomed to range more widely in this manner: "What indeed is this sweet and yellow body which <term>imagination</term><note>In Ficino's system, 'phantasia' or imagination is the faculty that processes sensory images before reason analyzes them.</note> now offers to me? Why is it sweet? Is it sweeter than wine?" Here, <term>reason</term> <margin>D</margin> asks three things which, as it seems to the Platonists, had been hidden from the imagination. First, it asks about the substance of the thing, when it asks: "What is this?" Second, it seeks the cause of that quality, when it inquires: "Why is it sweet?" Third, it seeks its relationship to other things, when it asks whether it is sweeter than wine. After this, reason answers these three questions for itself. First: "This is honey." Second: "It is sweet for this reason: because its moisture is rich and moderately cooked." <note>Ficino uses the medical language of his time, where 'concoction' or cooking refers to the heat of the body or nature ripening a substance.</note> Third: "It is sweeter than wine because its sweetness soothes the tongue more effectively and for a longer time." Because these discourses of human reason follow the impulse of the imagination, they are particular and wander through individual things.

Indeed, reason even approaches other questions: "What is honey? What is sweetness?" Now it asks no more about *this* specific honey than about any other; likewise, it asks about any sweetness whatsoever. And having neglected that specific image of honey which the imagination brought forward, it examines the common nature of all honey and of sweetness in general. <margin>E</margin> From this comes a universal question, and the answer becomes universal as well. Thus: "Honey is the juice of bees, hot in the second degree, <note>In Renaissance medicine, qualities like heat were measured in four degrees; honey was considered 'moderately hot.'</note> cleansing in its power, sweetest in taste, and rich to the touch." Again: "Sweetness is a flavor resulting from the moderate ripening of airy moisture." Reason sought these common definitions of honey and sweetness for a long time, and finally found them.

If it sought them for a long time, it did not possess them within itself. For it received from elsewhere that which it arrived at through this process of reasoning. Where then did it receive it? Not from the imagination. For if the imagination had possessed those definitions, it clearly would have offered them immediately, just as it offered the sensory images. Especially since that light of a common definition—to the extent that it is more brilliant and more divine than sensory images—should have shone more clearly to the "eyes" of reason adapted to it. Therefore, reason receives those definitions from the <term>Mind</term>. <note>Ficino distinguishes the 'Mind' (Mens) as the highest part of the soul that stays in contact with divine truths, while 'Reason' (Ratio) is the part that thinks through steps.</note> Because reason is so close to the Mind, it acquires that very power through which, sometimes neglecting individual questions, it applies itself to universal ones. 

And because it seeks definitions in a general way, it brings back common truths from the Mind. It was asked what profit comes to the soul from being in a body. Much, without a doubt! Indeed, if the soul remained outside the body from the moment it was first born, it would certainly know universal truths, but it would not perceive individual things—either by its own power or by the divine ray grasped through it. This is because its Mind would not descend beyond the ultimate <term>Ideas</term>, <note>The eternal, perfect blueprints of things in the divine realm.</note> and its Reason would rest in the simple intuition of the Mind. 

But in this body, because of the senses, reason becomes accustomed to run through individual things, to apply individuals to universal concepts, and to derive universals back into individuals. It runs through individuals in this way: "This is sweet and yellow, therefore it is honey." It applies individuals to universals like this: "This is sweet. All sweetness is moisture moderately cooked. Therefore, this is moisture so cooked." It applies universals to individuals here: "Everything sweet and yellow is honey. This, therefore, because it is such, is honey." 

Once reason has become accustomed to this in the body, when the soul is later separated from the body, it will easily distribute the common Ideas of the Mind into individual notions. Because just as here on earth, through its temporal reasoning, it provokes that divine and effective center of the soul (the "head" of the Mind) to lead the <term>formulas</term> <note>Latent principles or 'seeds' of knowledge within the soul.</note> hidden in the mind gradually into the light, so there after death—by a sudden and continuous impulse generated through long habit—it will "set fire" to those formulas. They will then flash from the Mind into the Reason like sparks struck from individual things. 

For this reason, Plato in his *Letters* and the *Laws*, and Plotinus also in his book *On the Immortality of Souls*, assert that separated souls possess some awareness of and care for our affairs. Plotinus wants this to be understood in this way: they notice human things only insofar as there remains in them some habit or affection turning toward bodily things. Once this is finally removed, they apply themselves to divine things with such intense attention that they either do not see individual things happening among us, or—as is common with people thinking very intently about something—they do not notice that they see them.

<summary>Ficino explains how the human soul uses sensory experiences, like tasting honey, to train the reason to connect individual objects with universal divine Ideas. This mental "exercise" in the body prepares the soul to retain a connection to individual things even after it has left the body and returned to a purely intellectual state.</summary>

<keywords>reason vs imagination, universal definitions, Platonic Ideas, immortality of the soul, Plotinus, honey metaphor, cognitive process, soul-body relationship</keywords>
