<meta>This page continues from the discussion of how human reason distinguishes between specific sensory experiences (like "this honey") and universal concepts (like "sweetness"). Ficino is now moving from the mechanics of perception to the metaphysical purpose of the soul's presence in the body: to act as a bridge that brings the physical world back to its divine source through "recollection."</meta>

## Platonic Book

This is roughly the reasoning regarding the recollection of human affairs. For Plato admits in one place that we can remember. In another, he says that the <term>River Lethe</term><note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld. Ficino uses it here to describe the transition of the soul between the divine realm and the physical body.</note> of oblivion flows between the region of this life and the next. For souls are moved toward those things which they sensed here for a long time; then, they are moved by them very little. Indeed, souls that slip into the body forget divine things to the same extent that they immerse themselves in the body. When they first emerge, and to the degree that they emerge, they then first and to that extent remember. However, there are many souls—as it pleases both the ancient and our own theologians—which <margin>A</margin> govern this or that, here or there, not by passion, but by a certain providence distributed by God. Add to this that in the *Republic*, Plato writes <margin>B</margin> that souls which knew each other here by some affection recognize each other there, and are affected toward each other in a nearly similar way. <margin>C</note> <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose Aristotelian and Neoplatonic commentaries were central to Renaissance philosophy.</note> also says in his *Metaphysics* that souls, both the blessed and the miserable, in the other life can imagine for a time—through a certain habit contracted from sensible things—those things which they previously imagined here with a more vehement passion. But let us dismiss these things for now as being less necessary.

<margin>C</margin> The second reason: So that particular forms may be reconciled with universal forms. Chapter 2.

<margin>D</margin> **W**onderful indeed is this power of human reason, proper to the rational soul, through which we are human beings. It receives individual things from the <term>imagination</term><note>Ficino uses 'phantasia' to mean the faculty that stores sensory images.</note> and common things from the mind; it gathers both into one. Just as in a human being mortal things are coupled with immortal things, so in this kind of reasoning, temporal images are joined to eternal <term>species</term><note>In this context, 'species' refers to the ideal, unchanging forms of things in the divine mind.</note>. Unless this were performed somewhere in the world, the series of forms would remain interrupted. Yet it cannot happen unless the rational soul is joined to a terrestrial body.

<margin>C</margin> The third reason: So that both the divine ray and its patterns may reflect back to God. Chapter 3.

<margin>E</margin> **I**t performs in this again another more wonderful thing. Since that divine ray is most full of <term>Ideas</term><note>The 'Ideas' (Ideae) are the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things existing in the mind of God.</note>, after it descends all the way to the soul, it passes through the vital power of the soul and through nature into the matter of the world. In this matter, it fashions certain final and shadowy likenesses of the Ideas, just as light fashions the images of colors in a mirror. Or rather, just as shadows of bodies are designated on the ground by light. Such likenesses or shadows depart very far from divinity itself. For from the pure they become impure, while they are stained by their opposites; from the unified, they become scattered. From the common, they become individual. From the stable, they become unstable according to their own nature. If every thing seeks its own origin—whence the ray of the sun striking the earth is reflected back toward the sun—is it any wonder that these shadowy likenesses of the Ideas also seek their ancient purity by a certain hidden instinct? And that the ray itself, their fashioner, after it descends, strives in turn to ascend? Will such a great effort be in vain? Not at all. Who will help? Not the souls of beasts, which gape only at individual images. Not those minds superior to ours <note>Ficino refers to angels or celestial intelligences.</note>, which, because they do not have bodies subject to all the storms of all bodies, do not receive any particular passions and forms of any bodies whatsoever. Only the soul of man remains, which, on account of its earthly body, is in a certain way struck by the individual disturbances of individual bodies. It indeed assumes through the senses these likenesses of Ideas stained by the matter of the world. It collects them through the imagination. It purifies and elevates them through reason. Then it binds them with the universal Ideas of the mind. Thus that celestial ray, which had flowed down to the depths, flows back to the heights, while the likenesses of the Ideas which had been scattered in matter are gathered in the imagination. The impure things are purified in reason, and the individual things finally emerge as universal in the mind. Thus the soul of man restores the world which was already falling into decay. Because by its service, the world which was once spiritual and has now been made corporeal is continually purified and daily emerges as spiritual. Rays sent down from the wide circle of the sun into a narrow opening of a very high wall make a cone through a pyramid, and are slanted in that very opening, until...

<summary>Ficino argues that the human soul acts as a metaphysical bridge, using reason to collect scattered, material "shadows" of divine Ideas and return them to their universal, spiritual source. He emphasizes that this restorative function is unique to humans because we possess both a physical body to experience individuals and a rational mind to grasp universals.</summary>
<keywords>reminiscence, Platonic Ideas, human reason, Avicenna, Lethe, divine ray, soul as mediator, universal vs particular forms</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the human mind acts as a spiritual mirror or lens. Ficino is using an optical analogy—likely inspired by the "camera obscura" effect—to explain how the vastness of the divine world is "compressed" into the smallness of the human body and then "expanded" again by the mind.</meta>

...so much so that they are led across by it: and when they fall upon the floor placed beneath, they form a shining circle, which is larger the further the floor is from the opening. There, they are seen to equal the width of the solar globe, if they fall at a distance from the opening equal to the distance they flowed down from the sun. This happens in our own eyes. For those [rays] which are compressed into a narrow space in the pupil are led from the pupil into the soul; and in the soul itself, they fulfill the magnitude of the sun, where the magnitude of the sun is truly judged. From this it appears that the soul is as far distant from the eyes as the solar orb stands above the eye. 

Therefore, in heaven—<margin>f</margin> according to the Egyptians—the mind is also celestial, for it stands above earthly eyes just as much as the heaven does. Likewise, the influx of <term>Ideas</term><note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the physical world.</note> sent down from higher minds into bodies becomes the narrowest from the widest; while through use they turn out entirely particular, once they are reflected from bodies back into the human soul, they receive their original amplitude. From this, they clearly show that the human mind is almost as remote from bodies as the superior minds are. Therefore, since it is as separate from mortal things as the divine minds are, it exists as equally immortal. Especially since it restores forms from eternity to time, and restores the parts of time all the way back to eternity.

# Fourth reason. That the soul may become more blessed.
# Chapter 4.

<margin>B</margin>
**F**urthermore, the descent of the soul into the body contributes to the soul's own blessedness. For if someone were of a duller wit and always healthy in body, he would not know how much value should be placed on good health. He must eventually fall ill, so that by that comparison at least he may recognize the price of health, and having recovered his health, he may enjoy it more sweetly. The human soul, in comparison to all other minds, needs this "collision" <note>original: "obtrusione" - literally a thrusting against or bruising, implying the soul's contact with the physical world.</note> for a full judgment of the greatest things. Therefore, having been tossed by the storms of the world, it will predict more rightly here—and discern more sharply there—how quiet and sweet a harbor is found in God. It will cling more intensely and enjoy Him more sweetly. 

<margin>D</margin>
Indeed, <term>Plotinus</term><note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> seems to approve of this reasoning in no small way. But <term>Porphyry</term><note>A student of Plotinus who edited his works and wrote extensively on the soul's journey.</note> says it most of all: he says that the soul, having experienced these evils more often, finally clings entirely to the Parent [God], never to return to these things again. Perhaps God himself ordained that divine joys should fall to the higher ranks of minds by their very nature, but should be acquired by the lower ranks through labors. Thus, there would be those who are made blessed by being born, and those who make themselves blessed by living. Neither should the sublime spirits be esteemed more than they are when they obtain bliss from another source [nature], nor should the lower spirits be despised, since they themselves are the authors of their own bliss. 

What if the <margin>F</margin> angels, for instance—who are more remote from time—attained blessedness in a single moment through a sudden turning toward God as soon as they were created? We, however, achieve a similar happiness through a longer circuit. That which is lacking in our nature is repaid by our <term>industry</term><note>In this context, "industry" (industria) refers to purposeful human effort, study, and moral labor.</note>. And while the endurance of honest and pious labor compensates for the weakness of our origin, we equal the angelic excellence in a certain way, and we equal their rewards. Thus, four grades are found in "the Good": God has His good from Himself alone. Physical things have it from another alone. The angel and the soul have it not only from another (because from God), but also from themselves (because they provide the good for themselves). But the angel does this by an eternal act, the soul by a temporal one. Nor should we wonder that the soul can not only depart toward the extreme of evil, like the miserable, but can also progress toward the highest good, like the angels. For we give it free movement, which has its limit nowhere except in the infinite.

# Fifth reason. That the lower powers of the soul proceed to their effect. Chapter 5.

<margin>K</margin>
<margin>A H</margin>
**I**n addition, this dwelling [in the body] is conducive not only to reason and the mind, as we have explained, but also to those three lower powers of the soul: <term>phantasia</term><note>The "phantasia" was considered the faculty that stores and processes sensory images; the bridge between raw sensation and abstract thought.</note>, sense, and the power of nutrition. It is necessary that these be in the soul no less than the mind and reason.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul's experience of the physical world, including suffering and labor, actually enhances its eventual eternal happiness through contrast and personal effort. He compares the mind's ability to perceive the vast sun to an optical lens, suggesting the soul is inherently celestial and immortal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's relationship with the body, specifically why an eternal soul would "descend" into a temporary, physical form. He is transitioning from an optical analogy of light to a discussion of the soul's different powers and its "ethereal" or "astral" vehicle.</meta>

### Platonic Book

...if indeed it holds the middle ground between angels and beasts. That power is indeed empty and immense which never proceeds into action. For regarding the three powers <note>In the Platonic tradition, the soul's lower powers—the vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative—require a physical body to operate, unlike the higher intellect.</note>, there is no action without a body; or at least, action does not begin without a body—specifically a terrestrial body—without which they cannot perform their operations either individually or as a whole. Add to this what <margin>A</margin> **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated and admired.</note> says: the soul clearly perceives its own powers and nature through its actions, and unless all its actions are brought forth, the soul will not perfectly know itself or its own perfection. Since these powers are entirely mobile and temporal, it is only right that their acts and effects should operate for a certain time. Because that which acts temporally upon temporal things must operate for a time, a body of this kind is given to it for a duration. But since the operation of the mind and its follower, reason, can be continuous toward perpetual objects, they rightly operate perpetually with the other three powers remaining at leisure. <margin>B</margin> But for what reason is the soul’s habitation here so brief? **Plotinus** answers: So that, having laid down its burden <note>original: "sarcina," literally a soldier's pack or bundle of luggage.</note> more quickly, it may set out for better things. A short age suffices to fulfill these duties for whose sake the soul comes here. But in what way is it fitting for an eternal soul to now descend to the lands and now ascend? And, as if playing a game, to be now in the body and now outside the body? Perhaps it is as **Plotinus** thinks: there is no need for the soul to be moved in place or time through descent and ascent for these duties. For just as it is born from God above place and time—which are the sufferings of the body—so it remains outside the limits of place and time. It proceeds from God no differently than the whole of light from the sun is everywhere through the air. <margin>C</note> I believe **Plotinus** learned this from the Egyptians <note>Ficino often linked Platonic thought to ancient Egyptian wisdom, which he believed was part of a "perennial philosophy."</note>, who think that the soul, according to its essence, is a participant in the immense presence of God; since, according to its power and operation, it is a participant in the immense intelligence and divine will through an unending intuition of unending truth and an affection for goodness. Therefore, according to them, it should not be said that the soul now sits here and then passes there, but rather that it now gives life to the earth and later does not—just as light, not changed in place, now illuminates an open eye but does not illuminate a closed one.

But let them see to this themselves. To what end is this game of granting life to the body and taking it away? I believe we have said enough: it gives life so that it may fulfill those duties we have described; it takes it away so that it may not be vacant from better duties for too long due to the service of viler works. And just as the stars rise and set to our eyes to fulfill the duty enjoined upon them by God; and just as many spirits <term>demons</term><note>In this context, "demons" refers to *daemons*—spiritual intermediaries or guiding spirits—not necessarily evil entities.</note>, having often fashioned new bodies, now present themselves to our eyes and now withdraw; so the souls of men appear at times in bodies and at other times lie hidden. <margin>D</margin> Here a triple level of appearance is shown: The souls of the stars show themselves to the eyes of men always and continuously, though to different people at different times. The souls of the following spirits [show themselves] always, but not continuously—always, because they do this in every age; not continuously, because they pause. Our souls show themselves neither always nor continuously. But if it is not against nature for something to descend from sublime bodies every moment to lower things and then ascend again—like the rays of the stars and flames—it is also not against nature for some of the sublime spirits to, as it were, descend and ascend here daily. <margin>E</margin> Likewise, it seems agreeable to the Platonists that just as angelic lives are always separate from bodies, but blessed lives are never separate, there are two middle paths here: first, the happier souls, which are always partly separate and partly joined without any hindrance to action; and then the less happy ones, which are sometimes segregated and sometimes <margin>F</margin> joined—joined, I say, to an elemental body <note>The "elemental body" is the physical body made of earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, which in a way hinders intellectual action. The Platonists say these souls always possess an <term>ethereal body</term><note>Also known as the "astral body," a subtle, celestial vehicle that the soul inhabits between its divine state and its physical incarnation.</note>. <margin>G</margin> Among Christians, however, they will finally possess such a body forever <note>Ficino is reconciling the Platonic "ethereal vehicle" with the Christian doctrine of the "glorified body" at the Resurrection.</note>. This is because the Platonists think that not only our souls, but also the proper souls of many spirits, change bodies at certain times. Truly, they believe that divine goodness now pours itself out into other things, and then turns those other things back to itself. Hence, souls have the power to rule bodies, and hence they betake themselves to incorporeal things.

<summary>Ficino argues that the soul occupies a middle ground between angels and animals, using its physical body as a temporary tool for specific actions while remaining essentially linked to the divine. He compares the soul's presence in the body to light hitting an eye, suggesting the "descent" is more about a change in activity than a physical movement through space.</summary>

# Theology

...bear them; and those things which can perfectly do both <note>That is, maintain a relationship with both the spiritual and the physical realms simultaneously.</note> at the same time do not change bodies. <margin>D</margin> If, however, they are otherwise disposed, they deservedly exchange them. Here arises that common disbelief: "How is this? The dead do not return; they are not seen; they do nothing." The **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, particularly regarding the immortality and migration of the soul.</note> indeed think that they return under other forms. But in truth, what is the need for a veteran and retired soldier <note>original: "emeritus miles," a soldier who has completed his service and is entitled to rest.</note> to return to the fight? If a return to the battle were according to nature, everyone would surely return. If it is against nature, do not seek the return of anyone. It is certainly against nature to return unnecessarily, if it was according to the laws of providence for those who have fulfilled their duty to depart from here. The sphere of fire often ignites a flame in the air. <margin>E</margin> A little later, the flame returns to its sphere. Do not seek a more frequent descent of that flame. That perpetual circuit within its sphere is natural to it. It is against nature to descend again. And although the soul, by the nature of the <term>Third Essence</term> <note>Ficino defines the Soul as the "Third Essence," the middle link in the five-step hierarchy of reality: God, Angel, Soul, Quality, and Matter.</note>, looks toward both—the corporeal and the incorporeal—like a two-faced **Janus** <note>The Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, yet because a broader providence belongs to higher minds and a narrower one to lower ones, and our soul is the lowest of all those <note>Meaning it is the lowest of the rational spirits compared to angels or celestial souls.</note>, a very narrow providence is suited to it. For this reason, it rules a celestial body for a short time, and a terrestrial one for a short time. And when it looks upon the corporeal and the incorporeal equally, it performs each duty of the Third Essence moderately. This happens in this life. But when, after this life, its attention dwells upon incorporeal things because of its purity, then it looks upon corporeal things more negligently; or, if because of impurity it is submerged in the lowest bodies, then it is deprived of the authority of human <margin>G</margin> governance. Indeed, since human life is the middle ground between the divine and the bestial, while the soul acts in the middle, it also touches both extremes. When it declines toward one of the extremes—which it indeed begins to do even now and fulfills later when it has departed—it touches the middle ground only slightly and the other extreme <margin>H</margin> not at all. But why are the souls of the dead not seen? You do not see God, or angels, or the air; yet you do not deny they exist because of this. Why do they not do anything? God does all things. The angels act. You do not notice their actions, just as you do not see them. What prevents souls, already released from the chains of earthly bodies, from moving an <term>ethereal or airy body</term> <note>The "astral vehicle" or "spiritus," a subtle body that the soul inhabits between its earthly life and its return to the stars.</note> that is invisible to our eyes? What prevents them from daily prompting our reason and imagination with thoughts, visions, and signs? We, however, are sometimes ignorant of where these things come from. For often the movements of invisible things are themselves invisible. <margin>L</margin> **Abenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous Arab physician from Al-Andalus.</note>, the son of **Abumaruan**, the Arab physician, writes that he received the best remedy for his own ailing eye from a recently deceased physician through a dream. Many things of this kind happen to us daily. <margin>M</margin> **Plato**, in the ninth book of the *Laws*, relates that the souls of those who have been killed often pursue their killers with hostility. From this, it perhaps happens that the wound of a slain man—even while the corpse is lying there—throws out blood again if the one who had wounded him stands nearby looking at the wound itself. **Lucretius** <note>A Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher; it is notable that Ficino cites him here to support a supernatural phenomenon.</note> affirms that this sometimes happens, and judges have observed it. **Posidonius the Stoic** <margin>N</margin> confirms **Plato’s** opinion with the story of two **Arcadians**, close friends, who had come to **Megara**. One turned aside to an innkeeper, the other to a host. When they had rested after dinner, the one who was at the host's house saw the other in a dream during the night, praying for help because a plot for his death was being prepared by the innkeeper. Terrified by the dream, he first got up. Then, when he had collected himself and decided the vision should be considered worthless, he lay back down. Then, as he slept, the same man appeared to him, asking that since he had not helped him while alive, he should at least not allow his death to go unavenged: he said he had been killed by the innkeeper, cast into a wagon, and covered with dung. He asked his friend to be at the gate in the morning before the wagon left the town. Moved by this in his sleep, the friend was ready at the gate for the plowman in the morning. He asked what was in the wagon. Terrified, the man fled. The dead man was dug out. The innkeeper, having been exposed, paid the penalty. Some of the **Stoics** conclude from this that the souls of the departed are also mindful of favors, as when **Simonides** <note>A Greek lyric poet; according to legend, he buried an unknown corpse and was later warned by the man's ghost not to sail on a doomed ship.</note> had taken care of a certain unknown person...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding the interaction between the living and the dead, specifically addressing why the souls of the departed remain relevant to the world of the living and how the universe is populated with rational beings to ensure constant worship of the Creator.</meta>

<header>Book of Platonic Philosophy</header>
<sig>a i</sig>

...had seen a dead body cast out; and after he had buried it, and was intending to board a ship, he seemed to be warned by the very man he had provided with burial not to do it. If he had sailed, he would have perished in a shipwreck. Simonides returned. The others were shipwrecked. All these things teach us that the souls of the deceased exert some influence over us.

### Sixth Reason. So that the world might be adorned and God might be worshipped. Chapter VI.

<margin>a</margin> But to conclude the previous discussion with a fitting end: the divine craftsman <note>original: "artifex," referring to God as the Architect of the Universe</note> willed the work of the world to be as similar to himself as possible. Such a work is most perfect if it is full of reason everywhere. Certainly, just as reason exists within God—being both uniform <margin>M</margin> and multiform at once—so in His handiwork He willed there to be one universal rational soul, and many individual souls belonging to that one. That is to say: one soul for the whole sphere of the universe, and many souls for the many individual spheres. And because any given sphere imitates the whole, He placed many souls in each individual sphere as well. Thus, just as a larger sphere contains a smaller sphere, so does a greater soul <margin>n</margin> contain lesser souls. Indeed, He established that there are at least as many other souls in the highest realm as there are stars; since each star imitates its own sphere, they each revolve around their own center, and they have been assigned their own proper movers for their own motions. For it is probable that those stars have their own lives beyond the life of the general sphere, especially if they are more excellent bodies than those of earthly animals, which have obtained lives of their own. <margin>B</margin> Know then that each of the celestial souls has its own intellectual motion centered on things that can be understood <note>original: "intelligibilia," the spiritual or platonic forms</note>, and a common "animal" motion centered on bodily things, shared with the universal soul of the sphere. These twin motions of the souls are followed by twin motions in the stars: one that is their own, and one that is shared. In this way, the smaller planetary spheres imitate the larger ones, because they similarly contain many rational souls, which have both a common condition in fate and a unique condition within themselves. Therefore, in every sphere of the world, beyond the common soul of each sphere, God established many rational living beings, as we have argued elsewhere. For this reason, it was necessary for there to be such beings in the middle seat of the world <note>the Earth</note> as well, so that there would be a great multitude of rational beings in all its members. This multitude adorns and worships this temple of God, and sings to and praises God the craftsman. Other minds do this in the higher spheres. Human

---

minds do this on earth. Nor shall this heart <note>original: "pectus," literally "chest" or "breast," used here as the seat of the soul and intellect</note> be mortal in the future, for it assiduously resonates with the eternal name of God. No one should lose heart because of this, or doubt that there are many inhabitants in the spheres of the planets simply because only a single planet is seen in each of them. Rather, because the number of inhabitants always increases as one descends from the summit (as the **Platonists** <note>Ficino refers to the school of Neoplatonists who believed in a hierarchy of being</note> believe), one soul—the soul of the sphere itself—is sufficient for the two or so stars in the highest heaven. But since more inhabitants live in the individual circles of the planets than in the highest heaven, and these are of a lower order, there is a need for more leaders. Therefore, God established two leaders in each: the soul of the sphere and the soul of the planet. These inhabitants are called angelic, demonic, heroic <note>original: "herotica," likely a variation of "heroica," referring to semi-divine beings or "heroes" in the Greek sense</note> animals, <margin>C</margin> and finally humans, composed of a rational soul and a body fitting for their sphere. Yet they are not seen, because they are either less bright or less solid than the stars and planets. Nor is this surprising, since the very spheres in which they exist are also not seen. They follow their planet in nature, motion, and name, just as the planet follows its sphere and soul, and the sphere follows the soul of the universe. Finally, they conclude: if there are many rational beings in the spheres at both extremes of the world, it is right that there are many in the middle ones as well. We, in turn, conclude that if God adorned the surrounding spheres with divine minds, He rightly adorned the middle one with divine minds as well. Nor should the habitation of the Earth be despised; it is the middle choir of the divine temple. It is the stable foundation of all the spheres. Nor should it be thought little of that the other spheres revolve around it as if around a hinge. What of the fact that the rays of all the celestial bodies, flowing together into the Earth, are mixed here, and their powers achieve a marvelous union? What of the fact that the face of the green earth, like a varied sky, is wrapped in three transparent bodies: water, air, and fire? Here, the rays of the stars are reflected and gathered in splendor. Therefore, if you were positioned on the moon and looked out at this globe from there, it would perhaps seem to you just as the moon now appears to you from the earth; and you would think that those who live here are celestial beings, and that they inhabit some star.

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe is a "divine temple" populated by a hierarchy of rational souls—from angels to humans—who exist to praise the Creator, asserting that Earth is a noble, celestial-like center where all heavenly influences converge.</summary>

# ->Theology<-

---

<margin>D</margin>...to inhabit. Therefore, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for their belief in a mathematical and harmonious universe.</note> called the globe of the earth—wrapped in water, air, and its own fire as if in its own veils—a single sphere of the world and a kind of star. **And Plato** calls the earth the oldest goddess of all the gods who exist within the heavens. **He adds** that vast regions of the earth are inhabited that are much higher than ours, where stones, metals, plants, and animals are far more excellent and beautiful than ours. **Where** very wealthy men live and are happily nourished by moderate food—since it is of the highest value—and by pleasant scents.

<margin>E</margin>**Add to this** what **Diodorus** and **Pliny** <note>Diodorus Siculus and Pliny the Elder, famous ancient historians and naturalists.</note> relate: that in some places men are nourished by soil and scent alone. **Certainly** that thing is wonderful which **Olympiodorus the Platonist** writes: that **Aristotle** saw a man who never slept and lived solely on air exposed to the sun's rays. **Nor** are those things much different from the idea that in the divine gardens, as if in the Elysian Fields <note>The ancient Greek version of paradise.</note>, men could have lived immortally just by tasting the tree of life.

**But** let us return to the established order. <margin>F</margin>**Timaeus** <note>Referring to the speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the universe.</note>, imitating **Moses**, says: in the beginning God created the fiery heaven and the earth as the principal members of the world; and so that he might bind these two more aptly together, he soon placed air and water between them, as if they were created not for their own sake, but for the sake of the others. **If** it were permitted to converse a little more broadly with our ancients—as we often do—I would indeed report that the principal and proper nature of fire is light rather than heat. **First**, because light is more divine. **Second**, because it acts more quickly. **Third**, it spreads itself most widely. **Fourth**, it is not like heat, which remains behind in a heated object when the fire is gone; **instead**, as a quality most proper to fire and mixed with nothing else, it follows its own fire everywhere. **Fifth**, because the more fire is mixed with foreign solidity, the more it seethes and the less it shines. **On the contrary**, insofar as it is restored to its own purity, it burns less and shines more. **To what purpose** is this? So that we may understand that heaven is fire, <margin>G</margin> whose proper nature is indeed to shine in actuality and to be hot in potentiality. Thus it can be said, not without merit, that celestial fire is light, whose heating power is harmful to no one of itself, but is gentle and health-giving to all.

**Hence** also the ethereal fire under the moon, following the celestial pattern in some way, does not consume the air closest to it. **However**, that power which in the highest fire is only health-giving and gentle, becomes biting—so to speak—in the lower fire, which differs in species from the higher. <margin>a</margin>**From this** it follows, either because it is mixed with earthly roughness—whence it burns more vehemently in more solid and drier material—or because it is driven by a certain reflection, and as if suffering violence, it also inflicts violence. **Therefore**, in freer air, fire is gentle to everything it touches; but between struck concavities, it strikes; and being reflected more violently by a concave mirror, it also reflects back more violently itself. **Although** the whole heaven is described chiefly through fire, yet the other elements are also joined to it, but in a celestial manner. **Therefore** fire prevails everywhere in heaven. **But** elsewhere it is combined with a certain celestial solidity of earth. **This** is evident in the more manifest stars, which, because they resist the rays of our eyes with a certain solidity, are clearly discerned even though they are very remote.

**Elsewhere**, indeed, fire flourishes with a certain celestial property of water joined to it, especially in the Milky Way <note>original: "orbe lacteo," the Milky Circle</note>; and therefore stars appear there insofar as the nature of water allows. **Finally**, fire reigns throughout with a certain airy transparency added. **By which** it results that in most spheres it is not seen, as long as it does not resist the eyes due to its own and the air's nature. **That** certain natures of the elements are in heaven, all astrologers confess. <margin>b</margin>**Hence** the Elysian fields among the poets. **Here** also that verse: **Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.** <note>original: "Beati mites: quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram," Matthew 5:5</note> **Hence also David and Moses** describe waters poured through the celestial regions. **Again**, to what purpose is this? So that we may conclude: if the elements are found in heaven in a certain celestial manner, then in turn celestial things can similarly be found in the elements in an elemental condition. **Most especially** <margin>c</margin> in the globe of the earth, which is the other foundation of the world besides heaven; in which, although earth prevails (just as fire does in heaven), yet water, air, and fire are added just as in heaven. **Finally**, fire is above the moon, and below...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's relationship with the physical world, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of providence and how the human soul, though divine, interacts with the "dregs" of the material Earth.</meta>

# ->The Platonic Book<-

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, earth reigns everywhere. And even near the center of the world itself, through the earthly gaps, rivers of fire, air, and water flow in every direction. For this reason, it should seem a wonder to no one that celestial souls are sent down to earthly things, and in turn, the foreign inhabitants of the earth are sometimes sent back to celestial things. Finally, whatever the earth may be, man is its lord. He is even a god on the lands. Nor should the human soul be thought less divine because it is surrounded by a fragile body; rather, it is most divine for this reason: that even in the dregs of the earth—if indeed the earth is considered base—it carries out such divine works against the nature of the place and the burden of the body, so that while it governs lower things, <margin>B</margin> it does not depart from higher ones. 

¶ All Platonists, with whom **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian who heavily integrated Neoplatonic philosophy into his works.</note> agrees, judge that the natural duty of divine minds is this: that they remain in their own nature; that they go forth by providing and acting; that they turn themselves back by recognizing themselves and their own origin; and that they turn back the things that follow them. Therefore, the soul, as a divine thing, fulfills these three tasks according to its strength. And it is drawn to this governance of lower things not so much by an amorous affection due to affinity as by a certain inborn zeal for providence due to the excellence of its nature. For all the most excellent things, by an exuberance of intimate perfection, propagate themselves most widely. <margin>C</margin> And as **Plotinus** <note>The 3rd-century philosopher who founded Neoplatonism; he viewed the universe as a series of emanations from "the One."</note> says: the Good itself, through poured-out splendor, procreates the Intellect. The Intellect also, while it unfolds the soul, expresses the rational soul. The soul itself, propagating itself, produces life and corporeal form. 

Hence **Dionysius the Areopagite** says: "Surely the divine unity, united to all things, in turn unites all things while it gathers into one those things which are equal among themselves through a similarity of quality by a certain mutual consent. But it turns lower things toward higher things through a desire for enjoyment because of their indigence. It bends higher things toward lower things through a zeal for providing, by which they imitate divine providence." 

<margin>D</margin> The Platonists argue that rational souls imitate divine providence in four ways. In the first grade they place the **World Soul** <note>Original: "anima mundi"; the concept of an intrinsic spirit that animates all nature in the universe.</note>, in which there is a universal providence over the world under God, through which all things are bestowed upon all. In the second grade are the souls of the twelve spheres <note>In ancient cosmology, the heavens were divided into rotating spheres carrying the planets and stars.</note>, in which there is a further particular providence, through which they distribute certain things to all worldly matters. In the third grade are the souls both of the stars and of whatever spirits <note>Original: "numinum"; refers to divine powers or guiding spirits of the spheres.</note> reign in any sphere of the world. Among these, they judge there is a further particular providence through which they bestow individual things upon certain members of the world, since they are fitting for them. In the fourth and final grade are particular souls: those, namely, which recur from the intelligible realm to the sensible realm and back again. They believe the providence of these is so particular that they now impart some things only to some people. Furthermore, they fulfill through many courses of time those things which superior beings accomplish in fewer periods, and which the first being completes in a single circuit. 

Certainly **Plotinus** and **Proclus** <note>A late antique Greek philosopher who systematized Neoplatonist thought.</note> <margin>E</margin> argue: just as one circuit of the world embraces many—those of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, and others in succession—so the one innermost circuit of the World Soul through its spheres contains many circuits of particular souls. Indeed, since a more sublime soul performs a longer orbit around intelligible things, an inferior one performs a shorter one. I have been rather lengthy in reciting these things because the Platonists believe that through these points especially, both those things in this chapter and those touched upon in the preceding chapter are explained and confirmed. But they themselves shall see to such matters. For me, let it suffice to have narrated them.

### Third question. For what reason are souls, if they are divine, affected by disturbances? Chapter 6.

<margin>F</margin> He asked thirdly: for what reason are souls, if they are divine, subject to disturbances? But no one would ever wonder at this if we also considered that no mind has been assigned a body more burdensome than the human one. Indeed, the minds of the spheres, stars, and more sublime spirits <note>Original: "demonum"; in this context, it refers to high spiritual beings or "daemons" in the Greek sense, not evil entities.</note> preside over simple bodies. These consist so much in their own unity of similar parts that nothing of themselves flows out. Therefore, it is not necessary that anything new flow in. Again, by a natural agility, they incline toward motion so that they live and are moved by the lightest nod of those minds.

# Theology

<margin>$\clubsuit$</margin> On the contrary, the human body is composed of four warring elements: water and earth; and it is slowed down by the weight of the earth. Because of the disagreement between its parts, it dissolves at almost every moment; it falls due to its weight; it is slow to move toward life and spirit. Because of this internal conflict in which the humors <note>original: "humores". In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) were the bodily fluids that needed to be balanced for health.</note> expel one another, something is always flowing out of the body. And again, work is needed so that something flows back in. Therefore, to reconcile, move, and restore a body of this kind, the most intense attention of our soul is required. This brings us back to that **Platonic** saying.

<margin>B</margin> Sublime bodies approach sublime souls. Lower souls approach bodies because, clearly, the former yield most easily to the latter. Not so for these [human souls], which yield with great difficulty. ¶ If any of those higher minds were enclosed in our body for a decade, it would perhaps be fatigued by the burden and troubled by care no less than our soul; and we would doubt its divinity, just as we now doubt our own.

<margin>C</margin> But someone will say: the soul of the world <note>original: "mudi anima". The *Anima Mundi*, a concept from Plato's Timaeus describing an intrinsic spirit that brings life and order to the universe.</note> has a body composed of the four opposing elements, yet it is not fatigued by that care as our soul is by our body. This is clearly true. But the elements themselves, which are the members of the world's body, are not merely parts of other elements, but whole and entire elements; they are not outside their natural places, but each is arranged in its own region. They are not confused with each other everywhere, but are separated into their own seats. They are not subject to external bodies. For there is no body outside the world. Conversely, the fire in our body is not the whole of fire, but some part of a larger whole. So it is with the other three. Therefore, the elements of this body are fractured. They are also outside their own proper places; for this reason, the fire and air within us always flee toward the heights, while water and earth fall toward the depths. It is very difficult to make imperfect things perfect, to reconcile warring things, or to keep bodies outside their natural place. Moreover, those four elements are mixed within us in every tiny particle of the body. As a result, the fight rages more violently

<margin>B</margin> everywhere; in the world, however, they are distinguished in various places; they rest in a somewhat more peaceful way. ¶ There are also many huge things outside us which, threatening us from all sides, afflict the body. The soul of the world is not weighed down by these burdens and labors. Nor are the souls of the elements, for whatever approaches or leaves their bodies has scarcely the weight of a single atom. Restoration is also expected from every side, nor does the natural harmony ever disagree—that harmony, I say, of the spheres <note>The Pythagorean and Platonic concept that the movement of celestial bodies produces a divine, mathematical music or harmony.</note> which leads to health. But not even those souls, however divine, can restrain the force of the spheres to such an extent that the parts of the elements and composite bodies do not devour and destroy each other. Eruptions of fire and water often disturb the world. Yet qualities of this conflicting kind could not be produced and guided by heaven in any way unless their powers were in it. Nor would they be in heaven unless they were in the movers and the creator of the heavens. But in God, they are a single form, distinct only by reason; in angels, however, they are further distinguished by forms. In souls, they are further distinguished by motion and time. In heaven, they are distinguished by place and power simultaneously. Finally, below heaven, they are distinguished by effect and conflict. Why all this? So we may understand that the souls of the elemental spheres do not have such great power that they can moderate and reconcile qualities—which do not fight each other in heaven—in such a way that they do not fight and kill each other below heaven. There are those who say that the celestial substance reconciles them by its excellence. But matter, which is beneath the elements, is shapeless, unstable, and ineffective; it can neither contain them all at once nor reconcile them. However it may be, it appears that the souls of the elements, if they have souls, cannot pacify them all at once. Even the soul of the world cannot do this. So it is no wonder that our souls labor so much in tempering the humors and are "out of tune" in this region of dissonance. In every way, a government that is both easier and happier has been assigned to the higher souls. But if our soul were in charge of the rudders of the world's body, as that soul is, perhaps it would be directed with the same ease as that one is.

It contrasts the chaotic "region of dissonance" on Earth with the perfect harmony of the celestial spheres.</summary>

<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Platonic

...would provide. But some divine minds also had to be sent into the particles of the earth, so that the King of the World <note>A common Neoplatonic reference to God or the Demiurge.</note> would be celebrated no less in the parts of the earth than in the heavens and all the elements. <margin>A</margin> This destiny fell to our souls. Hippocrates writes that sudden changes—especially those to the opposite state—bring about the greatest and most lasting diseases. Plato, however, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, considers that the soul, falling into the body, rushes suddenly from the highest light into extreme darkness. Thus, it is no wonder that the soul remains blind for a long time and is troubled. Proclus <note>original: "Proculus". Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a massive commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> argues in his commentary on the *Timaeus* that its disturbance increases because it falls from unity into a discordant multitude, and from a state of stability into a change devoid of almost all rest. Wherefore it is always distracted, and as if affected by vertigo, it staggers and wavers. Nor does its own "vital shadow," naturally handed over to the body, allow it to emerge easily from so many waves and storms. Therefore, it is affected by a vehement love for the body, as if for its own offspring; and as the body suffers daily, the soul also suffers with it in its own way. Perhaps, as long as the soul does not notice itself, it thinks it is nothing other than a shadow appearing openly in the river of the body—just as Plato teaches in the seventh book of the *Republic*. And no differently, troubled by this shadow, the soul also troubles itself; just as if ignorant children, seeing their shadows blurred in the water, were to lament heavily.

<margin>B</margin> The Platonists place such an order among souls: Some, namely the divine or "proper" souls, never descend into generation <note>original: "generationem". In Platonic thought, "generation" refers to the physical world of birth, decay, and change, as opposed to the eternal world of Being.</note> (that is, the generable body). Others do indeed descend into generation, moving from a better life to one less good, yet in such a way that they are never infected by it nor undergo any evil; these are counted among the daemons <note>original: "demones". In the Greek sense, *daimones* are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and heroes. Others descend and are immediately, in a way, corrupted; but they can be purified again and return to better things. They add that in the highest souls, no vice is found either in essence or in action. But in the lowest "shadows" of souls, vice is found in both. In our [human] souls, however, action can indeed be corrupted, but the essence never is.

# Book

<margin>C</margin> Many think the difficulty of human life is further increased because the motion and habit of the soul—insofar as it is intellectual and rational—ought to be a circuit <note>original: "circuitus". Neoplatonists believed that the highest form of motion was circular, representing the intellect returning to its source.</note>. The motion and shape of its ethereal vehicle <note>original: "etheri vehiculi". The *pneuma* or "astral body" that carries the soul down from the stars into the physical body.</note> is also similar [to a circle]. But in a composite body, while the soul is animating, sensing, and moving forward, it undergoes a straight motion, setting aside its circular path. The vehicle is also compelled to change its motion and shape. And even if it is not destroyed in its substance (because, as some think, it lacks matter), <margin>a</margin> it is nevertheless troubled in its shape and habits. These it will only recover when the mind is first raised toward its "head"—that is, the intellect—and is restored to its proper habit. This habit it seems to have lost entirely for a long time, <margin>E</margin> because through intemperance it fixes its "head" (the mind) to the ground, while it raises its "feet" (the lower powers of the soul) high. No habit more deformed or laborious than this can be imagined.

<margin>D</margin> But why was an airy body not given to us, in which we might inhabit the earth and more freely contemplate celestial things? <margin>cn</margin> Because airy spirits <note>Daemons or angels inhabiting the element of Air.</note> are already present there. If the earth were left this way, it would be empty. And if simple bodies [the elements] are not without reason, then composite earthly bodies must also possess reason. Thus, this corporeal world is made entirely rational, just like that spiritual world in whose image this one was made: the whole of it is Reason.

Furthermore, that Best Father [God] willed that his priests <note>A metaphor for souls, who serve as "priests" of the divine within the temple of the universe.</note> who sing to him in the higher spheres should remain there always as the same individuals, because due to the happiness of that place, they lead their lives there without labor. <margin>E</margin> On earth, however, he did not want his priests to endure long delays, because perpetual or long labor is not owed to those who diligently praise God. Therefore, he sends them here daily and recalls them. Thus, through a succession of souls on earth, that which happens as a single eternal life in the heavens may happen always here too. I pass over the fact that many think the bodies of daemons and heroes in the air, though they change slowly, eventually change for the better. However that may be, it seems our soul has a more burdensome body than other minds, and therefore it is sometimes more anxious than others.

# Theology

<margin>A</margin> ...may be prohibited from contemplating. Why, then, does man have a more **fragile body** than the beasts? It is not because he has a more fragile body that he should be thought less divine. On the contrary, it is precisely because he is more divine that he has a more fragile body. We have argued elsewhere that our body is the most temperate <term>temperate: the ideal medical balance of the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness)</term> of all earthly things, and most similar to heaven. This is so that it may offer a more peaceful service to the duties of the celestial mind. This very temperance, however, is necessarily followed by weakness. In a <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio". The physiological makeup or temperament of a person based on their humors.</note> in which heat exceeds by too much, the body is hardly harmed by heat or cold. For an immense internal heat overcomes milder external heats, so that by comparison they barely appear, and it breaks the force of cold. Likewise, if cold excels in some complexion, any coldness applied from without is not felt, and the body easily tolerates heat. It is similar where moisture or dryness prevails. But in a body where the four qualities are moderate and <margin>C</margin> mixed in a harmonious tempering, whatever new quality arrives from the outside forces one of those four qualities to exceed its limit. When it exceeds, the harmony of the previous complexion perishes, and the natural state is dissipated. Therefore, because it was necessary for man to have the most temperate complexion of all earthly things, yet such a balance is harmed by even the smallest offenses, it followed that the nature of the human body would be weak. 

Yet the diligent industry of our arts comes to the aid of this weakness, through which it happens that our temperance persists longer against the storms of the world. For the <margin>D</margin> divine architect balanced all things in such a way that in beasts, along with a weakness of soul, he gave physical gifts of higher value. In us, however, he compensates for the weakness of the body with the strengths of the mind. And so he signifies that the souls of beasts are destined for the death of the body, but our souls are dedicated to the perpetual life of the mind. 

<margin>G</margin> Yet these souls must always labor while outside their homeland. For a temperate complexion—which, as we said, is most natural to the human species—is compelled to fall into discord from every side for innumerable reasons, both from the birth of many and daily in every individual. Therefore, even if we notice it very little, there is a need here for continuous and most intense attention to restore the temperance of nature itself. 

<margin>E</margin> This is the hardest and perpetual labor of the <term>vegetative power</term> <note>original: "vegetatricis potentie". The faculty of the soul responsible for biological maintenance, growth, and nutrition.</note>. This labor not only does not relax much and <margin>F</margin> interrupts the focus of the mind—whence it is as if we do not use our minds—but it also affects us with many calamities and disturbances, agitating us like people dreaming. Indeed, while the soul works more strenuously in balancing these or those qualities, using its own appropriate <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of the "seeds" or blueprints within the soul that guide the formation of matter.</note> for these tasks, it stirs the senses. In the higher sense, it stirs images and affections pertaining specifically to those physical qualities. Thus, while <term>bile</term> <note>original: "bile". Yellow bile, associated with the choleric temperament.</note> is being handled, a tendency toward anger secretly arises. In the agitation of the blood, a vain joy. In <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita".</note>, weariness and laziness. In <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bile". Melancholy.</note>, fear and sorrow. Often indeed, such images and affections grow so strong that, with reason being entirely idle concerning such matters, insanity follows. 

Furthermore, in many people, while the soul strives to thin out a thicker <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus". A subtle vapor believed to link the body and the soul.</note>, it proves them to be very dull. While in others it strives to gather spirits that are too loose, it shows them to be unfit for the steadiness of contemplation and memory. If we say that a certain dryness of spirits "gathers the mind," we want it to be understood not that the dryness acts upon the mind, but that the mind does not have to labor in gathering the spirits. Whence it is forced to be diverted from contemplation. Finally, just as the external sense is offended when it deals with troublesome things, so too the internal sense—perceiving many internal offenses of the spirits brought on by various humors and causes—stirs up troublesome images and affections. 

<margin>B</margin> **E**nough has been said regarding the causes of this burdensome governance of the body. Regarding the vices of the soul, if we have said a little, something more must be added. Since the soul was created at the middle boundary between minds and bodies, it not only gasps after divine things but is also joined by natural providence and love to matter. In matter, through a certain shadowy communion of its own life, it disposes the animated body. It then loves this body as its own work and offspring. Natural love joined the soul to the body. Natural love detains it in the body. This same love daily urges the soul to the care of the body...

It details how the soul's constant labor to maintain this biological balance results in emotional disturbances like anger or sorrow based on the movement of humors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the soul and the body. Previously, the author argued that the human body's fragility is a result of its divine-like "temperance" or balance. Here, he explores why the soul chooses to inhabit such a fragile vessel and how it eventually frees itself.</meta>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

...provokes the body. I pass over what Plato approves in the *Laws* <margin>A</margin> and what Plotinus corroborates: that since the soul precedes the body and is its mistress, it does not possess a corporeal affection derived from the body; rather, <margin>B</margin> through such an affection of its own, it immerses itself into the body. This opinion certainly agrees with Zoroaster and, in a certain way, with Moses, who say that the evils of the body proceed from the faults of the soul. 

But however it may be, the soul indeed loves the body. Yet the burdensome and fragile nature of the body requires that the vital power of the soul sustain and move it with the greatest effort. And just as the senses and the imagination <term>imagination: the faculty of "phantasia," which acts as a bridge between physical sensations and abstract thought</term> constantly watch for what might benefit or harm the body, so the soul desires, fears, rejoices, and grieves for the body as if it were its own child. 

From the very beginning, three such powers undertake this kind of work. There is so much focus <note>original: "intentio". This refers to the concentration of the soul's energy on a specific task.</note> required because of the construction of the new body that there is almost no attention left in the soul for reason. Only when the body is fully grown and the senses are purged does the intensity of this work diminish. Truly, as soon as reason begins to wake up, it weakens the imagination—which has been strengthened in the soul by long habit—only with the greatest difficulty. Indeed, it is hard to resist either nature or habit. Yet one must fight not so much against a habit formed against nature, but against natural affections. Nevertheless, through diligent rational discipline, one finally achieves this. 

But in the meantime, reason itself—because of a natural kinship and its own foresight <term>foresight: "prudentia," the wisdom used to manage practical life</term>—loves those three lower powers like sisters or daughters. Therefore, it often complies with them. Those powers naturally take care of the body. Reason also, through them, inclines toward the body out of love. From this long-term inclination, it contracts a habit for itself of leaning more easily. We call this kind of habit a "vice"; <margin>C</margin> indeed, we even call it a kind of "death," so to speak. 

For just as happens in many species of animals: after the lower power has involved itself in the natural threads of building the body, the higher power often continues the work begun with a more solid web, and at last secretly shuts itself inside that very hard texture; it loses itself, not to rise again into the light until the hardened texture is broken. For this reason, the divine soul is not corrupted by the body, nor is it forced; rather, out of love for the animated body—which is its own work and an instrument born for it—the soul voluntarily <sig>☩</sig>

---

<margin>C</margin> casts itself down so that it may lift the body up to itself. Nor are there lacking among the Platonists those who say—Hermias <note>Hermias of Alexandria, a Neoplatonic commentator.</note> mentions some—that there are certain demons who favor generation and naturally increase the soul's inclination toward the body. 

Certainly, Plato in the book on the beautiful <note>Likely referring to the *Phaedrus* or the *Symposium*.</note> says, just as Moses does, that a certain demon from the beginning mixed pleasure with many of the lowest evils. I pass over what he says in his *Letters*: that a demon disturbed public goods. But we shall speak of these in what follows. 

Let us return meanwhile to the soul’s foresight. Since it is the property of all divine minds to gaze upon higher things and provide for lower ones, the same is also property of our soul. It cares for and cultivates not only its own body, but also the bodies of all earthly things and the body of the earth itself. But the more serious this foresight is—caring for things that are more fragile and more prone to disorder—the more it distracts the soul from contemplating higher things. <margin>D</margin> Yet not entirely. For in every age, through the intellect, we seek all truth; through the will, we love all good; and through our actions, we worship God, who is the true Good. 

These three duties of honor signify that the soul, even in the midst of so great a tempest of this sea, always looks up to celestial things; by looking at them, it is seized daily by a more vehement love for them. As it glows with this kind of love, the love for the body—through which the soul had been corrupted—gradually cools, and the stains of vice are wiped away. Therefore, the soul is never forced from elsewhere; rather, by love it merges into the body, and by love it emerges from the body. To this <margin>E</margin> that divine saying tends: *He who loves his soul in this world loses it. He who hates it here, receives it in eternal life.* <note>original: "Qui amat aiam suaz in hoc mundo pdit eā..." A reference to the Gospel of John 12:25 or Matthew 16:25.</note> 

But you may see what the soul becomes in this sea, as Socrates expresses it here in the tenth book of the *Republic*. Just as if someone saw the sea-god Glaucus, worn down and distorted by the waves over a long time, and covered over with rocks, seaweed, and oysters, he would think him a wild beast rather than a sea creature; so we, when we see souls distracted by and surrounded by earthly affections and habits, think we see something earthly rather than celestial. Truly, if we strip them bare and consider their purity and their love of divine things already from this sea...

<summary>This page explores how the soul voluntarily descends into the body out of love and "prudentia" (foresight), but becomes trapped by the habits of physical care like a creature encrusted in sea-growth. It emphasizes that the soul's return to the divine is achieved through intellectual and moral discipline, which cools its attachment to the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's relationship with the material world. While the previous page discussed the soul's voluntary immersion into the body, this section focuses on the external spiritual threats (demons) that exploit the soul's physical connection and the methods for overcoming these influences through spiritual and philosophical discipline.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>☝️</margin>...emerging. Without a doubt, we shall recognize that souls—because they are kindred to things divine and eternal—desire such things when they have first escaped pure; then they touch them and live in serene light, and through that habit they escape entirely into divinity. Thus far Socrates <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates discusses the soul's affinity for the eternal</note>. Therefore, when we say the soul is corrupted, we do not mean that it loses its own properties, but rather that it admits foreign things—that is, lower things—into itself. 

<margin>S</margin> Man does not lose his natural vice, but occupies it. But lest anyone should think our soul is corporeal for the reason that it seems to be infected daily by corporeal causes, <margin>F</margin> it is worth hearing the divine Apostle Paul crying out: "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against many throngs of demons" <note>original: "non esse nobis colluctationem adversus carnem et sanguinem...". A reference to Ephesians 6:12</note> who dwell among us in this misty air. 

The ancient theologians—both Origen and Augustine—confirm this: they believe these demons are clothed in an airy body, agile in motion, keen in sense, and endowed with a marvelous knowledge of things. <margin>D</margin> They believe they slip entirely into our own <term>airy spirit: the "pneuma" or "spiritus," a subtle substance acting as a bridge between the soul and the physical body</term> through their own airy bodies. And just as men are somewhat restricted by external signs—even the most skilled—when it comes to internal affections, so these most sagacious demons observe us not only through external signs, but even through the very movements of our spirits, which are frequently incited by the <term>imagination: phantasia, the faculty that creates mental images</term>. They daily lie in wait for more attentive notions and sharper affections, from which the spirits themselves are properly moved. 

Thus it happens that they know most precisely by which path they can more easily disturb each person. And being affected by a certain perturbation themselves, they daily trouble us. We believe the movement of this perturbation happens in this way: 

<margin>B</margin> The airy demons certainly move the airy spirit within us. When this is shaken, as it were, they move the <term>humors: the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine physical and mental health</term> in the body, and images are excited in the imagination. But in what manner? 

<margin>B</margin> In a sanguine body, by frequently stirring up the blood and images somewhat similar to it, they allure the soul to empty pleasures. In the choleric person, however, by irritating the bile and images corresponding to bile, they stir up rages and battles. But in the phlegmatic, while they increase the phlegm, they occupy us with sluggish images and lethargy. Finally, when they incite the black bile in the melancholic, they strike them with fears and sorrows. 

They terrify the imagination with false shadows. They frequently deceive the mind with false opinions. That all of this can be done by demons—especially by the incitement of black bile—is something Serapion and Avicenna <note>Serapion the Elder and Avicenna were influential medical authorities in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> relate according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers; and they themselves do not deny it. For it is not fitting that the divine mind should be so deceived and attacked by the senses in any other way than by demons striving toward that same end. Rather, it is conquered by the violence of ambitious demons out of such envy. 

The Platonists think this can be overcome through philosophy and sacrifices, as the Orphic hymns demonstrate to us. But Christ, the true physician of souls, commands that this be done through fasting and prayer. If it were permitted to explain the oracle of God himself philosophically, I would interpret "fasting" as abstinence from those things that either increase this or that humor, or move certain images and affections. I would explain "prayer" as such a vehement turning toward God that the soul does not notice the prods of demons, and the demons lose confidence that they can conquer a mind dedicated to God. 

But let us now conclude the discussion. Therefore, let no one say that the human soul is less divine because it is troubled in caring for the body, or because it is corrupted. For no harder province <note>task or duty</note> is assigned to our mind than to other celestial minds. Neither is the soul corrupted *by* the body; rather, it corrupts itself by loving the body too much, and it purifies itself. Nor should we think our divinity comes from God only because we live much more anxiously than the beasts. On the contrary, we are most divine for this reason: that while we are deprived for a time of our dwelling and heavenly homeland—that is, as long as we are God's vicars <note>representatives</note> on earth—we are continually troubled, even if we do not at all oppose this with a desire for the heavenly homeland. Nor can any earthly delights console the human mind in this exile, for it is desirous of better things.

<summary>This page explores how demons exploit the body's humors and the 'airy spirit' to disturb the soul with false images and passions. It concludes that the soul's earthly suffering is a sign of its divine nature and its longing for its true heavenly home, achievable through fasting and prayer.</summary>

# ¶ Fourth question. Why souls depart the body unwillingly. Chapter 8.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
**T**he fourth question proposed to us was this: if souls are celestial, why do they depart from the earth so unwillingly? First of all, not all depart unwillingly. For Theramenes, Theodorus, Lyreneus, Cleombrotus, and indeed all the followers of Hegesias the Cyrenaic <note>Hegesias of Cyrene was a philosopher known as the "Death-Persuader" because he argued that life has more pain than pleasure</note> departed voluntarily and most gladly. So too the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics</note> among the Indians, and the Getae, a people of Thrace, among whom they used to mourn at births and weep for the newborn; yet funerals were festive and celebrated with games and song as if they were sacred rites. I pass over the innumerable other soldiers, citizens, and religious philosophers. I pass over the first-fruits of the Christians <note>the early martyrs</note>. I pass over the fact that not all who die mourn, nor do all who are born; they begin this earthly journey with tears as if unwillingly, as though entering into exile. Furthermore, even among those who dread death, it is not the "whole soul" (so to speak) that is terrified. For that part of us which, by departing, proceeds toward what is better, not only does not depart unwillingly on that one occasion, but even departs voluntarily every day. For what else do we aim for through moral philosophy but to separate the soul from the affections of the body? What else through speculative philosophy but to call the reason away from the senses? This entire study of philosophy, as Plato says, is a <term>meditation on death: "meditatio mortis," the practice of separating the mind from bodily concerns</term>. Indeed, death is the liberation of the soul from the body. Nor <margin>B</margin> is death terrible to philosophers and those like them, because it is familiar and domestic to them; nor is the state of a pure soul after its passing hidden from them. For it shall be such as they experience almost daily at the highest peak of contemplation: namely, tranquil and serene, surrounded by the <term>formulas of Ideas: the eternal archetypes or blueprints of reality in the Platonic mind</term> as if by stellar rays, and flashing with the splendor of the divine sun. ¶ Hence the prophet Daniel says: "The learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in justice, like the stars for all eternity" <note>original: "Fulgebunt docti tanq̄ splendor firmamenti..." from Daniel 12:3</note>. That part of the soul goes unwillingly which is assigned only to the nourishing and guarding of the body. For by departing, it is vacated from a certain natural duty and deserts its friend. Furthermore, reason in most men loves this lower part of the soul too much. Thus it happens that it grieves, in a sense, at its loss. ¶ Plotinus, however, does not <margin>C</margin> properly call this a "part" of the soul, but a "simulacrum" <note>an image or shadow-reflection</note>—a certain shadowy likeness of the substantial soul. ¶ For he proves that "man" is the rational soul itself, which, remaining in itself, generates the "animal" below itself. Nor is the animal properly composed as one thing out of the soul and the body, but rather out of such a body and a certain vital "simulacrum" of the soul infused into the limbs. In this animal reside those senses which perceive external bodies with a certain passion <note>here meaning "undergoing an effect" or "suffering"</note>. This substance is both passive and confused, and disturbed. But in the substance of the rational soul itself, let there be an "impassible" <note>incapable of suffering or being changed by external forces</note> and universal sense, looking not toward sensible things, but toward the images and passions which are in the senses of that animal. For let there be reason, which looks upward with the mind. And insofar as it is guided within itself and raised up into the mind, it achieves and rejoices in separation. ¶ But insofar as it both forms the animal by a certain gift of providence and <margin>D</margin> looks back upon it once formed, it is delighted by a certain commerce with the body. But let us proceed to the rest. ¶ Some are also tortured who, in the departure, fear the sensation of it more than the departure itself. Timaeus teaches that this will be sweet, like the onset of sleep, if it happens through a certain dissolution according to the maturity of nature, and not by suffocation due to intemperance. ¶ Very many, however, grieve at this departure because they do not think they have merited the divine vision by their works. Whence it happens that they dread the long-lasting or perpetual darkness of the mind. ¶ Add to this that very many leave the allurements of this life—in which they were ensnared from the beginning—with difficulty. ¶ There are also those who properly distrust the divine <margin>✥</margin> because they have never looked upon the divine with the splendor of a pure mind, but only upon the mortal mist of corporeal images infused into the soul through the senses. And those who sharply gaze upon the splendor of the mind with the eyes of reason—not yet purged by philosophy—are beaten back by its rays; they grow dim and waver. ¶ For since nothing is more <margin>E</margin> present to the eyes of reason than the substance of the mind itself, it is not likely that it is unknown to us because of its minimal light, but rather because of its maximal light. Whoever, therefore, [seeks] the pure mind...

<summary>Ficino explains that while the lower, body-focused part of the soul fears death, the higher rational soul—prepared by philosophy—views it as a return to divine light. He argues that the soul is most truly itself when separated from bodily distractions, comparing death to the peak of philosophical contemplation.</summary>
