<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument for the immortality of the soul from the previous page, specifically addressing why we possess an innate hope for eternal life despite the physical decay we witness with our eyes.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>C</margin>
**T**he person who looks with the purified eyes of reason will not only not distrust [this truth], but will revere it as if it were a divinity. But although some may distrust it, many nevertheless trust in it. And even those very people who seem to distrust it hope at the same time that they will be eternal. Nor can a hope of this kind ever be entirely uprooted from our soul, as it is naturally implanted in us. Those appearances that have their origin from the senses, whether by chance or through habit, are usually deceptive. Such is certainly not the case with the belief in eternity. 
<margin>C</margin>
Since the senses perceive nothing except what is fleeting <term>caducum: literally "falling," referring to physical things that decay</term> and force us sometimes to suspect that perhaps those who have departed from life are nothing more, after they are seen nowhere. Therefore, the hope of immortality follows the natural instinct of reason. For the soul hopes for it not only without the help of the senses, but even against their will. I certainly am accustomed to wonder at nothing more than that any of us should hope for this, since we always live among fleeting things. Yet we do not stop hoping. 
<margin>D</margin>
This signifies that this hope is established by the firmness of nature. I think this also should be considered: that it would not be surprising if men had even more certain arguments for immortality than for all other things; 
<margin>E</margin>
yet in this matter, they distrust those very reasons more than in other cases. For what we love much, we fear for much. We love nothing more than eternal life, for the greatest reason: because it is most natural to us. 
<margin>☛</margin>
Entirely from the fear of death itself we can guess that some sense remains for us after death. For a person fears death because they hate perpetual darkness; and since this hatred proceeds from a different nature, the soul must be perpetual light. Or at least, the soul discerns eternal darkness only through some eternal light; it cannot look upon this without an immense light. If the light of the soul, which is its mind, relates to that light just as the life of the soul relates to life itself, then the light of the soul is reflected upon that immense light. 

---

Necessarily, the life of the soul embraces infinite life. Also, because life agrees more with life than light agrees with life: if the light of the soul, in its own way—that is, by understanding—attains immense life, much more does the life of the soul, in its own way—that is, by living—achieve infinite life. Furthermore, he who dreads the darkness deliberates with himself: whether he will live forever without a body, or if he will perish. This deliberation signifies that the soul, having left the body, already then retreats into itself. For the body does not reflect upon itself, nor is it elevated into a life separate from the body. 
<margin>B</margin>
In that very deliberation, the soul judges how much more excellent eternal life, free from the mortal body, is than either the present life or the deprivation of life; and it desires it to be free and eternal. It could not judge or desire so unless it first experienced such a life within itself. If a free life is far different from a servile one, and yet the soul, enclosed in the body, experiences and exercises it, how much more will it be able to fulfill it when released from the body? Moreover, in the same deliberation the mind disputes whether it can do anything by itself once the body is laid aside. If it can, it does not doubt it will live apart from the body. Even now, though one leads life with the body, one still acts somewhat without it when judging what it is and what kind of thing it is that is said to operate without the body. For who, through the body, would reject every body? Who, with the body, would distinguish all bodies from each other? Who, while working with the body, would perform that operation which is done without the body? Yet one performs in a way an operation that is without the 
<margin>F</margin>
body when one thinks and imagines it. For thinking <note>original: *excogitatio*</note> is an act of the soul. If, while it is in the body, it does something without the 
<margin>G</margin>
body, it will be much better able to act without it when outside it. And yet, what is wonderful is that the soul is so invincible that whoever declares war on its eternity is overcome by it. For whether the Lucretians <note>Followers of the Roman poet Lucretius, who argued for the mortality of the soul based on Epicurean physics</note> fight lazily, the soul is not conquered; or whether others fight vigorously, because they fight with the soul's own weapons, [they are defeated].

<summary>Ficino argues that the universal human hope for immortality and the fear of death prove the soul's eternal nature, as the mind can conceive of and desire a life independent of the physical body. He posits that the soul acts as a "perpetual light" that can only recognize the "darkness" of death by comparison to its own inherent immortality.</summary>

...and they fight bravely with their stings; indeed, the soul itself fights. Therefore, the soul itself, when it sees itself sinking, then it most especially triumphs. For it excels in the highest degree. Even if it seems to be perishing, it eventually sees itself as having perished <note>Ficino's point is that the act of "seeing" or perceiving one's own death implies a surviving consciousness that witnesses the event.</note>. He who sees anything still breathes. From these things it is clear: if by reason the fear of death proceeds from a horror of darkness, immortality is shown in that very fact. Perhaps because the soul fears death, it does not so much dread the darkness as it foretells and fears either punishment or sorrow. I certainly believe the latter is the case. From this, immortality is also revealed. For just as no one desires those things which he does not hope will be beneficial, nor thinks they are beneficial unless they are perceived <note>original: *percipiantur*; referring to conscious experience</note>, so no one fears things he does not judge to be harmful, nor thinks they will be a hindrance unless they can be perceived. For desire looks toward pleasure in the attainment of good, or the avoidance of evil. Fear looks toward pain in the presence of evil, or the absence of good. But pleasure and pain do not occur without consciousness. Therefore, he who desires the state of life for the sake of the pleasure with which he is filled during his lifetime, likewise fears the state after death because of the pain which he expects to perceive at 그at time.

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence: Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls, dedicated to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici. Book Seventeen.

### Fifth question. What the state of the soul is before it enters the body, and what it is after its departure. Chapter 1.

<margin>B</margin>
But now let us approach the fifth discussion, through which that question may be resolved: what is the state of the soul before it enters <margin>B2</margin> the body, and what is its state when it has departed. In these matters pertaining to theology, six supreme theologians once reached an agreement.

The first of these is said to have been **Zoroaster**, the head of the Magi. The second was **Hermes Trismegistus**, the prince of the Egyptian priests. Hermes was succeeded by **Orpheus**. **Aglaophemus** was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus. Aglaophemus was succeeded in theology by **Pythagoras**, and Pythagoras by **Plato** <note>This lineage is known as the *Prisca Theologia* (Ancient Theology), a path of divine wisdom Ficino believed linked ancient prophets to Plato.</note>. Plato comprised all their wisdom in his writings, expanded it, and illustrated it. Because all of them used to cover the sacred mysteries of divine things with "poetic shadows" <note>original: *poeticis umbraculis*; metaphorical language used to hide truths from the uninitiated</note> so they would not become common to the profane, it happened that their successors interpreted theology in different ways. Hence, the crowd of Platonic interpreters divided into six Academies. Three of these were Attic <note>from Athens</note>; the others were foreign. Of the Attic ones, the **Old Academy** flourished under **Xenocrates**, the **Middle** under **Arcesilaus**, and the **New** under **Carneades**. Of the foreign ones, the **Egyptian** was under **Ammonius**, the **Roman** under **Plotinus**, and the **Lycian** under **Proclus**. But although there were six schools, those three Attic ones as well as the Egyptian interpreted whatever Plato wrote about the "circuit of souls" <note>the cycle of reincarnation or the soul's journey</note> differently than the words seemed to sound. However, the two following schools observed the face of the words themselves more carefully. Let us diligently review how these two schools explain the Platonic mysteries.

### The exposition of Plato regarding the soul according to the last two academies.
### On the composition of the soul. Chapter 2.

In the *Parmenides*, Plato calls God **Infinite**; but in the *Philebus*, he names Him the **Limit** <term>Terminus: a boundary or defining principle</term>. He is Infinite because He receives no limit from elsewhere. He is the Limit because, through forms and measures distributed everywhere, He limits all things. Here the Platonists argue: insofar as God, as the Infinite, excludes all limits from Himself, to that extent there seems to hang from Him a certain shadow, a "material power" as it were, which lacks any limit and is, by its nature, formless and—so to speak—indefinite. But insofar as God, as the Limit, looks upon His own shadow as if into a mirror, to that extent He results in that shadow as an image; and that very infinity—that is, the most common matter—is limited by forms in a most orderly way. He confirms the same thing again thus: If the power of the universe-to-be is always in God, then the universe is rightly always outside of God...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the psychological and moral arguments for the soul's immortality to a more rigorous metaphysical framework. Having previously discussed the soul's innate fear of death as a sign of its enduring nature, Ficino now begins a systematic analysis of "potentiality" and "act," drawing on both Neoplatonic traditions and medieval scholasticism to define the composition of created beings.</meta>

<header>Theology of the Seventeenth [Book].</header>
<page-num>175</page-num>

# Theology

I speak of becoming from potentiality <term>potentiality (potentia): the capacity for a thing to exist or change, which is not yet "actual"</term>. For He <note>Referring to God as the Creator</note> could not always do all things—as some think—unless all things could always be made. 
<margin>$\zeta$</margin> They call this kind of potentiality "the most common matter," that is, a force equally receptive to all forms. By its own nature, it neither inclines toward being itself—otherwise it would not need a supreme Form-giver <note>original: *formatore*</note>—nor toward non-being—otherwise it would not obey the Form-giver. Instead, it stands equally toward both being and non-being, as well as toward various forms, like a certain middle ground; it is determined by the Form-giver. It is also one in all things—not in number, nor species, nor genus, but rather by a certain analogy and proportion. This is because it depends on the One, and represents the infinity of the one God in whatever way it can, in a shadowy <note>original: *umbratili*; meaning a dim or reflected image</note> manner. 
<margin>$\zeta$</margin> Just as "act" <term>act (actus): the state of being real or complete, as opposed to mere potential</term> is also called "one" in all things in a certain way, because it comes from one Limiter <note>original: *terminatore*; the principle that gives bounds or "limits" to potentiality</note> and reflects the limitation of the One. And this kind of act surpasses potentiality, because it flows from God, not fleeing further but now regarding matter. This kind of potentiality in spirits seems to have something of the body in it; for indeed in minds it contains the principles <note>original: *rationes*</note> of bodies, and in addition, in souls, it contains motions—a faculty capable of being formed in both. Conversely, in bodies, something of the incorporeal seems to be present; for while it precedes quantity, it appears indivisible, and always sustains certain incorporeal powers, so to speak. 
<margin>$\zeta$</margin> From this infinity—that is, from this boundary consisting of receptive, formable potentiality and formal act—they believe all things under God persist. This is perhaps what the Moorish philosopher Avicebron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058), a Jewish philosopher whose work *Fons Vitae* (The Source of Life) was highly influential on Christian scholastics</note> signifies in his book *The Source of Life*. And our theologians briefly confirm it thus: if every creature, both individually and universally, receives its being from God, it certainly does not exist of itself; and if abandoned by Him, it would no longer exist. Therefore, it can be and not be. Thus, it is not its own being; rather, it is potentiality toward it. Nothing is potentiality toward itself, nor does it receive itself. For an agent, while it acts, always makes that which is potential into something actual. Therefore, a creature is produced, not because potentiality is impressed upon potentiality—otherwise nothing would yet be brought into act—nor because act is infused into act, or because it procures the same for itself—otherwise that which is produced would exist before it existed. But in the production itself, act is properly applied to potentiality. And these two must necessarily be distinguished in a creature. Otherwise, the very being of the creature, because it would subsist in itself, would be utterly infinite. Since, therefore, being differs from essence, is it from essence? 
<margin>$\zeta$</margin> By no means. For nothing, as an efficient cause, can bestow being upon itself. Thus, it receives being from elsewhere. From this, insofar as it receives, it is potentiality; but what it receives is called "act." 

# Of the Seventeenth [Book].

<margin>II</margin> Therefore, whatever is produced is composed of potentiality and act. Essence and being are combined: the Platonists relate "essence" and "potentiality" to infinity, but "being" and "act" to the limit <note>original: *terminum*</note>. 
<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, in the *Sophist*, the *Parmenides*, and the *Timaeus*, they list five genera of things <note>These are the "Great Kinds" (megista gene) from Plato's *Sophist*</note> from which all things besides the First <note>God or the One</note> are composed:

*   **Essence** (eſſentia)
*   **Sameness** (idē)
*   **Difference** (alterū)
*   **Stability** (ſtatus)
*   **Motion** (motus)

Essence clearly signifies the formal principle of each thing being considered; it also includes "being" as the proper act of essence. "Sameness" <note>original: *idem*</note> is so called because anything is consistent both with itself primarily and with others. Again, he adds "Difference" <note>original: *alterum*</note> because it has a certain distinction both within itself and toward others. Furthermore, "Stability" <note>original: *statum*</note>, since it retains its unity for some time. Finally, "Motion" in this place signifies a certain transition from potentiality to act, whether by existing, or by acting in any way internally or externally. 
<margin>J</margin> Therefore, the infinity of things is subject to divine infinity, and the limit of things is subject to the divine limit. Next, we refer three things primarily to the infinity of things: namely, **Essence**, **Difference**, and **Motion**. To the limit of things, we likewise reduce three by distributing them equally: namely, **Being**, **Sameness**, and **Stability**. What is called "the One" and "the many" in the *Parmenides*, and "indivisible" and "divisible" in the *Timaeus*, is to be understood thus: that the One and the indivisible are according to the "limit." Conversely, multiplicity and the divisible are propagated everywhere according to "infinity" through their own genera. Although each thing besides the First is composed of these as if from seeds and elements, incorporeal things are said to be fashioned from a more harmonious mixture of seeds than corporeal ones. For this reason, the former remain more indissoluble.

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical composition of all created things, arguing that they are a mixture of potentiality (infinity) and act (limit). Ficino synthesizes the ideas of Avicebron with Plato's "five genera" to explain why only God is pure being while creatures remain composite and dependent.</summary>
<keywords>potentiality and act, Avicebron, Fons Vitae, Plato's Sophist, five genera of being, essence, sameness and difference, stability and motion, metaphysics of the One, immortality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's metaphysical exploration of the soul’s nature. Following the previous discussion on potentiality and act, he now focuses on the soul as a "middle" being—a bridge between the eternal, indivisible realm of God and the temporal, divisible realm of matter. He draws heavily on the "Five Greatest Kinds" from Plato's Sophist to explain how the soul is composed.</meta>

### Platonic Matters, Book [D]

...are thought. 
<margin>g</margin>
...that they might produce a mixture of other things in their present distance. And for what reason the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, whom Ficino viewed as precursors to Plato’s wisdom</note> and Platonists mix the soul from these kinds <note>original: *generibus*; referring to the "Five Greatest Kinds" of being, rest, motion, same, and other</note>: I will soon explain. But first I should warn: lest we think that, even if most of these men say the soul has always existed, they believe it exists entirely from itself. For since the soul does not unfold its total operation all at once—through which it always operates—it is established that it does not possess this infinite power of operating all at once. For if it held it all at once, it would also produce a single and total operation all at once. For of God <note>original: *Dio.*, likely a shorthand for *Deo* (God)</note>, as they say: the operation of power is one and for one. Therefore, the soul always receives the power of acting always. Because of this, it does not act consistently, but now in one way, now in another. To summarize: whatever acts temporally <term>temporally (temporaliter): acting within the flow of time, step-by-step, rather than in a single eternal "now"</term>, whether it be a body or a soul, it certainly receives the power of operating continuously and gradually, but never possesses the whole of it entirely at once. For this reason, the soul is judged by the Platonists not only to "be" always, but also to be "generated" always <note>This is the concept of *semper gigni*, where the soul is in a state of perpetual becoming because it is always receiving new life from God</note>
<margin>h</margin>
—namely, insofar as it draws its force gradually, and unfolds its internal forms in various ways, and continuously varies its affects and actions. Therefore, insofar as it is the vital cause of its own motion, it supplies itself with a certain essential and indeterminate life. And thus it is judged to "be"; but insofar as it unfolds this in infinite time, it receives such paths gradually from higher things; truly, it is judged to be perpetually generated by another. To this is added the fact that the supreme Principle of things is present to all things, so that individual things participate in the Principle everywhere according to their own nature. Otherwise, they would suddenly vanish. The soul, however, is not present to all things. For not all things live. Likewise, it is necessary that the First itself be entirely the One. For if it were some multitude, it would undoubtedly have the cause of its union above itself. Since it is not the nature of a multitude to unite, but rather the duty of unity; truly, it is forbidden to say that the First is a scattered multitude. 
<margin>i</margin>
Yet every soul is a multitude. Again, the First is conceived as being above all essence. Since every essence suffers a multitude within itself—at least of the kind we have enumerated in the higher things. But the soul is a certain vital and life-giving essence. Finally, the First can be contaminated neither "anywhere," nor "anytime," nor in any way. Others, however, are infected in many ways, sometimes, and somewhere. For this reason, the soul necessarily has an essence composed in a certain way by its superior principle.

Furthermore, in the things composed by God above the soul, the gifts that pertain to the limit <note>original: *terminu*; the principle of definition and boundary</note> surpass the opposite kinds by a very long interval. But in the things following the soul, the opposite occurs. Yet in the composition of the soul, the kinds harmonize more equally. Since the soul is the truest "middle" of all things composed by God, it is agreeable that it be composed in a certain middle and most equal way, insofar as it can be done by reason. Therefore, in her—to pass over other things—the partible is harmonically tempered with the impartible <term>partible and impartible: the "divisible" (matter/senses) and "indivisible" (spirit/intellect)</term>, and the "other" with the "same," and motion with rest, just as a high pitch is tempered with a low one. 

Indeed, in those things which are above the soul, three things are chiefly considered: essence, life, and intelligence. In those things also which are below the soul, there are three in turn: quality, nature, and sense; so that sense is a likeness of intelligence, nature a likeness of life, and finally quality is the ultimate image of essence. In the higher things, according to essence, life, and intelligence, the impartible surpasses the partible. The same also exceeds the "other," and rest exceeds motion. In the lower things, however, it happens entirely the opposite way. But in the soul, as the middle of all things, a middle mode is observed through all things. 

Accordingly, whether you compare her to the extremes of the world—judging her as a middle between minds (as being entirely impartible) and qualities (as being entirely partible in time and place)—or to her own extremes—namely, toward her own mind on one side and her life merged with the body on the other—she is likewise judged to be the middle between the individual and the divisible. Or if you finally compare her to her own center, which is reason: even this reason, when it rises toward the intellect and universals, is called impartible; but when it declines toward the senses and singular things, it is called partible. And there it attains identity <note>original: *identitatem*; "sameness"</note> and rest. Here, in turn, it undergoes alterity <note>original: *alteritatem*; "otherness"</note> and motion. And while she discourses in a certain way in the consideration of eternal things, she [generates] the divisible in an indivisible state...

<summary>Ficino explains the soul as a metaphysical "middle," composed of both divisible and indivisible elements, which allows it to bridge the gap between God's eternal unity and the material world's temporal diversity. He argues that while the soul is eternal, it is also "perpetually generated" as it receives its power from God moment by moment.</summary>

# Theology

...exercises motion <note>The OCR "scet" is likely the completion of "exercet" (exercises) from the previous page</note>. Conversely, in reaching temporal things, it somehow remains in itself: it tempers a motion that is divisible in turn into a certain indivisible state. Furthermore, just as the World Soul <note>The *Anima Mundi*, the spirit that animates the entire universe in Platonic thought</note> in moving the heavens—which is called "unwandering," that is, the fixed stars—shows itself as the "Same" in that sphere; yet in moderating the planets, which are in a certain way "wanderers," it seems to preserve that same "Same" within the "Other" through the order of its motion. But thus far the Same overcomes the Other. Finally, in governing the lower realms, it now permits the Same 
<margin>c</margin>
to be overcome by the Other. Similarly, the human soul is seen to hold itself around three "vehicles," namely: the ethereal, the aerial, and the composite body. 
<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, what Timaeus <note>The speaker in Plato's *Timaeus* who explains the creation of the world and the soul</note> intends when he uses musical proportions in composing the soul can be sufficiently understood. For he means nothing else than that the soul is so composed—both from the types of things themselves and from its own powers—that it is most fittingly joined first to its own Ideas <note>The eternal, perfect forms in the mind of God</note>, then secondly to itself, and thirdly to other things.
<margin>S</margin>
The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> are accustomed to use both mathematical figures and numbers in describing the soul. This is because, just as mathematics stands in the middle, so the souls hold the middle rank between natural and divine forms. They therefore set up a triangle, at whose peak is placed unity, 
<margin>G</margin>
from which three numbers flow forth on each side. On this side are the even, and on that side similarly the odd, according to this ratio: on one side first two, then four, finally eight; on the other side first three, then nine, and lastly twenty-seven. By these numbers, they judge that all the parts, powers, and duties of the soul are designated. For those things which are above the soul are thought to be unified rather than numerous. But those things under the soul are indeed numerous, but by themselves greatly dissonant. Certainly, the soul is first called "numerous" because, since it is closest to bodily multiplicity, it is already understood to be manifold in its motions as well as its powers. 
<margin>T</margin>
Next, however, since it is the first principle of ordered motion and generation, it is concluded by probable reason that its "numerosity" is most consonant. From its consonance, the consonance of the body—both celestial and elemental—continuously depends, no differently than how 

the harmony in the mind of a musician is that which subsequently flows into voices and into the harmony perceived in sounds. Furthermore, Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher who believed the world was made of "limit" and "unlimited"</note> 
<margin>B</margin>
called God "Unity" in the Pythagorean manner, and soon named extended matter "Duality." This is because, just as the first division among numbers is quality itself, so the dimension of matter is such in the beginning that forms become distracted among themselves and repugnant. Therefore, they think the soul, hanging from divine Unity, pours itself into matter as if into Duality—no differently than a triangle starts from a single top angle and ends in two angles. Thus, in a composite body, it is always distracted and disturbed. For this reason, the soul is rightly represented by a triangle. Then they apply seven limits of numbers to this triangle. Truly, since we see that the generation of things is governed by the seven-fold <term>septenary (septenario): relating to the number seven</term> number of the planets, and that the highest of the planets, Saturn, makes changes in the life of men every seventh year; and that the Moon, the lowest of the planets, induces a change every seventh day—both in itself and in the bodily fluids—they rightly judge that the origin of motion and generation 
<margin>||</margin>
is described by the number seven. There are also those who think the fetus is perfected in the womb by sevens, and that once born, a person is led through ages in a similar way. They assert, moreover, that there are numbers on both sides, both even and odd, to declare that through the even numbers the soul is of a divisible nature, and through the odd, it is mixed from the indivisible. Again, they add linear, superficial, and solid numbers so that it might appear the soul pours itself most easily through the length, breadth, and depth of the body. But they choose only those numbers by whose mutual proportions musical consonance consists, to show that a soul harmoniously composed disposes and moves all things harmoniously. Indeed, between four and three there is a "sesquitertial" proportion <note>A 4:3 ratio</note>. 
<margin>J</margin>
From this is born the harmony which the Greeks name *diatessaron* <note>The musical interval of a fourth</note>. But between three and two is the "sesquialteral" proportion <note>A 3:2 ratio</note>. This procreates the harmony which they call *diapente* <note>The musical interval of a fifth</note>. Furthermore, between four...

and two; or four and eight, a double proportion: which completes the <term>diapason</term> <note>A musical interval of an octave.</note> harmony. 
<margin>A</margin>
Between one and three, or three and nine, or between nine and twenty-seven, there is a triple proportion, from which the melody of the <term>diapason-diapente</term> <note>An octave plus a perfect fifth (a 12th).</note> is composed. Furthermore, between four and one, or two and eight, a quadruple proportion is born, which generates the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave.</note> harmony. Finally, between eight and nine there is the <term>epogdous</term> <note>The 9:8 ratio, which defines a whole musical tone.</note>, by which a full tone is established. A sound that is more relaxed than a tone they call a <term>hemitone</term> <note>A half-step or semitone.</note>. For this reason, all the proportions we have described, which are most necessary to the musical art, are created by those numbers that are described in the "figure of the soul" <note>Referring to the mathematical construction of the soul in Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>. Through these, the soul's natural composition, its motion, and its natural action are signified to be more harmonious and rhythmic than all other things. Nor are there lacking those who measure the magnitudes of the celestial spheres among themselves, their intervals, their motions, and the positions and aspects of the planets by nearly similar proportions. They even arrange the vital spirit by a similar tempering of its qualities. I reasonably bypass many things that many people in this area treat lightly and curiously concerning the imagined virtues of numbers and shapes. This is the sum of the Pythagorean and Platonic mystery. I add 
<margin>B</margin>
that they are accustomed to calling the Understanding "Unity," because it occurs through a simple intuition. Knowledge they call "Duality," because it proves a conclusion from a principle. But Opinion they call "Trinity," because it additionally brings into the middle the opposite of the conclusion through a certain ambiguity. Finally, Sensation they call "Fourness" <note>original: *quaternitatem* (the OCR *qua trinitatẽ* is a common misreading of the abbreviation for 4); 4 represents the physical world of the four elements.</note>, because it seems to be most concerned with things composed of the four elements. I add again: they call the soul "curved" because it effects circular motions. Indeed, they place in it a certain straight line insofar as it moves and regards bodies. Then they describe a certain inferior circle, like the orbit of the planetary mouths, insofar as it returns into itself. Also a superior circle, like the orbit of the fixed stars, insofar as it is turned toward higher things. They add two others: namely, the instinct of the intellect toward the True itself, and of the will toward the Good itself. The Charioteer is the mind; the head of the charioteer is the divine unity superior to the mind. The superior horses are Sameness and Rest. The inferior horses are Otherness and Motion. Also, the horses of good and evil: namely, the natures of Anger and Desire. 
<margin>L</margin>
For Anger seems to be closer to reason than Lust is. Finally (to speak summarily), by this reasoning all Pythagoreans and Platonists judge that all rational souls—both ours and those superior to ours—are composed in almost the same way. 
<margin>C</margin>
From this they believe it follows that the celestial souls, in revolving the spheres, produce an inestimable melody, and our souls are wonderfully delighted by harmonies of this kind. But between the celestial and our own, they interpose three middle grades, composed in a middle way, as if across a great distance. 
<margin>E</margin>
These bind our souls with the divine ones in a certain way, and they believe these grades proceed according to the proportion of essence, life, and intelligence. For the **Angelic** souls, flashing out most closely from the intelligible world, pour intelligible light into those that follow, remaining in the manner of "Essence." Next, the **Demonic** <note>In the Platonic sense, *daimones* are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> souls proceed by the manner of "Interminable Life." Finally, the **Heroic** souls follow the manner of "Mind and Conversion" <note>The soul's act of turning back toward its source.</note>. 
<margin>E</margin>
I add that he judges the Angelic to proceed from God according to intellectual virtue; the Demonic according to craftsmanship and providence, and therefore they fabricate mundane things; the Heroic according to the specifically "convertive" faculty. Therefore, they perform the duty of purifying souls. All these are harmonically tempered and produce harmony, and they are wonderfully delighted by harmonic things. But we shall treat more appropriately of these kinds of souls in what follows.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature and hierarchy of souls. While the previous page focused on the mathematical and musical proportions that structure the soul, this page classifies different grades of souls—divine, demonic, heroic, and human—based on their ability to remain focused on God and the intelligible world.</meta>

<page-num>xvij. 177</page-num>

# Theology

-> Mars. fici. 3 <-

<margin>C</margin> Between these extremes there are two middle grounds. The first consists of those who always follow God. Such are the souls of <term>demons</term> <note>original: "demonum"; in the Platonic tradition, these are not "evil" spirits, but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>, of heroes, and of those in the highest realms. Although these are not strictly called "divine," they nonetheless never depart from God. In this first class of souls, the principles are so arranged that while "being" <note>original: "essentia"</note> exists there, here (so to speak) "identity" <note>original: "identitas"</note> and other principles somehow surpass it.

<margin>E</margin> Below these are the souls that sometimes follow God and sometimes leave Him. In these, the principle called "the other" <note>original: "alterum"; referring to the Platonic principle of 'Difference' or 'Otherness' from the *Timaeus*.</note> seems to somehow overcome the others. Such are the souls of the lower demons and heroes, but most clearly the souls of humans. Since these are the lowest of all minds, they do not possess the power to perfectly fulfill two very different tasks at the same time: namely, to behold divine things through human reason and to govern earthly bodies. Yet it is necessary for them to do both, since they were born for both.

<margin>S</margin> Therefore, they perform in turn what they cannot do at the same time. They use this alternation in three principal ways. First, they transfer themselves from the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and Ideas.</note> to the <term>sensible world</term> <note>The physical realm of the senses.</note>, and vice versa. Furthermore, within the intelligible world itself, they pass through various types of contemplation in turn. Again, in the sensible region, they change through different ways of living.

<margin>B</margin> Plato describes these alternations often elsewhere, but especially in the *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato's famous dialogues concerning the soul and beauty.</note>. He describes it most clearly where he says that souls are at times companions of different gods in heaven, and that in contemplating the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things.</note>, they carry out a mental journey with their own god according to their strength: sometimes above heaven concerning divine things, sometimes in heaven concerning celestial things, and sometimes below heaven to consider natural things step by step. And so far as they can imitate the gods, they remain among the higher beings. Likewise, since they repeat their circuits from causes to effects and back again, <margin>F</margin> he says that the soul which has gazed upon the Idea—which is the "head" of the circuit—continues within that circuit through the Ideas themselves and does not fall. 

But the soul falls when the "bad horse"—that is, the stimulated power of desire—growing strong in its own time for the sake of the power of procreation, diverts the soul from contemplation toward generating. Then he enumerates nine types of lives—not because there are only that many, but because they descend through the seven planets, fire, and air. Finally, he describes many transmigrations through lower things and a return to the higher ones, where many things are undoubtedly poetic rather than philosophical. 

Therefore, let us now turn to a more philosophical order. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, many Platonists think there is something that possesses infinite life from itself; something that has it from another; and something that has it from neither. Again, that which has life from another either inclines toward the highest, or rather toward the lowest, or possesses a middle ground entirely. Certainly, God possesses a staying infinity of life entirely from Himself. The Angel also possesses a staying life, but one received from God. 

Then, other divine souls superior to ours have an infinite life from elsewhere, but it is "running" <note>original: "currentem"; meaning discursive or moving from one thought to another rather than seeing all at once.</note>; it runs, however, in a certain fixed order by discoursing from species to species, free from all failure and forgetfulness. Finally, our souls likewise have an infinite life. But it is not only "running," but also disordered, and it changes from a better state to a worse one, and back again, sometimes by remembering and sometimes by forgetting. Other things below our souls do not partake in infinite life in any way.

<margin>J</margin> Here his followers confirm their own view: namely, that celestial souls discourse even while understanding; they occupy the middle ground between the gods (who look upon intelligible things always and while staying still) and particular souls (who look upon those things only sometimes and while running). These celestial and sublime souls always behold, but by passing from species to species. 

<margin>K</margin> Elsewhere, however, we have recounted the opinion of Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD).</note> on this matter. Accordingly, they wish there to be one thing infinite in both power and perseverance. Next, many things infinite in perseverance rather than power—perseverance, I say, either possessing all its things at once, or succeeding from some things to others, whether that happens in a greater or lesser order. Finally, there are many things which are infinite neither by their own power nor by a perseverance accepted from elsewhere. 

They place such an order among spirits. In the sensible world, however, the pole, as far as it can, reflects the first grade of that order. The axis reflects the second. The celestial sphere reflects the third. The elemental sphere the fourth. <margin>L</margin> Finally, the fifth consists of those things composed of the four elements. But by this digression...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul, moving from the classification of souls to the concept of reincarnation and the cycles of life. It specifically addresses how human souls, being the "lowest of minds," experience multiple lives to fulfill their divine and earthly duties.</meta>

# Platonic Book

-> Marsilio Ficino <-

Having set these things aside, let us return to our souls. Indeed, the soul of man will always exist, since it longs for the eternal. It has also always existed, as they say; for it would eventually have an end unless it lacked a beginning.

<margin>C</margin>
**The soul of Pythagoras before birth.** The soul of Pythagoras was at one time free from an earthly body. Afterward, it was enclosed when Pythagoras was born. Here there are two lives: one free, the other corporeal. That life which was free reached its end at the beginning of the corporeal life. Therefore, it also had some beginning earlier. For that which ceases must have begun; thus it was not always outside the body before Pythagoras, though it was so at some time. And after it began to be in the body, it will not remain in these bodies forever, because what begins also ends. From which it follows that an innumerable number of times before Pythagoras, his soul was both within an earthly body and outside of it. And again, after Pythagoras, it will be outside the body in its turn, and then in a body. And just as all the spheres of the world vary their forms through their own souls, but at last repeat their own proper returns—which we observe in the four seasons of the year and the four alternating phases of the moon—so our souls, similar to the celestial souls, put on various forms of bodies. In certain cycles of time, they are involved in the same bodies in which they were before. This <gloss>palingenesia</gloss> <note>original: "παλιγγενεσίαν"; a Greek term meaning "being born again" or "regeneration."</note> is what <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>An ancient Persian prophet whom Renaissance scholars like Ficino believed was a source of "ancient theology" that prefigured Plato.</note> calls "Regeneration." Regarding this, <term>Mercury</term> <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> disputes much with his son Tatius. And Plato, in the book *On the Kingdom* <note>original: "libro de regno"; likely referring to the *Politicus* (The Statesman), where Plato discusses the cosmic cycles of the universe.</note>, describes this resurrection as something that will occur at the end of the world’s revolution by God’s command, with demons ministering.

<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, what the world fulfills through one single life, our soul carries out through many. For Plato’s *Timaeus* <note>A foundational Platonic dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note> teaches that God, the maker of the world, cast into a certain bowl all the seeds of things and mixed them in turn (as we said above) tempering them with specific measures. From this tempering, He created rational souls distributed in three grades, so that in every soul all seeds are inserted. Thus, since the soul is mixed from every kind of thing, it can easily recognize all things through a certain kinship. It can move all things, and vivify them, and more easily experience a life that takes every form. What else do we understand God’s "bowl" to be than the <term>third essence</term> <note>In Ficino’s philosophy, the soul is the "third essence" because it sits exactly in the middle of the hierarchy of being—between the purely divine (Mind/Angel) and the purely physical (Body).</note>, the medium between divine and corporeal things, sparkling with the sparks of divine things and pregnant with the seeds of corporeal things.

<margin>C</margin>
From this source, three principal species of souls have flowed: the divine, which always follow God; those that sometimes follow God; [and those that rarely do]. To the first, the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who emphasized mathematics and the transmigration of souls.</note> assign "wisdom." To the second, "right opinion." To the third, "wavering opinion." From this, we gather what we have often said: that our souls are, in a way, all things. And therefore, the progression of all living things is contained within their inner depths. However, the soul does not unfold all these things individually at once. For the first souls perform more than the second, and the second more than the third. Therefore, although perhaps not to all, the soul of man seems appointed to many progressions of lives. This transfer from life to life is brought about neither by external violence nor by a deliberate plan, but by a certain natural instinct—much like how, in this life, teeth, hair, seed, and the rest come forth each in its own time. For just as in the nature of the universe itself, so in the natures of particular souls, individual things are ordered by a certain eternal law; they come into action in a way that is consistent both for the soul itself and for the whole of nature. Certainly, one harmony is made from all the members of the "world-animal," through which individual parts harmonize with each other and with the whole everywhere. Therefore, just as the soul of the world itself produces certain things at certain times, so also particular souls, with their implanted seeds, are naturally inclined and disposed toward certain ways of living at certain times.

<margin>D</margin>
But while the affections and acts of the past life gradually fade, those of the following life are intensified in turn, with the nature of the universe contributing to each everywhere. It must be remembered, as the tenth book of the *Republic* teaches, that souls descend by fate—that is, they desire generation. That they feel this desire at such a time arises from a natural instinct joined to the order of the universe. But by their own choice, they choose this or 그 life. For although they naturally desired and thought about a corporeal life, when they [choose] such or such a species of life...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transmigration of the soul, specifically focusing on the process by which a soul chooses its next life based on past habits, the role of the three Fates, and the philosophical debate over whether human souls can truly inhabit animal bodies.</meta>

# Theology XVII.

<margin>☞</margin> they consider what they might adopt. Most people, however, choose according to the habit and affection of their prior life. These habits and affections were once created by free acts. The same [Plato] says: the fault lies with the one choosing, not with God. "A <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "demon"; here referring to a guardian spirit or personal destiny, not an evil entity.</note> does not choose you; you choose the daemon." For virtue is free. But after someone has chosen a life and a daemon, the chosen virtue can arrange and compose the life rather than set it aside. For it is necessary that certain circuits of fate be fulfilled. Furthermore, regarding what is written in that same place—that the world revolves between necessity and the providence of God—we have explained elsewhere. For necessity is called the soul of the world because the universe is led by its fatal power. He says "between the knees," that is, by its lower power, which is adapted to the revolving spheres. Indeed, it rests upon divine mind and reason; and if the lower power is essentially one, it is nevertheless given a triple name.

<margin>☞</margin> **Lachesis**: that is, "allotment," because she assigns individual lots to each person. **Clotho**: that is, the "revolver," because she unwinds the lots that were rolled up from the beginning for each person in certain orders and times. **Atropos**: that is, the "unchangeable," because she proceeds with immutable reason in unwinding the lots. Plato asserts that the soul goes to all these goddesses when it inclines toward the lower realms, namely in this order: after Lachesis falls upon the soul with its lots, the soul naturally desires an elemental life. Then, with many examples of lives set before it, the soul chooses a certain life and its leader, a daemon, according to its own judgment; then Lachesis confirms the choice. From there, it is led by the same daemon to Clotho and Atropos, and to necessity. Who here does not see that the soul, solely because of its affection for this body, soon falls into the full power of the fates? Finally, it goes to the River **Lethe**, the river of oblivion—that is, into this body. From which it immediately forgets divine things.

<margin>3</margin> Accordingly, it signifies that the soul which has previously drunk from that river—that is, the soul which has adopted a body for itself with a more vehement affection—forgets the higher things more and remembers them more slowly; conversely, it is the opposite for the soul that does the opposite. 

<margin>⚘</margin> But let us now come to the diverse species of living. Sometimes the soul leads an **angelic life** in the ether near that star to which it is made more similar either by nature or by habit; and together with that star, it consents and concurs in the uncertain governance of the universe. But traveling gradually upward or downward through all the spheres, it spends a certain time in each life, governance, and contemplation suitable to that sphere and intellect. Sometimes it leads a **demonic life** in fire similarly, then a **heroic life** in the air, a **human life** on earth, and even a **wild beast’s life**. And often while it leads the life of a man, a life of a horse, or a lion, or similar creatures, bubbles up gradually from its seeds into its nature, instinct, and imagination. This signifies the affections and manners which arise within us, characteristic of such beasts. Finally, having set aside the human form, it enters the body of that beast to which it showed itself most similar in manners—whether it inserts itself into a beastly fetus and becomes the proper soul of the beast's body (as **Plotinus**, **Numenius**, and **Harpocratio Boethus** <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who debated the nature of the soul's descent into matter.</note> think), or whether it joins itself to a beastly soul and becomes a companion to the beast (as was pleasing to **Hermias**, **Syrianus**, and **Proclus**). And after it has migrated from one beast into another and has unfolded all those progressions of beastly life which it was more prone to unfold, it brings forth again human progressions, after those heroic, then demonic, and finally divine ones. 

Truly, some souls live more or less in different places, insofar as they are variously disposed by fate, fortune, choice, or habit. Plato designated these transmigrations and restitutions by periods of one thousand and three thousand years in his discussions and for the sake of example—rather, as **Hermias** says, than because he thought they could be precisely counted. For any of these numbers is not only very large but also more perfect according to a certain ratio. This is to show that souls require a certain long but fixed time for perfect purgation. And those that have sinned more lightly, or rather have practiced philosophy, will return more quickly to their homeland. However, it is not to be understood that the soul will commonly return to the exact same human being in number, unless the course of the whole world has finally been fulfilled, as is written in the book *On Kingship*; which course, as we have said elsewhere, astronomers compute to be completed in **thirty-six thousand years** <note>This refers to the "Great Year" or Platonic Year, the time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to their original positions.</note>. Meanwhile, however, the soul often returns to the same state.

He says in the same [place], specifically, that there is a species of life and a similar manner of living. That is, from the divine to the divine, from the human to the human, and likewise from the brute to the beastly. Just as the circuit of the world itself often returns to similar states in the interim, until it finally returns to the exact same points. Lest anyone think it is absurd for a soul to transfer itself into such diverse species, they [the Platonists] bid us to consider how many different affections and habits the soul often puts on even in this body—not just in other bodies, but in the same human being: namely, those of a plant, a brute, a human, or an angel. Again, lest anyone wonder why we do not remember those things we did in a previous life, they bid us observe not only how much we forget of our infancy in old age, but also how easily we forget yesterday’s affairs today. Nor do those critics trouble them to whom that prophetic saying is thrown: "The wicked walk in circles." <note>original: "In circuitu impii ambulant"; a reference to Psalm 12:8. Here, critics were using the Bible to claim that only the wicked believe in the "circles" or cycles of reincarnation.</note> It is as if he were saying those people should be judged as impious who introduce such a circuit of souls.

### Chapter 4. That Plato explains [this] more correctly according to the manner of the four preceding Academies, especially the first and the fourth.

<margin>a</margin> Indeed, the four older Academies <note>The "Academies" refer to the historical phases of Plato's school, ranging from the original dogmatic followers to the later Skeptics.</note> differed among themselves on this point, though they agreed on one thing: they thought Plato's writings were entirely poetic. But they differed in this: **Carneades** <note>A leader of the New Academy known for Skepticism.</note> thought that Plato both believed and treated everything as ambiguous in the manner of the Skeptics, and that he held no preference in any matters. **Archesilas**, however, believed that while Plato held nothing as certain, he did hold some things as likely and probable. **Xenocrates** as well as **Ammonius** <note>Xenocrates was the third head of the Academy; Ammonius was the teacher of Plutarch or Plotinus.</note> affirmed that he held some things not just as likely and probable, but even as true and certain; and those were a few specific things concerning the providence of God and the immortality of souls. Therefore, following in the footsteps of Xenocrates and Ammonius, we do not deny that Plato affirmed certain things about the soul; but many things regarding its "circuit" <note>the cycle of reincarnation</note> which are discussed by him, we understand as poetic—meaning differently than the words seem to signify. Especially since he did not invent such a circuit himself, but narrated the accounts
<margin>B</margin> of others. First, those fashioned by the Egyptian priests under the figure of souls being purged;

---

then those sung in poetic verses by **Orpheus**, **Empedocles**, and **Heraclitus**. I will pass over how **Pythagoras** inserted the transmigrations of souls into those familiar stories and symbols of his. For this reason, we shall smile at the latest Academies. They rely chiefly on two foundations: their own reason and Platonic authority. Regarding what they explain about the types of things and the musical composition of the soul, and again, what they assume in their argument, we admit there are four species of souls. Again, we grant that our soul can scarcely do both at once: namely, see divine things and govern bodies, especially the more unsuited ones. We also grant that. But we do not think it is necessary for this reason that the soul should perform innumerable turns up and down. Since it performs both duties sufficiently if, while it lives on earth, it sometimes cares for bodily things and sometimes cultivates itself and God. And when it has departed from here, it may more easily guide its vehicle <note>The "astral vehicle" or "spirit-body" that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul.</note> and more intently apply itself to divine matters. We concede that there is a life above the soul pregnant with the seeds of all things. And therefore, it can carry out the progressions of all various things. But only on this condition: that those seeds exist in this very soul according to the mode of the human soul's species, and from them sprout affections and habits agreeable to the other species, yet a true transmigration from one species to another never occurs. For whether the soul is compared to the body as a specific form to its own specific matter, or as a specific art to its own specific instrument, any soul will not be able to enter any body. For who would dare to say that the form of the moon could form the matter of a stone, or that the art of music could enter the instruments of a potter? Justly did the divine **Iamblichus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>
<margin>C</margin> reject the transmigration of the soul from a human into beasts. **Porphyry** also rejected the infinite circuit, and allowed it to wander only within the human species for certain ages; and finally, he asserted that the purged soul of a human stays forever with the heavenly Father, never to return to the misery of this life. Since it could never be happy if it either did not know it would return here...

Third, that those things he had written about such matters, he did not confirm in his old age. And in the *Letter to King Dionysius*, when he was quite old, he says: that he had never composed anything regarding divine matters. Nor was there any work of Plato’s concerning them, nor would there ever be. As if he had not opened his own mind, but had narrated the mind of another. Since, if the soul turned into a brute, it would not be purged thereby, but rather thoroughly infected. For purgation does not occur except where some outcry of conscience reigns. <meta>This page continues the investigation into Plato’s views on the soul, specifically addressing the "perpetual" nature of the world and whether the soul literally moves into the bodies of animals or if these are metaphors for human character.</meta>

# Platonic Book

**Iamblichus** and **Proclus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) and Proclus (412–485 AD) were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who sought to interpret Plato's works as a unified theological system.</note> wish for the perpetual generation of the world to be understood from Plato in that passage. But if by chance it must be explained in that way, it will be the opinion of **Timaeus the Pythagorean** rather than that of Plato himself. Indeed, Plato himself says in the *Epinomis*: the stars will either be immortal, or they are of such a long life that their own lifespan suffices for them and they lack nothing longer. This is consistent with what he says in the *Timaeus*: namely, that the stars would be dissolvable by their own nature because they were composed from a beginning, unless they are preserved by the will of the **Creator** <note>original: "componentis," referring to the Demiurge or God as the one who puts the universe together</note>. Again, in the sixth book of the *Laws*, he says: the human race has either existed forever or arose many ages ago. In this, he seems to prefer a beginning rather than eternity. **Aristotle** also, where he disputes the nature of such questions, says the question of the eternity of the world is "neutral"; as if to say it is not so much a demonstrable certainty as it is an opinion that is somehow probable on either side. Furthermore, when Plato says in the *Laws* that the soul exists before bodies, he perhaps intends this to refer to the **dignity of its nature** <note>Meaning the soul is "prior" in importance or rank, not necessarily in a chronological timeline</note> rather than to time. <margin>A</margin> Although even some Christians are of the opinion that souls precede bodies by some small interval of time.

That the souls of men pass into beasts is not confirmed in the *Laws*. However, in the ninth book, he says—according to the fables of the priests—that they go into other men. And in the seventh book, he declares how it ought to be explained when they say they "insert themselves into other bodies." There he teaches that he who ignores necessary doctrines will never be a **god**, a **daemon**, or a **hero** <note>In the Greek tradition, these represent levels of being between humanity and the ultimate Divine</note> among other men. It is as if they say these things by comparison to other men; and those things which they sometimes fable concerning the bodies of wild beasts are the same. For even in the *Phaedrus*, he does not say the soul of a man passes into the *body* of a beast, but into a **beastly life**; and in the *Timaeus*, into a **beastly nature**, not into the body of a wild animal. In the last book of the *Republic*, he writes that the soul [of Thersites] passed not into the body of an ape, but **into an ape**. In these phrases, it is understood to mean the habit and way of life rather than a permutation of the physical species or body.

Furthermore, in the *Phaedo*, after he recounted in the manner of poets the transition of souls into beasts as a punishment for sins, he adds that it is **not the part of a wise man to affirm such things as certain**. Instead, he says only this can be prudently asserted: that they pay some penalties for their outrages. He adds that souls purified by **true philosophy** <note>original: "legitimam philosophiam," referring to the disciplined pursuit of wisdom</note> will live forever with God without bodies. This is indeed confirmed in the *Epinomis*, saying the pious soul, separated from the body, spends the remaining time in the contemplation of the most beautiful of all things. In the *Gorgias* as well, and the *Theaetetus*, and the tenth book of *On Justice* <note>The *Republic*</note>, he describes the perpetual punishments of the impious for many sins which cannot be expiated; he asserts that such punishments were instituted for the sake of an **example of justice** rather than for the sake of a cure. There, he rejects those inexplicable errors regarding souls. <margin>B</margin> Through these things, it is clear: Plato, in the manner of Christians, signified an everlasting good or evil. As for what the Christians call **Purgatory**, Plato understood this where he says the soul to be purified is revolved several times through lower things: namely, not so much through bodies as through the lives and "commerce" of beasts. Finally, once purified, it is restored to heaven.

<margin>C</margin> In the ninth book of *On Justice* <note>The *Republic*, Book IX</note>, he figures the human soul in this manner: There is a certain mass of many heads of wild beasts, as if forced into a savage globe. From this multiple mass of beastly heads, a certain trunk sprouts out as if from roots. This trunk is a **lion** on one side, and a **dragon** <note>original: "drago," likely referring to a serpent or spirit of anger</note> on the other. Beneath this trunk, a certain **man** is placed, holding a club in his hand, with which he beats the beasts when they grow restless. Finally, the skin of a human body surrounds them all, so that it appears to be one animal, though it is a multiple animal. He intends the mass of many beasts to be the **insatiable part of desire** <note><term>Concupiscence</term>: the part of the soul driven by physical appetites</note>. The trunk composed of the lion and dragon is the force of **anger**. It is called a lion when it supports reason, and a dragon when it resists it. The "man" is **reason**. After this, Plato commands that we should nourish that inner man rather than those beasts, lest—the man failing because of hunger—only the beasts survive in us. By these things, we are warned to accept the transition of souls not into various physical species, but into **habits of character**. Thus, in Plato's view, he who is devoted to nutrition and sleeps day and night will be a **tree**. He who lives by prey through lust will be a **wolf**. He who serves with excellence in the military will be a **lion**. He who rages cruelly against the human race will be a **dragon**. He who lives by civil reason will be a **man**. He who searches out natural things will be a **hero**. He who [studies] mathematics... [will be a] **daemon**.

<summary>This page argues that Plato's descriptions of reincarnation into animals are metaphors for human character and moral habits rather than literal biological changes. The author aligns Plato's views on the afterlife and purification with Christian concepts of Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether Plato believed in the literal transmigration of souls into animal bodies, or if such descriptions were intended as metaphors for human moral character. It references a wide array of "ancient theologians" including Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus (Mercurius), and Zoroaster to argue for a more symbolic interpretation.</meta>

<page-num>xviij. 180</page-num>
<sig>3 4</sig>

# Theology

The Angel who [administers] divine things. For such a thing the soul becomes: just like the habit it puts on. Such it is in the body; such it is also outside the body. **Socrates** confirms the same in the *Phaedrus* <note>The *Phaedrus* is one of Plato's dialogues dealing with the soul, beauty, and the nature of love.</note>, saying: "I therefore consider whether I myself am a beast more complex than **Typhon** <note>A monstrous giant from Greek mythology; Socrates is asking if he is a wild, multicomplex creature or a simpler, divine one.</note>, or a more divine animal." And later in the same book, he places a charioteer and a pair of horses in the soul: one good and one evil. These represent **Reason**, and the powers of **Anger** <term>original: "irascendi," the spirited part of the soul</term> and **Desire** <term>original: "concupiscendi," the part of the soul driven by physical appetites</term>. Here it appears that within those very powers, there are both the "human" and the "beast." In the same way, <margin>D</margin> **Parmenides** the Pythagorean had depicted the soul in his book *On Nature*. **Timaeus** the Pythagorean, a most noble man, also says that the migration into beasts is "falsely introduced to strike terror into wicked men." But **Pythagoras** himself signified the whole matter thus: *If, having left the body, you come to the free ether, you will be an immortal god, undying, no longer mortal.* <note>original Greek: "ην δ’απολειψασ σωμα εσ αιθερ’ ελευθερον ελθησ εσ’εε αθανατοσ θεοσ αμβροτοσ ουκεti θνητοσ"</note> This means if, having laid aside the body, you ascend to the free heavens, you will be an immortal god—immortal and no longer subject to death. It is as if he were to say: "You will be made an immortal god in such a way that you will be entirely far from death, never again to return <margin>E</margin> to mortal things." **Orpheus** also, in his hymn to the "Terrestrial Mercury," says of Mercury: *inhabiting the irreversible path of necessity of Cocytus.* <note>original Greek: "κωκυτου καιιωκη ανυποστροπον οικον αναγχησ." Cocytus is one of the rivers of the underworld.</note> In these words, he places eternal punishments in the underworld and completely removes that "manifold return" from life to life. But not even <margin>F</margin> all the **Egyptian priests** truly believe that the transitions of souls happen from species to species. Rather, they want it to be understood as the "beastly" or "heroic" habit of the soul when they assert a man becomes a beast or a hero; for among them, man is the only animal [with a rational soul]. This was revealed by **Mercury** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, the high priest of the Egyptians. Who, <margin>G</margin> when he had described such a migration in a poetic ritual, added that divine law does not permit the migration of our souls into the bodies of beasts. He also assigns everlasting punishments to wicked souls in the lowest elements of this world. And he clearly asserts that the souls of the wicked are subjected to eternal suffering by an immortal sentence. He also gives thanks to God because He has consecrated good men to eternity. Likewise, he says that the mind is joined to God to such an extent that it is never further entangled in errors. Finally, **Zoroaster**, <margin>B</margin> the inventor of that ancient theology, speaks thus: *For the beasts of the earth will inhabit your vessel.* <note>original Greek: "σοι γαρ οφ’ ξειον θηρεσ χθονοσ οικησου σιν"</note> That is to say, if the beasts are within us, then we pass from man into beast and from beast into beast *inside* ourselves, not outside. Nor <margin>J</margin> are there lacking those who explain transmigration into beasts in this way: that the souls which led a life similar to brutes dwell among various crowds of beasts. **Olympiodorus** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator.</note> judges this to be quite consistent with Plato, because Plato held that the most purified souls dwell among the gods. However, the impure souls often revolve among tombs, and we are sometimes accustomed to seeing their shadows flitting about. Indeed, since they have drawn something of the corporeal around themselves as well as into themselves, <margin>K</margin> Plato wishes it to be so that they may sometimes be seen. Similar to this is what **Pliny the Younger** writes: that there was an infamous house in Athens in which both a noise was heard and the ghost of a shaggy old man was seen. And when **Athenodorus of Tarsus**, the philosopher, had rented the house, that ghost appeared, and with the ghost as a guide, he discovered bones entwined in chains in a grassy area of the house under the earth. These he buried, as was the custom, and after that, the house was freed from that noise. He adds that he believes this because many people affirmed it. It is therefore nothing strange if impure souls, if they dwell among these places, similarly dwell among brutes. From all these things, we conclude that <margin>L</margin> **Plato** affirmed only those things concerning divine matters which he approved in his *Epistles* and the *Laws*. In these, infinite circuits of souls are not approved. And those things which he judged only in other works as the inventions of the ancients, he held to be "probable" rather than certain. And if anyone should pretend that Plato also affirmed these things [literally], we too perhaps might affirm them for the sake of argument...

<summary>This page argues that the transmigration of souls into animal bodies is a metaphor for human character and moral habits, citing authorities like Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus, and Zoroaster to support a symbolic interpretation. It concludes that Plato likely viewed literal reincarnation as a "probable" myth or a deterrent for the wicked rather than a certain theological truth.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion—where Ficino argued that Plato’s talk of souls entering animal bodies was metaphorical—to a new section. He is now moving to reconcile Platonic philosophy with the monotheistic doctrine of a created universe, shared by Jews, Christians, and Muslims.</meta>

...we will yield. But we shall judge that things must be explained far differently than the words might designate, just as was declared a little while ago, both by the words of Plato and by the testimony of the ancient theologians <note>Ficino often groups "ancient theologians" like Orpheus, Hermes Trismegistus, and Zoroaster as precursors to Plato.</note>.

### ¶ Of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, on the Platonic
### Theology concerning the immortality of souls, addressed to
### Lorenzo de' Medici, a man of great soul.
### Book Eighteen.

## ¶ That Plato does not forbid placing faith in the common
## theology of the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs: that the
## world was created. Chapter One.

<margin>a</margin>
**P**lato, therefore, seems to forbid nothing <note>original: "nihil prohibere videtur"</note> in placing faith in the common theology of the Hebrews, Christians, and Arabs: namely, that the world began at some time, and that the angels were created from the beginning. Furthermore, that the immortal souls of men are created every day. We are compelled to this by divine authority, and we are led to this by reasons of this kind. The mass <term>original: "moles," referring to the physical bulk or matter of the universe</term> of the world cannot exist through itself, in such a way that it does not depend on something else, but establishes itself within itself; otherwise, it would in some way create itself. However, to create or "make" anything does not pertain to the body; for whatever a body seems to do, it executes through a certain incorporeal power lying within the subject. Rather, the power of creation looks entirely toward an incorporeal essence remaining within itself, which is the origin of both [the power and the subject]. Furthermore, a corporeal mass cannot contain itself. Indeed, it is unable to contain unless by doing something—especially since it cannot have the power to contain without union. But union seems to belong not to a divisible nature (which itself stands in need of union), but rather to a power that is ultimately and entirely indivisible. Again, this same mass cannot act or move through itself. Because if things cannot give existence to themselves, much less will they be able to provide action. And conversely, if it could act upon itself, it could also act through itself. How it is not able to operate through itself is also clear from the fact that it cannot move itself, as we proved in the sixth book. Moreover, we have shown elsewhere that the perpetual and most orderly motion of the world requires an infinite power, which a finite and determined nature of a body cannot have from itself. Therefore, the world—as if wandering and dissolvable by its own nature—borrows its indissoluble order from elsewhere. But from where does it borrow it? Certainly, if the world can neither subsist through itself, nor contain itself, nor act or move through itself, it necessarily depends on a cause that exists through itself and contains itself. I say it depends on that which is utterly indivisible, lest that cause likewise be dependent on another—that is, through parts or a gatherer of parts—or be contained by another—that is, by a unity connecting the parts to each other—or be insufficient because it needs parts, or have "non-existence" mixed into it, since a composite made of parts is none of the individual parts. Furthermore, since the world is composed of dissimilar things, it is necessary to examine the cause of such a composition. For a body does not compose itself, since it is the principle of neither action nor union. Nor should it be said that the parts of the world flowed together into such a composition by some motion of their own. For bodies do not move through themselves. Nor [did they flow together] as if driven toward it from elsewhere, or as if compelling one another. For what is it that impels them? And what impels the first <margin>B</margin> part? Furthermore, it is a sin to commit such a marvelous order to impulses that lack order. In what way is such great order and ornament fashioned out of things that are unordered and unadorned? For the agent is always accustomed to being more excellent than the effect. Besides, if you say the parts of the world are the material causes of this composition, we shall ask about the efficient cause <term>The "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; in this case, the Creator</term>. But if you say they are the efficient causes, we will again inquire: in what way is a rational work produced from things lacking reason? Therefore, if the world is composed neither by itself nor by chance, it certainly has a definite cause for its composition. Nor should anyone argue that it has only a final cause <note>The "final cause" is the purpose or goal (the "end") for which something is made.</note>. For it does have one, since it is rightly directed toward the Good as if toward an end. But since it is not moved toward that end in vain...

<summary>In this opening to Book 18, Ficino argues that Plato's philosophy supports the monotheistic doctrine of a created world, using metaphysical arguments to show that the material universe requires an incorporeal, indivisible, and rational First Cause to exist and maintain its order.</summary>
