--- Page 420 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter One of Book Eighteen. Ficino is building a logical and authoritative argument that the world was created by God’s will and reason, rather than by chance or necessity. He draws on "ancient theologians" like the Chaldean Oracles, Hermes Trismegistus, and Orpheus to support this view.</meta>

<margin>B</margin>
...anything certainly receives some good from that cause. It receives it either according to its essence, or because it desires and is moved according to its essence. Therefore, it receives its being from the same source from which it receives its essential goodness. Thus, that cause is as much the <term>efficient cause: the agent that brings something into being</term> as it is the <term>end: the final purpose or goal (telos)</term>. It is also the <term>exemplar: the perfect model or pattern in the mind of the creator</term>. For if the world is led toward the good by a certain reason, surely God continues to direct it toward that good by a certain reason, as if by an exemplar. But since leading toward an end and seeking the good is the duty of the will, God undoubtedly moves the world by His will, just as He also composed it by His will. This is further confirmed by the fact that what is accidental and contingent is usually posterior to that which is ordered—that is, it depends on determined causes. Therefore, the order of the world could not have happened by some prior chance. Moreover, if someone were to bring forward many causes for the effects of the world, he would be unable to explain why the world is one and united, despite being made of diverse parts, unless he reconciled all those causes under a single one. Why would one whole be better than many parts, unless he found one common cause more excellent than the many individual causes? By the power of this one cause, all things come together into one. Therefore, there is one cause for the universe and for its union, to which all things are coordinated. If this cause were devoid of reason, then human beings—who use reason and know themselves—would be more excellent than the first cause, and a human work would be rendered more perfect than a divine work. Therefore, God rationally knows His own infinite goodness as being able to be propagated through all things. Hence, His own goodness pleased Him, to be propagated through individual things. For it is the property of the good to please, and of the highest good to please in the highest degree. By this affection of the rational will, all things were both created and are continually arranged in a rational and optimal way.

<margin>C</margin>
That the world is arranged by divine reason and will is signified in the *Chaldean Oracles* <note>The *Chaldean Oracles* were a 2nd-century CE collection of mystical verses highly regarded by Neoplatonists like Proclus and Ficino as ancient wisdom.</note>, which Proclus recites in his second book with these words: "The intellect of the Father, emanating with perfect counsel, understands the ideas of all forms, which have all proceeded from a single source. For from the Father were both the will and the end. Indeed, they were distributed by a certain intellectual fire, and then divided into other intellectual powers. For the King set over the multiform world an unfailing intellectual figure. The second world is the trace of this, hastening along with the form; and the world, hung [from it], is endowed with ideas of every form. There is one fountain from which break forth other countless divided intelligences, producing things around the bodies of the world. These are carried along in a ritual circuit, turned in every direction; but here and there are different intelligences from the paternal source, like sparks from an ever-watchful fire around the primordial ideas. For the first idea flowed from the Father, as a voluntary fountain." Thus far the Oracle, in which mention is made of the Father, the Son, the Spirit, the ideas, the angels, and the voluntary arrangement of the world.

<margin>D</margin>
But let us now return to our established order. The elements and plants perform whatever they do by a certain necessary affection of their nature. This affection is only of one kind. Therefore, they each perform one specific thing. Beasts, moreover, operate through appetite, which attacks various things according to how it is provoked in different ways through the senses. And just as elements and plants act by an innate necessity, so beasts operate by a necessity brought upon them by their senses. The rational soul acts through the will, which is moved to work not by the physical forms of things (as appetite is), but by the notions and counsels of the intellect. This is a free operation, rightly suiting the perfection of the soul. Such an operation must belong to God above all others.

<margin>E</margin>
Wherefore Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the beneficent will of God was the most certain origin of things.

<margin>F</margin>
Mercurius <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note> also says that the world consists by the divine will, to which all effects are committed. Orpheus, where he speaks of the supreme Jove [Jupiter], says this:

> For having hidden all things, he then sent them forth again
> into the much-rejoicing light from his sacred heart,
> performing his pondered and wondrous deeds. <note>original Greek: πάντα γὰρ κρύψας αὖθις φάος ἐς πολυγηθὲς ἐξ ἱερῆς κραδίης ἀνέηκε σχέτλια μέρμερα ῥέζων.</note>

"When he had hidden all things, he thereafter sent them out into the pleasant light from his sacred heart, working out his thoughts and wonders." In these words, Orpheus aptly declares that the world had its beginning in time from the divine will.

<margin>G</margin>
Nature and appetite never [produce] a work...

<meta>This page continues Book Eighteen, Chapter One of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. Ficino is explaining how a changeless God can create a world that has a beginning in time without God Himself undergoing any change in His will or essence.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>Platonic Book</header>

# Platonic Book

Humans rarely attempt something new unless their nature is affected in a new way or their desire is stirred differently. However, even in a human, the intellect and the will often begin a new work without any change occurring within those faculties themselves. <margin>C</margin> For example, Plato clearly decides in the evening to summon <term>Xenocrates: a student of Plato and later head of the Academy</term>. This firm intention for a future summoning remains settled until the appointed hour arrives to call him. The change that eventually occurs is not in Plato’s mind or will, but in his voice and in the limbs of Xenocrates. Similarly, the <term>worldly machine: the structure or "engine" of the universe</term> was always prescribed in the mind of the Architect of the world. The exact moment of its beginning was marked in the Architect's will. At that very moment which He had pre-designated, the machine was begun, with no change occurring within God. From eternity, God had completed the <term>substantial world: the world of perfect Ideas or Forms</term> entirely within Himself. He then permitted the <term>shadowy world: the physical universe, seen as a dim reflection of the divine</term> to flow forth from that source at the time when it was best. It was "best" at the moment established by the will of divine goodness, through which all things are made good. For we desire things because they are good; however, things are good precisely because God wills them to be so. In whatever manner and at whatever time He wills them to come into being, they are good for that reason alone. Similarly, we understand things truly only when we understand them as they actually are; conversely, things actually exist in a certain way because God understands them to be so. Thus, the truth of things proceeds from the divine intelligence, and the goodness of things proceeds from the divine will.

<margin>E</margin> Where the first cause of things resides, there also is the highest reason of things. Therefore, it was necessary for the world to be made rationally, just as God understood and saw it. God understood and willed that this "shadow"—whose nature consists in motion and time—should flow from Him temporally, that is, from a beginning of time. And the motion of this worldly shadow had to be led from a temporal beginning toward an end, as it still must be; for the time of this shadow is at its beginning and end simultaneously in every individual moment. <note>Ficino is arguing that time is a "flowing now" where every moment is a point of transition.</note> Nor should we ask why the world began to flow forth at one moment rather than an earlier one. For if it had begun a thousand years earlier, we would still ask why it did not start sooner. Yet it had to have a beginning at some point. Furthermore, this questioning is a fallacy of the imagination. There are no moments of time prior to the first moment of the world <margin>A</margin> in which it "ought" to have been created. Whatever is thought of "before" the world is the single, stable point of eternity. Every sequence of temporal moments began with the world and continues as the world runs its course. Similarly, one should not investigate why the world is located here rather than there. This is also a fallacy of the imagination. There is no physical place outside the world. Time measures the entire course of the world; the entire physical place is completely filled by the magnitude of the world. As <margin>B</margin> Plato’s *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world by a divine craftsman or Demiurge.</note> shows, time is equal to the world’s course, and place is equal to its magnitude. 

He is deceived who imagines a physical place outside the world. He is deceived who invents "times" before the world began. And he will be deceived who believes that anything is added to or taken away from divine perfection whether the world flows from it or not; for the world is far less in comparison to God than a shadow is to the body that casts it. Nothing is ever added to or taken from a body by its shadow. Indeed, that spiritual world—the exemplar of this world and the first work of God—is a life equal to the Architect. It was always with Him and always will be. But the physical world, which is the second work of God, departs from the Maker in one respect: it was not always there. Yet it retains another quality: it will exist forever. <note>Ficino follows the Platonic view that the universe, once created, is maintained eternally by God.</note> Composite bodies, however, which are the third works of God, lose every part of eternity. It is reasonable that the world is not equal to God; it is not equal in life, just as it is not equal in substance. Nor is it infinite in every direction, so that it may yield to the divine infinity. 

<margin>L</margin> It is also fitting that, just as all things have two acts—one internal and one external—and the internal act is a life equal to the agent while the external is subsequent, so too the Maker of things contains within Himself an offspring of equal life <note>original: "fetum vita equalem" - referring to the Divine Word or the Intelligible World</note>. But He produces an external "birth" that is subsequent to Him, so that eternity, no less than His other perfections, remains distinct in its effect. And just as this world is produced as something finite in power and magnitude by an infinite God, so it seems likely that it is made "new" and circumscribed by a beginning by the eternal God.

<summary>Ficino argues that God creates the world through His unchanging will and intellect, comparing the universe to a shadow that does not affect the "body" of God. He asserts that time and space only exist within the world, making questions about what happened "before" or "outside" the universe logically impossible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Book Eighteen of Marsilio Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*. On the previous page, Ficino argued that God’s decision to create the world at a specific moment in time does not imply a change in God’s eternal will. Here, he provides further arguments for why the world must have had a beginning, drawing on physics, historical traditions, and the philosophy of Proclus.</meta>

# Theology #
### xviii. ###

<margin>A</margin> Just as the world is assigned a specific location—because it exists here in such a way that it does not occupy an infinite space—so too it is assigned a specific time. It exists in this time such that it did not exist for an infinite duration beforehand. If God exceeds the substance of the universe by infinite degrees of perfection, it is only right that He should exceed the duration of the universe by infinite degrees of duration. For in any given thing, the **substance** is more excellent than its **duration**.

<margin>D</margin> Anyone who considers <margin>B</margin> the parts of the world that exist below the moon—how they change from one state of being into another and back again—and the parts above the moon—how they pass from one state to another in turn—can see that because they change everywhere, they are inherently needy and imperfect. Furthermore, the universe itself consists of a specific <term>subject: the underlying matter or "stuff" of the world</term> and a **form**. Because the subject naturally exists before the form, it has the capacity both to take on such a form and to not take it on. <margin>C</margin> Likewise, the world consists not only of measurable parts but of parts that are in conflict with one another. Finally, the universal body does not exist through itself in any way, but entirely through another: namely, through its <term>efficient cause: the creator who brings it into being</term>, its end, its form, and its matter. Therefore, in its own nature, it is completely unstable. 

Anyone, I say, who considers these four points can clearly conclude that the entire mass of the world, by its own nature, is changeable from being to non-being. It would not be this way unless it had once transitioned from non-being into being.

<margin>E</margin> For this reason, almost all the <term>Democriteans: followers of Democritus, who believed the world was made of atoms</term>, the Cyrenaics, the Stoics, and the Cynics were forced to admit that the world had a beginning in time. The Egyptians say that the first day of the world dawned in such a way that **Aries** was in the middle of the sky and **Cancer** was rising. They claim the **Moon** was in Cancer, the **Sun** in Leo, **Mercury** in Virgo, **Venus** in Libra, **Mars** in Scorpio, **Jupiter** in Sagittarius, and **Saturn** in Capricorn. They say that the individual planets are the "lords" of those signs in which they were believed to be when the world was born. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia famous for astronomy and astrology</note> believe that when the world was born, the Sun was in Aries. Both groups believe that the world was born at a specific time; they call Aries the "head of the signs," either because the Sun was there or because it struck the middle of the sky. <margin>F</margin> For this reason, astronomers judge the fortune of the entire year primarily from the Sun's entry into Aries, as if almost everything depends on that moment. 

To this, the Egyptians added that they assigned only **Leo** to the Sun and only **Cancer** to the Moon. But to the remaining planets, besides the signs they then occupied, they joined the remaining five signs in such a way that the second order began where the first order ended. Thus **Aquarius**, which follows Capricorn, is given to Saturn (who had been last); then **Pisces** to Jupiter (who was next to Saturn); **Aries** to Mars; **Taurus** to Venus; and **Gemini** to Mercury. But let us leave these matters aside and return to the main point.

<margin>G</margin> **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who heavily influenced Ficino</note> demonstrates that because the world has an extended and composite essence, it is naturally scattered and liable to fall apart. Therefore, it is held together only by a certain indivisible power infused by the **Divine Unity**. Furthermore, because the world always moves in an orderly way toward the Good by a natural desire, the origin of such a desire and movement must have been received from the Divine Mind and Goodness. This power, through which the world is connected and moved, must be infinite so that it can be connected and moved without end. Since the world is finite, it cannot possess this power from within itself, but must always receive it from the **Divine Infinity**. It does not receive it all at once—for it cannot contain it—but rather, according to its temporal nature, it drinks it in <note>original: "quasi guttatim"</note> **drop by drop**, as it were, at every single moment. 

Proclus shows that this power flows away just like the passing moments, and is likewise drunk in momentarily along with those moments. In this way, as we have described, the corporeal world is always "flowing" and "becoming," but in truth it never simply "is." It is like the **shadow of a tall tree** in a rushing stream. Even though the tree is seen, the shadow is not the tree; and although it appears to be the same for a long time, it is nevertheless continually renewed as the waves are continually renewed. Why, then, should it seem strange to anyone that the world proceeded once from non-being into being at the beginning? Especially since, according to some, it is so shadow-like and unstable that it passes from being to non-being and back again in every single moment. But <margin>H</margin> Proclus himself has seen these things. **Plato**, in his book on the generation of the world <note>Plato’s *Timaeus*</note>...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the temporal beginning of the universe. Ficino concludes Book IV, Chapter 1 by citing historical authorities who link Platonic thought with Hermetic and Mosaic traditions, then transitions into Chapter 2 to discuss the hierarchy of spirits (God, angels, human souls, and animal souls) and their respective durations in time.</meta>

# Platonic Book #

<margin>A</margin>
...he shows by reason that the world was created by the grace of divine goodness. However, a work of this kind was not established for this purpose: to make God—who is goodness itself—any better. Rather, it was made to reflect the divine goodness. Just as parents do not beget children for any other reason than to see their own image reflected in their children. The world reflects the goodness of God its maker especially well if it demonstrates not only how **generous** He is, but also how **excellent** He is. How generous He is, He demonstrates by the fact that the world is always preserved unharmed by God—for if it were left to itself, it would dissolve. As Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Ut in Timeo inqt Plato"</note>. How excellent He is, the world testifies by the fact that it began to exist at a certain point; through this beginning, one clearly perceives that the world is not from itself, but from God. By an infinite interval, God exceeds the world, He who existed (so to speak) for an infinity before the world, who by infinite power produced the world out of <term>nothing: Latin "ex nihilo", the theological concept that God did not use pre-existing matter to create the universe</term>, and who acts by the freedom of His will, not by a necessity of nature. Such an origin of the world's generation was taught more clearly by **Trismegistus** and **Mercurius** <note>Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage whom Renaissance thinkers believed was a contemporary of Moses</note>. Nor should it seem a wonder that he knew such things, if this same Mercurius was also **Moses**, which the historian **Artapanus** <note>Artapanus of Alexandria was a 2nd-century BCE historian who famously identified Moses with the Greek figure Musaeus and the Egyptian Thoth/Hermes</note> has shown through many conjectures.

## Angels and souls have not always existed. Chapter 2. ##

<margin>B</margin>
**W**e have established the order among bodies; now let us establish the order among spirits. There is that supreme Spirit which always was and always will be. That is **God**. There are also the lowest spirits of beasts, which have not always been, nor will they always be. In the middle are certain spirits between these two extremes that differ so greatly. These middle spirits should have a part of that first Spirit and a part of the lowest spirits. In what way, then, shall we arrange these middle beings? Shall we say they have always existed, but will eventually cease? Not at all. For that which has always been has lived for an infinity through an infinite power. Infinite power is never diminished. Therefore, if they had always been, they would also always be. In that case, they would be equal to God in duration, not middle spirits. Therefore, so that they may be "middle" in their perseverance, it is necessary that they began at some time, but will never cease. Although they were made out of nothing, they will nonetheless not turn back into 

<margin>C</margin>
nothingness. Indeed, that which we call "nothingness" is, in their creation, neither the matter nor the <term>maker: the efficient cause</term> from which they are made. Rather, it is perhaps the "boundary point" from which they arise. And it is truly called a boundary point. They are not, therefore, forced to follow the nature of that "nothingness" so as to return into nothing—a nature which they had already rejected when they first came into being. On the contrary, they preserve the nature of their cause, from which they received their essence. Thus, through that same infinite power in which they are preserved in being, they remain far from nothingness; for by that power they emerged from nothing into being, leaving nothingness behind. It is not at all absurd to think that what is procreated directly by an infinite principle and an infinite end—that is, God—will have no end. For many things which proceed from a beginning and a certain finite limit are rightly considered to proceed without an end. For in this way, number proceeds from unity. In this way, a mathematical line proceeds from a point. In this way, future time is conceived to proceed from the present moment without end, with nothing preventing it. That something created should exist forever—especially the soul—

<margin>D</margin>
is proven not only by religion but also by **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age</note> and **Alganteles** <note>Latinized name for Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), the Persian theologian and philosopher</note> acting as philosophers. Thus, the angels occupy one middle position between God and the beasts. Human souls were allotted the second middle position immediately after the angels. These souls agree with the angel in that they will always exist, but they differ in that they have not existed for all time, as angels have. The angels, having arisen at the beginning of things in the natural order before the course of heaven (of which time is the companion), have existed through all time, even if they have not existed through all eternity. Our souls, born after the origin of time, are junior to the angels. Nevertheless, they are not temporal. For God, through that very point of His eternity which is always the same and towers over the universe, embraces the entire circuit of time; just as He procreated the angels through it, He also procreates the souls of men.

<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, the souls of men are created above the "passions" <note>in this context, "passions" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by external forces, like decay or aging</note> of time, even though they are created after the origin of time. The souls of brutes <note>animals</note>, however, are generated both after the origin of time and under the passions of time. This is because they are not made by God directly through His eternity, but through the rotations of the heavens and the powers of other souls. Hence it happens that they do not live forever. They are subject to the change of time...

<summary>Ficino argues that the world was created "ex nihilo" as a reflection of God's goodness and distinguishes the eternal nature of God from the immortal but created nature of angels and human souls. He posits that while angels were created with the beginning of time, human souls were created within time but remain immortal because they proceed directly from God's eternal power.</summary>
<keywords>divine goodness, creation ex nihilo, Hermes Trismegistus, Artapanus, hierarchy of spirits, immortality of the soul, angels, Avicenna, Al-Ghazali, eternity vs time</keywords>

--- Page 424 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the nature of the soul. Having previously discussed the creation of the world, he now transitions into the specific ontological status of the human soul—specifically why it is created "daily" (individually at birth) rather than all at once, and how it fits into the Platonic hierarchy between the eternal and the temporal.</meta>

...subject [to time]: those things which are made through the movement of the heavens within time. And if it possesses anything precious, it all flows continually from that very fountain of the **third essence** <note>In Ficino’s five-layered reality, the 'Third Essence' is the Soul, which sits exactly in the middle, connecting the divine/eternal realm with the physical/temporal realm</note>; of which <margin>E</margin> they are not the streams, but rather shadows. For this reason, <margin>a</margin> the Platonists believe these are certain images <note>original: 'idola', here meaning reflections or phantom-like likenesses</note> of the world-soul, or of the soul of that sphere in which it dwells; they position it as a middle ground between the third essence and the <margin>f</margin> qualities of bodies. To this essence, however, they trace them back like shadows. Hence Plotinus <margin>c</margin> says: just as many images are spread through many mirrors from a single face, <margin>v</margin> so from the soul of a sphere, many likenesses of one soul are spread into the bodies of **brutes** <note>original: 'brutorum', referring to non-rational animals</note>. The bodies of brutes, I say, in which human souls are not present. For where these [human souls] are, the irrational power follows the rational substance of our soul like a shadow.

### Souls are created every day. Chapter 3.

<margin>D</margin> Why are new souls created daily by God? Could God not have created all souls together once the world was constructed, just as He created all the angels at the beginning of the world? It was not fitting. For if they had lived for a long time released from the chains of bodies, they would have judged purely how much more precious a released life is than any other. Nor would they ever have wished to enter bodies, insofar as they are intellectual beings. Neither God nor an angel wishes to compel the free will of the soul. For the mind does not move in any other way than through persuasion. Indeed, the soul would not even have known each individual body that it could choose, since it lacks the sensory knowledge of individuals beforehand. Thus, this middle part of the divine temple would lack divine priests and sacred hymns. Yet it is necessary that in each circle of this temple a proper choir of priests be led to sing to God. Furthermore, it accords with reason that just as the souls or angels of the spheres were not created through some delays of time before their own spheres, so neither were our souls created before their <margin>h</margin> own bodies. Likewise, the soul is the form and <term>act: Latin 'actus', the state of being active or the realization of a thing's potential, as opposed to 'potency'</term> of the body. Although any act in the universe is prior to potential according to the order of nature, it is nonetheless posterior in time within the same subject. This is because movement is effected from <term>potential: the capacity to become something else, like a seed's capacity to become a tree</term> into act. Therefore, the seed—which is the potential for life—existed before the soul, which is the vital act. To this is added that for anything to be formal, it must be joined to its own matter. <margin>g</margin> Otherwise, that which is composed of matter and form would be a mere heap contrary to nature. Moreover, that which belongs to a thing according to its nature is granted to it before that which is contrary to nature. For what belongs according to nature is present in each thing through itself; what happens contrary to nature comes from some external accident. Therefore, for the soul, by the very reason that it is a soul, it is more natural to be joined to the body than to be separated. How then did it live before the body? Add to this that if there is any higher mind—as some believe—and it is one in species and immortal, while every corporal form is both multiple within the same species and mortal, then the human soul—which succeeds those minds and precedes these forms—will participate in both. Thus it would be either a single soul in the human species and mortal, or immortal and multiple. The first cannot be. If a single soul carries the whole species of souls, it would embrace with its own powers the innumerable souls that could be made under that species. Thus it would be of an almost immense power and immortal, especially since the species of things are eternal, and whatever contains an entire species is eternal. Again, because it would have no communion with these bodily things, it would be far removed from destruction. Indeed, if it were such, it would preserve the pure simplicity of its species. That species is separated from the falling body. Therefore, it would remain in its own purity, alien to mortal bodies, and would not provide life to them. From these points it is clear that the human soul cannot be one and the same in all humans. Again, it cannot be both one and mortal. Therefore, <margin>H</margin> it will be immortal and multiple. In its immortality, it will imitate the minds; in its multitude, it will imitate entirely corporal forms. Perhaps it will be consistent with the order of things that the first grade be held by those ideal species of things themselves. The second, however, by those which receive the species. And of those that receive them, first are those that receive their species according to the full capacity of the creature, and always. Second are those that do not receive the whole species, but do so always. Third are those that receive neither the whole nor always.

<summary>Ficino argues that human souls are created individually at the time of birth rather than all at once, asserting that the soul's natural state is to be the 'act' or form of a specific body. He concludes that the human soul is unique because it is both immortal (like the divine) and multiple (like physical forms).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s origin. Having established that the soul is a "third essence" between the eternal and temporal, Ficino now uses the analogy of light to explain how the soul relates to both the divine Mind and the physical body, and defines the specific terminology of its "creation."</meta>

# Platonice Liber

### Column 1

Just as in the highest rank we place the exemplar of lights, that is, the sun. In the second, the stars, each of which always receives its total light from there. In the third, the moon, which indeed always receives it but not the whole of it, and thus it undergoes eclipses; yet it suddenly recovers it—similarly with the air and water. In the fourth, those things composed of the elements which are in some way transparent and bright; such things indeed desire [light], but neither always nor in its entirety. Let us pass over the opposites <note>Ficino refers to opaque or "dark" matter</note>, which in no way admit light into themselves. But from where does this single species of the soul receive its manifold number?

Perhaps it is not from that which imitates minds <note>The "Minds" or Intellects are the higher angelic/divine ranks in the Platonic hierarchy</note>. Is it then from the fact that it imitates bodily forms? What kind are these? They begin with the body and they end with the body. Otherwise, if our soul were entirely of such a kind that it began and ended at the same time, it would not be imitating them, but would be of the same genus. And yet, if it possessed neither of these [qualities], it would not imitate them, would not be compatible, would not cling to them, and would not give them life. Therefore, it must have one or the other: either it will begin only with the body, or it will end only with the body. The mind—which directs itself toward eternal truth and goodness as its end—cannot end with the body.

<margin>A</margin> For it does all things for the sake of this. Just as we have a conjecture regarding the beginning of things from the efficient cause, so we are accustomed to take a conjecture regarding the perseverance of things from the end <note>The 'end' refers to the purpose or *telos* of a thing</note>. If, therefore, the mind is directed toward an eternal end by its own proper natural kinship, it is capable of eternal perseverance. For a proper end corresponds to a perpetual agent; the perseverance of a thing directed toward its end holds the middle ground between the two. Therefore, since the mind has a perpetual proper end, it also has a perpetual proper agent, and for that reason, it possesses life and perpetual perseverance from both sides. If it does not end with the body, it at least begins with the body. Truly, the soul of man becomes manifold in many bodies. This is indeed signified by the contrary opinions and affections of men. Such a soul does not become manifold from its own species—through which it is one—but, as some think, in a certain way from bodies. Or rather, it is from God, the reconciler of souls and bodies. Not because it is divided within the body; not because it is made of matter like the body; not because it is born from the body. From where then? Unless it is because by divine will it becomes a companion of the body when God provides a beginning to both at the same time. For

---

### Column 2

he provides the same beginning. He drives neither the same nature nor a similar end, but as we said, the same beginning. From this, number itself passes down the same thing. Hence the affection of the soul toward the nature of the body <margin>B</margin> is increased, because it accompanies the beginning of the body. And in the creation of this, the change—which appears as one—is actually triple. For the duration of the soul from nothing into being, made by God alone, is called **creation**; however, the change of a non-living body toward life itself to be received from the soul is called **formation** of the body; and the result is called the **generation** of the animal. The boundary of creation toward which the soul is directed is within itself, responding only to the divine eternity, which is the boundary from which creation proceeds. The boundary of formation toward which it happens is the soul, not staying within itself so much as in the body. The boundary from which it happens is nature as being. Finally, the boundary of generation toward which it tends is the animal, composed of soul and body. The boundary from which it begins is likewise nature—I say nature not only in the particular sense, but also the universal, by whose power the particular body is prepared for the soul. Indeed, universal nature is called a certain power, or the instrument of the **World Soul** <term>anima mundi: the living spirit that Platonists believed animated the entire universe</term>. Therefore, Plato said in the *Philebus*: "If the world lacked a soul, from where would we have ours?" Not because our soul comes from the <margin>C</margin> World Soul in its essence, but because it is placed in the body through its work. Otherwise, the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos</note> shows that our souls are made by the same God and from the same fountain as all the higher souls. Hence that which he shows: that the *Timaeus* says the rational soul comes from God alone, but the irrational life beneath it, which is enslaved to the body, hangs from the celestial gods by God's command. Because, clearly, they prepare the body for the soul, and they strengthen our soul to be infused into the body. But let us leave these things aside as if they were superfluous here.

<margin>D</margin> Let there be, therefore—someone might say—many souls. Let them even begin with bodies; this does not offend the ears. Yet one "scruple" <note>original: 'scrupulus', a small sharp stone, used here to mean a nagging philosophical or moral difficulty</note> remains. In what way is it fitting for God to procreate individual souls at every moment at the whim of those joined in lust? Copulation is not an evil thing, since it is naturally instituted for a good purpose.

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's origin through an analogy of light and distinguishes between "creation" (from God), "formation" (the body's readiness), and "generation" (the combined living being). He addresses the Platonic view that while the rational soul comes from God, the preparation of the body involves "universal nature" and celestial influences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of why God creates souls individually and continuously rather than all at once. Ficino is countering arguments that the "defect" or lust of parents is the cause of the soul, arguing instead that God acts according to a divine plan of providence, using the sun as a metaphor for His activity.</meta>

## Theology

## XVIII. 184

But the lack of moderation in the minds of those joining together <note>Referring to the act of procreation</note> does not cause it. Generation does not arise from a lack of moderation, but from the physical union of the body. God distributes souls to this generation not according to the lust of those joining, but according to the prescribed law of providence, which has seen the number and the times of such unions in eternity from the beginning of things. He has accepted these souls in eternity long ago. Why then does God bring forth souls daily? Because bodies were to be generated not all at once, but through succession. Add to this that He continuously illuminates the angels; and just as He never ceases to form the superior minds <note>The angelic ranks</note>, so He never ceases to procreate the lowest minds <note>Human souls</note>. There, a perpetual formation takes place; here, a perpetual procreation.

I say procreation is constant for as long as the sun—God’s vicar <note>original: "vicarius"; Ficino often describes the sun as the visible representative of God in the physical world</note>—continuously illuminates the higher bodies and continuously generates the lower ones. It befits the immense power of God to always show itself as powerful to the eyes of the mind, so that one may see God continuously procreating something out of nothing in the lowest rank of minds because of the world’s final place. Through this continuous effect, they may more clearly recognize the absolutely infinite power of God performing an infinite act of creation infinitely, if it should please Him. Let them venerate Him as He illuminates the heavens. Let them admire Him (if I may speak thus) as He creates upon the earth. To be sure, creation is a more excellent operation than illumination <note>term: "illustratio"; the process by which God grants divine light and understanding to higher beings</note>.

<margin>¶</margin> Therefore, the former [creation] even more than the latter [illumination] is suited to God; and the latter is done continuously by God. Therefore, the former is done continuously according to God's will. The ministers of God move the heavens. By this motion, subsequent things are generated, while any species of thing on earth performs an action and, in acting, becomes a minister of heaven. Does God Himself alone do nothing while all other things perform some work? Far be it that the First Act <note>A philosophical term for God as the source of all activity</note> should do nothing while others are acting. But you will say: it is enough that He acts insofar as He does not desert the remaining agents, but supplies them with the power of operating. That is not enough. Truly, from this, the works of other causes follow their own nature, and images of *those* causes are made in the world, not images of God. Why would God not also wish to continuously make His own works and His own images, by always procreating many things without a medium? Therefore, since creation is the proper

<meta>catchword: proper</meta>

---

operation of God, while external generation is the proper operation of others, God will not cease to create something as long as others do not cease to generate something. God is the true center of the world,

<margin>†</margin> as we discussed in the book *On Love* <note>original: "de amore"; this refers to Ficino's famous commentary on Plato's *Symposium*</note>, because He is one, simple, stable, and in all things. And any other things whatsoever, being many, composite, and mobile, are perpetually revolved around Him through their natural desire for Him. Thus, God is the center of all things because He is in all things, so much so that He is more internal to each thing than it is to itself. He is also the circumference of the world, because existing outside all things, He so towers over the universe that He excels the highest peak of every thing with His immense dignity. Likewise, as much as He is (if it is permitted to say) the smallest of all in quantity, He is the greatest of all in power. As He is the center, He is indeed in all things. As He is the circumference, He is truly outside all things. I say He is in all things, yet not included, because He is the circumference. He is also outside all things, yet not excluded, because He is also the center. What then is God? He is, so to speak, a spiritual circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. <note>This is a famous Neoplatonic and Hermetic definition of the divine nature.</note>

But if the divine center has some imaginary or visible seat of operation in some part of the world, it rules especially in the middle of things, like a king in the middle of a city. The heart is roughly in the middle of the body. The sun is in the middle of the planets. In the sun, therefore—that is, in the third and middle essence of things <note>Ficino's system places the Soul as the "Third Essence," the central link between the two higher realms (God/Mind) and the two lower realms (Quality/Body)</note>—God has placed His tabernacle. A tabernacle, I say, for His power to be demonstrated more frequently. This seat is familiar to God, not so much because it is the species of the soul, but because it is the middle of the divine city, the public treasury, and the harmonious moderation of the city's parts. We have already often declared that the soul of man is the middle of all things. In this region, therefore, the chief operation of God will more frequently prevail. Such is creation. Therefore, He creates the souls of men assiduously. Surely, because He is the stable center, He creates continuously. Because He is the circumference which encompasses the circumference of the world, He creates them, as the Platonists <note>original: "Platonici"</note> would say, in some manner in the circumference...

<summary>Ficino argues that God continuously creates human souls to match the ongoing generation of bodies, using the famous metaphor of God as a "spiritual circle" whose center is everywhere and circumference is nowhere. He positions the soul as the "middle essence" of the universe, making it the primary site of God's creative activity.</summary>

->Platonic Book<-

...the difference of the world. Again, because it is the center. Therefore it is the highest of things. Because it is the highest, it pours out individual things: both individuals once from the beginning of things, and all things collectively every day: just as by creating the soul, which is the middle of things, he pours out the universe from his own bosom: which are collectively gathered in the middle.

### Whence the soul descends into the body. Chapter 4.

<margin>A</margin>
**W**hence does the soul descend into the body?
**I**ndeed, since God is present to every place while being outside of place, the soul is not enclosed in a place at the moment it is created and becomes present; therefore, it is not properly said to "descend." Nor should one ask from where it descends. For, flowing from God himself, it is present to the body (if I may put it this way) just as a ray from the light of the sun is present to the eye. But it is pleasing sometimes to converse with the ancient sages. If, therefore,
<margin>B</margin>
we believe Zoroaster <note>The legendary Persian prophet, seen by Ficino as a source of ancient wisdom</note> and Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition</note>, it is sent down from the circuit of the world. And, to relate their opinion in order: the lowest mind <note>The human soul</note> first adheres to the highest body. Nor does it merely stick to it, but it is infused into it, through which—as if through a middle ground—it is coupled to thicker bodies. A simple and immortal <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to the soul's essence or its immediate ethereal covering</note> is not joined to a composite and mortal body in any other way than through a body that is itself simple and immortal. And this is not without reason: since the soul, through its own essence, provides life to the body. Its essence is eternal life. This eternal life, to which it first adheres, it adheres to forever. Especially since the essence of the soul is immutable. Thus it follows that it vivifies its first body immutably. Indeed, the proper act of perpetual life is eternal vivification. One might imagine that Aristotle thought something similar in his second book *On the Generation of Animals*. There, when he had proved that the intellectual soul is separable from the body because corporal operation does not share in its own operation, he added shortly after: that to this soul there belongs a certain body which is separable from the body of the offspring. From this also appears what we were seeking earlier against <term>Averroes</term> <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" Ficino opposed</note>: namely, that the intellectual soul is a form that gives life to the body. Especially because when Aristotle had proved there that of the three souls—namely the <term>vegetative</term>,

the <term>sensitive</term>, and the <term>intellectual</term>—only this last one comes from without and is separable from the body, since its operation alone can be fulfilled by itself without an instrument, he then added that all three of these souls are equally in the seed according to potential. But truly, if someone considers these things diligently, he will find that there cannot be any potential common to these by which the body is prepared for the three souls in the same way, unless there is a certain faculty through which it receives life and motion from the intellectual soul in the same way as from the others. But let us now return to the first body of the soul. The <term>Magi</term> <note>The ancient Eastern sages or Platonists</note> call this the <term>vehicle of the soul</term> <note>original: "vehiculum animae"; the ethereal or "astral" body that carries the soul down to the material world</note>: namely, an ethereal little body received from the ether, an immortal garment for the soul; naturally round in shape because of the region of the ether, but transforming itself into the human image when it enters the human body, and restoring itself to its former state when it departs. For this reason, the Magi judge it necessary: because angels are such that they are separable in power and are actually separate from bodies. Irrational souls are neither separable in power nor in act. From which it follows that rational souls, as intermediaries, ought to be such that they are always separable in power—because if bodies are taken away from them, they will not perish—but they are always joined in act, because they obtain a familiar body from the ether, which they preserve as immortal through their own immortality. Plato calls this the "chariot" of both gods and souls in the *Phaedrus*, and the "vehicle" in the *Timaeus*. The celestial souls use the purest spheres of this; the souls of <term>daemons</term> <note>Spiritual intermediaries, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note> use a less pure version; our souls also use a less pure version because of the mixture of the earthly body. For this reason, Zoroaster thus instructs: "Do not defile the spirit, nor deepen that which is a surface." <note>original Greek: "μη πνεύμα μολυνής μηδέ βαθύνης το επίπεδον"</note> That is, do not stain the spirit, nor increase the depth of what is flat. He calls the vehicle itself "spirit" and "flat/surface"—not because it is not a body and lacks depth, but because on account of its most thin and splendid purity, it is as if it were not a body. He therefore commands: do not, on account of too much affection for the elemental body, force the spirit to become filthy even after this life, and...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "ethereal vehicle," the subtle body that carries the soul from the divine realm into the physical world. It explores the nature of the "idol" (a lower reflection of the soul) and the different layers of existence the soul inhabits.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>E</margin>
...and heavy with a grave darkness from the addition of the elements. This "shadow," as the ancient theologians <note>original: "umbram prisci theologi"</note> called it, is what they spoke of. Yet they do not mean that the rational part of the soul is the first thing to cling to the <term>vehicle</term> <note>The "vehicle" (vehiculum) is a subtle, star-like body that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the heavy physical body.</note>. Rather, it is the rational soul itself—insofar as it is rational and a companion to the celestial souls—that puts forth a life-giving act into the vehicle. We have often called this act of the soul the <term>idol</term> <note>original: "idolum"; here meaning a "reflection" or "image" of the soul's power</note>. Plato, in his book on the generation of the world <note>Referring to the *Timaeus*</note>, calls this species of the soul "mortal." He does not mean that it literally dies, but rather, as some think, that it would collapse if the vehicle were withdrawn. For just as the moon’s splendor produces a paleness in a cloud from its own light,

<margin>F</margin>
so the soul in its celestial body emits an "idol" like the tail of a comet <note>original: "crinita comaz"; literally "hairy hair," a common way to describe a comet's trail</note>. This would vanish if that body vanished, just as the paleness of the cloud is extinguished when the clouds are scattered. However, because the vehicle is never actually withdrawn, **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Persian sage</note> says: **"There is also a portion for the image in the place that is all-shining,"** <note>original Greek: "εστί και ειδώλω μερίς εις τόπον αμφιφαντα"</note> that is, even the "idol" has a place in the luminous region. This is because it returns to heaven together with the vehicle and the rational soul. Plotinus, however, believes that this idol is simply immortal, even if the vehicle were to be withdrawn. Similarly, he says that the sun's light in the air—or rather, the light present to the air—is not extinguished even if the air is removed from the middle. For it depends on the sun alone as its perennial act. It is not a "passion" or suffering of the air, nor a quality proper to the air itself. Indeed, it is present in a moment and gone in a moment; nothing of the light remains in the air once the sun is removed. Nor is it only present in the air, but similarly in everything transparent, even if transparent things are of contrary natures, as if it does not depend on a specific nature of the subject. Nor does it depend on the transparent thing in any way because it is transparent; rather, it is present to it only because it is not prevented from being there, just as it seems to be prevented from being present to what is opaque.

<margin>G</margin>
For the sun always emits this act; it does not "let go" of it or "send it away" permanently. It simply happens that something sits beneath it which can receive it—or rather, seems to receive it. This act, in turn, accompanies the sun perpetually. The soul stands in the same relation to the body as a face does to a mirror.

<margin>D</margin>
These are the views of Plotinus. In this "idol," however, they believe there is a certain irrational and confused imagination. Furthermore, there are senses of such a kind that the soul sees and hears equally through the whole vehicle. 

<margin>rari-</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
Very few people—and then only rarely—possess these specific senses properly. Yet through them, the wonderful harmonies of the heavens <note>The "Music of the Spheres"</note> and the voices and bodies of <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are guardian spirits or intermediary beings, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> are often sensed.

<margin>2</margin>
This happens whenever someone, having left the earthly body for a time, retreats into their celestial body. Therefore Tatius, the son of Mercury <note>Characters from the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note>, when he had been purified by his father's sacred rites and expiations, immediately cried out that he had then been translated into an immortal body, and that he beheld and heard wonders.

<margin>3</margin>
Mercury himself relates that the same thing happened to him a little while before during an abstraction of the mind.

<margin>4</margin>
Olympiodorus the Platonist also relates that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker</note> used to see things happening in Egypt from the city of Rome by this method. Furthermore, many Platonists think the soul uses three vehicles. The first is immaterial and simple—that is, celestial. The second is material and simple—that is, aerial. The third is material and composite—that is, constituted from the four elements. From the first, the soul gives an irrational but immortal life. From the second, it gives an irrational but long-lived life, which survives for a certain time in the simple body after the composite body is dissolved. From the third, finally, it gives a life that is both irrational and destined to be dissolved along with the dissolved body. Furthermore, in the first life communicated to the vehicle, the sense is "common" and cannot be acted upon (impassible). In the second, the sense is "common" but can be acted upon (passible)—meaning the entire sense is equally present through the entire vehicle. Finally, in the third, the sense is both divided and can be acted upon.

<margin>3.4.</margin>
### In which part of the heaven souls are created, or from where they descend. Chapter 5.

Regarding the part of the heaven where souls are created: it is foolish to seek a location for things that are not enclosed by any location. Just as wherever the sun shines, a ray is sent, so wherever God is present, He sends souls. Yet it is pleasing sometimes to play poetically with the ancients. Therefore, Timaeus says in Plato that souls are sown among the various stars by the Maker of the world, so that they might become companions of those stars in life. The Platonists do not want this understood to mean that individual souls are assigned to stars, but rather legions of souls. He adds that God gives souls to his...

# Platonic Matters

...placed them in vehicles <note>The "vehicle" is the subtle, celestial body that carries the soul.</note> and taught them the laws of fate. For this reason, they say the souls descend from heaven primarily through **Cancer**, as the Platonists claim; conversely, they believe they ascend through **Capricorn**, which is opposite to Cancer. Thus, they call the former the "gate of men" and the latter the "gate of the gods." No one, however, should be so deceived as to take this "descent" or "ascent" literally according to physical position. Rather, because the Moon—the mistress of Cancer—is the primary ruler of generation, while Saturn—the ruler of Capricorn—is the most remote from the gods, they say souls descend through Cancer (that is, through lunar and vegetative instinct) and ascend through Capricorn (that is, through Saturn and intellectual instinct). 

<margin>A</margin>
For the ancients call Saturn "the Mind." It is by this power alone that they seek higher things. Added to this is the fact that the "dry" virtue of Capricorn and Saturn draws the spirit <note>original: "spiritum"</note> toward the innermost parts and collects it, constantly urging it toward contemplation. Lunar moisture, however, scatters and dilates, distracting the soul toward sensible things. In the descent itself, the soul receives certain "supports" or incitements to better perform contemplation: from the divinity of Saturn through itself, and from the light of Saturn through the ethereal body and the <term>idol</term> <note>The "idol" is a lower reflection or "shadow" of the soul's power.</note>. 

<margin>B</margin>
From the divinity and light of **Jupiter**, it likewise receives the power for the government of civil life; from <term>Mars</term>, it receives magnanimity for repelling injuries; from the **Sun**, it receives clarity of the imagination and senses; from <term>Venus</term>, it receives charity; from <term>Mercury</term>, it receives interpretation and eloquence; and from the **Moon**, it receives the power of generation. Although each of these qualities comes as a "good" from those sources, they can nevertheless degenerate into "evil" when mixed with earthly matter. A descent of this kind can happen almost as suddenly as the descent of rays from the sun; though they are sent down to earth instantly, they are nevertheless clothed in various colors by the clouds they pass through.

<margin>C</margin>
Some, however, think that souls live a life appropriate to each sphere for a certain time, as they are allotted specific vehicles by each sphere. At last, after many ages, they descend to the elements. They live a "demonic" <note>In the Platonic sense, "demonic" refers to spirits (daemons) that act as intermediaries, not necessarily evil beings.</note> life in fire and air, and a human or animal life on earth. Likewise, they eventually return to the higher realms by similar stages. These are their views. As for us, in everything we write, we wish it to be affirmed by ourselves and others only insofar as it seems fit to the assembly of Christian theologians.

¶ When the soul is infused into the body, and by what it is led while living in the body. Chapter 6.

<margin>D</margin>
**Question:** When is the soul infused into the body?

<margin>H.</margin>
After the seed, which had previously flowed from the man's whole body, is in the woman’s womb, it carries with it a formative power from the man's soul. Through this very power, over about forty-five days, it is affected in this way: for six days it turns out like milk. Soon, in the following days, it becomes blood. For another twelve days, it becomes flesh. In the remaining eighteen days, it is shaped. Then the soul is created and infused. 

Those who believe souls lived before entering the body say they naturally chose a <term>daemon</term> <note>A "daemon" here refers to a guiding spirit or "genius" assigned to a person's life.</note> as a leader of life at the very beginning of the descent, before they entered the body. Others, however, say that after they begin to use choice, they secretly choose a daemon as a leader of life by choosing their habits. Often, the same daemon is chosen by many; for many souls can use one "genius"—that is, one daemon who is a leader of their natural character. Those who believe the choice happens before birth want the soul to receive a daemon from that specific crowd of spirits that corresponds to the same star to which the soul was assigned by the Maker of the World. For there are as many legions of daemons and heroes as there are stars in number. From such a crowd, the soul is allotted the one who best suits the chosen life and the "figure of the heavens" <note>The astrological chart or alignment of the stars.</note> that is composed at that moment of choice and descent. 

For these reasons, a great difference arises in the characters and fortunes of men. Those who say that souls receive different geniuses after birth according to their changing habits also claim that these leaders are changed when habits are changed; they attribute more to counsel than to either fate or fortune. Whichever way it may be, we stand in perpetual need of the guardianship of the divine powers. Plato, while he mentions this in the *Symposium*, *Protagoras*, *Politicus*, and *Critias*, proves it thus in the *Laws*: namely, because we dwell among false goods and innumerable evils. From this, constant deception and perturbation are born. Therefore, like sheep, we always need the wonderful guardianship of divine shepherds. He adds that while our own vice destroys us, our own virtue (being so small) cannot save us. Therefore, only the virtue of the higher beings...

### By which part of the body the soul enters and exits; and by what guide it proceeds. Chapter 7.

<margin>G</margin> **T**he soul, which is the medium of things, by the command of God (who is the center of the world), is first infused into the middle point of the heart, which is the primary center of the body. From there, it pours itself through all the members of its body, as it joins its course to the natural heat. Through this heat, it joins to the **spirit** of the body. <margin>- )</margin> Through this spirit, it is immersed in the humors; and through the humors, it is inserted into the limbs. Finally, when these mediums are dissolved through disease, the soul immediately gathers itself (so to speak) with that **vehicle** of yours. It flows back into the heart from where it had first flowed out; once the heat of the heart is extinguished—which was the proper receptacle of that vehicle—it finally leaves the heart as its vehicle releases it. Just as when the eye is closed, the light of the sun which had flowed into it flows out entire, as its own heat releases it. And as **Plotinus** proves, it is not extinguished, but follows its own sun forever. <margin>□</margin> I say for the present: that the guardian spirits and their daemons lead all souls departing the body to the common judge. But once the sentence is delivered, the former daemons depart; a violent and evil daemon drags away the wicked, while God peacefully leads forth the good. This is found in the *Phaedo*.

### On the state of the pure soul, especially according to the Platonists. Chapter 8.

<margin>3</margin> **W**here then is the pure soul when it departs the dead body? Where is the light of the sun when the eye is closed? Indeed, the light is reflected back into the sun. So too the ethereal **chariot** <note>original: "currus"; the subtle, celestial body that carries the soul.</note> of the soul is reflected back into the ether, once the earthly burden is laid down. The soul, born once in the ether, aspires to the ether, as **Pythagoras** says. This is especially true if it has conceived in its mind a habit of living and thinking similar to the ethereal minds. For in this way, the soul is moved and acts by its **habit** <note>In medieval philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable internal disposition or quality.</note> just as nature acts by its forms. This is clear in those who, after they have acquired the habit of an art, operate almost naturally, without deliberation or attention, just as nature is accustomed to do. <margin>f.</margin> Indeed, **Plato** asserts in the *Phaedo* and the *Gorgias* that the habits <margin>K</margin> of both morals and disciplines—both good and bad—remain in the separated soul. Reason proves this because it says a habit is so converted into nature that an inclination proceeds from it just as it does from nature. This is most fully realized in souls separated from this mutability. <margin>L</margin> But why do the souls of the elements and their vehicles not also strive toward a celestial habitation? To answer according to the opinion of the Platonists rather than my own: a duty has been assigned to them by God to be there always. Souls yield to the divine will. <margin>X.</margin> Their vehicles also yield to the desire of the souls. Those souls do not lose a more excellent duty because of this present duty. Their vehicles maintain a circular motion around their souls without being hindered. And just as it is natural for the heavens to be turned there around their souls, so it is here for these vehicles around theirs. But our soul, having rightly performed the duty enjoined upon it for a time, chooses for itself above all others that region of the ether to which it had been assigned at birth. It rises up to that star and divinity, as Plato says, to which it rendered itself similar while living. But let them see to these matters. Furthermore, just as on earth it proceeded by considering individual things toward the common species of natural things, and from species toward divine reasons as if they were the causes of natural things; so in heaven, in turn, it converts itself from divine reasons (that is, the **Ideas**) toward natural species, and from these perfectly toward individuals in a certain way. And just as diligently as it inspected individuals here, so it perceives them there without effort. Conversely, what it perceived obscurely of divine things here, it perceives clearly there. And what it saw here one by one through instruments in external light, it sees there according to the species through itself in intrinsic light. Truly, as much as it once turned toward the senses, so much does it then turn toward the mind. In the eye of the mind, the divine light shines. This can indeed <margin>§</margin> be said to be intrinsic to minds even here; yet it is much more so there, depending always on God himself—just as a ray infused into the eye depends on the sun—and it is preserved, full of forms, just as...

**B**ut lest anyone should distrust that the separated soul can be raised to such a great light, because we see it surrounded by such great darkness in the body, the Platonists command us to compare the **intellect** <term>intellectus: the faculty of the mind that perceives spiritual or abstract truths</term> to sight, and the **intelligible** <term>intelligibile: that which can be understood by the mind, as opposed to "sensible" things seen by the eyes</term> to the visible. Sight never fully comprehends the light itself in the sun. For that light always exceeds its proportion. Sometimes, hindered by a **cataract** <note>original: "cataracta"; used here as a medical metaphor for a blockage or clouding of vision.</note>, it does not even see the light in colors. Sometimes it is clouded by a certain vapor, or red or yellow: and it judges obscurely and differently than the thing is. At other times, either because of a contraction toward the internal **imagination** <note>original: "imaginationem"</note>, it does not seem to see external things, or because of a distraction toward objects far distant from each other, it hardly discerns either one. So, if it proceeds a little more attentively toward one, meanwhile it turns more feebly, or in no way at all, toward the other. 

Similarly, the human intellect never fully comprehends the immense fullness of the divine light overflowing in the absolute nature of God. Indeed, since that light exceeds the capacity of the mind. Furthermore, some can clearly perceive that same light of God, whether determined in the **Ideas** <note>Platonic "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things.</note> of created things or already contracted in the angels: namely, when the mind has been so far removed from the contagion of the body as they are. But now, joined to the elemental body as if by a certain cataract, its proportion to those things is so hindered that it cannot at all comprehend the **ideal reasons** <note>original: "ideales rones"; the logical structures within the Platonic forms.</note> and angelic substances which are separated far indeed from matter. Therefore, as often as it thinks out certain of their properties according to its strength, being so joined to the **phantasy** <term>phantasie: the faculty of forming mental images, which Platonists often saw as a bridge—or a barrier—between the physical and spiritual.</term>, it sees them wrapped in the images of the phantasy—as if in vapors and clouds—so that it is forced to see them either very obscurely or differently than they are. Finally, even if it might briefly dispel the clouds of phantasy as much as it can, meanwhile, because it is contracted to the difficult ministry of ruling the body, and distracted by having to attend continuously to the encounter of sensible images and the intuition of intelligible things at the same time, for that reason it hardly looks up to the heavenly influences, and, as it were, does not see them clearly.

Therefore, it should seem a wonder to no one that here we perceive neither the clarity of divine things nor that sweetness itself, which is tasted there from them, or that we ourselves taste even a little. Surely the mind, on account of formless matter—which is most foreign both to the mind and to divine things—cannot taste the truth and pleasure of divine flavors, no differently than a tongue paralyzed by **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"; in medieval medicine, an excess of phlegm was thought to dull the senses.</note>. ### Theology XVIII.

But by what taste it may feed upon these flavors, we have argued elsewhere. <margin>D</margin> To this point tends that Platonic saying in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul.</note>: that souls which have emerged from the water of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology.</note> fly up higher. There, they first perform a celestial circuit along with the celestial gods, and then a supracelestial circuit with the supracelestial beings; that is, in that order: so that some wander around there with certain deities, and circuits of this kind are repeated in alternating turns. This means nothing other than that the souls, released from elemental bodies and now in celestial vehicles <note>The "astral body" or subtle spirit-vehicle that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul between the physical and divine realms.</note> restored to their own proper circular shape, dwell in the celestial region. And there, together with the stars and other inhabitants of heaven—to whom they are more familiar either by nature or by habit—they both harmonize in a certain governance of the world and likewise run through the species of things by reason. Again, with the supracelestial gods, that is, the angels, they suddenly harmonize in the very intuition of the Ideas <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in Platonic thought.</note> and, as if in a certain circuit, happily perform both [the celestial and supracelestial] along with both groups. He [Plato] adds that they are fed there together with the higher beings on nourishment: namely, ambrosia and <margin>☞</margin> nectar. He considers ambrosia to be the clear and sweet intuition of truth. Nectar, <margin>E</margin> however, he considers to be an excellent and most easy providence <note>The divine care and foresight through which the universe is governed.</note>.

Here is also opened that ancient secret celebrated by Plato in the book *On the Kingdom* <note>Referring to the dialogue *The Statesman* (Politicus).</note> above all others: that the present circuit of the world from east to west is "Jovian" [of Jupiter] and fated. But there will one day be another circuit opposite to this one under Saturn, moving in turn from west to east. In this state, humans will be born spontaneously and will proceed from old age into youth; and nourishment will be supplied to them freely under an eternal spring according to their <margin>☞</margin> wish. They call the "World Soul" Jupiter, I believe, by whose fatal law this manifest order of the manifest world is <margin>F:</margin> arranged. Furthermore, he wishes the life of souls in elemental bodies to be "Jovian": <margin>v:</margin> <margin>Time:</margin> devoted to the senses and to action. But Saturn <note>In Ficino's astrology and philosophy, Saturn represents the highest intellectual and contemplative faculty.</note> he wishes to be the supreme intellect among the angels, by whose rays souls are illuminated beyond the angels and are set on fire, and are continually raised toward the intellectual life according to their strength. Whenever they turn toward a life of this kind, they are said to live under the Saturnian reign to the extent that they live by intelligence. Therefore, in that life, they are said to be regenerated "spontaneously" because they are reformed for the better by their own choice. Again, they are said to "grow young daily," that is, if days are even counted there, they flourish more and <margin>Apostle:</margin> more. This is what the Apostle Paul meant: *The inner man is renewed day by day.* <note>original: "Homo interior renovatur in dies." 2 Corinthians 4:16.</note> Finally, nourishment is supplied to them "freely and in abundance under a perpetual spring" because they enjoy the wonderful spectacles of truth itself not through the senses or laborious study, but through an internal light, with the greatest tranquility and pleasure of life. The scent of such a life is <margin>clear</margin> sensed when the mind is separated [from the body] as much as possible; <margin>separated</margin> but the taste is enjoyed when the mind is entirely separated.

He adds here in the *Symposium* that purified souls, which have loved divine beauty above all else, finally immerse themselves entirely into the very ocean of divine beauty; and there they not only drink the divine liquids but even pour them out from themselves <margin>blessed</margin> upon others. He concludes the summit of happiness in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue often attributed to Plato, following the *Laws*.</note>, where he says that the most purified soul—once its mutability is made firm and its multiplicity is gathered—betakes itself entirely into its own unity, which is higher than the intellect. Through this, it is now transferred into the divine unity, which is higher than the intelligible world; it lives by God rather than by itself, to whom it is certainly joined by a certain wonderful reason that is above the intellect. Plato wishes this "knot" [union] to be effected by a certain divine light, which shines in the mind in no other way than if, being entirely set on fire by the love of God, the mind is transformed into God. Thus it happens that in the *Phaedo*, he placed divine love far above all grades of divine madness and good souls. Here, indeed, the Platonic mysteries lie hidden most of all; I will briefly summarize a few of them below. Surely, when segregated minds first turn toward themselves through their natural and proper ray, just as animals that see at night, they see only a few things.

# Platonic Philosophy

Then indeed, by turning themselves through their own ray into the light common to all species of sublime minds, they now clearly behold all things created by the author of this light, as if through the light of day. Yet they cannot attain the Light itself, the origin of this brightness—which they naturally yearn for and therefore do not desire in vain—simply by looking up. For even if that light is infinite in God, it becomes narrow within created minds. Although they perceive the Light obscurely, they are nonetheless inwardly set on fire by its heat through their ardent loving. And having been set on fire—which is the proper quality of love—they are transformed into light. By this they are finally strengthened, following through love what they could scarcely follow from afar through sight. Thus, the Light itself now becomes most easy to attain through love, which they previously struggled to pursue with their eyes. So great is the power of love, so great its ease, so great its happiness; or rather (to speak more correctly), so great is the power of the light that is loved. **For the mind**, in loving the light, does not so much set itself on fire and transfer itself, as it is set on fire, transferred, and made to shine by the light that sweetly allures it, vehemently strikes it, and penetrates it deeply. Since the total efficacy of perception and enjoyment that exists in the external senses is present much more in the imagination, and is again far more powerful in the mind—especially when it is freed from the body—and since the reasons <note>Latin: *rationes*. In this context, it refers to the ideal forms or blueprints of things existing in the divine mind.</note> of sensible things and pleasures exist most exactly in God, it follows that while the mind is freed, it places in God the highest and most sincere of all the pleasures of the senses, feeling them most fully in its own miraculous way. Nor is this only an imaginary delight regarding God, such as in seeing, hearing, and smelling. **For these** cannot fully satisfy; rather, it is also soothed by a certain substantial pleasure similar to taste and touch. I speak of a taste or touch not of some external contact, as occurs in the senses, but of one that penetrates deeply and is
