### The Nine Degrees in the Homeland. <note>The "Homeland" (*patria*) is a traditional theological term for Heaven, the true home of the soul.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
**A**ccordingly, there are nine degrees of the blessed arranged not only among Christians, but also among the Platonists, both among the angels and among souls. This is done for this reason, as I believe: because divine contemplation is perfected there in nine principal ways. Surely, just as we hunt for the power, wisdom, and goodness of God from the power, order, and utility of things with whatever sagacity we can, so they in turn recognize these same three things in objects from the divine goodness, power, and wisdom—as if from the final, efficient, and exemplary cause <note>Aristotelian categories of causation: the "final" is the purpose, "efficient" is the maker, and "exemplary" is the model or blueprint.</note> of the universe. They do so in such a way that some consider the divine goodness chiefly in itself; others refer it chiefly to things themselves; and others chiefly refer things to the goodness itself as if to their end. Yet each individual beholds all these things. Thus, a triple intuition of the divine goodness is fulfilled, through which the first three orders of the blessed are distinguished. In three ways they likewise contemplate Power, and in as many ways they contemplate Wisdom. From this, six additional orders of the blessed are 
<margin>B</margin>
enumerated. To these nine degrees of the happy ones among the Platonists, the eight regions of the heavens and the ninth region conceived above the heavens <note>The "supracelestial" realm, or the Empyrean.</note> seem to be fittingly accommodated. Among the followers of Orpheus <note>Refers to the Orphic mysteries, an ancient Greek religious tradition often cited by Neoplatonists.</note>, however, there are the eight heavens and the ethereal fire beneath the moon. Among Christians, there are nine circles beneath the Empyrean. For everyone is carried toward that particular region by a certain similar disposition, as if by a natural lightness, having rendered themselves especially similar in life to the angels who inhabit it. Similarly, Christians believe that the souls of the damned are precipitated into nine degrees of damned demons, to whom they made themselves similar while living, as if by a natural weight of similarity. But more on these things elsewhere. That there are nine degrees in beatitude <note>The state of perfect, eternal happiness in the presence of God.</note> is also, I believe, proven by reason. For we fear the divine power, we seek the divine wisdom, and we love the divine goodness. Only the love of goodness transforms the soul into God. Therefore, love—without the need for searching or fear—returns the soul to the homeland. But the opposite is by no means true. But now, let us arrange the degrees themselves, by which they ascend into heaven, in order.

# Theology

<margin>C</margin> **For** in the first rank are those who primarily love goodness. Next, they fear power; lastly, they seek wisdom. In the second are those who primarily delight in goodness, but regard the other two equally. In the third are those who are similarly affected by goodness first, then scrutinize wisdom, and lastly fear power. In the fourth are those who regard all three equally. In the fifth are those who love goodness first, then greatly dread power. In the sixth are those who similarly delight in goodness, but in the next degree they desire wisdom. In the seventh are those who love goodness absolutely and simply. In the eighth are those whom power moves first, goodness second, and wisdom third. In the ninth are those with whom wisdom prevails first, goodness second, and power third. I believe a mystery of this kind was signified in the Gospel <note>The author refers to the "Beatitudes" in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3–12).</note> where the divine oracle calls his followers "blessed" nine times; this is because, by nine degrees of merit and under the guidance of the God of heaven, nine orders of contemplation are blessedly sought. But behold, now the blessed commemoration of the Holy Gospel seems to warn us: that, having dismissed these philosophical windings, we should seek happiness by a shorter path, the way by which Christian theologians lead us—and Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was a Dominican friar and the most influential philosopher-theologian of the Middle Ages, known as the "Angelic Doctor."</note> first among them, the splendor of Christian theology.

## On the state of the pure soul, especially according to Christian theologians.

<margin>D</margin> Any created mind, whether looking into its own essence <note>original: "essentia" — the fundamental nature of what the soul is.</note> (which there differs from its actual being <term>existence: "esse"</term>) and which exists in a certain species <note>original: "specie" — here meaning a specific category or form of being.</note> at an infinite distance from God, or looking into its own private light, or into any light determined within it, cannot understand the divine substance. Since that substance is infinite, certainly what it is in itself cannot be represented by anything finite. <margin>E</margin> Indeed, it is only through those things we have mentioned that minds know both that God exists, and what He is *not* rather than what He *is*, and by what principle either He relates to other things or other things are referred back to Him. Plato proves this in the *Parmenides* <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of the "One" and the many.</note>. Likewise, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian Neoplatonist whose "Mystical Theology" argued that God is known through a "divine darkness" beyond all human concepts.</note> confirms this in his *Mystical Theology*, concluding that minds at the highest stage of natural knowledge are joined to God as if to something unknown, like an eye growing dark beneath the light of the sun. In such knowledge, however, natural desire is not fulfilled.

For whatever is contained within a certain species carries out the perfection of that species. But such knowledge is judged to be incomplete in the act of knowing itself. For we are not accustomed to rest in any mode of knowledge until we think we have known what the thing itself is according to its substance. Furthermore, it is natural for reason to engage in continuous discourse through arguments until it reaches the highest reason; and since that is infinite, it alone can halt the discourse of reason, which would otherwise wander pointlessly without end. Indeed, beyond any finite thing, the mind always devises something further. This is evident in the pursuit of innumerable lines, figures, and proportions. From this it follows that the mind can only come to rest in the substance of God, which alone is infinite. This should be judged to happen for this reason: both the sharpness of natural intelligence and the heat of the will are a kind of ray infused from the first divine light itself through its own light, and they naturally spring back into that same light; nor does the movement cease until it has finally restored itself to its own sun. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, the closer something is to its natural end, the more vehemently it approaches that end. This is manifest in the movements of the elements <note>A reference to Aristotelian physics, where elements like fire or earth move faster as they approach their "natural place."</note>. Separated minds <note>Pure spirits or souls freed from the body.</note>, through natural knowledge, turn out to be closer to God and joined to Him. Therefore, if our minds are not content with the boundaries of their natural knowledge, certainly those are much less so. Since the appetite of any natural species, directed by universal nature, cannot be altogether in vain, it follows that all minds must be able to see the divine substance, without which nothing is seen perfectly. But since they cannot see it in any created form, there is nonetheless a need for a form through which they may see—a form, I say, proper to the Divine substance itself, through which they may discern it not through the imagination, but properly. It is necessary that they be so coupled to the divine substance that they may now behold it through itself. Something similar appears in the sense of sight, which perceives colors through their images under the light, but cannot see light itself through anything other than light. <margin>G</margin> But lest anyone should think it absurd for God to be joined to the intellect like a "form," one must remember that the perfection of the mind consists in Truth.

<summary>The author classifies nine ranks of souls based on their priorities of goodness, power, and wisdom, linking them to the Gospel Beatitudes. He then argues via Thomas Aquinas and Dionysius that the soul's infinite longing can only be satisfied by a direct, supernatural vision of God's essence, rather than through any finite or natural knowledge.</summary>

The author synthesizes Neoplatonic ideas about "Being" and "Truth" with the Scholastic doctrine of the "Light of Glory."</meta>

# Platonic Book

Truth and being are the same as the "intelligible" <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "intelligible" refers to things that can be understood by the mind but not perceived by the physical senses.</note>. Whatever in this category is composed of essence and existence is more a "being" and "true" than "Truth" and "Existence" in itself. No created mind can serve as the form <note>In this context, "form" refers to the organizing principle that gives something its nature and allows it to be understood.</note> for other minds, because its form is already limited to its own specific "matter." Therefore, only God stands in relation to the whole category of minds as their form; He alone is **existence itself** and the simplest truth. He is a form, I say, not as a part of a composite mixture, but as the principle of operation. In this way, the mind acts as God rather than the mind acting as itself. It is like gold heated by fire, which acts more like the fire than the gold. This is the kind of gold the **Apocalypse of John** <note>A reference to Revelation 3:18: "I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire."</note> commands us to buy.

### In what manner the mind is joined to God.

<margin>A</margin>
**A**S for the mind putting on the divine substance as if it were a form, it is not led to this by its own power, but is drawn by divine action. Indeed, an inferior nature cannot attain the property or form of a superior one without the action of that superior being itself. This is evident in the elements, where air does not become fire unless fire acts upon it. Furthermore, nothing can be led toward a more excellent action unless its power is first strengthened. If a thing is to be led toward a familiar type of action, but one that is somewhat more intense, it is enough for its usual power to be increased; for example, if air, which naturally heats by one degree, is to heat by two degrees, it is sufficient to intensify the quality of its natural heat. However, if the air is to claim an action of a superior species or genus—namely, if it were to give off light, which is the property of the **ethereal body** <note>The "ethereal body" or "quintessence" was believed to be the substance of the stars and heavens, which naturally emits light.</note>—it must then receive a new form from the ether itself. Why mention this? So we may understand that the mind cannot be raised to behold the divine substance through its own power by a mere increase in natural virtue and light. Such an operation differs from the natural operation of the mind by more than just degree; it requires a new power and a new light descending from <margin>D</margin> a higher principle.

# Book

<margin>B</margin>
They call this both the **light of grace** and the **light of glory**. Once the mind is illuminated—and much more, set on fire—by this light, it puts on the divine substance (in whose heat it now glows) like a flame. I say a flame, not like the dry vapor lifted from the earth that turns into a comet <note>original: "crinita," literally "long-haired star." Pre-modern observers believed comets were atmospheric vapors that caught fire near the sphere of fire.</note> when it reaches the sphere of fire, though that seems very similar; rather, it is a super-celestial flame that shines healthily and does not burn. Someone might perhaps deny that minds can be led to perceive God by any light at all, arguing that there is no proportion between sight and sound; likewise, there is no proportion between the finite mind (or the light received by it) and the immense God. But we respond: although God exceeds the faculty of the intellect, He is not as alien to the intellect as sound is to sight, or as an imperceptible thing is to the senses. For God is, as Christian theologians prefer, the **first intelligible** <margin>C</margin>: the principle, the middle, and the end of all intellectual power and action. There is, therefore, a certain proportion between the intellect and God—not that there is any shared measurement, but rather a relationship, like that of intellectual "matter" toward an intelligible form, or an effect toward its cause. Furthermore, although that infused light becomes finite when it enters the mind, it is infused by God with the power <margin>E</margin> to couple the mind to the divine substance—not by a natural bond, but by an intellectual one. A natural ray of light cannot accomplish this, because from the beginning it has already passed entirely into the nature of the recipient, which was previously formless. Thus, the natural ray itself becomes shadowy and weak. Nor can the mind, since it has degenerated far from divine simplicity, obtain its total perfection through that same natural ray. Therefore, the natural ray is one thing in the mind, through which it understands things according to its own species; but the light infused by God is another, which, by lifting the mind, wonderfully raises it to a most eminent degree beyond anything that can be imagined. Finally, the infinity of God does not signify a lack of form (such as the <margin>F</margin> infinity that belongs to matter, which is powerless and...)

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the human mind is joined to God. On the previous page, Ficino argued that God acts as the "form" or organizing principle of the mind during contemplation. Here, he clarifies the limits of this union: though the mind "sees" God, it does not "comprehend" Him as fully as He comprehends Himself.</meta>

# Theology

forms: he rightly judges it unsuitable for cognition.
But it signifies an absolute excellence, narrowed down by no subject at all. This, just as the sun has this by its nature: in a marvelous way, by remaining silent and by illuminating, it can most of all move the intellectual sight and be seen. And by that same power through which it exceeds minds, it can raise the mind above its own proper strengths. Yet, one must not think that because the mind is formed by the divine essence—in that it understands what that essence is—it therefore "comprehends" it completely. The mind's power is limited, and the light within it is determined; thus, when it enters the divine essence, it is not formed by the *entirety* of the divine power. What then?

<margin>D</margin> Does it perhaps see one part of the divine substance while not seeing another part? We certainly should not say so, since God cannot be divided. Rather, one should think that the mind gazes upon God, yet does not "comprehend" Him—that is, it does not perceive God with as many perspectives, or with as much certainty and perfection, as God is perceived by Himself. Added to this is the fact that the mind cannot see all the things that God sees and is able to see. For God sees and is able to see infinite things beyond those He has established in nature, as we have proven elsewhere. If the mind does not comprehend God's substance, it certainly does not comprehend His intelligence or His power. Therefore, it does not understand all that God understands and can do. Otherwise, since power is usually estimated by what it can achieve, if the mind saw and could completely comprehend all things, it would equally comprehend the power of seeing and acting, and thus the substance of God. What more? The higher an intellect is, the more things it ought to understand, whether in number or by reason. From this it follows that the divine mind, looking upon itself from every side, sees both more things and through more perspectives than any other intellect sees.

->**All types of minds can be joined**<-
->**to God.**<-

<margin>E</margin> **N**o one ought to doubt that human minds—despite being the lowest in the very category of minds—can be led to the contemplation of the divine substance itself. For neither do the angelic minds themselves reach that point by any natural power; rather, they are drawn there by a divine and (so to speak) <term>supernatural</term> <note>original: "supernaturali". Ficino uses this to describe actions that exceed the "built-in" capabilities of a created being, requiring a direct "boost" from God.</note> power. A work that is carried out by a supernatural power cannot be hindered by the diversity of natures. Indeed, nothing anywhere can resist the immense power of God. The divine power moves the entire machine of the universe as easily as it moves the smallest part of the world. It heals a person who is gravely ill as easily as one who is only lightly ill. For this reason, by a faculty infused by God, the highest minds and the lowest are equally snatched up to the heights.

Furthermore, the highest of created minds is distant from God by an immense space. However, the lowest mind is separated from the highest mind by a finite interval, since both are finite. The proportion of this finite interval to that infinite one is judged to be nothing. But if a finite addition to an infinite gap brings no real difference (as it seems), what prevents the power of God—which instantly traverses the immense space to reach an angel—from then embracing the tiny gap between the angel and the human soul? Thus, the soul and the angel may be snatched up together.

<margin>F</margin> Finally, if there is a natural instinct in the category of minds (by virtue of them being minds) to see the "highest intelligible" <note>The "highest intelligible" is God, the ultimate object that the mind is designed to understand.</note>—which they seek in seeking any understandable thing, and which they desire in all desiring—it follows that such a natural instinct belongs to the lowest minds as much as the highest. And thus both these and those can naturally reach their desired end. Our own natural "appetite" or longing shows us this: since it draws us toward the infinite, it cannot be implanted or moved by anything other than the infinite itself, and finally, it can only be satisfied by the infinite. If inferior things moved by nature are not moved in vain, how much less so are those led by the Supreme Power? The ray of this Power, transferring itself through all the orders of minds, both illuminates each one so that they may see, and sets them on fire so that they may love. Since fire and the sun usually propagate their light further than their heat, it is logical that wherever the ray of the divine sun reaches by "heating" (inspiring love), it can much more reach by "illuminating" (granting vision). Therefore, just as human minds, being set on fire from that source, daily desire the divine Good, so too may they eventually reach the divine Truth.

<summary>Ficino explains that while human and angelic minds can see God, they cannot "comprehend" Him fully because His nature is infinite. He argues that because this union is a supernatural gift, even the "lowly" human mind can be raised to the same vision of God as the angels.</summary>

¶ **Different degrees in the homeland: and how all see all created things.**
¶ Other minds, however, can behold the divine substance more clearly and fully to the extent that they receive the light itself from that source under different degrees of perfection, preparing themselves as if they were the "matter" for that light. They prepare themselves in different ways either by their natural capacity or by the diversity of their acquired disposition. Indeed, the greatest variety for our minds proceeds from the different degrees of love. Fittingly, different degrees of vision—and much more, degrees of joy—correspond to these degrees of love. 

Perhaps, indeed, although individual souls see all created things (as we shall prove), some nevertheless reach more things than others among those that are not created; and they are affected by more reasons regarding what they see. Nevertheless, God is perceived through a true account. And since joy responds as the boundary of love, those who have loved more ardently are joined more closely—as love is accustomed to do—and clinging more deeply, they are transformed into the Good. Thus, with the very habit of love contributing, they enjoy it more sweetly. 

Furthermore, if the end of minds is to arrive at the divine substance, necessarily every desire of the minds is entirely filled there, as if in the ultimate goal. However, it would not be filled unless they understood the entire created order of the universe from every side.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ Indeed, such is the habit and pursuit of the intellect: that it resolves particulars into universals, reaching all the way to the most common principles. It describes "being" itself under an absolute account and divides it most distinctly through all its degrees. It is as if the intellect were born specifically for this: so that it might one day be formed by the very form of the universe. What, then, prevents the intellect, while it gazes at the source of the universe, from perceiving the universe flowing out from there? This is especially true since the intellect is not hindered by the highest "intelligible" object from seeing lesser things—unlike the senses, which are temporarily blinded by the highest "sensible" object (like the sun)—but is instead wonderfully strengthened. Furthermore, the "intelligible" genus is broader than the "natural" genus. For many things can be understood beyond those that nature actually makes. Therefore,

# Book

whatever is necessarily required to complete a "natural being," even more things are required to complete an "intelligible being." <note>Ficino distinguishes between "natural being" (physical reality) and "intelligible being" (reality as understood by the mind). The mind's reality is "larger" because it can conceive of things that don't exist in the physical world.</note> But "intelligible being" is only then made absolute when the intellect has reached its highest end. Just as the perfection of natural being consists in the constitution of all things, for this reason, whatever God produced for the perfection of the universe, He also produces in the intellect joined to Him. 

Again, although one may see God more perfectly than another, each person nevertheless sees Him in such a way that their natural capacity is filled to their wish. This capacity in any mind extends to all the genera and species of the universe. Add to this, moreover, the individual things placed everywhere under those species. For we do not desire beyond this. 

Thus, minds in God discern even individual things distinctly. Surely, since a superior power can do whatever an inferior power can—and even more eminently—and since souls joined to bodies know both universals and particulars, it is consistent that minds joined to Truth itself should comprehend both through a single power and a single intuition. This is especially true because the species of things themselves are most fully present in those minds, and they attain the most effective power there, through which they derive knowledge from genera and species all the way down to individual things. 

To be sure, the species of things reach the "joined" intellect and the "separate" intellect in a certain opposite order. <note>The "joined" intellect refers to the soul while in the body; the "separate" intellect refers to the soul after death or in pure contemplation.</note> In the former, it happens by a certain resolution, separating the species from the individual conditions of matter. In the latter, however, it happens from a certain conjunction of the mind with the **Divine Form**, which is the maker of all things and the judge of even individual things. This Form is not abstracted from individual things, but is everywhere the creator of individuals—not only of their form, but also of their matter, in which the origin of individuality resides. For this reason, the forms flowing into the mind represent more than just commonalities; they represent individual things to the joined minds. This is also confirmed by this: if angelic minds move celestial bodies through the intellect, it is necessary that they are not ignorant of that very thing which they move, and which in turn is changed by their motion. Our minds, indeed, can be led to angelic perfection, especially regarding knowledge of motion—particularly if they obtain some office of governance there.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument from the previous section, moving from how the mind sees all created things in God to the permanent, unchanging nature of that vision. It explores why this "state" of the soul is stable and how different human archetypes find their ultimate fulfillment in the divine presence.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>D</margin>
¶ **The state of the soul with God is immovable.**
**S**ince minds there see the forms of created things in the single form of God, it is fitting that they all see with a single vision. If this vision is indeed most perfect, it is possessed in a **fixed state** <note>original: "statu"; referring to a permanent condition of rest as opposed to the constant change of the physical world</note> rather than being sought through **succession** <note>original: "successione"; the step-by-step process of learning or moving through time</note>. For it is probable that minds, which are eager for rest rather than motion, will rest firmly once they have reached their end. This is especially true because if they know all the species of the universe there—and since under certain genera <note>categories</note> there proceed innumerable species, or species according to number, figure, and proportion—it seems to follow that they see species that are, in some way, infinite. But since it is not permitted to pass through infinite things one by one, they do not count them by passing through them, but behold them while remaining still. 

Again, if the perpetual intelligence is a kind of life for the one who understands, and if there the intelligence, because of its stability, becomes a participant in eternity, it follows that the blessed mind is rightly said to be translated into **eternal life**. And rightly so. For the human mind is placed as a medium between eternal and temporal things. Just as its operation, by which it is joined to temporal things, is accustomed to becoming temporal, so also that operation which is joined to eternal things becomes eternal. 

Finally, I do not see how that vision there could be mobile <note>subject to change or movement</note>, where the power of seeing transcends time from the very beginning (and most especially now), and where the object which is seen, as well as the form through which it is seen, is **Stability** itself and **Eternity** itself. From this it follows that souls, once adhering to God, will never depart from Him, provided they have already transcended motion and fulfilled their natural desire. Since this desire is founded in a stable substance and is naturally directed toward a stable object, it surely desires nothing other than a stable possession as its final goal. What wonder is it if the everlasting mind desires what it desires—not for the sake of something else, but for its own sake—and desires to hold it forever? 

Furthermore, since the mind is ignorant of no natural things beneath itself, it certainly is not unaware of the nature of its own possession. Therefore, if it were ever to be lacking it, it would foresee its future loss and would live unhappily, thinking that it would eventually—or rather soon—lack such a dear possession. Add to this that whatever naturally adheres to an end is not torn away except by some applied force. Therefore, since the mind, like light, is joined to God as its end—naturally, above all else, and by choice—and since God Himself is the efficient cause of this union, and no greater opposing force can exist that might violently separate what God has freely joined, without doubt the mind will never be compelled by anything to withdraw from that place. 

Moreover, it cannot be imagined how the mind would turn away, either from certain truth through deception, or from the pure and total Good through its own will. Truly, neither is the substance of the mind changed, nor does the clarity of its understanding fail under the light that continually strengthens it. Nor is that light ever withdrawn, which is poured out from eternity into eternity. Nor does the will withdraw from the possession of the Whole due to the stimulus of something else, or segregate itself from that Object due to boredom or satiety. Because that Object <note>God</note> cannot be fully encompassed, it always presents itself as something new and with the highest wonder; therefore, it is possessed with continual desire. Finally, if it is true that the closer something is to the highest state of God, the more immovable it becomes, then it is necessary that minds already formed by the divine substance must become entirely immovable.

¶ **Individuals are satisfied in God.**
<margin>E</margin>
**H**ere, indeed, individuals achieve whatever they desire. **Philosophers**, who are greatly devoted to truth, here perceive all true things within Truth itself, the mother of all truths. Here **statesmen** <note>original: "viri ciuiles"; those devoted to the "active life" of governing and civic duty</note> devoted to government and power become the most powerful governors alongside the omnipotent Governor of the world. Here, those who desire victory and glory have now conquered all adversaries. They have moved everyone; they are known to all the blessed. Here, the followers of pleasures—if only they reach the source of pleasures—will enjoy total pleasure. For just as physical bodies are but shadows of divine things, so also the delights of the senses are but shadows of divine joy. For the mind is far more effective than the senses, and perceives the true and total Good more than the senses perceive a certain false good...

He explains that in this state, all types of people—philosophers, leaders, and pleasure-seekers—find their specific ultimate satisfaction in the divine essence.</summary>

Moreover, the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus"; the highest part of the human mind that perceives spiritual truths directly</note> is accustomed to penetrate its object from all sides, since it distinguishes intrinsic things from extrinsic ones, and things that are its own from those belonging to others. This is something the senses never accomplish. Likewise, the **intelligible object** <note>the non-physical truth being thought about</note>, on account of its wonderful purity and power, flows entirely into the inner recesses of the intellect itself. This is something a physical object cannot do for the physical senses. 

For this reason, the pleasure of the pure intellect regarding the highest intelligible truth is not only continuous and pure—of a kind that does not exist in the senses—but it is also grasped as intimate, whole, and entirely complete all at once. It surpasses the pleasure of the senses by much more than the sweetness of flavors surpasses the empty allurements of smells. We are accustomed, when we are restored to our proper state, in whatever way that happens, to be filled with pleasure. Truly, no restoration can be thought greater than when the soul, which had fallen away from the **Ideas** <note>the eternal, divine blueprints of all things</note>—or rather from itself—restores itself entirely into its own Idea, or rather into itself. 

There, again, the soul rejoices in the very Idea of joy. In that one Good, it enjoys all goods. And since those things delight us which we desire, and we desire all things that are good, there we are bathed in the highest pleasure; for since every good is present there, we perfectly obtain whatever can be sought. 

Truly, clear minds enjoy every good primarily according to the essence of the Good itself; however, they enjoy the various "grades" of the good according to their own specific Ideas. They do this insofar as they love different levels of the total Good and set out toward that Good by various paths. Finally, to speak summarily: there is entirely one thing which all the blessed enjoy, even if some enjoy it in different ways and for different reasons, just as each person is drawn by their own pleasure, whether varying by their own affection or by the different way the object allures them.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>As Plato says: "All envy is absent from the divine choir."</margin>
Thus therefore, as Plato says, all envy is absent from the divine choir. For the common charity in that choir ensures that they congratulate each individual's happiness as if it were their own. Furthermore, when everyone already attains their heart's desire—attaining what they loved, for the reason they chose it, and to the extent they desired it—everyone there lives without envy and far from its sting, entirely content and full. **Ficino**.

The capacity of the soul, both natural and acquired, is entirely filled; nor is a greater capacity desired by anyone. For one's own things are naturally most dear to each. Added to this is that nothing is more pleasing to the blessed, who burn with divine love, than to will that very thing which they know God wills: and to take possession of the beloved God in the measure they can receive Him, for the reason they desire Him, and in the manner in which God offers Himself to be possessed. But they recognize that their Good cannot be entirely comprehended there, and they are wonderfully delighted by this very fact: namely, choosing that their treasure be infinite rather than finite.

### Concerning the Bodies of the Blessed. Chapter IX.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>To pure souls, a double happiness belongs. One from itself, which we have discussed. The other from the body, which, among the Platonists, is of this kind.</margin>
It is better to think of this by a certain example. Your eye is indeed round, clear, bright, and very swift in motion. It has a wonderful sharp-sightedness. It sees my eye, and beholds itself reflected in mine. It gives shape to each of your soul's affections within itself and transfers them into mine; and in turn, it receives my affections through my own eye. Such are those **chariots of the souls** <note>original: "animorum currus"; a famous metaphor from Plato's Phaedrus where the soul is depicted as a charioteer driving two horses</note>, both in themselves and toward one another. For each of them is entirely an "eye." 

And in almost all things, it is as we see the eyes themselves to be. Therefore, since they are like certain round, clear, bright eyes, very swift in motion, they look around at all things from every side with great ease. They display the affections and thoughts of their souls and indicate them to other souls very easily by a kind of "nod," as it were. They also receive, in a similar way, the signs of others' affections and thoughts. 

And not only do they see most sharply from afar and from all sides, but they also hear. This is likewise true for all the stars and **spirits** <note>original: "demones"; in Neoplatonism, these are not evil demons, but rational, spiritual beings that mediate between gods and humans</note>. They easily form effortless voices; and just as the senses there are without any "passion" <note>original: "passione"; meaning suffering or being passively affected by external pain</note>, so also are the voices: certainly of another species and kind than ours. Thus say **Plotinus** and **Hermias** <note>Plotinus (3rd century) and Hermias (5th century) were major Neoplatonic philosophers who commented on the nature of the soul</note>.

# Theology

...in his **Metaphysics** <note>original: "metaphysicis"; a major work by the Persian philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina)</note> Avicenna proves that the soul, separated from the contagion of the body, uses a certain celestial instrument in the heavens, as if it were received from the body of the heaven itself; and through this instrument, the soul exercises the function of **imagination** <note>the faculty that allows the soul to form mental images even without physical eyes</note>. Indeed, following the opinion of **Plato**, he wishes for the intellectual soul to preside over the entire physical mass of the universe with natural dignity and command. Finally, those **chariots** <note>a reference to Plato's "Phaedrus," where souls are described as riding in horse-drawn chariots through the heavens</note> are filled with the overflowing splendor of their minds and shine wonderfully. The whole heaven is accessible to them, as if by certain rays. And as is pleasing to many followers of Plato, they sparkle like stars, especially in the **Milky Way** <note>original: "orbe lacteo"</note>. For this reason, ancient poets used to say that when happy souls flew back to the powers above, new stars shone in heaven. But let them look to those matters. Added to these things are the arguments of the followers of **Zoroaster**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato**—chiefly **Plotinus** and **Proclus**—who argue that since the same causes return in every way, the same individual people are destined to return through the same experiences. And Plato writes in his book **On Kingship** <note>original: "de regno"; likely referring to the "Statesman" (Politicus), where Plato discusses the cosmic cycles of the world</note> that after the present and fated course of the world, the souls of men, by God’s command and by raising up their bodies which they lost in this current course, will receive them back. He argues that just as human bodies once fell into the earth under the power of **fate**, so under the command of divine **providence** they shall rise again from the earth and live again. 
<margin>D</margin> These mysteries of the ancient philosophers do not differ much from the mysteries of the Hebrews and Christians, which are also confirmed by the **followers of Muhammad** <note>original: "maumethenſibus"; Muslims</note>. 
<margin>E</margin> For the opinion common to these three laws <note>the "three laws" refers to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam</note> is that the whole of this movement cannot truly be the end, because it always flows from one thing into another. Indeed, this very tendency toward something else is utterly foreign to the definition of an **end**, especially the **ultimate end** <note>the final purpose or resting place of a thing</note>. Therefore, the highest and ultimate end of the universe—which the world must eventually reach, since even individual things smaller than the world pursue their own proper ends—will not be **motion**, but **rest** <note>original: "statum"; a state of permanence or stability</note>. For rest is more perfect than motion, and all individual things move for the sake of reaching a state of rest. Furthermore, the body of the world will be most beautiful in that state, being most perfected. When the course of heaven is finally finished, through which all things are currently born, nothing further will be generated. Instead, the individual bodies of men, for whose sake everything was previously generated, will all rise from the earth at God’s command. They confirm this resurrection first by divine authority.

For so God has often predicted through the **Prophets** and **Apostles**, and in various ages, He has raised many from the dead. Furthermore, holy men, even after they have departed this life, have performed miracles and continue to do so daily. I pass over the rest, for they are innumerable. Certainly, in our own time, in the year 1467, in December and January, certain relics of **Peter the Apostle** <note>referring to a reported discovery of relics in Volterra during the 15th century</note> were found in the city of **Volterra**; they showed twelve miracles, and indeed huge ones, manifest to all the people. These and similar things are the most powerful signs of the resurrection, so much so that Avicenna asserts in his **Metaphysics** 
<margin>⏹</margin> that one must believe in the divine authority that guarantees the resurrection. And if Avicenna does not attempt to bring forward any logical reasons for such a great matter, Christian theologians nevertheless persuade us with arguments of this kind. 
<margin>§</margin> The **first reason** is this: because from the human soul and body, one single natural **composite** <note>a thing made of two parts that belong together by nature</note> is formed, and the soul is attracted to the body by a natural instinct. Therefore, it is clear that the soul is coupled to the body not only by the order of the universe, but also according to the order of its own nature. It follows that it is contrary to the order of both universal and proper nature for the soul to remain permanently separated from the body. However, after the death of the body, souls remain eternal. Since that which is **against nature** <note>original: "contra naturam"</note> cannot be eternal, it follows that souls will eventually receive their bodies back. 
<margin>⏹</margin> The **second reason**: individual souls are naturally inclined toward vivifying and ruling their individual bodies. For so nature and providence are balanced between the eternity of life and time, having an inclination partly toward eternal things and partly toward temporal things by nature. But a natural inclination remains as long as the nature itself remains. Therefore, souls separated from their bodies will always naturally incline toward them. A natural inclination or tendency should not be in vain forever; for that is utterly foreign to the order of the universe. Therefore, souls will eventually receive those very bodies for which they always have a natural affection.

# Platonic

# Book

Insofar as it belongs to the soul: it is imperfect, just as a part usually is when it is outside of its whole. It was established for the purpose of constituting that whole. Therefore, its natural appetite will never be at rest. No soul will ever be truly blessed unless it is led back to its whole—having resumed its body—and it hopes to be led back. 

<margin>A</margin> **The fourth reason.** Rewards are owed for virtues, and worthy punishments for vices. Since these are not fully granted in this life, they must be granted in the next. Furthermore, the body is a participant alongside the soul in both virtues and vices. Therefore, so that it may simultaneously share in the rewards or punishments, it is eventually restored to the soul; nor should it seem absurd that souls, after they have departed from their natural habit <note>The "natural habit" refers to the soul's innate state of being joined to a physical body</note>, should return to that same state again. 

Indeed, the planets both leave and seek out their natural houses <note>In ancient astrology, "houses" were the specific zodiac signs where a planet's influence was strongest</note>. Likewise, small particles of the elements, often expelled outside their own proper place and separated for a long time, meanwhile continually lean toward it, and finally return. Nor is it difficult for the infinite power of God, present everywhere, who created the whole from nothing, to reclaim bodies dissolved into elements from those very elements, which in turn bear witness to them. 

Indeed, He will reweave the same body because the **form** <note>In Platonic and Aristotelian thought, the soul is the "form" or organizing principle that makes a body what it is</note> will be the same as it once was—that is, the soul—and the primary matter <note>original: "materia sempiterna"; the basic, eternal substance that underlies all physical things</note> will also be the same, which underlies all things. Finally, the same indeterminate dimension remains as the companion of matter. Indeed, in this life, we have the same body from childhood to old age, even though it flows out and flows back in continually. 

<margin>B</margin> The body will rise again entirely immortal. For from the beginning, God so tempered the order of things that for the rational soul—which is eternal life and the natural form of the body—its matter (that is, the body) would correspond in this very respect: so that through the soul itself, which lives forever and naturally desires to give life forever, the body might similarly be able to live forever. 

Potency of this kind is a certain good, most consistent with the order of the universe. Therefore, since God, who created it from the beginning and created it such that it could live forever, when He recreates it in reality, He will undoubtedly fulfill what is most fitting, lest a potency so good and so fitting to the universe be forever in vain. Furthermore, that creation made by God, once the motion of the world has ceased—which was established for the sake of the perfection of some eventual rest—will be directed toward something lasting and stable. Thus, the body will remain forever joined to the soul. 

Again, the intention of nature in generating is directed toward the perpetuity of at least the species. And it received this from God Himself, in whom the first root of perpetuity flourishes. Therefore, the intention of God in **regenerating** <note>Referring here to the resurrection as a second, divine "birth"</note> is directed toward something perpetual much more than nature is. He will therefore recreate man incorruptible: not only in species—for that could be sufficiently fulfilled through ordinary generation—but also as an eternal individual <note>original: "numero sempiternum"; literally "eternal in number," a technical term meaning the specific, individual person is preserved, not just the "human" category</note>. 

Not according to the soul alone—for it had this even before—but also according to the body. To this is added: in daily generation, the soul comes to a body already made. In that regeneration, conversely, the body comes to the soul. Therefore, just as the present life of the composite human follows the condition of the falling body, so that future life of the composite will in turn follow the condition of the immortal soul. So that deprivation may finally cease in a state that is at least the most perfect natural species. And death, as if very weak—as the prophets say—may be swallowed up by life <note>A reference to the biblical passage in 1 Corinthians 15:54: "Death is swallowed up in victory"</note>. 

Likewise, bodies rise again for this reason: so that eternal rewards and punishments may be paid out forever to the bodies that earned them. Therefore, it shall rise again eternal. Add that they are also raised so that souls do not remain forever imperfect. Since, therefore, in this matter, He consults the perfection of the soul itself above all else, such a body will be returned as is fitting for the soul. To an eternal soul, an eternal body is fitting. 

<margin>C</margin> Sacred scriptures <note>original: "littere sacre"</note> testify that this was granted even from the very beginning of things. Indeed, this gift, which was interrupted for a time in a certain ordered movement, will finally be restored by God to the whole, ordering it as is best. That the natural state of man was such from the beginning is shown by this: that the more perfect man is than the beasts, the more easily, perfectly, and frequently he ought to be able to attain his end than they attain theirs. In the present state, however, the opposite occurs. From which it is clear...

...humans are characterized by this: because they have departed from their first temperament <note>original: "temperatione"; this refers to the perfectly balanced mixture of elements or "humors" that Renaissance thinkers believed humans possessed before the Fall or their descent into materiality</note>, they strive toward their own happiness with the greatest difficulty. They will finally achieve it most easily only when they have been restored to their prior state.

<margin>D</margin> This indeed is the opinion of Zoroaster, Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note>, and in the mysteries of Plato, and among the poets singing of the Golden Age; it seems most consistent of all. But let us now return to the resurrection. Ultimately, the immense power of God is the efficient cause of the resurrection. Therefore, by the same infinity of life with which He rouses the dead, He most fittingly preserves them as free from death forever. For it seems proper that such a great miracle of returning to life should be followed only by everlasting life. In this matter, Almighty God renders bodies so subject to the command of their souls that the eternal life of the soul overflows into the body. This is naturally fitting for the most excellent form <note>In Platonic philosophy, the soul is the "form" that gives the "matter" of the body its shape and life</note> in relation to the matter subjected to it, and it is most consistent with the order of nature. Indeed, as theologians teach, it is consistent with the order of merits. It is also highly appropriate that bodies are joined—not so much according to the general life shared by all human souls—but according to the specific quality of that life: that is, to souls that are pure and joined to God through their qualities and actions, just as those souls themselves are joined to God. 

Therefore, the intellect—full of divine light—and the will—filled with joy and incomparable power—completely transfer that splendor, power, and marvelous motion into the body. Thus, just as those souls are raised to the level of celestial minds, so too are their bodies raised to the clarity and virtue of the heavenly bodies <note>The stars and planets, which were thought to be made of a perfected, incorruptible fifth element called "aether"</note>. Nor should it seem strange that the human body—which by its nature is already somewhat similar to the heavens due to its balanced temperament—should suddenly be lifted up to the celestial region when it puts on a certain heavenly form by a divine gift, drawn by the soul which is supported by the infinite power of God. Even now on earth, though separated from God, the soul binds, sustains, and lifts the body against the nature of its own elements; how much more then, when joined to the super-celestial God, can it lift the body with itself to the high ethereal region. In that penetration, the body neither strikes the ether nor is it struck by it, for that most pure body has already been made ethereal in virtue and quality.

### The State of the Impure Soul. Chapter 10.

<margin>E</margin> **S**o that we may understand what the state of the impure soul is after death, we must observe what the habits and character of the living are. For just as the character of youth largely becomes the habit of old age, so too are the affections of the dead. In this present life, virtue and vice are born. With virtue, the reward begins; with vice, the punishment. In the future life, virtue and vice are perfected. There, the reward is fulfilled, and the punishment is completed. Virtue is reward in its beginning; reward is virtue in its adulthood. Vice is punishment being born; punishment is vice perfected. For the seed is the same as that which becomes the harvest, and the harvest is the same as that which becomes the fodder. 

<margin>F</margin> Therefore, what we sow in this autumn <note>Metaphor for this mortal life</note>, we shall reap in 그 summer <note>Metaphor for the eternal life</note>. We shall either be fed in the dusky night of the Stygian marsh <note>The Styx, a river or swamp in the classical underworld</note>, or we shall feast in the serene day of the Elysian fields <note>The paradise of the classical afterlife</note>. Just as Nature, the minister of divine Providence, moves light bodies upward and heavy bodies downward by an internal weight, so too Providence leads all things by an internal law and a certain natural inclination. By this law, the high minds and the souls themselves, being implanted with it, govern the universe under the First Governor. By this same implanted law, human minds lead themselves to the places suitable for their way of life.

<margin>G</margin> And just as the humors in an animal have two principles of motion: the natural and the animate. By the natural principle, light things move upward and heavy things move downward quite often. By the animate principle, they move toward those members that need them most, as the life of the living being requires. So too, souls possess two principles of motion within them. From...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the fate of souls from Chapter 10. # Platonic

# Book

Again indeed, it is either by their own impulse or by judgment. The other is indeed the law of divine providence, entirely implanted in the soul's innermost parts. By the former <note>referring to their own impulse</note>, they transfer themselves into these or those habits <term>mores: character or habitual ways of acting</term>. By the latter, once these habits have been contracted, they are led into places of punishment or rewards suited to those habits by a certain intrinsic and occult inclination. Plato very often approves of this opinion, received from the ancients. All the Platonists everywhere confirm this. <margin>a</margin> They distinguish this law—which is always good in itself and divine—in such a way that they call it "Grace" and a "Good Spirit" <note>original: "bonū demonē"; in Platonic thought, a 'daemon' is a mediating spirit, not necessarily an evil entity</note> when it returns good things for good merits. Conversely, some call it "Nemesis," or a "Fury," or an "Evil Spirit" when it leads sinners to punishments. That law leads from within in the manner of nature, and so gently, that no one feels any violence from providence until they reach the final end. And meanwhile the universe—which would very often be dissonant due to the first principle of the actors' motions—is restored to its harmony everywhere through this second principle of motion, while individuals gradually receive their merits through their own movement. Furthermore, there is no lack of <margin>B</margin> good spirits for us, who are called "genii" <note>guiding spirits assigned to a person at birth</note>, constant leaders of our character, who lead not by force but by persuasion. There are also evil ones, not as naturally ordained leaders, but as adversaries—or, as I might say, strangers. The Platonists think these are driven away in this life through philosophy and sacrifices. <margin>C</margin> But both Plato and Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> say that after this life, wicked souls, having changed their "genius," fall into the power of an evil spirit. That is, after they have been led by their own genius to a judge who cannot be deceived. This is especially so since everything appears clearly in separated souls: both those things which were there by nature and those which were there from the passions. Hence Socrates says in the *Gorgias*: "Setting aside all other things, I focus on this: how I may show the judge a most healthy soul." For the greatest of evils is to descend to the underworld with a soul filled with sins. He adds both there, and in the *Theaetetus*, and in the *Republic*, that these things are not to be mocked as if they were fables. For indeed, whoever denies such things always introduces ridiculous things themselves into public view. Therefore, he teaches that we must strive for this above all: that <margin>D</margin> the best habits be acquired. For he says that habits are <margin>a</margin> the paths leading either to the lower regions or to the upper ones.

I think it will be worthwhile to repeat more broadly what he writes about these matters in the *Republic* and in the book *On Knowledge* <note>The *Theaetetus*</note>. Truly, he says those people are to be utterly mocked who think that either justice should be pursued or injustice avoided for the sake of human rewards or punishments. Rather, that opinion is true which asserts that those are not the real rewards or punishments which some people receive, perhaps by chance, but those which always and by a necessary order follow virtues and vices. He adds in the book *On Knowledge* that God is justice itself, and nothing is more similar to Him than a just man, and nothing is more dissimilar than an unjust one. Furthermore, we must consider that to be clear wisdom and power which knows this and pursues it according to one's will. The opposite habit must be judged as extreme ignorance and weakness. Accordingly, he places two extreme models in the universe. At the highest point, indeed, is the most blessed divinity. At the lowest, however, is the opposite of divinity—void of it and most miserable. He affirms that the unjust, on account of their extreme ignorance, never notice that because of their injustice they become daily more dissimilar to the most blessed and more similar to the most miserable. He judges that such dissimilarity or similarity is the proper punishment for injustice, while the reward for justice is properly the similarity to the most blessed and dissimilarity to the most miserable. To these he adds that the unjust are not received into the homeland of blessedness itself, either in this or the other life, inasmuch as they are dissimilar; rather, by a certain perverse habit, they are congruously drawn back to the lowest place of misery, to which they have become similar, and they always wander in a malignant region very like themselves among the wicked who are similar to them. Finally, he adds that these things are often mocked by some out of ambition. But if they were compelled to give and receive reasons for these things diligently, they would finally depart, as we have indicated above, truly convicted and mocked like children. But let us now return to the habits; once these are distributed in order, we will understand by what reasoning rewards or punishments are distributed. But before we distinguish them, it is necessary to remember that good habits are only so...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the soul's journey after death from Marsilio Ficino’s 'Platonic Theology'. While the previous page discussed the soul's internal law and the role of guiding spirits (genii), this page categorizes the moral state of souls into four specific types to explain why some ascend immediately to the heavens while others remain trapped in 'shadows'.</meta>

# Theology

...are sought for the purpose of leading to happiness through a special love toward God, the author of happiness. <margin>☞</margin> However, other things are accustomed to plunge those souls especially into misery in which all love of God is extinguished. Hence Plato’s saying: "For the wise man, God is the only law; but for the fool, it is lust." <note>original: "unicum illud Sapienti viro lex deus est. Inspicienti vero libido." This draws from Plato's Laws, suggesting that the wise follow divine order while others follow passing desires.</note> Likewise: "He will be blessed who humbly submits himself to divine law; but wretched is he who proudly despises it." There are, moreover, four characters of the living. There is the **temperate** man, the **continent**, the **incontinent**, and the **intemperate**.

The **temperate** is one whose reason judges truly and whose sensory appetite willingly obeys reason. The **continent** is one whose reason also judges truly, but the appetite obeys with difficulty. The **incontinent** is one in whom reason does not judge poorly, yet bodily disturbance prevails. The **intemperate** is one in whom reason is either lulled to sleep or depraved by a too-dominant appetite—where everything is done at the command of the <term>phantasia: the faculty of imagination that produces mental images</term>. Reason does not oppose the appetite. When we speak here of temperance or continence, we are understood to be "composing" or "arranging" the soul in the Platonic rite <note>meaning: following the specific traditions and methods of Plato</note> against all species of disturbances, so that the duties of all moral virtues are included in these.

<margin>☞</margin> Furthermore, when we place the <term>phantasia</term> in the separated soul, we understand it either in the Platonic rite as the internal sense which they place in a <term>vehicle: a spiritual or "astral" body that carries the soul</term>, both ethereal and aerial; though with passion properly in the aerial one. Or, according to the manner of the <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle</term>, especially **Avicenna**, as the affect and habit of even the rational part, which the soul conceived within itself by obeying the senses, declining toward bodily passions and dragging toward matter. Whereby Avicenna says: the soul, as if by a certain nature and without choice or meditation, is distorted and tormented—both here and in the next life—from the intelligible mode to the sensible.

To return now to our purpose: In the **temperate** soul, only the nutritive power stays with the body. The imagination does not love the body; reason hates it. Therefore, once the ministry of caring for this body is completed, that life-giving power is, as it were, content with its vehicle. The remaining powers of the soul, whichever survive, just as they were accustomed in this temperate man, give themselves over to considering the truth of all things. And they do so all the more fervently than before, as they have been made more free. Therefore, all at once with a common effort and in an **ethereal chariot**, they run back into the ether.

The soul of the **continent** man is indeed carried into heaven, like the former, but not suddenly. For in this man, the appetite of the imagination was accustomed to obey reason only with difficulty because of the allurements or irritations of the body. Therefore, it leaves bodily things in the mind with sorrow. This sorrow occupies the sharp edge of reason for a little while. Yet reason, which had been accustomed to conquer that appetite, commands it to stand. Hence, once the complaint of the imagination is settled and the darkness expelled, the celestial spark shines forth; and with all the powers of the soul consenting, the supernal fatherland is revisited.

The **incontinent** man, however, is liberated late from these prisons. But the **intemperate** man is never freed. Indeed, the souls of these men, infected by bodily passions, fell into such madness in this life that they rashly preferred the shadows of goods to the goods themselves; they loved shadows, or feared shadows. And after this life, they are driven by a similar madness—the former for a long time, the latter forever.

Certainly, the madness of the incontinent finds some medicine. Because, although the disturbance of the imagination was accustomed to dominate, reason was nevertheless accustomed to oppose it at some point in life. Similarly, even after death, it cries out against the madness of a certain raging imagination and grieves that it is deprived of the possession of sublime things. This outcry and repentance gradually weakens the force and act of that imagination, especially since those bodily incitements are not present which might nourish such an imagination. And such a soul would willingly listen to a physician about to cure the affection of a long-lasting weariness—just as in the case of one who is troubled by horrific nightmares. Sometimes, when he is not pressed by the deepest sleep, he says to himself: "Perhaps I am dreaming then, and being tortured by empty cares." Whence the fear and labor are diminished. The same perhaps happens in the lower regions for the incontinent man: the noise of the raving imagination is diminished, and the absolute clarity of reason is increased.

# Platonic Book

...command. Thus at last the freed soul attains happiness. In the intemperate soul, however, while it lived the life of a man, reason was entirely asleep or completely obeyed the passions. From this, it carries with it a persistent habit of inclining toward bodily things as if it were its own nature. Such is the state of this soul, about which
<margin>A</margin> Orpheus sang: **"With unspeakable cries, among the people of evil dreams."** <note>original Greek: ἀρρήτοις δʼ ἰάχουσι κακῶν δήμῳ ὀνείρων. This refers to the souls of the wicked being trapped in a dream-like state after death.</note> That is, the gates of Pluto cannot be closed. Inside is a crowd of dreams. <term>In the seventh book of the Republic, Plato says this soul sleeps deeply in this life.</term> And it departs before it wakes up. After death, it is weighed down by a deeper sleep and disturbed by sharper dreams, which is properly designated by the name Tartarus <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment</note>. It is carried, as Plato wishes, by an excessive love for the elemental body. Therefore, when the earthly body is dissolved, it weaves for itself another body from the vapors of the elements. It weaves it from easy matter by a mere nod, as it were. By a single draught, it refreshes that constantly vanishing body daily, as if by breathing. He adds that a soul of this kind revolves around the elemental body and the region toward which it was inclined, with its passion persevering. Nor should it seem a wonder, they wish, that the soul forms a vaporous body, as it were, and perceives through it. What could be easier or closer to the soul? And in this body, through such a spirit, it provides life and sensation to the body. If one asks what the shape
<margin>B</margin> of that body is, we will respond according to the magi <note>referring to ancient Persian or Neoplatonic wise men</note> that various images of different animals are formed from these vapors. For just as a life has imitated the habits of any animal, it primarily makes itself such; and entirely such would its passion and disposition appear if it were perceived by some sense. It also fashions such a figure in a way in its own shadowy body, if only the light body can be colored and shaped by the vehement passion and habit of the soul. And just as it felt the passions of the flesh in life, so it feels the passions of that [vaporous] body—and all the more sharply as the body is purer. But those sensations are of one kind, and those of the flesh are of another. And thus, perhaps, is how the transformation of men into beasts among the ancients is to be understood <note>Ficino suggests that "turning into an animal" after death is a psychological or "astral" transformation based on the soul's behavior, rather than a literal physical change</note>. Some, however, say that the soul does not properly form such a body and perceive through it.
<margin>C</margin> Rather, just as by magical art through a certain arrangement of statues suited to certain demons, they are bound to the statues of the demon—as **Mercurius** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> and **Plotinus** confess—so by divine law, souls that have surrendered themselves to bodies are enslaved, even to fire. And indeed so servilely that they are vehemently indignant and grieved by this. But let this passion in both cases be called the fury <term>Tisiphone</term> <note>One of the three Furies; her name means "avenging murder"</note> by Orpheus: the one who afflicts them from the body. He adds two other furies to her: who torment them from within their disposition. <term>Megaera</term> <note>The "jealous" Fury</note> indeed because of hatred and the fear of imaginary evil. <term>Allecto</term> <note>The "unceasing" Fury</note>, however, because of the desire for imaginary good. Plato says these furies are incited by avenging demons, and **Plotinus** proves it; and **Orpheus** himself describes a great avenging demon in his own hymn. For such are the first disturbances of this soul, like those who rave in a frenzy due to fever, or those who are terrified by melancholic humor. Even **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian philosopher and physician</note> admits this happens, as does **Proclus**; when he says there are certain irrational demons, he
<margin>D</margin> signifies that it is no wonder if the souls of the wretched turn out irrational. For when the actions of the five senses cease, the internal actions are greatly increased. And if you are accustomed to using reason the most, then you will contemplate most diligently. If you use the <term>phantasia</term> <gloss>the faculty of imagination</gloss>, then you will imagine most vehemently. And this happens in sleep to such an extent that we think images of things are real things. Terrified by horrible visions, we tremble, sweat, cry out, and wake up. Much more so does the deception of terrible images happen to the impious in death and after death. For then the various duties of nourishing cease, as do the multiple actions of the external senses, the occupations of human actions, and the comforts of things. There remains only, as the Platonists think, the command of the raging
<margin>E</margin> <term>phantasia</term> or the phantastic reason in the impious man. Which, moved by the hatred I mentioned and by fear, turns over within itself a long sequence of sad images. Now it sees the sky falling on its head...

<summary>This page describes the fate of the "intemperate" soul, which remains trapped near the physical world after death in a "vaporous" body shaped by its animalistic passions. Ficino interprets the Greek Furies not as literal monsters, but as psychological torments (hatred, fear, and lust) that plague the soul’s imagination like a permanent nightmare.</summary>

--- Page 446 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the soul's journey after death, specifically how its psychological "habits" and "phantasy" (imagination) dictate its experiences in the afterlife. Having established that the intemperate soul is trapped in a dream-like state, he now maps these states onto classical mythological landscapes and philosophical hierarchies.</meta>

# Theology

<margin>E</margin>
The soul imagines itself being swallowed up by the deep chasms of the earth. Then, it is snatched up by the force of flames. Next, it is submerged in a vast whirlpool of water, or seized by the shadows of demons. Thus, the soul drives its own body through the lowest places wherever the force of its raging <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of imagination which, for Ficino, can create vivid, subjective realities for the soul after death.</note> pushes it. Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom.</note> says to Plato that these demons are the "salvation" of the soul; he wants there to be two types of them, who act as ministers of divine law—even if people do not notice it. The wicked soul suffers this through the fury Megaera <note>One of the Furies, representing vengeful anger.</note> out of hatred and fear. But through Alecto <note>Another Fury, representing unceasing anger or obsession.</note>, certain thoughts and affections creep in again due to the habit of love which they had contracted toward the body, and from which they cannot be weakened.
<margin>F</margin>
Indeed, just as old men who lived lustfully in their youth are burned by a double penalty in old age—namely, they burn with a desire for pleasures, yet are deprived of all hope of obtaining them (unless they are truly senile)—so the miserable ones among the dead are troubled by various desires for human things because of their past habits. For the most part, they do not hope to achieve them. Although sometimes, like madmen, they seem to themselves to almost reach their delights, they are immediately driven away from them by even sharper pains.
<margin>G</margin>
Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for his decadence and luxury.</note> is driven far from his embrace. An angry man is kept from his gold. Tantalus is kept from the banquet. Sisyphus is kept from the summit. Such is the power of the imagination, such is its force, when either it rules alone, or when some imaginative habit and affection, contracted from long-standing commerce with the body, rules alone in the reason.
<margin>H</margin>
The order we established above is confirmed by <term>Olympiodorus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist commentator on Plato.</note> in his commentaries on the *Phaedo*, where he posits three types of vices according to Plato's opinion. First are those that are easily curable, namely those that lack a settled habit. Second, he says, are those that can be cured only with difficulty, as they are committed out of habit, but they carry with them a certain resistance and repentance as a companion. Finally, the third cannot be cured; these are performed by habit and are utterly lacking in resistance or repentance.
<margin>I</margin>
Therefore, the Platonists assign the first type to Acheron, the second to Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus <note>Rivers of the underworld representing sorrow (Acheron), fire (Pyriphlegethon), and wailing (Cocytus).</note>, and the third to Tartarus. Regarding these, <term>Plato</term> says that no one can ever escape. Just as many levels are distributed to the good in the *Phaedo*.
<margin>B</margin>
There he asserts that innocent and pious souls, but those unskilled in philosophy, live easily in the air along with "airy" bodies. Others, who are additionally endowed with "civil philosophy" <note>The virtue required for living well in a community or state.</note>, live in heaven with celestial and luminous vehicles. Finally, the most purified souls live most blessedly above heaven without any bodies at all. <term>Orpheus</term> however
<margin>R</margin>
distributes nine primary regions to souls. For us, these are either the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, the planets, or the ether below the planets. These spheres are indeed nine, if you divide them carefully into the nine levels of contemplation which we have discussed elsewhere. For those in the middle, he assigns the air, the water, or the earth. Finally, for the reprobate, he assigns Acheron, Cocytus, and Pyriphlegethon. "Styx, flowing between nine times, hems them in," as the poet says. This number nine is taken from this:
<margin>C</margin>
they sinned either by a certain affection, or by a changeable habit, or by an unchangeable habit. And in whichever of these ways they failed, they sinned either in thought, or in speech, or additionally in action. Hence, nine levels of faults and nine levels of punishments are deservedly calculated.
<margin>The oracle of Maro <note>Referring to Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note></margin>
<margin>L</margin>
That oracle of <term>Maro</term> <note>Virgil</note> in the sixth book of the *Aeneid* is by no means to be despised as if it were merely poetic; in it, following partly Mercury and partly Plato, he describes four affections which follow the four <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm) believed to control health and temperament.</note>. From fiery bile arises <margin>Appetite, Pleasure, Fear, Sorrow</margin> appetite; from airy blood, pleasures; from earthy black bile, fear; and from watery phlegm, sorrow and softness. It seems consistent that from these four affections, four such habits are conceived in the soul, inclining it toward corporeal things. The miserable carry these with them after death to be purged throughout the four elements. In this purgation, Virgil arranges four primary regions in the underworld in the Platonic manner. Just as it seems consistent to hear the noise and bellowing of Acheron, Cocytus, Phlegethon, and Tartarus, he likewise arranges four regions in the Elysian fields; namely, the four "triplicities" of signs in the Zodiac. <note>Groups of three Zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic argument that the soul’s experience after death is a direct result of its internal state and habits developed during life.
