# Platonic
## Book

<margin>A</margin> These four things agree with the four kinds of virtues. By these four, the <term>passions</term> <note>In this context, the "affectus" or passions are the irrational disturbances of the soul, like fear and lust, that cloud the mind.</note> are conquered; from which the soul, with a serene mind, receives the celestial light. One must remember, however, that those should not be admitted among the Platonists who think that souls living in the spheres of the planets, and in fire and pure air, are to be counted among those in the underworld. In what way are they assigned to the underworld? <margin>B</margin> For if they are among the blessed, they exist in bodies so light and obedient to the command of the mind that they are not diverted from the contemplation of divine things.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, we should call only that region of the world—where the tumultuous confusion of the elements clashes—by the name "underworld" in the Platonic sense. Finally, to understand the opinion of the ancient theologians regarding the state of the soul after death in a few words: they think that only divine things (as we have said elsewhere) exist as true realities. The rest are but images and shadows of those truths. Wise men, who devote themselves to divine things, are "awake"; but the unwise, who pursue other things, are entirely deluded by dreams, as if they were sleeping. And if they should be awakened in the midst of this sleep and rest, they "die" <note>Meaning they experience the shock of leaving the physical world they mistook for reality.</note>; after their departure, they are tormented by similar and even sharper visions. Just as he who devoted himself to truth in life possesses the highest truth after death, so he who followed falsehood is tortured by extreme deceit. The former is delighted by true things; the latter is vexed by false phantoms. Therefore, Christ, the master of life, often commands thus: "Watch, I say, watch, lest the Lord find you sleeping." Again he says: "Arise, and let us go from here." <note>original: "Vigilate... surgite... hinc abeamus." Ficino interprets these biblical exhortations as calls to philosophical awakening from the "dream" of material life.</note> What else is it to "wake up" than to recognize that one is merely dreaming while in the senses?

<margin>C</margin> What else is it to "rise and depart" but to bring oneself to God with the mind? I do not think the cause of punishment should be passed over in silence—hidden indeed to those suffering, but most powerful—which Plato indicated in the *Timaeus*, *Gorgias*, and *Republic*, and which Origen <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian who attempted to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> interpreted. God tempered the soul from its beginning with a certain harmony of spiritual parts, powers, and movements. This kind of tempering in men of integrity is gradually loosened by instinct, and in the damned, it is mostly dissolved. It is necessary that from this loosening and dissolution, a moderate annoyance and pain arise in the soul, even if it does not know why or for what reason it suffers. Just as when the natural temperament of bodily spirits, humors, and limbs is loosened, pain <margin>D</margin> necessarily follows, even if the sick person does not know the medical reason for his pain. Christian theologians will not entirely deny this. But they will add, I think, some penalty from a true judgment of the damned soul. For it will think that it is forever deprived of the divine vision. This is the greatest penalty because God is the "end" <note>The Greek "telos" or ultimate purpose of existence.</note> for which we were born. For His sake we desire and do all things. Therefore, the natural thirst for Him is much sharper than the thirst that moves a parched man toward drink. But just as if someone were numbed by a sleep-inducing opium: although he might be dying of thirst, he will not feel the sting or the harm of thirst. But when the effect of the opium is dissolved, he will perceive it, and it will vex him more vehemently. So the soul, which has swallowed the <term>Lethean</term> <note>Referring to Lethe, the mythological river of forgetfulness; here, it represents the "drunkenness" of being immersed in physical matter.</note> river of matter, is so utterly occupied with a stupor regarding the sense of divine things that it does not feel the torments of its natural thirst toward God; but once the stupor is finally expelled, it both feels most acutely and is tormented most vehemently. And if in some way we can think of this in our lives, even though we are far from God, yet because we are occupied by the solaces of life, we rarely notice this; and when we do notice, we hope to return shortly to the Father. There, neither solace nor any hope delights the wretched; because the power of <term>Acheron</term> <margin>E</margin> <note>A river in the underworld, here representing the lack of joy.</note> increases the penalty. It increases the penalty because the soul thinks itself deprived of such a great good by its own fault; therefore they are perpetually indignant with themselves, which can be signified by the name of <term>Styx</term> <note>The river of hatred; for Ficino, it represents the soul's self-hatred and anger.</note>. To this is added the habitation of "Tartarean" places: either lowly or most foul. And finally, the torment of this human body. Which in the sense of the soul is seen to be <term>Phlegethon</term> <note>The river of fire; representing burning passion.</note>, and in the spirit is <term>Cocytus</term> <note>The river of wailing; representing lamentation.</note>.

### ¶ On the middle state of souls, especially according to the philosophers.

<margin>F</margin> **I**t is often customary to inquire about the souls of those who died from their bodies before the age of choice <note>Referring to children or those who died before reaching the "age of reason" to choose between good and evil.</note>. Plato writes that Er the Pamphylian, who rose from death, said many things about the state of other souls...

<summary>Ficino argues that 'Hell' is not a physical location but the material world and the psychological state of a soul that has lost its internal harmony. He explains that the pain of the damned is the sudden, acute realization of their separation from God once the numbing distractions of the physical body are removed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Platonic Theology, specifically examining the middle states of the soul after death. Ficino moves from discussing the "underworld" as a state of the soul to exploring the hierarchy of afterlife experiences, drawing on Avicenna and Plato to explain the fate of those who are neither fully holy nor fully wicked, such as infants.</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>Theology XVIII</header>

# Theology

...many and stupendous things have been told. Regarding these matters, however, there are other things not very worthy of memory. But **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Metaphysics" deeply influenced Scholastic and Renaissance thought.</note> indeed says in his *Metaphysics*: that those souls who have not yet contracted either a good or a bad <term>habit</term> <note>In Aristotelian and Scholastic terms, a "habit" (habitus) is a settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up.</note> <margin>✠</margin> receive something good from the abundance of divine mercy. Therefore, if we were allowed to proceed by the conjectures of natural philosophers in this matter, we might perhaps say that the order of things runs in such a way that fates of this kind happened to them, in a certain sense, outside the apparent order. But by **Divine Wisdom**, which permits nothing anywhere to be entirely devoid of order, they are reduced into a certain order—hidden to us, indeed, but most manifest to those above. 

What if? Just as Nature always interposes several middle points between all extremes that are furthest distant from each other, so has she inserted as many levels as possible between the lots of the most blessed and the most miserable, as if they were the most distant of all? So that there would exist no fewer levels in the hidden orders of souls than in the manifest levels of bodies; and thus there would be many who are most blessed on one side, and many most miserable on the other. Again, here some are less blessed, and there others are less miserable. In the middle of all, equally, are those who are neither properly miserable <margin>B</margin> nor blessed. For indeed, he is **blessed** who enjoys the divine flavors in God. But he is **miserable** who nowhere senses any divine scent and always <margin>C</margin> burns. On the one hand, he is "less blessed" who enjoys fewer things in Him. Conversely, he is "less miserable" who burns with less pain. Finally, there is the one who senses certain scents of the Creator within the creature, and is content with that divine scent. 

For which reason, philosophers will perhaps say that the souls of **infants** ought not to complain about divine justice. Even if they are perhaps deprived of the faculty of the **Highest Good**, they are also liberated from the danger of the extreme evil. Again, it is probable they do not complain if only—into the clarity of the soul, obscured by no clouds of bodily affections—the light of the divine sun flows, creating the fullness of natural forms; so that, as **Timaeus** <note>A reference to the speaker in Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, who describes the mathematical and rational ordering of the cosmos.</note> says, it may demonstrate the order of the universe to them, and at the same time show the Ordainer within the order, as much as the order itself can grasp the Ordainer; and by this good, He may command and cause the soul to be content. 

Therefore, just as <margin>D</margin> in man between the gross body and the soul there is the **spirit**, and in the <term>affections</term> <note>The emotional or irrational parts of the soul.</note> between pain and pleasure there is "indolence" <note>Here meaning a state of neutrality or lack of pain.</note>; likewise in reason, between science and ignorance there is "right opinion." Again, in the visible universe between the bright and the opaque, there is the translucent; so in separated spirits there seem to be those who are blessedly cherished in the heavens by the light of the shining God, and conversely those who miserably lack both around the earth. Between these, however, are the "middle ones" in the purer air, to whom, even if the Light itself does not properly breathe upon them, the **Luster** <note>Ficino distinguishes between *lux* (the source), *lumen* (the diffused light), and *radius* (the specific ray).</note> does. 

One must remember, however, what we signify elsewhere: just as **Light** remaining in the sun is one thing, and the **Luster** flowing from it and diffused through all things is another, and the **Ray** directed toward the eyes is another; so there is one infinite **Light** in God, through which only the soul and God enjoy Himself, and the blessed minds enjoy the divine goodness. There is another "common luster" spreading abundantly from there through all clear minds, through which individual minds—provided they do not turn away from it—behold all created things as if they were external and created; but they do not see the Creator Himself properly in Himself, unless they are transferred into the Light by an enkindled luster. There is yet another "ray," proper to each soul and made natural to the minds from the beginning, remaining in them in some way even when they turn away and depart. 

<margin>ℐ</margin> In the first grade, indeed, they are **blessed**. In the second, they are neither properly blessed nor miserable, provided they live content with this very state. In the third, finally, are the **human souls**, bound either to bodies or to the affections of the body; and by this very fact they are now almost miserable, happy only in hope. Below this very grade are those for whom only a "ray" remains, and that one now gloomy and burning, and destitute of the confidence of pure light. 

<margin>K</margin> Perhaps some **Platonist** will conjecture thus: If God created minds for the sake of the primary Light, and He Himself is prepared to grant it for the sake of attaining it—both through the recognition of divine goodness and especially through love—since recognition is formed by the luster from there, and love reforms the soul back to the light from here; it would be likely that divine justice wills that the faculty and opportunity of knowing and loving God should never be entirely lacking to any of the minds. But since many die before the use of reason, and again some are dull from the beginning by a malignant fate...

<summary>Ficino argues for a hierarchical afterlife where souls exist in various states of "light" between total blessedness and total misery. He specifically addresses the neutral state of infants and the philosophical distinction between the source of divine Light and its diffused luster.</summary>
<keywords>hierarchy of souls, Avicenna, Timaeus, divine light, infants in the afterlife, Neoplatonism, Marsilio Ficino, states of the soul</keywords>

--- Page 449 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book XVIII of Marsilio Ficino’s "Platonic Theology." Having previously established that there are middle states for the soul, Ficino here addresses the specific cases of infants and the "stolid" (those born without the use of reason), debating how they might achieve salvation or progress toward God despite lacking the capacity for moral "merit" or "habit" during their earthly lives.</meta>

# Platonic Book [XVIII]

[...necessity] withdraws: therefore it would be consistent that a faculty of this kind, through divine providence, either in this life—by some wondrous pact—or at least in the other life, be repaid. Nor should one, without his own fault, be deprived of the principal part of hope. For this reason, we have said that the souls of these people—even if never here—are nevertheless separated from their bodies and placed in that light where they recognize the creator in his creatures; they are gradually kindled by so much love for the creator that they are prepared at a certain time to attain the light. I say "at a certain time" because only angelic minds, being entirely in eternity, as it were, progress or fall away in a single moment. But souls, which by nature already incline toward temporal things, perform their works in time; though they do so over a longer time while in the body, they do so in a much shorter time outside the body. Indeed, it lasts but a moment once they have been translated into the order of the angelic nature. Thus, if souls placed in the punishments of <term>purgatory</term> <note>original: "purgatorijs", refers to the state of purification before reaching heaven</note>—even though they are in a worse condition and place—nevertheless rise up to blessedness, it should not seem strange that the souls of those placed in the middle region of "indolence" <note>A state of rest or lack of pain, often associated in this context with the Limbo of infants</note> and closer to blessedness, are able to progress toward that same blessedness.

<margin>pointing hand</margin>
These things are what the philosophers would chiefly think concerning infants. Nor does the question concerning those who are entirely stolid <note>meaning those born with severe intellectual disabilities or "fools" by nature</note> by their very nature seem much more difficult than the question concerning infants. For if they have lived a long time, they contract a certain <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitũ", a settled disposition of the soul acquired through repeated actions</note> regarding the "machine" <note>the physical body or the material world</note> which is the lowest part of the universe; such a habit is accustomed to turn away from God, who is the highest part of the universe. This "stodgy" habit of the soul, and even the soul when separated, perhaps still turns toward matter and, in the meantime, turns away from God. But <term>blessedness</term> <note>original: "Beatitudo", the ultimate state of happiness in God</note> is judged to come to none except those turned toward God. Yet if these people are miserable, and could in no way be turned toward the Highest because fate prohibited it, they were not miserable by any fault of their own; and God would have commanded them to turn to Him in vain, if they were unable to do so.

<margin>a</margin>
Perhaps some <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>original: "peripateticus", a follower of the philosophy of Aristotle</note> will respond here: that in fools, because of the excessive intensity of the <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: "phãtasie", the faculty of the soul that processes sensory images</note> itself, reason was so empty that, by not acting, it did not create a habit. They might assert that the proper habit of the phantasy—which is not so much in the soul as in the body—ceases immediately when the body is dissolved. By this it would happen that the mind, with nothing prohibiting it, would naturally turn by its own ray—

into God; and receiving the divine light, which is present everywhere, it would be kindled. Then, once kindled, it would love, and by loving it would turn itself more vehemently, and in a short time, by meriting something, it would attain blessedness.

<margin>B</margin>
But the Platonists, who think that the habit remains in some way even in the phantasy, would respond that if reason consented to it in any way—even if it consented then by compulsion—it is necessary that the habit which turns it toward opposites be first entirely deleted before the soul can be raised higher. But in deleting this, they say that both the <term>genius</term> <note>a guardian spirit or guiding intelligence</note> and the power of God work marvelously. For it is not less provided for under divine providence that souls be purest in minds and bodies. Therefore, just as in sick bodies, where nature cannot expel the disease and return to health by its own power, it is accustomed to expel it through the confirmed art of doctors; similarly in minds, where the natural faculty for purging and relaxing the habits of the body is lacking, the Almighty Physician acts—either by His own power or through the happy ministry of His servants. Nor will they think that this lacks order. So that divine clemency—which is most proved in a prince—may shine most aptly here: while no one is condemned without their own fault, even he who is deprived of the faculty of merit through no fault of his own for a time, may eventually be restored to that faculty by divine power—a faculty, I say, such that it cannot err, and with God’s help, may merit much in a short time.

<margin>C</margin>
These are their views. But lest we think childishly about children, or foolishly about fools, it seems that we should conclude thus: The way of the philosophers leads us nearly to this conjecture. But since human conjecture is often and greatly deceived concerning divine matters, let us judge it much better and safer to commit ourselves with obedient humility to the holier leaders among the Christians.

### Conclusion.

After the end of life was granted to us by God—not the same end as for the other living creatures—as we have shown first by common reasons, second by specific arguments, and third by both signs and the solutions to questions: I believe we must take the greatest care, lest this uncertain and fleeting [life...]

<insert>LIBRARY OF THE VITTORIO EMANUELE NATIONAL LIBRARY, ROME</insert>

<summary>Ficino explores whether infants and those born without reason can reach heaven, weighing Aristotelian and Platonic theories before ultimately deferring to Christian doctrine. He suggests that divine providence acts as a "physician" to heal souls that could not develop moral habits in life.</summary>
<keywords>infants, fools, divine providence, habit, phantasy, Peripatetics, Platonists, salvation, purgatory, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the final book (Book XVIII) of Marsilio Ficino’s magnum opus. Following the discussion on the souls of infants and the "stolid," Ficino concludes with a grand exhortation on the soul’s ultimate return to its divine source, followed by the formal colophon of the 1524 Venetian edition.</meta>

# Theology

...prefer the moment of this life to infinite ages. 
¶ Let us remember, moreover, if we are wise, that we cannot exist well for eternity, nor live perfectly, nor understand happily, unless we are formed by His <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental, divine nature of God from which all things derive their existence.</note>; for we received our being from His act of creation, and we live by His life, by whose breath we breathe and move. By His intelligence let us understand Him, and all things through Him, by whose enlightenment we daily consider created things and seek even the Creator. We shall reach, with God as our guide, this highest degree of nature, if only we separate the affection of our soul, as much as we are able, from matter itself, which is the lowest degree of nature. Thus, as much as we depart from matter, so much may we approach God; and for Him—having now set aside the fleeting moment of this deceptive life—we live as far as we can, so that at last we may live by His life forever.

-> THE END. <-

# 164 VIII. Theology

<unclear>... also of the soul ... ...</unclear>
<unclear>... ... ... ... ... ...</unclear>

...it is necessary that there be one branch of philosophy that pursues this ultimate goal. For since it is clear that "the one" <note>In Platonic thought, "The One" is the supreme, indivisible source of all reality.</note> is nothing in itself, the question is investigated: both seem to be beneficial, since that which we hold toward God for the sake of other things does not depend on itself; also, to possess from another that which is nothing in terms of <term>reason</term> <note>The specific faculty of the human mind (ratio) that distinguishes man from animals.</note>, which properly belongs to man; for since it is nothing in itself, when

it might use its power, it would rattle <unclear>noise</unclear> into the infinite. However, after it [the soul] has directed itself toward those things which are eternal and true, it seems to worthily exhaust the worship of religion for the glory of its creator, if that be the ultimate end of souls. It has provided the light of understanding to our souls, as something else which exists through itself: but let there be something which exists through itself...
